options.text: Score all three projects on business value and cost, then share the funding rule.
Fund all three for now and move the shortfall into next quarter's budget.
Cut each team's budget by the same 15% so the rule stays simple and fair.
Fund the team with the most urgent deadline first and let the others wait.

basic.situation: A staff member says her laptop has been very slow since this morning, and she has a client presentation at 2 p.m. You are the nearest IT person on the floor.

options.text: Restart the laptop and tell her to call you again if the slowness comes back.
Reinstall the operating system now, since that clears most slowness, and restore her files afterwards.
Check which program is hogging the memory, close it, and confirm her slides open.
Install a popular free cleaner tool from the internet since it usually speeds laptops up.

advanced.situation: Staff in two branches cannot log in to the shared finance system, and payroll cut-off is in three hours. Your helpdesk team has already tried password resets with no result.

options.text: Find what changed today, like an update or access setting, and test reversing it.
Give the payroll team one shared administrator login so they can finish the cut-off.
Arrange a temporary approved backup route for payroll staff, then investigate the cause after cut-off.
Reset the passwords again for both branches and ask staff to try another browser.

basic.situation: Your junior programmer finished a small report script and wants it released today. You have not yet looked at his work, and the report goes to senior management.

options.text: Ask another programmer to glance at it and release it if they are happy.
Test the script on sample data against last month's figures, and read through the code.
Release it today as he asked, because he has been reliable and fixes can follow.
Ask him to walk you through the logic and sample output, then approve it.

advanced.situation: A vendor proposes a RM1.2 million system to replace your company's inventory software. Their demo looked good, but they gave no reference sites, and the quote leaves out data migration.

options.text: Map the proposal to the warehouse's requirements and ask the vendor to price migration.
Sign the vendor's letter of intent to hold the price while the team studies it.
Recommend approval based on the strong demo, with migration costs to be settled afterwards.
Get reference sites and a migration quote, then compare the total cost to budget.

basic.situation: You run a small helpdesk. At 9 a.m. three requests arrive: a password reset, a jammed printer for one person, and a slow server affecting a whole team.

options.text: Handle requests in the order they arrived so that nobody can say you played favourites.
Put the slow server first because it affects most people, then clear the quick ones.
Do the password reset first since it takes two minutes, then look at the server.
Wait for the slow server to settle itself while you finish the printer and reset.

advanced.situation: The company wants to move customer records to a cloud service by quarter-end. You must plan data security and disaster recovery, but the vendor's standard package has no tested recovery plan.

options.text: Keep an offline backup of customer records on site and write the restore steps.
Accept the vendor's standard package and trust their assurance that data is replicated across regions.
Migrate the customer records now to meet quarter-end and add the recovery plan afterwards.
Agree recovery targets with the business, then require a restore test before migrating.

basic.situation: Your manager mentions a new AI coding assistant that other IT teams are testing. You have one spare hour this week and are asked to learn about it for the team.

options.text: Watch the vendor's launch video and share its main selling points with the team.
Read independent reviews and the vendor's documentation, then summarise the main points for your manager.
Try it on a sample project with no real data and note strengths and limits.
Paste a section of company source code into the public tool to see its answers.

advanced.situation: A new policy says all staff laptops must be encrypted. A senior engineer says his test devices are exempt, but the policy does not mention test devices. Others are watching your response.

options.text: Write a company-wide notice stating that test devices are exempt, so the issue is settled.
Ask the policy owner for a written ruling on test devices before the next audit.
Treat test devices as exempt since the policy does not list them and move on.
Encrypt test devices holding company data and ask the policy owner about the rest.

basic.situation: Your team needs ten replacement monitors. Two suppliers quote RM480 and RM520 each, and the dearer one delivers in two days. Your team can wait a week.

options.text: Split the order into smaller purchases under your approval limit to skip the sign-off.
Confirm both quotes cover the same specifications and warranty, then order from the cheaper one.
Order from the cheaper supplier since the team can wait, and check specifications on delivery.
Order from the faster supplier at RM520 so nobody has to wait for monitors.

advanced.situation: Two department heads both want your team's server upgrade this month, but you have capacity for one. Each says their work is critical to company revenue.

options.text: Tell each head privately that theirs comes first, and sort out the clash later.
Schedule the upgrade for whoever asked first and tell the other head it is unavoidable.
Choose the department with higher revenue and offer the other head a later date.
Meet both heads together, compare business impact and risk openly, and agree the order.

basic.situation: You are closing the branch counter at 5 p.m. The cash in the teller's till is RM300 less than the teller system shows.

options.text: Recount with a colleague, trace the day's slips against the system, and record any gap.
Seal the till and ask the teller to recheck her slips tomorrow morning.
Top up the till with RM300 of your own money so the books balance.
Recount the cash yourself and, if the gap remains, record it and tell your supervisor.

advanced.situation: Your branch now handles more bank drafts and cheques for business clients. You must set the team's handling rule, because one cheque was nearly released to another person last week.

options.text: Release cheques and drafts at the counter on request, and match records after closing.
Set two-person checks on payee and amount, and log every instrument at each handoff.
Let the most experienced teller handle all cheques and drafts since she makes few errors.
Brief the team on last week's near miss and remind them to double-check payee names.

basic.situation: You are helping plan next year's branch budget. Over the past 12 months the electricity bill was steady, except March, which is far higher than the rest.

options.text: Delete the March bill from the records so the yearly trend looks steady.
Find what caused the March spike, then budget from normal months plus any repeating cause.
Use the lowest month's bill times twelve, as it shows what is truly needed.
Use the 12-month average as the base since it reflects real bills for the year.

advanced.situation: A junior analyst's budget model shows a 20% saving next year, based on a vendor's quoted rate. You suspect the rate leaves out service charges, and the model has no checks on assumptions.

options.text: Submit the model as it is, since the 20% saving matches what management hopes for.
Have him confirm what the rate covers and re-run the model with higher costs.
Add a margin for extra charges to the model yourself and send it on.
Trim a few other cost lines slightly so the 20% saving holds if charges appear.

basic.situation: A small-business customer calls, upset that a RM8,000 transfer to his supplier has not arrived after two days. He asks you to fix it today.

options.text: Trace the transfer, tell him its status, and set a time to update him.
Apologise sincerely, take his details, and promise that the operations team will call him back.
Move RM8,000 from the branch's own account to his supplier to settle the matter today.
Explain that transfers can take several days and ask him to check again next week.

advanced.situation: A long-standing business client says a RM2,500 fee error last month has damaged her trust and she may move her accounts. You can refund the error, but a fee waiver needs head office approval.

options.text: Refund the error and apologise, then explain that waivers are not available at branch level.
Refund the error, then forward her fee request to head office with her account history.
Waive her fees in the system for a year and inform head office afterwards.
Send a short apology email and ask her to wait while you check options.

basic.situation: Two tellers called in sick and the lunchtime queue is long. You have one back-office clerk and one teller from the next counter free to help.

options.text: Call the regional office and ask them to send extra staff, then wait for them.
Let the clerk run a till for cash transactions since he has watched tellers.
Tell the queue about the delay and ask the teller to keep chats short.
Put the clerk on enquiries and forms, and keep the available teller on cash.

advanced.situation: Month-end close needs the loans, treasury and branch teams to submit reconciliations on the same day. Treasury says it will be two days late, which blocks the others.

options.text: Find what is blocking treasury, agree a firm date, and resequence the other teams' tasks.
Have the loans and branch teams enter estimated balances so the close finishes on time.
Ask treasury to send partial figures so the others can start, then update later.
Push the close date back by two days for all teams to match treasury.

basic.situation: A new teller starts on Monday and you must arrange her first-week training. The branch has a standard checklist, but the usual trainer is on leave.

options.text: Pair her with an experienced teller on the checklist and check progress daily.
Give her the checklist and manuals to study and answer questions when you can.
Put her on a live cash drawer from day one, since the queues need help.
Let her shadow a teller all week since real customers teach faster than manuals.

advanced.situation: You must plan next year's compliance training for 40 staff. Last year everyone completed the course, yet errors in customer ID checks have not dropped.

options.text: Report to management that the course has worked since every employee completed it.
Add a short quiz to the course and require staff to pass before receiving certificates.
Repeat the course with a livelier trainer and remind staff to take more care.
Study the ID error records, build training around them, and track error rates afterwards.

basic.situation: You need to hire a loan officer. Ten applications arrived, and the shortlist meeting with your manager is tomorrow. Three look strong, and seven are unclear.

options.text: Shortlist applicants from well-known universities, since their standards are more familiar to the team.
Phone the strongest applicant and offer her the job today so no competitor takes her.
Shortlist the three strong applicants and keep the other seven on file for later.
Score all ten against the job requirements and call unclear ones to confirm details.

advanced.situation: Your branch lost three relationship managers in six months and needs five hires within fixed salary bands. You are asked to set the team's hiring approach, not just fill posts.

options.text: Review why people left, define must-have criteria, and set a structured interview and scoring process.
Hire quickly from the first five acceptable applicants to fill the gaps before month-end.
Promise each candidate a higher package than the band to close the hires this week.
Post all five roles widely and ask current staff to refer people they trust.

basic.situation: Policy says every payment needs an approved purchase order. A department head sends a RM4,800 invoice from a new supplier, no purchase order on file, and asks you to pay today.

options.text: Log the invoice as pending and email the department head asking for the purchase order.
Return the invoice to the department head and ask them to resubmit it later.
Pay the invoice today and ask the department head to raise the purchase order afterwards.
Log it as pending, help the department head raise the purchase order today, then schedule payment.

advanced.situation: You find that petty cash claims of up to RM300 are approved by the same person who holds the cash box. Your manager asks you to propose a control fix for the branch offices.

options.text: Ask each branch to sign a yearly declaration confirming that all claims were properly approved.
Send every petty cash claim to head office for approval before the branch pays out.
Have a second branch officer approve claims, and add surprise cash counts by head office staff.
Ask the cash box holder to photocopy each receipt and file it for the monthly review.

basic.situation: You have RM6,500 in cash and cheques from today's customers. The bank closes in 40 minutes, and the receipts are not yet matched to the day's collections.

options.text: Bank the receipt book total and keep any extra cash in the drawer as float.
Lock the takings in the office safe and bank them tomorrow after matching the receipts.
Count with a colleague, match the total to the receipt book, and bank it today.
Count the takings yourself, bank them today, and match them to the receipts tomorrow morning.

advanced.situation: The bank holds your company's salary payment file for an extra verification check. Salaries are due tomorrow morning, and your manager is travelling. The relationship officer's number is on your desk.

options.text: Call the relationship officer, ask what the bank needs, provide it today, and update your manager.
Upload the same salary file again through the portal in case the first attempt failed.
Tell the payroll team salaries may be late and wait for the bank to release them.
Email the relationship officer to ask why the file was held and wait for the reply.

basic.situation: You are helping prepare the monthly management report. The bank balance in the ledger is RM3,200 higher than the bank statement, and the report is due to the controller this afternoon.

options.text: Post a balancing entry to sundry expenses so the ledger agrees with the bank statement.
Ask the controller to move the deadline to tomorrow until the difference has been traced.
Reconcile the ledger to the bank statement and attach the unmatched items to the report.
Submit the report on time with a note that the RM3,200 difference is being checked.

advanced.situation: You supervise a small payments team and will be on leave for two weeks. Urgent supplier payments still need releasing, and your manager has asked you to arrange the cover.

options.text: Let the payments clerk both approve and release urgent supplier payments so nothing gets delayed.
Write a cover approval with dates and a payment limit, then have your manager sign it.
Give your bank token and password to the most senior clerk so payments run as usual.
Email the team naming a trusted colleague to approve urgent payments while you are away.

basic.situation: A sales executive wants to claim RM450 for a client dinner but has only a handwritten note. Company policy requires an official receipt for every expense claim.

options.text: Reject the claim and tell her to take the matter up with her own manager.
Explain the rule and show her how to request an official receipt from the restaurant.
Tell her an official receipt is required and ask her to resubmit when she has one.
Accept the handwritten note and add a remark so the claim is paid this month.

advanced.situation: The company expects RM2 million of surplus cash for six months before paying for machinery. Management asks you where to place it. The bank offers fixed deposits with early-withdrawal penalties.

options.text: Recommend keeping the surplus in the current account so the money stays available for payments.
Recommend placing the surplus in a higher-return equity fund, since six months will pass quickly.
Recommend staggered short deposits timed to the machinery payments, plus a cash buffer for daily needs.
Recommend the fixed deposit with the highest rate after comparing offers from three banks.

basic.situation: Your weekly cash flow check shows the bank balance will drop below the company's minimum cash level by Friday, because a large customer payment is overdue.

options.text: Prepare a day-by-day cash forecast showing the gap and movable payments, then show your supervisor.
Tell your supervisor that the balance will dip below the minimum and ask for instructions.
Chase the customer daily for the payment and see whether it arrives before Friday.
Hold back this week's supplier payments, since the late customer payment should arrive soon.

advanced.situation: Over three months, a payables clerk in your team has made repeated posting errors, while also covering a colleague on long leave. Her annual review is next week and you must rate her.

options.text: Sort the errors by type against her workload, then agree targets and support with her.
Give her a good rating for the extra work and review the errors next quarter.
Ask HR to issue a written warning based on the error count recorded over three months.
Rate her on the error count and tell her to be more careful with postings.

basic.situation: Auditors have asked you to pull supporting invoices for 25 sampled payments. You find that two invoices are missing from the files.

options.text: Tell your supervisor that two invoices are missing and wait for instructions on what to do.
Ask the two suppliers for copies, note the gap, and tell the auditors they are coming.
Print replacement invoices from the payment vouchers so the auditors receive a complete sample file.
Give the auditors the 23 available invoices first and mention the other two if asked.

advanced.situation: Your analysis shows overtime costs in one department rose 30% over six months while output stayed flat. The department head says it was a busy season.

options.text: Drop the overtime line from the report until the department head agrees with the figures.
Report the 30 percent rise to management and recommend a cap on overtime hours next quarter.
Accept the department head's explanation and note the rise as seasonal in the report.
Compare overtime with output and past seasons, then show management the findings and suggested checks.

basic.situation: Your senior manager asks you to shortlist stocks for the fund's income mandate. One Malaysian stock pays a 9% dividend yield, far above its sector peers. You have an hour before the meeting.

options.text: Check that earnings and cash flow cover the dividend, then shortlist it if payments look sustainable.
Leave the stock off the shortlist, because such high yields often signal trouble ahead.
Add the stock to the shortlist, since its yield beats every peer and the fund's target.
Look at the dividend record for five years and shortlist the stock if payments were steady.

advanced.situation: You must sell a large block of a thinly traded small-cap stock held by the fund. Selling it all today would likely push the share price down. Your manager has asked you to plan the execution.

options.text: Sell half the block at market price today and decide how to handle the rest later.
Sell the whole block at market price today so the fund exits in one go.
Split the sale into smaller orders over several days, tracking volume and price as you go.
Place one limit order near yesterday's closing price and leave it open until it fills.

basic.situation: You are analysing a plantation company for your senior analyst. Its latest profit jumped 40%, but the notes to the accounts show most of the gain came from a one-off land sale.

options.text: Strip out the land sale gain, find the underlying profit, and base the valuation on that.
Hold the analysis until next quarter's results show whether profit stays at the higher level.
Use the reported profit in the forecast, since the auditors already signed off the accounts.
Report the 40 percent rise and add a footnote saying part came from a land sale.

advanced.situation: A Malaysian solar-panel startup pitches the fund. Its plan forecasts 200% revenue growth, but most of it depends on one pending government tender. Your manager asks for your view on the opportunity.

options.text: Accept the projections as presented, since a government tender signals strong policy support for the sector.
Ask the startup to send five-year projections and review the opportunity again next month.
Check the founders' track record and the technology claims, then recommend investing if both look credible.
Model revenue for both a tender win and loss, and test what each means for returns.

basic.situation: At your weekly check, a stock has risen so much that it is now 7% of the portfolio. The fund's rules set a 5% limit for any single stock.

options.text: Add the breach to the weekly report so your manager sees it at the next review.
Watch the price for a few days in case it falls back under the limit.
Tell your manager today the weight is 7% and work out the sale needed to comply.
Raise the limit in the monitoring sheet to 8% so the report shows no breach.

advanced.situation: The regulator issues a draft proposal that would cap unrated bonds at 5% of a fund's value. Your fund holds 8% in unrated bonds, and no final date is announced.

options.text: Read the paper, estimate the effect on current holdings, and give your manager options and dates.
Wait for the final rule before analysing anything, because the draft may still change.
Forward the paper to your manager with a note saying it may affect the fund.
Sell the unrated bonds this week to stay clear of the limit, then brief your manager.

basic.situation: You are helping draft the fund's valuation policy. Your supervisor asks what the policy should say about a bond that has not traded for three weeks.

options.text: Draft a rule to use an independent pricing agency's quote, and record any fallback method used.
Draft a rule to value it at the last traded price until a new trade occurs.
Draft a rule to value it at purchase cost until the fund sells it.
Draft a rule to value it at the average of quotes from two dealing brokers.

advanced.situation: The fund's mandate is moderate risk. Your manager wants the policy to allow up to 20% in one sector that has performed strongly lately, and asks you to draft the sector limits.

options.text: Test a 20% sector cap against past falls, then draft limits that fit the risk target.
Draft the 20% cap as a guideline the manager may exceed if the sector keeps rising.
Draft the 20% sector cap as requested and add a quarterly review of the limit.
Draft sector limits by copying those of a rival fund in the same risk category.

basic.situation: A retail investor asks what it costs to hold the fund. The factsheet shows a 1.5% annual management fee and a 3% sales charge paid on purchase.

options.text: Explain the annual fee, since she asked about holding costs, and send the factsheet later.
Explain the sales charge and the annual fee, using a ringgit example for her amount.
Explain both charges using the percentages in the factsheet and offer to send her a copy.
Tell her the cost is 1.5% a year, as the sales charge is paid once.

advanced.situation: You present a fund that returned 4% last year against a 7% benchmark, though its three-year average is above it. A large investor asks if it is still worth holding.

options.text: Highlight the three-year average, which beats the benchmark, and move on to the outlook.
Show returns against the benchmark, explain what caused the shortfall, and describe the risks involved.
Show last year's figures against the benchmark and explain that market conditions caused the shortfall.
Tell the investor the shortfall is temporary and that returns should recover later this year.

basic.situation: A broker's morning briefing praises a stock your fund holds. A business newspaper article that same morning warned of weak earnings for that stock. Your manager asks for a summary.

options.text: Summarise the briefing for your manager and add a line that the newspaper disagreed.
Summarise the briefing and rely on the broker's view, since the broker regularly meets management.
Share the broker's summary with the team and leave the newspaper article out to avoid confusion.
Summarise both views for your manager and check their claims against the company's latest results.

advanced.situation: You are drafting the fund's brochure. The return chart starts at a year of strong performance, which makes the fund look better than its full record. Your manager wants it finished today.

options.text: Keep the chart as drafted, since the figures are accurate and marketing has approved the layout.
Keep the chart and add a footnote giving the return since the fund launched.
Keep the chart and add the usual past-performance disclaimer in the small print on each page.
Redraw the chart to show returns since launch against the benchmark, with the standard performance warning.

basic.situation: A production order for 5,000 plastic containers is due next Friday. You have the order sheet, the resin stock count, and the shift roster open on your desk.

options.text: Release the order to the line as planned, because the planner already approved it.
Calculate resin and labour needs from this order's quantity, then compare with stock and roster.
Confirm the resin stock covers the order, and leave staffing to the supervisor to sort out.
Use the figures from a similar order last month to check stock and the roster.

advanced.situation: Two rush orders are due the same Friday. Three operators are on leave, the overtime cap is nearly reached, and one order is for your biggest customer.

options.text: Run extra overtime shifts until both orders ship, since late delivery costs more than overtime.
Split the operators evenly across both orders so each customer gets equal progress.
Give the biggest customer's order full priority and run the other order with whatever hours remain.
Weigh each order's late penalty against its margin, then allocate the limited hours accordingly.

basic.situation: A new operator joins your packing line today. Your supervisor asks you to help with his first-week training on the machine, while the line target is high this week.

options.text: Let him run the machine now so the target is met, fixing mistakes later.
Give him the written machine manual to read and ask him to come back with questions.
Pair him with a fast operator to teach him the machine while they work.
Show him the steps, let him practise while you watch, and give feedback after each run.

advanced.situation: Two operators on your shift each complain that the other gets easier tasks and better overtime. Both call the rotation unfair, and the shift output is dropping.

options.text: Tell them to settle it between themselves, because the shift target must come first.
Talk to both together, look at the records, and agree a fix on the spot.
Hear each one alone, check the rotation and overtime records, and post a clear rotation rule.
Swap the two operators' tasks for a week so each can see how the other works.

basic.situation: While logging hourly reject counts on the bottling line, you notice rejects rose from 2 to 6 per hour after the 10 a.m. changeover.

options.text: Leave the changeover rejects out of the log as settling-in losses, since they are expected.
Keep logging each hour and tell the supervisor about the rise at shift end.
Record when the rise began, check what changed at changeover, and report it to the supervisor.
Write the likely cause in the log from your own hunch, and carry on counting.

advanced.situation: Customer returns of your packaged snacks have doubled in three months. Each shift records defects on its own form with different categories, so you cannot compare shifts.

options.text: Create one shared defect form with agreed categories, trial it on every shift, and review weekly.
Ask each shift lead to explain their categories, then merge the forms into one sheet yourself.
Drop the shift forms and use the customer complaint list as the defect record instead.
Compare the total defect counts per shift and focus on the shift with the highest number.

basic.situation: You are checking a sample from a fresh batch of rice crackers against the standard. Moisture reads slightly above the allowed limit, but the sample looks and tastes fine.

options.text: Round the reading down to the limit on the sheet since the gap is small.
Record the average of two readings from the same sample and decide from that figure.
Record the reading, retest a second sample, and hold the batch if it is confirmed.
Record the reading and pass the result to the supervisor to decide on the batch.

advanced.situation: A supervisor asks you to approve RM18,000 for a new sealing machine because the old one often leaks. A repair quote is RM6,000, and your approval limit is RM20,000.

options.text: Approve whichever option the supervisor prefers, since the supervisor knows the machine well.
Turn down the request and keep the old machine running until the next budget round.
Approve the repair because it costs far less, and ask the supervisor to track leaks afterwards.
Compare repair and replacement over their lifetime, including leak and downtime costs, then approve the cheaper.

basic.situation: In the weekly meeting, a maintenance technician says the conveyor motor may fail within two weeks, which overlaps with your biggest order of the month.

options.text: Ask how likely the failure is and how long a spare takes, then plan around it.
Tell the sales team the order is on schedule since the motor has not failed yet.
Ask the technician to service the motor this week so it holds through the big order.
Record the warning in the notes and raise it again if the motor shows trouble.

advanced.situation: You chair a meeting for a new product variant due next month. Quality, purchasing, and the line team each raise a different concern, and the launch date cannot move easily.

options.text: Ask each team to send its concerns in writing, then draft the launch plan yourself.
List the concerns by risk, give each an owner and date, and schedule a trial run.
Hold the launch date and let each team solve its concern during the first run.
Address the quality concern first, since defects hurt the brand, and let the others follow later.

basic.situation: While preparing the daily production report, you notice the night shift count is 400 units lower than the packing-slip total. The report is due to the manager at 8 a.m.

options.text: Add 400 units to the night count so the report matches the slips.
Use the packing-slip total in the report, since slips come from the warehouse and look reliable.
Trace the gap in the shift log and slips, then report the confirmed figure.
Report the lower count and flag the 400-unit gap for the manager to check.

advanced.situation: Your filling machine has broken down four times in two months, each repair costing about RM3,000 and a day of lost output. The supplier offers a RM150,000 replacement.

options.text: Place the order for the replacement now to stop lost output, then seek approval later.
Keep repairing the machine and ask the supplier for a discount on parts each time.
Recommend replacement because four breakdowns in two months show the machine is near the end.
Find the repeat fault in the repair records, then compare repair and downtime costs with replacement.

basic.situation: A delivery of aluminium foil rolls arrives at 4 p.m. The supplier certificate matches the order, but the incoming-inspection standard calls for a thickness check on sample rolls.

options.text: Measure thickness on rolls from the front pallet and release the delivery if they pass.
Take sample rolls from different pallets, measure thickness against the standard, and record each result.
Accept the rolls on the strength of the matching certificate from a familiar supplier.
Send the rolls straight to production to meet the schedule and test them if problems appear.

advanced.situation: You oversee in-process testing on a three-shift line. The night shift missed two scheduled hourly checks this week because the lone technician was also covering the lab.

options.text: Rebuild the roster so each shift has cover, and re-test product made during the missed checks.
Fill in the missed checks from the next readings so the log stays consistent.
Ask for a second night technician and remind the team to keep to the check schedule.
Reduce the night checks to every two hours so one technician can manage them.

basic.situation: You are writing down the acidity test method for the sauce line. The technician explains it, but the old procedure sheet lists different titration volumes from those he uses.

options.text: Document the method as the technician performs it, since that is what the lab really does.
Copy the old sheet into the new document, since it was approved and staff know the steps.
Observe the test run, find out why the volumes differ, and write up the confirmed method.
Ask the technician to write the method in his own words and file it as submitted.

advanced.situation: You are setting up an inspection procedure for a new moulded-part line. Past data shows most defects arise at the cooling stage, but the draft plan puts equal checks at every stage.

options.text: Weight sampling toward the cooling stage by the defect data and set pass limits.
Keep equal checks at every stage because that is easier to teach and audit.
Add extra checks at the cooling stage and keep the equal checks everywhere else as planned.
Place all inspections at the final stage, where parts are easy to count and sort.

basic.situation: You are checking batch records before a customer audit tomorrow. One record has a missing operator signature on a critical step, though the test results look fine.

options.text: Log the gap as a deviation and attach the operator's dated statement for the audit file.
Keep the record in the audit pile and explain the missing signature if the auditor asks.
Ask the operator to sign with today's date and note that the entry is late.
Ask the operator to sign it dated yesterday, since the step was done then.

advanced.situation: Three customer complaints about loose caps arrived this month. Your manager wants a report by Friday, and production says it is just bad luck from one operator.

options.text: Trace the complaints to their lots, compare line, shift and supplier, and report any link.
Classify the complaints as customer handling issues, since the caps passed final inspection.
Interview the operator and the line leader, then write the report from what they explain.
Report the three complaints as isolated cases and recommend retraining the operator involved.

basic.situation: The authority has published an updated limit for a preservative in drinks like yours. Your supervisor forwards the notice and asks you to read it.

options.text: Summarise the new limit and its start date in a short note for the team.
Compare the new limit with current specifications and recent results, and list affected products.
Check whether competitors' labels mention the new limit and follow what most of them do.
File the notice for later, since our products pass now and the change looks small.

advanced.situation: Your final inspection stations reject 8% of cartons, yet customers still report defects the stations missed. Adding inspectors would cost about RM6,000 a month.

options.text: Ask for the extra inspectors, since more people looking should catch more defects.
Review the customer complaints by defect type and brief inspectors on the types most often missed.
Treat the returns as damage in transit, since the cartons passed inspection when they left.
Seed known-defect cartons through the stations, see which defects are missed, and adjust the method.

basic.situation: A new inspector is learning to use a digital caliper on shaft diameters. He tilts the caliper, and his readings vary when he measures the same shaft repeatedly.

options.text: Demonstrate the proper grip and alignment, then watch him repeat the measurements until they match yours.
Give him the caliper manual to read, then let him carry on measuring shafts.
Accept his readings as recorded, since small variation is normal in hand measurement.
Explain that tilting causes errors and ask him to hold the caliper straight next time.

advanced.situation: Two of your lab technicians report different pH results for the same product, and one blames the other's meter. A batch awaits release and the shift supervisor wants a quick answer.

options.text: Retest the batch sample yourself and use your result to release or hold the batch.
Have both read a known buffer on their meters, recalibrate if needed, then retest the sample.
Average the two results and release the batch if the average is within the limit.
Release the batch on the senior technician's result, since the other meter is probably faulty.

basic.situation: You are preparing next year's QC operating budget. Last year ran 12% over because of extra calibration and reagent costs that nobody tracked separately.

options.text: Increase last year's total by 12% to cover the overrun and submit it on time.
Copy last year's budget figure again and explain any overrun later if it happens.
Split last year's spend into categories, use actual calibration and reagent costs, and budget each line.
Cut the calibration and reagent lines to meet finance's target, as the overrun was a one-off.

advanced.situation: A contractor's quality plan for packing your products has no incoming-material check and no sampling plan. They say their record is clean and want sign-off today to start Monday.

options.text: Tell them the checks the plan needs, and approve the revised plan once those are added.
Approve the plan for the first run and ask them to add the missing checks afterwards.
Sign off the plan today as submitted, since their record is clean and Monday is fixed.
Ask them to show inspection records from their other customers' work, then decide on approval.

basic.situation: Your PLC screen shows brine flow to the separator drifting above its usual range this shift. No alarm has triggered yet, and shift handover is in one hour.

options.text: Widen the alarm band on the controller so small drifts stop cluttering the handover screen.
Compare the trend with a local gauge, then log the drift and brief the lead.
Log the drift and ask the incoming shift to keep watching the trend after handover.
Wait for the alarm to trigger, since the set limits were chosen by the engineers.

advanced.situation: Net output has slipped about four percent over three months with no single alarm. Cooling tower fan power and condenser pressure both look slightly worse, and you must find the cause.

options.text: Reset the output baseline to today's level so monthly reports stop showing a decline.
Trend output against condenser pressure, water temperature and fan power to see which explains the loss.
Compare current condenser performance with its design curve and fix whatever gap appears there.
Book a cooling tower fill cleaning, since fouling is a familiar cause of gradual losses.

basic.situation: Your supervisor assigns you this month's preventative maintenance on a standby brine pump. The checklist lists bearing greasing, but you notice a faint rattle when turning it by hand.

options.text: Grease the bearings as the checklist says and write the rattle in the maintenance record.
Close the job as routine, since a standby pump rarely runs and the rattle is faint.
Tag the pump out of standby and report the rattle so the bearings get inspected.
Run the pump briefly after greasing to see whether the rattle clears, then finish the checklist.

advanced.situation: A contractor crew is repairing a steam line valve on your shift. They skipped the lock-out step the site procedure requires, saying the valve already looks isolated.

options.text: Halt the job, send the crew away, and file a formal complaint with the contractor's manager.
Let the crew finish this valve, then raise lock-out at the next toolbox meeting.
Stop the work and let the crew resume once the leader confirms lock-out is on.
Stop the work and check the isolation points with the leader before the repair restarts.

basic.situation: A senior engineer asks you to help assess a possible well pad site on a hillside. You are to walk the area and record ground conditions before the afternoon rain.

options.text: Record slope, soil, drainage and access at marked points with photos and GPS locations.
Walk the main route and list obvious features such as slopes, streams and road access.
Copy the soil and slope notes from the neighbouring pad report to finish before the rain.
Fill in the sheet from last year's survey map and check a few changed spots.

advanced.situation: You must draft next quarter's operating schedule. Wells A and B both need scaling clean-outs, while the power buyer wants full output during a two-week high-demand period.

options.text: Defer both clean-outs until after the peak window, since the wells still flow acceptably now.
Do both clean-outs together before the peak window so the wells enter it freshly cleaned.
Drop the clean-outs from the plan and commit to full output, adding them if flow falls.
Put the clean-outs before and after the peak window, staggered so remaining wells cover output.

basic.situation: At the end of your shift you are completing the daily log and realise you did not note the time of a small, routine separator pressure adjustment.

options.text: Leave the adjustment out of the log, since it was routine and would clutter the record.
Write that a small pressure adjustment was made this shift and leave the time blank.
Check the controller event history for the time and enter it marked as a late entry.
Ask a nearby colleague what time they recall and enter their answer in the log.

advanced.situation: Reviewing the week's daily logs, you find two shifts recorded different injection flow figures for the same hour. The monthly report goes to management tomorrow morning.

options.text: Replace both entries with the design flow rate, so the report looks consistent for management.
Ask both operators to explain their figures and use whichever value they jointly agree on.
Check both figures against the meter's stored data, then amend the log with a dated note.
Use the average of the two figures in the report and mention the gap later.

basic.situation: You assist the shift supervisor. A new operator is walking the injection well field without his gas detector, which site rules require, saying it is a short check.

options.text: Let him finish the short check and raise it at the crew meeting next week.
Call him back to the control room and let the supervisor decide the next step.
Walk with him to collect the detector and explain why gas can collect near wellheads.
Tell him to fetch the detector before going out, then carry on with your own tasks.

advanced.situation: An experienced operator on your crew has made three small logging errors this month, but he is also the person others ask for help. Appraisal discussions are due this week.

options.text: Praise his helpfulness in the appraisal and mention the errors briefly as something to watch.
Show him the three entries, ask what caused them, and agree a fix to review later.
Leave the errors out of his appraisal, since the crew trusts him and they were small.
Wait until the errors repeat next month, so the evidence is clear before you raise them.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to help prepare next month's consumables budget. You have last year's invoices, but the chemical supplier has just sent a revised price list.

options.text: Wait for the supplier to confirm the new prices in writing before starting any figures.
Keep the old prices in the budget, since the new list may change before ordering.
Apply the revised rates to last year's usage quantities and note how the total changes.
Use last year's invoice totals and add a ten percent margin to cover any price rise.

advanced.situation: Mid-year, your well field maintenance budget is eighty percent spent. An unplanned pump replacement costing about RM 60,000 is now needed, and spare funds are tight.

options.text: Request extra funds from management, explaining that the pump is needed and funds are spent.
Identify deferrable planned jobs, then present the pump cost with failure risk and proposed offsets.
Charge the pump to next year's budget code so this year's figures stay within plan.
Cancel next quarter's routine inspections to fund the pump and update the budget at year end.

basic.situation: During your shift the biodiesel reactor temperature sits a few degrees below the required range on the batch sheet. The steam valve is part of your duties.

options.text: Open the steam valve fully to recover the lost temperature, then close it near range.
Lower the low-temperature alarm limit so the reading counts as in range and the batch continues.
Set the steam valve to last batch's opening and check the reading again in ten minutes.
Open the steam valve in small steps, waiting to see the reading settle within range.

advanced.situation: A technician proposes a larger RM 40,000 feed pump to raise biodiesel throughput, which falls within your approval limit. Throughput is limited, but product quality has also slipped over recent weeks.

options.text: Reject the proposal and keep the current pump until quality returns to normal.
Approve it as the technician knows the plant, and add the cost to this month's spending.
Ask the technician to trial a temporary rental pump first and report flow and quality results.
Request flow and quality data to confirm the pump is the limit before approving the purchase.

basic.situation: You are asked to draw a biodiesel sample from the storage tank for the lab. The sample valve has dried residue around its outlet.

options.text: Flush a little product from the valve, then fill a clean bottle and label it.
Fill the bottle from the nearby transfer line and record it as the tank sample.
Wipe the outlet with a cloth, then fill a clean bottle and label it.
Dip a bottle in the top hatch instead, since that avoids the dirty valve.

advanced.situation: Management asks whether a second methanol recovery unit is worth buying. You have six months of data on methanol use per tonne of biodiesel, but the figures vary widely between batches.

options.text: Check why batches differ first, then estimate savings using a realistic range of usage.
Use the three months with the highest methanol use, since they show the payback most clearly.
Use the supplier's stated recovery rate to estimate payback and send it up quickly.
Calculate savings from the average methanol use and compare it with the unit's quoted price.

basic.situation: Site rules require earthing before any methanol transfer. A tanker driver arrives and says the transfer will take ten minutes, so the earthing clamp is a waste of time.

options.text: Let the short transfer go ahead, since ten minutes is brief and the bay is outdoors.
Tell the driver earthing is required and watch him attach the clamp before he starts.
Refuse the delivery and send the tanker away, then email the supplier about the driver's attitude.
Hold the transfer until the clamp sits on bare metal and its indicator light is on.

advanced.situation: At night a methanol leak alarm sounds at the reactor skid. You are the senior person on shift, and the batch is nearly finished. Stopping would waste about RM 50,000 of product.

options.text: Run the full emergency shutdown, sound the alarm, and keep staff clear of the skid.
Bypass the alarm trip so the batch can finish its last minutes, then shut down.
Send an operator with a handheld detector to confirm the leak before starting any shutdown steps.
Shut down the reactor skid and watch the gas readings for signs the leak is spreading.

basic.situation: You supervise the wash-and-dry crew. Two operators disagree about who covers a missing colleague's wash station, which needs trained hands, and the transfer is due in an hour.

options.text: Let the two operators settle it between themselves and report the outcome before the transfer.
Put whichever operator is free first on the station, since the transfer is due soon.
Give the station to the operator trained on it, and rebalance the other's tasks to match.
Take the station yourself to keep things moving, and let both operators stay on their tasks.

advanced.situation: A new operator has twice mixed up the valve order when switching feed tanks, and a wrong sequence could send methanol into the wrong line. Production targets are high this week.

options.text: Pair him with the fastest operator so he picks up the routine by watching during shifts.
Leave him on tank switching alone and check the log for mistakes at shift end.
Walk him through the tank switch with the written sequence, then watch him do it.
Give him the written valve sequence to study and ask him to follow it next time.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to help prepare the unit's monthly cost report. Your unit used more steam than planned, and the overspend is about RM 8,000.

options.text: Show the overspend in the report with steam hours and the likely cause from operating records.
Move the steam cost to another unit's cost code so your unit stays on budget.
Report the overspend figure and add a note that steam use will be reviewed later.
Spread the extra steam cost across the next three months so the monthly figure looks steadier.

advanced.situation: Your unit has RM 120,000 left this year. A heat exchanger is fouling and will need replacing within a year, but a cheaper cleaning contract could delay replacement. You must plan the spend.

options.text: Buy the replacement now from the remaining funds, since it is needed within a year.
Choose the cheaper cleaning contract and revisit replacement next year when funds are clearer.
Leave both out of the budget and treat any exchanger failure as a breakdown repair.
Compare repeated cleaning costs against replacement over three years, including lost output, then choose.

basic.situation: A customer's tanker is booked to collect biodiesel at 3 pm. At noon the lab has not yet released the batch, and the loading bay crew asks whether to start.

options.text: Move the customer's booking to tomorrow morning so the lab is not rushed.
Ask the lab for a release time, hold loading until then, and update the customer.
Hold loading until lab release and let the customer's driver find out when he arrives.
Start loading now and let the lab results follow, since most batches pass anyway.

advanced.situation: Two weeks before month-end, you must meet a large export order. Feedstock delivery is late, the dryer needs scheduled maintenance, and quality checks are already behind.

options.text: Postpone the dryer maintenance past month-end so the plant can keep running for the order.
Rank the constraints by effect on the order, then rebuild the schedule around the tightest one.
Warn the customer the order may slip and ask whether a partial shipment would suit them.
Release product with shortened quality checks so the shipment leaves on the original date.

basic.situation: A radio call from the fuel yard reports smoke near the conveyor, but static breaks up the message. You are on the control room radio during the afternoon shift.

options.text: Wait for the caller to radio again, since a second message should be clearer.
Ask the caller to repeat the spot, confirm it back, then send the nearest operator.
Send the nearest operator to the conveyor area and wait for a clearer radio update.
Tell the caller it is probably conveyor dust and carry on with the shift log.

advanced.situation: Two near-miss reports this month involve workers clearing jams at the fuel feeder before isolating it. You help run the plant's safety programme and must decide the follow-up.

options.text: Remind the feeder crew at the next toolbox talk to isolate the feeder before clearing jams.
Trace the shared cause of both near misses, then revise the isolation steps for all shifts.
Close both near-miss reports as no injury occurred, and note the crew cleared the jams quickly.
Ask the feeder supervisor to name the two workers and give them a written warning.

basic.situation: A fitter on your shift is greasing the boiler feed pump bearings and skips the logged lockout step, saying the pump is already off. You supervise the crew.

options.text: Sign the lockout entry for him, since the pump is off and the job is short.
Pause the job, verify the isolation together, and have him fit his own lock and tag.
Trust his judgement on the pump, as he is experienced, and check the lockout log later.
Confirm the breaker is off yourself, let him continue, and remind him of the lockout after.

advanced.situation: A generator overhaul is running two days late. Technicians lent by a sister plant use different torque and sign-off steps from yours, and your own crew is unhappy about it.

options.text: Let the sister plant's lead set the sign-off steps, since his team has overhaul experience.
Let each team follow its own steps on separate sections, then inspect the joins yourself.
Shorten the final checks to win back the two lost days and sign off on time.
Agree one written sequence and sign-off standard with both leads, then brief all technicians.

basic.situation: The weekly status report is due at 5 p.m. The fuel consumption figure from the weighbridge log is about double last week's. You are compiling the report.

options.text: Compare the weighbridge entries with delivery tickets, fix any slip, and report the confirmed figure.
Report the logged figure and add a note that it looks high and will be checked.
Hold the report until tomorrow so all the numbers can be rechecked with the weighbridge clerk.
Use last week's figure, as fuel use is steady and the new one looks odd.

advanced.situation: Next year's budget is due this week. Boiler tubes are wearing faster than planned, yet a manager asks you to cut the maintenance line by 10 percent to hit the plant's savings target.

options.text: Remove the tube inspection line and cover any failures later from the contingency fund budget.
Apply the cut and note the tube wear risk in the budget remarks for later review.
Present the tube wear data and propose savings from other lines, keeping tube work funded.
Spread the cut evenly across all maintenance items so no single task takes the full reduction.

basic.situation: On your morning round you see a small oil drip under the induced draft fan bearing. Panel readings look normal and the fan is carrying full load.

options.text: Check the oil level and bearing temperature, then log the drip and raise a work order.
Mention the drip to the next shift verbally at handover and leave the logging to them.
Wipe the drip away and top up the oil yourself, then carry on with the round.
Log the drip on the round sheet and watch it again on the next round.

advanced.situation: Gasifier output has slowly dropped about 8 percent over two months while fuel cost stays the same. You are asked to find the cause and suggest improvements.

options.text: Set the gasifier air supply to match a sister plant's settings and see if output rises.
Inspect the gasifier and clean the grate, filters and feed screw, then see whether output recovers.
Raise the fuel feed rate to restore output and watch the cost figures for a month.
Compare fuel moisture and size records with the output trend, then trial a feed adjustment.

basic.situation: Monthly stack dust readings are close to the limit in the plant's licence, though still under it. You are reviewing the monthly performance sheet.

options.text: Plot recent months against the licence limit and alert your manager if the trend is rising.
Mark the sheet compliant and file it, since the readings are still under the licence limit.
Mark the month compliant and ask the operators to check the dust control equipment this week.
Average this month's readings with last month's lower ones so the sheet shows a safer margin.

advanced.situation: Dispatch records from the grid operator show your plant is asked to cut output most middays and raise it in the evenings. You are asked to suggest how operations should adapt.

options.text: Suggest raising boiler output in the evenings to meet demand, based on this month's records.
Analyse the hourly dispatch records over months, then propose scheduling maintenance in the midday dips.
Keep midday output at full level despite the dispatch requests, since the fuel is already delivered.
Keep steady output all day as before, since changes may upset the boiler and fuel plan.

basic.situation: While counting spares, you find just two of the usual six conveyor chain links in stock. The supplier normally needs two weeks to deliver.

options.text: Check past usage to set a reorder level, then order the links and update the sheet.
Order four more links to bring stock back to six and update the stock sheet.
Take chain links from the spare conveyor in the yard and record the change later.
Tell the maintenance crew to take care of the conveyor chain until the next stock count.

advanced.situation: Heavy monsoon rain is forecast. Wood chip deliveries, an ash removal truck and a planned boiler inspection all fall on the same two days this week, and you plan the schedule.

options.text: Postpone the boiler inspection to next week and keep the fuel and ash schedule as planned.
Cancel the chip deliveries on those days to avoid rain delays and use the stockpile instead.
Work out the fuel days in stock, then move ash removal and inspection around the deliveries.
Record the boiler inspection as done this week and carry out the check next month instead.

basic.situation: The grid dispatcher asks for extra output tomorrow evening, but the reservoir is lower than usual after a dry week. You are helping draft the daily production schedule.

options.text: Draft the schedule for the full request and plan to cut back if the level falls.
Adjust the minimum level figure in the planning sheet so the full request fits the schedule.
Keep the usual schedule and tell the dispatcher the plant cannot give extra output tomorrow.
Calculate the extra output the water level and inflow forecast allow, then draft the schedule.

advanced.situation: A turbine runner replacement is planned for the dry season, but the contractor wants to start four weeks earlier. Some customer contracts need full output until then.

options.text: Compare lost generation and contract penalties for both start dates, then present the options.
Hold off replying to the contractor until customers raise supply concerns about an earlier start.
Confirm the earlier start in writing to the contractor and sort out the contracts afterwards.
Keep the original start and ask the contractor what early preparation work could proceed meanwhile.

basic.situation: A technician starts stripping a generator bearing before the lead signs the work permit, saying approval was given verbally. Plant rules require the signed permit first. You are documenting the job.

options.text: Ask the technician to pause and raise the permit issue at tomorrow's team meeting instead.
Ask the technician to pause and record the missing permit in the notes for the lead.
Ask the technician to pause, get the lead to sign the permit, then let him resume.
Sign the permit for the lead, since he approved the job and the delay is costly.

advanced.situation: During commissioning of a new governor system, the vendor engineer suggests shortening the tests to meet the handover date. Your manager wants the unit online on schedule.

options.text: Record the load rejection test as passed using the factory results to meet the handover date.
Run all the specified tests in full and tell the manager the handover date may slip.
Check which tests the specification requires, then agree a tighter sequence with the vendor.
Accept the vendor's shortened plan, as his firm knows the system and has done similar jobs.

basic.situation: On your checklist round, a generator winding temperature reads just above the usual limit on the sheet. The unit is still carrying load.

options.text: Note the reading on the checklist and see whether it settles before the next round.
Re-read the gauge, compare it with the control room display, and report to the supervisor.
Tick the item as within limits since the margin is small and load is steady.
Report the high reading to the shift supervisor and wait for instructions beside the unit.

advanced.situation: A transformer oil leak in the switchyard is spreading toward a drain that leads to the river. You are first on site and the supervisor is thirty minutes away.

options.text: Phone the supervisor and the environmental officer first, then contain the leak once instructed.
Cover the drain with the spill kit and phone the supervisor, then wait for the team.
Block the drain and boom the oil using the spill kit, then phone the supervisor.
Hose the oil away to clear the switchyard and report the leak once the supervisor arrives.

basic.situation: On your hourly round, turbine bearing vibration reads slightly higher than the last two rounds. The senior engineer is in a meeting and you are monitoring under his guidance.

options.text: Check the vibration trend against the alarm level and message the engineer with the figures.
Record the figure on the round sheet and recheck it at the next hourly round.
Reset the vibration monitor baseline so the display reads normal and no nuisance alarm sounds.
Message the engineer that vibration is higher and ask him to look after his meeting.

advanced.situation: At 2 a.m. a transmission line trips and the alarms show the plant has lost its grid connection. You hold the shift and the duty manager's phone is off.

options.text: Confirm which breakers opened, tell the grid dispatcher the unit status, and use the call list.
Tell the grid dispatcher about the trip and keep the units steady until the manager answers.
Close the line breaker again to restore supply to the villages and watch for a repeat.
Keep calling the duty manager until he answers, and log each alarm as it appears.

basic.situation: You are filing last month's maintenance job cards and find one with no technician signature or date. The technician is on leave for two weeks.

options.text: Leave the card out of the file until the technician returns and can sign it.
Flag the card as incomplete and ask the supervising lead to confirm the job details.
Sign and date the card yourself from the work order, since the job was clearly done.
File the card with a note saying the signature is missing until the technician returns.

advanced.situation: A state agency writes asking why downstream river levels fell last Tuesday. Your logs show a planned gate release was cut short when a unit tripped, and villagers have complained.

options.text: Pass the letter to the communications office and let them answer, as it involves public complaints.
Reply briefly that a unit trip shortened the release and that more details will follow.
Gather the gate and trip records and draft a factual timeline reply offering a briefing meeting.
Reply that river levels depend on rainfall and the plant's releases are not the main cause.

basic.situation: While reviewing the annual budget draft with the finance lead, you notice the spare parts line matches last year although two new units are being added.

options.text: Estimate extra spares for the new units from the maker's list and show the gap.
Raise the spares line by 20 percent for the new units then review the rest.
Sign off the draft as reviewed to meet the deadline and fix the spares gap mid-year.
Tell the finance lead the spares line looks low for the new units and ask why.

advanced.situation: You are asked to lead a small efficiency project. The older unit runs poorly at part load, a drainage pump uses much electricity, and the budget covers one study.

options.text: Choose the pump study because it is cheaper and quicker to finish within the budget.
Estimate each option's saving and cost from plant data, then choose the higher return.
Use the study budget to buy a new pump straight away, then measure the savings afterwards.
Study the older unit first since its part-load losses are well known and likely large.

basic.situation: You are receiving 200 cartons of printer paper, but the delivery order says 220. The driver is waiting and wants your signature on his copy.

options.text: Count the cartons, log 200 received, and email the buyer about the gap later.
Count the cartons with the driver, note the shortfall on his copy, and log 200.
Sign to release the driver, then count the cartons later and log the total.
Sign and log 220 as received, since the vendor will probably send the missing cartons soon.

advanced.situation: A new packaging supplier quotes 12 percent below your current vendor. Your junior buyer wants to switch this week, but you know little about the supplier's capacity, payment terms or track record.

options.text: Request a company profile and product sample, then compare the unit price with the current vendor's.
Let the junior buyer switch the next order, since a 12 percent saving is worth testing.
Interview the supplier on capacity and terms, call references, and score it by our vendor criteria.
Move the whole account to the new supplier, since price decides most buying choices.

basic.situation: You are reviewing a purchase order for RM 8,000 of office chairs. It lacks the second quotation that company policy requires above RM 5,000, and the requester says the chairs are urgent.

options.text: Return the order to the requester marked incomplete and carry on with your other work.
Split it into two orders of RM 4,000 each, so the chairs arrive quickly.
Hold the order and tell the requester exactly which quotation is missing and why.
Check the policy on urgent buys, then prepare an exception form or request the quote.

advanced.situation: Engineering sends you a draft bid specification for forklift tyres that names one brand's product dimensions and tread code. Three suppliers are due to bid by Friday, and the engineer wants it issued today.

options.text: Ask the engineer for the performance needs behind the code, then rewrite the spec around them.
Add 'or equivalent' after the brand details so other makes can bid, then issue the document.
Issue the spec as drafted and let suppliers raise questions during the clarification period.
Send the draft to the brand's local agent to check the technical details before issuing.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to draft a one-page instruction for staff on raising urgent purchase requests after office hours. You have the old procedure and two staff complaints about it.

options.text: Write the steps from your own experience of urgent requests and give them to your supervisor.
Tidy the wording of the old procedure and send the cleaned version to your supervisor.
Use the complaints to find where the old steps failed, then redraft those steps.
Send the draft to all staff to save time, as the steps are common sense.

advanced.situation: A warehouse audit finds 40 pallets of obsolete spare parts. A scrap dealer offers you RM 6,000 for all of them and wants to collect them tomorrow.

options.text: Send the pallets to the scrap yard to free up space, since the parts are obsolete.
Get approval from your manager and finance, then sell the parts to the dealer who called.
Accept the dealer's offer, since RM 6,000 beats paying to store the parts any longer.
Confirm the write-off rules with finance, then invite quotes from several dealers before choosing a buyer.

basic.situation: You are compiling A4 paper costs for a report due this afternoon. One vendor invoices per ream, another per carton of five reams, and you bought different quantities from each.

options.text: Convert both to cost per ream, then average the two prices to show the quarter's cost.
Report the lower price as the quarter's cost, since that is the target level.
Convert both to cost per ream, then weight each by quantity bought to find the average.
List both invoice prices side by side in the report and let the reader compare them.

advanced.situation: You are preparing a board paper on a plan to switch two suppliers and save RM 90,000 a year. One switch triggers a contract exit penalty and raises delivery risk.

options.text: Take the lower-risk switch to the board and hold the other for a later paper.
Show the full RM 90,000 saving and list the penalty and delivery risk in the notes.
Present the RM 90,000 saving and deal with the exit penalty after the board approves.
Show the net saving after the penalty, flag the delivery risk, and offer a phased switch.

basic.situation: The stationery budget is 85 percent spent with two months left. A colleague asks you to raise a RM 1,500 order for new binders, and some earlier orders are still unbilled.

options.text: Check the remaining balance in the ledger, and raise the order if RM 1,500 still fits.
Tell the colleague to wait until the next review so the budget is not stretched.
Compare open orders and monthly use with the remaining balance before saying yes or no.
Raise the order and charge it to the cleaning budget, which has plenty of room.

advanced.situation: The online purchasing system lets any buyer approve orders up to RM 20,000 with no second approval. Two orders last month were duplicated by mistake. You are asked to tighten the controls.

options.text: Give all buyers edit rights to cancel and re-enter orders so mistakes can be fixed fast.
Lower the approval limit to RM 5,000 for all buyers and email them about the change.
Ask the buyers to check the order list daily for duplicates and report any they find.
Review recent orders to see where duplicates arose, then set approval tiers and a duplicate-check alert.

basic.situation: A small vendor phones you upset because a RM 3,200 invoice has been unpaid for 45 days. Finance put it on hold because the delivery order copy has no receiving signature.

options.text: Tell the vendor finance has a query and that you will chase finance for an answer.
Apologise to the vendor for the delay and promise that payment will go out this week.
Ask finance to release the payment this week and sort out the signature paperwork afterwards.
Explain the signature query, request a signed copy, and promise the vendor an update by Friday.

advanced.situation: You are leading a contract renewal with a key bracket supplier who wants a 10 percent price rise, citing raw material costs. The rival quote you hold is slightly above their current price.

options.text: Trade a committed annual volume for a rate freeze, citing material price movements as the test.
Accept the 10 percent rise for one year to protect supply while you look elsewhere.
Tell the supplier a rival quoted lower, so it should hold this year's price.
Counter with a 5 percent increase and ask the supplier to justify anything above that.

basic.situation: During your morning check you find a forklift hydraulic hose leaking oil onto the bay floor. It is peak dispatch hour and the only other forklift is already in use.

options.text: Top up the hydraulic oil and carry on, since the forklift still lifts loads normally.
Put a drip tray under the hose and use the forklift until the peak hour ends.
Tag the forklift out of use, clean and mark the spill, and log a repair request.
Tag the forklift out of use and tell the supervisor, then carry on with dispatch duties.

advanced.situation: The lowest quote for your container runs comes from a haulage contractor with no written safety record. Its manager says the drivers are experienced, and your team wants to award the work this week.

options.text: Accept the manager's word on safety and award the runs, since the quote saves money.
Visit the contractor's yard to see the trucks and speak to a few drivers before deciding.
Request its accident log and vehicle inspection records, then score it on the team's safety checklist.
Award a three-month trial run and watch how the drivers perform before signing the longer contract.

basic.situation: You are checking a supplier's commercial invoice for imported spare parts. It lists nine cartons, but the shipping manifest shows eight, and the customs declaration is due tomorrow.

options.text: File the declaration using the manifest's eight cartons, since the carrier prepared that document.
Email the supplier about the carton difference and wait for a revised invoice before filing.
Amend the invoice yourself to show eight cartons so both documents match, then file on time.
Check the packing list for the carton count, then ask the forwarder to confirm before filing.

advanced.situation: You review a proposal to switch one long-haul route from road to rail, claiming a 15 percent saving. The figures leave out terminal handling charges and the longer transit time for customers.

options.text: Accept the 15 percent saving and cut next year's road budget by that amount.
Rebuild the comparison with terminal charges and transit time included, then show the net saving.
Get the rail operator's charge list and add those costs to the proposal's saving calculation.
Ask the proposer to recheck the 15 percent figure and support the switch if it holds.

basic.situation: You are shortlisting for a forklift operator. One candidate has strong experience but a certificate that lapsed six months ago; the other is certified with less experience. Company rules require valid certificates.

options.text: Offer the job to the experienced candidate, since skills are harder to teach than paperwork.
Hire the experienced candidate and let them operate the forklift while the renewal is being processed.
Select the candidate with the valid certificate, as the role starts soon and training takes time.
Ask about the lapse and renewal plan, then score both candidates against the same job criteria.

advanced.situation: Two night-shift supervisors disagree on how to stack and label chemical drums. Your procedure is unclear on this, and last week a wrongly labelled drum almost went out on a truck.

options.text: Set one stacking and labelling method from the data sheets and rules, then brief both supervisors.
Choose the method of the more senior supervisor and tell the whole shift to follow it.
Let each supervisor keep their own method and check the dispatch labels yourself each night.
Have the dispatch clerk sign off drum labels at loading so the supervisors need not agree.

basic.situation: Fuel reports show two delivery vans leaving half empty on the same Klang Valley morning route, an hour apart. You are asked to cut fuel use on this route.

options.text: Merge both vans' loads into one van and tell the customers their delivery times may change.
Compare drop lists and customer time windows, then merge loads into one van where possible.
Cancel the later van's run and move its customers to the next day's schedule.
Ask both drivers to avoid idling and drive steadily so each van uses less fuel.

advanced.situation: Sales forecast a 30 percent rise in volume next year. You must recommend adding racking in your warehouse or renting a second unit, and the racking would block two loading bays.

options.text: Order the racking now to secure the contractor's price and sort out the loading bays afterwards.
Get a racking contractor's quote and compare its price with the rent of a second unit.
Compare both choices on cost, bay access and peak-day throughput, then recommend with the numbers.
Recommend adding racking, since it looks cheaper than rent and the bays can be rearranged later.

basic.situation: Sales keep promising next-day delivery to Kuching customers, but your sea freight shipments take about three days. Customers are complaining and the sales team says logistics is too slow.

options.text: Give sales a table of real transit times and agree how they will quote from it.
Email the sales manager about the complaints and ask the team to promise realistic delivery times.
Phone each unhappy customer yourself and explain that sea freight takes three days.
Book air freight for late orders from the department budget so the promises are kept.

advanced.situation: A key customer disputes a RM 2,400 transport charge, saying sales quoted RM 1,800. Billing applied the current tariff, and the sales rep asks you to tell billing to match the quote.

options.text: Ask billing to hold the invoice while sales and the customer settle the price between them.
Tell billing to match RM 1,800 and record the RM 600 gap as a discount.
Compare the written quote with the tariff, find the cause, and advise both teams.
Advise billing that the tariff applies and ask sales to explain the quote to the customer.

basic.situation: Your weekly count shows 60 cartons of instant noodles on the system but 52 on the shelf. The next outbound order needs 55 cartons, and picking starts in an hour.

options.text: Ship the 52 cartons, send the balance later, and look at the difference next week.
Recount the shelf, check recent picks and receipts for entry errors, then amend the record.
Pick the order from the system's 60, as the missing eight are probably in another bay.
Recount the shelf, update the system to 52, and warn the planner about the shortfall.

advanced.situation: Your main carrier proposes a 7 percent rate rise at renewal, though your volume grew 20 percent this year. A second carrier quotes lower but offers less coverage on the northern route.

options.text: Ask the main carrier for a smaller rise in view of the 20 percent volume growth.
Switch freight to the second carrier for its lower rate, then tell the main carrier.
Trade a committed annual volume for a rate freeze, citing the second carrier's lower quote.
Accept the 7 percent rise to keep the northern route coverage and avoid a messy changeover.

basic.situation: Two local suppliers meet the stated quality criteria, but one has a shorter delivery window and a higher quoted price.

options.text: Ask both suppliers to confirm lead times before recommending one.
Recommend the faster supplier because production needs the stock soon.
Choose the lower quote and confirm the delivery date later.
Compare delivered cost and reliability against the evaluation criteria.

advanced.situation: A new packaging supplier offers a lower price, but quality and finance teams disagree about acceptable defects and payment terms.

options.text: Accept the lower price and revisit defects after the first shipment.
Ask each team to send its preferred terms for your review.
Align defect criteria and payment limits before negotiating the offer.
Negotiate a trial order while quality and finance continue reviewing.

basic.situation: A delivery is due at the warehouse just as two workers begin unloading another truck with the available pallet jack.

options.text: Ask the driver to wait until the pallet jack is free.
Check the first load's finish time before confirming the next unloading slot.
Check arrival timing and assign suitable equipment and workers to each load.
