Start both unloads with the available crew to clear the yard.

advanced.situation: Your team is redesigning deliveries for a growing product line, with tight stock targets and a company goal to reduce packaging waste.

options.text: Model stock needs, delivery routes, and reusable packaging against the growth plan.
Increase safety stock and ask suppliers to use less packaging.
Keep current routes and raise stock targets for the new product line.
Ask sales for growth estimates before changing replenishment plans.

basic.situation: You are helping choose a measure for comparing suppliers after teams report different views of late deliveries and product defects.

options.text: Rank suppliers by the measure showing the strongest result this month.
Set shared delivery and defect measures using consistent time periods and verified data sources.
Ask each team to explain its preferred measure and supporting data.
Compare suppliers using monthly delivery delays and recorded product defect rates.

advanced.situation: Warehouse teams use separate tracking tools, and missing scans make it difficult to explain stock differences between locations.

options.text: Choose the tool with the quickest setup and migrate one warehouse.
Document the missing scans and request a systems review.
Ask technology vendors to demonstrate their latest tracking features.
Map scan gaps and compare systems against shared tracking and reporting needs.

basic.situation: A planner asks for your input because a supplier's updated lead time may affect next month's stock availability.

options.text: Forward the supplier's update to the planner for review.
Ask the planner whether the longer lead time changes the supply plan.
Compare the updated lead time with demand plans and flag likely shortages.
Keep the current plan until the supplier confirms another change.

advanced.situation: Engineering has moved a component change forward, while production still holds the previous date for the first batch of a new product.

options.text: Share the new date with production and ask whether stock needs review.
Ask production to confirm its first-batch date before updating the plan.
Align change dates, inventory cutoffs, and production readiness across teams.
Update the component order to match engineering's earlier date.

basic.situation: Several clean offcuts from production are collected for disposal, though a nearby process may be able to use them.

options.text: Ask production whether it can use the offcuts next week.
Check the offcuts' condition and quantify possible reuse with production.
Send the offcuts with the regular waste pickup to clear space.
Store the offcuts beside the line until someone requests them.

advanced.situation: A revised environmental requirement may affect packaging returns, but suppliers have not yet confirmed how their current processes work.

options.text: Keep existing return steps until the next supplier review meeting.
Map return flows against the updated requirements and identify supplier gaps.
Flag the possible change and ask procurement to check supplier responses.
Ask suppliers to confirm whether their current process has changed.

basic.situation: A new warehouse colleague asks how returned cartons move from the receiving bay to their storage location.

options.text: Trace the carton route and record handoffs, timing, and assigned roles.
Send the colleague the warehouse map and let them follow it.
Ask the colleague which steps seemed unclear during the first shift.
Sketch the route from the receiving bay to storage.

advanced.situation: A supplier has missed two delivery windows, and a revised receiving process is being considered before a seasonal demand increase.

options.text: Request a supplier recovery plan and assess its impact on warehouse routines.
Maintain the current flow and review the supplier's next delivery estimate against actual arrivals.
Track delivery trends and trial a revised receiving flow using agreed measures.
Schedule extra receiving staff for peak demand while monitoring queue times.

basic.situation: You are reviewing the annual health benefits summary and notice several employees have asked about dental coverage. Your manager asks you to help assess the current program.

options.text: Ask the broker to prepare a fresh summary of dental coverage.
Send the existing summary again so employees can check their coverage.
Group recurring questions, check plan details, and summarize possible improvements for review.
Compare employee questions with the current plan summary and flag unclear coverage.

advanced.situation: After an acquisition, two employee groups have different medical and leave benefits. You are asked to help map the programs before a proposed integration is reviewed.

options.text: Choose the larger group's plan as the standard for everyone.
Ask each provider to recommend one plan for both groups.
Compare coverage, costs, and employee needs, then outline transition choices for review.
List both groups' coverage and flag differences for the integration review.

basic.situation: Employees at your site say the current wellness allowance does not cover activities they use. Your manager asks you to gather ideas for improving quality of life.

options.text: Share a short survey about preferred wellness activities.
Keep the allowance unchanged until the next annual review.
Ask employees which wellbeing costs the current allowance misses.
Compare employee suggestions with broker options and summarize feasible changes.

advanced.situation: A benefits policy is due for renewal, and a broker flags a possible compliance gap while employees report weaker coverage than nearby employers offer.

options.text: Check the policy requirements and market options, then draft changes for review.
Ask the broker to clarify the compliance concern and policy wording.
Renew the current policy while the concern remains under review.
Compare the renewal quote with nearby employers' benefit summaries.

basic.situation: A manager asks you to compare the company's technician pay with current local wage data before the next compensation review.

options.text: Collect current technician wage figures from one salary website.
Use last year's figures to keep the review moving.
Check role scope and local wage sources, then summarize pay positioning.
Compare local wage figures for similar technician roles and locations.

advanced.situation: A proposed pay review coincides with new industry guidance and a recent arbitration decision. Your manager asks what these developments may mean for pay planning.

options.text: Ask peers about similar changes and share their observations during pay planning.
Compare guidance, arbitration, and contracts to identify emerging pay planning trends.
Summarize guidance and arbitration implications for the upcoming pay planning discussion.
Maintain the current pay approach while monitoring developments for the next cycle.

basic.situation: Your team is updating its onboarding checklist, and a new manager asks you to draft a basic procedure for confirming equipment and orientation needs.

options.text: Draft steps for equipment requests and orientation handoffs.
Set out owners, timing, and handoffs for equipment and orientation.
Copy the old checklist into the new policy template.
Ask the manager to list the procedure steps for you.

advanced.situation: Several departments report delays in approving job changes, and managers say the current process creates inconsistent employee experiences. You are asked to suggest improvements.

options.text: Tell teams to submit requests earlier in the month.
Map each approval step and summarize where requests pause across departments.
Compare department workflows and recommend a simpler shared approval route.
Ask managers to remind their teams about submission deadlines.

basic.situation: A department is hiring a new coordinator, and your manager asks you to prepare a job description from notes supplied by the team lead.

options.text: Ask the team lead to write the full description.
Confirm duties, reporting line, and required skills before drafting the description.
Turn the notes into a clear list of duties and qualifications.
Reuse a similar role description and change the job title.

advanced.situation: Two teams use different titles for similar analyst roles, while their managers propose several new levels. You are asked to help define job families.

options.text: Retain current team titles and proposed levels pending a shared review.
Ask managers to rank roles by seniority and explain their criteria.
List current titles and compare responsibilities across both teams and proposed levels.
Compare scope and decision duties, then draft shared levels for manager review.

basic.situation: An employee says a recent benefits statement does not match their expected coverage. You are helping handle questions while the benefits specialist is away.

options.text: Check plan details and explain coverage that addresses the employee's question.
Send the question to the provider and include the employee's stated concern.
Compare statement and plan details, then route the discrepancy with useful context.
Ask the employee to review the next statement when it arrives.

advanced.situation: A manager is choosing between two pay adjustment proposals for a team, and employees have raised questions about how performance and benefits were considered.

options.text: Compare both proposals and explain how each treats performance and benefits.
Ask the manager which proposal may be clearer to explain, then note employee concerns.
Support the proposal with the larger average increase for the team.
Explain the pay guidance and acknowledge employee questions about performance and benefits.

basic.situation: Your team lead says a customer support vacancy is affecting shift coverage and asks you to help recruit suitable applicants.

options.text: Confirm shift needs and screen applicants against the role requirements.
Check shift coverage needs, then shortlist applicants against agreed criteria.
Invite the first applicants who meet the listed experience requirement.
Post the vacancy again on the usual job boards.

advanced.situation: Two employees dispute a shift allocation, and one has made repeated attendance errors. Your manager asks you to help document the issue before any staffing action.

options.text: Move the employee to another shift and close the issue.
Separate the roster dispute from attendance concerns and document each fairly.
Record each employee's account and check the shift allocation history.
Ask the team lead to decide which employee should move.

basic.situation: A new employee asks when their health coverage begins, and you are helping update the benefits enrolment tracker under supervision.

options.text: Check the enrolment record and share the stated coverage start date.
Forward the question to payroll for a reply.
Compare the enrolment record with plan dates and flag any mismatch.
Tell the employee to check again after the next payroll run.

advanced.situation: A market review suggests your company's allowance is falling behind, while a policy check raises a question about eligibility rules. Your manager requests options.

options.text: Assess market positioning and eligibility, then outline balanced policy options.
Ask the broker for a view on allowance levels.
Recommend matching the highest allowance in the market review.
Compare peer allowance figures and note the eligibility question.

basic.situation: A prospective employee asks about weekend shifts and promotion opportunities during a recruitment call. You have access to the current role information.

options.text: Send them the general careers page after the call.
Share the stated terms and invite specific questions about the role.
Tell them the role has flexible hours and good prospects.
Explain the stated schedule and promotion paths from current materials.

advanced.situation: You are supporting an employee hearing about a disputed workplace decision. The employee representative asks you to explain the organization's position using the case records.

options.text: Repeat the manager's account as the organization's full position.
Organize the records by issue and present the supported position fairly.
Present the documented position and answer questions within your brief.
Ask the representative to send their concerns in writing.

basic.situation: Several new starters begin next week, and your manager asks you to help prepare their orientation session and materials.

options.text: Prepare the room, test equipment, and align orientation materials with the session goals.
Use last month's slides and agenda as a starting point for new starters.
Ask a recent starter which materials helped them settle into the workplace.
Update materials to match session goals, then confirm the planned sequence.

advanced.situation: A needs review shows recurring equipment handling errors across shifts. You are asked to propose development and safety training for affected employees.

options.text: Ask supervisors to repeat the equipment rules at briefings.
Schedule targeted refresher training and practice sessions for employees on affected shifts.
Design practical sessions using review findings for each shift.
Share the safety slides with all staff by email.

basic.situation: Your manager needs a monthly report of hires, transfers, and departures. You are asked to compile the figures from personnel records.

options.text: Count each movement type from the current personnel records.
Ask each team to send its own movement totals.
Reconcile movement entries with records before summarizing monthly totals.
Copy last month's totals into the report template.

advanced.situation: Absence figures have risen in one department for three months. Your manager asks you to analyze the trend and suggest what to examine next.

options.text: Compare absence trends with shift and role data to identify useful context.
Ask the department manager whether staff morale seems lower across the teams.
Review attendance records and recommend a stricter policy after checking the rise.
Group absences by team and role, then compare patterns across three months.

basic.situation: Your manager is drafting next quarter's staffing budget and asks you to help estimate personnel costs using the current headcount plan.

options.text: Reuse last quarter's personnel budget totals as the estimate.
Ask team leads to send their preferred budget amounts.
Apply current staffing figures and salary assumptions to the personnel budget template.
Check planned hires and exits, then estimate costs by team.

advanced.situation: A manager asks whether a proposed role redesign could create staffing issues. You are reviewing workforce plans alongside relevant industry agreements and legislation.

options.text: Summarize relevant agreements and legislation, then note possible staffing effects by role.
Review agreements and legislation, then map implications for workforce planning.
Proceed with the redesign using the current workforce plan.
Ask managers whether similar redesigns worked at other employers.

basic.situation: A new hire starts tomorrow, but the department has not named an on-the-job trainer. You have the orientation checklist ready.

options.text: Assign the new hire to shadow whichever team member is free on the first day.
Get the department to name a trainer today and brief that person on the plan.
Put the new hire on a work station so co-workers can teach tasks as they come.
Run the orientation as planned and ask the department to name a trainer afterwards.

advanced.situation: A new supervisor and twelve operators start together across two departments. Each department wants different orientation content, and the plant manager wants everyone productive by Friday.

options.text: Use the standard orientation for everyone and let each department add its own content later.
Run separate orientations for each department, and let the supervisor join one of them.
Cut the orientation to one hour of company history and send everyone to their stations.
Run one shared day-one session on safety and policy, then split into department sessions.

basic.situation: Several staff ask for a basic Excel class. Your manager says it can run next month within a small budget, and you must arrange it.

options.text: Send staff a free online Excel video list and let them learn at their own pace.
Book your cousin's training company because it can start early, and arrange the payment.
Check staff skill levels first, then book a trainer to suit that level within budget.
Get quotes from two trainers and book the cheaper one for next month.

advanced.situation: Management wants a leadership programme for 40 supervisors across three sites, some on night shifts. The budget is tight, and you must choose how to deliver it.

options.text: Buy the cheapest video package and mark supervisors as trained once they log in.
Combine short shift-timed workshops with online modules and pilot them at one site.
Hold a two-day classroom workshop at head office and ask each site to release supervisors.
Send all 40 supervisors the leadership e-book and ask each to report what they learned.

basic.situation: You observed a new trainer's first class. He read the slides aloud, and participants looked bored. You are asked to give him feedback.

options.text: Mention in the trainers' group chat that the next class needs more interaction.
Tell his manager he is not suited to training and suggest using another trainer.
Share one thing he did well and one change, such as adding questions, in private.
Give him a training techniques checklist and ask him to read it before next class.

advanced.situation: You must set performance standards for your twelve trainers. Several senior trainers resist, saying their years of experience speak for themselves, and the director wants standards in place this quarter.

options.text: Adopt a standards template from a respected training body and present it to all trainers.
Apply the standards to new trainers first and exempt senior ones until they accept them.
Announce the standards by email and tell trainers below target they will lose their bonus.
Draft standards from learner feedback and observation criteria, then refine them with senior trainers.

basic.situation: A new packing machine arrives next quarter. You are asked to survey operators about training needs, and the draft survey has one question: 'Do you need training?'

options.text: Send the draft survey with an open comment box and sort the answers by section.
Use the topics from the last machine rollout and report them as the survey results.
Ask the production supervisor to name operators needing training and skip the survey.
Change the survey to ask operators to rate their confidence in each machine task.

advanced.situation: Half the line will switch to a new product next year, and the current machine-operation course may no longer fit. Managers disagree on how much to change.

options.text: Keep the current course and add a short module on the new product after launch.
Survey operators about what they would like added and update the course to match.
Map the new product's tasks with planners, compare them to the course, and revise where needed.
Cancel the current course for the whole line this quarter and wait for the new product training.

basic.situation: You are checking a safety training handout against the company's training standards checklist. One required topic, emergency exits, is missing from the handout.

options.text: Record the missing topic on the checklist and return the handout to its author.
Tick the emergency exits item as covered, since trainers mention exits in class.
Add the missing topic to the handout using the standard wording and tell the author.
Ask the trainer if exits are covered in class and note the answer on the checklist.

advanced.situation: While reviewing an apprenticeship programme against government standards, you find logbooks showing fewer on-the-job hours than required for several apprentices. The provider says it is just paperwork lag.

options.text: Note the provider's explanation in the report and rate the programme as conditionally compliant.
Check site attendance records against the logbooks, then report the verified gap and fixes.
Give the provider a deadline to update the logbooks, then recheck before reporting.
Accept the provider's explanation, mark the programme compliant, and revisit it at the next review.

basic.situation: You are organising the training manual for a forklift course. The author's pages are in different layouts, and some of the photos are blurry.

options.text: Print the manuals as they are and list the problems for the next edition.
Apply one layout to all pages and keep the photos, since the text explains each step.
Use one layout for all pages, retake blurry photos, and send the author the draft.
Replace blurry photos with pictures copied from the forklift maker's website to save time.

advanced.situation: Finance cuts your training budget request by 20 percent, yet the mandatory safety courses are already scheduled. You must submit a revised budget this week.

options.text: Fund mandatory safety courses first, then rank the other programmes by need and trim the lowest.
Move classroom courses to cheaper online versions so all planned programmes still run.
Resubmit the original request to finance with a longer explanation of why it is needed.
Cancel the booked safety courses and let supervisors brief staff informally to stay within budget.

basic.situation: You are setting irrigation for a new bed, and the schedule lists two zones with different watering times.

options.text: Keep yesterday's settings through the shift to save time.
Ask a grower to confirm the zone before changing flow.
Compare moisture across beds, then adjust the affected zone.
Set the timer from the schedule and check the first bed.

advanced.situation: Soil results vary across a field, and fertilizer is costly. You must recommend a plan before planting next week.

options.text: Use the field's average result to set one fertilizer rate.
Map the results by zone and match rates to crop needs.
Apply last season's rate across the whole field again.
Use the lowest result to set a cautious field rate.

basic.situation: You are checking an incubator of fish eggs and notice that the water flow seems weaker than yesterday.

options.text: Ask a colleague to inspect the incubator when available.
Check the flow and eggs, then alert the hatchery lead promptly.
Record the change and check the flow against the routine.
Leave the settings unchanged until the next scheduled check.

advanced.situation: Hatching rates fall across two batches, and a few fry appear sluggish. You are helping plan the next hatchery cycle.

options.text: Separate sluggish fry and ask the lead about treatment options.
Keep the current routine so both batches stay comparable.
Review hatch records and water conditions, then trial a controlled change.
Increase water flow for the next batch and track results.

basic.situation: You are recording weekly crop growth and greenhouse temperature, but one day's readings are missing.

options.text: Copy the previous day's reading to complete the weekly table.
Ask a coworker whether they recall that day's temperature.
Check the sensor log, then record any gap as missing.
Enter the available readings and mark the missing date clearly.

advanced.situation: A state reporting deadline is near, and production figures from one block do not match the harvest records. You prepare the farm report.

options.text: Use the production sheet and note that records differ.
Submit the larger figure to avoid understating production.
Reconcile both records and flag any unresolved difference in the report.
Use the harvest total because it appears more complete.

basic.situation: A customer asks how often to water a newly planted shrub during a hot, dry week.

options.text: Suggest deep watering and invite them to return with questions.
Recommend watering each morning based on the week's heat.
Repeat the label's watering advice without checking the planting conditions.
Ask about soil, then explain how to check moisture.

advanced.situation: A buyer wants a fixed price and delivery window for several crop loads, but harvest timing may shift.

options.text: Agree to the buyer's window and let dispatch handle shipment details.
Negotiate volume, price, and flexible delivery terms against the harvest outlook.
Offer a firm price and delivery date to secure the order.
Discuss a price range and ask the buyer to confirm volumes.

basic.situation: You inspect a packing shed and find a loose hinge on a frequently used door.

options.text: Tighten the hinge if the routine maintenance kit is available.
Ask another worker to watch the door during busy periods.
Leave the door as it is until the next inspection round.
Inspect the hinge, then repair it or report needed parts.

advanced.situation: A contractor is building a drainage channel near crop beds, and the latest section slopes toward them. You are monitoring the work.

options.text: Mark the low point and request a review at day's end.
Check the drawings and agree a safer route with the crew.
Ask the crew to pause that section while you check the plan.
Let the crew finish, then see whether water reaches the beds.

basic.situation: You find fresh insect damage in one crop row, while nearby plants look healthy.

options.text: Check the area, then report its size to supervisors.
Record the row and inspect nearby plants for spread.
Treat the whole field using the usual pest routine.
Set aside time to check the row again tomorrow.

advanced.situation: Market prices differ for two crops, and water is limited for the coming planting cycle. You must recommend how to divide acreage.

options.text: Repeat last season's acreage split to avoid disrupting operations.
Compare likely returns, water needs, and demand before recommending acreage.
Shift a small area toward the higher-priced crop and review later.
Plant more of the crop with the higher current price.

basic.situation: A concrete delivery is running late, and two crews need the same access route. You are helping update today’s site schedule.

options.text: Move the affected crew after checking access and tell nearby trades.
Re-sequence crews around the delayed delivery and confirm shared access.
Keep the original sequence and ask each crew to fit around delays.
Check the trade sequence with the supervisor, then update today's site board.

advanced.situation: Heavy rain makes the planned roof work unsafe and delays a key delivery. You need to revise the sequence while keeping other trades moving.

options.text: Shift roof work and tell each crew to follow the revised schedule.
Move crews to indoor tasks and update the daily programme for review.
Ask the supervisor to choose new tasks while crews wait near the work area.
Check site conditions, resequence safe tasks, and confirm crews understand the changes.

basic.situation: Your manager asks you to help estimate the cost of tiling a small area and compare it with the project allowance.

options.text: Use the last tiling estimate and adjust it for the larger area.
Use the allowance as the expected cost and report that figure.
Count the area, check recent material prices, and show your estimate assumptions.
Ask the supplier for a price and pass the figure to your manager.

advanced.situation: A subcontractor requests a price revision after a design change, while the client wants the cost impact before approving the work.

options.text: Accept the subcontractor's new price and include it in the next report.
Use the original rate for now and discuss the difference at the next meeting.
Compare the requested change with the contract scope and price impact before proposing terms.
Ask the subcontractor to provide a breakdown, then share it with the client.

basic.situation: You are checking a work area against the site safety checklist and notice a temporary walkway partly blocked by materials.

options.text: Leave the materials where they are until the next scheduled site review.
Ask the crew to clear the route and record the issue for the supervisor.
Note the blockage on the checklist and continue checking nearby areas.
Move the materials aside and confirm the walkway is clear for workers.

advanced.situation: A worker is hurt near a recently altered scaffold, and the team is unsure whether the approved work method was followed.

options.text: Ask the supervisor to handle the incident while you resume site coordination.
Photograph the scaffold and review the work method with the site team.
Record the injury and ask the scaffold crew to explain the work sequence.
Secure the area, document conditions and accounts, then compare them with the approved method.

basic.situation: You are reviewing environmental requirements for a small renovation and see that the work plan mentions waste removal but not sorting.

options.text: Add labelled waste areas to the work plan and brief the site team.
Ask the waste contractor which materials can go in each container.
Check the project requirements and ask how the waste should be separated.
Use the usual skip for all waste and mention it in the site notes.

advanced.situation: Your project is seeking third-party green certification, and a review finds that several material records are missing before the assessor’s visit.

options.text: Request the missing records and keep preparing the certification submission.
Send the available records to the assessor and explain that others are pending.
Map each certification requirement to evidence, assign gaps, and check the completed records.
Ask the supplier for material certificates and file them for the review.

basic.situation: A new worker is unsure which drawing applies to a task, and the crew is waiting for direction before starting.

options.text: Find the latest drawing and brief the crew on the relevant task.
Show the current drawing, explain the task, and check the worker's understanding.
Ask an experienced worker to explain the drawing while you direct the crew.
Tell the worker to follow the drawing already pinned near the work area.

advanced.situation: The owner and subcontractor disagree about who must complete a disputed handover task, and the disagreement is delaying follow-on work.

options.text: Summarize each position and arrange a discussion around the contract wording.
Ask the subcontractor to complete the task while you record the owner's concern.
Review the contract wording with both parties and agree the handover responsibility.
Refer both parties to the project manager and pause the handover discussion.

basic.situation: You are listing materials for a small partition job and discover that the delivery note shows fewer boards than the task requires.

options.text: Count the remaining boards, check the task quantity, and request the shortage.
Ask the store for more boards and update the materials list afterward.
Use the delivery note quantity and tell the crew to start with those boards.
Check the site stack against the delivery note and report the difference.

advanced.situation: A computer model shows two construction methods with similar costs, but one uses more labour and may disrupt nearby work.

options.text: Choose the lower model estimate and share it with the project team.
Compare model assumptions, labour demand, and site disruption before recommending a method.
Review the labour figures and ask the planner about nearby work clashes.
Ask the estimator which method is usually used on similar projects.

basic.situation: Your manager asks you to track this week’s supply spending and prepare a purchase request for classroom art materials.

options.text: Check the receipts against the budget and list quantities for approval.
Use last week's amounts to estimate this request and send it for review.
Ask the supplier for a quote and forward it to your manager.
Order the usual art pack and enter its cost in the tracker.

advanced.situation: Enrolment enquiries are rising, but confirmed registrations remain steady. You are preparing next term’s staffing and supply forecast.

options.text: Raise the forecast from enquiries and hold the same supply budget for now.
Ask registration staff to summarize enquiries before updating the forecast.
Compare enquiries, registrations, and past enrolment patterns before revising allocations.
Keep the current forecast and mention the enquiries in the planning notes.

basic.situation: A senior teacher asks you to draft next week’s preschool activity schedule around a planned music session and outdoor play.

options.text: Copy last week's schedule and replace the music activity with this session.
Check staff and space availability, then draft a balanced activity schedule.
Reuse the usual schedule and add the music session at the end.
Draft the schedule with activity times and send it for staff review.

advanced.situation: Recent feedback says children enjoy an after-school activity, but attendance is low and staff preparation takes longer than planned.

options.text: Compare attendance and preparation time, then suggest a focused schedule change.
Review attendance and feedback, then discuss possible changes with the team.
Ask staff whether a shorter session could make preparation easier.
Keep the activity unchanged and share the positive feedback with staff.

basic.situation: Your centre is sharing information about an upcoming parent activity day, and you are asked to prepare a short leaflet for nearby families.

options.text: Check the event details and write a clear leaflet for families to take home.
Reuse the old leaflet and hand it out at the centre entrance.
Use last term's leaflet and change the activity date before printing.
Ask a teacher to check your draft before sharing it with families.

advanced.situation: A community group asks how your centre’s programme could support children whose families have limited access to early learning.

options.text: Explain how usual activities may support families with different early learning needs.
Share the programme outline and ask which access needs the group sees locally.
Invite the group to share questions about programmes for families with limited access.
Describe current activities and offer the group a copy of the programme leaflet.

basic.situation: A teacher applicant submits a missing training certificate after an interview, and you are helping prepare the hiring file.

options.text: Check the file requirements and update the applicant's record for review.
Tell the hiring manager the certificate has arrived and file it later.
Mark the applicant's file complete based on the interview notes.
Add the certificate to the file and note when it was received.

advanced.situation: Two preschool sites have conflicting plans for teacher coverage during a training day, and you are coordinating activities across both locations.

options.text: Ask each site to keep its current roster and report any shortages later.
Compare both rosters, resolve coverage gaps, and confirm the agreed site plans.
Collect both rosters and send the differences to the administrator.
Review the rosters together with both site leads and propose coverage changes.

basic.situation: You are checking the centre’s safety checklist and notice a cleaning trolley left near the classroom exit during pick-up.

options.text: Tell the cleaner about the trolley and continue checking the rooms.
Ask a colleague to watch the exit until the cleaner finishes.
Note the trolley location and report it to the centre manager.
Move the trolley to its storage area and record the checklist finding.

advanced.situation: A new government code requirement affects how a centre stores maintenance chemicals. You are asked to help update the facility procedure.

options.text: Check the requirement, identify affected storage steps, and draft a practical procedure update.
Copy the storage procedure from another centre and send it for approval.
Keep the existing procedure and mention the new code at the next meeting.
Ask the manager which storage steps should change under the new requirement.

basic.situation: During class, a child struggles to join a counting activity and becomes upset when the other children move ahead.

options.text: Tell the child to watch the group and try again after the activity.
Encourage the child to try the next counting item with you nearby.
Sit with the child, offer a simpler counting activity, and observe their response.
Ask another child to show the counting activity while you help the group.

advanced.situation: Teachers report that several children are struggling with early literacy, and families have asked how learning goals are chosen for the term.

options.text: Review classroom progress and explain the proposed literacy goals to families.
Set one literacy target for every child and share it with families.
Review progress with teachers and set clear literacy goals with suitable support.
Ask teachers to choose targets and send families a general update.

basic.situation: A teacher asks you to draft next term’s course descriptions, but two subjects appear to overlap in the proposed schedule.

options.text: Draft both descriptions and flag the overlap for the senior administrator.
Ask both teachers to settle the overlap before drafting descriptions.
Compare subject aims, draft distinct descriptions, and note the scheduling conflict.
Copy last term’s descriptions and send the draft for approval.

advanced.situation: A district review shows uneven learning outcomes across schools, and you must propose common curriculum standards for the next academic year.

options.text: Compare school curricula, then select shared elements for district standards.
Ask each school to submit its current curriculum for district review.
Draft common standards using existing district course documents and school feedback.
Use outcome gaps to set shared standards and phase in teacher guidance.

basic.situation: You are updating attendance records before a monthly report, and one class register is missing several entries.

options.text: Check the register with the class teacher before finalising the report.
Fill gaps using the previous week’s attendance pattern.
Enter the recorded attendance and mark missing entries for follow-up.
Leave the class out of this month’s attendance summary.

advanced.situation: Several school requests exceed the available equipment budget, and you need to allocate funds while keeping essential teaching needs covered.

options.text: Fund the earliest requests before the remaining balance runs out.
Rank requests by teaching need, cost, and available alternatives before allocation.
Prioritise requests that describe the clearest teaching need.
Split the funds evenly across all school requests.

basic.situation: A new teaching assistant starts next week, and you are helping prepare their induction with guidance from the administrator.

options.text: Share the timetable and ask a colleague to explain daily routines.
Give them last year’s induction notes and arrange a classroom visit.
Ask the assistant to follow another aide during the first week.
Prepare current role guidance and pair it with a trained staff mentor.

advanced.situation: Two staff members disagree over shared duties, disrupting lesson support, and you must coordinate their work while maintaining coverage.

options.text: Move one staff member to another class for the full academic term.
Map lesson needs, agree handoffs, and review daily coverage with both staff members together.
Meet with each staff member to clarify shared duties, lesson needs, and daily coverage expectations.
Keep the current rota and ask both staff members to coordinate their coverage.

basic.situation: A student tells you they are falling behind in several subjects and feel unsure how to ask teachers for help.

options.text: Explore the student’s concerns and plan a teacher check-in together.
Suggest focusing on the easiest subject to rebuild confidence.
Help the student list subjects and plan questions for teachers.
Share a general study tip and encourage the student to try it.

advanced.situation: A special education meeting reveals that classroom support plans are being applied unevenly, and teachers ask you to help coordinate improvements.

options.text: Review agreed supports with educators and coordinate consistent classroom routines.
Send the plan again and ask teachers to read it before class.
Tell teachers to use the plan that fits their classroom needs.
Ask teachers to share examples of where the plans differ.

basic.situation: You are helping collect assessment results for a school improvement review, but one year group has submitted incomplete data.

options.text: Enter the results received and flag the missing year group.
Estimate missing results from the previous assessment report.
Compile the submitted results and leave the year group section blank.
Check the missing entries with the year lead before compiling results.

advanced.situation: Student results show persistent reading gaps, and the school improvement plan must identify actions that staff can track next term.

options.text: Repeat last year’s reading activities across all classes.
Use subgroup results to target teaching actions and set review measures.
Set a reading target and ask staff to report progress monthly.
Add extra reading sessions and monitor overall scores next term.

basic.situation: Your school is hosting an open day, and you are asked to distribute programme leaflets and help visitors find the right rooms.

options.text: Place leaflets near the entrance and answer questions as they come.
Check room labels, arrange leaflets by programme, and guide arriving families.
Set out leaflets and direct visitors using the printed room list.
Hand out leaflets at the entrance and let visitors explore.

advanced.situation: Parents report confusion about a new after-school programme, while staff need a clear event plan before community registration opens.

options.text: Revise the flyer and ask families to contact the office with questions.
Publish the current flyer and open registration for interested families.
Align staff messaging, clarify programme details, and coordinate a parent information event.
Ask staff to share the programme details at their next parent meetings.

basic.situation: A faculty office needs a room schedule for orientation week, and you are asked to prepare a draft with guidance.

options.text: Reuse last year’s schedule and send it to the faculty office.
Check room availability and draft a schedule for staff review.
Draft a schedule from the requested times and note open questions.
Ask the office for preferred times before drafting the schedule.

advanced.situation: Enrolment patterns and room use have shifted, and senior leaders ask you to prepare a strategic plan for future academic services.

options.text: Extend current services in line with projected enrolment growth and available campus capacity.
Use enrolment and space trends to set priorities and phase future service plans.
Retain the current strategic plan while updating timelines to reflect emerging academic service needs.
Invite departments to outline service needs, expected demand, and proposed implementation timelines.

basic.situation: A support team is short-staffed during enrolment, and you are asked to help coordinate its daily activities.

options.text: Match enrolment duties to staff roles, then review workload and coverage at set intervals.
List urgent tasks, assign them across available staff, and check coverage during peak enrolment periods.
Ask the team lead to assign remaining tasks based on staff availability and priorities.
Let staff choose from a shared task list as enrolment requests arrive throughout the day.

advanced.situation: A programme review finds students are missing key learning outcomes, and you must choose an assessment approach for the next cohort.

options.text: Ask lecturers to suggest questions for a common assessment.
Keep existing assessments and use student feedback to judge learning.
Use the same end-of-term exam and compare overall pass rates.
Map each outcome to assessment items and review results by cohort.

basic.situation: You are preparing a monthly expense report, and several receipts are missing from the department’s records.

options.text: List recorded expenses and flag receipts needing confirmation.
Estimate receipt amounts from similar purchases last month.
Submit recorded expenses and leave missing items for later.
Reconcile ledger entries with available invoices and query missing receipts.

advanced.situation: The finance committee needs a forecast before approving next semester’s spending, but department requests exceed projected funds.

options.text: Use last semester’s spending as the forecast baseline.
Cut each department request by the same percentage.
Compare commitments, enrolment needs, and requests when modelling budget options.
Ask departments to rank requested spending by urgency.

basic.situation: You will represent your institution at a local community education fair and need to answer visitors’ questions about campus services.

options.text: Describe services from memory and collect visitors’ contact details.
Review approved service information and prepare a short visitor handout.
Attend with a colleague and ask them to handle service questions.
Bring the usual brochures and direct unfamiliar questions to the office.

advanced.situation: An industry group invites your university to discuss student placements, while an upcoming accreditation review needs clear evidence of external engagement.

options.text: Share the invitation with faculty and ask for placement ideas.
Discuss placement needs and document agreed partnership evidence for review.
Send the group a brochure and request details by email.
Accept the placement offer and mention it in the review materials.

basic.situation: A faculty committee is reviewing course sequencing, and you are asked to help organise its meeting materials.

options.text: Prepare agenda papers by topic, highlight decisions, and record follow-up owners afterward.
Bring course documents and invite members to select discussion topics during the meeting.
Use prior minutes to draft an agenda, without checking current committee priorities.
Group papers by decision, then circulate them early so members can prepare.

advanced.situation: A student nearing graduation is choosing between two career paths, and faculty committee members ask you to help with their course progress.

options.text: Clarify career priorities, check graduation progress, and map suitable courses.
Review completed credits and help compare remaining course options.
Share both course lists and suggest the student choose one.
Recommend the path with the most available course places.

basic.situation: Your department is hiring an administrative assistant, and you are asked to help coordinate applications and interview arrangements.

options.text: Forward applications in the order they arrived for review.
Check applications for required documents and share the shortlist.
Ask the hiring panel to arrange interviews from the applicant list.
Sort applications against stated criteria and prepare interview schedules.

advanced.situation: A new hire is struggling with department systems after induction, and you must support their training while documenting the role concern.

options.text: Extend their induction, then review role expectations and available support with them.
Identify system gaps, provide focused practice, and review progress against role needs.
Send the system guide and schedule a later check-in with the new hire.
Ask a colleague to cover routine systems while you document concerns and arrange training.

basic.situation: A client asks whether a proposed pump upgrade is viable, but the team has gathered little data on demand or available equipment.

options.text: Recommend the upgrade based on the client's enthusiasm and a rough cost.
Check recent demand figures and ask the equipment team about available capacity.
Use last year's demand and equipment list to draft a quick feasibility note.
Compare current demand, equipment capacity, and resource needs before summarizing feasibility.

advanced.situation: A high-risk bridge project may need a design change after new ground data conflicts with the original assumptions.

options.text: Ask the design team to explain the ground data and outline the proposed revision.
Compare the ground data, safety implications, and resource impacts before deciding on the change.
Approve the revised design from the consultant's summary to protect the schedule.
Review the updated drawings and ask the geotechnical team to confirm its findings.

basic.situation: Your engineering office is binning reusable offcuts from a routine prototype run. You are asked to help reduce workshop waste.

options.text: Put the clean offcuts beside the bins for anyone who wants them.
Ask the workshop to keep useful offcuts in a labelled reuse area and track them.
Suggest separating reusable offcuts and ask the workshop lead to monitor the bins.
Remind staff to sort offcuts and mention the waste issue at the next meeting.

advanced.situation: Several sites report rising material waste, but their processes differ. Senior managers ask you to shape a shared reduction programme.

options.text: Set a single waste target and circulate it to all site managers.
Compare site waste streams, set shared measures, and tailor reduction actions to each process.
Announce a company-wide ban on disposable materials before checking operational needs.
Ask each site to report its waste and let local teams choose improvements.

basic.situation: A supplier's estimate for routine design materials is higher than last month's, and your manager asks you to review it.

options.text: Compare the quantities and unit prices with the project list and recent quotes.
Check the total against the budget and flag the increase to your manager.
Approve the estimate using last month's price as a reasonable guide.
Ask the supplier to confirm the new total and expected delivery date.

advanced.situation: A large materials contract is due for review, and two bids use different specifications and delivery terms.

options.text: Ask both suppliers to restate their prices using the same delivery window.
Check each bid against the specification and ask procurement to clarify delivery terms.
Compare specification fit, delivery terms, and total cost, then document the recommendation.
Choose the lower bid and approve it before the quoted price expires.

basic.situation: New staff are recording inspection results differently, making routine equipment checks hard to compare. You are helping draft a procedure.

options.text: Ask experienced staff to share their preferred inspection format for the draft.
Draft shared recording fields and ask the team lead to check them.
Define common fields and recording steps, then ask users to review a sample.
Copy the format from the last project and circulate it as the procedure.

advanced.situation: Senior management asks you to set technical goals for a department facing tighter resources and several competing project needs.

options.text: Set ambitious targets for every team and share them at the next meeting.
Translate management priorities into measurable goals, checking capacity and dependencies with team leads.
Use last year's targets as a starting point and adjust for current staffing.
Ask team leads to propose goals that align with management's stated priorities.

basic.situation: You are preparing a budget draft for a small engineering proposal, and one material quote is missing.

options.text: Ask procurement for a current quote and delay the draft until it arrives.
Leave the material line out and present the remaining budget.
Use the last project price and note that supplier pricing may differ.
Use a recent similar quote and label it as a provisional estimate.

advanced.situation: Senior stakeholders question a proposal's cost assumptions during a review, while the client is waiting for your findings.

options.text: Show the budget breakdown and offer to clarify any disputed line items.
Share the detailed spreadsheet and ask stakeholders to review it after the meeting.
Walk through key assumptions, show the cost drivers, and explain remaining uncertainties.
Defend the total using the headline estimate and return to the schedule.

basic.situation: A design task is slipping because engineering and production staff have different understandings of the project specification.

options.text: Ask the engineering lead which version production should use for now.
Bring both teams together to compare the specification and agree on the open points.
Send the latest specification to both teams and ask them to flag differences.
Ask production to follow the latest drawing while engineering resolves its notes.

advanced.situation: A client changes an important project requirement while two technical teams are integrating their work.

options.text: Ask both team leads to assess the change and send the client their questions.
Update the project specification from the client's message and share it with both teams.
Clarify the client's priority and constraints, then align both teams on the revised specification.
Tell both teams to pause affected tasks until the client confirms the change.

basic.situation: You are helping plan a biodiesel filtration trial, and the team needs a clear way to compare two filter settings.

options.text: Use last month's plan and change the filter setting in its notes.
Ask the researcher which settings to test, then note their answer.
List the settings, measurements, and sample labels in the draft plan.
Set out the question, controls, measurements, and sample sequence for review.

advanced.situation: A pilot study shows a biomass residue could yield useful fuel, but its variable composition may affect production costs.

options.text: Recommend a product concept and flag the feedstock variation for follow-up.
Ask the project lead which product idea they prefer to pursue.
Compare the yield data with likely uses, constraints, and validation needs.
Promote the residue as a ready fuel based on the strongest trial.

basic.situation: You are assisting with a biomass pretreatment run, and two samples look different after the same heating step.

options.text: Blend both samples together so the run can stay on schedule.
Repeat the heating step on the darker sample before measuring.
Label each sample, record the difference, and follow the protocol separately.
Record the appearance and continue with the planned measurements.

advanced.situation: A new fermentation feedstock gives higher yield in early runs, but foaming varies and could affect scale-up estimates.

options.text: Repeat the strongest run and use its yield for the process estimate.
Plan a controlled set of feedstock and operating conditions, including foam measures.
Track feedstock, foam, and yield across controlled repeat runs.
Ask the team to suggest which fermentation conditions to vary next.

basic.situation: You are helping build a lab-scale fermentation model, and one batch has a much longer lag phase than expected.

options.text: Adjust the lag value until the model matches the expected curve.
Ask a colleague to choose a lag value for this batch.
Enter the batch data and note the longer lag phase.
Check batch records, then update inputs and compare the model output.

advanced.situation: Your solvent recovery model predicts strong performance at plant scale, but the lab data cover only a narrow flow range.

options.text: Ask the process lead whether the plant estimate seems reasonable.
Use the strongest recovery result as the plant-wide performance estimate.
Present the forecast with a note about the tested flow range.
Model a broader flow range and show uncertainty in the scale-up forecast.

basic.situation: You are drafting a section of a biodiesel research report, and one trial produced an unexpected low yield.

options.text: Ask the researcher how they want the low yield described.
Describe the low yield and include the recorded operating conditions.
Report the result, conditions, and comparison with the other trial.
Leave out the low result so the report reads more clearly.

advanced.situation: Senior managers need a decision on a biodiesel prototype, while the latest report shows promising yield but incomplete cost data.

options.text: Summarize the yield findings and ask managers what they need next.
Compare yield, missing cost evidence, and decision risks in the recommendation.
Present the yield result as proof the prototype is commercially viable.
Recommend continued development and mention that cost data remain incomplete.

basic.situation: A new technician asks how to label samples during a routine biodiesel viscosity test, and the bench is busy.

options.text: Show the technician the label format and check their first sample.
Explain the format and point them to the written bench procedure.
Tell them to copy labels from the previous batch.
Ask another technician to show them the sample labels.

advanced.situation: Two researchers are running linked pretreatment trials, but they use different sample logging methods that complicate the comparison.

options.text: Suggest they include the same sample fields in both logs.
Review both logs with the team and ask which feels easier.
Ask each researcher to keep their current logging method for now.
Agree a shared sample log and explain how to record deviations.

basic.situation: You are tracking a biodiesel prototype, and a supplier delay may push the next test beyond its planned week.

options.text: Mark the test complete based on the team's earlier estimate.
Update the tracker with the delay and revised test date.
Log the delay, its test dependency, and the schedule impact for review.
Ask the supplier for a date and leave the tracker unchanged.

advanced.situation: Two biodiesel prototypes meet yield targets, but one has rising material costs and the other needs more durability testing.

options.text: Compare performance, cost exposure, and validation needs against intended uses.
Summarize yield, cost trend, and outstanding durability work for both prototypes.
Ask the project leads which prototype they want to prioritize.
Rank both projects by yield and recommend the stronger result.

basic.situation: You taste a curry batch before lunch service and notice it is milder than the approved sample.

options.text: Compare the curry with the approved sample and ask the cook to adjust seasoning.
Serve the batch and invite lunch customers to share comments about its seasoning.
Take a second tasting, compare notes, and tell the cook the curry tastes milder.
Add extra spice to the pot based on your own taste preference.

advanced.situation: Several cooks plate the same lunch special differently, and guests have started commenting on uneven portions.

options.text: Let each cook plate according to their usual station style.
Set a portion and garnish reference, then coach cooks using sample plates.
Ask the head cook to select the plating style for today's lunch special.
Show the cooks a reference plate and portion guide during service.

basic.situation: A server calls in sick before dinner, and you are helping prepare the shift roster with the manager.

options.text: Move a trained server to the open section and update the roster.
Ask the manager which shift member should cover the section.
Assign the nearest available server to the section for dinner.
Suggest a trained server cover, then tell the team at briefing.

advanced.situation: New kitchen staff make repeated portioning errors during busy service, and food costs are rising this month.

options.text: Reduce serving sizes across the menu to lower food costs.
Remind cooks about portions during the next pre-shift briefing.
Create a short portioning demonstration and observe each cook practising.
Post the portion chart beside the serving line for cooks.

basic.situation: You are updating the sanitation log after a routine kitchen cleaning, and one temperature entry is missing.

options.text: Ask the cleaner what they remember and add their estimate.
Check the cleaning notes and enter the recorded temperature with time.
Check the notes and flag the missing entry for follow-up.
Leave the entry blank and tell the supervisor at closing.

advanced.situation: During a kitchen walk-through, you notice a fire exit partly blocked by stacked beverage cartons before the dinner rush.

options.text: Tell the delivery team to move the cartons after dinner service.
Move the cartons to nearby storage and record the correction.
Ask a nearby staff member to clear the cartons before service.
Notify the manager and wait for their direction on the cartons.

basic.situation: You are counting the till after lunch, and the cash total differs slightly from the recorded sales.

options.text: Recount the cash and compare it with the transaction record.
Recount the till and note the amount for the manager.
Write down the difference and finish the deposit paperwork.
Use the sales total as the cash figure for the deposit.

advanced.situation: Your weekly stock review shows rising vegetable waste and frequent emergency orders for the dinner menu.

options.text: Review waste records and suggest smaller orders for weekdays.
Order extra vegetables to prevent another shortage during dinner.
Compare usage, waste, and order timing before adjusting par levels.
Share the waste and shortage figures with the kitchen lead.

basic.situation: A guest says their rice arrived cold, and the dining room is busy with several tables waiting.

options.text: Ask the guest to wait while you finish serving other tables.
Apologize, check the dish, and arrange a fresh hot portion.
Offer a replacement portion and let the kitchen know about the temperature.
Tell the guest the kitchen is busy and the rice cools quickly.

advanced.situation: Guests give mixed feedback about slow service, and new servers handle complaints in different ways during busy evenings.

options.text: Ask servers to use their own approach when guests complain.
Set a simple complaint response guide and practise it with servers.
Discuss the feedback at briefing and remind servers to listen carefully.
Collect more guest comments before changing how servers respond.

basic.situation: A beverage delivery arrives before lunch, and several cartons look damp while the invoice lists the expected quantity.

options.text: Count the cartons and note the damp packaging on the delivery record.
Ask the driver whether the damp cartons are safe to store.
Sign for the full delivery and sort the cartons after lunch.
Check quantities and product condition, then report the damaged cartons.

advanced.situation: The kitchen's main mixer needs repair, while a scheduled pest-control visit overlaps with a busy catering preparation window.

options.text: Keep the repair booking and request a different pest-control visit time.
Reschedule both services for the next quiet period that suits the kitchen.
Confirm the mixer repair window and tell pest control about the clash.
Ask the kitchen lead which service can move, then coordinate a suitable time.

basic.situation: A new dealer asks you to clarify a table's maximum bet before opening.

options.text: I check the posted limit and explain it using the table guide.
I ask a nearby dealer what limit they usually quote players.
I tell the dealer to follow the limit used on yesterday's shift.
I match the rule sheet to the sign and explain the limit.

advanced.situation: Management asks you to draft an updated credit policy after staff report inconsistent requests from players.

options.text: I ask floor staff what credit limits would make their shifts easier.
I summarize common requests and suggest a few policy changes to management.
I review recent requests and draft clear credit steps for management to assess.
I adapt the policy from a nearby property and circulate it for use.

basic.situation: You are asked to sit in on an interview for a dealer vacancy and note how the candidate handles game questions.

options.text: I use the agreed questions and record examples from each answer.
I chat about casino work and share my overall impression afterward.
I ask the listed questions and note the candidate's strongest answers.
I ask about the candidate's favourite games and note their confidence.

advanced.situation: New dealers make inconsistent calls during busy shifts, and you are asked to propose facility-wide training standards.

options.text: I ask experienced dealers to coach newcomers during quieter periods.
I define observable game procedures and assess them with shared practice scenarios.
I circulate a list of common mistakes for dealers to review before shifts.
I send each dealer the current manual and ask them to study it.

basic.situation: A guest says the payout on a completed hand seems lower than the table rules promised.

options.text: I review the hand with the dealer and check the payout against the posted rules.
I check the payout record and explain the result to the guest.
I ask the dealer what happened and repeat their explanation to the guest.
I apologize and offer a small meal voucher to settle the concern.

advanced.situation: A quiet weekday follows several guest complaints about confusing promotions, and management wants a marketing strategy to lift visits.

options.text: I ask regular guests which weekday games or offers would interest them.
I compare visit patterns, test a targeted offer, and track guest response.
I extend the popular weekend promotion to weekdays and track guest attendance.
I share a broad weekday discount online to attract more guests.

basic.situation: A player repeatedly tracks exposed cards and changes bets, drawing a dealer's concern during a routine game.

options.text: I record unusual bets and brief the floor lead after the round ends.
I ask the player about the betting pattern while play continues.
I ask the dealer to monitor the player's betting pattern during play.
I observe the play, note betting patterns, and discreetly alert the floor lead.

advanced.situation: Two players use coordinated signals across tables, and their play resembles a known method for shifting game odds.

options.text: I stop their play and tell them to leave the gaming area.
I document the signals and alert security to follow the response procedure.
I ask nearby dealers to monitor both players and report further signals.
I move the dealers to different tables and keep both players under observation.

basic.situation: You receive chips for a table and must complete the shift's money-supply paperwork with a supervisor nearby.

options.text: I count the chips against the issue record and complete each required field.
I enter the amount from the slip and finish the form before opening.
I copy the last shift's figures and adjust them to match the new slip.
I count the chips and enter the total on the issue form.

advanced.situation: The table's recorded chip issue differs from the return slip, and you are preparing the shift paperwork for review.

options.text: I compare the issue and return totals, then flag the difference to my supervisor.
I compare both slips, recount the return, and note any unresolved difference for review.
I use the return slip total to close the paperwork and meet the deadline.
I recount the returned chips and update the paperwork to match my count.

basic.situation: A dealer calls in sick before the evening shift, and you are helping prepare the table schedule with guidance.

options.text: I ask the available dealers who can stay later to cover the table.
I move the next scheduled dealer to the vacant table and update attendance later.
I check the roster and break plan, then suggest a covered shift change.
I check who is present and ask the shift lead about a replacement.

advanced.situation: Player visit data shows uneven demand across shifts, while the team must balance table coverage, breaks, and complimentary meal offers.

options.text: I adjust the roster to demand and ask staff where meal offers may help.
I increase meal offers on quiet shifts and reduce staffing there to save costs.
I add dealers to the busiest shift and keep meal offers unchanged.
I align staffing and meal offers with shift demand, then review coverage and redemption patterns.

basic.situation: You are helping budget a weekend sports programme and have last month's venue and equipment costs.

options.text: I list expected costs by item and check the figures against last month's records.
I list venue and equipment costs using the previous programme as a guide.
I use the old budget total as this weekend's figure and submit it.
I copy last month's total and add a small amount for price changes.

advanced.situation: Customer counts are rising for evening classes while staff overtime costs climb, and management asks for a programming strategy.

options.text: I present attendance and overtime trends with a few possible programme changes.
I compare attendance and overtime by class, then propose schedule changes with expected costs.
I cut evening classes to reduce overtime and present the savings estimate.
I add more evening classes to meet demand and share the idea with management.

basic.situation: Two activity areas need opening help, and you are assisting with the weekend roster under your manager's guidance.

options.text: I split opening tasks evenly across staff and check their usual hours.
I assign the earliest arrivals to opening tasks and post the roster.
I match staff availability to opening tasks and share the draft roster for review.
I ask staff which opening task they prefer and note their responses.

advanced.situation: Several new recreation assistants start before a busy school holiday, and you are asked to train them on facility procedures.

options.text: I ask an experienced assistant to show the newcomers the usual routine.
I demonstrate each procedure, then have new assistants practise and explain the key steps.
I give each assistant the procedure handbook to read before the holiday begins.
I send a short message listing the procedures and start times for opening day.

basic.situation: You are asked to retrieve radios for a community event and return them to storage after the shift.

options.text: I count the radios before use and put them back on the same shelf.
I take enough radios for the team and leave the return count for tomorrow.
I take the radios from the usual shelf and return them after the event.
I check the storage list, sign out the radios, and return them to their labelled spaces.

advanced.situation: A vehicle, radios, and ride components are needed at overlapping events, and newer staff ask where to store returns.

options.text: I label storage shelves and send staff a list of where equipment belongs.
I map storage locations and sign-out records, then show staff how to return each item.
I group items by event and ask staff to return them to those areas.
I tell staff to put each return wherever similar equipment is stored.

basic.situation: A family activity day has three short sessions, and you are helping arrange their order with guidance.

options.text: I list all three sessions in a timetable and share it with the team.
I place the most popular session first and fit the others around it.
I sequence sessions with setup time between them and confirm the activity leads.
I copy the previous event's timetable and change the activity names.

advanced.situation: You are leading a mixed-age group through a long outdoor activity, and a late start has reduced the available time.

options.text: I keep the schedule and ask participants to move faster through each activity.
I shorten one activity and explain the revised timing to participants.
I split the activity into stages, brief everyone, and check progress throughout.
I remove the final activity and keep the remaining sessions on schedule.

basic.situation: A visitor asks whether children may use a climbing attraction without an adult beside them.

options.text: I check the attraction rules and explain the supervision requirement in plain language.
I explain the rule from memory and offer to check the posted notice.
I tell the visitor what families usually do at the attraction.
I read the posted rule aloud and answer the visitor's question.

advanced.situation: A parent says an instructor spoke sharply to their child and wants a refund after a crowded class.

options.text: I offer a future class place and ask what would address the parent's concern today.
I ask the instructor what happened and relay their account to the parent.
I listen, apologize for the experience, and record the complaint for follow-up.
I hear the parent's account, check the service details, and explain the available response.

basic.situation: During setup, a coworker asks over the radio where to bring the first-aid kit for the activity area.

options.text: I direct them to the marked activity area beside the main entrance.
I repeat the area name and describe its nearest entrance.
I confirm the area and ask them to repeat it back.
I name the activity area and ask them to call if lost.

advanced.situation: A participant collapses during a crowded activity, and nearby staff are unsure who should respond or contact emergency help.

options.text: I start the response plan, assign a caller, and provide trained first aid.
I call the trained first aider and keep other participants back.
I move the participant aside and ask staff to restart the activity.
I ask nearby staff to support the participant while I guide others away.

basic.situation: A guest arrives during a busy check-in period. You have the arrival list and registration screen but need to confirm a booking detail.

options.text: Check the guest's name against the arrival list and ask a colleague about mismatches.
Match the booking reference and guest ID, then enter verified details and explain the next step.
Ask the guest to confirm the booking name, then enter details using the registration screen.
Use the name on the first booking shown and finish check-in before the queue grows.

advanced.situation: A guest disputes a room charge after a delayed room change. Other arrivals report similar confusion, and the front desk is getting busy.

options.text: Review the charge with the guest and offer a clear explanation of the room change.
Hear both accounts, check the service record, and agree on a practical remedy with duty staff.
Apologize and remove the disputed charge to calm the guest and clear the queue.
Explain the room-change policy and ask the guest to wait while you find the manager.

basic.situation: You are checking a newly cleaned guest room before arrival. The checklist covers the bathroom, bedding, surfaces, and supplies.

options.text: Check the bathroom, bedding, surfaces, and supplies, then flag any failed item for correction.
Glance around, then mark the room ready so housekeeping can move to the next room.
Follow the checklist, checking each area and noting anything that needs attention.
Check the bathroom and bedding first, then ask housekeeping about any unclear checklist item.

advanced.situation: Several rooms and a public corridor have recurring cleanliness complaints despite routine inspections. You are guiding housekeeping staff during a busy turnover.

options.text: Ask staff to repeat the usual room routine and focus on rooms due for arrival.
Show staff the reported rooms and have them copy the cleaning approach used there.
Tell the team to speed up turnover and check complaints again after the weekend.
Set observable standards for each area, walk through examples, and review results with the team.

basic.situation: Two housekeepers arrive for the morning shift, and three rooms need inspection before guests check in. You have the daily task list.

options.text: Give each worker a room and let them choose what to inspect after finishing.
Review the task list, assign rooms by location, and confirm each worker understands their duties.
Split the rooms evenly and check with your supervisor about the last inspection.
Assign two rooms to one worker and ask the other to handle the third room.

advanced.situation: A meeting group has added an early setup, while two staff members are unavailable. You need to adjust today's shift coverage and room preparation duties.

options.text: Rework shift coverage around setup and service peaks, then confirm duties with affected staff.
Map setup and service times, then assign available staff to the tasks needing coverage first.
Move one staff member from a later shift and ask the team to share remaining duties.
Keep the original roster and ask the meeting group to use the standard setup time.

basic.situation: A guest pays a deposit for a future stay. You have the receipt, booking reference, and payment system open.

options.text: Enter the deposit against the booking reference and compare the amount with the receipt.
Record the amount under today's deposits and keep the receipt with the shift papers.
Copy the receipt amount into the payment screen and move on to the next arrival.
Check the booking reference and receipt, then ask a colleague where to record the deposit.

advanced.situation: Monthly room revenue is below forecast, while weekend occupancy is rising and departments request extra funds. You are preparing figures for the manager's review.

options.text: Raise weekend rates based on stronger occupancy and trim each department's supply budget.
Summarize the revenue gap and ask department leads where spending can be reduced.
Compare occupancy and revenue by period, then propose rate and budget adjustments for review.
Review monthly revenue and occupancy, then share the main trend with the manager.

basic.situation: Your department needs a standard form for a laundry delivery and outside repair request. A colleague has shared the current paperwork template.

options.text: Use the last completed form as a guide and replace its date with today's date.
Copy the service and date from the request into the form and send it onward.
Complete the template fields and ask a colleague to review the paperwork before sending.
Fill the template with the service, delivery details, and department information, then check it against the request.

advanced.situation: Laundry deliveries are repeatedly late, disrupting room turnover. Staff use different request details, and you are asked to improve the department's procedure.

options.text: Set a standard request template with delivery details and explain it at the team briefing.
Tell staff to use the quickest request method and handle late deliveries as they arise.
Ask staff to call the laundry provider earlier and remind them at the next shift handover.
Compare recent requests, define required details and timing, then brief staff and review delivery results.

basic.situation: You are interviewing an entry-level housekeeping applicant with a manager present. The applicant has answered questions about availability and previous work.

options.text: Recommend the applicant because they seem friendly and can start next week.
Ask the applicant to describe a time they helped keep a shared guest space tidy.
Ask whether the applicant can start soon, then record the answer for your manager.
