I would enter the time and fault note using the usual form fields.
I would enter the time and note, then leave the cause field blank.

advanced.situation: A weekly downtime report differs from the control-room log, and the cause codes vary between sites. Management wants a fair performance comparison.

options.text: I would align event definitions, reconcile source logs, and document each adjustment.
I would use each site's existing codes and note that methods differ.
I would publish the totals and ask site leads to explain the differences.
I would replace the higher downtime figures with the control-room totals.

basic.situation: A new technician needs a refresher on the site's lockout briefing. You have been asked to help coordinate the next session.

options.text: I would send the time, location, and briefing topic to the technicians.
I would mark the team trained after sending the briefing slides.
I would check the roster, arrange a trainer, and track attendance.
I would book a room and ask the trainer to share available times.

advanced.situation: Contractors and employees report different hazards during seasonal work, while a landowner asks how the site protects nearby habitats. You are shaping a training programme.

options.text: I would reuse last year's slides and add the landowner's question.
I would build role-based safety and environmental modules around site hazards.
I would schedule one refresher covering the shared hazards and habitat rules.
I would gather site hazards, tailor practice by role, and check learning.

basic.situation: During a routine inspection, you notice a subcontractor preparing to work near a turbine. Your supervisor is nearby, and you have been asked to observe work practices.

options.text: I would note the setup and tell my supervisor what I observed.
I would watch the briefing, check the agreed steps, and record facts.
I would ask the subcontractor to explain the planned work sequence.
I would sign the observation sheet based on the crew's usual practice.

advanced.situation: At one site, a subcontractor's inspection records repeatedly miss required checks, though no defect has yet been found. You oversee work quality across sites.

options.text: I would pause acceptance, review samples, and agree corrective checks with the lead.
I would accept the records and remind the crew to be more careful.
I would flag the pattern and request a corrective action plan.
I would ask the crew to repeat the checks and update the records.

basic.situation: A routine equipment check shows an unusual vibration reading on a turbine. Your lead asks you to assist with the inspection.

options.text: I would record the reading, time, and equipment ID for the lead.
I would copy the previous reading to complete the inspection sheet.
I would retake the reading and note whether the vibration persists.
I would record the reading and compare it with the checklist range.

advanced.situation: A gearbox repair may be covered by warranty, but a contractor proposes a faster paid repair. The turbine is losing output, and you oversee maintenance planning.

options.text: I would check coverage, preserve evidence, and compare safe repair options.
I would compare repair timing and cost, then ask the contractor to proceed.
I would approve the paid repair to restore output before the weekend.
I would confirm likely coverage and request a repair quotation.

basic.situation: A planned inspection finds that two common filter sizes are running low. Your supervisor asks you to list what the site should order.

options.text: I would check work orders, stock, and lead times before drafting quantities.
I would order the usual monthly quantity for both filter sizes.
I would list both filter sizes and the current shelf quantities.
I would count the filters and draft an order for the low sizes.

advanced.situation: Parts orders often arrive after scheduled maintenance, and packaging waste is rising. You are asked to propose a sustainable procurement process for site operations.

options.text: I would add sustainability checks to each order form for buyers.
I would bulk order popular parts to reduce packaging and delivery trips.
I would map demand and lead times, then set reuse and waste criteria.
I would require recyclable packaging and retain the current ordering cycle.

basic.situation: A survey delay shifts two project milestones, and the senior manager asks you to update the schedule and cost estimate.

options.text: I would move the dates and carry forward the existing cost estimate.
I would update dates, affected costs, and assumptions for review.
I would keep the published dates and adjust the forecast later.
I would revise the milestone dates and note the survey delay.

advanced.situation: Several work packages are trending over budget, and teams use different forecast assumptions. You are asked to guide cost controls for a large wind project.

options.text: I would freeze discretionary purchases until teams explain their variances.
I would set shared forecast rules and review variances by work package.
I would consolidate the forecasts and highlight the largest overruns.
I would ask each team to reduce spending by the same percentage.

basic.situation: An equipment bid includes a drawing and materials list that do not seem to match. The engineer asks you to check the documents before review.

options.text: I would ask the bidder to confirm which materials they priced.
I would check revision identifiers and flag the mismatch for engineering review.
I would choose the newer-looking file and mark the bid complete.
I would compare drawing revisions and list the mismatched items.

advanced.situation: Two bids meet the headline capacity, but one omits details needed to compare foundation design compliance. The review team needs consistent technical recommendations.

options.text: I would use a common compliance matrix and mark evidence gaps for clarification.
I would compare the available designs and note the missing foundation details.
I would recommend the lower bid and request details after award.
I would ask the engineer to judge the incomplete foundation information.

basic.situation: You are helping prepare a building permit application, and the site layout has a revised access road. The project lead asks you to update the form package.

options.text: I would send the old package and explain the road change by email.
I would add a note about the road and leave the drawing unchanged.
I would update the layout and check the form fields against it.
I would replace the layout page and flag the change to the lead.

advanced.situation: An environmental permit submission depends on a seasonal survey, and the review team has raised questions about the study boundary. You coordinate the application strategy.

options.text: I would submit the current draft and answer boundary questions later.
I would extend the schedule to allow another seasonal survey.
I would ask the team for a revised survey and update the application.
I would map the concern, confirm evidence needs, and sequence submission steps.

basic.situation: A project lead asks you to help draft an RFP for site survey work. The scope and response deadline are already agreed.

options.text: I would state the scope, deliverables, response format, and deadline.
I would reuse the last survey RFP and change the project name.
I would add the scope and deadline, then invite questions by email.
I would draft the agreed scope, deliverables, and response deadline.

advanced.situation: A construction subcontractor is behind schedule and has submitted extra costs for changed access conditions. You oversee quality and conformance to the project terms.

options.text: I would approve part of the claim to keep the crew moving.
I would review the claim and ask the site lead to confirm progress.
I would compare the change evidence with scope, budget, and quality records.
I would reject the extra cost and ask the subcontractor to catch up.

basic.situation: A project manager asks you to list tasks and resources for an initial site assessment. The team has shared likely survey and access needs.

options.text: I would list the survey tasks and ask who can support each one.
I would group tasks, owners, and access needs for the manager to review.
I would copy the previous project's task list and assign its resources.
I would list survey tasks and the resources named by the team.

advanced.situation: A wind project scope must accommodate uncertain survey access and seasonal environmental studies. You are guiding teams as they build a plan and contingency.

options.text: I would include both studies and add a general time contingency.
I would set scope boundaries, dependencies, owners, and decision points.
I would hold the scope open until all survey results arrive.
I would schedule both studies and track access as a planning risk.

basic.situation: You join a site assessment visit and must send a status update. The survey team has completed the access review but is still checking ground conditions.

options.text: I would report the access review and pending ground checks with dates.
I would note the access review and mention ground checks are pending.
I would report that the assessment is nearly complete.
I would say the team completed the site assessment.

advanced.situation: Construction access planning conflicts with a seasonal study boundary, and commissioning dates are approaching. You coordinate development, engineering, and site activities.

options.text: I would ask engineering and the study team to propose revised dates.
I would keep construction on schedule and move the study boundary later.
I would map constraints, align affected teams, and stage work around evidence.
I would pause access work until the study team provides its findings.

basic.situation: You are helping start cleanup at an abandoned workshop, and the crew asks which approved steps to follow first.

options.text: Move visible debris to clear machinery access after checking site controls.
Stay within marked work areas and report any unexpected material.
Ask the site lead which area crews should clear first.
Review the approved cleanup plan, then brief the crew on initial safety steps.

advanced.situation: A proposed brownfield renewal could reduce contamination but may shift runoff toward nearby homes and waterways.

options.text: Shape regeneration around cleanup outcomes, runoff pathways, and nearby community needs.
Present the cleaner design as settled and ask neighbors to support it.
Ask the design team to compare runoff options before choosing a layout.
Keep the design within the site boundary and prioritize its planned end use.

basic.situation: A consultant proposes soil treatment at a site, and your supervisor asks you to review the proposal's main assumptions.

options.text: Accept the treatment method because the proposal includes a cost estimate.
Check the stated contaminants, treatment approach, and evidence against the site brief.
Review the proposed schedule and note questions for your supervisor.
Ask the consultant to explain the treatment method and expected duration.

advanced.situation: Two cleanup methods have different costs and residual risks, while the redevelopment team needs a defensible recommendation.

options.text: Compare the risk estimates and discuss the higher-risk method with the team.
Choose the lower-cost method and ask the team to manage its residual risks.
Compare lifecycle costs and quantified risks across both methods before recommending a path.
List the main risks and ask the consultant which method is safer.

basic.situation: You walk a redevelopment plot and notice a stained patch beside a drain during a routine inspection.

options.text: Mark the location, photograph it, and record nearby drains for the site file.
Photograph the patch and tell the site lead where you found it.
Note the stain in your inspection log and continue the walk.
Cover the stain with soil to keep the walkway clear.

advanced.situation: Cleanup readings vary between visits, and the team asks you to improve how progress is monitored across the plot.

options.text: Use the latest readings to describe the cleanup trend in the update.
Set repeatable sampling points, dates, and field notes for each monitoring round.
Ask the team to revisit the same areas and record new readings.
Choose the cleanest readings to show that remediation is progressing.

basic.situation: A delivery crew arrives while cleanup equipment is using the same access road, and your site lead is nearby.

options.text: Ask the driver to wait while you tell the lead about the arrival.
Let the delivery crew unload beside the equipment staging area.
Check the day's sequence with the site lead and stagger both activities.
Direct the truck to the nearest open space until the road clears.

advanced.situation: A contractor's draft cleanup contract leaves waste tracking and site access responsibilities unclear before a large project begins.

options.text: Ask procurement to compare the price with another contractor's offer.
Discuss the unclear duties with the contractor and note proposed changes.
Accept the draft terms and ask the contractor to settle details on site.
Clarify scope, tracking records, and access duties in the draft before negotiating price.

basic.situation: A design decision changes the cleanup sequence, and the project file needs an updated record before the weekly meeting.

options.text: Replace the old schedule with the new dates for the meeting.
Save the revised schedule and note that the design team requested it.
Record the decision, reason, owner, and resulting schedule change in the project file.
Add the new dates to your notes and share them with the team.

advanced.situation: Several cleanup projects face funding gaps, and leadership wants a clear view of current applications and supporting records.

options.text: Review each application file and flag missing documents to the project leads.
List possible funding routes and ask project leads which to pursue.
Reuse the strongest application narrative across every project to save time.
Rank funding routes by project fit and reconcile each application with its evidence file.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks for a short progress update on soil cleanup before the project meeting tomorrow.

options.text: Summarize completed cleanup, current status, and the next milestone using site records.
Report that cleanup remains on schedule, citing this week's crew activity and recorded progress.
List this week's activities, dates, crew progress, and delays for your supervisor to review.
Use the latest schedule to report upcoming cleanup tasks, dates, and expected crew needs.

advanced.situation: Several teams prepare applications for demolition and remediation, but their drafts use different formats and omit recurring details.

options.text: Compare drafts, identify repeated missing details, and circulate a summary for every team to review.
Create a shared checklist from permit requirements and train teams to use it.
Send the previous project's application as a reference template for all project teams.
Ask each team to list details it usually includes in its draft applications.

basic.situation: At a music industry event, you meet a festival organiser who leaves in a few minutes. Your agency's young singer-songwriter has no other offers yet.

options.text: Introduce yourself and your singer, ask what acts they need, and swap contact details.
Praise the festival and ask for a booking slot for your singer this year.
Hand over a card and a link to the singer's songs, and say you will call.
Tell the organiser your singer has other festival offers so they must decide today.

advanced.situation: You mentor a junior agent who wants to land a headline act. A big industry conference is next week, and the act's manager will be there.

options.text: Help them research the manager's recent deals, plan a warm introduction, and agree follow-up steps.
Advise them to hand out as many cards as possible and talk to everyone there.
Suggest they say they already work with a famous act to get the manager's attention.
Tell them to attend the manager's panel talk and speak to the manager afterwards.

basic.situation: A promoter sends your supervisor's client a standard performance contract. Your supervisor asks you to go through the pay and cancellation clauses.

options.text: Read the pay and cancellation clauses, note what they mean for the client, and list questions.
Read the pay and cancellation clauses and tell your supervisor that they look standard.
Sign the contract for the client to secure the date, since the promoter needs it back.
Check the fee amount against the quote and mention the other clauses are long.

advanced.situation: A promoter says your client breached a contract by cancelling a show due to illness. The promoter demands full payment and a public apology.

options.text: Pay the promoter in full from the client's account to close the matter quickly.
Check the contract's illness terms, gather the doctor's note, and propose a partial settlement.
Share the doctor's note with the promoter and ask them to drop the payment demand.
Offer a public apology to calm the promoter and then discuss the payment later.

basic.situation: Your agent asks you to send a client's showreel to three casting directors for an audition. You have the showreel link and a contact list.

options.text: Check the showreel link works, personalise each email, and record whom you sent it to.
Send each director a short email with the link and your client's name.
Send the showreel to all casting directors in your contact list, in one big batch.
Send the link to the directors you know and add the others when there is time.

advanced.situation: A sports brand may sponsor your client, a young athlete. You are asked to design a pitch for a major endorsement within a month.

options.text: Offer the brand a discount on the endorsement fee to win the deal before others.
Send the brand the athlete's results and social media numbers with a short proposal.
Promise the brand the athlete will post daily and wear its logo at every event.
Study the brand's audience and build a campaign around the athlete's story, agreed with the client.

basic.situation: Your client has a concert on Saturday night. A radio station asks for an interview on Saturday afternoon in another town. You help book dates.

options.text: Ask the client if Saturday afternoon is free, and confirm with the radio station if so.
Move the concert soundcheck to later in the evening to fit in the Saturday interview.
Accept the Saturday slot and arrange a driver, as radio exposure helps the concert.
Check the travel time and the client's soundcheck time, then suggest an interview slot on Friday.

advanced.situation: You coordinate a three-city tour for a band within one week. A venue in the second city has cancelled, and the band's flights are non-refundable.

options.text: Ask the cancelling venue to move the show to next month and tell the band to wait.
Tell the band the venue cancelled and ask the other cities if they can add a show.
Book the first free club nearby at any price and confirm it to ticket holders today.
Contact nearby venues for the date, check travel options, and update the band and promoters.

basic.situation: You sit in a meeting where your senior agent tells a young actor why a TV role was declined. The actor looks upset. You take notes.

options.text: Write down the main decision and tell the actor the role was not the right fit.
Note the decision and the reason given, and leave the actor's feelings out of your notes.
Change the reason in your notes to something kinder so that the actor feels better.
Note the reasons given, the actor's questions, and next steps, then share them.

advanced.situation: A mid-career actor wants to move into directing. You are building a five-year career roadmap and training a junior agent on how to explain it.

options.text: Give the junior a roadmap template and ask them to explain it to the actor.
Tell the actor directing roles will come soon, so the junior can promise results.
Write the roadmap yourself and let the junior watch you present it to the actor.
Agree goals with the actor, set yearly steps, and coach the junior to explain each step.

basic.situation: You help organise an audition day for new talent. Your supervisor asks you to arrange the interview schedule and watch the auditions.

options.text: Build a timetable with gaps between auditions, confirm times with each performer, and note impressions.
Book all performers for the same morning hour and watch the auditions as they come.
Set the timetable and send it to the performers, then watch each audition.
Give the earliest audition slots to your friends first and fill the rest afterwards.

advanced.situation: You lead a panel auditioning new clients. A talented singer asks for a lower commission than the agency's standard rate and wants a quick decision.

options.text: Score singers on the agreed criteria and refer the lower commission request to management.
Tell the singer the standard rate is fixed and ask for a decision by tonight.
Sign the singer at their proposed rate and note the deal in the file later.
Agree a small discount in the commission to sign the singer before rivals do.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to buy 2 tonnes of fresh milk for the dairy plant this week. The usual farm can supply 1.5 tonnes.

options.text: Buy 2 tonnes from the nearest farm that has stock, whatever its quality grade is.
Buy the 1.5 tonnes and tell the supervisor the rest will be bought next week.
Buy the 1.5 tonnes now and ask the supervisor which other farm to try.
Pay the farm for 2 tonnes in advance so it finds the extra milk elsewhere.

advanced.situation: You set the quality standard for buying durian from many small growers. Junior buyers accept fruit differently, and the processor complains about uneven grades.

options.text: Write grade criteria with photos, train junior buyers, and spot-check what they accept.
Write a one-page grade guide and email it to the junior buyers to follow.
Accept every lot offered and pay growers a single flat price for all grades.
Tell junior buyers to accept just the ripest fruit and call you when in doubt.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to draft a simple purchase agreement for 5 tonnes of cabbages from a local farmer. You have last year's agreement as a sample.

options.text: Reuse last year's structure, update quantity, price and delivery date, and send it for review.
Change the names and quantity in last year's agreement and send it for review.
Write a short note listing the quantity and price and have the farmer sign it.
Have the farmer sign a blank agreement now, then fill in the price after delivery.

advanced.situation: A palm oil mill wants a three-year supply contract with a smallholder group. Prices could swing widely, and the group asks for one fixed price for all three years.

options.text: Agree to the fixed price for all three years to secure the supply for the mill.
Propose a price linked to a market reference with a floor and ceiling.
Offer a fixed price for the first year and negotiate the later years when they come.
Promise the group the mill will cover any losses, to get them to sign quickly.

basic.situation: You check this week's supermarket orders for tomatoes. Two orders ask for 500 kg each, and a third asks for 300 kg and is marked urgent.

options.text: Fill the two larger orders first and mention the urgent one when supply allows.
Cancel the urgent order yourself and tell the supermarket to order again next week.
Add up the orders, note the urgent one, and tell the supervisor the total needed.
Add up the three orders and tell the supervisor the total quantity needed.

advanced.situation: Rice demand has changed after a new government subsidy. You must decide how much of each rice type to forecast and order for the next quarter.

options.text: Compare past orders with subsidy dates, forecast each rice type, and review monthly.
Double all rice orders for the quarter in case the subsidy raises demand sharply.
Raise last year's order quantities by the subsidy percentage for every rice type next quarter.
Order the same quantities as last quarter and adjust once the new demand shows up.

basic.situation: You enter today's purchase of paddy into the records. The weighing slip says 780 kg, but the seller's invoice says 800 kg.

options.text: Record the weighed 780 kg, note the difference with the invoice, and tell your supervisor.
Record 780 kg from the weighing slip and file the invoice with the paperwork.
Change the weighing slip to read 800 kg so the records and invoice agree.
Record 800 kg as invoiced because the seller's figure is the one being paid.

advanced.situation: Your company must report quarterly farm product stock and purchases to a government agency. Stock figures sit in three spreadsheets, and the numbers do not match.

options.text: Reconcile the spreadsheets against receipts, set one master format, and submit the verified report.
Average the three sets of numbers and submit the result with a short note.
Submit the lowest purchase figures so the company is less likely to face questions.
Pick the most recent spreadsheet as the master and submit its figures on time.

basic.situation: A buyer asks you to book a truck for 400 kg of fresh vegetables from a farm to a wholesale market. They must arrive by morning.

options.text: Book the cheapest truck available for tonight and tell the farm the pickup time.
Book a covered truck, confirm pickup time with the farm, and send the driver the address.
Ask the farm to arrange its own transport and send the vegetables when ready.
Load the vegetables onto a spare open pickup and drive them to the market yourself.

advanced.situation: A buyer must store 50 tonnes of grain for two months before a processing contract starts. Warehouse space is tight, and the grain is slightly damp.

options.text: Store the grain in the cheapest space available and move it if mould appears.
Dry the grain to a safe level, then reserve a ventilated warehouse and inspect it weekly.
Pack the damp grain with the dry stock to save warehouse space during the two months.
Reserve the largest ventilated warehouse available and check the grain at the end of each month.

basic.situation: A farm delivers 200 kg of ripe mangoes that must be sold or processed within three days. You decide where to send them.

options.text: Hold the mangoes in the warehouse for a few days until the market price improves.
Sell all mangoes to a street trader today for cash and log the sale next week.
Ask the processor which ripeness it accepts, send what fits, and sell the rest at market.
Send all the mangoes to the juice processor you used last month and confirm receipt.

advanced.situation: Your company buys large amounts of sweet corn each season. Prices drop at the harvest peak, and processing capacity is limited. You design the resale plan.

options.text: Split the corn between fresh sales, freezing and canning by price forecasts, and book slots.
Sell most of the corn fresh at peak and process the remainder when slots open.
Freeze as much corn as the warehouse holds and sell it whenever prices recover.
Sign a fixed resale price with one supermarket for the whole season before checking costs.

basic.situation: Your manager asks you to review last quarter's supermarket sales records and spot basic trends before a buying meeting tomorrow.

options.text: Use last year's trend for the same quarter and tell the manager it is likely similar.
Pick out the five products with the highest sales and tell the manager they are the trend.
Tell the manager the trend follows what is in the news and order stock for it.
Compare sales by product across the months, note risers and fallers, and share a summary.

advanced.situation: A junior buyer asks how to use inflation data and a falling ringgit when planning next quarter's imported snack stock. You guide them.

options.text: Tell them to double orders now since import prices will certainly climb this quarter.
Show them how to turn import cost changes into low and high price scenarios for orders.
Tell them to read the central bank's monthly report and adjust orders by the headline figures.
Tell them to wait for prices to settle before placing the next quarter's orders.

basic.situation: A new batch of cotton shirts costs RM20 each, and the usual mark-up is 50 percent. Your supervisor asks you to suggest a selling price.

options.text: Put RM30 on the labels yourself and tell the supervisor after the shirts are out.
Suggest RM30, compare it with similar shirts, and show your supervisor the working.
Suggest RM35 because the shirts look better than the ones the shop sold last season.
Suggest RM30 from the usual mark-up and tell the supervisor it is the standard price.

advanced.situation: You train staff to inspect imported watches priced above RM5,000. A recent batch included fakes that passed a quick visual check.

options.text: Compare each watch with photos on the brand's website and note any differences.
Set a checklist with serial number checks, papers and supplier checks, and train staff on it.
Add a second person to approve each watch and ask staff to look more closely.
Accept watches from long-standing suppliers on trust and inspect stock from new suppliers carefully.

basic.situation: Your manager asks you to find out from shop staff what customers have been asking for in the sports shoe section. You talk to three staff members.

options.text: Report the requests you heard most recently, since they show what customers want now.
Ask each staff member about common requests and complaints, then write one summary.
Ask the most experienced staff member what customers want and report it to the manager.
Write up what customers prefer from your own view and say the staff agreed.

advanced.situation: You design a way to capture customer preferences across 20 stores. Staff are busy, and past paper surveys were mostly left blank.

options.text: Pilot a one-question checkout prompt in three stores, review the answers, and train staff.
Print a feedback link on every receipt and review the responses once a month.
Use sales data from the busiest store as the preference for all 20 stores.
Ask each store manager to send in a monthly list of what customers asked for.

basic.situation: You must reorder A4 paper using the senior buyer's checklist. Stock stands at 10 boxes, and the checklist says to reorder at 15.

options.text: Order the checklist quantity from the approved supplier and remember to log it later.
Order from the cheaper supplier you found online and tell your senior buyer afterwards.
Order the checklist quantity from the approved supplier and log the order date.
Order a smaller quantity than the checklist says, since ten boxes will last a while.

advanced.situation: You define selection criteria for a new line of eco-friendly kitchenware. Every supplier claims its products are sustainable, and you mentor a junior buyer.

options.text: Define criteria on materials, certifications and packaging, and teach the junior to ask for proof.
Choose the supplier with the lowest price and ask the junior to check the claims later.
Label every product as sustainable in the catalogue so the junior can order them confidently.
Use the suppliers' own sustainability claims as the criteria and teach the junior to compare them.

basic.situation: You process an invoice for 200 cartons of canned drinks. The delivery note says 180 cartons were received. Your supervisor sits nearby.

options.text: Hold the payment, tell the supervisor about the 20 cartons, and ask for an amended invoice.
Hold the payment and ask the supplier to explain the difference in the quantity.
Pay the full invoice and change the delivery note to show 200 cartons received.
Pay the full invoice because this supplier has delivered on time for many years now.

advanced.situation: You set the policy for approving returns of damaged goods. Returns are rising, and some suppliers refuse credit when the damage is not clearly documented.

options.text: Require photos, a damage report and a time limit, and agree it with finance.
Require a damage report for every return and send suppliers a copy with the goods.
Approve returns when store staff call them damaged and sort out credit with suppliers later.
Return all slow-selling goods to suppliers as damaged to claim credit for the stock.

basic.situation: You observe a senior buyer negotiating prices with a rice supplier. Afterwards, the supplier calls you directly and offers a lower price if you confirm today.

options.text: Ask the supplier to send the offer in writing and tell the senior buyer later today.
Agree to the price in principle and mention it to the senior buyer next week.
Thank the supplier, say the senior buyer handles prices, and pass the offer on.
Confirm the new price and a bigger order today to lock the supplier's discount.

advanced.situation: You lead talks for a two-year snack supply deal. The supplier offers a volume discount, but the larger orders would exceed your warehouse space.

options.text: Decline the discount and keep ordering current volumes at the standard price for now.
Accept the volume discount and rent extra storage to hold the larger orders for two years.
Sign the volume discount deal and sort out the storage problem after the first delivery.
Ask for staged deliveries at the discounted price and agree a review clause.

basic.situation: Your manager needs 50 safety helmets for a building project. You search catalogs and directories to find suppliers.

options.text: Find the lowest-priced helmet in the first catalog and send your manager the details.
Shortlist three suppliers, check each helmet's safety standard, and send your manager the list.
Order the helmets from an online seller with good reviews and tell your manager later.
Shortlist three suppliers from the catalogs and send your manager the list with their prices.

advanced.situation: You set standards for evaluating suppliers of imported electronic parts. Two suppliers have similar prices but different delivery records and support.

options.text: Define weighted criteria for quality, delivery, support and price, and teach staff to score.
Choose the supplier with the better delivery record and tell staff to use that as a guide.
Ask each supplier to rate itself on quality and support and compare the answers.
Pick the supplier a trusted colleague uses and write it up as the evaluated choice.

basic.situation: You monitor cooking oil prices. This week your usual supplier's price rose 8 percent, while the market index rose 2 percent.

options.text: Report the 8 percent rise to your supervisor and mention that prices are moving.
Cancel the usual supplier's standing order and buy from the cheapest spot seller this week.
Compare the supplier's price with the index and report the gap to your supervisor.
Accept the new price because the market is rising and update the price sheet.

advanced.situation: Your company plans a three-year steel contract. A supplier's price proposal looks low, but a regulator recently changed the rules on imported steel standards.

options.text: Compare the proposal with market prices and recommend it if it is lower than the average.
Recommend the proposal now because the price is low and rules usually take time to apply.
Accept the low proposal and ask the supplier to confirm it meets the new rules.
Check the new rules against the proposal, ask for a cost breakdown, and compare market prices.

basic.situation: A shipment of printer paper arrived with damp, unusable reams. Your supervisor asks you to contact the vendor about the defective goods.

options.text: Call the vendor, describe the damp reams, and ask for a replacement delivery this week.
Send the vendor photos and delivery details, and ask how they will resolve it.
Withhold payment for all of this month's orders until the vendor apologises in writing.
Throw out the damp reams and order a new batch from the same vendor.

advanced.situation: A key supplier repeatedly delivers late, and a junior buyer asks how to handle it. The contract has a delivery clause but no penalty, and production is affected.

options.text: Send the supplier a formal letter listing the late deliveries and asking it to improve.
Log each late delivery, review the clause, and meet the supplier to agree dated improvements.
Terminate the contract by email today and tell the junior to find another supplier.
Start buying from a second supplier and tell the first one when stock arrives.

basic.situation: You prepare a purchase order for 100 office chairs from a requisition signed by the department head. The requisition has no delivery address.

options.text: Use the company's main address as the delivery address and note it on the order.
Ask the department head for the delivery address, add it, and attach the requisition.
Copy a delivery address from an old order to the same department and send it.
Send the order and ask the vendor to phone for the address when it is ready.

advanced.situation: You design the purchasing workflow and train new team members. Orders are often delayed because approvals travel through long email chains.

options.text: Ask managers to reply to approval emails within a day and remind them weekly.
Write a step-by-step guide for email approvals and train new members to follow it.
Map the approval steps, set up one order system with clear limits, and train new staff.
Let new staff place orders directly with vendors and collect approvals once the goods arrive.

basic.situation: You update the delivery record for printer toner. The supplier's slip lists 20 cartridges, but the box count today shows 18.

options.text: Record 20 and take two cartridges from another department's stock to make up the count.
Record 18 as received and file the slip with the rest of the delivery paperwork.
Record 20 as the slip says, since this supplier has packed boxes carefully before.
Record 18 as received, note the slip difference, and tell the supplier and your supervisor.

advanced.situation: A sudden road closure delays a critical packaging shipment for a product launch. Stock covers four days, and the supplier says delivery may take ten.

options.text: Ask the supplier about partial shipments, find a backup source, and brief production on the options.
Ask the supplier to rush the shipment and tell production the stock should last.
Tell production the shipment is still on time and wait to see what happens by Friday.
Place an urgent order for double the packaging from a second supplier at any price.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to help draft a product specification for 500 laptop bags for staff. You have last year's order and a vendor sample.

options.text: List size, material, strength and branding needs from the request, and attach the sample.
Copy last year's specification and change the quantity and date for this order.
Write the specification as bags suitable for staff and let the vendor choose the details.
Describe the vendor's sample in detail and use that description as the specification.

advanced.situation: You write the bid policy for purchases above RM100,000 and review technical specifications. Managers want faster approvals, and auditors want competitive bids.

options.text: Require three bids above the limit, set a fast track with approval, and check specifications.
Require three bids above the limit and keep the current approval steps in place for now.
Let managers split large purchases into smaller orders to stay under the bid limit.
Allow managers to skip bids above the limit when they confirm the vendor is trusted.

basic.situation: A claimant reports a stolen laptop. Your supervisor asks you to call him and collect the basic information for the file.

options.text: Ask him to describe what happened and note the answers he gives in the file.
Tell him to email the details and you will add them to the file when they arrive.
Fill in the missing details with typical figures for similar claims to complete the file.
Ask when and where it happened, the laptop details, and whether he reported it to police.

advanced.situation: A doctor's report on an injury claim conflicts with the claimant's account of when the injury happened. You interview the specialist and guide a junior on questions.

options.text: Ask the doctor to confirm the injury date and tell the junior to record the reply.
Prepare neutral questions on the report's dates, interview the doctor, and have the junior take notes.
Tell the junior to ask the claimant to change the date to match the report.
Accept the doctor's date, since doctors are experts, and note it as the injury date.

basic.situation: A policyholder claims for flood damage to his shop. Your supervisor asks you to check the policy to see whether flood is covered.

options.text: Confirm to the policyholder that flood is covered so he can start repairs at once.
Search the policy for the word flood and tell your supervisor what you find.
Read the schedule and exclusions for flood cover, note any limit, and tell your supervisor.
Tell your supervisor flood is usually covered for shops, so the claim should go ahead.

advanced.situation: A factory fire claim is large, and the repair estimate is double the contractor's earlier quote. You set standards for checking damage evaluations.

options.text: Approve the new estimate since the damage was caused by fire and costs vary.
Compare the estimate with the earlier quote, ask for itemised costs, and appoint an assessor.
Ask the contractor to explain the higher figure and approve it if the reasons sound fair.
Pay half of the estimate now and settle the rest after the factory reopens.

basic.situation: You review a motor claim form and the attached repair bill. The accident date on the form is a Sunday, but the garage's job card shows the car arrived the previous Friday.

options.text: Change the accident date on the form to match the job card and approve the claim.
Note the date mismatch, compare the police report, and refer the file to your supervisor.
Ask the claimant to resubmit the form with the garage's date and process it.
Note the date mismatch on the file and continue processing the rest of the claim.

advanced.situation: Three claims from the same garage show near-identical photos. You lead the investigation and mentor an adjuster on evidence standards.

options.text: Ask the garage to explain the photos and approve the claims if the answer sounds reasonable.
Check the photo files, pause payment on the three claims, and refer them to investigators.
Warn the garage owner that his claims are under review so he can fix the photos.
Reject the three claims straight away and tell the claimants the photos were suspicious.

basic.situation: You are asked to attend a mediation for a disputed injury claim with a senior adjuster. This is your first mediation.

options.text: Attend, take notes during the session, and review them with the senior adjuster later.
Tell the claimant's lawyer the company's top settlement figure before the session to speed things up.
Read the file beforehand, sit with the adjuster, take notes, and ask questions afterwards.
Attend and join the discussion to offer your views on how the claim should settle.

advanced.situation: A disputed commercial fire claim may go to trial. You manage the litigation strategy, and the lawyers ask for evidence of the insured's maintenance.

options.text: Give counsel the records that support our position and keep the rest on file for now.
Send counsel the maintenance records the insured gave you and ask what else is needed.
Collect the maintenance records and inspection reports, secure originals, and brief counsel on what they show.
Ask the insured to prepare a summary of the records and send it to counsel.

basic.situation: You enter a new claim's reserve into the system from the adjuster's note. The note says RM12,000, but a medical report in the file suggests more.

options.text: Leave the reserve blank until the claim is paid so no figure can be questioned.
Enter RM12,000 as noted and trust the adjuster has already seen the medical report.
Enter RM12,000 as noted and ask the adjuster whether the medical report changes it.
Raise the reserve to RM20,000 yourself based on the medical report and tell the adjuster.

advanced.situation: You develop reserve policy for severe injury claims. Reserves are often set low early and then raised sharply, which upsets finance.

options.text: Spread large reserve increases over several months so that finance sees smaller changes each time.
Ask adjusters to set reserves carefully and explain any large increases in the notes.
Set higher starting reserves for all severe claims and review them at year end.
Set reserve guidelines by injury type with review points and audit a sample of files.

basic.situation: You input a claim payment of RM3,500 into the system. The system asks for file notes explaining the payment.

options.text: Copy the notes from another claim's payment and change the claim number to match.
Write a one-line note saying the claim was paid under the policy and save the entry.
Note the payment reason, who approved it, and the date in two short lines.
Leave the notes blank and tell your supervisor the payment details by chat message today.

advanced.situation: An audit found missing notes in many files and a few overpayments never reported. You design new documentation standards and must audit files.

options.text: Set a payment note checklist, audit a file sample, and require overpayments to be reported.
Ask adjusters to add missing notes to old files and raise overpayments at the next meeting.
Set a note checklist for every payment and ask adjusters to follow it from now.
Write the missing notes into the old files from memory and leave out the overpayments.

basic.situation: You inspect a car after a rear collision. The senior appraiser asks you to list the visible body and mechanical problems.

options.text: Start the engine and drive the car around the yard to check how it runs.
List the visible dents and broken lights and tell the senior appraiser the rest looks fine.
Walk around the car, photograph each damaged area, and list dents, lights and leaks.
Use the owner's description of the damage and add it to your list with a photo.

advanced.situation: A car with a mild front dent has the airbag warning light on after a collision. The owner wants a quick, cheap repair.

options.text: Clear the warning light and note the car as repairable with a cosmetic fix.
Approve the body repair and tell the owner to see a dealer about the light.
Scan for fault codes, inspect the airbag system and wiring, and list the repairs needed.
Recommend resetting the warning light and test-driving the car before approving the body repair.

basic.situation: You use the standard parts and labour manual to estimate a bumper replacement. The manual lists 3 hours of labour, but the shop quoted 5.

options.text: Use the manual's 3 hours, add parts, and note the shop's 5 hours for review.
Average the two labour figures and write it as the manual's rate on the estimate.
Use the shop's 5 hours, because the shop knows the job better than the manual.
Use the manual's 3 hours and add the parts cost to prepare the estimate.

advanced.situation: You set cost standards for repairing hybrid battery housings, a complex job. Junior appraisers estimate widely different amounts for the same damage.

options.text: Use the highest estimate from the juniors as the standard to avoid underpaying shops.
Set the standard from the manual's figures and tell juniors to follow it from next week.
Let the juniors agree among themselves on a typical figure and send it to you.
Gather manuals and recent shop invoices, set a standard cost range, and walk juniors through two examples.

basic.situation: A ten-year-old sedan is a total loss. Your senior asks you to look up its market value as a starting point for the salvage value.

options.text: Quote the price of a newer model of the same car as the market value.
Check three similar listings by model and year, note the prices, and give the range.
Use the price the owner paid ten years ago and adjust it down a little.
Look up the model's price in one used-car guide and give the senior that figure.

advanced.situation: The owner disputes your salvage value for a flood-damaged SUV, saying a buyer offered more. The owner has no written proof of that offer.

options.text: Raise the salvage value halfway towards the owner's figure to settle the dispute quickly.
Explain how you valued the SUV and ask the owner to find the buyer's written offer.
Record the owner's higher figure as the salvage value on the form and close the dispute.
Compare recent auction results for similar flood vehicles and ask for the offer in writing.

basic.situation: A car worth RM30,000 needs RM12,000 of repairs. Your checklist says to declare a total loss if repairs exceed 70 percent of the value.

options.text: Compare RM12,000 with 70 percent of RM30,000, mark the car repairable, and record the working.
Mark the car as a total loss so the owner is paid and the claim closes.
Mark the car repairable because RM12,000 looks small compared with the car's value overall.
Mark the car as a total loss because the damage looks serious in the photos.

advanced.situation: A rare classic car's repair cost is RM85,000 against a pre-accident market value of RM90,000. Parts are scarce, and the owner wants it restored.

options.text: Get a specialist valuation, check parts availability and time, and set out repair and payout options.
Recommend a payout of RM90,000 since the repair cost is so close to the value.
Approve the repair now to keep the owner satisfied and review the cost afterwards.
Recommend repair because the cost is below the market value and the owner prefers it.

basic.situation: You copy details from an approved estimate onto the insurer's standard claim form. The estimate shows RM4,250 for repairs and RM300 for a rental car.

options.text: Enter both amounts in their boxes and submit the form, as the numbers are copied.
Round both amounts up to the nearest hundred ringgit so the form looks neat.
Enter the repair amount and add the rental figure later if the insurer asks for it.
Enter both amounts in their boxes and check the totals against the estimate before submitting.

advanced.situation: Several claim forms show repair costs that do not match the attached estimates. You audit the forms and train staff on proper documentation.

options.text: Tell staff to type the estimate total on every form, whatever the repair invoice says.
Fix the mismatched forms yourself and send staff a reminder to check their entries.
Ask each staff member to recheck their own forms and report any errors found.
Sample recent forms against estimates, find the common cause, then train staff with a short checklist.

basic.situation: A repair shop quotes RM2,800 for a door repair, while your estimate was RM2,200. The senior appraiser sits beside you as you review the shop's estimate.

options.text: Ask the senior appraiser to talk to the shop, since you are still learning.
Agree to the shop's RM2,800 quote on the spot so the repair can start today.
Compare the shop's parts and labour lines with yours and ask about each difference.
Tell the shop your estimate is RM2,200 and ask whether it can match that.

advanced.situation: You and a repair shop still disagree after two rounds on a RM9,000 repair estimate. The owner is waiting for the car.

options.text: Meet the shop a third time and offer a small increase to your estimate.
Approve the shop's full estimate to release the car and note the gap as an error.
Tell the owner to pay the shop the difference and claim it back later.
Arrange another appraiser to inspect the car, share both estimates, and tell the owner the plan.

basic.situation: You check a business licence application against the checklist. It is complete except for the applicant's insurance certificate, which is missing.

options.text: Fill in the certificate details from last year's application and send it for approval.
Pass the application to the next stage and note that the certificate may follow.
Hold the application and tell your supervisor that the insurance certificate is still missing.
Mark the application incomplete, list the missing certificate, and request it from the applicant.

advanced.situation: You design an audit protocol for import permits from several countries. Formats and languages differ, and past reviews missed forged stamps.

options.text: Use one checklist for all countries and ask reviewers to flag anything that looks unusual.
Ask reviewers to compare each stamp with the samples they remember from earlier permits.
Accept any permit with an official-looking stamp and review complaints when they come in.
Build a checklist per country, add checks with issuing authorities, and train reviewers on forgery signs.

basic.situation: Your supervisor gives you a template and asks for a short summary of this week's 12 inspections, of which 3 found problems.

options.text: Fill in the template with the totals and list the 3 inspections that found problems.
Fill in the template with all 12 inspections, name the 3 problem sites, and add dates.
Leave out the 3 problem inspections from the summary so the week looks clean.
Write that the week went smoothly, with a few small matters to follow up.

advanced.situation: You set reporting standards and train junior staff. Reports vary in length, and decision-makers say they cannot find the recommendations.

options.text: Tell staff to remove the evidence sections from all reports so the recommendations stand out.
Ask readers what they need, create a template with recommendations first, and train staff on it.
Create a template with recommendations first and email it to the staff to use.
Ask staff to shorten their reports and bold the recommendations when they write them.

basic.situation: During a routine site check, you find a company storing chemicals without the required permit. You enter it in the tracking system.

options.text: Log the site, date and permit issue with photos, and tell your supervisor about the violation.
Delete the entry after the company promises it will apply for the permit tomorrow.
Tell the company to get the permit this week and log the case once it does.
Log the site, date and permit issue in the tracking system and move on.

advanced.situation: A company broke rules covering two agencies, environment and labour safety. You must report to both, but each wants the other to take the lead.

options.text: Wait for the two agencies to agree who leads before sending your report to either.
Report to both agencies with the same evidence, state which rules apply, and name one contact.
Report to the agency with the more serious rule and ask it to inform the other.
Send each agency a shorter version covering just its own rules and keep the full file.

basic.situation: A restaurant owner is late renewing a licence. Your supervisor asks you to read the standard penalty warning to him on the phone.

options.text: Tell him the fine is waived if he renews today, as it is his first.
Tell him a fine is coming and suggest he renew soon to avoid trouble.
Read the warning as written, state the deadline and fine, and ask him to confirm.
Read the warning as written and note on the file that you called him.

advanced.situation: A large company disputes a penalty notice, and one of its staff shouted at your team. Your juniors are shaken, and the company's lawyer wants a call today.

options.text: Offer to reduce the penalty if the company drops its complaint about your team.
Ask a senior colleague to join the call with the lawyer and explain the notice.
Let a junior take the call so the lawyer sees the team is calm.
Take the lawyer's call, restate the notice basis calmly, record it, and check on your juniors.

basic.situation: A caller asks what documents are needed to renew a food stall permit. You have the permit requirement sheet in front of you.

options.text: Tell the caller it is the same as last year, so the old documents will do.
Read the documents on the sheet and tell the caller to check the website for the rest.
Read the documents on the sheet, say where to submit, and offer to email it.
Tell the caller the renewal fee can be paid a few weeks after the permit expires.

advanced.situation: New rules change licensing conditions for all food factories from next month. Senior stakeholders ask you what changes and what they should do.

options.text: Compare old and new rules line by line, list changes and deadlines, and recommend actions.
Read the official summary of the new rules and send stakeholders its key points quickly.
Tell stakeholders the rules are mostly the same and they can wait for further notices.
Tell stakeholders that factories already licensed are exempt from the new conditions this year.

basic.situation: You sit in an interview where a senior officer questions a licence applicant about his business history. You take the notes.

options.text: Add answers you expect the applicant to give where your notes have small gaps.
Note the answers that seem important to the licence decision and skip small talk.
Write down dates, names and answers in his words, and mark anything unclear.
Write a summary of the answers in your own words after the interview ends.

advanced.situation: You lead an investigation into whether a licensed firm hid its ownership. Specialists from legal and finance give conflicting views on a shareholder structure.

options.text: Ask each specialist to explain their reasoning, test both views against documents, and record why.
Follow the legal specialist's view since the question concerns company law, and note the finance view.
Ask the two specialists to agree on one view and send it to you.
Adopt the view that fits the firm's explanation and tell the specialists to align.

basic.situation: A senior inspector asks you to draft a notice of violation for a factory that discharged oily water into a drain. You have the inspection notes.

options.text: Tell the factory manager there will be no notice if the drain is cleaned today.
Draft the notice with date, location, rule breached and required action for review.
Use an older notice for a similar factory and change the name and date.
Draft the notice from your inspection notes and describe the discharge in general terms.

advanced.situation: You lead an enforcement hearing for a company that failed to act on two notices about pesticide storage. Its lawyer claims the notices were not properly served.

options.text: Reissue the notices today with earlier dates so that the service claim has no effect.
Present the service records, inspection evidence and legal basis, and ask the chair to decide.
Offer to withdraw the case if the company agrees to fix the storage soon.
Present the inspection evidence and ask for a fine, noting that notices were sent.

basic.situation: At a river site, your supervisor asks you to record field conditions and take a flow meter reading near a factory outlet.

options.text: Record time, weather and location, take the reading three times, and note anything unusual.
Take the reading from the factory's own meter and record it as your measurement.
Take a reading and use the figure from the last inspection if it looks different.
Take one flow reading and write down the time and location on the sheet.

advanced.situation: You design an evidence plan for a suspected illegal dumping site. Witnesses are nervous about speaking, and the trucks come at night.

options.text: Give the witnesses' names to the site owner so he can confirm what they saw.
Ask the witnesses to film the trucks themselves at night and send you the videos.
Plan night observation with timestamped photos and ask witnesses to send written statements by post.
Plan night observation with timestamped photos, private witness interviews, and a chain of custody log.

basic.situation: You check one waste storage permit against a checklist. The permit expired last week, but the company says its renewal is in process.

options.text: Mark the permit expired and ask the company to stop storing waste until renewed.
Record the expiry date, check if renewal was filed, and tell your supervisor.
Extend the expiry date on your checklist by a month to match the company's timeline.
Note the permit as valid pending renewal, since the company says it has applied.

advanced.situation: You help develop a spill prevention programme for a chemical depot that has had repeated small leaks from old storage tanks.

options.text: Recommend cleaning each small leak quickly and recording each one in a daily logbook.
Review leak records, inspect the tanks, and recommend containment, replacement and regular checks.
Recommend containment trays under all the tanks and a monthly check by depot staff.
Recommend that the depot stop recording small leaks, since they are too minor to matter.

basic.situation: You collect a stream water sample for lab testing. The lab gave you a sterile bottle and said to keep samples cool.

options.text: Fill the bottle halfway at the stream and top it up with tap water later.
Fill the bottle below the surface, seal it, label it, and put it in a cooler.
Use a clean spare bottle you have, since the stream is clear and looks safe.
Fill the bottle, seal and label it, and keep it in the car until you finish.

advanced.situation: A large lake has several outflows near a mining area. You must pick sampling locations, and a recent rule change affects the permitted levels.

options.text: Check the updated limits, map the outflows, and choose upstream and downstream sites with reasons.
Sample at the point where the mine's own monitoring is done, and use the mine's methods.
Sample at the easiest-to-reach outflow, since the water should be much the same around the lake.
Sample at each outflow and compare the results with the limits you used last year.

basic.situation: You organise this week's inspection records into the case file. A photo log, three sample forms and a field notebook need filing.

options.text: File the records by date and tell your supervisor once you have finished the file.
Throw away the field notebook once you have typed the notes into the file.
File records by site and date, check sample forms are signed, and list missing items.
Put the records in one folder and rely on the notebook's dates to find them.

advanced.situation: You create a chain of custody template for samples and guide other inspectors. A court case last month questioned a gap in sample handling.

options.text: Ask inspectors to keep a personal diary of where each sample was at all times.
Design a form for each sample's collection and lab delivery times, and share it.
Fill in the missing handover details on past sample forms from the inspectors' memories.
Design a form recording each handover with names, times and seals, and train inspectors.

basic.situation: You explain a simple waste disposal rule to workshop owners using a prepared script. One owner asks a question the script does not cover.

options.text: Repeat the relevant part of the script and move on to the next question.
Tell the owner the rule does not apply to small workshops, from what you recall.
Answer from what you know of the rule and mention you may need to check.
Say you will check, note the question, and reply after confirming with a senior inspector.

advanced.situation: Two agencies plan separate enforcement visits to the same riverside plants in the same week. You coordinate multi-agency strategy and public education on the rules.

options.text: Share your visit dates with the other agency and ask it to avoid your sites.
Carry on with your visits as planned and compare findings with the other agency later.
Contact the other agency, agree a joint visit plan, and plan a briefing for plant owners.
Visit the plants a day before the other agency and take their documents first.

basic.situation: An employee files a complaint saying her manager gives all overtime to men. You are asked to read it and clarify the main issues.

options.text: Read the complaint and summarise it as an overtime issue for your supervisor to review.
Ask the manager for his side first and then decide what the complaint is about.
Tell the employee her complaint is too general and suggest she withdraw it for now.
Read the complaint, list the claims, dates and people named, and mark what is unclear.

advanced.situation: You lead an investigation into claims that a company's promotion tests disadvantage older applicants. Records show a pattern, but HR says it is coincidence.

options.text: Collect promotion data by age group, analyse the pattern, and document each factor found.
Remove the age column from the company records before they reach the investigation file.
Interview HR and several older applicants and write up the different explanations they give.
Accept HR's explanation and record the pattern as coincidence unless more complaints arrive later.

basic.situation: You are asked to interview a worker named in a complaint about unfair shift allocation, to verify the basic case details.

options.text: Ask the worker what happened and write down the main details he gives you.
Ask yes or no questions based on the complaint wording so the interview ends quickly.
Tell the worker what other staff have said about him before you ask any questions.
Confirm his name, role and shift, ask what happened and when, and read back the notes.

advanced.situation: You must settle a dispute between a pregnant employee and her supervisor over a transfer to a lower-paid role. Both are angry, and a meeting is tomorrow.

options.text: Suggest the employee accept the transfer for now, since the supervisor has the authority.
Hold the joint meeting and let both sides present their positions before you suggest terms.
Meet each side separately, review the policy and facts, then propose options at the joint meeting.
Tell the employee she will lose her job if she does not accept the transfer.

basic.situation: A manager asks you to help draft hiring guidelines so job adverts are fair. You have the company's hiring policy and a sample advert.

options.text: Copy the policy's hiring section into the guidelines and add the sample advert as an example.
Write short guidelines saying all job adverts should be fair, and leave the detail to managers.
Draft guidelines that allow managers to ask for a preferred age or gender in adverts.
List the policy points, then draft advert wording rules on skills, age and gender for review.

advanced.situation: You set the organisation-wide non-discrimination policy. Departments ask for exceptions, and the legal team wants one clear standard.

options.text: Approve every exception departments request so that none of them object to the policy.
Let each department write its own version, and collect them into one shared folder.
Draft one standard with no exceptions and ask departments to follow it from next quarter.
Draft one standard with a clear exception process, consult legal and departments, and plan rollout.

basic.situation: You assist with a report on an equal opportunity investigation. Your supervisor gives you the interview notes and complaint and asks you to prepare the facts section.

options.text: Summarise the complaint and the interviews in order, using the notes as they were written.
Summarise the complaint, list the interviews with dates, and mark where accounts agree or differ.
Write the facts as the complaint describes them, and add interview points that agree.
Rewrite unclear parts of the interview notes in clearer words that support the main point.

advanced.situation: You review compliance data on an anti-bias hiring guideline six months after rollout. Numbers look good, but departments use different data formats.

options.text: Estimate the missing figures from the good departments and report them as complete data.
Combine the data as submitted and report the overall improvement to leadership next week.
Standardise the formats, check figures against source records, and set reporting standards for departments.
Report on the departments with consistent formats and leave the others for the next review cycle.

basic.situation: An employee asks whether the company can refuse to hire him because of his religion. The senior officer is away, and you have the company policy.

options.text: Tell him it depends on the job and he should ask the hiring manager.
Read him the policy on religion and arrange a follow-up with the senior officer.
Tell him the company can refuse him if the role involves working with customers.
Tell him religious discrimination is against the policy and ask him to wait for the officer.

advanced.situation: A large employer asks whether its flexible-hours rule for parents could be unfair to staff without children. The regulations are ambiguous, and you advise leadership.

options.text: Advise that the rule is probably fine and recommend watching for complaints from staff.
Advise leadership to extend the flexible hours to everyone at once to avoid any risk.
Tell leadership the rule is lawful because many other employers use the same rule.
Review the rule against the wording and guidance, set out the risks, and suggest options.

basic.situation: You are asked to give new employees basic information on how to file a workplace grievance. You have the HR handout.

options.text: Walk through the handout steps, explain who to contact and time limits, and invite questions.
Tell employees to talk to their managers first about any grievance and see what happens.
Give each employee the handout and ask them to read it and call you.
Tell employees that filing a grievance can hurt their careers, so they should think carefully.

advanced.situation: You design a training programme for managers on handling discrimination complaints. Attendance is low, and past sessions were long lectures.

options.text: Record attendance for managers who did not attend, so the report shows full completion.
Send managers the slides by email and ask them to confirm they read them.
Build short scenario-based sessions, gather feedback from past attendees, and train other trainers to deliver them.
Shorten the lectures to one hour and make attendance a yearly requirement for all managers.

basic.situation: Government laptops were found in a contractor's storeroom. Your supervisor asks you to help collect and label the laptops as evidence.

options.text: Switch on each laptop to see what is stored on it, then label them afterwards.
Photograph each laptop in place, then bag and label it with date, place and initials.
Bag and label each laptop with the date and place, then hand them to your supervisor.
Pile all the laptops into one box and label the box with the date and place.

advanced.situation: You oversee evidence handling in a fraud case. A colleague searched a contractor's office without a warrant after a verbal tip and seized files.

options.text: Set the files aside, record how they were obtained, and ask legal counsel for advice.
Use the files and describe the search as a routine inspection in the report.
Keep the files in the case but mark them as obtained during the visit.
Return the files to the contractor quietly and start the evidence collection again from scratch.

basic.situation: You review a special permit application using a supervisor's checklist. The applicant's business address differs from the address on the attached lease.

options.text: Note the address difference, ask the applicant to explain in writing, and inform your supervisor.
Change the address on the application to match the lease and continue the review.
Use the lease address in the review, as leases are stronger evidence than forms.
Tick the address item as checked and note that two addresses appear in the file.

advanced.situation: You set standards for investigating complex licence violations. A construction firm holds several permits, and its subcontractors may have breached conditions without the firm knowing.

options.text: Investigate the subcontractors one by one and report each case to the firm separately.
Define steps to trace each breach to its responsible party and train junior staff on them.
Hold the firm responsible for every breach on its permits and train juniors to do likewise.
Close any case where the firm says it did not know about the breach.

basic.situation: You write a one-page summary of a property inspection using the template. You noted two broken fences, one missing sign, and a blocked drain.

options.text: List the four findings with locations in the template and send it to your supervisor.
Write that the site has minor maintenance problems, with details in the full notes.
List the four findings with locations and photo numbers in template order, for review.
Leave the drain out of the summary, since it can be cleaned before anyone reads it.

advanced.situation: You prepare to testify at an administrative hearing about an inspection finding. The contractor's lawyer says your report is inconsistent with your photos.

options.text: Update the report to match the photos now and bring the new version to the hearing.
Re-read your report several times and rehearse the answers it gives before the hearing day.
Ask the contractor's lawyer which photos he means and prepare your answers in advance.
Compare the report and photos, note any differences, and prepare a clear account of your observations.

basic.situation: You join a mentor to inspect a public housing site and note compliance issues. In a stairwell, you see a cracked wall.

options.text: Photograph the crack with a tape beside it, note its location, and tell your mentor.
Wait to see whether the mentor notices the crack before saying anything about it yourself.
Fill the crack with filler from the site's storeroom so it does not worsen.
Note the crack in your inspection notes and mention it to your mentor at the end.

advanced.situation: You develop inspection standards for contractors holding government equipment on high-risk sites. Some equipment has gone missing, and contractors keep records differently.

options.text: Require every contractor to send a monthly equipment list and check the lists yearly.
Visit each high-risk site once and count the equipment against the contract list.
Accept the contractors' own statements about missing items and write them off as lost.
Set standards for equipment registers, spot checks and reporting, and train new inspectors to follow them.

basic.situation: You check a delivery record for government supplies against the invoice. The quantities match, but the date on the record is a Sunday.

options.text: Change the date on the record to the Saturday before so it looks normal.
Note the unusual date, check the site log for that day, and tell your guide.
Accept the record because the quantities match the invoice and the date is minor.
Note the unusual date on the record and continue checking the next document in the pile.

advanced.situation: You design audit procedures to detect subtle discrepancies in large supply datasets. Past audits checked totals alone, and a contractor repeatedly inflated small items.

options.text: Ask contractors to sign a statement that their invoices contain no inflated items, then pay.
Add random item sampling to each audit and compare unit prices to market rates.
Design item-level checks for repeated small amounts, test them on past data, and document them.
Lower the total-value limit that triggers a detailed review of invoices each quarter.

basic.situation: A police officer calls asking for a contractor's inspection file, saying it relates to a theft. You are asked to help coordinate.

options.text: Say you will pass the request to your supervisor, and note the officer's name and case.
Ask the officer to put the request in writing and send it to the office email.
Read parts of the file to the officer by phone while you look for your supervisor.
Send the file now by email since police matters are urgent and the officer sounds genuine.

advanced.situation: You advise senior management after an inspection found a contractor selling spare parts from government vehicles. Management wants quick action.

options.text: Recommend a formal warning letter to the contractor and a follow-up inspection next quarter.
Preserve the evidence, recommend suspending the contract, and advise referring the case to enforcement.
Recommend that management seize the contractor's bank account to recover the value of the parts.
Recommend suspending the contract and demanding that the contractor return all parts it has sold.

basic.situation: You assist at a death scene in a flat. A senior officer asks you to record the position of the body and nearby items before anything is moved.

options.text: Photograph the body and items from several angles, sketch their positions, and note the time.
Ask the family to describe where things were and use that instead of recording.
Take a few photos of the body and write down where the main items are.
Move nearby items aside to see the body better, then photograph everything in the room.

advanced.situation: You set evidence handling standards for death scenes. Recently, medication containers and a note were collected by different staff, and the note's location was not recorded.

options.text: Add the note's location to the record from the officer's memory and move on.
Remind all staff by email to record the locations before collecting items at death scenes.
Require staff to log each item when collected and sign the log at the scene.
Set a sequence to photograph, tag and log each item in place, and train junior staff.

basic.situation: You assist a pathologist with a preliminary examination of an unidentified body. Your task is to help identify the person and note signs of trauma.

options.text: Photograph and measure visible marks, tattoos and scars, then give the notes to the pathologist.
Clean the body surface first so the marks are easier to see and describe.
Tell the pathologist who you think the victim is based on a missing person report.
Note the visible marks, tattoos and scars in writing and give the notes to the pathologist.

advanced.situation: You direct a team conducting autopsies. Toxicology results conflict with the pathologist's first impression of the cause of death.

options.text: Ask the pathologist to update the cause of death to match the toxicology results.
Finalise the cause of death from the first impression, because it was written down first.
Record both findings in the file and ask the pathologist to explain the difference.
Review both findings with the pathologist, ask for repeat tests on retained samples, and document it.

basic.situation: You interview a neighbour who found a man unresponsive at home. A senior coroner asks you to get basic information on the circumstances.

options.text: Tell the neighbour the man likely died of a heart attack to calm them before asking.
Ask the neighbour to tell the story in their own words and note the main points.
Ask when and how they found him, who else was present, and note what they touched.
Ask the neighbour whether they think it was natural, and record their opinion in the file.
