advanced.situation: You write the test schedule for a new online store. The team wants to test on the three browsers the developers use. Analytics show 30 percent of visitors use others, mostly phones.

options.text: Add the most common phone browser to the plan and test it once before launch.
Build the test plan from analytics, covering main browsers and phones, and retest after changes.
Test on the three developer browsers and ask users to report problems on other devices.
Mark the store as tested on all devices because the three browsers share the same engine.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to build a simple event page using the team's page builder tool. It needs a title, date, map and sign-up link for this month's event.

options.text: Build the page from the template and check that the title, date and map show up.
Copy an old event page with its sign-up link and change the title and date.
Build the page from the template, check the sign-up link works, and preview it on a phone.
Build the page from scratch with your own code, since it gives you more control.

advanced.situation: You are choosing a programming language for a large web application. The team knows one language well, but another has better libraries for the payment features.

options.text: Choose the newest language that people are talking about online and learn it while building.
Choose the language with the better payment libraries and plan training for the team.
Choose the language the team knows well, since it keeps the schedule safe for now.
Compare both languages on libraries, team skill and upkeep, then test a small prototype.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to document basic style guidelines for the website's blog posts. Writers currently use different heading sizes and tones.

options.text: Write rules from the three most recent posts and share them with the writers.
Edit all published posts yourself to match your own style and update their dates.
Check recent posts, list heading sizes, tone and image rules, and ask your supervisor to review.
Write rules from your own preference and share them with the writers for feedback.

advanced.situation: You set accessibility and privacy standards for a new public site. Marketing wants a visitor tracking tool and a video background with no captions.

options.text: Require captions and keyboard access, and ask marketing to check privacy with legal later.
Approve both features for launch, since competitors use them, and write the standards afterwards.
Require captions and keyboard access, add a tracking consent notice, and explain the reasons.
Approve the tracking tool with a privacy notice in the footer and add captions later.

basic.situation: You are asked to create a simple page template for a news blog with a headline, image and body text. A lead will review it.

options.text: Build the template with clear spacing, test long headlines, and show it to the lead.
Build the template with clear spacing and show it to the lead with a sample headline.
Use the template from another company's site, change the colours, and publish it live today.
Build the template to look good for one sample article and send it for review.

advanced.situation: You direct pre-production for a campaign site. The client has not agreed on a visual direction, but the developers want to start in two weeks.

options.text: Pick the direction yourself, tell the client it is final, and ask developers to begin.
Create moodboards with two directions, get the client's choice, and set the timeline.
Create a moodboard from your own taste and start the storyboards while waiting for feedback.
Tell the developers to start building the pages and update the design as it evolves.

basic.situation: You must tell the back-end developer which form fields the new sign-up page will send. Your lead asked you to share the details with the team.

options.text: Send the developer the field names and types, and confirm they received them.
Rename the fields yourself in the back-end code to match the design and tell them later.
Post the field list in the team chat and wait for questions from the developer.
Tell the developer the fields are the usual ones and they can check the design.

advanced.situation: Marketing wants a pop-up discount offer on the shop homepage. The developers say it will slow the page. You must resolve this and tie the offer to the site.

options.text: Measure the pop-up's effect on speed, share the numbers, and agree a lighter design.
Side with marketing and add the pop-up, since sales matter more than a slight delay.
Add the pop-up to the live site tonight and tell the developers in the morning.
Ask the developers to make the pop-up load faster and add it once they confirm.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to check all links on the company's services page before Monday. Several links lead to partner sites.

options.text: Remove every link that opens slowly from the page so visitors do not see problems.
Run a link-checking tool, send the lead the list of broken links, and wait for guidance.
Check the first few links on the page and assume the others still work.
Click every link, list any that fail, fix those you can, and report the rest.

advanced.situation: You direct a big update to the site's navigation, which will change many page addresses. The business relies on search traffic, and launch is next week.

options.text: Launch the update and rely on search engines to find the new addresses over time.
Map old addresses to new ones, set redirects, test them, and submit a sitemap.
Delete the old pages the day of launch to avoid duplicate content in search results.
Set redirects for the main pages and watch search traffic for a week after launch.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to write short dialogue for a shopkeeper character in a village level of a family-friendly adventure game.

options.text: Write short lines in the shopkeeper's voice that suit the level's tone.
Write friendly generic lines for the shopkeeper and send them to your lead.
Reuse lines from your previous game's shopkeeper and change a few names.
Use memorable dialogue lines from a popular film that suit the scene.

advanced.situation: You are asked to create core features for a new game franchise: storyline, role-play mechanics and character biographies. The publisher expects a pitch in two weeks.

options.text: Define the central idea, build a mechanics prototype, and write one strong character biography.
Take the storyline and characters from a small unknown game and rename them.
Combine popular features from successful games into one pitch for the publisher.
Write the full storyline first and develop the mechanics after the pitch is approved.

basic.situation: You add a new jump mechanic to a prototype. Your senior asks you to update the design document.

options.text: Tell the team about the jump in the daily meeting and update later.
Describe the planned jump instead of the one you built, since it is neater.
Add a short paragraph and a screenshot of the new jump to the document.
Describe the mechanic, its values, and how it interacts with other mechanics.

advanced.situation: You coordinate documentation and schedules with the production team for a game due in six months. Design changes keep arriving without notice.

options.text: Ask designers to inform you of changes by email and note them in the document.
Keep the original schedule and tell the team to absorb all the changes.
Update the schedule every Friday based on the changes you have heard about.
Set a change request process and update the schedule when changes are agreed.

basic.situation: Your art lead asks you to sketch an initial layout for a new level's village in 2D software.

options.text: Sketch one detailed layout over two days and send it for approval.
Paste artwork from an online asset site into the layout and send it.
Sketch a few rough layouts and revise them from your lead's feedback.
Trace over a screenshot from a similar game and change some buildings.

advanced.situation: Management and engineers want to see a playable prototype of a new combat idea in two weeks. The art assets are not ready.

options.text: Present slides explaining the combat idea with sketches and written descriptions of each move.
Show a prototype using combat footage recorded from a competitor's game and call it ours.
Create a video mock-up of the combat using final-quality art from the art team.
Build a placeholder-art prototype focused on how the combat feels and demonstrate it.

basic.situation: A colleague shows you a new menu layout for the game. You think the buttons are too small for mobile screens.

options.text: Keep quiet in the meeting and wait to see what players say.
Resize the buttons in the colleague's shared file yourself and tell nobody about it.
Tell the colleague politely that the menu needs larger buttons for mobile players.
Explain which buttons are small and why, and suggest a larger size.

advanced.situation: Two development teams disagree about whether the crafting system should be handled by the economy team or the inventory team, delaying a milestone.

options.text: Bring both teams together, clarify needs and dependencies, and record who owns what.
Suggest that each team builds its own version of the system for now.
Assign the crafting system to the team that shouted louder in the meeting.
Ask the producer to decide who owns the crafting system and tell both teams.

basic.situation: QA staff ask you what to check in a new level. You have a design document describing the level's intended behaviour.

options.text: Tell them to play the level and report anything that feels strange.
Tell them the level is finished and ask them to approve it quickly.
Send them the design document and ask them to work out the tests.
Send them test specifications listing expected behaviour, key paths and known limits.

advanced.situation: External playtesters finish the tutorial in half the expected time and say it feels dull. Your original vision is a slow, careful pace.

options.text: Add extra tutorial steps to slow players down and run another test.
Remove the playtesters' recordings and re-run the test with friends of the team.
Accept the faster pace as players' preference and rewrite the vision document.
Review recordings and feedback, find where pace diverges, and adjust to fit the vision.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to play a competitor's puzzle game and note ideas that could improve your own game.

options.text: Read the competitor's reviews and plan to copy their most praised features.
Play the first two levels and list all the features you liked.
Play several levels, note what works and what frustrates, and list original ideas.
Extract the competitor's art files from the game and use them as references.

advanced.situation: Playtest data shows new players quit after level three because it is too hard, while hardcore fans like the challenge. Revenue depends on both groups.

options.text: Keep the difficulty and add a paid hint item for struggling new players.
Hide the quit data from the team and keep the difficulty unchanged for launch.
Make level three easier for all players and release the update soon.
Analyse quit points, adjust the difficulty with options, and retest with both groups.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to install web server software on a new test machine and set up the site folders.

options.text: Install the software and give every user full access to the site folders.
Create public and private folders, then set permissions after the site is live.
Use the default folder layout from the installer and tidy it up later.
Set up separate public and private folders and apply the permissions list.

advanced.situation: The company site will move to a larger server before a major sale. You must evaluate server options and recommend one with secure, scalable features.

options.text: Estimate peak traffic, compare options on scale and security, and recommend one.
Recommend the server your friend's company sells, since you can get it quickly.
Recommend the most powerful server that the budget allows for this sale.
Recommend the cheapest cloud plan with automatic scaling and review security later.

basic.situation: You are asked to back up the website files and database before a plugin update, following the usual steps.

options.text: Back up the website files, then start the plugin update on the live site.
Update the plugin first to see if it works, then back up if needed.
Back up files and database, check the backups open, then update.
Copy the old plugin folder to your desktop and then update the plugin.

advanced.situation: Your company has backup and recovery plans but has not tested a full restore. The e-commerce site makes money every hour.

options.text: Restore a single file from the backup and report that the plan works.
Schedule a restore test on a copy, time it, fix gaps, and repeat regularly.
Restore the full backup over the live site this weekend to prove the plan.
Check the backup logs weekly and confirm they show successful completion each time.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to check the web server's log files each morning for errors.

options.text: Check the end of the log file for errors and report any you find.
Delete the previous day's log files after glancing at them to save disk space.
Run a script that counts errors and report the total to your senior.
Scan for errors and unusual requests, and report anything unclear to your senior.

advanced.situation: A colleague's test routine for the payment pages passes every time, but a customer reports a failed payment that the routine did not catch.

options.text: Review the routine's coverage, add the missed case, and test realistic payments.
Add a test for the reported payment problem and rerun the whole routine again.
Tell the customer to retry the payment and wait for more reports.
Mark the customer's report as a one-off error and close it today.

basic.situation: You just finished configuring a web server with your senior's guidance. The team wants the setup documented so it can be repeated.

options.text: Save the configuration file in the team folder and tell the team.
Write the main steps from memory and save them in the team folder.
Write each step with settings and commands, and have a colleague repeat it.
Copy the setup notes from an online tutorial and say they describe your server.

advanced.situation: The website is updated by different people every week, and mistakes reach the live site. You are asked to develop a procedure for ongoing revisions.

options.text: Define a draft, review and approval path with rollback steps, and train editors.
Ask editors to check each other's changes before they publish to the live site.
Limit publishing rights to one person who handles all weekly changes alone.
Let editors edit the live site directly and fix mistakes when users report them.

basic.situation: A form on the website will be down for maintenance tonight from 11 pm to 1 am. Your senior asks you to inform users.

options.text: Put up a notice saying the whole site is down until tomorrow morning.
Email the users on the mailing list the night of the maintenance work.
Update the support team's calendar and wait for users to ask about it.
Post a notice on the site with the times and tell support.

advanced.situation: The marketing team asks for a site redesign, but servers need upgrading. You must recommend improvements and build a budget.

options.text: Budget for both using the highest vendor quotes to avoid being short later.
Budget for the redesign first since marketing has asked for it urgently.
Split the budget evenly between the redesign and the server upgrade this year.
Cost both items, rank them by benefit, and present a phased budget.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to compile last week's page visit numbers from the analytics tool into a table.

options.text: Copy the numbers from the dashboard summary into a table and send it.
Export visits for the set dates, check the totals, and make the table.
Adjust a few figures upward so that the week looks stronger in the table.
Use the monthly total divided by four as an estimate for last week.

advanced.situation: Management asks for performance metrics for the company site. The team currently checks whether the site is up.

options.text: Define metrics the site already meets so management sees good results each quarter.
Track every metric the analytics tool can produce and share the full list.
Add page load time and error rate to the weekly report for management.
Choose measures tied to goals, such as speed and sign-ups, and set targets.

basic.situation: Your senior gives you a spreadsheet of 200 street light locations to add to the council's GIS database.

options.text: Check coordinates on a map, import a small batch, then load the rest.
Delete the old street light layer, then import the spreadsheet into the live database.
Import the full spreadsheet and check that the point count is 200 after loading.
Type the coordinates in by hand to keep control over each single point.

advanced.situation: A department needs 50,000 old land records converted and loaded into the GIS database. The records have mixed formats and some errors.

options.text: Remove the records with errors from the source files before converting the rest.
Design a staged conversion with automated checks and a sample review by users.
Convert the cleanest records first and leave the difficult ones to be done later.
Convert everything with one script and fix any errors that are reported afterwards.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to produce a map layer showing schools in a district using the standard GIS software.

options.text: Use last year's map layer of schools and change its title to this year.
Load the school data, add labels, and export the default map layout.
Draw school points by eye on a base map and save it as official.
Load the school data, check the projection, and save the styled layer.

advanced.situation: A client asks for a 3D visualisation of flood risk for a neighbourhood to present to council members. The elevation data has gaps.

options.text: Use a smooth surface across the gaps so the model looks complete to the council.
Raise the elevation values near the gaps so the risk areas look worse.
Produce the 3D view from the existing data and note that gaps exist.
Fill the elevation gaps with documented methods and state assumptions on the model.

basic.situation: You are asked to find buildings in an aerial photograph that are not on the current map layer.

options.text: Mark the obvious large buildings that you can see in the photograph.
Add every building seen in the photograph straight to the official property layer.
Compare the photo with the layer, mark each missing building, and note dates.
Count the buildings in the photograph and report the difference in total numbers.

advanced.situation: A health agency wants a model showing where to place new clinics, using population, roads and travel times. Data sources use different coordinate systems.

options.text: Overlay the layers as they are and report the result as final to the agency.
Build the model with the largest dataset and match the others to it later.
Use straight-line distances instead of travel times to simplify the whole model.
Align coordinate systems, build the model, and test it against known catchments.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to test an existing GIS web map app after a software update and note any problems.

options.text: Follow the test list, record each result, and log any problems found.
Open the map, pan, zoom, and tell your supervisor whether it loads properly.
Test the features you use most often and assume the rest still work.
Tell your supervisor it works because the update notes say nothing was changed there.

advanced.situation: The council wants a public web map showing planning applications. Some data is internal and must not be shown. The deadline is tight.

options.text: Publish a version containing the public fields and review the rest next month.
Hide the internal fields in the map's display settings and publish the full dataset.
Delay publishing until the council agrees on a data policy for all fields.
Design separate public and internal data layers, test access rules, then publish.

basic.situation: A planner calls to say a map layer will not display in her GIS software. She is in a hurry.

options.text: Ask what she sees, check the layer path, and walk her through the fix.
Restart her computer remotely and ask her to open the software again.
Replace her saved project file with a colleague's file that shows the layer.
Send her the steps for adding a layer and ask her to try again.

advanced.situation: You must prepare training for 30 council staff with different GIS skill levels, from beginners to analysts.

options.text: Run one session at intermediate level and share all the slides afterwards.
Assess skill levels, build tiered materials with exercises, and collect feedback after.
Hand out the software vendor's technical manual and cancel the live sessions altogether.
Prepare detailed materials for beginners and tell the analysts to study alone.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to document the tables and fields of the current planning database and any data quality issues you notice.

options.text: List each table and field, and record issues such as blanks and duplicates.
List each table and its purpose in a short summary document for your senior.
Copy the vendor's generic schema document and add your own notes at the end.
Fix the data quality issues in the live tables as you find them.

advanced.situation: The council's GIS software will lose vendor support next year. A newer version changes file formats, and several departments have custom tools.

options.text: Recommend switching to a free GIS package this year to avoid upgrade fees.
Recommend staying on the current version since the custom tools work well.
Recommend upgrading all departments at once to keep the systems consistent for support.
Assess impacts on formats and custom tools, and recommend a phased tested upgrade.

basic.situation: You are asked to scan a box of signed contracts and import them into the document system following the team's steps.

options.text: Scan the whole box into one large file so the import is faster.
Throw out the paper contracts after scanning to free up the shelf space.
Scan at the set quality, name files by the rule, and check imports.
Scan the contracts, import them in one batch, and check a few files open.

advanced.situation: You must configure a new document system for legal, finance and HR, each needing different access profiles and approval workflows.

options.text: Give all users the same broad access so approvals are not held up.
Use the vendor's default profiles and workflows and give users access next week.
Configure one standard workflow for all three teams and adjust the access later.
Gather each team's needs, configure profiles and workflows, and test with pilot users.

basic.situation: Your manager asks you to help list who may open the HR files folder in the document system.

options.text: List all HR staff as users and send the list to your manager.
Copy the access list from the finance folder and send it for approval.
Ask HR who needs each folder, and draft an access list for approval.
Let every department head open the folder in case they need something later.

advanced.situation: The company has five different ways of naming and filing documents. You are asked to develop system usage standards.

options.text: Review current practices, agree one naming and filing standard, and publish usage procedures.
Adopt the naming method of the largest department and ask others to follow it.
Rename all existing documents to the new standard in the live system overnight.
Write a long rulebook covering every case anyone in the company can imagine.

basic.situation: Your senior gives you a batch of new documents to label by confidentiality level using the company's guide.

options.text: Check each document against the guide and add its label and metadata.
Label them by the folder they came from and tell your senior.
Label every document as internal because that is the usual middle level.
Label the documents by their file names, assuming confidential files have obvious names.

advanced.situation: Audit logs show unusual numbers of document copies being printed in the archive room after hours. Staff are anxious about being watched.

options.text: Install a camera in the archive room and review the footage each week.
Review the logs, consult the archive manager, and report findings with controls.
Send staff a reminder about printing rules and review again next quarter.
Accuse the night staff in a team message and ask them to explain.

basic.situation: A manager asks you to find the retention period for supplier invoices. You have a records policy and a folder of legal guidance.

options.text: Search the policy and guidance, note the period and source, and tell her.
Search online and give the manager the first period you find on any website.
Tell the manager the usual retention period for invoices from your memory.
Check the records policy and tell the manager the retention period it states.

advanced.situation: New privacy rules are announced that may change how long personal records can be kept. Your company stores records in several systems.

options.text: Read the rules, map affected records and systems, and propose policy updates.
Delete all personal records older than one year in every system to be safe.
Wait for the system vendor to announce changes for the new rules.
Ask the legal team to summarise the rules and update the policy later.

basic.situation: Staff keep asking how to check a document in and out. You are asked to prepare a short support guide.

options.text: Write the steps from memory and share the guide in the team folder.
Share a tutorial video from another company's system and say it applies here.
Write simple steps with screenshots and test them with a new staff member.
Copy the relevant chapters of the vendor's long manual into the guide.

advanced.situation: Staff complain that searching in the content system is slow and results are poor. You are asked to propose improvements to stakeholders.

options.text: Collect examples of poor searches, identify causes, and propose ranked fixes with costs.
Propose training staff to use search better and leave the system unchanged.
Propose hiding the search function and giving staff direct folder links instead.
Propose replacing the whole content system with a newer product from the vendor.

basic.situation: A colleague asks for a copy of last year's board paper from the document repository.

options.text: Retrieve the paper and email it to the colleague with a short note.
Tell the colleague where the repository is and let them search on their own.
Check their access rights, retrieve the paper, and log the request.
Download the board paper to a shared USB drive and hand it over now.

advanced.situation: Legal asks you to update an official policy document with new clauses and record the change. Compliance must confirm before it is published.

options.text: Make the changes and send them to compliance, assuming legal has already agreed.
Draft the new clauses and wait for legal to send the final wording back.
Make tracked changes, send them to both teams, and publish after they confirm.
Publish the update now to save time and record compliance's confirmation later.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to set up a new test server for a client so it has only the services the project needs.

options.text: Leave the default services running in case the project needs them later.
Give the project team administrator accounts so they do not need to ask.
List the needed services, switch off the rest, and limit account access.
Install the standard build and switch off services you know are risky.

advanced.situation: You must design a wireless security test for a client's offices. The client's written scope covers the staff network but not the neighbouring tenant's network.

options.text: Limit the plan to the staff network, record the boundary, and brief the team.
Include the neighbour's network in the plan since signals overlap and it saves time.
Delay the plan until the client confirms who else is affected by the test.
Plan tests on the staff network and ask the team to avoid the neighbour's signals.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to gather public information about a client's exposed systems before a scheduled test.

options.text: Ask a client employee for passwords so you can check what is exposed.
Search public sources on the client's main domain and send notes to your senior.
Use public sources within the agreed scope and record what you find.
Collect what you can on the client's staff from social media profiles.

advanced.situation: A security bulletin describes a new technique used against companies like your client. Your team lead asks if it affects your testing plans.

options.text: Share the bulletin with the team and suggest adding the technique to plans.
Add the technique to the plan since new techniques are usually effective.
Verify the bulletin, assess its relevance to the client, and brief the team.
Tell the client the bulletin proves they are at risk, and offer more tests.

basic.situation: A staff member reports a strange email. Your senior asks you to help collect basic information for the incident record.

options.text: Take a screenshot of the email and note who else received it.
Record times and details and keep the original email unchanged for analysis.
Ask the staff member what the email said and write that in the record.
Delete the email from the inbox and describe it from memory for the record.

advanced.situation: Servers show signs of compromise on a Friday evening. Management wants them restored to reopen on Monday. Logs have not been copied.

options.text: Restore on new servers and keep the old ones for later review.
Wipe and restore the servers as management asked and delete the old logs.
Copy the logs, wipe the servers, and restore them from last week's backup.
Preserve images and logs first, then investigate the root cause before restoring.

basic.situation: You are testing a client's web application under a signed agreement listing three web addresses. You find a fourth address that looks linked.

options.text: Ask the client's developer informally whether you may test the fourth address.
Test the fourth address too since it appears linked to the same system.
Stay within the three addresses and ask your lead about the fourth.
Note the fourth address in your log and finish the three first.

advanced.situation: During an approved test, you reach a database holding real customer records. The test goal was to show that access was possible.

options.text: Download a sample of records to show the client how serious the finding is.
Stop at proof of access, capture minimal evidence, and alert your lead.
Copy the full database to your laptop to analyse the risk later.
Stop and tell your lead, keeping screenshots that show some customer records.

basic.situation: You completed a simple scan on a client's test server. Your senior asks you to document the findings.

options.text: Rate all findings as low severity so the client is not alarmed.
Paste the scan tool's report into a document and add your name.
List each finding with evidence, system, date and severity, then send for review.
Write a short summary of the main findings and attach the scan output.

advanced.situation: You must write an audit report for a client's board. Technical staff want every detail, while the board wants a short summary with clear actions.

options.text: Write an executive summary with prioritised actions and an appendix with technical detail.
Remove the findings that embarrass the client's managers from the board version.
Write a technical report and add a short covering note for the board.
Write a one-page summary for the board and share details on request.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to check the server room at a client site for obvious physical risks such as heat or unlocked doors.

options.text: Walk the room with a checklist, note each risk, and photograph issues.
Ask the client's staff whether they know of any physical risks in the room.
Check that the door is locked and the temperature looks normal today.
Try to enter the server room after hours to see whether anyone notices.

advanced.situation: A client asks for a mitigation strategy after tests found weak points in several systems. Stakeholders list different business priorities and limited budgets.

options.text: Propose fixing all high-severity findings first, whatever the business impact is.
Collect stakeholder priorities, rank risks by impact, and propose mitigations that fit budgets.
Propose the cheapest fixes first so that most findings are closed quickly.
Propose accepting all the risks and tell stakeholders that testing was enough.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to draft a one-page policy on screen locking for office laptops.

options.text: Write that screen locks are optional for senior managers to avoid complaints today.
Write that staff should lock screens when away, with no time limit.
Copy the screen lock rule from a template and send it to your senior.
Check the company standard, draft clear rules, and send them for review.

advanced.situation: A company has no plan for a data breach. Management asks you to develop response and recovery strategies, and the legal team must approve all notifications.

options.text: Define roles, containment, legal notification paths and recovery steps, then run a drill.
Plan to inform customers directly from IT in a breach before legal reviews it.
Adopt a generic response plan from the internet and rename the company.
Write a response checklist for IT staff and add recovery steps later.

basic.situation: Your senior gives you step-by-step instructions to install and enable a host firewall on ten staff laptops.

options.text: Follow the steps on one laptop, test it, then repeat on the rest.
Enable the firewall with every rule set to allow so that nothing breaks.
Follow the steps on all ten laptops and confirm each shows as enabled.
Switch the firewall on and turn off the antivirus to prevent conflicts.

advanced.situation: You are asked to develop a tool that flags unusual login patterns across several systems. Too many false alarms will make analysts ignore it.

options.text: Define what unusual means with analysts, test on past logs, and tune alert thresholds.
Alert on logins from new countries and treat everything else as normal.
Alert on every failed login and let analysts filter the alerts themselves.
Auto-lock any account that triggers an alert and notify the user afterwards.

basic.situation: You are asked to help run a 20-minute awareness session on password habits for a small group of staff.

options.text: Ask each staff member to say aloud the password they use at work.
Present the policy slides and read the password rules aloud to the group.
Send the group a poster about passwords instead of holding the session.
Show real examples, explain a simple passphrase method, and let staff try it.

advanced.situation: Audits find staff often break security rules. You oversee the training program, and managers say staff have no time for long sessions.

options.text: Mark staff as trained after they click through the slides in a minute.
Send monthly emails with rules and require staff to reply to confirm reading.
Offer short role-based modules, track completion and behaviour, and report results to managers.
Hold one annual long session for everyone and record attendance for audits.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to set up a basic alert for repeated failed logins on the file server.

options.text: Set the alert at a high number so it rarely fires and bothers nobody.
Set the threshold as advised, trigger a test, and confirm the team gets it.
Switch off the lockout rule so failed logins can be counted freely.
Set an alert for any failed login and send it to your senior.

advanced.situation: You oversee vulnerability assessments for a payment system. The test team proposes testing the live system during peak hours to save time.

options.text: Schedule tests in a low-traffic window with rollback plans and monitoring agreed with operations.
Test a copy of the system and apply the results to the live one.
Approve the full test at peak hours and inform operations after it starts.
Run the lightest checks on the live system during peak hours for speed.

basic.situation: You helped gather initial evidence on a small incident. Your senior asks you to write up what you found.

options.text: Write the facts in time order, mark confirmed items, and cite sources.
List the evidence files and leave the explanation for your senior to write.
Write a brief summary of what happened and the likely cause, then send it.
Write what you think the cause was and present it as established.

advanced.situation: A breach exposed customer data. The investigation shows two possible entry routes, and the business wants a final answer in 24 hours.

options.text: Evaluate both routes with evidence, state confidence levels, and report damage and next steps.
Report the route that fits the damage most closely and note the other one.
Ask the business for another week and hold all findings until then.
Choose the route that blames the vendor and present it as final.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to check whether the weekly patch report shows all laptops meeting the company's patch target of 95 percent.

options.text: Rerun the report after excluding laptops that failed so the target is met.
Check the overall patch percentage and tell your senior if it is below 95.
Compare the report with the target, then list the laptops below it.
Check last week's report and assume this week is about the same.

advanced.situation: Performance data shows security controls cost more each year while incidents are flat. Management asks you to recommend enhancements.

options.text: Analyse control cost and effectiveness, then recommend changes that fit the data.
Recommend adding new tools since incident numbers are not falling this year.
Recommend cutting the security budget since incidents have stayed flat so far.
Recommend switching off monitoring tools that generate the most alerts to cut costs.

basic.situation: Your supervisor gives you a seized laptop and asks you to make a copy of its drive for analysis.

options.text: Start the laptop and copy its files over the network to your computer.
Copy the folders you need to a USB drive and return the laptop sealed.
Use a write blocker, image the drive, verify the hash, and reseal it.
Run a cleanup tool on the laptop first so the copy is smaller and faster.

advanced.situation: Evidence for a fraud case spans a phone, two laptops and cloud accounts held by different custodians. You must set how it is preserved and tracked.

options.text: Set imaging, labelling and storage rules with a custody log for each item.
Image the laptops and phone first and deal with the cloud accounts later.
Collect everything into one shared folder so that all analysts can reach it.
Let each custodian preserve their own devices and send you the results.

basic.situation: You are asked to check whether a folder of files labelled as photos has hidden documents inside.

options.text: Sort the files by size and look closely at the largest ones.
Open each file on the working copy and note any that fail.
Rename the extensions on the original files so that they all open.
Compare each file's signature with its extension on a copy, and list mismatches.

advanced.situation: A server's file system was damaged during an incident, and parts of the logs are missing. The investigator wants to know what happened.

options.text: Run recovery tools on the original server and report what comes back.
Rebuild the missing log lines from the pattern of the nearby entries.
Work on an image, recover what you can, and document gaps clearly.
Report the available logs and say the missing parts show nothing happened.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to look through a firewall log for connections from one suspicious address to the company's web server.

options.text: Search for the address and count how many times it appears in the log.
Filter the log for the address, list times and ports, and report.
Block the address on the live firewall and clear its log entries.
Search for the address and tell your senior it is the attacker.

advanced.situation: Traffic analysis shows a small, regular outbound data flow from one workstation at night. It might be a backup tool, or something harmful.

options.text: Compare with known backup schedules, inspect flow details, and report both possibilities.
Wipe the workstation to remove it, and report that the issue is resolved.
Ask the workstation owner whether they run any backup tool at night.
Treat it as a backup tool since the timing is so regular.

basic.situation: Your supervisor gives you a script that parses a log file into columns. You need to run it on a new log file.

options.text: Edit the original log file so it fits the script's expected format.
Run it on a copy, compare output with a few lines, and save results.
Edit the script to match the new file and run it right away.
Run it on the new log file and check that the output looks tidy.

advanced.situation: Analysts spend days parsing large evidence files by hand. You are asked to build automation, and the output may be used in court.

options.text: Build a repeatable script, validate it on known data, and keep raw files untouched.
Use a popular open script from the internet that does very similar parsing.
Write a script that produces the summary tables quickly and share it with analysts.
Have the script drop records it cannot parse so the output looks clean.

basic.situation: You have finished analysing a laptop and must write a technical summary of your findings for your supervisor.

options.text: Remove findings that do not support the case theory from the summary.
Describe what you did, what you found, and the limits of the analysis.
Write the conclusion you expect the investigator wants to read and add some detail.
List the files you found that relate to the case, with their dates.

advanced.situation: You are asked to sign an affidavit about your findings for a court case. The lawyer wants stronger wording than your analysis supports.

options.text: Keep to what the analysis supports and explain its limits to the lawyer.
Offer the lawyer a neutral wording of the findings and ask for time to review.
Sign the affidavit as drafted since the lawyer knows what the court needs.
Add details from your memory of similar cases to support the lawyer's wording.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to help list the steps for investigating a report that an employee copied customer files to a personal drive.

options.text: List steps that begin with confronting the employee and checking their drive.
List the questions to ask the employee at the first meeting with them.
List scope, authority, evidence sources, preservation steps, and who must be informed.
List the devices to examine and the order of examination for the team.

advanced.situation: The company wants policies for how digital evidence is collected, processed and reported across all branches. Branches now follow their own habits.

options.text: Write a short policy listing principles and let branches decide the details.
Draft common requirements with branch input, cover custody and reporting, and pilot them.
Write the policy from a template and tell branches it is already approved.
Adopt the procedure of the biggest branch for every branch in the company.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to draft a design pattern for recording certificate issue events on a shared ledger so entries cannot be changed.

options.text: Add a timestamp to every entry and have staff check the list monthly.
Hash-link the entries and keep the whole ledger on one office server.
Allow the issuing office to edit old entries later and keep a private edit log.
Define the fields, hash-link each entry to the last, and ask for review.

advanced.situation: A bank consortium wants a blockchain for trade finance records. Members disagree about who may read which records and who may validate transactions.

options.text: Run workshops to agree roles, design permissions and validation rules, and prototype them.
Choose a permissioned design where all members validate and read everything equally.
Let the largest bank run all validation and set read rights for the others.
Build a public network so that no member controls who reads the records.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to set up a simple data store that copies transaction hashes from a test blockchain for reporting.

options.text: Create the table and load the test data from an exported file.
Store the data in a spreadsheet and update it by hand each day.
Create a table for hash, time and block, load test data, and check counts.
Connect the reporting tool directly to the live node's internal database files.

advanced.situation: Executives want a dashboard of cross-border payments from several blockchain and non-blockchain systems. The sources show different totals for the same day.

options.text: Show each source side by side on the dashboard with a clear note.
Average the totals from all sources and present the figure as exact.
Pick the source with the highest total since it is the most complete.
Reconcile the sources with owners, document definitions, then build the dashboard.

basic.situation: Your senior gives coding guidelines for a smart contract helper library. You are asked to add one small function.

options.text: Add the function directly to the deployed library and test it after.
Copy a similar function from an online example and adjust the names.
Follow the guidelines, write a test with the function, and request a review.
Write the function in the guideline style and test it once yourself.

advanced.situation: You must set coding standards for a team updating client and server applications that handle business rules and signing of transactions.

options.text: Allow developers to store signing keys in the code repository during development tests.
Define review, testing and key-handling rules with the team, and enforce them.
Adopt a well-known open standard and ask the team to read it.
Write a short list of dos and don'ts and email it to the team.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to deploy a software update to three test nodes using the team's deployment script.

options.text: Run the script against the production nodes since they run the same software now.
Run the script on all three nodes at once and check they restart.
Update the nodes by hand in case the script has a fault.
Run the script on one node, check the logs, then update the others.

advanced.situation: Your company runs validator nodes in six countries. Updates must be applied to all of them quickly, but a bad update could halt the network.

options.text: Automate updates but ask regional teams to apply them when convenient for them.
Design staged, automated rollouts with health checks and automatic rollback for each region.
Automate the rollout in two waves, half the nodes first, then the rest.
Push the update to every node at once and fix failures as reported.

basic.situation: A teammate's smart contract draft includes a private key written directly in the code file. You review it.

options.text: Ask the teammate to be careful with keys in all future code drafts.
Leave it for now and add a code comment saying to replace the key later.
Tell the teammate, retire that key, and keep new keys in secure storage.
Remove the key from the file and ask the teammate to fix the rest.

advanced.situation: A risk review finds that a custody service holds client keys in one location with limited access logs. The business wants to launch next month.

options.text: Rate the risk as low in the report to avoid delaying the launch.
Rate the risk, recommend split key storage and logging, and set conditions.
Recommend adding more access logging before launch and keep the schedule as planned.
Accept the risk because the single location already has limited access for staff.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to run the standard infrastructure test on a small test network of ten nodes.

options.text: Run the test script, record node behaviour and errors, and share the results.
Run the test script and report whether it finished on every node.
Run the test on the live network since it has more nodes to try.
Run the test on two nodes and assume the other eight behave the same.

advanced.situation: You must design catastrophic failure handlers for a payment network, covering a node compromise and a data corruption event.

options.text: Build a handler that deletes the affected node data so the problem cannot spread.
Build a handler that halts the whole network when any warning appears.
Define triggers, isolation steps and recovery paths for each case, then test.
Add alerts for both events and write down what staff should do.

basic.situation: A department wants a simple booking tool for meeting rooms. Your senior asks you to identify the hardware and software parts needed.

options.text: Ask about users and rooms, then list the server, database and software needed.
List the parts used for the last booking tool your team built.
List a server and a database, then ask your senior if more is needed.
Order a high-end server now so the department has plenty of capacity.

advanced.situation: You must design a distributed system architecture for a nationwide ticketing service that must stay available when one data centre fails.

options.text: Use two data centres with a documented manual switch-over procedure for operators.
Design redundancy across sites, define failover tests, and document the trade-offs and standards.
Use two data centres but send all traffic to the main one for now.
Keep one data centre and plan to rebuild quickly if it fails there.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to configure a new file server to a written specification listing shares and permissions.

options.text: Follow the specification, apply each share and permission, and test with sample accounts.
Apply the shares and permissions and confirm the server is online and reachable.
Copy the configuration of the old server and adjust it afterwards if needed.
Give all users full access to every share to avoid support calls.

advanced.situation: You need to explain a major system redesign to senior management in a technical report. They have limited time and need a decision.

options.text: Present the design using diagrams and ask managers to read the detail later.
Lead with a one-page recommendation and cost, then attach the technical detail.
Write the full technical report and highlight the key sections for managers.
Present the benefits in a short summary and leave out the technical risks.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to watch the monitoring screen of a new system for the first day after launch.

options.text: Leave the screen open on your desk and rely on email alerts if needed.
Check the screen each hour and report any red alerts to your senior.
Watch the key measures, log anything unusual with times, and report it.
Silence the alerts that keep appearing so the monitoring screen stays quiet.

advanced.situation: A critical payment application must be verified for security and scalability before launch. The test window is short and the team wants to cut steps.

options.text: Prioritise tests by risk, run security and load tests on critical paths.
Sign off the architecture based on the vendor's own test summary alone.
Run the full load test and skip the security tests this time.
Run the security tests and assume the application will scale as expected.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to compare two backup products for cost and compatibility with the company's servers.

options.text: List prices and supported systems for both, and check compatibility with the vendors.
Compare the prices and recommend the cheaper product to your senior today.
Choose the product from the vendor whose salesperson you already know well.
Choose the product that has the most positive reviews on the internet.

advanced.situation: You must approve a project plan and budget for migrating systems to a new platform. The project manager's schedule looks optimistic and omits testing time.

options.text: Approve the plan as submitted to keep the project manager motivated.
Return the plan, ask for testing time and a risk reserve, then approve.
Approve the plan and ask the manager to add testing time if needed.
Approve the plan but cut the budget by ten percent to encourage care.

basic.situation: A junior colleague asks why a test environment keeps losing network connection. You have time to help.

options.text: Check the logs with them and test the connection step by step.
Take over the environment and rebuild it yourself from scratch over the weekend.
Suggest they restart the environment and report back if it happens again.
Tell them which setting you think is the cause and move on.

advanced.situation: Management asks if the order system still meets organisational needs. Users complain, but performance data looks acceptable.

options.text: Report that performance is acceptable and that complaints are anecdotal opinions.
Recommend replacing the order system to settle the complaints once and for all.
Combine performance data with user interviews, identify gaps, and propose targeted changes.
Survey users about their complaints and report the survey results to management.

basic.situation: You are asked to show two new staff how to restart the monitoring server using the written procedure.

options.text: Let them restart it alone on the live server as their first attempt.
Give them the written procedure and ask them to try it later.
Walk through the procedure, let them do it with you watching, and answer questions.
Demonstrate the restart while they watch and then give them the document.

advanced.situation: You direct a team building and operating a new system. Two senior engineers disagree on the operating approach, and operations staff are waiting for a decision.

options.text: Choose the approach of the engineer with longer experience on the team.
Ask a third engineer to choose between the two approaches and report back.
Tell operations staff to run both approaches in parallel on the live system.
Hear both approaches, compare them against requirements and risks, and decide with reasons.

basic.situation: Your senior manager asks you to draft the schedule for a staff portal rollout. You have the scope document but no team availability yet.

options.text: Draft it from the scope, flag availability as unconfirmed, then check dates with the leads.
Reuse the timeline from the last portal project and shift the dates to fit.
Draft the schedule from the scope and send it to your manager for comments.
Pick tight dates for each task so the schedule meets the launch date your manager wants.

advanced.situation: Leadership wants to approve a new ticketing system. Your plan shows costs clearly, but the savings figures came from the vendor's own brochure.

options.text: Ask the vendor for two customer references and add their reported savings to the plan.
Halve the vendor's savings figure to be safe and present that as the return.
Check the savings against your own ticket data, then present a range with assumptions.
Use the brochure figures as they are, since the vendor knows its own product.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to assign this week's test cases to three team members. One of them is new and has not used the test tool before.

options.text: Give all the cases to the two experienced members to finish the week faster.
Assign the new member the cases that need the tool and let them learn by doing.
Split the cases evenly and tell the new member to ask questions if stuck.
Pair the new member with a colleague on fewer cases and share the split.

advanced.situation: Your server supplier says delivery will slip three weeks. Two of your engineers are blaming each other over who ordered late. The go-live date is fixed by the client.

options.text: Reassign the ordering duty to a third engineer and point the team to recovery work.
Ask the supplier for a firm new date and tell the client about the delay.
Settle the facts with both engineers, then ask the supplier for partial delivery or loan units.
Cancel the supplier order and buy servers from a local reseller on the company card.

basic.situation: While updating the expense spreadsheet, you see the cloud hosting line is already at 85 percent of budget with six weeks of the project left.

options.text: Hold the hosting line back from the update until the next monthly bill arrives.
Move part of the hosting cost to another line that still has spare room.
Record the figure as it is and mention it at the next weekly meeting.
Record it, estimate the likely overspend, and report it to your manager today.

advanced.situation: You are preparing next year's IT project budget. Finance asks for a flat 10 percent cut, but two projects have fixed vendor contracts for the full year.

options.text: Apply the cut to flexible items, show locked contract costs, and propose options for the gap.
Cut the flexible items, send finance the new total, and mention the contracts are fixed.
Apply the 10 percent cut across all projects evenly and ask vendors for discounts later.
Trim the budget by 10 percent and leave out the contract costs so the total fits.

basic.situation: You are asked to take notes at a project meeting. The discussion moves fast, and two people give different dates for the testing phase.

options.text: Pick the date from the project plan and record it as the agreed date.
Note both dates, check with the project manager afterwards, then circulate the notes.
Note both dates as said and circulate the notes that afternoon for attendees to comment.
Leave the testing dates out of the notes since they were not settled in the meeting.

advanced.situation: Your project has three vendors, two internal teams and a client sponsor. Updates go out in different formats, and the sponsor says they no longer know where things stand.

options.text: Call a weekly review meeting with all parties to go through every update together.
Send the sponsor a weekly summary yourself and let others keep their own formats.
Forward every vendor email to the sponsor as it arrives so nothing is missed.
Agree one weekly update format and named contacts with the sponsor, then brief everyone.

basic.situation: Your manager asks you to list the people needed for a small app update. The plan has design, coding and testing work, but you are unsure about testing effort.

options.text: List design and coding resources now and add testing later when the plan is clearer.
Leave testing off the list, since developers can check their own work as they go.
Estimate one tester for the whole period and note that the figure is rough.
Ask testers how long similar updates took and list testing hours from their figures.

advanced.situation: You must pick a hosting vendor. The cheapest bidder's price is 30 percent lower, but references show two of its clients had long outages last year.

options.text: Choose the second cheapest bidder because its references look clean and present it to your manager.
Ask the cheapest bidder about the outages, then score every bid on price and uptime.
Choose the cheapest bidder and keep the outage reports out of the evaluation file.
Pick the cheapest bidder and add a service credit clause for outages to the contract.

basic.situation: You are asked to collect data for the weekly status report. Two task owners have not updated their progress in the tracker, and the report is due at noon.

options.text: Mark both tasks as complete so the report shows no delays at noon.
Message both owners for progress, use their replies, and mark any gap as pending.
Estimate their progress from the time the tasks have been open and submit the report.
Use the progress shown last week and note that two tasks were not updated.

advanced.situation: Deliverables from your team vary in quality, and the client has rejected two documents this month. You are asked to set a standard the team will follow.

options.text: Write a checklist yourself from an online template and email it to the team.
Ask each team member to check their own work more carefully before submitting it.
Build a checklist with the team from the rejection reasons, then review against it.
Resubmit the rejected documents with a note saying they now meet the client's standard.

basic.situation: A senior actuary asks you to calculate premium rates for a new term life product. Your mortality table is five years old, and a newer one is on the shared drive.

options.text: Ask the senior actuary which table to use and wait for the answer before starting.
Price on the newer table, show the gap to the old one, and flag it.
Use the older table, since the pricing sheet you were given was built around it.
Blend both tables and adjust the result until the premium matches a competitor's price.

advanced.situation: A mutual insurer has a surplus to share among participating policyholders. Your manager asks you to propose the split, and older policies have different contribution histories.

options.text: Base the split on each class's contribution, document the method, and test samples.
Share the surplus in proportion to premiums paid and show the method in your note.
Share the surplus equally across all policies to avoid disputes from older policyholders.
Allocate more surplus to the largest policyholders so they stay with the company next year.

basic.situation: You compare last year's claim counts with expected mortality. One age band with few policyholders shows claims 40 percent above expected.

options.text: Remove that age band from the comparison report since its numbers are too small to use.
Combine that age band with the next one so the gap looks smaller and steadier.
Report the 40 percent gap to your senior along with the band's policyholder count.
Check the band's exposure, measure the uncertainty, then report the gap to your senior.

advanced.situation: You must build a probability table for flood-related property claims. Eight years of data exist, and the last two years were unusually severe.

options.text: Build the table with and excluding the severe years, then show both with limits.
Use all eight years, include the severe ones, and mention the short history in your report.
Use the six calmer years and treat the two severe years as exceptions in a footnote.
Take the two severe years as the standard and delete the older data from the file.

basic.situation: A client bank offers a bond fund with a high yield. Your manager asks you to list its risks. The factsheet shows most holdings are rated below investment grade.

options.text: List credit, liquidity and rate risks, and link each to holdings in the factsheet.
Note that the high yield rewards the risk and mark the fund as acceptable.
List the credit risk from the low-rated holdings and send the note to your manager today.
Keep the risk list short so the client bank is not discouraged from buying it.

advanced.situation: A credit union wants to raise returns on its loans. Its loan book is concentrated in one sector, and the CEO wants a higher yield next quarter.

options.text: Recommend raising rates on the loans in the concentrated sector to lift yield.
Model returns in a downturn, then show how to cut concentration and keep yield.
Show the yield projections from the strongest quarters so the CEO approves the plan.
Recommend adding riskier loans in other sectors to lift yield and spread the book.

basic.situation: Your team is updating a pricing policy. Your manager asks you to summarize three changes for the sales team, who are not technical.

options.text: Summarize the changes from memory in a short chat message to save time.
Forward the technical memo to the sales team with a note to ask questions.
Write a one page summary in the technical terms and attach a short glossary of them.
Write each change in plain words with an example, then test it on a colleague.

advanced.situation: You must explain to shareholders why reserves are rising when claims look stable. Several of them have little finance training.

options.text: Say the rise is a temporary adjustment that will reverse once next year's claims settle.
Present the reserve calculation steps clearly and invite shareholders to ask questions at the meeting.
Chart reserves against the longer claims trend and explain the main driver in plain words.
Tell shareholders the rise follows standard practice and offer the full report for details.

basic.situation: Underwriters invite you to a meeting about a new travel insurance plan. They use many sales terms you do not know.

options.text: Take notes in the meeting and read about the terms afterwards on your own.
Take notes, mark unfamiliar terms, and ask an underwriter to explain them later.
Leave the meeting early, since the plan details will reach you by email later.
Stay quiet during the meeting and ask your manager for a summary of it afterwards.

advanced.situation: You lead actuaries, claims staff and underwriters on a motor insurance line review. Claims staff and underwriters disagree on why loss ratios rose.

options.text: Back the underwriters' view, since pricing is their area, and draft changes now.
Set up a shared review of claim causes and agree findings before changing rates.
Propose a rate increase on all motor policies first and sort out causes later.
Ask each group for a written explanation and choose whichever case looks stronger.

basic.situation: As a junior consultant, you review a client's reinsurance contract for your senior. A clause on claim notice periods looks shorter than the client's usual terms.

options.text: Mark the clause as acceptable because the rest of the contract looks standard overall.
Edit the clause to match the client's usual terms and send the copy back.
Tell the client the clause looks short and suggest they ask the reinsurer about it.
Flag the clause, compare it with the usual terms, and ask your senior for guidance.

advanced.situation: You negotiate reinsurance terms for a portfolio. The reinsurer offers lower premiums if your company accepts a higher retention and a cap on payouts after a large event.

options.text: Accept the offer and leave the cap out of the summary for your manager.
Model the retention and cap against past events, then counter with terms you can support.
Accept the higher retention and ask the reinsurer to drop the payout cap.
Accept the offer because the lower premium will improve this year's reported results.

basic.situation: A logistics manager asks you to find a delivery route plan that cuts fuel use. You have the distances between twelve depots and a formula your senior suggested.

options.text: Choose the shortest links between depots by eye and hand over the route list.
Adjust some distances in the data until the new route shows a large saving.
Apply the formula and send the manager the route list with the total distance.
Apply the formula, compare with last month's routes, and report the saving.

advanced.situation: A factory team faces a scheduling problem that existing methods do not fit. They ask you to guide them in choosing a mathematical approach.

options.text: Adapt the closest existing method and tell the team it should work.
Help the team state the problem formally, then trial two methods on small cases.
Choose the most advanced method available and ask the team to trust the output.
Pick the method you know well and walk the team through applying it.

basic.situation: Your senior gives you a spreadsheet of sensor readings and steps to compute averages. One column has a few readings far larger than the rest.

options.text: Replace the large readings with the column average and report the result as measured.
Remove the large readings from the column since they would distort the averages.
Finish the computations as instructed and report the averages with those readings included.
Finish the sums, flag the large readings, and ask your senior whether to keep them.

advanced.situation: You are building an analysis framework for a large demand forecast. The result depends strongly on two uncertain assumptions about growth and prices.

options.text: Run the forecast with a low, middle and high case and report the middle one.
Choose the assumptions that give the result the sponsor expects and run the forecast.
Test a grid of growth and price values and show what drives the result.
Take the most likely growth and price values from the last report and run once.

basic.situation: You are asked to build a simple model of how a water tank fills. Your supervisor gives you the inflow rate and the tank size.

options.text: Take a formula from a similar tank and change constants until the result looks right.
Write the fill equation from the rates and give it to your supervisor to check.
Write the fill equation, test it on a measured fill time, and show your supervisor.
Fit a straight line through two data points and use it for every range.

advanced.situation: You must design a simulation of airflow in a new building. Earlier simulations were off by 15 percent against measurements, and the client wants tighter accuracy.

options.text: Refine the grid resolution across the whole model and rerun it against old measurements.
Trace the earlier error to its source, refine the model there, and check fresh measurements.
Apply a 15 percent correction factor to the results so they match the measurements.
Report the simulation results as accurate and drop the old measurement comparison from the file.

basic.situation: Your team asks you to keep up with recent work in numerical methods. A colleague shares a new journal paper on solving large linear systems.

options.text: Ask the colleague to explain the paper in a short chat and skip reading it.
Cite the paper in your next report after reading its title and abstract.
Read the abstract and conclusion, then share the paper with the whole team.
Read the paper, summarize its main idea, and note how it could help.

advanced.situation: While researching a proof, you find a result that seems to link two known theorems. You have a sketch of the argument, but one step is unproven.

options.text: Write up the sketch as a conjecture and share it with colleagues for comments.
Describe the link as proven in your draft so the result can be submitted soon.
Treat the link as established and build the next steps of your research on it.
Test the link on examples, work on the gap, and discuss it with a senior.

basic.situation: You help format a research report for publication. The journal template requires specific heading styles, and your tables are wider than the page.

options.text: Check the heading rules, resize the tables, and send the draft to your senior.
Remove the tables that do not fit and note that they are available on request.
Shrink the table text until it fits and keep your original headings as drafted.
Resize the tables to fit and send the draft back to your senior.

advanced.situation: You lead publication of a high-profile paper with two junior authors. A reviewer questions your main result a week before the deadline.

options.text: Reply to the reviewer with an explanation and keep the paper as written.
Reword the main result to sound less certain and submit by the deadline.
Reproduce the analysis with the juniors, answer the reviewer, and revise the paper.
Ask the journal for a longer deadline and rework the paper afterwards on your own.

basic.situation: A colleague asks you to explain standard deviation. They need it for a report and look confused by the formula.

options.text: Walk through the formula step by step on the whiteboard and check they follow.
Send them a textbook chapter on the formula and offer to answer questions.
Explain it as the typical distance from average, with a small example from their data.
Tell them to use the spreadsheet function and not to worry about the meaning.

advanced.situation: You are asked to design a training program on advanced numerical techniques for new analysts with varied backgrounds.

options.text: Assign the analysts a list of papers and check who has finished at the end.
Test their skills first, then build staged modules with exercises per group.
Build a course from a university syllabus and run it for all analysts together.
Collect slides from past talks and present them all in one long session.

basic.situation: A manager tells you the warehouse is too slow but gives no details. You are asked to define the problem for an analysis.

options.text: Ask which orders are delayed and restate the problem in measurable terms.
Visit the warehouse, watch the process for an hour, and write down what looks slow.
Define the problem as too few staff and ask the manager to approve more hires.
Pick the busiest shelf area as the problem and start building a model around it.

advanced.situation: Sales wants lower stock and operations wants faster delivery. Both say the planning problem is theirs, and the director wants one clear problem statement.

options.text: Choose the lower stock goal since it saves money and brief the teams afterwards.
Ask the director to pick one team's goal and define the problem around it.
Meet both teams, list their goals, and draft one statement for the director.
Define two separate problems and run an analysis for each team on its own.

basic.situation: You built a simple queue model for a clinic. It predicts a waiting time of 12 minutes, but the clinic's records show an average of 20.

options.text: Add eight minutes to every predicted wait so the output matches the records.
Report the 12 minute result to the clinic since your model's logic is sound.
Ask your supervisor to review the model and tell you what to change.
Compare the model inputs with clinic records, find the gap, and adjust it.

advanced.situation: A client wants to know how a new self-service kiosk will change queues, but no similar system exists to copy. You must design an experimental approach.

options.text: Build a model from published queue studies of staffed counters and adjust it.
Pilot one kiosk, record queue data, and build the model from the results.
Ask the client to describe expected usage and model the kiosk on those figures.
Use the kiosk vendor's expected queue figures as your results and submit the report.

basic.situation: You are asked to study a bank's loan approval process. You can see five steps, but staff give different times for each step.

options.text: Use the times from the process manual, since it is the official source.
Time each step on real cases for a week, then use the averages as values.
Take the average of the times the staff gave you and use those values.
Use the times from the fastest staff member so the process looks efficient.

advanced.situation: Three vendors offer different routing software. Their demos used their own data, and each claims the largest saving. You must evaluate them for a senior team.

options.text: Ask each vendor to re-run its demo on a sample of your routes and compare.
Pick the vendor with the largest claimed saving and draft the recommendation.
Compare the three vendors' claimed savings and the cost of each product.
Run all three on one shared set of your own routes and compare.

basic.situation: You help plan a three-month office relocation. Your supervisor asks you to draft the task timeline, and two tasks cannot start until the electrical work is done.

options.text: List all tasks in date order and mark the electrical work as the first job.
Leave dependencies off the timeline for now and show the shortest possible duration.
Link both tasks after the electrical work and compute the total duration.
Schedule both tasks at the same time as the electrical work to save days.

advanced.situation: A retailer's three distribution centres each use different picking methods, and costs vary widely. You are asked to design a standard logistics process for all of them.

options.text: Design a standard method from industry articles and send it to all three centres.
Compare costs across the centres, design a common method, and pilot it at one.
Order all three centres to switch to a method you designed and skip any trial.
Adopt the lowest-cost centre's method for all three and roll it out next month.

basic.situation: Your manager asks you to prepare a short report on why order errors rose last month. Your data shows errors rose mainly in one shift.

options.text: Leave the shift detail out of the report to avoid blaming any one team.
Report the shift pattern with numbers and suggest a check on the causes.
Report the total rise in errors and mention the shift in one line.
Report that the night shift staff caused the rise and suggest retraining them.

advanced.situation: You present a complex simulation result to senior leadership. They want a yes or no on a new depot, but the model shows a wide range of outcomes.

options.text: Give a recommendation, show the range, and name the assumptions behind it.
Give a yes based on the average outcome and keep the range for questions.
Give a yes based on the most favourable run since leaders want one answer.
Show the range of outcomes and let the leaders decide what to do next.

basic.situation: A new scheduling method has been approved. Your team must apply it next week, and a colleague worries it will confuse the packers.

options.text: Tell your colleague the method is approved and the packers will adjust soon.
Change the method on your own to the old schedule where packers feel comfortable.
Offer to prepare a one page guide and join the packers' first shift to help.
Forward the method steps to the packers and ask them to read before Monday.

advanced.situation: Senior managers disagree on whether to adopt your recommended inventory policy. Some fear job changes and others want to start at once.

options.text: Present the analysis results again to all managers and ask for a vote.
Meet each group, address its concerns in the plan, and agree a phased start.
Start with the managers who support it and let the others follow later.
Describe the policy as approved by the board and begin the rollout on schedule.

basic.situation: Your senior asks for a sample size for a customer satisfaction survey of 5,000 customers. She wants a margin of error of 5 percent.

options.text: Set the sample at 50 and report a 5 percent margin to match her request.
Use a sample size from a similar past survey and send it to her.
Pick 500 customers, which is a tenth of the list, as the sample.
Calculate it from the margin and confidence level and show your working.

advanced.situation: You design a national household survey. Rural areas hold 20 percent of homes but are expensive to reach, and the budget is fixed.

options.text: Sample households at random nationwide and accept whatever rural numbers come in.
Sample mostly urban homes and treat the results as covering the whole country.
