Record rural answers by copying urban answers to meet the quota within budget.
Stratify by rural and urban areas and weight results to match their shares.

basic.situation: You assist a senior in testing a survey form. Two questions seem to confuse respondents in a small trial of 20 people.

options.text: Note the confusing questions, suggest clearer wording, and re-test with more people.
Reword the two questions yourself and update the survey form for all the respondents now.
Report the two confusing questions to your senior and wait for a decision.
Delete the two questions from the trial data and report the remaining answers.

advanced.situation: You are asked to write a custom program to fit a complex model for a bank's risk team. Results differ slightly from the standard package's output.

options.text: Round your program's outputs to match the package and move on to documentation.
Ask a colleague to review your code and the package settings before continuing.
Deliver the results to the bank, since small differences are normal for custom code.
Check the program against the package on test data and trace where results differ.

basic.situation: You prepare survey data for analysis. Some respondents gave ages of 150 and 999, and a few rows have empty income fields.

options.text: Fill the empty income fields with the highest income in the file to be safe.
Flag the impossible ages and blanks, check the source forms, and record fixes.
Replace the impossible ages with the average age and leave blanks as they are.
Delete rows with impossible ages and keep the rows that have empty income fields.

advanced.situation: A national dataset you must use has a response rate of 35 percent, and responses are skewed toward older people. Your team wants a plan for this.

options.text: Weight responses by age group and describe the method in the report.
Report the results as given and mention the low response rate in a footnote.
Weight to known population shares, test the sensitivity, and state the limits.
Drop the oldest respondents until the age mix looks balanced, and report the rest.

basic.situation: A mentor asks you to look at monthly sales data and find a trend. Sales rise each December and fall in January.

options.text: Report that January shows a sales decline and recommend a review of the staff.
Compare several years of December and January sales to see if the pattern repeats.
Report that sales are rising overall since December is higher than the months before.
Describe the rise and fall as a seasonal pattern and report it to your mentor.

advanced.situation: A hospital researcher asks you to analyse patient recovery times that are heavily skewed, with some cases still in treatment. Standard averages seem misleading.

options.text: Set the recovery time of patients still in treatment at the current average.
Use survival analysis suited to censored data and explain the choice.
Remove the patients still in treatment and compute the usual average recovery time.
Use medians instead of averages and list the censored patients in a separate note.

basic.situation: You make a chart of survey results for a weekly report. Responses are ranked from 1 to 5, and the audience is not technical.

options.text: Start the chart's vertical axis near the top rating so small differences look large.
Use a bar chart of rating shares with clear labels and one summary line.
Show the average rating as one large number with a clear title.
Use a pie chart with five slices and add the raw counts below.

advanced.situation: You are to present findings from a multi-year study at a conference. The audience is expert, and one result is statistically weak.

options.text: Present the weak result with its interval and say what more data would settle it.
Present the weak result as a trend and say more years should confirm it.
Present the strong results first and mention the weak result briefly at the end.
Re-run the analysis with other methods until the weak result reaches significance and present that.

basic.situation: You assist in supervising three data entry clerks. One clerk's entries show frequent typing errors in the number fields.

options.text: Tell the clerk to be more careful and check the entries next week.
Check a sample of entries, show the clerk the errors, and teach the checks.
Re-enter the clerk's work yourself each evening so the data stays clean.
Report the clerk to your manager for poor work after seeing the first few errors.

advanced.situation: You manage a 12-person data team. Workflows are delayed because analysts wait for cleaned data, and two analysts are blaming the cleaning team.

options.text: Tell the cleaning team the delays are theirs and ask them to work overtime.
Map the workflow with both teams, find the waits, and agree on handovers.
Set a daily deadline for cleaned data and ask both teams to meet it.
Move one analyst to the cleaning team and see if the delays go down.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to prepare tables for a data monitoring committee report. One table's adverse event count differs by two from the clinical database.

options.text: Keep the table's count, since it was already checked, and finish the report.
Edit the database count to match the table so the two sources agree.
Send the table to your senior with a note that the counts differ by two.
Trace the two events to source records, fix the table, and record why.

advanced.situation: A flu outbreak model you built predicts a peak in three weeks, but two weeks of new data run below the forecast. A health agency relies on it.

options.text: Lower the forecast by the size of the gap and send it to the agency.
Keep sending the original forecast to the agency so its plans stay stable.
Refit the model on the new data and tell the agency the revised forecast.
Keep the model and tell the agency the low counts may be reporting delays.

basic.situation: Your team plans to use a new method for handling missing data. A colleague mentions a recent paper that criticizes it.

options.text: Switch the whole study to the method in the paper after reading the abstract.
Keep using the method, since your team already chose it for the study.
Read the paper, note the criticism, and share what it means for your study.
Ask the colleague to summarize the paper and decide from that summary.

advanced.situation: A physician wants a trial of a new drug with 40 patients to show a modest effect. You calculate that this is too few.

options.text: Run the trial with 40 patients and report that the study is exploratory.
Plan the analysis around the one outcome most likely to reach significance with 40 patients.
Show the power calculation and offer options such as more patients or a different design.
Tell the physician the sample is too small and ask for a bigger budget.

basic.situation: You collect survey data on paper forms at a community clinic. A respondent leaves the age box empty and says it is private.

options.text: Estimate the age from the respondent's appearance and enter it on the form.
Copy the age from another respondent in the same household and enter it.
Record the age as declined with a note, and finish the form.
Leave the age box blank and finish the rest of the form.

advanced.situation: A trial measured blood pressure on 200 patients monthly for a year, but 30 percent missed some visits. Your manager wants a simple average comparison between groups.

options.text: Average each patient's available readings across the year and compare the group means.
Fill each missed visit with the other group's average and compare the group means.
Use a mixed-effects model for repeated visits and explain why it suits the gaps.
Compare group averages at each visit and report how many patients are missing.

basic.situation: You must calculate the sample size for a pilot clinical study. The effect size is uncertain, and the budget allows about 60 patients.

options.text: Calculate sizes for plausible effects and show what 60 patients can detect.
Report 60 patients as the sample size since it fits the available budget.
Choose an effect size large enough that 60 patients appear to be sufficient.
Calculate the size for the effect your supervisor expects and report it.

advanced.situation: A research protocol proposes a t-test for survival times in cancer patients, with many patients still alive at the end. You review the analysis plan.

options.text: Recommend a nonparametric test on the observed times and list the limits.
Approve the plan and pick the analysis later after seeing how the results look.
Approve the t-test since it is widely used and easy for readers to follow.
Recommend a survival method for censored times and explain why to the team.

basic.situation: You write code in statistical software to run a regression for your senior. The script runs but gives a warning about a variable with missing values.

options.text: Find which variable triggers the warning, count its missing values, and report.
Re-run the script, add a comment about the warning, and send the output.
Turn off the warning messages in the script so the output looks clean.
Drop the variable from the regression and send the results to your senior today.

advanced.situation: You write the statistical analysis plan for a vaccine trial. The sponsor asks you to leave the primary endpoint open until the data are in.

options.text: Specify the primary endpoint and method in the plan before any data are unblinded.
Specify the primary endpoint and describe the method generally to leave some flexibility.
List several candidate endpoints in the plan and choose one after interim results arrive.
Leave the endpoint open as the sponsor asked and finalize the plan after unblinding.

basic.situation: You must assign three programming tasks to two assistants. One task checks patient data used in a regulatory report; the others are routine formatting.

options.text: Give the data check to the experienced assistant and review the output yourself.
Give the data check to the newer assistant for training and send it on unreviewed.
Split the three tasks by workload and ask both to report problems.
Give the data check to whoever finishes first and review it later.

advanced.situation: A lab scientist asks you to confirm that her result is significant at 5 percent. You find that p equals 0.07 after testing six outcomes.

options.text: Say the result is close to significant and suggest adding a few more samples.
Explain the p value and multiple testing, and suggest a confirmatory study.
Report the one outcome that reached significance and leave the other five out.
Report the p value of 0.07 and say it is not significant at 5 percent.

basic.situation: You are cleaning a customer file for a model. The phone number column mixes formats like 012-3456789 and +60123456789.

options.text: Standardize the numbers by script and check a sample of rows.
Remove all rows with a plus sign so the column looks consistent.
Fix the formats by hand in a spreadsheet for the first hundred rows.
Keep both formats as they are and let the model treat them as different.

advanced.situation: Your team repeats the same cleaning steps on weekly sales files, with small manual changes each time. You are asked to build a reusable tool for it.

options.text: Write one script with the current file's changes built in and share it.
Write a function that deletes rows it cannot read and run it on new files.
Write a documented function with parameters, then test it on past files.
Copy last week's script and adjust the steps for each new file.

basic.situation: A marketing lead wants to survey 200 of your 20,000 customers. Your supervisor tells you to use sampling, and age groups differ greatly in size.

options.text: Pick 200 customers from the largest age group since it dominates the file.
Sample at random within each age group in proportion to its size.
Pick the 200 customers who bought most recently as they are easiest to reach.
Select 200 customers at random from the full list and note the age mix.

advanced.situation: A retail manager says sales are falling and asks for a model to predict next month's sales. You suspect the real issue is losing repeat customers.

options.text: Build the sales forecast as requested and add a note on repeat customers.
Tell the manager repeat customers are the cause and change the project to match.
Check repeat customer rates in the data, then propose a model for the problem.
Build the forecast and wait for the manager to ask about the causes.

basic.situation: You trained two models to predict customer churn. Model A has slightly higher accuracy, but Model B scores better on the metric your supervisor chose.

options.text: Compare both models on the chosen metric and on held-out data, then report.
Pick a new metric on which Model A scores higher and report the comparison.
Report Model B since it scores higher on the metric your supervisor chose.
Report Model A since accuracy is the metric most readers already understand well.

advanced.situation: Your demand forecast model scored well in testing but is missing actuals badly in the first live month. The manager wants a quick patch.

options.text: Retrain the model on the latest live month of data and redeploy it.
Check how test and live data differ, retrain if needed, and report the cause.
Tell the manager the testing score proves the model is sound and live data is odd.
Add a fixed correction to each forecast to match the gap seen so far.

basic.situation: While looking at sales data, you notice ice cream sales and swimming pool visits rise together. Your supervisor asks if one drives the other.

options.text: Explain that both likely follow hot weather and test it by adding temperature.
Recommend ice cream promotions at pools based on the link in the data.
Report that rising pool visits seem to lead to higher ice cream sales.
Report the strong link and say you cannot tell the cause from the data alone.

advanced.situation: An engineering team has noisy sensor readings and wants a method to detect early machine failures. Existing alarms trigger too often to be useful.

options.text: Filter the noise, test a change-detection method on past failures, and tune the threshold.
Smooth the readings with a moving average and use the existing alarm rules.
Raise the alarm threshold until the number of false alerts is manageable.
Switch off the alarms for the noisiest sensors so engineers are not disturbed.

basic.situation: A manager asks for help deciding how many staff to schedule on weekends. You have two years of hourly customer counts.

options.text: Copy the weekday staffing level and add one extra person for each weekend shift.
Find the busy weekend hours in the data and suggest a staffing range.
Recommend cutting weekend staff because the average count looks low across the whole week.
Calculate the average weekend customers per hour and suggest a single staffing number.

advanced.situation: Your analysis recommends dropping a product line that executives love. The data are clear, but the executives challenge your conclusions in a meeting.

options.text: Repeat your conclusion with a summary slide and ask the group for a decision.
Offer to soften the recommendation to keep the product line for another quarter.
Remove the weakest figures from your slides so the data look more persuasive.
Walk through the data and assumptions, invite their challenges, and offer a follow-up test.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks for a chart showing monthly revenue for five regions over two years. The first draft has ten overlapping lines.

options.text: Split the chart into small panels per region that share one axis scale.
Keep one chart but use different colours and thicker lines for each region.
Show the latest year alone so there are fewer lines on the chart.
Plot a single average line for all regions and hide the regional details.

advanced.situation: You present model results to department heads. One head asks a technical question about model assumptions that you cannot answer right now.

options.text: Say the assumption is standard and suggest the question is not important for decisions.
Answer from general knowledge and add that it may need confirming later.
Ask a colleague in the room to answer and move on to the next point.
Say you will check the assumption and send a written answer by Friday.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to list current customers in a region using the BI tool. The tool shows two accounts with almost the same name and address.

options.text: Compare the two accounts' details, flag the pair, and ask how to merge.
Merge the two accounts in the tool so the customer list looks clean.
List the account with more recent activity and drop the other from the list.
List both accounts and add a note that they may be one customer.

advanced.situation: Industry reports suggest demand is shifting from desktop to mobile in Southeast Asia, but your own regional sales show the opposite. A product team awaits your view.

options.text: Present both sources side by side and let the product team decide which to trust.
Compare how each source measured demand, then give the team a reasoned view.
Follow your own sales data and leave the industry report out of the summary.
Follow the industry report since it covers more markets than your sales data.

basic.situation: You maintain the team's library of report templates. A colleague uploads a new template that uses a different naming style from the others.

options.text: Rename it to match the library's rules and tell your colleague.
Replace an older template with the new one to keep the library small.
Add the template as uploaded and mention the naming style to your supervisor.
Leave the new template as uploaded since the older ones can be renamed later.

advanced.situation: You build a sales dashboard that pulls from three databases. In testing, regional totals differ by 3 percent between the dashboard and the finance system.

options.text: Match the dashboard to finance by adjusting the regional totals with a fixed factor.
Release the dashboard on schedule and ask users to report any differences they see.
Trace the gap to its feed, fix it, and re-test before release.
Add a note on the dashboard that totals may differ slightly from finance.

basic.situation: A manager asks for a new weekly report on overdue invoices. You are asked to draft the specification, but she has described it in two sentences.

options.text: List the fields you understand, mark the gaps, and confirm with the manager.
Build the report first from your own idea and write the specification after.
Copy the specification from a similar report and change the title and date.
Draft the specification from the two sentences and send it for approval.

advanced.situation: Your team's report designs are documented in different ways, and developers keep misreading them. You are asked to set a documentation standard.

options.text: Ask each developer to add notes to their documents wherever they find gaps.
Write a standard template yourself and send it to the team to follow.
Pick the clearest existing document and tell the team to follow it from now on.
Draft a template with developers, trial it on one report, and refine it.

basic.situation: You are given instructions to update a dashboard's data source to a new table. After the change, one chart shows blank values.

options.text: Fill the blank values with the previous month's numbers and report the update done.
Revert to the old data source and tell your supervisor it did not work.
Check the field mapping, repair the chart, and tell your supervisor.
Hide the blank chart from the dashboard and report the update as complete.

advanced.situation: Several departments rely on a nightly data refresh for their morning reports. This morning the refresh failed halfway, and some reports show old numbers.

options.text: Add a banner to the reports about the failure and wait for tonight's refresh.
Copy yesterday's numbers into the failed tables so every report looks complete.
Tell users which reports are stale, restart the refresh, and confirm the fix.
Restart the refresh and send users a message once all reports are updated.

basic.situation: A colleague tells you a dashboard filter shows no data for last week. You know how to check the filter settings.

options.text: Tell your colleague how to reset the filter and ask them to try again.
Check the filter settings, fix the date range, and tell your colleague.
Rebuild the filter from scratch on the live dashboard and tell them afterwards.
Tell your colleague to wait until the end of the week for data to appear.

advanced.situation: You added new metadata fields to a shared sales report. Several departments use the report, and a team lead asks if they need to change anything.

options.text: Tell the team lead that nothing needs to change because the old fields remain.
Remove the old fields next week and tell people to find the new ones.
Post the field list on the team page and answer questions as they come.
Send a note listing the new fields, what changed, and who to contact.

basic.situation: You generate the standard monthly report for a manager. The revenue total looks 20 percent lower than usual because of a missing region.

options.text: Send the report as generated and explain the drop if the manager asks.
Check the load for the missing region, rerun the report, and tell the manager.
Send the report with a note that one region is missing from the data.
Add an estimate for the missing region based on last month and send the report.

advanced.situation: Executives want a custom report showing which products to cut. Your data covers sales, but not support costs, which change the picture.

options.text: Build the report from sales data and mention that support costs are missing.
Estimate support costs from an industry average and include them in the report.
Rank products by sales and describe the ranking as the full cost picture.
Request the support cost data first, then build the report and state the gaps.

basic.situation: A site sends you paper case report forms to enter into the clinical database. One form has a lab value that looks ten times higher than the usual range.

options.text: Leave the value out of the database and file the form with the others.
Enter the value as written, raise a query to the site, and log it.
Enter the value divided by ten, since it looks like a misplaced decimal.
Enter the value as written and highlight it for the team to review later.

advanced.situation: You design edit checks for a new trial database. Your supervisor wants fewer checks to speed up site entry, but a key safety field has several likely entry errors.

options.text: Keep every check and ask sites to enter data more slowly.
Keep strong checks on the safety field and cut low-risk ones elsewhere.
Remove the safety field checks and add a monthly review of entries.
Remove all edit checks and rely on data review after the trial finishes.

basic.situation: While reviewing entered data, you notice a patient's visit date is earlier than the consent date. Your SOP says to raise a data query to the site.

options.text: Raise a query to the site asking them to confirm both dates.
Mention the dates to the study coordinator at the next weekly team meeting.
Delete the visit record since the date order cannot be valid.
Change the visit date to the consent date so the order is valid.

advanced.situation: During an audit you find that three sites entered adverse events late, and two have missing sign-offs. You are leading the audit report for the sponsor.

options.text: Add the missing sign-offs yourself with the coordinators' names to close the findings.
Report the late events and the missing sign-offs as minor issues to avoid delay.
List all findings in the report and leave the actions to the sites.
Document each finding with evidence, rate its risk, and request corrective actions.

basic.situation: A statistician asks you to format a data set for analysis. The date columns use three different formats across sites.

options.text: Send the data set as it is and describe the three formats in a note.
Convert the dates to the largest site's format and leave the rest as they are.
Delete the date columns from the data set since they cause formatting problems.
Convert all dates to one standard format and check a sample of rows.

advanced.situation: Query resolution takes an average of 14 days, and sites complain. Your manager asks you to suggest changes that speed it up while keeping data quality.

options.text: Suggest sending weekly reminders to all sites for every open query older than a week.
Find where queries wait longest, then suggest targeted fixes and clearer wording.
Suggest closing queries automatically after ten days if the site has not responded.
Suggest cutting the number of data checks by half so fewer queries are raised.

basic.situation: You help design a form to collect patient vital signs. Your supervisor asks for clear fields, and the draft has one box for all readings.

options.text: Make every field free text so sites can record whatever they want to.
Keep the single box and add a line of instructions on how to enter readings.
Create separate labelled fields with units for each vital sign and show it.
Split the box into two fields, one for numbers and one for notes.

advanced.situation: End users ask for a data export in a new format for a regulator. The programmers say the current structure cannot produce it directly.

options.text: Write a specification from the users' request and send it to the programmers.
Tell the users that the regulator's format cannot be produced and close the request.
Ask the programmers to propose a format and tell the users to accept it.
Meet users and programmers, agree the fields and format, then write the specification.

basic.situation: You draft a work instruction for entering lab results. A colleague who read it says step four is unclear.

options.text: Add an example to step four and send the revised version to your supervisor.
Ask what confused them, rewrite step four, and have another colleague read it.
Remove step four from the instruction since it causes confusion among colleagues.
Leave the step as written because it follows the department template exactly.

advanced.situation: You write the data management plan for a trial across five countries. Sites use different coding dictionaries for adverse events and medicines.

options.text: Choose the dictionary used at the largest site and leave the others to adapt later.
Specify one dictionary and version for coding, with a review process for coders.
Leave coding out of the plan and decide the approach when the data arrive.
Let each country use its own dictionary and convert the codes at the end.

basic.situation: You track paper forms moving between sites and the data centre. Today you notice 12 forms sent last week have not been received.

options.text: Check the tracking log, contact the sites, and report the missing forms.
Remove the 12 forms from the tracking log so the weekly count matches.
Wait another week to see whether the forms arrive before telling anyone.
Report the 12 missing forms to your supervisor and wait for instructions.

advanced.situation: A data entry staff member keeps making the same coding error. Another staff member says the first one is careless, and morale is dropping.

options.text: Move the staff member to filing work and tell the team the reason for it.
Review the errors with the staff member, retrain on the rule, and check later.
Remind the whole team of the coding rule at the next weekly meeting.
Ask the other staff member to fix the errors in the data each day.

basic.situation: A researcher asks you to retrieve all known variants of one gene from the standard mutation database. The search returns 4,000 records, with some marked low confidence.

options.text: Retrieve the first 500 records and send those since the list is too long.
Retrieve the records that support the researcher's expected result and send those.
Filter by confidence and source, retrieve the matches, and record the filters.
Retrieve all 4,000 records and note which ones are marked low confidence.

advanced.situation: A biologist asks whether a protein domain found in a plant also appears in a fungus linked to crop disease. The answer needs three databases with different formats.

options.text: Query each database separately and send the biologist the three result lists.
Plan the queries across the three databases, map shared identifiers, and check the matches.
Merge entries from the three databases by name similarity and report the matches as confirmed.
Query the largest database and assume the other two would give the same answer.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to write a short script that pulls sequence records by accession number from a database. You have an example script from another project.

options.text: Write the script to pull records and skip any accession numbers that cause errors.
Run the example script as it is and send the records it returns.
Adapt the example and send the script to your supervisor to try.
Adapt the example, test it on three known accessions, and show the output.

advanced.situation: Your lab's sequence tracking tool must now handle a new file format from a sequencer. Other teams use the tool daily, and a change could break their imports.

options.text: Add the format on a test copy, check old and new imports, then release.
Write a separate converter script for the new format and leave the tool alone.
Replace the tool's import code with a new version and tell the teams to adapt.
Add the new format to the live tool and fix any problems users report.

basic.situation: A sequence alignment you ran shows a large gap in coverage across one region. Your colleague says it is probably fine.

options.text: Ask a senior analyst whether the gap is expected for this kind of sample.
Mark the region as low coverage in the results and continue with the analysis.
Check read quality and coverage for that region and report what you find.
Fill the gap by copying bases from the reference sequence into your results.

advanced.situation: A prediction model's outputs look excellent on your lab data, but the input files came from three sequencers with different quality settings. The team plans to publish.

options.text: Send the results as they are since the model's scores are strong.
Compare input quality across sequencers, test each, and report the limits.
Add a note that input quality varied and send the results to the team.
Re-run the model on one sequencer's data to see if the results hold.

basic.situation: You changed a field name in a shared database to fix a typo. A colleague says their query stopped working this morning.

options.text: Log the rename with its reason, tell the colleague, and help fix the query.
Tell your colleague about the rename and help them fix the query.
Rename the field back to the typo and explain the reason in your email today.
Rename the field back and remove today's changes from the change log.

advanced.situation: Your team's database has no standard procedure for checking incoming data, and each person checks differently. You are asked to write one that everyone will follow.

options.text: Draft checks with the team, test them on old data, and add a short manual.
Write the checks you use yourself as the standard and send them to the team.
List the common checks in a short memo and ask people to use their favourites.
Adopt the checks from a published tool unchanged and tell the team to comply.

basic.situation: Researchers are discussing what data they need from a new sequencing project. They use terms you do not know, and your supervisor asked you to attend.

options.text: Take notes and look up the terms later in the project papers.
Stay quiet in the meeting and ask your supervisor for a summary later.
Agree to provide the data they ask for and sort out details later.
Take notes, mark unfamiliar terms, and ask the researchers to explain later.

advanced.situation: A research team wants a database for single-cell data, but members disagree on which fields matter. The clinician wants patient details, while the biologists want raw reads.

options.text: Run a session to rank needs, agree on required fields, and note privacy limits.
Include patient details in the database for everyone to see to settle the dispute.
Follow the biologists' list since raw reads make up most of the data volume.
Collect each member's field list and build a database that includes all of them.

basic.situation: You help prepare a methods section for a paper. The lead author asks you to list the software versions used, but you cannot find some.

options.text: Write the latest versions of each program, since they are probably what was used.
Leave the unknown versions out of the section so the list looks complete.
List the versions you remember using and ask the lead author to check.
Check the analysis logs for versions, and mark any that remain unknown.

advanced.situation: You lead the writing of a scientific paper. A collaborator's figure supports your main claim, but you notice the analysis used a different reference genome from the rest.

options.text: Keep the figure since the claim holds and mention the difference in the cover letter.
Remove the mention of the reference genome from the methods so the figures match.
Ask the collaborator to rerun it on the shared reference and update the figure.
Add a note in the figure legend that a different reference genome was used.

basic.situation: A senior architect asks you to plan the layout of a small two-storey shophouse renovation. The client wants the staircase moved, but a load-bearing wall sits in its path.

options.text: Remove the wall in the sketch since it can be replaced with a beam later.
Sketch options that keep the wall and show your senior the choices.
Sketch the staircase in its new position and note the wall for the engineer.
Draw the staircase in the new position and leave the wall off the drawing.

advanced.situation: A client wants a certified green office building. Your engineer says the target rating needs a costly glazing system that exceeds the budget.

options.text: Model the glazing's savings, compare cheaper ways to earn points, and present options.
Specify the cheaper glass in the drawings and claim the target rating in the brochure.
Choose cheaper glass and tell the client the green rating is still likely.
Present the costly glazing as the way to reach the rating and ask for budget.

basic.situation: You prepare the specification for floor finishes in a clinic. Your senior gave you a list of products, and one is no longer available.

options.text: Keep the unavailable product in the specification and let the contractor sort it out.
Tell your senior the product is unavailable and wait for a new instruction.
Substitute a similar looking product and mention the change in the specification notes.
Check the supplier for a replacement, compare it, and tell your senior.

advanced.situation: A contractor claims extra payment because the client changed the third floor layout. The contract requires written approval for variations, and none was issued.

options.text: Check the records, then advise the client on the claim under the clause.
Reject the claim because no written approval exists and inform the contractor.
Approve the claim in full and ask the client to sign the variation later.
Pay the claim in part to keep the contractor on site and the project moving.

basic.situation: A senior asks for a floor plan in CAD at a scale of 1:100. After plotting, the dimensions on the printed sheet look too small.

options.text: Check the plot scale, replot at 1:100, and measure a known length.
Replot the sheet on a larger paper size and send it to the senior.
Resize the drawing on the sheet by eye until the plan appears to fit.
Increase the text and dimension size so the drawing looks more readable.

advanced.situation: Your studio wants a standard for 3D models shared with consultants. Models arrive in different layering and naming styles, and the clash checks keep failing.

options.text: Ask consultants to tidy their models before sending them over for each clash check.
Draft a layer and naming standard with consultants and test it on one project.
Write a standard from your own model setup and send it to consultants.
Skip the clash checks that fail and report that the models are coordinated.

basic.situation: A client explains that their family needs a prayer room, a large kitchen and space for visiting relatives. You are taking notes for the senior architect.

options.text: Write the rooms down and add extra ones you think the family will like.
Write down each need exactly as said and share the notes afterwards.
Note the main points and fill in the gaps from similar houses you know.
Write down each need, ask who uses each space, and share the notes.

advanced.situation: You are preparing a proposal to win a school design project. A rival firm has a lower fee, and your team's fee is higher because of a longer design review.

options.text: Keep the fee and explain the value of the design review in the proposal.
Match the rival's fee and reduce the design review to cover the cost.
Match the rival's fee and bill extra for design changes after winning the work.
Show how the review cuts later changes and offer a shorter review option.

basic.situation: During a site visit, you see the contractor has used a thinner wall panel than the drawings show. The site supervisor says the change was approved.

options.text: Report the difference to the architect and mention what the supervisor said.
Accept the supervisor's word and note the thinner panel in your visit report.
Tell the contractor to replace the panels this week on your own authority.
Photograph the panel, ask for the approval record, and tell the architect.

advanced.situation: You lead a feasibility study for a hillside housing site. Early checks show the slope may need drainage works near a stream, which could breach environmental conditions.

options.text: Move the housing layout away from the stream and note it in the report.
Describe the drainage works as minor in the report so the client proceeds.
Report the stream risk to the client and recommend a further study first.
Finish the drainage assessment, consult the authority, and report the options.

basic.situation: You help two technicians prepare drawing sets for submission. One tells you he will finish his sheets by Friday, but the submission is Thursday.

options.text: Finish his sheets yourself on Thursday night and tell the team afterwards.
Submit the drawing set on Thursday and mark his unfinished sheets as final.
Check the sheets left, share them with the other technician, and tell your architect.
Remind the technician that the deadline is Thursday and ask for his progress by noon.

advanced.situation: The mechanical engineer's duct layout clashes with the structural beams in the design. The engineer says it is the architect's job to solve it.

options.text: Tell the engineers the clash is minor and ask them to resolve it on site.
Ask the structural engineer to change the beam level and inform the mechanical engineer.
Convene the engineers, review the clash on the model, and agree changes with both.
Move the duct yourself in the drawings and send both engineers the new version.

basic.situation: A client wants a small front garden with low water use. Your senior suggests drought-resistant plants, but the client loves a large lawn.

options.text: Draw the full lawn and add a few drought-resistant plants along the edges.
Draw the lawn as asked and suggest watering at night to save water.
Show a smaller lawn with drought-resistant beds, and the water saved.
Replace the lawn with plain gravel and show the client the result later.

advanced.situation: A resort project aims to use indigenous plants and recycled materials. The contractor offers cheaper imported stone and says local plant supply is limited.

options.text: Check local nursery supply and recycled stone options, then present costed choices.
Accept the imported stone for the paths and keep the indigenous planting list.
Switch to common imported plants that are easy to get from suppliers.
List the imported stone as recycled in the specification to keep the project's green claim.

basic.situation: You inspect a proposed park site with your supervisor. You see an old retaining wall at the back that is not on the survey plan.

options.text: Mention the wall in your site notes and move on to the other checks.
Tell your supervisor about the wall and wait for instructions on the plan.
Leave the wall off your notes since the survey plan does not show it.
Photograph the wall, mark it in your notes, and tell your supervisor.

advanced.situation: A client asks you to advise on persistent flooding at a new housing site. Rain drains toward the lowest lot, and the developer wants a quick fix.

options.text: Analyse the drainage data, propose options, and explain the trade-offs.
Recommend raising the level of the lowest lot with extra fill soil.
Recommend a larger drain for the lowest lot and report the cost.
Recommend directing the extra water to the neighbouring lot's boundary drain.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks for a simple sketch plan of a courtyard showing paths and planting areas. You have the dimensions but no drawing standard.

options.text: Copy a layout from a similar courtyard and change the sizes to fit.
Draw the plan neatly by hand and label the main areas for review.
Draw the paths in detail and leave the planting areas to be added later.
Draw it to scale with a north arrow and legend, then ask for a check.

advanced.situation: You must show a client how a new campus landscape will develop over ten years. They worry the first-year images will look bare.

options.text: Show year one with extra mature plants so the first images look full.
Prepare one drawing of year ten and explain how the plants will grow in.
Prepare drawings of years one, five and ten, with plant sizes shown to scale.
Use pictures of finished gardens from other projects and describe them as this design.

basic.situation: You attend a meeting with a client and an architect. The client says the pond should be larger, but the architect says the building edge is fixed.

options.text: Note both views, check the site dimensions, and tell your supervisor.
Note the client's request and pass it to the architect after the meeting.
Enlarge the pond in the drawings and let the architect find out later.
Note the architect's limit and tell the client the pond size cannot change.

advanced.situation: A building team asks you to help cut the energy use of a new office tower. Your idea of green walls adds weight, and the structural engineer is uneasy.

options.text: Test lighter green walls with the engineer and model the cooling benefit.
Add the green walls to the plans and leave the structural check for later.
Keep the green walls and ask the engineer to find a way to support them.
Propose trees and shading on the ground level instead and present the savings.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to help make slides for a community meeting on a new park design. You have drawings, plant lists and cost tables.

options.text: Paste the drawings and cost tables onto slides and send them for review.
Add attractive renderings from other parks to make the design look more finished.
Copy slides from a previous project and swap in the new park name and images.
Choose a few clear images, write short plain captions, and ask for a review.

advanced.situation: You lead a bid to design a city waterfront park. A rival is known for flashy images, while your strength is detailed flood and community planning.

options.text: Show your flood and community planning clearly, backed by strong images.
Describe past projects by other firms as your own to look more experienced.
Match the rival's flashy imagery and add a short page on flood planning.
Offer the lowest fee and list flood planning as an optional extra.

basic.situation: You watch a paving subcontractor lay stones. Some joints are wider than the specification, and the foreman says they will settle.

options.text: Sign the inspection form as passed so the paving crew can continue.
Accept the foreman's view and note the joints for review after settling.
Tell the foreman the joints look wide and ask him to check them.
Measure and photograph the joints, report the difference, and request rework.

advanced.situation: Three subcontractors maintain a large hotel garden, and you must set long-term care standards. Their crews differ in how often they prune and water.

options.text: Write a maintenance schedule with tasks and frequencies, and brief all crews.
Cut the maintenance frequencies to save money and review the garden later.
Give all crews the supplier's care sheets and ask them to follow it.
Let each crew continue its routine and check results at the end of the year.

basic.situation: A senior gives you a town map to revise. You notice a road name on the map differs from the name in the latest council records.

options.text: Update the road name from the council record and send the map back.
Change the name to the one shown on a popular online map and move on.
Check the council record, update the road name, and note the source.
Keep the old name and mention the difference to your senior at the weekly meeting.

advanced.situation: Your team produces maps in three different scales and colour styles, and customers complain about inconsistency. You are asked to set production standards.

options.text: Agree standard scales, projections and colours with the team and write them down.
Pick the scale and colours you prefer and apply them to every map.
Write a standard colour palette and leave the scales to each mapmaker.
Choose the style of the most popular map and tell the team to copy it.

basic.situation: You trace rivers and roads from an aerial photo. Part of a river is hidden under cloud shadow, and your supervisor is away.

options.text: Trace the visible parts, mark the hidden part uncertain, and request a new photo.
Trace the visible parts and flag the hidden section for your supervisor's return.
Draw the hidden section as a straight line joining the two visible parts.
Copy the river course from an old map and label it as traced.

advanced.situation: A client needs a 3D terrain model of a hill for a flood study. Your photo pairs overlap poorly in one area, which leaves holes in the model.

options.text: Capture extra photos for the poor area, rebuild the model there, and check heights.
Deliver the model with the holes and tell the client to avoid that area.
Fill the holes with heights from a different hill's model so the surface looks complete.
Fill the holes by smoothing between nearby heights and mark the area.

basic.situation: You collect survey notes and aerial photos for a new district map. One set of survey notes uses feet while the others use metres.

options.text: Convert the feet to metres, mark the change, and check a few points.
Assume all the notes use metres and enter the numbers into the database.
Use the numbers as they are and add a note about the units later.
Ask the surveyor which units were used and wait for a reply before using it.

advanced.situation: Two land title records give different boundary lines for the same lot, and the neighbours dispute the edge. You must draw the boundary on a planning map.

options.text: Draw the boundary from the record that favours the larger landowner on the lot.
Compare both records with the survey plan, show the dispute, and report it.
Draw the boundary halfway between the two lines to settle the matter fairly.
Draw the boundary from the newer record and note the conflict in the file.

basic.situation: You are scaling a set of elevation points for a topographic map using a standard formula. Your result for one point looks much higher than its neighbours.

options.text: Delete the point from the data set so it does not affect the map.
Average the point with its neighbours so the surface looks smooth on the map.
Recheck the inputs and arithmetic for that point and compare with neighbours.
Mark the point as unusual and move on to scaling the remaining points.

advanced.situation: Your team needs a faster way to scale features from drone photos, since the current method takes a week per area. You are asked to develop an improved method.

options.text: Test an automated method against the current one on a known area.
Reduce the number of control points used so each area is processed faster.
Adopt a method from a software tutorial and apply it to the next area.
Skip the accuracy check on the new method and report that it works.

basic.situation: Using a checklist, you inspect a finished tourist map. The checklist passes, but you notice a hospital icon sits across a river from its real location.

options.text: Pass the map since the checklist items are met and the icon is minor.
Move the icon to what looks like the proper place and pass the map.
Mark the icon error, verify the position with the source data, and report it.
Complete the checklist, pass the map, and mention the icon to your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You set accuracy standards for your department and train new staff on inspection. Staff disagree on how much position error is acceptable for city maps.

options.text: Let each inspector set a tolerance and record it in the inspection report.
Set a loose tolerance so that nearly every map passes inspection on time.
Adopt the tolerance of the strictest colleague and train staff on it.
Base the tolerance on the map's purpose and standards, then train staff.

basic.situation: A supervisor asks you to examine satellite images for new buildings in a district. Some images show cloud cover over a corner of the area.

options.text: List visible buildings, mark the cloudy corner unchecked, and request new images.
Copy building shapes from last year's map into the cloudy corner as new.
List visible buildings in the images and note the cloud cover in the final report.
Assume the cloudy corner has no new buildings and finish the building list.

advanced.situation: You are asked to design an algorithm to detect land cover change across thousands of satellite scenes. A first test flags many shadows as water.

options.text: Accept the shadow errors and remove false water areas manually after the run.
Add shadow and slope filters, test on labelled samples, and measure errors.
Report the first test as successful and run the algorithm on all scenes.
Raise the water threshold until fewer shadows are flagged and run it again.

basic.situation: You set up a total station to establish a control point for a road survey. The instrument's bubble level drifts slightly after you start recording.

options.text: Adjust the readings by a small amount to cancel the drift and keep going.
Re-level the instrument and continue recording from the next control point on the road.
Stop, re-level the instrument, and repeat the readings since the drift began.
Continue recording and note the small drift in your field book afterwards.

advanced.situation: You direct an aerial survey to set baselines for a long pipeline route. The pilot says wind may disrupt the planned flight lines tomorrow.

options.text: Fly the planned lines tomorrow as scheduled and record the wind conditions at each leg.
Fly shorter lines in the wind and join the data afterwards in the office.
Check the forecast, agree a backup window with the pilot, and prepare control.
Cancel the flight and use old photos of the route to set the baselines.

basic.situation: You calculate the height difference between two benchmarks from level readings. Your total misses the known benchmark height by 12 millimetres.

options.text: Report the misclosure to your supervisor and wait before using any values.
Check the field book for arithmetic errors, then repeat doubtful readings.
Adjust the last reading by 12 millimetres to force the line to close.
Spread the 12 millimetres evenly across the readings and note the misclosure.

advanced.situation: Survey data for a hillside shows two stations whose computed positions disagree with a satellite fix by half a metre. The client needs positions for slope studies.

options.text: Average the two position sets for those stations and report the mean values.
Use the satellite fix for those two stations and note the change in the report.
Review the geodetic computation and datum used, find the cause, and recompute.
Report the computed positions and describe the difference as within normal limits.

basic.situation: A client wants the boundary of a lot. At the land office you find the title, but the plan attached is faded and hard to read.

options.text: Redraw the faded plan from memory and note it as copied from the office.
Use the lot dimensions from the title and skip the faded plan for now.
Photograph the faded plan and work from that image after reading the title.
Request a clear copy of the plan, check it with the title, and record it.

advanced.situation: You are surveying a river channel for a planned jetty. Water levels are unusually high after rain, and the client wants the survey completed this week.

options.text: Use depth figures from a ten-year-old chart and mark the survey as complete.
Survey at the high water level and note the level on every sheet.
Record the level, reschedule the depth work, and tell the client.
Survey from the bank and estimate the channel depths from the bank profile.

basic.situation: You prepare a sketch map of a lot for a survey report. Your supervisor notes that the bearings on the sketch are listed in two different formats.

options.text: Add a short note explaining both bearing formats on the sketch and resubmit it.
Remove the bearings from the sketch so the formats do not conflict.
Convert all bearings to one format, recheck them, and resubmit the sketch.
Change the bearings that look unusual to the main format and resubmit.

advanced.situation: You must certify a survey and write the legal description for a deed. The client's lawyer asks you to describe the boundary using a fence that is not on your survey.

options.text: Use the fence in the description as requested and certify the survey as complete.
Include the fence in the description after a quick visit to confirm its position.
Describe the boundary from your measurements and explain why the fence is excluded.
Describe the boundary from your measurements and add a note about the fence.

basic.situation: Your levelling instrument's readings seem to drift a little over the day. The calibration due date is next week.

options.text: Test it on a known baseline, adjust if needed, and tell your supervisor.
Stop using the instrument and ask your supervisor to arrange a replacement.
Keep using the instrument until the calibration date next week and note the drift.
Adjust the readings in your notes at day end to remove the drift.

advanced.situation: You are asked to develop criteria for survey methods for a new rail corridor. The client's budget favours a cheaper method that gives lower accuracy.

options.text: Set criteria from the design's accuracy needs, then compare methods and costs.
Choose the cheaper method and lower the accuracy target in the proposal.
Choose the cheaper method and keep the accuracy claims from the accurate one.
Choose the more accurate method and ask the client to raise the budget.

basic.situation: You deliver survey findings to an engineering team. The engineer asks for the elevation of a point you have not measured.

options.text: Give a likely value from a similar site and describe it as measured.
Say the point was not measured, offer to survey it, and give nearby elevations.
Interpolate from the nearest points and give the engineer the value with a note.
Give the elevation of the nearest measured point as the engineer's answer.

advanced.situation: You are called as an expert witness in a boundary case. The opposing lawyer asks whether a survey by another firm could also be right.

options.text: Say your result is certain and refuse to discuss any other firm's survey.
Say you have not reviewed it, so you cannot say if it is right.
Say the other survey is probably flawed, since yours used newer instruments.
Answer from your methods and data, and state what checks would resolve it.

basic.situation: You measure elevations at twelve points with a digital level for a dam monitoring survey. Rain starts halfway through, and the display begins to fog.

options.text: Finish all the points quickly and note the weather in your field book.
Pause, shelter the instrument, and repeat the last points after the rain.
Cover the instrument and keep measuring the remaining points through the rain.
Wipe the display and keep measuring, then adjust any odd readings later by eye.

advanced.situation: A client's tract has old boundary marks that do not fit the deed dimensions. Your theodolite and satellite readings agree with each other but not with the deed.

options.text: Use the deed dimensions and reset the boundary marks to match them.
Use your readings for the boundary and note the deed difference in the report.
Compare marks, deed and readings, document the conflict, and refer it upward.
Keep the old marks as the boundary and describe the readings as matching the deed.

basic.situation: You compute coordinates for a control point from field observations. The computed height differs from a nearby published benchmark by 8 millimetres.

options.text: Edit a few observations slightly so the computed height agrees with the benchmark.
Recheck the computation and observations, then report the difference with working.
Report the 8 millimetre difference to your supervisor with the raw observations.
Use the published benchmark height and adjust your computed height to match it.

advanced.situation: You must adjust an old highway alignment survey to fit the national geodetic grid. The old survey used a local datum, and the two do not match at several points.

options.text: Shift the whole survey by the average offset and report the new coordinates.
Adjust the points that are furthest from the grid and leave the rest.
Transform using official parameters, check the residuals, and document it.
Keep the local datum values and label them as national grid coordinates.

basic.situation: A field crew sends you traverse data to verify before it goes to the client. The angles do not sum to the expected total.

options.text: Return the data to the crew and ask them to resurvey all the angles.
Mark the data as verified and pass it on to the client today.
Check the angle sums, then ask the crew to recheck doubtful angles.
Share the angle error equally among the angles and pass the data on.

advanced.situation: Control data for a bridge project has uneven quality, with some stations observed once and others several times. The engineers need positions within 10 millimetres.

options.text: Request extra observations at every station before the design starts.
Accept all stations as they are and state that 10 millimetres is met.
Assess quality, find the weak stations, and request more observations there.
Use the stations observed several times and drop the weaker ones.

basic.situation: You review a completed control survey against the project specification. The specification calls for 1:10,000 closure, and the survey achieved 1:8,000.

options.text: Report the shortfall to your supervisor and suggest checks to meet the specification.
Report that the survey nearly meets the specification and recommend acceptance today.
Accept the survey because the closure is close to the required specification.
Round the closure up to 1:10,000 in the report and approve the survey.

advanced.situation: Your section's old total station has been giving poorer results each year. A manager asks whether to upgrade or keep using it.

options.text: Recommend keeping it since it still works and the budget is tight this year.
Recommend lowering the accuracy goals in the project standards to match the instrument.
Compare recent accuracy with project needs, cost the upgrade, and advise on a change.
Recommend buying the newest model available to keep your section up to date.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks for a weekly progress report on a network survey. You have finished 6 of 10 stations, but two days were lost to rain.

options.text: Report that 6 of 10 stations are done and leave the schedule as it is.
Report that 8 of 10 stations are done, expecting to catch up this week.
Report the survey as on schedule and plan to make up the time later.
Report stations done, days lost to rain, and a revised completion date.

advanced.situation: You maintain a database of control point coordinates used by many surveyors. A user reports a coordinate that differs from a recent survey result by 20 millimetres.

options.text: Add the recent result as a second value and tell the user both exist.
Check the source records, update the value with a note, and flag its quality.
Replace the value with the user's result and delete the old record from history.
Leave the database value as it is until the next scheduled quality review.

basic.situation: You train two new assistants to observe a control network. One keeps reading the instrument scale too quickly and recording the numbers loosely.

options.text: Pair the assistant with a faster colleague and review notes at day end.
Tell the assistant to read faster and trust the instrument to catch mistakes.
Give the assistant a written checklist and ask them to follow it.
Demonstrate the steps, watch their first observations, and give feedback.

advanced.situation: You lead a team of five on a large geodetic project. Two experienced members disagree over observation methods, and work slows down.

options.text: Split the team so each member can use the preferred method on separate areas.
Meet both, review the specification, and decide the method with reasons.
Let the two test both methods on one area and compare their results.
Choose the more senior member's method and tell the team to follow it.

basic.situation: You run a vibration test on a small wing model with a supervisor's test plan. Midway, one sensor reading jumps well beyond the expected range.

options.text: Replace the odd reading with the average of nearby sensors and continue.
Remove that sensor from the test data and report the results as complete.
Continue the test and mark the odd reading for review after the run.
Pause the test, check the sensor, and tell your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You set test criteria for a new composite fuselage panel. Management wants a shorter test schedule, but fatigue failures often appear late in the cycle.

options.text: Shorten the test and apply a safety factor to the final results.
Keep the full fatigue cycle count, then add test rigs to save time.
End the test at the first scheduled review and report the panel as passed.
Test fewer panels for the full cycle count and extend the results to the rest.

basic.situation: You check a bracket design against the engineering standard. The drawing shows a hole closer to the edge than the standard allows.

options.text: Change the hole position on the drawing yourself and approve the bracket.
Note the issue in your review and ask a senior engineer for advice.
Approve the bracket since the margin is small and the part is minor.
Flag the hole position as non-conforming and send it to the designer.

advanced.situation: Inspection reports show a supplier's turbine blades meet size limits but have surface marks. A programme manager wants the delivery accepted this week.

options.text: Accept the blades and record the marks as cosmetic in the quality file.
Reject the whole delivery and ask the supplier to rework every blade now.
Evaluate the marks against criteria, consult the stress team, and decide.
Accept the blades with a note on the marks for follow-up inspection.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks for a rough concept sketch of a small drone for crop monitoring. The customer wants long flight time and low cost.

options.text: Sketch one concept with a large battery and a long wing for endurance.
Sketch two concepts that trade wing size against battery life.
Sketch a concept with the cheapest parts and list flight time as long.
Sketch a drone like a popular commercial model and adjust its size slightly.

advanced.situation: A computer model of a wing structure disagrees with ground test strain readings by 18 percent in one region. A design change decision is due tomorrow.

options.text: Present the model results as validated and note the test data are noisy.
Scale the model results up by 18 percent in that region and then proceed.
Check mesh and loads there, update the model, and state the confidence.
Report the 18 percent gap and ask for the decision to be delayed.

basic.situation: You file performance reports from flight tests for future reference. One report is missing a page, and the test lead is on leave.

options.text: Hold the report outside the filing system until the missing page is found.
File the report as received and wait for the test lead to return.
Recreate the missing page from the test summary and file it as original.
Note the missing page in the record and ask the test lead's deputy.

advanced.situation: You are asked to write a handbook for technicians on a new engine inspection method. Different teams document similar steps in inconsistent ways.

options.text: Write the handbook from the most detailed team's steps and share it.
Publish the manufacturer's manual as the handbook and tell all teams to comply.
Draft a standard template with the teams and test it on one procedure.
Collect each team's documents into one binder and add an index page.

basic.situation: You help coordinate a small test setup with two technicians. One needs a part that another team is holding, and the test is tomorrow.

options.text: Ask the other team when the part is free and tell your engineer.
Order a replacement part and charge it to the other team's budget.
Borrow the part from the other team's bench and tell them afterwards.
Tell the technician to wait and check with the other team tomorrow.

advanced.situation: You direct a team designing a landing gear component. A junior engineer proposes a lighter design, but a senior engineer says it overlooks fatigue loads.

options.text: Let the junior proceed and ask for a fatigue check at the end.
Support the senior engineer's view and ask the junior to learn from it.
Have the two review the fatigue loads together, then decide and say why.
Approve the lighter design and tell the junior to sign off the fatigue check.

basic.situation: You log customer reports of cabin noise on a small aircraft model. Three reports describe the same noise but use different words.

options.text: Close all three reports as normal noise to keep the log tidy.
Log the clearest report and close the other two as duplicates.
Log the three reports separately and mention the similarity in a note.
Group the reports in one entry, keep each wording, and tell your engineer.

advanced.situation: A customer reports an engine control fault on two aircraft. Initial checks show different symptoms, and the customer wants an answer within days.

options.text: Plan the investigation, collect fault logs from both, and update the customer.
Tell the customer the fault is a known software issue and send a patch.
Treat the two faults as one problem and apply a known fix to both.
Investigate one aircraft first and tell the customer the second one follows later.

basic.situation: You draft a plan for a small goat shelter. Your supervisor reminds you to allow for ventilation and drainage, but the farmer wants it built cheaply.

options.text: Draw the shelter as the farmer wants it and add a note on drainage.
Draw the shelter with a closed roof and solid walls to keep costs down.
Include vents and a sloped floor drain, and show the extra cost.
Draw the cheap design as requested and add a vent on the front wall.

advanced.situation: You lead design of a grain storage and drying facility for a cooperative. The site is flood-prone, and the cooperative wants the lowest construction cost.

options.text: Build at ground level as planned and add flood barriers at the doors.
Raise the floor above flood level, compare costs, and explain the risk.
Leave the flood risk out of the design report to keep the cost low.
Build at ground level and set aside money to repair damage after any flood.

basic.situation: Using CAD, you sketch a bracket for a seed planter. Your supervisor says the hole spacing must match an existing part, but the dimensions are missing.

options.text: Estimate the spacing by eye from a photo and finish the sketch.
Use standard hole spacing from a catalogue and finish the sketch today.
Ask your supervisor for the drawing and pause the sketch until it arrives.
Measure the existing part, match the hole spacing, and confirm it.

advanced.situation: A university asks you to design a soil moisture sensor system for field trials. The first prototype drifts in hot weather and gives unreliable readings.

options.text: Test across temperatures, find the drift source, and add compensation.
Replace the sensor with a higher priced model and use it in trials.
Apply a fixed correction to all readings and describe the data as reliable.
Add a manual calibration step before each reading and train the users.

basic.situation: You help plan an irrigation layout for a small plantation. Your supervisor gave you a field sketch, and one corner lies higher than the water source.

options.text: Draw the layout from the sketch and ask your supervisor about the high corner.
Draw the pipes to that corner and expect the water to reach it.
Check elevations, flag the high corner, and propose a pump route.
Draw the layout as if the whole field is level and skip the corner.

advanced.situation: You direct a land reclamation project on a former mining site for crops. Test pits show acidic soil, and the client wants planting to start next month.

options.text: Report the soil as suitable and start planting next month as the client wants.
Plan soil treatment first, then agree a revised planting date with the client.
Plant the originally planned crops and add fertiliser to offset the soil acidity.
Start planting acid-tolerant crops next month and treat the soil as they grow.

basic.situation: You prepare a short report with sketches for a small farm drainage project. The supervisor asks you to add a cost estimate, and prices for pipes have changed.

options.text: Use last year's price list and tell your supervisor it is out of date.
Get current pipe prices, build the estimate, and state the price date.
Use last year's prices raised by a flat ten percent and present the estimate.
Leave pipe costs out of the estimate and present the other costs as the total.

advanced.situation: You prepare the budget and specifications for a multi-site irrigation scheme across four farms. Each farm has a different soil and water source, and the funder wants one total.

options.text: Cost each site separately, add shared items, and state your assumptions.
Use the average cost per hectare from one farm for all four sites.
Cost the largest farm in detail and scale its figure up to the others.
Give the funder the lowest quote for each item across all four sites.

basic.situation: On a site visit to a farm, you see muddy runoff flowing from a freshly ploughed field into a stream. Your supervisor is unreachable.

options.text: Tell the farmer about the runoff and leave a message for your supervisor.
Leave the runoff out of the report so the farm is not in trouble.
Photograph the runoff, note where and when, and tell your supervisor.
Mention the runoff in your visit notes and move on to your other checks.

advanced.situation: A harvester that you tested keeps overheating during long runs in the field. The dealer wants a quick sign-off, and the busy season is near.

options.text: Sign off now and ask the dealer to report any overheating cases later.
Sign off with a warning about long runs and a note to the dealer.
Log temperatures in a longer test, find the cause, and hold the sign-off.
Sign off and describe the overheating as normal for this type of harvester.

basic.situation: You attend a meeting where a farmer explains a drainage problem to you and a contractor. You are there to listen and take notes.

options.text: Write down what you think the problem is and share that version of the notes.
Write down the main points and send the notes to your supervisor later.
Write down the contractor's solutions and add the farmer's points if time allows.
Write down the farmer's points, confirm them back to him, and share the notes.

advanced.situation: A regional council asks you to advise on a river that has become polluted by farm run-off. Farmers say any new rules will raise their costs.

options.text: Review the water data, propose practical controls with costs, and consult farmers.
Recommend voluntary guidelines for farmers and a review of the river after one year.
Recommend strict limits on fertiliser use across the catchment based on the data.
Advise the council that the pollution likely comes from other sources, not farms.

basic.situation: You help evaluate a new infusion pump prototype. During your test, the alarm sounds two seconds late on one of ten trials.

options.text: Record the delay, repeat the trial several times, and report it.
Count the late alarm as a one-off and report the pump as passing.
Leave the late trial out of the results since nine trials passed.
Report the late alarm to your supervisor and continue with the remaining trials.

advanced.situation: You lead the design of a handheld blood glucose monitor. Early tests show results vary with room temperature, and a launch date is near.

options.text: Fix the test conditions to one room temperature and report those results.
Add a warning label about room temperature and keep the launch date.
Report the temperature variation as normal for such devices in the design file.
Measure the temperature effect, add compensation, and validate before launch.

basic.situation: You run a simple simulation of blood flow in a narrowed artery. Your supervisor gave you the settings, but the output shows a pressure value that seems far too high.

options.text: Check the units and settings, rerun the simulation, and tell your supervisor.
Report the high value to your supervisor and wait for further guidance on it.
Report the output as it is and note that the supervisor set the inputs.
Scale the pressure values down to a typical range and report the output.

advanced.situation: You build a statistical model of how a growth factor affects cell culture yield. The model fits well on your data, but it is based on 12 batches.

options.text: Present the model as proven for production use based on the fit.
Add more variables to improve the fit until the model explains the data.
Report the good fit and mention that the data came from 12 batches.
Validate on new batches, report the uncertainty, and state the limits.

basic.situation: You help write the steps for moving a cell culture process from the lab to a pilot bioreactor. A step uses a glass vessel that does not scale.

options.text: Flag the glass vessel step and ask the team for a scalable option.
Replace the vessel with a larger glass one and keep other steps the same.
Remove the vessel step from the document to keep the transfer simple.
Write the steps as they are done in the lab and flag the vessel.

advanced.situation: You set the standards for moving a biological process from lab to commercial production. Yield dropped 20 percent in the first scale-up trial.

options.text: Set a standard that accepts yield drops up to 20 percent at scale-up.
Remove the pilot stage from the standard and scale straight to commercial volume.
Require staged scale-up checks and study the yield drop before moving on.
Repeat the same scale-up trial with the process unchanged to check the result.

basic.situation: You draft a user manual for a hospital ventilator accessory. The safety sheet from the supplier lists a cleaning agent that damages the plastic.

options.text: Flag the cleaning agent, ask the supplier for a safe option, and tell your supervisor.
Copy the supplier's cleaning steps into the manual and add a general warning.
Remove the cleaning section from the manual to avoid raising the problem.
Ask the supplier about a safe cleaning agent and wait before drafting that section.

advanced.situation: A regulator asks your company for added test data on an implant. Your manager wants a short, general reply to avoid delays.

options.text: Send the data you already have and promise the remaining data later.
Tell the regulator the requested data is confidential and decline to provide it.
Send the short general reply your manager wants and wait for follow-up questions.
Review the request, supply the data, and agree timelines with the regulator.

basic.situation: You maintain a database of experiment results. A colleague sends data in a spreadsheet with units missing for one column.

options.text: Enter the data using the units from the previous experiment in the database.
Enter the data and fill the units with whatever the other columns use.
Enter the data and note that the units are missing in the comments.
Ask the colleague for the units and hold the entry until confirmed.

advanced.situation: You write a research article on a new tissue scaffold. A key figure supports your claim, but one trial run gave a different outcome.

options.text: Include the figure and mention the different run in the methods section.
Include all trials, explain the odd run, and show the full data.
Remove the different run from the dataset and publish the figure as is.
Add a footnote that one run was unusual and exclude it from the figure.

basic.situation: You help make a timeline for installing a new lab incubator. The vendor's delivery date has slipped by two weeks.

options.text: Update the timeline, check which tasks depend on delivery, and tell your manager.
Cut the testing tasks by two weeks so the end date stays the same.
Keep the original timeline and ask the vendor to speed up the delivery.
Shift all later tasks by two weeks and send the timeline to your manager.

advanced.situation: A hospital administrator asks whether to buy a new imaging machine or upgrade the old one. The new machine costs twice as much.

options.text: Recommend the new machine since newer devices are generally more reliable overall.
Recommend the upgrade since it costs less and avoids changes in staff training.
Compare costs, usage, support and clinical needs, then advise in writing.
Recommend the option the vendor's sales team suggests and share their brochure.

basic.situation: You monitor data from a lab reactor run. The temperature trace shows a steady rise above the setpoint for 10 minutes.

options.text: Check the controller and cooling flow, log the deviation, and tell your supervisor.
Log the deviation and tell your supervisor once the run has finished.
Raise the setpoint to match the new temperature and continue the run.
Delete the high temperature readings from the log so the run looks stable.
