advanced.situation: You lead a team developing a new process to cut solvent use. A promising trial gave 15 percent higher yield, but just one batch was run.

options.text: Replicate the trial, check the data, and plan scale-up if it holds.
Report the 15 percent gain to management and propose a scale-up now.
Change the plant settings to the trial conditions across all current batches.
Run two more batches next week and report the results to management.

basic.situation: You assist with a lab study of a new mixing step. Your protocol says to hold 60 degrees, but the heater struggles above 55.

options.text: Run at 55 degrees and note the change in your lab book afterwards.
Use a second heater from another lab to reach 60 degrees and continue.
Record 60 degrees in your lab book as the temperature held for the run.
Record the temperature reached, tell your supervisor, and wait for a decision.

advanced.situation: Your pilot plant trial for a new product shows a different by-product level than the lab study. The customer wants a decision on the process by Friday.

options.text: Use the pilot level for the customer decision and change the lab report.
Report both sets of results and recommend further pilot runs before deciding.
Investigate the by-product difference, share interim findings, and propose a decision timeline.
Use the lab results for the decision and note the pilot difference.

basic.situation: You help prepare a production cost estimate. A supplier's quote for a solvent is missing, and your manager needs the estimate today.

options.text: Use a low solvent price so the total looks competitive for management.
Ask the supplier to rush the quote and delay the estimate until it arrives.
Use the last invoice price, label it an estimate, and update it later.
Leave the solvent cost out of the estimate and note it is pending.

advanced.situation: You set the format for monthly cost reports across three plants. Plants count labour and energy costs differently, which makes comparison hard.

options.text: Use the largest plant's cost categories for all three plants from next month.
Ask each plant to add a note explaining how it counts its costs.
Agree one cost category list with the plants and test it on last month.
Convert all costs to the cheapest plant's method and adjust the reported numbers.

basic.situation: You monitor pressure in a distillation column during a shift. The pressure drifts slowly upward but stays within the alarm limit.

options.text: Raise the alarm limit slightly so the drift stays inside the range.
Adjust the controller setpoint downward on your own to bring the pressure back.
Keep watching the pressure and report the trend if it reaches the limit.
Note the trend, check the condenser, and tell the shift lead.

advanced.situation: Product purity has been falling for three weeks in a plant process. Operators blame the new raw material, while the supplier says it meets specification.

options.text: Ask the supplier for fresh batch certificates and re-check the purity trends.
Review process data and lab results, test the raw material, and find the cause.
Switch back to the old raw material for now while you study the problem.
Tell operators to adjust settings until the purity reading looks normal on the log.

basic.situation: You help decide the order of mixing and heating steps for a small batch process. Two arrangements seem possible, and your senior asked for your view.

options.text: Compare both arrangements on time, energy and safety, and explain your choice.
Pick the faster arrangement and tell your senior the safety checks can follow.
Pick the arrangement with fewer steps and send it to your senior for comment.
Pick the arrangement used in the last plant you visited and send it on.

advanced.situation: You are asked to design the safety system for a new reactor handling a toxic gas. The budget allows one gas detector per room.

options.text: Place the detector at the likeliest leak point and add a manual alarm.
Use a lower-grade detector in each room to fit more rooms in the budget.
Follow the budget and add warning signs near the reactor door and exit.
Assess leak scenarios, justify extra detectors and shutoffs, and present the risk.

basic.situation: You assist in developing a procedure to separate two liquids by distillation. Early runs give a mixed product, and the senior suggests changing the reflux ratio.

options.text: Report the purest sample from the early runs as the typical product quality.
Test a higher reflux ratio in a controlled run and record the purity.
Cut the feed rate by half and check whether the product is purer.
Change the reflux ratio on the main unit and see whether purity improves.

advanced.situation: You direct workers building an absorption unit. A crew leader says a weld test failed and wants to carry on to meet the handover date.

options.text: Accept the weld and mark the test as passed to protect the handover date.
Retest the weld in the afternoon and continue with other sections meanwhile today.
Stop work on that section, repair and retest the weld, and inform management.
Continue the build and plan to repair the weld during the first shutdown.

basic.situation: On a site visit, you see the contractor has placed rebar at wider spacing than the drawings show for a slab. The foreman says it is the same strength.

options.text: Measure the spacing, record it in your report, and tell the engineer.
Ask the foreman for the contractor's calculation and wait before reporting back.
Tell the contractor to pour the slab so the schedule is not delayed.
Accept the foreman's word and note the wider spacing in your visit report.

advanced.situation: You lead a survey to set grades for a drainage channel. The crew's benchmark was set from a point that a loader may have moved yesterday.

options.text: Ask the crew to confirm the benchmark is stable and continue the survey.
Continue the survey and compare the results with the earlier survey this week.
Reset the benchmark to the design elevation so the new grades match the plan.
Check the benchmark against a second reference and resurvey if they disagree.

basic.situation: You estimate concrete quantity for a small retaining wall using your supervisor's template. The drawing shows a footing you cannot find in the template.

options.text: Leave the footing out of the estimate since the template does not list it.
Add ten percent to the wall volume to allow for the footing.
Add a footing line, calculate its volume, and show your supervisor.
Estimate the wall part and tell your supervisor the footing is missing.

advanced.situation: You build a cost model for a coastal highway feasibility study. Land prices could change a lot, and the sponsor wants a single cost figure.

options.text: Model low, expected and high land costs, and present the range.
Use a low land price so the project appears affordable to the sponsor.
Use the expected land price and add a ten percent contingency to the total.
Use last year's land prices because they are already verified by the office.

basic.situation: You read a site plan to find where a pipeline crosses a road. The plan's scale bar and the printed scale give different values.

options.text: Check against the survey data and ask the drafter which scale applies.
Use the printed scale since it is written on the title block of the plan.
Measure the crossing with a ruler and assume the scale is close to 1:500.
Use the scale bar and note the doubt on your calculation sheet.

advanced.situation: Borehole logs show a soft clay layer under part of a planned building. The structural design assumed uniform firm soil across the whole footprint.

options.text: Order more boreholes and hold the whole design until all results arrive.
Keep the design and list the clay layer as a minor risk in the report.
Review the logs, brief the designer, and propose options for that zone.
Increase footing sizes across the whole building to cover the weaker soil.

basic.situation: You draw a culvert section in CAD under supervision. Your supervisor's sketch shows the pipe diameter, but the dimension is missing for the headwall.

options.text: Scale the headwall from the sketch with a ruler and draw it in.
Draw the headwall using a standard size and flag it in the notes.
Make up a headwall size that looks reasonable and submit the drawing.
Ask your supervisor for the headwall size, then draw it once confirmed.

advanced.situation: You lead a design team for a school building and must reduce energy use. The client wants a glass facade, which raises cooling needs.

options.text: Reduce the glass area in the drawings and inform the client later on.
Keep the glass facade and add a larger air conditioning plant to cope.
Model the cooling load and propose shading and glazing options to the client.
Keep the glass facade and report the cooling load using a lower value.

basic.situation: You help prepare a bid report with your supervisor. A table of quantities uses two different totals for the same item.

options.text: Use the lower total so the bid price looks competitive to the client.
Remove the item from the table so the totals do not conflict.
Use the higher total to stay safe and tell your supervisor.
Check both totals against the drawings, then fix the table.

advanced.situation: You direct a building site where heavy rain has flooded the excavation. The schedule is tight, and subcontractors are waiting to start.

options.text: Start subcontractors on dry areas while the excavation is pumped out.
Pump out the water, check the walls, and re-plan the work sequence.
Order work to resume at once in the flooded excavation to recover time.
Wait for the water to drain naturally and resume work when it clears.

basic.situation: You review a site plan against basic safety rules. Scaffolding is erected next to a road, and the walkway for pedestrians is blocked.

options.text: Report the blocked walkway to the safety officer and note it in writing.
Add a note to your report suggesting a signboard to guide pedestrians.
Mention the blocked walkway to the foreman and check it again tomorrow.
Leave the walkway issue to be raised at the monthly safety review.

advanced.situation: A senior manager asks whether a cracked bridge pier should be repaired or replaced. Inspection data show the crack is growing slowly.

options.text: Recommend replacement since it removes the long-term risk of cracking.
Recommend waiting until the crack becomes visible to the people using the bridge.
Recommend repair now and ask for monthly crack measurements afterwards.
Compare repair and replacement on safety and cost, and propose monitoring limits.

basic.situation: A developer submits plans for a 200-unit housing block near a school. You are asked to review them for possible traffic impact.

options.text: Note that the road is already busy and ask the developer to reduce units.
Approve the traffic section since the developer's consultant already prepared one.
Compare the unit count with similar developments and report the likely trips.
Check expected trips against the road capacity and flag the school access.

advanced.situation: A town council asks you to study a junction with many crashes. The signal timings are old, and drivers complain about long waits.

options.text: Add a stop sign at the busiest entrance to slow the traffic.
Retime the signals using the typical rush hour pattern and monitor crashes afterwards.
Shorten the waits for drivers by lengthening the green phase on every approach.
Collect crash and traffic data, model new signal timings, and recommend changes.

basic.situation: You check a draft cost estimate for a road widening. The totals sheet adds up, but one line item has a unit rate that seems very low.

options.text: Accept the estimate because the totals sheet adds up and looks neat.
Compare the rate with recent tenders, flag it, and ask the estimator.
Tell the estimator the rate seems low and ask for a supplier quote.
Raise the unit rate to a figure that makes the total look reasonable.

advanced.situation: Your team's design checking varies by engineer, and two bridge designs went to tender with missed errors. You are asked to set a checking protocol.

options.text: Require a senior sign-off stamp on each design and drop the detailed checks.
Draft a protocol with checklists and independent checks, and trial it.
Ask each engineer to double check their own work before sending designs.
Assign the most experienced engineer to review every design from now on.

basic.situation: You inspect delivered asphalt documents for a road job. The supplier's certificate shows the mix, but a required environmental test result is missing.

options.text: Check the mix details against the contract and accept the delivery today.
Ask the supplier for the test result and hold the material until it arrives.
Accept the material and note the missing result in your inspection log.
Mark the environmental test as received to match the other delivery documents.

advanced.situation: An environmental impact statement for a new highway ramp underestimates noise at a nearby school. The project team wants to keep to the programme.

options.text: Accept the statement as written and mark the noise issue as resolved.
Accept the statement and recommend monitoring noise after the ramp opens to traffic.
Request a noise re-assessment, document the gap, and propose mitigation.
Note the concern in your review and ask for a noise barrier.

basic.situation: You prepare a final layout drawing for a bus stop with stress calculations for the shelter slab. Your supervisor's numbers use a load you think is too low.

options.text: Use your supervisor's load and add a note questioning the value in the drawing.
Use the higher load in your own calculation and keep both versions on file.
Compare the load with the design code and ask your supervisor to confirm.
Use your supervisor's load and delete the calculation notes that show it.

advanced.situation: You design a rural road using recycled materials to cut cost and emissions. The contractor doubts the recycled base will meet strength requirements.

options.text: Use the recycled base on shorter test sections and compare performance over time.
Use the recycled base with a thicker layer chosen by general judgement.
Test recycled samples against strength requirements and adjust the mix or thickness.
Specify the recycled base and state in the report that testing is complete.

basic.situation: You help prepare a monthly report on traffic counts. The count at one junction is far above the usual level because of a road closure nearby.

options.text: Report the count, explain the closure, and show the usual level.
Report the count and add a short note about the road closure.
Replace the count with last month's average and report that figure instead.
Remove the junction from the report so the monthly trend looks steady.

advanced.situation: You lead a public hearing on a new bypass. Residents are angry about noise, and the traffic data you present is technical.

options.text: Tell residents that noise levels are within limits and move to other items.
Present the full technical data and offer written answers after the hearing.
Present simple maps and clear figures, explain assumptions, and record resident concerns.
Shorten the presentation and refer residents to the website for more details.

basic.situation: You assist a survey crew staking out a culvert. The crew leader gives you stake positions, and one position falls on an existing buried cable marker.

options.text: Stake it as given and tell the contractor to take extra care digging.
Remove the cable marker so the stake can stay in the planned position.
Hold that stake, tell the crew leader, and wait for the cable check.
Move the stake slightly away from the marker and record the shift.

advanced.situation: A school entrance road has frequent near misses at drop-off time. Parents blame drivers, and the school wants a quick fix.

options.text: Recommend closing the entrance road permanently and sending all parents elsewhere.
Observe drop-off, record conflicts, and recommend separating cars from walking children.
Recommend a lower speed limit and signs along the entrance road at drop-off.
Recommend that the school staggers class end times to reduce the crowding.

basic.situation: You are asked to pick a standard pump for a small wastewater lift station. Two catalogue models meet the flow, but one has a higher power rating.

options.text: Pick the pump with the higher rating to keep a safety margin in hand.
Pick the pump you used on your last project and mark it as checked.
Pick the cheaper pump and note that it meets the minimum flow needed.
Check head, flow and site rules, and recommend one with reasons.

advanced.situation: You design a treatment plant extension for an industrial estate. The factory wastes include metals that the standard process may not remove.

options.text: Identify the metals, test treatment options, and add a removal stage.
Design the standard process and state in the report that metals are removed.
Design the standard process and ask each factory to pre-treat its wastewater.
Design the standard process and plan to check the effluent after startup.

basic.situation: You help forecast water demand for a housing area. The utility's meter data has gaps for two months because of a billing system fault.

options.text: Fill the gap months with the average of all the other months.
Mark the gap months, use similar past months, and state the assumption.
Calculate demand from the months available and report the shorter data period.
Set the gap months to zero and calculate the average demand from that.

advanced.situation: You lead the environmental impact assessment for a new sewage treatment outfall. A fisher group says discharge will harm their fishing area.

options.text: Include the fishing area, model the discharge dispersion, and meet the group.
Describe the fishing area as unaffected in the assessment based on assumptions.
Note that the outfall meets standard limits and leave the fishing area out.
Report the group's concern in the assessment and refer it to the authority.

basic.situation: You review a water supply model result for a small town. The model shows low pressure at one hilltop street at peak demand.

options.text: Check the inputs for that street and confirm the pressure in the field.
Add a note about the low pressure and finish your review of the model.
Tell your senior about the low pressure and wait for a clear decision.
Raise the pump pressure setting in the model so the street shows adequate pressure.

advanced.situation: A riverbank is eroding near a village after repeated floods. The council wants a stabilization plan, and the cheapest option is a concrete wall.

options.text: Recommend moving the village's drainage outlet onto the riverbank slope to reduce flow.
Recommend the concrete wall and add planting on the bank above it.
Recommend placing rock fill along the whole bank based on past practice here.
Analyse flows and bank conditions, compare options, and propose a design.

basic.situation: You help identify options for a new village water source. Your senior lists a river intake and a borehole, and asks you to suggest others.

options.text: Suggest trucking in water from a neighbouring town until a source is found.
Add a second borehole to the list since it is similar to the first.
Suggest a larger river intake since the river is the nearest water source.
Review nearby sources and rainwater harvesting, and list pros and cons.

advanced.situation: You must model how a chemical spill would spread in a reservoir that supplies a town. The 3D model needs lake depth data, but the survey is old.

options.text: Update depth data with a quick survey, run the model, and state uncertainty.
Run the model with the old data and mention that the survey is dated.
Use depth data from a different reservoir and report the dispersion as accurate.
Assume a uniform depth for the whole reservoir and run a simple model.

basic.situation: You draft a short report on household water use for a small township. Your data is a table of monthly usage by district.

options.text: Replace the district figures with a national average so the report is complete.
Describe the data source, summarise usage by district, and state the limits.
Copy the table into the report and write a one sentence summary.
Describe the usage with a chart and leave out the data source.

advanced.situation: You oversee construction of septic-style systems for twenty rural homes. An installer wants to place a tank close to a well to save piping.

options.text: Approve the placement and plan to test the well water after a month.
Accept the placement if the installer adds extra sealing to the tank lid.
Check the separation distance, stop that placement, and agree a new position.
Ask the installer to move the tank a few metres from the well.

basic.situation: A junior technician asks you how to check a pipe layout for a pump station. Your senior has gone to a site meeting.

options.text: Tell the technician to copy a previous layout and adjust the pipe sizes.
Ask the technician to wait until your senior returns before starting the check.
Explain the checking steps, review the layout together, and tell your senior.
Tell the technician to mark the layout as checked to keep things moving.

advanced.situation: You supervise a team recommending a treatment method for a food factory's wastewater. Two engineers favour biological treatment, while one prefers chemical dosing.

options.text: Compare methods on pilot results, cost and sludge, and guide a team decision.
Choose biological treatment since two engineers prefer it and move ahead with design.
Let each engineer prepare a design and send all of them to the client.
Choose chemical dosing since it is faster to start up and easier to control.

basic.situation: You select a memory chip for a product with a spec sheet from your lead. The preferred chip has a long lead time, and a cheaper chip is in stock.

options.text: Choose the stocked chip and edit the spec sheet so the chip complies.
Compare the stocked chip with the spec and ask your lead.
Choose the stocked chip since it is cheaper and available right away.
Order the preferred chip and tell your lead about the long lead time.

advanced.situation: You lead the design of a custom chip. Late simulation shows a timing path that fails at the highest clock speed, with a tape-out date close.

options.text: Analyse the failing path, fix the design, and re-run timing before tape-out.
Lower the clock speed target and note the change in the product specification.
Tape out on schedule and plan to fix the timing in the next version.
Add a small timing margin to the failing path and move on to tape-out.

basic.situation: You record test data for a new circuit board under supervision. One board fails the power-on test, and the other nine pass.

options.text: Record the failure with board details and report it to your supervisor.
Leave the failed board out of the test record since nine others passed.
Record all ten results and tell your supervisor at the end of the day.
Retest the failed board until it passes and record that final result.

advanced.situation: Simulation data shows your prototype board overheats under heavy load. The standard limit is strict, and the product launch is in six weeks.

options.text: Ask for the temperature limit to be relaxed for this product launch.
Reduce the load in the test setup so the board stays within limits.
Locate the hot components, modify the layout or cooling, and retest the prototype.
Add a larger heat sink to the prototype and retest it under heavy load.

basic.situation: A marketing colleague asks which laptop hardware would suit a classroom of 30 students. You have budget figures but no details of usage.

options.text: Recommend the newest laptop model in the catalogue and let them check the budget.
Ask how the laptops will be used, then match specifications to those needs.
Recommend the laptop you use yourself since you know how it performs.
Recommend a mid-range laptop and mention that usage details would help refine it.

advanced.situation: A bank wants new servers. It wants high security, low cost and quick delivery, and the options trade these off differently.

options.text: Recommend the most secure option and explain that cost and delivery will be higher.
Recommend the cheapest option and list security features to add later on.
Recommend the quickest option and state that the security needs are met.
Rank the requirements with the bank, compare options, and recommend a configuration.

basic.situation: You draft a functional specification for a sensor board. The interface section needs a voltage level, and your notes list two different values.

options.text: Use the higher voltage in the draft because it covers both cases.
Leave the voltage blank in the draft and finish the other sections.
Check the datasheet, confirm the voltage with your lead, and update it.
Write both values in the draft and ask your lead which one applies.

advanced.situation: You set the documentation standard for several hardware teams. Teams write specifications in different formats, and reviewers struggle to compare them.

options.text: Require every team to keep all specifications to one page from now on.
Ask reviewers to convert each specification into a standard table before the reviews.
Draft a common template with team leads and trial it on one project.
Pick the cleanest team's format and ask the other teams to use it.

basic.situation: You assist two technicians testing a new power board. One asks you to skip a step in the test procedure because it takes an hour.

options.text: Tell the technician to ask your supervisor before deciding to skip that step.
Let the technician skip the step and note it in the test record.
Let the technician skip the step and sign the record as complete.
Explain that the step is required, and ask your supervisor if it can change.

advanced.situation: You train system designers on a new hardware platform. Two senior engineers are resistant and say the old platform works fine.

options.text: Train the younger designers first and let the seniors catch up later.
Tell the seniors the old platform will be switched off in a month.
Run the standard training session and ask the seniors to join later.
Show them the platform's benefits with a hands-on trial on their own project.

basic.situation: A sales colleague asks if your chip supports a wider voltage range for a customer. You think it does, but you have not checked the datasheet.

options.text: Say it probably does and offer to confirm after the customer call.
Say yes and let the customer test it on their own prototype boards.
Send the customer the voltage range of a similar older chip as ours.
Check the datasheet, then reply with the exact voltage range.

advanced.situation: Executives ask for a long-term hardware plan as chip rules and supplier markets keep changing. They want a firm five-year choice.

options.text: Recommend delaying the plan until the chip market settles down next year.
Present a plan with decision points, supplier risks, and compliance checks for review.
Recommend one supplier's roadmap for five years and update it each year.
Present the current supplier's marketing claims as the plan's compliance proof for executives.

basic.situation: You help design a small control panel with a supervisor. The supervisor's drawing shows a 10 amp breaker for a motor that is rated at 12 amps.

options.text: Ask your supervisor to check the motor rating on the drawing.
Show the rating mismatch to your supervisor and suggest a bigger breaker.
Keep the 10 amp breaker since the motor rarely runs at full load.
Change the motor rating on the drawing to match the 10 amp breaker.

advanced.situation: You lead a capital project programme to replace aging switchgear at three plants. The budget covers two plants, and each plant claims to be most urgent.

options.text: Rank the plants by risk and condition data, and propose a phased programme.
Replace the two largest plants first and defer the third to next year.
Ask the plant managers to vote on which two get the budget.
Split the budget equally across the three plants for small partial upgrades.

basic.situation: You prepare a purchase specification for cables for a building site. Your supervisor's list does not state the insulation rating needed.

options.text: Choose the cheapest insulation rating the supplier lists to save project money.
Leave the rating open in the specification and let the supplier propose one.
Use the rating from a previous project's specification and flag it for checking.
Ask your supervisor for the insulation rating, then complete the specification.

advanced.situation: You set standards for drawings across a large substation project. Teams use different symbols and title blocks, and contractors have misread two drawings.

options.text: Adopt a drawing standard with the teams, brief everyone, and audit sample drawings.
Publish a symbol list and require teams to follow it from now on.
Ask contractors to check the drawings themselves and report any mistakes they find.
Reissue the two misread drawings and keep the other formats as they are.

basic.situation: You calculate cable sizes for a factory line using the standard tables. The calculated current is between two table values.

options.text: Choose the larger cable size, show your working, and have it checked.
Choose any size from the table and adjust the current to fit it.
Interpolate between the table values and record the result as the size.
Round to the smaller cable size to save cost and record the reason.

advanced.situation: You plan a study of a new power conversion method for a plant. Early results look positive, but the test setup differs from plant conditions.

options.text: Run the study in the lab setup and extend the results to the plant.
Design tests that match plant conditions, define success measures, and run a pilot.
Report the early results to management as proof the method works at the plant.
Search published papers and adopt the method with the strongest reported claims.

basic.situation: You observe a newly installed motor starter panel for safety compliance. A warning label is missing from one cabinet door.

options.text: Mention it verbally to the installer and leave it out of the written report.
Pass the panel as complete since the label is a small item.
Ask the installer to add a label soon and record that he agreed.
Note the missing label, take a photo, and tell your supervisor.

advanced.situation: A vendor's new transformer is cheaper than the current model. You are asked to investigate it and define inspection standards for incoming units.

options.text: Test sample units, compare them with specifications, and define incoming inspection checks.
Review the vendor's datasheet and certificates and approve the product for purchase.
Approve the transformer and cut the incoming inspection checks to save money.
Approve the transformer because other companies in the region already use it.

basic.situation: You help estimate labour and material costs for a small rewiring job. Copper prices have risen since the last quote.

options.text: Keep the last quote's copper cost and add a note on rising prices.
Use the copper price from last year's job to keep the estimate low.
Add a ten percent increase to the copper cost from the last quote.
Get current copper prices from suppliers and update the estimate with the date.

advanced.situation: You oversee production on an electrical installation project that is two weeks behind. The client insists on the original completion date.

options.text: Tell the client the delay is caused by supplier problems and ask for time.
Reduce the testing and commissioning time to recover the lost two weeks.
Find critical tasks, add crews where possible, and update the client.
Add overtime across all tasks to try to hold the original completion date.

basic.situation: You compile data for a report on a feeder's voltage drops. Three readings look much lower than the rest.

options.text: Check the instrument for those readings and note the cause.
Report the average of all readings and leave the individual readings out.
Delete the three low readings and report the remaining voltage drops as typical.
Include all readings and mention the three low ones in the report notes.

advanced.situation: You train new team members on switching procedures for a live substation. One trainee wants to practise on the real equipment to learn faster.

options.text: Let the trainee watch an experienced worker perform the live switching on site.
Let the trainee practise on live equipment with a worker standing close by.
Let the trainee practise on live equipment once the written test is passed.
Start on a simulator, then supervise the trainee on live equipment.

basic.situation: You prepare a maintenance schedule for test equipment. The manufacturer says calibrate every six months, but the old schedule says yearly.

options.text: Keep the yearly schedule since changing it would create extra work for staff.
Use the six-month interval, cite the manual, and update the schedule.
Keep the yearly schedule and add a note about the manufacturer's advice.
Use six-month checks for busy equipment and yearly checks for the rest.

advanced.situation: You set rules for storing confidential circuit designs. Engineers email files to personal accounts to work from home, and a client requires confidentiality.

options.text: Ban personal email in the rules and tell engineers to work in the office.
Set a secure remote access method, brief engineers, and audit file transfers.
Ask engineers to password-protect the files before emailing them to themselves.
Allow personal email for routine files and leave the client uninformed of it.

basic.situation: You inspect a batch of power supplies against the specification. One unit's output is 5 percent above the allowed voltage.

options.text: Pass the unit because 5 percent is a small amount over the limit.
Adjust the unit's output setting and pass it as it was received.
Mark the unit as failed, record the reading, and report to your supervisor.
Quarantine the unit and ask the supplier for an explanation of the reading.

advanced.situation: You develop a test procedure for a new medical monitor. A test that checks alarm response takes four hours, and production wants it cut to one.

options.text: Run the full test on a sample from each batch and shorten the rest.
Keep the alarm checks that carry risk, and shorten the lower-risk steps.
Shorten the test to one hour by cutting the alarm response steps.
Report the alarm response as tested on every unit and run the short version.

basic.situation: You check the requirements and cost for a customer's request for a sensor system. The customer's budget is lower than your cost estimate.

options.text: Lower the cost estimate to match the budget and adjust the price later.
Tell your supervisor about the cost gap and wait for further guidance.
Compare the needs with the budget and show the customer what fits.
Offer the customer a cheaper sensor and keep the specification as it was written.

advanced.situation: You review a colleague's design for compatibility with a larger system. It works in the lab but may fail when connected to older equipment on site.

options.text: Ask the colleague to test the design on older equipment and report back.
Approve the design and ask the field team to report any problems.
Evaluate the interface with older equipment, set test criteria, and test before release.
Approve the design and remove the older equipment from the compatibility list.

basic.situation: You design a simple filter circuit with your mentor. Your calculated resistor value is not a standard value in the parts list.

options.text: Round the value to the nearest ten ohms and record it as calculated.
Order a custom resistor with the exact value you calculated for the circuit.
Choose the nearest standard value and show your mentor the finished design.
Choose the nearest standard value, recheck the response, and show your mentor.

advanced.situation: You design a communication board for a scientific instrument that works near strong radio noise. A basic design passes bench tests but is not noise tested.

options.text: Release the design and tell the scientists to avoid using it near noise.
Add filtering to the design and test it later on the instrument itself.
Release the design to the scientists since the bench tests were satisfactory.
Add shielding and filtering, then test the board in a representative noise environment.

basic.situation: You attend a meeting between engineers and a customer about a delayed delivery. The customer asks a pricing question you cannot answer.

options.text: Say you will check with sales and send a written reply by tomorrow.
Give a rough price from memory and mention that it may change.
Ask an engineer in the meeting to answer the pricing question for you.
Quote a price from an older order and say it is final.

advanced.situation: You direct a factory line and an installation team, and a customer changes a feature late. The change affects both teams' schedules.

options.text: Assess the effect on each team, agree a revised plan, and brief both.
Accept the change for the factory line and let the installers adapt.
Accept the change and promise the customer the original delivery date again.
Tell both teams to absorb the change within the current schedule and cost.

basic.situation: A customer calls about a handheld device that will not charge. You are asked to give basic support using the support script.

options.text: Tell the customer the battery is probably dead and needs replacing soon.
Follow the script, check the charger and cable, and record the call.
Ask the customer to send the device in for repair straight away.
Tell the customer to charge it from a stronger adapter of any brand.

advanced.situation: A field fault in a power controller keeps recurring. The cause may be a weak component, and customers want a quick repair, with staff needing training.

options.text: Analyse failed units, recommend a component change, and train staff on the fix.
Tell staff the fault is user error and close the repair cases.
Advise customers to reduce loading on the controller to avoid further faults.
Replace the failed component in each unit as it comes in and record it.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to connect a new handheld reader to the stockroom software before Monday. The vendor guide lists the reader settings.

options.text: Test it on the bench with the vendor settings and confirm reads reach the software.
Edit the stockroom database fields so the new reader connects quickly, then tell your senior.
Connect it to the live stockroom software and check that a sample tag shows up.
Copy the settings from the older reader beside it, since both models behave much alike.

advanced.situation: Your client plans 400 readers across three warehouses. You must model read coverage before the vendor quotes, and the floor plans have changed twice.

options.text: Simulate one warehouse in detail and scale the result to the other two sites.
Model coverage and interference from the latest floor plans and share your assumptions.
Send the client the vendor's quote for 400 readers now and adjust the layout during installation.
Apply the vendor's standard reader spacing at all three sites and flag it for review.

basic.situation: A client's receiving dock will get RFID gates. Your lead asks you to list the existing scanners, software and network points there for the plan.

options.text: Take photos of the dock equipment and fill in the versions from the vendor catalogue.
Request the client's IT asset list and copy the dock entries into your notes.
Walk the dock with the receiving supervisor and record each scanner, software version and network point.
Log in to the dock server with a shared admin password to read the software details.

advanced.situation: A cold-storage client wants RFID on frozen cartons. Two vendors offer very different solutions, one cheaper and one with better reads at low temperatures. You must prepare the comparison.

options.text: Present the cheaper solution as the match, since the client asked about budget first.
Rank both vendors on total cost over five years and attach the datasheets.
Recommend the vendor with the better low-temperature reads since the client's cartons are frozen.
Compare both on read rate in freezer conditions, total cost and downtime, and show the trade-offs.

basic.situation: You must choose tags for plastic crates of garments in a Shah Alam distribution centre. Your supervisor gave you three tag samples and wants a pick with placement spots.

options.text: Pick the smallest tag and stick it on the flat side of each crate.
Choose the sample with the longest advertised read range and place it near the handle.
Test each sample on a real crate and pick the one that reads steadily.
Order the cheapest tags for all crates now and test a few once they arrive.

advanced.situation: A vendor pitches new battery-assisted tags for tool tracking on a large site. Your manager asks if they are worth a trial, and the tools include metal items in outdoor yards.

options.text: Ask other customers of the vendor how the tags performed and report what they say.
Recommend a site-wide order for the new tags, since their longer range suits large yards.
Define the tracking need, then trial a few tags on metal tools in the yard.
Compare the vendor's datasheet claims with passive tag options and recommend whichever fits the budget.

basic.situation: You printed 200 new RFID labels for carton sets. Your supervisor asks you to confirm they read before the labels go on the shelves.

options.text: Release the labels now and ask the shelf staff to report any that fail to scan.
Scan a sample of twenty labels and release the batch if all of them read.
Check the printer's status report showing it encoded every label and release the batch.
Scan all labels with a handheld reader, log any failed ones, and reprint those before release.

advanced.situation: A developer hands over the RFID tracking application before go-live. Your company has architectural standards for interfaces and logging, and the handover note says the application follows them.

options.text: Run the application through its test cases and confirm it matches the handover note.
Approve the application and plan to fix any standards gaps after it goes live.
Read the developer's note and sign off, since the same team built the last two applications.
Review the code and interface design against the standards checklist and send findings back before go-live.

basic.situation: Your lead gives you a step-by-step sheet to mount a fixed RFID reader and antenna above a conveyor. The antenna cable looks shorter than the sheet says.

options.text: Borrow the longer cable from the running line next door and replace it later.
Mount the antenna lower on the frame so the short cable reaches the reader.
Stop before mounting, measure the run, tell your lead, and get the right cable.
Extend the cable by joining a spare length from the toolbox with tape.

advanced.situation: The warehouse software is old and cannot take reader data in the format the new RFID readers send. The vendor suggests a small adapter. Go-live is in two weeks.

options.text: Alter the old software's database tables directly so it accepts the reader format by go-live.
Use the vendor's adapter as supplied and run a pilot with live reads in one aisle.
Export the reader data to spreadsheets each day and have clerks key it into the software.
Build the adapter, test it on a copy of the system, and plan the cutover.

basic.situation: After installing six fixed readers, your supervisor asks you to write down the equipment details for the handover file.

options.text: Photograph each reader and file the pictures with a short note on where it sits.
Reuse the previous site's handover file and update the site name and date.
Record each reader's model, serial number, location, IP address and settings from the units and configuration.
Copy the model list from the purchase order and add each reader's location.

advanced.situation: You wrote a procedure for the new RFID gate system at a distribution centre. Shift supervisors must run it from next week, including handling failed reads and gate faults.

options.text: Email the procedure to every supervisor and ask them to reply if anything is unclear.
Run hands-on sessions at the gate for each shift, using real failed reads, and collect questions.
Pin the procedure beside the gate and let supervisors learn it from the first live shift.
Hold one classroom briefing for all supervisors and give each a printed copy.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to update the site's spill response procedure after a new storage tank was added. The old version is on the shared drive.

options.text: Overwrite the old procedure on the shared drive with the tank supplier's safety sheet.
Attach a short note about the new tank to the front of the old procedure.
Add the new tank's details to the procedure and email the updated file to the team.
Edit a copy with the new tank's details, get it reviewed, then replace the old version.

advanced.situation: An audit found two sampling records missing signatures because the QA procedure does not say who checks them. You must revise the procedure and get four technicians using it.

options.text: Remind the technicians to sign each record and send the audit finding to all of them.
Add a checker line to the procedure and post the revised version on the notice board.
Revise the procedure to name the checker and a deadline, then brief the technicians on it.
Sign the two records yourself from lab notebook entries so the audit file looks complete.

basic.situation: Your manager needs bids for monthly groundwater sampling at a factory site. She asks you to send the request to consultants and collect the quotes.

options.text: Send the request to the consultant used last year and compare it with last year's price.
Share the factory's budget figure with the consultants so they can price close to it.
Send each consultant a different description of the work so they can propose their own approach.
Send one scope of work to three qualified consultants and compare their quotes.

advanced.situation: You manage a river-bank conservation programme with three field teams. One team keeps missing monitoring dates, while the others finish on schedule.

options.text: Remove that team from the programme and recruit a new one before the next cycle.
Move some of that team's sites to the other two teams and tell all three.
Send all teams a weekly table of completion rates so the slower team sees the gap.
Meet the team lead, find what is blocking the dates, and agree a plan with check-ins.

basic.situation: You are monitoring a stormwater pond clean-up. The plan says to collect water samples at three points, but one point is under a fallen branch.

options.text: Take the third sample from the nearest open spot and mark its location in the log.
Leave the third point out of this week's run and raise it at the next meeting.
Sample the other two points, note why the third was missed, and tell your lead.
Record all three points as sampled so the weekly progress report stays on schedule.

advanced.situation: You help plan a multimedia inspection at a chemical plant covering air, water and waste. The team has four people and the plant has a confined-space tank farm.

options.text: Plan the air and water sampling first and add tank farm steps once access is confirmed.
Draft safety rules for tank farm entry and sampling and have the team review them.
Use the plant's own safety induction for the tank farm and assign sampling roles on site.
Send two people into the tank farm to sample while the others cover air and water.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to help draft a spill contingency plan for a new chemical drum store. You have the drum list and the site map.

options.text: List each chemical's hazards, mark kits and exits on the map, then send it for review.
Tell staff to wash any spill into the floor drain and report it later.
Adapt the spill plan from another store and update the drum names and quantities.
Write the plan around the largest drum, since smaller spills would follow the same steps.

advanced.situation: A factory's wastewater pond keeps failing the ammonia limit. Your team is designing an upgrade, and a junior engineer proposes a cheaper aeration layout than the one vendors recommend.

options.text: Approve the cheaper layout for construction and report the savings to management this week.
Choose the vendors' layout, as it is proven, and thank the junior for the idea.
Review the junior's oxygen and ammonia calculations and pilot the layout before choosing.
Adopt the cheaper layout and plan to add more aerators if the ammonia stays high.

basic.situation: Your team is building a database to track waste manifests across five sites. You are asked to help check the table design and which regulations apply to each field.

options.text: Ask the database developer which fields they think the regulations require and use those.
Compare each field with the waste regulation requirements and list gaps for the team lead.
Check the fields against last year's manifests and note any that are missing.
Approve the table design as drafted so developers can load the manifests this week.

advanced.situation: Residents complain about landfill odour. The gas engineer, the planner and the lawyer each give different advice, and the council wants a plan in a month.

options.text: Follow the gas engineer's advice, since odour is a technical problem, and inform the others.
Ask each specialist for a written proposal and pick the one the council can afford.
Send the council the gas engineer's plan as the team view and sort out differences later.
Bring them together, set out each constraint, and agree one plan with owners and dates.

basic.situation: A factory's new staff ask why the plant sorts its waste into six bins. Your supervisor asks you to explain the basics at tomorrow's induction.

options.text: Tell them mixed waste is fine when bins are full, since staff can sort it later.
Tell them the bins follow company policy and ask them to read the policy document.
Show real examples of each bin's waste and explain why mixing raises costs and risks.
Hand out the bin colour chart and explain which waste goes into which bin.

advanced.situation: A state agency asks your firm to comment on a draft effluent standard. It sets a tighter limit for a metal that your industrial clients' treatment plants cannot meet yet.

options.text: Tell the agency the limit is unrealistic and that clients will relocate if it stays.
Support the tighter limit in principle and ask the agency for a longer deadline.
Gather client plant data, show what limit is achievable, and propose a phase-in with monitoring.
Submit the clients' internal plant results to the agency as proof the limit cannot be met.

basic.situation: A company plans a new portable space heater. Your senior asks you to check the draft design for safety hazards before the prototype is built.

options.text: Compare the design with the safety features of the company's older heater model.
Mark the draft as safety-reviewed so the prototype can start and review it during testing.
Check that the heater's wattage and plug type match the target market's requirements.
Check the drawings for tip-over, overheating and cord risks and list concerns for designers.

advanced.situation: Injury records show a rise in hand injuries on the packing line over six months. Your manager wants to know if it is a real trend or a result of more staff and longer shifts.

options.text: Tell the manager the rise is just from longer shifts, as that explains most workplace injuries.
Report the rise in injuries to the manager and recommend extra hand protection on the line.
Compare injury rates per hours worked by month and shift, and test the rise statistically.
Count injuries per month against headcount and report the trend with a chart.

basic.situation: A worker was burned in a boiler room last week. Your lead asks you to join the interview with the worker and take notes.

options.text: Tell the worker the burn was caused by a mistake and ask them to confirm it.
Ask open questions about the steps taken before the burn, note the answers, and avoid blaming.
Note the worker's account and add what you think happened where the story has gaps.
Follow your lead's questions and write down what the worker says word for word.

advanced.situation: A client's noise survey shows readings near the legal limit in a stamping hall. You direct the retest, and production wants it done during a quiet shift.

options.text: Report the quiet shift readings as the hall's usual levels to keep production running.
Test during normal production at the loudest stations with calibrated meters, and record the conditions.
Use the supplier's published machine noise figures to estimate levels for the hall.
Retest during the quiet shift with calibrated meters at the usual stations and log the results.

basic.situation: A plant sends plans for a new press machine. Your task is to check that the guarding and emergency stops meet the safety requirements.

options.text: Compare the guard and stop designs with each requirement in the standard and list the gaps.
Rely on the machine maker's compliance certificate and file the plans with a short note.
Check that the plans show guards and emergency stops, then return them with your approval.
Approve the plans now and add the guard checks to the commissioning list.

advanced.situation: A new robotic loader is entering factories, and no safety code covers shared work areas with people. Your industry group asks you to help write a draft safety rule.

options.text: Publish guidance saying the loader is safe in shared areas until incidents say otherwise.
Draft rules based on the loader maker's own safety manual and ask members to comment.
Review incident data and international practice, draft rules with risk levels, and consult makers and workers.
Copy the safety rules for older fixed robots and add a section on shared areas.

basic.situation: A new industrial cleaner is going on sale. You are asked to help draft the precaution label and the usage steps for workers.

options.text: Copy the warnings from the safety data sheet and write the usage steps below them.
Draft clear steps and warnings from the safety data sheet, then test the wording with workers.
Write short, friendly instructions and keep the hazard details in the data sheet.
Base the label on a similar cleaner's label and change the product name and size.

advanced.situation: You are asked to testify as an expert in a case where a worker lost a hand at an unguarded press. The company's lawyer suggests you keep your opinion narrow to help their side.

options.text: Give your findings from the inspection records and standards, including points that hurt the company's case.
Change the inspection report to say the press guard was fitted, since the company will settle.
Agree to the lawyer's narrow framing and mention the guard problem if asked directly.
Answer the questions put to you and stay within the facts you have inspected.

basic.situation: A warehouse is introducing new harnesses for work at height. You are asked to help arrange training for 30 workers across two shifts.

options.text: Issue the harnesses to workers now and let experienced colleagues show new ones on the job.
Arrange one demonstration session for the first shift and hand out the manufacturer's leaflets.
Send the harness video to all workers and ask supervisors to confirm they watched it.
Book hands-on fitting sessions on both shifts, keep an attendance list, and follow up with absentees.

advanced.situation: A food plant has repeated back injuries and sick leave in its lifting areas. Management asks you to advise on fixing the problem, not just treating each case.

options.text: Advise management to replace workers who have repeated back injuries with fit new hires.
Suggest the plant offer physiotherapy to affected workers and track their return to work.
Review injury data, observe the lifting tasks, and recommend layout, equipment and rotation changes.
Recommend training on safe lifting for all lifting staff and review injuries again in six months.

basic.situation: Your plant's emergency contact sheet for the fire department and rescue team is two years old. Your lead asks you to bring it up to date.

options.text: Remove the old sheet from the control room now and post a new one next week.
Call each organisation to confirm numbers, update the sheet, and post it at the gate.
Check the organisations' websites for current numbers and update the sheet with them.
Keep the old sheet and add any new numbers that colleagues mention in passing.

advanced.situation: Several workers at a chemical plant report headaches and dizziness near one mixing area. You must meet the company doctor and a hygienist to plan how to manage the risk.

options.text: Ask the hygienist to measure the air and move workers away until results arrive.
Share the exposure readings and symptom timeline, then agree testing, controls and worker monitoring with both.
Ask the doctor to examine the affected workers and keep the area running meanwhile.
Tell workers the symptoms come from the heat and give them extra water breaks.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to sketch a layout for a new packing table and two shelves in a small bakery workroom. Workers move boxes from the oven side to the door.

options.text: Draw the layout in CAD from the wall dimensions and put the table by the door.
Draw the layout in CAD along the box route from oven to door, and share it.
Copy the layout from the bakery's other branch and adjust the shelves to fit.
Mark the floor with tape to match your sketch and have workers start using it.

advanced.situation: A plant will add a second shift, and the current layout makes workers walk long distances to get parts. You must propose a new layout and labour standards that your team can use.

options.text: Redesign the layout around the busiest parts and use last year's standards for the second shift.
Copy the layout of a similar plant and apply its labour standards to your workers.
Study material flow and walk times, redesign the layout, and set standards from timed observations.
Set tighter labour standards for the second shift now and fix the layout later if needed.

basic.situation: Your supervisor gives you a form and sampling instructions to record the weight of ten bags from each hour's run. One bag at 2 pm is clearly underweight.

options.text: Record the underweight reading but leave the sampling decision to the next shift supervisor.
Record every bag as measured, mark the underweight one, and tell your supervisor straight away.
Change the underweight reading to the target weight so the hour's average looks normal.
Replace the underweight bag with another from the same run and record that weight.

advanced.situation: A batch of 2,000 brackets has hairline cracks from a supplier's casting. Production wants to use them, and finance wants to know who pays for the loss.

options.text: Rework the cracked brackets with filler and ship them to the customer with the good ones.
Use the brackets on low-load products first and watch for returns while you contact the supplier.
Reject the whole batch, send it back to the supplier, and ask for a replacement.
Quarantine the batch, sample the defect rate, and cost the loss against the supplier contract.

basic.situation: Your lead gives you next week's production schedule for a furniture line and asks you to work out the basic material and labour cost per chair.

options.text: Use last month's cost per chair and adjust it for next week's order quantities.
Take the price from the sales brochure and subtract a profit margin to get the cost.
Read the schedule and specifications, list materials and run times per chair, and calculate the cost.
Divide the line's total weekly spend by the number of chairs in the schedule.

advanced.situation: Engineering proposes a thinner steel plate for a product to save material, but it would need an extra welding step. Management wants a cost view before deciding.

options.text: Model material, welding, scrap and rework costs for both designs and show the net saving.
Calculate the material saving per unit and subtract the extra welding labour cost.
Report the material saving per unit and note that welding will add some cost.
Tell management the thinner plate saves money, since steel is the largest cost item.

basic.situation: Your lead asks how many packers a line needs to pack 1,200 boxes in a shift. One packer packs 150 boxes per shift, before breaks and absences.

options.text: Round down to seven packers to save labour cost and expect overtime to cover the gap.
Divide 1,200 by 150, get eight packers, and report that number as the requirement.
Divide 1,200 by 150 for eight packers, then ask your lead how to allow for breaks.
Use nine packers, because the neighbouring line packing similar boxes runs with nine.

advanced.situation: Complaints rose for a bottle-filling line. You must set a fill-weight standard for the whole factory from six months of data across five lines with different fill machines.

options.text: Drop the highest and lowest fills from each line, then set the standard from what remains.
Check each line's variation, then set limits from each machine's capability and test them.
Pool all five lines' data and set limits at three standard deviations from the overall mean.
Use the top line's average as the standard and ask the others to match it.

basic.situation: You direct three workers measuring part lengths at the end of a line. One worker keeps rounding readings to the nearest centimetre, though the form asks for millimetres.

options.text: Show the worker how to read in millimetres, check a few readings together, and recheck later.
Remind the worker that the form needs millimetres and ask them to follow it.
Convert the rounded readings to millimetres yourself and enter them on the form as measured.
Take over that worker's measuring for the rest of the shift and say nothing more.

advanced.situation: Three departments blame each other for late deliveries. Purchasing says parts arrive late, assembly says paint is slow, and quality says rework is high. You coordinate quality control.

options.text: Collect delay data from each stage, review the main causes together, and assign actions.
Ask each head to send a written explanation and forward all three to the plant manager.
Pick the stage with the longest delays last month and ask that team to fix it.
Tell the plant manager that purchasing is the cause and ask for tougher supplier penalties.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to prepare the weekly production report and a purchase order for 50 replacement tool bits, using the company templates.

options.text: Copy last week's report with updated totals and reuse last month's purchase order.
Fill both templates from the logs and approved quote, then pass them to your lead.
Fill the report from the logs and send the purchase order to the supplier directly.
Round the output figures up to match the weekly target, then order the 50 bits.

advanced.situation: Engineering drawings on the shop floor are often out of date because changes are logged in emails. You are asked to set a standard for how changes are recorded.

options.text: Define a change record form, require drawing updates before release, and train the team on it.
Tell shop staff to work from the latest email and discard the printed drawings.
Appoint one engineer to scan the emails weekly and update the drawings that changed.
Ask engineers to attach the changed drawing to every change email and file the emails.

basic.situation: Your senior sends you to a call centre with a checklist for desk height, chair setting and screen distance. Two agents' desks are already adjusted for their own height.

options.text: Enter standard values for those two desks on the checklist so the ten results look uniform.
Measure the other desks and note that those two were adjusted by the agents.
Reset the two desks to standard values and then record all ten desks consistently.
Record each desk as found, note the agents' own adjustments, and ask how they use them.

advanced.situation: You must design an observation study of nurses moving patients on a ward, capturing posture, lifting force, interruptions and time pressure. Observers can watch only a few shifts.

options.text: Define the measures, pilot the protocol on one shift, and schedule observers across tasks and shifts.
Ask nurses to rate their effort and interruptions on a daily form and compare the ratings.
Film patients being moved on every shift and review the videos when time allows.
Record video of the day shift lifts and score posture and force from the footage.

basic.situation: Your lead gives you a year of accident reports from a bottling plant and asks you to find the common safety issues.

options.text: Tell your lead the main cause is worker error, since most reports describe people slipping.
Count the reports by month and report which months had the most accidents.
Read the three most serious reports and describe the issues you find in them.
Group the reports by task, body part and location, and list the issues that repeat.

advanced.situation: You review injury data and job descriptions for a logistics company. Jobs with the most injuries also have the most overtime and the newest staff.

options.text: Recommend limiting overtime and adding training for new staff in all the injury-prone jobs.
Rank jobs by injury rate and recommend redesigning the three highest ones first.
Compare injury rates by job after adjusting for hours and experience, then observe the tasks directly.
Conclude that new staff cause the injuries and recommend removing them from those jobs.

basic.situation: A packing worker complains of shoulder pain from reaching to a high shelf. Your senior asks you to propose a basic workstation adjustment.

options.text: Give the worker a step stool so they can reach the high shelf safely.
Tell the worker to stretch before shifts and keep the shelf where it is.
Lower the shelf to a height that suits the worker who complained, then log the change.
Measure the reach, move frequently used items to waist-to-shoulder height, and check back with the worker.

advanced.situation: A rail company is adding a new driver display to its trains. The hardware team says the screen layout is fixed, but drivers' tests show they miss alarms during night runs.

options.text: Share the test data, set alarm visibility requirements, and agree display changes with the hardware team.
Write a training note telling drivers where alarms appear and to scan the screen more often.
Ask for a louder sound alert and keep the screen layout the hardware team has fixed.
Accept the fixed layout and log the missed alarms as driver attention issues in the file.

basic.situation: You collected task times from 12 workers using an old tool and 12 using a new tool. Your lead asks you to test with the software whether the new tool is faster.

options.text: Check for outliers, run a suitable test in the software, and report the result and limits.
Remove the slowest old-tool times so the groups look similar, then run the test.
Run the test in the software and report whatever its summary says about the tool.
Compare the two averages and report the new tool as faster if its average is lower.

advanced.situation: A city agency asks you to forecast how commuters will respond to a new bus lane. Survey data is limited and many answers are stated intentions.

options.text: Report the survey results as they are and let the agency interpret likely behaviour.
Fit a simple model to last year's trip counts and adjust it by the survey rates.
Build an agent-based model from survey rules, test the weak inputs, and report a range.
Forecast that most commuters will switch to buses, since that is what respondents said.

basic.situation: After a field visit, your supervisor asks you to draft a short report on ergonomic findings at a laundry, including awkward postures and repetitive tasks.

options.text: Summarise the findings with photos, rank issues by risk, and send the draft for comment.
Write that the laundry has ergonomic problems and recommend a full assessment by a specialist.
List the issues you saw in the order you saw them and attach the visit notes.
Reuse the recommendations from a previous laundry report and change the company name and date.

advanced.situation: Control room operators of a water plant must follow a 20-step shutdown during alarms, and errors have occurred under stress. You are asked to design a cognitive aid.

options.text: Turn the 20 steps into a laminated checklist and add it to each operator's console.
Observe a drill, design a step-by-step aid with checkpoints, and test it under simulated alarms.
Ask the most experienced operator to design the aid and issue it after one review.
Cut the shutdown to the five steps operators remember most and drop the others.

basic.situation: A new office worker asks you how to set up their desk and chair. You have an ergonomics guide from your company.

options.text: Give them the guide and point out the pages on chair and screen settings.
Tell them to copy the way colleagues nearby sit, since their desks work for them.
Tell them posture matters little for office work and to sit however feels comfortable.
Go through the guide at their desk, adjust the chair and screen together, and invite questions.

advanced.situation: In a design meeting for a new factory control panel, engineers and the product manager want to cut a feature that operators asked for to meet the launch date.

options.text: Agree to cut it and suggest adding it in a later release if operators complain.
Say operators asked for it and request that the feature be kept in the launch.
Present the operator findings and error risks, then propose a lower-cost way to keep the feature.
Agree to cut it and tell operators in training that the feature was not required.

basic.situation: A senior engineer asks you to draft the validation protocol for a new tablet-coating machine at a pharmaceutical plant. You have the machine manual and the company template.

options.text: Draft the protocol after the first production runs so you can copy the actual settings.
Reuse a protocol from a similar machine and change the machine name and settings.
Write the protocol from the manual's installation checks and send it to the line for approval.
Fill the template with test steps and acceptance criteria from the manual, then ask for review.

advanced.situation: Your company is adding a new sterile filling line. You lead the validation protocol work, and the engineering team wants to start testing next week before the master plan is approved.

options.text: Finish the master plan and protocols, get them approved, then agree a test schedule.
Start installation checks next week under the draft plan and complete approval before process tests.
Approve a short protocol for the key tests now and add the rest after startup.
Let engineering test next week and write the protocols afterwards from the recorded results.

basic.situation: You must draw samples of a raw powder from 12 drums for a validation test. The sampling plan says to take a scoop from the top, middle and bottom of each drum.

options.text: Follow the plan, use a clean scoop for each drum, and label and record each sample.
Take top samples from each drum and add a note that the rest looked the same.
Take top, middle and bottom samples from each drum with the same scoop and label them.
Fill the sample bags from three drums and label them as coming from all twelve.

advanced.situation: You validate a biodegradable packaging film using an electronic tester that gives tensile and barrier readings. In one run the barrier readings drift upward during the test.

options.text: Complete the run, then repeat it and report the average of both sets of readings.
Stop the run, check calibration and conditions, repeat the test with controls, and record the deviation.
Report the readings from the first half of the run, before the drift appeared.
Adjust the later readings down by the drift amount and report the full run.

basic.situation: You are entering 40 results from a cleaning validation run into the tracking database. A swab result on the printout is smudged and could be 0.5 or 0.8.

options.text: Enter 0.5 because it is the first digit that is clearly readable on the printout.
Confirm the value with the analyst or lab record, then enter it and note the query.
Enter 0.8 as the higher figure and flag it for the analyst to confirm later.
Leave the smudged value out of the database so the batch record stays tidy.

advanced.situation: Three batches from a new mixing process failed content uniformity, but equipment checks passed. You have validation test data and must find the likely root cause.

options.text: Pass the process since equipment checks met limits, and note the failed batches as outliers.
Plot the failed batches' results over time and look for the point where they shifted.
Compare mixing time, speed and loading across batches, then confirm the likely factor with a trial.
Suspect the raw material lots and ask the supplier for new ones before further trials.

basic.situation: A mentor asks you to review a completed qualification file for a freezer before audit. The file has all signatures, but one test date differs between two pages.

options.text: Tell your mentor about the mismatch and ask which date to use in the file.
Tick the file as reviewed since all signatures are present and the dates are close.
Fix the page with the later date and initial the change as the reviewer.
Note the mismatch, check the raw test records, and raise it with your mentor.

advanced.situation: A regulator emails your company asking why a validation was repeated and wants the report within five days. The repeat followed an unexplained failure, and your manager is away.

options.text: Reply within five days that a response is in preparation and ask for more time.
Gather the investigation and repeat results, draft a factual reply, and get it approved before sending.
Send the repeat validation report and explain that the first run had an equipment fault.
Say the first result was a test error and remove the failed run from the file.

basic.situation: You ran a temperature mapping test of a warehouse and your supervisor asks you to prepare a simple report from the logger data.

options.text: Delete the two out-of-limit readings and report the rest as the full data set.
Report the average, highest and lowest temperatures and state whether they meet the limits.
Write that the warehouse passed since the average temperature stayed inside the limits during the test.
Summarise the logger readings against the limits, list any excursions with times, and attach the data.

advanced.situation: You are the final reviewer for a validation package on a new autoclave. The author reports all tests passed, but one cycle record shows a temperature dip below the specification.

options.text: Request a written explanation of the dip from the author and approve if it sounds reasonable.
Hold the approval, ask for a deviation investigation of the dip, and review the updated package.
Approve the package as submitted since the author has signed off all other cycles.
Ask the author to repeat that cycle and replace the record in the package.

basic.situation: You help schedule a validation test of a packaging line. The test needs the line stopped for four hours, and production has a customer order due that week.

options.text: Book the next free slot on the line and ask production to move the customer order.
Ask production for a four-hour window that fits the order plan and confirm it with maintenance.
Stop the line on the morning of the test and let production find the time later.
Book the test for the weekend and email production and quality to tell them.

advanced.situation: You direct validation work on a new cleaning procedure. Two operators have started the new method but still follow the old steps for the final rinse, and the protocol was just revised.

options.text: Let the operators use whichever rinse they prefer and compare results at the end.
Send the revised protocol to both operators and ask them to confirm they have read it.
Walk the operators through the revised rinse step on the line and observe their next run.
Put a new sign beside the sink about the rinse step and expect operators to notice.

basic.situation: A designer sends you a bracket drawing to check against the specification before it goes to the shop. The specification lists a 2 mm minimum wall thickness.

options.text: Compare the bracket with a similar part already in production and pass it if close.
Pass the drawing to the shop and ask machinists to report any thin walls.
Check every wall against 2 mm, flag hard-to-make features, and send comments back.
Check the main walls against 2 mm and return the drawing marked as acceptable.

advanced.situation: You lead a design review for a plastic housing family with six variants. The designer's tooling plan is complete, but two variants have undercuts that need costly mould actions.

options.text: Ask the designer to remove the undercuts from the two variants and resubmit the plan.
List issues across all variants, cost the mould actions, and agree design changes with the designer.
Approve the tooling plan for the four clean variants and defer the two problem ones.
Approve the plan as complete and let the toolmaker propose fixes for the undercuts.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to list the main environmental impacts of the metal parts washing step in a factory, using the usage logs and safety data sheets.

options.text: Report the washing step's electricity use from the meter and add a note on water.
Read the logs and data sheets, list water, solvent and energy use, and note waste.
List the solvents from the data sheets and note their hazard labels and amounts used.
Tell your lead the washing step is low impact because the parts are small.

advanced.situation: Management wants to cut a plant's greenhouse gas emissions from its curing ovens and replace a toxic solvent in the coating line. You are asked to develop the technology approach.

options.text: Ask the coating supplier to recommend a non-toxic solvent and adopt its suggestion for all lines.
Buy carbon credits to cover the emissions and keep the current solvent until it runs out.
Trial low-energy curing and water-based coatings, then compare emissions, cost and quality results.
Switch the ovens to a cleaner fuel now and test water-based coatings after the next audit.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to propose a layout for two new CNC machines in a bay with limited floor space. Operators need clear access for loading and maintenance.

options.text: Sketch the machines with loading and maintenance zones, then check it with operators.
Place both machines along the wall to save floor space and leave a walkway.
