Copy the machine arrangement from the manufacturer's brochure for the same two models.
Place the machines tight together to fit a third machine later, with access at the ends.

advanced.situation: A new welding process must be proven capable before the customer approves it. You must design tests of finished welds to set standards and show the process meets the requirement.

options.text: Test thirty welds under ideal settings and use the average strength as the standard.
Choose five good-looking welds for testing and report them to the customer as the process capability.
Define the weld measures, test across normal variation, and set limits from the results.
Use the strength standard from the customer's drawing and test five welds to confirm.

basic.situation: Your lead notices that a machining cell uses 8% more aluminium than planned each week. She asks you to find out why.

options.text: Ask the operators why they use extra material and note what they say.
Raise the planned material allowance by 8% so the variance disappears from the weekly report.
Check the scrap bin records for the past month and report the main scrap reason.
Compare scrap records and cutting programs with the plan, then measure offcuts on the next run.

advanced.situation: Fatigue cracks keep appearing in a pressed steel part after about 50,000 cycles. You have inspection data from 300 failed parts and can request changes to tolerances or the process.

options.text: Tighten the thickness tolerance on the part and monitor failures over the next quarter.
Switch to a harder steel grade for the part and run the same process.
Analyse crack positions against thickness, press force and heat treatment, then trial the recommended changes.
Add a thicker coating over the crack-prone area so the cracks are less visible.

basic.situation: A customer asks for a quote on 5,000 units of a new plastic cover. Your senior asks you to estimate the production time and cost from the drawing.

options.text: Take the cost of the most similar cover and scale it to 5,000 units.
Estimate cycle time, material and labour, add setup and scrap, and show workings.
Estimate material cost by weight and add a fixed percentage for labour and everything else.
Quote the same price as the earlier cover order, since that customer accepted it before.

advanced.situation: Operators of a stamping line spend 20 minutes per shift changing dies, which limits output. You are asked to cut costs by improving the process, within the fixed die set.

options.text: Train operators to change dies faster and set a target time for each changeover.
Record the changeovers, do preparation outside stoppage, and trial quick-change clamps on one die.
Skip the die alignment checks after each change to cut the time and review scrap later.
Add a second shift to make up for the lost minutes and keep the current method.

basic.situation: A new assembly procedure for a pump has been approved. Your lead asks you to prepare the documentation for the shop floor, using the engineering notes.

options.text: Issue the old pump procedure for now and update it once the new method settles.
Convert the engineering notes into numbered steps and issue them to the assembly area.
Write ordered steps with tools, torque values and checks, and have an operator try them.
Give the assembly area the engineering notes and explain the changes at the morning briefing.

advanced.situation: You supervise four technicians who disagree on how to set up a new robotic welding cell. Each has a different method, and the cell has to start production on Monday.

options.text: Choose the quickest setup to meet Monday and handle weld quality problems when they appear.
Let each technician set up the cell on their own shift and compare outputs later.
Pick the method of the most experienced technician and ask the others to follow it.
Test each method on sample parts, choose on weld results, and document the setup.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to draft the interior layout of a small passenger ferry's lower deck, with seats, a luggage area and a stairway. Exits must meet the vessel's safety plan.

options.text: Put the luggage area at the stairway foot to shorten the crew's loading walk.
Place the seats to fit the most passengers and add exit routes around them afterwards.
Draft the layout from the general arrangement, keep exit routes clear, and send it for review.
Copy the layout of a similar ferry and scale the seating area to this deck.

advanced.situation: You are designing the hull of a 30-metre patrol boat. The customer wants more speed, but weight limits and stability criteria leave little margin.

options.text: Scale the hull of a faster existing boat and check stability once the drawings are done.
Compare hull form variants for resistance, weight and stability, then present the trade-offs.
Promise the customer the higher speed and relax the stability margin in the calculations.
Slim the hull to reduce resistance and trim ballast to stay within the weight limit.

basic.situation: You help test a new bilge pump on the workshop bench. Your lead gives you the test sheet with flow rate and pressure checks.

options.text: Run the pump for ten minutes and note that it sounded normal on the sheet.
Run each check in order, record the readings, and tell your lead about any shortfall.
Run the flow test, record the result, and pass the pump to the next stage.
Record the manufacturer's rated flow and pressure on the sheet as the test results.

advanced.situation: A coaster's owner adds a deck crane, and you must lead the stability and weight analysis. The lightship weight and centre of gravity records are from the original build.

options.text: Do an inclining test to update lightship data, then recalculate stability with crane loads.
Check the crane maker's stability advice for similar vessels and apply it to this coaster.
Approve the crane fit on the original stability booklet and note that loads are small.
Add the crane's weight and height to the original records and recalculate stability curves.

basic.situation: You review a vessel's life-saving equipment records before a port inspection. The liferaft service certificate expired last month, though the raft looks fine.

options.text: Flag the expired certificate to your senior and request raft servicing before the inspection.
List the expired certificate in your review notes and finish checking the other records.
Change the expiry date on the certificate copy to a later date so it passes.
Check the raft visually and mark the certificate as acceptable because it looks fine.

advanced.situation: A shipowner needs urgent repairs at a foreign port, and the class surveyor wants extra checks that would add cost. You coordinate between the shipowner and the surveyor.

options.text: Argue that the repairs already cover the surveyor's concerns and ask to drop the extra checks.
Agree to all the surveyor's checks and tell the shipowner to approve the added cost.
Ask the surveyor which checks are required, combine them with the repairs, and agree the scope.
Complete the repairs and delay the surveyor's checks until the vessel's next scheduled survey date.

basic.situation: A boatyard sends a proposal for a 12-metre workboat. Your senior asks you to read it and list the size, weight, speed and draft figures the design must meet.

options.text: Read the proposal and specification, list each figure, and flag any that conflict.
Take the figures from the boatyard's brochure for the same class of workboat.
Fill in the missing figures with typical values for a workboat of that length.
List the size, weight, speed and draft figures stated on the proposal's summary page.

advanced.situation: You plan sea trials for a new tug covering speed, manoeuvring and bollard pull. The weather window is short, and trials cannot be repeated cheaply.

options.text: Run all tests at full power in one outing and review the data once they end.
Follow the shipyard's usual trial order from its last tug and adjust if weather changes.
Order tests by weather need and risk, set pass conditions in advance, and brief the crew.
Run the bollard pull test first as the buyer values it, then fit the others.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to check an automatic bilge alarm on a cargo boat at the quay. The alarm is wired to a float switch in the bilge.

options.text: Mute the alarm to stop it disturbing the crew and turn it back on before sailing.
Lift the float to trigger the alarm, check the panel display, and log the result.
Check that the alarm panel shows no faults and record the alarm as working today.
Look at the float switch and wiring for damage and log that they look sound.

advanced.situation: A ferry operator has had three engine alarm failures in a year. You are asked to define inspection standards for alarm and control systems across its six vessels.

options.text: Add alarm tests to the monthly checklist of the vessel that had the three failures.
Adopt the alarm makers' recommended inspection intervals for all six vessels and track them monthly.
Review the failure records, set inspection items and intervals by criticality, and agree them with engineers.
Set the alarm check interval to once a year to cut the maintenance workload.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to write a one-page technical summary of a completed pump replacement for the sales team to use. You have the work order and test results.

options.text: Summarise the work and test results in plain terms, check the figures, and send for review.
Write about the pump's benefits from the manufacturer's brochure and add the test result.
Add a line saying the new pump will save fuel, since newer pumps usually do.
Copy the work order text into a one-page document and attach the test results.

advanced.situation: A shipowner's board asks for a report on your design package, which is two weeks behind. One cause was your own team's late stability check.

options.text: State the delay and its causes plainly, give a recovery plan with dates, and agree check-ins.
Send a short progress note stressing the work completed and promising a new date soon.
Report the delay and give a revised completion date, with the causes summarised briefly.
Report that the delay came from the client's late approvals and leave out the stability check.

basic.situation: A batch of steel bars arrives at your plant. Your supervisor asks you to run the hardness test on five bars from the batch and record the results.

options.text: Test two bars and record their average as the result for the whole batch of five.
Record the hardness values from the supplier's certificate as your own test results for the batch.
Prepare the surfaces, check the tester on the reference block, test each bar, and record readings.
Test each bar at one spot as received and record the readings against the specification.

advanced.situation: Your foundry has changed alloy supply. You must design the testing plan for castings, covering chemistry, tensile strength and porosity, with limited test equipment time.

options.text: Rely on the new supplier's test certificates and begin testing castings after customers complain.
Keep the previous testing plan and add chemistry checks for the new alloy supplier.
Test tensile strength on a few castings per lot, since strength decides most failures.
Rank tests by failure risk, set sample sizes and limits, then trial the plan once.

basic.situation: Tensile test results for twenty aluminium sheet samples show four below the minimum strength. Your lead asks you to review the results and point out simple problems.

options.text: Report the four failures with their sample numbers and compare them to the specification.
Release the sheets to the customer since sixteen of the twenty samples passed the minimum.
Report the average strength of all twenty samples and note that it meets the minimum.
Check if the weak samples share a coil, position or test date, and report the pattern.

advanced.situation: A pressure vessel weld cracked in service. Operations, the supplier and the fabricator each blame another party, and you must lead the investigation of the materials failure.

options.text: Compare the failed weld with the supplier's data sheet and decide who is responsible.
Replace the cracked section with new material and report the cause as an installation fault.
Preserve the fracture, gather certificates and weld records, then test and analyse to find the cause.
Examine the fracture under a microscope and share the likely crack mechanism with everyone.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to review the specification for a plastic housing. It asks for heat resistance of 120 degrees, but the datasheet of the chosen resin says 105.

options.text: Update the specification to 105 degrees so the resin matches and note the change later.
Compare the specification with the datasheet, mark the 15 degree gap, and ask your supervisor.
Accept the datasheet figure and ask whether 105 degrees will do for the housing.
Note the resin datasheet figure and suggest a higher grade resin from the same supplier.

advanced.situation: A product team wants to switch a bicycle frame from steel to a new magnesium alloy to cut weight. Executives want a decision in a month.

options.text: Define strength, corrosion and cost needs, test alloy samples, and brief executives on results.
Compare the alloy datasheet with the steel's properties and recommend the switch if it is lighter.
Ask the alloy supplier to provide a technical report and present its conclusions as ours.
Tell executives the new alloy is stronger per kilogram and put it into production planning.

basic.situation: You assist in planning a laboratory trial of a new coating on steel panels. The trial needs coating weights, cure times and a test for adhesion.

options.text: Plan the cure times and coating weights and decide the adhesion test after the first panels.
List the variables, coating weights and cure times, plus the adhesion test, for your supervisor.
Start coating the panels with the settings from the supplier's brochure and plan tests later.
Copy the plan used for the previous coating and change the coating name and panel numbers.

advanced.situation: You must model how a new polymer composite behaves under heat for an automotive part, using computer simulation. The supplier gave only room-temperature property data.

options.text: Use property values for a similar composite from a published paper in the model.
Extend the room-temperature properties in a straight line to the operating temperature and report it safe.
Test high-temperature properties, build the model with them, and check it against a physical sample.
Model the composite using the room-temperature data and apply a safety factor for the heat.

basic.situation: Your manager asks you to help write a report with a budget for a trial of a new alloy. You have last year's lab costs and current quotes.

options.text: Build the budget from quotes and lab hours, compare with last year, and write it up.
Update last year's budget figures for inflation and add the report text around them.
Cut the budget lines by 20% to make the trial look attractive and fix numbers later.
Use the highest current quote for each item and leave labour costs to the manager.

advanced.situation: You are invited to present your team's results on a new corrosion-resistant alloy at a conference. A competitor will attend, and your company has a pending patent filing.

options.text: Ask the patent attorney and your manager what can be shared, then present approved results.
Present the full results and composition, since sharing it will build the company's reputation.
Present all your team's results but skip the slide that lists the alloy composition.
Present the general test method and benefits, and decline to answer questions on composition.

basic.situation: You assist the senior technician supervising a heat treatment shift. A newer technician is unsure which furnace setting to use for a batch of tool steel.

options.text: Give the technician the setting used for the last tool steel batch and let them proceed.
Tell the technician to start the batch and adjust the furnace when it looks right.
Check the work order and procedure with the technician, confirm the setting, and log it.
Tell the technician to choose a middle setting that should suit most tool steels.

advanced.situation: A customer's staff keep misusing a new ceramic coating, applying it too thick, which causes cracking. You are asked to train them on the product and application method.

options.text: Run a classroom session on the coating properties and give staff the application guide.
Email the thickness limits and the application guide to the customer's manager and offer a call.
Visit their plant, demonstrate thickness limits with samples, and let staff practise while you coach.
Advise the customer to apply thinner layers than the guide says and skip the cure checks.

basic.situation: Your senior gives you a blueprint of a motor mount and asks you to prepare the part for machining. The drawing shows a 12 mm hole with a tolerance of plus or minus 0.05.

options.text: Use the 12 mm size and apply the shop's standard tolerance since it is usually close.
Tell the machinist to drill a 12 mm hole and match the old mount.
Read the hole size and tolerance, then pass the drawing to the machinist with a note.
Read the dimensions, tolerance and notes on the drawing, and ask the drafter about anything unclear.

advanced.situation: You assist a drafter on a pressure vessel support frame. The CAD model passes the checks, but you notice the weld symbols do not match the stress report's requirements.

options.text: Release the model since it passes the checks and mention the symbols in the cover note.
Compare the weld symbols with the stress report, mark mismatches for the drafter, and confirm updates.
Edit the stress report's weld requirements to match the model so both documents agree.
Tell the drafter the symbols look different from the report and let them decide.

basic.situation: You help design a small conveyor for a packing line. Your supervisor sets a load of 20 kg per tray and asks you to select a motor.

options.text: Order the cheapest motor that fits the frame and tune the belt speed to suit it.
Pick the motor used on a similar conveyor in the catalogue and confirm its torque rating.
Choose a motor one size larger than the catalogue's smallest option and test it later.
Calculate torque and power from load, speed and friction, add a margin, and select a motor.

advanced.situation: A supplier offers a cheaper pump for your cooling system. You must specify components that still meet the performance specification and the plant's noise limit.

options.text: Accept the supplier's statement that the pump is equivalent and record it in the specification.
Check the pump's flow and head against the specification and accept it if they match.
Compare the pump's flow, head and noise data with the specification and approve if all pass.
Order the cheaper pump now and adjust the system after it is installed if needed.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to test whether a new bearing holds its rated load in a small gearbox. You have a test rig and the bearing's datasheet.

options.text: Check that the bearing dimensions fit the gearbox and trust the rated load on the datasheet.
Run the bearing at rated load, record temperature and vibration, and compare with the datasheet.
Run the bearing on the rig at light load first and extrapolate to the rated load.
Run the bearing at double the rated load to finish quickly and report the result.

advanced.situation: You are developing a lighter alternative design for a bicycle crank arm and must assess sustainability and feasibility. Prototype tests are costly, so you can build only a few.

options.text: Choose the alternative with the lowest material cost and build several prototypes of it.
Model the alternatives for stress and material impact, then build prototypes for the most promising two.
Drop the sustainability assessment and test one prototype of the lightest design to save budget.
Build prototypes of the two lightest alternatives and test them for fatigue and weight saved.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to estimate the cost of fabricating a steel platform. You have the drawing, steel weights and the shop's labour rate.

options.text: Take the lowest quote you can find for the steel and leave labour for later.
Total material by weight and price, add labour at the shop rate, and add a margin.
Estimate the steel cost from weights and prices and double it for labour and other costs.
Use the price per kilogram from a previous platform job and multiply by the new weight.

advanced.situation: Your firm is bidding for a large extraction-plant construction contract with a tight deadline. Your estimate shows a thin margin, and the customer's specification has unclear sections.

options.text: Submit the bid at the thin margin and include a note that variations will be charged.
List unclear sections as clarification questions, price the risks, and submit the bid with stated assumptions.
Submit the bid with the lowest figures to win the contract and handle cost overruns later.
Raise the margin by a fixed percentage to cover the unclear sections and submit the bid.

basic.situation: A cooling fan on a machine trips its breaker after ten minutes. Your supervisor asks you to find out why and suggest a fix.

options.text: Compare the fan's rating with the breaker rating and tell your supervisor if they differ.
Swap the breaker for a higher-rated one so the fan keeps running through the shift.
Measure the fan current, check for blocked airflow and bearing drag, and report the likely cause.
Replace the fan with the spare one from the stores and see if it still trips.

advanced.situation: A pump in your product keeps failing at the shaft seal, and customers complain. Tests show the seal gets hot because of shaft vibration. You must recommend design modifications.

options.text: Trace the vibration source, recommend a balance or shaft support change, and test it before release.
Reply that customers install the pump badly and keep the design unchanged for the next batch.
Recommend more frequent seal replacement in the maintenance manual to reduce customer failures.
Recommend a seal rated for higher temperatures and add a temperature alarm to the housing.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to write the performance requirements for a new automatic labelling machine, using the customer's request and your plant's line speed.

options.text: Copy the requirements of the plant's existing labeller and change the line speed to match.
Write that the machine must be fast, accurate and reliable and add details later.
List speed, accuracy, uptime and safety requirements with measurable values, then review with your lead.
Use the machine maker's brochure figures as the requirements and send them to suppliers.

advanced.situation: Your gearbox design moves to batch production. The machine shop proposes a faster method that changes the surface finish on gear faces.

options.text: Approve the faster method to protect the delivery date and check gears after assembly.
Ask the shop to show surface finish readings from the method on one part and decide.
Run trial parts with the faster method, test noise and wear, and approve if specifications hold.
Approve the faster method for the first batch and inspect gear faces on every tenth part.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to draft a short report on a week of stack testing showing voltage against current. One test run was restarted after a power dip.

options.text: Report the results from the completed runs and attach the full data file for reference.
Describe the tests and results, note the restarted run, and send the draft for review.
Replace the restarted run's values with the previous week's values to keep the curve smooth.
Leave the restarted run out of the report since the power dip spoiled it.

advanced.situation: You lead engineers, a supplier and a customer representative in cutting a fuel cell stack's cost by 15%. The supplier resists changes to the membrane and plates.

options.text: Lower the specification limits so cheaper parts pass and tell the customer after delivery.
Ask the supplier for a price cut on both parts and review the stack design later.
Change to the cheapest membrane on the market and update the specification to match.
Break down stack cost, test lower-cost membrane and plate options with the supplier, and agree trade-offs.

basic.situation: You help set up a test station for a fuel cell stack. Your lead gives you a connection diagram for the gas lines, humidifier and data logger.

options.text: Connect the lines per the diagram and run nitrogen through them to check for leaks.
Connect the lines per the diagram, leak-check the gas fittings, and have your lead check them.
Connect the lines per the diagram and re-tighten each fitting by hand before the test starts.
Connect the lines per the diagram and open the hydrogen supply to see if pressure holds.

advanced.situation: Your team proposes a new hydrogen fuel cell design with a rare metal catalyst. You must evaluate its power output, system cost and environmental impact before the funding review.

options.text: Report the peak power from the tests and the catalyst cost per stack to the review.
Combine test power data with a cost model and a life-cycle estimate, and state the uncertainties.
Use the highest power from one run and the lowest metal price in the review.
Present the catalyst's low loading as proof of low cost and low environmental impact.

basic.situation: You get data from a test of a 5 kW fuel cell system: hydrogen flow, voltage and current. Your lead asks you to calculate its electrical efficiency.

options.text: Multiply voltage and current for power, divide by the hydrogen energy input, and state the units.
Take the efficiency from the manufacturer's datasheet for the 5 kW class of system.
Divide the hydrogen flow by the voltage and report the result as a percentage.
Calculate power from voltage and current and divide it by the system's rated 5 kW.

advanced.situation: A fuel cell bus lost power after 2,000 hours. You lead the failure analysis, and the bus maker says the fuel cell is at fault.

options.text: Collect operating logs, inspect the stack and bus interfaces, and test hypotheses before assigning a cause.
Take the stack apart and examine the cells for membrane and catalyst damage, then report.
Return the failed stack to service after cleaning it and watch whether power drops again.
Agree the fuel cell is at fault and offer the bus maker a replacement stack.

basic.situation: You help connect a new motor controller to a fuel cell vehicle's power bus using the wiring specification. One connector on the controller does not match the harness.

options.text: Stop, report the mismatch to your supervisor, and wait for an approved adapter or wiring change.
Fit a similar-looking connector from the stores and test the controller at low power.
Connect the matching leads first and ask your supervisor about the odd connector later.
Cut off the harness connector and splice the wires to the controller terminals to save time.

advanced.situation: You manage the sizing of a fuel cell and battery hybrid for a delivery truck. Customers want a 400 km range, but heavy battery and fuel cell options both raise weight and cost.

options.text: Size the fuel cell for the average load and the battery for the peak power.
Choose the largest battery that fits and a small fuel cell to extend range.
Simulate duty cycles to size the fuel cell and battery together, then compare cost and durability.
Size components to a flat road range of 400 km and add a note about hills.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to run a standard simulation of a small fuel cell motor drive in the team's software and report the efficiency curve. The tutorial uses default parameters.

options.text: Enter the real motor parameters, run the model, and report the curve to your lead.
Enter the real motor parameters, run the model, and compare the curve with a test result.
Adjust the model's losses until the curve looks like the brochure curve, then report it.
Run the model with the tutorial's default parameters and report the efficiency curve it gives.

advanced.situation: Your company wants a new testing programme for fuel cell durability, but its test stations cannot cycle temperature and humidity fast enough. You are asked to design the programme.

options.text: Run the existing stations at their limit and extend the test time to make up.
Rent faster test stations from another lab and use their standard test programme as it is.
Cut the cycling steps from the programme and count the shortened tests as durability proof.
Define durability goals, design the test sequence, and specify new equipment that cycles conditions quickly.

basic.situation: Your fuel cell test needs the factory crane on Thursday, but manufacturing has a launch run that day. Your supervisor asks you to help coordinate.

options.text: Take the crane during the launch run while the operators are busy elsewhere on the floor.
Tell your supervisor the crane is not available and push the test to next month.
Ask manufacturing which crane times are free, offer to move the test, and confirm in writing.
Book the crane for Thursday afternoon and send manufacturing an email about the booking.

advanced.situation: A new fuel cell stack variant has passed its tests. The production team wants parts released now, but a durability test on one component is still running with early signs of wear.

options.text: Hold the release, review the wear data with the test lead, and agree release conditions.
Release the parts in a small pilot batch and watch the durability test results.
Release the parts and ask production to track any returns from the first customers.
Release the parts and mark the durability test as passed so the records are complete.

basic.situation: Your team lead asks you to propose design alternatives for a car door hinge bracket to reduce weight. The current part is steel and must pass the same crash load tests.

options.text: Propose a thinner steel bracket with the same shape and update the drawing for review.
Sketch lighter material options, estimate each against the crash load, and share them with your lead.
Propose an aluminium bracket of the same shape and ask others to check strength.
Propose removing the reinforcing ribs to cut weight and check strength on the prototype.

advanced.situation: You are designing the brake system for a small electric van. In wet-road tests the first design misses the stopping distance target, though regenerative braking works well.

options.text: Analyse the wet-road data, adjust brake blending and friction materials, and retest against the target.
Reduce the regenerative share on wet roads and note that the target is nearly met.
Increase the brake disc size and recheck the stopping distance on the wet road.
Revise the target to match the first design's stopping distance and update the safety file.

basic.situation: A lead engineer asks you to help write control feature requirements for an automatic parking brake. You have the system description and a list of customer complaints.

options.text: Write requirements from the customer complaints and leave the technical limits to the software team.
Convert the system description into requirement statements and ask your lead to add limits.
Copy the old manual parking brake requirements and rename them automatic for the new system.
List each trigger and response, add limits and fault cases, then review it with your lead.

advanced.situation: You develop an emissions control algorithm for a diesel engine. It reduces nitrogen oxides in lab tests, but on road drives particle emissions rise and fuel economy falls.

options.text: Detect the lab test pattern in the software and run the clean mode during that test.
Keep the lab-optimised algorithm and report the road results as ordinary test variation in the summary.
Analyse the road data, tune the algorithm across operating ranges, and have a colleague review it.
Tune the algorithm for the lab test cycle and add a limit for particle output.

basic.situation: Your team lead asks you to study whether reshaping a car's wing mirror cuts wind noise. You have a two-hour wind tunnel booking.

options.text: Test old and new mirrors at the same speeds, record noise levels, and report the difference.
Test the new mirror once and report that it is quieter if you hear less noise.
Skip the tunnel and report that the new shape is quieter because it looks smoother.
Test the new mirror at highway speed and compare the noise with last year's figures.

advanced.situation: You direct system-level testing of a new lane-keeping assist. Early road tests show it works on marked roads, but the project plan has no tests on faded or missing markings.

options.text: Follow the plan as written and mention the missing marking cases in the final report.
Run extra tests on faded markings on a closed track and record the results.
Tell sales the system works on all roads, based on the marked-road results from the track.
Add faded and missing marking tests in varied weather, set pass criteria, and update the plan.

basic.situation: Several windscreen wiper motors from the field show burnt windings. Your lead asks you to do a basic root cause analysis using the returned parts and failure reports.

options.text: Scrap the returned motors to clear bench space and write the cause from similar past cases.
Read the failure reports and list the most common condition recorded for each failure.
Conclude that the motors overheated from overload because burnt windings usually mean overload.
Inspect the returned motors, group failures by condition in the reports, and list likely causes.

advanced.situation: You lead a design review for a suspension arm. The designer's analysis shows adequate strength, but the test team reports a fatigue crack in a prototype after only 40% of the target life.

options.text: Remove the crack finding from the review pack so the design stays on schedule.
Compare analysis assumptions with the crack location and load data, then decide the next steps.
Ask the designer to increase the arm thickness near the crack and rerun the analysis.
Approve the design since the analysis shows adequate strength and treat the crack as a one-off.

basic.situation: Your project manager asks you to help prepare a cost estimate for a new door trim design, using the drawing, material prices and the supplier's tooling quote.

options.text: Use the lowest material price quoted and state it as the full unit cost.
Add material, tooling per unit, labour and scrap, and note each assumption in the estimate.
Add material and tooling per unit from the quote and ask the manager about labour.
Use the cost per unit of the previous door trim and scale it by weight.

advanced.situation: Your company will launch a hydrogen-powered van. You must develop specifications for the fuel storage and supply system, and safety reviewers are concerned about leaks in crashes.

options.text: Write the specification around one tank supplier's brochure and release it to other suppliers.
Define pressure, leak detection and crash shut-off requirements from standards, then review with safety.
Copy the specification of a hydrogen bus tank system and adjust sizes for the van.
Specify a larger tank wall thickness and ask safety to approve the leak details later.

basic.situation: You are asked to prepare the monthly status report for a seat frame project and update the engineering documents. Two drawings show an old part number.

options.text: Edit the two drawings directly to the new part number and save over the originals.
Note the old part numbers in the status report and ask the drafter to update them.
Write the report using the part numbers the supplier uses on its delivery notes.
Update the drawings to the current part number through change control, then write the status report.

advanced.situation: A junior engineer presents test results to your project review but misreads a graph, and the manager starts to decide on that basis. You are the team's technical lead.

options.text: Wait until the meeting ends and then explain the misreading to the junior privately.
Let the junior finish, then email the manager an updated graph reading after the decision.
Pause politely, show what the graph says using the data, and let the junior continue.
Say nothing and let the decision stand, so the junior is not embarrassed in the meeting.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to suggest a location for a new haul road and stockpile at a granite quarry. The area has a stream on one side and houses beyond the other.

options.text: Mark options on the map, check distances to the stream and houses, and compare haul lengths.
Place the road and stockpile at the shortest haul route from the pit to the crusher.
Place the stockpile next to the stream so water can wet the pile and cut dust.
Use the same layout as the neighbouring quarry, where it has worked for years.

advanced.situation: A tin deposit lies beneath a river terrace. You must select an extraction method, weighing safety, cost, deposit shape and flood risk.

options.text: Choose the method used at the nearest tin mine and adapt the plan to this deposit.
Pick the method with the highest recovery and drop flood risk from the summary.
Score each method on safety, cost, recovery and flood risk from drill data, then recommend.
Choose open pit as the cheapest method and plan flood walls once the design is set.

basic.situation: Your senior gives you a map with six drill hole locations at a bauxite prospect and the core logs. You are asked to describe the deposit's basic thickness and extent.

options.text: Average the ore thickness across the six holes and report it as the deposit thickness.
Mark the deposit boundary as the edge of the map and report its size.
Plot ore thickness at each hole, mark where it thins out, and note the hole spacing.
Use the thickest hole's ore thickness for the whole area since it shows the potential.

advanced.situation: You assess whether to develop a copper-gold deposit with steep, narrow veins and poor road access. Drill data are sparse, and the owner wants a profit answer within two weeks.

options.text: Report that profit looks good because the veins carry high grades in several holes.
Build a simple model from drill data, test access and recovery cases, and report profit ranges.
Estimate the average grade from the holes and report profit using the standard metal price.
Report the highest grade hole as the typical grade and the profit that follows from it.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to monitor daily ore production at a gold mine and flag when it falls. Today's tonnage is 15% below the weekly average.

options.text: Record the shortfall in the daily report and compare it with last week's tonnage.
Adjust the day's tonnage record up to the weekly average to avoid questions from management.
Check the shift logs for downtime and delays, record the cause, and tell your supervisor.
Treat the dip as normal variation and watch whether tomorrow's tonnage recovers before reporting.

advanced.situation: You coordinate development of a new underground mine ventilation system. The fan contractor delivers fans with a lower rating than specified, but says the airflow will be enough.

options.text: Hold acceptance, check airflow against the specification with modelling, and agree a fix with the contractor.
Start the mine using the lower-rated fans and add extra fans if gas readings rise.
Accept the fans if the contractor gives a written statement on the airflow they will deliver.
Install the fans and measure airflow after installation, then decide whether changes are needed.

basic.situation: On a quarry inspection with your supervisor, you notice a conveyor guard is missing near a drive roller, and the conveyor is running.

options.text: Tell your supervisor, request the conveyor be stopped and locked off, and record the finding.
Reach past the exposed roller to check its bearing quickly while the conveyor keeps running.
Warn the nearby workers to keep clear of the roller and finish the inspection.
Tell your supervisor and record the missing guard in the inspection list for follow-up.

advanced.situation: You set inspection standards for slope stability at a pit with weak clay layers. Heavy rain is forecast, and inspectors disagree about how often to check the highwall.

options.text: Keep the current weekly inspections and add one check after the heaviest rain day.
Let the most senior inspector decide when to check and record the decisions later.
Set inspection triggers from rainfall and movement readings, define stop-work levels, and brief inspectors.
Order daily highwall inspections for the whole rain season and write a simple checklist.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to prepare a simple schedule of monthly costs for running a small sand quarry, using equipment lists and fuel and labour prices.

options.text: Take last year's monthly costs and increase them by the usual yearly price rise.
Cost the fuel and labour from the lists and add a round figure for the rest.
Use the lowest equipment hire rates quoted for all months to keep the schedule attractive.
List equipment hours, fuel, labour and maintenance by month, apply prices, and check totals.

advanced.situation: You prepare detailed cost estimates for developing a deep limestone mine. The owner asks you to drop the contingency so the project passes the bank's approval.

options.text: Keep the contingency but phase the costs so the early years look smaller to the bank.
Remove the contingency and hold the unit costs low in the bank version of the estimate.
Keep a risk-based contingency, show the estimate range, and explain the reasons to the owner.
Reduce the contingency a little and list the added risks in the estimate notes.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to write a short technical summary of last month's drilling results for the mine manager. You have the drill logs and a survey map.

options.text: Summarise hole depths and ore intersections in a table and attach the drill logs and map.
Report the average grade of the richest holes as the average for the whole programme.
Summarise hole depths, ore intersections and grades, attach the map, and note any missed holes.
Write a paragraph on the richest holes and attach the logs for the manager to read.

advanced.situation: Two junior survey technicians you supervise produce pit surveys with errors. One struggles with the instrument and the other rushes. You are responsible for their training.

options.text: Observe each at work, coach their specific errors, set a checking routine, and review later.
Run a group training session on the instrument and set a rule to double-check all surveys.
Move the weaker technician to office work and ask the other to slow down.
Mark both down in their evaluations and warn them that errors will end their contracts.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to draft a design for a lead shielding wall around a new radiation source in a research lab. You have the source activity and the dose limit for the adjacent corridor.

options.text: Calculate the thickness that keeps the corridor dose below the limit and send it for review.
Use the wall thickness from a similar lab and check it against the dose limit.
Choose a thick lead wall that looks generous and record the thickness in the draft.
Size the wall for the source's weakest radiation type since the corridor is rarely used.

advanced.situation: You lead design of a spent-fuel handling process for a research reactor. The current process creates large volumes of contaminated rinse water, and the operator wants less waste while keeping safety.

options.text: Reduce the rinse volumes by half in the process and monitor the contamination levels afterwards.
Add a filter step to reuse the rinse water and update the process diagram for review.
Map the waste streams, assess options that cut water use, and check each one's safety effect.
Release the lightly contaminated rinse water to the drain to cut the stored waste volume.

basic.situation: You assist the shift supervisor in monitoring a research reactor's daily operation. On your rounds, a coolant temperature reading is above its normal band but within the limit.

options.text: Record the reading, compare it with earlier shifts, and tell the shift supervisor about the trend.
Adjust the cooling flow valve yourself a little to bring the temperature back into band.
Record the reading and mention it at the end-of-shift handover with the other notes.
Note that the reading is within the limit and continue the rest of your rounds.

advanced.situation: At night in a research reactor, a radiation alarm trips in the experiment hall for no clear reason. You are duty engineer, and the manager cannot be reached for fifteen minutes.

options.text: Reset the alarm and wait for the plant manager to call back before acting.
Check the alarm detector for faults first and keep the reactor running at power meanwhile.
Clear the hall and monitor the readings while you keep trying to reach the manager.
Follow the emergency procedure: shut down, clear the hall, and notify the manager and regulator.

basic.situation: On a walkdown of a research reactor hall, you notice a radiation sign is missing at a door to a controlled area. Your supervisor is nearby.

options.text: Assume the sign was removed on purpose for work and carry on with the walkdown.
Record the missing sign in your walkdown notes and report it in the weekly summary.
Fetch a spare sign from the store and fix it up yourself before telling anyone.
Tell your supervisor, record the location, and ask for a temporary sign to be placed now.

advanced.situation: You direct environmental compliance for a nuclear facility. A routine sample shows tritium in a drainage ditch at 70% of the discharge limit, up from 20% last quarter.

options.text: Note that the level is still under the limit and review it again next quarter.
Move the sampling point upstream where the readings are lower so the trend looks stable.
Increase sampling to monthly and report the rising trend in the next quarterly report.
Investigate the source, increase sampling, restrict related discharges, and inform the regulator as required.

basic.situation: You assist an experiment on how well a ceramic container holds radioactive samples. The sample count is higher than the procedure allows in the hood.

options.text: Place the extra samples on the bench beside the hood for the day and log them.
Run all the samples in two batches and update the log with the batch times.
Hold the extra samples, tell your supervisor, and run the number the procedure allows.
Load all the samples into the hood together to finish the experiment on time.

advanced.situation: You direct a research project testing a new fuel cladding material. Early results are promising, but the sponsor wants to publish and promote the material before irradiation tests finish.

options.text: Finish the irradiation tests first, share interim data with limits stated, and agree timing.
Share the results with the sponsor privately and delay public statements until a later date.
Describe the material as proven in the paper and add the irradiation results in an update.
Publish the promising results now with a note that irradiation tests are still running.

basic.situation: A senior colleague asks you to help write an operating instruction for transferring radioactive samples between labs. You have the existing transfer notes.

options.text: Write the steps from memory of the last transfer and file them as the instruction.
Tidy the existing notes into a clean document and leave the safety points as they are.
Convert the notes into numbered steps and send them to the colleague for approval.
Rewrite the notes as ordered steps, add shielding and monitoring checks, and ask for review.

advanced.situation: Your team prepares an environmental impact statement for a planned isotope production facility. The draft understates traffic and waste volumes compared with the engineering data.

options.text: Submit the draft as written, since the regulator checks the figures after approval anyway.
Keep the draft figures and add a note that actual volumes may be higher.
Align the statement with the engineering data, state assumptions, and have specialists review it.
Update the traffic and waste figures to the engineering data and submit on schedule.

basic.situation: You attend a team meeting on specifications for a new cooling pump system. The draft gives a flow rate that does not match the heat load figure shown earlier.

options.text: Raise the mismatch politely in the meeting, show both figures, and note who will check them.
Say nothing in the meeting because the senior engineers must have checked the figures.
Note the mismatch in your own notebook and check it again before the next meeting.
Mention the mismatch to the chair after the meeting and share both of the figures.

advanced.situation: You lead a discussion with a vendor and a safety review board on replacing a reactor cooling pump with a cheaper model. The vendor says the pump is equivalent, but the board wants proof.

options.text: Ask the vendor for a safety case on the pump and send it to the board.
Order the pump now so delivery fits the shutdown and send paperwork to the board later.
Compare the vendor's data with requirements, ask the board what evidence it needs, and plan tests.
Tell the board the vendor is a trusted supplier and ask for approval on that basis.

basic.situation: A drilling supervisor asks you to explain the mud weight and pore pressure chart to the new rig crew before the next section. You have the chart and today's drilling data.

options.text: Hand out the chart and explain the mud weight line and the pore pressure line.
Explain each line against today's depth, say what a deviation means, and check the crew understands.
Tell the crew the numbers are on the chart and they should ask the supervisor.
Tell the crew to adjust mud weight by feel, since the chart is a rough guide.

advanced.situation: At 3,000 m the rig sees unexpected gas and pressure rises. You lead a call with the geologist and rig engineer, and each standby hour is costly.

options.text: Raise mud weight to the geologist's expected pressure and resume drilling slowly while monitoring.
Keep drilling at the planned speed to get through the zone and avoid standby cost.
Wait for the next bit run to see whether the readings settle before changing anything.
Review the pressure and gas logs together, agree a safe response, and update the drilling plan.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to monitor an oil well's daily production and flag when it drops. Today's rate is 12% below last week, and the water cut has risen.

options.text: Increase the choke setting to push the rate back up and mention it later.
Compare rate, pressure and water cut with last week, flag the drop, and suggest a review.
Flag the drop to your supervisor and attach the rate and water cut figures.
Wait two more days to see if the rate recovers before mentioning it to your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You analyse reservoir data to place a new well in an oil field with a gas cap and water below. The richest-looking zone sits close to the gas-oil contact, and this year's budget allows one well.

options.text: Place the well in the same spot as the nearest producing well since it works there.
Place the well in the thickest oil zone and set a lower rate to reduce coning.
Model coning at candidate spots, rank them by recovery and risk, and recommend one.
Place the well close to the gas-oil contact to capture the richest zone first.

basic.situation: A small operator asks you to help estimate the cost and expected production of a shallow onshore well. You have costs from three nearby wells.

options.text: Average the nearby wells' costs and production rates and report one figure for each.
Use the nearby wells' costs and decline curves, adjust for depth, and show the range.
Take the cost and rate of the most productive nearby well as your estimate.
Use the operator's hoped-for production rate as the estimate and calculate the economics from it.

advanced.situation: You set the method your team uses to evaluate offshore drilling sites. Teams currently use different oil price and cost assumptions, so their rankings are hard to compare.

options.text: Require every evaluation to show a positive value by using the optimistic price case.
Define common price, cost and risk assumptions, publish a template, and brief teams on using it.
Ask each team to state its assumptions clearly at the top of every evaluation.
Fix a single oil price for all evaluations and ask teams to keep their own costs.

basic.situation: You help prepare a drilling plan for a new development well. Your senior gives you the target depth and offset well data, and one offset well lost circulation at 1,800 m.

options.text: Draft the casing and mud plans from offset data and mention losses in the notes.
Plan to drill through the loss zone at full mud weight and see what happens.
Draft the plan using the standard design for the field and add the target depth.
Draft casing and mud plans from offset data, flag the loss zone, and ask for review.

advanced.situation: You supervise a well stimulation programme. A planned acid job on a carbonate well is about to start, but the service company's pump trucks have a lower pressure rating than the design requires.

options.text: Run the job at the design pressure with the lower-rated trucks to keep to the schedule.
Ask the service company to confirm the trucks' ratings by phone and start if they agree.
Hold the job, check pump ratings against the design, and get suitable equipment or a revision.
Start the job at a lower pressure and extend the pumping time to place the acid.

basic.situation: You keep the daily drilling record for a well. At shift end the driller's depth is 15 m less than this morning's entry, and you are not sure why.

options.text: Keep the morning depth in the record because the driller probably misread the new one.
Enter the new depth and overwrite the morning figure so the record shows one value.
Check the pipe tally with the driller, find why depths differ, and note it.
Enter the new depth and add a comment that it differs from the morning figure.

advanced.situation: Management asks you to create a template for weekly technical reports on drilling and production so teams report consistently. Past reports vary a lot in detail and in how problems are recorded.

options.text: Ask each team to write reports in their own style but include a summary paragraph.
Review past reports, set required fields and definitions, pilot the template with teams, and revise it.
Build the template from the most detailed past report and send it to all teams.
Make the template a one-line status form so reports are short and easy to produce.

basic.situation: You assist in monitoring a well test. The test crew reports the flowing pressure is steady, but the choke size in the report does not match the field notes.

options.text: Use the choke size in the report and add a note about the mismatch.
Ask the test lead which choke was used, compare the notes, and record the confirmed value.
Use the choke size in the field notes since it was written at the time.
Use the larger choke size so the flow rate calculation shows a higher production.

advanced.situation: You coordinate engineers and technicians on a field development study. Two groups produce reports with conflicting reservoir models, and the deadline for the board is next week.

options.text: Ask both groups to run the board case on their models and present the range.
Send both reports to the board as they are and let directors choose between them.
Pick the model from the more experienced group and tell the other group to align.
Bring both groups together, compare data and assumptions, agree one model, and document the differences.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to collect data for an energy audit of a shopping mall's air conditioning. You can walk the plant room, read sub-meters, and talk to the technician.

options.text: Read the sub-meters once at midday and note the chiller set points from the controller.
Adjust the chiller controller to a lower set point to see how the readings change.
Log sub-meter readings for a full week with chiller schedules and set points.
Take the chiller's rated power from the nameplate and assume it runs all day.

advanced.situation: You lead an energy audit of a factory with compressed air, boilers and lighting. The owner has budget for one major upgrade this year and wants the audit to justify a new boiler.

options.text: Audit the boiler in depth and give the other two systems a quick walkthrough.
Report savings from the boiler upgrade at the highest possible figure to justify the purchase.
Audit all three systems and give the boiler upgrade a high priority as the owner wishes.
Measure each system, rank savings by payback, and report the ranking even if boiler ranks low.

basic.situation: You are asked to verify the electricity bill for a school against its meter readings. The bill shows 18,400 kWh, but your reading of the meter shows about 16,900 kWh for the same period.

options.text: Compare dates and readings, check multipliers and estimated reads, and query the utility.
Change your reading record to match the bill so the school's file is consistent.
Report the difference to the school and suggest they ask the utility to check.
Assume the bill is right since utility meters are checked and note your reading differs.

advanced.situation: You created an energy model of a new office tower to verify its design performance. After commissioning, measured energy use is 30% higher than the model predicted.

options.text: Tell the owner real buildings often use more than models predict, so the gap is normal.
Compare model inputs with as-built systems, calibrate the model, and find the causes.
Scale the model results up by 30% so they match the measured use in the report.
Lower the measured energy figures by 30% in the verification report to match the model.

basic.situation: A client's facility team asks you to explain basic energy management at a short session. Most attendees are technicians who do not know what a demand charge is.

options.text: Tell attendees that demand charges are a management matter and need no action from them.
Tell attendees to turn off equipment when not in use and leave out the tariff details.
Explain demand charges with a slide and give the attendees a copy of the tariff sheet.
Explain demand charges using a real bill, show which start-ups raise peaks, and take questions.

advanced.situation: Your company is negotiating a power purchase agreement for a factory. The supplier offers a lower tariff for a ten-year fixed volume commitment, though the factory plans to cut consumption soon.

options.text: Model consumption with planned savings, compare take-or-pay exposure, and negotiate flexible volume terms.
Accept the offer because the tariff is lower and savings can be handled later.
Recommend signing now to lock the tariff and tell management the savings plan will fit.
Ask for a lower volume commitment at the same tariff and accept if the supplier agrees.

basic.situation: You monitor construction of a hospital wing. The drawings call for LED lighting with occupancy sensors, but the contractor's delivery note lists standard fittings and no sensors.

options.text: Approve the delivery note as complete, since the fittings are LED, and close the item.
Let the installation continue and plan to add sensors during the first maintenance round.
Compare the delivery note with the specification and raise the mismatch with the project manager.
Ask the contractor if sensors will be added later and record the answer in the log.

advanced.situation: You direct the rollout of an energy management project across six hospitals. One hospital's building manager resists, saying the new controls could affect patient comfort, and the schedule is tight.

options.text: Install the controls at night when the manager is away and explain the change afterwards.
Ask your director to instruct the building manager to accept the controls on schedule.
Meet the manager, address comfort concerns with a pilot and set limits, and adjust the plan.
Delay that hospital to the end of the rollout and proceed with the other five.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to draft a short report on a bakery's energy use after an audit. You have the meter data, the equipment list and photos.

options.text: Copy savings figures from another bakery's report and state them as this bakery's potential.
List the equipment with its nameplate power and leave the savings to the supervisor.
Summarise the total monthly energy use and attach the photos and equipment list to it.
Summarise energy use by equipment, highlight the largest users, list savings ideas, and send for review.

advanced.situation: You write an energy management routine for a building automation system in an office block. It will shut down air handlers after hours, but a data room on the same system needs cooling around the clock.

options.text: Program the office floors' shutdown now and handle the data room in a later change.
Program the schedule with a data room exception, simulate it, and test it before going live.
Program the shutdown for all zones and ask the data room staff to report overheating.
Program shutdown for all zones and mute the data room alarm to avoid false alerts.

basic.situation: A shop owner asks you why their air conditioner uses so much power and whether setting it to 16 degrees will cool the shop faster.

options.text: Tell the owner that 16 degrees works faster and saves power in hot weather.
Tell the owner to set 16 degrees for an hour and then raise it.
Explain that 16 degrees will not cool faster, suggest 24, and check filters and door seals.
Tell the owner that a higher set point saves power and suggest cleaning the filters.

advanced.situation: A hotel chain asks you to recommend a fuel for a new laundry and kitchen boiler at a remote island site. Piped gas is not available, and diesel, LPG and biomass pellets are possible.

options.text: Recommend diesel because the hotel already has delivery arrangements for its generators and fuel tanks.
Compare delivered cost, supply reliability, emissions and storage for each fuel, then recommend one.
Recommend biomass pellets because they are renewable and have no supply issues on islands.
Recommend LPG because it burns cleanly and is easy to store in cylinders on site.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to create the mechanical design document for a small bracket that holds a sensor on an automated filling machine. You have the sensor datasheet and the machine drawing.

options.text: Draw the bracket with the datasheet's hole positions and tolerances, and have your senior check it.
Draw the bracket to fit the machine frame and add the sensor's mounting hole sizes.
Send a sketch to the workshop and draw it up after the part is built.
Copy an older sensor bracket drawing and change the title, part number and date.

advanced.situation: You build a mechanical model to simulate a robotic pick-and-place arm for a new line. The simulation shows vibration at the gripper at high speed, though the line needs that speed.

options.text: Reduce the arm speed in the model until the vibration disappears and report that speed.
Add flexibility and joint stiffness to the model, test damping and speed profiles, and validate it.
Smooth the vibration plot in the report and state that the model meets the speed target.
Add a heavier base in the model to reduce the vibration and keep the speed.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to upgrade an existing manual door latch tester by adding a sensor that counts cycles. You have the tester drawings and a sensor kit.

options.text: Fit the sensor where it fits easily and compare the count with a manual count.
Drill into the tester frame where the sensor sits conveniently and check the drawings later.
Pick a mounting point from the drawings, fit and wire the sensor, and test the count.
Fit the sensor to the tester and trust the counter display once it lights up.

advanced.situation: Your plant moves finished glass bottles from a filler to packing. You must design automated handling, but bottles are fragile, and the line speed varies with the filler.

options.text: Design a gentle transfer with sensors and buffers, simulate speed changes, and test with real bottles.
Use plastic bottle handling parts from another line and adjust the speed until bottles stop breaking.
Use a standard conveyor and robot gripper rated for glass and set a fixed speed.
Design the transfer for the maximum line speed and use hard stops to position bottles.

basic.situation: A factory technician asks you whether a stepper motor or a servo motor suits a small label applicator. Your supervisor is available for questions.

options.text: Explain that servos cost more but are more precise, and suggest a servo for the applicator.
Ask about speed, accuracy and load, explain the trade-offs, and confirm with your supervisor.
Tell the technician either motor will work and to buy whichever the supplier has in stock.
Suggest the stepper because it is cheaper and most small machines like it use one.

advanced.situation: A packaging line wastes 6% of its products at the sealing station. Operators blame sealing temperature, but sensor data point to inconsistent film feeding. You must suggest improvements.

options.text: Compare temperature and film feed data with defects, trial a feed fix, and propose changes.
Follow the operators' view, raise the sealing temperature, and see whether waste falls later.
Replace the sealing unit with a new model and drop the film feed from the review.
Adjust the film feed tension and monitor the waste rate over a full week of production.

basic.situation: You implement a simple fix on a conveyor sorting gate: a limit switch and a relay your supervisor specified. The wiring diagram is in the pack.

options.text: Install per the diagram, check continuity, test the gate with the supply isolated, then run it.
Wire the switch your own way if it seems simpler, and test whether the gate works.
Bypass the switch with a temporary jumper to keep the line running and fit it later.
Wire the switch and relay per the diagram and run the gate on the line.

advanced.situation: Your company considers a new robotic palletiser costing RM900,000. You must judge its feasibility, cost and performance benefits against the current manual palletising.

options.text: Recommend purchase now because competitors use robots, and settle cost questions during installation later.
Use the vendor's throughput claims and the labour savings to calculate the payback period.
Judge it by the robot's brochure features and recommend a demonstration visit to the vendor.
Measure current throughput and cost, check vendor data against references or a trial, and model payback.

basic.situation: You must choose a sensor to detect when a cardboard box reaches the end of a conveyor. Your supervisor gives you a shortlist of an inductive, a photoelectric and an ultrasonic sensor.

options.text: Choose the ultrasonic sensor because it detects any material at a distance and order two.
Choose the photoelectric sensor since it detects cardboard, check its range, and confirm with your supervisor.
Choose the cheapest sensor on the shortlist and test it on the conveyor when it arrives.
Choose the inductive sensor because it is rugged and most factories use it on conveyors.

advanced.situation: You specify materials for the housing of a mechatronic sensor that works in a hot, humid, oily factory zone. The cheaper plastic option has passed room-temperature tests.

options.text: Use the cheaper plastic since it passed testing, and note that room temperature is representative.
Use the cheaper plastic and add a protective coating in case of oil exposure in service.
Compare materials for heat, humidity and oil resistance, and test samples in factory conditions.
Choose an aluminium housing for strength and heat and check the cost against the budget.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to maintain the project files for a robot cell upgrade. You have drawings, emails, test sheets and an old file list, and some files have similar names.

options.text: Move the files into one folder and add the latest versions to the file list.
Keep files where they are and add a note on the file list pointing to them.
Name files by type, version and date, store them together, and update the file list.
Delete the older-looking files to keep the folder tidy and rename the rest for the project.

advanced.situation: You publish the engineering report on qualification tests for a new motion controller. A test passed only after a second attempt that followed a settings change, and the customer will read the report.

options.text: Remove the first attempt's data from the test records so the report shows a clean pass.
Report the passing attempt and mention the earlier attempt and settings change in an appendix.
Report the passing attempt and state that the controller met the specification at test.
Report both attempts and the settings change with reasons, and show the qualifying evidence.

basic.situation: A senior engineer asks you to draft a schematic and layout for a small MEMS pressure sensor die. The foundry's design rules set a 3 micrometre minimum gap between membrane features.

options.text: Draw the layout to the foundry rules, run the rule check, and fix violations before review.
Reduce the membrane gaps to 2 micrometres for sensitivity and tell the foundry afterwards.
Reuse the layout from the last sensor die and resize features by eye to fit.
Draw the layout with 3 micrometre gaps throughout and send it to the senior for review.

advanced.situation: You create the layout for a MEMS accelerometer with a fragile proof mass that must also fit a tiny package. The package supplier's keep-out rules conflict with the proof mass size.

options.text: Shrink the proof mass to fit the keep-out rules and note the effect on sensitivity.
Compare constraints, test layouts with a smaller mass or other package, and agree the trade-off.
Place the proof mass partly inside the keep-out zone and submit the layout as compliant.
Ask the package supplier to relax the rules and keep the proof mass as is.

basic.situation: You help collect data for a failure analysis of MEMS gyros that drift after thermal cycling. Your supervisor gives you a test log template and the failed units.

options.text: Record each unit's drift, cycle count and conditions in the template, and keep failed units labelled.
Open the failed units for a quick look inside and bag the parts together.
Record the drift of the three worst units and note that the others looked similar.
Record the drift of each unit in the template and add the cycle counts later.

advanced.situation: Yield on a MEMS microphone line has dropped from 92% to 81% in two weeks. You lead the reliability and yield study, and production wants a quick answer.

options.text: Split yield loss by step and lot, find process changes, and verify with a controlled run.
Compare the process settings before and after the drop and adjust the one that changed most.
Loosen the final test limits to bring the yield back to 92% and ship the units.
Raise the final test limits so weaker units are rejected and shipping quality holds.

basic.situation: A senior engineer asks you to update the bill of materials for a MEMS module after a supplier changed a capacitor's part number. The datasheet shows a different package size.

options.text: Update the part number and keep the old footprint since capacitors are all similar.
Update the part number in the bill of materials and attach the new datasheet.
Update the part number, check the new footprint against the layout, and flag the change.
Edit the datasheet package size to match the old footprint and update the bill of materials.

advanced.situation: You establish documentation standards for a MEMS group where engineers keep drawings, process notes and bills of materials in different formats. A new product is about to be transferred to a partner.

options.text: Pick the format used by the largest team and ask everyone to switch within a month.
Define required documents, create templates, convert the new product's files, and add a release check.
Hand the partner the full process files for all products to avoid reformatting work.
Send the partner each engineer's files as they are with a list of formats.

basic.situation: You help fill out the process control checklist for a MEMS etch step, collecting etch depth data from five wafers. Wafer 4's depth is slightly outside the control limit.

options.text: Record all five depths and mention wafer 4 at the end-of-shift handover to the next team.
Measure wafer 4 again until the depth falls inside the limit and record that value.
Record wafer 4's depth as the limit value so the checklist shows all wafers in control.
Record all five depths, mark wafer 4 out of limit, and tell your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You design quality control protocols and data reporting for a new MEMS microphone line. The customer requires traceability by lot and wafer, but the test equipment reports lot-level data.

options.text: Treat each lot as one wafer in the reports and explain this in the notes.
Report lot-level data to the customer now and ask the vendor for wafer-level output later.
Define wafer-level tracking at key steps, specify data reports, and validate it on a pilot lot.
Assign wafer numbers to lot data in the reports by assumption to satisfy the customer.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to run a basic simulation of a MEMS cantilever's resonant frequency using the group's model template and the design dimensions.

options.text: Enter the dimensions and materials, run the model, and compare the result with a hand estimate.
Use the previous cantilever's frequency and scale it by the length ratio of the two designs.
Change the template's material values until the frequency matches the target, then report it.
Enter the dimensions, run the model with default materials, and report the frequency from the output.

advanced.situation: You model a MEMS pressure sensor to balance cost and performance. Die size drives cost, membrane thickness drives sensitivity, and the two pull in opposite directions.

options.text: Pick the smallest die size and adjust the membrane until the simulation looks acceptable.
Pick the thinnest membrane that passes the sensitivity target and report its die size.
Simulate die sizes and thicknesses with process variation, and present the cost and performance curve.
Fit the model to match the target cost and performance, then report the design as optimised.

basic.situation: A project lead asks you to help schedule simple research tasks for a MEMS sensor test, including wafer fabrication at a foundry with a six-week lead time.

options.text: List tasks and dependencies, allow the foundry lead time, and share the draft with your lead.
Schedule the tasks from the earliest date and assume the foundry can deliver sooner.
Give the project lead a schedule with the foundry lead time cut to two weeks.
Schedule the test tasks to start right after the wafers are due and share the dates.

advanced.situation: Your group plans a new MEMS flow sensor and must define research methods and the development schedule. Market data suggest customers need two sensitivity ranges, but the budget covers one design.

options.text: Promise customers both ranges in the proposal and plan to find the budget during development.
Design for the range in the largest customer's request and schedule the rest later.
Design a single sensor that tries to cover both ranges and plan a long development.
Find which range more customers need, design for it first, and plan milestones toward the second.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to design a simple electro-optical sensor that detects a bottle on a conveyor, using an LED, a photodiode and a bench power supply.

options.text: Copy a circuit from the internet and adjust the resistor values until the LED lights.
Match LED and photodiode wavelengths to the bottle, build it on the bench, and test detection.
Connect the LED straight to the bench supply at full voltage to get the strongest light.
Build it with the kit's LED and photodiode and check it detects a bottle.

advanced.situation: You lead design of an LED display backlight for a laptop maker who wants 20% lower power at the same brightness. Thermal and colour uniformity limits make this difficult.

options.text: Reduce the drive current by 20% and try a more reflective film behind the panel.
Model LED, optics and driver options, prototype the top two, and measure power and uniformity.
Switch to the most efficient LED in the catalogue and check the colour uniformity.
Report the 20% saving using power measured at a dimmer setting than the specified brightness.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to list possible uses of a new infrared sensing module in a food factory. You have its datasheet and a short factory tour.

options.text: List the uses that the vendor's salesperson suggested and present them as your findings today.
List uses from the datasheet's application section and mark those seen on the tour.
List uses of infrared sensing seen in other factories and assume the module fits them.
List uses that match its range and sensitivity, such as fill detection, and note limits.

advanced.situation: A client wants a compact sensor to detect tiny gas leaks in a refinery. You must decide which photonics approach, such as laser absorption or fibre sensing, meets sensitivity, safety and cost targets.

options.text: Recommend the approach used by the client's competitor in a similar plant and cost it.
Compare the approaches on sensitivity, safety and cost, test a short list, and recommend one.
Recommend the cheapest fibre sensing option and say it meets the refinery safety needs.
Choose laser absorption since it is the most sensitive and check the safety rating later.

basic.situation: You test a short fibre-optic link between two switches. Your lead gives you a light source, a power meter and the link's loss budget of 3 dB.

options.text: Measure sent and received power, compare loss with 3 dB, and clean connectors if high.
Look into the fibre end while the laser source is on to see if it works.
Measure the received power and compare it with the receiver's minimum level on the datasheet.
Shine a flashlight through the fibre and call the link fine if light comes out.

advanced.situation: Your team's prototype laser sensor works in the lab, but you must establish its performance limits for temperature and vibration before the customer demo. Test time is two weeks.

options.text: Define the operating envelope, test at temperature and vibration extremes, and record where it fails.
Test the lab conditions that matter to the customer and quote the results as limits.
