Quote the laser component datasheet limits as the prototype's performance limits in the demo.
Test at room temperature with vibration and extrapolate the limits for higher temperatures.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to analyse system performance requirements for a photonic sensor going to production. The customer lists accuracy, response time and operating temperature.

options.text: Copy the requirements from the customer's email into a table and send it to your senior.
Check the requirements against the prototype's results and note which ones it meets today.
List each requirement as a measurable value, link it to the design, and query unclear items.
Remove the requirements the prototype cannot meet from the list before sending it on.

advanced.situation: You oversee transition of a photonic transceiver prototype to production. Yield in the pilot run is 70%, mostly from fibre alignment, and the factory wants to start volume next month.

options.text: Ship the pilot units that fail alignment at lower prices to hit the volume target.
Move to volume next month and add extra inspection steps to catch misaligned units.
Analyse the alignment losses, develop fixtures with the factory, and set a yield gate for volume.
Start volume on schedule and put an engineer on the line to adjust alignment.

basic.situation: You are asked to document the design process for a photodiode amplifier, including objectives and issues, using your notes from the work.

options.text: Write the process as having gone smoothly and leave the difficult issues out of it.
Paste your working notes into the design document and tidy up the headings and fonts.
Write the objective and design steps in order and attach your raw notes at the end.
Write the objective, design steps, issues met and how each was resolved, then ask for review.

advanced.situation: You create the design history for a photonic module that was redesigned three times. Records of why changes were made are scattered across emails and lab notebooks.

options.text: Fill the missing reasons with likely explanations so the history looks complete to the auditor.
Build the history from the final design files and note the revision numbers and dates.
Write a short summary of why the design changed based on what you remember.
Collect the reasons and test evidence for each revision, build a dated history, and confirm gaps.

basic.situation: A new operator joins the photonics assembly line. Your lead asks you to train them on a basic fibre splicing procedure, using the work instruction.

options.text: Let the operator watch an experienced colleague for an hour then splice customer fibres alone.
Give the operator the work instruction and tell them to ask if anything is unclear.
Demonstrate each step from the work instruction, let them practise with feedback, and check splice loss.
Demonstrate the splice once and let the operator start on production fibres with checks.

advanced.situation: You oversee fabrication of precision optical components. A shift lead proposes shortening the polishing time to meet an order, which may cause surface defects that are hard to see.

options.text: Approve the shorter time and rely on the customer to report any defects they find.
Approve the shorter time and record the normal polishing time in the batch record.
Test the shorter polishing on samples for surface quality, share the results, and agree the process.
Allow the shorter time on this order and add an extra inspection step at the end.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to back up the programs and parameters of a welding robot before a controller software update. The robot is in production and will be stopped for the update.

options.text: Run the update first and restore programs from the supplier's defaults if anything is lost.
Copy the programs to the controller's internal memory since the update keeps that storage.
Save the programs to a USB drive and update the controller software straight after.
Save programs and parameters externally, label with date and robot ID, and verify the files.

advanced.situation: You write code for a robot arm that sorts irregular parcels using a camera. The algorithm works in tests but fails when parcels overlap, and the customer's start date is close.

options.text: Deliver the code and tell the customer the arm will sort overlapping parcels reliably.
Add overlap detection, handle failures by re-presenting the parcel, and test with overlap cases.
Tune the camera thresholds until the test overlaps pass, then deliver the code on time.
Add a rule that rejects overlapping parcels into a manual bin and test it.

basic.situation: You changed a robot's pick position by 5 mm to fix a missed grip. Your supervisor reminds you that robot changes need to be recorded.

options.text: Leave the log as it is, since the grip now works and the program is saved.
Log the date, reason, old and new values, and save the new program version.
Add a short note in the log saying the pick position was changed by 5 mm.
Tell the supervisor verbally about the change and record it when you have time.

advanced.situation: You set documentation standards for robot application changes at a plant with twelve cells. Changes are noted in different places, and an outage was traced to an undocumented parameter edit.

options.text: Ask each cell owner to keep a change log in a shared folder for later review.
Restrict program edits to one engineer and let that person decide what is recorded.
Email all staff a reminder to document their changes and share the outage lesson.
Define a change record with required fields and approval, link it to backups, and audit it.

basic.situation: A packaging robot's gripper stopped closing during the night shift. Your lead asks you to investigate the mechanical failure with the maintenance records and the gripper itself.

options.text: Inspect the gripper and air line, check the maintenance record for wear history, and report.
Grease the gripper joints and return it to production to see if it holds.
Ask the night shift operator what happened and record their explanation as the cause.
Replace the gripper's seals, which commonly wear, and watch whether it works through the shift.

advanced.situation: Your lab explores a soft gripper for handling fragile fruit. Early prototypes bruise ripe mangoes, and the research manager asks you to lead the next research steps.

options.text: Study published soft gripper designs and copy the most popular one for the next prototype.
Test a softer silicone version of the gripper and record whether the mangoes still bruise.
Change the mango test to firm green fruit so the next prototype appears to work.
Measure the bruise pressure limits of the fruit, test soft materials and grip patterns, and compare.

basic.situation: Your lead gives you raw data from a distance sensor on a mobile robot and asks you to process it for a simple obstacle alert. The data has occasional wild spikes.

options.text: Filter the spikes with a median filter, check alerts at known distances, and log the settings.
Delete readings above a high number as errors and set the alert on what remains.
Lower the alert trigger distance until the spikes stop setting it off and mark it done.
Average the readings over a short window and set the alert to trigger below a distance.

advanced.situation: You review a design and cost estimate from a junior engineer for a robotic palletising cell. The cost looks low, and the reach calculations assume lighter boxes than the customer will use.

options.text: Send the estimate back asking the junior to use heavier boxes in the reach calculations.
Approve the estimate and add a note that box weights should be confirmed later.
Recheck reach and payload with real box weights, ask for revised costs, and approve when consistent.
Approve the estimate since the low cost will help win the contract and fix reach later.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to design end-of-arm tooling for a robot that picks flat metal brackets off a conveyor. You have the bracket drawing and the robot's payload rating.

options.text: Design a gripper for the bracket, check its weight against payload, and calculate grip force.
Buy a standard gripper from the catalogue that is advertised for flat metal parts.
Design a gripper for the bracket and test it on the robot with sample brackets.
Design a heavy steel gripper for strength and set the robot to run slowly with it.

advanced.situation: You design control software for a robot that works close to people in a warehouse. The software must stop the robot safely if a person enters its zone, but tests show a slow stop at full speed.

options.text: Limit speed by distance to people, use safety-rated sensors, verify stopping distances, and review with safety.
Enlarge the safety zone in the software and keep the robot's full speed in the aisles.
Reduce the robot's top speed so the stopping distance fits the safety zone and test it.
Shorten the stop delay by skipping the sensor confirmation check so the robot meets the target.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to build and configure a small training robot arm from a kit. The kit includes a controller, motors and a setup manual.

options.text: Assemble it in the order that seems logical and check the manual when stuck.
Power up the controller before connecting the motors to see which parts respond to commands.
Assemble per the manual, set joint limits, and run a slow test near the emergency stop.
Assemble it per the manual and run the full-speed demo program from the kit.

advanced.situation: You supervise two technicians commissioning a robot cell with a welder. One technician reports that the welder's interlock does not stop the robot when the door opens, and the customer inspection is tomorrow.

options.text: Lock out the cell, fix the interlock fault, retest the door stop, and inform the customer.
Bypass the interlock for the inspection and tell the customer the cell is working properly.
Put a warning sign on the door and fix the interlock after the customer inspection.
Ask the technician to retest the interlock to see if it was a one-off.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to measure the surface roughness of a thin film sample using an atomic force microscope. The sample surface looks slightly dusty.

options.text: Scan the sample as it is and remove obvious dust spots from the image afterwards.
Blow the dust off with clean air and scan one area at the default settings.
Clean the sample by the approved method, check calibration, and scan several areas, recording settings.
Wipe the film with a tissue and solvent from the bench to remove the dust.

advanced.situation: You lead research on dispersing nanoparticles in a polymer for heat transfer. Tests show clumping at higher loadings, and the funder expects a publication.

options.text: Characterise the clumping, test surface treatments and mixing methods, and report the results as found.
Reduce the loading to avoid clumping and report the improved heat transfer at that level.
Report heat transfer values from the clump-free samples and drop the others from the paper.
Describe the dispersion as uniform in the paper, since the funder expects strong results.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to make a simple 3D CAD model of a nanodevice holder from a sketch with micrometre dimensions. The sketch lacks one dimension.

options.text: Model the holder with a round number for the missing size and send it to fabrication.
Model the holder with a reasonable value for the missing dimension and note the assumption.
Model the holder by scaling the sketch from the dimensions that are given and save it.
Model the known dimensions, flag the missing one, and ask your senior for its value.

advanced.situation: You set design standards for nano-enabled food packaging film. Silver nanoparticles improve shelf life, but migration into food is unclear, and marketing wants a launch next quarter.

options.text: Approve the standard as it is and keep migration questions out of marketing material.
Allow the launch with a low silver loading and decide on migration tests afterwards.
Set the standard at the supplier's recommended silver loading and add a review in a year.
Require migration tests and a comparison with lower-risk materials before launch, and set limits.

basic.situation: You prepare a weekly report for your supervisor on lab activities with nanoparticle synthesis. Two batches were made, and one batch had an unexpected colour change.

options.text: Report both batches with methods and results, describe the colour change, and flag it.
Report the normal batch in detail and mention the colour change in one line.
Report the two batches as complete and discuss the colour change at the next meeting.
Leave the changed batch out of the report and discard it to avoid questions.

advanced.situation: You write a proposal to secure external funding for a nanofabrication workflow. The funder's call asks for evidence of readiness, and your preliminary data covers two trial runs.

options.text: Describe the trial runs positively and promise further results during the first year of funding.
Present the two trial runs plainly, plan more data, and cite related published work.
Include the stronger run's data as representative and mention the second run in passing.
Add projected results from a competitor's paper as if they were your own trial data.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to identify the equipment needed for a pilot run of a nanoparticle coating process, using the lab recipe and the target batch size.

options.text: Order the same equipment as the lab uses, in a quantity matching the pilot batch size.
Choose equipment from a catalogue by price and order it before checking the recipe.
List each step with equipment, capacity and cleanliness needs from the recipe, and flag gaps.
List the lab equipment used in the recipe and ask the supplier for larger versions.

advanced.situation: You optimise a commercial-scale nanoscale coating line. The coating thickness varies by 15% across the web, the customer needs 5%, and the line speed is already at the production target.

options.text: Replace the coating head with a newer model and keep the other settings the same.
Slow the line to improve thickness uniformity and measure the result at each speed.
Exclude the web edges from the thickness data so the variation shows within 5%.
Map thickness across the web, study drying and head settings, and trial changes systematically.

basic.situation: You help coordinate two lab technicians preparing nanoparticle samples. One technician asks if they can skip the fume hood step to save time because the solvent amount is small.

options.text: Ask the technician to check the solvent's safety data sheet before deciding on the hood step.
Say the hood step stays, explain the solvent risk, and reorder the tasks to save time.
Allow it and tell the technician to finish quickly so both samples are ready today.
Allow it for the small amount and ask the technician to open a window.

advanced.situation: You oversee three vendors building parts for a nano-probe system. One vendor's lens arrives with scratches, and another vendor's delivery date depends on that lens for final testing.

options.text: Accept the lens to keep the schedule and ask the vendor for a discount.
Ask the lens vendor if the scratches affect performance and decide from the reply.
Pass the scratched lens to the other vendor for testing and report results as normal.
Reject the lens with photos, agree a replacement date, and update the dependent vendor.

basic.situation: A customer calls with a basic question about how to store a nanoparticle suspension after opening. The product sheet says to keep it cool and sealed.

options.text: Tell the customer to keep it cool and sealed and to read the product sheet.
Tell the customer a fridge is fine for any nanoparticle product and not to worry.
Tell the customer to freeze the suspension to make it last longer between uses.
Explain the sheet's storage steps, say why they matter, and offer to send it.

advanced.situation: A colleague asks you for advice on integrating a nanoparticle sensor layer into a microfluidic chip. The layer degrades when exposed to the chip's cleaning solvent.

options.text: Suggest rinsing the chip quickly with the solvent and drying it straight away to limit exposure.
Review the layer and solvent chemistry, suggest another solvent or a barrier, and propose a test.
Suggest skipping the cleaning step on the chips that will be used for the demonstration.
Suggest a thicker sensor layer so enough of it survives each cleaning with the solvent.

basic.situation: You assist a test engineer measuring strain on a wind turbine blade component using strain gauges and a data logger. One gauge reads zero while the others show values.

options.text: Check the gauge wiring, test it with a known load, and log the fault before continuing.
Copy the reading from the neighbouring gauge for the zero channel and continue the test.
Record zero as the real strain at that point and report the component as unloaded there.
Mark that channel as faulty in the log and continue with the other gauges.

advanced.situation: You lead the failure investigation for an experimental turbine rotor that showed unexpected vibration and noise at high wind speeds. The design team believes it is a sensor fault.

options.text: Check the sensors, analyse the vibration and noise data, inspect the rotor, and run controlled tests.
Replace the sensors and see whether the vibration and noise continue at high speed.
Accept the sensor fault explanation and continue the high wind tests at full speed.
Accept the sensor fault explanation and limit turbine speed as a precaution during tests.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to help draft specifications for a gearbox oil cooler for a wind turbine. You have the gearbox losses, the nacelle size and the site temperature range.

options.text: Calculate the heat load, specify capacity, flow, size limits and temperature range, and send for review.
Copy the specification of the cooler used on another turbine and change the title.
Specify a very large cooler so site temperature does not matter, and fit it later.
Specify the cooler capacity from the gearbox losses and state the size limit from the nacelle.

advanced.situation: You define technical standards for a wind farm collector system that connects fifty turbines. The terrain includes rocky ground and a river crossing, and designers use differing cable depth rules.

options.text: Let each designer keep their own depth rule and require a note explaining the choice.
Set standards for cable rating, burial depth, crossings and protection by ground type, with designer input.
Adopt the deepest burial rule used by any designer for all ground types and crossings.
Set a shallow burial depth for all ground types to cut cost on the rocky sections.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to help write a report on test results for a wind farm's collector cables. The test sheet shows one cable section with insulation resistance below the limit.

options.text: Include all results, highlight the low section against its limit, and recommend repair and retest.
Record the low section's value as the limit value so the cable section is marked passed.
Report that the cables passed overall, since most sections were well above the limit.
Include all results and mention the low section in the summary paragraph at the end.

advanced.situation: You recommend infrastructure changes to improve a wind farm's performance and cut costs. Data show wake losses between rows and high maintenance travel time, and the budget supports one change.

options.text: Recommend repositioning the worst-affected turbines since wake loss reduces energy output across the farm.
Recommend stretching the turbine maintenance intervals to cut travel costs and keep the budget.
Recommend a new access road to cut travel time, since it is the easier change.
Quantify wake loss and travel cost, model each option's payback, and recommend the strongest return.

basic.situation: You help analyse a month of data from a wind farm and check availability against the contract specification of 97%. Your calculation gives 96.4%.

options.text: Report 96.4% to your senior and note that it is close to the specification.
Recheck the downtime records and formula, confirm the figure, and report the shortfall to your senior.
Wait for next month's data to see if the average reaches 97% before reporting.
Remove the longest outage from the data so availability shows above 97% in the report.

advanced.situation: You lead root cause analysis on a wind turbine tower bolt that failed in service. Three other turbines of the same batch are operating, and the operator wants to avoid shutting them down.

options.text: Preserve the bolt, inspect the others, check torque and material records, and advise on shutdown.
Replace the failed bolt and re-tighten the others to the specified torque on the next visit.
Keep the three turbines running and discard the failed bolt to clear the site.
Test the failed bolt's material and report whether it met the specification, then close.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to prepare a basic wind farm layout drawing showing twelve turbine positions from a coordinates list. Two coordinates fall inside a marked no-build area.

options.text: Plot all positions, flag the two in the no-build area, and ask your senior about them.
Plot ten positions and leave the other two off the drawing with a note.
Move the two positions just outside the area and plot all twelve on the drawing.
Plot all twelve as listed and remove the no-build area from the drawing to avoid clashes.

advanced.situation: You build a model to optimise access roads and crane pads for a hilly wind farm. The shortest road route crosses steep slopes and a stream, and the crane needs gentle gradients.

options.text: Add slope, stream and crane gradient limits, compare route costs, and review with the civil team.
Use the shortest route and set the steep slope sections as flat in the model.
Choose the shortest route in the model and have contractors adapt it on site.
Choose the route with the gentlest gradients and add the stream crossing cost to the model.

basic.situation: You monitor wind farm construction and see a contractor washing concrete trucks beside a stream. The environmental permit requires washouts to be contained and away from watercourses.

options.text: Ask the contractor to stop, photograph and record it, report to your supervisor, and follow up.
Leave the washout as it is because the stream is small and the concrete will settle.
Remind the contractor of the permit rule at the next weekly site meeting with the others.
Report it to your supervisor at the end of the day with the site photos.

advanced.situation: You direct commissioning of a wind farm substation and SCADA system. A last test shows communication drops to three turbines, but the grid operator expects energisation tomorrow.

options.text: Energise the farm and keep the three turbines offline until the communication is fixed.
Ask the grid operator for a short delay and promise details when the test is done.
Energise the farm on schedule and tell the operator the SCADA test is complete.
Isolate the cause with the vendor, retest communications, and give the grid operator the true status.

basic.situation: A homeowner in Johor wants a rooftop solar system. Your senior asks you to draft basic design specifications using the roof area, monthly bills and the inverter datasheet.

options.text: Fill the roof with as many panels as fit and choose an inverter to match.
Copy the specification of a similar house nearby and change the address and date.
Size the array from the bills and roof area, check inverter limits, and draft for review.
Specify the largest system the inverter takes and tell the homeowner it will cover the bill.

advanced.situation: You lead the specification for a 2 MW rooftop solar system on a factory. The roof has older sections of uncertain load capacity, and the owner wants installation to start in six weeks.

options.text: Use standard panel weights for all sections and mark the old roof as to be confirmed.
Assume the old sections carry the same load as the new ones and finish the specification.
Specify the array on the newer roof sections and review the old sections later.
Get the roof assessed, set array layout and weight per section, and then finalise the specification.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to run a basic simulation of a 5 kW rooftop PV system in the design software, using the roof tilt, orientation and the local weather file.

options.text: Enter tilt, orientation, losses and the weather file, run it, and compare yield with similar systems.
Use the default tilt and orientation in the software and report the yearly output.
Raise the panel efficiency in the software until the output looks attractive and report that.
Enter the tilt and orientation, run it with default losses, and report the yearly output.

advanced.situation: You analyse thermal and stress effects for a ground-mounted solar array at a hot, windy site. Cell temperatures reduce output, and the frame must handle wind loads with a thin design.

options.text: Use a thinner frame than the wind check allows to cut cost, and call it acceptable.
Use a standard frame from the supplier catalogue and assume the temperature loss is small.
Model cell temperature and wind load, compare frame options on cost and output, and verify.
Use the thinnest frame that passes the wind load check and note the temperature loss.

basic.situation: You do a site visit to a shop house for a rooftop solar design. Your supervisor gave you a checklist for roof type, structure, shading and the electrical panel.

options.text: Open the live panel and test the busbars with your own meter to find the rating.
Complete the roof items and photograph the electrical panel but leave the rating blank.
Complete the checklist from what you can see from the ground and the owner's description.
Complete each checklist item with measurements and photos, and note shading and panel limits.

advanced.situation: You design inspection checklists for finished solar installations. Past checklists missed loose DC connectors at several sites, and installers say the current list is already too long.

options.text: Add a line reminding inspectors to check all connectors and leave the list otherwise unchanged.
Shorten the list by removing electrical checks that installers say take the most time.
Review past defects, rank checks by risk, and trial a revised list at two sites.
Add a DC connector torque check to the list and remove a low-value item.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to draw a single-line diagram of a small 5 kW solar system in CAD. You have the equipment list and a hand sketch.

options.text: Leave the protection devices off the diagram to keep it simple and clear for the owner.
Reuse a single-line diagram from another project and edit the system size and title.
Draw the array, inverter and grid connection from the sketch and add ratings later.
Draw the array, inverter, protection devices and grid connection with ratings, and send for review.

advanced.situation: You coordinate the design and CAD drawings for a 500 kW rooftop solar system on a commercial building. A junior drafter's drawings show cable runs through a fire-rated wall.

options.text: Approve the drawings and ask the installer to sort out the wall on site.
Review the drawings against fire and electrical rules, mark the wall issue, and redesign the route.
Approve the drawings and tell the junior that fire walls are the contractor's responsibility.
Ask the junior to add a note about firestopping at the wall penetration on the drawing.

basic.situation: You are installing panels with your team lead on a roof, following the standard procedure. After rain the roof is wet, and the procedure calls for fall protection and dry surfaces.

options.text: Work on the wet roof in rubber shoes and move carefully to stay on schedule.
Start on the dry section of the roof and wear the harness as the procedure says.
Skip the harness on the wet roof because it slows movement and finish the panels.
Wait for the roof to dry, wear the harness, and tell your lead about the delay.

advanced.situation: You establish and audit quality and safety standards for a network of fifteen solar installers. An audit finds one installer regularly skips torque checks on mounting bolts, though its work is fast and popular.

options.text: Warn the installer verbally to do torque checks and review it at the next audit.
Document the finding, require corrective action with a re-audit, and link further work to compliance.
Add a torque check reminder to the installer's work sheets and continue using it.
Remove the torque check from the standard for all installers so they are treated alike.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to help create a basic monitoring plan for a new 50 kW solar system, listing what to measure and how often. The inverter provides a data portal.

options.text: Plan to check the system when the owner reports a drop in output or a fault.
Turn off the inverter alarms to avoid false alerts and review output once a year.
List the inverter portal's standard data points and set a weekly check by email.
List output, alarms and weather data to log, set check frequency, and agree alert limits.

advanced.situation: You provide technical direction to installation teams at a 10 MW solar farm. During commissioning, two strings show lower voltage than expected, and the grid connection date is fixed.

options.text: Isolate the strings, trace the cause with the team, fix and retest, and report the risk.
Connect the rest of the farm and fix the two strings after the grid connection date.
Ask the team to recheck the string connections quickly and continue commissioning if it improves.
Report the two strings as normal in the commissioning sheet and plan to investigate later.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to draw a plan of a small single-storey storeroom in CAD from a hand sketch with dimensions. One wall dimension on the sketch looks smudged.

options.text: Draw the plan using the closest-looking value for the smudged dimension and note it.
Work the smudged dimension out from the other walls so the plan closes up.
Draw the plan with a standard wall length for the smudged one and issue it.
Draw the clear parts in CAD, flag the smudged dimension, and ask your senior.

advanced.situation: Drawings in your office use mixed layer names and line styles. A junior's structural layout for a three-storey building also shows beams clashing with ducts.

options.text: Set a layer and line standard, then show the junior how to run a clash check.
Ask the junior to fix the clashes and discuss the layer names at the next meeting.
Fix the clashes in the junior's file yourself and send the layer standard to everyone.
Release the layout to the engineer and let them find the clashes during their review.

basic.situation: You prepare a set of finished architectural drawings for printing and copying. The client requires A1 prints and a PDF set, and the title blocks need the latest revision letter.

options.text: Update title blocks, plot A1 at scale, export the PDF, and check the prints.
Plot the sheets on A3 for quick checking and tell the client A1 will follow.
Plot the drawings to A1 and export the PDF from the same files, then deliver both.
Send the client last month's PDF set and say the new prints are being plotted.

advanced.situation: You coordinate structural, electrical and mechanical drawings into one presentation set for a hospital extension. The three disciplines use different grid references and level names.

options.text: Convert all drawings to the structural grid and level names and tell the others.
Agree common grid and level names with each discipline, update drawings, and check the combined set.
Issue the set as it is with a table that matches each discipline's references.
Rename the grid and levels on the other teams' drawings yourself and issue the set.

basic.situation: You visit a job site to measure rooms for a renovation drawing. The owner says one wall can be moved, but the wall may be load-bearing.

options.text: Measure the rooms and draw the wall moved as the owner asked, then continue.
Measure all rooms, mark the wall as possibly load-bearing, and tell your senior about it.
Tell the owner the thin wall is safe to remove, then measure the rooms.
Measure all rooms and draw the wall as it is now, with a note.

advanced.situation: You lead a field investigation for a road drainage drawing revision. Survey levels at a culvert differ from the drawing by 400 mm, and the contractor is waiting for revised drawings.

options.text: Revise the drawing to the new survey levels and note that it is under verification.
Tell the contractor to build to the drawing and report any difference they find.
Revise the culvert level on the drawing by 400 mm to match the contractor's request.
Recheck the culvert levels with the surveyor, then revise the drawing from the verified data.

basic.situation: Your senior gives you the dimensions of a concrete slab, 6 m by 4 m and 150 mm thick, and asks you to calculate the concrete volume for the materials list.

options.text: Use the volume of the previous slab on a similar job and scale it by area.
Multiply length, width and thickness in metres for 3.6 cubic metres, and enter it with units.
Calculate 3.6 cubic metres and enter it in the list rounded up to 4 cubic metres.
Multiply 6 by 4 by 150 and enter 3,600 in the list as the volume.

advanced.situation: You develop the method for calculating excavation and fill tonnage for a highway cut-and-fill section, and verify results for another team. Their numbers differ from yours by 8%.

options.text: Adopt the lower tonnage figure to keep the cost estimate down and issue it as checked.
Compare cross-sections, swell factors and densities, find the source of the 8%, and agree one method.
Recheck your own calculation and send the other team your results with your assumptions listed.
Take the average of the two sets of tonnage figures and issue it as the result.

basic.situation: Your senior gives you a materials list and the drawing for a stairway and asks you to check the listed step widths and handrail lengths against the drawing.

options.text: Check a few items from each list and sign the list if they match.
Check the step widths against the drawing and assume the handrail lengths are right.
Compare each width and length with the drawing, mark mismatches, and return the list.
Change the list figures to match the drawing and return it as checked and complete.

advanced.situation: You analyse building by-laws for a commercial building design. The architect's layout has two corridors narrower than the fire escape by-law requires, and the drawing deadline is near.

options.text: Cite the by-law clauses with corridor widths, brief the architect on options, and revise after agreement.
Widen the two corridors on the drawing yourself to meet the by-law, then inform the architect.
Tell the architect the two corridors are too narrow and wait for new instructions.
Draw the corridors as designed and add a note that the authority will check the by-law.

basic.situation: A site supervisor calls you about a drawing detail for a retaining wall. Your senior is out, and the supervisor asks you to explain how the drainage layer is built.

options.text: Explain the detail from the drawing and notes, and send a marked-up sketch to the supervisor.
Tell the supervisor to follow the general method for retaining walls in the area.
Describe the layers listed on the drawing and offer to ask your senior about the rest.
Tell the supervisor to build what looks right and the drawing will be updated later.

advanced.situation: You manage a drafting team. Two drafters dispute who should fix a clash between roadworks and a drain layout, and the construction crew is waiting for an answer.

options.text: Tell the crew to wait while the drafters settle it between themselves by tomorrow.
Hear both, check the clash with the engineer, assign one fix owner, and set a deadline.
Assign the fix to the more experienced drafter and tell both to move on.
Tell the crew to build the roadworks as drawn and let the drain be altered afterwards.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to draft a simple wiring diagram for a motor starter panel from the engineer's sketch. The sketch shows the overload relay but not its rating.

options.text: Draw the diagram and add the overload rating from a similar panel's drawing in the files.
Draw the diagram with the overload relay left unrated and issue it for installation.
Draw the diagram and pick a high overload rating so the motor trips less often.
Draw the diagram, mark the overload rating as to be confirmed, and ask the engineer.

advanced.situation: You draft assembly drawings for a printed circuit board with fine-pitch parts. The manufacturer's standard needs minimum clearances, and the engineer's layout has three places that are too tight.

options.text: Mark the three tight places against the standard, send them to the engineer, and update after.
Move the parts apart slightly on the assembly drawing and tell the engineer afterwards.
Reduce the clearance values in the standard table so the board layout passes the check.
Draw the board as laid out and add a note on the drawing about the clearances.

basic.situation: An engineer asks you to sketch a basic lighting layout for a small office, using the floor plan and a lux level table. The plan shows 12 m by 8 m.

options.text: Copy the lighting layout from another office of similar size and adjust the outline.
Place a few luminaires near the windows to save power and leave the centre dark.
Place luminaires evenly around the room and note that lux levels are to be checked.
Place luminaires on a grid to meet the lux table and have the engineer check.

advanced.situation: You draw master sketches for a new electrical installation that connects to an existing building. Old as-built drawings of the switchroom conflict with what you saw on a site visit.

options.text: Use the site visit sketch and add a note that the as-built drawings differ.
Draw the new installation to the as-built drawings and issue it to the contractor.
Use the old as-built drawings since they are the official record, and list the differences.
Verify the switchroom by measurement, mark the conflicts, and base the sketch on verified site data.

basic.situation: You read a work order for an installation. It asks for a power supply for the workshop but does not say whether the load is single-phase or three-phase.

options.text: Assume a single-phase supply because it is the most common and proceed with the drawing.
Check the order against the site details, ask which supply is needed, and note the answer.
Look at the workshop's equipment list to find the likely supply type and note it.
Choose three-phase to be safe and tell the installer to order three-phase equipment today.

advanced.situation: A work order and the schematic disagree on a breaker rating, and the vendor's manual gives a third value. The design engineer is on leave until next week, and installation starts Monday.

options.text: Use the vendor's manual value since it comes from the maker and note the discrepancy.
Use the schematic value and tell the installer the work order will be updated later.
Compare the three values with the load data, confirm with the vendor and a covering engineer.
Use the highest of the three ratings so the breaker will not trip during testing.

basic.situation: You are asked to measure the distance for a cable run across a factory floor between two panels. Machines and a walkway lie between them.

options.text: Walk the route and estimate the distance by steps, then order the cable to that length.
Read the distance off the floor plan and order the cable to that length.
Measure the actual route around the machines, add allowances, and mark the route on a sketch.
Measure the straight-line distance between the panels and add ten percent for the route.

advanced.situation: You calculate cable lengths and adjust specifications for an installation across a multi-level plant. Your measured vertical runs add 18 m of cable compared with the drawing's estimate.

options.text: Add 18 m to the cable length in the specification and keep the cable size.
Keep the drawing's cable length and tell the installer to join shorter pieces where needed.
Keep the drawing's estimate and order extra cable to cover any shortfall on site.
Recalculate lengths from the measured routes, check voltage drop, and update the specification and list.

basic.situation: Your senior gives you a checklist and a completed drawing of a distribution board layout to check for obvious errors before it goes to the engineer.

options.text: Check the labels and breaker ratings and pass the drawing if they look consistent.
Go through each checklist item, mark errors on the drawing, and return it to your senior.
Look over the drawing quickly and pass it, since the drafter is very experienced.
Fix the errors you find directly in the drawing and send it on as the original.

advanced.situation: You guide a drafter who compares a control panel's logic element configuration on screen with the engineering schematic. The two disagree, and the drafter insists the screen is right.

options.text: Trace both to the latest approved change, find which is current, and align them.
Ask the drafter to recheck the schematic against the screen and report back to you.
Tell the drafter to change the live screen configuration to match the schematic right away.
Accept the drafter's view that the screen is right and update the schematic to match.

basic.situation: You finish a drawing job. Your supervisor asks you to locate the project files in the library database, load the program and record the completed job data.

options.text: Find the files, load the program, and record the job data at week's end.
Load the program from a copy on your own drive and record the job data.
Record the job as complete in the database before loading the program, to save time.
Find the project files in the library, load the program, record the job data, and confirm.

advanced.situation: A lighting design and ceiling layout conflict in a mall, and the engineer, architect and contractor each want a different fix. You lead the meeting to finalise the documentation.

options.text: Follow the engineer's fix since lighting drives the electrical drawings, and inform the others.
Ask each party to submit a written proposal and select the cheapest to document.
Finalise the drawings with the fix that you prefer and release them before the meeting ends.
Show the conflict on drawings, compare each fix's impact, agree one fix, and record the actions.

basic.situation: Your senior drafter asks for front, top and side views of a simple bracket from a hand sketch. The sketch gives no hole depth, and the drawing goes to the shop today.

options.text: Copy the hole depth from a similar bracket in the project folder and carry on.
Ask your senior drafter for the hole depth while you draw the other views.
Choose a common hole depth, complete the drawing and release it to the shop.
Draw the views with a note asking for the depth and send it for checking.

advanced.situation: You are building the 3D model and full-size drawing of a chassis cross-member. The customer changed the mounting hole pattern after approval, and the supplier is still quoting from the old drawing.

options.text: Update the model, send the supplier a revised drawing and confirm the change.
Let the supplier work from the old drawing and fix the holes when parts arrive.
Hand-mark the new holes on the old drawing and send it to the supplier.
Update the model and the drawing, and tell the supplier the new pattern is coming.

basic.situation: A senior drafter hands you a finished layout and asks you to add the notes and dimension callouts. Some notes would cover a dimension line on the drawing.

options.text: Shrink the note text a little so it fits beside the dimension lines.
Move the notes to clear space with leader lines so dimensions stay readable.
Place the notes over the lines since the shop knows how such parts are made.
Delete the overlapped dimension lines so the notes show clearly on the sheet.

advanced.situation: You must lay out illustrations for a maintenance manual on a pump assembly. The senior editor wants every step image to match the real part, but the drawings show an older pump version.

options.text: Redraw the illustrations after comparing them with a pump from the workshop floor.
Check the current pump drawings and redraw the affected views for the editor.
Reuse the older drawings as they are since the maintenance steps stay the same.
Keep the older drawings and add a note that some parts may differ slightly.

basic.situation: You are checking steel plate dimensions against the cutting list and giving each plate a part number. One plate on the list is 4 mm thinner than the order sheet says.

options.text: Number the other plates and ask the store which thickness was actually delivered.
Use the cutting list thickness since drafters usually update it before the order sheet.
Hold that part number and show both documents to your supervisor now.
Number the plate to match the order sheet and amend the cutting list to agree.

advanced.situation: A client's spec for a rotating shaft gives a power rating that looks too low for the load in the sketch. The release date is tomorrow.

options.text: Draw to the spec as given, since the client is responsible for the numbers it supplies.
Ask the client to confirm the power rating and keep drawing in the meantime.
Increase the shaft diameter on the drawing yourself to leave a safe margin.
Recalculate the load from the sketch and raise any gap with the client's engineer.

basic.situation: A machinist reports that a cover plate slot is slightly too narrow for the bolt head. Your supervisor asks you to fix the drawing.

options.text: Widen the slot by a generous margin so the bolt cannot jam again.
Change the bolt size in the notes so the existing plate fits as made.
Widen the slot by the amount the machinist suggests and update the drawing.
Check the bolt head size, widen the slot and mark the revision.

advanced.situation: Vibration keeps loosening parts on a packing line, and the conveyor frame, motor mount and guard drawings all need changes. You lead the revision, and production wants the line running Monday.

options.text: Release the three revised drawings to the shop and let the teams find clashes later.
Revise the motor mount first since it vibrates most and handle the others later.
Find the cause in each system and revise all three drawings together.
Add thicker stiffeners to all three drawings and release them to the shop together.

basic.situation: You are laying out a duct bracket and need to know where the electrician will run cables. The electrical drawing is not yet issued.

options.text: Place the bracket where it looks clear and let the electrician work around it.
Ask the electrician for the planned cable route and adjust the bracket position.
Leave extra clearance around the bracket and mention it to your senior drafter.
Fix the bracket position in the issued drawing and ask the electrician to reroute.

advanced.situation: A customer's installer says your pipe layout clashes with their duct run on site. The mechanical, piping and electrical teams each point at another team's drawing.

options.text: Tell the installer to proceed as their duct run is already in place.
Ask each team for its latest drawing and compare them yourself to find the clash.
Meet the teams and installer, mark the clash on one layout and agree revisions.
Move your pipes clear of the duct on the layout and tell the installer.

basic.situation: A new drafter on your team asks you how to set the layers and line weights before starting a drawing. You have a deadline later today.

options.text: Show the new drafter the company template and layer standard, then check their first sheet.
Tell the new drafter to pick the weights that look good and fix them later.
Send the new drafter an older drawing to copy the layer settings from.
Tell the new drafter to follow the settings in the software defaults.

advanced.situation: You lead a small drafting team whose drawings keep returning from checkers with missing title blocks and unclear notes. Your manager asks you to raise quality across the team.

options.text: Agree a written standard and checklist with the team and sample-review weekly.
Fix the faults yourself before the checkers see them and say nothing to the team.
Return each faulty drawing to its drafter with comments and let them improve themselves.
Run a single training session on title blocks and notes and remind everyone of it.

basic.situation: During your morning inspection of a vibration test rig, you notice a small oil stain under the hydraulic pump. The rig is booked for a test run in one hour.

options.text: Leave the stain, since small drips are normal, and start the test run on time.
Report the stain to your supervisor, then continue the pre-test checks on the rig.
Wipe the stain, top up the oil and run the test as booked.
Isolate the pump, tag the rig out of service and tell your supervisor.

advanced.situation: A strain gauge amplifier on the wing-fatigue rig drifts again after two repairs. The test program is behind schedule and the amplifier is costly to replace.

options.text: Recalibrate the amplifier offset each morning and carry on with the fatigue test.
Find what drives the drift, repair that part and verify the amplifier before testing.
Swap in a spare amplifier and send the faulty unit to the maker for analysis.
Apply an offset to the logged readings and keep the rig running.

basic.situation: Following the checklist, you finish a pre-operational checkout of an aircraft pressure system. One reading is just outside the limit printed on the checklist.

options.text: Stop the checkout, record the reading and report it to the senior technician.
Round the reading to the nearest value and mark the item as passed.
Repeat the reading and report it if it stays outside the limit.
Mark the item as passed, noting that the aircraft flew fine with it last month.

advanced.situation: You must define design limits for a new landing-gear actuator by testing it under simulated flight loads. Your first runs give results that disagree with the engineer's model.

options.text: Record the model's values as the design limits and file the test as complete.
Share the results with the engineer and let the model be adjusted to fit them.
Verify the setup and sensors, rerun and share both results with the engineer.
Run the loads until the results settle near the model and report those runs.

basic.situation: You record temperature readings from a bearing test every 10 minutes. The log sheet has a box for each reading, and one reading looks much higher than the others.

options.text: Take the next reading and use the average of the two for the box.
Record the reading as shown and add a note beside it.
Record the reading as shown, circle it and tell the test engineer.
Write a typical value from earlier readings in that box and move on.

advanced.situation: The project lead asks how many extra test hours and technicians the next phase needs. Your first-phase data shows scatter, so any estimate carries real uncertainty.

options.text: Ask for the maximum hours and staff so the phase cannot run short.
Analyse the scatter, give an estimate with a stated range and list your assumptions.
Quote the lowest hours seen in the first phase so the plan is approved.
Give the lead the average from the first phase and offer to refine it.

basic.situation: You are setting up a strain test on a bracket from the engineer's sheet of sensors and sample rate. The sheet lists a sample rate your logger cannot reach.

options.text: Set the closest rate you can find in the logger menu and keep going.
Use the logger's highest rate and note the change on the test sheet.
Tell the engineer the logger limit and ask for a rate it can reach.
Run at the logger's highest rate and report it as the requested rate.

advanced.situation: You are setting data acquisition standards for a new engine test program. Teams use different sample rates and file formats, so results from different rigs cannot be compared.

options.text: Set one rate and format per measurement type, write them down and train each team.
Let each team keep its own setup and write a script to merge the files.
Choose the rate and format your own team uses and ask other teams to adopt them.
Ask each team to convert its files to a common format after testing.

basic.situation: You are asked to fit a pressure sensor into a test fixture using hand tools while a technician is away. The sensor's thread looks slightly different from the port.

options.text: Compare the thread with the drawing and fit it if the sizes look close.
Force the sensor in with a wrench since the fixture can be re-tapped later.
Hold the sensor back, compare the thread with the drawing and ask the technician.
Start the sensor by hand and tighten it once it feels snug.

advanced.situation: You guide two junior technicians fabricating and installing a test rig for a new gearbox. The mounting plate they made sits 2 mm out of position, and the test starts this afternoon.

options.text: Check the plate against the drawing, then rework or remake it before installing.
Hold the install and ask the engineer whether a 2 mm offset is acceptable.
Shim the gearbox into position, run the test and tell the engineer afterwards.
Enlarge the mounting holes yourself and begin the test as scheduled.

basic.situation: You start the data acquisition computer for a routine engine test. The system shows a calibration warning, but the test starts in ten minutes and the engineer is in a meeting.

options.text: Run a quick check with a known input and start if the reading looks fine.
Hold the test, note the warning and ask the engineer to confirm the calibration.
Disable the warning in the software settings so it cannot interrupt the test.
Clear the warning message and start since it came up last week too.

advanced.situation: A new test specification demands tighter tolerances than your acquisition system's current calibration supports. The first run is tomorrow, and the test engineers are waiting on your advice.

options.text: Tell the engineers the system meets it and calibrate after the first run.
Tell the engineers the system meets the new tolerance based on the maker's brochure.
Calibrate to traceable references, confirm the tolerance and brief the engineers.
Calibrate with the maker's procedure and confirm tolerance during tomorrow's first run.

basic.situation: You are drafting a dimensioned drawing of a drain cover from a supervisor's template. One dimension on the template differs from the site survey sheet.

options.text: Ask your supervisor which dimension is current, then finish the drawing.
Use the survey sheet figure since it comes from measuring the actual site.
Draw to the template and note the difference from the survey sheet.
Pick the larger of the two figures so the cover is sure to fit.

advanced.situation: You must draw a layout and site map showing flood-prone areas for a drainage upgrade. Two survey data sets give different ground levels near the proposed culvert.

options.text: Use the newer data set on the map and list the older set in notes.
Check both sets against survey benchmarks and show the difference on the map.
Use whichever data set shows fewer flood-prone areas so the plan looks affordable.
Average the two ground levels and draw the culvert using that single level.

basic.situation: You read a blueprint to find the length of a retaining wall. A symbol beside the wall dimension is not in the standard legend you were shown.

options.text: Check the dimension against the plan scale and carry on if it fits.
Treat the symbol as a normal wall mark and use the length shown.
Look for the drawing's own legend or ask your supervisor what the symbol means.
Skip the dimension and estimate the wall length from the plan's overall width.

advanced.situation: A structural specification calls for one concrete grade, but the blueprint notes a different grade for the same beam. Ordering is due today and the supplier needs a mix.

options.text: Order the lower grade since it is cheaper and the beam may not need more.
Raise the conflict with the engineer and hold that beam's order for now.
Order the grade in the specification and mention the blueprint note in your email.
Order the higher of the two grades and tell the engineer afterwards.

basic.situation: You calculate the floor area of a 6.2 m by 4.5 m room to order tiles. Your calculator shows 2.79, which looks small to you.

options.text: Redo the multiplication, compare it with a rough estimate and then order.
Use 2.79 as shown because the calculator rarely makes mistakes in simple sums.
Ask a colleague to do the same sum on theirs and use their answer.
Round the area up to a convenient figure and order tiles for that.

advanced.situation: You calculate concrete and steel quantities for a 12-storey car park from the plans. Your concrete volume is 8 percent below the contractor's figure, and the order is due tomorrow.

options.text: Order your quantity and add 8 percent as a margin for the difference.
Order to the contractor's larger figure and review your own sums after delivery.
Order your lower quantity since the contractor has every reason to overstate its volumes.
Rework your quantities by element, compare with the contractor's and resolve the gap.

basic.situation: You keep the daily site log on a road resurfacing job. At day's end you remember that rain stopped paving for two hours this morning.

options.text: Record the rain stoppage in the log with start and end times.
Write that paving ran all day to match the planned schedule.
Note in the log that rain delayed work during the morning.
Leave it out since the paving finished on schedule in the end.

advanced.situation: You compile the handover report for a completed drainage system. The maintenance team will rely on it, but the as-built changes sit in several people's emails.

options.text: Write the report from the original drawings and add the changes you remember.
Collect all changes, update the drawings and list each as-built difference.
Submit the original design report since it was already approved by the client.
Attach the email threads to the report and let the team find the changes.

basic.situation: You notice water pooling beside a newly laid pipe trench at the project site. Your supervisor is across the site.

options.text: Pump the water into a nearby drain yourself to keep the trench clear.
Mention it to the site foreman and carry on with your task.
Wait to see whether the pooling drains away before reporting it to anyone.
Take a photo, note the location and report the pooling to your supervisor.

advanced.situation: A pump station layout conflicts with an existing water main found on site. The contractor wants to shift the pump station sideways, which would affect the electrical connection plan.

options.text: Tell the contractor to build over the main since it is a small pipe.
Accept the contractor's sideways move and update the electrical plan to suit.
Ask the contractor to proceed while you work out the electrical changes.
Document the conflict and agree a change with the design engineer first.

basic.situation: You are unsure which version of the plan to use for preparing a section drawing. Your supervisor has just left for a site visit.

options.text: Check the project folder for the latest dated plan and use that.
Message your supervisor to ask which plan version applies and wait.
Start with the version that has fewer changes on it to save time.
Use the version you printed last week as it matches your earlier work.

advanced.situation: You are preparing a meeting with your supervisor on acceptance testing for a new culvert. Field conditions have changed since the plan was written, and the schedule is tight.

options.text: Summarise the changed conditions and agree revised tests with your supervisor.
Tell your supervisor the conditions are similar and skip the field evaluation.
Bring the original plan and mention the changed conditions during the meeting.
Propose keeping the original test plan and note field changes after the tests.

basic.situation: You are assembling a prototype control board from a wiring diagram. One resistor on the parts tray is marked with a different value from the one on the bill of materials.

options.text: Measure the resistor and fit it if it reads the listed value.
Fit the part marked on the tray since the bill of materials may be outdated.
Hold that resistor back and ask the engineer which value the design needs.
Swap the other resistors around until the board's voltages look about right.

advanced.situation: You must integrate a new motor controller with an existing PLC and its control software. During the first power-up test, the controller resets whenever the motor starts.

options.text: Replace the controller with the spare unit and test whether the resets continue.
Add a delay in the software so the controller restarts quickly after each reset.
Disable the controller's reset protection in its settings so the test can finish.
Log when resets occur, check the supply and wiring, then adjust the integration.

basic.situation: You set up an oscilloscope and a power supply to test a sensor board for the first time. Your supervisor is away, and the scope manual and standard test sheet are on the bench.

options.text: Set up the scope from memory of an earlier test and check the results.
Apply a higher supply voltage so the sensor signal shows clearly on the scope.
Follow the standard test sheet step by step and record each reading.
Connect the supply at the board's rated voltage and use scope autoset to save time.

advanced.situation: You review an electrical plan for a small factory extension against the design specification and applicable electrical codes. Its cable sizes meet the specification but look undersized for the stated load.

options.text: Approve the plan since it meets the specification and add a comment about the cables.
Pass the plan because cable sizing is the designer's responsibility, not the reviewer's.
Ask the installer to use larger cables than drawn once the work starts.
Check the load current against code cable ratings and raise the gap.

basic.situation: You log the operating hours and a fault code each shift on a testing bench. The fault code reader shows a code that is not in the manual.

options.text: Record the code as shown and plan to look up its meaning later this week.
Record the code exactly as shown and ask your supervisor what it means.
Enter a similar code from the manual so the log looks complete.
Log the fault as unknown and leave the code field blank for later.

advanced.situation: You set the documentation standard for a new product line's test records. Technicians currently store schematics, repair notes and parts used in separate folders and spreadsheets.

options.text: Ask each technician to email a monthly summary of what they recorded.
Move all files into one shared folder and let technicians name them as they like.
Define one record format for schematics, repairs and parts, then train technicians.
Keep records in the separate spreadsheets and rebuild them when an audit happens.

basic.situation: You are asked to list the components needed for a simple LED driver circuit from its schematic. The schematic shows an LED but not its current rating.

options.text: List a standard resistor that many LED circuits use and order it.
Check the LED datasheet and list the matching resistor and driver parts.
Leave the resistor off the list since the schematic does not show it.
List the parts shown and ask the engineer for the missing rating later.

advanced.situation: You prepare the budget and schedule for upgrading six production lines' control panels. Quotes from two suppliers differ in price and delivery time, and the project manager needs numbers by Friday.

options.text: Compare total cost and delivery for both quotes and state your assumptions.
Choose the cheaper supplier and tell the manager the delivery time is longer.
Submit the lower price with the faster delivery date taken from the other quote.
Choose the faster supplier and keep the cost difference out of the budget summary.

basic.situation: A prototype amplifier board gives too little gain. Your senior technician asks you to change one resistor, and gave you the new value.

options.text: Change the resistor and a second one nearby that looks related to gain.
Pick a larger value than given so the gain clearly improves on the first try.
Change the resistor and tell your senior technician the modification is finished.
Change the resistor, then retest the gain and note the result for the technician.

advanced.situation: You produce drawings for an industrial control network linking sensors to a plant controller. Two sensor types in the layout use incompatible signal standards.

options.text: Draw the sensors as designed and add a note that the signals are incompatible.
Add converters, label each interface and confirm them with the engineer.
Change one sensor type on the drawing to match the other and file it.
Draw the sensors connected directly since the controller may accept both types.

basic.situation: You assist in supervising the installation of a new motor drive. The installer says the earth connection is not needed because the cabinet is already metal.

options.text: Ask the installer to show where the manual allows leaving it out.
Check the instructions, require the earth connection and tell your supervisor.
Let the installer proceed and add the earth connection during the final check.
Accept the installer's view because they have fitted many such drives.

advanced.situation: You design a quality assurance program for a new batch of power supply units. Early units pass the final test but have failed in customer use.

options.text: Add burn-in tests, trace field failures to causes and set pass criteria from them.
Tighten the final test limits and sample more units from each batch.
Keep the current test since all shipped units passed it as required.
Send customers a note on suitable operating conditions for the units.

basic.situation: You select a motor for a small conveyor from a sheet requiring 0.5 kW at 24 V. The catalogue lists a 0.55 kW motor at 24 V and a 0.5 kW motor at 48 V.

options.text: Pick the 0.55 kW, 24 V motor since it matches the voltage and power.
Pick the 48 V motor and plan to run it from the 24 V supply anyway.
Pick whichever motor is cheaper in the catalogue and check the voltage during installation.
Pick the 0.5 kW motor and add a voltage converter to the order.

advanced.situation: You set technical standards and the document system for an electromechanical project with five suppliers. Suppliers email datasheets in different formats, and revisions are getting mixed up.

options.text: Keep the latest emails in a shared mailbox so people can search them.
Set up one document register with revision numbers and make suppliers use it.
Let engineers store the datasheets they trust on their own computers.
Ask each supplier to put the revision date in every file name.

basic.situation: You read a schematic to plan the assembly order of a small relay panel. Two sequences seem possible: wiring the terminals before or after mounting the relay.

options.text: Check the technical order, or ask a senior technician which sequence applies.
Mount the relay first since that is how earlier panels were built.
Pick the order that leaves more room to reach the terminals with tools.
Wire the terminals first and then mount the relay with the wires attached.

advanced.situation: A servo drive assembly shows a noisy feedback signal under load on your oscilloscope. The design engineer wants a pass or fail result today and a repeatable test protocol.

options.text: Repeat with shielded probes, check grounding and write the test limits down.
Filter the signal on the oscilloscope and pass the drive if it looks clean.
Pass the drive because noise under load is common in servo assemblies.
Fail the drive and tell the engineer the feedback sensor is the cause.

basic.situation: You inspect small motor housings for surface defects under good light. One housing has a light scratch near the sealing face.

options.text: Polish the scratch off yourself and return the housing to the batch.
Pass the housing if the scratch cannot be felt with a fingernail.
Pass the housing because the scratch is too small to matter for sealing.
Set the housing aside, note the scratch position and ask the inspector.

advanced.situation: You are setting quality control standards for precision shafts and training inspectors on tolerances. Inspectors using different micrometers get readings that differ by 0.01 mm.

options.text: Tell inspectors to average their readings from two different micrometers.
Check the micrometers against a gauge block, then fix one method for all.
Tell inspectors to use the same micrometer for every part within each batch.
Widen the tolerance by 0.01 mm so the differences no longer matter.

basic.situation: A small cooling fan in a test cabinet has stopped. Your supervisor asks you to get it working again, and you find its connector is loose.

options.text: Solder the wires directly to the fan terminals to hold them firm.
Reseat the connector and tell your supervisor that the fan is now fixed.
Reseat the connector, test the fan and record what you found.
Replace the fan with a spare from the store to be safe.

advanced.situation: You lead the redesign of a packing machine's drive system and must produce its CAD drawings. Two older drawings of the gearbox mount disagree with the machine on the floor.

options.text: Draw the mount from the older drawing and check it during commissioning.
Use the drawing with the later date and note the other as superseded.
Combine features from both drawings into one mount that seems sensible.
Measure the machine, update the CAD model to match and mark the drawing revision.

basic.situation: You fit a bearing into a housing using a hand press. The bearing seems tight and does not slide in.

options.text: Heat the housing with a torch until the bearing drops in.
Tap the bearing in with a hammer until it seats fully.
Apply a thin film of oil to the bearing seat and press again.
Stop pressing, check the bearing and housing sizes and look for burrs.

advanced.situation: You develop a new assembly method for a sensor module and train three technicians on it. The first trial shows connector alignment varies from unit to unit.

options.text: Design an alignment fixture, trial it and update the training.
Tell technicians to align the connector carefully by eye and trust their judgement.
Add an alignment check to the training and have technicians measure each unit.
Keep the method unchanged and set looser connector limits in the test.

basic.situation: You solder a connector onto a small control board. The soldering iron tip looks dirty and the joint looks dull and grainy.

options.text: Leave the joint as it is since it conducts in a continuity test.
Cover the dull joint with heat-shrink tubing and send the board on.
Reheat the joint and add fresh solder until it looks smooth.
Clean and tin the tip, then redo the joint and check its shine.

advanced.situation: You set the safety standards for soldering and installation in your team's workshop and mentor two juniors. One junior has been working on boards with the bench supply switched on.

options.text: Tell the junior that experienced technicians often work on live boards this way.
Let the junior finish the board and mention the rule afterwards.
Remind the junior to be careful around live boards at team briefings.
Stop the work, explain the isolation rule and add a written safe-working step.

basic.situation: You connect wires between two robot controllers following a wiring list. One wire on the list has a colour you cannot find in the cable bundle.

options.text: Stop, check the list against the wiring diagram and ask the lead technician.
Connect the nearest wire to the terminal and power up to check it.
Wire the other connections first and look for that colour somewhere later in the day.
Use a wire of a similar colour and mark the change on the list.

advanced.situation: You build a six-axis robot arm from scratch using fixtures and templates. The base plate holes from the template do not line up with the shoulder joint housing.

options.text: Remake the template from the drawing and then continue the build.
Stop, check the template and housing against the drawing and inform the lead.
Enlarge the holes slightly so the housing bolts can fit through.
Drill new holes where the housing sits and continue the build.

basic.situation: You help lower a new robot arm onto its stationary base in a packing cell. The crane is free but the lead technician is called away for ten minutes.

options.text: Lower the arm onto the base with the crane and bolt down one corner.
Prepare the bolts and tools and have everything ready for the lead.
Lower the arm onto the base and unhook it so the crane is free.
Wait for the lead technician to return before lifting the arm into position.

advanced.situation: You install a new robot on a floor track for a production line that restarts Monday. During final alignment, the track is 3 mm out of level over two metres.

options.text: Adjust the robot's position programme to compensate for the slope in the track.
Shim the track to the supplier's tolerance, recheck the alignment and then release it.
Release the robot to production because a 3 mm slope is within the usual play.
Shim the track level and release the robot, then check alignment during production.

basic.situation: You help an engineer set up a robot arm, and its gripper sensor reads nothing. The engineer asks you to look for a basic electronic fault.

options.text: Check the sensor's power, cable and connector with a meter and report.
Swap in a spare sensor and tell the engineer if it reads.
Restart the controller a few times and see if the reading returns.
Bypass the sensor input in the controller so the arm can move.

advanced.situation: A hydraulic robot arm loses force halfway through its cycle, then recovers. Production is waiting, and the pressure gauge dips during each loss.

options.text: Log the pressure through a cycle, then test the pump, valves and fluid level.
Top up the hydraulic fluid and log the pressure during the next few cycles.
Replace the main valve first and watch whether the dips continue.
Raise the pump pressure setting until the dips are no longer visible.

basic.situation: You use a voltmeter to check the output of a robot's servo drive before it goes to the customer. The reading is 0.3 V below the datasheet value.

options.text: Recheck the range setting and connections, then report the reading.
Write the datasheet value in the report and ship the drive.
Adjust the drive output until the meter shows the datasheet value.
Log the reading and say it is close enough to the datasheet value.

advanced.situation: You evaluate a welding robot line whose reliability has dropped, and may reprogram or calibrate it. Output is high but scrap has doubled over two weeks.

options.text: Compare scrap data with calibration records and recalibrate the axes at fault.
Reprogram the robots to skip the weld quality check that rejects parts.
Slow the whole line down until scrap falls back to the usual level again.
Recalibrate every robot on the line over the weekend and see what changes.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to move a pick-and-place robot's drop-off point 5 cm to the right. You open the program to edit the movement.

options.text: Shift every point in the program 5 cm so the movements stay consistent.
Edit the drop-off point and run one slow cycle to check the new position.
Edit the movement while the robot is running to save restart time.
Back up the program, edit that one point and test it at slow speed.

advanced.situation: You reprogram the controller of a palletising robot to improve efficiency. Faster moves raise output by 12 percent but make the gripper drop boxes occasionally.

options.text: Keep the faster moves and add an extra operator to catch dropped boxes.
Tune the speed and gripper timing, then test for dropped boxes.
Keep the faster moves and report the dropped boxes as operator errors.
Use the faster moves in the daytime shift when staff can watch.

basic.situation: You top up a robot gearbox's oil during routine service. The service record sheet has a tick box for 'oil changed' but not for 'oil topped up'.

options.text: Note 'oil topped up' in the comments and keep the 'changed' box empty.
Tick 'oil changed' and note the top-up in the comments column for the lead.
Tick 'oil changed' because the gearbox now holds fresh oil from the top-up.
Leave the record unchanged and tell the lead the sheet has no matching box.

advanced.situation: You train a customer's staff to maintain and repair your robots. A trainee proposes replacing a servomotor with the power still connected to save time.

options.text: Stop the job, show the lock-out steps and have the trainee repeat them back.
Tell the trainee that experienced maintenance staff can decide when to isolate.
Let the trainee try it and talk about any problem at the end of shift.
Explain the power risks and let the trainee proceed with a colleague watching.

basic.situation: You check pH and flow readings at a wastewater treatment unit each hour against limits on a supervisor's sheet. Today the pH reading is just above the upper limit.

options.text: Recheck the probe, then report the reading to your supervisor if it stays high.
Wait for the next hourly reading to see if the pH comes down.
Record the reading and mention it to your supervisor at the end of shift.
Lower the pH by adding chemicals from the store to bring the unit in line.

advanced.situation: You lead a compliance check of a factory's discharge permit. The records show a monthly discharge sample above the permitted limit, and the plant manager says it was a one-off.

options.text: Ask the plant manager for written reasons and file them with the permit records.
Leave the exceedance out of the audit report since the manager explained it.
Note the exceedance in your audit and wait for the next monthly sample.
Verify the result and trend, then report the exceedance as the permit requires.

basic.situation: You check a project's environmental document against a completeness checklist. All items are present except a map that the checklist says must show monitoring well locations.

options.text: Tick the map item since the text lists the well locations.
Draw the well locations on a rough map yourself and tick the item.
Request the map from the author but pass the rest of the document.
Mark the map as missing and return the document to the author.
