advanced.situation: You review work plans for three field crews and must schedule their sampling for next month. Two crews need the same sampling vehicle in the same week.

options.text: Check each crew's sampling window and permit dates, then assign the vehicle.
Give the vehicle to the crew whose plan arrived first and move the other.
Ask the crews to agree among themselves who uses the vehicle.
Schedule both crews in the same week and see which one cancels.

basic.situation: A new water-level logger arrives from the supplier for your field kit. You must receive it, set it up and test it before it goes out tomorrow.

options.text: Put the logger in the kit since the supplier tests every unit before shipping.
Set up the unit and run a test log, then file the delivery note.
Check the delivery against the order, set up the unit and run a test log.
Send the logger out with the crew and test it on site.

advanced.situation: You troubleshoot a groundwater sampling pump that failed in the field. It holds traces of contaminated water, and a crew needs it back in service for a site next week.

options.text: Rinse the pump with clean water, test it and tell the crew what you did.
Hand the pump to the crew and say it was cleaned at the last site.
Decontaminate the pump to protocol, test it and brief the crew on the steps.
Test the pump as it is and decontaminate it if the test fails.

basic.situation: You package water samples for the laboratory using a guide. One bottle label has smudged ink, and the courier collects the cooler in ten minutes.

options.text: Pack the bottle and email the lab to say the label is smudged.
Write a label from memory and pack the bottle before the courier arrives.
Relabel the bottle using the field sheet details and record that you did.
Pack the bottle and trust the lab to match it by position in the cooler.

advanced.situation: You design the sample handling steps for a new groundwater monitoring project and train new technicians. Past samples lost holding time because the lab was closed on collection days.

options.text: Record the lab delivery time as the collection time when samples arrive late.
Freeze the samples overnight so they last until the lab reopens next day.
Plan collections around lab hours, set chilled storage rules and train technicians.
Tell technicians to deliver samples as soon as the lab reopens each day.

basic.situation: You enter field readings into the project's computer file from handwritten sheets. One sheet has a number you cannot read.

options.text: Check the neighbouring readings and choose the most likely value, then flag it.
Ask the technician who wrote the sheet what the number is.
Enter the number you think it is and move on.
Enter zero so the file calculates properly and carry on with the rest.

advanced.situation: You audit the record-keeping for an air monitoring programme. Logbook entries and the computer file disagree on 6 percent of readings, and corrections are not dated.

options.text: Ask staff to be more careful when copying entries from the logbook.
Delete the mismatched entries so the file and logbook seem to agree.
Update the file to match the logbook and note it in your audit.
Trace each mismatch to its source and set a rule requiring dated, signed corrections.

basic.situation: You record rainfall, temperature and a short note on water colour at a monitoring site, using a template. The water looks unusually brown today.

options.text: Write 'normal' since the water colour changes with the rain every year.
Write 'brown' in the note and move on to the next site.
Note the colour as seen, add a photo and mention it to your supervisor.
Leave the note field blank since the template mainly asks for numbers.

advanced.situation: You create a template for recording field observations across five sites and coach new staff. Staff describe water clarity in different words, so records cannot be compared.

options.text: Remind staff verbally to use the same words as the first site.
Define a fixed scale with photo examples, add it to the template and train staff.
Add a free-text box and ask staff to be consistent in their wording.
Tell staff to describe clarity however they like since all records get filed.

basic.situation: You time a worker assembling a gearbox for a time study. Midway, the worker pauses to help a colleague for two minutes.

options.text: Stop the clock for the help, note the pause and continue timing the cycle.
Discard that cycle and start timing a fresh one later in the day.
Cut two minutes from the total and record it as a normal cycle.
Note the interruption on the sheet and time the cycle as a whole.

advanced.situation: You design a motion study to set a standard rate for packing boxes across three shifts. Night shift workers are 15 percent slower than the day shift.

options.text: Observe all three shifts, find why night work is slower and set the rate.
Set the standard from the fastest worker you timed across all the shifts.
Set the standard at the average of the three shifts' measured times.
Set the standard from the day shift and review night shift later.

basic.situation: You observe a press operator using the machine to check it follows the quality procedure. The operator skips the hourly tool wear check printed on the procedure sheet.

options.text: Do the tool wear check yourself and record it as the operator's.
Note the skipped check, remind the operator and tell the supervisor.
Take it that the operator knows the machine and watch another worker.
Remind the operator of the check and carry on with the observation.

advanced.situation: You audit how press operators maintain a stamping machine against the quality standards. Operators follow the steps, but the lubrication log shows the same entry every day for two weeks.

options.text: Watch a lubrication job in person, compare it with the log and raise gaps.
Ask the operators to confirm the log entries are true and sign it.
Mark the audit as compliant and recommend that the log format be reviewed.
Accept the log since the machine is still running within its limits.

basic.situation: You read a worker's log against the specification sheet and find the entered torque value is 25 where the sheet allows 20 to 22.

options.text: Accept the entry because a higher torque is safer than a lower one.
Ask the worker to recheck the torque on the product and update the log.
Flag the entry as out of specification and pass the log to your supervisor.
Change the value to 22 in the log so it meets the sheet.

advanced.situation: Before a customer audit, you find that batch records and the test sheets disagree on the production dates for four lots.

options.text: Trace each date to machine logs, amend the records with notes and get sign-off.
Change the test sheets to match the batch records before the audit.
Use the dates on the test sheets since they were written later.
Ask the shift leaders which dates they remember and update the batch records.

basic.situation: You test sample products at the polishing stage using a checklist of gloss and thickness limits. The thickness gauge shows a reading slightly above the upper limit.

options.text: Retake the reading once and pass the product if it comes back lower.
Check the gauge on a reference piece, retake the reading and then decide.
Pass the product because gauge readings often vary by small amounts.
Round the reading down on the checklist so the product passes.

advanced.situation: You develop a new test protocol for the sealing strength of food pouches. Existing tests check leaks at room temperature, but customers report seals opening in cold storage.

options.text: Add cold-storage conditioning, set pass limits from trials and document the test.
Keep the protocol as it is since pouches pass the room temperature test.
Tell customers to warm pouches to room temperature before opening them.
Add one cold test to the protocol and use the same limits.

basic.situation: You compile defect counts from five production reports into a weekly summary table. One report shows 120 defects on a day when the line made only 80 units.

options.text: Check that report with the line leader before using the figure.
Cap the defect count at 80 so it cannot exceed production.
Include the figure and add a footnote saying it looks high.
Replace the figure with the average of the other four reports.

advanced.situation: You must predict reliability of a new motor model from two years of failure data. Early data suggest failures rise after 3,000 running hours, but samples are small.

options.text: Use the failure rate from the older motor model since it is known.
Fit a statistical model with confidence limits and note the sample size.
Report the average failure time and note that samples are small.
State that failures will stay low since few have occurred so far.

basic.situation: Next week's schedule needs two operators on a drilling machine. You have a list showing who is available and which machines each person can run.

options.text: Assign the two available operators who are trained on the drilling machine.
Assign any two operators who are free and train them on the job.
Assign whoever finished last week's job on the machine and ask later.
Assign the two most senior operators on the list to the machine.

advanced.situation: A rush order arrives while the schedule already has a machine breakdown, and two operators are on leave. You must adjust work assignments for the week.

options.text: Promise the customer the original delivery date and sort the plan out later.
Move the rush order ahead of all other orders and keep the same staff.
Re-plan around machine capacity and staff, then tell the supervisor what slips.
Ask operators to work extra hours until all the orders are completed.

basic.situation: You run a nanoparticle compounding machine following the standard operating procedure. Step 6 says to wait until the chamber reaches 80 C, but production is waiting.

options.text: Wait until the chamber reaches 80 C and record the reading before starting.
Raise the heater setting well above 80 C to reach temperature faster.
Ask a colleague to confirm the reading is close enough, then start.
Start now since the chamber keeps heating during the first few minutes of the run.

advanced.situation: You implement an improved mixing process for a nanocoating, which your team lead approved on paper. A pilot run makes coatings thicker than the specification allows.

options.text: Continue the pilot and sand the coatings down to the specified thickness.
Stop the pilot, review the settings with the lead and rerun after adjusting.
Finish the pilot and tell the lead the coating thickness is high.
Record the specified thickness on the batch sheet and ship the pilot coatings.

basic.situation: You measure and mix two chemicals for a nanoparticle solution using a written formula. Your balance shows 5.12 g where the formula says 5.00 g.

options.text: Adjust the other chemical to match the extra 5.12 g by eye.
Record 5.12 g and note the difference in the batch record.
Use the 5.12 g since the extra amount is too small to matter.
Remove a little of the chemical until the balance reads 5.00 g.

advanced.situation: You modify a wet chemical method from standard lab scale to suit nanoscale particles. Your first batch gives uneven particle sizes, and the senior scientist is away for two days.

options.text: Pick the batch with the most even sizes and report the method as complete.
Change one variable at a time, log each trial and share the results on return.
Change the mixing speed, temperature and time together to find a better recipe.
Pause the work and wait for the senior scientist to return before running more.

basic.situation: You take an image of nanoparticles with an optical microscope and measure their sizes. The image looks blurred at the magnification in the instructions.

options.text: Refocus the microscope, clean the lens if needed and retake the image.
Increase the magnification until the image looks sharp and record that setting.
Measure sizes from the blurred image and note that it is unclear.
Pick the sharpest-looking part of the image and report that as typical.

advanced.situation: You help an engineer characterise a thin carbon nanotube film. Two methods, atomic force microscopy and scanning electron microscopy, give thickness values 15 percent apart.

options.text: Report the average of the two thickness values to the engineer.
Compare how each method measures, check calibration and report both values with notes.
Report the value from the method the engineer used last time.
Report the thinner value because it fits the target specification.

basic.situation: You monitor a coating machine's pressure and flow every 15 minutes against a specification sheet. The pressure drifts slightly toward the upper limit.

options.text: Record the reading and mention the drift at the end of the shift.
Pause the readings until the pressure settles back to its normal level again.
Record the trend and alert the operator if the next readings keep rising.
Adjust the pressure valve slightly yourself to bring the reading down.

advanced.situation: You monitor a hazardous waste cleanup using nanocomposites. The contractor's crew applies the material faster than the procedure allows, to finish before the rain.

options.text: Tell the contractor's supervisor, record the rate used and ask for the specified rate.
Record the faster rate in the log and report it in the weekly summary.
Let the crew finish before the rain and check results afterwards.
Sign off the work as done at the specified rate to avoid conflict.

basic.situation: You fill in the batch record for a nanoparticle run. After the run, you notice you forgot to write down the start time.

options.text: Copy the start time from the previous batch record into the box.
Write the time you think the run began and initial it.
Leave the box blank and tell your supervisor you forgot it.
Enter the start time from the machine log as a dated late entry.

advanced.situation: You prepare capability data and training notes to transfer a nanocoating process to the production team. Your pilot capability data used just ten samples.

options.text: State the sample size, add samples if you can and write training notes.
Round the pilot data up to look stable and attach training notes.
Present the ten-sample data as the capability and add brief training notes.
Copy capability figures from a similar process and write the training notes.

basic.situation: A scientist asks you to compile measurement data from three days of nanoparticle experiments into one spreadsheet. Two files use different units for particle size.

options.text: Combine the files as they are and list the units in the notes.
Drop the file that uses different units and compile the rest.
Use the units from the first file for all the data.
Convert the sizes to one unit, label it clearly and tell the scientist.

advanced.situation: You must prepare a presentation for upper management on a nanomaterial scale-up that is two months late. The data show the delay comes from a supplier's particle quality.

options.text: Focus on the technical results and say the delay is a normal risk.
Blame the production team for the delay since management will accept that.
Present the revised timeline and mention the supplier issue in one slide.
Present the cause with supplier data, the revised timeline and options for recovery.

basic.situation: You set up a tensile test on a steel sample using written instructions. The instructions give a pull speed in one unit, but the machine's display uses a different unit.

options.text: Choose the nearest speed setting on the machine and start the test straight away.
Convert the speed yourself using a chart and start the test.
Start at the machine's default speed since results are similar anyway.
Ask the engineer to confirm the conversion before you start the test.

advanced.situation: You test a redesigned pump housing under working pressure to investigate a proposal for better performance. A small leak appears at a seam, and the proposal deadline is today.

options.text: Raise the pressure further to see whether the leak gets worse before the deadline.
Seal the seam with tape and continue the test to complete the data.
Stop the test safely, record the leak location and pressure, and report it.
Finish the planned test run and note the leak in the report afterwards.

basic.situation: You read a voltmeter and an ammeter on a motor test to record voltage and amperage at operating temperature. The ammeter needle shows a value beyond the rated amperage.

options.text: Record the rated amperage in the log so the test looks normal.
Tap the meter to settle the needle and record the new reading.
Pause the test, note the reading and tell your supervisor.
Record the reading and continue the test while watching the needle closely.

advanced.situation: A compressor test shows output 6 percent below rating, and the maker's rating has a 5 percent tolerance. You must adjust it to meet specification and plan the follow-up inspections.

options.text: Adjust the unit until the output reaches the rating and keep to normal inspections.
Record the unit as within tolerance since the shortfall is near 5 percent.
Widen the tolerance in the report to 6 percent so the unit passes.
Investigate the shortfall, adjust the unit, retest and plan earlier inspections.

basic.situation: You help an engineer prepare a prototype pulley for testing by sketching its key dimensions. You have a rough drawing and the pulley itself on the bench.

options.text: Take the dimensions from a similar pulley sketch in the file.
Estimate the dimensions by eye from the pulley and sketch it quickly.
Measure the pulley with calipers and compare it with the drawing first.
Copy the dimensions from the rough drawing into your sketch and carry on.

advanced.situation: You design a jig for holding thin aluminium panels during drilling. The panels bend slightly under clamp pressure, and drilled holes drift out of position.

options.text: Clamp harder to stop the panel bending and drill the full batch.
Reduce the clamp pressure and keep the same jig layout for the batch.
Add support under the drilling area, spread the clamp load and test a panel.
Tell the drill operator to slow down and check each hole position.

basic.situation: You draft a detail drawing of a bracket for the sheet metal shop. The senior technician's sketch shows the bend angle but not the bend radius.

options.text: Use the shop's standard bend radius and note it on the drawing.
Ask the senior technician for the bend radius before releasing the drawing.
Leave the radius off and let the shop pick what suits them.
Draw a sharp corner so the radius no longer matters.

advanced.situation: You prepare the layout of a new pump room and set drafting standards for the team. Piping, electrical and mechanical drawings use different scales and symbols.

options.text: Keep each drawing as is and tell the contractor to sort out clashes.
Set one drafting standard for scales and symbols and apply it to all drawings.
Redraw this layout in one scale and tell the team to follow it.
Add a legend to each drawing explaining its own scale and symbols.

basic.situation: You disassemble a small gearbox for a technician who will inspect it. The parts are not labelled and the assembly order is not obvious.

options.text: Mix the small parts in one tray to save time and sort them later.
Remember the order and reassemble from memory since the gearbox is small.
Photograph each step and label the parts as they come off.
Lay the parts out on the bench in the order you removed them.

advanced.situation: You lead a failure analysis on a conveyor shaft that broke twice in a month. The factory wants to replace it with a thicker shaft today.

options.text: Report the breaks as bad luck since the shafts are within specification.
Replace the shaft with an identical one and watch it carefully.
Examine the fracture, check loads and alignment and recommend a fix.
Fit the thicker shaft and monitor it for cracks over the next month.

basic.situation: A senior engineer gives you a sketch with a note, 'TYP 4X', next to a hole. You are not sure whether it means four holes or four times the diameter.

options.text: Make a hole four times the diameter and see if anyone complains.
Make one hole and wait for the inspector to say if it is acceptable.
Make four holes since that is the usual meaning of that note.
Ask the senior engineer what the note means before making the part.

advanced.situation: Management asks you to advise whether a complex housing should be machined in-house or outsourced. A junior technician asks you to explain how you would decide.

options.text: List tolerance, volume and cost factors and explain how each affects the choice.
Give management your recommendation and offer the juniors your reasoning later.
Tell the junior the decision is management's and not for technicians.
Recommend what the last similar job used and tell the junior it worked.

basic.situation: You install an engine on a test stand following the setup sheet. The sheet lists four mounting bolts, but the engine has a fifth threaded mounting hole.

options.text: Fit the four listed bolts and note the fifth hole on the sheet.
Start the engine to see whether the four bolts hold it steady.
Ask the test engineer whether the fifth mount is needed.
Fit a bolt in the fifth hole too, since more mounting points help.

advanced.situation: You modify a prototype bracket to hold a new sensor for a durability test. The sensor sits 4 mm too close to the exhaust, and testing begins tomorrow.

options.text: Make a revised bracket that moves the sensor, then check fit and heat exposure.
Bend the existing bracket by hand until it looks far enough away.
Run the first day's test and watch the sensor temperature for problems.
Add a heat shield around the sensor and leave the bracket as built.

basic.situation: You run a manual brake test on a bench rig and must record stopping distances for five runs. After the third run the distance is much longer than the first two.

options.text: Record all five runs as measured and mention the long run to the engineer.
Change the third value to match the first two runs in the log.
Drop the third result and record the other four runs as the data.
Check the rig for a cause, rerun that test and record both results.

advanced.situation: You help test a lane-keeping function that uses machine learning, running it on a closed track. In one run the car drifts across a faded lane marking with no warning.

options.text: Repeat the test on fresh markings and report it if it fails again.
Mark that run invalid because the markings were poor and delete its data.
Log the run data and conditions, repeat the test and report the failure.
Note the faded marking as the cause and carry on with the test plan.

basic.situation: You read the blueprint for a test of an alcohol-blend fuel line. The drawing calls for a seal material you do not recognise.

options.text: Use the seal type from your last fuel line test and continue.
Fit the nearest-looking seal from the stores and write it in the log.
Look up the seal material in the specification or ask the test engineer.
Leave the seal out of the line to test the rest of the layout.

advanced.situation: You evaluate a hydrogen fuel cell prototype in a small test vehicle. During a range test, the cell output falls sharply when the outside temperature drops.

options.text: Heat the cell with a portable heater during the test and report the range.
Repeat the range test on a warmer day and compare the results.
Log temperature against output, check cooling controls and report the pattern.
Report that the cell fails in cold weather and stop the evaluation.

basic.situation: You monitor a computer-controlled dynamometer during an engine run. Written instructions say to stop if oil pressure falls below 2 bar, and the display shows 1.8 bar.

options.text: Lower the alarm limit on the display so the run can continue.
Stop the run as instructed and tell the test engineer the reading.
Keep running to the end of the stage and stop the run after that.
Check the reading with the backup gauge and stop the run if it matches.

advanced.situation: You analyze test data from a redesigned dual-clutch gearbox. Fuel efficiency improved 3 percent in the lab but just 1 percent in road tests.

options.text: Report the 3 percent lab figure and leave the road test out.
Compare lab and road load, temperature and shift patterns, then explain the gap.
Report the lab result as the main figure and the road test as extra.
Report the average of the lab and road results as the improvement.

basic.situation: You document a brake test with photos and a spreadsheet. A photo of the disc wear is blurred, and the test rig has been dismantled.

options.text: Attach the blurred photo and write that the wear looked normal to you.
Use a clear photo from an earlier test and keep it in the file.
Use the blurred photo and add a written description of the wear.
Record the blurred photo as unusable in the spreadsheet and tell the engineer.

advanced.situation: A customer asks for a durability test of a door hinge. You recommend test conditions and later suggest design changes, but the customer's cycle count is below the industry standard.

options.text: Reduce the cycle count further so the hinge is certain to pass.
Run the customer's cycle count and report that the hinge passed the durability test.
Run the customer's cycle count and mention the standard in your report.
Recommend the standard cycle count and suggest design improvements from the data.

basic.situation: You do routine maintenance on a test-bench pressure sensor. The calibration sticker shows it is due next week, but the sensor reads normally.

options.text: Replace the calibration sticker with a new date to avoid a reminder.
Skip the calibration because the sensor reads normally against the other gauge.
Do the routine checks and book the calibration before the due date.
Do the routine checks and tell the lead the calibration is due soon.

advanced.situation: You manage buying test equipment and supplies for the lab for the year. The budget allows either one expensive data logger or three cheaper ones, and four rigs are scheduled.

options.text: Order the three cheaper loggers so each of three rigs can run at once.
Compare rig needs and accuracy, then order what covers the schedule.
Order the cheapest quote available and see which rigs it suits.
Order the expensive logger and share it between rigs when needed.

basic.situation: You read a technical order to find the tolerance for calibrating a pressure gauge. The order lists tolerance in kPa but your test gauge reads in psi.

options.text: Convert the tolerance with an online tool and use the result.
Read the tolerance off an older order for the same gauge type.
Convert the tolerance with the standard factor and have a colleague check it.
Use the kPa number as if it were psi, since gauges are similar.

advanced.situation: You write the report on calibration tests for a flow meter that failed its as-found check. The customer's quality manager will review it before deciding whether past batches need re-testing.

options.text: Report the as-found error, the adjustment made and the affected period.
Report the as-found error and the final calibration result in a short summary.
Report that the meter passed and keep the as-found error out.
Report the final result as in tolerance and attach the full data sheet.

basic.situation: You plan the order of calibration tests for a temperature probe. The specification asks for checks at three set points from low to high.

options.text: Test at the high set point first, then the others, to save time.
Test at one set point and sign off for all three.
Test at the middle point and estimate the other two from it.
Test at the low, middle and high set points in the order specified.

advanced.situation: You develop a new calibration method for a humidity sensor after test data show drift above 70 percent humidity. A quick fix would use the maker's standard method with a correction factor.

options.text: Apply the factor to the drifting sensors and note it on the certificate.
Apply the factor to every sensor and issue the certificates this week.
Use the maker's method unchanged and record that drift was seen above 70 percent.
Test the correction factor against reference standards over the whole range first.

basic.situation: You calibrate a room thermometer against a reference thermometer at 25 C. The reference reads 25.0 and the device reads 25.4, and the allowed error is 0.3.

options.text: Mark the device as failed and return it to the customer.
Record the as-found reading, adjust the device, then record the as-left reading.
Mark the device as within limits since 0.4 is a small error.
Adjust the device to read 25.0 and record the new reading.

advanced.situation: You test the reliability of a hydraulic press gauge for a customer who uses it for safety checks. The gauge passes at five points, but it sticks slightly when pressure falls.

options.text: Pass the gauge and advise the customer to tap it before reading.
Pass the gauge and clean the glass so the needle looks smoother.
Pass the gauge since all five calibration points are within tolerance.
Test with falling pressure too, record the hysteresis and tell the customer.

basic.situation: You visually inspect a micrometer returned for calibration. You see a faint scratch on the measuring face and a worn thimble marking.

options.text: Record the scratch and calibrate it, since the markings are still readable.
Calibrate the micrometer and mention the scratch if the readings fail.
Polish out the scratch on the face before calibrating it.
Record both defects on the receipt and tell the customer first.

advanced.situation: You disassemble a precision torque wrench for detailed inspection. After you remove the spring, the adjustment mechanism looks worn, and the owner needs it back today.

options.text: Photograph the wear, measure it and report to the owner that it needs repair.
Reassemble and calibrate it, then tell the owner the mechanism is worn.
Reassemble and calibrate it, and tell the owner the wear is minor.
Reassemble it and apply a calibration label so it can be used today.

basic.situation: You repair a handheld calibrator whose display flickers. The cause looks like a loose ribbon cable inside, and the unit is used for customer certificates.

options.text: Reseat the ribbon cable, then verify the unit against a reference before use.
Reseat the ribbon cable and use the unit if the display stays steady.
Tape the ribbon cable in place and return the unit to the bench.
Replace the display module with a spare one from stock and use the unit.

advanced.situation: You must make a metal housing for a calibration sensor on the lathe and mill, working from your own sketch. The sensor will be used in a wet environment.

options.text: Machine the housing from your sketch and check fit later with the sensor.
Machine the housing from your sketch and add a seal if it fits.
Draw plans with seal details, have a senior review them, then machine.
Use a thinner wall than planned so the housing is finished sooner.

basic.situation: Your company sends you to a one-day workshop on a new torque calibration tool. Back at work, your supervisor is busy and the tool is already in the lab.

options.text: Wait until the next workshop to use the tool in real jobs.
Review your workshop notes and try the tool with a supervisor watching.
Read the tool manual and try it on a spare device first.
Use the tool on customer devices now, based on what you remember from the workshop.

advanced.situation: You are asked to guide your team on a new calibration tool and method you learned at a training session. Two colleagues doubt it gives better results than the old method.

options.text: Tell the doubting colleagues to follow the new method or be reassigned.
Present the maker's claims and training slides and let the team decide.
Run a side-by-side comparison with both methods and share the data with the team.
Switch the team to the new method since you learned it directly from the trainers.

basic.situation: You visually examine a welded pipe joint with a torch and mirror. You see a short dark line along the weld edge that could be a crack or a scratch.

options.text: Pass the joint since weld edges often show dark lines like this.
Clean the area, view it magnified and report the indication.
Mark the spot and ask a colleague for a second opinion.
Record it as a scratch if it does not catch your fingernail.

advanced.situation: You supervise two trainees inspecting a bridge girder for fatigue cracks. One trainee reports a crack near a bolt hole and the other sees nothing at the same place.

options.text: Inspect the spot yourself with magnification and penetrant, then brief both trainees.
Record the crack and tell the other trainee to be more observant.
Record no crack since one of two inspectors found nothing.
Ask both trainees to look again and record whichever view they agree on.

basic.situation: You use an infrared camera to check a concrete wall for hidden voids, as taught. The picture shows one cooler patch, but the sun is shining on that side.

options.text: Repeat the scan in shade or at another time of day and compare the images.
Report a void under the patch and recommend breaking the wall open to check.
Dismiss the patch as a sun effect and scan the next wall.
Mark the cool patch as a possible void and tell your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You map imperfections in a thick steel plate with sonic measurements and ultrasonic testing. Echoes from the back wall are weak in one area, so the map there is uncertain.

options.text: Fill in that area by copying the pattern from the nearby readings.
Check the probe coupling, rescan the area and map the weak zone separately.
Show the weak area as sound metal because no flaw echo appeared.
Mark the area as uncertain on the map and tell the engineer.

basic.situation: You expose film to image a small cast part with the radiographic setup from the procedure sheet. The processed film looks very dark overall.

options.text: Check the exposure setting against the sheet and retake the film.
Lighten the film image with a viewer lamp and report the part as sound.
Retake the film with a shorter exposure that you estimate yourself.
Read the dark film as it is and note that it is overexposed.

advanced.situation: You make radiographic images of a pipeline weld to find flaws, working near a public footpath. The exposure area is not yet fully cordoned off.

options.text: Complete the cordon and radiation checks, then expose the weld as planned.
Begin the full exposure and watch the footpath for approaching people.
Post a warning sign at the footpath and begin the exposure.
Start with a short exposure to test the setup and finish the cordon after.

basic.situation: You select and calibrate a basic ultrasonic thickness gauge under supervision. The calibration block shows 10.0 mm, but your gauge reads 10.3 mm on the block.

options.text: Recalibrate the gauge on the block until it reads 10.0 mm.
Use the gauge as it is, since 0.3 mm is small for thick parts.
Change the block's stated thickness to 10.3 mm in the log and carry on.
Note the 0.3 mm offset and subtract it from every later reading.

advanced.situation: You develop a leak testing method for a new fuel tank design and choose the equipment. The usual method needs pressurising to a level the thin tank walls may not tolerate.

options.text: Trial a helium test at lower pressure and compare it with known leaks.
Use the usual method at a lower pressure and note the change in your report.
Use the usual method on the real tank and watch for bulging.
Use the usual method at full pressure on a spare tank first.

basic.situation: You compare a magnetic particle indication on a shaft with the acceptance table in the code. The indication is 2 mm long and the table allows up to 1.5 mm.

options.text: Measure it again carefully and report the new length if it differs.
Round the length down to 1.5 mm in the report.
Accept it, since the difference is less than one millimetre and small.
Reject the indication per the code and report it to your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You interpret results from leak, penetrant and acoustic emission tests on a pressure vessel. The three methods point to different weak areas.

options.text: Report the area that is cheapest to repair and skip the other areas.
Report the area that two of the three methods flagged.
Correlate the results by location and sensitivity, then recommend a rescan.
Report the area from the most recent test and skip the other areas.

basic.situation: You document the steps and results of an eddy current test you performed with guidance. You realise you forgot to write down the probe frequency.

options.text: Copy the frequency from the last test report you filed for this part.
Check the frequency in the equipment settings and add a dated late entry.
Add a likely frequency from the procedure and mark it as an estimate.
Leave the frequency out of the report since the results are recorded.

advanced.situation: You prepare the report on ultrasonic testing of a crane hook for the owner. Your method is complex, and the owner will use the report to decide on retirement.

options.text: Give a pass or fail decision with the technician's signature.
Send the raw instrument printout and let the owner read it.
Describe the method, calibration, findings and limits with annotated images.
Give the findings and a summary of the method with key images.

basic.situation: You enter the clean room to start a shift. You find a colleague's cardboard box of parts left on the bench near the laser assembly area.

options.text: Cover the box with a clean-room cloth and carry on with your work.
Take the box out via the airlock and wipe the bench with approved wipes.
Wipe the bench around the box and leave the box where it is.
Open the box and unpack the parts to put them away in the cabinet there.

advanced.situation: You train two new technicians on clean room protocols. One keeps wearing gloves over uncovered wrist cuffs, and the supervisor says the whole team must follow the same gowning steps.

options.text: Demonstrate the gowning sequence, watch both do it and give feedback.
Tell the trainee to follow the gowning guide once the shift is over.
Post the gowning steps at the entrance and remind them to follow them.
Let the trainee carry on since the gloves cover most of the wrist.

basic.situation: You set up a test console, a collimator and cables for a lens test with guidance. The cable ends for the detector are not labelled.

options.text: Test each cable end on the console with the detector switched off.
Plug the cables into any free ports and switch on to see what works.
Match the cable ends by size and plug in the detector cable.
Look up the cable pairing in the setup guide or ask your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You configure a die bonder and a wire bonder for a new laser module and troubleshoot the setup. Bond strength is low on every unit from the first run.

options.text: Run the whole lot and sort the weak units out at final test.
Run the rest of the lot at a higher temperature to speed things up.
Check bonding temperature, force and tool wear one at a time and retest.
Increase the bond force a little and retest a few units.

basic.situation: You adjust the power setting on a laser used for alignment, as shown in the procedure. The power meter reads slightly above the allowed power.

options.text: Lower the setting in small steps and recheck the meter each time.
Cover the laser aperture partly with tape to reduce the output.
Lower the setting once and record the value you set on the log sheet.
Leave the setting as it is since the meter may read high.

advanced.situation: You define calibration standards for the team's beam analysers and guide technicians on maintenance. Two analysers give beam widths that differ by 5 percent for the same laser.

options.text: Tell technicians to use whichever analyser gives the narrower beam width.
Compare both against a reference, set a calibration interval and note it.
Calibrate both analysers so their readings match the average of the two beams.
Mark the newer analyser as the reference since it is newer.

basic.situation: You record photonic test data for a fibre coupler. The sheet asks for insertion loss in dB, but the meter shows values in mW.

options.text: Record the mW numbers as dB since the units look similar.
Record the mW numbers in the dB column and add a note.
Record the mW values and ask your supervisor to convert them later.
Convert the readings to dB using the formula on the sheet.

advanced.situation: You design a test plan for failure analysis of optoelectrical modules returned by a customer. Some modules stop working after a few hours of operation.

options.text: Report the failure as customer misuse and close the case.
Run extended burn-in tests, log temperature and current, and inspect failures.
Run a short functional test on all returned modules and sort them.
Open every failed module first and look for visible damage.

basic.situation: A scientist asks you to help with a photonics experiment and to note the lab bench readings every five minutes. After 20 minutes the readings start to drift.

options.text: Adjust the optical alignment yourself until the readings look steady again.
Pause the experiment and wait for the scientist to come back.
Keep recording, tell the scientist about the drift and ask what to do.
Keep recording and mention the drift in your notes at the end.

advanced.situation: You assist engineers in building a new fixture for aligning fibre arrays. Your trial shows it holds fibres well but is slow to load, and the engineers want a decision on whether to continue.

options.text: Recommend dropping the fixture and going back to the old manual alignment method.
Tell the engineers the fixture works and loading speed can be tuned later.
Time the loading steps, suggest design changes and share the data.
Suggest adding a second operator to load the fixture faster for now.

basic.situation: You document the steps for calibrating a fibre optic power meter, with guidance. The senior technician gives you rough notes in an order that differs from the actual procedure.

options.text: Copy the notes into the document as they are and file it.
Write the steps in the notes' order and add the procedure's page numbers.
Write the steps in the procedure's order and check them with the senior.
Write the steps from memory of an earlier calibration and tidy them later.

advanced.situation: You write the standard operating procedure for a new fibre alignment process and recommend ways to cut costs and cycle time. A cheaper epoxy cures faster but is untested on your parts.

options.text: Write the procedure with the current epoxy and propose a trial of the cheaper one.
Switch to the cheaper epoxy and claim the cost saving in the report.
Switch the procedure to the cheaper epoxy and note the change in the document.
Write both epoxies into the procedure as options and let operators choose freely.

basic.situation: You hold the vertical rod for a theodolite operator on a sloping site. The operator signals to move the rod, but you cannot tell which direction was meant.

options.text: Place the rod on the nearest mark and let the operator adjust the reading.
Move the rod in the direction that looks flatter and hold it.
Keep the rod still and signal back to ask the operator to repeat it.
Move the rod a little each way until the operator stops signalling.

advanced.situation: You help develop a faster method for a boundary survey, and you calculate coordinates from the field notes. A trial of the new method gives points that differ 4 cm from the old method.

options.text: Recommend the new method since 4 cm is small for boundary work.
Average the two sets of coordinates and recommend the new method.
Recommend the new method but keep using the old coordinates in the official records.
Compare both methods against a known control point and report the deviation.

basic.situation: You trace contours from a field sketch to produce a map showing property locations. Two contour lines in your sketch cross each other near a stream.

options.text: Delete one of the crossing lines so the map looks clean.
Check the field notes for the elevations and ask the surveyor.
Trace the lines as drawn and mark the crossing for review.
Join the lines at the crossing point into a single smooth contour.

advanced.situation: You design a geographic database for a council's drainage maps and set print scales for the plots. Staff want one scale for all sheets, but small culverts disappear at that scale.

options.text: Keep the small scale and remove the tiny culverts from the database altogether.
Use the single scale and list the missing culverts in a separate table.
Set the scale by feature size, use layers and test one printed sheet.
Print all sheets at the larger scale and accept the extra pages.

basic.situation: You compare contour lines on a draft map with an old aerial photograph to check accuracy. A hill's shape on the map is slightly different from the photograph.

options.text: Leave the hill as it is since the map came from a field survey.
Redraw the hill to match the photograph and delete the surveyed contours.
Check the survey data for that hill and note the difference.
Mark the difference on a copy of the map and move on.

advanced.situation: You compare survey computations for a road project against the applicable standards to decide whether the data is adequate. Closure error on one traverse is within the standard but close to the limit.

options.text: Accept the traverse as it is within the standard and note the figure.
Recheck the computation, record the margin and recommend a repeat measurement.
Accept the traverse and tell the supervisor it passed with room to spare.
Adjust one angle slightly to bring the closure error well under the limit allowed.

basic.situation: You compile information from engineering plans to stake the corners of a small building plot. The plan lists the plot width but the site plan shows a slightly different width.

options.text: Stake the plot using the engineering plan and tell the surveyor about the difference.
Stake the narrower width so the building is sure to fit inside.
Ask the project engineer which plan is current before you set any stakes.
Stake the width from the site plan since it was drawn from the ground.

advanced.situation: You research property records to describe a boundary after a parcel was split and one part merged with a neighbour. The old deed and the new title give slightly different frontage lengths.

options.text: Trace the split and merger records, then note any unresolved gap.
Use the new title's frontage and attach the old deed to the property file.
Average the two frontage lengths and use that in the description.
Use the old deed's frontage since it describes the original boundary.

basic.situation: You trim and join aerial photo prints into a mosaic. The edge of one print does not line up with the neighbouring print at the road.

options.text: Check the reference points on both prints and realign them to the scale.
Stretch one print slightly so the road joins up neatly.
Trim a little off one edge until the road lines match up.
Draw the missing section of road over the gap by hand.

advanced.situation: You analyze aerial photographs of an industrial area to find resource and industrial features for a planning map. Part of the photo is in deep shadow, hiding an area near a factory.

options.text: Show the shadowed area as empty land since no buildings are visible.
Mark the shadowed area as unverified on the map and carry on with the rest.
Request photos from another time or sun angle and mark the area unverified.
Infer the hidden features from similar nearby factories and show them on the map.

basic.situation: You enter new survey points into the land-information system and then query it for points near a lot. The query returns no results, though you just saved the points.

options.text: Run the same query again after a few minutes to see the points.
Enter the points a second time in case the first save failed.
Delete the new points and re-import the whole survey file.
Check the coordinate system and search area settings, then query again.

advanced.situation: You manage the land-information system for a district office. Staff request a complex plot showing parcels, utilities and contours, but the system times out on the full dataset.

options.text: Ask staff to request each layer separately and join the prints by hand.
Restart the server repeatedly during office hours until the full plot completes.
Plot a reduced dataset and tell staff the rest can follow later.
Split the plot by area or layer, test the output and document the steps.

basic.situation: A small dairy farm in Perak asks what a milking cow needs to eat. You have the feed label of a new pellet and a standard requirement table.

options.text: Compare the protein value with the table and tell the farmer.
Compare the pellet's protein and energy with the table and show the farmer.
Tell the farmer the pellet suits dairy cows because the label says so.
Tell the farmer to feed more pellets until the milk yield rises.

advanced.situation: You design a feeding trial to test two feeds on egg quality in laying hens. The farm manager wants to start next week using all hens in one house with the new feed.

options.text: Split the hens into matched groups, give each feed to one group and measure both.
Give the new feed to all hens and record the manager's impressions.
Feed one house the new feed and compare its eggs with last month's.
Feed the new feed to the strongest hens and compare them with the rest.

basic.situation: You explain heritability to a farm trainee using milk yield data from your station's herd. The trainee assumes every high-yielding cow has high-yielding daughters.

options.text: Agree that yield is mostly inherited and tell the trainee to select by yield.
Explain that heritability is partial, and show several dam and daughter yields.
Tell the trainee that feed decides everything and genes do not matter.
Explain that heritability is partial and refer the trainee to a textbook.

advanced.situation: You manage a breeding program to raise growth in goats. Fast-growing bucks are producing kids with weak legs, and the farm owner wants to keep using the same bucks.

options.text: Use the bucks on a small group of does to see the effect.
Review the pedigrees, limit use of those bucks and bring in unrelated sires.
Keep the bucks but pair them with does that have strong legs.
Keep using the same bucks and cull the weak kids at birth.

basic.situation: You help record feeding and housing conditions in a poultry house. The shed's water drinkers are dirty, and the guideline says to clean them daily.

options.text: Clean the drinkers and note in the log that they were dirty.
Add disinfectant to the water to cover the dirt and leave the drinkers.
Clean the drinkers now, log it and tell the farm supervisor.
Leave the drinkers until the weekly cleaning since the birds are drinking.

advanced.situation: You develop new housing and disease control standards for a pig farm after repeated parasite outbreaks. The owner wants a low-cost plan that can start within a week.

options.text: Add a second dose of dewormer to the feed for all pigs.
Start a deworming programme for all pigs and review housing next quarter.
Map outbreak patterns, set cleaning rules and start monitoring with the vet.
Move sick pigs to a spare pen and keep housing the same.

basic.situation: You write a half-page summary of a feeding trial for the farm staff. The trial found a 4 percent weight gain with a new feed, but only in one of three pens.

options.text: Report the 4 percent gain and add that more trials are planned.
Report the 4 percent gain for the whole trial to keep it simple.
Say that the new feed raised weight gain on the farm by 4 percent.
State the 4 percent gain, name the one pen and note the limits.

advanced.situation: You present findings on a new feed additive to producers, government officers and fellow scientists in one session. The data are strong for milk yield but weak for animal health.

options.text: Present the yield result and keep the health data in the appendix.
Present both results with limits, and adapt the examples for each audience.
Present the yield result in full and mention the health data briefly.
Present the yield result and say more health work is under way.

basic.situation: You observe and record daily management practices on a goat farm for a study. You notice workers feed in different orders, which the study protocol does not mention.

options.text: Record the different feeding orders as seen and ask the study lead.
Record the most common feeding order and mention the difference in notes.
Record the order given in the protocol since that is the standard.
Ask the workers to feed in one order so the records look consistent.

advanced.situation: You lead a research project to improve overall production in a dairy herd. Early results show a feed change raises milk, but two cows lost weight and one had a calving problem.

options.text: Roll the feed out to the whole herd to confirm the milk result.
Report that the feed raises milk and treat the other cases as chance.
Continue the trial as planned and report the weight loss at the end.
Extend the trial with controls, track body condition and calving, and consult the vet.

basic.situation: A smallholder asks how to raise chick survival in cold weather. You know brooder lamps help but not how many a flock of 200 needs.

options.text: Tell the smallholder to use as many lamps as the power supply allows.
Explain brooder lamps and suggest a number that worked for another farmer's flock.
Tell the smallholder one lamp per hundred chicks is the standard figure.
Explain the purpose of brooder lamps and check the lamp number with your senior.

advanced.situation: You advise a large producer on adopting a new automated feeding system. The producer wants to install it across all barns at once to meet a contract deadline.

options.text: Propose a pilot in one barn, show expected returns and agree a staged rollout.
Advise installing in half the barns first and the rest after a month.
Promise the producer that the system will meet the contract deadline.
Support the full installation and offer to check the system after a month.

basic.situation: You analyze a batch of fruit jam for sugar and moisture using the lab method sheet. The moisture result is much higher than the last three batches.

options.text: Re-dry the same sample for longer until the moisture number comes down to normal.
Average it with the last three batches and report the average.
Report the high result to your supervisor and attach the lab sheet.
Repeat the test on a fresh sample and check the oven and balance records.

advanced.situation: You lead research to replace nitrite in a cured chicken product with a plant-based alternative. Early samples are safe in lab tests but their colour fades after a week.

options.text: Add a little nitrite back to hold the colour and keep the label unchanged.
Trial other curing agents and packaging, checking safety and colour over shelf life.
Add a small amount of colouring to the plant-based sample to hold the colour.
Shorten the stated shelf life to five days and proceed to launch with the current recipe.

basic.situation: You follow the standard procedure to seal and pack bottled sauce. The sealing machine's temperature display reads 5 degrees below the set point.

options.text: Wait a few minutes for the temperature to reach the set point.
Stop packing, tell your supervisor and wait for the machine to be checked.
Keep packing and check the seals by eye every ten bottles.
Raise the set point by 5 degrees to make up the difference.

advanced.situation: You design a new preservation method for a coconut milk drink to extend its shelf life to 90 days. A lab trial with mild heat treatment keeps microbes low but changes the taste.

options.text: Reduce the shelf life target to 30 days and keep the process.
Keep the mild heat treatment and add preservatives above the usual limit.
Test milder heat, acidity control and packaging with taste and microbial checks.
Keep the mild heat treatment and add natural flavouring to cover the taste change.

basic.situation: You run a sensory test on a new biscuit for flavour and texture with ten staff tasters. Two tasters score the biscuit much lower than the other eight.

options.text: Record all ten scores, note the two low ones and ask them for comments.
Replace the two low scores with the group average in the report.
Remove the two low scores from the data since eight tasters agreed with each other.
Record all ten scores and report the average for the whole team.

advanced.situation: You check raw mango puree for stability and finished cans for safety and nutrition before release. One can in the sample shows a slight bulge, but the lab results are within limits.

options.text: Hold the batch, test more cans for spoilage and trace the puree lot.
Open the bulged can, taste it and release the batch if it is fine.
Release the batch but test the bulged can further and report the result.
Release the batch since the lab results are within the limits.

basic.situation: You review recent food safety regulations and scientific articles for your team. The team lead asks for a short update on labelling rules for allergens.

options.text: Read the current official labelling rule and summarize it with its source.
Summarize a recent trade magazine article on allergen labelling rules for the team.
Tell the lead that allergen labelling rules are unlikely to have changed.
Use last year's team summary on allergen rules and add today's date.

advanced.situation: You develop food standards and production specifications for a new infant cereal, using consumer feedback asking for less sugar and a shorter ingredient list.

options.text: Draft lower-sugar specifications, check them against regulations and test with parents.
Draft the specification by copying the sugar level from a competing product.
Draft the specification with the shortest ingredient list and leave sugar unchanged.
Draft the specification with lower sugar and send it to the regulatory team afterwards.

basic.situation: You inspect a food processing area for sanitation using a checklist. You find a drain cover in the packing room with food residue around it.

options.text: Tick the item as passed since drains usually have some residue.
Ask a worker to wipe the cover and tick the item as done.
Note the residue in comments but tick the item as passed.
Mark the item as failed, ask for cleaning and note it for follow-up.

advanced.situation: You help develop a quality assurance program for a sauce plant and evaluate its storage operations. The cold store door is opened often, and temperature logs show brief rises above the set limit.

options.text: Analyse the logs, find the causes and set door rules, alarms and checks.
Move the temperature probe to a colder spot in the store.
Raise the temperature limit in the program to match the observed readings.
Add an alarm to the cold store and keep the current door habits.

basic.situation: You attend a weekly meeting with engineers and plant operators to share updates on a new snack. Your test results show the snack's crispness drops after two days.

options.text: Mention the snack is fine for now and give the results later.
Share the results briefly and let the engineers ask for details.
Leave out the crispness result because the launch date is close.
Share the crispness results, answer questions and note any actions agreed.

advanced.situation: A client tasting of your new drink shows a bitter aftertaste. Your flavour expert blames processing, the process engineer blames the flavour, and the client wants answers this week.

options.text: Tell the client the aftertaste is a normal feature of natural ingredients.
Ask the flavour expert to reformulate and update the client on progress.
Run a joint trial changing one factor at a time and update the client.
Tell the client the sample was from an old batch and send another.

basic.situation: You collect soil samples from an oil palm plot and record colour and texture under supervision. The sampling plan says five points, but one point is waterlogged.

options.text: Sample the four other points and mention the fifth in your notes.
Take the sample from the waterlogged point and dry it in the sun.
Tell your supervisor, then sample the nearest dry spot and mark its location.
Copy the fifth point's colour and texture from the neighbouring point on the map.

advanced.situation: A farm reports poor water quality in a stream beside a field, and you need a better soil sampling method to trace the source. Your usual auger reaches 30 cm, but runoff pathways may lie deeper.

options.text: Design a deeper sampling method, test it on one transect and compare.
Use the 30 cm auger at more points across the field.
Blame fertilizer use on the farm since it is the usual cause of runoff.
Rent a deeper drill and sample random spots around the stream.

basic.situation: You help set up a pot experiment on fertilizer and plant growth and record the first observations. Two pots show slower germination than the others, though the same seeds and soil were used.

options.text: Leave the two pots out of the table since they look unusual.
Record the same germination date for all pots to keep the table tidy.
Record the delay and replace the two pots with new ones.
Record the delayed germination as observed and tell the researcher about the pots.

advanced.situation: You lead experiments to develop a rice variety with better disease resistance. A promising line yields 10 percent more but shows leaf blast in one of three field trials.

options.text: Advance the line and plan a blast test during the next season.
Repeat the trial at more sites and measure blast incidence first.
Record the blast trial as failed due to bad weather and advance the line.
Advance the line since the blast appeared at a single trial site.

basic.situation: You help plant, spray and harvest test plots of chilli following a written procedure. The procedure says to spray in the early morning, but the wind is strong at that time.

options.text: Delay the spraying until the wind drops and record the time and weather.
Spray at midday instead because the wind is usually lower then.
Hold the spraying, ask your supervisor and record the weather conditions.
Spray from further away so the wind carries the mist across all plots.

advanced.situation: You develop a new composting method for oil palm waste to promote sustainable farming. A trial pile reached 70 C, which kills pathogens, but nitrogen is being lost.

options.text: Add chemical nitrogen fertilizer to the compost and call it a new method.
Adjust turning and cover the pile, then measure nitrogen loss against a control.
Accept the nitrogen loss since the pile killed pathogens and finished early.
Lower the pile temperature by turning it more and see what changes.

basic.situation: You apply lime to trial plots as instructed. The instructions give a rate per hectare, but your plots are measured in square metres.

options.text: Apply a small amount to one plot and see what happens.
Convert the rate for each plot area and have your supervisor check the figure.
Apply the full per hectare amount to each plot to be safe.
Convert the rate to the plot size yourself and apply it to each plot.

advanced.situation: You develop an environmentally safe method to control weeds on a vegetable farm near a river. A promising herbicide works but could wash into the water.

options.text: Use the herbicide since the river is not on the farm's land.
Use the herbicide on dry days and tell the farmer about the river.
Use the herbicide with a wide buffer strip left beside the river.
Test non-chemical options such as mulch and targeted weeding, and measure runoff.

basic.situation: You walk a hillside plot with a senior soil scientist to identify signs of soil degradation. You see small channels forming and pale patches of exposed soil.

options.text: Say the plot looks healthy since the crop on it is still green.
Photograph and map the channels and bare patches for the scientist today.
Tell the scientist the pale patches are just a colour change.
Note the channels in your notebook and mention the patches later.

advanced.situation: You advise a government agency on regulatory standards for reclaiming a former tin mining site. The agency proposes a single topsoil depth for the whole area, but soil quality varies widely.

options.text: Support the single depth and suggest it be set at the shallowest figure.
Support the single depth because it is simple for officers to inspect.
Recommend the deepest topsoil layer for the whole area so all zones are covered.
Recommend depth ranges by soil zone, supported by sampling data and test plots.

basic.situation: You write a one-page summary of a trial's results for a group of village farmers. The report contains terms like cation exchange capacity and statistical significance.

options.text: Send the technical report with a note to ask if there are questions.
Keep the terms but add a short glossary at the end.
Replace the terms with plain words and test the page on one farmer.
Shorten the summary to the main yield number and leave out the conditions.

advanced.situation: You consult with engineers on a housing project built on soft clay soil. They plan to start piling next week, and your tests show the clay layer is thicker than their drawings assume.

options.text: Send the test data to the engineers and leave the decision to them.
Tell the engineers to add a safety margin to the pile lengths.
Keep the findings for your report after piling since the plans are approved.
Share your test data, explain settlement risk and propose more boreholes first.

basic.situation: You use an electron microscope with guidance to view a protein sample on a grid. The image looks streaky and the grid appears to have ice crystals on it.

options.text: Image the streaky area and filter the streaks out in the software afterwards.
Warm the grid inside the microscope to melt the ice and keep imaging.
Stop imaging, tell your supervisor and prepare a new grid with the standard method.
Image a clearer corner of the grid and note the ice in your log.

advanced.situation: You help determine the 3D structure of a large protein complex from diffraction data. The model fits the data well overall, but one region shows poor density.

options.text: Flag the poor region, test alternatives and draw no conclusions from it.
Build the region from a related structure and report the model as complete.
Describe the mechanism using the whole model and mention the poor region later.
Delete the poor region from the model and report the rest as complete.

basic.situation: You observe yeast cell growth under a microscope and count budding cells every hour for a supervisor. At hour four, the counts drop sharply.

options.text: Replace the hour four count with the average of hours three and five.
Record the drop and mention it at the end of the experiment.
Recount the field of view, record the drop and tell your supervisor.
Record the drop and note it as a probable counting error.

advanced.situation: You study mutations that may lead to cancer in cell lines. Your data suggest a mutation increases growth, but the result comes from a single experiment with no repeat.

options.text: Repeat with replicates and controls before claiming the mutation drives growth.
Present the mutation as a cause of cancer growth in the group meeting.
Share the finding with your team as preliminary and plan a repeat.
Write the finding into the draft paper and add a repeat later.

basic.situation: You run a simple blood glucose test with step-by-step help. The control sample gives a result outside its expected range.

options.text: Adjust the patient results by the control's error and report them.
Test the patient samples and flag them as needing a recheck.
Stop, tell your supervisor and repeat the control before testing samples.
Repeat the control once and continue if it falls inside the range.

advanced.situation: You design tests to detect a rare genetic disorder from blood samples. Your first test misses some known positive samples, but it has not given a false positive.

options.text: Use the test as it is, since false positives are the greater risk.
Report the test as fully sensitive after removing the missed samples from the set.
Adjust the assay conditions and validate against known samples before any use.
Use the test as a screen and confirm negatives with a second test.

basic.situation: You set up a standard assay using an existing protocol and plate reader. The protocol calls for 10 minutes of incubation, but the incubator is already booked.

options.text: Check the booking calendar and book the incubator for the required time.
Incubate for 5 minutes instead and double the reagent amount.
Use a nearby incubator at the same temperature and note the change.
Skip the incubation step since the plate reader can read at once.

advanced.situation: You develop a new method to study how an enzyme changes shape in living cells. Your first design needs a dye that may disturb the enzyme's normal activity.

options.text: Test the dye's effect on activity first and compare a dye-free approach.
Run the method with the dye and add a note about possible effects on activity.
Change the dye amount until the enzyme result matches the expected value.
Describe the method as validated after one successful run with the dye.

basic.situation: You assemble a small gel electrophoresis tank following the instruction sheet. One of the electrode leads is shorter than the drawing shows.

options.text: Check the parts list and ask your supervisor about the short lead.
Assemble the tank and test the short lead with a low voltage.
Join the short lead to a spare wire with tape to extend it.
Stretch the lead and tape it so it reaches the terminal.

advanced.situation: You write a competitive grant proposal for research on enzyme inhibitors. The deadline is in three days and your preliminary data are limited to one assay.

options.text: State the data's limits, add a feasibility plan and ask a mentor to review.
Describe the data as conclusive and promise that further assays will confirm them.
Include the data with a strong aims section and send it in.
Add figures from a published paper as if they were your preliminary data.

basic.situation: You write a short report summarizing the results of a protein purification run. The yield was lower than expected, and your senior asks for a clear summary.

options.text: State the lower yield, give likely reasons from the logs and suggest next steps.
Report the yield from an earlier successful run in place of this one.
Report the yield as in line with expectations and add the steps.
State the lower yield and list the purification steps you followed.

advanced.situation: You manage a small lab team and supervise a graduate student whose experiments keep failing at the same step. Two other projects also need your time this week.

options.text: Review the student's protocol together, find the faulty step and agree a plan.
Give the student a paper on the technique and offer to check in later.
Ask the student to repeat the experiment a few more times to see.
Take over the student's experiment and finish it yourself this week.

basic.situation: You identify bacteria in a water sample under a light microscope, with guidance. You see rod-shaped cells in chains, but your reference chart shows two similar species.

options.text: Report the species whose reference picture looks closest to what you see in the field.
Report the more common of the two species and note the other.
Report the more harmless species to avoid raising a false alarm in the ward.
Check stain and culture results against the chart and confirm the species.

advanced.situation: You classify a bacterial strain from a clinical specimen to guide treatment. The strain's tests match two pathogens, and the doctor's request is urgent.

options.text: Report the less dangerous pathogen so treatment stays simple and cheap.
Run further tests to separate the pathogens and update the doctor.
Report the pathogen that is more common in your hospital's past cases.
Report both possible pathogens and say that the result is not final.

basic.situation: You observe how a fungus grows on a plant leaf over several days under supervision. On day three the control leaf in the other tray also shows a patch of mould.

options.text: Record the control's mould and tell your supervisor about it.
Remove the mouldy control leaf and continue as if nothing changed.
Record the control as clean since the mould came late.
Record the mould on the control leaf and carry on with observations.

advanced.situation: You investigate how an antibiotic affects bacteria that cause a hospital outbreak. The antibiotic stops most bacteria in the lab, but a few colonies keep growing.

options.text: Record the survivors and repeat the test with a higher dose.
Report the antibiotic as effective since most of the bacteria were stopped.
Remove the surviving colonies from the plate before reporting the results.
Isolate the survivors, test their resistance and tell infection control.

basic.situation: You test a water sample from a school canteen for harmful bacteria using a standard method with instructions. The incubator temperature reads 4 degrees above the method's setting.

options.text: Write the method's temperature in the record and continue.
Reset the incubator to the method's temperature and restart the test.
Continue the test and shorten the incubation time to balance the heat.
Continue the test and note the temperature difference in the record.

advanced.situation: You design tests to trace the source of contamination in a river used for drinking water. Bacteria counts rise downstream of a factory and a farm, and both deny responsibility.

options.text: Sample just downstream of each site and compare the counts with the river.
Name the factory in your report since factories cause most pollution.
Name the farm in your report since the owner cannot afford a lawyer.
Sample upstream, between and downstream, test for source markers and share the data.

basic.situation: You analyze alcohol content in a fermented drink under supervision. The method needs a fresh standard solution, but the bottle on the shelf is a month old.

options.text: Run the standard from the shelf and note its age in the record.
Prepare a fresh standard as the method says or ask your supervisor for one.
Run the old standard and add a correction based on its age.
Dilute the old standard with water until it reads the expected value.

advanced.situation: You develop a new procedure to detect microbial contamination in packaged milk. The method works on lab samples, but plant staff say it takes too long for their production line.

options.text: Tell the plant staff the method is mandatory and the line must wait.
Test rapid detection options against the current method using real plant samples.
Recommend the plant uses the method on a few random batches.
Recommend the plant takes fewer samples so the method fits the time.

basic.situation: You prepare bacterial cultures in nutrient broth following the lab guide. The guide says to incubate at 37 C, but the label on the flask rack shows 30 C.

options.text: Incubate at the guide's 37 C and ask your supervisor about the label.
Incubate at 30 C since the rack label is right in front of you.
Incubate at 37 C and plan to mention the label next week.
Incubate at 33 C as a compromise between the two figures.

advanced.situation: You use a flow cytometer on your own for the first time and it reports no signal from a stained sample. The senior user is away and the instrument is shared.

options.text: Run a bead control, check the lasers and fluidics, then log the result.
Restart the cytometer, wait for it to warm up and run the sample again.
Increase the detector gain to maximum and run the sample again.
Open the instrument cover to look at the laser path yourself.

basic.situation: You draft a short technical summary of lab results for a supervisor to review. The results show contamination in one of six samples.

options.text: Leave out the contaminated sample since the other five were clear.
Describe the results as mostly clean and attach the data table.
State the contamination, name the sample and list the checks you made.
State that five samples were clear and mention one problem sample.

advanced.situation: You supervise a team of scientists and set standards for lab operations. Two scientists use different cleaning steps between runs, and results from their benches vary.

options.text: Compare both methods with a test, set one written procedure and train everyone.
Tell both scientists to follow their own method but record it carefully.
Pick the method used by the more senior scientist and tell everyone.
Accept the variation since each scientist can explain their steps.

basic.situation: You count bird species along a forest trail using a checklist. Midway, you hear a call you cannot identify and see nothing.

options.text: Log the call as unidentified with time and place, and tell the team lead.
Add a common species to the checklist to keep the count complete.
Record the call on your phone and try to identify it later.
Tick the species on the checklist whose call sounds closest to this one.

advanced.situation: You design a population model for a hornbill colony to guide long-term habitat plans. Your data cover three years, but nesting numbers swing sharply between years.

options.text: Use the three-year average as the colony size and plan from it.
Use the highest year as the population so the habitat plan is generous.
Drop the lowest year from the data so the swing looks smaller.
Collect more years of data, show uncertainty ranges and test the model.

basic.situation: You identify mammals from camera trap photos using a field guide. One photo shows a blurred animal that looks like either a civet or a small cat.

options.text: Mark it unidentified, note the visible features and ask a senior.
Check the next photos from the same camera for a clearer view.
Record the species whose photo in the guide looks most similar.
Record it as a common civet since that species is more frequent.

advanced.situation: You interpret genetic data to explain how two island squirrel populations are related. The data suggest a recent split, but fur and skull features suggest a much older one.

options.text: Report the older split since physical features are easier to observe.
Report the recent split and describe the physical features as unreliable.
Report the genetic result and mention the physical features in a short footnote.
Present both lines of evidence, note the conflict and propose more sampling.

basic.situation: You walk along a river bank where animals drink and note visible changes. You see a new pipe discharging cloudy water upstream of a nesting site.
