options.text: Block the pipe with rocks to stop the cloudy water reaching the nesting site.
Take a water sample and keep it in your bag for later.
Note the pipe in your field book and look again next week.
Photograph the pipe and water, note the location and report it to your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You assess how a palm oil mill's night operations affect nearby leopard cat activity and recommend alternative operating conditions. Camera data show fewer visits on nights when the mill runs.

options.text: Compare mill and quiet nights, then recommend lighting and timing changes.
Report that the cats have simply moved elsewhere and need no action.
Report the drop in visits and leave the mill to decide on changes.
Recommend the mill stops all night operations to protect the cats in the area.

basic.situation: You read and summarize key points from scientific articles on wildlife trade rules for your supervisor. One article contradicts the summary you wrote last week.

options.text: Keep last week's summary as written since it was already submitted.
Check both sources' dates and methods, then update your summary and tell your supervisor.
Replace last week's summary with the new article's key points quietly.
Add the new article to your summary as another point of view.

advanced.situation: You lead a compliance check at a quarry near a protected forest. You find the nest of an endangered bird in the cleared area, and the manager says work cannot stop.

options.text: Agree to let the work continue until the chicks have flown from the nest.
Record the evidence, explain the legal duty and notify the authority.
Ask the manager to move the nest to a safer tree nearby.
Photograph the nest and report it to the authority later in the week.

basic.situation: A school group asks you to explain why sun bears should not be fed in a park. You prepare a short talk.

options.text: Tell them feeding is against park rules and that bears might bite visitors.
Explain how feeding changes bear behaviour and puts people at risk.
Say that feeding is fine if the food is natural fruit.
Tell the students that bears will be sad if people feed them.

advanced.situation: You design a public education program on pangolin conservation for towns near a trafficking route. Many residents believe pangolin scales have medicinal value.

options.text: Distribute posters about pangolins in local shops and markets for a month.
Tell residents that people who buy scales are criminals who will be reported.
Use local speakers and evidence on scales, and offer ways to report.
Run a talk on pangolin biology and ask residents to stop buying scales.

basic.situation: You help organize notes from a wildlife management meeting between rangers and village leaders. Two people gave conflicting versions of an agreed patrol schedule.

options.text: Include both versions in the notes and leave the choice to readers.
Use the version the ranger gave since rangers run the patrols.
Ask both which version was agreed and mark the item unresolved until then.
Choose the version that sounds more reasonable and write it as agreed.

advanced.situation: You lead stakeholder consultations to finalize a habitat management plan for an elephant corridor. Plantation owners, villagers and conservationists disagree on where the corridor should run.

options.text: Hold separate meetings with each group and combine their favourite points.
Finalize the route preferred by the plantation owners to avoid delays.
Choose the route backed by the strongest data and present it to all groups.
Share the movement data, hold joint meetings and test route options with all groups.

basic.situation: You run a sequence alignment with a standard dynamic programming tool, with a senior's guidance. The default gap penalty gives an alignment that looks odd for your protein family.

options.text: Try two other gap penalties and ask your senior which result looks plausible.
Check the tool's documentation and ask your senior about the gap penalty.
Edit the alignment by hand so it matches what you expect to see.
Pick the gap penalty that gives the highest alignment score and use it.

advanced.situation: A researcher needs a new way to cluster single-cell data where standard methods merge two rare cell types. You guide a junior analyst on the approach.

options.text: Tell the junior to remove the rare cells so the clusters look clean.
Tell the junior to try several clustering tools and pick the clearest output.
Tell the junior to split the merged cluster by hand using known markers.
Benchmark standard methods on labelled data, then validate a custom approach.

basic.situation: You compile expression data from five samples into a table for gene expression profiling, following step-by-step instructions. Two sample files list gene names in different formats.

options.text: Map the names to one standard format using the reference list.
Convert the names with a quick script and check a few at random.
Drop genes that do not match across files and carry on.
Merge the files as they are and let the software match the names.

advanced.situation: You analyze a large proteomics dataset for a clinical study. After normalization, one patient group shows a strong signal that disappears when you check the batch dates.

options.text: Remove the samples from the odd batch and report the remaining signal.
Report the strong signal and mention the batch dates in a footnote.
Model the batch effect, rerun the analysis and report both results.
Keep the strong signal and drop the batch dates from the metadata.

basic.situation: You query a public genomic database for a gene's sequence using an example from your senior. Your query returns hundreds of records, with several versions of the gene.

options.text: Merge all the records into one sequence to cover every version.
Take the longest record since it likely holds the most information.
Filter by the reference entry and check the version and species.
Take the first record and tell your senior what the query returned.

advanced.situation: You design the data model for a database that will store sequencing runs, samples and results from three labs. The labs use different sample ID formats.

options.text: Define a unique internal ID, map each lab's format to it and document it.
Use the order of upload as the sample ID for every run from each lab.
Store each lab's ID in a free text field and let users search by it later.
Ask the three labs to switch to one common ID format from next quarter.

basic.situation: You modify a small web-based tool that plots gene expression, with guidance. A user reports that the plot's labels overlap when many genes are chosen.

options.text: Limit the number of genes a user can pick to a small number.
Edit the live tool to shrink the label font and tell the user.
Hide the labels completely in the live tool for every user right now.
Reproduce it on a test copy, adjust the labels and ask for review.

advanced.situation: You create a new web-based tool for researchers to run a statistical test on their gene lists. Early testers get slightly different p-values from the tool and from their own software.

options.text: Tell testers to use their own software when the values differ.
Add a note that p-values may differ slightly between different software tools.
Round the p-values in the tool so they match their own software.
Compare the tool with trusted software on test data and note the gap.

basic.situation: You draft a project report with feedback from senior colleagues. A senior asks you to add a figure of results that you have not yet checked.

options.text: Add a figure from last month's report with updated axis labels.
Check the data behind the figure first, then add it.
Add the figure and mark it as preliminary in the caption.
Add the figure as requested and keep your doubts to yourself.

advanced.situation: A research team asks you to recommend a computational strategy for analyzing a very large metagenomic dataset on a limited server. They want results in two weeks.

options.text: Promise the full analysis in two weeks and ask for more server time.
Propose a lighter pipeline with subsampling and test it first.
Suggest the team analyzes a small slice of the data and stops there.
Run the full analysis on the shared server during the working day.

basic.situation: You assist technicians in using a bioinformatics tool under supervision. A technician runs the tool on a file in the wrong format and gets an error.

options.text: Show the technician the accepted formats and how to convert the file.
Convert the file yourself and give it back to the technician to run.
Tell the technician to rename the file extension and run it again.
Tell the technician to try another tool that accepts the file.

advanced.situation: You direct technicians and IT staff running bioinformatics tools for a metagenomics project. A new software version changes some outputs, and the technicians want to keep the old version.

options.text: Switch everyone to the new version since it is the latest release.
Keep the old version for this project and review the new one later on.
Compare outputs from both versions on test data, then brief the team.
Let each technician pick a version and merge the results afterwards.

basic.situation: You extract DNA from tissue samples following a written protocol. The protocol says to incubate for one hour, but you realise you took the tubes out after 45 minutes.

options.text: Continue with extraction and compare the DNA yield with an earlier sample later.
Continue the protocol and record the shorter incubation in your notes.
Write one hour in your notebook since the protocol requires it.
Return the tubes for the missing time and tell your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You develop a guideline for handling a new virus in your lab. Colleagues disagree on whether the usual containment level is enough for this virus.

options.text: Apply the usual containment level and add extra glove changes for staff.
Assess published risk data and agree the level with the biosafety officer.
Apply the usual containment level since colleagues have used it safely for years.
Apply the next higher containment level to be careful and update later.

basic.situation: You compile data from a cell growth experiment and prepare simple slides for a team meeting. One data point looks far outside the others on your chart.

options.text: Move the point closer to the others so the chart looks smooth.
Check the raw data for that point and mark it on the slide.
Leave that point off the chart since it looks like an error.
Show the chart as it is and ask the team about the point.

advanced.situation: You adjust your experimental design after peer feedback on a cell signalling study. Reviewers say your sample size is too small, and the lab can afford about half the extra samples they ask for.

options.text: Add the samples the lab can afford and describe the limits in the paper.
Run a power calculation, add the samples it supports and explain the limits.
Keep the design and argue that the effect is large enough.
Duplicate some existing measurements in the table to reach the sample size.

basic.situation: You keep the lab records for an ongoing experiment. You notice you pipetted 5 microlitres instead of the 10 written in the entry for a plate you already logged.

options.text: Tell your supervisor but leave the original entry as it is.
Leave the entry as written because the plate is already in the incubator.
Overwrite the original number with the actual volume and remove the page.
Amend the record with a dated, signed note showing the actual volume.

advanced.situation: You evaluate a new brand of centrifuge tubes for your lab's cell work. A trial run shows slightly lower cell recovery than with the current tubes, but the new tubes cost half as much.

options.text: Run a replicated comparison on recovery and viability, then report back.
Order the new tubes and tell the lab that cell recovery is the same.
Adopt the new tubes for all work since the cost saving is large.
Adopt the new tubes for routine work and keep old ones for key tests.

basic.situation: You help track the supplies and hours charged to a research project, as planned. The plan allows 40 hours of equipment time, and you see 52 hours logged.

options.text: Reduce the logged hours to 40 so the report matches the plan.
Report the 52 hours to the project lead at the next meeting.
Check the log, find the cause and report the overrun to the lead.
Move 12 hours to another project's budget code to balance it.

advanced.situation: You provide scientific direction to a team testing a drug on cells and disease models. Colleagues in another field want to use your cell line, which is sensitive to contamination.

options.text: Refuse to share it and tell them to order their own line.
Agree shared handling and testing protocols and keep a log of its use.
Send the cell line with a short note on handling.
Give them the cell line and let them handle it as they like.

basic.situation: You read documents to understand cell differentiation for your team. A review article says one thing about a signalling pathway and a newer paper says the opposite.

options.text: Use the review article since reviews summarise many studies in one place.
Compare the methods and dates of both, then summarise the disagreement for the team.
Pick the paper whose conclusion fits what your team already expects.
Use the newer paper and mention the review article in a note.

advanced.situation: You lead applied research to improve a microbe that recycles waste. A strain breaks down waste faster but makes a gas that smells strongly near neighbouring houses.

options.text: Continue scale-up and add air filters if neighbours complain about it.
Pause scale-up, test ways to reduce the gas and consult neighbours.
Scale up the strain and tell neighbours the smell is harmless.
Run the strain at night when fewer neighbours are at home.

basic.situation: You help draft sections of a grant application for funding. The lead asks for a one-paragraph summary of your pilot results, and the results are modest.

options.text: Describe the results as promising and leave the numbers for the appendix.
Describe the results as strong, since reviewers favour confident wording.
Describe the results briefly and focus mostly on the future plans.
Describe the results accurately and explain why they support the next stage.

advanced.situation: You supervise a postdoctoral fellow and two technicians, and also teach a graduate course. A technician reports that the fellow has been recording data after experiments from memory.

options.text: Talk to the fellow about record rules, review notebooks and set expectations.
Ask the technician to check the fellow's data quietly each week.
Remind the whole team about record rules at the next meeting.
Leave it alone since the fellow is senior and knows the field.

basic.situation: You calculate allele frequencies from genotype counts in a study of 200 people, with guidance. Your calculated frequencies add up to 1.05 instead of 1.

options.text: Recheck the counts and formula and ask your senior if still unsure.
Reduce the largest frequency by 0.05 so the total equals one.
Report the frequencies with a note that they add to 1.05.
Divide each frequency by 1.05 so they add to one, and report them.

advanced.situation: You build a statistical model to find genes linked to a trait in a large sample. The model flags 300 genes, and most are probably false positives because of the many tests run.

options.text: Report the genes that fit the pathway the team already expected.
Report the 20 genes with the smallest p-values as the findings.
Apply multiple-testing control and validate the top genes in a second sample.
Report all 300 genes and note that some may be false.

basic.situation: You extract DNA from blood samples and run a gel under supervision. The gel shows a smeared band instead of a clear one.

options.text: Rerun the gel with the same DNA and a fresh buffer.
Report the smeared band as the result of a degraded sample.
Check the extraction notes and gel setup, then rerun and report to your supervisor.
Cut out the smeared band and use it for the next test.

advanced.situation: You develop a protocol to improve an existing genetic test for a common variant. Your change raises sensitivity but takes twice as long, and the clinic runs 80 tests a day.

options.text: Offer the new protocol as an option for difficult cases and keep the old one.
Validate the new protocol on known samples and test options to cut run time.
Replace the old protocol and tell the clinic to cut the daily tests.
Replace the old protocol and ask the clinic to add a machine later.

basic.situation: You help collect tissue specimens in the field following a sampling plan. The plan calls for ten samples per site, but a landowner allows only three at one site.

options.text: Collect three samples and ten at the next site to make up the total.
Collect the three samples, record the shortfall and report it to the project lead.
Collect the other seven samples from the neighbouring land next to it.
Collect three samples and enter the site as complete in the log.

advanced.situation: You analyze determinants of an inherited trait in a crop and devise a method to alter it. A promising edit improves the trait but also changes a nearby gene involved in disease resistance.

options.text: Proceed with the edit because the trait improvement is the main goal.
Remove the resistance tests from the plan to avoid delays.
Test edit variants for effects on the nearby gene and keep resistance.
Proceed with the edit and note the resistance risk in your report.

basic.situation: You attend a laboratory safety training session and then work on a bench with a new chemical. The label lists a hazard that was not covered in the training.

options.text: Read the safety data sheet and ask your safety officer before starting.
Start the work and read the data sheet if a problem appears.
Ask a colleague what the hazard symbol means and then begin working.
Start the work since the training said the bench was safe.

advanced.situation: You supervise geneticists and technicians and teach medical students about managing genetic disorders. A student asks to see a real patient's genetic report for practice.

options.text: Describe the patient's case in words and leave the report out of the session.
Let the student read the report on the screen in the lab.
Offer an anonymized sample report and explain the privacy rules to the student.
Show the report with the name hidden to the student in your office.

basic.situation: You keep a laboratory notebook for a genetics project. After a long day, you finish an experiment and must write up the method and the results.

options.text: Write the results tonight and add the method details tomorrow morning.
Write the method and results the same day, in order, with dates and initials.
Keep the key numbers on loose paper and copy them into the notebook later.
Write the final results and leave the method out of the notebook.

advanced.situation: You write a grant to fund research on a gene variant. A reviewer says your preliminary data are interesting but do not support your main claim.

options.text: Narrow the claim to match the data and add a plan to collect stronger evidence.
Keep the claim and add more references from other research groups to support it.
Add a new figure from a related study as if it was your data.
Keep the claim and describe the data as preliminary but very promising.

basic.situation: You assist biologists with a basic biochemical analysis of a gene product. A biologist asks you to prepare a sample using a method you have not done before.

options.text: Tell the biologist you are familiar with the method and start.
Prepare the sample the way you think it is usually done.
Say you have not used it, read the method and ask for a demonstration.
Read the method and try it first on a test sample.

advanced.situation: You confer with IT specialists to develop an application for analyzing genetic data. They propose storing patient genotypes in a cloud database with shared access for the whole company.

options.text: Agree to the cloud database for now and plan a security review later.
Agree to the cloud database and ask for encryption to be added.
Agree to shared access since the IT team knows storage well.
Explain the privacy needs and require access controls and anonymized records.

basic.situation: You collect data on insects and soil moisture at a forest plot with guidance. The meter shows moisture readings that jump between 20 and 60 percent in the same spot.

options.text: Record the average of the jumping readings and carry on with the plot.
Record the highest reading since the soil may have been wet.
Record a typical value from the previous plot in the table.
Recheck the meter, take repeat readings and tell your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You design a study of how pesticide runoff affects insects in a stream and its banks. The site has steep banks, and the stream floods suddenly after rain.

options.text: Sample the banks during storms to catch the peak runoff directly.
Sample at the stream centre in dry weather and extend the study later.
Sample near the road at the access point where it is easy.
Plan sampling at several distances from the stream with rain-day safety rules.

basic.situation: You identify plant species from a field sample using a provided key. Your sample has flowers, but the key's second question asks about fruit.

options.text: Ask a senior or find a fruiting plant of the same type to continue.
Choose the answer that the species in the last sample had.
Skip the question and try the next step of the key.
Choose the answer that leads to a species you already know.

advanced.situation: You define classification standards for a group of beetles where two forms look different but may be one species with seasonal variants. The collection database needs an entry rule soon.

options.text: Treat them as whichever species already has more entries in the database.
Treat them as one species since seasonal variants are fairly common in beetles.
Check structure and behaviour across seasons, then agree the rule.
Treat them as two species until more evidence shows otherwise in the data.

basic.situation: You describe basic principles of plant and animal life to a trainee, with help. The trainee asks why fish gills work in water but not in air.

options.text: Explain gill structure and oxygen exchange and check with a senior.
Tell the trainee that fish simply cannot breathe air at all.
Explain that gills need water to stay open and leave out the other parts.
Tell the trainee that gills take in water instead of oxygen.

advanced.situation: You explain complex biological principles to a team of new staff. They struggle with how natural selection acts on traits in a changing environment.

options.text: Use a local example, walk through each step and ask them to explain.
Tell them to read a textbook chapter and come back with questions.
Give a clear lecture on selection with definitions, diagrams and a handout.
Tell them that natural selection means species change when they need to.

basic.situation: You use a spreadsheet to store and sort species count data from a survey, following step-by-step instructions. After sorting, the totals column no longer matches the earlier total.

options.text: Retype the totals by hand so they match the earlier figure.
Undo the sort, check that all columns were selected and sort again.
Delete the rows that cause the mismatch and update the total.
Sort again by another column and see if the totals match.

advanced.situation: You review a land use report and a recreational development proposal for accuracy and adherence to policy. The report's wildlife counts are lower than your own survey data for the same area.

options.text: Approve the report because the authors are respected and experienced experts.
Approve the report and attach your survey data as a comment.
Reject the report and replace its counts with your own survey data.
Compare methods and dates, request the raw data and note the gap.

basic.situation: You help prepare a technical report on a small environmental impact study and present findings to a supervisor. A chart in the report has no axis labels.

options.text: Add axis labels with units and check them against the data before presenting.
Copy axis labels from a similar chart in another report and move on.
Remove the chart from the report since the text describes the results anyway.
Explain the chart in your talk and add the labels later.

advanced.situation: You represent your employer at a conference and present an environmental impact report to industry and government. A questioner asks about a finding you are unsure of.

options.text: Say you will check the data and follow up in writing after the session.
Give the likeliest answer you can and add a note that it is unconfirmed.
Redirect the question to another topic and carry on with the talk.
Answer confidently using figures from a similar study that you recall.

basic.situation: You help draft a statement of work for a small biodiversity grant, with guidance. The funder's template asks for deliverables, but your project outputs are still vague.

options.text: Promise extra deliverables that will sound impressive to the funder.
List the main activities and leave the deliverables to be defined later.
Copy the deliverables from a previous grant and change the title.
List concrete deliverables with dates and ask your senior to review.

advanced.situation: You develop the grant strategy for your team's biological research and mentor two juniors. A call for proposals fits your work, but the deadline is in six days and your team's capacity is limited.

options.text: Skip this call and wait for a call with a longer deadline.
Copy sections from another group's funded proposal and submit them as yours.
Judge fit and workload, then apply with a focused scope.
Apply with the full project scope and ask the juniors to work late.

basic.situation: You are helping plan a vegetable plot in Cameron Highlands where one crop has been grown for years. Your supervisor asks you for a rotation idea.

options.text: Advise the farmer to leave the slope bare for a season so the soil can rest.
Propose a legume because it adds nitrogen, and send the idea to your supervisor.
Propose a legume after checking the soil test, then list labour and seed costs for the farmer.
Copy the rotation used on the neighbouring estate, since nearby plots usually respond the same way.

advanced.situation: You lead a small team drafting a wetland and groundwater plan. A paddy cooperative wants to pump more, while a nearby village well has dropped this dry season.

options.text: Draft a plan holding pumping at current levels until the village well has been studied.
Compile well and pumping records, then convene both groups to agree a shared extraction limit.
Draft the plan around the cooperative's figures and drop the village well data from the draft.
Approve the cooperative's request, since food output matters and one dry well is a single complaint.

basic.situation: You visit a roadside slope in Hulu Langat with gullies after heavy rain. Your supervisor asked you to note what is causing the erosion.

options.text: Photograph the gullies and measure their depth, then leave the cause to your supervisor.
Photograph the gullies, note slope, ground cover and water paths, and record the GPS location.
Tell the roadside workers to fill the gullies with loose soil before your supervisor visits.
Report heavy rain as the cause, since the gullies appeared after last week's storm.

advanced.situation: Soil tests, a farmer survey and rainfall records for a degraded hillside disagree about the main cause. You must propose long-term restoration measures by Friday.

options.text: Pick the cause the farmer reports and propose measures that suit it, then close the file.
Average the three sources into one cause and propose standard measures that fit the average.
Compare the three sources, note where they conflict, then propose measures that fit the strongest evidence.
Rely on the soil tests as measured data and propose terracing and cover crops.

basic.situation: A paddy farmer in Kedah asks why you want him to leave a grass strip along his canal. He thinks it wastes planting space.

options.text: Explain the strip filters runoff and protects the bank, then ask your supervisor to follow up.
Tell him the strip is optional and he can plant up to the canal edge.
Tell him the conservation plan requires the strip and that it cannot be changed.
Explain the strip filters runoff and holds the bank, then offer a nearby farm to visit.

advanced.situation: A state agency asks for your technical view on a wetland restoration easement. The draft map covers a peat swamp edge, and the boundary survey is two years old.

options.text: Approve the map as drawn on your own and tell the agency the boundaries are confirmed.
Support the easement because restoring any peat edge helps, and leave boundary details to the agency.
Recommend the easement as drawn and note that the survey is two years old.
Advise a fresh boundary check first and state what the old survey does not cover.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to compile wetland bird counts from three field sheets into one table. Two sheets use different units for the survey area.

options.text: Use the two sheets that match and leave out the third until there is time.
Adjust the third sheet's areas until its bird densities look similar to the other two.
Convert the areas to one unit and put the finished table in the report folder.
Convert areas to one unit, note the conversion under the table, and tell your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You review a watershed organisation's annual report for certification today. It is complete, except the sediment results for one quarter are missing.

options.text: Certify the report with a note asking the organisation to add the missing quarter later.
Fill the missing quarter with the average of the other three and certify the report.
Ask for the missing results today and hold certification until they arrive, recording the reason.
Hold certification and tell your supervisor the organisation missed one quarter of results.

basic.situation: You enter soil nitrate readings into the department's web decision tool. One reading, 480 mg/kg, looks about ten times higher than the other plots.

options.text: Check the field sheet for a typing slip, then enter the value and flag it.
Change the reading to 48 because the decimal is likely misplaced, then run the tool.
Enter the reading as recorded and mention the high value to your supervisor afterwards.
Leave that plot out of the tool run so the other results are not distorted.

advanced.situation: You manage a small field office. A district council wants a technical assistance programme to start next month, but two of your four staff are on leave.

options.text: Tell the council what two staff can deliver next month and agree phased steps in writing.
Accept the council's date and list the programme as fully staffed in your monthly report.
Start the full programme and ask the staff on leave to check email for urgent issues.
Ask the council to move the start by a month and offer a preparation meeting meanwhile.

basic.situation: A landowner phones the office asking whether the low, damp corner of his plot counts as a protected wetland. You are not sure of the local rule.

options.text: Tell him damp corners are usually not covered, so he can go ahead with his plans.
Tell him it is not a wetland and email him a note saying so.
Take his lot details, explain how sites are assessed, and ask a senior to confirm.
Explain that wetland status depends on a site assessment and offer to book one.

advanced.situation: You lead a session between a district office and landowners over who maintains a drainage channel that floods farms. Both sides blame each other, and one landowner is shouting.

options.text: Propose that the landowners pay for the channel work now to end the argument.
Pause the session, speak to the landowner privately, and reschedule once everyone has calmed down.
Set ground rules, hear each side in turn, then list shared interests before discussing cost.
Ask the district office to present its maintenance record so landowners see the facts.

basic.situation: A landowner in Pahang wants a conservation plan for his cattle pasture, and a small trail for eco-tourists. Your supervisor asks you to draft the first outline.

options.text: List his goals, then outline rested paddocks and a trail routed away from the water points.
Outline rested paddocks for the cattle and note that the trail can be planned later.
Reuse the plan from a previous cattle farm and change the owner's name and lot number.
Route the trail through the stream crossing since it is the most scenic spot.

advanced.situation: You are drafting a technical standard for how long grazing land must rest after use in your state. Field data from wet and dry seasons show very different regrowth rates.

options.text: Set one rest period from the wetter season average, since most grazing happens when rain falls.
Copy another climate's rest period standard and publish it as the state rule.
Set separate wet and dry season rest periods from the regrowth data and circulate for review.
Set one rest period from the slower dry season rate to protect the land all year.

basic.situation: A wildlife corridor beside a pasture has bare patches after trampling. Your supervisor asks you to help stabilise the soil before the monsoon.

options.text: Sow native cover on the bare patches and tell your supervisor when the seeds are down.
Spread sand over the bare patches to firm the surface before the rains arrive.
Burn the dry grass around the patches so new growth comes through before the monsoon.
Fence off the bare patches, sow native cover, and check them after the first heavy rain.

advanced.situation: Invasive weeds are spreading across a leased pasture, and the owner asks you to choose between herbicide, a controlled burn or reseeding. A stream runs along one edge.

options.text: Burn the thickest weeds along the stream edge today, since the owner has approved it.
Spray herbicide across the whole pasture since it is the fastest way to stop the spread.
Spot-treat weeds away from the stream, reseed cleared areas, and review results next season.
Reseed the whole pasture with a competitive forage grass and watch how the weeds respond.

basic.situation: You measure vegetation cover on set transects for a monitoring programme. Halfway through, rain starts and the rest of the transect has tall wet grass that is hard to read.

options.text: Stop, finish the transect on a dry day, and note the weather on the sheet.
Copy last season's cover values for the wet section so the record is complete.
Finish the transect in the rain, taking extra care, and write the weather on the sheet.
Estimate the wet section from the plots already measured and move to the next site.

advanced.situation: A rancher's herd has grown and the pasture looks thin in places. You are asked to study grazing patterns and advise a stocking number before the next dry season.

options.text: Map heavily grazed areas, measure forage across zones, and propose a stocking number from the results.
Count the herd, compare it with the district's recommended stocking rate, and advise a number.
Advise reducing the herd by half now, since thin patches suggest the pasture cannot carry it.
Advise adding more cattle, because thin patches will recover once manure spreads across the pasture.

basic.situation: You help direct a crew building a fence to keep cattle out of a stream. The crew leader wants wider post spacing to finish before dark.

options.text: Keep the specified spacing and tell your supervisor the fence will finish a day late.
Let the crew use wider spacing tonight and sign the fence off as built to plan.
Keep the specified spacing, mark the last finished post, and plan tomorrow's start with the leader.
Agree to wider spacing and add an extra wire strand to make up the difference.

advanced.situation: A rancher applies for a grazing permit on a forest edge lease. His herd is within the limit, but your last inspection found overgrazed patches near the water point.

options.text: Hold the permit until the overgrazed patches have recovered, and explain the reason to the rancher.
Refuse the permit and tell his neighbours which patches he overgrazed so they can complain.
Grant the permit with a rotation condition near the water point and book a follow-up inspection.
Grant the permit since the herd is within the limit and raise the patches at renewal.

basic.situation: A forest reserve manager from the state forestry department calls about cattle straying across your boundary fence. You are asked to coordinate.

options.text: Take down the details and promise to check the fence line and call back.
Agree who inspects the fence line with the manager and send a written summary afterwards.
Tell the manager the cattle belong to the ranch owner, so the owner should handle it.
Open the reserve gate yourself so the cattle can walk back to the pasture this afternoon.

advanced.situation: Cattle owners and a conservation group disagree over seasonal grazing in a wetland meadow. You are asked to mediate a written agreement, and both sides want their own wording.

options.text: Use the conservation group's draft since the wetland is fragile and ask owners to sign.
Meet each side first, find where they overlap, then draft one text for both to review.
Tell each side that the other has already agreed, so that both sign the draft.
Combine both sides' wording into one draft and send it to everyone to comment on.

basic.situation: A smallholder asks how to raise forage production on his small paddock. You have a simple guide, but he also mentions the soil gets waterlogged after rain.

options.text: Recommend he plant a thicker stand of the grass he has now, which usually raises yield.
Advise him to apply extra fertiliser before the rains so the grass outgrows the water.
Share the guide's tips on forage varieties and fertiliser as written, and offer to answer questions.
Share the guide's tips on forage varieties and fertiliser, and flag the waterlogging for your supervisor.

advanced.situation: A rancher asks for advice on controlling brush spreading around his stock-watering reservoir. You know the reservoir feeds a stream used downstream.

options.text: Advise cutting all brush by hand around the reservoir and the pasture each year.
Advise hand-clearing brush near the reservoir, targeted treatment further out, and regrowth checks each season.
Advise spraying the brush around the reservoir with a broad herbicide, since it works fast.
Advise burning the brush right up to the water line, since ash will enrich the soil.

basic.situation: A visitor at the park entrance wants to fly a drone to film hornbills. Park rules require a written permit for drones, and he has none.

options.text: Explain the permit rule and ask him to keep the drone in its bag today.
Let him fly it near the hornbill trees, since the clip may help promote the park.
Tell him the rule exists and point him to the visitor centre for more details.
Explain the permit rule, say how to apply, and suggest a spot to watch the hornbills.

advanced.situation: You lead a night walk for school children, elderly visitors and two wheelchair users. The planned trail has steep steps and a narrow bridge.

options.text: Switch to the boardwalk loop, adapt the stops for all abilities, and brief the group first.
Use the boardwalk loop for everyone and keep the talk as planned for the original trail.
Keep the planned trail and ask the wheelchair users to wait with a ranger.
Take the whole group over the narrow bridge and carry the wheelchairs across by hand.

basic.situation: You draft a brochure on the park's bird trail. Your supervisor's notes say 250 species, but the park's official checklist says 232.

options.text: Write that the park has over 300 species, a round number that nobody will question.
Check which figure is current with your supervisor, use the confirmed one, and cite the source.
Use the higher figure of 250, since it came from your supervisor's own notes.
Use the official checklist figure of 232 and mention the difference to your supervisor later.

advanced.situation: A school asks you to build a three-term environmental programme for Year 5 classes. The teachers want it to fit the national syllabus, but you have two weeks.

options.text: Write all three terms from your own park programmes and send them for teachers to adjust.
Reuse a programme from another park and replace its place names with ours.
Tell the school the programme is syllabus-aligned and fill in the actual links after it starts.
Get the syllabus topics from teachers, map park activities to them, and pilot one term.

basic.situation: You photograph a rare orchid in bloom for the park records. A visitor wants to pick a flower from the same plant for his own photo.

options.text: Take your photos and leave the visitor to decide, since the orchid may seed anyway.
Pick one flower yourself for a cleaner close-up, then let the visitor photograph the rest.
Ask the visitor to step back, take your record photos, and offer to share a copy.
Take your record photos first, then explain to the visitor that plants must not be picked.

advanced.situation: You oversee a contractor building an interactive display on the park's river ecosystem. A week before opening, a touchscreen module keeps freezing during testing.

options.text: Ask the contractor to fix it before opening and check the module again the day before.
Sign off the display as complete and release the contractor's final payment before opening day.
Open on schedule and tell staff to restart the touchscreen whenever it freezes.
Log the fault, get a fix date from the contractor, and prepare a backup panel.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to draft next month's programme schedule. The ranger team says the weekend slot you planned for the cave tour clashes with a trail repair.

options.text: Keep the weekend slot, since tours earn money and the repair crew can work around visitors.
Move the cave tour to a free weekday slot and update the draft schedule.
Get the repair dates, move the cave tour to a free slot, and tell your supervisor.
Tell the rangers to push the trail repair back a month so the tour can run.

advanced.situation: You coordinate a Hari Alam Sekitar event expecting 800 visitors at the park. Two days before, the forecast shows heavy afternoon rain and the main stage is open-air.

options.text: Prepare a wet-weather plan with a covered stage and earlier programme, and message registered visitors.
Keep the plan unchanged and have staff hand out ponchos if rain starts at the stage.
Move the whole event to the morning and post the new time on the park's page.
Keep the programme as planned and run the sound system through the rain on open ground.

basic.situation: During a routine check you find a loose handrail on a viewing platform. Your supervisor is at a meeting and school groups are due in an hour.

options.text: Pull the loose rail off to stop it rattling, and reopen the platform for the groups.
Close the platform with tape and a sign, then message your supervisor to arrange the repair.
Tighten the rail screws with your toolkit and note the platform for a later check.
Leave a note on your supervisor's desk and keep the platform open for the school groups.

advanced.situation: A visitor collapses on a trail with heat exhaustion while you are the nearest ranger. Your radio works, but you are at an unmarked junction.

options.text: Radio your grid reference and stay with the visitor, checking breathing until help arrives.
Radio your grid reference, move the visitor into shade, give water, and stay until help arrives.
Carry the visitor down the trail yourself to the car park before calling anyone.
Leave the visitor resting and walk to the nearest marked post to name the location.

basic.situation: You help train a new seasonal guide on the park's visitor safety briefing. He wants to skip the section on the river crossing because he finds it dull.

options.text: Explain that the crossing section is required and ask him to read it before tomorrow.
Let him drop the crossing section, since visitors remember the rest of the briefing more anyway.
Let him shorten the crossing section to two sentences, since visitors rarely listen to long briefings.
Explain why the crossing briefing matters, have him practise it aloud, and give feedback.

advanced.situation: Senior rangers keep adding their own steps to the school-programme briefing, so new guides hear different things. You are asked to settle one standard for training.

options.text: Collect their versions, agree one checklist with the senior rangers, and use it in training.
Pick the version used by the longest-serving ranger and tell the others to follow it.
Write one checklist from the park's official briefing notes and give it to all the trainers.
Cut every extra step the seniors added and tell the new guides to follow your version.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to draft the next six months of work for a 200-hectare plantation block. You have the planting dates and a list of crew leave days.

options.text: Schedule crews on their leave days, since the planting dates cannot move, and tell them later.
Copy last year's six-month plan for the block and change the dates to this year.
Build the schedule around the planting dates and send it to your supervisor for approval.
Build the schedule around planting dates and leave days, then ask your supervisor to review.

advanced.situation: You lead a forest inventory survey for a licence renewal. Halfway through, a team reports that about a tenth of the sample plots were measured with a faulty diameter tape.

options.text: Remove the affected plots from the data and report results from the remaining plots.
Adjust the affected plots by the average error the tape seems to show and carry on.
Keep all the measurements as recorded and submit the report, since the deadline is fixed.
Identify the affected plots, remeasure them with a checked tape, and record the correction.

basic.situation: You inspect a forest nursery and find a bed of seedlings with yellowing leaves. You are asked to record conditions for the supervisor.

options.text: Record the bed number, count the affected seedlings, check watering and drainage, and photograph the leaves.
Apply extra fertiliser to the bed, since yellow leaves usually point to a nutrient shortage.
Photograph the yellowing leaves and note the bed number, then report them to your supervisor.
Pull the yellowing seedlings out and throw them away before the supervisor sees the bed.

advanced.situation: You map a hill forest block to estimate standing timber. Satellite data shows dense canopy, but your plots on the steep side show many small stems and few large trees.

options.text: Report the satellite estimate with a note that the steep side may have fewer large trees.
Drop the steep-side plots as outliers and map the block from the satellite data.
Use the satellite estimate for the whole block, since it covers every hectare consistently.
Add field plots on the steep side and adjust the satellite estimate using the plot data.

basic.situation: You check a logging contractor's site against the contract, which says logs must not be dragged through stream buffers. You see drag marks near a stream.

options.text: Tell the foreman to stop dragging near the stream and note it in your diary.
Record the site as mostly compliant and mention the drag marks in your monthly summary.
Ask the foreman to rake over the drag marks so the report shows a clean buffer.
Photograph the marks, record their location and buffer depth, and report to your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You are trialling a drone-photo method to estimate tree height, to replace a slow manual method. Early results are within 3% of manual readings in open stands.

options.text: Retire the manual method now and tell the team the drone method has been fully validated.
Test it in dense and steep stands, compare against manual readings, and write down its limits.
Repeat the open-stand test on more plots to confirm the 3% result before using the method.
Adopt the method for all stands now, since 3% is close enough for forest inventory work.

basic.situation: You help clear brush from a planting site with hand tools. The plan says to stack debris for collection and not burn it, but a crew member suggests burning the dry pile.

options.text: Burn the pile at the edge since it is dry, and tell your supervisor afterwards.
Scatter the debris thinly across the site so it rots away and no pile is needed.
Stack the debris as planned, tell the crew member why, and mark the pile for collection.
Stack the debris as planned and ask your supervisor to speak to the crew member.

advanced.situation: You negotiate a harvesting contract with a timber company. They want a longer harvest period and lower replanting duties, while state rules require replanting after each harvest.

options.text: Agree to the longer harvest period now and leave the replanting terms for later.
Accept the lower replanting duties and record them as the state's standard terms.
Trade a longer harvest period for a firm replanting schedule, and clear it with your superior.
Hold firm on replanting duties and say you will consider the harvest period after their offer.

basic.situation: You help supervise a planting crew today. Site rules require safety boots, but two workers arrive without them and your supervisor has already left.

options.text: Let them plant on the slope in their sandals, since the day's target is tight.
Send them home for the day and note their names for your supervisor.
Ask the crew leader to decide, since he knows these workers and the site well.
Give them yard tasks off the slope, find spare boots, and tell your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You guide a team of twelve on a thinning project on steep ground. Two experienced workers say the new spacing standard slows them down and want their own method back.

options.text: Let those two workers use their own method while the others follow the standard.
Trial both methods on one plot with the team, then decide the standard from the results.
Cut the standard from the briefing and let each worker space trees as they prefer.
Explain why the spacing standard was set and ask them to follow it for two weeks.

basic.situation: A private woodlot owner in Perak asks whether he should thin his dense rubberwood stand. You are asked to help prepare simple advice for him.

options.text: Check stand density on sample plots, explain what thinning does, and give him a short note.
Tell him dense stands grow faster together, so thinning will cut his future income.
Tell him to thin out a third of the trees from the poorest rows this month.
Explain that thinning gives remaining trees more light and room, and suggest he thin soon.

advanced.situation: A state agency asks for your recommendation on opening a degraded forest block for plantation use. Your survey shows part of it is a water catchment.

options.text: Advise against any use of the block until the catchment boundary is mapped.
Leave the catchment finding out of the report so the agency's plan is not delayed.
Recommend excluding the catchment section, propose plantation use on the rest, and attach your survey map.
Recommend plantation use on the whole block and add a note that part is a catchment.

basic.situation: Eight diarrhoea cases are reported from a school hostel. Your supervisor asks you to help collect data on what students ate and when symptoms began.

options.text: Advise the hostel to dispose of the leftover food now to prevent more illness.
Interview the eight affected students and record what each ate and when symptoms began.
Ask the hostel warden what the students ate and take his list as the exposure data.
Interview affected and unaffected students with the same food-history form, and record onset times for each.

advanced.situation: Typhoid cases appear in three districts with no clear link. Lab results, water maps and food-stall records point to different sources, and you must set the investigation plan.

options.text: Name the food stall with the most cases as the source in the first report.
Set one case definition and questionnaire for all districts, then test each suspected source.
Follow the water supply lead first, since piped water reaches the most people.
Let each district investigate its own cases and combine their reports at the end.

basic.situation: You help prepare a questionnaire for a survey on mosquito-net use in villages. Your supervisor asks you to draft questions on net use in the past week.

options.text: Word the questions around how useful nets are, so respondents agree and finish quickly.
Write short questions with set answer choices and send the draft to your supervisor.
Write short questions with set answer choices and test them on two villagers first.
Reuse a questionnaire from a foreign study and print it in English for all villages.

advanced.situation: You analyse reports of a parasite linked to raw freshwater fish dishes. Your findings could shape advice to markets, but only 30 cases are confirmed.

options.text: Recommend a market-wide warning on raw fish now, based on the 30 confirmed cases.
Report the findings and wait for more cases before saying anything about the risk.
Report that raw fish is the proven source and name the two markets that sold it.
State what the 30 cases show, flag the small number, and propose more interviews before advice.

basic.situation: You help run a weekly dengue surveillance report for a district. This week two clinics have not sent their case counts by the Monday noon deadline.

options.text: Call both clinics for counts, log the delay, and tell your supervisor if any stay missing.
Use last week's counts for the two clinics so the weekly total looks complete.
Hold the report until both clinics send their counts, even if it takes several days.
Send the report on time with a note that two clinics have not sent counts.

advanced.situation: You direct a study on a rise in leptospirosis cases after floods. A junior officer proposes dropping the follow-up of recovered patients to finish before the budget year ends.

options.text: Follow up a sample of recovered patients, trim other questions, and record the change.
Keep the full follow-up and ask for a budget extension to cover the extra weeks.
Agree to drop the follow-up and describe the study as limited to acute illness.
Drop the follow-up and report the outcomes as complete in the final summary.

basic.situation: You draft the methods section of a journal article on a school measles outbreak. Your co-author's notes list 62 cases, but the line list you used has 58.

options.text: Use 62 because your co-author's notes are senior, and edit the line list to match.
Use 58 from the line list in the draft and tell your co-author about the difference.
Ask where 62 came from, reconcile it with the line list, and use one total.
Write about 60 cases in the draft so the text fits both sets of notes.

advanced.situation: A junior colleague asks you to review a diabetes screening grant application due in two days. Its aims are strong, but the budget section claims results the pilot data do not show.

options.text: Keep the claims as written, since reviewers like bold results and the deadline is close.
Mark the strong claims in the draft and ask them to revise before another read.
Fix the claims yourself overnight and send the application on under both your names.
Point out where claims exceed the pilot data, help reword them, and check the budget.

basic.situation: You log notifiable disease reports into the district register. A clinic reports a suspected case of cholera by phone, but its written form has not arrived.

options.text: Log the case once the written form arrives, then report it to your supervisor.
Record it as a routine diarrhoea case, since cholera needs a lab result to be reported.
Ask the clinic to confirm the diagnosis with a lab test before you log anything.
Log it as suspected, tell your supervisor now, and ask the clinic to send the form.

advanced.situation: You must brief state health officials on an outbreak model with wide uncertainty about next month's cases. They ask for a single number to plan hospital beds.

options.text: Give a range with a planning figure, name the key assumptions, and say what changes it.
Give the middle estimate as a single number and mention that it is uncertain.
Give the lowest estimate as a firm forecast, since officials prefer clear answers.
Give the highest estimate as the number, so the hospitals are certainly ready.

basic.situation: At a clinic talk on dengue prevention, a mother says she was told fogging alone keeps mosquitoes away. You are asked to answer, with guidance.

options.text: Tell her fogging is the council's job and that she should wait for the next round.
Explain that fogging has a short effect, and show her how to clear standing water.
Explain that fogging has a short effect and give her a leaflet on clearing standing water.
Agree that regular fogging is enough and tell her she need not check for standing water.

advanced.situation: A state health director asks whether a new imaging technology based on physics could help screen workers for lung disease. You know the basics, not the cost or accuracy.

options.text: Explain how it works, say cost and accuracy are unknown, and offer to review the evidence.
Explain how it works and promise cost and accuracy figures by the end of the week.
Recommend buying the machines for the state's clinics now, since early screening saves lives.
Say the technology is promising for screening, since similar imaging has helped in other diseases.

basic.situation: You are weighing a toxic reagent when your glove tears. Lab rules require changing torn gloves before touching anything else.

options.text: Finish weighing with the torn glove on, since the reagent is already open on the bench.
Cover the reagent, change gloves and decide later whether the contact needs reporting.
Seal the reagent, change gloves, wash your hands, and log the tear and any contact.
Change gloves, finish weighing, then wash your hands and mention it to a colleague.

advanced.situation: You are designing a handling protocol for a new bacterial strain whose risk group is unclear. The team wants to start experiments next week.

options.text: Copy the protocol of a similar strain and ask the safety officer to approve it.
Start experiments next week at the lower level and write the protocol while they run.
Write the protocol at the higher containment level until the risk assessment is finished.
Write the protocol at the lower level and add a plan to upgrade if problems appear.

basic.situation: You draft the results section of an article. One experiment gave a result opposite to your team's hypothesis, and your senior author suggests leaving it out for space.

options.text: Include the result with the others, state it plainly, and discuss it with your senior author.
Move the result to the supplementary material and mention it in one sentence in the text.
Repeat the experiment until it supports the hypothesis, then report that run in the article.
Leave it out as suggested and keep a record of the result in the lab notebook.

advanced.situation: Your team's paper is accepted with revisions. A reviewer asks for an extra experiment that needs three weeks, and the revision deadline is in four.

options.text: Answer the reviewer with published evidence and explain that the experiment is beyond this paper.
Start the experiment now and write the response letter once the results are ready.
Report the expected result of the extra experiment in the revision and run it after resubmission.
Start the experiment now, reserve time for revisions, and warn the editor early if it slips.

basic.situation: You prepare cell samples for a toxicity test. Your culture dish looks slightly cloudy, which can mean contamination, and the experiment slot is booked for this afternoon.

options.text: Check the dish under the microscope, set it aside if contaminated, and tell your supervisor.
Add extra antibiotic to the dish to clear the cloudiness and run the experiment on time.
Move the booking to a later day and prepare a fresh dish from frozen stock.
Use the dish as planned and add a note on the record that it looked cloudy.

advanced.situation: Your team's tissue sample analysis gives inconsistent results between two technicians using the same method. You are asked to find the cause and train others.

options.text: Send a reminder to both technicians to follow the written protocol more carefully.
Average the two technicians' results and report that figure as the sample value in the study.
Rerun the samples yourself and tell the team which technician's results match yours.
Watch both technicians run the method, compare steps with the protocol, and retrain on any difference.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to outline a study testing whether a vitamin supplement lowers infection rates in children. You have a list of 40 volunteer children.

options.text: Outline control and supplement groups, assign children by random draw, and list outcomes to count.
Let parents choose which group their child joins, then compare the infection rates after.
Place the healthiest-looking children in the supplement group and the rest in the other group.
Give all 40 children the supplement and compare their infection rates with last year's rates.

advanced.situation: You direct a multi-site trial on a new vaccine. Midway, one site reports unexpectedly high mild side effects, and the sponsor wants recruitment to continue without delay.

options.text: Send the data to the safety board, pause that site, and keep the others running meanwhile.
Send the data to the safety board and keep all sites recruiting while it decides.
Ask the site staff to recheck their reporting forms before telling anyone else about the numbers.
Note the side effects as site variation in the interim report and keep recruiting everywhere.

basic.situation: You draft the background section of a research grant. The funder's guide caps it at 500 words, and your draft is 700 words long.

options.text: Cut the draft to 500 words by removing whole paragraphs from the end, then share it.
Reduce the font size and margins so the 700 words fit the space on the form.
Ask your supervisor whether the funder will accept a longer section before you cut anything.
Cut it to 500 words, keep the points that support the aims, and ask for comments.

advanced.situation: A junior researcher's grant was rejected, and they want to resubmit unchanged next round. The reviewer comments raise concerns about sample size and a missing budget item.

options.text: Tell them to resubmit unchanged and complain to the funder that the reviewers misread it.
Advise sending it to a different funder unchanged, since the same reviewers may be harsh again.
Suggest they revise the sample size and budget item before resubmitting to the same funder.
Go through each comment together, revise sample size and budget, and add a response to reviewers.

basic.situation: You demonstrate pipetting to first-year students. One student keeps placing used tips back in the clean tip box, which could contaminate it.

options.text: Pause the group, show how used tips contaminate the box, and watch her dispose of them.
Remind her quietly to use the waste container and replace the tip box yourself later.
Continue the demonstration and give a general reminder about tip disposal at the end.
Let the whole group keep using the same tip box for the session to save time.

advanced.situation: You are asked to design a lab training course for hospital technicians on a new test method. The hospital wants it in a month, and technicians have mixed experience.

options.text: Run one lecture on the method and sign everyone off as trained straight afterwards.
Reuse a course from another hospital and add a section on this method.
Check what technicians know, build modules for the gaps, and pilot one with a small group.
Build the course from the method's manual and run a short written quiz at the end.

basic.situation: You analyse a night's photometry for a variable star. The software gives a 2% brightness dip, but two frames were taken as thin cloud passed.

options.text: Report the 2% dip as found, since the software already averages over all frames.
Delete the two cloudy frames from the archive so no one reanalyses them.
Flag the two cloudy frames, run the analysis both ways, and report how the dip changes.
Drop the two cloudy frames and report the dip from the remaining data.

advanced.situation: Your observations of a young star show an infrared excess that a published disc model does not explain. A colleague's team has data suggesting a second dust ring.

options.text: Publish the two-ring idea as your own theory using your colleague's numbers from the talk.
Fit the two-ring model to your own data and cite the colleague's talk as supporting it.
Adjust the published disc model's parameters until it matches your infrared excess closely.
Request their data, test a two-ring model against both datasets, and write up the comparison.

basic.situation: Your team's shared observing script mislabels exposure times. A colleague posted a fix in a public code repository last month, but nobody has tested it here.

options.text: Use the fix on the shared observatory script tonight and tell the other observers tomorrow.
Test the fix on a copy and use it in your own runs from now.
Edit the exposure labels in your data files by hand and leave the shared script alone.
Test the fix on a copy, then share the result with the team before updating.

advanced.situation: You lead a small team building software to process data from a new spectrograph. Two members disagree on using an older proven code or writing a new pipeline.

options.text: Let each member build their own version and submit whichever finishes first for the survey.
Compare both on a test dataset, list costs and risks, and decide with the team.
Choose the new pipeline because it can be tailored to the spectrograph from the start.
Choose the proven code now and plan to add new features to it over time.

basic.situation: At a public stargazing night, a child asks if a black hole could swallow the Earth. Parents are listening, and you are not sure how to answer simply.

options.text: Praise the question and promise to look up the answer for the next stargazing night.
Tell her it could happen one day but nobody knows when, so enjoy the sky.
Explain how black holes form from collapsed stars in full detail so her parents hear everything.
Say known black holes are far too distant to reach us, then show her a chart.

advanced.situation: A school for visually impaired students books your planetarium show, which depends on projected images of the night sky. The show date is in three weeks.

options.text: Run the usual show and tell the school it is suitable for all students.
Give the teachers printed star charts to explain the show to students after it ends.
Ask the school about the students' needs, add touch models and spoken description, and trial it.
Add spoken description of every image to the usual show and run it as scheduled.

basic.situation: A first-year graduate student you mentor tells you she is struggling to finish her data reduction and has not told her supervisor.

options.text: Share your own reduction scripts with her and tell her to ask if she gets stuck.
Ask what blocks her, work through one example together, and suggest she update her supervisor.
Finish the data reduction for her over the weekend so she can present results on time.
Tell her all students find data reduction hard and that she will get used to it.

advanced.situation: A doctoral student you supervise finds that a key result in her thesis chapter depends on one noisy observation night. Her defence is in two months.

options.text: Remove the noisy night from the dataset so the result holds up at the defence.
Keep the result in the chapter and add a footnote that one night dominates the signal.
Ask her to rerun the analysis on the other nights and report what changes.
Review the data with her, plan a robustness test or extra nights, and adjust the claims.

basic.situation: You calibrate a radio telescope measurement of a source. The calibration star's reading today is 15% lower than its usual value, but the weather looks clear.

options.text: Repeat the calibration on the same star in an hour and compare the two readings.
Use the usual calibration value and record today's low reading as a typing error.
Repeat the calibration on a second star, check the receiver log, and mark the data pending.
Apply a 15% correction to all target readings tonight so they match the usual calibration.

advanced.situation: Your orbit fit for a newly found asteroid uses only a week of observations. The uncertainty range is wide, and a colleague wants to post a close-approach date online today.

options.text: Post the central date as a firm prediction, since the media will find it anyway.
Rerun the fit with just the sharpest nights to shrink the range before posting.
Send the fit and its range to the reporting centre and ask for follow-up observations.
Report the full uncertainty range, hold public dates until more observations narrow it, and request follow-up.

basic.situation: You are presenting a poster at a regional astronomy conference. A senior researcher points out a possible flaw in your error bars during the session.

options.text: Tell the researcher the error bars are fine, then shrink them on the printed poster tonight.
Thank them, explain how you calculated the error bars, and say you will recheck that step.
Thank them and say you will look into the error bars after the conference ends.
Explain that the method is standard in the field and move on to the next visitor.

advanced.situation: You sit on a funding panel and must score a proposal from a former student. Panel rules require members to declare close links before scoring.

options.text: Score the proposal as usual and say nothing, since the panel will not know the connection.
Score it fairly and mention in your comment that you taught the applicant years ago.
Declare the link and step out of scoring that proposal, then score the others as usual.
Declare the link to the chair and let the chair decide whether you score it.

basic.situation: You record the swing times of a pendulum, and your supervisor asks you to express the relation between length and period.

options.text: Quote the textbook formula for a pendulum and note that your readings roughly agree.
Plot period squared against length, fit a straight line, and state the relation with its uncertainty.
Plot period against length and draw a smooth curve through the points by eye.
Adjust two readings that sit off the line so the data fit the textbook formula neatly.

advanced.situation: A colleague's paper calls a measured decay rate roughly proportional to temperature, though the data look exponential. They ask you to check the wording before submission.

options.text: Keep the wording and add a sentence saying the data may follow a curved trend.
Suggest changing the wording to exponential, and ask the colleague to confirm with a fit.
Replace the wording with a precise equation copied from a similar paper and cite its authors.
Fit both forms to the data, compare them, and suggest wording that states the supported model.

basic.situation: You draft a short report of experimental results for your supervisor. Your run gave a value 8% below the accepted value, and you suspect a calibration issue.

options.text: Report the accepted value in the summary and put your measurement in a separate appendix.
Report the measured value and 8% gap, and name the calibration issue as a possible cause.
Report the measured value and the 8% gap, and leave the cause for your supervisor.
Scale your measurement up by 8% and report it as agreeing with the accepted value.

advanced.situation: A junior researcher plans a 15-minute conference talk with 40 slides, mostly equations, and asks you for advice a day before the talk.

options.text: Help them cut to about 15 slides around one main result and rehearse the opening.
Suggest they speak faster and shorten the introduction so most of the 40 slides fit.
Tell them to keep all 40 slides and ask the chair for more time.
Tell them to cut the slides to fit and trust their judgement on what to remove.

basic.situation: You analyse provided detector counts to measure a signal peak. Your supervisor gave step-by-step instructions, but your fit shows two peaks where one was expected.

options.text: Check the residuals and data for a second source, then show your supervisor both fits.
Refit with a single-peak model as the instructions expect, and report the fit value.
Remove the data points around the second peak until the single-peak fit looks clean.
Report the two-peak result to your supervisor and ask whether the instructions need a change.

advanced.situation: You are asked to find a weak periodic signal buried in noisy detector data. Your first method finds a candidate period, but it also appears in randomly shuffled data.

options.text: Collect more data and check whether the candidate period still shows up as before.
Measure how often shuffled data produce such peaks, then redesign the method to reduce false ones.
Report the candidate period as a detection, since the peak is clear in the real data.
Report the candidate period with a note that it may be a statistical fluctuation.

basic.situation: Your instructions say to run a curve-fitting script on the file named run_final. Two files have similar names, run_final and run_final2.

options.text: Run the script on both files and send both sets of results to your supervisor.
Pick the file with the later date since it is likely the updated one.
Delete the older file to avoid confusion, then run the script on the other one.
Ask your supervisor which file the instructions mean, and note the answer before running the script.

advanced.situation: You develop a faster algorithm for evaluating a physics integral. It matches the old code on test cases, but the old code has been trusted for years.

options.text: Switch the group's projects to the new code and delete the old code to avoid confusion.
Run the new code alongside the old for a month on real work, then switch over.
Replace the old code now since the test cases match and the speed gain is large.
Compare both across a wide range of inputs, extremes included, and document any differences.

basic.situation: You run an existing simulation of heat flow in a metal rod. The output shows temperatures rising above the heater's maximum, which is physically impossible.

options.text: Check the inputs against the model guide, rerun, and tell your supervisor what you found.
Use the simulation's results as they are since the model is already approved for use.
Cap the output temperatures at the heater's maximum and use the capped values.
Rerun the simulation with a smaller time step and see whether the numbers settle.

advanced.situation: Your group has three simulation models of the same experiment that give different results. You are asked to propose a standard for which model future work should use.

options.text: Choose the model that most people in the group already use and document it.
Validate all three against measured data and set a standard with documented checks and stated limits.
Choose the model with the most detailed physics, since more detail suggests greater accuracy.
Average the three models' results and make that average the group's standard output.

basic.situation: You help draft the expected outcomes section of a proposal for a detector upgrade. Your mentor's notes say sensitivity will double, but test data show a 40% gain.

options.text: Write the 40% gain from the test data and mention it to your mentor later.
Write the 40% gain, note what could raise it, and show your mentor the test data.
Write that sensitivity will roughly double, as your mentor's notes say, and cite the test data.
Write that sensitivity will double and delete the 40% figure from the shared test sheet.

advanced.situation: A colleague asks you to improve their grant application the evening before the deadline. The science is sound, but the budget justification is vague and the form asks for itemised costs.

options.text: Add typical cost figures for similar equipment to the justification, based on your own past grants.
Rewrite the justification in clearer language and tell them to add itemised costs if time allows.
Get their cost details, rewrite the justification item by item, and check totals match the table.
Write itemised costs that add up to the budget total, and send the application on tonight.

basic.situation: You launch a weather balloon for the afternoon upper-air reading. The ground station is missing the first minutes of wind data because of a radio dropout.

options.text: Send the data as received and mention the gap to your supervisor afterwards.
Hold the whole profile back until you can launch another balloon the next day.
Fill the missing minutes with the previous day's wind values so the profile looks complete.
Log the dropout time, check the receiver, and flag the gap when you send the data.

advanced.situation: You write a program to collect data from twelve automatic weather stations. Two stations send in a different time format, and the monsoon season starts next week.

options.text: Assume the two stations use the same format and let the program label their data.
Add a time-format check that converts or flags odd entries, and test it on past data.
Drop the two stations from the program until their time format is fixed by the vendor.
Convert the two stations' times by hand each morning until the program is updated later.

basic.situation: You analyse 30 years of monthly rainfall for a Pahang station. One year shows zero rainfall in March, which your supervisor says is unlikely for that month.

options.text: Check the station log and nearby stations, and flag the value as missing if faulty.
Replace the zero with the March average and describe the series as complete.
Keep the zero in the data, since the real record may include an unusually dry month.
Remove that month from the analysis and mention the removal to your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You test a new method for spotting trends in 50 years of rainfall records. It shows a strong trend, but the records come from stations that moved sites twice.

options.text: Report the trend and add a general caution that station moves may affect the records.
Rerun the method on the longest unbroken stretch of each record and compare the trends.
Report the strong trend as confirmed by the new method and omit the station move history.
Adjust for the station moves using overlapping records, rerun the method, and state the remaining uncertainty.
