basic.situation: A standard model run shows heavy rain over Kota Bharu tomorrow night, but a second run shows light showers. Your senior forecaster asks for your reading.

options.text: Average the two rainfall amounts and present the result as your reading of the forecast.
Call the second run a model error and remove it from the shared files.
Suggest using the heavy rain run, since a cautious forecast is safer for the public.
Compare both runs with current radar and satellite, then give your reading and the doubt.

advanced.situation: You are building a statistical correction for a rain forecast model that over-predicts coastal rain. It improves coastal accuracy on last year's data but you have not tested it elsewhere.

options.text: Test it on another coastal year and put it into use if the improvement holds.
Report last year's improvement as the model's accuracy gain in the monthly update.
Apply it to all forecasts from the next run, since coastal accuracy matters most.
Test it on other years and inland stations, then document where it helps and fails.

basic.situation: You read a scripted radio weather update. Minutes before air, the script says light rain for your area, but the latest radar shows a thunderstorm approaching.

options.text: Delay the update by ten minutes until the forecast office confirms the thunderstorm risk.
Tell the producer about the radar, get the script updated, and read the revised warning.
Read the script as written and tell the producer about the radar afterwards.
Announce thunderstorms on your own and name the districts you think will be hit.

advanced.situation: You design a flood-preparedness training for village heads on reading rainfall warnings. Many attendees cannot read the technical bulletin, and some speak mainly Malay or Iban.

options.text: Tell village heads to evacuate whenever it rains heavily, so they need not read the warnings.
Rewrite key warnings in simple Malay and Iban with local examples, and trial them first.
Translate the bulletin word for word into Malay and Iban and print copies for everyone.
Present the bulletin in English with slides and give each village head a printed copy.

basic.situation: You prepare a weather map for the evening broadcast. The graphics software shades a district red for heavy rain, but the forecast table says moderate.

options.text: Send the map as it is and edit the forecast table to say heavy.
Change the shading to match the table and send the map to the broadcast team.
Compare the map with the forecast table, fix the shading to match, and tell the forecaster.
Keep the red shading, since it is better to over-warn than to under-warn the public.

advanced.situation: You review a colleague's draft climate report where temperature trends use different baseline periods in different charts. A department deadline requires sign-off today.

options.text: Ask for one baseline in every chart, check the revision, and sign off once it matches.
Redraw the charts yourself with one baseline and sign off on your own version.
Sign off and shift the baselines yourself in the summary so the trend looks stronger.
Sign off with a comment asking the colleague to unify baselines in the next report.

basic.situation: A researcher asks you for a rainfall climatology for a river basin to use in a flood study. You have station data, but two stations have shifted locations.

options.text: Send the data with notes on the moved stations and offer to explain their use.
Send all the station data as it is and let the researcher decide what to use.
Send the data from the unmoved stations and say the moved ones need checking first.
Merge the moved stations' records into one series and send it as a single basin average.

advanced.situation: You manage a small forecasting office. Two forecasters are on leave during the monsoon peak, and a new graduate has joined who is untrained in the local model.

options.text: Give the graduate a self-study pack on the model and place them on shifts next week.
Put the new graduate on solo night shifts to cover gaps and learn the model.
Pair the graduate with a senior, book model training this week, and adjust the roster.
Keep the old roster and ask the remaining forecasters to cover extra shifts through the peak.

basic.situation: You run an HPLC test on a product sample following the method sheet. The first injection shows a peak in the right place but a baseline drift you have not seen before.

options.text: Pause, check the mobile phase and column against the method sheet, and tell your supervisor.
Run the remaining samples and draw the baseline by hand in the integration software.
Adjust the integration settings until the drift disappears and the peak area looks stable.
Let the system equilibrate for another twenty minutes, then rerun the same injection.

advanced.situation: A client's polymer sample gives results that the standard test cannot explain. The engineer suggests a nonstandard test, but no validated method exists for it.

options.text: Report the standard test results as they stand and note the engineer's idea for later.
Run the nonstandard test and issue its result under the lab's accredited method number.
Run the nonstandard test on the client's sample and report the result with a warning.
Design the test with the engineer, validate it on a reference sample, and record its limits.

basic.situation: You run a routine quality check on a batch of cleaning solution. The pH reads 8.9, outside the 7.0 to 8.5 specification, and the batch is due for shipment today.

options.text: Recalibrate the meter, retest, and hold and report the batch if still out of range.
Hold the batch and report the reading to your supervisor so a decision can be made.
Add a little acid to bring the pH down and record the reading as 8.5.
Release the batch and note the reading in the log, since the difference is small.

advanced.situation: While auditing your lab, you find that staff routinely handle a volatile solvent outside the fume hood because the hood is far from the bench. Nobody has been hurt.

options.text: Record the finding, measure solvent exposure, and propose moving the work or adding a nearer hood.
Note the practice in the audit and wait to see whether anyone reports problems.
Leave the practice out of the audit report since nobody has been harmed by it.
Remind staff of the hood rule at the next meeting and record that you did so.

basic.situation: You collect temperature and flow readings from a heat exchanger to help check its efficiency. Two readings were noted on the back of a glove instead of the log sheet.

options.text: Enter the two readings with a note on how they were noted, and remeasure if possible.
Remeasure both readings at the next stable operating point, then discard the glove notes.
Leave the two readings out of the data set, since they are not in the log.
Estimate the two readings from the ones either side and enter them as measured.

advanced.situation: You lead a project to cut energy use in a distillation process. Changing the reflux ratio saves energy in trials but slightly lowers product purity.

options.text: Keep the current setting and look for energy savings in the heating system first.
Adopt the trial setting for a month and watch whether complaints about purity come in.
Adopt the trial setting and lower the purity limit in the specification to match it.
Test several settings, find the lowest-energy one meeting purity limits, and confirm in a long run.

basic.situation: You draft a short report on a stability test of a coating. Your supervisor's notes list results from three batches, but the raw data file has results from four.

options.text: Report the three batches in the notes and delete the fourth from the raw data file.
Report all four batches from the raw file and drop the supervisor's notes from the draft.
Report on the three batches in the notes and mention the fourth in your cover email.
Ask your supervisor about the fourth batch, then report on the confirmed set of batches.

advanced.situation: You are asked to write a specification for a test method that several labs will adopt. Two labs report slightly different results using your draft procedure.

options.text: Run a small comparison between the labs, find where steps differ, and revise before release.
Ask both labs to follow the draft exactly and send their results again next month.
Add a tolerance wide enough that both labs' results count as agreeing with each other.
Release the method as written and tell the labs the differences come from their equipment.

basic.situation: You prepare a standard solution following the written method, which says to weigh 4.00 g of a reagent. The balance shows 4.21 g after your last pellet.

options.text: Use the 4.21 g and label the solution with the nominal strength written in the method.
Remove pellets to get near 4.00 g, record the actual mass, and calculate the true concentration.
Use the 4.21 g and record the actual mass in the notebook for your supervisor.
Remove pellets until the balance shows exactly 4.00 g, even if it takes several attempts.

advanced.situation: The lab's only gas chromatograph, needed for a client's urgent job, starts giving noisy baselines. The service engineer cannot visit for three days.

options.text: Dismantle the detector and rebuild it from the manual before the engineer's visit.
Check gas supply, septum, liner and detector, fix any fault, and verify with a standard.
Replace the septum and liner, then run the client samples and watch the baseline.
Run the client samples anyway and tell the client the baseline noise is within normal range.

basic.situation: You notice the lab's acetonitrile is down to one bottle, and the usual supplier needs a week for delivery. A big project starts in five days.

options.text: Take solvent from the neighbouring lab's cupboard and tell them once the order arrives.
Wait until the last bottle is opened, then order so the stock count is accurate.
Order today, ask the supplier for faster delivery, and tell the team how much is left.
Place the usual order today and mention it at the next team meeting.

advanced.situation: You direct a four-person team running tests for two urgent clients. One analyst repeatedly gets different results from the others on the same reference sample.

options.text: Watch the analyst alongside a colleague, find the technique difference, retrain, and rerun the reference sample.
Tell the analyst to follow the method sheet more closely and to review their own results.
Leave the analyst on the urgent tests and average their results with the others.
Move the analyst to non-urgent tests while you check their results against the others.

basic.situation: You record the hardness of ten aluminium alloy samples. Sample seven reads far higher than the others, and your supervisor is out for the day.

options.text: Remeasure sample seven at a second spot, record both readings, and flag it for your supervisor.
Leave sample seven out of the table, since it looks like a measurement error.
Replace the high reading with the average of the other nine and finish the table.
Record the high reading as measured and mention it to your supervisor tomorrow.

advanced.situation: You lead a project developing a ceramic with higher heat resistance. Samples fired at a higher temperature are stronger, but the furnace you need is booked by another team for two weeks.

options.text: Ask the other team for a slot and plan the firing variations while you wait.
Use the other team's furnace overnight when nobody is there and tell them later.
Fire the samples at a lower temperature in your own furnace and extrapolate the strength.
Wait the two weeks and report the delay to your manager at the next review.

basic.situation: You set up a simple tensile test on a polymer strip for a senior scientist. The sample's width varies along its length, and the test plan lists one fixed width.

options.text: Cut a new strip of even width and run the test on that.
Use the width in the test plan for the calculation, since the plan covers this test.
Measure the width at three points, record all of them, and tell the senior scientist.
Measure the widest point and enter that as the width so the stress comes out lower.

advanced.situation: You design experiments and a computer model to predict how a new alloy resists fatigue. The model fits your lab tests well, but you used all your data to tune it.

options.text: Report the close fit as proof that the model predicts fatigue life for this alloy.
Run a few new tests next month and compare the model's predictions with the results.
Set some tests aside, retune on the rest, and report accuracy on those held-out tests.
Tune the model further until it matches every test exactly and publish the model.

basic.situation: You help run a compression test on concrete additive samples. The method calls for 28-day cured samples, but one batch is only 21 days old and the client wants results today.

options.text: Test the 28-day batches, explain the curing rule, and give a date for the rest.
Ask your supervisor whether to test the younger batch early, and test the 28-day batches meanwhile.
Hold all the batches until the 21-day batch has also cured, then test them together.
Test the 21-day batch today and report its result as a 28-day result.

advanced.situation: A batch of steel bolts failed in service. Your tension tests on retained samples pass, but the failed bolts show crack marks near the thread root.

options.text: Repeat the tension tests on more retained samples to confirm they meet the specification.
Examine the fracture surface, test hardness near the thread root, and review the forming records.
Report that the bolts meet specification and blame the failure on how they were installed.
Sign the batch as acceptable since the tension tests passed, and close the investigation.

basic.situation: You write up a lab report on a corrosion test. Your mentor says your conclusion is stronger than your results, which showed a small difference between two coatings.

options.text: Keep the conclusion and omit the data from the two panels that disagree with it.
Keep the conclusion and add more detail to the results section to support it.
Rewrite the conclusion to state the small difference, give the data range, and suggest further tests.
Soften the wording of the conclusion and resend the report to your mentor.

advanced.situation: You are lead author on a paper on a new composite. A co-author wants to include data from a collaborator's lab that has not agreed to its use.

options.text: Leave the collaborator's data out of the paper and cite their earlier published work instead.
Hold the paper until the collaborator replies, even if a journal deadline passes.
Include the data and add the collaborator's name to the acknowledgements as thanks.
Ask the collaborator for permission and agree on credit, and include the data once they consent.

basic.situation: You take notes during a client meeting about a heat-resistant coating. The client mentions two requirements that conflict: low cost and very high temperature use.

options.text: Record both requirements as stated and send the notes to your lead after the meeting.
Record both requirements as stated, mark the conflict, and ask your lead to raise it.
Tell the client in the meeting that both requirements can be met within their budget.
Record the high temperature requirement in full, since technical needs matter more than cost.

advanced.situation: You lead a consultation with an electronics client who wants a new heat-spreading material. Their brief gives a target conductivity, but their engineers say it will run hot inside a sealed case.

options.text: Propose a material that meets the conductivity target and offer to discuss the sealed case later.
Agree the written brief as the specification and handle heat problems after the product is built.
Ask about the sealed case, operating limits and lifetime goals, then propose specification ranges.
Tell the client the target conductivity is achievable and suggest a trial sample to test it.

basic.situation: A technician asks which of two plastics can hold a hot liquid at 90 degrees Celsius. You find datasheets listing a heat deflection temperature of 85 degrees for one and 110 for the other.

options.text: Recommend the cheaper 85-degree plastic and tell him that the datasheet figures include a safety margin.
Recommend the plastic rated to 110 degrees and send the datasheet figures to the technician.
Recommend the 110-degree plastic, show the datasheet figures, and suggest the supplier confirm long exposure.
Say both plastics are usually fine, since 90 degrees is a little above 85.

advanced.situation: Senior engineers ask you to recommend a material for pump parts exposed to hot, salty, acidic fluid. Material A has the strongest corrosion data but costs more, while B is cheaper with little acid data at this temperature.

options.text: Recommend B because the cost saving is large and similar materials have done well in acid.
Recommend B and describe its acid performance at this temperature as proven in the report.
Recommend A for now, explain B's data gap, and propose testing B in the real fluid.
Recommend A because its corrosion data is stronger, and mention that B is cheaper.

basic.situation: You help collect data for an environmental audit of a palm oil mill's effluent pond. The mill manager offers to hand you his own readings instead of letting you sample the discharge.

options.text: Use his readings and sample later from the cleaner end of the pond to confirm them.
Use his readings for the audit, since the mill knows its pond better than you do.
Take your own samples as planned and mention his offer to your supervisor.
Take your own samples at the discharge point as planned, and record his readings separately.

advanced.situation: You lead an investigation into suspected illegal dumping near a river. A resident gives you photos, and the company named denies it. Findings may be used in enforcement.

options.text: Tell the company's neighbours that the company is dumping, so that pressure builds before the report.
Collect your own samples at the site and send the results to the enforcement officer.
Send the resident's photos to the enforcement officer as evidence and wait for their instructions.
Verify the photo details, take your own samples with custody records, and document every step.

basic.situation: You review a company's environmental report against its permit conditions. The report says wastewater pH is within limits but does not give the actual readings.

options.text: Fill in typical pH readings for the section from earlier reports and pass the review.
Accept the claim, since the company has met its limits in all earlier reports.
Request the pH readings from the company and mark the claim unverified until they arrive.
Pass the report as it is and add a reminder to ask for readings next year.

advanced.situation: A district council asks you to draft a code of practice for managing food-stall wastewater. Stall owners say a grease trap on every stall is too costly.

options.text: Require grease traps on every stall and offer a longer time to install them.
Write the code to match the stall owners' proposal and finish it before the meeting.
Drop the grease trap requirement and ask stalls to clean their drains weekly instead.
Check stall volumes, scale grease trap rules to them, and consult owners on the draft.

basic.situation: You organise air quality readings from five monitoring stations into a table for your supervisor. One station's file has a six-hour gap with no readings.

options.text: Leave the gap blank and send the table to your supervisor as it is.
Fill the gap with the average of the readings either side to keep the table continuous.
Copy the previous day's readings into the gap since the station is in a stable area.
Leave the gap blank, label it missing in the table, and ask the station operator why.

advanced.situation: You manage a database of river water quality from 40 sites, collected by three teams using different units and detection limits. A new report requires a combined trend analysis.

options.text: Standardise the units and drop all the below-detection values from the trend analysis.
Merge all data as reported and treat each below-detection value as zero in the analysis.
Standardise the units, treat below-detection values by a documented method, and log every change.
Analyse each team's data separately and place the three trend lines side by side.

basic.situation: You monitor a construction site beside a stream, as the permit requires monthly turbidity readings. This month's reading is the highest yet, but still under the permit limit.

options.text: Record the reading, note the upward trend, check the silt controls, and tell your supervisor.
Warn the contractor about the reading and offer to leave it out of your report.
Record the reading as within the limit and continue with the monthly schedule as planned.
Increase sampling to weekly on your own and tell the contractor to expect more visits.

advanced.situation: A factory's emissions fall after a filter upgrade, but nearby residents report worse odours. You must advise on whether the upgrade solved the problem.

options.text: Identify the odour compounds, sample near the homes, and compare with the emissions data before advising.
Advise the factory to stop reporting emission figures publicly until the residents' complaints end.
Report that emissions fell and recommend the factory investigate the odours on its own.
Advise that the upgrade solved the problem and the odours are likely from other sources.

basic.situation: You prepare a bar chart of monthly dust levels for a public leaflet. Starting the vertical axis at 40 instead of zero makes a small rise look dramatic.

options.text: Start the axis at 40 and add a red arrow on the rise to draw attention.
Start the axis at zero, add the limit line, and explain the rise plainly.
Start the axis at 40 and write the starting value in small print under the chart.
Start the axis at zero and add a title that describes the chart.

advanced.situation: You present at a public hearing about a proposed quarry. A resident asks if the dust will harm children. Your data show levels near the limit in normal winds but unknown in storms.

options.text: Tell her the levels stay within the limit, so children will be fine.
Give the levels under normal winds, say storm conditions are unknown, and explain the planned monitoring.
Say the quarry will produce no dust once permitted, so no one should worry.
Say the levels are near the limit and refer her to the health department.

basic.situation: You help train a new technician to collect river water samples. He leaves each sample bottle uncapped in his bag while he records the site number.

options.text: Explain why open bottles spoil samples, have him cap and label first, then watch again.
Take over sampling for the rest of the day and let him record the site numbers.
Tell him to cap each bottle before writing the site number, then check the next one.
Let him continue and use the bottle, then remove any odd results from the data afterwards.

advanced.situation: A state agency asks for guidance on setting up a river monitoring programme on a small budget. Wide coverage and frequent sampling cannot both be afforded.

options.text: Sample every site at the same low frequency so all sites get equal coverage.
Sample often at a few easy-to-reach sites and extend the results to the whole river.
Map the main risks, sample often at high-risk sites, check others less often, and review yearly.
Advise cheap test kits at every site and drop the quality checks to save money.

basic.situation: You gather studies on sea level rise for a coastal state policy brief. Two reports give very different projections: one from a research institute and one from an advocacy group's blog.

options.text: Present both projections as a range, since both sources describe the same coastline.
Cite the higher projection as the official estimate because it makes the case for action stronger.
Use the institute's report and leave the blog out of the brief entirely.
Use the institute's report as the main source and check the blog's sources before citing it.

advanced.situation: You lead a team reviewing 12 studies of heat-related deaths. The studies use different definitions of a heatwave, and your team is split on how to combine them.

options.text: Combine the studies as they stand and describe the differences in definition in an appendix.
Keep the studies sharing the most common definition and describe the result as a full review.
Pick the definition that gives the largest effect and re-label the other studies to match.
Agree one working definition, convert studies to it where possible, and list the exceptions.

basic.situation: You research how other states regulate cooling energy in building codes for a policy note. Most sources are government sites, but one useful comparison appears only in a news article.

options.text: Include the news comparison with the article's link so readers can judge it themselves.
Cite the news comparison as an official government finding to strengthen the note.
Use official sources, trace the news claim to its origin, and flag it if not found.
Use the official sources and leave the news article's comparison out of the note.

advanced.situation: A legislator's office asks for a one-page summary of research on carbon pricing, due tomorrow. You have forty pages of conflicting studies, and the legislator favours one position.

options.text: Summarise the findings, show where evidence is strong or weak, and tie any advice to it.
Write the summary around the legislator's position and describe the opposing studies as outdated.
Summarise the studies that support the legislator's position and list the others in a footnote.
Summarise the three most-cited studies and note briefly that the others differ in method.

basic.situation: You present climate adaptation data at a community meeting with your mentor present. A resident asks about flood risk for her street, which you cannot answer.

options.text: Tell her her street is safe, since the main flood zones are elsewhere in the district.
Give her the district's flood risk and say it should apply to her street.
Ask your mentor to answer the question and then carry on with the presentation.
Say you lack street-level data, offer to find out, and take her contact details.

advanced.situation: You present climate risk findings to a state executive council deciding on a flood barrier budget. You have ten minutes, and the findings include an important caveat on sea level uncertainty.

options.text: Present the worst-case estimate to make the council act, with the range in an appendix.
Present the central estimate clearly and leave the uncertainty details for question time.
Open with the decision, give the central estimate and range, and show the cost of waiting.
Leave the uncertainty caveat out of the presentation so the council can reach a clear decision.

basic.situation: Your team asks you to draft a suggestion for a state law encouraging rooftop solar. A teammate points out that a similar national incentive exists, and you are unsure how they interact.

options.text: Draft the suggestion as if the national scheme did not exist, to keep it simple.
Check the national scheme with your team, draft a complementary suggestion, and mark open questions.
Draft the suggestion as planned and add a note that the national scheme may overlap.
Copy the wording of the national scheme into your suggestion with the state's name added.

advanced.situation: You design a proposal to cut freight emissions by shifting some goods from road to rail. Hauliers warn it will raise their costs, and rail capacity is limited.

options.text: Propose a high road tax on hauliers to fund rail and leave the cost analysis out.
Propose a five-year rail-share target and let hauliers adjust in their own way.
Model emissions and costs, phase the shift to match rail capacity, and consult hauliers on support.
Propose moving all freight over 300 km to rail and review it when problems appear.

basic.situation: An environmental group asks you to help promote a tree-planting initiative with a government agency. Their flyer says it will remove 10,000 tonnes of carbon, but the agency's plan says 2,000.

options.text: Support the larger number at the launch because it will attract more volunteers.
Tell the group the agency's figure is 2,000 and ask them to update the flyer.
Print the group's flyer as it is since it is their publication, not the agency's.
Show the group the agency's figure, ask how they got theirs, and agree one number.

advanced.situation: You design an outreach campaign to reduce household energy use across a state with urban flats, rural villages and estates. The budget allows one national ad campaign.

options.text: Run the national ad campaign and add a hotline for people who want tips.
Segment households by type, test messages in each group, and pick channels that reach each one.
Run the national ad with a warning of fines for high usage to push people quickly.
Run one message about saving money on the bill in all channels and languages.

basic.situation: You help prepare a grant application's budget table. The funder's form limits equipment costs to 20% of the total, but your draft shows 27%.

options.text: Tell your lead the equipment share is over the limit and ask what to change.
Reduce the equipment line by 7% in the table and plan to find the money elsewhere.
Tell your lead, move costs that belong elsewhere, and rebalance the budget to the limit.
Rename some equipment items as services in the table so that the equipment share looks lower.

advanced.situation: You defend a climate research proposal before a funding panel. A panelist says your sampling plan is too small to detect the effect you claim, and she may be right.

options.text: Change the stated effect size in the slides so the plan looks adequate, then continue.
Acknowledge the concern and promise to send a revised sampling plan after the meeting.
Explain that similar studies used similar sample sizes and that reviewers have accepted them.
Acknowledge the concern, show your power calculation, and offer to expand sampling in year one.

basic.situation: You help collect soil and water data at a former tin mining pond to be restored. The sampling plan lists ten points, but two points are under deep standing water.

options.text: Sample the eight reachable points and tell your lead the other two will follow when possible.
Sample the eight reachable points, record why two were missed, and ask your lead about them.
Sample from the shore nearest each deep point and log them under the planned point numbers.
Copy values for the two points from the nearest sampled points and log them as measured.

advanced.situation: You lead a site assessment to certify a restored wetland as habitat. Plant cover looks good, but you saw few birds and your team has made only one visit in the dry season.

options.text: Delay certification and tell the restoration team that the habitat looks like it has failed.
Certify the habitat now, since the plant cover is good and the funder wants a decision.
Schedule visits across seasons, add bird and water-level surveys, and certify when evidence supports it.
Schedule a wet-season visit and certify based on the combined plant and visit results.

basic.situation: You help draft a restoration plan for a riverbank cleared of weeds. Your lead asks for a native tree list, and a nursery offers a cheaper mix that includes a fast-growing exotic species.

options.text: Plant the exotic species along the water edge first, since it will stabilise the soil quickest.
List the nursery's native species and leave the exotic out of the plan.
Use the nursery's cheaper mix, since it covers the bank faster and costs less.
List native species suited to the soil and flooding, and raise the exotic with your lead.

advanced.situation: You develop a restoration plan for land around a wind farm. Turbine access roads cut through key habitat, and the operator will fund work along the roads.

options.text: Plan restoration of the whole site and ask the operator to pay for all of it.
Propose road-side restoration plus habitat corridors, and cost the extra work separately for them.
Plan restoration along the roads and describe it as full habitat recovery for the site.
Plan restoration along the roads as funded and note that the wider habitat still needs work.

basic.situation: You help prepare a permit application for dredging a silted pond. The agency's form needs the pond's coordinates, volume and disposal site, but you lack the disposal site details.

options.text: Enter the nearest approved disposal site from a past application as the planned site.
Write that sediment will be reused on site and submit the form to meet the deadline.
Ask the agency whether it will accept the form with the disposal site added later.
Fill in what you can, ask your lead for the disposal site, and submit when complete.

advanced.situation: A pipeline repair will cross a stream with a protected fish species. The contractor offers three crossing methods, and the cheapest needs the longest in-water work.

options.text: Compare methods with permit conditions and the breeding season, then recommend the least in-water one.
Approve the cheapest method and let the contractor begin while the permit review continues.
Recommend the cheapest method and add a note that fish may be disturbed.
Recommend the method with the least in-water work and ask the contractor to confirm costs.

basic.situation: You make a GIS map showing where mangrove seedlings will be planted. The high tide line layer is from 2015, and a recent survey shows the shoreline has moved.

options.text: Redraw the 2015 line by eye to match the shoreline in a recent satellite photo.
Use the recent survey line, note its source on the map, and tell your lead.
Use the 2015 line and note on the map that the shoreline may have moved.
Use the 2015 line and label the map as based on current survey data.

advanced.situation: You build a flood model for a river restoration plan using GIS data. The model says restoring a floodplain will lower flooding downstream, but the elevation data is coarse.

options.text: Test the result against elevation error, get finer data for key areas, and report the uncertainty.
Rerun the model on a finer grid using the same elevation data for more detail.
Report the result and state that elevation data is coarse in the assumptions.
Present the flood reduction as a firm figure and leave elevation data out of the report.

basic.situation: You help write a grant for planting native trees on a degraded slope. The funder wants measurable outcomes, and your lead's draft says the project will restore the forest.

options.text: Suggest targets like seedling survival and canopy cover by set dates, and revise together.
Add a claim that the project will restore 500 hectares of forest within two years.
Add the hectares to be planted to the outcomes and keep the rest as drafted.
Keep the wording as drafted since funders like ambitious goals more than small numbers.

advanced.situation: You lead a feasibility study for restoring a coastal peatland. The cost-benefit analysis shows benefits exceed costs only if carbon credit prices stay high, which is uncertain.

options.text: Use a mid-range carbon price in the analysis and note that prices may change.
Add benefits from a larger area than the project covers to make the ratio look stronger.
Use the high carbon price in the analysis, as it is the price the funder expects.
Show results at low, medium and high carbon prices, name other benefits, and state the risk.

basic.situation: You are asked to review a remediation design for a polluted pond. The design's volume calculation uses a depth of 2 m, but your site notes record 3.5 m.

options.text: Send your site notes to the engineer and ask them to check the depth.
Recheck the depth against the survey, then send the difference and its effect to the engineer.
Approve the design since the rest looks sound and the depth error may be small.
Change the depth to 3.5 m in the design yourself and approve it for the engineer.

advanced.situation: Your biologists want to replant a stream bank with native shrubs, while the engineers want hard rock lining to stop erosion before the monsoon. You must give technical direction.

options.text: Propose rock at the bank toe with native planting above, and agree it with both teams.
Choose the rock lining for this monsoon and plan the native planting for next year.
Choose native planting because it costs less and the roots will hold the bank in time.
Order the rock lining for the whole bank and remove the existing shrubs to make room.

basic.situation: You monitor dust from a new factory construction site for a monthly report. The contractor's own log shows lower dust than your handheld meter.

options.text: Report the contractor's log, since it covers the whole month and your readings are spot checks.
Record both sets of readings, check your meter's calibration, and share the difference with your supervisor.
Average the two sets and report the result as a single measured value.
Report your meter's readings as the figures and mention the contractor's log in a footnote.

advanced.situation: You evaluate whether a company's waste-reduction programme worked. Waste fell 12% after launch, but production also fell 15% in the same months.

options.text: Report the 12% drop as the programme's result, since it was the goal that was set.
Compare waste per unit produced before and after, test the change, and report the result.
Report a 27% improvement by adding the two changes together to show the programme working.
Report the 12% drop and add a note that production also fell in those months.

basic.situation: You map how plastic packaging moves through one local factory for a flow chart. The purchasing records show 40 tonnes in, but the waste records show 52 tonnes out.

options.text: Scale the waste figure down to 40 tonnes so that the flow chart balances neatly.
Check units and periods in both records, ask about stock changes, and mark the gap.
Chart 40 tonnes for both in and out, since the purchase records are the official figure.
Chart the 40 tonnes in and 52 out and ask your supervisor about the gap later.

advanced.situation: A city plans to replace a plastic food container with a paper-coated one. You must analyse the change for unintended effects, with a council vote in two weeks.

options.text: Check whether the paper-coated container can be recycled locally and report what you find.
Support the change because paper is natural and plastic waste is a visible problem.
Report the paper-coated container as the lower-impact option, citing the supplier's brochure as evidence.
Compare both containers across their life cycles, including disposal, and report where problems may shift.

basic.situation: You review a metal plating workshop's practices to list possible environmental hazards. The workshop stores spent acid in unmarked drums beside a drain.

options.text: Neutralise the acid with lime from the workshop store and mark the hazard resolved.
List the drums and drain as hazards, photograph them, and report them to your supervisor today.
Ask the workshop owner to move the drums and mark the issue closed in your review.
Add a line to the review that drums should be labelled, and note the drain nearby.

advanced.situation: Participation in a new recycling scheme is low in a housing estate. Residents say the bins are far, collection days are confusing, and the sorting rules seem complicated.

options.text: Survey residents on each barrier, trial one fix per barrier, and compare participation afterwards.
Send a leaflet to every household explaining the sorting rules and the collection days.
Introduce a fine for unsorted bins and report the scheme as working once participation rises.
Move the bins closer to the flats and check participation after a few months.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks how a natural food web could help you understand an industrial park where one plant's waste feeds another. You have one ecology paper and a plant list.

options.text: Map waste exchanges, compare them with the food web paper, and note where it breaks down.
Summarise the food web paper and say that industrial parks work in the same way.
List the plants and describe each one as a producer, consumer or decomposer.
Explain that the industrial park is a natural ecosystem and does not need further study.

advanced.situation: You advise factories on sharing waste heat and water, based on industrial ecology ideas. Two factories agree, but the third fears giving away its process secrets.

options.text: Ask the third factory to share its full process data so the exchange can be designed.
Proceed with the two willing factories and invite the third to join later.
Obtain the third factory's process data from its supplier records and include it in the design.
Limit sharing to heat and water, protect process data in writing, and meet the third factory.

basic.situation: You maintain a database of pollutant data for an industrial area. A colleague sends a spreadsheet using ND for values below detection, while your database stores numbers.

options.text: Replace every ND with zero so that the column stays numeric and can be summed.
Replace every ND with the previous month's value for that site to keep the series going.
Check the detection limit behind ND, add a flag field, and document the rule.
Import the numeric values and add a comment field noting that ND values were removed.

advanced.situation: You are asked to redesign a food processing plant's linear flow, where peel and pulp waste is dumped, into a closed loop. The plant manager worries about cost and food safety.

options.text: Identify uses for the waste, check safety rules for each, and pilot the lowest-cost safe option.
Contract a composting company to take the waste and review costs after six months.
Mix the peel and pulp back into the plant's products at a small share to cut waste.
Keep dumping the waste and add a recycling section to the plant's sustainability report.

basic.situation: You help prepare a plan to manage a community's bamboo grove as a renewable resource. The villagers want to harvest as much as possible this year because prices are high.

options.text: Plan the harvest at the level villagers want and add monitoring for later years.
Estimate yearly regrowth, propose a harvest limit under it, and review the plan with the villagers.
Propose a harvest limit of half the grove and revisit the figure next year.
Plan to harvest the whole grove this year and replant it all at once next year.

advanced.situation: You promote an environmental management system to a mid-sized factory. The owner says certification costs too much and the system will add paperwork without cutting waste.

options.text: Explain that the system will cut waste over time and offer a free guide to begin.
Tell the owner the system is required by law and that fines will follow.
Show a similar factory's savings, start with the waste-heavy processes, and reuse existing records for paperwork.
Suggest the owner wait until customers ask for certification before looking at the system.

basic.situation: You interpret a well log showing a thick sandstone layer at 120 m. Your supervisor's map puts that layer at 150 m, and the two may use different depth reference points.

options.text: Check the depth reference of both, convert to a common datum, and tell your supervisor.
Edit the log's depth marks by 30 m so the layer matches the map.
Use the supervisor's map depth of 150 m since the map covers many wells.
Report the sandstone at 120 m as logged and mention the map difference to your supervisor.

advanced.situation: A hillside housing project sits below slopes that showed small slips after heavy rain. Borehole data, slope maps and rainfall records give mixed signals on landslide risk.

options.text: Use the borehole data to rate the risk, since it is the most direct measurement.
Rate the whole hillside high risk from the past slips and recommend a detailed study.
Rate the risk as low since no large slide has happened, calling the slips minor.
Combine slope, soil, rainfall and past slip data, rate risk by zone, and state the uncertainty.

basic.situation: You use geological charts to mark likely groundwater zones for a village well project. A fault line runs near the most promising zone, and you are unsure how it affects water flow.

options.text: Mark the zone as high potential and leave the fault off the map to avoid confusion.
Mark the zone and send the chart to your supervisor with the fault visible.
Mark both, flag the uncertainty, and ask your supervisor how the fault affects flow.
Choose a different zone far from the fault so you do not have to explain it.

advanced.situation: A developer wants to build a quarry-fed cement plant. Aerial photos and survey data suggest limestone, but a drilling result from one hole shows shale at the planned depth.

options.text: Treat the shale hole as a local anomaly and estimate the volume from the other data.
Combine all three data sets, estimate usable limestone, and recommend more drilling to resolve the shale.
Report the limestone estimate to the developer and drop the drilling result as unrepresentative.
Estimate the limestone volume from the aerial and survey data and note the one shale result.

basic.situation: You collect rock samples from an outcrop with your supervisor. She is called away, and you notice a second outcrop 50 m up the slope that looks different but is not on the plan.

options.text: Finish the planned samples and mention the second outcrop to your supervisor in passing.
Collect samples from the second outcrop too and label them with the first site's number.
Finish the planned samples, photograph and locate the second outcrop, and tell your supervisor.
Leave the planned samples and spend the day sampling the second outcrop, which looks more interesting.

advanced.situation: You design a drilling and testing programme for a bridge foundation site. The budget allows six boreholes, but the geology varies across the river and your team suggests twelve.

options.text: Plan six boreholes and describe the programme to the client as fully covering the site.
Drill the six boreholes on the easy-access bank and extend the findings across the river.
Space the six boreholes evenly across the site and note the limits of the coverage.
Place six boreholes at the main geology changes, add cheaper geophysical lines, and explain the uncertainty.

basic.situation: You operate a magnetometer on a survey line. A colleague walks past carrying a steel tool box, and the readings jump.

options.text: Pause, note the jump, ask the colleague to keep clear, and repeat that stretch.
Smooth the jump out of the data later using the readings on either side of it.
Note the time of the jump in your field book and carry on surveying.
Delete the readings from that stretch on the instrument and continue as if nothing happened.

advanced.situation: A gravimeter shows slow drift that exceeds the maker's specification between base readings. A survey crew is waiting, and the nearest service centre is far away.

options.text: Start the survey and compare results against known stations to judge the drift afterwards.
Check levelling, temperature and clamping, run drift tests at the base, and model any stable drift.
Apply a straight-line drift adjustment between base readings and go ahead with the survey.
Open the instrument case and adjust the internal spring yourself to stop the drift.

basic.situation: You draw a cross-section chart from bore logs for a hill road cut. Two logs disagree on where a clay layer lies, 4 m apart.

options.text: Draw the clay as a range between the logs, note the disagreement, and ask your supervisor.
Draw a smooth layer through the midpoint between the two logs and finish the chart.
Draw the clay where it looks consistent with the hill and omit the log labels.
Draw the clay layer at the position given by the nearer log and label the source.

advanced.situation: You review a colleague's geological report for a slope stabilisation project. It cites a soil strength value from a different site, and the client plans to rely on it for design.

options.text: Replace the value with a typical figure for similar soils and approve the report.
Flag the value, request site test data, and hold your approval until the report is updated.
Approve the report as written, since the author is senior and the client wants it today.
Approve the report with a comment that the strength value is from another site.

basic.situation: You are asked to find recent research on landslide triggers for your team. A search returns a popular article claiming a new method predicts landslides days ahead, with no data shown.

options.text: Cite the method as a proven way to predict landslides in your team's summary.
Add the article to the reading list, since it is recent and widely shared.
Find the original study, check its data and review status, and share your findings.
Share the article with the team and say that its claims still need checking.

advanced.situation: A local council asks whether to allow housing on a former mining area with ground subsidence risk. The council's own studies are two decades old.

options.text: Advise that the old studies are adequate and the council can approve the housing now.
Recommend new subsidence surveys first, explain what the old data show, and suggest building conditions.
Advise against any building on the site because the old data cannot be trusted.
Advise that housing can proceed if the foundations are made deeper than is usual.

basic.situation: You collect water samples from a river for a supervisor. At the third site the water is unusually cloudy after rain upstream, and the sampling plan prefers clear-flow conditions.

options.text: Wait an hour for the water to clear a little, then sample and move on.
Collect the sample, record the cloudiness and rain, and ask your supervisor whether to resample.
Sample from a clearer side channel and record it as the planned river site.
Skip the site today, note it as unsampled, and tell your supervisor you will return.

advanced.situation: You design an investigation for a proposed factory near a village that relies on wells. The factory would use groundwater, and the available data are from only two wells 5 km apart.

options.text: Use the regional groundwater map to predict the effects and add the two wells for detail.
Interpolate between the two wells and add a safety margin to the predicted drawdown.
Add monitoring wells near the village and site, run a pumping test, and model drawdown.
Use the two wells to declare the supply plentiful for both the factory and the village.

basic.situation: You record daily rainfall from a rain gauge for a storm study. One morning you find the gauge overturned and cannot tell how much rain fell overnight.

options.text: Mark the reading as missing and set the gauge upright for the next day.
Mark the reading missing, note why, compare with nearby gauges for reference, and tell your supervisor.
Enter the nearest official station's rainfall in the record as your own gauge's reading.
Enter the average of the last three days' rainfall in the record for that day.

advanced.situation: You lead a study of permafrost thaw at a mountain research site run with an overseas team. Instruments show ground temperature rising, but a near-surface sensor reads values that jump up and down.

options.text: Include the surface sensor's raw values and report the thaw rate as firmly confirmed.
Base the thaw estimate on the deeper sensors and mention the surface sensor in the notes.
Smooth the surface sensor's values with a moving average and include them in the analysis.
Check the sensor and logger, compare with neighbouring sensors, and flag suspect periods first.

basic.situation: You review treated water test results for a small town supply. One sample shows turbidity above the standard, while the next day's sample is normal.

options.text: Report the high reading to your supervisor and note that the next day was normal.
Flag the high reading, check the sampling records, and report it with the next day's result.
Treat the high reading as a one-off and record the supply as compliant for the week.
Remove the high reading from the dataset because the following day's sample was normal.

advanced.situation: You review an application to build a small hydroelectric plant on a stream. The flow data cover only one wet year, and a village downstream uses the stream for irrigation.

options.text: Recommend approval, since hydroelectric power is a public benefit and the data look adequate.
Recommend denial because the data cover one year and the village depends on the stream.
Recommend approval with a condition that flows for irrigation are maintained throughout the year.
Recommend further investigation: multi-year flow data and an irrigation impact study before any decision.

basic.situation: You install a water level logger in a stream with an engineer's guidance. The engineer leaves, and you find the logger's clock is set to the wrong time zone.

options.text: Set the clock to local time, log the change, and check it against a manual reading.
Set the clock to local time and log the change in the install record.
Leave the clock as it is and note the offset to apply when processing the data.
Install the logger as it is and assume the engineer set the time zone on purpose.

advanced.situation: You develop a river flow prediction model. It fits last year's data very well, but it overpredicts flows in the driest months and has not been tested on an extreme flood year.

options.text: Add an adjustment factor for the dry months and release the model for all seasons.
Test on other years including a flood, study the dry bias, and document limits.
Release the model for general flow forecasting and note the dry-month overprediction in the guide.
Release the model for flood warnings, since it fits last year's data so closely.

basic.situation: A homeowner phones to ask whether he may drill a private well in his garden. You know a permit is usually needed but are unsure of the exact local rules.

options.text: Tell him a permit is needed and give the fee you remember from last year.
Tell him to check the water office website for the current rules before drilling.
Tell him private wells in gardens do not need permits, so he can start drilling.
Say a permit is usually needed, take his details, and ask a senior to call him.

advanced.situation: A contractor sealing an abandoned well used an unapproved sealing material to save time. The well is next to a village water source, and the contractor says the work is finished.

options.text: Inspect the well, order resealing with approved material, document the breach, and notify the owner.
Issue a written warning to the contractor and ask them to explain the material used.
Record the well as properly sealed, since the contractor has already completed the work.
Accept the work after a test shows the water source is not affected at present.

basic.situation: You gather data at a construction site beside a stream after a villager complains the water is muddy. The contractor says the site's silt fence is working.

options.text: Photograph the fence, take turbidity readings upstream and downstream, and report to your supervisor.
Tell the villager the water is safe to drink since the silt fence is in place.
Accept the contractor's statement and record the complaint as resolved in the register.
Take a turbidity reading downstream and report it to your supervisor with the complaint.

advanced.situation: You lead a project to reduce erosion and sediment in a river basin where farms, logging and a quarry all contribute. The funding is enough to tackle one source this year.

options.text: Tackle the quarry first because it is the easiest source to regulate and monitor.
Tackle the farms first because they cover the largest land area in the basin.
Spread the funding thinly across all three sources and report all three as addressed.
Measure each source's sediment load, treat the largest first, and schedule the others for later.

basic.situation: You classify satellite imagery into a land cover map for a district. A cloud covers part of the image, and the classifier labels cloud shadows as water.

options.text: Reclassify the shadow areas as forest by hand so that the map looks complete.
Leave the shadows classed as water, since the map is for general use.
Mask the cloud and shadow areas and mark them as no data on the final map.
Mask cloud and shadows, fill them from a clearer date, and record this in the metadata.

advanced.situation: You develop an automated routine to remove ground vegetation effects from drone imagery. It works well on test plots but fails on steep, shaded slopes.

options.text: Test on varied slopes and shade, adjust the routine, and document where it fails.
Apply the routine everywhere and report all results as validated on the test plots.
Use the routine on flat areas and process the steep slopes by hand instead.
Apply the routine everywhere and flag steep slopes in the results as lower confidence.

basic.situation: You analyse satellite vegetation index values for a district following your supervisor's instructions. Your output shows a sharp drop in one month that your supervisor did not expect.

options.text: Remove the month from the analysis, since your supervisor did not expect a drop.
Replace the month's values with the average of the months either side and carry on.
Check the raw images for cloud or sensor errors in that month, then tell your supervisor.
Tell your supervisor about the drop and ask whether it should stay in the analysis.

advanced.situation: You manage a project combining radar and optical satellite images to map flooded areas. The two sources disagree over a large area where trees stand in water.

options.text: Use the radar result for the flooded forest, since radar can see through leaves.
Show the larger of the two flooded areas in the final map and label it verified.
Check both against field photos and flood records, set rules by land cover, and document them.
Use the optical result everywhere, since it is easier to explain to the client.

basic.situation: You use satellite bands to detect surface water in a delta region. Your water index marks some wet rice fields as lakes.

options.text: Report the water map as accurate, checking it against the same image used to make it.
Add an elevation layer, check against known lakes and fields, and explain the method.
Report the water map and note that wet rice fields may appear as lakes.
Remove all small water areas from the map, since lakes in the delta are usually large.

advanced.situation: You use satellite data to estimate forest loss for a carbon tracking report. Your estimate is 8% higher than the project developer's figure, and the developer wants the lower one used.

options.text: Check your estimate on high-resolution images for a sample and report it if it holds.
Use the developer's lower figure since they know the project area better than you.
Adjust your classification settings until your estimate matches the developer's lower reported figure.
Compare definitions and methods, check samples on high-resolution images, and present both figures with reasons.

basic.situation: You join fieldwork to collect ground reference points for a land cover map. Your GPS shows poor accuracy under thick canopy at the next point.

options.text: Leave out this point and move on to the next one on the list.
Record the point with the reading shown and note that accuracy was poor.
Record the planned coordinates as the point's location, since you are standing near it.
Take a fix from a nearby gap, record the offset, and note the accuracy.

advanced.situation: You maintain a network of ground weather and soil moisture stations used to check satellite data. Two stations stopped sending data, and the next scheduled visit is in three weeks.

options.text: Fill the gap from satellite data and mark it, though that weakens the check.
Wait for the scheduled visit, since remote checks suggest nothing urgent has failed.
Estimate the missing readings from nearby stations and store them as measured data.
Check the dashboard for faults, visit the two stations early, and flag the data gap.

basic.situation: You organise a folder of geospatial files for a project. Several files have no information on their source, date or coordinate system.

options.text: Fill in the missing metadata with the most likely values, based on the other files.
Rename the files clearly and add a note to the folder listing which have missing metadata.
Trace each file's source, fill in the metadata, and flag any you cannot trace.
Move the files lacking metadata into an archive folder to keep the project folder tidy.

advanced.situation: You monitor data quality from a drone mapping team. Over two weeks, the images show growing blur, and the team blames wind.

options.text: Ask the team to fly on calmer days and check whether the blur reduces.
Review flight logs, wind records and camera settings, test the camera, and act on the findings.
Sharpen the blurred images with software and pass them on as original data.
Accept the wind explanation and add a blur warning to the metadata of affected images.

basic.situation: You prepare a short report of a mapping project for a client meeting. The map's overall accuracy is 82%, one class is much weaker, and your lead says clients prefer a single number.

options.text: Round the accuracy up to 90% in the slide because the client expects a high figure.
Give the figure for the three strongest classes to show what the map does well.
Give the single 82% figure and keep the table available if the client asks.
Give the 82% figure, name the weaker class, and offer the full table on request.

advanced.situation: You direct testing of new image processing software before the team switches over. It runs faster, but results differ slightly from the old software on 5% of test images.

options.text: Run both programs side by side on live work for a month, then decide.
Check those images against ground data, find the cause, and set acceptance criteria before switching.
Switch to the new software now, since a 5% difference is within normal variation.
Switch to the new software and delete the old results to avoid confusing users.

basic.situation: You study monthly retail sales data for a ministry unit. This month's figure is 15% above trend, and you are unsure whether it reflects a real surge or a data change.

options.text: Adjust the figure down to the trend value and report it as the month's result.
Check the source for coverage changes, compare related series, and report the figure with your findings.
Report the figure as a strong month and mention it may be revised.
Leave the figure out of the summary until next month's data confirms the trend.

advanced.situation: Your team's forecasts of state tax revenue use different growth assumptions across departments, so results cannot be compared. You are asked to draft a common forecasting standard.

options.text: Ask each department to label its assumptions as standard and keep using its own method.
Adopt the assumptions of the largest department as the standard for every department.
Review the assumptions, propose shared baselines with allowed variations, and test them on last year.
Set one fixed growth rate for all departments, taken from the national average figure.

basic.situation: You review a think-tank paper arguing that a minimum wage rise will raise unemployment. Your supervisor asks for a summary of its economic argument.

options.text: Write that the paper is biased because of its funder and leave the evidence unreviewed.
Summarise the argument and evidence, list its assumptions and gaps, and note where other studies differ.
Give the paper's conclusion in one line, since your supervisor wants the answer quickly.
Summarise the paper's main argument and its conclusion in a short paragraph for your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You assess the economic impact of a proposed tax on sugary drinks. Studies elsewhere show demand falls, but local data on low-income households' spending are limited.

options.text: Report the average impact from other countries' studies and add that local data are limited.
Report the impact on revenue and health, and leave the low-income question for later.
Assume low-income households cut spending the same as others and report that as a finding.
Estimate impacts using elasticities from comparable studies, test low-income scenarios, and state the data gaps.

basic.situation: You draft the data section of a technical report on household income. Your supervisor's table gives mean income, while the survey notes say the distribution is highly skewed.

options.text: Report the mean as the typical household income, as the table gives it.
Report the mean as given and add a footnote that the distribution is skewed.
Add the median beside the mean, explain the skew, and check the wording with your supervisor.
Report a trimmed average that removes the top earners and call it the mean.

advanced.situation: You are asked to write an expert report for a competition dispute. The law firm that hired you suggests dropping an analysis showing their client's market share is higher than they claim.

options.text: Drop the analysis from the report and revise the market share figure to the client's claim.
Include the analysis and add a note that other methods give lower market share estimates.
Base the report on the firm's preferred methods and keep the other analysis in your files.
Include the analysis with its limits, and tell the firm your report must reflect all findings.

basic.situation: At a community briefing, you explain how a new road toll will affect household costs. A resident asks why her monthly costs will rise by RM60 when the notice says RM40.

options.text: Tell her the notice figure is the official one and her own calculation is mistaken.
Explain that the notice figure is an average and ask her to check the details online.
Explain that RM40 is an average, her trips may differ, and offer to work out hers.
Tell her the toll will cost RM40 for everyone and her trips do not matter.

advanced.situation: You testify at a legislative hearing on a proposed rent control law. Your cost-benefit estimate shows mixed effects, and a committee member wants a simple yes or no on whether it helps.

options.text: Set out tenant and landlord effects, give the net range, and name the key assumptions.
Say the effects are mixed and refer the committee to your written report.
Answer with a firm yes or no based on the larger of the two estimated effects.
Answer yes and tell the committee that the estimates show no downside for landlords at all.

basic.situation: You assist in a first-year economics tutorial. A student claims prices fall whenever supply rises, even in cases where demand rises more.

options.text: Explain that her claim holds when demand stays unchanged, but not when demand also moves.
Draw both curves, show supply and demand rising together, and ask her to predict the price.
Agree with her to keep the tutorial moving, since the lecturer will cover it later.
Tell her to check the textbook chapter on price changes and come back if still unsure.

advanced.situation: You supervise four students' research projects. Two projects need your data access approval this week, and one student has missed three meetings.

options.text: Approve the data requests on trust to free up time for the absent student.
Approve the data requests first, contact the absent student for a check-in, and fix meeting times.
Approve the data requests this week and wait for the absent student to contact you.
Meet the absent student first as long as needed, then handle approvals if time remains.

basic.situation: A small business owner asks whether raising prices by 10% will raise his profit. You have limited data on how his customers respond to price.

options.text: Explain it depends on customer response, estimate a range from his sales history, and state assumptions.
Tell him a 10% rise will raise profit by about 10%, since costs stay the same.
Tell him prices can safely be raised by 10% because competitors are doing the same.
Explain that the answer depends on how customers respond and suggest a trial in one shop.

advanced.situation: A state agency asks you to propose a plan to reduce volatility in local vegetable prices. Causes include weather shocks, middlemen margins and import dependence, on a limited budget.

options.text: Estimate each cause's contribution, rank options by cost and impact, and propose a phased plan.
Recommend a large subsidy for imports and report that it will end price volatility.
Recommend cutting middlemen margins by regulation, since they are the most visible cause of swings.
Focus on the weather-shock cause with storage and early-warning support, and review other causes later.

basic.situation: You calculate the costs and benefits of a rule requiring cleaner stoves in a district. Your supervisor gave you the compliance cost, but health benefits are listed as cases avoided, not in ringgit.

options.text: Pick a value per case that makes benefits exceed costs and present it as the standard.
Compare costs in ringgit with benefits as case counts and say benefits are larger.
Use a per-case value from a published study and state its source under the table.
Ask which value per case to use, apply it, and show the assumption and a range.

advanced.situation: You lead an assessment comparing three options to cut river pollution. A junior analyst's model shows option B as cheapest, but you notice it leaves out maintenance costs after year five.

options.text: Report option B as the cheapest option over its whole life, as the model shows.
Add the maintenance costs to the model yourself and send the updated results to the team.
Report option B as cheapest within five years and mention maintenance as a later issue.
Show the analyst the omission, add maintenance costs for all three options, and rerun it together.

basic.situation: You help draft a research plan to study how fishers respond to a fishing ban. Your supervisor wants a survey of 500 fishers, but the budget covers 300.

options.text: Draft the plan for 300 respondents and tell your supervisor that precision will be lower.
Draft the plan for 500 respondents and plan to find the extra budget later.
Check what 300 respondents can detect, sample by area, and ask your supervisor to decide.
Draft the plan for 300 respondents and report it as the 500-respondent design in the summary.

advanced.situation: You design a three-year research plan on wetland value for a multi-university team. A partner university asks to add a new data collection that would delay deliverables by six months.

options.text: Weigh the new data against the delay, agree milestone changes with the team, and update costs.
Accept the new collection and extend all deliverables by six months for every partner.
Add the new collection to the plan and keep the original deadlines in the reports.
Decline the new collection to protect the original timeline and tell the partner later.

basic.situation: You help identify sustainability goals for a resort's new building project. The resort wants goals guests can see, but the biggest environmental impact is in energy and waste behind the scenes.

options.text: Suggest a goal to become carbon neutral by next year, since it will be highly visible.
Suggest goals for energy and waste with measurable targets and send them to your lead.
Suggest measurable energy and waste goals plus one guest-visible goal, and consult your lead.
Suggest guest-visible goals such as reusable straws and a refill station, since they help the brand.

advanced.situation: You set a standard for how much sand can be extracted from a river each year. Construction demand is rising, and survey data on replenishment are uncertain.

options.text: Set the limit at the construction industry's expected demand and monitor the river bed.
Set no limit until the replenishment data are fully certain, and rely on voluntary industry reporting.
Set the limit below the low replenishment estimate, require monitoring, and revise it as data improve.
Set the limit at the central replenishment estimate and review it every five years.

basic.situation: You draft a summary of a study on fertiliser subsidies. The main finding is that farmer income rose by 4%, but the 95% range runs from -1% to 9%.

options.text: State the 4% average rise, give the range, and say the effect could be near zero.
State the 4% average rise and give the range in a table at the end.
State that incomes rose by up to 9% to make the result sound stronger.
State that incomes rose by 4% and describe the subsidy as effective for farmers.

advanced.situation: You write an economic impact statement for a proposed pesticide ban, to inform a ministry decision. The agrochemical industry has funded one of the studies you rely on.

options.text: Disclose the funding in a footnote and use the study as one of several sources.
Leave the study out of the statement, since industry-funded work cannot be trusted.
Disclose the funding, compare its methods with independent studies, and show results both ways.
Use the study's conclusions as they are and omit the funding details to avoid bias claims.

basic.situation: You run a forecast of electricity demand using your team's template. The template assumes 3% annual growth, but recent data show growth of 1%.

options.text: Run the template as given and describe the 3% growth as the observed trend.
Run it at 1% and 3% growth, show both, and ask your lead which to report.
Run the template as given and note in the report that recent growth was 1%.
Change the template to 1% and send the results on to the planning team.

advanced.situation: You build an integrated model linking fish stocks, fishing effort and market prices. It predicts stable stocks, but validation shows it misses sharp stock declines in two past years.

options.text: Study what drove the two declines, add the missing dynamics, and revalidate on separate years.
Report the stable prediction and state that the model missed two past declines.
Adjust the model parameters until it reproduces both declines and report it as validated.
Treat the two declines as one-off shocks and exclude those years from the validation.

basic.situation: You present simple findings on household water use to a small village group. A man asks you in front of everyone to say whether the price rise is fair.

options.text: Say you present data and cannot comment on whether the rise is fair.
Explain who pays more and who benefits, say fairness is a judgement, and invite their views.
Say fairness depends on your view and offer to show the cost data behind the rise.
Say the price rise is unfair, since the water company can easily afford to absorb it.

advanced.situation: You design a one-semester course on environmental economics for students with mixed maths backgrounds. A senior colleague suggests a heavy focus on advanced modelling.

options.text: Teach the course with minimal maths and describe the models in words throughout.
Build core concepts first, add optional modelling sessions, and check student backgrounds in week one.
Follow the colleague's suggestion and offer extra maths tutorials for the weaker students.
Teach the advanced models to everyone and move on if students struggle to follow along.

basic.situation: You enter survey answers into a data file. One respondent ticked two boxes on a question that allows one answer.

options.text: Flag the record, code a double response per the guide, and check with your supervisor.
Choose the box that matches the group's likely majority answer to keep the results consistent.
Choose the first box ticked, since respondents usually list their main answer first.
Leave the question blank for that respondent and note the reason in the data log.

advanced.situation: A client wants to know if their satisfaction score of 7.4 is better than last year's 7.2. Your output shows the difference is not statistically significant, and the client expects good news.

options.text: Say the gap is within error margins, show the interval, and advise on sample size.
Report that satisfaction improved from 7.2 to 7.4 and note that the sample was small.
Run the test again with a one-sided setting until the difference is significant, then report that.
Report that satisfaction is stable at about 7.3 and avoid overstating the change.

basic.situation: You are interviewing households by phone from a script. A respondent says she is busy and can answer only the first half now.

options.text: Fill in the second half with typical answers from similar households and mark the interview complete.
Record her answers, mark the interview partial, and offer a callback at a time she chooses.
Record her answers to the first half and end the call politely, thanking her.
Ask her the second half quickly in a faster voice so she can finish sooner.

advanced.situation: Your survey's response rate is 28% against a 45% target with two weeks left. Responses so far come mostly from urban respondents.

options.text: Break down response by area, target follow-up at low-response areas, and adjust contact times.
Weight the urban responses to represent rural areas and close the survey on time.
Send reminders to all non-respondents and extend the deadline by a week if allowed.
Ask staff to fill in forms for non-respondents from what they know of the households.

basic.situation: You help design a question on income for a household survey. Your team debates between asking for an exact amount and offering ranges.

options.text: Propose asking for exact amounts, since they allow more detailed analysis at the later stage.
Propose income ranges, since respondents usually find them less sensitive than exact amounts.
Propose estimating income from housing type and appliances to avoid asking the question at all.
Propose income bands with an optional exact-amount follow-up, and test the question on a few respondents.

advanced.situation: Midway through fieldwork, interviewers report that a question about religion is causing refusals, and some respondents are ending interviews. You can change the survey method.

options.text: Drop the religion question for the remaining interviews and analyse the others as planned.
Move the religion question to the end of the interview and tell all interviewers.
Let each interviewer decide whether to ask the question, and treat skipped ones as no answer.
Check refusals by question, test a reworded version, and roll it out with a methods note.

basic.situation: You prepare a fact sheet table of survey results by age group. The 60+ group has only 18 respondents, and your supervisor asks for percentages for each group.

options.text: Round the 60+ percentages to the nearest ten so they look steadier in the table.
Show percentages for all groups and add the number of respondents in a footnote.
Combine the 60+ group with the 45 to 59 group so the numbers look more reliable.
