Show percentages for all groups, flag the 60+ result as based on 18 people.

advanced.situation: You write a proposal to win a government survey project. The call asks for 5,000 interviews in 3 months, which your team believes is feasible only with a smaller sample.

options.text: Propose the smaller sample and explain clearly why 5,000 is not feasible in 3 months.
Propose 5,000 interviews and plan to ask for a deadline extension once the project starts.
Offer a plan for 5,000 interviews with realistic staffing and an alternative smaller sample, both priced.
Promise 5,000 interviews in 3 months and plan to count unfinished interviews as complete.

basic.situation: You record the details of how a survey sample was drawn for the methods file. Your notes show that 12% of selected addresses were replaced with nearby ones when interviewers could not reach them.

options.text: Record that the sample was drawn randomly, since replacements are a standard field practice.
Record the original selected addresses as the final sample to match the sampling plan.
Record the replacement rule, the 12% figure and the replaced addresses for later checks.
Record that addresses were drawn randomly and add a line noting some were replaced.

advanced.situation: You write a training manual for interviewers on a sensitive health survey. In pilot calls, interviewers explain questions in different ways, causing inconsistent answers.

options.text: Tell interviewers they may explain questions in whatever words they think will get an answer.
Add scripted wording, rules for allowed explanations, practice exercises, and call monitoring to the manual.
Add scripted wording for each question and ask interviewers to read exactly what is written.
Add a short section reminding interviewers to stay consistent and use their own judgement.

basic.situation: A client asks for a survey on customer satisfaction but cannot say who the customers are or what decisions the results will inform.

options.text: Decide the target group yourself from what looks sensible and start designing the survey.
Agree to a standard satisfaction survey and ask the client to send details later.
Ask for a customer list and suggest a standard satisfaction questionnaire from your files.
Ask who the customers are, what decisions depend on the results, and when they are needed.

advanced.situation: You must hire and train 30 data collectors in two weeks for a rural survey in Sabah. Many applicants are enthusiastic but have no experience, and training time is short.

options.text: Hire experienced collectors from other projects and shorten training since they know the work.
Hire the 30 most enthusiastic applicants and give all of them a one-day lecture.
Select applicants for local language skills, train them with practice interviews, and keep a reserve.
Hire the first 30 applicants and start fieldwork on day one, training them as they go.

basic.situation: You use a standard rating scale to assess customer service staff for a client company. One manager rates every person 5 out of 5, with no variation.

options.text: Use the ratings as given, since the manager knows the staff better than you do.
Include the manager's ratings in the analysis and tell your supervisor they show no variation.
Lower some of the manager's ratings to match the other managers' averages before analysing.
Flag the identical ratings, ask the manager for behaviour examples, and note it in the report.

advanced.situation: You validate a new personality-based screening test for a bank. It predicts job performance slightly, but it scores one ethnic group lower on average.

options.text: Report the test as valid because it predicts performance, and note the group difference as small.
Remove data from the lower-scoring group so the test results look fair across groups.
Test for bias, try alternative items or cut scores, and advise the bank on use.
Recommend the bank use the test alongside interviews so that it carries less weight.

basic.situation: You help identify training needs for a team of eight technicians. Their supervisor says they all need communication training but gives no examples.

options.text: Ask for specific incidents, observe a few shifts, and check findings with the team and supervisor.
Write the needs analysis from the supervisor's comments and record it as based on staff input.
Recommend a standard communication course from the training catalogue for all eight technicians.
Survey the technicians on which communication skills they find difficult and summarise the answers.

advanced.situation: You are asked to train a client's HR staff to run structured interviews. Several senior HR staff say unstructured chats work fine, and attendance is low.

options.text: Shorten the training to one hour so senior staff are more willing to attend.
Tell senior staff that attendance is required by management and will count in reviews.
Share evidence on structured interviews, practise on real cases, and agree how seniors will apply it.
Hold the training for the staff who attend and send the materials to the others.

basic.situation: You interview a warehouse worker as part of a job analysis. She describes a lifting task that your supervisor's job description does not mention.

options.text: Ask her to describe the task, record weight and frequency, and tell your supervisor.
Leave the lifting task out of your notes, since it is not in the job description.
Tell her the lifting task is not part of her job and she should stop.
Note the lifting task in your interview record and mention it to your supervisor later.

advanced.situation: You lead a study of whether a leadership programme raised team productivity at a factory. Teams that joined the programme were chosen by managers.

options.text: Compare productivity of programme teams with other teams after the programme and report the gap.
Survey programme participants about their satisfaction and report that productivity has clearly improved.
Report the productivity rise in programme teams as the programme's effect, since it followed the programme.
Compare teams before and after, adjust for team selection, and state the limits.

basic.situation: You draft a summary of survey findings on employee burnout for a client. The data show higher burnout in night shift workers, based on 25 people.

options.text: Report the higher night shift burnout, state the sample of 25, and say it needs confirming.
Report the higher night shift burnout and add a line that the sample was small.
Report that night shift work causes burnout, since the data point in that direction.
Report night shift burnout as a major company-wide problem to make the findings more important.

advanced.situation: A junior colleague wants to publish a white paper on remote work and productivity. Their analysis is sound, but they write long technical sentences and bury the main finding on page nine.

options.text: Show them how to lead with the finding, rewrite a section together, and let them revise.
Tell them readers will find the main finding if they read the whole paper.
Move the main finding to the first page yourself and send the revised paper back.
Rewrite the paper and publish it under your name, since you did most of the work.

basic.situation: You assist in a small team meeting about moving to a new scheduling system. Two members are vocal against it, while the others stay silent.

options.text: Invite quieter members to share, record every concern on a board, and sort them together.
Let the two vocal members explain their concerns fully and record them for the manager.
Ask the two vocal members to leave so the meeting can finish on time.
Move the discussion to the benefits of the new system to calm the vocal members.

advanced.situation: A company plans to merge two departments with different cultures within three months. Early surveys show staff in both fear job losses, and the CEO wants to announce the plan this week.

options.text: Advise telling staff that no jobs will be lost, to calm their fears before the merger.
Advise delaying the announcement until all details are finalised, to avoid unsettling staff.
Advise announcing this week and offering staff a question-and-answer session some weeks later.
Advise announcing with a clear timeline and job facts, plus staff forums and morale checks.

basic.situation: An employee asks you for career advice after being passed over for promotion. She is upset and wants to know whether to resign.

options.text: Listen and tell her that many people feel this way and that it passes in time.
Listen, help her list her goals and options, and suggest seeking feedback before deciding.
Offer to speak to her manager for her and say she is considering resigning.
Suggest she resign and look for a company that values her work more.

advanced.situation: You coach a senior executive whom his team rates poorly for listening. He insists the ratings are unfair, and his CEO wants progress within three months.

options.text: Agree the ratings may be unfair and coach him on managing his team's impressions.
Tell the CEO the executive is resistant and recommend replacing him within three months.
Review the feedback with him, pick two behaviours to change, and agree how to measure progress.
Share the full ratings with him and suggest he apologise to his team.

basic.situation: During an intake interview, a client describes low mood, poor sleep and loss of interest for three weeks after a job loss. You are asked to identify possible concerns under supervision.

options.text: Write a diagnosis of major depression in the file and start treatment planning on that basis.
Tell the client the low mood is a normal reaction to job loss and will pass.
Record the symptoms and timing and send your notes to your supervisor for review.
Record symptoms and timing, check the diagnostic manual, and discuss options with your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You help plan a psychological service for a hospital's cancer ward with psychiatrists and nurses. The ward has no budget for new staff, and demand for support is high.

options.text: Propose a leaflet and a helpline number for patients, since no extra staff can be hired.
Propose individual therapy sessions for all patients and ask hospital management for new staff.
Propose that nurses give psychological treatment on their own, using a written guide.
Map patient needs, propose stepped support with trained nurses and groups, and agree referral rules.

basic.situation: A new client asks whether counseling will fix his anger problems in a few sessions, and he doubts it will work.

options.text: Tell him that counseling is guaranteed to work if he commits to six sessions.
Tell him that a few sessions will usually solve anger problems if he follows advice.
Explain that counseling can help with anger and invite him to try a few sessions.
Explain what counseling involves and how long change takes, then agree goals and a review point.

advanced.situation: A seven-year-old child has stopped speaking at school after a family loss. Talking therapy has not worked, and you are considering play therapy, in which you have limited training.

options.text: Continue talking therapy for a few more months and wait for the child to respond.
Use play therapy techniques you have read about and tell the parents you are experienced.
Refer the child to a play therapist and stop your own sessions until they respond.
Consult a trained play therapist, arrange supervision or referral, and involve the parents in the plan.

basic.situation: You take a first interview with a client who gives short, vague answers about her family and seems reluctant. Your supervisor has asked you to complete the history form.

options.text: Complete the form with the answers she gave and mark the unanswered sections for next time.
Press her for fuller answers, explaining that the form must be finished today.
Fill in the blank sections with likely answers based on what other clients report.
Explain why you ask, let her skip some questions, and return to them as trust builds.

advanced.situation: A client in session says she has been thinking about ending her life and has a plan involving medication at home. She asks you to keep it secret.

options.text: Promise confidentiality as she asks and keep the conversation out of the formal file.
Assess intent, plan and means, explain the limits of confidentiality, and set up safety steps today.
Talk through her feelings, ask her to promise to stay safe, and book a session soon.
Give her a helpline number and suggest she talk to a family member about the medication.

basic.situation: A client you are counseling for stress mentions severe headaches and blurred vision that began last month. You are not a medical doctor.

options.text: Suggest she see a doctor soon and continue the stress sessions as planned.
Treat the symptoms as stress-related and teach relaxation techniques at the next two sessions.
Explain these symptoms need a medical check, help book a doctor's visit, and tell your supervisor.
Advise her to take pain medicine from the pharmacy for the headaches and carry on.

advanced.situation: You supervise an intern whose session notes are well written, but you notice she reassures clients too quickly when they describe distressing events, and a client has complained.

options.text: Review a session recording with her, discuss early reassurance, and agree on practice goals.
Reply to the complaint yourself saying the intern was acting on your instructions.
Tell her to reassure clients less and check her notes again next week.
Assign her cases with milder problems for a few months until the complaint is forgotten.

basic.situation: After a session, you write progress notes. The client mentioned a conflict with her employer and asked you not to record it because she fears others will read it.

options.text: Leave this session's progress notes unwritten for now to respect her request about privacy.
Record relevant content factually, tell her how notes are stored, and note her privacy concern.
Write full notes and send a copy to her employer's HR to help resolve the conflict.
Write brief notes on the clinical themes and leave out the employer details she mentioned.

advanced.situation: A court asks for your written evaluation of a defendant's competence to stand trial. Your assessment is incomplete because he missed the second session, and the court date is close.

options.text: Tell the court the assessment is incomplete, state what was covered, and request a short extension.
Submit a report from the first session and state that the second session was missed.
Use the defendant's lawyer's account of the second session to complete the report on time.
Submit the report based on the first session and give a firm conclusion on competence.

basic.situation: You administer a standard cognitive test to a client. Midway, a noisy construction drill starts outside and the client says she cannot concentrate.

options.text: Finish the test and score it normally, since the standard procedure is already set.
Continue the test and give her extra time on the later items to make up.
Continue the test and note on the score sheet that there was noise outside.
Pause the test, record the interruption, and move to a quieter room or reschedule.

advanced.situation: A university department asks you to discuss a therapy approach you use and share occupational information for a student programme. They also ask for anonymised client examples.

options.text: Share real case files with names blacked out, as the clients agreed to treatment generally.
Share anonymised examples with ages and occupations removed, but leave dates and places as they are.
Share the approach and occupational information and decline to give any client examples.
Share the approach and general occupational information, and offer composite examples that cannot identify any client.

basic.situation: You administer a standard reading test to a Year 3 pupil under supervision. Halfway through, he says he feels sick and wants to stop.

options.text: Finish the test quickly by skipping the remaining items and scoring what is done.
Pause the test, check on him, and reschedule with a note if he cannot continue.
Let him rest for a few minutes, then finish the test and note the break.
Encourage him to finish and record the full score as if there had been no problem.

advanced.situation: You interpret test results, teacher reports and parent input to decide whether a pupil is eligible for special education support. The test score is borderline, but teachers report clear difficulties daily.

options.text: Weigh all sources together, observe him in class, and base your recommendation on the combined evidence.
Decide by the test score, since it is the standard and most objective measure of eligibility.
Recommend support, since teacher reports show clear difficulties, and note the borderline score.
Raise the pupil's score a few points to meet the cut-off so he receives support.

basic.situation: You help draft an individualised educational plan for a pupil with attention difficulties. The teacher wants specific goals, while the parents have asked for more time outdoors.

options.text: Draft the plan from the teacher's goals and add the parents' request later if time allows.
Copy goals from another pupil's plan and paste them in after changing the name.
Draft measurable goals from the teacher's list and add the parents' request as a note.
Draft measurable goals, include the parents' outdoor time request, and review it with your senior.

advanced.situation: You lead the development of a schoolwide inclusion programme. Some teachers fear extra workload, and parents of other pupils worry that attention will shift away from their children.

options.text: Delay the programme until teachers and parents agree on it fully, which may take a year.
Hear teachers' and parents' concerns, pilot in two classes with teacher support, and share the results.
Launch the programme school-wide with a briefing for teachers and a letter to all parents.
Launch the programme and tell teachers that taking part is a condition of their contracts.

basic.situation: You file a pupil's confidential counselling record. The school clerk asks to keep it in the general office cabinet because your room is far away.

options.text: Agree to the general cabinet, since the clerk has handled school files for years.
Keep the record in your locked cabinet, explain why, and offer the clerk a non-confidential register.
Give the clerk a copy of the record so it can be found when needed.
Keep the record in a sealed envelope in the office cabinet, marked for your opening.

advanced.situation: A teacher tells you a pupil has bruises and said her father hits her. The teacher wants to keep it quiet because the family is respected in the community.

options.text: Record what was said and seen, report to the proper authority, and support the pupil.
Agree with the teacher to keep the matter within the school and record nothing.
Speak to the father first to hear his side before deciding whether to report.
Report to the authority and tell the teacher not to contact the family until advised.

basic.situation: A mother tells you at the school gate that her son's behaviour at home has worsened since the parents separated. She is tearful and asks what to do.

options.text: Listen and reassure her that children usually adjust to separation after some months.
Tell her the father's behaviour is the cause and that she should limit his visits.
Listen, acknowledge her worry, suggest simple supports, and offer a meeting with the counsellor.
Advise her on what to say to her son and how to handle the father.

advanced.situation: After a pupil's parent dies suddenly, many classmates and teachers are distressed. You are asked to set up a response and guide two junior counsellors who have not handled a loss like this.

options.text: Hand the two junior counsellors a loss-support guide and let them run the sessions.
Set up group and individual support, brief the junior counsellors, and arrange regular debriefs with them.
Run all the support sessions yourself and keep the junior counsellors out of them.
Tell the class what happened in detail so everyone understands why the pupil is absent.

basic.situation: In a staff meeting, a teacher asks why a bright pupil cannot sit still in class. You know some basics about child development but are not an expert on attention problems.

options.text: Tell the teacher that bright pupils who cannot sit still are usually just misbehaving.
Share basic points on attention and tell the teacher to try seating him near the front.
Share basic points on attention, say what needs assessment, and offer to observe him.
Tell the teacher he probably has attention deficit disorder and should be assessed for it.

advanced.situation: You lead a professional development session for teachers on behaviour management. The principal asks you to explain why suspensions have risen, and the data show most come from one teacher's classes.

options.text: Tell the staff that suspensions are mainly a problem of one teacher's classroom management.
Show the data with the teacher's name on the slide so the staff understand the cause.
Present the school-wide suspension data in the session and leave the individual pattern aside.
Present the school-wide data, raise the one-teacher pattern privately with the principal, and propose support.

basic.situation: You help collect attendance data to evaluate a school's breakfast programme. Records from two classes are missing for the first month.

options.text: Use the second month's attendance for the two classes as an estimate for the first month.
Fill in the missing attendance with the average of the other classes and report it normally.
Analyse the other classes and mention in the report that two classes had missing records.
Note the missing classes and weeks, ask teachers for the registers, and report the gaps.

advanced.situation: You design the evaluation of a schoolwide behaviour programme across eight schools. Principals want quick results and suggest using suspension counts as the only measure.

options.text: Use suspension counts as asked, since principals can act on them quickly and easily.
Use suspension counts and add a pupil survey at the end of the year.
Use whichever measure shows the programme working in each school and report those results.
Combine suspension, attendance and survey measures, set baselines first, and agree reporting dates with principals.

basic.situation: A patient brought in after a motorbike fall is alert but repeats the same questions every few minutes and cannot recall the accident. You are asked to note signs for your supervisor.

options.text: Tell the family the patient has a concussion and will recover in a few days.
Record the memory lapses, orientation and speech with times, and report them to your supervisor.
Note that the patient seems confused and tell your supervisor at the end of the shift.
Allow the patient to leave with relatives because he looks alert, and note it afterwards.

advanced.situation: A 62-year-old patient shows memory loss and mood changes, with a history of heavy alcohol use and a past head injury. Scans show mild changes, and his family wants one clear diagnosis today.

options.text: Tell the family the diagnosis is dementia so they can start planning care.
Give the diagnosis the family hopes for, a treatable condition, to spare them distress today.
Attribute the memory loss to alcohol use, which is the most likely cause, and plan treatment.
Explain that several factors may contribute, assess each, and give a working formulation with follow-up.

basic.situation: You administer a standard memory test to an older patient. He gets frustrated, says the test is pointless, and starts to give random answers.

options.text: Change the test items to easier ones so he feels successful and finishes the test.
Take a break, acknowledge his frustration, explain the test's purpose, and resume if he agrees.
Encourage him to try harder and continue, noting his frustration on the score sheet.
Stop the test and record the random answers as his score for the test.

advanced.situation: A patient who is deaf and uses sign language needs neuropsychological assessment, but your standard tests rely on spoken instructions.

options.text: Give the standard tests with written instructions and score them against the hearing norms.
Use the standard tests with a family member signing the instructions and note this.
Use a qualified interpreter, pick suitable tests, and state any adaptations in the report.
Give the nonverbal sections of the standard tests and report the findings as complete.

basic.situation: You draft a clinical summary after a patient's testing. The memory scores are low, but your supervisor's notes say the patient was anxious and slept poorly the night before.

options.text: Report the scores and recommend retesting at a later date when the patient is well rested.
Leave out the supervisor's notes and report the low scores as evidence of a memory disorder.
Report the scores as showing memory impairment and mention the anxiety in a footnote.
Report the scores, include the anxiety and poor sleep, and say they may have lowered results.

advanced.situation: You review a colleague's neuropsychological report for a legal case. It states permanent brain damage, but the test data included inconsistent effort indicators that the report does not mention.

options.text: Sign off the report and add a comment that effort indicators should be discussed in court.
Raise the effort indicators with the colleague informally and leave the final report as written.
Ask the colleague to address the effort indicators, recheck the conclusion, and hold sign-off.
Sign off the report, since the colleague is senior and the legal deadline is close.

basic.situation: You help create a recovery plan for a patient with attention problems after a stroke. The patient wants to return to driving soon, but his attention tests are still poor.

options.text: Tell the patient he may drive short distances in the daytime while he does the exercises.
Include attention exercises with goals, explain why driving waits for reassessment, and review with your supervisor.
Include driving as a goal for next month and plan weekly practice drives with his family.
Include attention exercises with goals and tell the patient to discuss driving with his doctor.

advanced.situation: You supervise recovery plans for patients with progressive disease, where baselines are needed to detect decline. Different clinicians use different tests and timings, so changes are hard to compare.

options.text: Circulate the preferred test list and ask clinicians to follow it where they can.
Let each clinician keep their own tests and convert the scores to a common scale later.
Set a standard baseline test set and schedule, train clinicians, and audit some cases.
Use the most recent test results for each patient as the baseline for decline.

basic.situation: A patient's daughter asks you to explain his test results, which show mild memory difficulties. She is worried and asks whether he has Alzheimer's disease.

options.text: Explain what the results show and do not show, say the doctor will discuss diagnosis.
Explain the results in simple words and tell her to ask the doctor about a diagnosis.
Tell her mild memory difficulties are a normal part of ageing and nothing to worry about.
Tell her the results point to early Alzheimer's and that she should plan for care.

advanced.situation: You lead a workshop for families of patients with traumatic brain injury. One father angrily says his son is doing this on purpose, referring to his irritability and poor planning.

options.text: Tell him his view is mistaken and he should attend the next session to learn more.
Acknowledge his frustration, explain how frontal injury affects mood and planning, and offer a private talk.
Share the son's test results with the group to show that his behaviour is not deliberate.
Explain to the whole group that irritability after brain injury is not deliberate behaviour.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to attend a workshop on a new cognitive screening tool and read two recent papers on it. The tool's maker is paying for the workshop.

options.text: Attend the workshop, read both papers, and summarise the tool's main strengths for your supervisor.
Attend the workshop, read both papers, look for independent evaluations, and summarise for your supervisor.
Recommend the tool to your supervisor on the basis of the maker's own accuracy figures.
Attend the workshop and summarise the maker's slides and handouts for your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You lead a small study of a new rehabilitation technique. A colleague you mentor suggests dropping patients who did not improve in the first month to show a clearer effect.

options.text: Drop the patients who did not improve and describe the sample as consecutive patients.
Tell him to keep all patients in the analysis because the journal will require it.
Explain how this biases results, show him analysis including all patients, and plan the method together.
Report both analyses and let readers decide which one reflects the technique better.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to screen a 70-year-old man whose family reports growing forgetfulness. His scores look mildly low, but he was tired and anxious during testing.

options.text: Mark anxiety and fatigue as possible factors and ask your supervisor to plan a retest.
Book a repeat session for when he is rested and compare the results yourself.
Record early dementia as the likely cause, since the family has noticed the decline.
Tell the family the scores point to dementia so they can start planning ahead.

advanced.situation: A patient has episodes of shaking and blank staring. Her scan is normal and she is under stress. You must judge whether the episodes are psychogenic or seizure-related.

options.text: Advise her family to treat every episode as a seizure and restrict her activities.
Conclude the episodes are stress-related since the scan is normal and refer her to counseling.
Request video-EEG monitoring and compare her described episodes with the recording before giving an opinion.
Review her diary and the neurologist's notes, then give a provisional view in your report.

basic.situation: You are giving a memory and attention battery to a child. Halfway through, she says she is tired and starts giving short answers.

options.text: Skip the remaining subtests and score the completed ones as if the battery was finished.
Offer a short break, note the change in her effort, and continue the standard instructions.
Continue testing at the usual pace and mention her fatigue to your supervisor afterward.
Rephrase the questions in simpler words to keep her answering and finish the battery today.

advanced.situation: A referral asks about attention and language after a mild stroke. The clinic's usual battery is long and the patient tires within an hour. You must choose the tests.

options.text: Run the clinic's usual full battery in one sitting and note fatigue in the report.
Give a brief screening test, then recommend a full battery if the results look low.
Pick shorter, targeted attention and language tests with good norms, and split them over two visits.
Give a quick screening test and write that the stroke has not affected thinking.

basic.situation: Your mentor asks you to draft a short summary of a client's test results. One score looks far lower than all the others, and you are not sure why.

options.text: Add the low score with a brief remark that it may need checking later.
Leave the low score out and let your mentor spot the gap during review.
Average the low score with the others so the summary reads smoothly for the reader.
Include the low score, mark the gap in your draft, and ask your mentor.

advanced.situation: As the senior reviewer, you read a junior colleague's report that blames a patient's poor scores on low motivation. The test data show validity indicators were never checked.

options.text: Soften the motivation sentence to say effort may have varied and sign off the report.
Run the validity indicators yourself and add the results as an appendix to the report.
Release the report as written because the colleague saw the patient and knows the case.
Ask them to check validity indicators and revise the conclusion before the report is released.

basic.situation: A patient with memory problems after a head injury keeps missing appointments. Your supervisor asks you to help set up a simple recovery plan.

options.text: Mark the missed appointments as non-compliance in the file and close the plan.
Draft reminders and a daily routine card, then review the plan with your supervisor.
Share a standard memory tips handout with the family and book a review visit.
Tell the patient to write everything down and call the clinic if appointments are missed.

advanced.situation: A man with early Parkinson-related dementia is expected to decline over years. The team asks you to set baseline measures so his progress can be tracked.

options.text: Begin testing once his symptoms get worse, so the scores show clear change.
Choose tests with alternate forms, record current scores, and schedule repeat testing every six months.
Record baseline scores from one brief screening test and compare them next year.
Rely on the family's description of his daily changes and review it each year.

basic.situation: A patient's wife asks what a diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment means. Your supervisor is in another session and the family is waiting.

options.text: Explain the results in simple terms, check her understanding, and book a supervisor visit.
Tell her the condition usually turns into dementia, so the family should prepare early.
Suggest she looks up the term online and writes down questions for the next visit.
Give her the printed leaflet on cognitive impairment and say the clinic will call later.

advanced.situation: You supervise a psychology intern who will lead a family session about a young patient's brain injury. The mother is angry and blames the hospital.

options.text: Plan the session with the intern, co-lead the opening part, and review it together afterward.
Give the intern a script and ask for a short summary the next day.
Agree with the mother that the hospital was at fault to calm her down.
Let the intern lead alone, since handling difficult families is how interns learn the role.

basic.situation: Your clinic offers a free workshop on a new memory test on the same day as your report deadline. Your supervisor has said you are free to attend.

options.text: Attend the workshop and copy last month's report text into the new one to save time.
Ask for a short extension, attend the workshop, and share your notes with the team.
Attend the workshop and finish the report late at night so both get done.
Skip the workshop and finish the report, then read the slides when you have time.

advanced.situation: You are asked to run an in-service session for colleagues on new research about cognitive testing in older adults. You have two weeks and know the topic well.

options.text: Share a reading list and invite colleagues to discuss it at the next meeting.
Choose two recent studies, relate them to your clinic's cases, and ask colleagues for questions beforehand.
Present the key points from a review article you read last year, with slides.
Present a manufacturer's brochure about the test, since it summarizes the research neatly for staff.

basic.situation: You are analyzing a household survey on neighborhood trust. One district shows far higher trust than the rest, and your supervisor is waiting for the summary.

options.text: Check the district's sample size and collection method, then report the result with a caveat.
Report the district's trust level as the main finding, since it is the strongest result.
Remove the district from the results so the overall pattern looks consistent for the summary.
Mention the district as unusual in the summary and suggest looking into it later.

advanced.situation: Research shows a town's youth crime and school dropout are linked to a shortage of after-school spaces. The council asks you to propose an approach to the problem.

options.text: Present the findings to the council and let its officers design the program.
Combine the crime and education findings, propose a pilot with measurable goals, and plan its evaluation.
Recommend building more after-school centers across the town, since the link in the data is clear.
Propose a curfew for teenagers because it addresses crime quickly and is cheap to run.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to prepare a short report on interview findings. Two participants' quotes could identify them because of their rare job titles.

options.text: Keep the quotes and titles as they are because the participants agreed to be interviewed.
Replace the job titles with general descriptions and confirm the quotes still read clearly.
Use the quotes but remove the participants' names and leave the titles in place.
Remove both quotes from the report so no one can be identified from it.

advanced.situation: You are drafting a grant application for a three-year study on aging and loneliness. The funder wants impact evidence, and your pilot data is small.

options.text: Include the pilot data and cite a few studies on loneliness to support the need.
Frame the pilot as preliminary, support the design with prior studies, and set realistic outcomes.
Describe the pilot results as strong evidence of impact so reviewers take the proposal seriously.
Promise large effects across several outcomes to match what the funder says it wants.

basic.situation: At a community talk, a resident asks what a sociological survey is and why anyone would trust results drawn from a few hundred people.

options.text: Say the results are certain because the university approved the survey method for this study.
Use a simple example to show how careful sampling lets a few hundred people represent many.
Describe how the survey was designed and note its limits, then take questions.
Tell the resident that the method is complicated and that the report has the details.

advanced.situation: A state legislator's aide asks if your poverty research supports cutting cash aid to families who miss school meetings. Your data does not cover that question.

options.text: Say the research supports the idea in general terms, since poverty and schooling are closely linked.
Tell the aide your data does not cover the proposal and suggest checking the library.
Send your latest poverty report and let the aide draw conclusions from it.
Explain what your data can and cannot show, cite related studies, and offer a review.

basic.situation: You are interviewing residents of a flat complex about shared facilities. One resident answers every question with a single word and keeps glancing at a neighbor nearby.

options.text: Fill in fuller answers yourself based on what you expect residents to say about facilities.
Offer to move to a private spot and remind the resident that answers are confidential.
Continue with the interview and record the one-word answers exactly as given by the resident.
Ask the neighbor what the resident probably means and note the neighbor's views as well.

advanced.situation: You are observing a community committee that keeps stalling on a repair fund. Two members dominate the talks while others stay silent, and a vote is due next week.

options.text: Tell the quiet members privately how to vote so the fund decision is settled quickly.
Interview the two dominant members and base your conclusions on their account of the stalling.
Log who speaks and who defers, then share the patterns with the chair for next steps.
Record the stalling in your notes and report it after the vote has been taken.

basic.situation: You are helping design a questionnaire on commuter satisfaction. One draft question asks, How much do you enjoy the excellent new train service?

options.text: Flag the loaded wording to your supervisor and wait for new text before sending.
Reword it neutrally, for example asking how satisfied the respondent is with the train service.
Keep the question since the supervisor wrote it and add a comment box underneath.
Send the survey out as drafted, since respondents will understand what the question means.

advanced.situation: A factory team has strained relations between shifts. You are asked to design an intervention to improve cooperation before a new production line starts in a month.

options.text: Hold a team-building dinner for both shifts using the format that worked at another firm.
Run a company-wide survey and share the average satisfaction score at the next meeting.
Observe both shifts, interview supervisors, and pilot a role-play session built on what you find.
Reassign workers between shifts next week and tell them the change is final.

basic.situation: Your supervisor leaves you to compile survey results from three clerks. One clerk's spreadsheet has totals that do not match the raw entries.

options.text: Compare the totals with raw entries, mark the mismatches, and ask the clerk to explain.
Merge the three spreadsheets as they are and mention the mismatch in the summary.
Replace the clerk's totals with the average of the other two clerks' totals.
Merge the three spreadsheets and adjust the totals yourself to match the raw entries.

advanced.situation: Your poverty study with a statistician and an economist is behind schedule. The economist wants income measured from tax records, but the statistician wants survey self-reports.

options.text: Compare both sources on coverage and bias, then agree a choice with both of them.
Use the tax records because the economist has the stronger claim on measuring income.
Collect both sources separately and publish whichever result looks stronger in the final report.
Ask the project lead to decide between the two and follow whatever the lead says.

basic.situation: Your senior planner asks for a land use map overlaid with population density for a new housing area. The census file you have was last updated six years ago.

options.text: Scale up the old population figures by the national growth rate and present the map.
Build the map from the old census file and mention its age in your email.
Label the map with the census date and ask where newer population figures are held.
Fill the density layer with figures from a property agent's website and label them official data.

advanced.situation: You lead an impact study for a proposed industrial park near a village. At the public hearing officials expect your findings, but the traffic survey is half complete.

options.text: Ask the officials to postpone the hearing until the traffic survey is complete.
Extend the half-finished traffic results to the full study area and present them as measured.
Present the finished findings, say traffic work is incomplete, and give a date for it.
Use traffic figures from a similar park elsewhere to fill the gap and present all results.

basic.situation: A developer's application proposes a three-story shophouse on a lot zoned for two stories. Your senior planner asked you to check it against the zoning rules.

options.text: Tell the developer's agent the height is not allowed and ask them to revise the plans.
Record the height conflict, cite the zoning rule, and pass the application to your senior planner.
Approve the form because the developer's agent says a variance will be granted later.
Mark the application as compliant on other points and add a note about the height.

advanced.situation: Your team must evaluate a proposed housing project on a flood-prone riverbank. Junior planners ask how to judge its sustainability claims, and no set standard exists yet.

options.text: Accept the developer's sustainability rating since an outside consultant produced it for this project.
Tell each junior planner to review the developer's claims against the project's own documents.
Draft a checklist on flood risk, drainage and habitat, test it here, and brief the team.
Approve the sustainability section so the project stays on schedule and reassess it after construction starts.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to help draft a policy on water meter upgrades for a small town's public utilities. You have not written a policy before.

options.text: Post the draft on the council website so residents can comment before your supervisor reads it.
Review similar policies from other councils, draft a version, and list questions for your supervisor.
Copy the structure of a policy from another town and change the names and figures.
Write the policy from memory of a course lecture and send it for approval.

advanced.situation: You are asked to lead a regional plan to cut transport carbon over ten years. Two junior planners will help, and districts disagree on bus priority versus road widening.

options.text: Set emission targets, model both options for each district, and coach the juniors on the modeling.
Give each district the option it asked for and combine them into one document.
Adopt the bus priority approach everywhere because it has the clearest emissions benefit on paper.
Choose road widening in all districts to end the dispute and set targets afterward.

basic.situation: Your senior planner asks you to prepare a recommendation on a small rezoning request. The request meets the rules, but nearby residents have submitted three objection letters.

options.text: Draft a conditional approval, summarize the objections, and flag it for your senior planner.
Recommend approval and leave the objection letters out of the file to keep it simple.
Recommend denial because three objections suggest the neighborhood does not support the change.
Recommend approval because the request meets the rules, and attach the objection letters.

advanced.situation: You supervise two planning technicians preparing advice for officials on a costly bridge. Their cost estimate was never reviewed, and officials meet in two days.

options.text: Get the estimate reviewed by a qualified person and tell officials which parts are checked.
Present the estimate with a note that figures are provisional and ask officials to wait.
Send the estimate to officials as prepared, because the technicians have done similar costings before.
Tell the technicians to recheck the figures themselves and present the estimate as final.

basic.situation: You are asked to arrange a meeting between your team and a district planning officer about a new park. The officer's calendar is full for two weeks, and no rush has been requested.

options.text: Ask the officer's assistant for the first free slot and book it for the team.
Tell the officer's assistant the park project is urgent and has your director's approval.
Send the officer a calendar invitation for tomorrow and expect other items to move.
Offer two or three times, attach a short agenda, and ask the officer's assistant to confirm.

advanced.situation: You lead coordination for a rail link needing approval from three agencies. Two agencies send conflicting requirements, and the architect is waiting for a decision to finalize drawings.

options.text: Tell the architect to follow the stricter agency's requirements and sort out the other later.
Tell the architect to finalize drawings using whichever requirement is cheaper to build.
Convene the three agencies, record agreed requirements, and send the architect a written summary.
Ask each agency to state its priority in writing and forward the replies to the architect.

basic.situation: You are asked to help present a plan to cut waste to a residents' association. The plan has many technical terms and the audience includes elderly residents.

options.text: Promise residents that their fees will not rise, to win support for the plan.
Use plain words, a few large pictures and a printed one-page summary, then take questions.
Present the full technical plan slowly and offer to answer questions after the talk.
Send the written plan to the association chair and ask them to share it with residents.

advanced.situation: A plan for a new highway ramp divides a neighborhood. Residents oppose it, the developer insists, and the city wants an alternative within a month.

options.text: Tell the residents the ramp is approved and construction will start within a month.
Ask the residents to submit written objections and send them to the developer for response.
Pick the compromise you think is fair and present it to both sides as final.
Hold facilitated sessions with both sides, map their concerns, and develop two alternative designs.

basic.situation: You are interviewing elders about a village festival for a cultural study. One elder speaks quietly and you are not sure you caught an important date.

options.text: Write the date you think you heard and mark it uncertain in your notes.
Record the date from the usual festival calendar and write it as the elder's statement.
Look up the festival date in a tourist brochure and use that in your notes.
Ask the elder to repeat the date, then check it against another interviewee's account.

advanced.situation: You lead a student excavation crew at a field site. A volunteer begins digging through a layer faster than the trench plan allows, and others copy the pace.

options.text: Send everyone a written summary of excavation steps and ask them to follow it from tomorrow.
Pause the dig, demonstrate the layer method on a sample square, and supervise each volunteer's section.
Fill in the notes for the disturbed layer from the plan so records look complete.
Let the volunteers keep digging to protect the schedule and review finds during the final cleanup.

basic.situation: You are reading a colonial-era trader's diary to explain how local marriage customs developed. One passage describes a ritual in a way that conflicts with a village account.

options.text: Merge the two descriptions into a single ritual and present it as documented fact.
Note both accounts, consider the trader's bias, and seek a third source before concluding.
Use the village account because it comes from the community itself and drop the diary passage.
Use the diary as evidence because it was written at the time of events.

advanced.situation: You are testing a general rule that societies with shared water systems develop stronger kinship obligations. Two of your six cases contradict the rule.

options.text: Remove the two contradicting cases and publish the rule as a general finding across societies.
Present the rule as a strong tendency and list the two cases as exceptions.
Examine why the two cases differ, refine the rule's conditions, and test it on new cases.
Add more supporting cases from the same region until the contradicting ones are outnumbered.

basic.situation: You work with a clinic team to understand why few villagers attend vaccination days. A community elder says many people trust a traditional healer more than the clinic.

options.text: Ask the healer and elders about their views of the clinic, then report to the team.
Note the elder's comment in your report and recommend more posters about vaccination benefits.
Tell the clinic team that villagers hold outdated beliefs and need to be educated about vaccines.
Tell villagers at the next gathering that the healer's advice is dangerous and should be rejected.

advanced.situation: You run a participatory action study with a bakery's workers to redesign their shifts. Management wants quick results, and workers are cautious about speaking openly.

options.text: Form a worker group, agree ground rules on anonymity, and co-design shift options with them.
Observe the bakery floor for two days and design the shifts around the tasks you see.
Interview workers individually, summarize their concerns, and propose a new shift pattern to management.
Have managers sit in on worker meetings so they hear complaints directly and act on them.

basic.situation: You are recording a craftsperson's weaving process on video for your project records. Midway she asks you to stop filming because a neighbor has arrived.

options.text: Stop filming and offer to return another day when the neighbor is not present.
Stop filming at once, ask whether she is happy to continue later, and log her answer.
Lower the camera but keep recording audio to capture her explanation of each step.
Finish the current step on video and then stop, since the footage is nearly complete.

advanced.situation: You are writing a grant proposal for a two-year study of a community's land customs. The funder asks for deliverables, but the community has not yet agreed to publication.

options.text: State that the community has endorsed publication and attach the earlier letter of welcome as proof.
Leave out publication plans and describe the study as private research for the funder.
List planned outputs, make publication depend on community consent, and budget for consultation meetings.
Promise a book and two articles, and plan to seek community permission after the fieldwork ends.

basic.situation: A dispute arises between fishers and a resort over a shared shoreline. The fishers say their family-managed fishing grounds are being overlooked in the talks.

options.text: Summarize the resort's plan and the fishers' complaint in one page for the mediator.
Record the fishers' rules on grounds and seasons and share them with your supervisor.
Tell the resort the fishers' rules carry no weight and can be dropped from the talks.
Advise the fishers to claim the whole shoreline because it has been used for generations.

advanced.situation: A government agency asks you to assess how a proposed mining road will affect an indigenous community's sacred sites and food gathering. The consultation deadline is tight.

options.text: Work with community representatives to map sites and gathering areas, then assess impacts and route options.
Mark the sacred sites as low impact because the road avoids the main village.
Review published ethnographies of the region and write an impact assessment based on them.
Request a longer deadline from the agency and explain what consultation is still required.

basic.situation: A teacher asks you to review a Year 5 social studies lesson on festivals. It describes one community's customs as strange and the others as normal.

options.text: Tell the teacher the lesson is fine because pupils at that age will not notice wording.
Point out the word strange to the teacher and suggest she replaces it herself.
Rewrite the lesson yourself to remove the community's customs, since they cause the most confusion.
Suggest neutral wording for every festival and a class task on what each custom means.

advanced.situation: You are training a company's product team in ethnographic interviewing. After the first session, one participant plans to interview customers using leading yes-or-no questions.

options.text: Let the participant run the interviews and present the themes to executives as customer findings.
Demonstrate open questions through a short role-play, then have the participant practice with feedback.
Tell the team to proceed, as practice in the field will teach them better than classes.
Send the participant a written guide to open-ended questions and ask them to follow it.

basic.situation: You need population data for a district map. A free national database has the figures, but its file notes say the boundaries changed after the figures were collected.

options.text: Use the data and redraw the districts to match your own estimates of the old boundaries.
Combine the figures with current boundaries and label the map as based on verified data.
Download it, check which boundaries it uses, and note any mismatch in the map's source.
Use the data as downloaded and add the collection year to the map legend.

advanced.situation: Global satellite data shows rapid urban growth in your region, but national census figures show slow growth. You are guiding a junior team in explaining the gap.

options.text: Compare how each source defines urban areas, test sample towns, and have juniors document the differences.
Report both figures side by side and note that they come from different methods.
Choose the satellite figures since they cover the whole region more consistently than census counts.
Average the two sources and present the result as the verified growth rate for the region.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks for a simple map of clinics in a district. The clinic coordinates use one coordinate system and the base map another, so the points land in the sea.

options.text: Ask your supervisor which coordinate system the clinic file uses and wait for the answer.
Move each clinic point by hand to its approximate location on the base map.
Delete the points that fall in the sea and send the map showing the rest.
Check each layer's coordinate system, reproject the clinic points, and confirm they sit on land.

advanced.situation: A private client wants a GIS portal that shows delivery routes. Their staff share one login and the data includes home addresses of drivers.

options.text: Keep the shared login and ask the client to limit who receives it within the firm.
Show the addresses on the map since drivers are employees and the client owns the data.
Publish the portal on a public link so the client's partners can view it easily.
Propose individual logins with role-based access, mask driver addresses by default, and document the setup.

basic.situation: You are compiling a land cover dataset from satellite images and an old paper map. The paper map shows a forest where the latest image shows a plantation.

options.text: Use the satellite image for the area and drop the paper map from the notes.
Record the plantation as current cover, note the conflict, and cite each source's date.
Record the area as mixed forest and plantation to avoid showing a conflict in the data.
Record the area as forest because the paper map is an official published source.

advanced.situation: You design a protocol for measuring river bank erosion across ten sites over a year. Equipment is limited to two sets and the sites are far apart.

options.text: Let each field team choose its own measuring method so work proceeds at every site.
Rotate the equipment on a schedule, use identical methods at each site, and log calibration.
Measure the sites nearest each other first and add the remote ones if time allows.
Measure three sites and apply the average erosion rate to the other seven sites.

basic.situation: You are summarizing a field study on flood-prone villages for your supervisor. Your results fit a pattern but rely on a survey with a low response rate.

options.text: Raise the reported response rate by counting partial replies as complete to look stronger.
State the pattern, report the response rate, and say the findings may not generalize.
State the pattern and add a footnote with the response rate for readers who check.
Describe the pattern as typical of flood-prone villages across the whole region, citing your survey.

advanced.situation: You must present research on coastal erosion to fishers, engineers and officials in one meeting. Their interests differ and the findings suggest costly protection works may fail.

options.text: Open with the main finding, tailor short points for each group, and pause for questions.
Leave out the findings about possible failure to avoid arguments with engineers and officials.
Focus on the findings that support protection works, since officials are funding the project.
Give the full technical presentation you prepared for scientists and offer a summary handout later.

basic.situation: You are helping a teacher explain latitude and longitude to a class. Several students keep mixing up which lines run east-west and which run north-south.

options.text: Move on to the next topic since the concept will become clear when they use atlases.
Tell students the two terms mean the same thing, so labels do not matter.
Use a globe and a grid on the board, and have students locate three places themselves.
Give students a simple memory trick and a printed list of definitions to learn tonight.

advanced.situation: You are designing a unit on climate and migration for senior students. You have six weeks, mixed ability, and a syllabus requiring students to analyze primary data.

options.text: Give the same advanced dataset to all students and mark them against the strongest group's work.
Use a textbook chapter on migration and let students pick any data source they like.
Build tasks around real datasets, scaffold analysis for weaker students, and end with a research project.
Teach the topic through lectures and readings, then set one data analysis task at the end.

basic.situation: A small business asks you to help prepare a one-page note on possible shop locations in a town. You have a base map and a list of existing competitors.

options.text: Recommend the busiest street because most shops in town have chosen that location.
Map competitors and busy areas, list pros and cons for three sites, and note data gaps.
Mark the competitors on the map and suggest the area with the fewest of them.
Promise the chosen location will triple sales, because the client expects strong figures from you.

advanced.situation: You lead a consulting project assessing flood hazard for a developer's riverside site. The developer hints that a lower risk rating would speed financing.

options.text: Report the rating the preliminary data supports and offer a fuller analysis later for a fee.
Present a range of ratings so the developer can pick the one that suits financing.
Give the lower rating and adjust the flood model inputs so the report supports it.
Complete the hazard analysis, report the rating the data supports, and document the method for review.

basic.situation: At a public archive you are copying pages of a 1950s court register. The reading room rules ban flash photography, and the pages are fragile.

options.text: Photograph the pages with your phone with flash turned off and skip asking staff first.
Photograph the pages with flash quickly while the reading room supervisor is busy, to save time.
Ask the archivist which copying methods are permitted, then use a flash-free camera or order scans.
Copy the key passages by hand in pencil and request scans for the rest later.

advanced.situation: You are researching a rural strike in 1947 where official records were destroyed in a fire. Time is short and three possible sources exist: a union newsletter, family diaries and elderly witnesses.

options.text: Interview the elderly witnesses first, then cross-check with the newsletter and diaries, recording origins.
Rely on the union newsletter, since printed material is easier to verify than memories.
Read the union newsletter and family diaries in full and note that witnesses were not reached.
Fill gaps in the strike timeline with plausible events from similar strikes elsewhere in that same decade.

basic.situation: You are organizing a spreadsheet of census entries from 1921. Some entries list the same family twice with different spellings of the surname.

options.text: Merge the likely duplicates yourself and add a note listing both surname spellings.
Delete the second entry for each family and standardize the surname to one spelling.
Leave the duplicates in the spreadsheet because the census recorded them as separate entries.
Flag the likely duplicates, keep both original entries, and ask your supervisor how to merge them.

advanced.situation: You guide a student tracing how a port town's trade guild changed political influence over two centuries. One source says the guild led a 1790 reform, but no other source mentions it.

options.text: Leave out the 1790 reform because one source cannot support an argument about the guild.
Build the guild's influence timeline around the 1790 reform and present it as established.
Include the 1790 reform in the account and add a footnote noting the single source.
Test the claim against town records, and show the student how to weigh single-source claims.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to research the old railway for a local history booklet. You find little material on it in the first week.

options.text: Write the railway section from general knowledge and invented details to fill the space.
Search archive catalogs and local newspapers for railway material, then report findings and gaps.
Tell your supervisor the topic has little material and ask for a different topic.
Switch to the town market history, which has plenty of sources, and tell your supervisor later.

advanced.situation: You mentor two junior historians choosing a thesis question about a city's wartime housing. One proposes a broad question, the other a narrow one that few sources can answer.

options.text: Choose the broad question for both historians because it can use more of the available sources.
Help each adjust the question to the available sources, and share criteria for a workable question.
Tell both to follow their personal interests and revise the question once research is underway.
Advise them to settle their conclusions now and gather sources that support those views.

basic.situation: You are reading a prepared summary about a local immigrant community to a small group at a library. A listener says the summary leaves out a group that lived there.

options.text: Add the group yourself with details recalled from the listener's comment as you read.
Say the summary was prepared by the society and give the listener its contact details.
Tell the listener the group was not significant enough to be included in the account.
Thank the listener, note the omission, and tell your supervisor so it can be reviewed.

advanced.situation: You lead a public talk on a town's founding story. A local group objects to your account of a conflict with a neighboring community, saying it is one-sided.

options.text: Keep your account and invite the group to submit a written response for the town archive.
Listen to the objection, compare it with your sources, and present both views with evidence.
Drop the conflict from the talk and present the founding as a peaceful partnership.
Soften the wording of the conflict to avoid offense while keeping the same overall account.

basic.situation: A curator asks you to help arrange items for a display about a village school. One photo label gives a date that conflicts with the school log.

options.text: Hang the photo with its original label and decide about the date after the opening.
Tell the curator about the date conflict and hold the photo until the date is confirmed.
Print a new label showing the log date and discard the old label as outdated.
Place the photo with its label and mention the date conflict to the curator later.

advanced.situation: You review a colleague's exhibit text on a revolt. It includes a famous quote that several historians think was attributed later, and the exhibit opens in a week.

options.text: Ask your colleague to recheck the quote and approve the text if they confirm it.
Approve the text as written since the quote appears in many popular history books and websites.
Keep the quote and add a small caption saying its origin is debated among historians.
Check the quote's earliest source, then revise the text to note the doubt and cite sources.

basic.situation: You are storing brittle letters from the 1930s. The preservation guidelines call for acid-free folders and a cool, dry cabinet, but the supply room has just plastic sleeves.

options.text: Fold the letters flat into the plastic sleeves and press the stack under heavy books.
Move the letters to the cool, dry cabinet and request acid-free folders from your supervisor.
Put each letter in a plastic sleeve and store them on the open shelf.
Move the letters to the cool, dry cabinet and keep them in their current box.

advanced.situation: A private collector asks you to confirm the authenticity of a rare diary said to be from 1850. The paper and ink look suitable, but the handwriting has not been compared.

options.text: Give a written opinion that the diary is likely genuine, based on how the paper and ink look.
Certify the diary as authentic so the collector can proceed with the sale this week.
Say the paper and ink fit the claimed date and suggest the collector ask another expert too.
Report what you checked, recommend handwriting comparison and lab testing, and state authenticity is unconfirmed.

basic.situation: You are organizing election results by constituency for a report. One constituency shows turnout above 100 percent in the figures you downloaded.

options.text: Include the row in the table with a footnote saying the turnout figure looks unusually high.
Check the source and voter roll figures, then flag the anomaly to your supervisor.
Cap the turnout at 100 percent for that constituency and carry on with the report.
Delete the constituency from the dataset so the report's averages stay tidy and believable.

advanced.situation: You forecast support for a policy using polling data. The latest poll, from an unfamiliar firm, shows a sharp jump that no other poll shows.

options.text: Check the firm's method, forecast with and excluding that poll, and report the range.
Treat the jump as real because it is the latest data and update the forecast.
Give the new poll a lower weight than the others and report a single forecast figure.
Publish the forecast with the jump as the headline trend before anyone else reviews it.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to summarize a new government housing policy for a briefing. The document is long and one clause on eligibility seems unclear to you.

options.text: Write what the clause probably means and present it as the policy's official position.
Explain the eligibility clause the way a news article described it earlier this week.
Summarize the clear parts, quote the unclear eligibility clause, and ask your supervisor about it.
Summarize the whole policy and mention in the briefing that the eligibility clause seems ambiguous.

advanced.situation: A company asks how a new data protection policy will affect its operations. The policy text is vague about cross-border transfers and the regulator has not issued guidance.

options.text: Confirm that transfers are permitted under the policy so the company can proceed as planned.
Advise the company to wait for the regulator's guidance before making changes to its transfer practices.
Advise that the policy probably does not affect transfers because it does not mention them clearly.
Set out the plausible readings, the risks under each, and a cautious plan pending guidance.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to identify research issues about youth voter turnout. You find many topics, from social media to school civics, and the deadline is next week.

options.text: Write the research question to match the conclusions your supervisor has favored in earlier reports.
List the candidate issues, check which have available data, and propose two to your supervisor.
Pick the issue you personally find most interesting and start collecting sources on that topic.
Send your supervisor the full list of topics and ask which one to research.

advanced.situation: You design a study testing whether coalition governments pass fewer reforms. Your two data sets disagree about which governments count as coalitions, and funding is fixed.

options.text: Use the larger data set and mention in the methods section that the other exists.
Define coalition by a documented rule, run tests on both data sets, and report differences.
Combine the two data sets and label a government a coalition if either source lists it.
Choose whichever data set shows a clearer difference, since it supports a stronger argument.

basic.situation: You track new government policy decisions for your office. This week you read about a tax change in a news article, but the official announcement is not yet published.

options.text: Leave it out of the tracker until more news outlets have reported the change next week.
Add the tax change to your tracker and list the article as the source.
Log the news report as unconfirmed and update your tracker when the announcement appears.
Tell your office the tax change is confirmed and in effect, based on the article.

advanced.situation: You guide colleagues in tracking emerging trends in election law across states. Everyone relies on the same two news feeds, and a new bill may be missed.

options.text: Set up a shared tracker fed by legislature sites and gazettes, with a monthly team review.
Subscribe to a commercial alert service and rely on its summaries of new bills.
Add two more news feeds to the colleagues' reading lists and ask for weekly summaries.
Tell colleagues to stop tracking state bills until they are passed to save effort.

basic.situation: You draft a short report on local budget priorities and hear that your main chart is hard to read. The report is due to the councilor in two days.

options.text: Simplify the chart, label the axes, and ask a colleague to read the draft first.
Crop the chart's axis to exaggerate the differences so the main point stands out.
Keep the chart as designed and add a paragraph explaining how to read it.
Replace the chart with a table of raw figures, which readers can check themselves.

advanced.situation: You must present research on public trust in courts at a public forum. Journalists are attending, and your findings are mixed, with some results that could be quoted selectively.

options.text: Present the strongest results and leave the mixed ones to the published full report.
State the finding and limits clearly, hand out a short summary, and offer the dataset.
Present the complete results in detail and ask the journalists to quote them with context.
Emphasize the most favorable numbers and tell journalists the others are not important.

basic.situation: A first-year student asks which political science courses to take next term and whether a semester abroad would delay graduation. You are not sure about the abroad credits.

options.text: Suggest suitable courses and tell the student to ask the registrar about credits abroad.
Suggest suitable courses, then check the credit rules with the registrar before answering on studying abroad.
Tell the student the semester abroad will not delay graduation and to sign up this week.
Say that studying abroad should be fine because most students manage to transfer their credits.

advanced.situation: You mentor a graduate student whose thesis on protest movements relies on one interview source. Their committee meets in a month, and the student says they are overwhelmed.

options.text: Suggest the student ask the committee for more time and explain the limits of the thesis.
Rewrite the weakest chapters yourself so the thesis is ready for the committee review.
Advise the student to describe the single source as representative of all protest movements.
Help the student list gaps, add two more data sources, and set a weekly plan.

basic.situation: Your senior planner asks you to draft a report recommending a pedestrian crossing near a school. Traffic counts exist for the morning, but the evening count has not been done.

options.text: Note the missing evening data in the draft and ask for a count to be scheduled.
Recommend the crossing using the morning counts and say evening conditions are probably similar.
Use last year's evening counts from a different street and attach them to the draft.
Estimate the evening count from the morning figures and label it as measured data.

advanced.situation: You lead an environmental assessment for a new bypass road. Late in the process, a survey finds a protected bird nesting area close to the planned route.

options.text: Keep the report on schedule and list the nesting area in an appendix for later review.
Add the finding to the assessment and propose planting trees near the route to compensate.
Leave the nesting area out of the report since it came after the main survey closed.
Add the finding to the assessment, assess route options with ecologists, and brief the approval authority.

basic.situation: A developer plans a 200-unit housing block. You are asked to check whether the plan includes the road access and parking the local transport rules require.

options.text: Confirm compliance because the developer's consultant submitted a statement saying the plan meets requirements.
Check the road access against the rules and tell the supervisor you will check parking later.
Approve the plan as compliant so the developer can proceed to the next stage of review.
Compare the plan with each rule, list what is missing, and send it to your supervisor.

advanced.situation: A national bill proposes cutting funding for rural bus services. Your regional authority asks you to assess the likely consequences for its transportation system over ten years.

options.text: Report that the cuts will save money and leave rural service effects to the sponsors.
Model ridership, access and cost effects under several funding scenarios, and state your assumptions.
Tell the authority the cuts will have little effect since few residents ride rural buses.
Estimate the effect using last year's ridership figures and report the expected savings and losses.

basic.situation: You help design a survey to learn residents' concerns about a planned bus lane. The first draft asks, Do you agree that the new bus lane will reduce harmful congestion?

options.text: Reword the one loaded question and send the survey to the existing mailing list.
Send the survey as drafted because the bus lane's benefits are well established.
Drop the question and let residents raise concerns in the general comments box.
Reword the questions neutrally, add a comment box, and test the survey with a few residents.

advanced.situation: Your team tests a new traffic demand model against last year's observed counts. The model underestimates peak flows on two corridors by 25 percent.

options.text: Investigate the corridor inputs and assumptions, recalibrate and retest the model, and log changes.
Release the model results to the client as validated and fix the peak flows later.
Use the model for other corridors and drop those two corridors from the study area.
Apply a 25 percent uplift to peak outputs on those corridors and note it.

basic.situation: You analyze counts from a week-long traffic counting program. Tuesday's counts at one junction are zero for six hours, while neighboring junctions show normal traffic.

options.text: Flag the six hours as a likely sensor fault and ask your supervisor how to treat them.
Replace the zeros with the average of neighboring junctions and carry on with the analysis.
Exclude the six hours from the weekly average and mention the exclusion in your notes.
Keep the zeros in the weekly average and report the junction as having very low traffic.

advanced.situation: Modeling software points to congestion at three junctions, but GIS data shows two of them are near new housing not yet included in the model. You must define regional priorities.

options.text: Prioritize the junction away from the new housing, since its model result is less uncertain.
Add an estimate of housing demand by hand and present the totals as model output.
