Rank the three junctions by current model results and flag the missing housing in the report.
Update the model with the new housing, rerun it, and rank priorities on the revised results.

basic.situation: At a public meeting on a bus route change, an angry resident says planners never listen. You are taking notes while the senior planner leads the meeting.

options.text: Tell the resident the route change is final and objections will not be considered.
Explain the reasons for the route change to the resident, using the report's arguments.
Record the resident's concerns accurately, thank them, and pass the notes to the senior planner.
Tell the resident the senior planner will answer questions at the end of the meeting.

advanced.situation: You lead a team with engineers and economists to draft a national sustainable transport strategy. The engineers favor rail upgrades, the economists favor bus lanes, and the deadline is fixed.

options.text: Choose the option with the lower upfront cost to settle the matter before the deadline.
Draft the strategy around your preferred option and describe the other as already rejected.
Agree shared criteria for emissions, cost and access, score both options together, and document trade-offs.
Split the strategy into rail and bus sections and let each group write its own.

basic.situation: You are assisting with an urban traffic counting program. A counter reports that two roadside machines were moved by workmen and may have recorded the wrong lanes.

options.text: Tell your supervisor about the report and ask whether the counts should be repeated that week.
Put the affected counts in the weekly summary and add a note that machines moved.
Mark the affected data, ask the counter for details of the move, and tell your supervisor.
Reassign the counts to the lanes that seem most likely and file the program data.

advanced.situation: You direct technical work on a program to recommend junction upgrades. Traffic projections and population forecasts differ, and a regulator asks for your recommendation this month.

options.text: Recommend upgrades from the traffic projections and note in your letter that population forecasts disagree.
Recommend the most expensive upgrades to be safe and say projections support them strongly.
Reconcile the two forecasts with their authors, state assumptions, and give a ranked recommendation with ranges.
Average the two sets of figures and recommend upgrades for the resulting demand level.

basic.situation: You must set up soil moisture sensors in a test plot before sunrise. The setup sheet shows three depths for the sensors, but one probe is missing.

options.text: Set up two depths, record the missing probe, and tell your supervisor before testing starts.
Install the sensors at one depth and label the readings as three-depth data for the trial.
Place the two working probes at the nearest depths and note the change in the log.
Borrow a probe from the neighboring plot and install it at the missing depth.

advanced.situation: You are asked to design a field testing protocol for a new drought-tolerant rice variety across three soil types. Past trials used different methods, so results cannot be compared.

options.text: Adopt the protocol from the most recent past trial and adjust it for the new variety.
Define plot sizes, sampling times and measures, pilot them in one soil, then document the protocol.
Let each trial site pick its own methods and combine the results into one table afterwards.
Plant the new variety on the most fertile plots to show strong results in the report.

basic.situation: You are collecting leaf samples from a banana plantation using a checklist. It asks for ten plants per block, but the last block has six plants you can reach.

options.text: Sample the six plants, record the shortfall on the checklist, and tell your supervisor.
Sample the six plants and take extra leaves from each to make up the amount.
Record all ten plants as sampled, since the missing four would look the same.
Take the remaining four samples from a nearby block and label them as the last block.

advanced.situation: Banana leaf disease detection varies a lot between regions because teams sample differently. You are asked to develop a standard sampling method for five district offices.

options.text: Ask each district to describe its method and adopt the one with the most farms.
Test sampling patterns on farms in two districts, compare detection rates, and write a guide.
Tell every district to sample the plants that already look diseased to raise detection numbers.
Adopt the sampling method used by a neighboring country's agency and send it to all districts.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to weed and prune a block of pepper plants. Rain is forecast this afternoon and the pruning shears have not been cleaned since use on a diseased block.

options.text: Weed the block now and leave the pruning for tomorrow, when you will have time.
Prune the diseased block first and then this block with the same shears to finish sooner.
Prune and weed before the rain and clean the shears at the end of the day.
Clean the shears with disinfectant, prune and weed while it is dry, and report disease signs.

advanced.situation: You manage land preparation for 20 hectares of new orchard on a slope. Heavy rain is expected next week, and plowing straight down the slope is the fastest method.

options.text: Plow down the slope as planned and cover exposed soil with mulch after the rain.
Plow the flat areas across the slope and delay the steep sections until after rain.
Contour the plowing across the slope, add drainage channels, and start on the steepest sections first.
Remove the remaining trees and ground cover on the slope before plowing to speed up work.

basic.situation: You are mowing a field edge on a small tractor under supervision. You notice a bystander's child has walked near the mower path.

options.text: Finish the pass quickly so the area is clear before the child comes closer.
Stop the mower, switch off the engine, and ask an adult to take the child away.
Slow the tractor and signal the child to move back while you keep mowing slowly.
Steer wide around the child and speed up to finish the field edge sooner.

advanced.situation: A combine harvester on your farm keeps stalling under load. Two newer workers also operate it, and one of them has already bypassed the safety cutout once.

options.text: Keep harvesting at a lower load and show both workers how the safety cutout works.
Tell the workers to restart after each stall and use the bypass to avoid delays.
Take the combine out of use, diagnose the stall, and retrain both workers on safety cutouts.
Keep the combine running and ask the workers to report stalls at day's end.

basic.situation: You are cleaning and checking hand tools in a farm shed with guidance. You find a spade with a cracked wooden handle.

options.text: Put the spade back with the other tools since the blade is still in good shape.
Lend the spade to a worker who needs one today and mention the crack later.
Take the spade out of use, tag it as damaged, and tell your supervisor.
Wrap the handle in strong tape and note it for repair when you finish cleaning.

advanced.situation: You are setting up a preventive maintenance schedule for tractors, pumps and sprayers across three farm sites. Records are scattered, and budgets allow few spare parts.

options.text: Service each machine after it breaks down and keep a list of repair costs.
Defer all servicing until the dry season to save budget and repair failures later.
Adopt the manufacturer's service intervals for every machine and review them once a year.
Gather service records, rank machines by use and failure risk, and set schedules with spare parts.

basic.situation: You record animal weights in a template during a feeding trial. One scale reading looks too high, and the animal has not been weighed again.

options.text: Enter the average weight of similar animals from the trial in place of the high reading.
Change the reading to what you expected and enter the new figure in the template.
Record the reading as shown, mark it doubtful, and weigh the animal again when possible.
Record the reading as shown and tell your supervisor later that it looks too high.

advanced.situation: You supervise a team of farm laborers recording pest counts. Their counts vary widely between workers, and a new trial starts on Monday.

options.text: Create a one-page counting guide, train the team on sample plants, and check each worker's first records.
Give the team a written counting guide and ask workers to call you with questions.
Keep the counts from the fastest workers and discard the others as unreliable data.
Average each worker's counts across the week to smooth out the differences in the trial.

basic.situation: You are collecting soil and yield data with a field recorder on a farm. The GPS signal drops for ten minutes, and the recorder stops logging positions.

options.text: Fill the missing section on the map by hand from where you remember driving.
Wait for the signal, re-drive the missed strip, and note the gap in the log.
Continue collecting and mark the gap in the file so the area can be revisited.
Copy the readings from the neighboring strip into the gap and save the file as complete.

advanced.situation: You must program a variable-rate sprayer from scouting data before spraying day tomorrow. Two GPS guidance sensors on the sprayer show slightly different positions.

options.text: Switch off one sensor and spray the field at a flat rate to meet the deadline.
Calibrate both sensors at a known reference point, then test the sprayer on a small area.
Average the two sensor positions and apply the prescription as programmed across the whole field.
Use the sensor that matches the field boundary map and report the difference to your supervisor.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to divide a field into management zones using GPS soil data. The data shows a clear change in soil type across the middle of the field.

options.text: Reuse the zone boundaries from last season because the farm manager already approved them.
Split the field in two equal halves along the middle and label each zone.
Draw the zones so the owner's favorite corner gets its own high-input zone, whatever the soil.
Draw zones along the soil change, label them, and compare them with the soil map.

advanced.situation: Yield maps show a low-yield patch in a field that was fertilized evenly. Weather data shows a late frost, and terrain data shows a low corner where cold air collects.

options.text: Increase the fertilizer rate on that patch next season to bring its yield up.
Report the patch as a fertilizer fault by the supplier and request a refund.
Attribute the patch to the frost and mention the low corner in your field report.
Overlay frost, terrain and soil layers on the yield map to test what explains the patch.

basic.situation: You are asked to read a soil map and a contour map to find where water collects in a field. The two maps use different scales.

options.text: Check each map's scale, note the difference, and match features on both before marking low areas.
Overlay the maps at the same size and mark the low areas that line up.
Mark the low areas from the soil map and skip the contour map to save time.
Read the contour map for low areas and mention the scale difference in your notes.

advanced.situation: A farm client wants one map showing yield, soil nutrients, drainage and input applications for the past three years. The data layers have different resolutions and dates.

options.text: Resample every layer to the coarsest resolution and describe the result as precise field data.
Standardize the layers to a common grid and date range, then build and check the map.
Stack the layers as received and adjust the transparency so all features are visible.
Create separate maps for each layer and give the client a short guide for comparing them.

basic.situation: You document precision agriculture records for a farm. A colleague gave you a spreadsheet of fertilizer applications with no dates in one column.

options.text: Insert the spreadsheet's creation date in all the empty cells and file it with the others.
Ask your colleague for the missing dates, mark the gaps, and fill them in when supplied.
Delete the rows that lack dates so the record looks complete and tidy for the farm.
File the spreadsheet as received and mention the missing dates in the cover note.

advanced.situation: You develop a management plan using satellite imagery and soil tests. Canopy density is low in one area, but the soil tests there look good and last month was very dry.

options.text: Compare imagery with weather history and soil data, check the area in person, then plan actions.
Add irrigation to the plan for that area and review the imagery again next month.
Mark the area as failed crop in the plan and recommend replanting it at once.
Apply extra fertilizer to that area because low canopy density suggests a nutrient shortage.

basic.situation: A farm's application map shows overlap where the sprayer applied chemical twice at field edges. Your supervisor asks you to suggest a way to reduce this.

options.text: Suggest the operator turns off the guidance system near the edges and sprays by eye.
Map the overlap areas, suggest turning on section control, and recheck after the next application.
Suggest lowering the spray rate across the whole field to offset the overlap areas.
Suggest the operator leave wider gaps at field edges when spraying to avoid overlap.

advanced.situation: Your company is developing an automated spot-spraying system to cut chemical use on weeds. Early tests show it misses small weeds near crop rows, and a launch event is next week.

options.text: Show the launch audience tests on large weeds and describe the system as fully reliable.
Proceed with the launch and tell clients about the miss rate in the sales briefing.
Report the miss rate, test improved camera settings and images, and adjust the launch claims.
Raise the spray area around crop rows so small weeds are covered at the event.

basic.situation: A farmer's GPS guidance display keeps freezing. Your supervisor asks you to contact the manufacturer for help, and the farmer needs it for planting in two days.

options.text: Open the display housing and swap in parts from a spare unit before planting day.
Note the model, serial number and error message, then call the manufacturer's support line.
Tell the farmer to keep resetting the display until it stops freezing on its own.
Email the manufacturer a short description and wait for a reply before doing more.

advanced.situation: A group of farmers complains that chemical drift from boom sprayers is reaching a neighbor's pond. You are asked to advise on improving boom-spray technology.

options.text: Advise spraying at night when nobody is around to see where the drift goes.
Recommend raising the boom higher so the spray covers a wider area on each pass.
Advise spraying in calm conditions and keeping a wider buffer strip around the pond.
Recommend drift-reducing nozzles, lower boom height and wind limits, and measure drift in a trial.

basic.situation: You compute the moisture content of a biscuit sample with guidance. Your result is above the limit, and you notice you used last week's oven weight in the formula.

options.text: Report the high result to your supervisor and suggest the batch be held for retest.
Redo the calculation with today's weights and enter the new figure in the record.
Record the result as within the limit, since last week's oven weight was also close.
Redo the calculation with today's weights and tell your supervisor about the first result.

advanced.situation: A microscope check of a juice sample shows unusual bacterial cells. The same line produced contaminated batches twice this year, and your supervisor is away until tomorrow.

options.text: Release the batch on schedule since the cells may be harmless and look similar to before.
Prepare a detailed report of the findings and send it to your supervisor for tomorrow.
Hold the affected batch, document findings with images, and alert the quality manager today.
Retest the sample tomorrow morning and release the batch if the second look seems normal.

basic.situation: You taste a vanilla sauce sample against a flavor specification with your supervisor. You have a mild cold and your sense of smell is reduced today.

options.text: Mark the flavor as meeting specification since earlier batches of this recipe have passed.
Taste the sample as usual and add a note about your cold to the record.
Assess the sample after a short rest and a glass of water to clear your senses.
Tell your supervisor about the cold and ask another trained taster to assess the sample.

advanced.situation: You design a sensory panel to select samples of a new chili sauce with a smoky taste. Panel members tire quickly with spicy samples, and the launch date is close.

options.text: Ask the sales team to pick the smokiest samples and call it the panel result.
Have panelists rate fewer samples per session and spread the sessions over several days.
Train a small panel on the smoky reference, limit samples per session, and add rest breaks.
Run all samples in one long session with the same panel to finish before launch.

basic.situation: You test a food coloring additive for color strength against a standard. The first reading is slightly off, and the instrument was calibrated last month.

options.text: Check the instrument's calibration record and then record the first reading as taken.
Adjust the instrument settings until the reading matches the standard and record that value.
Repeat the test on a fresh portion and ask your supervisor if readings still differ.
Record the first reading as a pass because it is close to the standard.

advanced.situation: Your lab must follow a revised national food safety regulation that lowers an allowed preservative limit. You audit the lab's testing protocols before the change takes effect next month.

options.text: Keep testing against the old limit until a customer complains about a failed result.
Update the preservative test method to the new limit and review other tests later.
Wait for the regulator to issue guidance notes before changing any of the test methods.
Compare each protocol with the revised limit, update methods and sensitivity checks, and record the audit.

basic.situation: You record pH results in a logbook during a shift. After writing a value, you realize you transposed two digits.

options.text: Strike through the entry with one line, write the right value, and initial it.
Cover the digits with white fluid and write the new value on top of it.
Cross out the digits and write the right value above them in the same ink.
Tear out the page and rewrite the whole page neatly with the right values.

advanced.situation: You set up record-keeping so the lab passes a government audit next quarter. Staff often fill logbooks days later from memory, and two staff share one login on the data system.

options.text: Backdate the late entries to the dates the tests were done so logbooks look current.
Have the supervisor review the logbooks before the audit and sign each page.
Write a procedure requiring same-day entries and email it to all staff before the audit.
Set same-day entry rules, give each person a login, and train staff on audit-ready records.

basic.situation: You are cleaning and sterilizing glass sample bottles using a checklist. The autoclave shows a temperature below the required setting halfway through a cycle.

options.text: Mark the bottles as sterilized on the checklist and store them for tomorrow's samples.
Stop the cycle, record the reading, tell your supervisor, and rerun the load once checked.
Let the cycle finish and add extra time to the next load to make up.
Let the cycle finish and use the bottles, since the low reading was brief.

advanced.situation: A food scientist reports that your lab's pH meter drifts after each calibration. You are asked to guide a junior technician and fix the maintenance schedule.

options.text: Delete the drift readings from the calibration log and keep using the meter as it is.
Check the electrode and buffers, log drift for a week, and revise the schedule together.
Order a new meter from the supplier and keep using the old one until it arrives.
Tell the junior to recalibrate the meter before each test and note the readings.

basic.situation: You order standard supplies for the lab storeroom under your manager's direction. The stock list shows the buffer solution is nearly finished, but your manager is away until Friday.

options.text: Wait for your manager to return on Friday and then order buffer solution.
Borrow buffer solution from the neighboring lab and plan to return it next week.
Order a large amount from a new supplier at a price you found online yourself.
Place the usual reorder for buffer solution and email your manager the order details.

advanced.situation: You supervise two food science technicians. One often leaves temperature records blank for cold-room checks, and the other covers for the colleague.

options.text: Do the missing cold-room checks yourself each day and leave the staff arrangement as it is.
Meet each separately, explain the record rules, and review the cold-room logs with them.
Send a reminder to the whole team about completing records and check logs next month.
Fill the blank entries with usual temperatures so the logs look complete at audit.

basic.situation: You are monitoring a cell culture experiment and recording temperature data hourly. At 2 a.m. the incubator reads two degrees above its set point.

options.text: Record the reading and mention the rise in your handover note in the morning.
Lower the set point by two degrees so the reading returns to normal for the cultures.
Record the reading, check the incubator controls, and tell the researcher in charge at once.
Leave the entry blank for that hour so the data shows no unusual temperature.

advanced.situation: You analyze growth data from a trial with five treatments. One treatment shows a large effect, but one replicate looks very different from its two partners.

options.text: Check the replicate's records for errors, run the analysis both ways, and report both results.
Keep all three replicates in the analysis and mention the odd one in your summary.
Run a quick outlier test and drop the odd replicate from the analysis if it fails.
Drop the odd replicate and describe the effect as consistent across all three replicates.

basic.situation: You are entering sample results from paper sheets into the lab database. One sheet has a smudged number that could be a 3 or an 8.

options.text: Enter the more likely number and add a comment that the sheet was smudged.
Enter the number that makes the sample result fit the expected range for the batch.
Leave that field open, flag the sheet, and ask the technician who wrote it.
Enter the average of the two numbers as a compromise and continue with the sheets.

advanced.situation: The lab's robotic liquid handler exports results to a shared database, but file naming differs between teams and some uploads overwrite earlier files. You are asked to improve the workflow.

options.text: Agree a naming rule with the teams, add timestamps to exports, and test on a trial run.
Email all teams a naming guide and ask them to follow it from next week.
Delete the older files from the shared database so just the latest versions remain.
Lock the shared folder so uploads go through you for checking at the end of the week.

basic.situation: You are preparing the work area before water sampling at a river. The sampling bottles are labeled, but you find one bottle with a cracked cap.

options.text: Set the bottle aside, replace it with a spare, and note the swap in your log.
Use the bottle and wrap the cap in tape to stop leaks on the way back.
Relabel a bottle from an earlier site with this site's name and use it for sampling.
Use the bottle for a sample and mention the cracked cap when handing it over.

advanced.situation: You design sampling protocols for a study of heavy metals in soil near an old factory. Funding covers 40 samples, and contamination may be patchy rather than uniform.

options.text: Place the 40 samples on a regular grid across the whole area and label each location.
Take a small pilot set to map variation, then place the 40 samples using a stratified design.
Take all 40 samples near the factory wall where contamination is most likely to be found.
Take eight samples at spots that look clean and report that average for the whole site.

basic.situation: You are setting up a microscope and preparing a blood specimen slide with step-by-step guidance. The slide shows air bubbles and uneven staining.

options.text: Examine the slide as prepared and describe the bubbles and staining in your notes.
Discard the slide safely, prepare a new one using the steps, and note the problem.
Add more stain over the existing stain to even it out and report the findings.
Scan around the bubbles and describe the clear areas as the specimen result.

advanced.situation: A spectrophotometer gives drifting readings during a time-sensitive run, and the lab must meet a standard. You are expected to troubleshoot and set the calibration standard for the lab.

options.text: Pause the run, check the lamp and cuvettes, recalibrate with a certified standard, and log it.
Finish the run and report the drifted readings as final results to meet the deadline.
Recalibrate with the standard you have and restart the run to save the samples.
Continue the run and apply a drift adjustment to all the readings afterward.

basic.situation: A scientist asks you to prepare 20 plant samples for analysis by tomorrow. While labeling, you see that two samples have no date on the field sheet.

options.text: Discard the two samples to avoid confusion and tell the scientist 18 were provided.
Prepare the 18 complete samples and tell the scientist about the other two tomorrow.
Prepare all 20 samples, flag the two missing dates, and ask the scientist to confirm them.
Write in the dates of the neighboring samples for the two missing dates and continue.

advanced.situation: You coordinate technical services for three research groups. Two groups ask for the same sequencing machine on the same day, and a junior technician is unsure what to do.

options.text: Give the machine to the group that asked first and tell the other group to wait.
Compare both groups' deadlines and sample stability, schedule the runs, and explain the reasoning.
Let the junior technician decide which group goes first, since the junior runs the samples.
Give the machine to the group with the senior head and delete the other booking.

basic.situation: You place a simple order for gloves and pipette tips from the approved checklist. The supplier's website shows a cheaper brand of tips that is not on the checklist.

options.text: Order the checklist brand and tell your supervisor about the cheaper tips for later.
Order the cheaper tips and list the checklist brand on the form to avoid questions.
Order the cheaper tips and note the change on the order form for the supervisor.
Order half the tips in each brand to test the cheaper ones in the lab.

advanced.situation: You manage supply ordering for a department with six labs. Suppliers offer a bulk discount for one-year contracts, but the labs' needs change often.

options.text: Sign one-year contracts for the items every lab uses and order the rest as needed.
Sign a contract for all labs now and tell lab heads their budgets will cover it.
Combine forecasts from all labs, negotiate bulk prices with flexible volumes, and review usage quarterly.
Sign the largest contract offered to get the lowest unit price for the whole department.

basic.situation: You are running a chromatography test under supervision. The first sample's peak is much smaller than the standard's, and the column was changed this morning.

options.text: Increase the injection volume for the samples so each peak matches the standard's size.
Run the remaining samples and flag the small peaks in your results for review.
Rerun the standard to check the column, then tell your supervisor before running more samples.
Scale the sample peak up in the report to match the standard and submit the results.

advanced.situation: A new product has an unexpected impurity peak in your spectroscopy results. No standard method exists for it, and the plant needs an answer within a week.

options.text: Design test runs with reference compounds, vary conditions to isolate the peak, and document the procedure.
Use the method for a similar impurity and report the result as provisional to the plant.
Tell the plant the peak is a harmless instrument artifact so production can continue.
Identify the peak by matching it to the closest library peak and report that as final.

basic.situation: You compile test results from five runs into a simple chart for your supervisor. Run 4 has a value written as 0.5 in the notes but 5.0 on the printout.

options.text: Check the printout and notebook entry, find out which is right, and flag the difference.
Use whichever value gives the smoother trend line for the chart and drop the other.
Plot both values on the chart as separate points and let your supervisor decide later.
Use the printout value, since it comes from the instrument, and mention the difference.

advanced.situation: Sample results show a slow upward trend in a contaminant across six months. Each value is within the limit, but the trend may reach the limit in three months.

options.text: Wait another three months to confirm the trend before raising it with anyone.
Report that all values are within limits and add a note about the upward trend.
Report that all values pass and leave the trend out so it does not cause alarm.
Chart the trend, check likely causes, and propose actions to management before the limit is reached.

basic.situation: You prepare a 0.1 M sodium hydroxide solution following a standard formula. After weighing, you realize the balance was not zeroed and the reading may be off.

options.text: Prepare the solution anyway and check its strength by titration before anyone uses it.
Adjust the final volume to make up for the difference you estimate in the weight.
Label it as 0.1 M and put it on the shelf for others to use today.
Discard the weighed amount, zero the balance, weigh again, and note the repeat in your notebook.

advanced.situation: You are asked to develop a new experimental formula for a cleaning solution and improve its preparation method. Early trials show the active ingredient dissolves slowly and sometimes clumps.

options.text: Use a stronger solvent from the stockroom and carry on if the ingredient dissolves.
Add the ingredient in larger amounts to compensate and approve the formula for production.
Heat the mixture to a higher temperature and keep stirring until the ingredient dissolves.
Test dissolving order, temperature and mixing speed in small batches and record each result.

basic.situation: You monitor the pH of a detergent batch against a specification of 8.0 to 9.0. Your first reading is 9.2 and the meter was calibrated this morning.

options.text: Record 9.2 as out of specification and carry on with the next batch tested.
Add acid to the batch until the pH reads 9.0 and release it as passed.
Round the reading down to 9.0 since the difference is small, then record it.
Retest with a fresh sample, and report to your supervisor if the pH is still above 9.0.

advanced.situation: You design a sampling program for incoming raw material from three suppliers. One supplier's lots have varied in purity, and testing every lot fully would exceed the lab's capacity.

options.text: Sample more often from the variable supplier, less from reliable ones, and review results monthly.
Test all lots from the variable supplier and stop sampling the other two suppliers.
Accept the variable supplier's own certificates of analysis and stop testing its lots at the lab.
Test the same number of lots from each supplier on a fixed monthly schedule.

basic.situation: A chemist asks you to assist with a distillation setup for a trial run. The chemist is called away, and the glassware is partly assembled.

options.text: Leave the heat off and ask another chemist to check the setup before it is used.
Finish assembling the setup and start heating at low power to save the chemist time.
Finish assembling the glassware from the procedure sheet and wait for the chemist before heating.
Fill the flask with the chemical and turn the heater to full to meet the schedule.

advanced.situation: You develop a training program for new technicians on handling a gas chromatograph. Two recent trainees damaged a column, and the lab has limited instrument time.

options.text: Combine a demonstration, supervised practice on an old column, and a checklist, then assess each trainee.
Let trainees learn on the live instrument while a senior technician works elsewhere in the lab.
Write a detailed manual and require trainees to read it before using the instrument.
Give trainees a short video and let them run samples alone the same day.

basic.situation: You inventory chemicals in the storeroom and order replacements. You find an unlabeled bottle of clear liquid on the shelf with the acids.

options.text: Leave the bottle where it is, tag it as unknown, and tell the safety officer.
Smell the liquid to work out what it is and then label it for the shelf.
Carry on with the inventory and tell your supervisor about the bottle when you finish.
Pour the liquid down the sink to clear the shelf and update the inventory sheet.

advanced.situation: You lead a safety audit of a chemical plant lab. You find that two fume hoods fail their airflow checks, and a client visit is scheduled in two days.

options.text: Postpone the airflow checks until after the client visit and list the hoods as passing.
Take the two hoods out of service, report the failures, and arrange repairs and alternative workspace.
Restrict use of the hoods to small volumes and plan repairs after the client visit.
Take the two hoods out of service and report the failures after the client visit.

basic.situation: You collect soil samples at a former petrol station using a checklist. Halfway through, you run out of the labeled sample bags the checklist requires.

options.text: Use plain bags and write the site details on tape stuck to each bag.
Combine the remaining samples into fewer bags and write all the locations on the label.
Stop sampling, ask your supervisor for more labeled bags, and note the delay.
Collect the remaining samples at one spot and label them as coming from different locations.

advanced.situation: You design a sampling strategy for an old industrial site with unknown pollution and train a new technician. The budget allows 30 samples, and the site has three distinct areas.

options.text: Take a few screening samples first, divide the site by use, and demonstrate each method.
Sample the area closest to the gate and state that the whole site was tested.
Divide the 30 samples evenly across the three areas and give the technician written steps.
Take all 30 samples from the area with the most visible staining and report them.

basic.situation: You prepare soil samples for a standard lead test. The balance shows a different weight for the same reference weight on two consecutive checks.

options.text: Carry on weighing since the difference is small and note it at the end of day.
Adjust all the recorded weights by the difference and carry on with the lead test.
Weigh each sample twice and use the average of the two readings for the test.
Stop weighing, recheck the balance with the reference weight, and report the difference.

advanced.situation: You must develop and validate a test procedure for a new pollutant that has no standard method. Early results from two analysts differ by 20 percent.

options.text: Adopt the more experienced analyst's method as the procedure and file it for use.
Compare their steps, run spiked samples to check recovery, and refine the method.
Ask both analysts to repeat their runs and use the average as the result.
Declare the procedure validated, citing the analyst whose results match your expected values.

basic.situation: You check an emission control device at a factory using the operating checklist. The pressure gauge reads outside the normal range, but production is at full speed.

options.text: Record the reading and mention it in your report at the end of the shift.
Write a normal reading on the checklist since the factory seems to be running well.
Record the reading, tell the plant supervisor, and ask for an inspection of the device.
Tap the gauge and recheck it, then record the new reading if it looks normal.

advanced.situation: A factory plans to switch to a new solvent to speed production. You analyze the environmental impacts and find its vapor may raise emissions, though the plant is within permits now.

options.text: Describe the switch as having no environmental impact in the report to speed approval.
Approve the switch since the plant is within permits now and monitor emissions afterward.
Recommend delaying the switch until the supplier provides complete emission data for the solvent.
Estimate emissions with the new solvent, compare them with limits, and recommend controls.

basic.situation: You inspect a workshop for hazards like noise and lighting. A worker says the grinder is loud, but your first sound meter reading is within the limit.

options.text: Accept the first reading and add the worker's comment in your inspection notes.
Measure the grinder noise while it runs and compare it with the limit.
Mark the grinder as safe and tell the worker the noise just seems louder up close.
Tell the worker to wear ear plugs and mark the workshop as compliant overall.

advanced.situation: A chemical spill at a plant forces an evacuation. You are sent to investigate and direct two laboratory staff collecting samples, but the wind has changed.

options.text: Send the two staff in to collect samples quickly while you coordinate by radio.
Check wind and safety data, plan upwind sampling, and brief staff on protective gear.
Collect the samples yourself to keep the staff safe and write the plan later.
Wait for the wind to change again and send staff in when the smell fades.

basic.situation: You record air quality test data and prepare a summary chart. A value from last Tuesday is missing because the monitor was unplugged that day.

options.text: Fill the missing day with the average of the days before and after it.
Leave the gap and add a footnote saying data is missing for that day.
Copy last Monday's values into Tuesday so the chart looks like a full week of data.
Leave the gap, note the unplugged monitor, and tell your supervisor about the gap.

advanced.situation: You are asked to create standard reporting templates and audit the hazardous waste database for the team. During the audit, you find chemical entries missing disposal dates.

options.text: Trace each missing date to its manifest, update entries, and make the field required.
Delete the incomplete entries so the database passes the completeness check before the audit.
Enter the date of the audit as the disposal date for each blank entry.
Add a check for blank dates to the template and fix entries as staff report them.

basic.situation: A customer asks you to explain a lab report showing lead in their well water above the guideline. They look worried and ask what to do.

options.text: Explain the result plainly, say it is above the guideline, and advise safe water.
Give the customer the report and a leaflet on lead in drinking water to read.
Tell the customer the level is slightly above the guideline and probably fine for adults.
Tell the customer the water is safe to drink and the report can be filed.

advanced.situation: A city asks you to help develop a program to monitor air pollution near schools. Your lab has monitors for four sites, but 12 schools are near busy roads.

options.text: Place the monitors at the schools the officials prefer and report results for all twelve.
Place the four monitors at the four schools nearest the busiest road and review later.
Rank schools by traffic and distance, place monitors at representative ones, and rotate them.
Ask the city to buy eight more monitors and delay the program until they arrive.

basic.situation: You join a drilling crew on a prospecting trip with supervision. The driller asks you to log core samples, but a box of cores has fallen and the order is mixed.

options.text: Number the cores in the sequence the plan expects and record that as their true order.
Arrange the cores by color and texture to match the drilling log, then record them.
Stop logging, tell your supervisor, and use depth marks to restore the order.
Log the cores in the order you find them and note that the box fell.

advanced.situation: You lead a small geophysical survey team in a remote forest. Halfway through the line, a team member twists an ankle and the satellite phone has no signal at the survey spot.

options.text: Stabilize the injury, move the team to the nearest signal point, and call for help.
Send one member to find a signal while the others continue the survey line.
Finish the survey line first since the equipment is already set up, then seek help.
Have the injured member walk out alone along the line while the team continues.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to read old exploration reports for a prospecting area and compile key data. Two reports give different depths for the same rock layer.

options.text: Average the two depths and enter the result as the compiled value for the layer.
Use the newer report's depth and note the older figure in your compiled notes.
List both depths with their report sources and ask your supervisor which to use.
Enter the deeper figure and delete the other report from the shared folder.

advanced.situation: You must gather information on groundwater problems near a quarry from public databases and local residents. The residents are upset, and the database records are incomplete.

options.text: Interview residents with a set question list, cross-check with records, and note gaps.
Rely on the public database records and invite residents to send written comments.
Talk to the most affected residents and use their accounts to fill the database gaps.
Fill the gaps with figures from a similar quarry and report them as local data.

basic.situation: You prepare water samples for analysis with supervision. One sample bottle arrived unlabeled, though it was packed with others from the same site.

options.text: Set the bottle aside, tell your supervisor, and ask the field team to confirm it.
Label it with the site name of the other bottles and test it with them.
Test the bottle and mark the result as source unconfirmed in the report.
Pour the contents into a labeled bottle from that site and discard the old bottle.

advanced.situation: You develop a new testing protocol and train a junior on analyzing rock samples for sulfur content. Results from two instruments differ, and the junior asks which one to trust.

options.text: Tell the junior to trust the newer instrument and record which one was used.
Tell the junior to use whichever instrument gives the result the client expects.
Run reference samples on both, find the cause of the difference, and teach the junior.
Tell the junior to average both instruments' readings for each sample going forward.

basic.situation: Your senior technician asks you to draft a short report on sampling results. One sample result is much higher than the rest, and no note explains why.

options.text: Lower the high result to match the others in the draft so the report looks consistent.
Report the result as measured, mark it unusual, and ask your senior technician.
Leave the high result out of the draft and add it if anyone asks.
Include the result in the table and add a line saying the cause is not known.

advanced.situation: You review a colleague's technical report recommending drilling at a site. The recommendation relies on one sample result, and the colleague insists the report must go to the client today.

options.text: Sign off the report as fully reviewed and ask the colleague to add more samples later.
Ask for the other sample data and hold sign-off until the recommendation is supported.
Sign off the report and add a note that the recommendation relies on one sample.
Send the report to the client today and offer to review the sample data next week.

basic.situation: You make field notes and a sketch of a rock outcrop with guidance. Your sketch scale is not marked, and the rock layers look tilted in two directions.

options.text: Add a scale bar, label the measured tilt directions, and ask your supervisor to check.
Copy the layer angles from a textbook diagram of a similar outcrop onto your sketch.
Redraw the sketch with all the layers tilted one way so it looks neater.
Add a scale bar and label the layers as tilted in two directions on the sketch.

advanced.situation: You create a geological cross-section from well logs and aerial photographs, and guide a junior. Two well logs disagree on the depth of a clay layer.

options.text: Check both logs against drilling records, mark the uncertainty, and explain it to the junior.
Draw the layer at the average depth and tell the junior this is standard practice.
Draw the layer at whichever depth makes the cross-section match the company's model.
Draw the layer at the shallower depth and write a note about the other log.

basic.situation: You record readings from a field gauge during a test and adjust it with guidance. After the adjustment, the readings jump by a fixed amount.

options.text: Change the earlier readings in the log to match the new level for a smooth record.
Note the time of the adjustment in the log and tell your supervisor about the jump.
Continue recording and mention the jump in your notes at the end of the test.
Subtract the jump from all later readings and carry on recording as normal.

advanced.situation: A well logging tool fails in the field, and the spare is a different model. You manage the team's data logging system, and the client wants results today.

options.text: Use the spare tool and tell the client the model changed after the work is done.
Repair the failed tool in the field using parts from the spare and resume logging.
Use the spare tool and log its readings under the failed tool's name.
Test the spare against known readings, document the differences, and tell the client.

basic.situation: You measure water level and flow at a stream gauge site with guidance. The river is higher than usual after rain, and the bank near the usual wading point is slippery.

options.text: Wade in carefully with a partner watching from the bank to take the flow reading.
Postpone the readings until the river drops, even if that takes several days.
Take level readings from the bridge and note why you avoided the bank.
Estimate the flow by eye from the bank and write it as a measured value.

advanced.situation: You investigate how a glacier-fed stream's flow has changed over several summers for a research project. Your gauge records show sudden jumps that may come from ice blocking the channel.

options.text: Report the jumps as measured and suggest in a note that ice may explain them.
Wait for next summer's data before looking into the jumps in the current records.
Compare the jumps with weather data and site photos, inspect the channel, and flag affected records.
Delete the readings around each jump and publish the rest as the true flow record.

basic.situation: You collect water samples to test for pH and oxygen. At the site, you notice an oily sheen on the water that is not on your sampling plan.

options.text: Move to a clear stretch of the stream and collect the planned samples there instead.
Collect the planned samples and mention the sheen in your field notes later.
Skim the sheen off the surface and dispose of it so the sample looks clean.
Collect the planned samples, add one of the sheen, and report it to your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You help design a program to ensure abandoned wells in a district are sealed properly. The district has 60 unmapped wells and a small team.

options.text: Seal the easiest wells first to show quick progress to the district and public.
Rank wells by contamination risk, pilot sealing methods on a few, and schedule the rest.
Fill the wells with soil from nearby and record them as sealed to meet the target.
Seal the wells in the order that residents report them to the district office.

basic.situation: You clean and prepare a stream flow gauge for installation with guidance. You find a small crack in the plastic casing of the water level recorder.

options.text: Install the recorder as it is, since the crack is small and above the line.
Seal the crack with waterproof tape and install it with a note in the log.
Set the recorder aside, label it as damaged, and ask your supervisor for a replacement.
Install the recorder and log it as new equipment that passed the inspection checklist.

advanced.situation: A stream gauge station stops sending data during a flood warning. You are expected to troubleshoot and repair it independently, but the site is partly submerged.

options.text: Check power and telemetry from dry ground and report the status to the control room.
Swim out to the station to reset the logger before more data is lost.
Wait for the water to drop and repair the station then, since the warning is out.
Wade to the station and repair it while a colleague watches from the bank.

basic.situation: You perform quality control checks on daily rainfall data for hydrologists. One station shows 250 mm for a day when neighboring stations show 25 mm.

options.text: Change 250 mm to 25 mm on the assumption that a zero was added by mistake.
Flag the value as suspect and pass the dataset on to the hydrologist with a note.
Flag the value, check the station log for faults, and tell the hydrologist about it.
Delete the whole day from every station's records to keep the data series consistent.

advanced.situation: You analyze ecological data on erosion and pollution in a river after floods. Your results suggest a factory discharge is part of the problem, but your data covers two sites.

options.text: Name the factory in the report as the cause and send it to local media.
Omit the factory from the report since two sites cannot prove anything about the river.
Report the link as preliminary, state the data limits, and propose added sampling sites.
Report the link as likely and recommend that the regulator investigate the factory.

basic.situation: You draft a table summarizing river temperature readings for a research report. Your table includes values from a thermometer later found to read one degree high.

options.text: Leave the table unchanged and mention the thermometer problem in the cover email.
Subtract one degree from those values and add a note explaining the change in the table.
Mark those values, note the thermometer fault, and ask your supervisor how to treat them.
Leave the table as it is since the error is small and the report is due.

advanced.situation: You write a groundwater contamination report on a suspected hazardous waste site. Test results show elevated levels in one well, and the site owner asks you to wait for retesting before sending.

options.text: Send the report with current results, state the uncertainty, and plan retesting as follow-up.
Wait for the retest results from the owner's chosen lab before sending the report.
Remove the elevated well from the report until the owner's retest is finished.
Send the report with the owner's earlier clean results averaged into the current ones.

basic.situation: A water conservation planner asks you a technical question about last year's stream flow. You have the figures, but they have not yet been quality checked.

options.text: Give the figures with a clear note that they are unchecked and offer to confirm later.
Give the figures and say they are final because the planner needs them quickly.
Give a rough estimate from memory and tell the planner to check the records.
Tell the planner you will answer after the figures have been checked next week.

advanced.situation: During a flood event, emergency staff ask for real time river data while a landowner complains that a neighbor's dam is raising water levels on their land.

options.text: Tell the landowner the neighbor must remove the dam and delay data for the emergency staff.
Send the flood data to emergency staff now, log the complaint, and schedule an investigation afterward.
Send the flood data to emergency staff and ask the landowner to write to the agency.
Visit the dam first to settle the complaint, then send the flood data to staff.

basic.situation: You calculate safe working time for a maintenance worker entering a contaminated area. The reading is 4 units per hour and the worker's remaining allowance is 6 units.

options.text: Give the worker the same time as the last worker who entered the area.
Divide the allowance by the reading, apply the plant's margin, and get it checked.
Round the time up to two hours so the worker can finish the job.
Divide the allowance by the reading and tell the worker the full time calculated.

advanced.situation: A repair in a high-radiation area would take longer than the exposure limit allows for one worker. You set the exposure plan and guide the crew.

options.text: Record the planned exposure as within the limit and assign one worker for the full task.
Split the task into timed shifts across workers, set dose alarms, and brief the crew.
Shorten the task by preparing parts outside the area, then recalculate the exposure time.
Start with one worker and swap in a second if the dose alarm sounds.

basic.situation: A radiation monitor alarm sounds while you are on shift. You have not seen this alarm before, and your supervisor is in a meeting.

options.text: Check the alarm display and readings, then report them to your supervisor afterward.
Follow the alarm procedure, keep people away from the area, and call your supervisor.
Switch off the monitor so the alarm stops disturbing workers working nearby in the area.
Reset the alarm and watch the monitor for a few minutes to see if it repeats.

advanced.situation: Several alarms sound at once in different areas of a facility. You are leading the response with a new technician beside you, and information from the control room is unclear.

options.text: Rank alarms by reading, send protected teams to the highest first, and explain each step.
Send the trainee alone to check the nearest alarm area and report back by radio.
Wait for the control room to clarify before sending any team to the alarm areas.
Send teams to the alarms in the order they sounded and ask control to clarify.

basic.situation: You place radioactive waste, including broken sample bottles, into disposal containers with supervision. One container is nearly full and the next bottle fragments are sharp.

options.text: Leave the fragments on the tray and ask your supervisor for a new container.
Press the fragments down into the container with a gloved hand to make them fit.
Put the fragments in the ordinary trash bin so the container does not overflow.
Seal and label the full container, then use a new one with tongs.

advanced.situation: You design a sampling strategy for suspected contamination in a facility's drainage system and advise on disposing of the waste. The drain has three branches with different histories.

options.text: Sample each branch on its own history, keep waste separate by branch, and advise on disposal.
Sample the branch with the highest past activity and treat the others as similar.
Sample the cleanest branch and declare the whole drain safe for ordinary disposal.
Mix samples from all three branches into one container and test the mixture once.

basic.situation: You clean a tool contaminated with radioactive material using soap and water under direct supervision. After cleaning, the monitor still reads above the clean limit.

options.text: Repeat the cleaning, recheck with the monitor, and tell your supervisor if needed.
Tag the tool as contaminated and ask your supervisor what to do next.
Wrap the tool in plastic and return it to the toolbox for later cleaning.
Release the tool for general use since most of the contamination was removed.

advanced.situation: You recommend a decontamination method for a large pump with heavy contamination in its internal parts. Abrasive blasting would work quickly but spreads particles, and the pump is needed soon.

options.text: Recommend abrasive blasting in the open work area to meet the pump's deadline.
Recommend a contained method such as chemical flushing, with air monitoring and waste capture.
Recommend abrasive blasting inside an enclosure with filtered air and extra air monitoring.
Recommend wiping the pump's outer surface and returning it to service if readings fall.

basic.situation: You collect an air sample from a work area to measure radioactivity. The sampling pump is running, but the flow rate display reads lower than the set value.

options.text: Stop sampling, check the pump and filter, then restart when the flow is steady.
Continue sampling and record the actual flow rate with a note on the form.
Continue sampling for a longer time to make up for the lower flow rate.
Record the set flow rate on the form as if the pump had run normally.

advanced.situation: You calibrate area radiation detection systems for a precise monitoring program and troubleshoot a unit that reads 15 percent lower than a reference source. The unit protects a work area in use today.

options.text: Leave the unit as it is and log its readings as accurate for the shift.
Remove the unit, set up a temporary monitor, and troubleshoot it with the reference source.
Keep the unit in service and add a 15 percent adjustment factor to its readings.
Recalibrate the unit in place while workers continue in the area and check it afterward.

basic.situation: You monitor personnel exposure. At midday, one worker's dosimeter shows exposure approaching the maximum permissible limit for the period, and the worker has another task planned this afternoon.

options.text: Tell your supervisor now and recommend moving the worker away from radiation areas.
Tell the worker to watch the dosimeter and stop if it reaches the limit.
Adjust the worker's dose record so the afternoon task can go ahead as planned.
Note the reading and report it to your supervisor at the end of the shift.

advanced.situation: You develop a radiation safety training program and a standard format for contamination reports. Staff say the current reports are inconsistent, and a new group starts next month.

options.text: Review past reports, draft a standard template, pilot it, and build training on it.
Write a template and email it to all staff with instructions to use it.
Use the report format from a plant you worked at earlier and train staff on it.
Rewrite the inconsistent past reports so they all look the same and skip the training.

basic.situation: You help a survey crew by measuring distances and clearing sightlines. The chief asks you to call out readings, and you notice the tape sagged between points on a slope.

options.text: Subtract a few centimeters from the reading to allow for the sag and call it out.
Call out the reading and mention the sag to the chief after the next point.
Tell the chief about the sag, hold the tape level, and remeasure the distance.
Call out the distance the chief expects from the plan to keep the crew moving.

advanced.situation: You design a digital database for forest tract data across several districts. Each district uses different tree species codes and survey dates, and a mapping deadline is near.

options.text: Delete records that do not fit the new format so the database loads cleanly.
Import each district's data as is and add a column with its original codes.
Use the largest district's codes for all and convert the others by similar names.
Agree common species codes with each district, set date fields, and test mapping with samples.

basic.situation: You plant seedlings on a cleared slope under supervision. Rain has made the soil heavy, and the planting plan asks for 3-meter spacing.

options.text: Wait for the soil to dry a day and then plant at the planned spacing.
Plant closer together than planned to save time since some seedlings may not survive.
Pack the wet soil hard around each seedling and plant at any spacing that fits.
Plant at the planned spacing, firm the soil lightly, and tell your supervisor about conditions.

advanced.situation: You supervise a forest nursery with a large order due this month. Workers report a fungus on a section of seedlings, and shipping them would meet the order.

options.text: Spray all the seedlings with fungicide and ship the whole order on schedule as planned.
Isolate the section, identify the fungus, and tell the buyer about the delay.
Ship the healthy sections on time and treat the affected section for a later order.
Ship the whole order on time and tell buyers any fungus will clear after planting.

basic.situation: You inspect trees and collect bark samples to find insect damage. You find small holes in several pine trunks with fresh sawdust at their bases.

options.text: Collect one bark sample from the worst tree and report it with your notes.
Brush away the sawdust and seal the holes to stop the damage spreading.
Photograph the holes, collect labeled bark samples from several trees, and report the finding.
Mark the trees for cutting right away and record the cause as insect damage.

advanced.situation: You design a field experiment to test whether a thinning method reduces insect outbreaks. The forest has varied soils, and three plots are available.

options.text: Thin the plot with the healthiest trees and report the method as proven effective.
Match plots by soil, assign treatments at random, keep one as control, and record conditions.
Thin two plots and compare them with the third using the same insect counts.
Thin all three plots and compare outbreak levels with last year's records from the area.

basic.situation: You patrol a park during the dry season. You see a small campfire still burning near dry grass, with no campers nearby.

options.text: Cover the fire with dry leaves so it burns out slowly while you continue patrolling.
Call the ranger station to report the fire and wait nearby until help comes.
Put out the fire with water and soil, then report it to the station.
Note the location and keep patrolling, planning to tell a ranger at the end.

advanced.situation: You coordinate fire detection and public education for a forest district. Lookouts report smoke from two locations, while a school visit is due this morning.

options.text: Send a crew to the larger smoke report and hold the second for confirmation.
Tell the lookouts to confirm with local farmers by phone before alerting any crew.
Dispatch crews to both smoke reports, then assign a colleague to reschedule the school visit.
Go to the school visit as planned and ask the crew to check smoke later.

basic.situation: You prepare documents for a forest use permit request. The applicant has submitted a form with the date section left empty and says they cannot recall the planned date.

options.text: Fill in the usual start date used for most permits and send the form on.
Issue the permit with the date left open so the applicant can start whenever they like.
Return the form, ask for a planned date, and note the request in the file.
Hold the form and phone the applicant tomorrow to ask for the date.

advanced.situation: A logging crew has cut trees inside the no-cutting buffer beside a stream. The foreman says the permit map was unclear, and the crew plans to continue tomorrow.

options.text: Warn the foreman and return in a week to see if cutting has stopped.
Stop the cutting in the buffer, record the damage, and report to your supervisor.
Agree that the permit is unclear and allow cutting to continue until it is clarified.
Ask the foreman to mark the buffer on the permit map before cutting resumes.

basic.situation: A woodlot owner asks you which tree species to plant on a wet patch of land. You know a few species well, but you are not sure about this soil.

options.text: Tell the owner you will ask a senior forester and call back with an answer.
Tell the owner any species will do, since trees can adapt to wet soil.
Suggest species for wet soil, say what you are unsure of, and offer to check.
Recommend the species you know most about since it grows well in most places nearby.

advanced.situation: You provide technical support to a seed orchard program. A researcher wants to remove a block of trees for a disease survey, but those trees hold genetic lines needed for the program.

options.text: Propose sampling a few trees, save seed from key lines, and discuss it first.
Let the researcher remove the trees and plan to reorder the lost genetic lines later.
Suggest the researcher survey trees outside the orchard and compare the results later.
Approve removing the block since disease surveys matter to the whole orchard program.

basic.situation: You collect evidence at a burglary scene under supervision. A bloodstained cloth is damp, and the evidence bags in your kit are plastic.

options.text: Ask for a paper bag, let the cloth air-dry, then package and label it.
Seal the cloth in plastic and leave it in the car until the scene is cleared.
Rinse the blood from the cloth to stop it spoiling and seal it in plastic.
Seal the cloth in plastic and take it straight to the lab for repacking.

advanced.situation: You lead evidence collection at a house fire scene with two junior technicians. Firefighters want to start cleanup to reopen the road within an hour.

options.text: Ask for a short delay, secure key areas, assign collectors, and log the chain of custody.
Release the scene to firefighters and collect items from the debris pile later.
Photograph the whole scene quickly and release it to firefighters for cleanup within the hour.
Collect the largest items first and let firefighters begin cleaning the smaller areas.

basic.situation: You lift a fingerprint from a glass at a scene with dust and tape. The lifted print looks smudged at one edge.

options.text: Submit the smudged lift and note which edge is unclear on the card.
Photograph the print on the glass first, try a second lift, and record both attempts.
Redraw the unclear ridges in ink on the card to match a suspect's known print.
Trace the smudged edge on the card with a pencil to clarify the pattern.

advanced.situation: You examine a latent print on a curved plastic bag and a partial shoe impression on soil at one scene. Your database comparison returns several close candidates for the print.

options.text: Report the candidates as possible, request a second examiner's review, and cast the impression.
Report the closest candidate as the likely match and cast the shoe impression too.
Declare a definite match with the closest candidate to speed up the investigation.
Choose the candidate with a criminal record since the print is a partial.

basic.situation: You analyze gunshot residue samples with supervision. You notice your own sleeve may have brushed the sample tray while labeling.

options.text: Wipe the tray with a clean cloth and analyze the samples as planned.
Tell your supervisor, document the contact, and ask about retesting the samples.
Analyze the samples as planned and mention the possible contact in your report.
Analyze the samples and leave the contact out since nothing visible was transferred.

advanced.situation: You reconstruct a shooting from bullet paths and blood stain patterns. The two lines of evidence suggest different shooter positions, and a detective wants a single conclusion today.

options.text: Report both findings, explain the conflict, and consult ballistics and pattern experts first.
Give the detective the bullet path result and say the blood pattern is unclear.
Pick the position supported by more blood stains and report it as the finding.
Combine both into one position that fits the detective's theory and state it as certain.

basic.situation: You prepare reagents for a blood presumptive test under instruction. The instructions call for a fresh solution each day, but yesterday's solution is still in the fridge.

options.text: Top up yesterday's solution with fresh reagent and log it as freshly made.
Discard yesterday's solution, prepare a fresh batch, and record the time in the log.
Test the old solution on a known control and use it if it works.
Use yesterday's solution and add a note to the log saying it was reused.

advanced.situation: A gas chromatograph in the lab shows baseline noise during an urgent drug analysis. You must troubleshoot it and improve sample preparation protocols for the team.

options.text: Move the samples to an older instrument that lacks a calibration record and report results.
Check the gas supply, column and vials, fix the source, then update the protocol.
Run a blank to check the baseline and continue if the noise looks stable.
Continue the analysis and apply a smoothing filter to the final data afterward.

basic.situation: You photograph a crime scene with guidance. A supervisor asks for overall and close-up photos of a window, but the scale marker has been left at another spot.

options.text: Place the scale beside the window, retake the close-ups, and note the retakes.
Take the close-ups and note in the log that the scale was missing from them.
Take the close-ups and add a scale to the photos later on a computer.
Skip the close-ups and use zoomed-in crops from the overall photos to save time.

advanced.situation: You prepare scene sketches and photographic records for a court case. The defense questions your sketch measurements, since some were estimated by eye. The scene is still accessible.

options.text: Replace the estimated values with rounded figures that look more precise in court.
Re-measure the estimated items with a tape, mark both sets in the records, and explain.
Mark the estimated measurements clearly on the sketch and state how they were obtained.
Redraw the sketch with exact-looking measurements and date it as the original sketch.

basic.situation: Before a hearing, a prosecutor asks you to confirm a detail in a report you helped prepare. You do not remember checking that detail.

options.text: Confirm the detail and add a note in the file saying you checked it.
Tell the prosecutor you are unsure and ask your senior colleague to answer.
Confirm the detail because it is probably right and the report was reviewed.
Check your notes and the case file, then tell the prosecutor what the records show.

advanced.situation: You testify as an expert witness. On cross-examination, the defense lawyer asks whether your analytical method can ever give a false result.

options.text: Say the method is very reliable and refer the lawyer to the validation report.
Say the method has not failed in your experience and move on to the next question.
Answer that all methods have limits, explain the error rate and controls, and stay calm.
Answer that false results are impossible with your equipment and your training record.

basic.situation: You run a routine assay on a raw material lot. The result is just outside the specification range, and you have enough sample for one more test.

options.text: Record the result as within range since the difference is within instrument error.
Rerun the test and record the second result if it falls within the range.
Report the first result to your supervisor and ask whether to use the spare sample.
Follow the retest procedure, record both results, and tell your supervisor about the first.

advanced.situation: A stability sample shows an unexpected result trend, and an analyst says the method was not followed exactly. You lead the failure investigation, and the batch awaits release.

options.text: Hold the batch, review the analyst's steps and records, and recommend actions.
Accept the original result and record the deviation as minor to close the case.
Release the batch with a note on file and complete the investigation next week.
Hold the batch and ask the analyst to repeat the test using the method.

basic.situation: You compile lab test data into a summary table for the weekly review. One result is missing because the instrument file did not save.

options.text: Fill the cell with the average of previous results and mark it estimated.
Fill the cell with the target value so the table looks complete and on time.
List the result as not available, tell your supervisor, and ask for a retest.
Leave the cell empty and mention the missing file in your weekly summary email.

advanced.situation: You lead an internal assessment of the lab's out-of-specification investigations. You find three recent investigations closed with no documented root cause, though each batch was released.

options.text: Add likely root causes to the three closed files yourself and finish the assessment.
Reopen the three files, review each case's root cause, and recommend fixes to the procedure.
Report the three findings to the quality head and propose training for investigators.
Note the gaps in the report and recommend a stricter checklist for new cases.

basic.situation: You complete an equipment logbook entry after using a balance. You realize you forgot to record the start time of your session.

options.text: Add a late entry with today's date, explain the omission, and sign it.
Leave the start time blank since the end time and the results are recorded.
Estimate the start time and enter it as if you had written it then.
Write the start time in the margin and tell your supervisor about it later today.

advanced.situation: You prepare quality control data for a regulatory submission and write the deviation report. The data includes one result later found to come from an uncalibrated instrument.

options.text: Include the result and add a short footnote that the instrument was recalibrated later.
Flag the result, document the instrument issue in the deviation report, and tell the lead.
Rerun the sample on a calibrated instrument and replace the old result in the data.
Exclude the result from the submission and describe the whole dataset as complete.

basic.situation: You perform a visual inspection of finished tablets with guidance. You see a few tablets with small chips that the inspection guide does not mention.

options.text: Pass the batch and mention the chipped tablets in your inspection notes for review.
Pass the batch since the guide does not list chips as a defect.
Set aside the chipped tablets, record how many, and ask your supervisor to classify them.
Remove the chipped tablets from the sample and pass the batch on the rest.

advanced.situation: You evaluate an analytical method that takes two hours per sample and has caused a backlog. A shorter method exists in the literature but has not been validated in your lab.

options.text: Run the shorter method on a few samples and use it if results look similar.
Switch to the shorter method for all samples and update the procedure afterward.
Add a second analyst to run samples with the current method to clear the backlog.
Validate the shorter method against the current one and update the procedure.

basic.situation: You assist in training a new analyst on a pH meter procedure. The new analyst skips the buffer check, saying it takes too long.

options.text: Sign the analyst's training record as complete since the rest of the steps were done.
Let the analyst skip the check this time and remind them next week.
Tell the analyst the buffer check is required and point to the written procedure.
Explain why the buffer check matters, watch the analyst do it, and answer questions.

advanced.situation: You find a recurring contamination problem in incoming vendor material. Production wants to keep using the lots, and the vendor says its own tests pass.

options.text: Accept the vendor's test results since they pass and note your concern in the file.
Allow production to continue and keep your contamination data out of the vendor talks.
Share your data with the vendor and production, request a joint review, and hold lots.
Recommend that production switch to another approved vendor until the vendor review is complete.

basic.situation: You use a pipette that gives inconsistent volumes during a routine test. A spare pipette is available on the shelf.

options.text: Stop using the pipette, tag it as faulty, use the spare, and report the fault.
Keep using the pipette and delete the replicate results that vary too much.
Keep using the pipette but take extra replicates to average out the variation.
Switch to the spare pipette and tell your supervisor at the end of the day.

advanced.situation: You set equipment validation standards for the lab. An analyst suggests extending calibration intervals on key balances to save time, citing three months of stable results.

options.text: Keep the current intervals for all the balances since any change is risky for audits.
Approve the longer interval for one balance first and review it after three months.
Approve the longer interval for every balance based on the analyst's three months of data.
Review calibration data and guidance, trial a longer interval, and set risk-based criteria.

basic.situation: You merge scanned aerial images into a photo mosaic using software with guidance. The seam between two images shows a visible brightness difference.

options.text: Apply the software's color balancing to both images, then check the seam.
Darken the brighter image by hand until both sides look the same in the mosaic.
Cover the seam with a clone patch copied from a different part of the area.
Blend the seam edge with the feathering tool and save the mosaic for review.

advanced.situation: You adjust remotely sensed images to show vegetation stress for a scientific category map. The default processing routine hides subtle differences in the dry zone.

options.text: Use the default routine and describe the dry zone differences in the map text.
Increase the contrast on the whole image until the dry zone differences become visible.
Paint the dry zone in a stress color by hand so the map matches expectations.
Test different band combinations and stretches, define the categories, and document the routine.

basic.situation: You integrate satellite imagery with a road layer under supervision. The two layers do not line up, and roads appear offset by about 30 meters.

options.text: Check both layers' coordinate systems, reproject if needed, and confirm the roads line up.
Shift the road layer by 30 meters and note the shift in the metadata.
Shift the road layer by 30 meters and delete the original file to save space.
Use the imagery as the base and drop the road layer from the project.

advanced.situation: During a remote sensing flight you process raw data to improve interpretation of a flooded area. The sensor shows noise streaks, and the pilot says the flight window closes in 20 minutes.

options.text: Continue the flight and filter out the streaks later on a copy of the files.
