Adjust the sensor gain, check a test strip, and refly the line if noise remains.
Continue the flight and overwrite the raw files with a filtered version afterward.
Continue the flight and note in the log that the streaks are normal for this sensor.

basic.situation: You verify data accuracy in a remote sensing image analysis system using a checklist. One image's metadata lists an acquisition date that does not match its file name.

options.text: Flag the mismatch on the checklist and move on to check the next image.
Change the metadata date to match the file name and note it on the checklist.
Mark the image as verified since the file name and metadata are close enough.
Compare the metadata with source records, flag the mismatch, and ask who can update it.

advanced.situation: You establish standards to verify data integrity across the team's remote sensing analysis system. Past errors came from file transfers, manual edits and software updates.

options.text: Turn off the edit logs to speed up analysts' file changes and reduce storage use.
Ask each analyst to verify their own files and report problems when found.
Write a standard requiring a second person to review every transferred file by hand.
Define checks for each error source, add checksums and edit logs, and train the team.

basic.situation: You join the planning of a mapping project for a coastal area. A senior planner asks you to list data needed, and you are unsure how recent the available imagery is.

options.text: List the imagery as available and assume it is recent enough for the project.
List the imagery as recent in the plan so the project can be approved quickly.
List the data needed, check the imagery's dates, and flag any old coverage.
List the data needed and ask the senior planner about the imagery dates later.

advanced.situation: You lead planning for a mapping project covering a city. Surveyors need ground control points, engineers need elevation accuracy, and the cartographer wants a single standard. The budget is fixed.

options.text: Ask each group to send written requirements and combine them into a single plan.
Follow the cartographer's standard for the whole project and tell the others later.
Meet all three, record each need, and agree a shared specification with priorities.
Choose the cheapest specification and tell each group it meets its stated requirements.

basic.situation: You collect aerial photos with a drone following step-by-step instructions. Wind picks up and the drone starts to drift from its planned flight line.

options.text: Land the drone, wait for calmer wind, and tell your supervisor before restarting.
Continue the flight and fill any gaps with photos from last month's earlier flight.
Continue the flight at a lower speed and check the photos for gaps afterward.
Switch off the drone's position hold and fly it manually to finish the line.

advanced.situation: You configure a multi-sensor aircraft system for a mission mapping forest canopy and heat loss. Two sensors share a mount, and their data cables could interfere.

options.text: Fly the mission with both cables taped together to save mounting time on site.
Plan the layout, test for interference on the ground, and fly a short test.
Fly the mission and label any unusable sensor data as test data afterward.
Mount both sensors as designed and check the first flight's data for noise afterward.

basic.situation: You prepare a presentation with charts and photos using a template. One chart shows land cover change, but the legend colors are the same for two classes.

options.text: Change one class color, check the legend against the data, and show your supervisor.
Merge the two classes into one in the chart and leave the totals unchanged.
Leave the chart as it is and explain the difference verbally in the meeting.
Add labels directly on the chart areas and keep the colors as they are.

advanced.situation: You design a presentation of mapping results for senior stakeholders. The images show a flood risk area that overlaps a politically sensitive development, and you have 10 minutes.

options.text: Present the flood risk map and leave out the development outlines to avoid controversy.
Lead with the key finding, use clear visuals, and state data limits.
Show all the findings in detail and run over time if stakeholders have questions.
Change the flood risk class on the development area so the map looks acceptable.

basic.situation: You inspect a factory floor to check fire and first-aid supplies. A fire extinguisher's gauge is in the red zone, and the next inspection is not for three months.

options.text: Mark the extinguisher as passed on the form to keep the inspection record complete.
Tag the extinguisher as out of service, report it, and arrange a replacement today.
Shake the extinguisher and recheck the gauge, then log it as working if it moves.
Report the low gauge to the supervisor and note it for the next inspection.

advanced.situation: A year of incident data shows many hand injuries on three production lines. Managers want a quick fix, but the injuries seem to come from different causes.

options.text: Report the injuries as worker mistakes and recommend written warnings for those involved.
Break down the injuries by line, task and cause, then recommend fixes for each source.
Recommend retraining workers on the lines with the most injuries and monitor the results.
Recommend gloves for all workers on the three lines and review results next year.

basic.situation: You collect a dust sample for lab analysis in a workshop. The sampling pump alarm shows low battery halfway through the sampling period.

options.text: Record the full planned sampling time on the form and send the sample to the lab.
Stop the sample, record the time, swap the battery, and restart a full sampling period.
Swap the battery and continue sampling, treating the short pause as part of the period.
Continue until the pump stops and note the actual sampling time on the form.

advanced.situation: You audit a hazardous waste storage site. You find leaking drums and incomplete labeling, and the site manager asks you to leave out the labeling issue because a client is visiting.

options.text: Document both findings, require the leaks to be contained now, and report the labeling gap as found.
Report the leaks and give the manager a week to fix the labeling first.
Leave both findings out of the audit report until after the client visit ends.
Report the leaks and leave out the labeling issue as the site manager asked.

basic.situation: You help maintain a noise survey program in a bottling plant. A new machine is installed, and the last noise map does not include it.

options.text: Measure noise around the new machine, update the map, and report any hearing protection needs.
Use the manufacturer's stated noise level for the new machine on the existing map.
Copy the noise level from the nearest machine onto the map and mark it measured.
Add the machine to the survey planned for next quarter and tell the supervisor.

advanced.situation: You develop a medical monitoring program for workers exposed to solvents. Some workers fear that abnormal results could cost them their jobs, and attendance is low.

options.text: Agree confidentiality rules with management, explain them to workers, and share results with consent.
Share each worker's abnormal results with supervisors so they can adjust job duties quickly.
Give managers the list of workers who skip checks so they can discipline them.
Send reminders to all workers about the benefits of attending the medical checks.

basic.situation: You demonstrate the use of safety goggles and ear protection to a group of new workers. A worker says the goggles fog up and wants to remove them.

options.text: Tell the worker to keep the goggles on and wipe them when they fog up.
Let the worker remove the goggles when working in areas with low splash risk.
Show anti-fog options or a better-fitting pair, and explain why eye protection is needed.
Tell the worker to remove the goggles and wear ordinary glasses instead for comfort.

advanced.situation: You coordinate a right-to-know program and develop training for a new hazardous chemical. The supplier's safety data sheet is in English, but many workers read Bahasa Malaysia more easily.

options.text: Tell workers the chemical is low risk so the training can be kept short.
Show a short video about the chemical from the supplier with English subtitles.
Translate key hazards and precautions into Bahasa Malaysia, add pictograms, and check understanding.
Give workers the English data sheet and ask supervisors to explain it during shifts.

basic.situation: You recommend measures to protect workers from a hazardous work method. Workers cut metal with a grinder that throws sparks near stored cardboard.

options.text: Recommend that workers wet the cardboard before grinding to reduce the fire risk.
Recommend moving the cardboard away, using a spark screen, and posting a fire watcher.
Recommend covering the cardboard with a fire blanket whenever grinding takes place.
Recommend grinding at night when fewer people are around to notice the sparks.

advanced.situation: A hospital laboratory worker shows symptoms that may be linked to a chemical vapor. You work with an engineer and the occupational physician to set controls while the lab keeps operating.

options.text: Tell the worker the symptoms are probably unrelated to work and take sick leave.
Ask the engineer to improve ventilation and tell the worker to see the physician.
Meet both, review exposure data, add local exhaust, and monitor the worker's health.
Give the worker a mask and keep the lab running as normal while you investigate.

basic.situation: You write a short report on your daily safety walkthrough. You saw a spill on a walkway that was cleaned up before you finished your walk.

options.text: Mention the spill briefly in the report and note that it was cleaned up.
Leave the spill out of the report since it was cleaned up before you finished.
Include the spill, the time it was cleaned, and the likely cause in the report.
Write that the walkway was dry and clear during your whole walkthrough to avoid questions.

advanced.situation: You must present research findings on repetitive strain injuries to senior management and a regulator. The findings show a costly redesign of workstations is needed.

options.text: Present a cheaper partial fix as the main recommendation to avoid management resistance.
Present the injury data, options with costs, and a phased plan with expected benefits.
Describe the injury rates as lower than measured so the regulator does not intervene.
Present the injury data and recommend the full redesign, leaving costs to finance.

basic.situation: You review an order for safety helmets for a construction site. The order lists helmets that lack the required standard mark, since the cheaper supplier does not certify them.

options.text: Return the order to purchasing, explain the missing mark, and request certified helmets.
Approve the order and write the standard mark into the paperwork yourself to save time.
Hold the order and call the supplier to confirm which helmet models are certified.
Approve the order and ask the supplier to send proof of certification afterward.

advanced.situation: At a night market you find a stall selling cooked food. The operator's food handler certificate has expired, and a crowd of customers is waiting.

options.text: Issue a written notice and give the operator seven days to renew the certificate.
Accept a small payment from the operator to overlook the expired certificate tonight.
Warn the operator verbally and check the certificate again at your next visit.
Explain the requirement, issue the notice, and have the stall stop selling until renewed.

basic.situation: You review sanitation reports and floor plans to gather information for a health inspection plan. One kitchen's sanitation report is missing, though its floor plan is on file.

options.text: Use last year's report for that kitchen in place of the missing report.
Ask the kitchen for the report, list it as missing, and inspect that kitchen first.
Fill in a satisfactory result for that kitchen so the plan can be completed.
Plan the inspection from the other reports and request the missing one when convenient.

advanced.situation: Several workers at a plant report skin rashes. You conduct a study to see if the illness is job-related, but the plant manager says it is due to their home soap.

options.text: Accept the manager's explanation and write that the rashes are not related to work.
Compare rash cases by work area and chemical exposure, review medical notes, and report findings.
Ask the workers whether they changed home products and base the report on that.
Interview the affected workers and list their work tasks and symptoms in the report.

basic.situation: You check that respirators are available and being used in a paint workshop. A worker pushes the respirator up on the head while spraying, saying it makes breathing hard.

options.text: Tell the worker to spray from farther away so the respirator is not necessary.
Remind the worker that the respirator must be worn at all times during spraying.
Stop the spraying, check the respirator's fit and filter, and have the worker retry.
Let the worker take the respirator off for short spraying jobs near the open door.

advanced.situation: A small company asks you to advise on applying safety principles in its workshop. The owner says safety rules slow work and wants just a few quick changes.

options.text: Agree that the rules slow work and suggest removing machine guards that block production.
Give the owner a general safety checklist found online and ask them to follow it.
Suggest the owner choose five quick changes and review how they work in three months.
Assess the workshop risks, rank them, and propose quick changes for the biggest risks.

basic.situation: You inspect fire suppression equipment in a storeroom. One portable extinguisher has a broken safety pin seal and its inspection tag is a year old.

options.text: Note the broken seal in your report and recommend a service at the next visit.
Replace the seal yourself and leave the old inspection tag in place for now.
Tag the extinguisher for service, record the findings, and tell the supervisor today.
Update the inspection tag with today's date and mark the extinguisher as fully serviced.

advanced.situation: Air tests at a printing plant show solvent levels above the exposure limit near one press. You recommend measures, and the plant says production cannot stop.

options.text: Recommend local exhaust at the press, interim respirators, and a retest after installation.
Recommend rotating workers away from the press every hour to cut each person's exposure.
Recommend opening the windows near the press and reporting that levels are acceptable.
Recommend respirators for all workers at the press and a retest in three months.

basic.situation: You supply and maintain personal protective equipment for a warehouse. A worker returns a harness with frayed stitching and asks for another one right away.

options.text: Remove the frayed harness from use, record it, and issue a new one.
Tell the worker to keep using the harness for now and check it next week.
Issue a new harness and hand the frayed one to the worker's supervisor.
Stitch the frayed section with strong thread and issue the same harness again.

advanced.situation: A worker refuses to enter a tank, saying the air smells odd. The supervisor says the tank was cleaned and wants the job done this afternoon.

options.text: Send a different worker into the tank since the supervisor says it is clean.
Keep the worker out, test the tank air, and clear entry once readings are safe.
Ask the worker to wait while you review the tank's cleaning records and past tests.
Tell the worker the refusal will be recorded as absence if the tank is not entered.

basic.situation: You maintain a logbook of your daily activities, including areas visited. At the end of the day, you realize you did not visit the loading dock listed on your plan.

options.text: Leave the dock line blank in the log and plan to visit tomorrow.
Record the loading dock as not visited and schedule the visit for tomorrow morning.
Write a short note about the dock conditions based on your last visit.
Skip the logbook entry for today and catch up on all entries next week.

advanced.situation: You prepare documents for a legal proceeding about a workplace accident and may be asked to testify. Your inspection notes from the day are incomplete and handwritten.

options.text: Fill in the missing details from memory and date the notes as written that day.
Type up the notes as they are and submit them with the other documents.
Organize the original notes, add a dated clarification for gaps, and prepare to explain them.
Rewrite the notes more clearly and submit the new version in place of the originals.

basic.situation: You draft a treatment plan for a new client with alcohol dependence, with guidance from a senior counselor. The client's history shows a past relapse after a job loss.

options.text: Use the clinic's standard plan template and add the client's name and stated goals.
Show the client another client's plan as an example and change details afterward.
Include job stress as a relapse trigger and review the draft with your senior counselor.
Copy the plan from a similar client in the files and change the name.

advanced.situation: You help evaluate a community drug prevention program with a school and a local clinic. The data show few teenagers attend the sessions, but the school wants the program unchanged.

options.text: Survey teenagers on barriers, adjust session timing, and re-evaluate attendance.
Keep the program unchanged as the school wants and review attendance next year.
Report the program as successful using attendance figures from the parent meetings instead.
Promote the sessions more widely through posters and the school newsletter this term.

basic.situation: You complete a client history form with supervision. The client gives a detail about past drug use that conflicts with a clinic referral note.

options.text: Change the referral note to match what the client said today and file both.
Record the client's statement on the form and leave the referral note as it is.
Record the detail from the referral note since it came from a professional.
Record the client's statement, note the conflict, and discuss it with your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You review a colleague's client records before an external audit. Several progress notes were written weeks after sessions, and some details appear copied between clients.

options.text: Remove the suspect notes from the files so the auditor sees consistent records.
Remind all counselors by email about timely and accurate notes before the external audit.
Ask the colleague to update the notes and return them before the audit starts.
Flag the notes, discuss them with the colleague and supervisor, and set a note standard.

basic.situation: A client's mother calls the clinic and asks what addiction services are available for her son. He has not signed a release allowing you to discuss his case.

options.text: Tell her about his plan and test results so she can support him.
Share general service information, say you cannot discuss his case, and take her number.
Confirm that her son is a client and say he is doing well in treatment.
Tell her you cannot discuss anything about the clinic and end the call politely.

advanced.situation: You act as liaison between a client, his family and the hospital doctor. The client wants his drug use kept from his family, and the family is demanding full information.

options.text: Tell the family the client wants privacy and refer their questions to the doctor.
Explain confidentiality limits to all, get the client's consent, and arrange a joint meeting.
Share the key facts with the family to calm them since they will find out anyway.
Ask the doctor to leave the drug use out of the notes the family can see.

basic.situation: You attend a staff case conference and take notes. The group discusses a client's possible suicidal thoughts, and a nurse suggests waiting before informing the family.

options.text: Record the discussion and decisions and leave the safety concern to the nurse.
Record the discussion and decisions, and flag the safety concern to the lead counselor.
Leave the suicidal thoughts out of the meeting notes to protect the client's privacy.
Record the discussion and decisions and raise the safety concern after the meeting ends.

advanced.situation: You coordinate post-treatment support for a client with the court, a probation officer and a community agency. The court date moves earlier, and the agency has no place for two weeks.

options.text: Tell the client to attend the court date and look for a place himself meanwhile.
Ask the community agency to find an earlier place and update the court afterward.
Inform the court of the gap, ask for time, and arrange interim support.
Tell the court the client has already started with the agency to avoid delays.

basic.situation: You collect a urine sample for dependency assessment under direct supervision. The client says the sample cup was already used when handed to him.

options.text: Rinse the cup and use it since the client is waiting and the sample is needed.
Stop, get a new sealed cup, restart the collection, and note what happened.
Collect the sample in the used cup and send it to the lab as normal.
Ask a colleague to check the cup before collecting the sample from the client.

advanced.situation: You analyze follow-up data on discharged clients to judge whether a treatment works. Results show clients who left early did worse, but many discharged clients cannot be reached.

options.text: Assume the unreachable clients did as well as those reached and report the total.
Count the unreachable clients as successes in the report to show the treatment works.
Report the results from clients reached and note that many could not be contacted.
Report the missing follow-up rate, test for bias, and suggest better tracking.

basic.situation: You conduct a program orientation for new clients with a lead counselor. A new client becomes upset, shouting that he does not want to be there, and others look uneasy.

options.text: Tell the group the client has been in treatment before and has failed before.
Stay calm, offer the client a private talk, and let the lead counselor continue.
Pause the orientation and ask the client to step outside and calm down first.
Tell the client he must stay and finish the orientation or leave the program.

advanced.situation: You supervise a student intern who will lead a first group session alone next week. The intern seems anxious and has not yet led a group with a counselor present.

options.text: Give the intern clients' case files to read at home before the session.
Give the intern a session guide and sit at the back of the first session.
Let the intern run the session alone and review the notes afterward as arranged.
Have the intern co-lead a session with you first, then decide on solo work.

basic.situation: You review a student's transcript to check graduation requirements. The student is one course short but wants a signed letter confirming eligibility today for a scholarship.

options.text: Write the letter saying the student is expected to meet all requirements very soon.
Sign the letter confirming full eligibility since the student plans to finish the course.
Explain the missing course, note when it can be completed, and offer a status letter.
Tell the student to ask the registrar for the letter once the course is done.

advanced.situation: You design an assessment of student interests for a school with limited counseling time. Teachers say the current test is long and many students do not finish it.

options.text: Give the current test in two sessions and score the answers that were completed.
Use a shorter published interest inventory and train teachers to give it in class.
Fill blank answers with the most common responses so every student gets a result.
Draft a shorter version, pilot it with a few classes, and check its usefulness.

basic.situation: A student asks you about college degree programs and admission requirements for engineering. You have last year's brochure, and you are not sure the entry grades are unchanged.

options.text: Share the brochure details and tell the student to confirm them with the college.
Tell the student the entry grades are fixed and no further checks are needed.
Tell the student the entry grades are probably about the same as last year's.
Share the brochure details, say they may have changed, and check the college website.

advanced.situation: Teachers ask you how to guide students toward careers. Several teachers push every student to university, though some students would suit technical training better.

options.text: Run a short session on career pathways, share local job data, and offer conversation tools.
Tell teachers to let students choose for themselves and avoid giving advice on options.
Support the teachers and tell students that university is the route to a good career.
Send teachers a handout listing university options and technical training courses nearby.

basic.situation: You instruct a small group of students in resume writing. One student lists a job on her resume that she never held, thinking it will impress employers.

options.text: Tell her it is fine since many applicants add jobs and employers rarely check.
Explain why the entry should be removed and show how to present real skills.
Tell her to remove the entry and move on to helping the next student.
Suggest she lists it as a short project, which sounds less like a job.

advanced.situation: You develop and lead a career workshop for 200 students. The hall has a weak microphone, and you have 45 minutes.

options.text: Show a long video about careers so students can watch comfortably from their seats.
Give one lecture on resumes and interviews and share the slides with students afterward.
Ask students to share their family income aloud in front of everyone to start discussion.
Plan short activities in small groups, give clear handouts, and test the microphone beforehand.

basic.situation: You help organize an orientation for new college students. The venue holds 100, and 130 students have confirmed, with the date fixed.

options.text: Split the orientation into two sessions, inform students of their slot, and tell your supervisor.
Let all 130 students attend and ask the extra students to stand at the back.
Ask your supervisor to find a bigger venue and wait for their reply.
Tell the last 30 students who confirmed that their places are cancelled now.

advanced.situation: You lead a recruitment and enrollment campaign for a vocational program. Admissions staff want to promise job placement, but past placement rates were about 60 percent.

options.text: Promise job placement to the first 50 enrollees to encourage early registration this term.
Use the actual placement rate, share student stories, and host sessions with employers.
Advertise a job placement guarantee for all students since competing programs already do.
Say most graduates find work and give the 60 percent figure to anyone who asks.

basic.situation: A student likes drawing and mathematics and asks which degree to take. Her assessment shows strengths in spatial and design skills.

options.text: Suggest architecture or design programs, explain entry requirements, and arrange a campus visit.
Suggest architecture and give her a printed list of universities that offer it.
Suggest accounting because it uses mathematics and has many job openings nationwide.
Tell her to choose the degree her friends are choosing to feel comfortable.

advanced.situation: A student shows signs of severe anxiety and has missed financial aid forms. You want a referral partnership with a local counseling clinic, but the clinic has a waiting list.

options.text: Tell the student to wait for the clinic and handle the aid forms alone.
Counsel the student yourself for several weeks while the clinic waiting list moves.
Meet the clinic, agree a priority referral route, refer the student, and arrange aid help.
Refer the student to the clinic and help with aid forms while the student waits.

basic.situation: A student comes to you upset about repeated absence and low marks at school. The student says things at home are difficult and then goes quiet.

options.text: Listen and suggest the student talk to a teacher they trust about home problems.
Listen calmly, ask open questions, and tell the school's lead counselor about your concern.
Tell the student to focus on marks and that home matters will settle in time.
Call the parents at once to say the student has been complaining about home.

advanced.situation: A serious incident occurs at school, and students are very distressed. You lead the counseling response and need staff to support students in classrooms.

options.text: Meet distressed students one by one in your office in the order they arrive.
Brief staff on a simple protocol, set up a quiet room, and identify students needing help.
Send an email to all teachers with advice and ask them to call if needed.
Tell students the incident is not a big deal and to return to class.

basic.situation: At the first session with a couple, you are using the clinic's standard intake questions. The husband keeps answering for his wife, who stays quiet.

options.text: Carry on with the husband's answers and plan to hear from the wife next session.
Continue with the husband's answers and tell your supervisor the wife stayed quiet.
Record the wife's answers as 'no concerns' on the form since she did not object.
Turn to the wife and ask the next questions to her directly, then to him.

advanced.situation: A mother says her teenage son threatens his younger sister at home. The usual intake form has no safety section, and the family wants to start therapy this week.

options.text: Reassure the family that such threats are common in teenagers and begin the usual sessions.
Start therapy as the family wants and gather safety details as trust grows.
Use the standard form and ask the mother extra questions about the threats.
Add a safety screen to the intake and see each member separately before planning therapy.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to draft a treatment plan for a family where the parents argue loudly in front of the children. You have the intake notes.

options.text: Reuse another family's plan, change the names and start sessions with this family.
Use the clinic's standard template with general goals and ask your supervisor to add specifics.
Write a short plan on reducing arguments and start sessions before your supervisor reads it.
Draft goals tied to the intake findings, list methods, and take the plan to supervision.

advanced.situation: A family's conflict pattern has not changed after eight sessions of the agreed plan. Each parent blames the other, and their child has started missing school.

options.text: Add extra weekly sessions to the current plan to work harder on the same goals.
Review progress with the family and your supervisor, then redesign the plan's goals and methods.
End sessions and refer the family elsewhere, saying their lack of effort caused the stall.
Keep the plan as it is, since change takes time, and review in eight sessions.

basic.situation: You finish a session with a family and must add your progress note to the case file before the next client arrives in ten minutes.

options.text: Jot short reminders today and complete the full note later this week when you have time.
Write a brief factual note covering activities, observations and next steps, then file it today.
Write this note and next session's note together once the next meeting is done.
Copy the previous session's note into the file and change the date at the top.

advanced.situation: An audit shows three junior therapists write progress notes in very different ways, and some leave out recommendations. You are asked to raise the standard.

options.text: Add recommendations to the old notes in the therapists' names so the audit passes.
Circulate one well-written note as a model and let each therapist adapt it to their style.
Agree one template with the team, review sample files with each therapist, and recheck next month.
Send all therapists an email listing the items every progress note must include.

basic.situation: A couple has finished their last planned session and say they feel better. You have a few minutes left to talk about what comes next.

options.text: Close the file and remove their contact details from the clinic system to save space.
Ask what has helped them, then agree on simple steps and a follow-up check-in date.
Suggest practices they can use at home and offer to answer questions by phone.
Tell them to contact the clinic if problems return and close the file today.

advanced.situation: A client who has relapsed into harmful family conflict several times is ending therapy. The family lives far from the clinic and has a low income.

options.text: Book a monthly in-person review at the clinic for the next twelve months.
Build a written relapse plan together: warning signs, free local supports and scheduled phone check-ins.
Give the family a booklet on managing conflict and invite them to call when needed.
Explain that follow-up is not possible given the distance and cost, then close the case.

basic.situation: A family's doctor phones to ask how therapy is going. The parents have signed a consent form that allows you to share basic progress.

options.text: Read out your session notes so the doctor has the full picture of the family.
Share attendance and general progress by phone once the doctor states his name and clinic.
Tell the doctor to ask the parents directly because therapy matters are private.
Confirm the consent on file, then share attendance and general progress, keeping details private.

advanced.situation: You lead a case conference for a child who refuses to attend school. The teacher, a paediatrician and the parents disagree about the cause and the plan.

options.text: Ask the paediatrician to decide the main cause and share a plan with the others.
Support the parents' view, close the meeting and tell the others the plan is final.
Set an agenda, let each person state their view, then agree shared goals and roles.
Summarise each view in a follow-up email and let people reply in their own time.

basic.situation: A client tells you she cannot pay rent after separating from her husband. She asks where to get help in her area.

options.text: Tell her to search online for housing support and return with questions next week.
Tell her money problems are outside therapy so she should not raise them again.
Suggest she ask relatives for a loan, since agencies are often slow to respond.
Give her the welfare office and legal aid centre contacts and explain how to apply.

advanced.situation: A client planning a divorce has debts, two children and unclear property ownership. She asks you what she should claim from her husband.

options.text: Tell her which assets to claim, based on what you read about similar cases.
Explain you cannot advise on claims, refer her to legal aid, and help her list questions.
Suggest she settle the money questions with her husband first and see a lawyer later.
Give her a general overview of how property is usually divided and suggest seeing a lawyer.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to draft a treatment plan for a client with anxiety. You have the intake form and the client's past records.

options.text: Write goals from the intake form and share them with the client first.
Give the client a plan copied from an online article and adjust it later.
Draft goals from the records, note your reasoning, and review them with your supervisor before sharing.
Use the clinic's standard anxiety plan, add the client's name, and pass it to your supervisor.

advanced.situation: A client with depression has stopped improving and mentions heavy drinking for the first time. The current plan covers mood alone.

options.text: Keep the plan unchanged for now and see whether mood improves with more sessions.
Add a goal about drinking to the plan and continue with the same weekly sessions.
Tell the client to stop drinking before treatment continues and pause the sessions.
Reassess the client including the drinking, adjust the plan, and discuss changes with your supervisor.

basic.situation: A client in session says she feels hopeless and has thought about ending her life. Your clinic has a written safety protocol.

options.text: Stay with her, ask directly about her plans, follow the protocol and call your supervisor.
Let her leave when she wishes and phone her family to say she is unwell.
Reassure her that these feelings pass and carry on with the planned session.
Stay with her, ask about her thoughts, and book an earlier next session.

advanced.situation: During a group session, a client becomes very agitated and threatens another member. The others look frightened and no security staff are nearby.

options.text: Grab the agitated client and hold him down on the floor until he calms.
End the session, tell everyone to go home, and write an incident report.
Calmly ask the group to leave, stay with the agitated client, and call for help.
Calm the client with a steady voice and ask the threatened member to step out.

basic.situation: A new client finds it hard to talk about her recent divorce and answers your questions with one word. You want to help her open up.

options.text: Slow down, use open questions, accept silences, and reflect back what she says.
Tell her most clients find talking helpful and she should try harder to share.
Ask a series of specific yes or no questions to find the main issue.
Tell her what to do about the divorce, based on what worked for you.

advanced.situation: A client with a gambling problem has relapsed twice since joining group sessions. She says she is ashamed and wants to stop coming.

options.text: Explore the shame, review her gambling triggers, and build a longer-term coping plan together.
Respect her wish and close her file with a note that she left.
Encourage her to stay and give her a worksheet of strategies to practise at home.
Tell her family about both relapses so they can monitor how she spends money.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to help run a weekly craft activity for clients at the centre. Several clients are new and shy.

options.text: Set up the activity, start on time, and leave shy clients to your supervisor.
Pick the clients most likely to take part and give them the main tasks.
Prepare materials, welcome each person warmly, and let them join at their own pace.
Tell the shy clients they must take part or they will lose their place.

advanced.situation: Your director asks you to run a workshop on mental health for factory employees. Many fear their managers will hear about anything they share.

options.text: Ask each employee to share a personal example so the group learns from it.
Invite the managers to sit in and note which employees seem to be struggling.
Present the topic using slides and clear statistics, and take questions at the end.
Open by explaining confidentiality, use anonymous question cards, and agree ground rules with the group.

basic.situation: At the end of a session you must complete the client's progress form. You are unsure how to fill the diagnostic section.

options.text: Copy the diagnostic wording from another client with similar symptoms and submit the form.
Complete the parts you know and ask your supervisor how to fill the diagnostic section.
Enter the diagnosis you think fits and ask your supervisor to check it next week.
Leave the diagnostic part blank and email your supervisor about it before you leave.

advanced.situation: While reviewing a colleague's files, you find client notes kept in a shared drive that all staff, including the front desk, can open.

options.text: Print the notes for your own drawer and delete the folder from the drive.
Post a reminder on the drive telling front desk staff to avoid opening the notes.
Ask your colleague to move the notes soon and check the drive next month.
Limit access to the treating team, explain why to your colleague, and tell the manager.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to interview a new teenage client for background information. The teenager looks nervous and avoids eye contact.

options.text: Start with light topics, explain what you will record, then ask harder questions.
Press for answers to every question until the teenager stops avoiding your eyes.
Read the clinic's standard questionnaire in order and record each answer carefully.
Ask the parents to answer most questions for the teenager and confirm key points.

advanced.situation: Six months into a stress programme, many clients still drop out after three sessions. Your manager asks you to review how well it works.

options.text: Send clients a short survey asking if they liked the programme and share the results.
Report that dropouts reflect clients' motivation, so the programme stays as it is.
Take the dropouts out of the attendance records so the programme's results look stronger.
Compare attendance and progress data with client feedback, then suggest specific changes to the programme.

basic.situation: A client with a back injury applies for services. You are reviewing her medical and school records to check basic eligibility, but one medical report is missing.

options.text: Ask the client to bring the report herself and finish the review when she does.
Request the missing report from her doctor with her consent and continue checking the rest.
Write in the likely findings of the report based on similar back injury cases.
Decide eligibility from the records you have and note that the report is pending.

advanced.situation: Several clients with disabilities decline jobs at a nearby factory. Buses stop at 8 pm, shifts end later, and the site has stairs and no lift.

options.text: Tell clients to accept the factory's conditions or be removed from the programme.
Look for other employers for each client one by one and drop this factory.
Meet the factory, transport provider and clients to agree changes to shifts, access and transport.
Ask the factory to add a ramp and let each client sort out transport.

basic.situation: A young client wants to open a small food stall. Your senior counsellor has not yet reviewed his options, and he asks what services he can get.

options.text: Tell him about services you know and promise a plan once your senior agrees.
Say a food stall is not realistic and suggest he choose an office job.
Promise him a start-up grant for the stall so he stays in the programme.
Explain the services available, note his goal, and say your senior will confirm next steps.

advanced.situation: A client with a brain injury has been aggressive at home. His family wants him in a residential centre, but he wants to stay home.

options.text: Support the client's wish to stay and tell the family it is his decision.
Meet the family and client together, agree supports at home, and review residential care later.
Book the residential place now and tell the client after the family moves him.
Explain the residential centre to the family and let them decide on it this week.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to book a hearing test and a vocational assessment for a client. Hospital appointments are three months away.

options.text: Arrange the vocational assessment alone and add the hearing test after the plan is made.
Book the first available hospital slot and tell the client about the delay.
Write the client's hearing as normal in the file so the plan can go ahead.
Ask the hospital about cancellations, book the earliest slot, and check private or community options.

advanced.situation: A company has hired six of your clients over two years. Your manager asks how well the placements have worked, but you hold only hiring dates.

options.text: Call the employer for current staff numbers and report how many still work there.
Contact the clients and the employer, compare retention and satisfaction, then propose improvements.
Report the hiring figures as the success rate and mention that follow-up will come.
Tell your manager all six are doing well, since the company has not complained.

basic.situation: A client phones to say she moved house and changed her phone number. You are updating her case file.

options.text: Write the new address on a sticky note for the file and update it later.
Wait to update the file until she sends written proof of the new address.
Delete her old details and her earlier service notes to keep the file tidy.
Update the address and number, note the date of the change, and save the file.

advanced.situation: You must audit ten case files before an agency inspection. Several lack signed consent forms, and some progress notes were written months after the sessions.

options.text: Send staff a list of files with gaps and ask them to update them soon.
Back-date the missing consent forms and have the clients sign them before the inspection.
Fix the notes yourself from memory and leave the consent forms for later.
List the gaps per file, get missing consents from clients, and teach staff the recording deadline.

basic.situation: At a team meeting with the physiotherapist and psychologist, you must update them on a client's attendance and goals.

options.text: Share her family and money problems in detail to explain the missed sessions.
Share her attendance and agreed goals, then ask what each professional needs to see next.
Pass round her whole case file, including old records, for everyone to keep.
Give the attendance figures and say your supervisor will cover her goals later on.

advanced.situation: Your agency wants to set up a supported work centre for adults with disabilities. A local council, a charity and a bank each expect different things.

options.text: Call a joint meeting, clarify expectations, and draft shared goals, roles and a timeline.
Write a proposal based on the council's expectations and send it to the others.
Accept the bank's funding terms and tell the others the plan is already fixed.
Ask each party to send written comments and merge them as they arrive.

basic.situation: A client in job training calls you upset that a trainer shouted at her. She says she may quit the course.

options.text: Tell her to give it another week and phone you if it happens again.
Listen to her, ask what happened, and arrange to speak with the trainer.
Tell the trainer who complained and that she wants to leave the course.
Tell her trainers are strict and that she should not take it personally.

advanced.situation: Three clients placed at the same bakery have left within two months, each giving different reasons. New counsellors will place more clients there next month.

options.text: Review the three cases for patterns, ask the bakery, and write steps for new counsellors.
Stop placing clients at the bakery and tell new counsellors to avoid it.
Tell new counsellors the three clients lacked commitment and to choose more motivated ones.
Visit the bakery to ask the owner what happened and share it with new counsellors.

basic.situation: You interview a mother about her family's situation while your supervisor observes. Her young daughter sits beside her and keeps interrupting.

options.text: Ask a colleague to occupy the child, then continue the interview privately.
Cut the interview short and finish the rest by phone next week.
Ask the daughter the questions instead, since she seems to know the household well.
Let the daughter stay, carry on, and write down what the mother says.

advanced.situation: A father refuses to let you interview his son, saying the school's report of bruises is exaggerated. You were assigned to assess the boy's safety.

options.text: Explain your role, ask to see the child, and inform your supervisor of the refusal.
Accept the father's explanation and record the school report as unconfirmed for now.
Interview the mother instead, record the bruise report, and revisit the father next month.
Close the file after the father signs a note saying the bruises were accidental.

basic.situation: A single mother of three needs after-school child care while she works. Your senior worker told you to find options near her home.

options.text: Give her the number of the welfare office and ask her to call them.
Arrange with a neighbour you know to mind the children and tell the mother afterwards.
Check nearby registered centres and subsidy schemes, then give her a short list with contacts.
Suggest she leave the eldest child in charge after school until a place opens.

advanced.situation: A family of five has lost its home in a fire. They need housing, school places and medical care, and several agencies say it is not their area.

options.text: Contact each agency, agree who does what, and keep a follow-up list with deadlines.
Tell the family their needs are beyond your authority and close the referral.
Give the family a list of agency numbers and ask them to apply themselves.
Arrange emergency housing first and tell the family to approach the other agencies later.

basic.situation: After a home visit you must update a child's case history and send a short report to your manager by noon. You took notes in the car.

options.text: Copy details from last month's report so the case history looks complete.
Update the history from your notes, mark any gaps, and send the report by noon.
Write a short report from memory and update the case history next week.
Send your handwritten notes to the manager and say the full report will follow later.

advanced.situation: A boy in your case faces a school expulsion hearing. His carers, the school, a clinic and the police each hold different information.

options.text: Send the police report and clinic notes to the school to help its decision.
Write to each party asking for their report and compile one summary.
Attend the hearing and speak for the boy based on the school's report.
Bring the parties together, share what each needs to know, and agree shared actions.

basic.situation: A teacher tells you a pupil has missed twelve days of school this term. You are asked to find out why.

options.text: Report the parents to the authorities for failing to send the child to school.
Speak with the pupil's parents and teacher, listen to each, and note possible reasons.
Ask the teacher for the attendance record and give it to your supervisor.
Advise the teacher to add detention for each missed day until attendance improves.

advanced.situation: Truancy and fighting have risen among Form Two pupils. The head teacher asks you to propose a plan and help staff apply it.

options.text: Recommend that repeat offenders be suspended and their parents be fined by the school.
Hold a talk for all Form Two pupils on the school's discipline rules and consequences.
Review data with staff and parents, set support steps for at-risk groups, and guide teachers.
Ask teachers to refer repeat offenders to you and give each of them counselling.

basic.situation: Your senior worker is preparing for a child protection hearing and asks you to compile the child's documents. Some reports are still with the clinic.

options.text: Draft summaries of the clinic reports yourself from what the carer remembers.
Ask the child's carer to collect the clinic reports and bring them to you.
List every document needed, collect what you hold, and request the clinic's reports in writing.
Compile what you have and tell your senior that the clinic reports are still missing.

advanced.situation: You are asked to give evidence in a custody dispute. The father's lawyer wants you to say the mother is unfit, though your reports show mixed findings.

options.text: Say the mother is unfit as the lawyer suggests, since that may help the child.
Give your findings as recorded, state their limits, and decline opinions beyond them.
Describe the mother's problems in stronger terms so the court understands the risks.
Answer the questions briefly and let your supervisor's written report cover the rest.

basic.situation: A teenage client tells you she has been sad since her parents split. She then goes silent and looks at the floor.

options.text: Fill the silence by telling her many teenagers feel the same way.
Stay calm, allow the silence, then reflect what she said and invite her to continue.
Tell her she has no reason to be sad and should focus on school.
Ask her several direct questions about how the split affected her at home and school.

advanced.situation: A village near a rubber estate faces job losses, rising alcohol use and domestic violence. You are asked to run group sessions for residents.

options.text: Meet leaders first, run open coping sessions, and link families to jobs and clinics.
Name the heaviest drinkers in the group so that others can pressure them.
Run group sessions on stress and coping and refer severe cases to the clinic.
Invite the families you already know so the sessions stay small and calm.

basic.situation: An elderly stroke patient is medically ready for discharge on Friday. He lives alone in a flat on the fourth floor with no lift.

options.text: Check his home access and support, then plan discharge with his family and ward team.
Send him home by taxi alone and ask the neighbours to look in on him.
Give his family the discharge date and tell them to arrange help at home.
Discharge him on Friday as the ward needs the bed and review him at home.

advanced.situation: A cancer patient's condition worsens and she can no longer care for herself at home. Her care plan assumes she manages her own medication and meals.

options.text: Reassess her needs with her doctor and family, then revise the plan for daily support.
Note in her file that the plan was reviewed and still suits her needs.
Ask her daughter to take over her medication and meals from now on, starting today.
Keep the plan and visit her more often to check how she manages.

basic.situation: Your team is starting a talk on diabetes for patients' families at the hospital. You are asked to help prepare materials.

options.text: Use English slides from a medical conference and ask the nurses to present them.
Collect simple leaflets in local languages and ask nurses what families often ask.
Copy a private clinic's leaflet and add the hospital's name and logo.
Print the standard diabetes leaflets from the hospital file and set up the room.

advanced.situation: A district with high smoking rates needs a programme to reduce relapse among patients who quit. Funding is small and staff are few.

options.text: Tell staff to warn patients they will lose treatment if they smoke again.
Run a one-time talk for patients and hand out quit-smoking leaflets and posters now.
Plan a large campaign with posters and events and apply for funds afterwards.
Pilot a low-cost peer group, track quit rates, and use results to seek funding.

basic.situation: A young woman recovering from surgery tells you she feels lost since losing her job. She asks you to listen for a while.

options.text: Listen for a few minutes, then tell her to stay positive and look ahead.
Listen to her and then give her a list of job vacancies.
Listen, then tell her family she is depressed so they can watch her.
Listen to her, reflect her feelings, and later ask what support she would like.

advanced.situation: A man with advanced lung disease asks what to expect near the end of life. His family wants you to avoid the subject.

options.text: Ask what he wants to know, explain expected symptoms and options, and inform the team.
Give him a leaflet on end-of-life care and offer to talk again.
Follow the family's wish and tell him he is improving and will recover.
Tell him his doctors will explain everything when the time comes nearer.

basic.situation: The wife of a patient with dementia tells you she is tired and does not understand why he keeps forgetting. You have ten minutes.

options.text: Tell her he forgets because of age and she should rest more.
Give her a leaflet on dementia and ask her to call if she has questions.
Tell her to be firm with him each time he forgets so he learns.
Explain in simple words how dementia affects memory, and give her a caregiver support contact.

advanced.situation: A mother of a child with a serious illness learns that her insurance has expired. Treatment starts next week and she cannot pay.

options.text: Advise her to borrow money from relatives to pay the clinic this week.
Tell the clinic she can pay and promise the hospital will cover any shortfall.
Help her fill in applications for aid and ask her to follow up herself.
Contact the clinic and aid funds for her, protect the treatment date, and record steps.

basic.situation: A patient keeps missing physiotherapy after a hip operation. Your supervisor asks you to find out what is stopping him.

options.text: Talk with him about transport, cost and pain, and check his records for notes.
Tell the physiotherapist he lacks motivation and may need to be taken off the list.
Mark him as having refused treatment in his record so the sessions are cancelled.
Phone him to remind him of the next session and ask if he can attend.

advanced.situation: Your department wants evidence that home visits cut readmissions. You can use two years of patient records and must design a small study.

options.text: Count the readmissions of visited patients and report the number to the department soon.
Compare readmission rates for visited and other patients, anonymise records, and get approval first.
Select the patients who improved and report their results as the study's findings.
Ask visited patients whether the visits helped and summarise their replies for the department.

basic.situation: A patient discharged after a heart attack needs help paying for medicine. Your senior asks you to refer him to financial help.

options.text: Give him the welfare department's address and tell him to apply this month.
Tell him to stop taking some medicines to save money until he gets help.
Explain the aid schemes, help him apply to the right one, and note the referral.
Tell him to ask the pharmacy for a discount and return if refused.

advanced.situation: You supervise two new junior workers on a ward. One discussed a patient's diagnosis in a corridor where visitors were passing.

options.text: Raise it at the next team meeting and let the juniors work it out.
Report the junior to the hospital director before asking for an explanation.
Speak with that worker privately, explain the privacy duty, and brief both juniors.
Send both juniors a message reminding them to keep voices low around visitors.

basic.situation: A client in a drug rehabilitation programme has missed two appointments because he has no money for the bus. His next appointment is on Thursday.

options.text: Tell him that missing a third appointment will end his place in the programme.
Call him, ask about transport, and arrange a pickup or help with bus fare.
Remind him of Thursday's appointment and encourage him to find a way.
Mark him as non-compliant in the file and tell the clinic to stop his medication.

advanced.situation: A client in treatment for schizophrenia reports new voices and is sleeping little. His plan was written when he was stable and sets weekly visits.

options.text: Tell him to rest and keep the weekly visits until his next review.
Tell him the voices are not real and that he should stop reporting them.
Meet him sooner, review his status with the psychiatrist, and adjust the plan's supports.
Increase visits to twice weekly and leave the rest of the plan unchanged.

basic.situation: After a session with a client recovering from alcohol dependence, your supervisor asks you to write the progress note. He reached one of his goals.

options.text: Write that the session went well and that he is doing fine this month overall.
Record what happened, his progress on each goal, and the plan for next session.
Copy last week's progress note and add that he reached his goal.
Record that he has recovered from dependence so his case can be closed.

advanced.situation: Your unit's relapse rate has risen among patients on a new treatment approach. A seminar on this topic takes place next week.

options.text: Read recent studies on the approach, attend the seminar, and share findings.
Tell your team the relapse figures are unreliable and stop recording them for now.
Attend the seminar and pass on your notes to your supervisor afterwards.
Keep using the approach since the unit has already spent time training for it.

basic.situation: You are reviewing a new client's records before an interview. They show a past hospital stay, but the discharge summary is not in the file.

options.text: Interview him about the stay from his memory and note it as confirmed.
Interview him as planned, ask about the stay, and request the summary.
Assume the stay was for substance use and note that in his assessment.
Ask your supervisor to chase the summary and postpone the interview until it arrives.

advanced.situation: A pregnant woman with opioid dependence is referred to you. She fears doctors will report her. The physician and nurse want a treatment plan this week.

options.text: Build the plan with the physician and nurse and tell her about it afterwards.
Tell the doctor she is afraid and ask the doctor to talk to her first.
Promise her that nobody outside the clinic will be told, then arrange treatment.
Explain confidentiality limits to her, then plan with the physician and nurse for safe treatment.

basic.situation: You lead a small group session for people recovering from drug use. One member dominates and the others stay silent.

options.text: Ask him quietly after the session to speak less in the group.
Tell him in front of the group that he is stopping others from speaking.
Let the group manage him on its own, since members often learn from each other.
Thank him for sharing, invite quieter members by name, and set a turn-taking rule.

advanced.situation: A client's wife tells you she wants to leave because his depression and anger are too much. The client does not know she is speaking to you.

options.text: Listen, explain depression and available family support, and encourage her to join a session with him.
Give her the number of a family helpline and keep the conversation private.
Advise her to wait until he has recovered before making any decision about leaving.
Tell the client his wife is planning to leave so he can prepare.

basic.situation: A community centre asks you to give a short talk to parents about the signs of drug use in teenagers. Your agency gave you a script.

options.text: Deliver the script, add local examples, and give parents the agency's helpline details.
Read the script as written and answer questions at the end if time allows.
Describe the signs in very strong terms to push parents to act quickly.
Tell parents to search their teenagers' rooms and phones every week for drugs.

advanced.situation: You are asked to design a community programme about mental illness for a rural area. Many villagers believe spirits cause illness and avoid clinics.

options.text: Run talks at the clinic explaining mental illness and the services offered.
Work with village leaders and traditional healers, share simple facts, and show clinic services.
Warn villagers that parents who avoid clinics may be reported and lose their children.
Tell villagers directly that spirit beliefs are false and that clinics are the answer.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to observe a counsellor's group session this morning and take notes. The counsellor seems nervous about being watched.

options.text: Greet the counsellor, explain the purpose of the visit, and keep notes for your supervisor.
Sit in the back, take notes, and give them to your supervisor.
Tell the counsellor your supervisor sent you to look for mistakes in the session.
Interrupt the session when you notice a mistake to show what to change.

advanced.situation: Two of your workers write very different assessments of similar clients, and one regularly misses risk factors. You are asked to raise service quality across the team.

options.text: Send the team the checklist from the national guidelines and ask them to follow it.
Take the worker who misses risks off assessments and give those to the stronger worker.
Rewrite the weaker worker's assessments yourself and file them under their name today.
Agree a standard checklist, review samples with each worker, and coach the one missing risks.

basic.situation: Your senior specialist asks you to help collect survey answers on dengue prevention from households in a housing estate. Some residents are not at home.

options.text: Ask neighbours to answer on behalf of the residents who are away.
Return at different times, record each visit, and keep to the survey questions.
Fill in missing households' forms using the typical replies from nearby homes.
Leave the form at their doors and collect it a few days later.

advanced.situation: Your unit has run a school anti-smoking programme for three years. The director asks you to design a study showing whether it lowers smoking rates.

options.text: Compare smoking rates in participating and similar non-participating schools before and after the programme.
Survey participating pupils now about their smoking habits and views on the programme.
Report the results from the schools where smoking fell and leave out the others.
Report the number of talks given and pupils reached each year as results.

basic.situation: After a health talk at a community hall, your supervisor asks you to record the number of attendees and who joined the blood-pressure screening.

options.text: Estimate attendance from the number of chairs used and enter that figure in the log.
Record the numbers planned in the proposal, because the hall looked about full.
Count attendees at the door, take screening numbers from the nurses' sheet, and file them.
Add extra names to the list so the talk meets its target.

advanced.situation: Your programme needs funding for a three-year diabetes education project. A state grant asks for a budget, a partner letter and outcome targets by Friday.

options.text: Submit the budget and targets on time and add the partner letter if time allows.
Use another organisation's budget and partner letter and swap in your programme's name.
Set high outcome targets to make the proposal look stronger to the reviewers.
Draft the budget and targets from past data, request the partner letter, and check requirements.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to prepare a short press release for a vaccination drive at the district clinic next week.

options.text: Write that the vaccine is completely safe for everyone and send it to newspapers.
State the date, place, who can attend and contact details, then ask your supervisor.
Copy last year's release and update the date, clinic name and contact number.
Write a catchy headline and a long story about the clinic's many achievements.

advanced.situation: A rumour spreads on social media that a vaccine in your district causes illness. Clinic attendance has dropped, and the page you manage reaches thousands.

options.text: Post clear facts from the ministry, reply to questions politely, and brief staff.
Post a short statement that the rumour is false and move on.
Delete comments that repeat the rumour and block the people who posted them.
Post a warning that people who skip vaccines will lose clinic services.

basic.situation: You are helping to organise an induction day for new clinic staff. The trainer cancels on the morning of the session.

options.text: Move the session to next week and tell the staff to come back.
Show a recorded video from last year and let the staff leave early today.
Present the trainer's slides yourself, including topics you have not studied before.
Tell your supervisor, ask a senior colleague to cover key topics, and inform staff.

advanced.situation: Staff across several clinics give inconsistent diabetes advice. The ministry asks you to set a continuing education plan for 200 staff in the state.

options.text: Set core competencies, offer short blended modules, assess staff, and review yearly with doctors.
Email the latest guidelines to every clinic and ask managers to share them.
Make staff who give inconsistent advice repeat the training at their own cost.
Run one two-day workshop for all staff and issue attendance certificates to everyone afterwards.

basic.situation: You assist in monitoring two outreach officers who run weekly school talks. One has stopped sending activity reports for the past month.

options.text: Ask him why, listen, and agree a date for the reports with your supervisor.
Tell the schools to stop the talks until he sends his reports.
Write the missing reports yourself from the school timetable and file them as his.
Remind the whole team by email that all activity reports are due weekly.

advanced.situation: A district NGO asks your advice on health education for migrant workers in dormitories. They have little funding, and workers speak six languages.

options.text: Assess needs with a short survey, suggest peer educators, and share translated materials.
Advise them to hold one large annual event with expert speakers from outside.
Tell them the workers are too diverse to teach and to wait for funds.
Give them your own programme materials in English and suggest they translate them.

basic.situation: You help send leaflets on quitting smoking to clinics. A box printed last year lists a helpline number that has now changed.

options.text: Cross out the old number by hand on each leaflet and send them.
Send them as they are, since patients can find the number online.
Set the box aside, tell your supervisor, and send updated leaflets to the clinics.
Send the box with a note telling the clinics that the number has changed.

advanced.situation: Your agency's health library has hundreds of pamphlets, some outdated, in several formats. Community agencies say they cannot find what they need.

options.text: Put the newest pamphlets on a front shelf and keep the rest as is.
Ask each agency to bring a list of the topics it wants.
Throw away everything printed before last year to clear the shelves quickly this week.
Audit the stock, retire outdated items, sort by topic and language, and train agencies.

basic.situation: You prepare a background report on a young offender. His mother says he is a good boy but gives few details when you interview her.

options.text: Accept her description and add a line to the report that he has family support.
Ask open questions about his school, friends and routines, and note answers that need checking.
Ask her for a character letter from a relative instead of more details.
Write that he has no history of trouble, since his mother said so.

advanced.situation: An informant says a parolee sells drugs and hides cash at his flat. Your supervisor is away, and a search of the flat is not covered by your orders.

options.text: Wait for your supervisor to return next week before taking any step on the tip.
Visit the parolee and ask him about the tip when he opens the door.
Log the tip, check it against his record, and seek your supervisor's approval for any search.
Enter the flat with a colleague and search it to confirm the tip.

basic.situation: You conduct a random urine test on a probationer at the office. He says he cannot pass urine and asks to leave and return tomorrow.

options.text: Let him leave and return tomorrow, and note the reason in his file.
Ask him to wait in the lobby and call you when he can provide a sample.
Record the test as negative since he could not give a sample today.
Offer him water, wait a reasonable time within the procedure, and record the outcome.

advanced.situation: A probationer on home detention has three curfew alerts from his electronic tag this week. He blames a tag fault, and his employer says he works late.

options.text: Accept the tag fault explanation and ask the vendor to replace the tag.
Visit his home that night to see whether he is in at curfew time or not.
Check the tag logs, confirm work hours with his employer, and decide on a violation report.
Report him as a violator to the court tonight based on the alerts.

basic.situation: A probationer convicted of assault says he hits people when he is drunk. You are meant to explore how drink affected his offence.

options.text: Explain that being drunk is no excuse and tell him to stop drinking right now.
Ask when he drinks, what triggers his anger, and how it linked to the offence.
Tell him he will be jailed again if he drinks and gets angry.
Agree that alcohol explains the offence and move to the next topic.

advanced.situation: A junior officer asks how to discuss drug use and anger with a parolee who denies both. You have handled many similar cases.

options.text: Join one meeting, model how to link drugs and anger to the offence, then debrief.
Give the junior a checklist of questions and ask him to use it.
Tell the junior to confront him in public about his drug use to shame him.
Tell the junior to be firm and warn the parolee of the consequences.

basic.situation: You are preparing a case folder for a new probationer. His court order, ID copy and earlier reports arrive at different times from different offices.

options.text: Keep the papers in your own drawer until all of them have arrived.
Open the folder with a checklist, file items as they arrive, and report any missing ones.
Throw away duplicate and older reports from other offices to keep the folder neat.
File the documents in date order and check for any missing ones early next month.

advanced.situation: You write a presentencing report for a first-time offender. The prosecutor wants a custodial recommendation, but you found strong family support and a stable job.

options.text: Recommend a lighter option and omit the prosecutor's concerns from the report.
Report your findings accurately and leave the sentencing recommendation to your senior officer.
Recommend custody as the prosecutor wants and drop the family support details.
Report your findings accurately and recommend what the evidence supports, including family and job.

basic.situation: A court order requires a probationer to attend substance abuse treatment. The nearest centre has a six-week waiting list.

options.text: Find a cheaper private counselling service and treat it as meeting the order.
Report him as non-compliant with the order because no treatment has started yet.
Place him on the waiting list and tell him to attend when called.
Ask the centre for an urgent place, book the earliest slot, and inform the court.

advanced.situation: Many released offenders in your district relapse within a year because they lack work, housing or counselling. Existing agencies work separately.

options.text: Ask one large housing agency to take all your released offenders and report back.
Create a list of agency contacts and give it to each released offender.
Tell released offenders to find work on their own or return to custody.
Bring agencies together, agree referral steps, and track outcomes of released offenders over time.

basic.situation: A newly released parolee asks what he must do now. You explain his conditions, which include weekly office visits and monthly payments.

options.text: Tell him to just visit weekly and the rest will be explained later.
Tell him the payments can be skipped for now if he cannot pay them.
Go through each condition, give written dates, and ask him to repeat them back.
Give him the order and tell him to read it before next week.

advanced.situation: Your office has no standard information pack for new probationers, and each officer explains services differently. You must create one and train three new officers.

options.text: Copy another country's pack and tell the new officers to use it as is.
Compile verified service details into one pack, test it with colleagues, and train new officers.
Collect leaflets from agencies into a folder and give a copy to each officer.
Write the pack yourself from memory and send it to the three officers.

basic.situation: You interview an elderly man at a welfare centre to record his family and education history. He gets tired and loses track of his answers.

options.text: Write the answers you think are likely and read them to him quickly to confirm.
Offer a break, ask short questions one at a time, and repeat answers back.
Skip the questions he cannot answer and fill them in from a neighbour's account.
Complete the form from his old file, then ask him to sign at the end.

advanced.situation: A new assistant asks for help compiling the history of a teenage girl involved with her school, a clinic and the police. The sources conflict on dates.

options.text: Suggest they write the most commonly repeated account and drop the other versions.
Show them how to list each source, mark conflicts, and confirm key facts.
Tell them to use the clinic's version because medical records are official.
Tell them to fix the dates so the sources agree and the history reads smoothly.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to use the agency's checklist to assess a client's basic physical needs, such as food, clothing and a safe place to sleep.

options.text: Fill the checklist from the previous worker's last notes and update later.
Go through each checklist item with her, observe the room, and note what she needs.
Hand her the checklist to tick herself and collect it the next day.
Mark all items as met since she looks well and did not complain.

advanced.situation: A man with a stroke and depression is referred for rehabilitation, but his family says he needs nothing. You must set out how to assess him.

options.text: Ask the family to describe his abilities and record their answers as his.
Follow his family's view and assess his physical needs before looking at anything else.
Use the agency's standard checklist and add a few questions about his mood.
Plan a structured assessment of movement, memory, mood and daily tasks with his consent.

basic.situation: After visiting a client's home, you must give your supervisor a short report. You remember that the client's electricity was cut off.

options.text: Add that the client's home was in good condition so the visit looks routine.
Write what you saw and heard, including the electricity cut-off, and send it today.
Leave the electricity out of the report since the client did not ask for help.
Mention the electricity cut-off by phone and write the report later this week.

advanced.situation: You notice a colleague's visit reports repeat the same sentences each month, as if copied. You must review the problem with your superior.

options.text: Tell your superior the reports look repetitive but you cannot say why.
Rewrite your colleague's reports yourself and file them under your colleague's name.
Show your superior examples from the files and ask how to verify the visits.
Ask your colleague to rewrite the reports and tell your superior if it continues.

basic.situation: A social worker asks you to draft a simple care plan for a boy who hits other children at the day centre. You know him well.
