options.text: Draft a plan based on what worked with other children and submit it.
Write a plan allowing staff to smack him lightly whenever he hits another child.
Draft triggers, goals and calm responses, then ask the social worker to review.
Write a plan saying he will be kept apart from the other children.

advanced.situation: A junior assistant's behaviour plan for a girl with autism uses punishments that upset her more, and her family has complained. You are asked to mentor them.

options.text: Review the plan with them, explain why punishments fail, and practise positive strategies together.
Tell them the plan needs more time and the family should be patient.
Give them a guide on positive behaviour strategies and ask them to revise it.
Tell them to add stricter punishments, so she learns the rules quickly.

basic.situation: A man who lost his job asks where to find help with unpaid utility bills. You have a directory of local agencies.

options.text: Give him the number of an unlicensed lender who helps people quickly with cash.
Hand him the whole directory and tell him to look through it himself.
Tell him to ask the utility company to waive the bills completely.
Look up suitable agencies, explain what each offers, and write down the contacts.

advanced.situation: An elderly widow with dementia has no relatives. She needs housing, medical care and legal help to protect her savings from a scam, and several agencies are involved.

options.text: Ask a friendly neighbour to manage her savings and handle the referrals for her.
Contact each agency, agree one lead, arrange the referrals together, and track progress.
Give her a list of all agencies and ask her to call each one.
Refer her to the housing agency first and tell the others later.

basic.situation: A mother on welfare asks how to apply for a school meal programme for her two children. You have the application form.

options.text: Explain who qualifies, go through the form with her, and list the documents she needs.
Fill in the form for her yourself using the details you assume apply.
Give her the form and tell her to ask at the school office.
Tell her the rules change often and she should check again next school term.

advanced.situation: Your centre wants a group workshop on money management for young adults who recently left foster care. Many have debts and little experience with budgeting.

options.text: Invite a bank speaker to explain the loan and credit products on offer.
Design short, practical sessions with budgeting exercises, local debt advice, and a follow-up check-in.
Show them a stock market trading app and encourage them to invest their savings.
Present a talk on saving and spending habits and share a budget template.

basic.situation: You phone a client with high blood pressure to check whether she collected her medicine from the clinic. She says she was too busy.

options.text: Ask what stopped her, suggest pickup options, and call again in two days.
Record in the follow-up list that she collected the medicine as advised today.
Remind her how important the medicine is and ask her to collect it.
Tell her you will check again at her next appointment in three months.

advanced.situation: Several clients with diabetes and kidney disease keep missing follow-ups. You are asked to design a routine for 40 such clients with two assistants.

options.text: Visit the clients who live closest, since travel takes much less time.
Group clients by risk, set contact schedules, and review missed follow-ups weekly.
Remove clients who miss two follow-ups from the list to keep workloads low.
Phone all forty clients every week using the same short reminder script.

basic.situation: After a home visit, your supervisor asks you to fill in the client's health form. Her weight and blood pressure readings are on a scrap of paper.

options.text: Enter the readings from memory because the handwriting on the scrap is hard to read.
Fill in the form and keep the scrap of paper in your bag as proof.
Fill in normal readings for her age and update them at the next visit.
Copy the readings onto the form, add the date, and check them with your supervisor.

advanced.situation: An audit shows your team's client records are filled in differently: some lack dates, some use nicknames, and others are kept on loose sheets.

options.text: Send a message to the team asking them to add dates and real names.
Agree a standard form and filing method, train the team, and spot-check records monthly.
Collect all loose sheets and file them in one box by date.
Discard loose sheets that lack dates, since the records cannot be checked later.

basic.situation: Your team lead asks you to list pregnant women in your area who have not attended antenatal checks. You have a list from the clinic.

options.text: Check the clinic list, visit the women politely, and record who needs follow-up.
Send one general message to the village group asking pregnant women to come forward.
Post the names of the women who missed checks on the village notice board.
Call the women on the clinic list and ask them to visit the clinic.

advanced.situation: Undocumented migrant workers living at a construction site rarely visit clinics because they fear being reported. You must plan how to reach them.

options.text: Put up posters at the site entrance about free clinic services and hours.
Ask the contractor to send sick workers to the clinic when needed.
Ask each worker for his documents on arrival and note down who has none.
Meet the site supervisor, explain confidentiality, and offer health checks on site.

basic.situation: You attend a village committee meeting to listen and take notes. Several residents complain about piles of rubbish near the clinic.

options.text: Listen, note the concerns and who raised them, and report to your team lead.
Write down the rubbish complaint and leave the other issues for another meeting.
Promise the residents that the clinic will clear the rubbish by the weekend.
Tell the residents the rubbish is the committee's fault and they should demand action.

advanced.situation: Villagers disagree angrily about whether to allow a fogging programme against dengue. You are asked to lead the next community meeting.

options.text: Present the official dengue figures and ask the villagers to vote on fogging this week.
Invite health officers, hear concerns, explain benefits and risks plainly, and agree next steps.
Tell the angry villagers that those who refuse will not get clinic care.
Meet the supportive villagers first and tell the others the decision later.

basic.situation: A man at the market tells you he has had a cough for a month and is losing weight. You carry a printed list of nearby clinics.

options.text: Advise him to attend the nearest clinic soon, and give its address.
Tell him to rest at home first and return if the cough worsens.
Tell him he definitely has tuberculosis and must stay away from the market.
Suggest a cough syrup and tell him to return if the cough continues.

advanced.situation: A teenager tells you in confidence that she is pregnant and being threatened by her boyfriend. She needs medical care, shelter and legal advice.

options.text: Refer her to the clinic and give her the number of a helpline.
Tell her parents about the pregnancy and threats so they can arrange her care.
Visit the boyfriend and tell him to stop threatening her or face the police.
Listen, explain which services can help, arrange referrals with her consent, and follow up.

basic.situation: You hand out leaflets on healthy eating at the Saturday market. A stall owner says he does not want leaflets near his stall.

options.text: Argue that the market permits leaflets and place them on his counter.
Thank him, move nearby, and offer leaflets to people who want one.
Hand leaflets to people you think are overweight and tell them to diet.
Leave a pile of leaflets on every other stall and move on.

advanced.situation: A factory asks you to design a six-week wellness programme for 150 workers who sit all day and eat late at night.

options.text: Survey workers' habits, plan weekly diet and exercise sessions, and measure change.
Weigh workers in front of colleagues and post their results on the notice board.
Give all workers the same strict diet plan taken from a health magazine.
Hold one talk on healthy eating and give each worker an exercise chart.

basic.situation: You are helping lead the weekly service. The sound system fails ten minutes before it starts, and the hall is filling with elderly worshippers.

options.text: Ask a worshipper to open the amplifier and rewire it while people wait.
Cancel the service and send the worshippers home with a short notice on the door.
Start on time and speak louder, hoping those at the back can follow.
Tell the senior leader, test the backup microphone, and seat the elderly near the front.

advanced.situation: A family asks you to conduct a funeral tomorrow for a relative from a different tradition. The family is divided about the rites to follow.

options.text: Let the family members vote at the service and follow the majority.
Meet the family, agree which rites apply, and consult the other faith's leader.
Decline to attend and tell the family to find another leader tomorrow.
Follow your own tradition's standard rites and explain this to the family beforehand.

basic.situation: You must prepare a ten-minute talk for the youth group on honesty. Your senior leader suggests a story from the scriptures.

options.text: Choose a story, link it to examples from teenagers' lives, and practise it aloud.
Read the story from the scriptures and add a short moral at the end.
Use a famous speaker's talk from the internet and read out the main points.
Present a speaker's talk from the internet as your own and change the opening.

advanced.situation: Volunteer teachers in the youth group keep quitting after a few weeks, saying they feel unprepared and unsupported. You are asked to train new leaders.

options.text: Ask all volunteers to sign a two-year commitment and pay a penalty if they leave.
Ask former teachers what they lacked, design short training with mentoring, and check in monthly.
Run a one-day course for the new leaders covering lesson planning and discipline.
Recruit more volunteers so that no single teacher carries too heavy a load.

basic.situation: A member tells you after the service that she feels lonely since her husband died. She wants to talk for a while.

options.text: Listen patiently, acknowledge her loss, offer a prayer if she wishes.
Suggest she find a new husband soon so that she is no longer alone.
Offer a short prayer, tell her to keep her faith, and wish her well.
Tell her that grief passes with time and suggest she stay busy.

advanced.situation: Late at night, a member calls to say her husband has collapsed at home and is not breathing. You are the nearest to their house.

options.text: Tell her to wait for him to wake up and keep her phone free.
Go to their house first and ask her to call the ambulance later.
Tell her to call emergency services now, go to help, and keep her calm.
Tell her you will pray for him and come as soon as you can.

basic.situation: The office has run out of printer paper and cleaning supplies ahead of a festival weekend. The usual supplier is closed today.

options.text: Use the congregation's cash box to buy the supplies and record it later.
Ask a member to bring supplies from home and cover the cost later.
Order a large amount from a new online seller to avoid running short again.
Check the approved suppliers list, buy from another shop within budget, keep the receipt.

advanced.situation: The finance committee finds the congregation's repair fund has fallen by a third, with several receipts missing. Members will ask questions at the next meeting.

options.text: Tell members that the fund is stable and the issue is being handled.
Share the figures openly, ask the treasurer for receipts, and agree an independent review.
Ask the treasurer privately to explain the gap and then report to the committee.
Adjust the records and accounts so the figures appear to match the cash.

basic.situation: You are asked to read a passage from the sacred text at the service. A word in it is hard to pronounce, and you are unsure of its meaning.

options.text: Read the passage and pass quickly over the word you cannot pronounce.
Explain the word to the congregation as you personally think it should mean.
Replace the hard word with an easier word that seems close in meaning.
Ask a senior leader about the word and practise the passage beforehand.

advanced.situation: A member tells you he has not slept for weeks and is having thoughts of ending his life. He says he trusts only you.

options.text: Stay with him, urge professional help, and help him contact a doctor.
Pray with him and ask him to see a doctor when he feels ready.
Keep his words private and meet him every week to strengthen his faith.
Tell him that such thoughts show weak faith and he must pray harder.

basic.situation: A member of your congregation is in hospital after an operation. You have been asked to visit him for comfort.

options.text: Visit and ask about his medical condition to share in the congregation's newsletter.
Send a card and flowers to his ward on behalf of the whole congregation.
Visit late in the evening so that you can stay a long time with him.
Visit during visiting hours, ask how he feels, listen, and offer a prayer if welcome.

advanced.situation: Attendance at your congregation has fallen by a quarter over three years. Many young families live nearby but rarely attend. You are asked for ways to grow.

options.text: Start a new weekly children's programme and advertise it on local social media.
Increase the number of services each week to give families more choice.
Publish the names of families who stopped attending and ask members to visit them.
Talk with nearby families about their needs, then plan activities that respond to them.

basic.situation: You are helping organise a weekend youth camp. The speaker is confirmed by phone, but the campsite booking is unpaid and the deadline is tomorrow.

options.text: Pay the deposit from your own savings and claim it back later.
Tell your supervisor, confirm the speaker in writing, and ask for payment approval.
Phone the campsite to ask for a short extension and note their reply.
Book a second campsite at once and tell your supervisor after the camp.

advanced.situation: A two-day interfaith seminar is planned. A senior clergy member objects to the guest speaker, and the donors will withdraw funds if the programme changes.

options.text: Postpone the seminar for six months and hope the matter settles by itself.
Keep the speaker and tell the clergy member the seminar will continue.
Replace the speaker and tell the donors that nothing has changed in the programme.
Meet the clergy member to hear the concern, then consult the donors and speaker.

basic.situation: You need to pick materials for a new eight-week course on basic scriptures for adults who have never studied them. Three textbooks are available.

options.text: Choose the shortest book so that the course can finish early and cost less.
Compare the books for reading level and length, then pick one fitting eight weeks.
Choose the advanced scholarly book so that participants are challenged from the first lesson.
Choose the book that most other centres use, as it is tested elsewhere.

advanced.situation: Over two years, adult class attendance has fallen while youth classes have grown. You are asked to redesign the education programme for next year.

options.text: Analyse attendance by group and survey members, then redesign courses to match demand.
Move the adult classes to weekends and add one more youth class.
Close the adult classes entirely and tell members to join the youth classes.
Keep the programme as it is and tell members to attend more regularly.

basic.situation: You are drafting the monthly bulletin. A teacher gives you the date and time of a new class, but the venue is not yet confirmed.

options.text: Delay the whole item until the venue is confirmed in the next issue.
Print the usual hall as the venue since classes are normally held there.
Print that registration is closed to stop calls while the venue is unconfirmed.
Include the date and time, mark the venue as to be confirmed.

advanced.situation: Your denomination asks you to lead a project helping three small rural congregations that have no full-time leader. You have a small budget.

options.text: Assign a visiting leader to the largest congregation and review after one year.
Merge the three congregations into one building and close the other two buildings.
Visit each congregation, list their needs, and partner with nearby groups.
Send each small congregation a package of materials and the name of a contact.

basic.situation: A new part-time religious education teacher starts on Sunday. You are asked to help train them on class routines and safeguarding rules.

options.text: Give them the teacher handbook and answer any questions they raise on Sunday.
Walk them through routines, share the safeguarding rules, and let them observe first.
Tell them the safeguarding rules are meant for large classes, not small ones.
Let them take their first class alone so they learn quickly from practice.

advanced.situation: Donations to the education programme fell by a fifth this year while teacher costs rose. You must set next year's budget priorities.

options.text: Compare costs per programme with attendance, rank priorities, and consult leaders.
Cut every programme's budget by twenty percent to match the lower donations.
Keep the budget the same and expect donations to recover by midyear.
Cut teacher training and safeguarding checks first since they bring no income.

basic.situation: A member of the parents' group tells you privately that she is worried about her teenage son's anger. She wants some guidance.

options.text: Listen, ask what is happening, and suggest a school counsellor if it worsens.
Offer a prayer for the family and say the anger will pass.
Tell the boy's teacher about the mother's worry in front of other parents.
Tell her to punish him firmly each time so that he learns control.

advanced.situation: A member is facing both a divorce and heavy debts, and says he feels hopeless. He asks your advice on both religious and money problems.

options.text: Offer spiritual guidance and encourage him to speak to a lawyer about the debts.
Listen, ask about his safety, offer spiritual support, and refer him to professional help.
Advise him to reconcile with his wife and settle the debts later.
Lend him money from the congregation fund to settle the debts quickly.

basic.situation: The class needs two more volunteer helpers for the holiday programme. A parent offers to help, but you do not know her well.

options.text: Thank her, have her complete the form and checks, then pair her with a helper.
Ask a trusted member to confirm she is reliable, then let her start with them.
Give her the youngest group because they need the most help from helpers.
Let her take a group alone from the first day to cover the gap.

advanced.situation: Volunteers from eight congregations need teaching resources, but each orders from different suppliers and many materials sit unused. You are asked to improve how resources are shared.

options.text: Order a large stock from one supplier for all eight congregations this month.
List what each congregation holds, set up one shared catalogue, and agree joint ordering.
Ask each congregation to send you its spare materials so you can redistribute them.
Collect the unused materials and send them for recycling to clear storage space.

basic.situation: A senior partner asks you to find what a new regulation says about late payment interest in a client's supplier contract. The client call is in two hours.

options.text: Quote the clause from an older version saved in the shared folder to save time.
Pull the official text, check it is in force, and cite the clause.
Use the summary from a law firm blog, since the partner needs an answer quickly.
Read the regulation on the government website and send the senior partner the main paragraph.

advanced.situation: Two High Court decisions on the same contract term point in opposite directions. Your client's case turns on it, and the hearing is in three weeks.

options.text: Rely on the more recent decision and tell the client it is the stronger authority.
Check each decision's court level and facts, then build the argument around distinguishing the unfavourable one.
Ask a colleague which decision the court is likely to follow and adopt that view.
Build the draft submissions on the favourable decision and leave the other out of the bundle.

basic.situation: Your senior lawyer has a mention at the Magistrates' Court tomorrow. You are asked to prepare the file and confirm all documents were served.

options.text: Check the court portal shows the documents filed and tell the lawyer all is in order.
Tell the lawyer service was done based on the draft covering letters saved in the file.
Check proof of service for each document and flag any gap to the lawyer tonight.
Tell the lawyer service was done because the clerk said the letters went out last week.

advanced.situation: You are leading settlement talks for a client in a civil claim. The other side offers a low sum and says the offer expires in one hour.

options.text: Counter with a figure near the client's earlier target and see if the other side moves.
Accept the offer on the client's behalf to secure a result before it expires.
Call the client to explain the offer and ask whether to accept before the hour ends.
Ask for a short extension, then compare the offer with the client's likely outcome and instructions.

basic.situation: A client tells you his version of a road accident. A senior lawyer asked you to take his statement and record the basic facts.

options.text: Let the client tell it in order, note dates and names, and read the notes back.
Suggest to the client which details help his claim, then write down his agreed version.
Ask the client the questions on the firm's accident form and note each answer he gives.
Record the statement in your own words afterwards so it reads clearly for the senior lawyer.

advanced.situation: A client says he owns a plot of land, but the seller's title papers look incomplete. You must confirm the registered owner before the dispute goes further.

options.text: Ask the seller's lawyer to confirm the ownership details and rely on the written reply.
Ask the client for his copy of the title and check it against the sale agreement.
Order an official land registry search and compare the registered owner with the client's papers.
Tell the court the client is the owner, since the sale agreement names him as buyer.

basic.situation: A senior lawyer asks you to draft a one-year tenancy agreement for a shop unit, using the firm's template, ready for review this afternoon.

options.text: Fill in the template from the agreed terms and leave the senior lawyer to spot gaps.
Download a free online tenancy form and adjust it, since it saves time on the draft.
Copy an earlier shop tenancy from the firm's archive and change the names and rent.
Fill in the template from the agreed terms and highlight any detail you had to assume.

advanced.situation: A client wants a joint venture agreement with tax and employment points outside your field. The partner wants a first draft by Friday.

options.text: Use tax and employment clauses from an old deal and describe them as standard terms.
Draft the core terms, then ask the tax and employment colleagues to review their parts.
Send the partner a term sheet and explain that the full draft needs more time.
Draft all clauses from precedents and list the tax and employment points in the cover note.

basic.situation: A legal assistant has fallen behind on filing client letters. A partner needs all of this week's letters filed by 5 pm today.

options.text: Help the assistant finish the pile and check each letter is in the right client file.
File the letters in the nearest folders quickly and fix any mistakes the partner mentions later.
Split the pile with the assistant, agree who files which client, and check the result.
Tell the assistant to stay late and finish the letters, then spot-check a few files.

advanced.situation: Your firm's junior lawyers keep missing court filing deadlines. You manage the practice's operations, and the partners want it fixed this quarter.

options.text: Send a firm-wide email reminding juniors that deadlines are strict and missed dates will be recorded.
Record the missed filings as delays caused by the court registry in the practice's incident log.
Introduce a shared diary with reminders and ask all juniors to enter their filing dates.
Find the common causes of the missed deadlines, then set up a shared diary with reminders.

basic.situation: A client asks if she can end her office lease early. The lawyer is in another meeting and asked you to explain her basic position.

options.text: Tell her what leases usually allow and ask her to wait for the lawyer's view.
Tell her she can stop paying rent from next month, since the landlord cannot sue.
Say she can leave early if she gives a month's notice, as most landlords accept that.
Read the termination clause with her, explain it plainly, and say the lawyer will confirm.

advanced.situation: A manufacturer asks whether a new safety regulation covers its imported machines. The wording is unclear, and a mistake could mean a costly recall.

options.text: Tell the client the rule does not cover imported machines, since the regulation mentions factories.
Give the client the plainest reading of the wording and suggest it ask the regulator.
Tell the client the rule probably applies, so it should prepare to comply with it.
Check official guidance and regulator comments, then give a reasoned view stating its limits.

basic.situation: You are entering today's hearing outcomes into the court case management system. The judge's handwritten note gives the next mention date, but it could be read as 14 or 19 November.

options.text: Match the date to the signed order or hearing minutes, then enter that date.
Leave the next-date field empty for now and carry on with the other entries today.
Enter the later date, 19 November, since a longer gap gives everyone more time to prepare.
Ask the judge's secretary which date was meant and enter the date they confirm.

advanced.situation: You are checking the file for tomorrow's trial. The pleadings bundle lacks the defendant's amended defence, though counsel says it was filed last week and the index lists it.

options.text: Put the original defence from the system into the bundle as a stand-in for now.
Ask counsel to email a copy of the amended defence and place it in the bundle.
Trace the amended defence in the filing record, then insert it or report the gap.
Leave the bundle as it is and mention the missing paper to the judge tomorrow.

basic.situation: You are proofreading a draft order before the judge signs it. The case number in the heading differs by one digit from the number on the filed papers.

options.text: Move on to the rest of the draft, since the names and hearing date all match.
Check the number against the filed papers and the system, then amend the draft heading.
Compare the heading with the previous order in the file and amend it to match.
Leave the number as typed and put a query note on the cover for the judge.

advanced.situation: The judge asks for a short memo on whether to allow an application to strike out a claim. Counsel's authorities point both ways, and one cited decision comes from a lower court.

options.text: Test each authority on its facts and court level, then recommend an outcome with reasons.
Recommend the side with more recent decisions and attach their cases as supporting authority.
Copy the headnotes of the leading cases into the memo and call the law unsettled.
Summarise each side's authorities fairly in the memo and leave the recommendation to the judge.

basic.situation: You are reading a newly filed notice of motion to prepare a note for the judge. The prayers ask for an injunction, but the supporting affidavit mostly describes unpaid rent.

options.text: List each prayer, match it to affidavit facts, and note any prayer lacking a stated basis.
Take the issue from the motion's title, since it already sums up the dispute.
Treat the unpaid rent as the real issue and describe the injunction as a side request.
Summarise the affidavit's main facts in the note and mention that an injunction is requested.

advanced.situation: You notice a newly gazetted amendment to an Act that applies to a case reserved for decision. It is unclear whether it covers cases filed before it took effect.

options.text: Send the judge the amendment text with a note that it may affect this case.
Assume the old provisions still apply, since a filed case keeps the law it began under.
Tell a senior clerk about the amendment during tea and leave the follow-up to them.
Read the commencement and transitional provisions, then tell the judge whether the amendment reaches this case.

basic.situation: A new registry staff member asks you what 'ex parte' means after a lawyer used the term at the counter. You are in the middle of a deadline task.

options.text: Say it means an urgent application, since that is how it usually comes up here.
Suggest asking the lawyer who used it, since the lawyer knows what the application involves.
Tell the staff member to look it up in the law dictionary in the library.
Explain in simple words that it means one side applies while the other side is absent.

advanced.situation: In a chambers conference, counsel disagree on how a procedural rule applies, and the judge turns to you. The rule's text is in the rules book on the desk.

options.text: Tell the judge you will check the rule and revert after the conference ends.
Let counsel argue the point out and record whatever ruling the judge gives for the file.
Read out the rule's wording, then explain how each counsel's reading would affect the case.
Offer how a similar case went last year from memory, to keep the meeting moving.

basic.situation: The judge wants a 30-minute meeting tomorrow with a visiting colleague who leaves at 3 p.m. A 2 p.m. hearing may overrun. The morning diary is clear.

options.text: Book 2.30 p.m. after the hearing and ask the colleague to wait if it runs over.
Book a 1 p.m. slot before the hearing and tell both that the time is tight.
Ask the colleague to come another day, since the afternoon diary looks too full.
Propose the free 9 a.m. slot to both, then update the diary once they agree.

advanced.situation: Three matters are listed before the judge this morning. Counsel for the second says his client is stuck in traffic, and counsel for the third is ready with a witness waiting.

options.text: Move the third matter ahead since its counsel is ready, and tell the second to follow.
Call matters in the listed order and let the judge decide about the late party.
Ask the judge whether to call matters one and three first while the second waits.
Mark the second matter absent in the system and carry on with the third.

basic.situation: You receive a new reprint of a statute for the judge's library. The shelf already holds an older reprint of the same statute, which the judge's notes cite.

options.text: Replace the older reprint on the shelf with the new one and discard the old copy.
Leave the shelf as it is and keep the new reprint in your drawer for now.
Place the new reprint on the shelf beside the older one so both stay available.
Shelve the new reprint and move the older one to a labelled archive shelf, logging both.

advanced.situation: A volunteer law student you supervise drafts a hearing summary for the judge's file. It states the judge's reasons for an adjournment that you do not recall hearing. The deadline is tight.

options.text: Tell the student to recheck the summary and file it themselves once they are satisfied.
Compare it with your own hearing notes, amend it yourself, and file it for the judge.
Review the summary against the hearing notes with the student and show how to record sources.
Trust the student's account since students usually take careful notes, and file the summary as drafted.

basic.situation: You are preparing for a hearing on a worker's compensation claim. A regulation you need was amended last year, but your reference book shows the older text.

options.text: Use the older text and decide the claim on it, since it is on your desk.
Ask the claimant's lawyer to tell you which version of the regulation applies now.
Find the current amended text from the official source and base your preparation on it.
Use the older text in your notes and flag that an amendment may exist.

advanced.situation: Two earlier decisions of your tribunal conflict on whether late notice bars a claim. A junior officer asks how to handle a case turning on this.

options.text: Adjourn the case indefinitely until a higher court settles the conflict.
Tell the junior officer to follow the more recent of the two decisions.
Tell the junior officer to pick whichever decision favours the claimant's side.
Compare both decisions and the rules, explain the difference, and record reasoning.

basic.situation: A claimant submits a birth certificate and an employer letter for a benefits claim. The date of birth on the certificate differs by one day from the claim form.

options.text: Reject the claim because the documents do not match, and close the file.
Treat it as a typing error and carry on with the claim review.
Ask the claimant to explain the difference and provide supporting documents.
Change the date on the claim form to match the certificate yourself.

advanced.situation: A claim file holds employer records, doctor's reports and photographs with signs of editing. You are asked to set a checking method for such files.

options.text: Ask staff to examine photographs closely and report anything that looks suspicious.
Set steps to verify originals with issuers and flag edited items.
Reject every claim that includes photographs, since edited photographs cannot be trusted.
Accept the documents unless the other side raises an objection to them.

basic.situation: The claimant's key witness has refused to attend a hearing voluntarily. Your supervisor told you to prepare the hearing paperwork.

options.text: Prepare the draft summons for your supervisor's approval and record the witness's refusal.
Proceed with the hearing and decide the claim on the evidence already submitted.
Sign and issue the summons yourself today, since the witness is refusing to attend.
Ask the claimant to persuade the witness to attend and report back to you.

advanced.situation: At a multi-party hearing, a respondent's lawyer asks to cross-examine a claimant who has no lawyer and seems frightened. The other side objects to any delay.

options.text: Refuse the cross-examination because the claimant has no lawyer and seems distressed.
Let the lawyer continue and tell the claimant to answer or lose the claim.
Allow questioning but limit it to ten minutes in the interest of time.
Allow the questioning, explain it to the claimant, and permit short breaks.

basic.situation: You take notes while an investigator interviews an employer about a workplace accident. The employer's answers about the date are vague.

options.text: Interrupt the interview to ask the employer to state the exact date.
Write the date from last month's report to complete your notes of the interview.
Note the vague answers exactly and tell the investigator the date needs checking.
Note that the employer gave the date and enter your own estimate of it.

advanced.situation: A difficult case involves a company that blocks employee witnesses from speaking to you. You are asked to guide a new officer on collecting evidence.

options.text: Tell them to ask the company's lawyer to arrange witness statements for you.
Show them how to request records formally, interview witnesses elsewhere, and document refusals.
Tell them to rely on the company's own HR reports and add short notes.
Tell them to record workers' conversations with their phones and not tell anyone.

basic.situation: You are drafting a decision on a clear-cut claim. The evidence and the rules both show the claimant is entitled, and the rules set out the amount.

options.text: Draft the decision applying the rules, state the amount, and send it for review.
Draft the decision and leave the amount for the finance unit to decide.
Approve payment yourself and send the money before your senior reviews the draft.
Draft the decision and add a larger amount since the claimant is poor.

advanced.situation: In a complex hearing, one side offers a recorded phone call as evidence. The other side objects, saying it was recorded secretly and is incomplete.

options.text: Exclude the recording at once and move on to the remaining evidence.
Hear both sides on admissibility, check how it was recorded, and give reasons.
Admit the recording and tell the objecting side to prove it is incomplete.
Admit the recording for now and decide later how much weight it deserves.

basic.situation: A claimant whose claim was rejected asks how to appeal. You have a script explaining the appeal steps and the deadline.

options.text: Give her a copy of the script and tell her to read it later.
Tell her the deadline is flexible, so she can appeal whenever she is ready.
Tell her appeals rarely succeed and advise her to accept the decision.
Go through the script, state the deadline, and say where appeals are sent.

advanced.situation: Your office rejects many claims, and claimants say the decisions are confusing and the appeal steps unclear. You are asked to improve guidance and train new staff.

options.text: Tell new staff to refer all confused claimants to the legal aid office.
Approve more marginal claims on first review to reduce the number of appeals.
Rewrite decision letters in plain language, add an appeal guide, and train staff.
Add a short paragraph about the appeal steps to every decision letter.

basic.situation: A tenant files a deposit claim with her tenancy agreement and bank slip attached. The slip shows a payment date that differs from the date she states.

options.text: Edit the date on your copy of the slip to match her claim.
Ask her to clarify the dates and note which document supports each date.
Use the date on the bank slip and mention the difference in the file.
Use the date she states, since she signed the claim form herself.

advanced.situation: A construction dispute turns on conflicting precedents about who bears delay costs when weather and a supplier both caused delay. The parties want a ruling next week.

options.text: Study the precedents, compare their facts, and identify the principle that applies here.
Rely on the most recent precedent and cite it in the ruling.
Ask each party's lawyer to send their preferred cases and choose between them.
Split the delay costs equally between the parties to avoid researching the conflict.

basic.situation: During a hearing, a party objects to a photograph shown by the other side. You are unsure of the rule for admitting photographs in your forum.

options.text: Allow the photograph and warn the objecting party against making further objections.
Reject the photograph because the objection was raised before it was explained.
Pause briefly, check the forum rules on photographs, then rule on the objection.
Admit the photograph for now but note the objection clearly in the record.

advanced.situation: A claim involves an employer's liability for a worker's injury, with an unclear contract, partial safety records and a past decision with similar but different facts.

options.text: Ask the employer's lawyer to draft your reasons and sign them as your own.
Follow the earlier decision since the cases look similar, and note small differences.
Compare the facts with the earlier decision and explain how the rules apply.
Decide against the employer because the safety records are incomplete and unclear.

basic.situation: The parties have agreed on payment terms in mediation. You must prepare the settlement agreement for them to sign using the standard template.

options.text: Fill the template with the agreed terms, check names and amounts with both parties.
Use the template from a previous case and change the names and amounts.
Fill in the template and send it to both parties to sign by post.
Add a clause favouring the party you dealt with more, since she was cooperative.

advanced.situation: You must write a formal opinion on a complex contract dispute. One party raised a point in its long submission that the hearing did not cover.

options.text: Decide the new point in favour of the party who raised it to avoid delay.
Mention the new point briefly in the opinion and say it was not argued.
Leave the new point out of the opinion since the hearing did not cover it.
Invite short submissions on the new point from both sides, then write full reasons.

basic.situation: In a neighbour dispute over noise, one neighbour says the other is simply rude. You are asked to clarify the issues under supervision.

options.text: Tell them both that noise rules are the housing office's job.
Warn the neighbours that the police and housing office will act if noise continues.
Ask each neighbour what happens, when it occurs, and what they want changed.
Ask the neighbour called rude to apologise first, then move on to terms.

advanced.situation: In a family business dispute, two brothers have not spoken in a year, and each says the other cheated him. A lot of money and family ties are at stake.

options.text: Tell them which brother's version seems more believable to you and propose terms.
Meet them separately first, learn their interests, then bring them together for options.
Start with a joint session and ask each to state his case.
Suggest that they split the business assets equally and sign this week.

basic.situation: You check a simple claim against your checklist. All items are met except one faint signature that appears to match the earlier forms.

options.text: Trace over the faint signature with a pen so that it looks clearer.
Approve the claim and mention the faint signature in the file notes.
Return the whole claim to the claimant and ask him to sign again.
Note the faint signature, ask your supervisor to confirm it, then approve if confirmed.

advanced.situation: The insurer offers a lower compromise settlement on a disputed injury claim. Medical reports are mixed, and the claimant needs money for treatment.

options.text: Recommend acceptance after the insurer offers you a small consultation fee on the side.
Recommend rejection since the offer is lower than the amount claimed.
Review all reports and the law, then recommend acceptance or rejection with reasons.
Recommend acceptance because the claimant needs money for treatment and cannot wait.

basic.situation: Two parties agree to mediate. One can meet only on Fridays, while the other works shifts and has not given any available dates.

options.text: Ask the second party for shift dates, then offer matching Friday slots in writing.
Ask the first party whether another weekday could work and wait for his reply.
Book the next free Friday and ask the second party to adjust.
Book a Friday and tell the second party the claim ends if he misses it.

advanced.situation: A dispute involves five parties with lawyers across three states. Two are unavailable most of the month, and one is travelling abroad.

options.text: Choose a date yourself and tell lawyers that absent parties will lose their say.
Schedule a session on the date most parties choose and update the rest.
Poll all parties for dates and propose online attendance for those who are far away.
Hold separate sessions for each party through the month and relay offers between them.

basic.situation: You are a new magistrate sentencing a first-time offender for minor theft. The law sets a range, and he has apologised and repaid the victim.

options.text: Pick the middle of the range as the usual starting point for all offenders.
Impose a sentence above the legal range to deter other people from stealing.
Apply the legal range, weigh the apology and repayment, and give written reasons.
Follow your senior's advice on the sentence and record the reasons he gives.

advanced.situation: In a complex case, several statutes point to different sentencing ranges. A fellow judge asks you how to read the overlapping provisions.

options.text: Suggest they follow how the last judge sentenced a similar case.
Tell them to apply the statute with the heavier penalty to stay safe.
Compare the statutes' wording and purposes, explain how they fit together, and cite decisions.
Suggest they choose the range that matches the public mood on social media.

basic.situation: In a simple civil case the court finds a contractor damaged a house. The two repair quotes presented differ, and both are reasonable.

options.text: Award the average of the two quotes since both seem reasonable to the court.
Review both quotes, award the amount the evidence supports, and explain why.
Award nothing and tell the parties to settle the repair cost between themselves.
Award the higher quote because the house owner suffered the damage first.

advanced.situation: Before a civil trial, one side asks for an order freezing the other's bank account, claiming he will move his money abroad. The other side denies it.

options.text: Hear both sides, weigh the evidence of risk, and limit any order you make.
Refuse the order because the allegation has not been proven by trial.
Freeze all his accounts and business assets and set the hearing for next year.
Order a short freeze on the account until a full hearing can be held.

basic.situation: You are presiding over your first jury trial under a senior judge. You must give the standard instruction on the burden of proof before deliberations.

options.text: Summarise the instruction in your own words to save the jury time.
Read the standard wording slowly, check the jury understands, and answer their questions.
Tell the jury to convict if they feel the defendant is probably guilty.
Read the standard wording as printed and then send the jury out to deliberate.

advanced.situation: During deliberations, a jury asks in a note whether they can treat a defendant's silence as a sign of guilt. The lawyers disagree on how to answer.

options.text: Tell the jury that silence can be treated as guilt in serious cases.
Repeat the earlier instructions exactly and add nothing further to the note.
Tell the jury to rely on their common sense and the earlier instructions.
Hear both lawyers, check the law on silence, and answer the jury in writing.

basic.situation: Two lawyers keep interrupting each other during a witness's testimony. Court staff remind you that the standard rule is one person speaks at a time.

options.text: Let them finish arguing, then ask the witness to restart his testimony.
Remind both lawyers of the rule, ask one to wait, and continue in order.
Fine both lawyers a large amount on the spot and warn them about contempt.
Adjourn the hearing for the day so the lawyers can calm down.

advanced.situation: A trial raises a new kind of online evidence for which no rule of procedure exists. Both lawyers ask you how it should be handled.

options.text: Hear both sides, set interim procedures based on similar rules, and record your reasons.
Ask the lawyers to agree rules between themselves and follow whatever they decide.
Admit the evidence in full and let the lawyers argue about its weight later.
Exclude the evidence because no rule covers it and move to the next witness.

basic.situation: You are given the pleadings and motions in a land dispute and must prepare a summary of the facts and issues for the judge before the hearing.

options.text: Summarise the facts from the first pleading and list the issues raised there.
Copy the plaintiff's lawyer's summary of the case into your note for the judge.
Read the documents, list undisputed facts and disputed points, and cite page numbers.
Write the facts you would expect for this type of case and verify later.

advanced.situation: Your court must decide a new question about liability for online platform content. You are told to research it and write an opinion that will guide later cases.

options.text: Research statutes and decisions, address both sides' arguments, and give reasons that can apply broadly.
Follow the closest earlier decision and apply it to the facts before you.
Copy the reasoning from a foreign article and cite it as binding law.
Decide the question narrowly on the facts and say nothing about the principle.

basic.situation: You must write a short decision in a simple case after the hearing. The senior judge reminds you that reasons must be written clearly for the parties.

options.text: State the outcome in a line and omit reasons so that appeals are harder.
State the facts found, the rule applied, and your reasons in plain language.
Write the result and a one-line reason and expand the details if requested.
Copy the reasons from a similar earlier decision and change the party names.

advanced.situation: As a senior judge you notice that court staff issue arrest warrants with missing details, and two junior judges handle similar applications very differently.

options.text: Set a standard checklist for warrants, brief staff and judges, and spot-check later.
Send a circular reminding staff and judges to complete all details on warrants.
Take over all warrant applications yourself for the next three months.
Tell staff to issue warrants in blank so judges can fill them later.

basic.situation: A senior lawyer asks you to draft a letter of demand for an unpaid invoice. The client gave you the amount owed but not the invoice date.

options.text: Leave the date out of the letter and send it to the lawyer anyway.
Fill in a plausible invoice date so the letter looks complete for the lawyer.
Draft the letter, mark the invoice date missing, and ask the client for it.
Use the date the client's last email was sent as the invoice date.

advanced.situation: You review a team member's draft pleading in a complex case and find an outdated provision and inconsistent party names. The filing deadline is in two days.

options.text: Send the draft to the lawyer and mention that it may need some checking.
Submit the draft to the court to meet the deadline and amend it afterwards.
Fix the errors yourself and pass the draft to the lawyer for review.
Mark the errors, return the draft with notes, and add a team template check.

basic.situation: A lawyer asks you to find the statute on notice periods for ending a tenancy. You find two online versions, one dated last year and one older.

options.text: Use the newer-dated version you found and tell the lawyer it came from online.
Use the older version because it is the one cited in the textbook.
Send the lawyer both versions and ask him which one he wants to use.
Check the official database for the latest version and tell the lawyer.

advanced.situation: A client believes a developer committed fraud on a housing project. The facts are spread across company filings, news reports and court records, and the lawyer wants a research plan.

options.text: Map the questions, list public sources for each, verify key facts, and build a timeline.
Search the developer's name in one database and send the lawyer whatever results appear.
Collect all news reports first and summarise them in date order for the lawyer.
Ask a friend inside the company for private documents and add them to the file.

basic.situation: A hearing is next week. A lawyer asks you to organise the exhibits in the order they will be presented. Several copies are missing page numbers.

options.text: Arrange the exhibits by file name and leave the numbering for the court.
Number the pages, arrange exhibits in the lawyer's order, and note missing copies.
Arrange the exhibits in date order and tell the lawyer about missing pages.
Remove the copies with missing pages from the bundle to keep it tidy.

advanced.situation: Two days before trial, a key witness says she is unwilling to testify because she fears her employer. The lawyer asks you to contact her.

options.text: Tell her that her employer will not find out what she says in court.
Remind her of the court date and tell her that she must attend.
Listen to her concerns, explain the process and protections, and report back to the lawyer.
Tell the lawyer she will not attend and suggest dropping her evidence.

basic.situation: A lawyer asks you to list the items in a deceased client's home for the estate. A family member asks if she can take some jewellery first.

options.text: Leave the jewellery off the list and let her take it home that day.
Let her take the jewellery if she signs a note promising to return it.
List the items with photos and descriptions, and refer the request to the lawyer.
Allow her to take items that seem of little value and note them.

advanced.situation: While reviewing a title search for a property closing, you find a bank charge the seller did not mention. Closing is in three days.

options.text: Remove the charge from the search summary so the closing is not delayed.
Tell the buyer's agent about the charge and ask him to raise it with the seller.
Note the charge in the file and carry on preparing the closing papers.
Alert the lawyer, obtain the charge details, and ask how it will be discharged.

basic.situation: You attend a client meeting with a lawyer to take notes. The client describes events out of order and mentions several dates.

options.text: Record points in order of events, mark unclear dates, and check them with the lawyer.
Fill in the missing dates from what you remember of similar clients' files.
Ask the client to stop and repeat everything slowly so you can write neatly.
Write down the points that sound important to you and skip the rest.

advanced.situation: A distressed client arrives without an appointment and says she wants to withdraw her case. Her lawyer is in court all day.

options.text: Ask her to return tomorrow when the lawyer is in and book an appointment.
Prepare the withdrawal form and get her signature before the lawyer returns.
Explain how a case is usually withdrawn and what forms she must sign.
Listen, record her wishes, say you cannot advise, and reach the lawyer through the clerk.

basic.situation: You file a lawyer's pleading with the court registry. The registry clerk says the copy is missing a stamp and asks you to wait.

options.text: Ask which stamp is needed, call the lawyer's office, and refile once added.
Stamp the copy yourself with the firm's own stamp and file it again.
Leave the copy with the clerk and promise to bring the stamp tomorrow.
Offer the clerk a small tip to accept it and fix the stamp later.

advanced.situation: The firm's law library has outdated volumes, uncatalogued books and unpaid online subscriptions. You are asked to improve how it is run and train a new clerk.

options.text: Cancel the paid online subscriptions and use free websites for all research.
Audit the volumes, update the catalogue, renew key subscriptions, and train the clerk.
Order the newest editions of the main volumes and shelve them first.
Discard every book older than five years to clear the shelves this week.

basic.situation: A search request lists the owner as Tan Ah Kow, but the attached sale agreement says Tan Ah Kau. The requester wants the result today.

options.text: Change the owner's name in the request to match the sale agreement and search.
Note the name difference, check the lot record, and ask the requester to confirm.
Search under the spelling in the request form and send the result back.
Search under both spellings and report the results together to the requester.

advanced.situation: A request for an old estate land parcel gives a vague description and a family name, and the land has been subdivided several times. You must define the evidence needed.

options.text: Pick one subdivided lot that seems likely and report on it as the property.
Search the family name across all land records and report everything you find.
Search the original parcel record and report the result for that lot.
List each subdivision, define the evidence needed per lot, and confirm scope.

basic.situation: You are asked to obtain the plan for a property from the survey office. The clerk says it is not in the system and offers a similar neighbouring plan.

options.text: Use the neighbouring plan as the property plan and submit it with the search.
Ask the clerk to check older survey records, and record the plan number received.
Take the neighbouring plan and mark clearly that it is a different lot.
Tell the requester that no plan exists for the property in the survey office.

advanced.situation: A closing file for a commercial property shows the transfer was signed, but the stamping receipt is dated after registration. Regulations require stamping first.

options.text: Assume the receipt date is a typing error and mark the file as complete.
Change the receipt date in the file to match the registration date.
Flag the file as non-compliant, check the registry dates, and refer it on.
Note the date difference in the file and continue to the next file.

basic.situation: You check a sale contract to verify the legal description of a property. The lot number in the contract differs from the lot number in the land record.

options.text: Use the lot number in the contract since the parties signed it.
Alter the lot number in your copy of the contract so the two match.
Compare the descriptions line by line, note the lot difference, and tell your supervisor.
Use the lot number in the land record and mention the contract was different.

advanced.situation: A title shows land tax arrears for three years and a charge to a bank. The buyer wants to build on the land, and the lawyer asks which restrictions matter.

options.text: Report the arrears and the charge to the lawyer with no comment on building.
Leave both items out of the report since the buyer plans to settle them later.
Report the bank charge as the main issue since it involves more money.
Report the arrears and the charge, and explain how each could limit building.

basic.situation: A lawyer asks you to summarise a recorded mortgage for the title file. The document is long and has several schedules.

options.text: Copy the summary from a similar mortgage you handled and update the names.
Summarise parties, property, amount and key terms, and check figures against the original.
Summarise the first pages and the main terms, and note that schedules follow.
Write the summary from the title on the cover and add typical terms.

advanced.situation: While searching a title you find an old lien and an unresolved private caveat. The buyer's lawyer asks for a report on what is needed to clear the title.

options.text: Advise the buyer's lawyer to lift the caveat by filing a form himself.
Describe both encumbrances and say they need to be removed before closing.
Describe each encumbrance, state who can remove it, and outline realistic clearing steps.
State that the lien is old and probably no longer valid, and mention the caveat.

basic.situation: You check a land document submitted for registration. The seller's signature is present, but the witness page is blank.

options.text: Ask the applicant to find any person nearby to sign as witness today.
Mark it incomplete, prepare the rejection notice, and pass it on.
Accept the document and ask the applicant to bring the witness page later.
Sign the witness page yourself so that the document can be registered today.

advanced.situation: Your office rejects many land documents, and applicants complain that the reasons are unclear. A new colleague asks you how to handle complex rejections.

options.text: Set a standard notice format that cites the specific defect.
Tell the colleague to reject documents from applicants who have complained often.
Tell the colleague to copy the rejection reasons used by others last month.
Tell the colleague to keep reasons brief so applicants have little to argue.

basic.situation: You enter new title details into the record system from a document. The lot area field is in square feet, but the document gives hectares.

options.text: Enter the number as given and leave the unit for the supervisor to fix.
Enter the number from the document and add a note about the unit.
Convert the area to the field's unit, enter it, and note the conversion.
Round the area to a neat number in square feet and enter that figure.

advanced.situation: Two parties dispute who owns a strip of land between their lots. The buyer's lawyer, a surveyor and a bank give conflicting information about the boundary.

options.text: Give the buyer's lawyer the official record and let him contact the others.
Side with the surveyor because his plan looks the most professional to you.
Compare each document with the official record and suggest a joint survey to all.
Tell the bank the strip belongs to the seller and the lawyer is mistaken.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared lecture on financial accounting. Halfway through, several students look lost and one says the examples are too advanced.

options.text: Pause, ask where they got lost, and work through a simpler example before continuing.
Continue with the slides and say you will upload extra examples after class.
Skip to the end of the slides so you finish the lecture on time.
Tell the class the material is in the textbook and they must read ahead.

advanced.situation: In a graduate marketing seminar, two students argue heatedly over a controversial advertising case, and others stop participating. You want to keep the discussion productive.

options.text: Move on to the next topic and continue with the prepared lecture.
Ask the two students to continue their debate after class and move on.
Acknowledge both views, restate the issue, set ground rules, and invite quieter students in.
Tell the louder student he will lose marks if he argues in class again.

basic.situation: You are preparing a syllabus for an introductory operations management course. A senior colleague gives you last year's syllabus and says the assessment weights can be adjusted.

options.text: Remove the group assignment and reduce the weights to keep your workload low.
Set the final exam at one hundred percent of the grade to simplify marking.
Copy last year's syllabus and change the dates, venue and lecturer name.
Update the schedule and readings, set the weights, and ask your colleague to review.

advanced.situation: You manage a course website for three sections. Students report broken links, and some slides show older policy dates. A colleague wants to add a discussion forum.

options.text: Remove the pages with old policy dates and tell students to ask in class.
Audit broken links and outdated content, set an update schedule, then add the forum.
Add the forum first because students will use it more than slides.
Fix the broken links this week and add the forum before the exam period.

basic.situation: You are grading 40 short business-report assignments with the rubric. One report is excellent but exceeds the page limit by two pages.

options.text: Apply the rubric's length penalty as stated and explain the deduction in the feedback.
Let this student resubmit a shorter version after the others have been graded.
Give full marks this time because the report is clearly excellent overall.
Mark the pages within the limit and tell the student the rest was not read.

advanced.situation: Exam results show that 60 percent of students failed the same finance topic over three semesters. The head of department asks you to revise the course.

options.text: Add two extra lectures on the topic and keep the materials the same.
Review the topic's teaching and assessment, redesign the materials, and pilot the changes.
Remove the topic from the syllabus and the exam and inform the department later.
Make the exam questions on that topic easier to raise the pass rate.

basic.situation: A first-year student comes to your office hours worried about failing accounting. He says he works night shifts and misses early classes.

options.text: Tell him that students who work night shifts rarely pass accounting.
Advise him to withdraw from the course before the deadline passes this week.
Give him your lecture slides and tell him to study at home.
Ask about his schedule, identify missed topics, and suggest a catch-up plan.

advanced.situation: A new lecturer in your department has had several student complaints about unclear marking and rushed feedback. The lecturer asks you to mentor them.

options.text: Tell them complaints are normal for new lecturers and will pass.
Tell the students the lecturer is inexperienced and that you will check the marks.
Share your own marking guide and ask them to follow it this semester.
Review their marking together, agree a feedback routine, and observe one class.

basic.situation: A colleague mentions a new journal article that changes how your field teaches pricing strategy. The article is behind a paywall.

options.text: Ask your colleague to explain the article's main points over coffee this week.
Read the free abstract and update your slides based on it right away.
Get the article through the library, read it, and note possible lecture changes.
Download the article from an unofficial site that shares paid journal papers free.

advanced.situation: You lead a small study on student entrepreneurship, and the results are mixed. A co-author wants to publish just the supportive findings in a journal.

options.text: Agree with your co-author and publish just the supportive findings in the paper.
Delay publication until you can collect new data that gives clearer results.
Publish both sets of results but place the mixed ones in an appendix.
Report all findings, explain the mixed results, and discuss the limits openly with your co-author.

basic.situation: You are asked to serve on the department's textbook selection committee. At the first meeting, a publisher's representative offers each member a free laptop bag.

options.text: Accept the bag since it is low in value and unlikely to affect decisions.
Accept the bag and recommend the publisher's textbook to show your appreciation.
Decline the gift politely and ask the chair to note the offer.
Accept the bag but declare it to the committee at the start.

advanced.situation: A local bank offers internships to your students if you design a new fintech module with its staff. The module needs faculty approval, and the bank wants to see the content first.

options.text: Promise the bank that students will receive credit while approval is still pending.
Run the module as an informal workshop outside the formal approval process.
Draft a joint proposal with the bank, seek faculty approval, and agree internship terms.
Design the module yourself and let the bank review it before approval.

basic.situation: You grade programming assignments with the department rubric. Two students' programs look almost identical, including the same unusual variable names and comments.

options.text: Grade both normally and mention the similarity in your private marking notes.
Give both students a zero and tell them to contact you for questions.
Grade by the rubric, report the similarity to the coordinator, and follow procedure.
Ask one student in front of the class whether they copied from the other.

advanced.situation: End-of-course surveys and exam results show students struggle with data structures and later fail the algorithms course. You are asked to revise the curriculum.

options.text: Analyse results and feedback, realign prerequisites and content, and review the changes next year.
Drop data structures from the programme and tell students to study it themselves.
Lower the pass mark in the algorithms course to reduce the number of failures.
Add extra tutorials for data structures and keep the rest of the content.

basic.situation: Your lab needs ten more laptops for a programming course starting in three weeks. The budget is fixed, and your department has an approved supplier list.

options.text: Ask students to bring their own laptops to labs for the whole semester.
Order cheaper laptops from an unlisted online seller and claim the cost later.
Order from the first approved supplier on the list and submit the invoice.
Request quotes from approved suppliers, compare specifications and price, and submit for approval.

advanced.situation: Your online programming course site must support automatic code submission and testing. Students report slow uploads and failed tests during peak times.

options.text: Switch off automatic testing for this week and mark the code by hand.
Tell students to submit earlier and increase the upload size limit as well.
Review server logs, add a test queue, run a load test, and inform students.
Remove the submission deadline so students can upload whenever the site is quiet.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared lecture on recursion. A student asks a question that is not in your notes, and you are unsure of the answer.

options.text: Tell the student the question shows they have not read the notes.
Say you are unsure, explain the related idea, and post the answer later.
Give a quick answer based on how you think the concept works.
Say the question is outside the syllabus and move on with the lecture.

advanced.situation: On the curriculum committee, members disagree on making cybersecurity compulsory. Industry feedback supports it, but staff say they lack teaching capacity.

options.text: Vote for the course and assign teaching to colleagues who were absent from the meeting.
Vote for the course and let the staffing issue be solved later.
Vote against the course because staff are already stretched thin this year.
Gather staffing and demand data and propose a phased rollout with costs.

basic.situation: You enter this week's attendance and quiz marks into the department's grade system. A student complains that his quiz mark is lower than the one on his paper.

options.text: Tell him that the system mark is final and cannot be changed now.
Compare the paper with the system, fix any entry error, and tell him.
Tell him to bring the paper to your office next week and wait.
Change the system mark to match his paper and delete the old entry.

advanced.situation: A final-year student wants to switch from software engineering to data science for a job offer, but prerequisite courses are missing and graduation is at risk.

options.text: Promise him the department will waive the missing prerequisites if he asks politely.
Tell him the switch is possible and he should apply for it now.
Check graduation rules and outline course options and risks for him.
Tell him to finish his current course and think about data science later.

basic.situation: You want to keep up with developments in machine learning for your courses. You have little time this month, and a conference discount offer arrives.

options.text: Pick a few relevant papers, join one conference session, and schedule reading time.
Register for the full conference and plan to see which talks matter later.
Read the conference programme and note the talks that look interesting to you.
Skip the reading this month and rely on what students tell you.

advanced.situation: Two colleagues disagree on whether students may use online code-sharing sites in take-home assessments, and complaints are rising. You are asked to help the department decide.

options.text: Support the more senior colleague's view and write the policy yourself this week.
Let each lecturer set their own rule for their course and tell students.
Gather views and evidence, discuss options at a meeting, and agree a policy.
Ask the IT office to block all code sharing sites on campus to end it.

basic.situation: You are preparing a weekly handout and homework for your first-year Java class. The textbook examples are too long for a one-page handout.

options.text: Copy examples from a student forum post and present them as your own work.
Skip the handout this week and give students the homework as a list.
Hand out the chapter summary page and tell students to read examples at home.
Select key examples, rewrite them briefly in your own words, and cite the textbook.

advanced.situation: You lead computer science recruitment at school fairs and registration day. Past events had long queues and few sign-ups.

options.text: Promise visitors guaranteed scholarships and graduate jobs to attract more sign-ups.
Survey past visitors, redesign booth and queue flow, add hands-on demos, and track sign-ups.
Offer a prize draw for everyone who signs up on the day.
Bring more brochures and extra staff to the next fair and registration day.

basic.situation: You are grading calculus assignments with a rubric. A student's final answer is wrong, but the method is sound apart from one arithmetic slip.

options.text: Give zero for the final answer and add a short comment on the slip.
Give full marks because the method is sound and the slip is small.
Award method marks per the rubric, deduct for the slip as stated, and add feedback.
Mark the student down further to keep the class average near last year's.

advanced.situation: You are asked to design a new final exam for a statistics course and validate it for the department. Past exams were criticised as inconsistent in difficulty.

options.text: Write harder questions than before to show that the course is rigorous.
Reuse questions from past exams and balance topics evenly across the paper.
Test the draft by letting a few current students attempt it and keep their copies.
Map questions to outcomes, pilot the exam, check item difficulty, and refine before use.

basic.situation: A senior colleague asks you to review the materials for a linear algebra course for accuracy and clarity. You find one worked example with a sign error.

options.text: Leave the example as it is since students may spot the sign error themselves.
Fix the example, check similar ones, and tell your colleague what changed and why.
Delete the example from the shared file and renumber the later ones quietly.
Tell your colleague about the sign error and leave the fix to them.

advanced.situation: Your department's calculus curriculum has not changed in ten years, and employers say graduates lack data skills. You are asked to lead the revision.

options.text: Survey employers and alumni, map skills to courses, and consult staff on changes.
Add a data analysis module to the final year and keep the rest.
Remove the proof-based courses to make room for programming and data skills.
Copy the curriculum of a top overseas university and adopt it in full.

basic.situation: You are asked to order a textbook for next semester's discrete mathematics course. Your colleague suggests the edition she used, but a newer edition is available.

options.text: Order the newer edition because newer editions usually have more up-to-date content.
Order the older edition because your colleague recommended it from experience.
Order both editions for every student and charge the department twice over.
Compare both editions, check cost and availability, and order the one fitting the syllabus.

advanced.situation: You are asked to set standards for choosing mathematics resources, including online tools, for all first-year courses. Lecturers disagree, and some prefer free materials.

options.text: Define criteria for accuracy, accessibility and cost, then test samples and consult lecturers.
Let each lecturer choose resources freely and report their choices at year end.
Choose the resources from the publisher that offers you personal incentives.
Adopt free materials for all first-year courses to reduce student costs.

basic.situation: Your department sponsors you to attend a mathematics education conference. You have one afternoon free between talks.

options.text: Skip the afternoon sessions to rest and prepare next week's lessons instead.
Attend relevant sessions, take notes, meet other lecturers, and share a summary with colleagues.
Spend the afternoon sightseeing and claim full conference attendance for the department.
Attend the sessions and keep your notes for your own later use.

advanced.situation: First-year mathematics has high dropout rates, and colleagues disagree on the causes. You are asked to lead an initiative to improve teaching practices.

options.text: Collect dropout and feedback data, form a small team, and test changes.
Introduce a peer teaching observation scheme for all first-year lecturers this term.
Blame the students' school results and ask admissions to raise entry grades.
Ask colleagues to email their ideas and then implement the most common one.

basic.situation: You are entering attendance and grades into the system. Two students have identical names, and the sign-in sheet shows just their surnames.

options.text: Enter the records by matching first names with the order they sat.
Enter both students' grades under the first name found and tell them later.
Average the two students' attendance and grades and enter the result for both.
Check student ID numbers, enter the records, and flag the duplicate names.

advanced.situation: An audit shows that some lecturers keep attendance in spreadsheets and some on paper, with different grade formats. You are asked to improve the department's record-keeping.

options.text: Agree one format, set backup and access rules, and train lecturers.
Ask the office to collect all paper records and keep them in a cabinet.
Move every record to a free online tool of your own choice today.
Send all lecturers a template spreadsheet and ask them to use it.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared lecture on differential equations from your notes. Ten minutes in, you notice a mistake in a formula on your slide.

options.text: Continue the lecture and mention the mistake at the start of the next one.
Tell students that the formula is right and ask them to copy it.
Tell the class, fix the formula on the board, and upload the new slide.
Write the fixed formula on the board silently and carry on teaching.

advanced.situation: You mentor a new lecturer whose office hours are full of last-minute exam requests. They ask how to advise students better.

options.text: Advise them to reduce office hours to one hour a week to save time.
Advise them to tell students to email questions instead of coming in person.
Advise them to turn away any student who arrives unannounced during office hours.
Suggest booked slots, pre-exam group sessions, and written study advice, then review together.

basic.situation: You grade studio design models using the department rubric. One student's model is striking but ignores the brief's site constraints, which the rubric weights heavily.

options.text: Give a middle mark to balance the strong design and the weak response.
Give the student a pass and ask them to resubmit privately for a better mark.
Give a high mark since the model is the most striking in the studio.
Mark against the rubric, score the constraints low, and give feedback on the strengths.
