advanced.situation: As studio coordinator, you find tutors give very different marks for similar projects, and students complain. You must set grading standards and guide the tutors.

options.text: Average every tutor's marks to remove the differences between their student groups.
Replace the tutors with the lowest marks and announce it to the students.
Create a shared rubric with exemplars and hold a moderation session.
Send all tutors a reminder to follow the department rubric more closely.

basic.situation: A senior colleague asks you to help prepare exam questions on building structures. You write one and notice it matches an example in a popular textbook.

options.text: Copy the textbook question and its figure into the paper and credit nobody.
Rewrite the question with new values and context, and note the source concept.
Change a few numbers in the question and keep the rest of it.
Use the question as written since structure problems are fairly standard anyway.

advanced.situation: Graduates say the architecture programme teaches little on sustainable design, and the accrediting body reviews the curriculum next year. You are asked to lead revisions.

options.text: Review the curriculum against accreditation criteria, consult industry, and draft changes.
Wait for the accrediting body to list what should change before acting.
Add a sustainability elective and describe it in the accreditation report.
Add sustainability wording to the course descriptions so the report looks complete.

basic.situation: You want to learn about new low-carbon building methods for your lectures. A colleague invites you to a local seminar the evening before your marking deadline.

options.text: Attend the seminar and mark the studio work in a rush the next morning.
Attend the whole seminar and ask the department for an extension on marking.
Attend part of the seminar, note useful points, and plan your marking time.
Skip the seminar and ask your colleague to share her notes.

advanced.situation: You lead a research team studying heat in housing. A junior colleague wants to publish the first findings now, but the data covers just one season.

options.text: Share early findings as a working paper, state the limits, and collect more seasons.
Publish now and describe the findings as proven for housing across the country.
Wait until the second season ends and publish the study with all the data.
Publish now as a final study and add the second season later.

basic.situation: You record attendance for a large lecture with a sign-in sheet. At the end, you notice that some names are in the same handwriting.

options.text: Remove all names written in the same handwriting from the attendance record.
Note the issue, ask the department how to verify, and change method next lecture.
Count all names as present this time and warn students that sheets will be checked.
Mark the whole class as present for the lecture to avoid any disputes.

advanced.situation: A funding body invites proposals for research on affordable housing. Your department has limited experience with the topic, and the deadline is in three weeks.

options.text: Form a team with an experienced partner and define a clear scope.
Write the proposal alone and ask a senior colleague to review it.
Reuse a previous unsuccessful proposal and change the topic and title.
Describe your department as experienced in affordable housing projects to impress reviewers.

basic.situation: A second-year student comes to your office hours upset about a low studio mark and says she wants to quit architecture.

options.text: Tell her low marks are common in second year and she should continue.
Show her other students' higher marks and projects to motivate her to improve.
Listen, review the feedback with her, and suggest steps to improve.
Tell her quitting might suit her if she is not enjoying it.

advanced.situation: A final-year thesis project with an industry partner has stalled. The firm wants extra unpaid work from the student, who is under stress, and you supervise internships.

options.text: Meet the student and firm, clarify scope in writing, and agree a plan.
Cancel the partnership with the firm and record the student's work as incomplete.
Advise the student to follow the firm's requests to keep the partnership.
Tell the student to stop contacting the firm and complete the thesis alone.

basic.situation: In a design history lecture, you invite comments, but just two students speak and the rest stay quiet.

options.text: Continue the lecture and let the two active students lead the discussion.
Call on students at random to answer questions about the reading.
Ask a question, let students discuss in pairs, then invite pairs to share.
Tell the quiet students that participation now counts for half of their marks.

advanced.situation: You are designing a new first-year lecture on architectural design methods for a class of 200. Resources are tight, and the hall is not suited to sketching.

options.text: Give a long lecture with images and set sketching as homework for students.
Split the content into short talks and sketching sessions in a suitable space.
Reduce the class to forty by capping attendance at random on the day.
Show a series of recorded videos instead of speaking yourself to the class.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared lecture on fluid mechanics. A student points out that a unit in your worked example does not match the formula.

options.text: Tell the student the units are usually interchangeable in this topic anyway.
Check the working, thank the student, and fix the unit for the class.
Say you will check it later and continue with the next example.
Tell the class to disregard that student's comment and keep the units as written.

advanced.situation: You lead a seminar for engineering lecturers on running discussions in large classes. A senior lecturer says discussion wastes time in a content-heavy course.

options.text: Present evidence, demonstrate a structured discussion, and let them try it.
Tell the senior lecturer his teaching approach is outdated in front of everyone.
Share a research article and ask them to read it later this month.
Agree that content comes first and shorten the discussion part of the seminar.

basic.situation: You grade lab reports with a supervisor's rubric. Three reports share an identical results table, including the same measurement errors.

options.text: Grade them all normally and add a comment about the identical tables.
Give the three reports half marks each as a cautious middle option.
Give all three students zero and post their names on the lab notice board.
Grade each by the rubric and report the identical tables to your supervisor.

advanced.situation: Most students pass the theory questions on your exam but fail the design problems. You are asked to revise the assessment strategy and guide other staff.

options.text: Analyse results by question type, align assessment to outcomes, and share grading standards.
Add a few more design tutorials and keep the exam unchanged.
Remove the design problems from the exam to raise the overall pass rate.
Raise all design marks by ten percent to hide the gap between topics.

basic.situation: A lead lecturer asks you to prepare a one-page handout and a homework set on beam bending. The textbook problems are very similar to last year's.

options.text: Take ready-made problems and solutions from students' shared online study notes and reuse them.
Select key ideas, write fresh problems, and ask the lead to review them.
Reuse last year's homework set and change the numbers in each question slightly.
Copy the textbook problems directly into the new homework set and add a title.

advanced.situation: Employers say engineering graduates lack teamwork and communication skills. You are asked to lead a curriculum revision, set content standards and brief colleagues.

options.text: Ask lecturers to add group projects to their courses at their own discretion.
Replace several technical subjects with soft-skill courses in every year this semester.
Gather employer and student feedback, map skills across courses, and draft changes.
Add a communication course in the final year and keep others the same.

basic.situation: You help a professor collect data for a research project on solar panel efficiency. A sensor gives one odd reading that is far from the rest.

options.text: Repeat the measurement and note the odd reading in your own log.
Adjust the odd reading to fit the trend of the other readings.
Leave the odd reading out of the data table and carry on collecting.
Record the odd reading, check the sensor setup, and tell the professor.

advanced.situation: You are writing a major research grant proposal with a junior researcher who suggests inflating the expected impact figures to make the proposal more competitive.

options.text: Use realistic evidence-based figures, state uncertainties, and strengthen the methods.
Use the more optimistic end of the range of realistic estimates.
Use the inflated figures but add a note on uncertainty in the appendix.
Use the inflated figures and remove any mention of how they were calculated.

basic.situation: You monitor a student lab session under a professor's direction. A student starts a welding task without wearing the required eye protection.

options.text: Remind him to put on eye protection soon and carry on monitoring others.
Tell him to hurry and finish the weld before the professor arrives.
Wait until he finishes the weld and then talk to him.
Stop the task, make sure he wears eye protection, and tell the professor.

advanced.situation: You oversee several graduate students' projects. One student's supervisor has left the university, and her experiments need costly equipment for months.

options.text: Assign a new supervisor with the student's consent and secure equipment access.
Ask the student to carry on alone until a supervisor is found.
Suspend the student's project until a new academic year begins next intake.
Tell the student to submit the thesis now under the departed supervisor's name.

basic.situation: You record the semester's attendance and grades. The registration office sends a revised class list that adds three students who joined late.

options.text: Add the three students and ask the office about missed work.
Leave the three students out of the records until the exam period.
Copy marks from classmates to the late students for the earlier assessments.
Add the three students with zero marks for the work they missed.

advanced.situation: You chair a committee that sets a new attendance policy. Lecturers want a strict rule, while students and the counselling unit argue for flexibility.

options.text: Write a policy yourself and announce it as the committee's unanimous decision.
Collect evidence from both groups, draft options, and set a review date.
Adopt the lecturers' strict rule and add a short appeal process for students.
Hold a quick vote in the first meeting and apply whatever the result is.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared lecture on soil chemistry. Students seem confused by the section on nutrient uptake, and the lecture is running over time.

options.text: Pause, give one clear example of uptake, and carry the rest over.
Continue at the same pace and tell students that confusion is their problem.
Speed up through the remaining slides so that you finish the topic on time.
Tell students to study uptake from the textbook and end the lecture.

advanced.situation: In a graduate seminar on food security, two students disagree sharply about pesticides and organic farming. A guest speaker from industry is present.

options.text: Close the discussion for now because it is getting too heated for the seminar.
Welcome both views, ask each for evidence, and guide the group to compare trade-offs.
Side with the guest speaker and tell the students to accept the industry view.
Let the guest speaker answer both students and then carry on with the agenda.

basic.situation: You grade a lab report on plant growth. The student's data table is neat, but the conclusion does not match the data.

options.text: Mark the conclusion as written and give the table no separate marks.
Give a middle mark for the whole report and write a brief note.
Give full marks because the report looks tidy and the student worked hard.
Give the table full marks, deduct on the conclusion, and explain why.

advanced.situation: Exam results show graduates struggle with farm record-keeping and basic business skills. You are asked to evaluate and revise the agribusiness course.

options.text: Add a business skills lecture series open to all final year students.
Make the existing exam easier so that more students are able to pass.
Review content and assessments, consult farmers and employers, and redesign modules.
Remove record-keeping from the syllabus because students find it too difficult to learn.

basic.situation: During office hours, a student asks whether she should take a plant breeding elective or an animal nutrition elective. She likes both.

options.text: Ask about her interests and goals, explain each elective, and let her decide.
Tell her to pick the elective that you teach yourself since you know it.
Tell her either elective will give her a job in any agriculture field.
Tell her to choose the elective that has the easier exams this year.

advanced.situation: A state agency asks you to advise on reducing soil erosion on hill farms. You know the topic well but have not studied this district's soil conditions.

options.text: Give the agency your standard recommendations from studies in other districts.
Ask the agency to supply the soil data and then advise on erosion.
Promise the agency a specific percentage drop in erosion in one year.
Review district soil data, visit sample farms, and give options with stated assumptions.

basic.situation: You want to learn about recent advances in rice disease resistance. You have two hours free and access to the library and a conference proceedings book.

options.text: Ask a colleague to summarise the advances in five minutes.
Skim the conference proceedings and note the titles that interest you most.
Read recent review papers from the library and note relevant findings.
Read a blog post on rice diseases and add it to your slides.

advanced.situation: You lead a team preparing a large grant to study climate-resilient crops. A partner lab offers to share unpublished data in return for co-authorship that is not in the proposal.

options.text: Use the partner's unpublished data and promise authorship when the paper is written.
Agree data sharing and authorship in writing, and name the partner.
Use the partner's data in the proposal and leave the partner's name out.
Leave the partner out of the proposal and discuss authorship afterwards.

basic.situation: You assist a senior lecturer during a field visit with 25 students to a vegetable farm. A student wanders off toward the livestock area.

options.text: Let him explore for a while and count the group at the bus later.
Ask a student standing near him to bring him back to the group.
Shout at the student in front of the group and send him to the bus.
Call the student back, check where everyone is, and tell the senior lecturer.

advanced.situation: A graduate student's field experiment on fertiliser trials has failed because of heavy flooding. The student is distressed and the funding deadline is near.

options.text: Advise the student to repeat the experiment next season on a new site.
Tell the student to complete the analysis using the flooded results anyway.
Support the student, review the surviving data, and discuss options with the funder.
Tell the student to adjust the results to look like a normal season.

basic.situation: You update attendance after a farm field day. A student was marked absent but says she was there, and her friend confirms it.

options.text: Tell her the record is final and she should have signed in.
Mark her present and mark the friend absent to balance the total.
Mark her present because her friend confirmed she was there that day.
Check the sign-in sheet and notes, then update the record if confirmed.

advanced.situation: You serve on a faculty committee reviewing the budget for field equipment. Departments request twice the available funds, and your own department is among them.

options.text: Declare your department's interest, compare requests against teaching needs, and support fairness.
Lobby members privately before the meeting to approve your department's request in full.
Support priority for your department since you know its needs the most.
Support an equal split of the available funds among all the departments.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared lecture on photosynthesis from a script. A student asks a question about a recent discovery that is not in your script.

options.text: Welcome the question, share what you know, and promise to follow up.
Say it is not in the syllabus and continue with the script.
Tell the student to stop asking questions that are outside the script.
Answer confidently with what you vaguely remember reading in the news recently.

advanced.situation: You lead a seminar for new biology instructors on discussing ethically sensitive topics like gene editing. Some participants fear students' strong reactions.

options.text: Give them a written list of tips on managing sensitive class discussions.
Tell them to end any discussion that becomes emotional and mark students down.
Model a ground-rules opening, run a practice discussion, and debrief on handling reactions.
Advise them to avoid sensitive topics in class altogether and stick to facts.

basic.situation: A student visits your office hours confused about cell division and has an assignment due tomorrow. You have a 15-minute slot.

options.text: Write out the answers to the assignment for her to copy tonight.
Show her the page in the textbook where the answers to the questions appear.
Give her the lecture notes and tell her to read them tonight.
Ask what she understands, explain key points with a diagram, and give her resources.

advanced.situation: Several first-year biology students are failing quizzes, and some have not attended extra help sessions. You are asked to design a support programme and mentor junior advisors.

options.text: Publish the list of failing students so they feel pressure to attend.
Identify at-risk students early, offer tailored help, and train advisors to follow up.
Email all first-year students a reminder about the help sessions this week.
Open more extra help sessions at different times and advertise them widely.

basic.situation: You enter quiz grades into the university system. One student's name appears in two classes with different marks on the same quiz.

options.text: Check the quiz papers, confirm which entry is accurate, and report the other.
Delete both entries and enter a new mark from what you remember.
Leave both entries in the system until the end of semester.
Enter the higher of the two marks and tell the student about it.

advanced.situation: You manage a large research grant. The funder's rules cap equipment spending, but a lab needs a costly microscope that would exceed the cap.

options.text: Buy a cheaper microscope within the cap and adjust the planned experiments.
Split the purchase across two invoices so each stays under the cap.
Check the rules, ask the funder about variation, and consider shared equipment.
Delay the purchase until the funding period is nearly finished.

basic.situation: You prepare materials for a student lab on enzyme activity. The supply room is short of one chemical that the protocol requires.

options.text: Tell the lab coordinator, check for an approved substitute, and revise the protocol.
Use a similar-looking chemical from another lab and adjust the protocol yourself.
Order the chemical urgently and run the lab a week later.
Mix a replacement from household chemicals and let students use it in the lab.

advanced.situation: A shared lab microscope shows faults, and several users have tried quick repairs. You are asked to set maintenance standards and train the staff.

options.text: Let each user clean and adjust the microscope as they see fit.
Open the microscope housing yourself and repair it using online videos.
Ask a technician to repair it and put up a warning sign beside it.
Log the faults, arrange a certified repair, and train staff on maintenance rules.

basic.situation: You observe a student lab session on microbiology. A student pours culture waste into the normal sink instead of the biohazard container.

options.text: Let her continue since it was just a small amount of waste.
Tell the class to use the biohazard bin from now on.
Wash the sink well yourself after class and mention it to no one.
Stop her, explain the disposal rule, and inform the lab supervisor.

advanced.situation: A graduate student's complex experiment keeps giving inconsistent results. The student thinks the design is fine, but the controls look weak.

options.text: Review the design with the student, find the weak controls, and plan a pilot.
Tell the student to drop the inconsistent runs from the data set.
Let the student continue and judge the results at the end.
Tell the student to repeat the experiment three more times and average results.

basic.situation: You grade lab reports using a provided rubric. One report is well written but lists data that seems to be copied from the lab manual.

options.text: Give full marks because the writing is excellent and the structure is clear.
Mark the report on writing quality and mention the data concern in notes.
Give zero marks and tell the student that he is a cheat.
Grade by the rubric, flag the suspected copying to the instructor, and wait.

advanced.situation: A journal asks you to review a paper by a researcher you know well from a past project. The conclusions look overstated.

options.text: Review the paper and mention in your comments that you know the author.
Declare the connection to the editor, assess the evidence, and give balanced comments.
Review the paper and soften your comments because you know the author.
Review the paper and ask the researcher to explain the results before you write.

basic.situation: You grade a forest mapping assignment. One student's map is accurate but arrived two days late, and you do not know how the course treats late work.

options.text: Give the map zero because it was late and tell the student to appeal.
Grade the map on accuracy and take off a few marks as you see fit.
Check the course policy on late work, apply it, and explain the mark.
Grade the map on its accuracy and ask the lecturer about the late policy.

advanced.situation: Course evaluations show forestry students find the GIS module outdated, and the field trip is poorly linked to the lectures. You are asked to revise the course methods.

options.text: Replace the GIS module with free online videos and inform the department later.
Update the GIS software and leave the rest of the course as it is.
Cancel the field trip to free time for more classroom teaching sessions.
Gather more evidence, update the GIS module, link field trips to lectures, and pilot.

basic.situation: You want to follow developments in peatland conservation. You have limited time and many journal alerts in your inbox.

options.text: Unsubscribe from the alerts and ask colleagues to tell you of news.
Pick relevant alerts weekly, read the abstracts, and note papers to read in full.
Read the titles each month and open the ones that interest you.
Rely on social media headlines about conservation to keep up with the field.

advanced.situation: A senior colleague asks you to review a draft paper on mangrove restoration before submission. The methods are unclear, but the conclusions are striking.

options.text: Give respectful written comments on the methods, suggest specific changes, and offer to discuss.
Rewrite the methods section yourself and add your own name as a co-author.
Mention that the methods could be clearer and approve the rest of the paper.
Tell the colleague the paper is fine because the conclusions are striking.

basic.situation: You prepare a handout for a lecture on tropical timber species. Your colleague gives you a page from a book to copy as the handout.

options.text: Copy the page for the handout and cite the book at the bottom.
Hand out the copied page and tell students to buy the book later.
Copy the page and remove the book's title so the handout looks original.
Summarise the main points in your own words and cite the book.

advanced.situation: A village near a forest reserve asks for a workshop on sustainable harvesting of non-timber products. Many villagers cannot read well, and some depend on illegal harvesting.

options.text: Report the villagers who depend on illegal harvesting to the forestry officers first.
Give a lecture with slides on the harvesting laws and the penalties involved.
Hand out a written booklet and ask them to read it at home.
Co-design a visual, practical workshop with villagers and explain legal harvesting clearly.

basic.situation: You help draft the budget section of a research grant proposal on forest carbon. The lead researcher gives you rough numbers, and some items are unclear.

options.text: Copy numbers from a previous successful grant's budget and change the project title.
Ask the lead what unclear items cover, check quotes, and draft the budget.
Draft the budget from the rough numbers and mark the unclear items clearly.
Round the unclear items up generously to be safe in case of cost increases.

advanced.situation: Researchers from two departments disagree on how to design a joint study of forest fire risk, and the funding deadline is close. You are asked to lead the collaboration.

options.text: Split the study into two separate projects with little coordination between them.
Submit the proposal under your preferred design and fill in the other team's names.
Meet both teams, clarify shared aims, agree a design, and set a decision rule.
Choose the design from the larger department and inform the other team.

basic.situation: You maintain attendance and fieldwork records for a week-long forest practical. One student is absent without notice on day three.

options.text: Mark the student as present to avoid trouble for him with the department.
Record the absence, try to contact the student, and inform the lecturer in charge.
Leave the record blank and fill it in at the end of the week.
Record the absence and wait to see if the student returns the next day.

advanced.situation: You supervise a graduate student's fieldwork deep in a forest reserve. Heavy rain begins, rivers are rising, and the student wants to finish the day's sampling.

options.text: Let the student continue the sampling alone while you wait at the camp.
Allow the team one more nearby sample site and then leave the forest.
Stop the sampling, move the team to safe ground, and inform the department.
Continue sampling but stay close to the camp and watch the river level.

basic.situation: During office hours, a first-year student asks what jobs a forestry degree leads to. You have a brochure from the careers office.

options.text: Tell him forestry jobs are scarce and he should consider another degree.
Promise him a government job after graduation if his marks are good.
Give him the brochure and tell him to read it and return.
Explain common paths, ask what interests him, and point him to the careers office.

advanced.situation: You advise the student forestry club and sit on the faculty committee. The club wants a tree-felling demonstration on campus, and the committee has safety worries.

options.text: Take the club's plan to the committee, address safety, and add trained supervisors.
Approve the demonstration yourself and tell the committee after it has taken place.
Advise the club to hold a smaller demonstration using hand tools instead.
Tell the club to cancel the demonstration this year and plan one later.

basic.situation: You are grading forty meteorology lab reports before Friday. One report has accurate data, but its conclusion contradicts its own data table.

options.text: Score the conclusion by the rubric and explain the data conflict in your comments.
Give the usual deduction for the conclusion and move on to the next report.
Edit the student's conclusion to match the data yourself, then grade the report.
Award full marks because the data table is accurate and the student clearly did the work.

advanced.situation: Exam results show most of your atmospheric thermodynamics class failed the same unit. The course outline is shared with two other sections.

options.text: Drop the hardest questions from the released marks file and recalculate every student's grade.
Scale all the exam marks upward so the pass rate matches the other sections.
Review which questions failed, compare other sections' results, and revise the unit with those lecturers.
Rewrite the unit's lecture notes using your own view of what students found hard.

basic.situation: Your head of department wants your next lecture to reflect current monsoon forecasting research. A major conference is next month.

options.text: Read the most recent review article and add its main findings to your slides.
Copy a summary from an online forum and present it to the class as current research.
Reuse last year's slides and mention the new research after the conference has taken place.
Skim recent journal articles on monsoon forecasting, note what changed, and discuss it with a colleague.

advanced.situation: A physics colleague says rain gauge readings in a joint student project differ from your lab's by ten percent. Neither of you knows why.

options.text: Re-check your own lab's gauge calibration and report the result to your colleague.
Tell the students to use your lab's readings because your equipment is newer.
Average the two sets of readings and publish the result in the project report.
Propose a joint calibration check of both setups and agree the next steps together.

basic.situation: You are making a homework sheet on cloud types. The lecturer's syllabus lists four learning outcomes for that week.

options.text: Write questions that match each of the four learning outcomes and check the answers yourself.
Write ten questions from the textbook chapter on clouds and check the answers yourself.
Take questions from a paid online exam bank and hand them out as your own.
Reuse last year's homework sheet from the department folder and update the dates.

advanced.situation: You must order equipment for a new atmospheric instruments course. The budget covers either one costly sensor set or ten basic kits.

options.text: Order both and move the extra cost into next term's consumables budget line.
Order the costly sensor set because the supplier said it is more accurate.
Match the course outcomes to group size, then order the option giving every group hands-on use.
Order ten basic kits because more groups can use them at the same time.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared micrometeorology lecture while a senior colleague observes. A student says your wind profile slide looks different from the textbook.

options.text: Tell the student the slide came from your senior colleague, so it should hold up.
Delete the slide from the shared course folder so nobody questions it again.
Tell the student you will check after class and carry on with the lecture.
Compare the slide with the textbook now, thank the student, and note any fix needed.

advanced.situation: In a graduate seminar on climate policy, two students argue heatedly over whether a hurricane study supports their view, and the others go quiet.

options.text: Pause the argument and summarise both positions, then move on to the next topic.
Ask both students to cite the data behind their claims, and invite quieter voices.
Remove both students from the seminar list to protect the quieter ones in class.
Side with the student whose view matches the textbook and close the debate.

basic.situation: You supervise a student running an experiment in a weather chamber. They notice the door seal is cracked and the readout looks unstable.

options.text: Stop the student from using the chamber and put a note on the door.
Tape over the cracked seal and let the student carry on with the experiment.
Let the student finish the run and flag the seal when you next pass by.
Stop the run, tell the lab technician about the seal, and log the issue.

advanced.situation: Your faculty committee reviews a proposal to cut field trip hours from the earth science degree to save money. Several lecturers oppose it.

options.text: Ask for cost and learning outcome data from past cohorts before the committee votes.
Tell student representatives the cut is approved before the committee has voted.
Argue against the cut by describing how useful field trips were in your studies.
Vote with the chair's recommendation so the meeting finishes on schedule today.

basic.situation: At the end of term you update the attendance sheet. A student says they attended a missed day, but the register shows them absent.

options.text: Change the record to present as the student asked, to avoid an argument.
Leave the record as it is and tell the student to speak to the registrar.
Ask the student to bring a note and change the record once received.
Check the signed register and your notes, and change the record if they confirm it.

advanced.situation: A final-year student says they want to leave the earth science degree for a job in carbon trading and asks if that is wise.

options.text: Advise them to withdraw this week since the degree will not matter there.
Tell them carbon trading is risky and advise them to stay in research.
Explore their goals, link degree skills to carbon trading, and refer them to careers staff.
Encourage them to finish the degree first and then look at carbon trading jobs.

basic.situation: You are grading titration lab reports. One student's concentration is wrong because of an arithmetic slip, though the method is sound.

options.text: Deduct for the slip and give method marks, then mention the error in class.
Give full marks because the method is sound and the student will learn later.
Give method marks, deduct for the slip, and point out the error in comments.
Rework the student's calculation yourself and change the figure in their submitted report.

advanced.situation: Over three semesters, students have scored poorly on spectroscopy questions. Your coordinator asks you to revise that part of the course.

options.text: Replace the spectroscopy section with an easier topic that students already enjoy.
Compare results by question, trial a revised spectroscopy block, and measure the change.
Remove spectroscopy questions from future exams so results look better in the report.
Add two extra spectroscopy lectures to the course and ask students if they help.

basic.situation: You are preparing a handout for an organic chemistry lab on recrystallisation. The syllabus lists the experiment steps and the solvents used.

options.text: Reuse last year's handout and change the date and room before printing.
Copy the steps from the lab manual onto one page and print enough copies.
Estimate the solvent amounts from memory so the handout is ready before class.
Write the steps in order from the lab manual and add each solvent's hazards.

advanced.situation: You are drafting a grant proposal for a new mass spectrometer. The deadline is in five days and the budget section is unfinished.

options.text: List equipment the lab already owns as new purchases to make the request look stronger.
Get supplier quotes, link each cost to a research aim, and have finance check it.
Use the supplier's brochure prices and add ten percent for extras and delivery.
Round the total up to a large figure so there is room if costs change.

basic.situation: After a teaching lab, you clean the benches and glassware. One beaker holds a clear liquid and has no label.

options.text: Pour the liquid down the sink with plenty of water and wash the beaker.
Move the beaker to the fume hood, mark it unknown, and tell the technician.
Ask the last students at the bench what it holds, and note their answer.
Smell the liquid to identify it and then pour it into the nearest waste bottle.

advanced.situation: A postgraduate student wants to use a new reagent that your lab's hazardous materials rules do not yet cover. Their experiment is due tomorrow.

options.text: Ask the student to write a risk assessment and approve it yourself.
Hold the experiment until the safety officer has reviewed the reagent's data sheet.
Let the student start with small amounts while you read the data sheet.
Sign the log as approved so the student can start and meet the deadline.

basic.situation: At next week's group meeting, each member brings one recent paper on chromatography. You have two hours to prepare.

options.text: Pick a recent journal paper, read its methods and results, and prepare two questions.
Bring a news article about chromatography and present it as a recent paper.
Read the abstract and conclusion of a recent paper and bring a printed copy.
Bring a paper a colleague recommended last year and say you remember its main point.

advanced.situation: Your results on a new extraction method are ready to publish, but a student supplied the key data and is not listed as an author.

options.text: Replace the student's data with a repeat run you do yourself, then publish alone.
Thank the student in the acknowledgements section and submit the paper on schedule.
Submit the paper now and add the student's name later if a reviewer asks.
Discuss authorship with the student and your supervisor using the journal's authorship criteria before submitting.

basic.situation: You supervise undergraduates in a distillation practical. One student leaves a hot plate on and walks to the balance room.

options.text: Wait for the student to return and remind them to switch it off.
Switch off the hot plate and carry on supervising the rest of the group.
Cool the hot plate with water so the apparatus is safe to leave.
Switch off the hot plate, call the student back, and review the rules.

advanced.situation: A graduate teaching assistant you supervise has twice been late to tutorials, and students have complained to you.

options.text: Report the assistant to the dean as unreliable and remove them from the course.
Take over the assistant's tutorials for the rest of the term to protect students.
Meet the assistant privately, hear their reasons, agree a plan, and review it later.
Remind the assistant by email about tutorial start times and ask them to confirm.

basic.situation: During office hours a student asks you to explain how to balance a redox equation. Three more students are waiting outside.

options.text: Give the student the answers to the next homework set so they can check.
Spend the full time on the first student until they understand every step.
Tell the student to read the textbook chapter and come back next week.
Do one worked example, then set a practice question and help the next student.

advanced.situation: A third-year chemistry student asks whether to do a research master's degree or take a job offer in a food testing lab.

options.text: Tell them to take the job because lab experience matters more than any degree.
Discuss their goals, outline what each path offers, and suggest they speak to alumni.
Explain the benefits of a master's degree and encourage them to apply this year.
Say the job offer is probably poor and tell them to turn it down today.

basic.situation: Your department meets monthly to share new findings. You must summarise a recent paper on microplastics in rivers.

options.text: Summarise the paper from its press release, since journalists already simplified the results.
Present the paper's figures as your own results since the group will not check.
Read the full paper, note its limits, and summarise methods and findings for the group.
Read the abstract and discussion and summarise the main finding for the group.

advanced.situation: A junior colleague's river pollution study was rejected twice. They ask you to help them choose a journal and revise the paper.

options.text: Read the paper and comments, then suggest edits and let them make the journal choice.
Advise them to remove the weaker sampling sites from the data before resubmitting.
Offer to rewrite the paper yourself and add your name as lead author.
Review reviewer comments together, fix the weaknesses, and pick a fitting journal.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared lecture on hazardous waste management. Midway, a student asks about disposal rules you have not covered.

options.text: Give the rule you remember from another country's guidelines and move on.
Check the course notes quickly during the break and give the student an answer.
Invent a plausible rule on the spot so the lecture keeps its pace.
Admit you are unsure, check the course notes, and answer next session.

advanced.situation: In a toxicology seminar, a student says industrial safety rules are exaggerated, and a classmate who works at a factory disagrees angrily.

options.text: Invite both to bring incident report evidence, then let the class compare it.
Tell the classmate that workplace experience is not evidence and move to the next point.
Thank both for their views and continue with the planned slides on toxicology.
Ask both to leave the room until they calm down, then continue the seminar.

basic.situation: A student tells you in office hours that they missed the field trip sign-up deadline, and the places are already full.

options.text: Add the student's name to the final sign-up list yourself to save time.
Say the deadline is firm and suggest they join the trip next year.
Tell the student to email the coordinator and explain the missed deadline.
Ask the trip coordinator about a spare place and update the student.

advanced.situation: A final-year student says they love fieldwork, but their family wants them to take a safe office job. They ask what you think.

options.text: Advise them to accept the office job now and give up fieldwork for good.
Describe the office jobs and field jobs you know, then let them make the decision.
Ask what they want, outline both paths, and suggest talking to recent graduates.
Tell them to follow their passion for fieldwork because jobs will appear.

basic.situation: You help supervise a group sampling a stream. One student steps onto a slippery rock beside fast water to collect a sample.

options.text: Hold the student's arm to steady them while they lean out for the sample.
Call the student back to the bank, offer a long sampler, and brief the group.
Call the student back to the bank and ask them to sample from there.
Tell the student to be careful and finish the sample, then review safety later in class.

advanced.situation: You sit on a committee reviewing a new field safety policy. One draft rule would ban all river sampling by students in the wet season.

options.text: Oppose the ban and say wet-season sampling is essential for every course.
Tell students privately that field sampling will continue whatever the committee decides in the end.
Support the ban because student safety matters and rules are simple to enforce.
Ask for incident data and propose limits with trained supervisors, not a full ban.

basic.situation: You grade water-quality lab reports with the rubric. Two students' reports show the same unusual error in one calculation.

options.text: Tell the two students they copied each other and report them for plagiarism.
Apply the rubric to both reports and add a comment on the error.
Give both students full marks because two students making it suggests it is a minor issue.
Check if the handout caused the error, apply the rubric, and tell the course lead.

advanced.situation: A former student asks you for a scholarship recommendation letter. Their grades were average, but they led a strong river clean-up project.

options.text: Decline politely and suggest they ask a lecturer who knows their grades better.
Write that the student ranked top of the class so the application stands out.
Write a short letter that praises the project and leaves out the student's average grades.
Describe the clean-up project and skills you observed, and keep claims to what you saw.

basic.situation: You are asked to prepare next semester's ecology lab syllabus. The coordinator gave you last year's version and the new calendar.

options.text: Update the dates, check topics against the outline, and send the draft to the coordinator.
Add new topics you find interesting and drop last year's assessment section.
Post the draft online to students before the coordinator has seen it.
Update the dates from the new calendar and print copies for the first week.

advanced.situation: Your department can apply for a wetland restoration research grant due in three weeks. Three colleagues could join the proposal.

options.text: Write the whole proposal yourself and send it to the colleagues for comments.
List the three colleagues as team members before they agree, to strengthen the application.
Reuse a funded proposal from another topic and adjust the title and the budget.
Meet the colleagues, agree roles and a timeline, then draft the proposal against the agency's criteria.

basic.situation: You deliver a standard optics lecture while a senior colleague observes. Halfway through, you notice the lens formula on your slide has a sign error.

options.text: Finish the lecture and then email students an updated slide with the sign fixed.
Pause, point out the sign error, and fix the formula on the board.
Adjust the numbers in the worked example so the final answer matches the old sign.
Leave the slide as it is, because the colleague observing did not mention it.

advanced.situation: In your graduate particle physics seminar, a student challenges a published result and others begin to side with them. You are unsure the challenge is sound.

options.text: Email the department that the student is spreading false claims about a published paper.
Ask the student to lay out the reasoning and test it against the paper together.
Back the student strongly to encourage questioning, and tell the class the paper is flawed.
Say the published result is peer reviewed and suggest the student write to the authors.

basic.situation: You assist in a first-year optics lab under direct instruction. A student points a laser at eye level while adjusting a mirror.

options.text: Tell the student to wear goggles on the bench next time they adjust the mirror.
Switch the laser off at the wall and let the student restart the setup.
Move the student's head aside with your hand while they finish aligning the mirror.
Ask the student to switch the laser off and lower the beam, then explain why.

advanced.situation: A graduate student you guide has finished an experiment with a single measurement run per setting, and the results look noisy.

options.text: Ask how they would estimate uncertainty, then plan repeat runs and report the spread.
Choose the cleanest-looking run for each setting and report those as the results.
Suggest they repeat the noisiest settings and report the average of those runs.
Tell them to smooth the data with a trend line and report that in the draft.

basic.situation: You grade mechanics homework with the answer key. One answer matches the key's final number, but the student's working is missing.

options.text: Mark the answer as copied and report the student for an academic offence.
Give full marks because the final number matches the answer key exactly, as expected.
Give the answer marks and move on, as the key lists the final numbers.
Follow the rubric, give answer marks, deduct for missing working, and comment.

advanced.situation: You must design the final exam for a large modern physics course, and past papers suggest too many questions test only recall.

options.text: Add several harder problem questions to the old paper and keep the same marking scheme.
Ask a colleague for last year's questions and copy a selection into your paper.
Map questions to learning outcomes and mix recall, application, and reasoning tasks.
Reuse the paper from two years ago since the department already approved it.

basic.situation: You help choose a textbook for first-year mechanics. Your supervisor gives you three options and a budget per student.

options.text: Order a class set of the book you prefer from the budget before asking.
Pick the cheapest of the three and tell your supervisor it fits the budget.
Pick the book whose author you know and tell your supervisor it is popular.
Compare coverage, price, and library copies, then recommend one to your supervisor.

advanced.situation: The physics department wants to revise its first-year curriculum after a drop in pass rates. Senior staff disagree about adding more maths support.

options.text: Analyse results by topic and background, then pilot a change in one tutorial group.
Add maths support sessions for all first-year students from next term, as proposed.
Remove the hardest topics from the first-year syllabus so pass rates recover quickly.
Lower the pass mark for first-year physics in the department rules, to fix the numbers.

basic.situation: You attend your first physics conference with a mentor. One talk presents results that seem to conflict with what you teach.

options.text: Update your lecture notes to match the talk before you check the paper.
Take notes on the claim and look it up in the literature after the conference.
Note the claim and method, then ask your mentor and the speaker about it.
Tell your students the textbook is out of date and the speaker is right.

advanced.situation: You lead a small project measuring cosmic muon rates. Your co-author thinks one result in the draft paper is a detector artefact, but you disagree.

options.text: Run a shielded control, share the data with your co-author, and agree the wording.
Rerun the analysis with artefact cuts yourself and send the result to the co-author.
Publish your interpretation and add a line saying a co-author sees it differently.
Submit the paper under your name alone and let your co-author find out later.

basic.situation: You enter grades for a physics tutorial group. You notice one grade you typed last week went to the wrong student.

options.text: Swap the two grades in the system today and mention it to the coordinator later.
Tell the coordinator, fix the entry by the change procedure, and tell both students.
Leave the entry and clear your tutorial notes so the records stay consistent.
Wait until the end of term and fix it when the final grades are entered.

advanced.situation: As the department's committee representative, you hear a proposal to let students skip the physics lab requirement if they have work experience.

options.text: Support the proposal in principle because many of our students have useful work experience.
Oppose the proposal in the meeting because lab skills must be taught in a lab.
Ask how lab learning outcomes would be met and gather department views first.
Promise students in your tutorials the lab requirement will be waived before the committee decides.

basic.situation: You help a senior researcher collect field data at an excavation. A student labels a pottery find with the wrong layer number.

options.text: Throw away the find's bag and write a new tag with the layer you assume.
Leave the label for now and sort out layer numbers when cataloguing begins.
Tell the supervisor, check the context sheet with the student, and fix the label.
Fix the label from memory of the layer and remind the student to take care.

advanced.situation: You plan interviews in a rural community for an ethnographic study. A community elder asks that recordings not be shared outside the village.

options.text: Accept the request verbally and promise the elder you will remember it when writing up.
Record the interviews as planned and share clips later if the elder does not hear.
Write the elder's limits into the consent form and get ethics approval.
Explain that funders require shared data and ask the elder to relax the request.

basic.situation: You prepare handouts for an urban anthropology lecture. A senior colleague gave you one article and a reading list.

options.text: Summarise the article, list the readings, and ask your colleague to review.
Copy the article's abstract and the reading list onto a single handout page.
Paste long extracts from the article into the handout to save students' time.
Add quotes from an online post you found, and list your colleague as the source.

advanced.situation: You lead the department's curriculum review. Feedback says the research methods course is too theoretical, but two professors want to keep it as it is.

options.text: Replace the theory lectures with practical sessions as the feedback asks, starting next term.
Add a fieldwork assignment to the course and keep every existing lecture in place.
Approve the new course outline yourself and send it to the registrar this week.
Review learning outcomes with both groups and trial a practical module first.

basic.situation: You record attendance for a field methods class. A student asks you to mark them present for a session they missed because of a clinic visit.

options.text: Mark them present and add their signature to the sign-in sheet to match the register.
Mark them present this once, and note it in your own diary for the coordinator.
Mark them absent and explain how to submit a medical note for the session.
Mark them absent and tell them the rule is strict, with no exceptions.

advanced.situation: You design a final exam for a large anthropology course. Last year's exam had inconsistent marking across the five tutors who graded it.

options.text: Change the marks recorded for scripts you suspect were marked harshly, then tell tutors later.
Switch the whole exam to multiple-choice questions so tutors cannot mark differently.
Give each tutor the same written guide and ask them to follow it closely.
Write a marking guide with sample answers and hold a calibration session for tutors.

basic.situation: A student arrives at office hours confused about the difference between emic and etic approaches. Your lecturer is away this week.

options.text: Say the difference will not be examined and suggest the student skip it.
Read out the textbook definitions of both terms and ask if that helps.
Explain both using a course reading example and ask the student to try one.
Tell the student to wait until the lecturer returns next week to ask.

advanced.situation: You advise the anthropology student society planning a cultural exhibition. Members disagree about displaying sacred items from a local community.

options.text: Suggest they consult community representatives first and help them draft a display plan.
Advise them to display photographs of the items instead and add a short explanation.
Tell them to borrow the items from the community this week to settle the debate.
Let the members vote on it and accept whatever majority decision they reach.

basic.situation: You help format a colleague's conference paper. The reference list mixes two citation styles and some page numbers are missing.

options.text: Convert the references to the required style and leave the missing page numbers blank.
Delete the references with missing page numbers so the list looks complete.
Add page numbers that seem likely for the missing ones so the list looks complete.
Convert references to the required style and list missing details for the author.

advanced.situation: You lead a grant application on heritage conservation. A reviewer on a previous round said your budget justification was weak.

options.text: Link every budget line to a project activity and have a colleague review it.
Add a longer narrative to the budget section explaining why costs are reasonable.
Contact the previous reviewer directly and ask them to support the new application.
Cut the budget by twenty percent across all lines so reviewers see modest costs.

basic.situation: You help organise a small campus open day for the anthropology programme. The room booking confirmation has not yet arrived.

options.text: Print the posters with the planned room and wait for the confirmation email.
Move the event to an empty classroom you saw on the timetable that morning.
Call the booking office to confirm the room, then update the poster.
Tell the invited visitors the booking is confirmed so they can plan their trip.

advanced.situation: You chair the hiring panel for a new lecturer. A strong candidate is your close friend, and the other panel members do not know.

options.text: Give the friend the interview questions beforehand since they deserve a fair chance.
Tell the panel about the friendship but stay in the room to score fairly.
Declare the friendship to the panel and the department head, and step back from scoring.
Score the candidate strictly by the criteria and keep the friendship to yourself.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared lecture on race and ethnic relations while a senior colleague observes. A student asks if you personally agree with a controversial theory you just described.

options.text: Give your personal opinion at length, since the students asked and want honesty.
Say your personal view is not relevant and move straight on to the next slide.
Present the evidence and critics of the theory and keep to course material.
Call the student's question disrespectful and tell the class to focus on the slides.

advanced.situation: In a seminar on cross-cultural perspectives, a student makes a stereotyped remark about a minority group present in the room. Several students look uncomfortable.

options.text: Ask the student to apologise publicly to the minority students in the room right now.
Let the remark pass and ask the group a general question about respect later.
Tell the student the remark is inappropriate and move on to the next reading.
Address the remark calmly, ask for evidence, and guide the group to examine stereotypes.

basic.situation: A student in your office hours is unsure whether they must take the area studies methods course this semester. You are not sure either.

options.text: Tell the student the course is optional and they can drop it from the timetable.
Check the handbook with the student and confirm with the programme coordinator.
Say it is usually taken in year two and tell them to check the handbook.
Advise the student to skip the course this semester and take it when convenient.

advanced.situation: You advise a student society planning a cultural festival. Two member groups argue over who should lead the opening ceremony, and the date is close.

options.text: Choose the group that you think is more experienced and inform the other group.
Cancel the opening ceremony from the festival programme and publish the revised schedule.
Meet both groups, agree criteria for roles, and propose a shared opening.
Ask the society president to decide the leader and tell both groups to accept it.

basic.situation: You are asked to choose a textbook for an introductory Southeast Asian studies course. Your supervisor must approve the final choice.

options.text: Choose the book you used as a student and tell the bookshop to stock it.
Order a class set of an old edition from a second-hand seller before approval.
Shortlist two books that cover the syllabus and let your supervisor choose.
Choose the book with the top online ratings and send the title to your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You are adding a site visit to a course on cultural heritage. The visit is to a living community temple, and the class has forty students.

options.text: Book a coach for the whole class and send the temple a notification letter.
Arrange the visit with a tour company and let them handle contact with the temple.
Ask temple leaders for permission, agree group sizes, and brief the students.
Take all forty students into the temple at once and photograph the ceremony for coursework.

basic.situation: You submit attendance and grades for an area studies course using the department template. You notice two rows have the same student ID.

options.text: Change one of the repeated IDs to an unused number so the template accepts it.
Delete the second row with the repeated ID and submit the sheet on time.
Check the enrolment list for the duplicate, fix the template, and tell the office.
Submit the sheet as it is and let the department office sort out duplicates.

advanced.situation: You design the final exam for a course that two other lecturers will also grade. In past years, the three of you gave very different marks for similar essays.

options.text: Change the exam to a single essay so there is less to compare between markers.
Write a shared rubric and have all three of you mark sample essays together.
Ask the other lecturers to send you their marks and adjust them to match yours.
Write a detailed rubric yourself and email it to the other two lecturers.

basic.situation: A colleague asks you to summarise a recent article on diaspora communities for a reading group. You have not read in this field before.

options.text: Read the article, note its main sources, and write a short summary.
Quote passages from a blog review and attribute them to the article's author.
Ask a colleague who knows the field to give you a summary to present.
Read the abstract and conclusion and write a short summary of the main argument.

advanced.situation: You are writing a grant proposal on migrant labour histories. The funder limits applications to ten pages, and your draft is fourteen.

options.text: Cut background text, keep research questions and budget, and have a colleague read it.
Submit the fourteen-page draft anyway and hope the funder accepts the extra pages.
Cut the methods section to a paragraph so the proposal fits within ten pages.
Cut the background section and the literature review until the draft fits ten pages.

basic.situation: You help staff the registration desk for new students in the area studies programme. A student says they cannot find their name on the list.

options.text: Enrol the student in the records system yourself and issue them a temporary card.
Ask for their ID, check the list and office records, and explain what you find.
Tell the student to email the programme office and come back when they reply.
Tell the student the list is probably incomplete and they can join orientation.

advanced.situation: As acting head of department, you learn a lecturer is late returning marks for three modules. Students are waiting close to the appeals deadline.

options.text: Meet the lecturer, agree a return date before appeals close, and inform students.
Release marks from the lecturer's draft spreadsheet you found so students can see results.
Email the lecturer a firm reminder and wait for the marks to arrive.
Hand the scripts to another lecturer this week and tell the lecturer afterwards.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared lecture on basic supply and demand. A student points out that the axes on your graph are swapped.

options.text: Tell the student that the axes were set by the department and cannot change.
Explain that both layouts are used in some textbooks and keep going.
Check the graph, thank the student, and redraw the axes on the board.
Say you will check the slides after class and carry on with the lecture.

advanced.situation: In a graduate price theory seminar, two students disagree sharply about whether minimum wage laws raise unemployment, and each cites different studies.

options.text: Tell the class that economists agree on this and ask the students to stop debating.
Side with the student whose study is more recent and close the discussion.
Summarise both positions on the board and then move on to the next topic.
Ask each to explain their study's data and method, then compare the evidence.

basic.situation: You grade a first-year economics essay. The argument is clear, but there is no reference list, and the rubric awards ten percent for sources.

options.text: Deduct the source marks and return the essay with the other marks as they are.
Give full marks for sources because the argument shows good understanding of the topic.
Deduct the source marks by the rubric and comment on how to cite.
Find a few sources online and add them to the student's essay before grading.

advanced.situation: Your introductory economics course has a high fail rate in the statistics section. You have exam data and student surveys from the past two years.

options.text: Link failed questions to survey comments and redesign that section with a colleague.
Redesign the statistics section based on what students wrote in the surveys this year.
Lower the difficulty of the statistics questions on the exam until the fail rate drops.
Remove the failing students' statistics scores from the records and recompute class averages.

basic.situation: You attend an economics conference with your supervisor. You have two free hours between sessions and a list of talks.

options.text: Rest in the hotel room and read the conference abstracts online later.
Attend a talk on your teaching topic, note key points, and ask a question.
Leave the conference early and tell your supervisor you attended every planned talk.
Use the break to talk with colleagues from other universities about their courses.

advanced.situation: You lead a research project on household savings with two junior colleagues. The new data contradicts a result in your earlier published work.

options.text: Delay the paper until a future dataset appears that fits your earlier work.
Re-run the analysis yourself and send the new results to your junior colleagues.
Drop the survey years that conflict with your earlier work and publish what remains.
Check the data and method with your team, then report the finding and its limits.

basic.situation: You help staff a recruitment fair booth for the economics department. A parent asks about scholarships and you are not certain of the details.

options.text: Say you are unsure, note their contact details, and ask admissions to reply.
Promise the parent a scholarship place for their child if the application is strong.
Give the parent the scholarship rules you remember from last year's printed brochure.
Tell the parent to look on the university website or visit the office again.

advanced.situation: You sit on a committee deciding whether to raise the minimum grade for entry into advanced economics. The change would affect forty current students.

options.text: Ask for performance data, consult affected students, and propose a phase-in.
Tell the forty students privately that the new grade will apply to them.
Vote against the change to protect the forty students already on the pathway.
Support raising the entry grade because higher standards will improve the course reputation.

basic.situation: You prepare a homework set on inflation for first-year students. The lecturer gave you three learning outcomes and a data table.

options.text: Reuse a set from another university's online course and replace the university name.
Write questions that match the outcomes, use the table, and solve them yourself.
Write questions from the textbook chapter and send them to the lecturer to check.
Use questions from the upcoming exam paper as homework so students learn the style.

advanced.situation: You are writing a grant proposal for a study on rural microcredit. The funder asks for a data sharing plan, but your survey includes personal financial details.

options.text: Describe how data is anonymised, how consent works, and who can access it.
Say data cannot be shared because it is personal and offer a summary report.
Say all personal details are removed from the survey data, to meet the funder's rule.
Promise to share the full dataset openly on the project website because funders prefer it.

basic.situation: A student visits your office hours asking how to prepare for the macroeconomics midterm. You have fifteen minutes before a lecture.

options.text: Tell the student which topics and questions appear on the draft midterm paper.
Share the key topics and past questions and suggest a short study plan.
Say the midterm covers everything and suggest the student read the whole textbook.
Tell the student to review all lecture slides and come back with questions.

advanced.situation: A final-year economics student asks whether to apply for a policy job or a PhD. They are anxious and unsure of their strengths.

options.text: Describe your own career path in detail and what you found useful about it.
Tell the student to take the policy job because most PhD students end up quitting.
Explore what they enjoy, outline both paths, and refer them to the careers service.
Suggest the PhD because it keeps more doors open and the student is bright.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared lecture on urbanization from a provided script. A student asks for a population figure for a city that is not in your script.

options.text: Estimate a figure from the city's size and tell the student it is approximate.
Say you will check the official census data and share the figure next class.
Give the figure from a news article you read last week and carry on teaching.
State a precise figure with confidence to avoid looking unprepared in front of the class.

advanced.situation: Your seminar discusses a planned dam that would flood farmland and displace villagers. Some students support it for energy and others strongly oppose it.

options.text: Let students argue freely until time is up and then summarise the main views.
Ask groups to map who gains and loses, then test each side's claims.
Ask the students from affected villages to speak for the opposition on behalf of everyone.
Share your own view of the dam first to give the discussion a starting point.

basic.situation: You grade geography map assignments with a rubric. One student's map is excellent but is missing the required scale bar.

options.text: Deduct the scale bar marks by the rubric and explain how to add one.
Deduct the scale bar marks and return the map with the final grade shown.
Give full marks because the map is excellent and the missing bar is minor.
Draw a scale bar onto the student's map yourself and grade it as submitted.

advanced.situation: Your department's GIS course has had falling student marks for two years. Exit surveys say labs feel rushed, and exams show weak spatial analysis skills.

options.text: Add an extra hour to each lab session starting next week for all students.
Raise all student marks by ten percent in the system so the trend appears stable.
Match survey comments to exam results, then redesign the labs and test them.
Remove the spatial analysis topics that students find hardest from the course outline.

basic.situation: You run a buffer analysis in GIS software, following a step-by-step guide. The output layer looks much larger than expected.

options.text: Send the output layer to your supervisor and ask whether it looks acceptable.
Reduce the buffer layer by hand-editing its boundary until it looks about right.
Check the distance units and input layer, then rerun the buffer tool.
Use the output as it is, since the software did what the guide said.

advanced.situation: A student's GIS project combines flood maps with population data, but the two layers use different coordinate systems. The results will go into a council report.

options.text: Reproject the population layer to match the flood layer and run the analysis.
Let the software align the layers on the fly and use the overlay results.
Shift the population layer by hand until the boundaries line up on the map view.
Reproject both layers to one system, record the steps, and check known locations.

basic.situation: You are asked to keep up with new research on urban heat islands, but you have limited time each week.

options.text: Read one recent paper each week and note how it links to your lectures.
Read the headlines of a research newsletter each week and save articles for later.
Add statements from a social media post to your lecture slides as established facts.
Rely on social media posts from well-known scientists to learn about new findings.

advanced.situation: You lead a collaboration with a sociology colleague on a housing study. Your data is spatial and theirs is interviews, and your first meeting ended with no plan.

options.text: Analyse your spatial data first and send your colleague the results to build on.
Wait for your colleague to propose a plan since they raised the idea.
Agree a shared question, each person's role, and regular check-ins in writing.
Start writing the paper using both datasets and add your colleague as co-author later.

basic.situation: You supervise a student doing a soil analysis in the lab with a detailed checklist. They skip a step that requires wearing gloves.

options.text: Let them finish the sample and mention the gloves at the end of the session.
Tell them gloves are optional for soil work and drop the step from the checklist.
Stop the work, ask them to put on gloves, and review the checklist together.
Pass them gloves and tell them to wear them from the next sample onward.

advanced.situation: You oversee six student research projects for a geography course. One group has collected interview data from residents without signing the ethics consent forms.

options.text: Let the group use the data this term and fix the paperwork next term.
Date the consent forms yourself and sign them as witness so the files look complete.
Pause use of the data, tell the ethics office, and plan how to get consent.
Ask the group to get signed forms from residents now and then carry on.

basic.situation: You update attendance for a geography class. Eight students were on a university-approved field trip and show as absent on the system.

options.text: Mark them present for the day, since they were away on university business all day.
Leave them as absent and tell the eight students to explain to the office.
Mark them as excused using the approved trip list and add the trip reference.
Delete the attendance column for that day so no student appears absent in the records.

advanced.situation: You chair a committee setting standards for student advising and recruitment. Staff disagree about whether to cap recruitment to protect advising quality.

options.text: Collect advising workload and satisfaction data, then draft options for staff to review.
Propose a cap based on what the advisers said at the next committee meeting.
Reject the cap because recruitment targets are set by the dean's office anyway.
Announce a recruitment cap to the public before the committee has approved it.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared lecture on classical political thought. A student asks whether Plato would have supported modern democracy, and you are unsure.

options.text: Say Plato opposed democracy in general and move on to Aristotle as planned.
Explain Plato's critique of democracy from the text and ask the class to compare.
Give a confident yes, because many modern thinkers praise Plato's political ideas today.
Say the question is off topic and ask the student to stop interrupting lectures.

advanced.situation: In a seminar on international relations, two students from opposing nations argue emotionally about a border dispute, and others avoid eye contact.

options.text: Pause the discussion and ask the two students to speak with you after class.
Restate ground rules, ask for sources on both sides, and invite others in.
Ask the class to vote on which student's account of the dispute seems stronger.
Tell both students that their emotional arguments reflect poorly on their home countries.

basic.situation: You prepare a handout for a lecture on electoral systems. The lecturer wants a one-page comparison of first-past-the-post and proportional representation.

options.text: Draft a comparison table with one example for each and send it for review.
Paste a comparison from a news website into the handout under your colleague's name.
Write the comparison from memory and print it before the lecture starts today.
Copy the comparison section from the textbook chapter onto a single page handout.

advanced.situation: Your department wants a revised comparative politics course. Students say it focuses too much on Western systems, but two lecturers are against changes.

options.text: Add one extra week on non-Western systems at the end of the course outline.
Approve the revised outline yourself and tell the two lecturers to follow it.
Replace the Western case studies with non-Western ones across all units this term.
Audit the syllabus against outcomes, draft wider readings, and consult both lecturers.

basic.situation: You record grades for a political science tutorial group. You notice one student's participation mark is missing from the spreadsheet.

options.text: Ask the student what mark they received and enter the number they tell you.
Enter a high mark for the student to avoid any complaint from them later.
Find the mark in your tutorial notes, enter it, and tell the lecturer.
Enter the class average for the missing mark so the total looks complete.

advanced.situation: You must set a final exam for a course taught across three campuses. Past exams gave very different average marks on each campus.

options.text: Let each campus set its own exam so the questions suit their students.
Scale each campus's marks up or down so every campus has the same average.
Use one shared exam blueprint and rubric, then compare marking samples across campuses.
Write one exam for all three campuses and let each campus mark its own.

basic.situation: A student at your office hours asks whether late assignments are accepted. The syllabus deducts ten percent per day, and the lecturer is away.

options.text: Say late work is usually accepted if the student gives a good reason.
Promise the student no penalty and tell them you will arrange it with the lecturer.
Tell the student to ask the lecturer, who is away, when they return.
Show the syllabus late-penalty rule and offer to pass on any request.

advanced.situation: You advise a student political society that wants to invite a controversial speaker. Members expect protest, and university policy requires prior notice.

options.text: Tell the society to notify the university and let them handle the protest.
Advise the society to cancel the invitation because protests would be a risk.
Check the university policy, notify the right office, and agree a safety plan.
Suggest announcing the event late so that protesters have little time to organise.

basic.situation: You read a new article on voter turnout and discuss it with a colleague. They argue the data shows the opposite of what you read.

options.text: Read the article again by yourself and email your colleague your final conclusion.
Tell the reading group that the article's data was misreported by its authors.
Accept your colleague's reading, since they have taught the topic for much longer.
Reread the article's data and methods together, then note where your readings differ.

advanced.situation: You lead a small research team on campaign finance. A junior researcher finds a data point that does not fit your hypothesis, one week before submission.

options.text: Delay submission by a month to collect more data that might fit your hypothesis.
Remove the data point and tell the junior researcher it was a typing mistake.
