Check whether it is a data error, then report it and explain its effect.
Rerun the analysis both with the data point included and left out, then pick one.

basic.situation: You help with registration for new political science students. A student asks to change from the evening group to the morning group, which is nearly full.

options.text: Remove another student from the morning list to make space for the request.
Tell the student the morning group is nearly full and suggest they stay evening.
Check the morning group's capacity and pass the request to the office.
Move the student's name to the morning list and tell the office later.

advanced.situation: As department head, you must set next year's teaching loads. Two senior staff ask for reduced loads for research, which would raise loads for junior staff.

options.text: Grant one senior staff member's request and keep the other's load unchanged this year.
Compare loads and outputs, consult all staff, and set a clear allocation rule.
Announce loads that favour senior staff by email and treat the matter as closed.
Keep last year's loads unchanged to avoid any argument among the staff this year.

basic.situation: You grade first-year psychology lab reports with a rubric. One report has very good analysis but copies a paragraph from the textbook word for word.

options.text: Grade by the rubric and report the copied text to the module leader.
Rewrite the copied paragraph in your own words to protect the student's grade.
Deduct marks for the copied paragraph and write a comment about citing sources.
Give full marks because the analysis is strong and the copied part is short.

advanced.situation: You design a new assessment for a research methods course. Students report on a survey they design, and you worry some may fabricate the data.

options.text: Require students to submit their survey questions to you for approval before collecting data.
Require raw data files and a short viva on how the survey was run.
Tell students you will fail any report with suspicious results, whatever the data shows.
Switch to a written exam so that no data can be fabricated by anyone.

basic.situation: You prepare a handout for a lecture on memory. The lecturer wants a short summary of three key experiments and their findings.

options.text: Summarise each experiment's method and main finding, citing the textbook pages used.
Write findings you think were reported, since you remember the studies fairly well.
List the three experiment names and the main finding of each in one line.
Use a memory infographic from a website and add your own title at the top.

advanced.situation: Your department wants to add online learning to the abnormal psychology course. Past feedback shows low student engagement with recorded lectures.

options.text: Delete the in-person lecture slots from the timetable before the department has agreed.
Record all the lectures again with better video quality and upload them soon.
Pilot short interactive online units with one class and compare engagement and marks.
Move the whole course online next term because students already use their phones.

basic.situation: A colleague asks you to help with a literature search and survey data entry for a psychology study. You are new to the topic.

options.text: Ask for the search terms and inclusion rules, then log each paper you read.
Search a few keywords you choose and send your colleague the first results.
Fill in skipped survey answers yourself using what similar participants usually said.
Tell your colleague you need a month to learn the topic before starting.

advanced.situation: You lead a grant application for a study of adolescent anxiety. The funder requires a participant protection plan, and you plan to recruit through schools you have not yet approached.

options.text: Say school principals have agreed to the study, to show the funder it is feasible.
Describe ethics approval, parental consent, and a referral route for distressed participants.
Promise confidentiality for all participants in every circumstance, as funders like clear guarantees.
State that the university ethics committee will review the study before any recruitment.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared lecture on cognitive processes with senior staff support. Halfway through, you realise you misdescribed a key experiment's result.

options.text: Mention the mistake at the end of the lecture and email the updated slide.
Pause, tell the class, state the accurate result, and update the slide later.
Continue the lecture and fix the slide before you share the notes later.
Insist the result was as you described it and move on if students ask again.

advanced.situation: In a discussion on work motivation, a student shares a painful experience of burnout, and another student dismisses it as laziness.

options.text: Tell the dismissive student to apologise and then continue with the planned content.
Ask the first student to explain exactly what caused their burnout to the whole class.
Thank the sharer, restate respect norms, and link the experience to theory.
Move on quickly to the next theory so nobody dwells on personal stories.

basic.situation: In office hours, a student says they feel overwhelmed and are thinking of dropping psychology. You have only ten minutes.

options.text: Listen, ask what is causing the pressure, and point them to counselling.
Offer to drop their hardest assignment so they feel more comfortable in the course.
Encourage them to push through because most students feel this way at some point.
Tell them to talk to their academic adviser about their course load this week.

advanced.situation: A student tells you they want to become a clinical psychologist but have low grades in statistics, which the programme requires.

options.text: Suggest they switch to an easier psychology specialism that needs less statistics.
Tell them clinical psychology is too competitive for anyone with grades like theirs.
Tell them to retake the statistics module and apply for clinical training next year.
Outline the entry requirements, plan statistics support, and suggest related roles to explore.

basic.situation: You maintain attendance for a psychology tutorial. A student asks you to remove a late mark from last week because their bus broke down.

options.text: Change last week's register and the sign-in sheet to show the student arrived on time.
Keep the late mark and tell the student that lateness is recorded for everyone.
Ask for proof of the breakdown and apply the department's lateness rule.
Remove the mark because bus breakdowns happen and the student seems honest to you.

advanced.situation: As department head, you learn a student has complained about unfair marking by a lecturer, who says the complaint is a grudge.

options.text: Have a second marker review the scripts and hear both sides in writing.
Change the student's mark in the system yourself to avoid a long formal process.
Ask the lecturer to explain the marking to the student at a face-to-face meeting.
Dismiss the complaint because the lecturer has taught the course for many years.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared sociology lecture on race and ethnic relations using your supervisor's slides. A student says one statistic on a slide seems outdated.

options.text: Say the slides come from your supervisor and the figure is probably fine.
Thank the student, note the source year, and check for a newer figure.
Tell the student to find a newer figure and bring it to the next class.
Change the date on the slide to this year so the figure looks current.

advanced.situation: In a seminar on ethnic discrimination in hiring, one student says it does not exist in Malaysia, and others react strongly.

options.text: Mark the student down for participation and move on to the next question.
Tell the student the claim is offensive and ask them to leave the discussion.
Ask for evidence, bring in published studies, and let the class compare them.
Say the claim is disputed and ask students to read about it for next week.

basic.situation: You grade sociology essays with a rubric. One essay has a strong argument but quotes sources without the page numbers the guideline requires.

options.text: Deduct the citation marks and return the essay with a short general comment on style.
Deduct citation marks by the rubric and show how to add page numbers.
Add page numbers to the essay yourself after checking the sources, then grade it.
Give full marks because the argument is strong and page numbers are a detail.

advanced.situation: You revise the exam process for a large sociology course. Two exams last year had marking errors that students found themselves.

options.text: Ask all markers to check their own totals twice before they submit marks to you.
Close the mark query route and release marks as final once the exam is over.
Let students mark each other's papers so that errors are spotted more quickly.
Add double-marking of a sample, a clear mark scheme, and a mark-query route.

basic.situation: You prepare a syllabus draft for an introductory sociology course. The coordinator gave you the topics and the assessment dates.

options.text: Add extra assessment tasks you think are useful and set your own due dates.
Fill in topics and dates and hand the syllabus to students at the first class.
Copy last year's syllabus from another lecturer and keep the grading rules as they were.
Enter the topics, dates, and readings, then send the draft to the coordinator.

advanced.situation: You lead a revision of the sociology curriculum across two departments. They use different reading lists and assessment standards for similar courses.

options.text: Cancel the courses that overlap and move their students into one course next term.
Compare outcomes, hold joint workshops with both departments, and agree standards first.
Write the new curriculum yourself and circulate it for comments after sign-off.
Adopt one department's reading list for both courses and keep separate assessments.

basic.situation: You assist a professor with a sociology survey on student housing. You are asked to enter responses from paper forms into a spreadsheet.

options.text: Enter the answer you think the respondent meant whenever the handwriting is unclear.
Enter responses as written, flag unclear answers, and re-check a sample.
Fill in blank responses with the most common answer so the data looks complete.
Enter the responses as written and leave unclear answers blank in the sheet.

advanced.situation: You write a grant proposal on workplace discrimination. The funder's reviewers value a clear impact plan, but your research is at an early stage.

options.text: Claim that the findings will shape national policy within the first year of the grant.
Describe the full potential impact in detail and mention risks briefly at the end.
Copy the impact section from a funded proposal in a different field and adjust it.
Describe realistic outputs, a staged sharing plan, and the study's early-stage limits.

basic.situation: During office hours, a student asks how to improve their sociology essay marks. They show you a returned essay with comments.

options.text: Tell the student to read more journal articles and to write more drafts early.
Offer to raise the student's essay mark if they agree to take the next module.
Go through the comments together and set two goals for the next essay.
Suggest the student ask a classmate with higher marks to share their essays.

advanced.situation: A new lecturer you are mentoring says they are overwhelmed by marking and research and are thinking of leaving the university.

options.text: Share how you coped with your own first year and suggest they be patient.
Help them rank priorities and introduce them to workload support and a peer.
Suggest they give all students the same pass mark this term to reduce marking.
Suggest they drop research for a year and focus on teaching and marking.

basic.situation: You maintain attendance for a sociology lecture. The sign-in sheet shows one student's name signed twice in different handwriting.

options.text: Note the discrepancy, ask the lecturer how to handle it, and record as advised.
Cross out one of the signatures in pen and record the student as present anyway.
Record the student as present once and keep the original sheet in the course file.
Record the student as absent because the sheet cannot be trusted for that name.

advanced.situation: You chair a departmental committee drafting a policy on student supervision. Some staff want a strict meeting schedule, others say research needs flexibility.

options.text: Present the strict schedule to the dean as the committee's agreed policy now.
Leave the policy vague so each supervisor can decide how to meet their students.
Review outcome data, draft a minimum standard with flexibility, and consult staff.
Adopt the strict schedule because clear rules are easier to enforce and explain.

basic.situation: You draft a syllabus and pick a textbook for a first aid course with guidance. Your senior colleague gave you the learning outcomes.

options.text: Order a class set of a book from your preferred publisher before the colleague approves.
Compare candidate books against the outcomes and send your colleague a short note.
Pick the textbook your own teacher used years ago and add it to the syllabus.
Pick the textbook with the most chapters and tell your colleague it covers everything.

advanced.situation: Your department sees many students failing the practical component of a clinical skills course. You must revise the curriculum for next year.

options.text: Remove the practical component from the course and assess students by written test.
Review practical results and feedback, then pilot extra supervised practice sessions.
Make the practical assessment easier so that more students pass in the first attempt.
Add more lecture hours on the practical skills and keep the assessment unchanged.

basic.situation: You grade written assignments for a public health course under a lead instructor. One assignment arrived two days late with no explanation.

options.text: Grade the assignment as normal and mention the lateness in a brief comment.
Change the submission date in the system so it shows the work arrived on time.
Apply the late policy from the syllabus and tell the student the penalty.
Give the assignment zero because it missed the deadline and the student gave no reason.

advanced.situation: You design an assessment for clinical decision-making in a medical course, and you must guide two junior staff on grading standards.

options.text: Write down your own grading standards and email them to both junior staff members.
Let each junior staff member grade using their own judgement and compare totals.
Tell the junior staff to give high marks so that students stay motivated.
Create a clear rubric and run a joint grading session on sample answers.

basic.situation: You lead a short class discussion on infection control from a prepared question list. Only two students are speaking while the rest stay silent.

options.text: Thank the two active students and carry on using their answers to teach.
Tell the class that their silence will affect their participation marks this week.
Have pairs discuss first, then invite each pair to share one point.
Call on silent students by name and require an answer from each of them.

advanced.situation: A new faculty member you mentor says their discussions keep drifting into personal clinical stories and students stop learning the theory.

options.text: Tell them stories are how students learn in health fields, so the drift is fine.
Suggest they stop all personal stories in class and keep to the planned slides.
Observe a class, then agree on prompts that link stories to the learning outcomes.
Take over their classes for a month and tell the students you are replacing them.

basic.situation: You attend a health education conference with your supervisor, who asks you to bring back notes on one session.

options.text: Copy another attendee's notes and share them with your supervisor as your own.
Collect the session handouts and write your summary from them after the trip.
Take notes on the slides of the busiest session and share them by email.
Choose a session on a topic you teach, take structured notes, and share them.

advanced.situation: You lead a study on hand hygiene in a student clinic. Your results are positive, but the sample was small and there was no control group.

options.text: Add extra participants from a different study to enlarge the sample size quickly.
Publish with the limits stated clearly and describe the findings as preliminary.
Publish the results as showing that the programme works for all student clinics.
Extend the study to a larger sample with a control group before writing anything up.

basic.situation: A student comes to your office hours with a checklist and asks which elective counts toward the diploma.

options.text: Sign the student's form to say the elective counts, to save them a second visit.
Use the checklist to answer, and confirm the elective with the coordinator.
Tell the student to ask a senior student who completed the diploma last year.
Tell the student which electives you think count and suggest they register early.

advanced.situation: A student wants to become a nurse educator but has no clinical work experience yet. They ask you to help build a career plan.

options.text: Outline the usual route, set clinical and study goals, and refer them to a mentor.
Tell them to gain a few years of clinical work first and come back later.
Offer to list them as having clinical experience on their application to help.
Suggest they apply for educator roles now since many schools need more teachers.

basic.situation: You update attendance for a lab group. One student left early with a nurse's note, so their attendance is unclear.

options.text: Alter the nurse's note so that the leaving time matches your register entry exactly.
Mark the student absent because they did not stay for the whole session.
Record the early departure with the time and keep the note on file.
Mark the student present for the full session since they were there most of it.

advanced.situation: You oversee a clinical lab where students practise injections on mannequins. A senior student reports that a junior used a needle on a classmate as a joke.

options.text: Warn the whole class about needle safety and ask the senior student to keep watch.
Speak to the junior student privately about safe practice and then keep teaching.
Tell the senior student that it was a joke and not to spread the story.
Stop the session, check for injury, secure the needles, and report to the head.

basic.situation: You demonstrate taking a blood pressure reading to a nursing student on a hospital ward, with a senior instructor present. The patient seems nervous.

options.text: Explain to the patient, demonstrate step by step, and then guide the student.
Move the demonstration to the calm patient in the next bed and begin right away.
Have the student take the reading on the patient while you watch from the doorway.
Demonstrate the reading quickly so the patient is not kept waiting and explain after.

advanced.situation: You supervise six nursing students on a ward. One student is about to give a medication, but the charted dose looks higher than the usual range.

options.text: Stop the student, verify the order with the nurse in charge, and debrief.
Tell the student to give half the dose and report the chart for review.
Let the student give the dose as charted since the doctor wrote the order.
Check the dose in the drug guide yourself and let the student continue if it fits.

basic.situation: You grade nursing students' care plans with provided rubrics. One care plan leaves out the required patient allergy section.

options.text: Give full marks because the rest of the care plan is detailed and well written.
Add a short allergy section to the student's care plan yourself before grading it.
Deduct by the rubric and comment on why allergy details protect patients.
Deduct the marks for the section and return the care plan with the grade.

advanced.situation: Clinical placement feedback shows graduates struggle with documenting patient handovers. You are asked to revise part of the curriculum.

options.text: Add one lecture on handover documentation to the existing course schedule this term.
Review placement feedback, add a simulated handover module, and check results next cohort.
Remove handover documentation from the assessed outcomes since it is hard to measure.
Ask placement sites to teach handover documentation, since they see it in practice.

basic.situation: You help prepare a syllabus for a nursing fundamentals course under senior faculty guidance. They give you a template and the learning outcomes.

options.text: Take the topics from a syllabus you found at another nursing school and use them.
Fill in the template with the weekly topics and print copies for the class.
Fill in the template with outcomes and weekly topics, then ask faculty to review.
Change the learning outcomes so they match the topics you find easiest to teach.

advanced.situation: You must choose simulation equipment for an advanced critical care course. Two suppliers offer similar mannequins, one cheaper and the other with better training support.

options.text: Accept a free demonstration set from one supplier and then order from that supplier.
Choose the lower price and ask that supplier about extra training after purchase.
Choose the supplier with better training support and cover the extra cost from supplies.
Trial both with staff, compare against course outcomes and total cost, and recommend one.

basic.situation: You attend a nursing education conference with a mentor. One session presents a simulation method you have not used before.

options.text: Take notes, ask the presenter a question, and discuss it with your mentor.
Tell your students you will use the new method next week before checking its evidence.
Decide the method is not suited to your students and attend another session.
Take photos of the slides and look at them again when you return to work.

advanced.situation: You lead a team project on improving clinical placement assessment. Two colleagues disagree on how to measure student competence.

options.text: Use your own measure and report the project as unanimous in the final summary.
Choose the measure most nursing schools use and tell both colleagues to adopt it.
Ask the head of school to decide which measure to use in the project.
Ask each to state the evidence for their measure, then pilot both and compare.

basic.situation: During office hours, a nursing student tells you they are struggling to balance placement shifts and assignments.

options.text: Offer to extend their assignment deadlines by two weeks and tell the course leader later.
Tell them everyone struggles with placement and the first term is the hardest.
Suggest the student make a weekly timetable and come back if things worsen.
Listen, review their deadlines together, and point them to study support services.

advanced.situation: A junior adjunct instructor you mentor received poor student feedback about unclear explanations. They are discouraged and ask whether to quit teaching.

options.text: Tell them the feedback is common for new instructors and to pay it little attention.
Ask the students who complained to name themselves so the instructor can respond to them.
Review the feedback together, observe a class, and agree two specific changes to try.
Share a few teaching resources and tell them to try again next term.

basic.situation: You help staff the nursing programme registration desk. A student asks for their clinical placement group, but you cannot find their name on the list.

options.text: Assign the student to the placement group that has the most open places today.
Tell the student they have no placement this term and should plan for next year.
Tell the student to come back after lunch when the list may be updated.
Check the list by student ID and ask the coordinator to look up their record.

advanced.situation: You coordinate a training programme with three hospitals and two clinics. Capacity differs, and one hospital wants to reduce its student numbers next semester.

options.text: Accept the hospital's reduction and move the displaced students to the two clinics.
Meet the hospital, review all site capacities, and redistribute placements by written agreement.
Reassign students at the clinics yourself and inform the sites after term begins.
Refuse the reduction because the existing agreement covers all students already assigned.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared lecture on reading instruction using a senior colleague's slides. A student asks about a research claim whose source you do not know.

options.text: Say the claim is well known in the field and go on with the lecture.
Delete the claim from the shared slide file and tell students it was not included.
Give a source you think it might be from and then move on quickly.
Say you will ask your colleague for the source and share it next class.

advanced.situation: In a graduate seminar on learning and development, two students strongly disagree about whether standardised testing helps children. Their exchange is turning personal.

options.text: Ask the class to vote on which student made the stronger argument so far.
Tell the two students to settle it outside and skip the seminar until they have.
Stop the exchange, summarise the two positions, and move to the next topic.
Refocus on research evidence, set speaking rules, and have each restate the other's view.

basic.situation: You grade education students' lesson plans with a rubric. One plan is creative but has no assessment section, which the rubric requires.

options.text: Give full marks because the plan is creative and the student clearly worked hard.
Deduct the marks for the missing section and return the plan with a grade.
Apply the rubric deduction and comment on how to add an assessment section.
Write an assessment section into the student's plan yourself and then grade it.

advanced.situation: You are designing an exam for a large education course, and four tutors will mark it. Last year students complained about inconsistent marks.

options.text: Give the tutors a detailed mark scheme and ask them to follow it carefully.
Write a mark scheme, train tutors on sample scripts, and double-mark a sample.
Split the scripts by student surname so each tutor marks a similar number.
Allow each tutor to change marks after results are released if students complain.

basic.situation: You help choose textbooks for a child development course with supervision. Your supervisor gives you a budget and a short list.

options.text: Choose the book with the nicest cover and the most pictures for students.
Order a book that is not on the list because the reviews are better online.
Check the short list against the syllabus and prices, then recommend one.
Choose the cheapest book on the list and tell your supervisor it fits the budget.

advanced.situation: You lead a project to update the teaching practice course. Surveys show graduates want more classroom experience, but placements are limited.

options.text: Promise graduates a longer placement in the next brochure before any plans are agreed.
Increase placement length for all students and ask schools to find more places.
Replace the placements with classroom videos so every student gets the same experience.
Analyse survey and placement data, then pilot simulated teaching alongside shorter placements.

basic.situation: At your office hours, a student asks how to prepare for the teaching practicum interview. You have the programme handbook open.

options.text: Give the student the interview questions another candidate told you were asked last year.
Share the handbook tips and practise two interview questions with the student.
Tell the student to read the handbook closely and come back with questions.
Say the interview is informal and they should just relax and be themselves.

advanced.situation: A student asks whether to pursue a teaching career or work in educational policy. They are torn and hold offers for further study in both.

options.text: Describe your own path in education and say what you would do again.
Tell the student to accept both offers and decide after the first term.
Recommend teaching because classroom experience is useful in almost any education job.
Explore their motives, outline both paths, and suggest talking with practitioners in each.

basic.situation: You are asked to read recent articles on reading instruction before a department meeting. You have limited time.

options.text: Ask a colleague what the articles say and share it as your own reading.
Quote a conclusion from an article you have not read because the title looked relevant.
Choose two recent articles, note their main findings, and prepare a question.
Read the abstracts of ten articles and mention a few at the meeting.

advanced.situation: You lead a team studying classroom discipline. Your findings are mixed, but a journal editor says clearer results would improve acceptance chances.

options.text: Report the main findings and leave the weaker sections out to keep the paper short.
Submit the mixed findings with a cover letter that stresses the strongest results.
Edit the survey responses that muddy the pattern so the results are clearer.
Report the mixed findings as they are, discuss why, and choose a suitable journal.

basic.situation: You update attendance and grade records for an education course. A student asks you to fix a grade they believe was entered wrongly, but you only enter marks given to you.

options.text: Compare the record with the lecturer's sheet and ask them to confirm any change.
Tell the student the record is final and refuse to look at the mark sheet.
Tell the student to take the question to the lecturer, since you cannot check marks.
Change the grade to what the student says, since they know their own result.

advanced.situation: You lead a grant application for a literacy programme with two colleagues. The funder's deadline is in a week, and one colleague has not sent their section.

options.text: Write the missing section yourself from their old reports and submit under their name.
Wait for the colleague to send their section and submit whatever arrives on time.
Contact the colleague for a firm date and draft a backup version of that section.
Apply for a deadline extension and tell the funder the team is still working.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared lecture on collection development. A student asks how libraries decide to remove old books, which your notes do not cover.

options.text: Give a firm rule, such as removing any book that is older than ten years.
Tell the student that weeding rules differ everywhere and cannot really be taught.
Say you will check standard library weeding guidelines and explain them next session.
Give an example from the library you used as a student and move on.

advanced.situation: You are building an online course on indexing for library science students. Test users say the video lessons are long and they lose focus.

options.text: Remove the practice tasks to shorten each lesson and keep the videos as they are.
Keep the videos but add a transcript and a short summary for each lesson.
Split lessons into short segments with practice tasks and test them with a small group.
Lock the course so students cannot move on until each video has fully played.

basic.situation: You grade a library science class paper with a rubric. The paper has good ideas but uses an inconsistent citation style.

options.text: Deduct citation marks by the rubric and show how to use one style.
Reformat the references into one style yourself and then grade the revised version.
Deduct the citation marks and add a note that style matters in this field.
Give full marks because the ideas are good and style is easy to learn.

advanced.situation: You compile a specialised reading list on digital archives for a graduate course. Several sources you found sit behind paywalls that students cannot access.

options.text: Drop every paywalled item from the list, even those central to the topic.
List all the sources and tell students to request copies through interlibrary loan.
Check library licences, swap paywalled items for open-access ones, and flag any gaps.
Upload the paywalled articles to the course page so students can download them.

basic.situation: A student visits your office hours to ask about library school application requirements. You are not sure about one deadline.

options.text: Tell the student the deadline is probably the same as it was last year.
Say you are unsure, check the admissions page together, and note the date.
Tell the student to ask the admissions office, since admissions is not your area.
State a deadline from memory with confidence and tell the student to plan around it.

advanced.situation: A student wants to move from library work into data management but has no technical background. They ask for a realistic plan.

options.text: Say a library degree is enough for data management and no new study is needed.
Tell them to apply for data jobs now and learn technical skills on the job.
Suggest they stay in library work because technical skills are hard to learn later.
Map their skills to data roles, suggest short courses, and connect them with practitioners.

basic.situation: You supervise a first-year student on a short internship at the campus library. For the second day, they have shelved returned books in the wrong sections.

options.text: Re-shelve the books yourself each evening so that the collection stays in order.
Tell them to take more care and re-check the shelves at day's end.
Move the student to the returns desk and record the shelving task as completed.
Show them how the call numbers work and check the next trolley together.

advanced.situation: As acting head of the library science department, you must decide whether to approve an internship partnership with a company that wants access to student project data.

options.text: Have legal staff review the terms, protect student data in writing, and consult staff.
Decline the partnership to avoid any risk to student data or the department's name.
Approve the partnership on condition that all students sign a data sharing waiver.
Approve the partnership and hand over the project data to start quickly this term.

basic.situation: A colleague asks for your help with a teaching issue: students seem confused about database search skills. You are to suggest ideas.

options.text: Suggest adding a longer lecture on database search to the schedule next term.
Tell your colleague that students should have learned this at school years ago.
Ask what confuses students, look at sample work, and suggest a short practice exercise.
Offer to change the students' search marks so the confusion does not show in results.

advanced.situation: You present research on library use at a professional conference. A listener says your sample is biased, and you suspect they may be partly right.

options.text: Acknowledge the point, explain your sampling, and add a limitations section to the paper.
Thank the listener and say you will think about the point after the conference.
Defend the sample as representative and move on quickly to the next question.
Edit the sample numbers in your slides and paper so the groups look more balanced.

basic.situation: You prepare a syllabus and handouts for a library skills workshop. The coordinator gave you the topic list and a one-hour limit.

options.text: Print another library's handouts with your library's name and logo on them.
Write handouts for all the topics, even if they take longer than an hour.
Fit the topics into one hour and send the draft handouts to the coordinator.
Use last term's syllabus as it is, though its topics are slightly different.

advanced.situation: You write a grant proposal to digitise a local history collection. The funder wants proof of community support, and you have letters from only two groups.

options.text: Ask the two groups to write several letters each under different names to boost it.
Request more support letters and describe the current level of support honestly.
Submit the two letters and say more groups are likely to support the project.
Delay the application a year to gather more letters, though the funder's round closes soon.

basic.situation: You deliver a standard criminal law lecture from a senior colleague's slides. A student asks whether an example would be decided differently locally, which you have not studied.

options.text: Tell the student that local law is outside the course and to stop raising it.
Say you are unsure, note the question, and check with your colleague.
Say the principle is similar in most countries and carry on with the lecture.
Offer your own view on how the example would probably be decided locally.

advanced.situation: In a policing seminar, a former police officer says a controversial practice was necessary, and a classmate who was once stopped by police disagrees emotionally.

options.text: Tell the classmate to keep personal experiences out of the seminar and mark them down.
Ask both to cite evidence, then have the class weigh the competing arguments.
Thank both students for sharing and go on with the planned lecture slides.
Ask the former officer to explain the practice as the class's expert on policing.

basic.situation: You grade criminal justice assignments with a checklist. One student's answer is accurate but copies sentences from a textbook without quotation marks.

options.text: Grade by the checklist and report the copied sentences to the module leader.
Deduct marks for the copied sentences and write a comment on quotation marks.
Add quotation marks to the student's text yourself and then grade the answer.
Give full marks because the answer is accurate and shows good understanding of the topic.

advanced.situation: You set an exam for a large criminal justice course. Students complain that last exam's multiple-choice questions were ambiguous and unfair.

options.text: Review question statistics, rewrite unclear items, and test them with a small group.
Use the same questions again, since most students passed the earlier exam last year.
Replace all the multiple-choice questions with essay questions for this exam and next.
Recompute last exam's marks after dropping the disputed items and replace published results.

basic.situation: You help select a textbook for an introductory criminology course. Your supervisor wants a recommendation by Friday.

options.text: Compare two books against the syllabus and price, then send a recommendation.
Recommend the book written by your former professor and say it is popular.
Ask the publisher for a free class set in return for a positive recommendation.
Recommend the book most universities use and attach the publisher's current price list.

advanced.situation: You lead a curriculum revision for the criminal justice degree. Employers say graduates lack digital evidence skills, but the course hours are fixed.

options.text: Add a short guest talk on digital evidence and leave the curriculum as it is.
Cut the fixed course hours of other subjects by announcement and start the new module.
Add a digital evidence module and extend each semester by two extra weeks.
Gather employer input, then swap overlapping content for a short digital evidence module.

basic.situation: A student comes to office hours asking how to prepare for the criminal procedure exam. A line of students waits outside.

options.text: Tell the student which cases and topics are on the exam paper you wrote.
Tell the student to read all the lecture slides and come back later.
Give a study outline, set a practice question, and offer a follow-up time.
Spend the whole hour helping this student until they feel fully ready for the exam.

advanced.situation: A strong student asks you for a recommendation letter for a police training programme. You have concerns about their temper after an incident in class last year.

options.text: Discuss your concerns with them, then write a letter based on what you saw.
Write a glowing letter that leaves out the incident, since the student has improved.
Decline to write the letter and suggest the student ask another lecturer instead.
Write a positive letter and send the programme a separate note about the incident.

basic.situation: You attend a criminal justice conference with your supervisor. One session covers new research on sentencing disparities, a topic you teach.

options.text: Take a copy of the slides and read them when you are back at work.
Listen to the session and rely on your memory of the main points later.
Take notes on findings and methods, ask a question, and plan how to use them.
Tell your students next week that the new research proves sentencing disparity is fixed.

advanced.situation: You lead a collaboration with a law faculty colleague on a joint cybercrime course. You disagree on how much technical content to include.

options.text: Let the law colleague decide on content since they know the legal side.
Write the course outline alone and present it to the dean as a joint proposal.
Include all the technical content you prefer and let the law colleague adapt later.
Agree learning outcomes first, then map topics to them and trial a draft unit.

basic.situation: You record attendance and grades for a criminal justice class using a template. You notice a grade that does not match the marked paper.

options.text: Leave the grade as entered because the lecturer may have changed it after marking.
Change the marked paper to match the template so that both records agree.
Check the paper against the entry and tell the lecturer before you fix anything.
Change the template to match the marked paper and save the file for submission.

advanced.situation: You sit on a committee reviewing a policy that would let students retake any failed module unlimited times. Staff worry about standards and costs.

options.text: Tell students the policy has been approved before the committee has made its vote.
Ask for retake outcome and cost data, then propose a limit with student support.
Support the policy because students deserve every chance to complete their degree here.
Oppose the policy because it will lower the standard of the whole degree.

basic.situation: You help select textbooks for a contract law course with guidance from your supervisor. The faculty library holds two editions of the main textbook.

options.text: Check which edition the syllabus cites and which is current, then ask your supervisor.
Choose the newer edition because it is probably more up to date than the other.
Choose the cheaper edition and tell students to use it for the course.
Order a class set of both editions on the library account to be safe.

advanced.situation: You revise the legal ethics curriculum after the licensing body updates its competency requirements. Your course hours stay the same.

options.text: Add the new requirements as an extra reading list at the end of the course.
Wait until the next academic year to see if the licensing body changes its mind.
Tell students the new requirements are already covered in the existing course materials.
Map the new requirements to current units, find gaps, and revise with colleagues.

basic.situation: You grade first-year law students' case briefs with a rubric. One brief is well argued but cites a case name you cannot find in any database.

options.text: Add a similar real case to the student's brief yourself and grade the result.
Deduct citation marks and write a comment that the case could not be found.
Give full marks because the argument is strong and the case may be real.
Search the databases, ask the student for the citation, and apply the rubric.

advanced.situation: You design a law exam for a course taught by three lecturers. Grades varied widely between groups last year, and students said the marking criteria were unclear.

options.text: Ask each lecturer to explain their marking criteria to their own group in class.
Mark all the scripts yourself to remove any differences between the three lecturers.
Adjust each group's grades to fit a standard curve after the results are released.
Publish marking criteria, give graders a shared guide, and moderate a sample.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared lecture on contract formation under supervision. A student asks about an example from a news story that your notes do not explain.

options.text: Give a quick answer based on the news report and move on to the next slide.
Say you will review the facts and answer next session using proper sources.
Say news stories are not law and decline to discuss any example from them.
Present a confident legal conclusion on the news story's facts as settled law.

advanced.situation: In a seminar, students debate a high-profile criminal case still before the courts. One student says the accused is clearly guilty, and others object.

options.text: Move on to another topic quickly since the case is still before the courts.
Tell the class what you personally think the likely verdict will be and why.
Ask the student who said guilty to present the evidence for that view.
Remind the class of the presumption of innocence and redirect to the legal issues.

basic.situation: A student asks in office hours whether they can borrow your marked exam papers from last year as examples.

options.text: Hand over the box of marked papers and ask the student to return it Friday.
Tell the student to ask the department office about borrowing the marked papers.
Explain marked papers are private and point them to the library's past papers.
Lend the student one paper after removing the name of the original author.

advanced.situation: You advise the law students' moot court society. Two officers accuse each other of unfair selection of team members for a national competition.

options.text: Meet both officers, review the selection criteria, and agree a transparent process.
Pick the team yourself since you know which students are strongest in moot court.
Remove both officers from their posts and appoint two new officers yourself today.
Ask the society's president to settle it and tell the two officers to accept.

basic.situation: You read new legal journal articles to keep up with contract law developments. One article disagrees with your lecture notes.

options.text: Tell your students the article is unreliable simply because it contradicts your notes.
Read it closely, compare its reasoning with your notes, and discuss it with a colleague.
Note the article's title and update your lecture notes when you have time.
Change your lecture notes to match the article since it is more recent.

advanced.situation: You lead a collaborative paper on legal reform with two colleagues. One colleague wants to include a controversial claim that the others consider poorly supported.

options.text: Include the claim in a footnote and avoid discussing it with the colleague.
Review the evidence together and include the claim if it meets the standard.
Remove the claim to keep the paper uncontroversial and finish on time as planned.
Include the claim and list the other colleagues as supporting it in the paper.

basic.situation: You maintain attendance and grade records for a law class. A student's grade in the system is lower than the mark on their paper.

options.text: Leave the system grade and tell the student to take the paper to the office.
Compare with the lecturer's marks, report the difference, and update after confirmation.
Update the grade to the mark on the paper and tell the lecturer afterwards.
Raise the system grade to the higher mark and delete the entry history afterwards.

advanced.situation: You serve on a committee deciding academic standards for plagiarism cases in law courses. Members disagree on whether first offences should be treated lightly.

options.text: Review past cases, compare other faculties' standards, and propose graded responses by severity.
Support strict penalties for every case to protect the reputation of the profession.
Support lenient treatment of all first offences because students are still learning the rules.
Share the committee's draft proposal with the student newspaper before it is final.

basic.situation: You deliver a lecture on child and adolescent mental health with a senior colleague's guidance. A student says a case in your lecture mirrors their own family and becomes upset.

options.text: Pause, check the student is okay, offer a break, and follow up after class.
Move on to a different case study quickly so the class is not disturbed.
Ask the student to share more of their family story so the class can learn.
Continue the lecture and speak to the student privately at the end of class.

advanced.situation: In a graduate seminar on evaluating social interventions, two students argue about whether a popular community programme works. Neither has read the full evaluation report.

options.text: Tell both students that unprepared opinions will be graded as low-quality participation today.
Summarise what you know about the programme and then give the class your conclusion.
Pause, share key pages from the report, and have both discuss what the data shows.
Let the debate continue to its natural end and then move to the next topic.

basic.situation: You grade social work students' reflective papers with a rubric. One paper is honest and thoughtful but runs well over the word limit.

options.text: Apply the rubric's length penalty and comment on the quality of the reflection.
Give full marks because the reflection is honest and the extra length shows effort.
Cut the paper to the word limit yourself and then grade the shortened version.
Grade the first part within the word limit and leave the rest unread.

advanced.situation: Student surveys and exam results show weak understanding of ethics in social work practice. You must revise the course.

options.text: Add a new lecture on ethics at the start of the course for everyone.
Remove ethics from the assessed content since it is hard to measure fairly.
Replace the ethics exam questions with easier ones so the results look better.
Find where students struggle, add case-based activities, and compare with the next cohort.

basic.situation: You prepare a handout on family assessment tools for a social work tutorial. The course lead gave you three required tools to cover.

options.text: Describe each of the three tools with an example and cite sources.
Paste pages from a published guide into the handout and omit the source.
Add five more tools you like and shorten the descriptions of the required ones.
List the three tools by name with a one-line description of each for students.

advanced.situation: You must choose specialised materials for an advanced social work research course. Two software packages differ in price and in support for qualitative analysis.

options.text: Install an unlicensed copy of the stronger package to avoid paying for licences.
Choose the cheaper package and tell students to use free tools for the rest.
Choose the package that is most popular among researchers and order it now.
Test both against the course tasks, compare total costs including licences, and recommend one.

basic.situation: At office hours, a social work student asks how to apply for a field placement. You have the placement handbook open.

options.text: Arrange a placement for the student at an agency you know to speed things up.
Walk them through the handbook steps, point out the deadline, and offer to review.
Tell the student to read the handbook and email you any questions that remain.
Say placements are usually arranged by the department, so there is no need to apply.

advanced.situation: You advise a student social work society planning a fundraising event. A member proposes sharing real client stories from their placement to attract donations.

options.text: Explain confidentiality duties and suggest consented or composite stories, checked with the placement.
Tell the society to avoid stories altogether and rely on statistics to raise funds.
Approve the plan because donors respond strongly to real stories from the field.
Tell the member to remove names and share the stories at the event.

basic.situation: You observe a student in the lab practising an interview skills exercise with a supervisor present. The student gives advice to a role-play client that sounds judgemental.

options.text: Tell the other students in the lab that the student's advice was inappropriate and unprofessional.
Stop the role-play and tell the student to start again from the beginning.
Note the moment, discuss it with the student afterwards, and suggest a neutral alternative.
Wait for the final grade and mention then that the interview was judgemental.

advanced.situation: You oversee graduate students' field placements. A student reports that their placement agency asks them to do tasks outside their role, such as handling client cash.

options.text: Tell the student the tasks are part of real practice and they should adapt.
Tell the student to politely refuse the cash tasks and continue with other duties.
Move the student to another agency this week and cancel the agreement yourself.
Review the placement agreement, contact the agency supervisor, and confirm task limits in writing.

basic.situation: You update attendance and grade records for a social work module. A student asks you to hide an absence because they fear it will harm a scholarship.

options.text: Explain you must record it accurately and refer them to the scholarship office.
Record the absence and tell the student you cannot discuss the scholarship rules.
Mark the student as late rather than absent, which is a less serious record.
Remove the absence from the record and tell the student to keep this between you.

advanced.situation: You lead a departmental committee that decides how social work students are matched with placement agencies. Students complain the process is unfair, and agencies want more say.

options.text: Gather student and agency input, draft transparent matching criteria, and pilot them.
Keep the current process and tell students the matching decisions are now final.
Let agencies pick their students first and fill the remaining places by lottery.
Let agencies choose students privately and inform the committee at the term's end.

basic.situation: You demonstrate a watercolour wash technique to a first-year class, guided by a senior colleague. Several students say the paper is buckling when wet.

options.text: Tell students that buckling is part of the technique and cannot be avoided.
Suggest students switch to thicker paper from their own supplies and keep painting.
Show how to stretch and tape the paper, then help students try it.
Tell students to use less water next time and continue with the demonstration.

advanced.situation: You lead a workshop for peer instructors on teaching improvisation in drama. Two instructors disagree about critiquing students during exercises or waiting until afterwards.

options.text: Present your own approach as the standard and move on to the next topic.
Adopt the approach most instructors prefer and ask the two to follow it.
Tell the instructors to settle the disagreement in front of the students next class.
Demonstrate both approaches, gather peer observations, and agree guidelines by exercise type.

basic.situation: You grade first-year music students' performance recordings with a rubric. One recording has strong expression but several missed notes.

options.text: Give a low grade because missed notes matter more than any feeling in the playing.
Re-record the difficult passages yourself and mix them into the student's file before grading.
Give a good overall grade because the expression stands out and the notes are close.
Score each rubric criterion separately and comment on expression and note accuracy.

advanced.situation: You lead a revision of the department's studio art curriculum after graduates say they lacked business skills. Faculty fear losing studio hours.

options.text: Cut a studio course in the final year to make room for a business course.
Add a business elective that students can take in addition to studio work.
Announce the new business requirement to students before faculty have agreed to it.
Survey graduates and employers, then pilot a short business unit within existing hours.

basic.situation: You maintain attendance sheets and grade records for an art history class. A student asks you to add a missing grade from a quiz they say they took.

options.text: Enter a pass mark for the quiz so the student has no gaps in the record.
Add the grade the student gives you and note the date you entered it.
Ask the lecturer for the quiz record and add the grade once they confirm.
Tell the student the quiz probably did not count and leave the sheet alone.

advanced.situation: You organise a student art exhibition at a gallery. The gallery asks for insurance values for each work, and some students are unsure what their pieces are worth.

options.text: Agree a simple valuation method, photograph each work, and confirm insurance cover with the gallery.
Tell the gallery the works are covered by university insurance, to finish the paperwork.
Ask students to estimate values themselves and submit the list to the gallery.
Give every work the same low value so the gallery paperwork is simple.

basic.situation: You attend a regional music education conference with a mentor. A workshop shows a teaching method you have not seen before.

options.text: Take notes, try the method with the group, and discuss it with your mentor.
Teach the method next week from memory and describe it as your own idea.
Collect the workshop handout and read it carefully when you return to work.
Decide the method is too different from your style and leave the session.

advanced.situation: You lead a faculty group designing a joint music and theatre project. Two colleagues disagree about how to split the budget between their departments.

options.text: Ask both for costs and aims, then propose a split based on project needs.
Ask the dean to decide the split and accept whatever the dean chooses.
Split the budget equally between the departments to keep things fair and simple.
Assign the larger share to your own department and tell the other colleague later.

basic.situation: A student comes to your office hours to ask about audition requirements for the end-of-year performance. You have the handbook open.

options.text: Go through the handbook requirements and dates, and suggest a practice plan.
Give the student a copy of the handbook page and wish them good luck.
Say the requirements may still change, so they should wait to start preparing.
Offer to arrange the student a private audition slot before the other students.

advanced.situation: You advise a student drama society that wants to stage a play with sensitive themes. Some members worry about complaints, and university approval is required.

options.text: Help them follow the approval process and prepare audience notes and support information.
Suggest they stage the play before approval is decided so the date is secured.
Advise them to choose a different play to avoid any chance of complaints.
Tell them to submit the script for approval and wait for the decision.

basic.situation: You help at an arts programme recruitment table during a school visit. A parent asks if the course guarantees a job after graduation.

options.text: Tell the parent that talented students nearly all find work in the arts.
Promise the parent a guaranteed job placement through the department's industry contacts.
Say most graduates find work in the arts and hand over a course brochure.
Say there is no guarantee, but explain typical careers and share outcome data.

advanced.situation: You lead a committee drafting arts policy for the institution. Members disagree on whether to prioritise funding for public performances or classroom resources.

options.text: Draft a split from what members said in the meeting and circulate it for comment.
Gather usage and cost data, consult staff and students, and propose a reviewed split.
Fund public performances first because they raise the institution's profile in the community.
Divide the funds to match your own department's current budget needs this year.

basic.situation: You prepare syllabi and handouts for a public speaking course with guidance from senior staff. They give you the learning outcomes and assessment dates.

options.text: Add assignments you like to the syllabus and adjust the assessment dates yourself.
Copy last year's syllabus and update the dates and the room number for this term.
Post the draft syllabus to all students online before senior staff have reviewed it.
Draft from the outcomes and dates, then ask senior staff to review it.

advanced.situation: You revise a media studies course after evaluations show students find the theory units disconnected from practice. Two colleagues teach the same course and prefer the current format.

options.text: Add a practical project to your own section and compare results at term's end.
Review the evaluations with both colleagues and pilot linked theory units in one section.
Change the shared course outline yourself and tell your colleagues the new version.
Replace the theory units with practical workshops in all sections from next term.

basic.situation: You start a short discussion in a communications class with instructor support. No one answers your first question.

options.text: Wait quietly for a minute and then ask again in the same words.
Rephrase the question, give a short example, and let pairs talk before sharing.
Pick a student at random and require them to answer in front of the class.
Answer the question yourself and move on to the next point on the slide.

advanced.situation: In a media ethics discussion, a student defends sharing an unverified viral video of a local incident, and another says that is harmful. The class is divided.

options.text: Summarise both views and tell the class to follow the textbook's ethics code.
Ask both to explain their reasoning, then test the video against a verification checklist.
Share the viral video yourself on the class page and ask the students to comment.
Side with the harm-concerned student to model responsible media behaviour for the class.

basic.situation: You grade public speaking assignments with a clear rubric. One student's speech is excellent but exceeded the time limit by two minutes.

options.text: Give a low mark because breaking the time limit shows poor respect for the audience.
Change the recorded time in your notes so the speech appears within the limit.
Mention the time limit in the feedback but keep the full mark for delivery.
Apply the rubric's time penalty and give feedback on the strong delivery.

advanced.situation: You write an exam for a communications course taught in three sections by different instructors. Past exams were graded very differently across sections.

options.text: Write a shared rubric, calibrate on sample answers, and compare section results.
Raise the marks in the harshest section after results are posted to match the others.
Grade every section yourself to keep the marks consistent for this one semester.
Give all instructors the same exam and let each grade their own section.

basic.situation: A student comes to your office hours with a question about a media assignment. The brief is ambiguous about the word count.

options.text: Tell the student any length is fine since the brief did not give one.
Agree the brief is unclear and confirm the word count with the course lead.
Give the student your preferred word count and say it applies to everyone.
Tell the student to aim for roughly the word count used in last year's brief.

advanced.situation: You advise the campus radio society, which plans to broadcast live interviews. Members disagree about who checks content for defamation and bias before broadcast.

options.text: Help them set a written review process with named roles, guided by university policy.
Tell the society that live shows carry too much risk and should be recorded first.
Suggest that one experienced member checks everything before each live broadcast starts.
Tell them to broadcast first and review the content if listeners complain later.

basic.situation: You read recent articles on changes in digital communication to keep current. One article makes a claim that conflicts with your lecture.

options.text: Read the article's evidence, compare it with your lecture, and discuss it with a colleague.
Mark the article to read later and keep your lecture as it is for now.
Update your lecture to match the article since it was published more recently.
Tell students that the article's claim is false and that you have checked it.

advanced.situation: You lead a research project on social media use among students. A co-author wants to publish before the data cleaning is complete.

options.text: Agree to publish now, since the main patterns are unlikely to change much.
Publish a short preliminary report now and add the full results to it later.
Explain the risks, agree a short deadline for cleaning, and publish after the checks.
Publish now under your name alone and describe the data as fully cleaned.

basic.situation: You help at a student recruitment fair for the communications programme. A student asks about internship options, and you know of only one.

options.text: Say internships are easy to find in communications, so there is nothing to worry about.
Describe the one internship you know in detail and suggest they ask staff later.
Share the one you know, say others exist, and refer them to careers office.
Tell the student the programme guarantees an internship for every student who enrols.

advanced.situation: You lead a committee drafting a policy on student use of editing services for assignments. Staff views range from banning them to encouraging them.

options.text: Define acceptable help with examples, consult students and staff, and review after a term.
Adopt a full ban because it is the easiest rule to explain and enforce.
Apply the draft ban to students' past assignments and reopen their earlier marks.
Leave the decision to each lecturer and publish no common policy for the department.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared lecture on poetry using a senior colleague's notes. A student asks what a line means, and you read it differently from the notes.

options.text: Present your own reading as the main one, since you are teaching the class.
Tell the student that poetry has no fixed meaning so the question does not matter.
Stick to the notes' reading and tell the student to ask your colleague.
Give the notes' reading, offer yours as another, and ask the class to compare.

advanced.situation: You lead a graduate seminar on translation and adaptation. A student presents a poem translation that drops a culturally sensitive term, and others object.

options.text: Ask the student to explain the choice, then compare other translations of the term.
Tell the student to restore the term and resubmit by the next class.
Defend the student's choice in front of the class and end the discussion there.
Let the objections stand and move on to the next presenter's work in the seminar.

basic.situation: You grade English essays with a rubric. One essay has strong ideas but many grammar errors that the rubric penalises.

options.text: Give a high mark since the ideas matter more than small grammar slips.
Fix the grammar in the essay yourself and then grade the improved version.
Score ideas and grammar separately by the rubric and show examples of repeated errors.
Deduct the grammar marks and add a general comment about proofreading before submission.

advanced.situation: You revise evaluation methods for a department-wide writing course. Students report that feedback is inconsistent between instructors, and results vary by section.

options.text: Switch to one standard exam for all sections so marking is the same.
Ask instructors to write more detailed feedback and send you a sample each week.
Create shared rubrics, run joint marking sessions, and compare section results after a term.
Tell instructors to adjust their marks so every section ends with the same average.

basic.situation: You help choose a poetry anthology for a first-year course. Your supervisor gave you three options and a limit on the price.

options.text: Order a class set of a fourth anthology that is above the price limit.
Choose the cheapest option and tell your supervisor it meets the price limit.
Choose the anthology you used as a student and say it is a classic.
Compare content, price, and available editions, then recommend one to your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You compile a bibliography for an advanced reading assignment on postcolonial literature. Many key texts are out of print and hard to find.

options.text: Check library holdings, list accessible editions, and note alternatives for rare works.
Scan the out-of-print books in full and upload them to the course page.
Remove the out-of-print texts and use titles that are easy to buy instead.
Include all the key texts and tell students to find copies by themselves online.

basic.situation: You are asked to keep up with new work in Victorian literature studies, but you have limited time each month.

options.text: Cite recent articles in your lecture from their titles alone to look current.
Skim the contents pages of journals each month and save any interesting titles.
Set a regular time to read one new article and note ideas for class.
Wait for colleagues to tell you about important new work during lunch breaks.

advanced.situation: You lead a collaborative project with a history colleague on literature and empire. Your colleague wants to use archival material that you suspect has copyright restrictions.

options.text: Check the archive's copyright terms together and seek permission before using the material.
Use short extracts from the material, since small quotations are usually considered fine.
Remove the copyright notices from the images before including them in the paper.
Use the material in the project and fix any issues if the archive objects.

basic.situation: A student comes to your office hours to ask what you expect from their next essay. You have the assignment brief.

options.text: Go through the brief and rubric together and show a sample introduction.
Tell the student which essay topics will come up on the final exam paper.
Tell the student to read the brief again and come back with specific questions.
Describe your own favourite essays and say the student should write something similar.

advanced.situation: A student asks you for a graduate programme recommendation letter, but you taught them in one large class and know little about their work.

options.text: Write a detailed letter with classroom examples that make the student sound stronger.
Decline and suggest they ask a lecturer who knows their work much better.
Write a short generic letter praising the student's potential in very general terms.
Explain your limited knowledge, review their work and CV, and write what you can support.

basic.situation: You maintain attendance for an English class. A student asks you to mark them present for a day missed because they were at a university-organised event.

options.text: Remove the absence from the sheet and tell the student to keep it private.
Check the event list and record an excused absence if the student is on it.
Leave the absence as recorded and tell the student to speak to the event organiser.
Record the day as present since the student was on official university business.

advanced.situation: You serve on a committee reviewing the English department's grading policy. One proposal would remove the pass mark for coursework to reduce failures.

options.text: Ask for failure and outcome data, then propose support measures instead of removing the mark.
Support the proposal because lower failure rates will improve the department's public image.
Oppose the proposal because pass marks must stay as they are in every course.
Tell students the pass mark is already removed before the committee has decided.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared beginner lecture on Spanish pronunciation from a provided script. A student asks about a regional variation your script does not cover.

options.text: Demonstrate a pronunciation you half remember with confidence so the class stays engaged.
Give the variation you think is common and ask the student to confirm it later.
Say regional variations are not part of this course and move on quickly.
Say you will check a reliable guide and answer at the next class.

advanced.situation: In an advanced class on cultural aspects of a language area, a student describes a local custom in a stereotyping way. Native speakers in the class are visibly upset.

options.text: Remind the class to be respectful and return to the planned material quickly.
Acknowledge the concern, ask for sources, and invite native speakers to add context.
Tell the student to apologise to the native speakers in front of everyone.
Ask the native speakers to explain the custom to the class on the spot.

basic.situation: You grade beginner writing assignments in a foreign language with a checklist. One student's text is clear but uses grammar well beyond the level taught so far.

options.text: Grade the text as submitted and add a note about sticking to taught grammar.
Give full marks because the text is clear and shows real ambition in the language.
Grade by the checklist and ask the student to explain their grammar choices.
Tell the student they cheated and give zero before hearing any explanation from them.

advanced.situation: You develop an oral exam for a language course taught by four instructors. Last year, examiners' scores varied widely for similar performances.

options.text: Tell examiners to give most students similar scores so the differences do not show.
Assign each examiner a fixed group of students so differences stay within groups.
Write a shared scoring guide, train examiners on recorded samples, and double-score some exams.
Give all examiners the same scoring guide and ask them to apply it.

basic.situation: You prepare handouts and homework for a beginner French class from a provided template. The lecturer gave you the vocabulary list.

options.text: Use the template, add simple exercises, and check the spellings in a dictionary.
Add extra words you think are useful and drop a few from the lecturer's list.
Fill the template with the vocabulary list and print copies for the class.
Copy exercises from a published workbook into the homework sheet as your own.

advanced.situation: You revise the intermediate language curriculum after students report weak speaking skills. Colleagues prefer to keep the grammar-heavy structure.

options.text: Rewrite the exam to test speaking and tell colleagues after students sit it.
Add a weekly conversation hour and keep all the existing grammar units unchanged.
Replace most grammar units with conversation practice across all the classes next term.
Review speaking results with colleagues and pilot more speaking tasks in one class.

basic.situation: You attend a language teaching conference with a mentor. A session presents a new method for vocabulary practice.

options.text: Take notes, ask about the evidence, and discuss with your mentor how to try it.
Decide the method suits advanced classes and leave to attend another session instead.
Tell your students the method is proven, based on what the presenter claimed.
Take a photo of the slides and look at them again after the conference.

advanced.situation: You lead a research project with two colleagues on language learning apps. One colleague wants to include a conclusion that your data supports only weakly.

options.text: Remove the conclusion from the paper to avoid disagreement and submit on time.
Include the strong conclusion and state that all authors fully agree with it.
Let your colleague write the conclusion as they prefer and review it afterwards.
Review the statistics together and word the conclusion to match the strength of the evidence.

basic.situation: At office hours, a student asks how to improve their speaking fluency before an exam. You have fifteen minutes.

options.text: Say fluency comes with time and that exams are mostly about written accuracy anyway.
Suggest daily speaking habits, practise a short exchange together, and share resources.
Tell the student the exam speaking questions you remember from last year's paper.
Tell the student to speak with classmates more and to listen to recordings often.

advanced.situation: A student asks whether to study abroad for a year or finish the degree quickly and enter the job market. They are unsure which helps a language career.

options.text: Recommend finishing quickly since most employers prefer candidates who graduate on schedule.
Describe your own experience abroad and say it was very useful for you.
Tell the student to go abroad since the degree has little value on its own.
Explore their goals, compare both options, and suggest talking with recent graduates.

basic.situation: You maintain attendance for a language class. The register still lists a student who dropped the course last month.

options.text: Keep marking the student absent each week until the end of term arrives.
Check the withdrawal record and confirm with the office before changing the register.
Remove the student from the register since they no longer attend your class.
Mark the student present for all past weeks so the register looks consistent.

advanced.situation: You organise a study abroad programme for twenty students. A week before departure, the partner university cancels the accommodation booking.

options.text: Book cheap rooms online in a location that looks convenient and send students there.
Tell students to find their own housing near the partner university and claim costs.
Postpone departure by a month and tell students to wait for further news.
Contact the partner, secure alternative housing, update students, and inform the head.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared lecture on ancient history using your supervisor's notes. A student says a date on your slide differs from their textbook.

options.text: Check the date against reliable sources, thank the student, and fix the slide.
Change the date in the shared slide file and leave your supervisor to notice.
Tell the student the supervisor's notes are the official version for this course.
Say historians sometimes disagree on dates and carry on with the lecture today.

advanced.situation: In a seminar on postwar civilisations, a student argues that a colonial regime was beneficial, and a classmate whose family suffered under it responds angrily.

options.text: Pause the discussion and remind everyone to be respectful of each other's views.
Ask for evidence, give space for the response, and compare sources from different perspectives.
Ask the classmate to describe their family's suffering to the class as evidence.
Tell the first student their view is outdated and ask the class to move on.
