basic.situation: You grade history essays with a rubric. One essay is well argued but uses a single source for all its claims.

options.text: Deduct source marks and write a short note on using more sources next time.
Add references from other books to the essay's bibliography yourself before grading it.
Give full marks since the argument is well built and the source is reputable.
Apply the rubric for source range and suggest other types of sources.

advanced.situation: Exam results in the history department show weak source analysis skills across three courses. You are asked to revise the curriculum.

options.text: Map source analysis across the courses, find gaps, and pilot a shared skills unit.
Add a source analysis lecture to each course at the start of term.
Remove source analysis questions from the exams to improve overall results this year.
Adjust the exam results upward in the system so the department report looks stronger.

basic.situation: You prepare a syllabus and homework assignments for a modern history survey course using a template from your supervisor.

options.text: Set the homework to ask for the answers to next week's exam questions in full.
Replace the supervisor's topics with a syllabus you once saw at another university.
Fill in the template with the topics and dates, then send it for review.
Fill in the template and email it directly to the students as the final syllabus.

advanced.situation: You select specialised materials for a research seminar on archival methods. A rare document collection costs more than the seminar budget.

options.text: Buy part of the collection within budget and ask students to share copies.
Ask the library about digital access, request extra funds, and plan fallback sources.
Order the full collection and charge the extra cost to another department's account.
Drop the collection and build the seminar around easier sources of any kind.

basic.situation: A colleague asks you to review a book manuscript for a publisher, with their guidance. You find the introduction unclear.

options.text: Mark the unclear passages, suggest changes, and share your notes with your colleague.
Send the manuscript to a friend in the field and use their comments as yours.
Write that the introduction is unclear and recommend the author rewrite it fully.
Rewrite the introduction yourself and send it to the publisher as part of your review.

advanced.situation: You write a grant proposal for a multi-year archive digitisation project. The funder wants measurable outcomes, but historical impact is hard to quantify.

options.text: Define concrete outputs and usage targets, state assumptions, and describe how you will track them.
Report outcome figures from another institution's project as your own expected results here.
Promise large visitor numbers for the archive based on a similar famous project.
List the documents to be digitised and describe the project's wide cultural value.

basic.situation: A student comes to your office hours to ask how to find primary sources for an essay. You are about to teach.

options.text: Tell them to use any online sources that look old and original for their essay.
Point to the library's primary sources page and tell them to explore it.
Write the essay's source list for the student so they can finish quickly.
Show them the library catalogue and archive search, and invite them back with questions.

advanced.situation: You supervise a graduate student whose research uses documents from a restricted archive collection. The student has copied more pages than the archive permits.

options.text: Keep the copies for the research but tell the student to follow limits later.
Stop further copying, explain the limits, and tell the archive and the department.
Tell the student to return the extra copies and not to copy any more pages.
Use the copied pages in the thesis and cite a different source for them.

basic.situation: You maintain attendance and grade records for a history course. A grade entry has a typing error that you made last week.

options.text: Leave the entry as it is and tell the student to raise it if needed.
Fix the entry, log the change with the date, and tell the lecturer.
Fix the entry in the spreadsheet and send the lecturer the new version.
Overwrite last week's backup file with the new version to keep one clean copy.

advanced.situation: As department head, you must respond to a complaint that a lecturer's course unfairly excludes certain historical perspectives. The lecturer says the course is balanced.

options.text: Ask the lecturer to write a response and forward it to the complainant.
Have an independent colleague review the syllabus, then meet both sides and agree actions.
Order the lecturer to add specific topics next week and skip the usual review.
Tell the complainant that academic freedom means the lecturer alone decides course content.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared ethics lecture to students and community members, guided by a senior colleague. A community member asks you to say which religion is true.

options.text: Say that is a personal matter and return to the planned material straight away.
Explain the course compares traditions instead of ranking them, and invite discussion.
Share your own religious view briefly since the community member asked you directly.
Argue that one tradition is superior and invite the class to challenge you.

advanced.situation: In a graduate ethics seminar, two students argue about whether euthanasia is ever justified. One reveals a painful family experience, and the exchange turns personal.

options.text: Ask the student who shared to explain their experience to support their argument.
Pause the seminar for five minutes and then continue with the planned topic.
End the discussion and tell both students that personal topics are not allowed.
Acknowledge the story, restate ground rules, and refocus on arguments and sources.

basic.situation: You prepare a handout for an introductory philosophy class. The course lead asked for a one-page summary of three classical arguments about the existence of God.

options.text: Summarise each argument neutrally with its main objection and cite the textbook pages.
Summarise each argument from the textbook and leave out the objections to save space.
Write the summaries from memory and print the handout before checking them against texts.
Copy a summary from a website and add your colleague's name as the author.

advanced.situation: You compile a specialised bibliography on contemporary religious thought for an advanced seminar. Students come from several faith backgrounds.

options.text: Build the list from the traditions you know well and add a few others.
Leave out sources that challenge religious belief to avoid upsetting any students.
Cover several traditions, include primary and critical sources, and ask a colleague to review.
Include the main works from each major tradition and add a short note on each.

basic.situation: You grade philosophy essays with a rubric. One essay argues clearly but misreads a key text.

options.text: Rewrite the student's interpretation to fit the text and grade the revised essay.
Give full marks because the argument is clear and the misreading is minor.
Apply the rubric for interpretation and point the student to the relevant passage.
Deduct interpretation marks and note that the student should reread the text carefully.

advanced.situation: You design the final exam for a logic course with 200 students sitting in two rooms. Some students may share questions between sessions.

options.text: Use one paper in both sessions and collect phones at the door beforehand.
Write two equal-difficulty versions, run both sessions together, and use one mark scheme.
Use one paper and ask the first session students to promise not to share it.
Give the second room's students the first room's questions in advance to be fair.

basic.situation: You read a new journal article on moral philosophy to keep your knowledge current. The argument is dense and you are not sure you follow it.

options.text: Cite the article in your lecture notes as supporting a claim you want to make.
Outline the argument in your own words and discuss unclear steps with a colleague.
Read a blog summary of the article instead and use that in your teaching.
Read the abstract and conclusion and treat the middle section as background detail.

advanced.situation: You are about to publish a paper on religious ethics. A reviewer says your argument misrepresents a living tradition, and your co-author wants to dismiss the comment.

options.text: Agree with your co-author and thank the reviewer while keeping the paper as it is.
Add a note in the paper that it reflects one reading of the tradition.
Consult scholars from the tradition, revise where needed, and explain the changes to the reviewer.
Remove the reviewer's comments from the file before sending the paper to the editor.

basic.situation: At office hours, a student asks whether they need to believe in a religion to do well in your religion class. You have ten minutes.

options.text: Explain the course studies religion academically and grades reward argument and evidence.
Say students who share your beliefs usually find the course easier to pass.
Tell the student beliefs do not matter and move on to their essay plan.
Suggest the student keep their own views out of discussions and essays this term.

advanced.situation: You advise a student society that wants to host a debate between religious and secular speakers. Members fear it could cause conflict on campus.

options.text: Advise them to cancel the event because it could cause unrest on campus.
Tell them to hold the debate and inform the university after it takes place.
Review university event rules, agree ground rules with speakers, and arrange a neutral moderator.
Suggest they hold the debate online and keep the comments section turned off.

basic.situation: You help with recruitment at a campus open day for the department. A visitor asks which job the programme leads to, and you have limited information.

options.text: Say graduates can work in many areas and leave it at that for now.
Promise the visitor a job in a field of their choice after graduation.
Hand over the department brochure and suggest they look at the website later.
Describe typical paths you know, say what you do not know, and offer contact details.

advanced.situation: You chair a thesis committee. Two members disagree sharply about whether the student's interpretation of a sacred text meets scholarly standards.

options.text: Follow the senior member's view and tell the student to revise the thesis accordingly.
Pass the thesis yourself to avoid the disagreement and report it as unanimous.
Take a vote among the committee at once and tell the student the result.
Ask each member to state criteria, check them against department standards, and guide revisions.

basic.situation: You facilitate a classroom discussion on food labels with a prepared script and instructor support. One student dominates while others stay silent.

options.text: Tell the active student to stop contributing for the rest of the term.
Let the discussion continue since active talkers keep the whole class moving along.
Thank the active student, then invite pairs to discuss and share with the class.
Ask the active student to give others a turn before speaking again in the session.

advanced.situation: You teach graduate students food science and nutrition. A student cites a popular diet claim that research does not support, and several classmates agree.

options.text: Support the claim in class to keep students engaged and test their reaction.
Let the claim stand since diet advice differs widely between experts and countries.
Tell the class the claim is unsupported and give them a reading list.
Have the class review the evidence and compare the claim with published studies.

basic.situation: You prepare a handout on child care safety for a lecture, using the course lead's checklist.

options.text: Copy the checklist onto a single page and print enough copies for the class.
Include safety figures from memory and present them as official statistics in the handout.
Add safety tips from your own home experience to the handout and skip the checklist.
Build the handout from the checklist and ask the course lead to review it.

advanced.situation: You compile a specialised reading list on sustainable consumption for a graduate seminar. Many strong sources are paywalled, and the budget is small.

options.text: List all the sources and tell students to request copies through interlibrary loan.
Choose sources that are free online, even if some of them are weaker.
Share the paywalled articles with students by giving them your own university login details.
Check library licences and open-access versions, request purchases for key items, and flag gaps.

basic.situation: You grade food science lab reports with a rubric. One report has good results but lacks the required safety section.

options.text: Write a safety section into the student's report yourself and then grade it fully.
Apply the rubric deduction for the safety section and explain why it is required.
Deduct the safety marks and return the report with the grade and a note.
Give full marks because the results are good and the lab ran safely.

advanced.situation: You design an exam for a nutrition course taught by three tutors. Last year, tutors graded similar answers very differently.

options.text: Change the whole exam to multiple-choice questions so that tutors cannot mark differently.
Ask tutors to adjust scores after marking so that the three averages match.
Give each tutor the mark scheme and ask them to follow it closely.
Write a detailed mark scheme, train tutors on sample answers, and double-mark a sample.

basic.situation: You help update a family studies course under a senior colleague's supervision. They ask you to refresh the examples in the budgeting unit.

options.text: Create examples with realistic figures and present them as official data in the unit.
Keep the old examples and change the dates and currency symbols in them.
Replace the examples with ones from a news article you remember reading recently.
Find current local examples from official sources and ask your colleague to review.

advanced.situation: You lead a revision of the department's curriculum so it meets new industry standards. Two lecturers resist changing their units.

options.text: Submit the revised curriculum for accreditation as if all the lecturers had agreed.
Revise the units yourself and ask the lecturers to teach them next term.
Leave the two resisting units unchanged and revise the rest of the units.
Compare the units with the standards, show the gaps, and agree changes with each lecturer.

basic.situation: A student at your office hours asks which elective fits their interest in child nutrition. You have the course catalogue open.

options.text: Recommend the elective you teach since you know its content and students well.
Add the student's name to a full elective's list to match their interest.
Point to the catalogue and suggest they pick the elective that sounds closest.
Ask about their interests, show matching electives in the catalogue, and note any prerequisites.

advanced.situation: A student asks you how to start a career in food safety consulting but has no industry contacts. They are anxious about finding a first job.

options.text: Offer to write that they have industry experience on their application to help them.
Tell them to apply to many food safety roles and learn on the job.
Discuss their strengths, outline entry roles and qualifications, and connect them with alumni.
Advise them to start their own consultancy since it avoids the need for contacts.

basic.situation: You help staff a student recruitment event for the department. A parent asks whether graduates find jobs easily, and you are unsure of the figures.

options.text: Give a general answer that graduates usually find jobs within about a year.
Say the department does not track outcomes and suggest they ask other schools.
Say you lack exact figures, share the published outcomes, and offer to follow up.
State a high employment percentage from memory to reassure the parent about the course.

advanced.situation: You sit on a committee deciding academic policy on internship hours. Employers want longer internships, but students worry about workload and pay.

options.text: Support longer internships because employers will then value our graduates much more.
Oppose any change because students are already overloaded with coursework this year.
Gather employer and student input, review workload data, and propose a flexible range of hours.
Tell employers in advance that longer internships are approved before the committee decides.

basic.situation: During your first anatomy lecture, a student asks about a muscle group your slides do not cover, and you are not sure of the answer.

options.text: Answer from memory in a confident tone so the lecture keeps its natural pace.
Give your recollection now and say it may need checking afterwards.
Ask the student to look it up and tell you what they find.
Note the question, check a reliable text, and tell the class next session.

advanced.situation: In your seminar on therapeutic recreation, two students argue loudly about an exercise approach while the rest of the room goes quiet.

options.text: Tell both students to continue after class so the seminar stays on its schedule.
Summarise both positions briefly and ask the group to carry on from there.
Declare the matter settled by your own view and close the discussion.
Ask each student to cite evidence for their view, then open it to the room.

basic.situation: You are grading forty assignments with a rubric. One paper has strong ideas but misses the rubric's referencing requirement.

options.text: Add a few marks for the strong ideas to balance out the missing part.
Give full marks since the work is clearly strong overall and move on to the rest.
Apply the rubric as written and return the mark with a brief comment.
Apply the rubric, note the missing part, and explain the mark in feedback.

advanced.situation: Exam results over three semesters show students scoring low on one conditioning topic. The teaching content for that topic has stayed unchanged for years.

options.text: Review the topic's content and teaching, revise it, and compare next semester's results.
Add extra evening revision sessions on that topic and remind students before the final exam.
Make the exam questions on that topic simpler so the results improve next semester.
Drop that topic from the final exam so the overall results look much healthier.

basic.situation: Your supervisor approves all handouts before they reach students. You have found a clear online diagram that fits next week's topic.

options.text: Check the diagram's usage terms, credit it, and send the draft for approval.
Send the draft for approval with the diagram and a note of its website.
Print the copies now so the class is ready, and show your supervisor later.
Pick a different diagram from your own course notes and send it for approval.

advanced.situation: You are writing a syllabus for a new course starting in six weeks. The department head's learning outcomes do not fully match your preferred topic list.

options.text: Keep your topic list and rewrite the learning outcomes so they fit it.
List the gaps, adjust your topics to the outcomes, and ask the head.
Follow the head's learning outcomes and leave out your own extra topics.
Submit your topic list as the syllabus and raise the gaps if anyone asks.

basic.situation: You are helping a senior lecturer with a literature review on exercise and older adults. Two of the studies you found report conflicting results.

options.text: Pass both studies to the lecturer with a short summary of each.
Average the two results into one figure and present it as the finding.
Include the study that supports the lecturer's current argument and mention it in the review.
Record both studies with their methods and sample sizes, then report the conflict.

advanced.situation: You are drafting a grant proposal for a community fitness study. The funder's deadline is Friday, but your pilot data is incomplete.

options.text: Fill the gaps with estimated figures that match what the pilot should show.
Present the pilot as ongoing, state its limits, and submit a realistic plan.
Submit on time and leave the pilot's limits out to keep the proposal strong.
Ask the funder whether the deadline can move so the pilot data is complete.

basic.situation: In office hours, a student asks whether an elective counts toward their degree requirements. You are not certain of the rule.

options.text: Check the handbook with the student, then confirm with the coordinator first.
Tell the student what you recall from last year's handbook and suggest checking later.
Tell the student it probably counts and suggest they go ahead and enrol.
Tell the student to enrol first and sort any problem out at graduation.

advanced.situation: A final-year student wants to move into physiotherapy after watching videos online. They know little about the entry route, and graduation is a year away.

options.text: Explain the entry route, arrange a talk with a practitioner, and plan next steps.
Tell the student to drop the fitness modules now to focus on the move.
Encourage the student to follow their passion and apply to any programme they like.
Point the student to the postgraduate admissions pages and wish them luck.

basic.situation: At registration week, a student asks to join a class that is already full. You are helping at the desk under a coordinator's supervision.

options.text: Tell the student to attend the first class and ask the lecturer directly.
Add the student to a waiting list and say someone will contact them.
Add the student to the class list yourself since seats are rarely all taken up.
Take their details, explain the class is full, and pass it to the coordinator.

advanced.situation: You chair a departmental committee reviewing recruitment standards. One member proposes lowering the fitness test requirement to attract more applicants.

options.text: Ask the members to vote on the proposal at their next scheduled meeting.
Lower the requirement in the next brochure and inform the committee afterwards.
Check how test results relate to later performance, then share the data.
Support lowering it, since higher enrolment helps the department's budget and its staffing.

basic.situation: A senior teacher asks you to draft a course outline for a new welding module. You have the college's template but not the module's goals.

options.text: Copy a welding outline from another college and submit it as your own draft.
Fill the template using last year's welding outline as your base and send it.
Write goals yourself from a quick online search and submit the outline for review.
Ask the senior teacher for the module goals before filling in the template.

advanced.situation: On the curriculum committee, you learn that a proposed change to the wiring programme cuts practical hours that industry supervisors call essential.

options.text: Voice your concern during the meeting and ask the committee to postpone the vote.
Gather the supervisors' feedback and bring the hours concern to the committee.
Raise your concern quietly with the chair and accept whatever they decide.
Vote through the change and tell the supervisors the decision is already final.

basic.situation: You present a lecture on hydraulic systems using a prepared script and slides. Midway, the projector fails and the slides go dark.

options.text: Give students an early break while you wait for the technician to arrive.
Pause briefly, sketch the key diagram on the whiteboard, and continue the script.
Keep reading the script aloud and promise to share the slides with students afterwards.
End the lecture now and record the topic as covered in the class log.

advanced.situation: You are asked to link the mathematics unit with the automotive workshop course so students see how formulas apply to engine work. The two timetables clash.

options.text: Add a few engine-related problems to the existing mathematics worksheets and keep both timetables.
Swap the two timetables yourself this week and tell the maths lecturer afterwards.
Map the formulas to workshop tasks, then adjust both schedules with the two lecturers.
Teach the maths yourself in the workshop for a month and see how it goes.

basic.situation: While watching a student assemble a circuit, you notice neat soldering but a wiring order that will not work. The student asks how they are doing.

options.text: Tell the student the wiring order needs work and suggest reading the manual again.
Say the circuit is done well so the student stays motivated and leave it there.
Praise the neat soldering, then show the student how to fix the wiring order.
Say the work looks fine overall and mention the order issue next lesson.

advanced.situation: Your programme wants a performance test to show whether the six-week plumbing course works. The available workshop slot is one hour per student.

options.text: Use a written quiz on plumbing terms and compare scores across the cohort.
Give a practical task on the key skills before and after the course.
Pass everyone who attended all six weeks and report a full success rate.
Ask students how confident they feel after the course and report the average.

basic.situation: During a workshop session, a student starts using a grinder with the guard removed because it is quicker. You are the only teacher in the room.

options.text: Let the student finish the cut and discuss safety at the end.
Leave the student to it and finish marking the other students' work.
Stop the student, refit the guard, and explain why it stays on during use.
Remind the student to be careful and stand beside the grinder until finished.

advanced.situation: You guide two junior staff who supervise students on a hotel kitchen placement. Last week a student burned their hand, and the placement has no written safety steps.

options.text: Ask the hotel to take over safety instructions and report back to the college.
Tell the junior staff to watch students more closely during every kitchen task.
Draft a safety protocol with the hotel supervisor, then train staff and students on it.
Keep the placement running as usual and note the burn as a minor event.

basic.situation: You attend a one-day seminar on new electric-vehicle servicing methods. Your senior teacher asks what you learned the next morning.

options.text: Share your seminar notes and the speaker's slides as they were given to you.
Share organised notes, highlight what applies to your courses, and suggest next steps.
Summarise the speaker's main points from memory during the staff tea break.
Say the seminar mostly repeated what you already knew and skip the details.

advanced.situation: A new safety standard for your trade starts next term. Your colleagues teach the old method, and the department cannot afford a full retraining day.

options.text: Wait for the department to announce the change before updating any lessons.
Rewrite your own unit first, then run a short peer session on the changes.
Email colleagues a link to the new standard and ask them to read it.
Teach the old method until students complain, since the standard has not started.

basic.situation: You must assemble the books and tools for a carpentry class using the course checklist. Two listed items are not in the store room.

options.text: Note the missing items, check for alternatives, and tell the lecturer before class.
Prepare what is available and let students find the rest in class.
Borrow similar tools from another workshop and mention it to the lecturer later.
Tick the two items off the checklist so the record looks complete.

advanced.situation: A lathe in the machine shop has broken, and repair quotes cost nearly half your annual equipment budget. Two classes need it next month.

options.text: Move both classes to theory lessons until the budget is renewed next year.
Order the repair from the vendor now and charge it to another budget line.
Compare repair and rental options and put the costs to your head.
Choose the lowest repair quote and ask the head to approve it before ordering.

basic.situation: You follow a provided lesson plan on shapes for a class of five-year-olds. The plan lists the aim, but the children seem unsure what they are meant to do.

options.text: Hold up each shape card and ask the children to name it aloud.
Give the children worksheets to complete alone while you prepare the next lesson.
Tell the children in simple words what they will do and show one example.
Start the activity and let the children work it out as they go.

advanced.situation: You and two teachers are revising the preschool programme. One colleague wants more academic drills, another wants more play, and the principal asked for a draft by Friday.

options.text: Split the week equally between drills and play and send the draft on time.
Submit the version you prefer under all three names to meet Friday's deadline.
Review the children's progress data together and draft a balance of drills and play.
Write the draft yourself in your preferred style and ask the others to sign it.

basic.situation: During free play, you notice a child who rarely speaks to others and often plays alone at the edge of the room.

options.text: Pair the child with a talkative classmate every day and see what happens.
Watch over a few days, write dated notes, and share them with your supervisor.
Write in the records that the child has a language problem and move on.
Make a note today and mention it to the child's parent at pickup.

advanced.situation: Two children in your class still cannot hold a crayon properly while their peers are drawing shapes. Their parents have not raised any concerns.

options.text: Give both children extra drawing worksheets to practise at home every night.
Plan short daily fine-motor games for them, track progress, and share it with parents.
Ask the principal to arrange an outside assessment for both children this term.
Tell the parents the two children are slow learners and may repeat the year.

basic.situation: A classroom rule says children must tidy toys before snack time. Today three children refuse and one starts to cry.

options.text: Stay calm, remind them of the rule, and help them tidy together.
Let the children go to snack today and remind them about tidying tomorrow.
Tell the whole class there is no snack today until every toy is tidy.
Remind them of the rule and tidy the toys yourself to save time.

advanced.situation: A parent volunteer keeps correcting children harshly during craft time, and two children now avoid joining in. You supervise the volunteers.

options.text: Place the volunteer at the supplies table so contact with children is limited.
Talk with the volunteer privately, model the tone you expect, and watch the next session.
Tell the volunteer in front of the parents that they are not welcome back.
Thank the volunteer in front of others and hope the tone improves.

basic.situation: You lead a storytelling and craft session. Halfway through, half the children lose interest and start wandering around the room.

options.text: Switch to a short action song, then return to the story with a prop.
Call the children back and read the rest of the story more loudly.
Let the children who lost interest play in the corner while the rest finish the craft.
End the session and tell the children they lost the right to craft time.

advanced.situation: You are planning a field trip to a local farm for twenty-four preschoolers. The farm has a pond and animals, and you have two adult helpers.

options.text: Send the consent forms home the day before and plan to go regardless.
Tell the children the safety rules on the bus and trust them to follow.
Ask parents to join so there are more adults watching the children.
Visit first, assign each helper a group, and set a head-count routine.

basic.situation: At pickup, a parent asks how their child's day went. The child was happy at play but refused to eat lunch.

options.text: Tell the parent the child ate lunch fine so they do not worry.
Tell the parent the child had a happy day and played well with friends.
Mention the lunch refusal and say the child needs to eat more at school.
Share the happy play and the lunch refusal, and ask about eating at home.

advanced.situation: A speech therapist asks to discuss a child in your class who struggles with speech. You also hold some notes the parents shared in confidence.

options.text: Share your classroom observations, and check with the parents before passing their notes.
Share your classroom observations and keep the parents' notes private for now.
Give the therapist the full file, including the parents' private notes, to save time.
Ask the therapist to request every detail from the parents directly instead.

basic.situation: A child spills juice on their uniform just before storytime. You are the only adult nearby, and spare clothes are in the cubby.

options.text: Take the child to the cubby, help change the clothes, and wash your hands.
Ask another child to help change the clothes while you start the story.
Hand the child the spare clothes and tell them to change quietly alone.
Wipe the uniform with a tissue and let the child sit through storytime.

advanced.situation: Your supply cupboard is nearly empty of paper and crayons, and the inventory record does not match what is on the shelves.

options.text: Count the stock, update the record, and submit a reorder request with the figures.
Adjust the record to match the shelves and say nothing about the earlier gap.
Send a reorder request using the old record figures and update it later.
Ask other classrooms to lend their crayons and paper until the next order arrives.

basic.situation: You are drafting a one-week lesson outline for kindergarten using the school's template. The curriculum guide lists topics but not their weekly order.

options.text: List the topics in the same order as the guide and submit it.
Copy a colleague's outline from last year and change the dates to this week.
Pick the topics you enjoy teaching and submit the outline for the week.
Order topics from simple to harder and ask your head to review it.

advanced.situation: The ministry updates the kindergarten curriculum guide. Three teachers in your team must revise their lesson plans, and one says the old plans still work fine.

options.text: Let that teacher keep the old plans and tell the head they were updated.
Send the team the new guide and ask them to update their plans.
Change the lesson titles to match the new guide and keep the old content.
Compare the old plans with the new guide and show the team the gaps.

basic.situation: You read a picture book to a class of twenty. A few children chat at the back and cannot see the pictures.

options.text: Hold the book higher and keep reading through the whole story.
Send the chatting children to sit apart outside the door for the story.
Read in a louder voice until the chatting at the back fades away.
Pause, invite the children to move closer, and ask a question about the story.

advanced.situation: Your class includes a child who learns slowly, two advanced readers, and many average learners. Today's phonics activity is the same for everyone.

options.text: Prepare three levels of the same activity and rotate support among the groups.
Keep the activity as planned and move the child who struggles to the back.
Give the advanced readers extra books and keep the activity as planned.
Slow the whole activity down to the pace of the slowest child.

basic.situation: Using a checklist, you observe children sharing blocks. One child grabs blocks from others twice in ten minutes.

options.text: Tick the checklist and tell the child to share the blocks next time.
Tick the checklist, add a short dated note, and keep observing.
Leave the checklist blank until you see a clearer pattern next week.
Mark the child as aggressive on the checklist and tell other teachers.

advanced.situation: Standardised results show half your class below the expected level in language. The head wants a plan, and many children speak another language at home.

options.text: Send the scores to parents with a note that the children are behind.
Compare results with classroom observations and home language, then plan targeted language groups.
Plan extra language drills for every child scoring below the expected level.
Report that the whole class is weak in language and ask for extra hours.

basic.situation: Before outdoor play, you prepare the playground. You see a loose swing chain and a wet slide, and class starts in ten minutes.

options.text: Dry the slide quickly and tell the children to use the swing gently.
Keep children off the swing and slide, mark them, and report the damage.
Cone off the swing and dry the slide, then start play on time.
Let the children play on both as usual and watch them from nearby.

advanced.situation: You supervise two new assistants. Yesterday one left a child alone in the toilet area for several minutes while helping another child.

options.text: Keep the incident between you and the assistant to avoid worrying parents.
Remind both assistants to keep eyes on every child in their care.
Tell the assistant to write a report about the incident for your records.
Set a written supervision rule with the assistants and check it during the week.

basic.situation: A parent greets you at the gate and asks how their child's day went. The child joined every activity and made a new friend.

options.text: Say the child did well and suggest they read the weekly newsletter.
Share the new friendship and activities, and ask what the child says at home.
Tell the parent the day was good and thank them for coming.
Tell the parent you have no time and walk to the next group.

advanced.situation: A parent is angry that their child was disciplined for hitting. They arrive early and ask to see you with the principal present.

options.text: Agree to a meeting, share your observation notes, and plan together how to help.
Promise the parent that the other child will be moved to another class.
Ask the principal to speak for you and stay out of the meeting.
Agree to meet but send a written report first so they can prepare.

basic.situation: At the staff meeting, the principal assigns tasks for the school open day. You are asked to help with the registration table.

options.text: Confirm your role, ask what is needed, and offer to prepare the sign-in sheet.
Accept the task and plan to work out the details when you arrive.
Accept the role and ask a colleague to explain what to do on the day.
Pass the task to a new assistant and tell the principal it is covered.

advanced.situation: You lead a committee to align the kindergarten programme with the year-one syllabus. Year-one teachers say your children arrive lacking basic number skills.

options.text: Add more number worksheets to the kindergarten timetable starting next month.
Tell the year-one teachers to adjust their own teaching to your programme.
Ask for examples, compare them with your outcomes, and agree changes together.
Explain that kindergarten should focus on play and refuse the request.

basic.situation: Your mentor asks you to draft a Year 3 science lesson outline with clear objectives for next week's class on plants.

options.text: Leave the objectives blank and let your mentor fill them in after the lesson.
Write the activities first and add the objectives at the end if time allows.
Write objectives as what pupils will do, then check them with your mentor.
Copy the objectives from the textbook chapter into your outline for review.

advanced.situation: Your school adopts new instructional standards for mathematics. Four teachers on your year team must change how they plan lessons, and two openly doubt the change.

options.text: Run a short workshop using one sample lesson and gather the doubters' concerns.
Tell the two doubters their plans will be marked down unless they comply.
Rewrite the team's lesson plans yourself so everyone uses the same format.
Email the new standards to the team and offer help when asked.

basic.situation: During science, two pupils start pushing each other at the back. Your class rule says hands stay to yourself.

options.text: Tell the whole class loudly to stop what they are doing and sit.
Tell the pupils to go outside and settle it between themselves.
Wait a moment to see whether the pushing stops by itself before acting.
Step over, remind them of the rule, and separate them for the activity.

advanced.situation: You are asked to draft safety steps for a new science corner with glassware and hot-water kettles, and to brief a new teacher on enforcing them.

options.text: Brief the new teacher verbally and rely on pupils to follow the rules.
Open the corner now and write the steps once pupils have settled in.
Draft steps with the safety officer and demonstrate them to the new teacher.
Post a rules list near the corner and ask the new teacher to read it.

basic.situation: You are reading a story to a small group while your supervisor watches. A pupil asks what a word means, and another interrupts with a joke.

options.text: Pause the story until the joking pupil agrees to be quiet.
Tell the group no questions are allowed during stories and read faster.
Answer the word question briefly, thank the second pupil, and continue the story.
Answer the question and ask the joking pupil to wait until later.

advanced.situation: You plan a class trip to a local recycling centre. Permission slips are due Monday, and the centre can host twenty pupils, but you have thirty.

options.text: Cancel the trip this term and show a recycling video in class instead.
Choose twenty pupils by lucky draw and tell the others they will do other work.
Take all thirty pupils and hope the centre allows the extra ten.
Ask the centre about two visit slots and plan matching activities for both groups.

basic.situation: You are marking twenty homework books with your mentor's marking guide. One pupil's answer is right but written in a different method.

options.text: Give full marks and write a note praising the pupil's different method.
Change the pupil's answer to match the guide and award the marks.
Check the method is sound, give credit, and tell your mentor.
Mark it down because it does not match the guide's method.

advanced.situation: Standardised results show Year 5 pupils across your school scoring low in reading comprehension, while their classroom grades are high. The head asks you for an explanation.

options.text: Say the test is unreliable and recommend setting this year's results aside.
Explain that classroom grades are inflated and ask teachers to mark harder.
Compare the test with class assessments, review a sample of scripts, then recommend changes.
Adjust this term's classroom grades downward to match the test results.

basic.situation: At the staff meeting, a colleague asks volunteers to help plan the sports day. You are free that week.

options.text: Stay quiet at the meeting and see whether enough other teachers volunteer first.
Volunteer for one clear task, confirm it in writing, and keep the team updated.
Tell the colleague you are busy that week although your diary is empty.
Volunteer and tell the colleague you will do whatever task is needed that day.

advanced.situation: Parents of two pupils complain to each other and the school that your class marking is unfair. They request a joint meeting with several teachers present.

options.text: Prepare marking evidence, listen to both parents, and agree on a follow-up plan.
Ask the head to meet the parents and keep your distance.
Tell the parents the marking scheme is confidential and cannot be discussed.
Meet each parent separately and explain your marking criteria to them in detail.

basic.situation: Your senior teacher asks you to label the shelves and storage boxes in the classroom before the new term starts.

options.text: Label everything in your own clear style so the room is ready early.
Label the shelves this week and leave the boxes for later.
Move supplies around to suit you and label them after term starts.
Ask what labelling style the senior teacher prefers, then label to match.

advanced.situation: You manage the classroom inventory and train two assistants on record-keeping. Last term, the stock record and actual counts differed by thirty items.

options.text: Set up a sign-out sheet and train both assistants to use it.
Ask the assistants to be more careful when they take items.
Write off the thirty missing items in the record and carry on.
Do a full recount yourself at each term end and update the record.

basic.situation: Your mentor gives you a lesson template. You must outline a Form 1 history unit on early Malay kingdoms using the curriculum document.

options.text: Reuse an old unit plan from another school and change the title.
Build the unit around interesting videos you found and add the standards later.
Match each lesson to a curriculum standard and ask your mentor to review.
Outline the lessons around the textbook chapters and check the standards afterwards.

advanced.situation: You are on a team revising the school-wide science curriculum. A senior teacher proposes cutting practical work to save time, and several junior teachers disagree but stay silent.

options.text: Record the proposal as agreed by all and send it to the head.
Invite the junior teachers to share their views, then bring examples to the team.
Ask the senior teacher to explain the reasons for the cut to the team.
Accept the proposal since the senior teacher has more experience in teaching.

basic.situation: You mark a stack of Form 2 maths homework. Several pupils made the same mistake on fractions.

options.text: Mark the work, note the common mistake, and reteach the fractions step next lesson.
Give those pupils full marks since so many made the same error.
Mark the work and mention the mistake briefly to the class at the end.
Mark the work and write the right answer on each pupil's page.

advanced.situation: Standardised results show your Form 3 science classes score well on facts but poorly on data analysis. Another teacher says the test is unfair.

options.text: Add more data tables to the weekly homework starting from next week.
Tell pupils the test results do not matter so they stay relaxed.
Check results by question type, then plan data-analysis practice for your classes.
Agree the test is unfair and stop using its results in planning.

basic.situation: At the start of class, three pupils are still talking loudly. Your class routine says pupils sit silently once the teacher raises a hand.

options.text: Raise your voice until the pupils are quiet and ready to begin.
Give the three pupils extra homework in front of the class straight away.
Wait calmly, praise pupils who are ready, and restate the routine.
Start the lesson and talk over the noise for a few minutes.

advanced.situation: You are mentoring a new teacher whose class uses the school workshop's saws and drills. Two pupils have been bumped by others near the machines.

options.text: Tell the new teacher to line pupils up and keep them calm.
Remind pupils at the start of each session to move carefully near machines.
Move the workshop sessions to the corridor where there is more space.
Draw a floor plan with safe zones, then walk the new teacher through it.

basic.situation: You plan to show a short video in class. When you start the lesson, the sound on the classroom computer does not work.

options.text: Play the video with subtitles on and hope pupils follow the story.
Skip the video and tell pupils it will be tested in the exam.
Ask a pupil to fetch the school technician while the class waits quietly.
Try the quick fixes, and if they fail, read the transcript aloud with pictures.

advanced.situation: You plan a visit by a guest speaker from a local company for 120 pupils, but the speaker may talk above their level and the hall is noisy.

options.text: Send the speaker the topic and ask them to keep it simple and short.
Meet the speaker beforehand, share the pupils' level, and prepare questions for them.
Let the speaker present freely and explain difficult words afterwards in class.
Skip the briefing and let the speaker decide how long they talk.

basic.situation: At a parent meeting, you must share a pupil's progress report with their parents. The report shows low marks in two subjects.

options.text: Present the marks with examples of work, and note the pupil's strengths too.
Tell the parents the pupil may be moved down a class next term.
Tell the parents the pupil is lazy and needs stronger discipline at home.
Hand over the report and ask the parents to read it carefully.

advanced.situation: A pupil's marks and attendance have dropped, and the counsellor says there are problems at home. Parents ask to see you and the counsellor together.

options.text: Meet the parents with the counsellor and focus on attendance and marks.
Plan the meeting with the counsellor first, then share concerns and agree support steps.
Share the counsellor's notes about the pupil's home problems during the meeting.
Let the counsellor handle the meeting while you send your marks beforehand.

basic.situation: You are asked to organise your classroom materials and file basic student records before inspection day. Your supervisor is away until tomorrow.

options.text: Organise the materials, file the records, and list gaps for your supervisor.
Fill the missing record entries from memory so the files look complete.
Ask a pupil to help file the records so you finish earlier.
File the records and leave the materials as they are until tomorrow.

advanced.situation: As a committee lead, you are asked to improve how extracurricular clubs get funds. Clubs complain of slow approvals and unclear amounts.

options.text: Map the approval steps, find the delays, and propose a clear funding timeline.
Approve every request yourself from now on to speed things up.
Skip the approval step for the clubs that have complained the most.
Set a fixed yearly amount for each club and announce it to everyone.

basic.situation: You are drafting a lesson outline for a Form 1 basic cooking unit using the curriculum guide. Your supervisor will review it.

options.text: Copy the textbook's cooking lessons in order and send them for review.
Plan fun recipes the class would like and fit the standards later.
Skip the outline and teach from memory, since the supervisor will watch later.
Align each lesson with a curriculum standard and note safety points for review.

advanced.situation: A new ministry curriculum standard for technical subjects arrives. Your colleagues must update their course outlines, and you have been asked to guide them.

options.text: Send colleagues the new standard and a blank outline template to complete.
Tell colleagues the old outlines remain valid until someone raises a complaint.
Update the outlines for them in one weekend and send them back.
Compare old outlines with the standard, then run a short gap session.

basic.situation: You demonstrate how to use a hand drill to Form 2 pupils. Some pupils at the back cannot see the demonstration.

options.text: Regroup the class around the bench and repeat the demonstration step by step.
Carry on with the demonstration and tell pupils to watch a video later.
Describe each step aloud louder and ask the back pupils to listen.
Ask the back pupils to stand on chairs to get a better view.

advanced.situation: Four pupils in your Form 2 class struggle to read the instructions in workshop manuals. The next project begins in two weeks.

options.text: Plan short reading support with picture steps and track progress each task.
Move the four pupils to a different class and tell the parents later.
Pair each struggling pupil with a stronger reader for the project.
Read all manual instructions aloud to the whole class during every lesson.

basic.situation: You grade a worksheet with an answer key. One pupil's answer is not on the key but looks reasonable.

options.text: Give the mark and add a comment inviting the pupil to explain.
Give all pupils full marks on that question so nobody complains later.
Mark it down since it does not appear on the answer key.
Check the answer against the lesson notes, then confirm with your supervisor.

advanced.situation: Your department's grading rewards the final project mark. Pupils who improve a lot but finish a weak project score low, and you are asked to propose a change.

options.text: Replace the final project mark with the average of two quick quizzes.
Add a participation score on top of the final project mark for everyone.
Raise every pupil's project mark by ten percent to be fair.
Pilot a rubric that scores progress and final work, then review the results.

basic.situation: A new pupil tells you privately that they feel lost in the workshop class because others already know the tools.

options.text: Tell the pupil to practise at home and ask questions if needed.
Reassure the pupil that everyone feels lost at first and carry on.
Listen, pair the pupil with a friendly classmate, and check in weekly.
Tell the class which pupil said they feel lost so others can help.

advanced.situation: A pupil's behaviour has worsened, and the parents blame the teachers, while the counsellor and the head each want different actions. You are asked to lead a meeting.

options.text: Share the facts with everyone, hear each view, and agree one plan with owners.
Meet the parents alone first and promise them a quick solution.
Write in the minutes that the counsellor caused the pupil's behaviour to worsen.
Let the head decide the action and inform the parents afterwards.

basic.situation: Before a sewing class, your assistant helps you set up. You have twenty machines, but three have loose needles.

options.text: Take the three machines out of use, tag them, and report them.
Use all twenty machines and tell the pupils to sew slowly and carefully.
Tighten the needles on the three machines yourself and start the class.
Tell pupils to avoid the three machines unless they have no choice.

advanced.situation: You are asked to review the full workshop equipment inventory and check safety standards before an inspection. Several tools are missing safety guards.

options.text: Remove unguarded tools from use, record them, and order replacement guards.
Remove the missing guards from the inventory list so the records look complete.
Order replacement guards for the tools and tell staff to wait for them.
Mark the unguarded tools with a warning sticker and keep them in service.

basic.situation: At the department meeting, the head asks everyone to help prepare a report for the school board. You are asked to assist with record-keeping.

options.text: Estimate the attendance numbers from memory so the report is ready sooner.
Ask what format is needed, collect the attendance records, and share a draft.
Wait for the head to give you more detailed instructions first.
Collect the attendance records and pass them to the head as they are.

advanced.situation: As lead on programme evaluation, you find that two teachers' student records do not meet the school's reporting policy. The report to the head is due soon.

options.text: Ask the two teachers to fix the records before the report goes out.
Meet the two teachers, agree a fix and timeline, and report the issue and plan.
Leave the issue out of the report and avoid any awkward conversation.
Fix the two teachers' records yourself and leave them out of the report.

basic.situation: You prepare a Form 4 chemistry lesson outline from the curriculum guidelines. Your head of department asks to see it on Friday.

options.text: Map each lesson to a guideline topic and share the draft by Thursday.
List the textbook chapters in order and share the draft on Friday.
Begin with experiments your class would enjoy and add the topics later.
Hand in an outline copied from the exam bank and rename its headings.

advanced.situation: You join a team revising the secondary school science programme. Teachers disagree on whether to add a project component, and the principal wants a proposal soon.

options.text: Write the proposal with your own option and present it as the team's view.
Ask the principal to choose between the options to settle the disagreement.
Support the option most teachers prefer and write up the proposal for the principal.
Gather pupils' needs, compare options with the team, and propose a pilot.

basic.situation: You are teaching a lecture on fractions in Form 1 maths with a teacher watching. Halfway through, you realise one example on the board has an error.

options.text: Leave the example as it is and mention the error after class.
Rub out the example quietly and write a new one while talking.
Pause, fix the example on the board, and tell the class what changed.
Tell the class the example was meant to trick them and carry on.

advanced.situation: You plan a field trip to a river for a geography project. The river has strong currents after rain, and the forecast shows storms on the trip day.

options.text: Check the forecast again, then move the date or offer a classroom alternative.
Keep the date and brief pupils on safety rules at the river.
Keep the date and let pupils decide how close they go to the water.
Keep the date but stay on the bank and keep pupils behind a rope.

basic.situation: You grade a class set of Form 3 homework. One pupil's answers look identical to a classmate's, down to the same spelling mistake.

options.text: Give both a low mark and tell the class not to copy.
Give the pupil you think copied zero and tell the class who it was.
Compare the two pieces, then speak to both pupils before deciding marks.
Mark both as normal and add a note asking them to work separately.

advanced.situation: Standardised results show weak performance in algebra across all Form 4 classes. The head asks you to identify student needs and report soon.

options.text: Remove the weakest classes' scores from the data so the average improves.
Report the overall average score and suggest extra algebra homework for all classes.
Break the results into algebra topics, then list needs for each topic.
Blame the previous year's teachers in the report and ask for new staff.

basic.situation: A pupil who uses a wheelchair cannot reach the ground-floor science lab through the usual door because a trolley blocks it.

options.text: Move the trolley, make sure the path is clear, and tell the pupil.
Ask the pupil to use a different door and wait outside meanwhile.
Ask two classmates to lift the wheelchair over the trolley to save time.
Hold the class in a different room until the trolley is moved.

advanced.situation: A pupil keeps failing tests and skipping classes. The counsellor, the parents and another teacher each suggest a different action, and the pupil says nothing.

options.text: Call a short meeting, share what each person sees, and agree a plan.
Tell the pupil they will fail the year if they do not change.
Wait until the end of term to see whether marks improve.
Follow the counsellor's advice and tell the others about it later.

basic.situation: At parents' day, a parent asks how their child is doing. The child is average in most subjects and good at art.

options.text: Say the child is doing fine and shows promise in art.
Tell the parent the child is among the top pupils in the class.
Share the average marks and the art strength, and ask about interests.
Show the marks sheet and ask the parent to read it later.

advanced.situation: You lead a meeting with parents about resources for pupils in the school's technical stream. Parents have different priorities, and the budget is limited.

options.text: Ask parents to rank priorities, then match them to the budget in the meeting.
Present the school's own priority list and invite parents' comments afterwards by email.
Promise parents everything they ask for and sort out the budget later.
Pick the priority supported by the loudest parents and plan for it.

basic.situation: Before a Form 2 science practical, you set up the lab. You find only twelve working microscopes for fifteen pupils.

options.text: Pair pupils on twelve microscopes, rotate turns, and report the faulty ones.
Pair pupils on twelve microscopes and carry on with the planned lesson.
Postpone the practical for a week and show a video in class.
Let three pupils use the broken microscopes and note the results anyway.

advanced.situation: A pupil with dyslexia and a pupil who learns English as a second language are in your Form 3 class. Your standard worksheets use long dense paragraphs.

options.text: Give the two pupils extra time and keep the worksheets as they are.
Ask the pupils' parents to help with the worksheets at home.
Rewrite the worksheets with shorter text and visuals, and test them with both.
Move both pupils to the back so they do not slow others.

basic.situation: You demonstrate how to measure and cut wood to a group of Form 4 pupils. Your step-by-step guide has ten steps, but time is short.

options.text: Skip the demonstration and let pupils start cutting using the written guide.
Talk through all ten steps quickly and let pupils practise later.
Show the first five steps and give the remaining steps on a sheet.
Show every key step, check understanding at two points, and shorten the practice.

advanced.situation: You are asked to design an occupational training programme for a new hospitality course and set standards other teachers will follow. Local hotels have different expectations.

options.text: Copy a programme from a college and adapt the course names.
Base the whole programme on the largest hotel's requirements and share it widely.
Survey the hotels, set shared skills standards, and test the plan with colleagues.
Tell other teachers to follow your own plan and skip the hotel feedback.

basic.situation: You grade a set of workshop theory homework. Some pupils handed work in two days late with no reason given.

options.text: Add marks to the late work so pupils and parents do not complain.
Grade the work and remind pupils about deadlines at the next lesson.
Grade the work, apply the school's late policy, and ask pupils for reasons.
Give the late pupils zero marks, since the deadline was clearly stated.

advanced.situation: You are building a standardised assessment for the electrical wiring course so other teachers can grade consistently. Early drafts get very different scores from two graders.

options.text: Raise the lower grader's marks to match the higher grader every time.
Use a single grader for all papers from now on to avoid differences.
Write a scoring guide with examples, then have graders mark sample work and compare.
Tell graders to discuss any differences and settle them using their own judgement.

basic.situation: In the metal workshop, pupils must wear goggles during grinding. One pupil forgets them while others are working at full speed.

options.text: Shout across the room for everyone to check that goggles are on.
Hand the pupil a spare pair later and let the work continue.
Stop the grinding, make sure the pupil puts goggles on, and then restart.
Call the pupil to the side and remind them to wear goggles next time.

advanced.situation: Your department has no written safety procedures for the automotive workshop, and two near-miss accidents occurred this term. You are asked to propose a policy.

options.text: Draft procedures with staff input, include training and records, and submit for approval.
Tell staff not to report near misses so the record stays clean.
Copy another school's safety policy and send it to the head today.
Post a list of warnings on the wall and brief pupils verbally.

basic.situation: Your teacher mentor asks you to prepare a draft outline for the Form 4 electronics course using the provided templates.

options.text: Follow the template, map each unit to a curriculum guideline, and ask for feedback.
Reuse last year's outline from another school and put your own name on it.
Follow the template and fill in the units straight from the textbook contents.
Fill in the template with units you personally find most interesting to teach.

advanced.situation: You lead the revision of the school's technical programme and plan work-experience placements. Local workshops offer fewer places than you have pupils.

options.text: Place pupils with the available workshops by a lucky draw this term.
Send extra pupils to placements that have not agreed to take them.
Let each pupil find a placement on their own and report back.
Contact more workshops, rotate pupils through placements, and rank placements by relevance.

basic.situation: A parent asks you about their child's progress in the carpentry class. You are new and your senior teacher is nearby.

options.text: Tell the parent the child will fail unless they get a private tutor.
Share the child's progress from your notes and ask your senior to add more.
Say the child is doing well and the senior teacher will add details.
Ask the parent to come back when the senior teacher is free.

advanced.situation: A final-year pupil in your welding class wants a job but has no certificate yet. A local workshop offers work, but its safety record is poor.

options.text: Tell the pupil about the workshop and wish them luck in the job.
Advise the pupil to wait for a certificate before looking for work.
Discuss the pupil's goals, check the workshop's safety, and use placement services.
Place the pupil at the workshop and leave out the safety record.

basic.situation: At a staff meeting, a senior teacher assigns a joint task to build a display for the school fair. You are told to collect materials.

options.text: Ask the senior teacher for a materials list and a deadline, then start.
Take the materials you need from the workshop store and record it later.
Collect materials you think will look good and bring them along.
Wait for another teacher to share the materials list with the group first.

advanced.situation: You mentor new teachers and lead a development session on working with administrators on programme revisions. A new teacher complains that the administrator does not listen to their ideas.

options.text: Show how to present ideas with evidence and invite the administrator into planning.
Tell the new teacher to send ideas by email to the administrator.
Advise the new teacher to wait until they have more experience.
Tell the new teacher to bypass administrators and take ideas to the parents.

basic.situation: A senior teacher asks you to draft the goals section of an individual education plan for a four-year-old with delayed speech.

options.text: Write small goals based on the child's observed skills and ask for review.
Write the goals from age norms and send them for review.
Write ambitious goals for the child to speak in full sentences within a month.
Use goals from another child's plan with similar delays and adjust names.

advanced.situation: You lead a meeting on a child's complex plan with the parents, a speech therapist and a social worker. The parents and the therapist disagree on priorities.

options.text: Follow the therapist's priorities since they hold the specialist training and records.
Ask each to explain their priorities, then agree on ordered goals with the parents.
Write the plan with your own priorities and ask everyone to sign.
Postpone the plan until the parents and therapist agree by themselves.

basic.situation: You arrange the classroom for a morning of play with children who have mobility needs. The room has toys and low tables close together.

options.text: Leave the room as arranged and ask the assistants to help children move around.
Stack extra toys on high shelves so the children stay seated and safe.
Widen the walkways, move extra furniture aside, and place toys within easy reach.
Move the tables to the walls and keep the toys on top.

advanced.situation: You must modify the preschool curriculum for a child with limited vision and train two assistants on adapted setups. The class theme this month is colours.

options.text: Skip the colour theme for the child and let them play alone.
Add touch, sound, and contrast activities to the colour theme and train assistants.
Give the child separate sound toys in a corner during colour time.
Describe the colours verbally to the child during each activity.

basic.situation: A child with special needs needs feeding help at lunch. You are new, and the child coughs when the spoon goes in too quickly.

options.text: Ask the child to eat alone at the table to avoid the coughing.
Slow down, sit the child upright, and ask a senior to show you.
Keep feeding at the same pace so lunch finishes before nap time.
Slow down and feed small spoonfuls to the child until lunch is finished.

advanced.situation: You guide assistants on the use of a child's walking frame and standing support. One assistant says the frame is unsafe, another says it is fine.

options.text: Check the device against the therapist's instructions and show both assistants safe use.
Put the frame away until the next therapy visit next month.
Tell the assistants to follow the more experienced person's advice.
Let the assistant who says it is fine continue using it unchecked.

basic.situation: During play, a child with autism covers their ears and cries when the music starts. You are asked to note incidents.

options.text: Record that the child cried and ask for the music to be turned down.
Record the time, trigger, and response, then share the notes with the teacher.
Record that the child was upset for the day and move on.
Stop the music for the whole class and skip recording the incident.

advanced.situation: Incident logs show most outbursts happen right after transitions between activities. You are asked to revise programme policies and coach staff.

options.text: Tell staff to remove children who have outbursts to a quiet room alone.
Remind staff to speak calmly when moving children to new activities.
Analyse the log pattern, add transition warnings and visual cues, and coach staff.
Shorten the day by cutting the activities that follow transitions.

basic.situation: You are teaching hand-washing steps to preschoolers with special needs, supported by your supervisor. One child refuses to put hands under water.

options.text: Wash your own hands slowly as an example and ask the child to copy.
Show the steps again, let the child touch water gently, and praise each step.
Wipe the child's hands with a wet cloth instead of using the sink.
Hold the child's hands under the running tap until they stop resisting.

advanced.situation: You develop a social-skills programme for children who push and grab. Another teacher wants a punishment chart, but the children are three years old.

options.text: Use the chart for a trial month and see whether it helps.
Use positive reinforcement with visual rewards and coach the other teacher on it.
Use the chart and display it by the door where all parents see it.
Add a sharing game and keep the chart for the worst cases.

basic.situation: At a team meeting with a parent, you take notes. The parent worries aloud about their child not speaking at home.

options.text: Stop writing and offer the parent your own advice from your experience.
Write down the exact concern, ask follow-up questions, and share notes after.
Write a short summary of the concern and tidy it later.
Write down what the parent says and pass the notes to the teacher.

advanced.situation: You advise administrators on revising the preschool programme after parent complaints about too little therapy time. The budget cannot grow.

options.text: Add therapy time by shortening free play across all classes.
Move some children to other programmes to free therapy hours quietly.
Review how therapy hours are used, trial a new schedule, and share data.
Tell parents the budget is fixed and therapy time cannot change.

basic.situation: You teach letter sounds to a kindergarten child with a learning disability, using a technique your mentor showed you. The child keeps mixing up two letters.

options.text: Move on to the next letters and return to these much later.
Repeat the same drill more times each day until the child gets it.
Tell the child to try harder and stop the lesson if they cry.
Repeat the sounds with pictures and touch, in short rounds, and note progress.

advanced.situation: You design strategies for a class with children who have autism, hearing loss and attention difficulties. You have one assistant and little planning time.

options.text: Plan lessons for the average child and let the assistant handle the rest.
Teach the whole class in the usual way and adapt later.
Use one strategy that works for the child with the greatest needs.
Group children by needs, set visual routines, and give the assistant clear roles.

basic.situation: You help test a kindergarten child's skills and record basic data. The score sheet has a blank for one section the child did not finish.

options.text: Fill in a middle score since the child did the first half.
Copy the answers from the child's previous test to complete the sheet.
Leave the section marked incomplete, add a note, and arrange another session.
Leave the section marked incomplete and hand the sheet to the teacher quickly.

advanced.situation: You review records for a child whose evaluation notes were written by different staff over a year. Some entries are missing dates, and the school must meet legal record rules.

options.text: Ask the writers to add the missing dates when they next have time.
Flag the missing dates, ask each writer to confirm entries, and update the file.
Store the file as it is and mention the gaps if someone asks.
Add the likely dates yourself from memory so the file looks complete.

basic.situation: You arrange materials for a morning free-play session for children with special needs. A shelf holds small beads and button toys beside blocks.

options.text: Add more beads to the shelf since the children enjoy sorting them.
Keep the beads where they are and tell children not to put them in mouths.
Put the beads in a box on the floor so children can explore.
Move the small beads to a high shelf and keep large blocks within reach.

advanced.situation: You modify the kindergarten curriculum for a child who uses sign language, while sharing limited resources among three special-needs groups.

options.text: Give the child with the most visible needs first use of resources.
Prepare sign cards for the child and keep resource sharing as before.
Add sign-supported lessons and rotate the shared resources on a posted schedule.
Take the newest resources for the child's group and share what remains.

basic.situation: You join an IEP meeting for a kindergarten child with a supervisor present. A parent asks you a question about the child's reading level.

options.text: Share what you observed, then pass the technical part to your supervisor.
Give a general answer from memory and move on to the next topic.
Tell the parent a reading level that you think sounds likely for age.
Say you are not sure and ask the parent to wait for the report.

advanced.situation: You lead IEP development for a child with several needs and guide a new teacher through it. The parents want goals the school cannot resource.

options.text: Set smaller goals than the parents asked for and explain later.
Write the goals as requested and ask the head to find resources.
Agree to all the goals in the meeting and leave resourcing to chance.
Explain resource limits openly and agree on goals the school can meet plus referrals.

basic.situation: A kindergarten child with special needs throws blocks during circle time. The class rule is gentle hands, and a lead teacher supervises you.

options.text: Calmly take the blocks, say gentle hands, and offer a quiet activity.
Take away the child's snack for the day so the rule is learned.
Tell the child firmly to stop and sit at the side of the circle.
Continue the circle time and let the lead teacher deal with it.

advanced.situation: You supervise two assistants and set behavior policies for a special-needs kindergarten class. One assistant physically holds a child's arms to calm them.

options.text: Ask the assistant to use holding when the child is very upset.
Say nothing, since the child calmed down and no one complained.
Remind the assistant to hold the children more gently when calming them.
Stop the practice, retrain the assistant on approved calming methods, and update the policy.

basic.situation: Your school sends you to a one-day workshop on teaching children with hearing loss. Your supervisor asks you to attend all sessions.

options.text: Attend all sessions, take notes, and share two ideas to try at school.
Attend all sessions and keep your notes to yourself until asked later.
Attend all sessions and place the handouts in the staff room folder.
Attend the interesting sessions and leave early to catch up on other work.

advanced.situation: You mentor teachers and help bring new assistive technology into your programme. A tablet communication app is available but costs a lot, and staff are unsure.

options.text: Buy a cheaper app with fewer features and tell staff to use it.
Ask the supplier for a demonstration for staff and then recommend buying it.
Order the app for every class this month and train the staff afterwards.
Run a short trial with two children, record results, and train staff first.

basic.situation: You prepare objectives and an outline for a Year 2 reading lesson for pupils with learning disabilities. The curriculum guideline lists broad outcomes.

options.text: Plan activities you like first and list objectives to match them.
Use last year's objectives from another class and change the date and title.
Break the outcomes into small steps for these pupils and ask your mentor.
Copy the outcomes from the curriculum guideline straight into the outline.

advanced.situation: You are asked to lead a school-wide programme for pupils with various disabilities. Teachers use different methods, and parents say pupils receive uneven support.

options.text: Survey current methods, set shared procedures with teachers, and review pupil results.
Choose the most popular method and tell all teachers to use it.
Tell parents the differences are normal and that support cannot be equal.
Write a long handbook of procedures and send it to every teacher.

basic.situation: You set up the classroom with exploration materials for pupils with learning disabilities. The supply list includes small magnets, and one pupil still puts items in their mouth.

options.text: Keep the magnets on a high shelf and hand them out when watching.
Give that pupil the magnets alone at a table to keep them calm.
Put out the magnets and remind that pupil not to chew things.
Swap the small magnets for larger safe items and tell your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You set behaviour rules for a diverse class, where one pupil with sensory needs reacts badly to loud bells and group clapping. Other pupils like clapping.

options.text: Stop clapping for the whole class so the pupil stays comfortable.
Allow the pupil to wear ear protection during clapping and bell times.
Tell the pupil to get used to the noise like everyone else.
