Add a quiet signal that works for everyone and explain it to the class.

basic.situation: You administer a standardised test to a pupil with special needs. The pupil becomes tired halfway and starts answering at random.

options.text: Offer water and a short stretch, then carry on with the test.
Pause the test, give a break, and continue later following the test rules.
Fill in the remaining answers yourself so the test finishes on time.
Finish the test as quickly as you can and record the score.

advanced.situation: Test results for a pupil show low reading but high listening comprehension. The parents think the child is lazy and want the results kept private.

options.text: Agree the child is lazy and note that in the pupil's file.
Explain the pattern, show strengths, and plan reading supports with the parents.
Tell the parents the pupil needs more practice at home.
Send the parents the test report with a short note.

basic.situation: You confer with other teachers to plan next week's lessons for pupils with special needs, following the approved curriculum.

options.text: Agree the schedule and plan your own lessons separately for each pupil.
Let the other teachers make the plan and join in on the day.
Share pupil notes, agree topics and times, and write the plan down.
Change the agreed timetable after the meeting and tell the others later.

advanced.situation: You coordinate placing a pupil with special needs into a mainstream class. The mainstream teacher is worried about the extra workload.

options.text: Plan the support together, define the teacher's role, and review after two weeks.
Place the pupil in the class and not tell the teacher about their needs.
Place the pupil and send a list of tips to the teacher.
Place the pupil and offer to answer questions as they arise.

basic.situation: You teach pupils with disabilities how to wash hands and stay safe in the canteen queue. One pupil forgets the steps each day.

options.text: Tell the pupil they cannot go to the canteen until they remember.
Repeat the verbal steps louder each time the pupil forgets.
Use picture cards at the sink, practise daily, and praise each finished step.
Do the hand washing for the pupil when they forget.

advanced.situation: A pupil wants to be independent but relies heavily on the teacher assistant. You teach goal setting and self-advocacy.

options.text: Remove the assistant completely tomorrow and see how the pupil copes.
Praise the pupil whenever they ask the assistant for help.
Set small independence goals with the pupil and reduce assistance step by step.
Tell the assistant to step back from the pupil gradually.

basic.situation: At a meeting, a parent of a pupil with special needs asks where they can find community support services.

options.text: Say you do not know of any services and end the meeting.
Give a short list of local services, explain each, and offer help.
Tell the parent to ask the school office for information.
Suggest the parent search online and try a few options.

advanced.situation: You monitor teacher assistants to make sure they follow the special education programme. One assistant often leaves pupils with disabilities alone while preparing materials.

options.text: Do the monitoring yourself and keep the incident out of the records.
Remind all assistants in the staff meeting to stay with pupils at all times.
Move the assistant to preparing materials full time away from pupils.
Observe a session, share notes with the assistant, and set supervision steps.

basic.situation: A senior teacher asks you to write the learning goals section of a Form 1 pupil's IEP using the assessment report.

options.text: Base each goal on the report, make it measurable, and ask for review.
Copy the goals from the pupil's last IEP and update the year.
Write general goals such as improve reading and do better in class.
Write goals from a template for the same disability and skip reading the report.

advanced.situation: You lead the team to finalise a complex IEP and guide a new teacher on compliance. The parents bring a private psychologist's report that disagrees with the school's testing.

options.text: Review both reports with the team, consult the psychologist, and update the plan.
Add the psychologist's report to the file and keep the school's plan.
Remove the psychologist's report from the file to avoid confusion at the meeting.
Tell the parents that the school's own testing is the one that counts.

basic.situation: You deliver a Form 2 science lesson with a prepared plan for pupils with learning disabilities. After five minutes, the class looks confused by the terminology.

options.text: Repeat the same explanation more slowly and carry on with the topic.
Stop, define the key terms with pictures, and check understanding quickly.
Hand out the glossary and ask the class to read quietly.
Speed up the lesson to finish the topic before the bell.

advanced.situation: You design new instructional strategies and mentor a peer. A pupil with a language disorder misses most spoken instructions but follows written ones.

options.text: Pair written instructions with visuals, trial it, and show your peer the results.
Stop speaking instructions to the whole class to suit the pupil.
Ask the pupil to find a classmate who will repeat the spoken instructions.
Give the pupil written instructions each lesson and keep other plans.

basic.situation: You give a simple spelling test to a pupil and record scores under supervision. The pupil seems nervous and scores lower than usual.

options.text: Record the score, add a note about nervousness, and tell your supervisor.
Record the score and tell the pupil to relax next time.
Record the usual score from last week instead of today's score.
Record the score and offer the pupil a chance to retake later.

advanced.situation: Standardised test data for your class shows strengths in maths and weakness in comprehension. You must guide a long-term development plan for each pupil.

options.text: Wait for next year's data before making any long-term plans.
Give every pupil the same plan to save time on preparation.
Review each pupil's profile, set short targets, and review progress every term.
Plan extra comprehension lessons for the whole class this term.

basic.situation: You assist in teaching hygiene routines to pupils with special needs. A pupil refuses to brush teeth after lunch and cries when you insist.

options.text: Stay calm, show the steps on a picture card, and try again later.
Hold the pupil's head still and brush their teeth to finish quickly.
Let the pupil watch a classmate brush first, then ask again.
Tell the pupil it is a school rule and they must brush.

advanced.situation: You design a life skills curriculum on food preparation and train staff. Some pupils have allergies, and kitchen sessions use real knives.

options.text: Train staff on knife use first and handle allergies when they come up.
Start the sessions this week and update the plan from what happens.
Check allergy records, set clear safety steps, and train staff on both first.
Use plastic knives and tell staff to watch the allergy list.

basic.situation: At a parent meeting, you take notes while the head of department talks with a parent about their child's progress.

options.text: Note the parent's priorities and questions, and share them with the teacher.
Write the head's comments and file the notes in the pupil's folder.
Record the meeting on your phone and keep the file for yourself.
Write a short summary of the head's comments in your own words.

advanced.situation: A family and a teacher are in conflict. The parents say the teacher ignores the pupil's needs, while the teacher says the parents expect too much.

options.text: Tell the teacher to apologise to the parents in writing.
Side with the parents in the meeting minutes to calm the situation.
Meet each side separately and report the answer back to the other.
Meet them together, set ground rules, and agree on actions for each side.

basic.situation: Following the teacher's step-by-step instructions, you label the shelves. One instruction says to label a shelf for glue, but that shelf already holds scissors.

options.text: Put the scissors in a drawer and label the shelf however you like.
Label the shelf for glue and leave the scissors where they are.
Ask the teacher what to do with the scissors, then label the shelf.
Label the shelf for glue and move the scissors to another shelf.

advanced.situation: You supervise teacher assistants on inclusive programme requirements. A new assistant treats a pupil with disabilities differently, giving less feedback than to others.

options.text: Ask the other assistants to cover that pupil from now on.
Tell the assistant in front of the pupils that they are being unfair.
Observe, share specific examples, and agree with the assistant on daily feedback goals.
Remind the assistant to give every pupil the same feedback.

basic.situation: A senior teacher asks you to help draft a Form 3 pupil's IEP using a learning-needs checklist.

options.text: List the checklist needs in the plan and add goals later on.
Write goals from the pupil's marks and skip the checklist items.
Match each need on the checklist to a goal, then ask for review.
Write goals from another pupil's plan that has a similar profile and submit.

advanced.situation: You coordinate placing a pupil with special needs into a mainstream Form 4 class. Two subject teachers refuse, saying they lack training, and the term begins Monday.

options.text: Arrange short training and support for both teachers, then phase the pupil in.
Escalate to the head and wait for a decision before doing anything.
Place the pupil in the other classes and revisit these two later.
Place the pupil in both classes and tell the teachers to adapt.

basic.situation: You use a special education technique under supervision to teach word recognition. A pupil gets frustrated and pushes the flash cards away.

options.text: Put the cards away and move on to a different subject.
Pause, switch to a picture-based game for the same words, and try again.
Return the cards after a pause and ask the pupil to keep trying.
Tell the pupil that pushing cards away means a lower grade.

advanced.situation: You modify the general curriculum with new technology for pupils with disabilities and train other teachers. Many teachers are reluctant to change their worksheets.

options.text: Send teachers a guide on modifying worksheets and ask for questions.
Modify the worksheets for the teachers yourself and send them back within days.
Tell the head which teachers are reluctant so they can be told to comply.
Model a modified worksheet, show the result for one pupil, and offer follow-up help.

basic.situation: You teach a daily living skill, making a simple sandwich, to a group with a mentor nearby. One pupil keeps putting on too much spread.

options.text: Take the knife and finish the sandwich for the pupil so lunch is ready.
Show the amount with a measuring card and let the pupil try again.
Tell the pupil to use less spread and show where to stop.
Let the pupil eat the sandwich as it is and skip the lesson.

advanced.situation: You create a life skills curriculum and mentor a peer. Pupils need to learn goal setting, but they struggle with long-term goals like finding a job.

options.text: Ask pupils to write a five-year plan and share it with the class.
Start with small weekly goals, track them visually, and share the method.
Give pupils a standard goal list and tell them to copy it.
Tell pupils that jobs are hard to find for them, so goals can wait.

basic.situation: You record pupils' progress in a log with administrative support. A teacher gives you attendance numbers that look like they include absent pupils.

options.text: Check the register against the numbers and ask the teacher about the difference.
Change the numbers to what you think the register says from memory.
Record the numbers and mention the doubt after finishing the log.
Record the numbers and add a note that they may need review.

advanced.situation: You interpret test data for a Form 5 pupil to set long-term support. The pupil scored high on one subtest and low on another, so the total misleads.

options.text: Average the two subtests and report the result as the pupil's level.
Use the total score to set goals and review next term.
Compare subtests with classroom work, list strengths and needs, and set support goals.
Use the highest subtest score to set goals for the pupil.

basic.situation: You set up the classroom for a Form 1 art lesson with assistance. A pupil with limited arm movement will use the usual desk.

options.text: Put the materials in the middle of the desk and see how it goes.
Ask the pupil's classmate to pass the materials to them during the lesson.
Leave the setup as usual and let the pupil ask if there is a problem.
Adjust the desk height and place materials within reach before the lesson starts.

advanced.situation: You choose assistive technology for pupils who struggle to write. Staff want an expensive tablet system, while a cheaper speech-to-text tool is available.

options.text: Order both tools for all pupils this term so nobody objects to the choice.
Trial both tools with two pupils, compare access and cost, then decide.
Pick the expensive system since staff prefer it and it has more features.
Pick the cheaper tool since it meets the needs of most pupils.

basic.situation: At a staff meeting, a coordinator shares an update about pupils' support. You are new and asked to note down what is said.

options.text: Write down just the parts that concern your own pupils.
Take clear notes, confirm unclear points afterwards, and share them with the team.
Take notes and keep them in your own file for later.
Skip the notes and trust your memory to repeat the update later.

advanced.situation: You lead a team to resolve a pupil's behavioural and academic problems. A parent wants the school to change the timetable, but two teachers say it is not possible.

options.text: Change the timetable partly to please the parent and inform the teachers.
Tell the parent what the teachers said and suggest alternatives later.
Check which timetable changes are possible, then agree a plan with everyone.
Promise the parent the change and tell the teachers to accept it.

basic.situation: During an adapted PE session in the hall, two pupils run across the mat while others do balance exercises. Your supervisor is at the other end.

options.text: Call the two pupils over and remind them to walk across the mat.
Move the balance group to a corner and let the running continue.
Pause the activity calmly, restate the hall rules, and mark clear paths.
Let the pupils burn off their energy first and give rules afterwards.

advanced.situation: You review the adapted PE programme against government regulations before an inspection. You find that equipment checks are logged on paper only and some entries are missing.

options.text: Trace the missing checks, repeat them now, and set a regular signed log.
Leave the log as it is and prepare answers in case inspectors ask.
Fill in the missing entries from memory so the log looks complete.
Tell the head about the gaps and ask for more time before inspection.

basic.situation: A senior colleague asks you to prepare a lesson plan for a pupil with cerebral palsy, based on the pupil's existing IEP.

options.text: Use last term's lesson plan for the same pupil and update the dates.
Write a plan from a video of another school's adapted PE class.
Use a standard class lesson plan and ask the pupil to follow along.
Read the IEP goals, choose matching activities, and check the plan with your senior.

advanced.situation: You modify the IEPs of pupils with intellectual and physical disabilities. A parent asks you to add a swimming goal, but the school has no pool and the IEP team has not met.

options.text: Take the request to the IEP team and look into local swimming options.
Tell the parent the school cannot add goals it has no facilities for.
Add the swimming goal to the IEP and tell the parent it is approved.
Add a land-based water-skills goal to the IEP and inform the team afterwards.

basic.situation: You record attendance for adapted PE sessions. A parent you meet in the corridor asks to see the sheet to check on another family's child.

options.text: Politely decline to share other pupils' records and offer their own child's.
Show the whole sheet since the parent is calm and polite.
Tell the parent to request the sheet from the head of department.
Show the sheet but cover the names of other pupils with your hand.

advanced.situation: You manage progress records for adapted PE pupils, with strict confidentiality. A teacher asks you to email a pupil's progress file to a private tutor.

options.text: Email the whole file to the tutor today as the teacher requested.
Check consent with the parents and the school policy before sharing any file.
Email the file with a password and tell the teacher it is sent.
Ask the tutor to contact the parents directly for any information.

basic.situation: You assist in observing pupils to assess basic motor needs under supervision. One pupil seems to avoid catching a ball, and you are asked for notes.

options.text: Record how the pupil reacted to the ball and pass the notes on.
Write a diagnosis of the pupil's problem based on a video you watched.
Write that the pupil is shy and does not like sports or games.
Write that the pupil cannot catch and leave the notes in the file.

advanced.situation: You lead the screening and placement of new pupils into adapted PE. The list has too many names for the available places this term.

options.text: Rank pupils by screened need, share the criteria, and set a waiting list.
Place the pupils whose parents have made the most requests this term.
Place pupils in the order in which they were referred to the programme.
Cancel the screening for this term and tell staff to wait next year.

basic.situation: During a ball skills session, a pupil with limited coordination finally catches the ball once after many attempts. The pupil looks to you.

options.text: Tell the pupil to do it again to be sure it was not luck.
Smile, name exactly what the pupil did well, and invite another try.
Tell the pupil that most of the class can catch much better.
Say well done and move straight on to the next pupil.

advanced.situation: You use advanced adapted techniques to improve gross motor skills for a group with mixed abilities. Some pupils tire quickly, and others find the exercises too easy.

options.text: Set tiered station activities with rest points, and rotate pupils based on progress.
Use the middle-level exercises for everyone and add extra time.
Split the group into two levels and keep the same plan for each.
Let each pupil choose any activity and watch from the side.

basic.situation: You must order new balls and hoops for adapted PE using the school's standard ordering form. The supplier list has three options.

options.text: Check stock first, compare the three options, and submit the form for approval.
Order from the supplier you used last time and submit the form.
Order by phone from a friend's shop and ask the school to reimburse.
Order from the cheapest supplier and send the form in after delivery.

advanced.situation: You advise teachers on accommodations for pupils with different disabilities in regular PE. A teacher argues that adapting the game makes the class unfair for other pupils.

options.text: Tell the teacher that school rules require them to adapt every game.
Explain the pupils' needs, show fair modifications, and invite the teacher to try one.
Suggest the teacher run adapted games for those pupils in a separate session.
Send the teacher a one-page guide to adapted games to read.

basic.situation: You meet a new adult learner who wants to improve English for work. Your supervisor asks you to record the learner's current level and goals.

options.text: Ask about work needs, give a short speaking task, and record both.
Ask the learner to fill in a form about their goals.
Record the level as intermediate since that is common for new learners.
Place the learner in the same class as their friends.

advanced.situation: You review a six-week ESL course using student evaluations and test results. Many learners say the speaking practice is too short, though tests show reading gains.

options.text: Remove the negative evaluations from the report to keep a positive tone.
Compare feedback with test results, then propose adding speaking time for next intake.
Recommend extra speaking classes after the course for any interested learners.
Report that learners are satisfied overall since the reading scores improved this term.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks for written evidence of your preparation for tomorrow's adult literacy class. You have planned in your head but written little.

options.text: Write a short lesson plan with aims and activities and send it tonight.
Copy a plan from last term's class and say you wrote it today.
Tell your supervisor the plan is in your head and offer to explain.
Send photos of the textbook pages and exercises you plan to use tomorrow.

advanced.situation: You plan a field trip to a bank branch for adult learners practising financial English. Two learners use wheelchairs, and the branch entrance has one step.

options.text: Keep the plan and tell the two learners to stay behind this time.
Confirm access with the branch beforehand, arrange a ramp, and brief all learners.
Ask the bank to move the visit to a ground-floor meeting room.
Ask other learners to carry the wheelchairs up the step on arrival.

basic.situation: You prepare the classroom for an evening literacy class. The projector bulb is dim and the class begins in twenty minutes.

options.text: Try the spare bulb, and if it fails, print the slides as handouts.
Ask the learners to sit near the screen and start as planned.
Start the class as planned and tell learners the slides will follow by email.
Cancel the class and send the learners home as they arrive.

advanced.situation: Your adult class includes learners with different reading levels and jobs. Your current worksheets use office vocabulary that confuses learners who work in factories.

options.text: Rewrite sections with workplace words from learners' jobs and test it next lesson.
Add a short glossary of office words to the existing worksheets.
Ask factory workers to join a lower class with simpler worksheets next term.
Keep the worksheets and explain the office words aloud as you go.

basic.situation: You give a basic grammar lecture to adult learners with guidance from a senior teacher. Several learners look lost after your first example.

options.text: Repeat the same example more slowly and move to the next point.
Tell the lost learners they should study at home before coming.
Pause, give a second example from daily life, and ask learners to try one.
Continue to the exercises and help those who put their hands up.

advanced.situation: An adult learner often arrives late and tired, and says they might drop out because of work and family stress. The learner has been doing well in class.

options.text: Tell the learner their seat will go to someone else if late again.
Encourage the learner to keep trying and promise to share the notes.
Tell the learner that people who drop out rarely get good jobs later.
Talk privately, listen to the constraints, and explore flexible options like catch-up materials.

basic.situation: You order books and supplies for next term's literacy course using the approved list. Two listed books are out of print.

options.text: Order the other books on the list and update the supervisor later.
Buy the two books second-hand from a seller and bill the school later.
Contact the supplier for suitable alternatives and ask your supervisor to approve.
Replace the two books with similar ones you saw in a bookshop.

advanced.situation: A group of adult learners is loud and teases a quieter learner during break. You are responsible for order in the class.

options.text: Remind the class of the rules at the start of the next session.
Speak to those involved privately, restate rules, and check on the quiet learner.
Ask the quiet learner to move seats away from the loud group.
Join the joking to keep the group friendly and let it continue.

basic.situation: You confer with a colleague to plan next week's lessons. The approved curriculum has a unit on banking vocabulary that you have never taught.

options.text: Ask your colleague for sample materials, then plan the unit within the curriculum.
Swap the unit for a topic you know better and inform the staff later.
Ask your colleague to teach that unit while you teach another.
Plan the unit alone using a dictionary and online banking pages.

advanced.situation: You help develop an instructional programme for migrant workers with a social worker. She proposes weekend classes, but your teachers are not available on weekends.

options.text: Survey workers' availability, ask about venues, and trial a weekend pilot class.
Offer to teach weekend classes yourself and ask the others to cover weekdays.
Agree to weekend classes and put the teachers' names on the roster yourself.
Tell the social worker that your teachers cannot teach on weekends.

basic.situation: You teach a beginner watercolour class and use the provided template to draft a lesson. The template asks for a clear objective.

options.text: Write one specific objective, such as mixing two colours, and share it.
Write an objective that says students will enjoy painting during the class.
Copy an objective from another painting course and adapt it for your class.
Leave the objective blank and decide it when you see the class.

advanced.situation: End-of-term feedback rates your cooking class unit on pastry low, while students praise the knife skills unit. You must revise or remove units.

options.text: Keep the pastry unit and shorten the praised knife skills unit to make room.
Replace the pastry unit with your own favourite one and tell students later.
Review the pastry feedback details and test results before deciding to revise it.
Ask a few students what they disliked about the pastry unit and note it.

basic.situation: You deliver a prepared yoga lesson using demonstration and short talks. A new student cannot follow the pose from the back row.

options.text: Move on to the next pose to keep the group in rhythm.
Tell the student to watch the others during the pose.
Demonstrate the pose again and continue with the class.
Move the student forward, demonstrate again slowly, and check posture afterwards.

advanced.situation: During a cooking class, you realise half the students are vegetarians and your prepared recipe is meat-based. Ingredients for each are limited.

options.text: Tell the vegetarians to cook the meat and remove it before eating.
Offer a vegetarian version of the recipe using the same techniques.
Switch to a plain rice dish that everyone in the class can cook.
Let vegetarian students watch while the others cook and taste the dish.

basic.situation: In a guitar class, you observe how each student holds the instrument and plays chords during practice.

options.text: Tell the students which ones are talented in front of the class.
Note each student's ability, then ask what songs they want to learn.
Note the quickest learners and teach the class to match their pace.
Note the students who struggle and plan to help them in later classes.

advanced.situation: Test scores for your English conversation course show weak results in listening. Students say the audio equipment is poor, and the course plan has little listening practice.

options.text: Report the course as successful since students attended all of the sessions.
Check both causes, test better equipment, and recommend adding listening practice.
Recommend adding more speaking practice to the course because students enjoy it.
Recommend replacing the audio equipment with a newer set before the next term.

basic.situation: You set up the art room and prepare materials for a scheduled class. Ten minutes before the session, you find a paint tin has leaked on the table.

options.text: Start the class and tell students to keep away from the table.
Let the students clean the spill themselves as part of the lesson.
Clean the spill, move materials aside, and set up fresh paint first.
Cover the spill with paper and start the class on time as planned.

advanced.situation: A student repeatedly interrupts others in your drumming class and ignores your reminders. Your centre's policy requires a written warning before removal, and records must be accurate.

options.text: Remove the student today and record the reason as non-attendance.
Give the written warning, record the incident accurately, and speak to the student.
Speak to the student after class and keep a private note.
Ask the student to sit out the next activity and then rejoin.

basic.situation: You order books and supplies for a calligraphy course from the list the centre gave you. The budget covers all items, but one is out of stock.

options.text: Order the other items first and mention the missing one to the centre later.
Buy a similar item from a shop at a higher price.
Contact the supplier for stock dates or alternatives and inform the centre.
Start the course and charge students extra fees for that item.

advanced.situation: You consider new recording equipment to improve your music class presentations. A salesperson offers a package costing more than the centre's yearly supplies budget.

options.text: Trial the equipment in one lesson, compare costs, and report to the centre.
Ask the salesperson to lower the price and accept the package.
Order the package and use the supplies budget to pay for it.
Buy the cheapest recorder in the package and try it out in class.

basic.situation: At a staff meeting, the centre manager lists tasks for the annual showcase. You are asked to serve on the committee.

options.text: Accept, ask what the committee needs from you, and note the dates.
Decline in front of everyone since your own classes come first this term.
Accept and wait for the manager to tell you exactly what to do.
Accept but say you can attend a single meeting because of classes.

advanced.situation: You lead a discussion with other instructors to align lesson plans. Two teachers share the same room and both plan loud activities at the same hour.

options.text: Suggest the louder teacher uses headphones for the activity to cut the noise.
Compare the plans, adjust the schedule together, and share a room calendar.
Tell both teachers to settle it between themselves after the meeting ends.
Ask one teacher to move their activity to another hour and thank them.

basic.situation: You cover a Year 4 maths class. The absent teacher's plan says to teach fractions, but the worksheet pages are missing from the desk.

options.text: Teach the planned fractions using board examples and leave a note for the teacher.
Check with the office for copies and start with a class review.
Teach a different topic you know well since the pages are missing today.
Give the class free reading time and leave a note about the missing pages.

advanced.situation: You substitute for a Form 2 science class and find the teacher's plan too hard, because the learners have not covered the prerequisite topic.

options.text: Follow the plan as written and note where the learners struggled afterwards.
Skip the hard parts of the plan and mark the lesson as covered.
Replace the plan with a quiz on any science topic they recall.
Teach a short review first, adapt the plan, and report the changes.

basic.situation: You supervise a Form 1 English class. A student asks for help with homework while others work on a worksheet.

options.text: Do the first question for the student and let them copy the pattern.
Give the student the full set of answers so they finish quickly.
Tell the student to ask the regular teacher when they return tomorrow.
Guide the student with hints on one question, then check back after a while.

advanced.situation: A student tells you privately they feel anxious about exams and cannot sleep. You will be in school only today.

options.text: Listen kindly, then tell the school counsellor and the class teacher what you heard.
Give the student your own tips for sleeping and studying well.
Listen kindly and suggest the student speaks to a trusted friend or relative.
Say that everyone feels anxious and that the student will be fine.

basic.situation: You cover a Form 3 class. Students are using phones, which the school rule bans in class.

options.text: Allow phones if students say they are using them for the lesson.
Remind the class of the phone rule and ask them to put phones away.
Tell the class to stop using their phones and carry on with teaching.
Take the phones from students and keep them until the end of the day.

advanced.situation: You supervise Year 6 students during a school field trip. A student leaves the group at the museum to buy a snack, and another follows.

options.text: Continue the tour and tell the museum guide to watch for them.
Keep the group together and phone the lead teacher to ask for help.
Wait ten minutes for them to return by themselves before acting.
Stop the group, count heads, locate both students, and tell the lead teacher.

basic.situation: The teacher's note says to hand out workbooks at the start of class. Thirty students are present, but there are twenty-eight workbooks.

options.text: Give workbooks to the first twenty-eight students and tell the rest to listen.
Ask the office for two more workbooks and wait until they arrive.
Share two workbooks between pairs and tell the teacher about the shortage afterwards.
Take two workbooks from a neighbouring class cupboard and return them later.

advanced.situation: You are asked to streamline how substitutes record attendance across your department. At present, three teachers use paper sheets, and some forget to submit them.

options.text: Email all teachers a reminder to submit their sheets on time.
Fill in missing attendance from the timetable so the records look complete.
Pilot one simple shared sheet for all, with a daily submission reminder.
Ask the office to collect sheets each afternoon from the classrooms.

basic.situation: A teacher asks you to explain basic etiquette rules to a class. You are to talk about greeting visitors politely.

options.text: Tell students that impolite people end up lonely and unsuccessful in life.
Write the rules on the board and tell students to copy them.
Read the rules from the handout slowly and ask if there are questions.
Role-play a polite greeting with a student, then let pairs practise it.

advanced.situation: You design and lead a workshop on conflict resolution for a school community of students and parents. Two groups hold opposing views about a recent incident.

options.text: Use the recent incident as the case and ask each side to speak.
Ask the parents to lead the discussion since they are older and experienced.
Hold separate sessions and share the summary with each group later.
Set ground rules, use a neutral case, and let each group state its view.

basic.situation: You are covering a class and the teacher left slides on the computer. The projector will not show the screen.

options.text: Check the cable and input, ask a neighbouring teacher, and teach from notes.
Show the slides on the small computer screen to the whole class.
Tell the class the lesson is cancelled and let them do free time.
Check the cable and input, then wait for the technician to arrive.

advanced.situation: You lead a short training session for other staff on a new classroom projector system. Some staff worry that they will break the equipment.

options.text: Start with a hands-on demo, let staff practise, and give a one-page guide.
Tell staff the system is simple and ask them to stop worrying.
Give staff a written guide and ask them to practise on their own.
Show the system once and tell staff they will learn quickly.

basic.situation: A senior tutor asks you to create a handout and short quiz for a Standard 5 maths lesson on decimals.

options.text: Copy a decimals worksheet from a workbook and add your centre's title.
Make the quiz long with many questions so pupils get more practice.
Use the pupils' common mistakes for examples and show the senior.
Reuse a quiz from last year's exam paper with the answers printed.

advanced.situation: You plan a multi-week module for a student who struggles with reading comprehension but excels in maths. The student's exam is in six weeks.

options.text: Give the student likely exam answers to memorise before the day itself.
Spend the six weeks on maths revision to protect the strong subject.
Plan weekly reading drills at the same difficulty level for all six weeks.
Set weekly reading goals that use maths strengths and adjust after checks.

basic.situation: You review a worksheet with a Standard 4 student under supervision. The student misses question five and asks you to just give the answer.

options.text: Show the working for question five and ask the student to try question six.
Give the answer for question five and move on to question six.
Tell the student the answer key might be mistaken so skip the review.
Ask the student to explain their working and guide them step by step.

advanced.situation: You prepare a Saturday workshop for six students on essay writing, mixing strong and weak writers. Weak writers fall behind when strong ones answer first.

options.text: Split the workshop into two rooms, one for strong and one for weak writers.
Ask the strong writers to wait until the weak writers have answered first.
Pair students by ability, give tiered tasks, and invite each pair to share.
Let the strong writers explain answers while weak writers copy the notes.

basic.situation: You help students in a computer lab at the tuition centre. A student has been silent for fifteen minutes and has not typed anything.

options.text: Tell the student to ask a friend sitting nearby for help.
Wait a few more minutes in case the student is thinking something through.
Walk over, ask what the student is stuck on, and offer a step.
Type the first paragraph for the student so the task is done.

advanced.situation: A student with learning difficulties is not improving after eight sessions. The parents have not shared any diagnosis or plan.

options.text: Tell the parents that the student must take a medical diagnosis soon.
Add more sessions of the same type each week for the student.
Review the results, try a new approach, and ask parents about support needs.
Tell the parents the student has dyslexia and needs special classes.

basic.situation: At the end of a session, you quiz a student and record the score in the progress sheet. The student scored lower than last week.

options.text: Record last week's score instead to avoid upsetting the student or parents.
Record the score and tell the student to study much harder next week.
Record the score but leave the notes section empty for the time being.
Record the score truthfully, note topics missed, and plan a revision next session.

advanced.situation: You work with a school counsellor and a student's parents to assess the student's needs. The parents want more homework, while the counsellor sees signs of burnout.

options.text: Share observations with both, agree a balanced plan, and review in a month.
Give extra homework as the parents asked and watch the student's mood.
Tell the student to hide tiredness from the parents and keep studying.
Follow the counsellor's advice and tell the parents the new rules.

basic.situation: A parent calls to book weekly tutoring slots for their child. Your administrator gave you the calendar, which shows two free evenings.

options.text: Offer the two free evenings, confirm one, and send a message with the time.
Book a slot that is already taken and sort out the clash later.
Book the first evening and tell the parent to adjust later if needed.
Offer the two free evenings and ask the parent to call back.

advanced.situation: You organise the tutoring room and lead a training session for other tutors. The room is noisy, and desks are crowded.

options.text: Ask students to bring their own headphones and carry on as before.
Close the room for a week and tell parents it is under repair.
Move the desks apart and ask all tutors to speak very softly.
Arrange quiet zones, set a noise rule, and share it with other tutors.

basic.situation: You send a template progress update to a parent after a Standard 6 student improves in spelling but still struggles with grammar.

options.text: Tell the parent the student is already good at grammar to please them.
Fill in the template with the spelling gain and leave grammar for next time.
Fill in the template with both the spelling gain and the grammar plan.
Send the blank template and ask the parent to read it later.

advanced.situation: Another tutor asks you how to handle a parent who wants to see all of their child's assessment records and also a classmate's results for comparison.

options.text: Suggest sharing the classmate's full results if the parent promises to keep them secret.
Share the child's own records and explain why classmates' results stay confidential.
Suggest sharing the classmate's average score to show where the child stands.
Tell the other tutor to refuse the parent and end the meeting.

basic.situation: A researcher asks for a 1950s land record in the archive's reading room. The record is fragile, and your supervisor is in a meeting.

options.text: Check access rules, offer a digital copy if available, and log the request.
Let the researcher photocopy the pages on the shared office machine today.
Fetch the original and let the researcher handle it with clean hands.
Ask the researcher to wait in the lobby until your supervisor is free.

advanced.situation: You direct two volunteers who arrange displays and propose acquiring a donated collection of family letters. The donor wants quick acceptance, but the letters' condition is unclear.

options.text: Inspect the letters, confirm the donor's rights, then recommend terms to your head.
Ask the volunteers to inspect the letters and decide for you this week.
Accept the letters now and inspect them properly during the sorting stage later.
Place the letters on public display this week to thank the donor.

basic.situation: You help appraise a box of old business ledgers. A senior archivist asks you to note which items look original.

options.text: Mark items as original if the dates and names look right to you.
Compare paper, ink, and handwriting with known originals and list any doubts.
Mark all the items as original to save the senior some time.
Ask the donor which items are original and list their answers down.

advanced.situation: You research the origin of a rare map that arrived without records. A dealer claims it dates from the 1800s, but the paper looks newer.

options.text: Ask the dealer for a certificate and file it with the map.
Record the map as an 1800s original to match the dealer's claim.
Examine the paper and ink, trace ownership records, and note findings with uncertainty.
Record the dealer's date in the catalogue and mark it as claimed.

basic.situation: You help maintain the archive's computer database under guidance. You notice two scanned files saved with the same name in one folder.

options.text: Rename one of the files and keep the other as it is.
Leave both files as they are and hope the system keeps them apart.
Check which files are which, rename them clearly, and tell your supervisor.
Delete one of the files to remove the duplicate name from the folder.

advanced.situation: You design a new database structure for the archive's photographs and must choose a file format for long-term storage. Staff suggest a popular format that may become unsupported.

options.text: Choose an open, well-documented format, keep originals, and plan periodic checks.
Store the photographs in a format that one vendor's software alone reads.
Choose whichever format your scanner produces and store it on one drive.
Choose the popular format and plan to convert files if it changes.

basic.situation: You assist in planning a school workshop on local history at the archive. Your supervisor asks you to prepare the document handling session.

options.text: Hand over the session to the volunteers and join the later talks.
Bring original documents for students to touch and pass around the room.
Prepare copies of documents and a short talk on how to read them.
Select copies of documents, prepare gloves and handling rules, and brief the volunteers.

advanced.situation: You coordinate public outreach and decide retention for a collection on a sensitive local event. Some families of those involved still live nearby, and a talk is planned.

options.text: Postpone the talk and keep the whole collection closed for several years.
Consult affected families, set retention and access limits, and plan the talk.
Proceed with the talk as planned and warn people it is sensitive.
Publish the names of those involved in the talk to attract attendance.

basic.situation: You help organise newly received records into series. The classification scheme has no category for a set of community photographs.

options.text: Ask your supervisor how to classify them and file them provisionally meanwhile.
Leave the photographs unfiled in a box at the back until someone asks.
Create a new category yourself and use it for all similar records.
File the photographs under the nearest existing category and add a note.

advanced.situation: You set policy guidelines for public access to a collection of old court files. A journalist demands immediate access to all files, including those with personal details.

options.text: Give the journalist all the files since the files are old.
Apply the policy, review files for personal data, and offer staged release.
Refuse all access until the policy is fully rewritten next year.
Allow access to the files but ask the journalist not to publish names.

basic.situation: You help prepare document descriptions for a new set of records. The file title is vague, and a note inside says minutes, 1962.

options.text: Write a short description based on the file title and the folder.
Use the title and date on the note as the description for now.
Write a description of what the minutes might contain from similar files.
Read the minutes, note the contents, and write a clear description.

advanced.situation: You direct the copying of fragile records to digital formats and set description standards. Funding allows half the collection to be scanned this year.

options.text: Scan the records that visitors request most and discard the damaged ones.
Rank records by fragility and value, scan those first, and document the rest.
Scan the records in alphabetical order until the funds run out.
Scan the records that are easiest to handle and leave the fragile ones.

basic.situation: A visitor asks about a ceramic bowl in your museum's collection. The catalogue entry lists its age and origin, but not who donated it.

options.text: Name a likely donor based on similar bowls to satisfy the visitor quickly.
Share the catalogue's age and origin, and offer to check on the donor.
Tell the visitor to look at the label next to the bowl.
Share the age and origin and tell the visitor the donor is unknown.

advanced.situation: You attend a civic event to seek financing for a new gallery. A company executive offers funds but wants a display of their products in the museum's front hall.

options.text: Decline politely and look for other donors at the same event.
Accept the offer in principle and report the display request to the board.
Accept the funds and promise the front hall display in writing.
Thank the executive, explain the museum's display policy, and propose a sponsor acknowledgement.

basic.situation: While checking the storage room with a colleague, you smell damp and see a small stain on a wall near the paper collection.

options.text: Cover the stain with paper and carry on with the inspection.
Move the nearby items to a dry area and report the leak to facilities.
Report the stain to facilities and leave the items where they are.
Wipe the wall dry yourself and check on it again next week.

advanced.situation: You set standards for climate and pest control across the facility. Pest traps show beetles in two galleries, and the budget for treatment is small.

options.text: Spray insecticide directly on the affected objects to stop the beetles fast.
Identify the beetles, isolate affected objects, and set a monitoring and treatment plan.
Ask the cleaners to vacuum the galleries more often and report any beetles.
Add more traps in the two galleries and check them every month.

basic.situation: A colleague asks you to examine a donated bronze figure and check its basic condition. You see greenish spots on the surface.

options.text: Photograph the spots, note their location, and report them to the conservator.
Note the spots in your condition report and leave the object in storage.
Rub the spots lightly with a dry cloth to see what happens.
Scrape one spot with a small knife to see what is underneath.

advanced.situation: You guide junior staff on a valuation case where a painting's signature looks genuine but the canvas type seems modern. The owner wants a quick valuation letter.

options.text: Value the painting based on the signature and add a note on the canvas.
Issue the quick letter with the full value to keep the owner happy.
Value the painting at the average price of similar paintings by the artist.
Arrange scientific analysis of the canvas and pigments and delay the valuation letter.

basic.situation: You enter new object details into the cataloguing database with help from a colleague. One object's donor name has two different spellings in the paperwork.

options.text: Enter the first spelling you see and update it later if needed.
Pick the shorter spelling to save typing and move to the next object.
Check the original donor form, ask your colleague, and then enter the name.
Enter both spellings in the donor name field separated by a slash.

advanced.situation: You review a grant proposal that claims your museum will digitise 10,000 objects in a year. Staff records show the team can scan about 3,000 a year.

options.text: Approve the proposal and tell the team to scan faster to meet it.
Ask the writer to adjust the target to match capacity or add resources.
Add a note in the proposal that the target is very ambitious.
Approve the proposal and plan to hire extra help if it is funded.

basic.situation: You assist a lead guide on a tour of a new exhibit for primary school pupils. Several pupils lean on a glass case.

options.text: Move the pupils to the next exhibit and say nothing about the glass.
Wait for the lead guide to deal with it after the tour.
Ask them kindly to step back and explain why the case is fragile.
Tell the whole group loudly to stop touching the glass case.

advanced.situation: You design an educational programme and research project on traditional weaving for school groups and the public. The two audiences need different levels of detail.

options.text: Prepare one version for the public and simplify it for schools.
Create two tiers from shared research and test each with a small group.
Skip the school groups for now and focus on the paying public.
Prepare a version for schools and hand the same version to the public.

basic.situation: You help organise storage for new collection items that arrived this week. The shelves are labelled by size, but several items are very delicate.

options.text: Place delicate items on the top shelf where there is free space.
Store delicate items by size with the others and label them delicate.
Stack all the delicate items together in one box to save shelf space.
Place delicate items in padded trays on lower shelves and update the location list.

advanced.situation: You supervise staff and authorise major collection exchanges. A foreign museum offers a loan swap, but your registrar warns the insurance values differ greatly.

options.text: Ask the registrar to reconcile values, agree insurance terms, and then authorise the swap.
Decline the swap and tell the foreign museum the matter is closed.
Approve the swap and ask the registrar to sort out the insurance later.
Authorise the loan at the foreign museum's values to avoid further delays.

basic.situation: You are cleaning a dusty painted ceramic plate under supervision, and the paint looks flaky in one area.

options.text: Wipe the whole plate with a damp cloth and dry it quickly.
Use household polish on the painted area to firm up the flakes.
Clean the plate with the approved solution and avoid scrubbing near the paint.
Dry-brush the dust, leave the flaking area untouched, and tell your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You must fabricate a missing handle for an antique wooden chest to restore its appearance. The curator wants it to look original.

options.text: Buy a modern handle that looks close and fix it with screws.
Make the part removable, mark it as new, and document the work.
Make the handle and age it so nobody can tell it is new.
Make a matching handle and glue it in firmly so it holds.

basic.situation: You help install a small silver bowl in a display case with guidance. The case lining feels slightly damp from cleaning.

options.text: Place the bowl and close the case to help the lining dry.
Place the bowl on a clean cloth over the damp lining for now.
Place the bowl and warm the case with a lamp to speed up drying.
Wait for the lining to dry fully, then place the bowl and report back.

advanced.situation: During installation, a painting arrives with a small crack in the paint layer that was not in the shipping report. The opening is tomorrow.

options.text: Hang the painting and tell the curator about the crack after opening.
Fill the crack with matching paint overnight so it cannot be seen.
Hang the painting in a corner where the crack is less visible.
Stop hanging it, photograph the crack, report it, and agree the next step.

basic.situation: You inspect textile pieces to see which need repair. One embroidered cloth has loose threads and small holes.

options.text: Record and photograph the damage, then pass repair options to your senior.
Record the damage on the form and write that the cloth seems stable.
Press the cloth with a hot iron to flatten the loose threads.
Stitch the loose threads at once with matching thread to stop further damage.

advanced.situation: You choose a repair method for a brittle ancient manuscript with torn edges. Two methods exist: a quick adhesive tape or a slower reversible paper repair.

options.text: Choose the reversible paper repair, test it on scrap, and record the method.
Choose the slower repair but skip testing since the method is well known.
Use strong household glue along the edges to fix the tears permanently.
Use the quick adhesive tape on the small tears to save time.

basic.situation: You photograph museum objects for documentation. Your assistant suggests using the camera flash on a faded silk banner to get a brighter picture.

options.text: Use the flash from far away so it is less strong.
Use the flash on its lowest setting for one photo of the banner.
Use several flash photos from different angles for a complete record.
Switch off the flash, use steady lights and a tripod, and add a scale.

advanced.situation: You manage complex database entries for the collection. Two records describe the same bronze vase with different dimensions and storage locations.

options.text: Add a note on each record pointing to the other one.
Edit both records to match the dimensions and location you remember.
Measure the vase, check storage, merge the records, and note the change history.
Keep the more recent record and delete the older record from the system.

basic.situation: You help lead a short museum tour for primary pupils. A pupil asks if the objects are real or copies, and you are not sure about one item.

options.text: Say all items are real and move on to the next room.
Answer for items you know and say you will check the other.
Say the unsure item is a copy so pupils do not touch it.
Ask the pupil to read the label and decide for themselves.

advanced.situation: You design a course for adult visitors on how museums protect fragile objects. The audience includes collectors who want to try restoring objects at home.

options.text: Avoid restoration topics completely and focus on display methods instead.
Teach basic cleaning methods and tell learners to practise on cheap items first.
Teach step-by-step restoration of old items so collectors can do it.
Teach preventive care, show what to avoid, and advise contacting a trained conservator.

basic.situation: While working on a damaged carving, you notice signs that the wood may be infested. You are not trained to treat infestations.

options.text: Isolate the carving in a sealed bag and notify your superior at once.
Treat the carving with a household pest spray from the cleaning cupboard.
Notify your superior about the signs after you finish the repair today.
Check the signs again tomorrow and report if they are worse.

advanced.situation: You advise curatorial staff on temperature and humidity for a gallery with historic textiles. The air conditioning is old, and humidity swings daily.

options.text: Tell staff the swings are normal for old buildings and need no action.
Recommend lowering the temperature to its lowest setting for all the textiles.
Monitor the conditions with loggers, recommend stable ranges, and coordinate an expert's visit.
Ask staff to open windows when the air feels too dry.

basic.situation: You help choose new books for the children's section using reviews and current holdings. The budget lets you buy ten titles.

options.text: Order the ten newest releases from the publisher's latest catalogue this month.
Buy ten copies of one popular series to please the readers.
Pick the ten titles with the most five-star reviews on a shop site.
Compare reviews with what the library already owns and choose varied titles.

advanced.situation: You consult teachers, parents and a community group to decide on new library services. One group wants a games room, another wants a quiet study area, and space is limited.

options.text: Choose the group with the most members and give it the space.
Ask the library manager to decide and then inform the groups afterwards.
Promise both groups their full requests and sort out space later on.
Gather needs from each group, survey usage, and propose a timed shared-space plan.

basic.situation: A patron asks for the opening hours of a government office near the library. You search the office's website and find two different hours listed.

options.text: Give the patron the hours listed on the first website result.
Check which page is current, confirm by phone, and tell the patron.
Tell the patron the office hours are usually nine to five on weekdays.
Give the patron both sets of hours and let them decide which applies.

advanced.situation: A patron needs a rare 1950s newspaper report about a village flood. The library's catalogue shows nothing, and the patron's deadline is next week.

options.text: Write a short summary of the flood from memory for the patron.
Suggest the patron look for a similar flood report from a later year.
Search archives and ask other libraries, then give the patron options with timelines.
Tell the patron to visit the national archive and give them directions.

basic.situation: You work the circulation desk. A patron returns three books, and the system shows one of them already marked as returned yesterday.

options.text: Scan all three books again and hope the system sorts itself out.
Check the record, update the status, and note the duplicate in the log.
Tell the patron they must have returned it already and refuse the book.
Scan the other two books and set the third aside for later.

advanced.situation: You compile a list of books and articles on climate change for a university researcher. The list is long, and many items are outdated or repeated.

options.text: Remove duplicates, check publication dates, group by theme, and mark the key sources.
Remove duplicates and give the researcher the full list in date order.
Give the researcher the full list and let them sort it themselves.
Cut the list to ten items at random to keep it short.

basic.situation: You set up a projector and microphone for a seminar in the library hall. The microphone makes a squealing noise when switched on.

options.text: Turn the volume up to cover the squeal and begin the seminar.
Ask the audience to tolerate the noise until the sound settles down.
Lower the volume, move the speaker away from the microphone, and test again.
Switch off the microphone and ask the speaker to talk very loudly.

advanced.situation: You develop and maintain an online tutorial and database guide for students. Students report that a link on the page leads to an error.

options.text: Check every link, replace broken ones, and set a monthly check.
Replace the broken link and email the students that it is fixed.
Add a note saying some links may not work at times.
Delete the page from the website so nobody finds the error.

basic.situation: A new patron asks how to borrow books and use the study rooms. The library has a borrowing limit and a room booking form.

options.text: Tell the patron the rules do not matter much for new members.
Tell the patron to read the notice boards for the rules.
Give the patron the library leaflet and wish them well in studying.
Explain borrowing limits and room booking, and show where the forms are.

advanced.situation: You plan a class on information literacy for secondary students. Many students trust the first search result and social media posts without checking.

options.text: Ask students to submit answers from their favourite websites and videos they like.
Warn students that the internet contains many false claims and fake news.
Teach source checks with real examples and let students practise in pairs.
Show slides on how search engines rank results and give a handout.

basic.situation: A patron complains that the study room is too loud because of a group at the next table, and asks you to act.

options.text: Ask the patron to talk to the noisy group directly and politely.
Tell the patron to move to a quieter table on the upper floor.
Listen, ask the group politely to keep it down, and check back.
Tell the patron that the library cannot control noise in open study areas.

advanced.situation: You supervise daily operations and plan next year's budget. Staff request overtime pay for evening events, but the budget is already tight.

options.text: Approve all overtime and cover the cost by cutting next month's book orders.
Review event attendance, compare costs, and propose a limited overtime plan for approval.
Approve overtime for the most popular events and cancel the lower ones.
Refuse all overtime requests and tell staff to manage within normal hours.

basic.situation: A new member registers at the desk. While you enter their details, you notice the phone number has one digit missing.

options.text: Ask the member to confirm the full number, then update the record.
Enter the number as given and add a note to check later.
Add a digit that seems most likely and continue with the registration.
Use the phone number from the last member you registered as a placeholder.

advanced.situation: You are asked to compile statistics on library usage and design a poster to promote reading programmes. Your data has two months with missing counts.

options.text: Ask other staff to recall the counts and fill them in the table.
Leave out the two months and show averages for the other months.
Copy the previous year's counts into the missing months in the table.
Mark the missing months clearly and base the poster on available trends.

basic.situation: A patron asks at the desk for a recommendation on research methods in psychology. You do not know the subject well.

options.text: Help locate the subject section and refer the patron to a librarian.
Recommend a book you saw on a display last week.
Search the catalogue for the topic and hand over the list to them.
Tell the patron the library does not hold anything on psychology today.

advanced.situation: A teacher and a student ask for help finding materials for a school science project on local rivers. They have a one-week deadline and limited internet access at home.

options.text: Give them a list of three online links to use at home.
Pull a few books on rivers from the shelves and hand them over.
Tell them to come back with a more specific question next month instead.
Search print and online sources, print key pages, and list further sources.

basic.situation: A patron asks how to use the library computers to find ebooks. You have helped with this before under guidance.

options.text: Show the search step by step, let them try, and stay nearby.
Show the search once at normal speed and return to your own work.
Write the steps on a note and let the patron try alone.
Search for the ebooks yourself and tell the patron the final title.

advanced.situation: You train new volunteers and schedule their work. Two volunteers are friends and keep chatting while shelving, and patrons have complained about the noise.

options.text: Remind all volunteers about the noise rule at the start of the shift.
Speak with them privately, explain the issue, and assign them to separate areas.
Move them to a back room task where they cannot be heard.
Tell them loudly in front of patrons to be quiet or leave.

basic.situation: A patron wants to renew a book that another member has reserved. The system shows the reservation, but the patron insists on renewing.

options.text: Explain the reservation, offer the next available copy, and apply the policy.
Renew the book for one week to keep the patron happy today.
Renew the book and delete the other member's reservation from the system.
Ask the patron to speak to the other member about the book.

advanced.situation: You process a donated box of books and DVDs for the collection. Some items have mould spots, and others have missing barcodes.

options.text: Shelve the items now and add barcodes when someone asks for them.
Add barcodes to all the items and shelve everything together on the cart.
Wipe the mould spots and shelve the items with the others.
Set the mouldy items aside, label the rest, and add barcodes before shelving.

basic.situation: While checking returned books with a checklist, you find a book with a torn page and a loose cover.

options.text: Place it in the repair tray, note the damage, and update the status.
Put the book back on the shelf with a note inside it.
Throw the book into the recycling bin and move on to the next.
Tape the page and the cover with any tape and shelve the book.

advanced.situation: A rare children's picture book has a water-damaged spine, and a school is waiting to borrow it. Your budget for repairs is small.

options.text: Offer the school another similar book and plan the repair for next month.
Quarantine the book, get repair advice, and offer the school a replacement copy.
Dry the book on a heater yourself and lend it out today.
Lend the book to the school with a warning to handle with care.

basic.situation: You deliver books to the upper floor using a pushcart. One wheel is sticking, and the cart leans to one side.

options.text: Use the cart carefully and report the wheel at the end of the day.
Pile fewer books on the cart so it stays balanced and level.
Push the cart faster so the wheel keeps turning on the way.
Stop using the cart, tag it as faulty, and carry smaller batches by hand.

advanced.situation: A photocopier, a computer and a projector all fail on the same morning before a public event. The repair technician will arrive after noon.

options.text: Cancel the event and tell visitors it is due to equipment failure.
Try restarting each device and wait for the technician to arrive later.
Open the casing of each device to check wiring before the technician arrives.
Rank the equipment by event need, fix what you can, and arrange substitutes.

basic.situation: You use the calendar and route map to schedule this week's farm visits. A farmer calls to say he cannot be home on Tuesday, when you planned to visit.

options.text: Move his visit to Friday and tell him the new day by phone.
Offer two other days on the same route and update the calendar.
Cancel his visit this month and move on to the next farm.
Visit his farm on Tuesday anyway and leave a note at the gate.

advanced.situation: You manage the regional visit schedule for twelve farms. Two farms with urgent pest problems are far apart, and your travel time and fuel budget are limited.

options.text: Rank farms by urgency, group nearby ones, and visit the urgent farms first.
Visit the nearest farms first to save fuel and the urgent ones last.
Visit the two urgent farms first and rearrange the rest after that.
Keep the original schedule and phone the two urgent farms with advice.

basic.situation: You help at a booth during a county fair and assist with registration. A visitor asks to register after the form period has closed.

options.text: Tell the visitor to come back next year and register early.
Explain the closing time, note their contact, and pass the request on.
Ask the visitor to write their details on a napkin for later.
Register the visitor on a spare form and keep it to yourself.

advanced.situation: You lead planning for a large state fair event and mentor junior coordinators. The event needs a parking plan, but local stalls and visitors will clash over space.

options.text: Tell junior coordinators to sell the closest parking spots to the highest bidder.
Map stall and visitor zones with juniors and test the plan with stall owners.
Reserve most of the parking for visitors and inform the stallholders afterwards.
Leave parking unmarked and let the junior coordinators handle problems on the day.

basic.situation: You collect soil samples and enter pH values into a spreadsheet under supervision. One reading looks much lower than the others in the same field.

options.text: Leave the reading out of the spreadsheet and continue with other samples.
Change the reading so it matches the average of the other samples.
Enter the reading and add a comment that it looks unusual to you.
Recheck the reading, note the sample location, and flag it up.

advanced.situation: You lead a study on a new fertiliser and prepare findings for a regional meeting. Results are positive on one farm but unclear on the others.

options.text: Report the average of all farms and call the result promising.
Present the positive farm as the typical result for the whole region.
Report all farms' results, state the limits, and propose a larger trial.
Wait a year for more data before sharing anything with farmers.

basic.situation: A farmer shows you yellowing leaves on his chilli plants. You are new, and your senior advisor is not available today.

options.text: Tell the farmer to pull up the yellow plants and burn them today.
Take photos and soil details, note the pattern, and ask your senior.
Tell the farmer to spray any pesticide he has at home.
Tell the farmer it is probably lack of water and suggest more watering.

advanced.situation: You develop a standard checklist for diagnosing common vegetable problems and train other educators on it. Educators disagree about whether to test the soil first or inspect the plants first.

options.text: Let each educator use the order they prefer and review it later on.
Trial both orders on several farms, compare outcomes, and adopt the better one.
Choose the plant inspection first because it is quicker to do.
Publish the checklist with your preferred order and tell others to follow it.

basic.situation: You assist at a field day, setting up equipment for a drip irrigation demonstration. The senior educator is late, and farmers are arriving.

options.text: Ask the farmers to come back later in the afternoon when ready.
Finish the set-up, greet farmers, and keep the demonstration for the senior.
Cancel the demonstration and send the farmers home as they arrive.
Start the demonstration from your notes and apologise for the senior's absence.

advanced.situation: You design a multi-day demonstration series on a new rice-drying technology for large groups of farmers. Many farmers have never used such machines, and the budget is small.

options.text: Let farmers operate the machine on their own to save on staff costs.
Hold one long session for everyone and show the machine once in action.
Hand out leaflets and a video link and skip the live demonstrations.
Start with a small pilot group, gather feedback, then scale to the full series.

basic.situation: A farmer tells you he is worried about unfair prices from a local buyer. You are asked to document his concerns for your supervisor.

options.text: Confront the buyer yourself and demand a better price for the farmer.
Write a short summary of his worry and submit it by the weekend.
Write down the details he gives, such as dates and amounts.
Tell him to speak to the buyer himself and see what happens.

advanced.situation: You represent a farmers' group in a state-level discussion on water access. The group asks you to demand a full guarantee, but officials hint at a partial plan.

options.text: Sign an agreement for the group before consulting any of the members.
Demand the full guarantee and refuse to discuss anything partial or phased.
Present the group's evidence, ask for staged commitments, and report back to members.
Accept the partial plan to end the discussion quickly and avoid conflict.

basic.situation: Your mentor asks you to review a sample Year 5 Science lesson plan. It says sound travels fastest through air, which does not match the textbook.

options.text: Tell your mentor about the mismatch and let the teacher decide how to change it.
Check the claim against the syllabus and textbook, then show your mentor the page references.
Pass the plan because its activities and timing match what other teachers use.
Rewrite the sentence in the plan yourself and return it to the teacher today.

advanced.situation: You lead a review of the Bahasa Melayu reading programme across 40 schools. Test scores are flat, but teachers say the method works. The district office wants a recommendation by month end.

options.text: Combine scores, classroom observations and teacher surveys, then recommend adjustments with a date to review again.
Recommend keeping the method because teachers report good results and scores may rise next term.
Break the score data down by school and report which schools improved or fell behind.
Recommend replacing the method with another popular one, since scores have not moved this year.

basic.situation: Your supervisor takes you to observe a Form 1 English class. You notice the teacher talks for most of the lesson while students sit quietly.

options.text: Write down that the teacher did most of the talking and tell your supervisor afterwards.
Tell the teacher after class to ask students more questions in future lessons.
Record talk time and student responses during the lesson, then go through them with your supervisor.
Report to the school head that the teacher is weak and should receive a warning.

advanced.situation: You are coaching a teacher who must move to group project lessons. Two observations show she reverts to lecturing, and she says the class gets restless.

options.text: Plan a short lesson together, then observe it and give feedback on the restless moments.
Recommend that she be taken off the programme since her class behaviour does not suit it.
Share written examples of group project lessons from another school and ask her to try one.
Tell her to follow the new format each lesson and say you will observe again soon.

basic.situation: A senior coordinator asks you to find which Ministry of Education circular applies when a school wants to change its class timetable.

options.text: Search the Ministry's official circular list and give the coordinator the number and date.
Tell the school to continue using the timetable rules from last year's circular.
Check the school's circular folder for a matching topic and show the coordinator what you found.
Approve the school's timetable change yourself, since the principal already agreed to it.

advanced.situation: A parent says a school broke Ministry rules by moving a Form 3 student to a lower class without notice. The principal says the circular allows it. You must advise.

options.text: Accept the principal's reading of the circular, since the school applies it every year.
Tell the parent the school broke the rules and say the student will be moved back.
Read the circular and compare it with the school's steps, then advise both sides in writing.
Ask the principal for the circular clause and notice records, then file them with the complaint.

basic.situation: A Year 3 teacher asks you to help choose a reading book for a class with mixed reading levels. You are working under the head of the English panel.

options.text: Order a class set of a popular novel online and send the teacher the invoice.
Pick a title you enjoyed as a child that is not on the approved list.
Shortlist three titles at different levels from the approved list and show the panel head.
Recommend one approved title at the middle reading level and tell the teacher to adapt it.

advanced.situation: A school head wants to start a coding programme next term. Teachers lack time, the Ministry guidelines require set outcomes, and the budget is small. You are asked to advise.

options.text: Fit coding outcomes into existing subjects and propose a phased start with free tools.
Recommend a coding club run by one enthusiastic teacher and report back on interest later.
Advise the head to buy tablets for every pupil so the programme starts on time.
Draft a timetable for the whole programme and send it to every teacher to follow.

basic.situation: Your supervisor gives you a list to order 300 exercise books for Year 4. When you check the store, you find 200 books already in stock.

options.text: Cancel the order and tell the teachers to share the 200 books already in stock.
Order the 300 as listed and tell your supervisor about the extra stock afterwards.
Tell your supervisor about the stock and ask whether to order fewer or follow the list.
Order 100 books to cover the gap and mention the change in your next update.

advanced.situation: You must set purchase standards for science kits costing over RM5,000 each across 30 schools. Schools want freedom to choose, but past kits were incompatible and overpriced.

options.text: Require three quotes for each kit and let a school panel pick the cheapest.
Let each school buy any kit it likes and report the price afterwards to the district.
Sign a contract with one supplier for all 30 schools this week to secure a discount.
Set an approved kit list with agreed specifications and let schools choose within it.

basic.situation: You are helping set up a Saturday teacher workshop on a new maths app for 25 teachers. The trainer sends the slides and asks you to prepare the room.

options.text: Set up the chairs and email the slides to teachers the night before instead of printing.
