Print copies, test the projector and internet with the app open, and set seats for 25.
Print the slides, set out 25 chairs and leave the equipment for the trainer to check.
Leave the room as it is, since hall staff usually prepare it for workshops.

advanced.situation: You are leading a two day conference for 300 teachers on new classroom tablets. Two weeks before, the keynote speaker cancels and registration shows many teachers have never used tablets.

options.text: Replace the keynote with a practical opening session and group teachers by experience level.
Find another keynote speaker quickly and keep the programme as planned for all teachers.
Shorten the conference to one day by dropping the practice sessions and keeping the talks.
Cancel the conference and hold it next year when a speaker and equipment are ready.

basic.situation: The teacher steps out for five minutes and asks you to watch a Year 2 class. Two children start pulling the same pair of scissors from each other.

options.text: Call the children's names and tell them to stop until the teacher returns.
Step in, take the scissors, and tell both children how turns will work.
Let them sort it out between themselves since the teacher is back soon.
Send both children to the corridor until the teacher comes back to sort it out.

advanced.situation: You are supervising a Year 6 group on a field trip. A boy walks towards the exit gate and refuses to return, saying the rules are silly.

options.text: Tell him loudly to return and warn that you will report him to the principal.
Let him go and note the time, since he is old enough to rejoin later.
Walk beside him and talk him back, planning to tell the teacher at the next stop.
Stay with him calmly, alert the teacher by phone, and have another adult take your group.

basic.situation: After the Year 1 art lesson, glue and paper scraps cover the tables. The teacher asks you to clean up and put the children's paintings on the wall before parents visit.

options.text: Clean the tables first, then hang the paintings with each at a child's eye level.
Wipe the tables, then hang the paintings in a neat row high on the board.
Mix a strong cleaner from the store cupboard to clear the glue and let children help.
Hang the paintings first because parents arrive soon, then clean the tables if time remains.

advanced.situation: Two new assistants will set up a Year 2 room for a pupil who uses a wheelchair. You have twenty minutes before school starts to show them how.

options.text: Walk the pupil's route with them, then agree reachable heights for materials and displays.
Set up the room yourself while they watch, then ask them to repeat it tomorrow.
Tell them to copy last year's layout since it passed inspection for another class.
Give them a written checklist on aisle width and shelf height and let them set up.

basic.situation: The teacher asks you to show a Year 4 group how to fold paper lanterns. Halfway through, you realise your folding differs from the teacher's sample.

options.text: Finish the demonstration your way, then show the teacher your lantern after the lesson.
Pause, compare with the teacher's sample, and ask which way the class should use.
Switch to the sample's folds mid lesson and let the children work out the difference.
Tell the children the teacher's sample is outdated and theirs should look like yours.

advanced.situation: Several Year 3 children keep leaving a new classmate out at break. The teacher asks you to plan and lead a short social skills series, with the teacher coaching you.

options.text: Seat the new child beside the excluding group and tell them to be friends.
Hold one talk on kindness with the whole class and ask the children to include everyone.
Plan short role play sessions on joining in, agree them with the teacher, and observe break.
Name the children who left the new child out when you address the class.

basic.situation: The teacher asks you to read a short story aloud to a Year 2 group. Two children at the side cannot see the pictures and start talking.

options.text: Pause, move the children closer so all can see the pictures, then carry on reading.
Keep reading louder so the talking children can still hear the story.
Stop the story and take away story time from the whole group for the day.
Ask the two children to sit at the back until they are ready to listen.

advanced.situation: Three Year 5 pupils are far behind in reading. The teacher asks you to propose a tutoring plan at the staff committee tomorrow, and you have today to prepare.

options.text: Review the pupils' reading records, draft a small group plan, and test it with the teacher.
Suggest daily one on one tutoring for each pupil, using a free hour you have.
Ask the committee at the meeting what they would like to do for the three pupils.
Skip the meeting and email the committee that the pupils need to repeat the year.

basic.situation: The teacher asks you to hand out workbooks to 30 pupils, but you count only 28 in the box.

options.text: Hand out the 28 books and tell the teacher about the shortage after class.
Take two workbooks from another class's shelf and hand them out before the lesson starts.
Photocopy two pages from a workbook for the missing pupils and hand those out.
Hand out the 28 books, tell the teacher, and let two pupils share for now.

advanced.situation: You manage the stock cupboard for six classrooms. Paper runs out every month before the next order arrives, and teachers complain. You are asked to fix the system and brief staff.

options.text: Ask teachers to bring in their own paper from home whenever the cupboard runs low.
Record the shortage in the stock book as damaged goods so the order is approved.
Order double the paper each month and keep a spare box in each room.
Track monthly use per class, set a reorder level, and teach staff to log stock.

basic.situation: The teacher asks you to make a Year 4 bulletin board about the water cycle. The teacher gave you a list of five labels and a sample picture.

options.text: Use the teacher's list and sample, and add two extra facts from the internet.
Follow the teacher's list, place the labels at pupils' eye level, and ask for a check.
Copy a finished water cycle poster from a website and print it for the board.
Rewrite the labels in your own words and put up the board before school opens.

advanced.situation: You are asked to set standards for digital teaching aids in your school. Teachers make slides with tiny text, flashing animations and unlicensed pictures.

options.text: Write a short standard on text size, motion and licences, then train staff.
Review each teacher's slides yourself and edit the ones you find hard to read.
Ban slides and animations across the school until a new policy is approved.
Email all teachers a reminder to use bigger text, fewer animations and licensed pictures.

basic.situation: A therapist's plan says a child with autism should follow a picture schedule for the morning routine. Today the child refuses to move from the carpet to the next picture.

options.text: Lift the child up and carry them to the next area to keep to the plan.
Point to the picture again, give the choice the plan allows, and wait calmly.
Skip that picture and move to the next activity so the morning stays on time.
Repeat the instruction in a firm voice and point to the next picture.

advanced.situation: A student with severe disabilities hits staff when frustrated. The behaviour specialist's programme is not working, and the teacher asks for your view before the review meeting.

options.text: Record what happens before each incident for a week and bring the pattern to the specialist.
Keep the student in the quiet room alone each time frustration starts, to protect staff.
Change the programme steps yourself for a week and report the results at the meeting.
Tell the teacher the programme looks too strict and suggest softer rules at the meeting.

basic.situation: The teacher asks you to hand out the Year 3 maths textbooks for today's lesson. You notice the box holds an older edition with different page numbers from the teacher's copy.

options.text: Hand out the old books and write the teacher's page numbers on the board.
Hand out the old books and tell the pupils the page numbers may be different.
Show the teacher the old books and ask whether to use them or fetch new ones.
Take the new edition from the Year 4 cupboard and bring it back after the lesson.

advanced.situation: You support a pupil with dyslexia in a class where the teacher and you give different instructions, confusing the pupil. The teacher is busy with exams, but you need to align support.

options.text: Ask the teacher for ten minutes to agree on shared instructions and who leads each task.
Keep using your own instructions for the pupil because they seem to work better.
Follow the teacher's instructions closely from now on and drop your own approach with the pupil.
Tell the pupil's parents that the teacher's instructions are unclear and need to change.

basic.situation: You are watching Year 1 pupils in the school canteen at recess. A child is walking around holding a hot bowl of soup, and others are running nearby.

options.text: Guide the child to a seat with the soup and tell the running pupils to walk.
Call out from across the room for the pupils to slow down and sit.
Stay at your spot near the door and step in if the soup spills.
Take the bowl from the child and carry it to a table yourself.

advanced.situation: A pupil with ADHD starts throwing chairs in the classroom. The teacher is out sick, a relief teacher is new to the class, and two other pupils begin to cry.

options.text: Grab the pupil firmly by the arms and hold them down until they stop.
Calm the pupil using the calming plan and ask the relief teacher to comfort the others.
Move the pupils to safety, use the pupil's calming plan, and call the senior teacher.
Tell the relief teacher what you know about the pupil and let them lead.

basic.situation: The teacher asks you to prepare picture cards for a sorting game about fruits. Some of the children in the group cannot yet read words.

options.text: Print large pictures of each fruit and cut them out ready for the group.
Print a list of fruit names and ask the children to sort the words.
Print the first fruit pictures from an image search and hand them out as they are.
Print large clear pictures with the fruit name underneath and check the set with the teacher.

advanced.situation: A pupil with low vision and poor hand control is learning shapes. The teacher asks you to adapt a tablet game and a hands on activity so both help build the pupil's skills.

options.text: Enlarge the shapes with high contrast colours, add textured pieces to feel, and try them.
Replace the shape work with colouring sheets so the pupil can stay busy.
Use the tablet game on the largest zoom and let the pupil play daily.
Keep the standard game and activity and give the pupil extra time to finish them.

basic.situation: At the end of the lesson, glue sticks, counters and picture cards are scattered across the tables. The teacher asks you to tidy up before the next group arrives in ten minutes.

options.text: Wipe the tables and leave the items stacked on the teacher's desk for later.
Return items to their labelled boxes, wipe the tables, and place boxes on low shelves.
Put all the items into one big box and wipe the tables clean.
Sweep the counters and cards into the bin to save time and wipe the tables.

advanced.situation: You are designing the layout for a new classroom with children who have different needs: two use walkers, one is sensitive to noise, and others need quiet corners. Space is tight.

options.text: Place the quiet corner next to the door so pupils can leave when needed.
Sketch a plan with wide paths, a quiet corner and reachable shelves, then try it out.
Copy the layout from another class that worked and fit the furniture around it as needed.
Arrange desks in rows with a gap on each side for the walkers.

basic.situation: A pupil with Down syndrome needs help washing hands before snack time. The teacher's plan says to show each step and let the pupil try.

options.text: Tell the pupil each step out loud from the doorway and watch until it ends.
Wash the pupil's hands for them quickly so snack time starts on schedule.
Skip handwashing today and give the pupil a wet tissue before the snack.
Show each step with soap and water, then let the pupil try it.

advanced.situation: You are asked to create a plan to teach a group of four teens with autism to buy snacks at the school shop. Each teen has different reading and money skills.

options.text: Take all four to the shop with a picture list and help whoever struggles.
Teach the whole group the same coin counting worksheet and test them next week.
Assess each teen's money skills, then plan shop role play with steps set for each.
Give each teen money and send them to the shop to learn by doing.

basic.situation: You are grading first-year essays with the lecturer's rubric. One essay is excellent but runs 300 words over the limit, and the rubric does not say what to do.

options.text: Stop reading at the word limit and mark the part you have read so far.
Grade it as written and add a note that the length went over the limit.
Cut the mark by ten percent for length since other markers are likely to do so.
Grade it on the rubric criteria and ask the lecturer how to treat the extra length.

advanced.situation: You help set marking standards for six assistants on a 400 student exam. Early scripts show assistants award very different marks for the same answer.

options.text: Ask the strictest assistant to mark all 400 scripts again so results look consistent.
Hold a calibration session using sample scripts, agree marks together, then spot check each assistant's batch.
Average each assistant's marks afterwards and adjust them to match the overall mean.
Write a detailed model answer with mark allocations and send it to all assistants.

basic.situation: You lead a tutorial for 20 first year students using the lecturer's discussion guide. Three students speak, and the rest look at their phones.

options.text: Call on students by name from the list and move through the guide's questions.
Ask the guide's next question to pairs first, then invite each pair to share.
Continue with the three active students and finish all the guide's questions on time.
Tell the class their participation marks will drop unless everyone speaks next week.

advanced.situation: A student in your lab section is failing and says they may quit the course. They ask you for help, but your office hours are full.

options.text: Do the next lab report together so the student passes this week and stays enrolled.
Book an extra session this week, plan their study steps, and suggest the support centre.
Give the student the lecturer's revision notes and say they can email you questions.
Tell the student to join the queue at your next office hours like everyone else.

basic.situation: The lecturer gives you detailed notes and asks you to type an answer key for a quiz of ten questions. You find that the answer to question 7 looks different from your textbook.

options.text: Type the answer from your textbook for question 7 and mention it in your email.
Leave question 7 out of the key so the problem does not come up.
Finish the key as given, mark question 7, and ask the lecturer to confirm it.
Type the lecturer's answer for question 7 and move on since the notes are official.

advanced.situation: You are asked to build the course website for a 300 student module. The lecturer wants fast delivery, but past sites were hard to navigate and often had broken links.

options.text: Upload all slides, readings and notes in one long page so students can scroll.
Copy last year's website layout and update the dates and links before launch.
Group content by week, test every link and ask three students to try the site first.
Link to public files on your personal drive so you can change them quickly.

basic.situation: A student asks during office hours how to submit a lab report. The course site says to upload a PDF by 5 pm on Friday.

options.text: Show them the upload page and tell them the PDF format and Friday deadline.
Tell the student late reports are accepted until Monday since most students submit then.
Offer to take the printed report and hand it to the lecturer yourself.
Tell the student to read the course site because the steps are written there.

advanced.situation: In peak week, 25 students arrive at your office hours with questions about extensions, resubmissions and a grading rule. You can see everyone for only a few minutes each.

options.text: See students in order and give each three minutes, then leave the rest for next week.
Approve every extension request on the spot to clear the queue faster this week.
Tell students to email their questions and cancel your office hours for the week.
Sort questions by type, answer common ones for the group, and book longer ones later.

basic.situation: While marking, you find that assignment question 4 refers to a chart that was left out of the handout.

options.text: Give every student full marks on question 4 and record it as a normal mark.
Draw the chart from memory and email it to students so they can finish.
Tell the lecturer today, with the question number, and wait to hear how to mark it.
Mark everyone's answers to question 4 as normal and mention the missing chart later.

advanced.situation: A student disputes a grade, saying you marked two similar answers differently. The lecturer asked you to meet your supervisor to settle it, and the form is due Friday.

options.text: Compare both answers with the rubric, bring them to your supervisor, and complete the form.
Explain to the student how you marked each answer and offer to review it again.
Raise the lower mark to match the higher one so the dispute ends.
Change the grade in the system yourself and fill in the form afterwards.

basic.situation: Before the 9 am tutorial the lecturer gives you a list: copy 40 handouts and bring them to the room. The copier is out of paper.

options.text: Refill the copier from the department store, print 40 copies, and carry them over.
Take paper from the lecturer's private office drawer to refill the copier this morning.
Send the file to students and ask them to print it before class.
Print 20 copies on the last sheets and ask students to share in pairs.

advanced.situation: You coordinate materials for six tutorial groups across two buildings. Textbook orders arrive late, and assignments must be returned to students by Monday as promised.

options.text: Return the assignments on Monday and tell groups the textbooks will come when they arrive.
Order the textbooks from an online shop using your own card to get them faster.
Photocopy chapters from the library copy for all groups and return assignments later.
List each group's needs, chase the supplier with dates, and return marked work by building.

basic.situation: A senior designer asks you to draft the layout for a Hari Raya promotion flyer. The brief gives A5 size, two photos and a headline, but no font size.

options.text: Use the same font sizes as the last flyer you worked on and send it.
Shrink the type to fit both photos and the headline, then send it for printing.
Draft the layout with readable type sizes, list your choices, and ask for sign off.
Wait until the senior has time to give you the exact font sizes.

advanced.situation: You must set design standards for a new campaign. Three illustrators propose very different styles, and the client's brand guide says only friendly and modern.

options.text: Let each illustrator keep their style and tell them to follow the brand colours.
Draft a one page style guide covering colour, type and illustration, then review it together.
Ask the client to choose one of the three styles and set rules from that.
Pick the style you like most and tell the other two to match it.

basic.situation: You are presenting final brochure layouts to a client with your supervisor present. The client points out a spelling mistake on page 3 that you missed.

options.text: Say the mistake is just from the draft and the final file will be fine.
Thank the client, note the fix, and say you will send an updated proof today.
Apologise, then promise to fix it and go on to the next page.
Fix the page on your laptop during the meeting and approve it for printing.

advanced.situation: A client's budget has dropped by 40 percent after you got approval. Their goals for the launch have not changed, and the creative team has already started work.

options.text: Keep the full plan and ask the client to find the remaining money.
Meet the client, rank their goals, and present two lower cost plans with the trade offs.
Cut the production quality across all items evenly to meet the new budget.
Promise the client the full plan at the lower budget and sort out the cost later.

basic.situation: You check illustrations for a children's book against the spec sheet. One image is 150 dpi, but the sheet asks for 300 dpi for print.

options.text: Approve all the images since the 150 dpi one looks fine on your screen.
Pass the other images and tell your supervisor one image looks low in quality.
Ask the printer whether 150 dpi would be acceptable for this book before deciding.
Flag the image, note the resolution, and ask the illustrator for a 300 dpi version.

advanced.situation: You set quality standards for proofs. Last month, three printed catalogues had colour shifts the team approved on screen. The printer says screens and press do not match.

options.text: Require a printed proof on final paper for colour critical jobs, with a sign off checklist.
Calibrate every team screen to the printer's profile and keep approving on screen.
Ask the printer to match colours to the screens in future and accept their promise.
Add a rule that reviewers must approve proofs within one hour to avoid delays.

basic.situation: You attend a product photo shoot for a skincare brand with your art director. The shot list has twelve images, and the photographer says the studio time ends in an hour.

options.text: Ask the photographer to skip the hard shots so the shoot finishes on time.
Watch the shoot and give the art director a full report once it ends.
Tick off shots as they are taken and tell the art director what remains.
Add extra studio time yourself by agreeing a new hourly rate with the photographer.

advanced.situation: In launch week, the copywriter's headline is longer than the layout allows, the printer needs files tomorrow, and the photographer's final images are one day late.

options.text: Shrink the headline type to fit and use the old images until the new ones come.
Ask the printer for an extra day and keep the headline and images as they are.
Hold a short meeting with copy, design and the photographer to agree cuts and timing.
Send the printer the files as they are and say changes will follow after printing.

basic.situation: A senior designer asks you to brief two junior staff on resizing banners to three sizes. One junior asks you to explain what safe margins are.

options.text: Explain that margins keep key content from being cut off, and show it on a banner.
Tell the junior to look up the term online and ask again later.
Tell the junior to follow the same margins used on the last banner.
Say that margins matter little for banners and tell them to fill the space.

advanced.situation: You are asked to train five new layout staff on a complex annual report design. Their skill levels differ, and the creative director wants the first pages in two weeks.

options.text: Give all five the same training deck and review their pages when they finish.
Let them learn by working on the live client file and fix problems as they appear.
Do the hardest pages yourself and give the new staff the simple ones.
Check each person's skills first, then set a two week plan with paired work and reviews.

basic.situation: You track the schedule for a poster project. The printer's quote is RM2,000, but your supervisor's budget sheet shows RM1,800 for printing.

options.text: Ask the printer for a discount to bring the quote down to RM1,800.
Tell your supervisor about the RM200 gap and ask how to cover it.
Change the quote figure in the sheet to RM1,800 so the budget looks balanced.
Move RM200 from another project's printing line to cover the gap in your sheet.

advanced.situation: You manage three projects, and a new software tool could cut production time by 30 percent. Two deadlines fall in the same fortnight, and the budget has no room for training.

options.text: Install the tool on all three projects this week to save time before the deadlines.
Trial the tool on one low risk job after the deadlines, then report the results.
Pass on the tool and ask the team to work extra hours to meet both deadlines.
Ask the director to approve the tool now and train the team after the deadlines.

basic.situation: You are making a batik tote bag and a customer asks for a small turtle motif. Your supervisor wants a sketch before any cloth is cut.

options.text: Sketch a quick turtle on your phone and send it to your supervisor for approval.
Cut the cloth to the bag pattern first so the turtle can be drawn on after.
Trace a turtle from a picture online onto the cloth and show the sketch later.
Sketch the turtle at actual size on paper, then show the customer and supervisor before cutting.

advanced.situation: Your studio plans a new line of handmade ceramic gift sets for Raya. Material costs rose 15 percent, and similar sets in the mall sell for RM60.

options.text: Match the mall price of RM60 and cut glaze and packaging to protect your margin.
Design a smaller set with a local motif, cost it fully, and price it by value.
Switch to a cheaper clay from a new supplier and keep the same price and design.
Keep the existing set design and raise the price by exactly 15 percent for Raya.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to make a brochure for a weekend craft fair. You have photos of five products and prices from the price list.

options.text: Use the five photos and write a short story about each product's origin.
Add prices that you think customers would pay, since the list may be old.
Print 500 copies today so they are ready before the fair starts on Saturday.
Use the five photos and list prices, add contact details, and ask your supervisor to check.

advanced.situation: You plan your studio's booth at a three day craft show. Last year foot traffic was high but sales were low, and customers often asked for custom orders.

options.text: Hand out more brochures at the entrance and stay close to the busiest aisle.
Add more low priced items to the table to lift the number of sales.
Offer made to order samples and a simple order form, and track which products draw questions.
Cut all prices by half on the first day to attract more crowds to the booth.

basic.situation: You are choosing wood for a small keepsake box. The supervisor says it should be light and easy to carve, and you have teak, meranti and rubberwood.

options.text: Pick the wood the supervisor used last time and check how it feels in the hand.
Use the cheapest offcut bin wood and glue pieces together to make the box.
Carve a small offcut from each lighter wood and pick the one that cuts cleanly.
Pick the darkest wood because it looks rich and strong for a keepsake box.

advanced.situation: You write specifications for 200 outdoor bamboo lanterns for a hotel. The hotel wants a matt finish, three years of wet weather use, and a fixed delivery date.

options.text: Leave dimensions flexible and let the workers choose sizes that suit available bamboo.
Specify treated bamboo and matt paint, and leave sealing to the hotel's maintenance team.
Choose the cheapest untreated bamboo and a glossy varnish since it is quickest to apply.
Specify treated bamboo, a water resistant matt sealant, set sizes, and an approved sample.

basic.situation: You are cutting thin brass sheet for earrings with hand snips. A piece curls and the edge looks rough, though your supervisor showed you the cutting method.

options.text: Use the grinder from the next bench to cut the remaining pieces much faster.
Stop, flatten the piece, file the edge smooth, and ask your supervisor how to avoid curling.
Press harder with the snips to get through the curl in one cut.
File the rough edge smooth and carry on cutting the other pieces the same way.

advanced.situation: You are asked to make a curved wooden bench with joints hidden inside. The first joint split along the grain, and the client's deadline is in four days.

options.text: Fill the crack with wood filler and stain over it so it cannot be seen.
Rebuild with the same joint and thicker wood to reduce the chance of splitting.
Glue and clamp the split joint and add a hidden screw for extra strength.
Test a new joint on scrap with the grain turned, then rebuild once it holds.

basic.situation: You are cutting a paper template for a set of ten leather coin purses. The supervisor gave you the measurements, and your first trace looks one centimetre too short.

options.text: Add a centimetre to the template and cut one test purse to see.
Cut all ten from leather using the short template and fix the size later.
Use the template as it is and make the purses a little larger when sewing.
Recheck the sheet's measurements, remeasure your trace, and remake the template if needed.

advanced.situation: A hotel orders 500 identical wooden soap dishes. Your first prototype looks good, but it tips over when wet and takes forty minutes to make.

options.text: Widen the base on the prototype and test it wet before starting the order.
Redesign the base, make a second prototype, time it, and cut a template.
Send the hotel the first prototype as the sample and negotiate the details after payment.
Start the order with the first design and fix the tipping on a later batch.

basic.situation: You are applying clear varnish to ten wooden spoons. The instructions say two thin coats with four hours between them, and it is already late afternoon.

options.text: Apply the first coat now and add the second coat after four hours or tomorrow.
Apply the varnish and pack the spoons into the boxes while they are still tacky.
Apply one thick coat now to save time and leave them to dry overnight.
Apply both coats within one hour and use a fan to dry them faster.

advanced.situation: You must pack 30 hand painted glass vases for courier shipping to Sabah. The courier handles parcels roughly, and last time three vases arrived cracked.

options.text: Pack the vases together in one large box with newspaper filling the gaps.
Wrap each vase, double box with padding, mark parcels fragile, and drop test one box.
Wrap each vase in bubble wrap and mark the boxes fragile in large letters.
Send them by courier in single thin cartons and replace any that break later.

basic.situation: A mentor asks you to visit a local art exhibition and bring back ideas for your next series of portraits. You have two hours and a notebook.

options.text: Walk through quickly and read the titles on the wall labels for ideas.
Take photos of the whole exhibition and review them at home later for ideas.
Sketch the most popular painting closely and use its composition for your series.
Pick three works, note how each was made, and share your notes.

advanced.situation: You guide two junior artists on how to research trends before a gallery proposal. One follows social media alone, and the other copies techniques from old masters.

options.text: Tell both to follow whatever sells well online and copy that style for the proposal.
Show them how to mix exhibitions, publications and technique study to develop their own ideas.
Let each continue their method and review the proposals when they are finished.
Tell the social media artist to visit galleries and the other to look at current work.

basic.situation: Your mentor asks you to paint a quiet evening scene of a kampung house. Your first sketch looks flat, with everything the same size.

options.text: Add more detail to the house so it stands out from the rest of the scene.
Enlarge the house in front, overlap trees behind it, and ask your mentor to look.
Trace a photo of a house in a similar scene and paint over the outline.
Add bright colours across the whole scene so that the picture feels livelier overall.

advanced.situation: A client wants a mural showing community unity, but calm and not busy. The wall is long and narrow, and you must choose colour, space and perspective.

options.text: Use bold bright colours across the mural so people notice it from far away.
Paint a single huge face across the wall in dark colours for strong effect.
Use a limited palette, repeat a few figures along the wall, and leave open space.
Fill the wall with many small figures in soft colours to show unity.

basic.situation: Your mentor asks you to draw a still life of fruit in charcoal. After an hour, the drawing looks smudged and the darks look grey.

options.text: Press firmer for the darks, rest your hand on clean paper, and spray fixative.
Spray the drawing with household paint to hold the charcoal in place before you continue.
Rub the smudged areas with your finger to blend the greys into smoother tones.
Start again on a new sheet using a softer charcoal stick for the darkest areas.

advanced.situation: You are teaching two younger artists to paint a glowing oil portrait with thin layers. One rushes and the paint cracks, and the other keeps overworking the face.

options.text: Finish both portraits yourself so the work looks strong for the coming exhibition.
Give both a printed guide on layering and overworking and let them practise.
Demonstrate fat over lean layers and drying times, then check each next layer.
Tell the first to wait longer and the second to stop when it looks finished.

basic.situation: You need reference photos of a wet market stall to paint later. Your mentor says to take clear shots of the produce, and the light is changing.

options.text: Take wide and close photos of the produce and check they are sharp.
Take a quick video and pick frames from it when you start painting.
Save a photo of a similar stall from the internet and use that as reference.
Take one wide photo of the stall and zoom in later on your computer.

advanced.situation: You plan a half day shoot at a fishing village to gather reference for a large painting series. You want portraits of fishermen and boats, and some people dislike being photographed.

options.text: Photograph the boats and landscape from the jetty and skip the people to avoid problems.
Take portraits from a distance with a zoom lens so nobody notices you.
Photograph the fishermen at work in close up and pay them later if anyone objects.
Visit first, ask permission, agree what to photograph, then shoot portraits and boats in soft light.

basic.situation: Your mentor asks you to prepare a folder of your artwork for a college interview. You have 25 pieces, some unfinished, and the folder allows 10.

options.text: Finish the unfinished pieces quickly in one night and include them with the others.
Choose the ten pieces that you like most and put them in the folder.
Include all 25 pieces in a larger folder so the panel can see everything.
Choose ten finished pieces that show different styles and ask your mentor to review.

advanced.situation: A student asks you to help build a portfolio for a design scholarship. Their strongest pieces are digital, but the panel asks for varied traditional media.

options.text: Check the criteria, choose a mix with traditional pieces, and plan new work for gaps.
Submit the digital work and explain in a note how each piece uses traditional skills.
Print the digital pieces and mount them so they look like traditional media.
Scan old school drawings from other students and add them to fill the gap.

basic.situation: An editor emails you to illustrate a short story for a school magazine. The email says two pages, soon, with no deadline or image size.

options.text: Reply asking for the deadline, image size, colour or black and white, and the story text.
Send a finished colour illustration at a large size to cover any need.
Quote a fixed price of RM500 and start work now so the editor sees your speed.
Start sketching from a general idea of the story and ask for details later.

advanced.situation: You have two illustration clients, and one wants exclusive rights to your style. You are also building a website and mailing list to market your art.

options.text: Decline the exclusivity and promise both clients you will keep styles very different.
Clarify what the exclusivity covers and for how long, then price it into the contract.
Agree to exclusivity today and update your website to say you no longer take other clients.
Accept the exclusivity for a short trial period and tell the other client the dates.

basic.situation: A senior artist asks you to model a simple 3D teapot for a cartoon scene. Your first model has jagged edges where the lid meets the body.

options.text: Send the model to the animator now and say the edges will be fixed in editing.
Hide the join with a decorative band around the lid and move on.
Increase the render quality settings so the jagged edges look softer in the final shot.
Add edge loops at the lid join, smooth it, and ask the senior to check.

advanced.situation: You must convert a real clay sculpture into an animated character that walks and talks. The scan has holes, and the rig folds badly at the knees.

options.text: Hide the knees in the shots by framing the character from the waist up.
Clean the scan holes, rebuild the knee topology with extra loops, and test the walk cycle.
Replace the character with a simpler model from the library so the scan is not needed.
Fill the holes automatically and add a helper shape at each knee fold.

basic.situation: You are asked to add a glow to a lantern in a night scene. Your supervisor wants it warm and soft, but your glow looks harsh and white.

options.text: Darken the whole scene lighting to make the glow stand out more clearly.
Paint a yellow circle over the lantern and flatten all the layers to save time.
Lower the glow strength, tint it warm orange, and widen the blur.
Lower the glow strength a bit and show your supervisor the result for approval.

advanced.situation: You lead the effects look for a rain scene. Each artist's rain, splashes and reflections look different, and the deadline is in three days.

options.text: Switch off reflections and splashes in every shot to match and meet the deadline.
Build one reference frame with agreed settings, then have each artist match it.
Review each shot yourself at the end and fix the ones that differ most.
Let artists keep their own looks and blend the shots with a colour grade.

basic.situation: A senior artist asks you to sketch a storyboard for a ten second scene where a cat jumps onto a table. You have drawn four panels.

options.text: Show the four panels to your friend first and send them after their comments.
Copy panels from a popular cat cartoon and change the colours slightly to fit.
Add four more panels showing the cat from different angles and share all eight.
Make sure the panels show the start, jump, landing and reaction, then share them.

advanced.situation: You must plan a 30 second animated ad in two days. The director wants a surprising ending, and the client changed the product name this morning.

options.text: Finish the storyboard with the old name and replace the name text at the end.
Ask the client to confirm the final name before you draw any more panels.
Thumbnail two endings with the new name and review them with the director.
Pick an ending you like and animate it fully before the director sees it.

basic.situation: You scan a hand drawn character and need to colour it. The scan has pencil smudges and a faint grey background.

options.text: Redraw the character on a tablet from scratch to avoid cleaning the scan.
Brighten the background with levels, erase smudges on a new layer, then colour below.
Colour straight onto the scan and erase the smudges on the same layer.
Apply a heavy blur filter to the whole scan until the smudges disappear.

advanced.situation: You manage the art files for a game trailer made by five artists. Files are named inconsistently, and last week an old version overwrote a finished scene.

options.text: Delete the old versions from the shared folder so they cannot be mixed up again.
Take over saving all final files yourself so nobody else can overwrite them.
Set file naming and version rules, add folder backups, and brief all five artists.
Send a message reminding everyone to name files clearly and save new versions.

basic.situation: You must make a simple label design for a juice carton from a supervisor's sketch. The printer needs CMYK colours, and your file is in RGB.

options.text: Convert the file to CMYK and send it to the printer the same day.
Send the RGB file and tell the printer to convert it during setup.
Convert the file to CMYK, check the colours, and have your supervisor approve it.
Change the colours by eye to bright shades so they will survive printing.

advanced.situation: A carton design prints with a wrong barcode and slightly shifted colours on test sheets, and the client expects 50,000 cartons next week.

options.text: Print the cartons as they are and offer the client a discount if scanning fails.
Ask the printer to add a sticker barcode over the printed one and carry on.
Fix the barcode file and send the shifted colours to the client for a decision.
Hold the run, check barcode and plates against the proof, then send a new sample.

basic.situation: Your manager asks you to help track an animation project's progress. You notice one scene is two days behind but nobody has mentioned it.

options.text: Ask the artist to work overnight to catch up before the next report.
Mark it in the tracker and wait to see whether the artist catches up.
Show the scene as on schedule in the tracker until the artist finishes it.
Mark it in the tracker and tell your manager which scene is two days behind.

advanced.situation: You manage budget and files for a 12 artist animation campaign. Two artists used different software versions, causing mismatched files, and the budget has RM3,000 left.

options.text: Fix one software version, convert the mismatched files, and log the change in version control.
Ask both artists to convert their own files and spend the budget on extra checking.
Ask the artists to keep their versions and fix the mismatch at the final edit.
Buy the latest software licences for all 12 artists using the remaining RM3,000 budget.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to check a kettle concept for safety and handling. Users say the handle gets warm, and the lid is hard to open.

options.text: Add a rubber grip to the handle and drop the lid issue for now.
Test how warm the handle gets and report the temperature to your supervisor.
Tell your supervisor the kettle is safe because the heating parts already passed testing.
List the handle and lid complaints, check the safety standard, and report to your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You lead research for a new lunch box for office workers. Early surveys show people want leak proof boxes, but production costs may rise by 25 percent.

options.text: Recommend the leak proof design and accept the cost rise as the market will follow.
Cancel the leak proof feature and select the cheapest design from earlier lunch boxes.
Run a larger survey on leak proof features and report the demand figures.
Ask users what they would pay, get supplier quotes, and compare the two.

basic.situation: A senior designer asks you to sketch three ideas for a desk lamp. You have one hour, and the budget limits you to plastic and aluminium.

options.text: Sketch three lamps in glass and brass since they look more premium to buyers.
Pick a lamp from a catalogue and trace it as your first idea.
Sketch three lamp forms in plastic and aluminium and note each one's features.
Sketch one detailed lamp in plastic and aluminium and describe two more variants.

advanced.situation: A client wants a folding stool that must hold 120 kg, cost under RM40 to make, and look modern. Your working model bends at the hinge when tested.

options.text: Use thicker material for the whole stool and tell the client the cost will rise.
Reduce the stated weight limit to 80 kg so the current model passes the test.
Reinforce the hinge, retest at full load, and recheck the cost per unit.
Send the current model to the client with a note that it can hold 120 kg.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to study three competing kettles and note their styles before a design meeting. You have the products and a notebook.

options.text: Compare the kettles by shape, material and features, and bring a summary.
Take photos of each kettle from several angles and share them at the meeting.
Read online reviews of the three kettles and report which one is most popular.
Copy the shape of the most popular kettle and present it as your own concept.

advanced.situation: A factory is making your plastic chair design. You see workers sanding rough edges by hand on a third of the chairs, which slows output and hurts quality.

options.text: Tell the workers to skip sanding on chairs that look acceptable to speed output.
Find what causes the rough edges, then agree a mould or process fix with the factory.
Suggest the factory adds another worker to sand the chairs and keep up with output.
Redesign the chair with softer edges and send the new design to the factory.

basic.situation: You are in a meeting with the engineering team about a new water bottle cap. Engineering says your cap design is too hard to mould, and you are unsure why.

options.text: Tell engineering the design is final because the client has already approved it.
Ask engineering which part is hard to mould and note their suggestions for the cap.
Say you will review the design and send the engineers a revised version.
Tell the client engineering rejected the cap and the project is behind schedule.

advanced.situation: You present a new appliance design to a committee. Two members want a bigger screen, and production says that adds RM15 per unit. The committee votes in ten minutes.

options.text: Say production can absorb the RM15 cost and confirm the bigger screen to win the vote.
Show the screen trade offs with costs and propose a medium size to vote on.
Agree to the bigger screen and note the RM15 cost in the minutes.
Defend the original screen size and ask the committee to approve it as drawn.

basic.situation: You are asked to build a foam model of a hand held fan. The supervisor shows you the sketch, and the foam is thick, rough cut stock.

options.text: Mark the sketch outline, cut slowly with a sharp blade, and sand the edges.
Cut the shape freehand with scissors, then sand the edges if they look rough.
Print a larger fan from the 3D printer instead and skip the foam model.
Use a heated wire cutter from the other workshop to cut the foam quickly.

advanced.situation: You are building a working model of a new door handle in metal, plastic and wood to test grip. Metal parts need machining, and you have used the lathe only twice.

options.text: Print the metal parts in plastic and test the shape, weight and feel by hand.
Machine the parts yourself slowly on the lathe and test the handle in the lab.
Ask the technician to supervise the machining, then assemble and test the grip.
Order cheap metal castings online and fit them as received to test the model.

basic.situation: You help direct the making of three model samples of a phone stand. The workshop asks which colour each sample should be, and the sketch does not say.

options.text: Tell the workshop to choose colours they have in stock to save time.
Pick three colours from the brand palette and tell the workshop to proceed.
Check the specification sheet, then ask the designer before telling the workshop.
Choose the colours you like and update the sketch to show them as final.

advanced.situation: You direct fabrication of ten sample sets. The workshop built from an older drawing, and the specification sheet lists dimensions that do not match the new drawing.

options.text: Stop work, reconcile the drawing and sheet with the designer, and reissue both.
Update the specification sheet to match the old drawing and carry on building.
Finish the ten sets as built and fix the drawings after the samples are done.
Send the sets to the client and tell them the drawing dimensions are approximate.

basic.situation: Your mentor asks you to review three fashion magazines and list the colours that appear most in this season's modest wear. You have an afternoon.

options.text: Note colours in each magazine, count the repeats, and share the list with your mentor.
List the colours from the first magazine, since trends are usually similar across all magazines.
Choose the colours you personally like and present them as this season's trend.
Copy a colour chart from a competitor's website and present it as your research.

advanced.situation: You lead the team deciding next season's direction for young working women. Fashion shows suggest bold prints, but your sales data shows customers prefer plain colours.

options.text: Ask the team to vote and release the winning direction across all stores.
Test a small print range with key customer groups and keep core plain items.
Follow the fashion shows and make bold prints the main theme this whole season.
Follow the sales data and design plain colours across the whole season's range.

basic.situation: A senior designer gives you a new cotton blend and asks you to help test it so a care label can be made. You have a washing machine and an iron.

options.text: Wash a swatch once and tell the designer how it looks and feels afterwards.
Write a care label saying machine wash hot since cotton usually handles heat.
Copy the care label from a similar cotton blend already in the shop.
Wash a small swatch following the planned label, then measure shrinkage and colour change.

advanced.situation: A new supplier offers a cheaper silk blend for 2,000 dresses. You must set a testing process before approval, and the supplier's own report covers colour fastness alone.

options.text: Order a small batch and test shrinkage yourself before deciding on the full order.
Accept the supplier's report and write labels based on those of similar silk blends.
Require independent tests for shrinkage, colour fastness and strength, then set labels.
Approve the fabric now to lock in the cheaper price and test after delivery.

basic.situation: Your mentor asks you to sketch a simple baju kurung design and write the specification. You are unsure which fabric weight and fastening to list.

options.text: Copy the specification from a different design and change the name at the top.
Sketch the front view and add the full specification after the first fitting is done.
Sketch front and back, list your suggested fabric and fastening, and ask for a review.
Leave the fabric and fastening blank and let the seamstress choose what suits.

advanced.situation: You prepare specifications for a 500 piece uniform order for a hotel. Housekeeping wants easy movement, the manager wants a formal look, and the budget is tight.

options.text: Choose the formal fabric the manager prefers and add pleats to allow some movement.
Choose a stretch blend, specify movement seams, and get sample feedback from both groups.
Choose the cheapest fabric available and list the style as formal in the specification.
Write a loose specification so the factory can pick fabric and details themselves.

basic.situation: You watch a fitting where a sample jacket looks tight across the shoulders on the model. Your supervisor is making notes.

options.text: Ask the model if the jacket feels tight and write down the answer.
Cut open a shoulder seam on the sample to give room before the supervisor decides.
Note where the fabric pulls when the model moves, and tell your supervisor.
Wait until the fitting is over and mention it to the pattern maker.

advanced.situation: A designer's couture gown must be adapted for a mass market line at one third of the cost. The hand beading and silk are too costly for the factory.

options.text: Keep the silhouette, swap in printed trim and crepe, and fit a sample to check.
Copy a competitor's mass market gown pattern and put your brand label on it.
Remove the beading and use the same silk, keeping the design otherwise unchanged.
Use a low cost polyester with a printed beading pattern and skip the sample fitting.

basic.situation: A sales agent needs three sample garments for tomorrow's meeting. You find that one sample has a loose button.

options.text: Sew the button on and hand the samples to the agent before closing time.
Give the agent all three and tell them to expect minor button issues.
Give the agent the two good samples and promise the third will follow later.
Sew the button on, check the other samples, and give all three to the agent.

advanced.situation: A store executive wants a special capsule line for Hari Raya in six weeks. Another designer is already making a similar line, and the executive wants exclusive designs.

options.text: Meet both, split the themes, and agree which pieces are exclusive to the store.
Promise the executive exclusive designs and reuse parts of the other designer's sketches.
Design your line quickly and release it first so the other designer cannot compete.
Tell the executive about the other line and let the store pick between them.

basic.situation: You are told to buy two metres of lace for a sample dress, up to RM60. The usual shop has lace at RM75.

options.text: Buy one metre at RM75 for now and tell your supervisor you need more.
Buy the lace at RM75 and ask the shop to write RM60 on the receipt.
Ask your supervisor whether to pay RM75 or check other shops for lace under RM60.
Buy a similar looking lace from a market stall at RM40 for the sample.

advanced.situation: You direct a team making 300 shirts. The cutters are behind, and the ordered buttons are out of stock, with delivery in two weeks and a deadline in ten days.

options.text: Wait for the original buttons and ask the client to move the deadline.
Source buttons from another supplier, add a cutting shift, and update the client.
Ship the shirts with plain safety pins and tell the client to sew buttons on.
Use buttons left over from an older order and tell the client later.

basic.situation: A customer wants a birthday bouquet in pink and white for RM80. The shop has a standard round bouquet pattern at RM70.

options.text: Use leftover flowers from yesterday's order in any colour and charge the full RM80.
Ask the customer to choose any flowers they like and price it afterwards.
Make a larger bouquet with extra flowers and charge RM80 even though it costs more.
Offer the standard round pattern in pink and white, and confirm the price.

advanced.situation: A bride wants a cascading orchid bouquet that is light enough to hold for two hours, priced at RM300. The orchids cost more than expected.

options.text: Make the full orchid bouquet and ask the bride to pay extra on the day.
Show a sketch using fewer orchids with light filler, and explain the weight and cost.
Accept RM300 and make the cascade heavy with wet foam, then fix the weight later.
Replace the orchids with cheaper flowers and tell her they look very similar.

basic.situation: You are asked to pick flowers and foliage for a small table arrangement in white and green. The shop has roses, baby's breath, ferns and eucalyptus.

options.text: Pick roses that are starting to wilt to use them up before they are thrown out.
Choose white roses and ferns since ferns are the cheapest foliage in the shop.
Choose white roses, eucalyptus and baby's breath, and check that stems are fresh and sturdy.
Choose all four types and fill the vase as full as it will go.

advanced.situation: You must create a new Merdeka arrangement using red, white and blue flowers. Blue flowers are rare, and the client wants something unlike last year.

options.text: Use the same flower combination as last year with a different ribbon and vase.
Dye white flowers blue with food colouring the night before and use them as they are.
Use artificial blue flowers mixed in with fresh ones and say all are fresh.
Test red and white blooms with blue accents, then show the client two versions.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to set up a small Mother's Day display on a table near the entrance, following the shop's guidelines.

options.text: Follow the guideline layout and add price cards later in the morning when there is time.
Block the entrance path with a large display so that every customer sees it.
Rearrange the table in your own style because the guideline layout looks rather dull.
Follow the guideline layout, group flowers by height, and add price cards before opening.

advanced.situation: You plan the shop window for the Chinese New Year season. Last year's red theme brought little extra traffic, and the window faces strong afternoon sun.

options.text: Cover the window with paper to block the sun and put the display behind it.
Design a new theme with sun tolerant flowers and artificial accents, and plan weekly changes.
Fill the window with fresh blooms at the start and replace them when they wilt.
Repeat last year's red theme with larger pieces and brighter lights to attract attention.

basic.situation: A box of fresh roses arrives at the shop. Your supervisor asks you to condition them for storage in the cooler.

options.text: Trim stems at an angle, strip lower leaves, and place them in clean water.
Place the roses in water straight from the box and strip leaves later.
Cut the stems very short with scissors and store them dry in the cooler.
Put the roses in the cooler in their box to avoid wetting the floor.

advanced.situation: You manage flower care for a shop that throws away about 20 percent of stock each week. Staff condition flowers in different ways, and the cooler is overfilled.

options.text: Order less stock each week so the cooler has room and flowers stay fresh longer.
Sell the older flowers as fresh at the usual price to cut the waste figure.
Tell staff to be more careful with flowers and check the bins each Friday.
Track which flowers are wasted, set one conditioning routine, and fix cooler space with staff.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to assemble five small hand tied bouquets with three stems each, using the shop's trimmers and floral tape.

options.text: Use the old trimmers from the back cupboard to cut the stems faster.
Make all five in the same style and show your supervisor when finished.
Make one bouquet first, show your supervisor, then copy it for the other four.
Make each bouquet differently so that every guest gets something unique to take home.

advanced.situation: A hotel wants twelve large wreaths and terrariums for a lobby launch tomorrow. Your two trainees are new, and you are short of floral foam.

options.text: Tell the hotel you can deliver eight pieces tomorrow and the rest next week.
Assign tasks by skill, demonstrate one wreath, and use moss frames when foam runs out.
Make all the wreaths yourself tonight and let the trainees prepare the terrariums alone.
Let the trainees make all twelve pieces and thin out the foam in each wreath.

basic.situation: A customer collects a bouquet you must wrap and price. The price list shows RM45 for this bouquet, but it has two extra stems.

options.text: Check the price list for extra stem charges and tell the customer the total before wrapping.
Charge RM60 for the bouquet since customers rarely check the price in the shop.
Remove the two extra stems from the bouquet to match the listed price.
Charge RM45 as listed and mention the two extra stems to your supervisor later.

advanced.situation: You oversee decoration of a church for a wedding on Saturday and the delivery of ten table arrangements to a hall. A delivery driver calls in sick that morning.

options.text: Ask a friend with a motorbike to carry the arrangements stacked in boxes.
Ask the hall to collect the arrangements from the shop when they are ready.
Deliver the arrangements yourself after the church work and phone the hall about the delay.
Move one staff member to deliveries and tell the hall the new arrival time.

basic.situation: You attend a first meeting with a client about a cafe menu. Your senior designer asks you to note down the client's layout requirements.

options.text: Note the size and page count the client mentions and send the notes to the designer.
Copy the layout of a rival cafe's menu into the brief as the client's requirement.
Take brief notes and fill in the layout details afterwards from what you remember.
Note the size, page count and must-have items, then read them back to the client.

advanced.situation: A bank asks for a rebrand, and your team must get final concepts approved. The board members disagree about the target audience and the style.

options.text: Follow the chairman's preferred style, since he signs the invoices, and adjust the audience later.
Tell each board member you agree with their view and produce concepts for every version.
Show three concept styles to the board and let them choose, noting the choice in writing.
Run a workshop on audience and goals, agree success measures, and record decisions for sign-off.

basic.situation: You are asked to create a simple sample layout for a school fair poster. The senior designer wants a clear order for title, date and venue.

options.text: Make the title largest, put date and venue below in smaller type, and leave space.
Use the same size for all text so everything is easy to read, and add a border.
Copy a published fair poster from the internet and swap in the school's name and date.
Fill the page with bright clip art and shrink the text to fit around the pictures.

advanced.situation: A client needs one logo that works on a website, a phone app icon and a billboard. The creative lead asks you to guide a junior on first drafts.

options.text: Ask the junior to test the sketches at icon and billboard size, then review them together.
Ask the junior to design for the website, then check how it adapts to the rest.
Give the junior a detailed sketch to copy so the drafts match your own idea.
Let the junior send the first drafts straight to the client to save a review round.

basic.situation: Your senior designer gives you step-by-step instructions to create a simple icon in the design software and then asks you to hand over the file.

options.text: Follow the steps in order, compare the icon with the instructions, then save and name it.
Follow the steps and send the icon to the senior designer as soon as it looks right.
Use an icon from a free website, trace over it, and save it as your own work.
Follow the first half of the steps and finish the icon by eye to save time.

advanced.situation: A TV news team needs an animated graphic for tonight's live bulletin. The figures change until the broadcast, and the control room needs the file in an hour.

options.text: Build the graphic with editable data fields, test it on the broadcast system, and prepare a fallback.
Send the unfinished animation to the control room and fix it live while the bulletin runs.
Make a static image of the current figures and tell the control room it replaces the animation.
Build the graphic with today's figures and test it on your own computer before sending.

basic.situation: A client's flyer is ready for print. The printer wants a PDF with bleed and runs the press as soon as the file arrives. You prepare the file.

options.text: Add the bleed, export a PDF with the printer's settings, and check the result on screen.
Send the working design file to the printer, since they can make a PDF from it.
Save the flyer as a small web image and send it to the printer to save time.
Export a PDF with the printer's settings and send it since the layout looks fine on screen.

advanced.situation: As print lead you set the checklist for final files. Last month two jobs came out dull because the files used screen colour mode instead of print colour mode.

options.text: Let the printer convert colour modes on arrival and add the cost to the client's invoice.
Write a preflight checklist covering colour mode, bleed, fonts and resolution, then train staff on it.
Ask staff to be more careful with colour settings and review each job at the end.
Add colour mode to the existing checklist and email the updated list to the team.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to study three product photos from a competitor's brochure and explain how they present the products.

options.text: Describe which photo you like most and explain why it stands out to you.
Note how each photo frames the product, uses space and colour, and share your notes.
Tell the senior that the brochure looks professional and suggest we copy its overall look.
Save the three photos in the shared folder and reuse them in the client's layout.

advanced.situation: A new layout tool promises faster work. Your team has a client pitch on Friday, and you must decide whether the team adopts the tool.

options.text: Read reviews and the tool's documentation, then recommend adoption if other designers rate it well.
Wait until other agencies adopt it, then follow whichever tool most of them choose.
Adopt it for the pitch layouts, since it is supposed to be faster, and review them afterwards.
Trial the tool on a small past project, compare time and quality, and decide after the pitch.

basic.situation: You finished a brochure project. The shared folder has a naming guide, and others will need to find the images later.

options.text: Delete the working images from the folder to free space and keep the final brochure.
Put the images in the project folder and give them clear names of your own.
Save the images on your own computer and tell colleagues you can send them if needed.
Name the images following the guide, put them in the project folder, and add the date.

advanced.situation: Your studio has a messy archive. Designers save work in personal folders, and clients sometimes ask for files from years ago. You are asked to design a proper system.

options.text: Set a folder structure and naming rules, then ask everyone to follow it from next month.
Ask each designer to tidy their personal folder and keep a list of what is inside.
Interview designers about how they search, then set a folder structure, naming rules and backups.
Move every personal folder into one shared drive and delete duplicates automatically to save space.

basic.situation: A couple asks you to design their small living room. Your supervisor told you to ask about their budget and style, but they only say they want it nice.

options.text: Say you will propose a design and ask for feedback after the first drawing.
Ask how they use the room and their budget, and show style photos to pick from.
Pick a modern style and quote a high price to cover possible changes.
Ask for their budget and note it, then choose a style you think suits them.

advanced.situation: A husband wants a dark, formal home office, while his wife wants a bright shared study. They have one RM20,000 budget and disagree openly in your meeting.

options.text: Present two separate designs with costs and ask the couple to choose one together.
Tell them you will design what you think looks good and surprise them.
Follow the spouse who is paying and adjust the plan after the first purchase.
Ask each to rank their needs, then propose a layout and lighting that serves both uses.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks for a paste up board for a bedroom showing paint colour, fabric and flooring. You have fabric samples, tiles and paint cards.

options.text: Take a photo of the samples laid on a table and send it to your supervisor.
Choose the three samples you like and paste just those on the board.
Use pictures from a magazine for the flooring because the tile is too heavy to mount.
Arrange the samples on one board, label each item, and show how they look together.

advanced.situation: You must produce CAD construction documents for a 20 unit hotel refurbishment. The contractor starts in a week, and the architect's floor plan changed twice.

options.text: Confirm the latest plan with the architect, then issue drawings with revision numbers.
Draw from the plan you have and update the drawings if the architect sends changes.
Copy the drawings from a similar hotel project and change the room numbers.
Send the contractor rough sketches now so they can start planning the work.

basic.situation: A mentor asks you to choose sofa fabric and cushion colours for a family living room with young children. The client likes cream.

options.text: Pick a delicate silk in cream because it feels luxurious to touch and looks elegant.
Pick the cheapest fabric you can find and tell the client it will last.
Pick pure cream cotton because it matches the client's wish and looks clean.
Pick a stain resistant fabric in warm cream and add colourful cushions, then check.

advanced.situation: A resort client wants a lobby with sustainable materials, but the budget is tight and the delivery date is fixed. Recycled timber costs 30 percent more.

options.text: Use recycled timber on one feature wall and lower cost sustainable finishes elsewhere.
Use ordinary timber and add plants and a few recycled accessories to suit the theme.
Choose the cheapest materials available and describe them as eco friendly in the proposal.
Use recycled timber for the whole lobby and ask the client to raise the budget.

basic.situation: You help coordinate a contractor to install shelves in a clinic waiting room. The contractor asks whether the wall can hold the load, and you are unsure.

options.text: Check the drawings for the wall type, then ask your supervisor to confirm with the engineer.
Ask the contractor to use heavier fixings and install the shelves today as planned.
Tell the contractor the wall should be fine because it looks like brick.
Tell the contractor to test one fixing in the wall and report what happens.

advanced.situation: On a condominium project, the contractor says the architect's ceiling height blocks your lighting plan. The architect says the lights can be moved. Work is held up two days.

options.text: Tell the contractor to proceed with the ceiling and cancel the lighting you designed.
Ask the client to decide between your lighting plan and the architect's ceiling.
Redesign the lighting yourself to suit the ceiling and send it to the contractor.
Meet both on site, review the drawings together, and record the agreed change.

basic.situation: You help estimate carpet for a 5 by 6 metre office. The carpet shop sells in 4 metre wide rolls, and your supervisor wants a quote for the client.

options.text: Multiply 5 by 6 metres and add ten percent to the carpet area.
Quote the lowest carpet price possible to win approval and fix the amount later.
Calculate the roll length needed with waste for cutting, and ask your supervisor to check it.
Use the total from a similar office and send that figure to the client.

advanced.situation: Your site visit shows the contractor installed cheaper tiles than the design plans specify, saving about RM8,000. The client has not been told, and the project is 80 percent done.

options.text: Record the difference, tell the client, and agree a replacement or a price reduction.
Ask the contractor to share the RM8,000 saving with you and keep it between you.
Raise it with the contractor and ask them to replace the tiles at their own cost.
Accept the tiles as a saving and tell the client the project is on track.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to find the basic fire safety requirements for a restaurant seating plan. You have access to council guidelines and a design manual.

options.text: Search online for fire safety tips and give your supervisor the first result.
Use the fire exit layout from the last restaurant you designed as a guide.
Tell your supervisor the seating plan is fine because the restaurant is small.
Read the council fire guidelines for seating and exits and note the points.

advanced.situation: A clinic client wants a narrow reception counter and a raised step at the entrance for style. Local accessibility rules require wheelchair access, and the client says rules are flexible.

options.text: Draw the entrance with a ramp on paper but leave it off the built plans.
Check the requirements, redesign with a ramp and lower counter, and explain why.
Follow the client's wishes and mention the rules in a note to the project file.
Keep the step and add a portable ramp for visitors who ask for one.

basic.situation: Your supervisor gives you ready made shelf parts and a diagram for a small gift stand. One screw hole does not line up.

options.text: Recheck the diagram and part order, and ask your supervisor before forcing any screw.
Force the screw in with a power drill until the parts fit together.
Leave out that screw and use glue to hold the part in place.
Drill a new hole beside the old one and finish assembling the stand.

advanced.situation: You must build a large hanging display of fabric panels for a mall promotion. The panels weigh 25 kg together, and the ceiling anchor points are rated lower.

options.text: Hang the panels from the anchors as planned and keep people from standing underneath.
Confirm anchor ratings with mall staff, use lighter panels, and spread the load.
Hang the panels in two sections from separate points and test with half the weight.
Add extra wire support under the panels to take some of the weight.

basic.situation: You are asked to place price signs on a shoe display. The price list changed this morning, and some signs show old prices.

options.text: Keep the old signs since customers usually pay the price at the till anyway.
Print new signs from the updated list, remove old ones, and check each shoe's price.
Place the old signs and tell staff to quote new prices at the counter.
Write the new prices by hand on the old signs with a pen.

advanced.situation: You are choosing the theme and lighting for a Deepavali window display. The product is jewellery, the window faces the street at night, and the budget is small.

options.text: Light the whole window brightly so the jewellery can be seen from any angle.
Use flashing coloured lights around the window to draw passers by on the street.
Fill the window with many Deepavali props to attract attention and add a few lights.
Pick a gold and red theme with spotlights on the jewellery and check it at night.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks for ideas to make a new bag display more appealing. The shop sells ten bag styles in four colours.

options.text: Place all ten styles in a single row on the shelf, sorted by price.
Place the most expensive bags on the floor so customers notice the display.
Group bags by colour, put two popular styles at eye level, and sketch it for approval.
Pile the bags together in a large basket so customers can browse freely.

advanced.situation: You plan displays for a major phone launch across three stores. The corporate meeting gave a theme, but each store has different space, and launch day is in ten days.

options.text: Pick the largest store's layout and tell the smaller stores to squeeze it in.
Wait for the corporate team to send exact layouts for each of the three stores.
Measure each store, adapt the theme into three layouts, and agree them with managers.
Use one layout for all three stores and trim items where space runs short.

basic.situation: You get a display plan from the display manager for a new cosmetics counter. You think a shelf in the plan blocks the cashier's view.

options.text: Remove the shelf from the display so the cashier can see the whole counter.
Mark where the view is blocked and discuss it with the display manager.
Move the shelf to a spot you prefer and build the rest as planned.
Build the display as planned and tell the manager about the shelf afterwards.

advanced.situation: The sales team wants a promotion display near the entrance on Friday, while housekeeping says the entrance must stay clear for a fire exit. The store manager is away.

options.text: Place the display at the entrance and move it later if housekeeping complains again.
Offer a spot beside the exit route, confirm clearance with housekeeping, and inform sales.
Put the display at the entrance and tell housekeeping to use the back door.
Tell sales the display cannot go up until the store manager is back.

basic.situation: While opening the shop, you notice a mannequin has a chipped arm and dusty clothes. The shop opens in 20 minutes.

options.text: Fill the chip with strong glue from the stockroom and press it on at once.
Dust the clothes and turn the chipped arm away from customers before opening time.
Move the mannequin to the back room and leave the space empty until later.
Dust the clothes, touch up the chip with matching paint, and tell your supervisor.

advanced.situation: You set maintenance schedules for 40 mannequins and props across three branches. Many have scratches, and staff clean them differently, sometimes with harsh chemicals that fade clothes.

options.text: Set a cleaning schedule by item type, approve gentle cleaners, and train branch staff.
Replace the most scratched mannequins at all branches with new ones this month.
Ban all cleaning of the mannequins so that staff stop damaging them with chemicals.
Write a simple cleaning guide and send it to the managers of all three branches.

basic.situation: You need three picture frames for a display tomorrow. The storeroom has two, and a colleague in another branch has more.

options.text: Ask your supervisor to arrange a third frame from the other branch.
Message your colleague and ask them to send a frame by courier today.
Take a frame off the wall in the shop's manager office for the display.
Use the two frames and place a flat picture in the third spot.

advanced.situation: You must source specialised festive lanterns for ten stores. The usual vendor delivers late, and a new vendor offers a lower price but has no photos of previous work.

options.text: Stay with the usual vendor and ask the stores to open their displays late.
Pay the new vendor a full deposit now to secure the lower price.
Request samples and references from the new vendor and keep the usual one as backup.
Order all lanterns from the new vendor and use the usual vendor if they fail.

basic.situation: A senior designer gives you the script scene and asks you to prepare a rough floor plan for a one room kampung house set. The stage is 8 by 6 metres.

options.text: Copy the floor plan of a house set from last year's show and resize it.
Sketch the room freehand with approximate sizes and refine it after rehearsals begin.
Draw the stage to scale, add doors and furniture from the script, and share it.
Make the room as large as the whole stage so actors have plenty of space.

advanced.situation: You build a scale model of a set for a film that needs a miniature river scene for background. The director wants water that looks real from a distance.

options.text: Use clear resin for the river and film the miniature close up to check it.
