Test resin, clear gel and rippled film on small samples, then build with the most convincing.
Run real water through the model from a pump while the set lights are on.
Paint the river blue on the model and add shine with spray varnish.

basic.situation: You are asked to choose furniture for a 1950s Malayan coffee shop scene. Your senior has given you three photo books and a prop store list.

options.text: Use furniture from a 1980s film set because it was easy to find.
Match furniture in the photos to the prop list, then show your senior the shortlist.
Choose modern cafe chairs and tell your senior the audience will not notice.
Pick furniture from the prop list that looks old and rustic to the eye.

advanced.situation: A play is set in a Melaka Peranakan house in the 1920s. You find sources that disagree on tile patterns, and the director wants authenticity. A museum expert is available.

options.text: Skip the research and paint a generic Chinese style pattern on the tiles.
Use the pattern shown in the most sources and note that experts may differ.
Compare the sources, ask the museum expert about tile patterns, and report to the director.
Choose the prettiest pattern and describe it as true to the period in the notes.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to list material costs for a small stage platform. The platform needs plywood, paint and screws, and you have a supplier price sheet.

options.text: List the plywood price from the sheet and estimate the paint and screws.
List each item with quantity and price, add a waste margin, and share the total.
Use the cost of the last platform and add ten percent for inflation.
Give a low total to get approval and say extras will be charged later.

advanced.situation: Your exhibit design for a science fair costs RM60,000, but the sponsor's approved budget is RM45,000. The exhibit opens in four weeks and has a fabrication limit on large metal parts.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to raise the budget to RM60,000 and wait for their reply.
Submit the original plan at RM45,000 and cover the difference from later invoices.
Cut the size of every feature by the same amount to reach RM45,000 exactly.
Rank features by visitor impact, replace costly metal parts, and submit a revised plan.

basic.situation: You read a script to list the sets needed for a short play. The script mentions a market, a bedroom and a riverbank.

options.text: List the three locations and decide the details when the rehearsals start next month.
Add a palace set to the list because plays like this usually have one.
Skim the first scenes and assume the rest repeat the same places as before.
List each location with scene numbers and named props, then check with your senior.

advanced.situation: A script describes a haunted house with scenes that change quickly, and the budget allows one fixed set. The director wants a creepy feel.

options.text: Build one detailed haunted room and use projections for all the other scenes.
Design one set with moving panels and lighting changes, and review it with the director.
Use real fire and smoke machines on stage to create the creepy feel.
Build several small sets and ask the budget to be raised after approval.

basic.situation: You arrange five old photographs and a clay pot for a school history display. The pot is fragile, and the photographs are different sizes.

options.text: Put the pot in a case and mount photos by size, then ask your senior.
Put the pot at the centre of the room and hang the photos around it.
Place the pot on a low table beside the photos so visitors can see it.
Let visitors hold the pot and add handwritten labels next to each photo.

advanced.situation: You design a night market display for a street festival with 5,000 visitors. The display uses fabric canopies, paper lanterns and electric lights along a narrow lane.

options.text: Place the lanterns and lights as planned and add a fire extinguisher at each end.
Hang the lanterns directly on the electric wires to save time and cable.
Use thicker fabric canopies to hold the lights up and away from visitors' heads.
Plan wide walkways, keep wires away from fabric, and check exits with safety staff.

basic.situation: You attend a production meeting for a stage play. The lighting team tells you a set wall will block a spotlight.

options.text: Tell the lighting team to move the spotlight, since the wall is already built.
Cut a hole in the wall so the light passes through before anyone notices.
Note the problem, ask lighting for the exact angle, and tell the set designer.
Tell the set designer after the meeting that the wall may block a light.

advanced.situation: During rehearsal you see the revolving set piece stick, and cast members must squeeze past it near the stage edge. The lighting team also needs to adjust cues.

options.text: Remove the revolving feature from the set during lunch and tell the director later.
Let the rehearsal continue and ask the cast to move carefully around the piece.
Pause rehearsal, inspect the mechanism, mark safe cast paths, and agree new lighting cues.
Oil the mechanism after rehearsal and mark where the cast should avoid standing.

basic.situation: The director gives you your lines for tomorrow's rehearsal. You have two hours tonight, and your cues in scene three are hard to remember.

options.text: Memorise your own lines first and learn the cues at the next rehearsal.
Read the scene aloud with cues, then test yourself with the script closed.
Record the other actors' lines on your phone and play them while you are sleeping tonight.
Ask the director to give you fewer lines in scene three before tomorrow's rehearsal.

advanced.situation: You are cast as a mother who has secretly lost her child, but the script says little about her past. You have three weeks, and the writer is available for questions.

options.text: Play the mother as simply sad in every scene since the script says little.
Read the script for clues about relationships, then ask the writer targeted questions.
Ask the writer to add more lines about the past before the next rehearsal.
Invent a full backstory yourself and use it in every rehearsal from tomorrow.

basic.situation: The director asks you to play a nervous student in a scene. You imagine the student as loud, but the director wants quiet.

options.text: Tell the director that a louder student would work better for the audience.
Try the quieter version once and then go back to your loud version.
Perform quietly in rehearsal but switch to your loud version on opening night.
Ask the director what makes the student nervous, then try a quieter version.

advanced.situation: In an ensemble play, you and two actors disagree about how the family should relate to each other. The director is away this week, and opening is in ten days.

options.text: Follow the most senior actor's reading and adjust your own performance to it.
Wait for the director to return and rehearse each reading separately until then.
Meet them, compare readings against the script, agree a shared approach, and update the director.
Perform your own reading in every rehearsal and ask the other two to adapt.

basic.situation: You must show surprise in a comic scene using only your face and body. The director says your first try looks forced.

options.text: Recall a real surprise, let your eyes and shoulders react, and try again for the director.
Add a loud gasp to the expression since sound helps the audience understand.
Open your mouth and eyes wider and raise your hands in the same way.
Hold the same expression for longer so the audience has time to notice.

advanced.situation: You perform a tragic monologue in a 1,000 seat theatre for a live and filmed show. Your voice was strained last night, and you must reach the back row.

options.text: Take a strong throat medicine before the show and perform at full volume.
Rest your voice until the show begins and perform at a lower volume.
Warm up gently, support with breath, and ask for a sound check beforehand.
Shout the monologue loudly to be sure the back row hears every word.

basic.situation: You must sing one verse in a school musical. You can sing it in the rehearsal room, but your voice shakes on stage.

options.text: Sing it louder in the next rehearsal to cover up the shaking in your voice.
Practise the verse standing on the stage, breathe slowly before it, and ask for notes.
Mime the verse on stage while a recording plays and tell nobody backstage.
Ask the director to give the verse to someone else for the show.

advanced.situation: You are asked to perform a stunt jumping down a short staircase in a stage fight. You have done similar falls before, and the stunt coordinator is unavailable for two days.

options.text: Perform the stunt on opening night first and adjust it if you get hurt.
Rehearse the fall at full speed on a mat and tell the coordinator afterwards.
Ask a fellow actor to watch you and perform the stunt at normal speed.
Rehearse slowly on a mat and wait for the coordinator before adding speed.

basic.situation: You tell a joke at a school event, and a few students look uncomfortable. The joke was about students' accents.

options.text: Move to a different joke and drop accent humour from the rest of your act.
Repeat the joke more slowly and loudly so that everyone in the hall understands it.
Make another joke about the uncomfortable students to lighten the mood in the hall.
Explain that you meant no harm and continue with the same type of jokes.

advanced.situation: You perform an illusion act that needs a volunteer to hold a box with a hidden compartment. At a family show, a young child volunteers eagerly.

options.text: Invite the child for a safe task and use an adult volunteer for the box.
Use the child for the box and keep a helper close to them on stage.
Use the child for the box and rely on their parents to watch from the seats.
Thank the child, send them back, and skip the trick to avoid risk.

basic.situation: A crew member is fitting your costume before a show and says the sleeves are too tight for you to lift your arms.

options.text: Say it is fine and plan to move your arms less in the scenes.
Raise your arms to show where it pulls and ask the crew to loosen the sleeves.
Take the costume home and cut the sleeves yourself with kitchen scissors tonight.
Wear your own jacket under the costume to stretch the sleeves before the show.

advanced.situation: You promote a new play on a radio interview. The host asks about a rumour that the lead actor quit, and you are unsure if it is true.

options.text: Say you do not know about the rumour and move on to the next question.
Say the producer can answer that, steer back to the play, and tell the producer later.
Confirm the rumour and describe what you heard about the lead actor's reasons.
Deny the rumour firmly on air to protect the play's ticket sales this month.

basic.situation: You are an assistant on a short film shoot. The camera operator and the lighting assistant give you different set up times for the first scene.

options.text: Check the call sheet, then agree one set up order with both crew members.
Give the camera operator the earlier time and tell lighting to catch up.
Let each crew member start when ready and fix delays when they appear.
Tell the director both teams are ready so the scene can begin on time.

advanced.situation: The heads of sound and lighting stop talking to each other after a quarrel over set time. Shooting is tomorrow, and the director and manager are waiting on both.

options.text: Ask the production manager to settle it and tell both departments to follow the decision.
Pass messages between the two heads and avoid getting involved in the quarrel.
Replace one of the two heads with someone from another production for tomorrow.
Meet each separately, then bring them together to agree shared times and who decides disputes.

basic.situation: You help plan shots for a short interview scene. The director wants two people at a table, and the room is small with a window behind them.

options.text: Place one camera in the middle of the room and film both people.
Film in the neighbour's garden instead and ask for permission once filming is done.
Keep the window behind them and fix the brightness in editing after filming.
Sketch camera positions, check the window light, and ask the director to approve the framing.

advanced.situation: You plan a five day shoot for a documentary with a small budget. Rain is forecast on days two and four, and one main interviewee is available only on day three.

options.text: Shoot outdoor scenes on days one and five and hope the forecast changes.
Film in the rain with the equipment covered by bin bags to keep to the dates.
Push the whole shoot back by a week to wait for dry weather.
Schedule indoor work for the rainy days, fix the day three interview, and keep a buffer.

basic.situation: You are assigned to read a script for a documentary about night market sellers. The director wants to know how to direct the interview scenes.

options.text: Watch a similar documentary online and copy how its interviews were filmed there.
Rewrite the interview questions in the script to suit how you would direct.
Read the script, mark the interview scenes and mood, and bring questions to the director.
Read the script once and tell the director which interview scenes you liked the most.

advanced.situation: In a script workshop, the lead actor wants to change a key scene, and the writer refuses. You have two days to finalise the draft before shooting.

options.text: Ask the writer to allow the actor to improvise in the scene during rehearsal.
Edit the scene yourself overnight and give the new draft to the actor.
Hold a reading of both versions with writer and actor, then decide with the director.
Side with the writer and tell the actor the script is final for this shoot.

basic.situation: You direct a short scene where an actor must walk to a window and look worried. The first take looks stiff, and you have time for two more.

options.text: Use the stiff take and say you will fix the mood in editing.
Tell the actor why the character is worried and where to pause, then shoot again.
Say the take was stiff and ask the actor to relax and be more natural.
Show the actor how to walk and look, and ask them to copy it.

advanced.situation: You direct a live broadcast of a charity concert. Ten minutes before going live, the opening singer loses their voice, and the audience is already seated.

options.text: Delay going live by ten minutes and tell the audience the show will start shortly.
Play a recording of the singer and let viewers think it is live.
Let the singer attempt the opening and prepare the host to fill in if needed.
Brief the producer, move a ready act to the opening, and brief the camera team again.

basic.situation: A prop master asks you to approve three lamps for a living room scene. The script says the room is set in the 1970s.

options.text: Pick the lamp that suits the 1970s and confirm it against the script.
Approve the cheapest lamp and charge it to the production account yourself today.
Approve the lamp that looks good on camera and mention the date later.
Approve all three lamps so the prop master has options on the day.

advanced.situation: You want to use 30 seconds of archive footage of a famous festival in your documentary. The archive owner has not replied, and the edit is due in five days.

options.text: Use the footage in the final edit and credit the archive in the titles.
Use a shorter clip of 10 seconds because smaller clips need no permission.
Chase the archive about licence terms and fees, and prepare a backup clip.
Use the footage in the draft edit and seek the licence before release.

basic.situation: You attend a meeting with the writer, the costume designer and the music lead. The writer says a scene moved from day to night, which affects costumes and music.

options.text: Change the scene back to day to avoid the extra work for the teams.
Say you will remind the teams of the change nearer the date of the shoot.
Note the change, ask each team what it needs, and share notes afterwards.
Tell the costume designer and music lead to adjust their work to night.

advanced.situation: You lead a weekly progress meeting for a TV drama that is two days behind. Department heads blame each other, and the broadcaster needs a progress report tomorrow.

options.text: Tell department heads to stop blaming each other and finish the work this week.
Report to the broadcaster that the production is on schedule to avoid worry.
Review each task, name delay owners, set a catch up plan, and report honestly.
Cancel the meeting and blame the slowest department in your report to the broadcaster.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to fill the daily schedule for the radio station. A 30 minute slot is empty after the 10 am news.

options.text: Check the template and ratings, fill the slot with a matching show, and share it.
Repeat the 9 am show in the slot and change the title on the schedule.
Leave the slot empty and ask the news team to extend their bulletin.
Fill the slot with music from the library and tell your supervisor later.

advanced.situation: A live football match runs into extra time, which will overlap the 8 pm drama and 9 pm news. The news team wants its slot, and sponsors paid for the drama.

options.text: Meet news and sales, agree what moves, inform the sponsor, and update the schedule.
Move the drama to tomorrow and give the sponsor a free spot later.
Cut the extra time of the match short to protect the drama slot.
Drop the drama this evening and run a repeat in its slot, then tell the sponsor.

basic.situation: Your team lead asks for simple ideas for a weekend show for teenagers. You have ten minutes at the meeting.

options.text: Suggest a music chart show because it is easy to make and fills time.
Suggest copying a popular show from another station with a new name and host.
Say you have no ideas yet and offer to bring a list tomorrow.
Offer two ideas tied to school life and say why teenagers would listen.

advanced.situation: Audience surveys show your station's morning show is losing listeners under 30. The host is popular with older listeners, and the owner wants new young listeners.

options.text: Study the survey comments, trial a youth segment, and keep the host's core slot.
Fire the host and change the show format entirely before the next survey.
Replace the host with a younger presenter and promote the change heavily on air.
Keep the show as it is and run ads aimed at younger listeners.

basic.situation: You are asked to record a five minute segment using the studio microphone. The meter shows the sound is too quiet.

options.text: Push the gain to maximum and record the segment while the room is noisy.
Ask the speaker to talk much louder than usual for the entire segment.
Move closer, raise the gain a little, test a short clip, then record.
Record the whole segment now and raise the volume in editing afterwards if needed.

advanced.situation: You set up a remote broadcast from a night market. The wireless link drops every few minutes, and the show goes live in two hours.

options.text: Cancel the live show and record a programme at the market for later.
Move the transmitter higher and check whether that improves the signal over time.
Go live as planned and let the studio play music when the link drops.
Test other spots, add a backup mobile connection, and brief the studio on a fallback.

basic.situation: You check a completed program log with a checklist. One entry shows a song played at 3:05 pm, but the schedule says a news bulletin ran then.

options.text: Mark the entry as inconsistent and ask the presenter and engineer what actually aired.
Flag the entry to your supervisor and wait for them to fix the log.
Change the log to show the news bulletin as scheduled and sign it off.
Assume the song entry is a typing mistake and leave the log unchanged.

advanced.situation: A sponsor wants a new jingle played in a children's show. The jingle sounds like a famous song, and the log must show legal clearances.

options.text: Play the jingle and record it in the log as an original station jingle.
Request written clearance for the music, record it in the log, and consult legal.
Play the jingle once as a trial and wait for any complaint to arrive.
Ask the sponsor to change a few notes so the jingle sounds different.

basic.situation: You read a prepared news script on air for the first time with a coach beside you. There is a hard name in the third story.

options.text: Skip the story with the hard name and read the other stories a little slower.
Read the name as you think it sounds and move quickly to the next line.
Change the name to a simpler one that sounds similar and read that.
Ask the coach to say the name, mark it on your script, and practise it.

advanced.situation: You mentor a new presenter. During a live interview, a guest becomes angry and begins shouting, and the presenter freezes while you watch from the control room.

options.text: Talk the presenter through the earpiece with a calm line, and prepare to cut to music.
Go on air yourself and take over the interview in the presenter's place.
Cut to a commercial break at once and speak to the presenter afterwards.
Let the interview run and review it with the presenter after the show.

basic.situation: You help schedule staff shifts for the weekend. A presenter asks to swap Saturday with a colleague, but both need your approval.

options.text: Tell them to ask your supervisor and avoid making any decision on this yourself.
Check coverage for both shifts, approve the swap, and update the roster.
Refuse the swap because weekend shifts are fixed and nobody can change them.
Approve the swap by message and update the roster at the end of the week.

advanced.situation: Two department heads, news and programming, argue over staff for an election special. You must direct operations, and one team is short of two people.

options.text: Hire two outside freelancers at your own rate and add the cost to the budget later.
Review both workloads, move two flexible staff, and confirm the arrangement in writing.
Give the election special priority and move two people from programming this week.
Ask each head to solve it among themselves and report back on Friday.

basic.situation: A senior director asks you to contact five agents and set audition times for Thursday. Two agents say their actors are free only after 3 pm.

options.text: Book all five actors in the morning and ask the two agents to adjust.
Give the two agents late slots, confirm all times in writing, and update the schedule.
Move the two actors to Friday and tell the senior director once it is done.
Tell the two agents their actors will be dropped if they cannot attend mornings.

advanced.situation: You must design screen tests for a lead role in a family drama. Five actors, two agents and the director have different availability, and one agent demands a private test.

options.text: Agree to the private test and book the others later around that slot.
Give each actor the same test and ask the demanding agent to join the group day.
Test the actors you already know and tell the other agents the role is cast.
Set one test format with fair slots, share it, and refer private requests to the director.

basic.situation: You review 40 actor resumes and photos for a small role and must shortlist ten for your supervisor. Several resumes have no photo.

options.text: Pick ten names at random from the pile to finish the task faster.
Shortlist ten by role fit and ask agents for the missing photos.
Shortlist ten from the resumes that include photos and tell your supervisor about the rest.
Shortlist the ten actors you have worked with before and send the list.

advanced.situation: You audition 12 actors for a role needing strong Hokkien dialogue. The director prefers a famous actor who is weak in Hokkien, and a newcomer is excellent.

options.text: Submit the newcomer alone and tell the director the famous actor was unavailable.
Submit both with no comment and let the director choose whichever they like.
Submit both with notes on Hokkien strength and recommend the newcomer, offering coaching if wanted.
Submit the famous actor to match the director's preference and add a note on Hokkien.

basic.situation: A producer shares a script and asks you to list the types of performers needed. The script has a grandfather, two teenagers and a baby.

options.text: List four roles and plan to use the same actor for both teenagers.
List the grandfather and teenagers and add the baby after the producer decides.
List each role with age range and scenes, and confirm needs with the producer.
List adult roles and leave out children because they are harder to cast.

advanced.situation: You must plan casting for a historical series needing 60 performers, including rare skills like traditional dance. You can watch live theatre and online clips for talent.

options.text: List the skills needed, watch live shows for dancers, and compile names from clips.
Post an open call online and accept the first 60 people who reply.
Contact the biggest talent agency and ask them to supply all 60 performers.
Reuse performers from your last series and ask them to learn the dance.

basic.situation: You update the talent file after an agent emails that an actor now speaks Mandarin and has moved to Johor. The file shows old details.

options.text: Delete the old file and rely on the agent's email in your inbox.
Update the language and location and leave the other details for another day.
Add a new entry for the actor and keep the old one in the file.
Update the language and location, note the date and source, and check the phone number.

advanced.situation: Your team's talent file has duplicates, missing availability dates and private notes about actors that anyone can read. You are asked to redesign it for 2,000 actors.

options.text: Delete the duplicate records and ask staff to fill missing dates when they can.
Keep the file as it is and add a warning about private notes at the top.
Design fields, merge duplicates, restrict private notes, and train staff on entry rules.
Delete all private notes and old availability dates to make the file smaller.

basic.situation: You are asked to draft standard terms for a one day shoot, with review from a legal advisor. The producer wants to offer RM500 and no overtime.

options.text: Use last year's contract and change the date and the fee before sending.
Draft standard terms with clear hours and overtime wording, then send to legal.
Send the draft contract to the agent today and show legal a copy afterwards.
Draft the standard terms exactly as the producer says and send them to legal.

advanced.situation: An actor's agent demands double the fee and a clause banning other work for a year. The producer's budget allows a 20 percent rise, and filming starts in a week.

options.text: Accept the demands and ask the producer to find the extra budget later.
Offer a modest fee rise and a shorter exclusivity tied to filming dates, with producer approval.
Tell the agent another actor is ready to take the role at half the fee.
Offer the full 20 percent rise and reject the exclusivity clause in the draft.

basic.situation: Using a checklist, you send scripts and role details to six actors for tomorrow's audition. One actor asks which scene to prepare.

options.text: Send the actor the full script and say they can choose any scene.
Tell the actor the scene will be given on the day of the audition.
Check the audition plan, give the actor the scene and character notes, and confirm.
Tell the actor to prepare whichever scene they find easiest and bring the script.

advanced.situation: A senior actor auditioning for a complex role has asked for coaching on the script's tone. The producer wants consistency across all actors in the process.

options.text: Coach the senior actor privately and keep the details from the other actors.
Write a prep guide for all actors and offer each the same coaching call.
Give the senior actor the sides and notes from other actors' auditions to compare.
Decline the coaching request and send just the script to every actor in the round.

basic.situation: A producer asks you to book Studio B for a recorded interview on Tuesday at 2 pm. You see the calendar already shows a maintenance check then.

options.text: Offer the producer another time that day, check with maintenance, and book once confirmed.
Book Studio B at 2 pm and ask maintenance to move their check.
Book Studio B and remove the maintenance check from the shared calendar today.
Tell the producer the studio is busy that day and suggest Wednesday instead.

advanced.situation: Two live shows and an urgent repair need the same studio on Friday evening. The engineering team says the repair takes three hours and cannot be moved.

options.text: Run both shows at once in the studio and have the repair proceed behind them.
Delay the repair until the following week and warn engineering about the risk.
Give the studio to the show with the larger audience and tell the other producer.
Meet both producers and engineering, find alternate rooms, and confirm a revised plan.

basic.situation: A producer tells you the interview show needs two extra microphones next week. You must relay this to the engineering staff under supervision.

options.text: Tell engineering the show needs more microphones soon and ask them to prepare.
Send engineering the date, studio, microphone count and contact name, and copy your supervisor.
Tell the producer to arrange the extra microphones directly with the engineering team.
Take two microphones from the news studio store and set them up yourself.

advanced.situation: The operations director wants a technical policy requiring all shows to use the new audio system. Producers say it breaks their workflow, and engineering says retraining takes a month.

options.text: Support the director's policy and tell producers to follow it from next month.
Collect concerns from both sides and propose a phased policy with training for the director.
Side with the producers and tell the director the policy is not practical now.
Write the policy yourself and publish it to all staff before the director reviews it.

basic.situation: You monitor a recorded segment against a station policy list with a mentor. The policy bans brand names on air, and you hear a brand name.

options.text: Mention it to the producer after the show has aired and let them decide.
Pass the segment since the brand name is said just once in twenty minutes.
Note the time of the brand name and ask your mentor how to handle it.
Edit out the brand name yourself and send the segment to air tonight.

advanced.situation: New regulator rules ban a type of advertising claim, effective next month. Your station already has 30 programmes with such claims. You must train staff and define standards.

options.text: Send all producers a copy of the new rules and ask them to comply.
Stop broadcasting all 30 programmes until the new rules are fully understood by staff.
List affected programmes, write a standard with examples, and train producers on checks.
Review the ten most popular programmes this month and leave the rest for later.

basic.situation: A senior technician sits beside you as you switch between two cameras during a rehearsal. The presenter moves to a new spot not on the plan.

options.text: Ask the senior which camera suits the new spot and switch on their cue.
Stay on the camera showing the old spot until the presenter moves back there.
Switch rapidly between both cameras in the live feed until the presenter settles.
Switch to the closest camera and adjust the shot yourself during the rehearsal.

advanced.situation: You design the switching plan for a live concert from a remote hall with six cameras. The main singer moves unpredictably, and a junior operator will switch the encore.

options.text: Mark key moments in a shot list, rehearse with the junior, and add backup shots.
Switch the entire encore yourself to avoid any mistakes from the junior operator.
Use one wide camera for the whole show to prevent switching mistakes at all.
Give the junior a simple list of cameras and let them follow the singer.

basic.situation: You watch the monitors during a rehearsal and give simple framing instructions from a script. The newsreader's head is cut off at the top of the frame.

options.text: Wait until the live show begins and fix it if any viewers complain online.
Tell the operator to zoom out so that the whole studio set is visible.
Ask the newsreader to sit lower so the head fits in the frame.
Ask the operator to tilt down slightly and leave space above the head.

advanced.situation: During a live sports show, the lead camera operator keeps framing too tight. You must coach them on composition while the show runs, and the director is busy.

options.text: Shout at the operator on the open channel until the framing improves a lot.
Take over the camera yourself and finish the show with wider framing throughout.
Wait until the next break and explain the composition problem to the operator.
Give short instructions through comms for wider frames, then review shots with them after.

basic.situation: You test the studio microphones before a show, and one gives no sound. Your job is to test equipment and then tell the supervisor.

options.text: Swap in a spare microphone and mention the faulty one later this week.
Check cable, battery and mixer channel, swap the faulty part, and log it.
Tell the presenter to use a different microphone that you know already works.
Open the microphone and try to repair it with tape before the show.

advanced.situation: You are asked to certify new staff on all major studio equipment, including switchers, cameras and lights. Staff learn at different speeds, and a live show needs two certified operators next week.

options.text: Create a skills checklist, train small groups on each item, test them, and certify passers.
Certify the two fastest learners now and train the others after the show.
Certify all new staff based on their resumes so the live show is covered.
Train everyone in one large session and certify those who attend the whole session today.

basic.situation: A senior coach asks you to teach a group of ten year olds the football rule about throw ins. Several keep throwing with one hand.

options.text: Let them throw the way they like and tell them the rule in the match.
Explain the throw in rule aloud and ask the children to remember it.
Demonstrate the two handed throw from behind the head, then watch each child try it.
Tell the children one handed throws will cost the team a point in practice.

advanced.situation: You prepare a 17 year old sprinter for a national meet in three weeks. The athlete's start is slow, nutrition is poor, and motivation is dropping after two losses.

options.text: Increase daily sprint practice to improve the start as soon as possible this month.
Give the athlete supplements from a friend's gym to boost speed quickly before the meet.
Analyse the start on video, set targeted drills and meals, and agree small goals together.
Tell the athlete to eat more protein and to forget the two recent losses.

basic.situation: A senior coach asks you to observe three players in a basketball trial and note their basic skills. One player dribbles well but misses most shots.

options.text: Give each player a score out of ten and share the scores with the senior coach.
Note the good dribbler as a promising star and skip the other players.
Note each player's dribbling, passing and shooting separately, and compare notes with the senior.
Write that the player who misses shots is not good enough and should leave.

advanced.situation: You develop a long term plan for a 15 year old gymnast with strong floor routines but weak landings. On video, you also notice the gymnast uses the springboard unsafely.

options.text: Analyse landings and board use on video, set a safe progression plan, and review progress monthly.
Keep the floor routine as the main focus and fix landings as they happen.
Enter the gymnast in a higher level meet to push faster improvement this season.
Focus the next three months on landings and mention the springboard issue later.

basic.situation: Your head coach asks you to find the opposing team's basic strengths and weaknesses before Saturday's match. You have one video of their last game.

options.text: Tell the coach the team looks weak because they lost their last game.
Watch the video, note scoring patterns and defensive gaps, and report to the coach.
Ask a friend on the other team to tell you their match plan.
Watch the first ten minutes of the video and tell the coach what you saw.

advanced.situation: In a final, your team loses 0 to 1 at half time because the opposing team uses a counter attack you did not expect. You choose the second half tactics and substitutes.

options.text: Tell the team to commit fouls early to stop the counter attacks in midfield.
Replace all the defenders with attackers to score as many goals as possible.
Keep the same plan and ask the players to attack with more energy.
Spot where the counter starts, tighten that area, and make two substitutions to match.

basic.situation: Your head coach asks you to set up equipment and schedule Tuesday practice for the under 12 team. Another group has the field booked from 5 to 6 pm.

options.text: Keep the 5 pm slot and ask the other group to share the field.
Start practice at 5 pm anyway and let the other group argue about it.
Check the booking sheet, offer the coach 6 pm or another field, and prepare cones.
Move practice to the school car park and set up there with cones and balls.

advanced.situation: You organise a three day tournament trip for 40 young players, with travel, hotel and meals. Two days before leaving, the coach company cancels, and parents have already paid.

options.text: Get quotes from other firms, tell parents and the club head, and confirm a replacement.
Cancel the trip and tell the parents their money will be refunded soon.
Ask parents to drive the players and give them the hotel address and schedule.
Hire a cheap bus driver you found online and pay in cash to save time.

basic.situation: You show new players how to use gym weights safely. A player starts lifting a heavy bar with no one nearby.

options.text: Let the player finish the lift and give safety advice afterwards in the changing room.
Tell the player to lower the bar and ask a friend to stand close.
Stop the lift, show the safe stance and spotter role, and use lighter weights.
Add more weight to the bar to show the player how serious safety is.

advanced.situation: You audit safety practice at a trampoline club where staff use gear differently. Some skip spotting, and a mat has a torn corner, but many coaches resist rules.

options.text: Write a short rule list, retire the torn mat, and train all coaches on spotting.
Retire the torn mat and send coaches a reminder about the spotting rules.
Tape the torn mat corner and observe the coaches over the next month.
Allow coaches to use their own methods to avoid arguments about club rules.

basic.situation: A parent asks you by message when Saturday's match starts and whether their child needs a white shirt. You are not sure about the shirt.

options.text: Tell the parent the match starts at noon and the child must wear white.
Give the start time and say you will confirm the shirt colour with the head coach.
Give the start time and say white is probably fine, as it was last match.
Reply that the head coach will send all the details later this week to everyone.

advanced.situation: A top student athlete is failing two subjects, which risks academic eligibility, and says they want to quit school for a pro contract offer. The athlete trusts you.

options.text: Advise the athlete to take the contract since sports careers are often short.
Meet the athlete and parents, check eligibility rules, arrange tutoring, and review the offer together.
Ask a teacher to raise the athlete's marks so that eligibility is kept this term.
Tell the athlete to focus on school and refuse the contract offer for now.

basic.situation: You start a 100 metre school race with guidance from the head official. One runner moves before the starting signal.

options.text: Restart the race and give the early runner a verbal warning before the next start.
Let the race continue and report the early move to the head official after.
Recall the runners, return them to their marks, and restart with standard commands.
Disqualify the early runner on the spot and send them off the track.

advanced.situation: In a rugby match, players argue after a hard tackle, and the stadium manager radios that a fire alarm test may start in five minutes. You must keep control.

options.text: Send both teams off the field until the alarm test is finished completely.
Continue the match and ask the manager to handle the alarm test alone.
Pause play, speak to both captains, and ask the manager to delay the test.
Abandon the match and write in the report that the players caused the problem.

basic.situation: In a youth badminton match, a player serves above the waist, which is a fault. It happens twice in one game, and your supervisor is watching.

options.text: Give the opponent two points to teach the player a lesson about serving.
Call the fault on the second serve and let the first one go.
Call the fault, explain the serve rule briefly, and award the point.
Warn the player after the game and do not call faults during play.

advanced.situation: After a close basketball final, a coach complains that your foul call decided the game and demands the result be changed. Fans are shouting, and the rule book is ambiguous.

options.text: Warn the coach that you will ban the team from the next season.
Explain your reasoning to the coach and tell them to write to the organisers.
Hear the complaint, check the rule with co officials, and send the protest upward.
Change the result to calm the crowd and avoid the coach's anger afterwards.

basic.situation: You time a school swimming relay and start the stopwatch at the signal. The watch freezes after the second swimmer.

options.text: Note the last time shown, switch to the backup watch, and tell the head official.
Stop the relay and ask the swimmers to start again from the beginning.
Restart the watch and estimate the first part of the time from memory.
Record the time as the average from the previous relay race for the same school.

advanced.situation: In a handball match with several timeouts, injuries and a protest, you must track the exact elapsed time. The scoreboard clock and your watch differ by 20 seconds.

options.text: Use your watch for the rest of the match and tell the other officials.
Average the two clocks and announce that time to both teams at the end.
Stop at the next break, compare clocks with other officials, and agree one time.
Use the scoreboard clock because the spectators can see it and trust it.

basic.situation: Before a youth cricket match, you check equipment with a list. One batting helmet has a crack in the shell.

options.text: Pass the equipment check since the helmet looks fine from a short distance away.
Tell the player to wear the helmet and report the crack after the match.
Take the helmet out of use and ask the team manager for a spare.
Tape the crack and let the player use the helmet today with a warning.

advanced.situation: You inspect a school athletics ground before a regional meet. The jump pit sand is hard, a hurdle base is loose, and heavy rain is forecast. The meet starts in two hours.

options.text: Report the problems after the meet and let the events run as scheduled.
Close the pit and loose hurdles, get them fixed, and agree a rain plan.
Fix the hurdles yourself and use the pit for warm ups before the start.
Pass the ground as safe because the organisers have already printed the programme.

basic.situation: After a school quiz competition you compile scores from three scoresheets. Two scoresheets have the same name spelled differently.

options.text: Treat them as two different students and give each a separate placing.
Use the spelling from the first scoresheet and combine the scores under that name.
Check the participant list, confirm which name is right, and record the combined score.
Record both names separately and mention the issue to the head official later.

advanced.situation: Before announcing winners of a regional diving event, you find one score total is higher than the sum of the judges' scores. A medal depends on it.

options.text: Hold the announcement, recheck scores with judges, and fix the total with the head official.
Announce the winners as listed because the diver with the higher total is local.
Announce the winners and say the total will be checked and updated after the ceremony.
Lower the total to match the sum and announce the winners as planned.

basic.situation: After a youth football match, a player was shown a red card. Your senior official asks you to complete the standard incident report.

options.text: Fill in the report from memory the next week when you have time.
Record the player, time, incident and rule applied, then have your senior check.
Write a short note saying the player was sent off for fighting during play.
Ask the player's coach to describe the incident and copy their account into the report.

advanced.situation: You mentor a junior referee and study match trends for a rival derby. Reports show repeated clashes between two teams' fans, and the junior writes vague reports that omit key details.

options.text: Rewrite the junior's reports yourself before submitting them to the regulator each week.
Teach a fact based report template, review past clashes together, and brief on trouble spots.
Leave out the fan clashes from reports to avoid trouble with the regulator.
Tell the junior to write longer reports and add more detail about each incident.

basic.situation: In rehearsal, the dance captain asks you to follow the beat of a new song. You keep arriving half a beat late on the turns.

options.text: Count the beat aloud, mark the turns slowly, and ask the captain to watch.
Follow the dancer beside you and copy their timing instead of the music.
Skip the turns during rehearsal and add them back on the day of the show.
Practise the turns faster at home and see if the timing improves by next week.

advanced.situation: You are the lead in an ensemble piece that also needs you to sing and act. Your partner's timing keeps slipping, and the singing cues clash with your lifts.

options.text: Drop the singing from the lifts and add it back when the dance is ready.
Adjust your lifts to your partner's timing and keep the singing cues as written.
Meet your partner, mark the clash points on the music, and rehearse them slowly.
Lift on the original beat and let your partner try to catch up.

basic.situation: You attend a technique class three times a week. Your teacher says you are stiff in the hips, and you have a show in a month.

options.text: Skip classes this week to rest your hips and return before the show.
Stretch hard once a week on your rest day to become more flexible.
Force your legs into a full split every day until your hips loosen.
Add daily gentle hip stretches and ask your teacher to check your form.

advanced.situation: You have a hip injury history and are offered a role with demanding jumps. The choreographer says you can say no, and you feel pressure to accept.

options.text: Decline the role right away and avoid talking about it with the choreographer.
Accept the role and keep your hip history from the choreographer and the director.
Accept the role and warm up for longer before each rehearsal and show.
Check with your physio, share your limits, and agree adapted jumps with the choreographer.

basic.situation: You arrive for a costume fitting before a recital. The costume is too tight at the waist, and the fitting is 15 minutes long.

options.text: Wear it as it is and mention the problem at the next fitting.
Show the staff where it is tight and ask them to let it out.
Stop eating all day before the show so that the costume fits properly.
Cut the seams at the waist yourself so you can move freely in the show.

advanced.situation: You are asked to advise on the look of a contemporary piece. Current trends use minimal costumes, but your conservative audience may be uncomfortable.

options.text: Suggest the trendiest costumes you found and let the director adjust them later.
Change the costume pieces yourself on show day to match the latest trend.
Study recent works, suggest modern but modest costumes, and discuss them with the director.
Suggest the same costumes used in the last show to keep things safe.

basic.situation: The choreographer asks you to refine a transition step with them. Your version feels smoother, but it changes the count of eight.

options.text: Show your version, explain the count change, and let the choreographer decide on it.
Dance your version in rehearsal and let the other dancers adjust to you.
Teach your version to the whole group while the choreographer is away from the room.
Use the choreographer's version in rehearsal and keep your idea in mind for later.

advanced.situation: You devise a group piece for eight dancers with different levels. Two beginners struggle with the quick formations, and the showcase is in three weeks.

options.text: Simplify the beginners' paths, keep the formation shapes, and test the piece with all dancers.
Slow down the whole piece so that the beginners can keep up with everyone.
Keep the piece as it is and tell the beginners to practise harder.
Replace the two beginners with more experienced dancers from another class before the showcase.

basic.situation: Your teacher shows you how to prepare pointe shoes. You sew the ribbons and notice one shoe's box feels too soft for the show tomorrow.

options.text: Pour strong glue into the shoe box to harden it quickly before tomorrow.
Sew the ribbons as shown and ask your teacher whether to use the soft pair.
Wear the soft pair for the show and bring a spare pair just in case.
Sew the ribbons and use the shoe for the show with extra glue.

advanced.situation: You customise pointe shoes for a dancer with a high arch and narrow heel, who performs long balances. The dancer wants a different shank than the usual.

options.text: Cut the shank down with scissors until the shoe feels flexible enough for the dancer.
Choose the stiffest shank because it gives the most support for long balances.
Use the usual shank and add padding in the heel to improve the fit.
Test two shank strengths with the dancer, adjust the heel fit, and record what works.

basic.situation: You teach beginners a simple step with a teacher watching. A student cannot copy the arm movement after three tries.

options.text: Split the step, show the arm part slowly, and let the student try beside you.
Move the student to the back row so the rest of the class can continue.
Repeat the same demonstration louder and with a clearer count for the student.
Tell the student to practise at home and move on with the class.

advanced.situation: You develop a ten week course for teens with mixed ability and mentor a junior teacher. The junior wants to teach advanced steps first to attract students.

options.text: Design a progression from basics to advanced steps and trial week one with the junior.
Follow the junior's plan and review it with them after the first two weeks.
Let the junior teach advanced steps to the strong students and basics to others.
Teach the course yourself and ask the junior to watch from the back.

basic.situation: A senior choreographer asks you to sketch ideas for a two minute folk dance to a new song. You have one afternoon.

options.text: Wait for the dancers to arrive and invent the dance on the spot.
Listen to the song several times, sketch formations and key steps, and record movement notes.
Copy formations from an old folk dance video and change the steps a little bit.
Use a finished dance from a competitor and say it is your own idea.

advanced.situation: You are designing a fashion show runway piece with dancers wearing long skirts. The designer wants flowing motion, but the runway is narrow and the music tempo is fast.

options.text: Shorten the skirts at the last minute so the dancers move more easily.
Test steps in costume on the runway, fit the tempo, and review with the designer.
Ask the sound team to slow the music down to suit the flowing motion.
Use wide sweeping movements that look elegant and rehearse them in normal clothes first.

basic.situation: You assist a choreographer by demonstrating basic steps to six dancers. A dancer keeps landing heavily on their heels in a jump.

options.text: Let the dancer continue and mention the heavy landing to the choreographer later.
Show a soft landing on the balls of the feet, then help them try.
Tell the dancer to jump lower so the landing is quieter for everyone.
Make the dancer repeat the jump twenty times on the hard studio floor today.

advanced.situation: In a full rehearsal of a lifting sequence, a dancer reports shoulder pain, but the show is in two days and the dancer insists on continuing.

options.text: Tell the dancer to take painkillers and continue the lifts as rehearsed today.
Let the dancer continue if they say they feel fine after a short rest.
Stop the lifts, send the dancer to the physio, and adjust the sequence or cover.
Reduce the lifts for that dancer and watch their shoulder closely in rehearsal.

basic.situation: You watch students in a class and note their abilities for a mentor. One student has good rhythm but weak balance.

options.text: Give the student a high score for rhythm and skip the other skills.
Note the good rhythm in your report and leave balance for the teacher.
Note strengths and weaknesses with examples, and suggest simple balance drills.
Tell the student their balance is poor and they should consider another class.

advanced.situation: You audition 60 dancers for a large production. Many are technically strong, but a few fit the unusual style. You must give useful feedback to everyone.

options.text: Tell each rejected dancer they lack talent so that they stop applying here.
Give feedback to the dancers you select and thank the others by email.
Choose the dancers with the strongest technique and send a general message to the others.
Score on set criteria, note one strength and one area to improve, and send feedback.

basic.situation: You help set up a stage for a school dance following a plan from the director. You see that the plan puts a prop in the exit path.

options.text: Place the prop as planned and tell the director after the first rehearsal.
Move the prop to a spot you think is better and say nothing.
Point it out to the director, suggest another spot, and wait for approval.
Leave the prop in the exit path and put a sign on it for dancers.

advanced.situation: You stage a dance drama in an old theatre with limited lighting. The lighting plan hides the dancers' feet, and dark costumes merge with the background.

options.text: Ask the lighting designer to add more lights and keep the costumes as they are.
Change the dark costumes to bright colours and leave the lighting plan unchanged.
Rearrange the dance so dancers stay at the front edge of the stage.
Review the stage with the designers, adjust lights and colours, and check on video.

basic.situation: A mentor asks you to read a short story and note its moods for a dance piece. The story moves from joy to sadness at the end.

options.text: Mark each mood change, link it to tempo and movement ideas, and share notes.
Choose the one mood you like and plan the whole dance around it.
Skip the story and use a dance from another piece that sounds happy.
Note the joyful beginning because it is the longest part of the whole story.

advanced.situation: You develop a concept for a new work, drawing on architecture and theatre. A senior colleague warns that mixing too many ideas may confuse the audience.

options.text: Dismiss the warning and add more influences from film and painting to the work.
Pick one architecture and one theatre idea, build from them, and test with viewers.
Use every idea you collected and explain the concept in the programme notes.
Drop the theatre influence and keep architecture alone to keep things much simpler.

basic.situation: You attend technique class daily to keep fit while helping at the studio. This week the studio is busy and you are tired.

options.text: Stop attending classes this month and focus fully on studio work and sleep.
Keep your class, lighten your studio tasks with the manager, and rest well at night.
Do a short stretch at home and rely on your fitness from last month.
Skip class for two days and make it up on the weekend with extra practice.

advanced.situation: You help manage a dance school with falling enrolment and rising rent. A parent group wants lower fees, and teachers want pay rises. The owner asks you for a plan.

options.text: Review the numbers, propose new classes and a fee structure, and consult parents and teachers.
Cut all fees by ten percent to attract more students and hold teachers' pay.
Raise fees to cover rent and pay rises and tell parents the reasons.
Cut the teachers' pay to keep fees low and tell them at month end.

basic.situation: A mentor asks you to write a simple eight bar melody and add chords for a school song. Your melody ends on a note that sounds unfinished.

options.text: End on the home note of the key, add the matching chord, and play it.
Keep the ending and add a loud final chord to make it sound complete.
Add two extra bars so the melody can find its own ending naturally.
Replace your melody with the first eight bars of a well known song.

advanced.situation: You compose a 30 second jingle and a film soundtrack cue for the same client. The client wants both fresh, but gives you little time, and the film cue needs a full orchestra.

options.text: Reuse the jingle theme in the film cue to save time and effort.
Sketch both themes at the keyboard, fit the orchestration to the cue, and share demos.
Use a famous song's chords for both pieces and change the rhythm slightly.
Write the jingle first for the client and finish the cue with leftover time.

basic.situation: A conductor asks you to copy the violin part from a full score for the first rehearsal. You find a few bars where notes are unclear.

options.text: Leave the unclear bars empty and hand the part out to the violinists anyway.
Copy the clear bars, mark the unclear ones, and ask the conductor about them.
Copy the part and fill in the unclear notes from what sounds likely.
Replace the unclear bars with notes from a similar piece you know well.

advanced.situation: You are asked to rewrite a classical piece for a school brass band in a jazz style. Several band members are beginners, and the show is in three weeks.

options.text: Use a ready made jazz arrangement from a website and print it for the band.
Write a very hard jazz version and expect the band to improve by the show.
Write the full jazz arrangement for advanced players and give beginners the melody.
Keep the melody, simplify beginner parts, add swing rhythm, and try it with the band.

basic.situation: In rehearsal, you use basic gestures to show tempo while a teacher watches. The students keep speeding up near the end.

options.text: Let the students speed up and fix the tempo in the final concert.
Wave your arms faster to match the students and hold them together at the end.
Give a steadier beat, show the tempo before entries, and hold it at the end.
Stop and tell the students to listen to the beat and not speed up.

advanced.situation: You conduct a youth orchestra in a new hall. The brass drowns out the strings in the first run, and a soloist cannot hear the cello section.

options.text: Ask the strings to play much louder and the soloist to listen more carefully.
Ask the brass to play softer in every section during the whole concert.
Reposition brass and cellos, rehearse a balance passage, and check with the soloist.
Cut the brass parts from the concert to protect the strings and soloist.

basic.situation: You help schedule rehearsals for a choir with eight singers. The hall is free only on Saturday morning, but three singers work that day.

options.text: Ask all eight for free times, find the most common slot, and check hall options.
Choose a time that suits you and tell all the singers to adjust.
Hold the rehearsal on Saturday morning and send notes to the three who miss it.
Cancel the three singers' places in the choir and keep the five who are free.

advanced.situation: You assign work to a copyist, an arranger and a vocal coach for a gala concert in two weeks. The arranger is behind, and the copyist cannot start until the arrangements are done.

options.text: Cancel the planned arrangements and perform simple versions found online, then tell the client.
Have the arranger send pages in batches, start copying early, and move vocal coaching forward.
Hire another arranger to work on half of the pieces from tomorrow morning.
Tell the arranger to work through the night until everything is completely finished.

basic.situation: You study a score to learn it before the first rehearsal. One section has many tempo changes you do not understand.

options.text: Ask the players to follow their own tempo in that section of the music.
Skip the section for now and focus on the parts you already understand well.
Mark the changes, listen to a recording, and ask your teacher about unclear ones.
Conduct the section at one steady tempo and fix the changes in rehearsal.

advanced.situation: A film director wants music over a quiet emotional scene, but the producer wants an upbeat track. You must define the music's placement before the edit locks in two days.

options.text: Follow the producer's view since the producer controls the budget for the music.
Follow the director's view and tell the producer the music suits the story.
Screen the scene with both, play two short demos, and agree one direction in writing.
Write both tracks quickly and decide which to use on the day of the edit.

basic.situation: You help pick music for a school band of 12 beginners and four advanced players. The band has two weeks to prepare for an assembly.

options.text: Choose a piece with easy main parts, a few harder lines, and available scores.
Choose a popular pop song that all the students know and enjoy playing.
Choose the hardest piece available to challenge the advanced players during the assembly.
Choose three long pieces so the band has plenty to play at the assembly.

advanced.situation: You apply for a grant to fund a youth orchestra tour. A guest soloist's agent quotes RM15,000, but your funding cap for artists is RM10,000.

options.text: Submit the budget with RM15,000 and explain your reasons to the funder.
Negotiate a lower fee or shorter slot, and submit a budget within the cap.
Cancel the grant application and plan a smaller tour paid from ticket sales.
List the soloist at RM10,000 on the form and pay the rest privately later.

basic.situation: You sing a song in front of a small group at a school gathering with your teacher guiding you. Halfway through, you forget the second verse.

options.text: Stop singing, apologise to the audience, and ask to start the song again.
Make up new words for the verse and keep singing until the chorus.
Walk off the stage quietly and refuse to sing in public again after that.
Stay calm, hum the tune, rejoin at the chorus, and tell your teacher afterwards.

advanced.situation: As a jazz guitarist, you improvise a solo in a concert. The audience seems bored, and the drummer signals to extend the solo another minute.

options.text: Change the rhythm and volume, quote the melody, and signal the band to build.
Stop the solo early and tell the audience to pay more attention to you.
Play faster and louder to grab the audience's attention until the solo finally ends.
Repeat your favourite phrase many times until the audience begins to respond.

basic.situation: You are asked to sing a short song from printed text and notation at a school event. The notation has a rest you are unsure about.

options.text: Skip the rest and join in again when the words continue in the next line.
Ask your teacher about the rest, practise counting it, and mark the page.
Assume the rest is quite short and sing through it quickly during the performance.
Change the song to a different one that you know by heart today.

advanced.situation: At a rehearsal, you sight read a hard clarinet part in an unfamiliar key. Others in the section are lost, and the conductor moves on quickly.

options.text: Copy the player beside you even when you hear they are playing different notes.
Check the key and rhythm first, play what you can cleanly, and mark trouble spots.
Play everything at full speed and hope to catch most of the notes.
Stop playing and wait for the next section to begin after this part.

basic.situation: You join a recording session with an engineer directing. After the first take, the engineer says your guitar is too loud in the headphones mix.

options.text: Turn the engineer's mixing dials yourself while the next take is recording live.
Take off the headphones and play by feel for the next take or two.
Play more softly in the next take and keep the same headphone mix.
Ask the engineer to adjust the headphone mix, play another take, and listen back together.

advanced.situation: A magazine offers a long interview about your new album, and your manager has a different message plan. The interviewer asks about a private dispute with a band member.

options.text: Skip the interview and promote the album on your own social media instead.
Tell the full dispute story to the interviewer to get a big headline.
Answer the dispute question carefully in general terms and avoid naming anyone involved.
Agree talking points with your manager, then politely decline questions about the private dispute.

basic.situation: A vocal coach asks you to transpose a short song down so you can sing it comfortably. The song is currently in the key of D.

options.text: Move every note down evenly, check it on an instrument, and sing it.
Change the key signature at the start and leave all the notes unchanged.
Sing the song an octave lower and see whether it works for you.
Raise the song one step instead because it is easier to write and read.

advanced.situation: You compose a vocal arrangement for a six voice group for a wedding. The couple wants a pop song, a hymn and a folk tune included in six minutes.

options.text: Choose the two songs that are easiest to arrange and drop the third.
Sing the three songs one after another in their original keys with short pauses.
Build a medley with shared keys and smooth links, then test it with the singers.
Use a recorded karaoke version and have the six singers sing along quietly.

basic.situation: You practise singing exercises with your vocal coach for an upcoming role. After 30 minutes, your throat feels dry and scratchy.

options.text: Stop, drink water, rest your voice, and tell your coach about it.
Sing louder to push through the scratchy feeling before the role audition tomorrow.
Continue softly for the rest of the session and rest your voice tomorrow.
Drink a cold drink and keep singing at the same volume as before.

advanced.situation: You are cast in a musical that needs singing, acting and dancing. You are strong at singing, weak at dancing, and rehearsals begin in two weeks.

options.text: Focus on your singing and acting and learn the dance during the rehearsals.
Ask the director to simplify the dance numbers for your character before rehearsals.
Book dance classes, get early steps from the choreographer, and practise them.
Tell the director you have dance experience and copy others in the first rehearsal.

basic.situation: You teach a beginner violin student using a school curriculum. The student keeps holding the bow too tightly and gets sore fingers.

options.text: Tell the student to loosen the grip and keep practising every day this week.
Move on to the next exercise and fix the grip later in the term.
Give the student a heavier bow to build strength in the hand quickly.
Show a relaxed bow hold, let the student copy it, and check each lesson.

advanced.situation: You direct a school orchestra of 40 players with mixed ability before a competition. The strings are strong, the winds are weak, and the principal wants you to set standards.

options.text: Set section standards, hold extra wind sectionals, and give the strings stretch parts.
Choose an easier piece so the weak winds can play it more safely.
Spend most rehearsal time on the winds and let the strings practise alone.
Remove the weakest wind players from the competition roster and replace them with strings.

basic.situation: You are preparing music for a small wedding and have a short playlist brief from the couple. What do you do?

options.text: Build a short playlist around the event theme, then check it with the lead DJ.
Preview the requested tracks and group clean versions by the event's planned mood.
Ask the client to choose every track, then follow their list in order.
Play familiar hits from memory to save preparation time before guests arrive.

advanced.situation: A junior DJ's set has abrupt transitions at a high-profile reception. You need to help raise the quality of the next set. What do you do?

options.text: Set clear transition standards, demonstrate techniques, and review a practice set together.
Tell the DJ to use popular tracks and keep the changes simple.
Ask the junior DJ to copy your last set for the reception.
Share a few transition tips and let the DJ choose which ones to try.

basic.situation: You are setting up speakers and a projector for a community hall event, using the venue's setup guide. What do you do?

options.text: Connect speakers and projector through labeled ports, then test both before guests arrive.
Ask the venue technician to connect equipment while you arrange chairs nearby.
Connect the listed cables and test the projector using the venue setup guide.
Use nearby cables, then power on the equipment and check each device.

advanced.situation: During a large dinner, one side of the room loses sound and the lighting console also responds slowly. What do you do?

options.text: Trace the signal path, check console load, isolate faults, and brief the crew.
Replace the silent speaker with a spare, then check its signal and output.
Ask a technician to troubleshoot while you keep the event program moving.
Lower the master volume, then retry lighting controls during the next song.

basic.situation: After a birthday event, you need to prepare an itemized invoice for the client's agreed services. What do you do?

options.text: Enter the agreed services and prices into the usual invoice template.
Copy the last invoice and update the client's name and event date.
Send the client one total based on the amount you remember discussing.
List the agreed services, hours, and charges, then compare the total with your notes.

advanced.situation: Several DJs share a growing music library, and duplicate files have caused set errors. You are asked to improve how the team organizes it. What do you do?

options.text: Move each DJ's files into a separate folder and ask them to manage updates.
Delete tracks that look duplicated and keep the newest file in each folder.
Ask everyone to rename their own files when they notice duplicates.
Create shared naming and tagging rules, then sort files into searchable event folders.

basic.situation: A client asks about paying the remaining balance for a small event. Your notes show the agreed amount and payment method. What do you do?

options.text: Confirm the recorded balance and send the usual payment instructions for the booking.
Tell the client the amount you recall and ask them to transfer it.
Check the booking notes, then explain the balance and available payment method.
Ask the client to pay the full package price again while you check.

advanced.situation: A venue wants to change the event timing and requests a lower fee, while your team has another booking that day. What do you do?

options.text: Accept the lower fee and adjust the schedule after confirming with the other client.
Review the booking details, clarify the new timing, and offer a fee tied to workable changes.
Decline the change and keep the original arrangement to protect the day's bookings.
Explain the schedule conflict and ask what timing and budget range they can accommodate.

basic.situation: Guests at a company dinner are making song requests while the dance floor is quiet. What do you do?

options.text: Sort requests by energy and fit, then weave suitable tracks into the set.
Take requests as they come and play the most familiar songs first.
Queue each request in arrival order so guests feel heard throughout the party.
Check each request against the event mood and promised playlist before choosing a transition.

advanced.situation: At a multicultural dinner, a dance-off is losing momentum and some guests are stepping away. What do you do?

options.text: Invite volunteers into short rounds, offer varied music, and keep judging light and welcoming.
Pause the contest and ask the host whether to switch to a group dance.
Keep the dance-off running and offer the prize to the next winner.
Change the music style and invite guests back for another round.

basic.situation: You are following a reception schedule, and the speeches are running five minutes late before the planned music set. What do you do?

options.text: Start the music at the printed time while guests finish the speeches.
Confirm the delay with the coordinator and shorten the next transition.
Wait until the speeches finish, then play the full set as planned.
Check with the coordinator, then adjust your start within the schedule they approve.

advanced.situation: At an outdoor event, wind changes the sound and a second DJ is unsure which checks to repeat before the next act. What do you do?

options.text: Recheck levels from the audience area, then tell the second DJ what you hear.
Move the speakers closer together, then repeat a microphone test before the next act.
Use a sound check for levels, microphones, coverage, and coach the second DJ.
Raise speaker levels and ask the second DJ to listen from the stage.

basic.situation: You are reading a prepared traffic update on air, but one place name is unfamiliar and your next line is coming up. What do you do?

options.text: Check the pronunciation note, then read the update at the planned pace.
Read the name as it looks and keep the update moving for listeners.
Pause briefly and ask the producer to pronounce the name for you.
Skip the place name and continue with the rest of the traffic update.

advanced.situation: A major event is unfolding during your live shift, and early reports give conflicting details about the location. What do you do?

options.text: Wait for a producer to resolve every detail before saying anything on air.
State what is verified, attribute the uncertainty, and update listeners as details are confirmed.
Report the conflicting locations and say that details are still being checked.
Choose the location mentioned most often and deliver the update confidently.

basic.situation: A local musician joins your morning show, and you have a short prepared question list. What do you do?

options.text: Start with a question about the guest's most popular song.
Ask the guest which topic they would most like to discuss first.
Read the questions in order and keep each answer within the planned time.
Review the guest notes, then ask the prepared questions in a conversational order.

advanced.situation: A senior guest gives a long answer that avoids your central question, and the program has time for one follow-up. What do you do?

options.text: Repeat the same question with a firmer tone before the segment ends.
Acknowledge their point, then restate the central question in a focused follow-up.
Move to the next planned topic to keep the interview on schedule.
Ask the guest to clarify the part of their answer that relates to your topic.

basic.situation: You are running a short interview on a studio console, and the guest's microphone sounds quieter than yours. What do you do?

options.text: Raise the guest fader until the voices sound closer in volume.
Check the guest channel meter and raise its level while monitoring both voices.
Ask the guest to speak louder while you continue the interview.
Turn up the program master so the guest reaches listeners more clearly.

advanced.situation: A console fault disrupted the previous shift, and a new presenter is unsure how to log the segment and monitor the channels. What do you do?

options.text: Let the presenter operate the console during the next segment to learn by doing.
Show the presenter the main faders and ask them to copy your settings.
Explain the channel meters and have them record the aired elements in the log.
Walk them through channel checks and the program log, then review one practice entry.

basic.situation: You are editing a short radio script, and a sentence has a confusing phrase that may be hard to read aloud. What do you do?

options.text: Ask another presenter to mark the confusing phrase before you change it.
Remove the sentence so the script is shorter for the presenter.
Rewrite the phrase in plain language and read the sentence aloud for flow.
Adjust the grammar while keeping the sentence structure for the presenter.

advanced.situation: Your team is building a broadcast series about several local issues, but drafts vary in tone and story structure. What do you do?

options.text: Set a story arc and tone guide, then shape each draft with it.
Combine the drafts into one script and trim repeated sections.
Ask each writer to follow the outline from their most recent episode.
Agree on a shared tone and let each writer develop their own structure.

basic.situation: You are helping prepare a small on-air quiz, and the producer asks you to set out the microphones and prize cards. What do you do?

options.text: Leave the prize cards with the host and check each microphone.
Place all items near the studio door for quick access before airtime.
Arrange the microphones and prize cards by the running order and test them.
Set out the microphones and prize cards within reach of the host and producer.

advanced.situation: A station fundraiser has several guests, a live contest, and a tight broadcast window. One guest cancels shortly before the show. What do you do?

options.text: Remove the interview and extend the contest through the remaining broadcast time.
Reshape the order around confirmed guests, brief the host, and keep the contest segment.
Invite a familiar guest to fill the gap and preserve the planned order.
Contact a suitable backup guest and tell the host the running order may change.

basic.situation: You are recording a short station promotion, and the script includes a sponsor name you have not seen before. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the producer how to say the sponsor name before you record.
Record a take using the pronunciation that seems most familiar.
Check the pronunciation note, then record the script at its planned pace.
