Record a take, then ask the producer whether the sponsor name sounded right.

advanced.situation: At a public station event, visitors ask about a new show while a sponsor recording is due before the next segment. What do you do?

options.text: Ask a colleague to record sponsor copy, then answer visitors about the new show.
Tell visitors to check the station schedule while you prepare the recording.
Introduce the show briefly, then record the sponsor copy in approved format.
Record the sponsor copy first, then answer visitors' questions about the show.

basic.situation: You are writing a background note and find two different dates for the same local event. What do you do?

options.text: I compare two reliable records, then flag any detail still uncertain.
I ask a colleague to review my notes before sending them to the editor.
I check the archive and confirm dates before drafting the background.
I use the first search result to finish the note quickly.

advanced.situation: After a flood, eyewitness accounts conflict with early official updates. You have footage and a live deadline. What do you do?

options.text: I publish the first account while details are still developing.
I separate confirmed facts from claims and keep checking each source.
I wait for an editor to decide which reports seem credible.
I verify eyewitness claims against official updates and timestamped footage.

basic.situation: A colleague sends you a short draft with several punctuation slips before the local news deadline. What do you do?

options.text: I revise every sentence to make the article sound more polished.
I smooth awkward lines quickly and send the draft onward.
I compare the draft with house style and mark clear errors.
I tidy punctuation and keep the writer's meaning intact throughout.

advanced.situation: Several reporters use different formats for the same recurring segment, delaying edits. You are asked to guide the desk's style. What do you do?

options.text: I review recurring edits and propose one standard for common cases.
I share a short style sheet and explain its use with examples.
I let each reporter choose formatting that suits their own draft.
I set the template, then invite questions about difficult style calls.

basic.situation: You need to write a short blog update about a council announcement using the desk's confirmed notes. What do you do?

options.text: I draft a brief update from the confirmed event notes.
I check names and dates, then save the draft for review.
I add my own take to make the post more lively.
I link the update to the source story and explain context.

advanced.situation: A new policy is drawing sharply different reactions, and your column is due today. You need to interpret its likely effects. What do you do?

options.text: I present two viewpoints and leave the implications for readers.
I weigh evidence from affected groups before drawing a measured conclusion.
I compare policy choices and explain who may be affected.
I argue from one striking example to keep the column punchy.

basic.situation: You are reading a prepared news link on camera, and two names are unfamiliar. What do you do?

options.text: I deliver the link naturally, pausing around key details.
I rush through the script to stay ahead of the rundown.
I mark names for pronunciation and rehearse the difficult lines.
I read the prepared link clearly and keep a steady pace.

advanced.situation: A remote reporter's audio drops just before a live handoff. The producer asks you to keep the broadcast moving. What do you do?

options.text: I introduce the reporter after a brief chat message says they are ready.
I pause the handoff until the reporter confirms audio is ready.
I agree a backup link with the producer and relay the updated timing.
I confirm the remote reporter's cue and tell the control room about delay.

basic.situation: A source can speak only during lunch, and the reporter has two possible interview times. What do you do?

options.text: I offer two time slots and confirm the guest's preferred contact method.
I explain the topic and ask which time suits the source.
I pencil in a time based on the source's usual availability.
I forward the guest's private number to the whole newsroom for quick replies.

advanced.situation: As duty editor, you have one reporter available for a developing story and another for routine coverage. What do you do?

options.text: I assign the story to the first available reporter on shift.
I send everyone the same assignment note and let them divide work.
I match the reporter's experience to the developing story's needs.
I split the reporting and photo duties around clear deadlines.

basic.situation: A reader emails asking when a council meeting mentioned in your story will take place. What do you do?

options.text: I reuse an old reply that covered a similar reader question.
I acknowledge the question and share the published contact details.
I forward the message to the desk that handles that topic.
I check the relevant article and answer within its stated facts.

advanced.situation: A regular contact offers an exclusive claim about a public project, but your deadline is close. What do you do?

options.text: I add every responsive contact to my list for future requests.
I message familiar contacts when a story needs a quick comment.
I keep a source log noting expertise, contact preferences, and past confirmations.
I publish the claim based on the contact's past reliability.

basic.situation: You are updating the contact list before scheduling a meeting with community representatives about a local campaign. What do you do?

options.text: I confirm each representative's availability before finalizing the calendar.
I update representatives' details and send meeting invitations with agendas.
I invite the whole community group to simplify scheduling.
I reuse last month's contact sheet and copy its meeting times.

advanced.situation: Two community partners disagree over a campaign's message, while managers want a joint plan this quarter. What do you do?

options.text: I ask both groups to send a joint statement before responding.
I map each group's concern and propose a shared discussion around overlap.
I give the loudest partner more space to calm the meeting.
I outline competing requests and brief managers on likely trade-offs.

basic.situation: A client asks whether customers support a proposed service, and you are organizing the survey results. What do you do?

options.text: I check the survey wording and group responses by key customer types.
I report the first percentage that supports the product launch.
I summarize response patterns and flag gaps in who replied.
I remove unclear answers before sending the spreadsheet to the client.

advanced.situation: A client wants to anticipate how public sentiment about a new service may change over several years. What do you do?

options.text: I extend this week's poll to more people for a larger sample.
I compare sentiment across time and test assumptions with varied groups.
I use current comments to forecast what most customers will want.
I combine repeated surveys, interviews, and trend indicators across audience groups.

basic.situation: A client shares goals for a new community campaign and asks you to draft an initial strategy outline. What do you do?

options.text: I list possible channels before checking the client's stated priorities.
I draft objectives, audiences, and measures from the client brief.
I connect the client's objective to a clear audience and outcome.
I adapt last quarter's outline and replace the campaign details.

advanced.situation: Your organization is setting a three-year reputation plan amid shifting public concerns and limited resources. What do you do?

options.text: I focus resources on this year's strongest media opportunity.
I link reputation goals to the organization's purpose and review measures yearly.
I set a broad public trust target and leave delivery details open.
I map priority audiences, risks, and milestones across the three-year plan.

basic.situation: You are preparing an internal newsletter with staff updates, links, and event dates before it goes to layout. What do you do?

options.text: I proofread dates and names, then apply the newsletter template.
I cut long updates to fit space and assume the details remain clear.
I tidy the layout and keep the team's wording unchanged.
I check headings, links, and figures against the supplied draft.

advanced.situation: A high-stakes external report is due soon, and reviewers have questioned several figures and claims. What do you do?

options.text: I apply the house template and smooth sections for readability.
I trace key figures to approved records and flag unresolved claims.
I review the full draft against its evidence and intended audience.
I reuse last year's approved report and update the cover date.

basic.situation: You are drafting a social post about an approved campaign for the company's website and social channels. What do you do?

options.text: I check the link and wording against the current campaign brief.
I draft a short post from the approved campaign message.
I reuse last week's caption and swap in today's product image.
I adapt a popular phrase to make today's post more engaging.

advanced.situation: Several writers produce releases and social posts in noticeably different voices. You are asked to set guidance for the team. What do you do?

options.text: I ask writers to copy one successful post for every channel.
I let each writer choose a tone that fits their audience.
I define voice rules and explain how they fit each channel.
I publish a voice guide with examples and coach writers on adapting it.

basic.situation: A client is making a small public appearance at a community hall, and you are arranging the event logistics. What do you do?

options.text: I reserve the usual room and send the client the details.
I book a larger venue to allow for unexpected attendance.
I check the client's availability before confirming the public event.
I confirm the venue, timing, access needs, and speaker arrival plan.

advanced.situation: A client representative will face difficult questions at a public meeting about a delayed service. How do you prepare them?

options.text: I rehearse likely questions and help the spokesperson answer in plain language.
I share the key messages and suggest keeping answers brief.
I run a mock interview and give feedback on unclear answers.
I prepare polished lines for the spokesperson to memorize before the event.

basic.situation: You are checking a short community newsletter with a spelling checklist before it goes to layout. You spot a misspelled place name and two misplaced commas.

options.text: Fix the obvious spelling and punctuation, then send it onward.
Mark the place name and commas, then check them against the checklist.
Check the name against the source, fix punctuation, and reread the short text.
Leave the marked-up page for the next editor to review.

advanced.situation: You oversee edits for a special issue, and two editors have applied different punctuation styles across several stories before the layout deadline.

options.text: Ask the editors to agree on punctuation before submitting their pages.
Set a brief style sheet, compare all pages against it, and resolve exceptions together.
Keep each editor's style so the pages can move into layout.
Choose one style, brief both editors, and review a shared sample.

basic.situation: An author submits a draft feature with a checklist attached. You notice the opening gives background but does not introduce the main point until the final paragraph.

options.text: Approve the draft because each paragraph reads clearly on its own.
Suggest moving the main point earlier and check the opening's flow.
Ask the author to shorten the final paragraph before review.
Flag the late main point and ask the author to move it earlier.

advanced.situation: A long manuscript has conflicting chapter order and a weak ending. The author wants to submit it soon, while the proofs team needs a stable draft.

options.text: Explain structural issues, rank revisions, and agree a stable handoff with the author.
Approve the current structure so the proofs team can begin layout.
Suggest a chapter reorder and ask the author to strengthen the ending.
Return the manuscript with notes outlining several needed structural revisions for the author.

basic.situation: A short profile lists a local event date and a public official's name. Your reference checklist includes the event programme and the organisation's directory.

options.text: Use the dates and names already printed in the draft.
Check the programme date and directory spelling, then mark both references.
Search the directory for the name and ask a colleague about the date.
Compare each detail with its listed source and record the page or entry.

advanced.situation: A feature includes several figures about a sensitive public service. Staff use different sources, and one figure conflicts with a published report before deadline.

options.text: Ask each writer to cite a source and review the conflicting figure together.
Set approved source rules, log each figure's evidence, and train staff on conflicts.
Replace the disputed figure with the number in the published report.
Keep the figure from the draft because it matches the feature's main point.

basic.situation: You are helping plan next week's community pages. Readers have asked about rising market costs, and your editor wants a few timely story ideas.

options.text: Pitch a local market costs guide with reader questions and practical advice.
Offer a general shopping story because prices are a current topic.
Reuse last week's popular food story with a new headline.
Suggest a market price explainer, then ask the editor which angle fits readers.

advanced.situation: Your publication is planning its next quarter, and several departments want space for unrelated topics. Readers have responded strongly to practical local service coverage.

options.text: Set audience-led priorities, explain the policy, and map coverage across the quarter.
Give each department the pages it requested for the quarter.
Ask department leads to trade pages until every team has some space.
Reserve regular space for service stories and review reader response each month.

basic.situation: A designer tells you that a photo is missing from a page due for print tomorrow. The layout team is waiting for your update on production progress.

options.text: Ask the designer to find any suitable replacement image today.
Check artwork status, flag the deadline risk, and agree a revised handoff.
Tell the printer the page is ready while the photo is pending.
Check the artwork list, update the designer, and confirm today's revised handoff plan.

advanced.situation: A late layout change would push a print run past its budget estimate. Marketing needs the page, while the production manager is awaiting your cost and timing update.

options.text: Approve the change and ask production to absorb the extra printing cost.
Assess print impacts, recommend a feasible option, and align teams on delivery.
Compare revised layout costs and timing, then present practical trade-offs to both teams.
Ask marketing to choose between the new layout and the existing page.

basic.situation: Your editor approves a simple local event assignment. Two writers are available, and one has already covered a similar event for the publication.

options.text: Ask both writers who wants the event and wait for their replies.
Offer the assignment to the available writer and confirm the deadline and brief.
Send both writers to cover the same event for more material.
Match the experienced writer, confirm the brief, and share the deadline.

advanced.situation: A developing local story could lead today's homepage, but reporters and editors disagree about its prominence. You are coordinating updates before the next edition closes.

options.text: Compare verified developments with audience value, then align desks on placement.
Ask each desk to send verified updates, placement preferences, and any deadline concerns.
Keep the current placement so the edition can close on time.
Let the homepage editor choose the placement after hearing both sides.

basic.situation: You are reading a pump drawing and operating specification to understand which valve the maintenance steps describe.

options.text: I compare the valve labels on the drawing with each specification step.
I trace the specified valve on the drawing, matching each step to its label.
I ask maintenance staff which valve they usually service first during routine work.
I draft steps from memory using the valve name I recognize.

advanced.situation: You are reviewing service manuals for a product line and notice repeated changes in operating procedures across newer models.

options.text: I update the manuals to match the newest model's procedure.
I compare manuals and discuss revision needs with engineering staff.
I map procedure changes by model and recommend targeted manual revisions.
I add a note that procedures may vary across models.

basic.situation: You are organizing a short setup guide whose steps repeat details and use different names for the same button.

options.text: I flag repeated steps and ask the writer which button name to retain.
I shorten the guide by removing repeated setup details from each step.
I follow house style and use one button name throughout the guide.
I remove repeated details while preserving the button names already used.

advanced.situation: Several teams publish user guides with conflicting terms for the same feature, and a new release is due across formats.

options.text: I choose the term used by the largest team for consistency.
I retain each team's terms and add a glossary to the release.
I publish a shared terminology list and ask teams to use it in drafts.
I assess terms against product usage and set a style guide for every format.

basic.situation: You are selecting images for a short guide showing how to clean a small office printer.

options.text: I match each step with a clear photo that supports its text.
I select images that show the printer's main cleaning parts clearly.
I choose the sharpest photos from the available folder for the guide.
I reuse printer photos from an older unrelated guide without checking relevance.

advanced.situation: A maintenance guide needs a sketch showing how a technician removes a jammed roller from a compact machine.

options.text: I draw the roller in place and let technicians infer removal order.
I adapt a similar machine's sketch and change its model label.
I sketch the main removal stages and ask maintenance to review them.
I sketch the roller sequence and label the access points from the supplied notes.

basic.situation: You are saving a revised troubleshooting page and need to keep a clear record of what changed from the prior draft.

options.text: I save the page in the shared folder using its topic name.
I replace the old file with the new page to reduce clutter.
I save the revised page with its date and a brief change note.
I retain both drafts and label each file with its date and changes.

advanced.situation: A help site has outdated pages across several product versions, and staff need to know which revisions remain current.

options.text: I add a banner directing users to check their product version before reading.
I record page owners, versions, review dates, and archive locations together.
I replace outdated pages while retaining earlier versions in the archive.
I map each page to its version, review cycle, owner, and archive.

basic.situation: A client asks for a quick guide to a new packing line but has not explained who will use it or for what tasks.

options.text: I ask the client to identify users, key tasks, and topics for the guide.
I reuse a guide from another packing line as the draft.
I ask who will use the guide and which tasks it should cover.
I request the machine model and begin a general operating guide.

advanced.situation: A publisher wants a multi-part maintenance manual for several machine models, but has not settled the deliverables or review schedule.

options.text: I define models, audiences, deliverables, and review points with the publisher.
I estimate a single manual covering every model and maintenance task.
I draft the first model's chapters while the publisher decides the rest.
I list the models and ask the publisher to rank priorities.

basic.situation: You are arranging typing and photocopying for a short safety handout needed at a staff briefing tomorrow.

options.text: I photocopy the current draft and hand copies out during tomorrow's briefing.
I book typing and duplication after confirming approval and the required copy count.
I send the approved draft for typing, noting copies needed and tomorrow's briefing deadline.
I confirm the approved file, copy count, and pickup time with the service desk.

advanced.situation: A revised product guide must reach service centres nationwide, and you are monitoring production and distribution dates.

options.text: I send the finished files to the usual distributor and wait for updates.
I check the schedule with production and list the centres needing copies.
I track production milestones and confirm quantities and dispatch dates with distributors.
I ask each centre to request copies when its stock runs low.

basic.situation: You are asked to help write a sales letter for a local bakery’s new lunch set, using a brief that names its audience and key benefits.

options.text: Ask the creative lead which tone to use before drafting any lines.
Draft a short letter around the brief's audience and one clear benefit.
Use the approved outline and explain the product's main benefit plainly.
Reuse last month's letter and change the product name and price.

advanced.situation: A client wants a name and slogan for a snack aimed at families in Malaysia and overseas, but early feedback shows different audiences value different things.

options.text: Keep the client's first name and polish its slogan for every market.
Choose the most popular name from the local feedback and extend it abroad.
Ask the client which audience matters most before suggesting a name.
Offer a short list of names with slogans suited to each audience.

basic.situation: You are helping interview shoppers about a new bottled drink and need to learn which feature most interests them.

options.text: Ask shoppers to compare the taste, price, and packaging, then note their choices.
Ask each shopper what they like about the drink and record their answers.
Ask whether they like the drink, then mark each answer as yes or no.
Mention the low price first and ask whether that makes them interested.

advanced.situation: A team needs consumer insight for a new home internet bundle, but households differ in budget, usage, and confidence choosing a plan.

options.text: Interview varied households about their routines, choices, and reasons for switching.
Ask the marketing team which customer group should answer a short survey.
Survey current customers about preferred prices and package features.
Interview a few colleagues who use home internet and summarize their views.

basic.situation: You are reviewing recent campaign examples and a consumer survey to help your team decide how to promote a new raincoat.

options.text: Pick the most eye-catching advertisement and recommend copying its style.
Summarize the recurring messages and survey findings for the team.
List the most frequent advertising styles and ask the lead what they mean.
Compare the examples with survey preferences and suggest a fitting message.

advanced.situation: A client’s sales are steady, but survey comments and recent campaign patterns suggest rainwear buyers may soon value durability over seasonal discounts.

options.text: Replace the discount theme with durability across every planned campaign.
Extend the discount message because it has supported steady sales.
Compare the signals over time and outline possible long-term messages.
Recommend emphasizing durable materials in the next campaign.

basic.situation: Your creative director asks you to help develop a campaign idea for a neighbourhood bookstore's weekend reading event.

options.text: Build a simple concept around local discovery and share it with the art director.
Draft a few campaign lines that fit the event and its readers.
Adapt a familiar book sale slogan and change the store details.
Ask the creative director for a sample campaign before writing ideas.

advanced.situation: A campaign for a new family service spans social posts, radio, and print, and junior writers are using different promises in their drafts.

options.text: Set one campaign promise, then align each channel's draft to it.
Collect the drafts and flag repeated phrases for the creative director.
Edit the social posts first and let the other writers finish their drafts.
Send the strongest radio line to every writer as the campaign message.

basic.situation: You are presenting a first draft of a café's new menu leaflet to the client with your supervisor in the meeting.

options.text: Walk through the draft and explain how its wording serves café customers.
Explain that this is a first draft, then ask which section needs discussion.
Read the leaflet aloud, then invite the client to share specific comments.
Show the headline first and ask what impression it gives the client.

advanced.situation: Senior stakeholders question why your campaign uses a plain-language explanation of a technical service instead of detailed product terminology.

options.text: Replace the plain explanation with the stakeholders' preferred technical wording.
Defend the plain wording by describing how customers may read the message.
Connect the wording choice to audience needs and the campaign's purpose.
Show the technical terms in the draft and ask which ones they prefer.

basic.situation: During a client meeting about a festive campaign, you are asked to note possible changes to its advertising theme.

options.text: Note each suggested change and ask the account lead to interpret them later.
Summarize the theme options and confirm which direction the client prefers.
Write down the first change mentioned and move to the next agenda item.
Record the client's requested changes and the reasons behind them.

advanced.situation: A client wants major copy changes two days before launch, but the new claims and tone pull the campaign away from its agreed theme.

options.text: Ask the client to choose between the current copy and their requested version.
Explain the theme conflict and offer one alternative line for review.
Clarify the client's priority, then discuss changes that fit the agreed theme.
Accept the new copy and send it for production to protect the launch date.

basic.situation: You are outlining a short story about a market stallholder who must decide whether to keep a family tradition or try a new idea.

options.text: Write the opening scene and decide the ending after feedback.
Map the choice, its consequences, and the ending before drafting scenes.
List the main events in order and add a few character notes.
Start with a market scene and follow whichever event feels interesting.

advanced.situation: Two writers are shaping a story that alternates between a grandmother’s past and a grandchild’s present, but their plot threads do not yet meet.

options.text: Choose a shared theme, then have both writers build scenes around it.
Ask each writer to outline their timeline, then connect their key events.
Compare both outlines and mark places where their timelines could intersect.
Link turning points across both timelines so each story changes the other.

basic.situation: You are writing a short descriptive piece about a rainy evening at a Penang bus stop for a local writing group.

options.text: Describe every sound and sight you remember from the bus stop.
Write a clear first draft, then ask the group what feels vivid.
Use familiar rainy-day phrases to finish the paragraph quickly.
Choose a few precise details and build the paragraph around them.

advanced.situation: An editor asks for a literary essay that moves between a flood memory and the present, while keeping your voice consistent across both periods.

options.text: Use recurring images to link the time shifts while keeping each scene distinct.
Keep the same sentence patterns throughout to maintain a consistent voice.
Write both periods in your usual voice, then review the transitions.
Draft the memories first and let the present-day sections explain them.

basic.situation: You are checking a short story draft against an editing checklist before sharing it with your writing group.

options.text: Check each paragraph for spelling, punctuation, and grammar before sharing.
Read the draft against the checklist and fix clear language errors.
Fix the opening page first and leave the remaining pages for the group.
Rely on spellcheck and send the draft once it shows no alerts.

advanced.situation: A small writing group submits linked stories with different styles, and the editor asks you to help them revise the collection consistently.

options.text: Agree shared revision criteria, then use examples to guide each writer's edits.
Edit each story into your own style and return the revised drafts.
Ask writers to fix grammar and spelling before the editor reviews the collection.
Share a checklist for recurring issues and invite writers to apply it.

basic.situation: You are preparing a short story for a publisher and have been given a template with formatting and file requirements.

options.text: Paste the story into the template and send the file right away.
Adjust the font and spacing to match your usual manuscript style.
Format the opening pages and ask the editor whether the layout works.
Apply the template and check the file against its submission requirements.

advanced.situation: A producer asks to use a story excerpt in a programme, and you are unsure whether your existing agreement covers that use.

options.text: Review the agreement's scope and seek qualified guidance before replying.
Ask the producer to send the proposed wording and usage details.
Offer a short excerpt and ask the producer to credit your name.
Agree to the excerpt use since the producer has described its purpose.

basic.situation: You are writing a story inspired by a local fishing village and need factual details about daily work there.

options.text: Read several articles and list details that could support the story.
Check local reporting and note which details need another source.
Search travel pages for vivid descriptions and adapt them to the setting.
Use the first article you find to describe a typical workday.

advanced.situation: Your writing team is developing a collection about migration, but the initial concepts repeat familiar stories and research approaches vary widely.

options.text: Set a shared research approach and invite concepts from underrepresented experiences.
Ask each writer to choose a migration story that interests them.
Compare the current ideas and suggest less familiar settings for revision.
Choose one striking interview and build the collection around its details.

basic.situation: An editor meets with you to discuss changes to a short story you submitted, and you have been asked to listen and take notes.

options.text: Note the requested changes and ask which concern matters most to the story.
Defend your draft's choices calmly as each suggestion comes up for discussion.
Write down each comment, then review your notes after the meeting.
Record the main edits and ask the editor to email any further suggestions.

advanced.situation: At a book launch, readers ask about a sensitive family story in your novel, while the publisher expects you to represent the project thoughtfully.

options.text: Share extra family details to keep the audience interested.
Ask the publisher's representative to answer the audience questions instead.
Answer within your knowledge and guide questions toward the novel's themes.
Thank the readers and invite them to ask about the writing process.

basic.situation: During a clinic visit, you are asked to interpret a short instruction, but one phrase is unclear and the senior interpreter is nearby.

options.text: I would interpret the message, then ask the senior to review it.
I would fill the unclear phrase from context and keep the visit moving.
I would interpret each point plainly and signal any phrase I cannot hear.
I would pause at the unclear phrase and request a repeat through the senior.

advanced.situation: At a community briefing, an interpreter uses a culturally specific expression that could sound insulting when translated literally, and the audience is reacting.

options.text: I would translate the phrase literally so listeners can judge its meaning themselves.
I would paraphrase the phrase neutrally and continue with the speaker’s next point.
I would ask the speaker to explain the phrase before translating it further.
I would render the intended meaning and briefly clarify the expression’s cultural context.

basic.situation: A client gives you a short appointment notice to translate, and the date and venue are easy to read.

options.text: I would translate the notice and check names, date, and venue against the source.
I would reuse a similar notice and replace its date and venue details.
I would translate the sentences, then ask a colleague to scan the wording.
I would translate the main message and send it for the client’s review.

advanced.situation: A technical manual uses one term for two related parts, and the client wants a translation that technicians can follow safely.

options.text: I would choose clearer terms for each part and note the choice for review.
I would define each part from the source context and apply distinct terms consistently.
I would use the closest dictionary terms and keep the manual’s original pattern.
I would retain one translated term throughout to match the source wording.

basic.situation: You are checking a translated event flyer against a checklist and spot a date that differs from the source.

options.text: I would leave the date as written because the flyer is nearly ready.
I would compare the date with the source and mark it for revision.
I would flag the date and ask the translator to confirm their source.
I would check the date against the event calendar before raising a query.

advanced.situation: A teammate’s translated health leaflet reads smoothly, but a key instruction uses a term inconsistently across pages.

options.text: I would standardize the term across pages using the first occurrence as reference.
I would leave the wording intact and tell the teammate about the variation.
I would mark the repeated term and ask the teammate to choose one form.
I would trace the term through the source and revise each matching passage consistently.

basic.situation: You are translating a short museum note and need a reliable equivalent for a local plant name.

options.text: I would check a bilingual dictionary and use its listed equivalent in context.
I would check a dictionary and record its source beside the chosen term.
I would choose the first familiar equivalent from an online search result.
I would consult two references and ask a colleague which term sounds natural.

advanced.situation: A client is preparing a multilingual glossary for a specialist field, and the same term appears differently in several reference documents.

options.text: I would record each term with field, source, context, and approved equivalent.
I would compare usage and discuss equivalents with the client before choosing.
I would adopt their first equivalent and flag it for client review.
I would sort terms by topic and review conflicting forms with the client.

basic.situation: A small business asks for a one-page brochure translation and wants to know the likely fee and delivery date.

options.text: I would quote the usual fee for a page and offer a likely date.
I would agree to the client’s suggested fee to secure the work.
I would discuss the page count and ask my supervisor about the fee.
I would confirm the language pair, scope, deadline, and fee basis before quoting.

advanced.situation: A client disputes your translation of a customary greeting, saying a literal version sounds disrespectful to local readers.

options.text: I would explain the possible readings and agree wording that preserves the greeting’s intent.
I would offer a natural alternative and invite the client to comment on tone.
I would ask the client for a preferred phrase and apply it to the brochure.
I would retain the literal wording because it follows the source phrase closely.

basic.situation: A school staff meeting asks you to explain when an educational interpreter should speak during a lesson.

options.text: I would outline the role and invite staff to ask about lesson situations.
I would explain the interpreter’s role and give a brief classroom example.
I would tell staff the interpreter can explain lesson content when needed.
I would describe the role using the wording from the school handout.

advanced.situation: A new interpreter is preparing for a school meeting with unfamiliar terminology, and you are assigned to guide their preparation.

options.text: I would have them review the agenda and bring questions to our check-in.
I would explain key terms and ask them to rehearse the meeting opening.
I would share the old glossary and let the interpreter prepare independently.
I would model preparation, then review their practice against the meeting context.

basic.situation: At a short committee meeting, two members speak at once while you record the discussion with a stenomask.

options.text: I would capture the louder member’s words and keep the recording flowing.
I would record the clearest words and flag the overlap in my notes.
I would pause briefly and ask the chair to have speakers take turns.
I would mark the overlap and continue recording each speaker as clearly as possible.

advanced.situation: During a hearing, counsel, a witness, and the judge begin speaking close together while your computerized recording equipment is running.

options.text: I would track each voice, mark overlap, and preserve the equipment recording for review.
I would prioritize counsel’s words because the witness can repeat answers later.
I would follow the judge’s voice and note where other speech overlaps.
I would switch attention between speakers and review the recording afterward.

basic.situation: You are formatting a short hearing transcript from a recording using the office template and notice one speaker label is missing.

options.text: I would use the most frequent speaker’s name for the missing label.
I would apply the template and verify the speaker label against the recording.
I would leave the label blank and finish the remaining formatting.
I would format the transcript and flag the missing label for review.

advanced.situation: A long transcript includes several speakers, quoted exhibits, and page breaks that differ from the court’s established format.

options.text: I would apply the established format consistently and track exhibit references across pages.
I would format the body first and ask a colleague about exhibit placement.
I would adjust page breaks to keep each speaker’s turn together.
I would preserve the recording order and use the nearest available template.

basic.situation: After a court session, you have shorthand notes to file in the designated case folder with several similar case names.

options.text: I would place the notes in the shared pending folder for later sorting.
I would check the case list and file the notes in the matching folder.
I would match the case identifier, label the notes, and file them in its folder.
I would file the notes under the case name that looks most familiar.

advanced.situation: Several case files include sensitive transcripts and shorthand notes, and your office is revising its storage workflow.

options.text: Sort files by case number, then place them in the assigned storage area.
I would group files by hearing date for quick retrieval.
I would separate transcripts from notes and store them together by case.
I would map access by case and follow the office retention process.

basic.situation: You are proofreading a short transcript and spot a surname that may be misspelled in the typed copy.

options.text: I would use the more familiar spelling to keep the transcript readable.
I would compare the surname with the recording or source record before editing.
I would flag the surname and ask a colleague to check the source record.
I would check the spelling against the case list before changing it.

advanced.situation: A draft transcript differs from the original proceeding record on a ruling, and the discrepancy could affect a party’s next filing.

options.text: I would compare the ruling passage against the record and flag discrepancies.
I would edit the ruling to match the draft discussion.
I would check the transcript against the record and note the difference.
I would mark the difference and alert the responsible court contact for review.

basic.situation: During a hearing, you cannot hear a witness’s final word clearly while preparing the verbatim record.

options.text: I would mark the word as unclear and alert the appropriate court contact.
I would ask the speaker to repeat the word through the court’s process.
I would check my notes and request clarification if the word remains unclear.
I would enter a likely word from context and continue recording.

advanced.situation: A lawyer asks during a hearing for an earlier passage, while the judge is speaking and the recording continues.

options.text: I would note the request and wait for a brief pause before responding.
I would acknowledge the request and keep listening to the judge.
I would keep the record clear and respond when the court directs.
I would read the earlier passage while the judge continues speaking.

basic.situation: A lawyer requests a transcript of a completed proceeding, and you find the file in the office system.

options.text: I would send the file to the email address in the request.
I would check the requester’s identity and prepare the transcript for approved release.
I would ask the requester to confirm the case number before sending.
I would confirm request details and provide the transcript through office channels.

advanced.situation: Several legal parties request transcripts from different sessions, and exhibits from those proceedings also need to be logged and stored.

options.text: I would list the requests by party and prepare each transcript in turn.
I would store the exhibits by date and keep transcript requests in a separate list.
I would log each request by case and session, then track each exhibit to storage.
I would send the most recent transcript first and sort the exhibits afterward.

basic.situation: During a studio segment, the senior cues you to switch from the wide camera to the presenter close-up.

options.text: Switch to the close-up as soon as the presenter moves.
Check the tally light, then switch on the senior's cue.
Hold the wide shot while checking the cue sheet again.
Follow the senior's cue and confirm the close-up tally.

advanced.situation: You plan a three-camera interview with a remote feed, and a junior operator is unfamiliar with the switching sequence.

options.text: Give the junior a cue sheet and explain the source order.
Let the junior follow the rehearsal and learn during transmission.
Use the usual camera order and ask the junior to watch your hands.
Map each source, cue, and fallback, then rehearse the handoffs together.

basic.situation: A producer asks you to record a short interview in a quiet room using the standard recorder and microphone.

options.text: Start recording at the default setting to save setup time.
Check the microphone connection and record a short sample first.
Record a quick test, check its playback, then capture the interview.
Set the microphone nearby and record at the default level.

advanced.situation: A client needs a clean dialogue edit by afternoon, but the room tone varies and several breaths sit close to the speech.

options.text: Compare dialogue with room tone, then edit breaths while preserving natural phrasing.
Mark noisy sections and ask the editor to smooth them later.
Remove every pause and breath to make the dialogue move faster.
Reduce the noise across the track and review the dialogue once.

basic.situation: At a community hall concert intermission, you are assigned to restore the stage lights and check the house sound against a checklist.

options.text: Raise the stage lights to full and leave sound unchanged.
Bring up the stage wash and check the house level against the list.
Restore the listed light level and listen for clear house audio.
Adjust the lighting first, then ask a colleague about the sound.

advanced.situation: A concert has a quiet opening, a sudden blackout, and a spoken announcement; you are drafting cues and coaching a new technician.

options.text: Write timed light and sound cues, then rehearse the blackout recovery together.
Ask the new technician to watch the console during rehearsal.
Mark the main transitions and explain them before doors open.
Use last month's cue sheet and let the new technician follow it.

basic.situation: A microphone has dust on its grille after a rehearsal, and your supervisor has asked you to clean it and inspect its cable.

options.text: Use a damp cloth on the grille and put the microphone away.
Wipe the grille gently and inspect the cable before storage.
Brush the grille and coil the cable for the next session.
Inspect the cable and clean the grille with a dry cloth.

advanced.situation: Several rooms share aging audio gear, and recurring faults are disrupting bookings; you are asked to propose upgrades and preventive checks.

options.text: Ask technicians which devices cause trouble and draft an upgrade list.
Compare fault records, room needs, and maintenance costs before proposing phased upgrades.
List recurring faults and suggest replacing every aging device this quarter.
Replace the most complained-about units and add a monthly cleaning reminder.

basic.situation: You must compress a finished interview clip with the supplied software template and store it in the project folder.

options.text: Compress the clip with the supplied template, then save a separate copy in its project folder.
Save the source and compressed clip together under one shared filename in the project folder.
Apply the template and compress the clip, saving over the original source file.
Use the template, inspect the output, then save it in the project folder.

advanced.situation: Your team stores clips for several productions, and staff have used inconsistent filenames and compression settings that make retrieval difficult.

options.text: Rename the current files and ask the team to follow your example.
Tell staff to use shorter filenames and the existing preset.
Set naming and compression rules, then demonstrate a sample folder workflow.
Move all clips into one folder and let staff choose settings.

basic.situation: During a presentation equipment training session, a projector repeatedly loses its image, and the facilitator asks you to alert the supervisor.

options.text: Let the facilitator know and carry on with the next topic.
Tell the group to keep reconnecting the projector until it works.
Notify the supervisor with the fault and affected equipment details.
Report the image loss to the supervisor after noting when it happens.

advanced.situation: You are coordinating assistants for a live presentation and training a new operator; a major audio fault appears during the speaker's introduction.

options.text: Have the new operator replace the cables while you continue the speaker's introduction.
Ask an assistant to alert the supervisor while you check and retrieve the spare microphone.
Have one assistant alert the supervisor and another fetch a spare microphone.
Keep the presentation moving while the new operator watches the fault response.

basic.situation: You monitor an incoming studio feed and notice its picture breaking up while the audio remains clear.

options.text: Ask the senior technician to inspect the picture before you act.
Note the breakup and adjust the receiver slightly while watching.
Turn up the signal control until the picture looks steady.
Check the source and signal readings before adjusting the feed.

advanced.situation: A station needs a modified equipment layout for a new incoming feed, and you are asked to propose changes within the station's specifications.

options.text: Change the input path and test the feed against the required specification.
Review the equipment manual and draft a change list for the engineer.
Use the nearest spare input and adjust gain until levels match.
Draw the signal path, compare equipment limits, then test a proposed configuration.

basic.situation: You are setting up a broadcast computer for an automated programme under a senior technician's checklist.

options.text: Set up the listed devices and check that the automation screen opens.
Follow the checklist and ask the senior to confirm each cable.
Connect the listed devices and test playback using the scheduled item.
Connect the computer and start playback with the first queued item.

advanced.situation: A broadcast computer loses access to the shared programme folder before a scheduled recording, and you are responsible for initial troubleshooting.

options.text: Save the schedule and ask the senior to inspect the network.
Check network access and folder permissions, then test a small recording.
Restart the computer and try recording from a local copy.
Change shared-folder settings until the recording system reconnects.

basic.situation: Before a scheduled bulletin, you preview the programme and see video on the monitor but hear no audio.

options.text: Start the bulletin and wait for the studio to notice the audio.
Replay the opening and ask a colleague whether audio is present.
Check the monitor volume and tell the producer what you hear.
Confirm the audio path and alert station staff before transmission.

advanced.situation: A live programme has several scheduled sources, and recent previews missed a silent opening; you are drafting a readiness check for the team.

options.text: List source, audio, and video checks, then test the sequence in rehearsal.
Rely on the programme slate and start on the scheduled minute.
Add an audio check to the existing preview checklist.
Ask each operator to inspect their own monitor before airtime.

basic.situation: Your shift checklist asks you to log transmitter readings, but one displayed reading changes while you are recording it.

options.text: Write down the earlier reading to finish the log faster.
Ask the next shift to confirm the reading before logging it.
Record the reading with its displayed time and recheck the value.
Wait for the reading to settle and enter the stable value.

advanced.situation: You are reviewing programming logs and transmitter readings before handover, and find several entries with missing times and unclear programme labels.

options.text: Fill gaps from memory and brief the next operator on your changes.
Flag missing times and ask staff to clarify their entries.
Mark unclear entries, compare source records, and brief staff on the pattern.
File the logs as received and mention the gaps at handover.

basic.situation: During a radio segment, the guest's voice becomes quieter than the host, and you are assisting with the audio controls.

options.text: Adjust the guest fader and check the meter with the senior.
Raise the guest channel slightly while monitoring both voices.
Ask the host to speak louder while you watch the meters.
Turn up the master volume so the guest is easier to hear.

advanced.situation: A live panel has guests at different microphone distances, and a new technician is handling the console during overlapping discussion.

options.text: Set a common fader position and let the technician manage the panel.
Raise all guest channels and lower the host to balance the panel.
Set channel targets, coach the new technician through overlap, and monitor the mix.
Show the technician the meters and ask them to keep levels even.

basic.situation: A studio monitor stops working during your shift, and a brief cable check does not restore sound.

options.text: Tell your supervisor the monitor is silent and ask how to arrange a repair.
Report the fault and monitor, then follow the studio repair process.
Keep testing the cable, then report whether the monitor produces any sound.
Connect a spare monitor, then label the faulty unit for the repair team.

advanced.situation: A transmitter room alarm appears during a shift, and the backup unit is available; you are trained for basic emergency checks.

options.text: Switch to backup under procedure and record the alarm for repair staff.
Switch to backup and silence the alarm before checking the display.
Check the alarm display and approved connections, then report the result.
Notify the supervisor and wait for instructions before touching equipment.

basic.situation: You are preparing a small interview room, and the guest arrives while you are choosing a microphone.

options.text: I would use the nearest microphone and turn up its gain to save time.
I would choose a handheld microphone and ask the engineer to check placement.
I would place the available microphone near the guest and listen for noise.
I would match a suitable microphone to the speaker, place it, then test levels.

advanced.situation: A hall recording needs separate speech, music, and audience channels, but the stage plan has changed and setup time is short.

options.text: I would revise the input list and run a brief check with the stage team.
I would follow the old channel list and adjust levels during the opening remarks.
I would map each source to a microphone and channel, then test separation and backup paths.
I would connect the main microphones first and leave spare channels for later.

basic.situation: During a recorded interview, the guest speaks more softly after the opening question, and the meter begins to fall.

options.text: I would ask the engineer to check the microphone while I monitor the meter.
I would add a little gain and listen for any background noise.
I would raise the master fader to bring the quieter reply back up.
I would raise the channel level slightly and watch the meter through the reply.

advanced.situation: At a live panel, two speakers, playback, and audience questions share the console; one microphone begins feeding back as the room fills.

options.text: I would mute the problem channel, identify its speaker, and adjust its gain and position.
I would reduce that channel and make a quick EQ adjustment while checking speech.
I would lower the microphone slightly and keep playback at its current level.
I would lower the master output until the feedback stops across the room.

basic.situation: You are combining a narrator and a music bed for a short training video, and the voice is hard to hear.

options.text: I would lower the music track and listen again to the narrator over it.
I would raise both tracks so the finished mix sounds fuller on speakers.
I would add more bass to the music and ask someone nearby to listen.
I would raise the narrator and lower the music a little on the board.

advanced.situation: A client review reveals that a dense scene has masked dialogue, and the export deadline leaves little time for mix changes.

options.text: I would boost the full mix and export the revised scene before the deadline.
I would lower the effects under dialogue and check a representative passage.
I would rebalance the dialogue and effects in context, then review the loudest passage.
I would reduce the music track and export a quick comparison for the client.

basic.situation: You are editing a short interview clip, and the recorded answer appears slightly out of sync with the speaker's mouth.

options.text: I would align the answer to the visible speech, then replay the edited section.
I would nudge the answer clip and check sync at the next sentence.
I would trim a few frames from the answer and watch the ending again.
I would shift the whole audio track until the opening looks aligned.

advanced.situation: A film scene has dialogue, music, and effects on separate tracks; a late picture edit changes several cuts before the delivery check.

options.text: I would shift all tracks together to match the first changed cut.
I would compare each changed cut against picture, then check sync across the scene.
I would replay the scene once and adjust the track that feels late.
I would check dialogue at key cuts and review the music against the picture.

basic.situation: A colleague gives you one audio recording to convert for editing and asks you to preserve the original.

options.text: I would duplicate the source, convert the copy, and tell editing where it is.
I would convert the source file directly and send that version to editing.
I would make a digital copy in the requested format and check that it opens.
I would save a second copy with a similar name and convert it for editing.

advanced.situation: You are converting a large archive of event recordings, and several source files have inconsistent names and unknown formats.

options.text: I would sample several files, choose a suitable format, and log the results.
I would rename unfamiliar files by date and convert them in smaller batches.
I would batch convert every file using the format from the first recording.
I would inventory the sources, test sample conversions, and record each output format.

basic.situation: A speaker's microphone cuts out during rehearsal, and the producer asks whether the sound can be ready for recording.

options.text: I would replace it with a spare microphone and resume the rehearsal.
I would note the dropout, test its cable, and report findings to the engineer.
I would tell the engineer about the dropout and request a setup check.
I would reseat the cable, then monitor the speaker through another rehearsal section.

advanced.situation: A concert soundcheck starts late after a console fault, while the producer and performers are still clarifying their preferred monitor mix.

options.text: I would log the fault, share soundcheck time, and confirm monitor priorities with performers.
I would ask performers for their priority monitor needs before restarting soundcheck.
I would keep troubleshooting the console and update the producer on the delay.
I would confirm key monitor requests and report the console fault to the producer.

basic.situation: You are checking a venue before setup and notice a cable crossing a damp walkway near the lighting position.

options.text: I would cover the cable with a mat and continue unloading the fixtures.
I would flag the cable route, keep people clear, and tell the site lead.
I would tell the site lead about the cable and ask for a safer route.
I would move the nearest case away and check whether the floor is dry.

advanced.situation: A venue walk-through reveals that the planned lighting position is beside an unfamiliar overhead structure and a crowded power route.

options.text: I would note the structure and power route, then brief the site lead.
I would inspect the power route and ask the site lead about overhead support.
I would use the planned position and ask crew to monitor overhead clearance.
I would move cases aside and check the power route before rigging.

basic.situation: A theatre cue needs a blue filter on one fixture, and the stage manager asks you to focus it on a doorway.

options.text: I would change the filter and adjust the beam until it covers the doorway.
I would fit the blue filter and aim the fixture while a colleague checks the doorway.
I would fit the blue filter, aim the fixture, and check the doorway from the stage.
I would point the fixture toward the doorway and leave its current filter in place.

advanced.situation: A concert plan adds fixtures above a narrow stage, and the crew must use scaffolding while keeping sightlines clear.

options.text: I would set the scaffolding near the stage edge and move fixtures around it.
I would place the fixtures where the old plan shows and adjust them during rehearsal.
I would check the sightlines and mark fixture positions for the crew to review.
I would review access and sightlines, then coordinate fixture positions with the rigging lead.

basic.situation: After a small theatre performance, you and a colleague are packing lighting cases into the store room.

options.text: I would stack cases by the door to clear the room quickly.
I would move heavy cases first, then gather small accessories for storage.
I would pack fixtures carefully and label cases with any missing parts.
I would coil loose leads, secure fixtures, and return cases to marked storage places.

advanced.situation: A touring production is loading out after the final show, and the next venue needs a clear equipment count before departure.

options.text: I would check cases against the load list, note shortages, and secure them by destination.
I would count the cases as they load and tell the crew about any mismatch.
I would load the cases in the usual order and count them at the next venue.
I would group cases by destination and ask the driver to confirm the load.

basic.situation: You are connecting one stage light to a dimmer, and the patch sheet identifies its assigned console channel.

options.text: I would connect the nearest dimmer and raise its fader to check output.
I would connect the listed dimmer and check for console response.
I would connect cable, patch its channel, and test the light at low output.
I would follow the patch sheet and ask a colleague to test output.

advanced.situation: Several fixtures on a large rig respond to the wrong console controls after a patch change, and rehearsal begins soon.

options.text: I would compare the console patch with the fixture labels and flag mismatches.
I would test the first affected fixture and copy its patch to the others.
I would compare the patch with fixture labels, isolate affected lines, then test each response.
I would repatch the affected fixtures to nearby channels and start rehearsal.

basic.situation: A rehearsal is about to start, and you need to load a prepared lighting cue onto the console for one scene.

options.text: I would open the cue and compare its title with the rehearsal sheet.
I would load the cue, check its fixture labels, and run it once with the operator.
I would load the cue and save over the previous scene file to keep things tidy.
I would load the cue and confirm its playback with the operator before rehearsal.

advanced.situation: A production adds automated movement cues to a revised sequence, and a relief operator will run the console during the show.

options.text: I would revise the sequence and run it with the relief operator before doors.
I would add the movement cues and check their timing from the console screen.
I would update the sequence, test transitions with the operator, and label the revised cues.
I would reuse the earlier sequence and tell the relief operator to follow the timing.

basic.situation: During a lighting check, one fixture fails to light and you find its lamp has burned out.

options.text: I would isolate the fixture, replace its lamp as trained, and test the output.
I would swap in a spare fixture and leave the failed one in the active rig.
I would notify the supervisor and use another fixture for the lighting check.
I would replace the lamp with the supervisor present and report the fixture status.

advanced.situation: Several fixtures show intermittent output during a technical rehearsal, and the lighting director needs the planned color and brightness maintained.

options.text: I would raise console brightness to mask the dropout and keep checking the fixtures.
I would report the intermittent output and ask the supervisor to arrange repairs.
I would test affected fixtures, record patterns, and tell the supervisor about repairs.
I would match fixture colors to the plan and watch for another dropout.

basic.situation: You are photographing a child indoors, and the first frame is blurred as they move. You need a clear portrait with some background detail.

options.text: I would open the aperture, then track autofocus across the child's face as they move.
I would match exposure from a similar indoor portrait before checking the result.
I would raise ISO slightly, then check focus on the moving child's face.
I would meter the scene, balancing shutter speed and aperture for motion and depth.

advanced.situation: You are guiding a colleague through a dim stage shoot where performers move quickly and the background must remain visible.

options.text: I would set a fast shutter and wide aperture for the moving performers.
I would demonstrate metering, then coach them to balance shutter, aperture, and ISO.
I would raise the ISO and ask the colleague to try a faster shutter.
I would keep the current settings and suggest they steady the camera between frames.

basic.situation: You are setting up a small family portrait, and the flash leaves harsh shadows on one side of the faces.

options.text: I would place the flash off-axis and use a reflector to balance shadows.
I would test a softer flash angle, then adjust the reflector after one frame.
I would point the flash straight at the group for even coverage.
I would angle a reflector toward the faces and soften the flash.

advanced.situation: You are assembling lighting for a product shoot with reflective packaging, a tight schedule, and a background that must stay evenly lit.

options.text: I would keep the existing lights and angle the product away from glare.
I would add a large softbox and move it until glare decreases.
I would use a diffuser and lower the flash power for softer reflections.
I would map the product and background lights, then test reflections before final placement.

basic.situation: You are checking a camera kit before a client portrait session, and the checklist calls for testing the flash and lens.

options.text: I would check the lens and flash against the checklist before packing.
I would test the flash and take a frame through the lens.
I would inspect the lens, then ask another photographer about the flash.
I would power on the camera and pack the kit for the session.

advanced.situation: You are helping maintain a shared camera kit after several shoots, and teammates report recurring loose connections and inconsistent battery checks.

options.text: I would set a shared checklist for cleaning, connection checks, and battery rotation.
I would replace the batteries and tape loose cables before the next booking.
I would remind the team to check batteries and connections after each shoot.
I would clean the contacts and record any loose connections for later review.

basic.situation: You are preparing a small set of event portraits, and the client asks for resized copies with a few minor blemishes retouched.

options.text: I would retouch the blemishes first and export copies at the requested size.
I would resize the whole folder and send the files for client selection.
I would select the clearest portraits, then resize and retouch the requested copies.
I would resize the selected portraits and retouch visible blemishes carefully.

advanced.situation: You are asked to train two colleagues on a new retouching workflow for a large portrait set with consistent colour and sizing requirements.

options.text: I would document the workflow, demonstrate a sample, and compare exports against the requirements.
I would ask each colleague to retouch a few portraits in their usual style.
I would edit one portrait and have the colleagues follow its settings.
I would share my preferred presets and let each colleague edit a sample.

basic.situation: You are mounting a finished portrait for a customer, and the print must sit straight inside a simple frame.

options.text: I would align one edge and ask the customer to review the frame.
I would centre the print, check its alignment, and secure the mount.
I would place the print by eye and close the frame for collection.
I would line up the print, then press the mount into place.

advanced.situation: You are finishing portraits for a premium order, and the prints will be mounted, framed, and archived for later reprints.

options.text: I would frame the prints quickly and keep the camera cards for reprints.
I would choose a clean frame and scan the prints before mounting them.
I would compare suitable mounts and frames, check each finish, and archive the image files.
I would use the usual mount and frame, then save scans of the finished prints.

basic.situation: You are helping a family plan a short studio portrait session, but they have not decided which group combinations they need.

options.text: I would suggest a standard group pose and book the usual session length.
I would reserve the studio and let the family choose poses on arrival.
I would ask who should appear together and note their preferred portrait style.
I would show a few sample poses and ask which ones they prefer.

advanced.situation: You are coordinating a location portrait project with several workers, changing light, and a client who has added group images to the brief.

options.text: I would revise the shot list and assign setup tasks around the light window.
I would add the group images to the list and keep the existing crew plan.
I would ask the client to rank the images and then update the schedule.
I would tell the crew to follow the original plan and fit groups in later.

basic.situation: You are recording a short interview on a standard video camera, and the speaker shifts position during the take.

options.text: I would leave the camera fixed and let the speaker move across frame.
I would zoom in quickly whenever the speaker moves away from centre.
I would follow the speaker with a measured zoom during the take.
I would reframe with a gentle pan and hold a steady medium shot.

advanced.situation: You are operating a track-mounted camera for a moving scene, but an actor's pace changes near the end of the planned move.

options.text: I would increase the track speed to catch up with the actor.
I would shorten the move and stop the camera before the actor reaches the mark.
I would hold the planned track speed and let the actor reach the mark.
I would rehearse the altered pace and adjust the track move to keep framing smooth.

basic.situation: You are framing a simple interview in a bright room, and a window behind the guest makes the face appear dark.

options.text: I would reframe away from the window and review exposure on a test shot.
I would tighten the shot and check whether the face remains visible.
I would keep the window behind the guest for a neat interview frame.
I would shift the frame from the window and check the guest's face.

advanced.situation: You are checking a location before filming, and passing vehicles create noise while afternoon sun crosses the planned frame.

options.text: I would inspect the frame at filming time and flag changing noise and sunlight.
I would note sun direction and check vehicle noise with the sound crew.
I would suggest a tighter angle to reduce traffic in the frame.
I would keep the location and let the crew adapt during filming.

basic.situation: You are positioning a camera for a seated interview, and the subject's face looks soft in the monitor.

options.text: I would widen the frame and leave the current focus setting in place.
I would refocus on the face, then check sharpness in the monitor.
I would adjust focus on the subject's eyes and check the monitor again.
I would turn the focus ring slightly and continue with the interview.

advanced.situation: You are setting exposure for a studio scene with bright windows and a darker foreground, and the test image loses detail in faces.

options.text: I would reduce exposure slightly, then review a fresh test image.
I would lower exposure and check whether faces and windows retain detail.
I would keep exposure and ask the subject to turn toward the window.
I would check exposure, adjust for faces, and review window detail in another test.

basic.situation: You are preparing a simple live stand-up shot outside a venue, and the reporter's microphone level is still being checked.

options.text: I would ask the reporter to speak louder as I adjust the frame.
I would frame the reporter and confirm the picture with control room.
I would begin the live shot while the sound check continues.
I would set the frame, check microphone signal, and confirm readiness with control room.

advanced.situation: You are setting up a live outdoor report as rain begins, and the scheduled start is close while the camera position is exposed.

options.text: I would keep the camera in place and shorten the report if rain worsens.
I would alert the control room and shift to a covered position before going live.
I would cover the camera and keep the planned position for the report.
I would move the camera under cover and check the live picture and sound again.

basic.situation: You are checking a camera kit before a short shoot, and the lens has fingerprints while the microphone has not been tested.

options.text: I would wipe the lens and pack the kit for the shoot.
I would pack the camera and use the microphone from the last shoot.
I would clean the lens and test the microphone before packing.
I would test the microphone and check the lens under the room light.

advanced.situation: You are diagnosing a broadcast camera that intermittently loses its microphone signal during a rehearsal, while another camera is available.

options.text: I would reset the camera settings and continue with the current microphone.
I would test the microphone path and connections, then document the fault before repair.
I would swap the microphone and send the faulty camera for repair.
I would use the spare camera for rehearsal and note when the signal drops.

basic.situation: You are discussing a short filming sequence with the director and sound crew, and their instructions place a microphone stand in the camera frame.

options.text: I would ask sound crew to move the stand after filming this take.
I would keep filming and ask the editor to crop out the stand later.
I would flag the visible stand and ask the director what to do.
I would coordinate with the director and sound crew before moving the stand.

advanced.situation: You are conferring with the director and lighting crew about a scene change, and the planned camera move conflicts with their reset timing.

options.text: I would suggest a shorter camera move to give lighting more reset time.
I would coordinate move timing with both crews and agree on a sequence.
I would run the planned move as lighting resets around the camera.
I would ask the director to keep the move and shorten lighting reset time.

basic.situation: The director's notes mark three usable takes for a short scene. You need to join the footage into a continuous sequence.

options.text: I follow the director's notes, then join the marked takes in script order.
I place the first usable takes together and leave uncertain shots for later.
I match each take to the notes and preserve scene continuity in order.
I group clips by scene and choose clear takes when notes are vague.

advanced.situation: Two junior editors have assembled overlapping camera angles for a scene, but their timelines differ. You need to guide them toward a coherent cut.

options.text: I teach cue syncing and have juniors check cross-angle continuity.
I use the earliest complete timeline and ask juniors to patch missing angles.
I assign scene ranges and compare the juniors' cuts against the director's notes.
I let each junior assemble a camera angle, then combine their timelines.

basic.situation: A dialogue scene has two camera angles, and the director marks where the view should change. You need to make the cuts feel smooth.

options.text: I cut at the marked lines and check how each angle change feels.
I hold the first angle through the exchange, then use the marked change.
I switch angles whenever the speaker changes to keep the scene moving.
I match each marked cut to action and check the transition in playback.

advanced.situation: A scene intercuts two timelines, and the director wants viewers to follow both without losing the emotional thread. You need to set cutting guidance.

options.text: I place the most dramatic shots first and let the sequence reveal context later.
I alternate the timelines at regular intervals so viewers can track both.
I define transitions around story cues and review whether each timeline remains clear.
I select the strongest shots and arrange them to keep the story understandable.

basic.situation: A short scene has dialogue and a music cue, but the cue masks a quiet line. You need to integrate the tracks into the edit.

options.text: I mute the music for the full scene and leave the dialogue as recorded.
I keep the music at its current level and raise the dialogue track.
I balance the cue under dialogue and replay the scene to check both tracks.
I place the dialogue and music, then lower the cue around the quiet line.

advanced.situation: A sequence needs new sound effects while the visual team changes shot timing. You are coordinating the edit across both teams.

options.text: I lock the sound effects to the current cut and let the picture team adapt.
I review the sound and picture versions together before passing on comments.
I ask both teams to send updates when their parts are ready.
I align effect cues to agreed picture points and share timing changes with both teams.

basic.situation: You are starting an edit on a shared workstation and have setup instructions for the project. You need to prepare the editing system.

options.text: I follow the setup notes and confirm the project opens before editing.
I change the display and playback settings until the timeline feels responsive.
I open the project with the workstation's existing settings and begin sorting clips.
I follow the setup notes and check the project settings before loading media.

advanced.situation: Several editors will use the same system for a project with titling and effects. You need to configure the setup for team use.

options.text: I document shared project settings and check that titling and effects work for each editor.
I let each editor set preferences before they begin their assigned scenes.
I set the project format and ask the team to report any setup problems.
I use one editor's saved setup and apply it to every workstation.

basic.situation: The export checklist asks you to verify a shot number and time code before delivery. You notice one entry differs from the edit notes.

options.text: I verify the shot and time code against source material, then update the checklist.
I check the nearby entries and use their numbering pattern to fill the gap.
I compare the entry with the edit notes and mark the discrepancy for checking.
I use the export list's value so the checklist can be completed on time.
