advanced.situation: A final review found inconsistent checks across several edits. You need to establish a review process the team can use before delivery.

options.text: I rely on the editor who finished last to catch any remaining issues.
I prepare one checklist of common export issues for the team to use.
I ask editors to watch their own exports and send any issues they notice.
I set shared review points for picture, sound, and time codes, with clear sign-off notes.

basic.situation: You receive a script with several locations and effects cues before editing starts. You need to understand the production requirements.

options.text: I read the script and note the locations and effects that shape the edit.
I read the script for locations, cues, and scene links before arranging the footage.
I start with the first scene and work out production needs as they arise.
I use the scene list as the edit order and leave effects for the finishing stage.

advanced.situation: The team is behind schedule, and a revised graphic cue affects several scenes. You need to coordinate the editing work and program the effect.

options.text: I map the cue across affected scenes, assign editing tasks, and review timing with the team.
I program the cue for the first scene and ask editors to copy it elsewhere.
I divide the remaining scenes among editors and let them adjust the graphic cue.
I list unfinished scenes, assign owners, and check progress at the next review.

basic.situation: A new patient mentions back pain and takes several medicines. You need to record their medical history before the appointment.

options.text: I record the patient's account, then confirm dates, medicines, and changes aloud.
I reuse the previous intake form and update its date during registration.
I follow the intake prompts and note the patient's main concern and medicines.
I ask about current symptoms, past conditions, medicines, and relevant treatment history.

advanced.situation: A junior staff member records a patient's medication and symptom history, but dates are unclear. You need to guide accurate history recording.

options.text: I copy the prior visit's medication list into the new record to save time.
I tell the junior to use the intake form and keep the interview moving.
I show the junior how to ask about dates, changes, and current medicines.
I review the entry, clarify unclear dates, and ask the patient to confirm them.

basic.situation: A patient reports stiffness when turning their neck. You need to assess movement and related physical findings during the examination.

options.text: I complete the guided checks and compare both sides for movement and tenderness.
I base the assessment on the patient's most painful movement and record that result.
I assess movement, strength, and symptom patterns before documenting the clinical picture.
I focus on the sore area and record the movement that feels most limited.

advanced.situation: A patient has recurring back stiffness and reduced movement on one side. You need to assess the neuromusculoskeletal findings consistently.

options.text: I repeat the most limited movement and use that result to describe the case.
I compare posture, movement, and symptoms, then record findings by body area.
I assess related movement and symptom patterns, then document how findings fit together.
I focus on the reduced side and use its movement to guide the assessment.

basic.situation: A patient's history and x-ray are available, and the reported pain does not match the first image finding. You need to interpret the information.

options.text: I compare the image with the symptoms and note where the findings do not align.
I ask more about the pain and use the image as supporting context.
I review the history and image together, then document findings that need clarification.
I treat the first image finding as the cause and document that conclusion.

advanced.situation: A patient's symptoms have changed, and the available x-ray does not clearly explain them. You need to interpret the findings and consider serious causes.

options.text: I focus on the x-ray report and record its main finding for the case.
I review the history and image, then note concerns that need further assessment.
I use the familiar image finding to explain the new symptoms in my notes.
I compare the symptom pattern and image for concerning findings before documenting my assessment.

basic.situation: A patient's symptoms need further imaging before you can complete your assessment. You need to arrange an appropriate diagnostic procedure.

options.text: I discuss the imaging need with the patient and arrange the indicated procedure.
I select a familiar scan and send the patient for the earliest available appointment.
I clarify the clinical question, then arrange suitable imaging and share the next steps.
I ask the patient which imaging centre is easiest for them to reach.

advanced.situation: A patient's findings call for input from another health practitioner and possible tests. You need to coordinate the referral and diagnostic needs.

options.text: I summarize the findings, state the clinical question, and coordinate relevant tests with the practitioner.
I order several available tests so the referral includes a broad set of results.
I share the patient's findings and arrange the test that seems most relevant.
I refer the patient and let the receiving practitioner choose any needed tests.

basic.situation: A patient is scheduled for a simple manual adjustment and reports mild discomfort during positioning. You need to apply the planned technique safely.

options.text: I continue with the adjustment at the planned force and finish the appointment.
I use the planned adjustment and check how the patient responds during positioning.
I reduce the force and complete the same adjustment as scheduled.
I pause, clarify the discomfort, and adjust the technique to the patient's response.

advanced.situation: A patient is uneasy about a support strap after an adjustment, though it may help with comfort. You need to decide how to apply it.

options.text: I explain the strap's purpose and check the fit with the patient.
I apply the strap as planned and review its fit at the next visit.
I ask what concerns the patient, then agree on a suitable support and fit.
I use the strap that worked for another patient with similar symptoms.

basic.situation: A patient asks how to manage stiffness between visits and mentions that poor sleep makes it worse. You need to offer relevant care advice.

options.text: I discuss manageable movement and sleep habits, then record the advice given.
I suggest resting more and mention sleep as a possible factor.
I ask about the patient's routine, agree on practical steps, and record the plan.
I recommend a routine that worked well for other patients with similar stiffness.

advanced.situation: A patient has ongoing discomfort and asks about changes to exercise, sleep, and stress. You need to counsel them and maintain an accurate case history.

options.text: I discuss exercise, sleep, and stress options, then update the case history.
I recommend cutting exercise and changing sleep habits to reduce discomfort quickly.
I review the patient's routine, agree on practical care steps, and record progress goals.
I note the concerns and repeat the same advice at the next appointment.

basic.situation: A patient reports sensitivity during a routine visit. You examine their teeth and gums with instruments and review the available x-rays under supervision.

options.text: Check the painful tooth with instruments and note the patient's symptoms for review.
Use the x-rays alone to mark the likely tooth and finish the chart.
Record the sensitive tooth and check nearby gums before summarising your findings.
Compare the x-rays with an instrument examination, then present the findings to your supervisor.

advanced.situation: Your clinic's monthly records show more patients with gum disease in one age group. You review the data before suggesting a protocol adjustment.

options.text: Ask the records clerk to verify age totals before sharing the monthly increase.
Review age trends across several months, relate them to findings, then propose a protocol adjustment.
Compare age-group figures across several months and check whether the increase persists.
Share the increase after reviewing this month's figures against earlier clinic records.

basic.situation: During a guided root canal, the supervisor asks you to fill the prepared canal with endodontic material. The patient is waiting for the next step.

options.text: Place the material to the depth you estimate from the preparation.
Confirm the prepared length, then fill the canal as your supervisor directs.
Ask your supervisor to recheck the length before you place the material.
Fill the canal and note any resistance for the supervisor to assess.

advanced.situation: A patient returns with persistent pain after root canal treatment, and the x-ray suggests a narrow canal. You are asked to plan the next treatment steps.

options.text: Ask a colleague to review the x-ray and discuss options before choosing treatment.
Review canal findings and choose an approach suited to the patient's anatomy.
Repeat the earlier technique, then reassess the filling if pain continues.
Assess canal anatomy, select an endodontic approach, and brief the assistant on handling points.

basic.situation: A patient needs a simple extraction and is anxious about pain. You are asked to administer local anesthetic while your supervisor is available.

options.text: Use the planned dose and begin once the patient says they feel numb.
Administer the planned anaesthetic and ask the patient whether it feels numb.
Inject at the usual site and start when the patient appears relaxed.
Explain the injection, administer the planned anaesthetic, and test numbness before starting.

advanced.situation: A complex oral surgery is scheduled, and the patient has a history of fainting during injections. You review the anaesthesia plan and clinic safety steps.

options.text: Ask the patient to wait while you check the clinic's usual protocol.
Adapt the monitoring and positioning plan to the history, and brief the team before anaesthesia.
Review the history and planned anaesthetic, then flag the fainting risk to the team.
Keep the standard plan and ask the patient to report feeling faint.

basic.situation: A child with newly erupted molars is due for sealants. You prepare the teeth and apply the sealant with step-by-step guidance.

options.text: Prepare the molars and ask the supervisor to apply the sealant.
Place sealant over the molars quickly before the child becomes restless.
Check each prepared surface, apply sealant, and confirm coverage before finishing.
Apply sealant after drying each tooth as shown in the clinic guide.

advanced.situation: Several patients have missed follow-up after fluoride treatment. You are asked to propose a prevention workflow and show staff how to polish teeth safely.

options.text: Review polishing suitability, demonstrate safe steps, and discuss reminders with staff.
Discuss the patient's polishing request and check suitability before offering treatment.
Ask reception to send follow-up reminders and distribute polishing guidance to staff.
Use missed visits to refine reminders and set safe polishing guidance for staff.

basic.situation: A patient has a fractured filling and mild gum inflammation. You help prepare a basic treatment plan for the dentist to review.

options.text: Plan the filling repair and leave the gum issue for another visit.
Ask the dentist which issue to include before drafting the plan.
Link both findings in a sequenced plan and note follow-up review items.
List the filling repair and schedule a separate review for the gum inflammation.

advanced.situation: A community clinic sees many children with early tooth decay, and several need space maintainers. You help plan a dental health programme and appliance instructions.

options.text: Estimate children's needs across clinic visits, draft programme priorities, and coordinate appliance referrals.
Order suitable space maintainers for children identified during today's clinic session.
Review decay patterns across visits and specify appliance cases for fabrication review.
Ask the clinic lead to set priorities before preparing the appliance list.

basic.situation: A patient arrives with a cough for a dental examination. You prepare your mask and gloves before using instruments.

options.text: Put on a fresh mask, gloves, and safety glasses before preparing instruments.
Ask the patient to cover their cough while you put on gloves.
Wear gloves and a mask, then prepare the examination instruments.
Reuse your mask and gloves from the previous patient to save time.

advanced.situation: A safety audit finds inconsistent glove changes and patients confused about home care. You are asked to review the findings and coach the team.

options.text: Ask the clinic lead to discuss the audit at the next meeting.
Share the audit findings and remind staff to explain home care clearly.
Send the audit figures to the team and let each person adjust their routine.
Show the glove-change gaps, demonstrate a clear routine, and practise patient advice with staff.

basic.situation: A patient with an impacted wisdom tooth is prepared for removal. You assist the surgeon by setting out instruments and tracking the tooth's position.

options.text: Review the x-ray and arrange instruments for the planned tooth removal.
Set out the extraction tray and wait for the surgeon's next instruction.
Confirm the tooth position with the surgeon, then arrange the needed instruments.
Start separating the tooth while the surgeon prepares the next instrument.

advanced.situation: A patient needs an implant after bone loss near the upper jaw. You review the case and plan surgery to prepare the site and regenerate tissue.

options.text: Schedule the implant preparation from the referral note and standard graft plan.
Ask the referring dentist to clarify the bone loss before drafting a plan.
Review the imaging and outline the grafting needs for the implant site.
Relate imaging to bone and gum deficits, then map the preparation and regeneration stages.

basic.situation: A patient presents with a small painful mouth ulcer and no other symptoms. You assess it and help plan treatment for the oral mucosa problem.

options.text: Describe the ulcer, check nearby oral tissue, and discuss care with the surgeon.
Consider symptoms and discuss a suitable mouth rinse with the patient.
Note the ulcer's location and appearance, and ask when the discomfort began.
Ask whether symptoms persist and arrange a suitable follow-up visit with the clinic.

advanced.situation: A patient has recurring mouth lesions and swelling near a salivary gland. You review the findings and help manage the complex oral disease case.

options.text: Compare lesion history with gland findings and develop a targeted review and treatment plan.
Document lesions and swelling, then arrange a focused review visit with the patient.
Treat the swelling as a simple infection and continue the previous care approach.
Ask the patient to track symptoms and bring notes to the next visit.

basic.situation: A child is scheduled for cleft palate repair. You assist the surgeon by preparing the instruments and supporting the planned surgical steps.

options.text: Prepare the general tray and wait for the surgeon to choose instruments.
Check the child's planned repair, then arrange instruments for each surgical stage.
Begin the first repair step while the surgeon reviews the chart.
Arrange the palate instruments and confirm the sequence with the surgeon.

advanced.situation: A patient needs jaw reconstruction after major tissue loss. You plan a transfer of bone and other tissue to restore facial form and function.

options.text: Ask the surgical team to select tissues before you outline the case.
Review the defect and list tissue options for the upcoming reconstruction meeting.
Match tissue choices to the defect and map support for facial form and function.
Choose a familiar tissue transfer and set the operation sequence from that.

basic.situation: A patient asks about a minor chin enhancement. You assist by preparing the treatment area and checking the planned procedure with the surgeon.

options.text: Set out the cosmetic tray and wait for the surgeon's final instructions.
Prepare chin materials from the booking note and begin when the patient arrives.
Prepare the treatment area and review the planned enhancement with the surgeon.
Confirm the requested chin area, then prepare the materials for the planned enhancement.

advanced.situation: Staff have varied approaches to facial rejuvenation with laser procedures. You help set practice standards and coach colleagues on safe patient assessment.

options.text: Let each clinician use a familiar rejuvenation method without shared review.
Set shared assessment points and coach staff through sample rejuvenation cases.
Share the clinic guide and invite staff to discuss laser questions.
Ask staff to read the laser guidance before their next clinic session.

basic.situation: A patient needs a local anaesthetic before a minor procedure. You administer it under direct supervision and check the patient's response.

options.text: Inject at the familiar site and begin once the patient settles.
Ask the supervisor to confirm the site before you prepare the injection.
Use the planned injection site and ask whether the area feels numb.
Give the planned anaesthetic and test the area before the procedure starts.

advanced.situation: A patient with several health concerns needs complex surgery, and imaging shows impacted wisdom teeth near important structures. You review anaesthesia and tooth position.

options.text: Link health history and imaging to anaesthesia, then brief juniors on risks.
Use the routine anaesthesia plan and note impacted wisdom teeth for surgery.
Review imaging, note nerve proximity and anaesthesia concerns, then brief the team.
Ask a senior to review the anaesthesia plan before the patient arrives.

basic.situation: A patient arrives with a minor facial cut after a fall. You assist with emergency treatment and contact the relevant dental colleague about follow-up care.

options.text: Record the fall and direct the patient to the next clinic session.
Clean the cut, check dental injury, then ask a colleague to review.
Support wound care, share injury details, and coordinate the needed dental review.
Close the cut alone while the surgeon treats another patient, then report back.

advanced.situation: A patient arrives with facial fractures and heavy bleeding after a road crash. You coordinate emergency support and communicate with colleagues involved in care.

options.text: Ask a colleague to notify the team while you document the patient's arrival.
Alert emergency colleagues, share key findings, and coordinate roles as care begins.
Wait for imaging before alerting colleagues about the facial injuries.
Contact the surgical team and share initial details plus current concerns.

basic.situation: You are fitting a patient with a prescribed retainer under supervision. It feels tight at one edge, and the patient says it is uncomfortable.

options.text: Remove the retainer and arrange another fitting when the clinic is quieter.
Ask the patient to wear it home and mention any soreness later.
Check the fit against the plan and tell the supervising orthodontist about the pressure point.
Recheck seating and the pressure point, then adjust only within the plan and supervision.

advanced.situation: During a review, a patient's appliance no longer seats evenly after a recent adjustment. The patient reports a changed bite, and your supervising orthodontist is treating another patient.

options.text: Ask the patient to remove it until the orthodontist is available.
Check seating and symptoms, pause further adjustment, and arrange the orthodontist's review.
Record the bite change and ask the orthodontist to review the appliance fit.
Bend the appliance until both sides seat and the bite feels familiar.

basic.situation: You are preparing a patient's treatment record from the visit notes. The appliance type is listed, but the adjustment date is missing from the draft.

options.text: Save the draft and tell reception the record needs another look.
Copy the last visit's date into the blank field to finish the form.
Leave the date pending, mark the field, and confirm it with the clinician.
Check the visit notes and ask the clinician to confirm the missing date.

advanced.situation: Several clinicians use different formats for diagnostic records, making treatment histories hard to compare. You are asked to help improve documentation across the clinic.

options.text: Agree required fields, create a shared template, and guide staff through sample records.
Share a sample record and ask clinicians which fields are useful.
Keep the current formats and let each clinician document in their own way.
Send a blank template to the team and invite optional suggestions.

basic.situation: At a review, you examine a patient's tooth position under supervision. The upper teeth appear crowded, and the patient's notes mention a recent change in their bite.

options.text: Record the crowding and bite concern, then share both with the orthodontist.
Examine tooth position and bite as directed, record findings, and flag the change.
Tell the patient the crowding is expected and continue the appointment.
Ask the patient to describe the bite change and note their answer.

advanced.situation: A patient has facial asymmetry and a changing bite, while previous notes describe stable tooth position. You are examining them before the orthodontist reviews the case.

options.text: Explain that facial differences can occur during treatment, and record the patient's concern.
Ask when the bite began changing, then add the patient's account to notes.
Document the asymmetry and bite change, then prepare notes for orthodontist review.
Compare facial and tooth findings with prior records, document changes, and flag concerns.

basic.situation: You review a patient's dental history, photos, and models with guidance. The records show a gap where a tooth has not yet emerged.

options.text: Compare the history, photos, and model, then discuss the finding before planning.
Request another photo before reviewing the existing history and model.
Note the unerupted tooth and ask the orthodontist how it affects planning.
Plan space closure because the gap is visible in the model.

advanced.situation: A patient's X-ray, photos, and dental history suggest a complex jaw and tooth-position problem. You are preparing a treatment plan for the orthodontist to review.

options.text: Choose a familiar appliance plan based on the X-ray appearance.
List the records and ask the orthodontist which ones matter most.
Integrate the history, images, and examination findings into options for orthodontist review.
Summarise the X-ray findings and ask the orthodontist to set the plan.

basic.situation: You are helping fabricate a retainer from the orthodontist's instructions. The model suggests one edge may need adjustment before the appliance is finished.

options.text: Compare the retainer with instructions and model, then confirm its edge before finishing.
Check the model and instructions, then show the edge concern to the orthodontist.
Follow the model's edge shape and finish the retainer as instructed.
Pause fabrication and ask the technician to review the model before proceeding.

advanced.situation: A custom appliance is needed for a patient with an unusual tooth position. The team has different views on its design, and the orthodontist has provided a treatment goal.

options.text: Draft a design from the goal, then ask a colleague to review it.
Ask the orthodontist to choose between the proposed designs and explain their preference.
Use the standard appliance pattern, adapting it to the patient's needs.
Translate the treatment goal into design requirements, agree checks, and document fabrication plans.

basic.situation: A patient asks what a proposed treatment plan may cost and how long it could take. You have the plan but need help explaining the estimate.

options.text: Review the plan and approved estimate, explain likely costs, and invite questions.
Explain the plan in plain language and check the estimate with the clinic team.
Give a rough figure from a similar patient's treatment and move on.
Tell the patient to ask reception about costs after the appointment.

advanced.situation: A patient with a complex orthodontic plan has missed several visits and asks whether they can continue treatment alongside care from another dental service.

options.text: Ask the orthodontist to explain both services at the next visit.
Tell the patient to stop the other service until orthodontic treatment ends.
Review the plan, discuss attendance barriers, and coordinate timing with the other service.
Explain the next orthodontic steps and ask the patient to contact the other service.

basic.situation: A patient says a new denture rubs while chewing. You are asked to make a simple adjustment under supervision.

options.text: Ask the patient to wear it longer before changing anything.
Mark the sore area, adjust the fitting surface, and recheck comfort.
Check the marked area with your supervisor, then make a small adjustment.
Smooth the edge that seems to rub and return the denture.

advanced.situation: A technician reports a cracked denture base after repair, while the patient needs it for an event tomorrow. You are guiding the repair.

options.text: Ask the technician to repeat the repair using the usual bench method.
Review the break with the technician and request a stronger repair.
Set the repair criteria, inspect the base and fit, then approve a tested repair.
Approve the repair after checking that the crack is no longer visible.

basic.situation: A patient asks about closing a small front-tooth gap with bonding. You are assisting during the procedure under direct supervision.

options.text: Roughen the tooth surface and apply bonding material as planned.
Confirm the planned shade and tooth shape with the patient and dentist.
Prepare the tooth as directed, then help check the bonded shape and bite.
Set out the bonding materials and wait for the dentist's instructions.

advanced.situation: A patient wants veneers for uneven front teeth, but the proposed design may affect their bite. You are planning the aesthetic restoration and coaching a colleague.

options.text: Use the preferred shape and send the design for fabrication after discussion.
Plan veneers around bite, proportions, and patient priorities, then coach bonding steps.
Review proportions with your colleague and refine the veneer outline together.
Select a shade, then ask the technician to match it to the planned restoration.

basic.situation: A prepared tooth is ready for a bridge abutment, but the provisional crown feels high. You are assisting with site preparation under guidance.

options.text: Recheck the bite, record the contact, and adjust the provisional as directed.
Reduce the high spot quickly so the bridge can proceed today.
Tell the dentist the crown feels high and prepare the instruments.
Check the contact and clearance with the dentist before proceeding.

advanced.situation: A patient with worn teeth and missing molars needs full-mouth rehabilitation, but their bite record is inconsistent. You are coordinating the prosthetic plan with junior staff.

options.text: Review the bite record with the team and outline staged treatment options.
Choose a familiar bite scheme and have the team begin the restorations without review.
Repeat the bite record and coordinate staged restorations around function and patient goals.
Ask a junior colleague to repeat the bite record and summarize the findings for planning.

basic.situation: A patient reports jaw clicking and tenderness when opening wide. You are assessing possible jaw joint problems with supervision.

options.text: Ask when symptoms occur, check opening gently, and document the findings.
Suggest avoiding chewy foods and review the symptoms at another visit.
Record the clicking and tell the patient it should settle soon.
Ask about pain and report the clicking to your supervising dentist.

advanced.situation: A patient with a prior facial injury has worsening jaw pain and limited opening that disrupts eating. You are developing care with the team.

options.text: Assess function and injury history, coordinate a tailored plan, and set progress measures.
Continue the current exercises and ask the patient to return if pain persists.
Discuss the worsening pain with the team and revise the exercise plan.
Plan care around pain relief and jaw exercises, then review later.

basic.situation: A lab request needs a simple partial prosthesis for a patient missing one tooth. You are assisting with the design under supervision.

options.text: Send the lab the impression and ask them to choose the design.
Copy the tooth position from the patient's old appliance and prepare the request.
Ask the dentist to confirm the tooth position before completing the request.
Check the impression and prescription, then sketch the proposed tooth position.

advanced.situation: Two technicians produce different fits for the same type of prosthesis. You are setting fabrication standards and supervising the next cases.

options.text: Compare finished devices and discuss fit differences with technicians before choosing a shared approach.
Discuss the different results with technicians and agree on consistent fitting steps.
Set shared fit checks, document them, and review sample cases with technicians.
Ask each technician to follow their preferred bench sequence for each case.

basic.situation: You are taking an impression for a new denture, but the patient gags when the tray is placed. A senior clinician is nearby for guidance.

options.text: Try a smaller tray and continue the impression before the patient loses confidence.
Reassure the patient and ask the clinician whether to change trays.
Pause, explain the next step, and adjust the tray approach with guidance.
Ask the clinician to take over while you prepare another tray.

advanced.situation: A patient with a complex bite history has an impression that conflicts with the examination. You are leading the assessment and coordinating input from the dental team.

options.text: Rely on impression measurements and begin planning the prosthesis without reconciling the examination.
Repeat key measurements, examine the bite, and reconcile findings with the dental team.
Discuss conflicting records with the team and arrange a repeat impression.
Ask a colleague to review the impression and advise the team on next steps.

basic.situation: A new patient reports stomach discomfort and takes several medicines. You are asked to record their food and health history before the dietitian reviews it.

options.text: Copy the referral summary into the history and ask the patient to confirm it.
Record the main symptom and usual meals to keep the intake brief.
Ask about meals, symptoms, allergies, and medicines, then record the patient's own words.
Use the prior patient's history as a template and change the name and age.

advanced.situation: Your clinic study finds a possible link between a local food pattern and rising blood sugar, but the sample is small and several participants missed follow-ups.

options.text: Present the link as a confirmed finding so the clinic can act on it.
Compare the available records and draft a short report for the clinic team.
Share the trend with colleagues and note that more participants would strengthen it.
Report the pattern as preliminary, explain missing follow-ups, and propose a larger study.

basic.situation: A patient with diabetes asks for help choosing lunch at the hospital café. Their clinician has set a meal plan for you to follow.

options.text: Review the meal plan, then compare café lunches with the patient’s usual preferences.
Share a relevant diabetes handout and discuss how its examples fit café choices.
Recommend a familiar balanced meal and ask how it fits the meal plan.
Ask about usual lunch choices and compare them with the agreed meal plan.

advanced.situation: A patient who fasts for religious reasons also has kidney disease and diabetes. Their family asks for a meal plan that fits shared evening meals.

options.text: Ask which evening dishes matter most and adapt portions within the existing plan.
Map fasting times and customary dishes against restrictions, then prepare meal options for review.
Advise ending the fast and using a standard clinic menu for meals.
Offer a kidney-friendly menu and invite the family to adapt familiar dishes.

basic.situation: A patient asks you to adapt a familiar noodle recipe because wheat triggers their diagnosed gluten intolerance.

options.text: Share a gluten-free recipe from the clinic handout for the patient to try.
Replace the wheat noodles with rice noodles and ask about the sauce ingredients.
Check each ingredient and suggest a gluten-free noodle with a similar texture.
Tell the patient to remove the noodles and keep the rest of the recipe.

advanced.situation: A care home needs a week of meals for residents with different food allergies and texture needs, while keeping the shared kitchen workflow manageable.

options.text: Draft allergy-aware meals and ask kitchen staff which texture changes they can manage.
Reuse the regular menu and mark dishes residents should avoid on each day.
Remove common allergens from every dish and serve the same soft meals to all residents.
Build a rotating menu, map allergens and textures per resident, and flag shared preparation risks.

basic.situation: You are helping prepare a one-page visual aid for a community session on adding vegetables to familiar meals.

options.text: Add several nutrition facts, even if the visual aid becomes crowded for participants.
Adapt the clinic poster into a handout, checking its examples match the session.
Select clear food images and brief captions showing vegetable portions in familiar dishes.
Use familiar meal pictures and a serving guide, then request dietitian feedback.

advanced.situation: Your study on meal patterns is ready for a professional report, but the results differ between two clinic sites and the team wants a clear summary.

options.text: Combine both sites and present one clear result for the professional audience.
Separate site findings, describe the methods and limits, and frame conclusions around the data.
Prepare a brief report using the strongest result as the main message.
Summarize the overall result and mention that the two sites differed.

basic.situation: A physician asks whether a patient recovering from surgery needs a texture-modified diet, but the referral gives no swallowing details.

options.text: Suggest soft foods based on the patient's recovery stage and usual preferences.
Ask the physician about swallowing guidance and review the patient's current diet needs together.
Recommend a standard recovery menu and let the ward team choose the texture.
Check the ward notes and share a cautious meal suggestion with the physician.

advanced.situation: New ward staff will counsel patients on nutrition, and recent handovers show inconsistent advice about meal plans and restrictions.

options.text: Build a short case-based session around common handover gaps and practice consistent counseling.
Review the current counseling guide with staff and invite questions about difficult cases.
Reuse the previous slide deck and cover the same nutrition topics again.
Send the ward team a summary of diet restrictions and ask them to read it.

basic.situation: A patient asks what to choose from a kopitiam menu while trying to follow the food plan discussed at clinic.

options.text: Ask about their usual order and compare it with the clinic food plan.
Share a healthy eating leaflet and highlight its meal examples for discussion.
Discuss several menu choices, including grilled fish, vegetables, and suitable alternatives based on their plan.
Suggest choosing the lowest-calorie dish, then ask how it fits their plan.

advanced.situation: You coordinate diet counseling across two clinic days, and a staff member reports patients are receiving different follow-up advice after group sessions.

options.text: Let each clinic day keep its routine and share the same leaflet with patients.
Create a shared counseling outline, assign follow-up roles, and review feedback.
Ask both teams to compare follow-up notes and discuss gaps in their advice.
Send the concern to the clinic lead and ask for guidance on consistency.

basic.situation: A patient says their new glasses slide down and blur when they look at the clinic appointment card. You are asked to check the fit.

options.text: Tighten the temples and ask whether the appointment card looks clearer afterward.
Offer a nose pad adjustment and suggest they return if the blur continues.
Check frame alignment and lens position, then adjust the fit and recheck the view.
Exchange the glasses for a tighter frame using the same lens measurements.

advanced.situation: A junior colleague struggles to fit a rigid lens for a patient with an irregular cornea, and the patient reports discomfort during the trial.

options.text: Ask the patient to keep the trial lens in place while the colleague practices.
Show the colleague the fitting guide and ask them to repeat the assessment.
Review the fit pattern with the colleague, then adjust the trial lens and reassess comfort.
Suggest a shorter wear trial and note the patient's discomfort for follow-up.

basic.situation: A patient describes a red, itchy eye and asks whether they need medicated drops. You are working under direct clinical supervision.

options.text: Check symptoms and history, then discuss possible drops with your supervising optometrist.
Ask when symptoms began and whether they affect vision before discussing options with your supervisor.
Explain that treatment depends on the cause, and arrange a routine clinic review.
Ask about discharge and pain, then report your findings to the supervising optometrist.

advanced.situation: Your clinic lead asks for input on a draft medication pathway for recurring eye complaints, including cases that may need medical review.

options.text: Adapt the existing clinic notes into a quick reference for recurring complaints.
Draft clear prescribing criteria and referral triggers for the lead to review against clinic scope.
Set a shared drop regimen for recurring complaints so staff can act consistently.
Summarize common treatments and ask the lead to confirm which cases need referral.

basic.situation: A patient has trouble tracking a moving target during a prescribed vision therapy session. You are assisting under guidance.

options.text: Add extra target movements so the patient can practice through the difficulty.
Pause the exercise and ask the patient to rest before trying again.
Repeat the target movement at a slower pace and check the patient's comfort.
Follow the prescribed exercise, observe tracking, and report the patient's response to the clinician.

advanced.situation: A patient with low vision cannot read bus signs after trying their current aids. You are asked to plan therapeutic support within the clinic service.

options.text: Review their current aids and add guided reading practice for bus signs at home.
Offer a magnifier and share printed tips for using it outdoors.
Assess tasks, trial aids, and plan practice for the patient's travel needs.
Suggest practising familiar routes with support while they learn to use their aids.

basic.situation: A patient is scheduled for cataract surgery and asks what to expect before leaving the clinic. You are helping with preparation under supervision.

options.text: Review the clinic's preparation instructions with the patient and check what questions remain.
Explain the appointment time and remind the patient to follow the clinic instructions.
Tell the patient to follow the same preparation routine as the previous patient.
Give the patient the printed surgery leaflet and offer to answer one question.

advanced.situation: The day after laser vision correction, a patient calls with worsening pain and reduced vision. You are supporting post-operative care at the clinic.

options.text: Reassure the patient that discomfort can follow surgery and keep the planned review.
Arrange urgent review through the clinic pathway and relay the symptoms to the treating clinician.
Review the discharge instructions with the patient and ask them to monitor symptoms.
Ask when symptoms began, how vision changed, and whether pain worsened before contacting the treating clinician.

basic.situation: A patient reports a speck on the white of their eye after gardening. You can see a loose surface particle during the supervised examination.

options.text: Irrigate the eye, check if the particle moves, and consult the supervisor before removing it.
Confirm the particle is loose and superficial, then remove it using the clinic's safe method.
Use a cotton tip to lift the speck while the patient holds still.
Ask the supervisor to assess the eye while you prepare removal supplies.

advanced.situation: A colleague asks you to demonstrate foreign body removal after a worker reports metal dust in one eye, but the particle appears embedded.

options.text: Stop the removal attempt, protect the eye, and arrange urgent assessment by the appropriate clinician.
Demonstrate a careful lift with a sterile instrument so the colleague can learn.
Show the colleague how to irrigate the eye while checking whether the particle shifts.
Explain the signs of an embedded particle and ask the colleague to prepare a referral.

basic.situation: A contact lens wearer says their eyes feel dry after a long shift and asks how to care for the lenses at home.

options.text: Hand the patient the clinic's contact lens leaflet and offer a new case.
Explain each cleaning step, ask about their lens case, and check how often they replace it.
Suggest wearing the lenses longer so the eyes can adjust to the dryness.
Review lens cleaning and wear habits, then explain when eye symptoms need clinic review.

advanced.situation: A patient reports flashes and a new shadow in their vision during a routine visit. You are preparing patient education and referrals within the clinic.

options.text: Give the patient a warning leaflet and advise them to call if symptoms change.
Reassure the patient that brief flashes can happen and keep the routine appointment.
Describe the symptoms to the clinic clinician and ask which referral route to use.
Explain the concern plainly and arrange prompt ophthalmology assessment through the clinic referral process.

basic.situation: A patient brings a prescription with a smudged dose. You need to check it before dispensing.

options.text: Check the patient profile and compare the dose with the prescription.
Pause dispensing and confirm the unclear dose with the prescriber.
Ask a colleague to inspect the writing and suggest a dose.
Read the smudge as the usual dose and prepare the medicine.

advanced.situation: An insurer rejects a claim because the quantity differs from its records. The prescription appears valid, and the patient is waiting.

options.text: Compare the claim with the prescription, clarify the mismatch, then resubmit.
Resubmit the claim with the quantity shown in the insurer's record.
Check the claim details and ask the insurer which field caused rejection.
Tell the patient the claim failed and ask them to return later.

basic.situation: You are packaging a routine medicine, and the standard procedure calls for a second label check before it leaves the bench.

options.text: Follow the packaging steps and verify the label before release.
Pack the medicine, then ask a colleague to check the label.
Use the previous package as a guide and finish this one quickly.
Check the medicine and label against the order before packing.

advanced.situation: A new liquid preparation has a different mixing sequence from the one used last month. You are updating the pharmacy procedure and label instructions.

options.text: Draft the mixing steps and ask a colleague to review the label.
Keep the current procedure and add a note for staff to take care.
Confirm approved preparation details, then revise and check both procedure and label.
Adapt last month's steps and update the label to match the new liquid.

basic.situation: A patient collecting tablets asks whether they should keep the bottle in the car between shifts.

options.text: Check the label, explain its storage directions, and ask where they can keep it.
Tell them the bottle can stay in the car during a short shift.
Suggest they ask a family member to store the bottle at home.
Explain the storage directions and suggest keeping the bottle in a cool place.

advanced.situation: A physician asks whether a patient's new medicine could interact with the existing regimen, which includes several medicines and a recent dose change.

options.text: Focus on the new medicine and share its usual side effects with the physician.
Review the regimen and flag the recent dose change for discussion.
Tell the physician the new medicine is commonly used with other treatments.
Check the medicines together, assess likely interactions, and discuss options with the physician.

basic.situation: During a routine count, the shelf quantity for a common medicine differs from the stock record. You are recording levels with guidance.

options.text: Enter the shelf count and note that it differs from the record.
Adjust the record to match the shelf count and continue the count.
Recount the item, check recent stock movements, and record the result.
Ask a colleague for the expected count before updating the record.

advanced.situation: Several medicines are nearing expiry while a delivery is delayed. You are reviewing supply levels and storage for the next order.

options.text: Review usage and expiry dates, then adjust the order and storage plan.
Reduce the next order based on the near-expiry stock on hand.
Order the usual quantities and move the older stock to the front.
Keep the standard order and store the delivery wherever space remains.

basic.situation: A sample's measured strength differs from the expected value during a routine check. You need to assess the result before recording it.

options.text: Record the first result and note that it differs from expected strength.
Check the equipment and method, repeat the measurement, then compare results.
Use the expected value to complete the record and move to the next sample.
Repeat the measurement with the same setup and record the second value.

advanced.situation: A monthly review shows rising use of one medicine alongside another with a possible interaction. You are checking prescribing trends for patient safety.

options.text: Check the prescribing data and highlight the rise in a summary.
Treat the rise as seasonal demand and update the monthly chart.
Share the rising use figure at the next routine team meeting.
Compare the trend with patient records and flag the pattern for clinical review.

basic.situation: A patient's profile is missing the date of a recent medicine change. You are updating the record with supervision.

options.text: Enter the medicine change and leave the date field for later.
Add the change using the date from the latest dispensing entry.
Ask the supervising pharmacist which date to use, then update the profile.
Check the source note, enter the change date, and review the saved profile.

advanced.situation: An intern is preparing a prescribed cream while the usual pharmacist is handling another patient. You are overseeing the compounding bench.

options.text: Demonstrate the key weighing and mixing steps, then observe the intern's work.
Ask the intern to follow the written procedure and bring the cream for review.
Prepare the cream yourself and let the intern watch from the bench.
Let the intern finish, then compare the final cream with the prescription.

basic.situation: During a clinic visit, you examine a patient reporting dizziness and need to check their physical condition with guidance.

options.text: I ask about symptoms and examine the patient using the clinic's routine sequence.
I check the patient's pulse and balance, then record what I observe.
I focus on the symptom the patient mentions and note that finding.
I record the patient's dizziness and use the last visit's findings as a guide.

advanced.situation: A junior colleague is unsure how to examine a patient with swelling and breathlessness, and you are asked to guide the examination.

options.text: I share my last similar case and suggest following its examination pattern.
I show the junior how to check the swelling and listen to the chest.
I ask the junior to repeat the routine examination while I observe.
I demonstrate a focused examination and explain which findings need careful comparison.

basic.situation: A patient's blood test shows a mildly abnormal result, and you are asked to interpret it with supervision.

options.text: I review the result, reference range, and symptoms before discussing its meaning.
I note the abnormal value and ask whether it needs follow-up.
I treat the mild result as routine and file it with the chart.
I compare the result with the reference range and flag the deviation.

advanced.situation: Several patients have unusual test results that may reflect either illness or sample problems, and you are asked to guide interpretation standards.

options.text: I compare trends, symptoms, and sample concerns, then document escalation criteria.
I ask staff to repeat tests when results look unlike the usual range.
I use the most common explanation to sort similar results for the team.
I review the unusual results with staff and note recurring patterns.

basic.situation: During a clinic visit, you take a patient's health history and need to record it with assistance.

options.text: I record the patient's symptoms, medicines, and relevant past conditions.
I ask about unclear dates and medicines, then record the patient's answers.
I note the main complaint and add the remaining history later.
I copy the previous history forward and update the current complaint.

advanced.situation: A chart audit finds inconsistent progress notes and examination results across the team, and you are asked to improve record quality.

options.text: I map recurring gaps, clarify documentation fields, and track whether they improve.
I remind staff to include examination findings in their progress notes.
I tidy the sampled charts and ask staff to use those as examples.
I review sample charts and share a clear format for notes and findings.

basic.situation: A patient needs a prescribed injection, and you are assisting with the procedure under supervision.

options.text: I confirm the order and patient details before preparing the injection.
I set out the supplies and check the label against the chart.
I use the familiar dose and prepare the injection from the chart.
I prepare the injection and ask the supervisor to confirm the details.

advanced.situation: During a complicated wound procedure, a technician is unsure about sterile supplies and you are asked to guide the team.

options.text: I pause the setup, clarify the sterile field, and assign checks before resuming.
I let the technician use the usual setup and monitor the wound care.
I explain sterile handling and watch the technician prepare the supplies.
I ask the technician to replace the uncertain items before the procedure.

basic.situation: A patient asks how to maintain their health while following a prescribed treatment plan, and you need to provide basic guidance.

options.text: I repeat the advice from the treatment sheet and invite questions.
I explain the routine advice and check what the patient already understands.
I suggest the patient follow the plan and discuss details at another visit.
I give the patient a simple health leaflet and summarize its main points.

advanced.situation: Patients with complex emotional concerns are struggling to follow treatment advice, and you are asked to develop a counseling approach for the team.

options.text: I group common barriers, draft tailored discussion prompts, and review patient feedback.
I collect staff suggestions and prepare shared talking points for counseling.
I ask staff to use the usual treatment script with these patients.
I adapt the existing advice sheet for patients who mention emotional concerns.

basic.situation: The clinic is running low on routine dressings, and you are asked to order supplies with guidance.

options.text: I order a full case so the clinic has extra dressings available.
I compare stock with upcoming use and confirm the quantity with the team.
I request a small top-up based on the last order's quantity.
I check the shelf count and place an order for the usual amount.

advanced.situation: Supply levels are tight while several patients need different therapies, and you are asked to coordinate technicians and review proposed treatment plans.

options.text: I ask technicians to prioritize the cases with the earliest appointments.
I allocate scarce supplies by routine and leave treatment plans unchanged.
I review the proposed plans and share the supply constraints with the physician.
I coordinate the technicians, check supply needs, and flag plans outside my approval authority.

basic.situation: Before a scheduled procedure, you are asked to administer an anesthetic drug under the anesthesiologist's direct supervision.

options.text: I check the prepared label and administer the drug as directed.
I confirm the drug and dose with the anesthesiologist before administration.
I use the prior case's drug setup to prepare this patient's dose.
I review the drug chart and prepare the usual anesthetic dose.

advanced.situation: A junior colleague is preparing several adjunct drugs for a longer procedure, and you are asked to guide administration under the anesthesiologist's direction.

options.text: I review each drug against the plan and teach the junior to track timing.
I show the junior the usual adjunct set used for longer procedures.
I ask the junior to prepare the adjunct drugs while I watch the setup.
I check the labels and review the planned sequence with the junior.

basic.situation: A patient has difficulty breathing in recovery, and you are asked to assist with airway support while a senior clinician guides you.

options.text: I bring airway equipment and wait for the senior to assign a task.
I check the airway and assist with the support the senior directs.
I assess breathing, assist with directed airway support, and report changes.
I use the routine recovery response and continue checking the patient.

advanced.situation: A patient deteriorates during recovery and the response team is assembling; you are asked to lead airway and life-support actions within your role.

options.text: I manage the airway while the team gathers around the patient.
I lead airway support and ask a colleague to prepare ventilation equipment.
I assign airway roles, call out patient changes, and coordinate directed support.
I follow the last emergency layout and ask the team to assist.

basic.situation: A patient is waking after anesthesia, and you are asked to monitor and document their progress with assistance.

options.text: I check the vital signs and enter them in the recovery chart.
I enter the last set of readings to keep the chart current.
I record the vital signs and note how the patient responds over time.
I ask a colleague to confirm the readings before I chart them.

advanced.situation: A complex patient has changing ECG and arterial pressure readings after anesthesia, and you are asked to guide the team's monitoring approach.

options.text: I review trends with the team and define which changes need prompt reporting.
I compare the readings with earlier values and discuss the pattern with staff.
I use the routine observation schedule and note unusual monitor values.
I ask staff to increase checks when a reading moves outside its range.

basic.situation: Before a procedure, you are asked to pretest the anesthesia delivery system with a supervisor and confirm needed supplies are available.

options.text: I check the gas supply and prepare the machine for the supervisor's test.
I use the prior case's check notes to prepare the same machine.
I pretest the delivery system and report any fault to my supervisor.
I run the equipment check and confirm the required gases and supplies.

advanced.situation: The unit is introducing an updated anesthesia delivery system, and you are asked to help develop calibration and pretest guidance for staff.

options.text: I adapt the old checklist and include the new system's main controls.
I draft a calibration checklist and ask experienced staff to review it.
I map the calibration checks, record acceptable readings, and review trial results.
I share the supplier's quick guide as the team's calibration procedure.

basic.situation: Before anesthesia, you collect the patient's health history and a blood sample for testing with help from a colleague.

options.text: I collect the sample and enter the patient's reported health history.
I record the main health conditions and prepare a sample label.
I confirm the patient's identity, collect the sample, and record key history.
I use the previous visit's history and label the sample from the chart.

advanced.situation: A records review finds gaps in pre-anesthetic histories and inconsistent specimen labels, and you are asked to improve the team's process.

options.text: I review examples with staff and share a clearer history and labeling guide.
I revise sampled records and use them as reference examples.
I trace recurring gaps, clarify identity and history fields, and check later records.
I remind staff to complete histories and match labels with the chart.

basic.situation: A departmental seminar covers an anesthesia practice relevant to your work, and you are attending to keep your knowledge current.

options.text: I read the seminar summary and ask a colleague what stood out.
I attend the session and write down the speaker's main recommendations.
I attend the seminar and note changes that may affect my clinical practice.
I keep using my current reference notes for this familiar topic.

advanced.situation: New staff need consistent preparation for anesthesia practices, and you are asked to design and deliver a clinical training session.

options.text: I share reference materials and ask staff to review them before their shifts.
I set learning goals, demonstrate key practices, and check staff understanding.
I prepare a practical session and invite staff to discuss their questions.
I repeat the last training session and update its opening slides.

basic.situation: You review a patient's history and foot x-ray, but the reported pain is on a different side from the charted injury.

options.text: Follow the charted side and record the x-ray findings for the senior podiatrist.
Use the patient's pain location to choose a likely diagnosis before checking the image.
Read the x-ray first and summarize its visible changes for the senior podiatrist.
Compare your notes with the history and x-ray, then flag any mismatch for review.

advanced.situation: A patient's persistent foot swelling has unusual laboratory results, and the common explanations do not fit the examination.

options.text: Check the result ranges and related findings, then clarify inconsistencies before documenting a differential.
Compare the abnormal results with the examination and history, then document possible patterns.
Treat one unusual result as the cause and document a rare condition for follow-up.
Review the unusual values and ask the laboratory to confirm the reported measurements.

basic.situation: A patient points to a painful corn, but the clinic note identifies a different foot for the planned removal.

options.text: Prepare the instruments and remove the corn at the site written in the note.
Review the clinic note and set out the instruments for the recorded site.
Confirm the painful site with the patient and chart before preparing the removal.
Ask the patient to point again, then prepare the instruments for that foot.

advanced.situation: You are assisting with care for a severe bunion, and the imaging shows joint changes beyond the expected deformity.

options.text: Prepare the usual bunion instruments and tell the surgeon about the imaging changes.
Review the imaging and help the surgeon connect the joint changes with the planned procedure.
Set out the routine instruments and proceed with the planned bunion correction.
Ask the patient about pain and stiffness before setting out the usual instruments.

basic.situation: You apply a plaster cast for a patient with a toe deformity, but the first wrap shifts as the patient moves.

options.text: Check the toe position and cast fit with the supervising podiatrist before finishing.
Adjust the wrap around the toe and secure it before the patient moves again.
Ask the supervising podiatrist to review the shifted cast before securing it.
Add another layer over the shifted wrap to hold the toe in place.

advanced.situation: A patient with partial foot loss says a trial prosthetic appliance slips when walking, although it feels secure while seated.

options.text: Ask where the appliance slips and adjust the contact points before another trial.
Review the appliance materials and request a different size for the next fitting.
Observe a walking trial and adjust the appliance fit around the patient's residual foot.
Add padding at the reported pressure point and let the patient try it later.

basic.situation: A patient with a mild foot strain asks whether a standard treatment plan can help them return to work comfortably.

options.text: Suggest the usual pain medicine and device so the patient can return to work.
Explain a standard treatment option and check whether it fits the patient's routine.
Review symptoms and work demands, then discuss suitable care choices with the patient.
Recommend rest and a supportive device based on the patient's description.

advanced.situation: A patient with long-standing foot pain has tried several treatments, and their current device worsens discomfort after long shifts.

options.text: Renew the current device and add pain medicine for the longer shifts.
Review prior responses and shift demands, then coordinate a revised plan across treatment options.
Replace the device with a familiar model and arrange a later review.
Discuss the previous treatments and consider a different device or therapy approach.

basic.situation: A patient with recurring heel irritation asks what changes might help prevent another episode during daily walks.

options.text: Suggest softer shoes and shorter walks until the irritation settles.
Show the patient how to check footwear and protect irritated skin during walks.
Explain footwear and skin care choices, then agree on a practical walking routine.
Recommend a heel insert and ask the patient to return if it hurts.

advanced.situation: You notice reduced foot sensation and a small wound in a patient who mentions managing diabetes with another clinic.

options.text: Advise daily foot checks and ask the patient to contact their physician soon.
Suggest a protective dressing and review the wound at the next routine visit.
Explain the wound concern and arrange referral to the patient's physician for review.
Cover the wound and explain signs that should prompt another clinic visit.

basic.situation: You are filing a patient's visit record and notice that the treatment note is missing from the scanned documents.

options.text: Mark the file as incomplete and tell the clinician which note is missing.
Complete the file with the scanned pages and leave the missing note unlisted.
Check the visit record and request the missing note before completing the file.
File the available pages and add a reminder to check the note later.

advanced.situation: You are preparing a public foot-care talk, and the clinic's supply order is due while the venue changes the session time.

options.text: Confirm the venue details, update the talk materials, and submit the checked supply order.
Use the revised talk time and order the regular supplies from last month's list.
Update the talk announcement and send the supply list to the clinic manager.
Keep the printed talk time and place the usual supply order before the cutoff.

basic.situation: A patient has practised dressing skills for two weeks, and you need to report their progress to the rehabilitation team.

options.text: Compare recent performance with the starting level and note specific changes in your report.
Describe the latest dressing session and share the patient's comments with the team.
Record whether the patient finished dressing and note how long the session took.
Write that dressing is improving based on the patient's confidence today.

advanced.situation: A patient has mixed strength, memory, and home-safety findings, and the team needs realistic goals for returning to meal preparation.

options.text: Set a meal-preparation goal from the patient's preferred task and current confidence.
Link test results to kitchen demands and set measurable goals around safe meal tasks.
Review the assessment results and suggest goals based on the patient's strongest abilities.
Prioritize strength exercises and revisit meal preparation after the next assessment.

basic.situation: A client wants to practise managing a simple work routine, and you are choosing activities suited to their current abilities.

options.text: Choose a short work routine with steps matched to the client's current abilities.
Select a longer task that includes several steps for realistic practice.
Use the same work worksheet as the previous client to save preparation time.
Offer a familiar sorting activity that practises attention and task completion.

advanced.situation: A community group asks you to plan sessions for adults adjusting to new mobility limits and returning to daily roles.

options.text: Plan peer discussions about adapting routines and managing changes in daily roles.
Arrange general wellness talks and invite participants to share questions afterward.
Repeat the clinic's standard group activities and invite the community group to attend.
Build group sessions around practical routines, shared problem-solving, and participants' stated goals.

basic.situation: A client struggles to hold a cup during therapy, and a senior therapist asks you to prepare a simple adapted handle.

options.text: Check the client's grip and assemble the handle to fit the cup securely.
Choose a standard adapted handle and ask the client to try holding the cup.
Use the thickest available grip so the client has more surface to hold.
Wrap a familiar foam grip around the cup for a quick trial.

advanced.situation: A client with limited hand movement needs computer access for work, but the standard adapted keyboard trial causes fatigue.

options.text: Order a larger-key keyboard so the client can target keys more easily.
Observe the client's work tasks and request equipment matched to reach, movement, and fatigue.
Request the same keyboard model used by another client with limited hand movement.
Discuss alternate keyboard layouts and request a trial for the client's work tasks.

basic.situation: After a session using puzzles and eating utensils, you are putting materials away and updating the clinical record.

options.text: Wipe the used tools and add a brief note about the completed activity.
Write the session summary and return the puzzles and utensils to storage.
Return the tools to storage and enter the session title in the record.
Clean and check each tool, then record the session and any equipment issue.

advanced.situation: During a records check, you find a missing session entry and a therapy tool with a loose handle before the next appointment.

options.text: Report the loose handle and add a reminder to complete the missing entry.
Complete the session entry and put the loose tool aside for later maintenance.
Tighten the handle and use the tool for the next appointment after a quick check.
Secure the tool from use, report its condition, and complete the missing session entry.

basic.situation: A client is practising memory tasks in occupational therapy and begins physiotherapy sessions that use similar activities.

options.text: Tell the physiotherapist which memory activities the client has already practised.
Continue your current memory activities and ask the client how physiotherapy is going.
Add more memory exercises so occupational therapy stays distinct from physiotherapy.
Compare activity goals with the physiotherapist and coordinate practice that supports both sessions.

advanced.situation: A client is working toward independent cooking with occupational therapy, physiotherapy, and nursing support, but their practice times conflict.

options.text: Agree shared cooking goals with the team and schedule practice around each discipline's input.
Coordinate the practice schedule with the team and share the client's latest progress.
Keep occupational therapy cooking practice and ask the client to attend other sessions later.
Move your cooking session to the earliest open slot on the client's calendar.

basic.situation: A client recovering at home struggles to reach kitchen items safely, and their caregiver asks what changes might help.

options.text: Move frequently used cups and plates to a lower, reachable shelf.
Offer a stable stool for reaching higher shelves, if safe for the client.
Ask the caregiver to place kitchen supplies on one accessible counter.
Discuss kitchen tasks and suggest reachable storage changes that suit the client's abilities.

advanced.situation: A caregiver will help a client practise dressing after discharge and asks how to support therapy goals safely at home.

options.text: Show the agreed dressing method, then let the caregiver practise safety cues.
Ask the caregiver to follow the client's usual dressing routine and report new difficulties.
Tell the caregiver to help with dressing whenever the client needs extra time.
Explain the dressing steps and give the caregiver a written practice guide.

basic.situation: You are teaching a client with visual impairment a two-point touch cane technique in a familiar corridor. They are unsure how wide each sweep should be.

options.text: Show the sweep, then check cane coverage as the client practises.
Demonstrate the sweep and have the client practise at a steady pace.
Describe the sweep and let the client practise along the corridor.
Ask the client to repeat the technique from memory during a walk.

advanced.situation: A client asks whether an electronic travel aid could help on unfamiliar routes. Device prompts may be hard to hear near traffic, so you need to recommend and train an option.

options.text: Recommend an electronic aid and practise its prompts indoors.
Demonstrate an electronic aid and discuss its route prompts with the client.
Recommend a long cane and practise the familiar route again.
Compare device prompts with the client's needs and practise in varied settings.

basic.situation: You are guiding a client through a simulated route from a clinic room to reception. They can follow familiar turns but lose track after a change in direction.

options.text: Walk the route for the client and describe each turn.
Ask the client to lead the route while you give prompts at turns.
Let the client lead, then discuss where the direction change caused difficulty.
Repeat the route with the client following your verbal directions.

advanced.situation: You are designing a simulated travel exercise for a client who manages familiar routes but struggles when a bus stop or walkway changes unexpectedly.

options.text: Add one detour and prompt the client at each decision point.
Repeat the familiar route until the client travels it smoothly.
Add a detour and observe how the client chooses a new route.
Use a familiar route and add a simulated detour with decision points.

basic.situation: You are showing a client how to use tactile and auditory cues in a familiar hallway. They can hear a doorway landmark but have trouble finding its position.

options.text: Ask the client to listen for the doorway sound during another pass.
Pair the doorway sound with a tactile landmark for practice.
Describe the doorway and ask the client to find it by sound.
Guide the client by the arm to the doorway landmark.

advanced.situation: A client has reduced hearing and inconsistent tactile sensitivity. You are planning sensory training for navigating a busy indoor setting with several distinct landmarks.

options.text: Build a training plan around tactile landmarks across the route.
Combine checked tactile and kinesthetic cues, then practise at key landmarks.
Discuss which cues feel useful and practise those in a quiet room.
Use the same auditory landmark exercise planned for other clients.

basic.situation: You are assisting a client with a basic adaptive eating technique during a supervised session. They spill when using a standard spoon and ask to try a wider grip.

options.text: Encourage the client to keep using the standard spoon.
Offer a wider grip and observe the client's next few bites.
Explain a wider grip and ask the client to try it.
Switch to a deeper spoon and finish the meal practice.

advanced.situation: You are developing an independent living plan with a client who has low vision and manages diabetes. They want to handle meals, medication routines, and home tasks more independently.

options.text: Agree on priorities for meals, medication routines, and home tasks with the client.
Write a broad home skills checklist for the client to follow.
Set staged practice for meals, medication routines, and home tasks with the client.
Focus the plan on meal preparation and revisit other tasks later.

basic.situation: You are documenting a client's assessment and progress after practising a familiar route. They needed fewer prompts today, and your supervisor asked you to prepare the notes.

options.text: Record the route and number of prompts used during practice.
Describe the route, prompts, and change since the previous session.
Copy the last note and update the appointment date.
Ask the client how the route felt and note their answer.

advanced.situation: A client's mobility progress has stalled on unfamiliar routes, although familiar travel is improving. You are reviewing assessment results with the client and team to adjust rehabilitation plans.

options.text: Ask the client which route they want to practise next.
Continue familiar route practice until the next scheduled review.
Discuss the assessment results and agree on a new route practice goal.
Agree on a route goal and track unfamiliar travel performance at reviews.

basic.situation: You are distributing large-print materials to a client who says the current pages are difficult to read. The client asks whether another available format can be tried.

options.text: Offer another available print size and ask the client to compare.
Give the client the standard large-print set for home use.
Show the client a larger print sample and explain its use.
Provide a reading stand with the current large-print materials.

advanced.situation: A client wants to communicate independently using an adaptive keyboard and feels unsure explaining this need at a service meeting. You are asked to plan instruction and support self-advocacy.

options.text: Teach keyboard functions and write a request for the client to use.
Demonstrate the keyboard and discuss what the client wants to communicate.
Ask a specialist to explain the client's equipment needs at the meeting.
Plan keyboard practice and help the client prepare points for the meeting.

basic.situation: A referral arrives for a patient with knee pain and limited walking. You are asked to draft a starter plan for the senior therapist to review.

options.text: I review the referral, check today's limits, and draft exercises for senior review.
I compare referral and records, link exercises to goals, and flag uncertainties for review.
I reuse a familiar plan and change repetitions to fit today's appointment.
I ask the patient what feels manageable, then choose common exercises for review.

advanced.situation: A patient with several conditions has conflicting mobility goals from different clinicians. You are leading a meeting to agree on a workable care strategy.

options.text: I settle on the quickest proposal and send the team my decision afterward.
I note the disagreement and ask the senior therapist to resolve the plan.
I circulate key records and an agenda, then guide agreement on goals, owners, and reviews.
I summarize competing goals and invite each clinician to explain their priorities.

basic.situation: A patient returning to lifting work asks how to reduce the chance of another back strain. You have time to share a few prevention tips.

options.text: I explain lifting and pacing, then ask the patient how they will use them.
I give the same quick lifting tip I use with most patients.
I mention common stretches and suggest the patient try them before work.
I share a simple prevention handout and invite questions about daily activities.

advanced.situation: A community group asks your clinic to help shape injury-prevention guidance for local workers, but its members describe very different job demands.

options.text: I circulate an unreviewed guideline as the community's agreed prevention policy.
I gather local injury concerns and work with agencies on practical prevention guidance.
I present clinic trends at a community meeting and collect feedback for future materials.
I draft broad advice from familiar clinic leaflets for local groups to review.

basic.situation: After several sessions for shoulder pain, a patient reports easier dressing but discomfort during an exercise. You are reviewing the effects with a senior therapist.

options.text: I compare today's function with baseline, note the response, and adapt the exercise dose.
I record the patient's response and ask the senior therapist whether the plan needs adjustment.
I repeat the same measure and keep the session routine unless symptoms change.
I record that the session went well based on the patient's brief comment.

advanced.situation: Your clinic is reviewing its approach to balance exercises. You find research with mixed results and are asked to recommend whether practice should change.

options.text: I share a promising paper and suggest trying its approach with a few patients.
I adopt the paper's main recommendation for our patients after a quick read.
I appraise relevant studies, compare them with clinic outcomes, and propose a measured practice update.
I summarize a recent study and ask colleagues whether its methods fit our patients.

basic.situation: A patient says a newly fitted ankle support rubs during walking. You are helping check its fit under the supervising therapist's guidance.

options.text: I use the usual fitting steps and note any obvious rubbing for review.
I tighten the straps until the device feels secure during a short walk.
I check alignment, comfort, and movement, then report fit concerns to my supervisor.
