I help fit the device and ask the patient about pressure or discomfort.

advanced.situation: A supportive device has a loose joint before a patient's session. You are trained to maintain clinic devices and must decide whether it is ready to use.

options.text: I tighten the joint and check that the support holds its shape by hand.
I inspect the device, identify the damaged part, and ask the orthotist about repair.
I patch the loose support with clinic tape so treatment can continue today.
I follow the device specifications to repair the joint, then test stability before use.

basic.situation: You are entering a patient's first-visit measurements from a paper worksheet into the clinic system, with a therapist available to help.

options.text: I copy the last visit's basic details, then update today's date and symptoms.
I use the patient's initials and room number to find the right chart.
I enter measured findings, confirm identifiers, and save the note for therapist review.
I enter the patient details and measurements from today's paper worksheet.

advanced.situation: Your team wants more reliable progress notes across several therapists. You are asked to review records and suggest documentation standards.

options.text: I reuse last month's checklist to mark records that look complete at a glance.
I review a set of charts and list recurring gaps for the team to discuss.
I check recent notes for missing fields and remind colleagues about common requirements.
I sample records against shared criteria, track patterns, and update staff guidance.

basic.situation: A patient is starting a gentle manual exercise for stiffness. You are asked to guide the movement while a therapist directly supervises.

options.text: I use the familiar exercise sequence to keep the session moving on time.
I guide the exercise at the planned pace and check how the patient feels.
I monitor pain and form, then adjust the exercise within the treatment plan.
I repeat the demonstrated movement and ask the patient to follow my count.

advanced.situation: A student is learning to teach home exercises, while a support worker helps with clinic sessions. You are asked to guide and assess their work.

options.text: I let students copy my sequence while I keep the clinic schedule on track.
I set clear tasks for students and review their technique after each session.
I observe learners, give specific feedback, and tailor practice to demonstrated gaps.
I pair a student with a routine task and share a brief demonstration.

basic.situation: A patient is ready for a routine session. You are entering the prescribed treatment data and setting the equipment controls with a senior technologist nearby.

options.text: I reuse a recent setup and change the treatment fields for today's patient.
I match the prescribed site and settings to the patient record, then verify the console display.
I enter the prescription details and confirm the fields with my senior before treatment.
I enter the listed settings and ask a colleague to review the display.

advanced.situation: A custom immobilization support no longer fits after a patient's position changes. You are asked to prepare a revised device and check it before use.

options.text: I compare the immobilization design with the setup and ask physics staff about the fault.
I secure the worn support with clinic tape and use it for the planned session.
I adjust the support using its usual fitting points and retest patient comfort.
I remake the support to match the planned setup, then test its fit and stability.

basic.situation: A patient arrives for a routine session with a clear treatment prescription. You are positioning them on the table under supervision.

options.text: I position the patient as last time and make small adjustments by eye.
I align the patient to the prescribed marks and check position before setup continues.
I place the patient in a comfortable position and begin setting up the room.
I use the usual position and ask the patient whether it feels comfortable.

advanced.situation: A difficult case needs tumor localization during dosimetry, and the patient's position is hard to reproduce. You are assisting the clinical team with setup.

options.text: I check reproducible landmarks with the team and document setup limits for localization.
I use the clearest visible mark and proceed with the localization steps.
I ask the patient to hold still while the team completes its usual checks.
I share the positioning limits with the team and help reproduce the planned setup.

basic.situation: Two patients with similar names are listed for treatment. You are reviewing the chart and prescription with guidance before bringing one into the treatment room.

options.text: I review the chart and ask the patient to confirm their appointment details.
I use the listed appointment time to decide which patient is due.
I select the first matching name on the treatment list and prepare the room.
I compare the patient's identifiers and prescription with the chart before proceeding.

advanced.situation: A treatment record shows a dose entry that differs from the expected session total. You are reviewing delivery data and asked to flag any safety concerns.

options.text: I compare delivered doses with the plan, trace the discrepancy, and flag a protocol gap.
I check the dose entry with a colleague and record the difference for review.
I review the session entries and note any values outside the usual range.
I carry forward the previous session's dose total to complete the record.

basic.situation: A physician asks you to help prepare the technical details for a straightforward treatment plan. You have the patient's records and a physicist's guidance.

options.text: I complete the familiar planning fields so the case can move forward today.
I assemble the technical details against the prescription and flag unclear items for review.
I collect the requested measurements and send them to the physician for review.
I use the previous plan as a template and update the patient's details.

advanced.situation: A complex plan has an unresolved technical setup issue and the junior technologist is waiting for direction. You are coordinating technical input with the physicist and support staff.

options.text: I outline the setup concern and ask the physicist which details need review.
I coordinate technical tasks, track open issues, and brief the junior technologist on next steps.
I refer the open issue to support staff and continue reviewing other plan details.
I compare a similar case's setup and keep the planning team informed of differences.

basic.situation: A patient looks tense before a routine session and asks what sensations to expect. You can answer general questions and reinforce the physician's explanation.

options.text: I explain what the patient may experience and invite questions about their concerns.
I offer a brief explanation and help the patient settle into position.
I tell the patient that most people manage the session without much trouble.
I reassure the patient and repeat the main points from the physician's explanation.

advanced.situation: A student technologist is supporting a patient who reports increasing nausea during a session. You are supervising the student's patient checks and response.

options.text: I ask the student to record the symptom and update me after the session.
I demonstrate a calm response and ask the student to repeat the key questions.
I tell the student to use the usual reassurance while I finish the session.
I review the student's response, coach symptom checks, and agree how to escalate changes.

basic.situation: A patient needs a series of routine appointments, and you are entering the session record and arranging times with guidance from the scheduling team.

options.text: I enter the session details and check available times against the treatment plan.
I reserve the usual slot and fill in the visit record later.
I copy the prior appointment pattern and update the dates in the system.
I enter the session details and offer the patient the next available time.

advanced.situation: Several treatment records have incomplete dose entries, and appointment slots are going unused. You are asked to review records and suggest scheduling improvements.

options.text: I note incomplete entries, review appointment patterns with colleagues, and suggest where coordination could improve.
I reuse last month's appointment template and mark incomplete records for later review.
I sample records for required fields, map unused slots, and suggest schedule changes.
I check recent records and move appointments into the earliest open slots.

basic.situation: You are drafting a plan for a new patient who enjoys music and wants to socialise more. The senior therapist asks for a first draft before the afternoon review.

options.text: Ask her to choose between two activities before writing goals.
Use the assessment notes to suggest an activity and one goal.
Draft goals around her interests, assessment notes, and social aims.
Copy last week's plan and change the activity name for today's file.

advanced.situation: You are preparing a discharge plan for a patient who wants to join community activities, but transport and family support remain uncertain.

options.text: Map a chosen group, transport options, and support needs with the patient.
List nearby groups and leave transport details for the family to arrange.
Ask the patient to name a preferred group before the discharge meeting.
Record a familiar activity and mark the patient ready for discharge.

basic.situation: At a care meeting, the team discusses a patient's response to group games and plans next week's sessions. You are taking notes for the treatment team.

options.text: Record the patient's reactions and the team's agreed session changes.
Write that the patient enjoyed games and leave out the discussion.
Note the reactions and ask the lead therapist to confirm changes.
List the activities discussed and the patient's attendance for next week.

advanced.situation: Group attendance is steady, but several patients seem less engaged. You are facilitating a team discussion about whether the therapy programme is helping.

options.text: Keep the programme unchanged until attendance begins to fall.
Review reactions and progress reports, then agree a measurable programme adjustment.
Ask staff which games they prefer and use the most popular one.
Compare attendance notes and ask the team for one possible change.

basic.situation: During a supervised art session, a patient joins briefly, then watches from the side. The lead therapist asks you to record the patient's participation and reaction.

options.text: Record when the patient joined, watched, and responded to prompts.
Write down the activity and the patient's attendance for the chart.
Mark the patient as uninterested because they left the activity early.
Note that the patient watched and seemed unsure about joining.

advanced.situation: During a movement session, a patient becomes tired and anxious after the planned activity starts. You are supporting the lead therapist, who asks what you observe.

options.text: Continue the planned movement and record the patient's discomfort afterward.
Suggest a seated variation and share the patient's observed response.
Pause the activity and tell the lead therapist what you observed.
Offer a different game while the lead therapist checks the plan.

basic.situation: The lead therapist asks you to help run a familiar music session. A patient arrives late and seems unsure about joining the group.

options.text: Explain the session and invite the patient to join when ready.
Start the group song and leave the patient to follow along.
Ask another patient to show them the song while you prepare materials.
Welcome the patient, explain the activity, and support their first song.

advanced.situation: A patient with limited stamina is due to join a planned group session. The lead therapist asks you to lead while they monitor the patient's response.

options.text: Replace the group activity with quiet music for everyone present.
Shorten the session and ask the lead therapist to monitor closely.
Break the session into short rounds and check the patient's response between them.
Run the full session as planned and report any difficulty afterward.

basic.situation: You are assisting with an art activity, and a patient asks how to make a simple paper collage. The lead therapist is nearby and has approved the materials.

options.text: Hand over the materials and let the patient work it out.
Explain the steps slowly and ask which part they want to try.
Finish a sample collage first so the patient can copy it.
Demonstrate each collage step, then invite the patient to try.

advanced.situation: A patient with limited hand movement wants to join a painting activity, but the usual brush is difficult to hold. You are asked to adapt the instruction.

options.text: Show a larger grip and invite the patient to try one stroke.
Ask a colleague to choose a different activity for the patient.
Offer a larger grip and test a short brush stroke together.
Keep the usual brush and ask the patient to practise longer.

basic.situation: A patient says they miss having a hobby but feel unsure about joining a leisure group. You are encouraging them to try an activity they might enjoy.

options.text: Encourage them to try a group and ask what feels comfortable.
Ask what they enjoyed before and suggest one manageable activity.
Suggest a popular hobby and offer to find its session time.
Tell them to join the busiest group to meet people quickly.

advanced.situation: A patient wants to return to a leisure group but worries others will judge their changed abilities. You are discussing ways to help them re-engage.

options.text: Reassure them about the group and ask what support might help.
Say the group will welcome them and book their return session.
Suggest they wait until they feel more confident before returning.
Explore the concern and plan a small, patient-chosen first step.

basic.situation: You are assisting with a prescribed arterial blood gas test. The patient's notes include a recent change, and your supervising therapist asks you to review the information first.

options.text: Read the prescription and ask your supervisor about the noted change before proceeding.
Prepare equipment and check the prescription before beginning the test with supervision.
Use a previous patient's details to prepare this sample without checking current notes.
Check the prescription and notes, then review the test steps with your supervisor.

advanced.situation: A patient has breathlessness that does not match the initial test results. The physician asks which available pulmonary tests may help clarify the findings.

options.text: Ask the physician which additional test they want considered.
Repeat the same test and report whichever result appears clearer.
Review the results and suggest a suitable available test for physician approval.
List the available tests and ask the physician to select one.

basic.situation: A patient is due to practise a breathing exercise after treatment. The lead therapist asks you to demonstrate it, then support the patient's practice.

options.text: Tell the patient to copy another patient's breathing exercise.
Give the patient a leaflet and offer to answer questions afterward.
Demonstrate the breathing steps, then watch the patient practise them.
Explain each step and ask the patient to practise with you.

advanced.situation: A new staff member is learning a respiratory care procedure, and you are asked to demonstrate it while the lead therapist observes the training.

options.text: Explain each stage, demonstrate the procedure, then ask the trainee to describe each step.
Give written steps and watch the trainee's first attempt without guidance.
Demonstrate the procedure and invite the trainee to ask questions during practice.
Rush through the demonstration so the trainee can practise without discussion.

basic.situation: You are setting up a prescribed oxygen delivery device using the written instructions. The patient is waiting, and the lead therapist is available nearby.

options.text: Follow the written instructions and ask the lead therapist about unclear steps.
Prepare the device, then compare its settings with the written instructions.
Reuse the last patient's device settings to save setup time.
Check the order and device instructions before setting up the equipment.

advanced.situation: A patient’s prescribed therapy needs adjustment after their condition changes. You are reviewing the treatment requirements with the physician’s updated order.

options.text: Adjust the device based on the patient's description of yesterday's treatment.
Review the updated order and ask the physician about unclear parameters.
Keep the earlier settings because the patient used them successfully yesterday.
Match the updated order to the device settings and confirm any unclear parameters.

basic.situation: You are cleaning respiratory equipment after a session. A routine inspection shows a loose connection, and the lead therapist asks you to check its condition.

options.text: Return the device to storage because it worked during the session.
Inspect the connection and tell the lead therapist about the looseness.
Clean the device, inspect the connection, and report the fault for repair.
Clean the device and label it clearly for another check by staff next week.

advanced.situation: During an equipment visit, a respiratory device fails its function check before the patient’s next session. You are asked to assess the problem and arrange a response.

options.text: Restart the device and note whether the warning appears again.
Return the device to service because its warning cleared after restarting.
Remove the device from use and report the fault for urgent repair.
Check the connection and report the failed function check to the lead therapist.

basic.situation: A blood analysis result is available during a patient's therapy. The physician asks you to relay the result, and the lead therapist is also present.

options.text: Wait until the next team meeting to mention the available result.
Tell the family the result and ask them to pass it along.
Relay the result clearly and confirm the physician received it.
Relay the result to the physician and note the time shared.

advanced.situation: A patient's response to therapy changes, and nurses and physicians are reviewing the care plan. You are asked to contribute respiratory observations to the discussion.

options.text: Keep using the same approach because the previous session appeared to go well.
Ask the nurse to explain the change before sharing your respiratory observations with the team.
Share the response trend and ask how it relates to the care plan.
Report the latest response and ask what the team recommends as the next step.

basic.situation: A patient looks anxious before a prescribed respiratory treatment. The lead therapist asks you to explain what will happen and help the patient cooperate.

options.text: Explain the main steps and reassure the patient that staff are nearby.
Describe the next steps plainly and invite the patient to raise concerns.
Start the treatment while the patient is still asking questions.
Ask the family to explain the procedure while you prepare the equipment.

advanced.situation: During a respiratory emergency, the patient becomes unresponsive and the lead therapist directs you to assist with the team's response.

options.text: Ask a nearby colleague to find the lead therapist first.
Alert the emergency team and tell the lead therapist what changed.
Wait for the lead therapist to return before alerting anyone.
Call for the emergency team and begin your assigned resuscitation support.

basic.situation: You are administering a standard speech test, and the patient seems unsure about one instruction. What do you do?

options.text: Record the response as uncertain and continue according to the test procedure.
Rephrase the instruction in simpler words and note the change afterward.
Repeat the instruction clearly, then record the response using the test procedure.
Continue with the next item and mark this response as unclear.

advanced.situation: A patient has unusual speech changes and a complex medical history. Your test results do not fit the referral notes. What do you do?

options.text: Integrate the speech results and history, then document a cautious differential for discussion.
Compare the test findings with the medical history and document the mismatch for review.
Select the rare disorder matching one unusual symptom and record it as confirmed.
Repeat the main speech test and use the new result to guide your report.

basic.situation: A client with mild stuttering is ready for home practice. You are drafting a simple exercise programme with guidance. What do you do?

options.text: Set short daily practice using the agreed speech exercise and a simple progress note.
Use the clinic handout and ask the client to practise its exercises each day.
Ask the client to practise speaking more slowly whenever time allows.
Copy last week's exercises into the plan and keep the same schedule.

advanced.situation: A patient with severe swallowing difficulty is tiring during meals, and the current exercise plan is not helping. What do you do?

options.text: Reduce the exercise repetitions and keep the existing meal routine for now.
Pause the hardest exercise and note the patient's fatigue for the review.
Keep the plan unchanged until the next scheduled review to preserve consistency.
Review the swallowing findings and revise the plan around the patient's current tolerance.

basic.situation: During a routine review, a client completes more speech exercises than last week. Your checklist has space for brief notes. What do you do?

options.text: Write that the client improved because more exercises were completed this week.
Copy last week's checklist marks to save time during the review.
Record completed exercises against the checklist and note the client's reported effort.
Mark the exercises completed and tell the client to keep practising.

advanced.situation: A client's long-term records show gains in speech clarity but rising fatigue during sessions. Your current treatment is intensive. What do you do?

options.text: Keep the same treatment because speech clarity has improved across recent sessions.
Ask the client whether they prefer shorter sessions before changing the routine.
Review the trend in clarity and fatigue, then adjust session demands to fit both.
Reduce the session length and document the fatigue trend for the next review.

basic.situation: A patient is learning a communication app but struggles to find familiar requests during practice. What do you do?

options.text: Guide the patient through the app and practise finding a familiar request together.
Tell the patient to explore the app menu until the requests feel familiar.
Show the patient where common requests appear and let them try the app.
Select a request for the patient and record that the app was practised.

advanced.situation: A patient with limited hand movement cannot reliably select the usual communication buttons. You are asked to adapt their communication strategy. What do you do?

options.text: Enlarge the buttons and ask the patient to practise with the revised screen.
Move the most used requests to the first screen for easier access.
Keep the current layout and encourage the patient to practise more often.
Trial an easier access method with the patient and record reliable choices.

basic.situation: A client is practising a voice technique but keeps lifting their shoulders while breathing in. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the client the technique is fine and move on to another exercise.
Remind the client to relax their shoulders during the next practice round.
Let the client finish the exercise and discuss breathing at the next visit.
Demonstrate the breathing technique again, then have the client practise it with feedback.

advanced.situation: A client's family reports that communication breakdowns at home are causing distress. You are teaching coping strategies alongside communication techniques. What do you do?

options.text: Suggest that family members speak for the client when conversations become difficult.
Share a general communication tip sheet and invite questions after they read it.
Practise an agreed strategy for difficult conversations and discuss when to use it.
Ask the family to describe difficult moments, then practise a suitable repair strategy together.

basic.situation: After a routine appointment, you need to complete the patient's standard progress form. The client reported practising twice this week. What do you do?

options.text: Record the client's report in the progress form and complete the required fields.
Enter the reported practice and mark the usual exercises as completed.
Fill in the form using the usual template and include the practice report.
Write a brief note about practice and leave the remaining fields for later.

advanced.situation: At a case meeting, educators and clinic staff disagree about a patient's progress. You are preparing the meeting record and clinical report. What do you do?

options.text: Note the disagreement and ask staff to send written comments after the meeting.
Record each team's observations and agreed actions, separating evidence from interpretation.
Use the most positive account in the report to keep the plan moving forward.
Summarise the team's shared view and list the next review date in the report.

basic.situation: A new client wants to build stamina and has approval for light exercise. You are drafting a basic plan with a senior physiologist. What do you do?

options.text: Suggest regular walks and ask the client to choose a comfortable pace.
Use a standard intense circuit from another client's programme to save preparation time.
Draft a gradual walking plan with clear session lengths for the senior's review.
Recommend extra activity whenever the client feels energetic during the week.

advanced.situation: A client returning after a long illness tires quickly, and their recovery goals include strength and endurance. What do you do?

options.text: Build a staged programme around assessed capacity, goals, and suitable equipment.
Start with light treadmill sessions and increase time as the client improves.
Set demanding sessions so the client regains fitness as quickly as possible.
Use the usual recovery programme and adjust it after the first few weeks.

basic.situation: A client is scheduled for a body fat measurement, and a senior physiologist is present. The tape measure is ready. What do you do?

options.text: Estimate the result from the client's previous measurement and save time.
Explain the measurement, follow the clinic method, and record the result clearly.
Ask the client to hold the tape while you check the reading.
Take the measurement and enter the result on the client's form.

advanced.situation: Before a busy testing session, a spirometer reading seems inconsistent with its recent checks. You are responsible for equipment calibration and upkeep. What do you do?

options.text: Start testing with the current reading and compare results after the session.
Repeat the spirometer check and note whether the new reading matches.
Ask a colleague to check the spirometer while you prepare the room.
Check calibration against the device procedure and arrange service if readings stay inconsistent.

basic.situation: A client is using an exercise bicycle for the first time while a trainer is present. What do you do?

options.text: Explain the controls and ask the client to begin at an easy pace.
Demonstrate the bicycle setup and have the client practise adjusting it safely.
Tell the client to copy another participant's bicycle settings for today's session.
Point out the resistance control and stay nearby during the first few minutes.

advanced.situation: You are training staff to lead a high-risk group exercise class. One trainee rushes the equipment demonstration while participants look uncertain. What do you do?

options.text: Model a paced demonstration, then coach the trainee to check each participant's understanding.
Remind the trainee to slow down and invite participant questions during class.
Ask the group to follow the trainee's demonstration and keep the class moving.
Let the trainee finish the class and provide general feedback afterward.

basic.situation: A new client arrives for an exercise assessment and seems unsure about sharing their medical history. You have a standard interview checklist. What do you do?

options.text: Skip the health questions and focus on the client's exercise goals today.
Ask the client to complete the checklist alone before you discuss their goals.
Work through the checklist and note any questions the client declines to answer.
Explain why the history matters, then use the checklist to record the client's answers.

advanced.situation: A group exercise trainee has several participants struggling with the routine, but their testing records show mixed results. You are reviewing staff performance. What do you do?

options.text: Rate the trainee poorly based on the participants' difficulty and file the result.
Check the records and ask the trainee how the group responded to the routine.
Review the testing records and observe the trainee's cues before giving focused feedback.
Repeat the participant tests before deciding whether the trainee needs feedback.

basic.situation: A client with a desk-based routine asks how to add more movement to ordinary days. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the client to begin strenuous daily workouts to improve fitness quickly.
Suggest a realistic walking break and help the client fit it into their routine.
Share a list of common ways to be more active during the day.
Recommend taking short walks during the week and see how it goes.

advanced.situation: An athlete reports unusual breathlessness during training and asks whether a stress test is needed. You can recommend diagnostic procedures. What do you do?

options.text: Explain that breathlessness can occur during training and suggest tracking it.
Recommend a stress test based on the breathlessness and document the request.
Record when breathlessness occurs and ask the athlete to discuss it with their clinician.
Discuss the symptoms and recommend clinical review to determine suitable testing.

basic.situation: During a supervised exercise session, a participant becomes dizzy and needs help. What do you do?

options.text: Offer water and encourage the participant to finish the session slowly.
Stop the activity, alert the supervising clinician, and provide care within your training.
Pause the session and wait nearby to see whether the dizziness passes.
Help the participant sit down and ask how they are feeling.

advanced.situation: You are presenting exercise research at a professional meeting, and an audience member questions how the findings apply to rehabilitation clients. What do you do?

options.text: Explain the study limits and relate findings to the rehabilitation group cautiously.
Read the key results again and offer to share the research paper afterward.
Summarise the main findings and invite the audience to discuss possible applications.
Present the findings as proof that the same programme will help rehabilitation clients.

basic.situation: A client at a community centre says they are unsure what to make in today's session. You have time to agree one simple goal together.

options.text: Reuse last week's collage plan and ask whether the client wants to continue.
Suggest a drawing goal based on the referral, then check the client's interest.
Agree one client-chosen art goal and document how the session will address it.
Ask the client which art activity feels useful, then record one agreed session goal.

advanced.situation: A client has become withdrawn during open-ended painting, while their treatment plan includes emotional expression and grounding. You are preparing their next individual session.

options.text: Adapt the plan around the client's goals, using grounding before open-ended painting.
Use the referral diagnosis to select a familiar exercise and record expected outcomes.
Keep the usual art sequence and add a brief check-in about feelings.
Combine a client-chosen art task with a counseling prompt tied to agreed goals.

basic.situation: During a quiet drawing session, a client pauses and says their picture feels different from last week. You have time to talk with them.

options.text: Tell the client the picture looks more confident than last week's work.
Praise the finished drawing and move on to the next activity.
Ask what feels different and reflect the progress the client describes.
Invite the client to describe one part of the picture that matters.

advanced.situation: A shelter asks you to explain art therapy to staff who may refer clients. You are leading a short information session and have limited time for questions.

options.text: Explain the service, referral route, and how staff can discuss it with clients.
Share a handout about art materials and collect staff names for follow-up.
Describe the referral process, client choice, and limits of what the session can promise.
Present a few successful art activities and invite questions at the end.

basic.situation: A new client's file has little detail about their communication needs. You are preparing an initial art session and can ask the client about their preferences.

options.text: Ask the client about preferred materials and note their responses for planning.
Review the file, then ask the client how they prefer to communicate.
Use the referral summary to choose a familiar activity for the first session.
Begin with a simple drawing task and observe how the client responds.

advanced.situation: After several sessions, a client's drawings and participation have changed, but their written goals remain the same. You need to assess current needs before planning further.

options.text: Compare recent work and observations with goals, then ask about the changes.
Ask the client whether the new drawings feel different from earlier work.
Interpret the darker colours as evidence that the client's mood has worsened.
Review the drawings alongside session notes and note possible changes in functioning.

basic.situation: A client stops painting when another participant enters the room, then resumes after a pause. You are completing the session note before the next appointment.

options.text: Mark the session as productive because the client finished their artwork.
Note the client's participation and mention that the artwork was completed.
Record the interruption, the client's pause, and their return to painting.
Write that the client was distracted but completed the painting.

advanced.situation: Across a month, a client attends regularly but speaks less and leaves several artworks unfinished. Your team asks whether the current approach is meeting their goals.

options.text: Compare attendance, session notes, and client feedback before recommending a plan review.
Ask the client about participation and share the answer with the team.
Review notes and unfinished work, then discuss possible adjustments with the team.
Recommend continuing the current approach because the client attends regularly.

basic.situation: A client wants to explore texture but tires easily when handling tools. You are preparing materials for a short session in a shared therapy room.

options.text: Use small beads because they provide several interesting textures to explore.
Offer soft clay and large tools, then check which feels manageable.
Set out the centre's usual paint and brushes for the session.
Choose soft clay and a few tools suited to the client's grip.

advanced.situation: Several clients need accessible materials for a group project, but the supply cupboard has limited adaptive tools. You are asked to recommend what to purchase within a modest budget.

options.text: Buy extra modelling clay and wider brushes to broaden material choices.
Order the most popular adaptive tools from the catalogue for the group.
Ask the team about client needs, then recommend versatile grips and stable supports.
List the missing grips and supports, then request quotes for suitable options.

basic.situation: A case manager asks for your assessment findings before a planning meeting. The client has agreed that relevant observations can be shared with the team.

options.text: Tell the case manager verbally that the client seems more settled.
Share key observations and describe how they relate to the client's goals.
Send a concise summary of observed needs and related recommendations to the team.
Forward the full session notes so the case manager has more detail.

advanced.situation: A practicum student is preparing clay for a client group but is unsure how to support safe, independent use. You are responsible for guiding the student during the session.

options.text: Demonstrate setup, ask the student to practise, and observe their support with clients.
Ask an experienced volunteer to help the student during the activity.
Give the student a written clay activity and let them lead the group.
Show the student how to prepare clay and explain the group's activity.

basic.situation: A client enjoys familiar songs but tires during long sessions. You are helping set a goal and plan the pacing for their next music therapy visit.

options.text: Set a longer music session so the client can build endurance through practice.
Suggest a shorter familiar-song session and check whether that goal suits them.
Use the last session's song list and repeat its order for pacing.
Ask which musical activity matters to the client and agree one achievable goal.

advanced.situation: A client with limited movement becomes more engaged when choosing songs, while the team wants progress on communication and coordination. You are revising their music therapy plan.

options.text: Use client-selected songs for communication turns and track responses over sessions.
Build song choice into short turn-taking and movement tasks tied to both goals.
Choose familiar songs with a steady beat to practise coordination during sessions.
Keep the current song routine and add extra movement practice at the end.

basic.situation: A client's referral mentions sound sensitivity, but gives little detail about its effect in sessions. You are preparing an initial assessment and can speak with the client.

options.text: Review the referral, then ask which sounds feel comfortable or difficult.
Use a familiar song to see whether the client stays engaged.
Start with several instruments and note which ones attract the client's attention.
Ask the client about sound preferences and record their examples for planning.

advanced.situation: A client communicates inconsistently during music sessions, and the standard rating form misses their responses. You are asked to recommend a way to assess their communication needs.

options.text: Use the standard form and infer unanswered items from the client's behaviour.
Review session notes and recommend a second observation in a familiar activity.
Adapt response choices with the team, then compare observations across familiar activities.
Ask a family member to describe communication at home and share examples.

basic.situation: A client asks to join a simple greeting song, but loses the beat when you play guitar. You can adjust your accompaniment during the session.

options.text: Play the guitar more softly and invite the client to sing along.
Keep the usual guitar tempo so the client hears a steady pattern.
Switch to a shaker and let the client follow its pulse.
Slow the guitar pattern and sing the greeting clearly for the client.

advanced.situation: A client with limited hand movement wants to take part in an improvisation, but a standard drum is hard to reach. You have several instruments and visual aids available.

options.text: Offer a hand-held shaker and invite the client to choose when to play.
Move the drum closer and use a visual cue for starting together.
Continue the planned guitar improvisation while the client listens and responds.
Position an accessible drum and improvise at the client's pace, following their cues.

basic.situation: A client appears tense during a music activity and relaxes when a slower song begins. You are exploring their responses to different musical experiences.

options.text: Offer another slow song and ask what changes the client notices.
Pause the music and ask whether the client wants to end the activity.
Note the client's response and offer a choice between two slower songs.
Continue the faster playlist to see whether the client adjusts over time.

advanced.situation: During a session, a client becomes unsteady and says they feel faint. You are the therapist in the room, and the centre's emergency procedure is posted nearby.

options.text: Offer water and wait a few minutes to see whether the feeling passes.
Stop the activity, support the client safely, and follow the centre's emergency procedure.
Move nearby instruments aside and ask the client to describe their symptoms.
Help the client sit safely and call the designated staff member for support.

basic.situation: A client smiled during a familiar song and turned away during a louder rhythm. You are writing a progress note before the next session.

options.text: Write that the client enjoyed music and participated well today.
Record the songs, observed responses, and timing in the progress note.
Mark the session as positive because the client smiled during a song.
Note the client's smile and turn away, then mention both activities.

advanced.situation: Your team is considering a new music activity, and a recent research summary may be relevant. You are asked to help decide whether it fits your clients' needs.

options.text: Review the study's population and methods, then discuss fit with current practice.
Adopt the activity because the summary reports encouraging results for participants.
Summarize the findings and note questions about applying them with your clients.
Ask a colleague whether they have tried the activity with similar clients.

basic.situation: A client says a familiar song helped them feel calmer after a difficult morning. You have a moment to acknowledge their response and build rapport.

options.text: Ask what in the song helped and reflect the client's own observation.
Tell the client that music usually helps people feel more settled.
Praise the client's song choice and ask whether they want another track.
Thank the client for sharing and note that they seemed calmer afterward.

advanced.situation: A new intern will lead part of a group, and a client's communication goal depends on coordinated support from the speech therapist. You are helping the team prepare.

options.text: Give the intern last month's activity sheet and ask them to lead it.
Coordinate the activity with the therapist, then coach and observe the intern's delivery.
Ask the therapist for suggestions and let the intern choose an activity.
Plan a shared music activity with the therapist and brief the intern beforehand.

basic.situation: A dog has a small paw wound, and the veterinarian asks you to clean and dress it while they supervise. What do you do?

options.text: Confirm the cleaning plan with the veterinarian, dress the wound, and observe the dog's response.
Rinse the paw, cover it with gauze, and advise the owner to keep it dry.
Clean the wound as directed, apply the dressing, and record the care provided.
Follow the clinic's routine dressing method, then continue with the next waiting animal.

advanced.situation: A cat with a suspected abdominal injury is deteriorating, and imaging suggests internal bleeding. You are the attending veterinarian. What do you do?

options.text: Proceed with the familiar abdominal approach and adapt once the cat is open.
Reassess stability and imaging, set an operative priority, and brief the team on contingencies.
Ask a colleague to review the images while you prepare theatre and the anaesthetic.
Stabilize the cat, review the findings, and prepare for surgery with the available team.

basic.situation: A first-time dog owner asks how often to wash a puppy's bedding and where to put its food bowl. What do you do?

options.text: Explain a simple bedding routine and food bowl placement, then invite questions.
Recommend weekly bedding washes and keeping food apart from the puppy's toilet area.
Copy a neighbour's routine, since puppies often have similar daily needs.
Change bedding daily and place the food bowl near the puppy's bed.

advanced.situation: A client asks whether to euthanize an elderly dog whose pain is hard to control. A new staff member gives conflicting advice nearby. What do you do?

options.text: Describe the likely costs and suggest a decision before the next appointment.
Invite the client to describe the dog's comfort and priorities, then discuss care choices calmly.
Explain the treatment choices and ask the client to decide after speaking with family.
Repeat the staff member's view so the client receives one clear recommendation.

basic.situation: A rabbit arrives with reduced appetite. Your senior asks you to perform its basic physical check and report what you find. What do you do?

options.text: Check the rabbit's weight and general signs, then share your findings with the senior.
Complete the clinic's basic check, note changes, and promptly report them to the senior.
Offer a treat to see if the rabbit eats, then reassure the owner if it does.
Look at its coat and ask the owner when it last ate before reporting back.

advanced.situation: A dairy herd has uneven body condition before breeding, and the farm manager asks you to revise its nutrition and reproduction plan. What do you do?

options.text: Adjust the ration for the thinner animals and keep the breeding calendar unchanged.
Use last season's ration and breeding schedule as the starting plan for this herd.
Check recent feed and breeding notes before suggesting a ration change to the manager.
Review herd condition and breeding records, then set nutrition targets and review dates.

basic.situation: A dog needs a radiograph of its front leg. Your supervisor asks you to set up the room and operate the machine under direct supervision. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the owner to hold the dog while taking a quick side-view image.
Position the plate and capture the requested image while your supervisor watches.
Reuse settings from a previous dog's image to save room setup time.
Set the plate after checking positioning with your supervisor, then take the guided image.

advanced.situation: A valuable breeding goat dies unexpectedly, and the owner asks you to investigate the cause before the herd is moved. What do you do?

options.text: Examine the main organs, note visible changes, and report a likely cause to the owner.
Document the findings, collect relevant samples, and interpret them with the case history.
Focus on the most abnormal organ and tell the owner that it explains the death.
Photograph the visible changes and ask the owner about recent feed changes.

basic.situation: Two clients request the same available appointment time, and one is waiting at reception. You are helping manage the clinic schedule. What do you do?

options.text: Check urgency and availability, offer suitable alternatives, and update the schedule clearly.
Book both clients into the slot and let the veterinarian sort out the overlap.
Offer the waiting client the slot and move the other request to the next opening.
Give the slot to the client who called first and note the other request.

advanced.situation: The clinic's monthly costs are rising, and the team has requested time for continuing education. You help manage the budget and staff development. What do you do?

options.text: Check recent spending, then ask staff which course should receive the available funds.
Review spending and training needs, then propose a budget that protects priority learning.
Pause new training requests and monitor supply costs for another month.
Approve the requested courses and reduce routine supply orders to cover the cost.

basic.situation: A dog needs a urine sample for examination, and your senior asks you to collect it while they supervise. What do you do?

options.text: Confirm the collection method, label the sample, and pass it to your senior for review.
Ask the owner to bring a sample from home at the next visit.
Use a container from the treatment room and write the dog's name afterward.
Collect a fresh sample, label it, and place it in the clinic's sample area.

advanced.situation: Several farm workers ask how to reduce infection risk after a suspected animal disease case. You are helping prepare public guidance. What do you do?

options.text: Share general handwashing and cleaning advice with the workers at the farm.
Suggest protective clothing and ask workers to avoid the affected pen for now.
Explain practical hygiene steps, identify exposure concerns, and direct workers to local health advice.
Tell workers the infection is unlikely to affect people and resume normal handling.

basic.situation: You are taking vital signs on a medical ward. Your patient's temperature is 38.4°C, up from 37.2°C at the last round, and he says he feels cold.

options.text: Give him a blanket for the chills and retake his temperature at the next round.
Recheck his temperature, add pulse and breathing, then tell the senior nurse all the readings.
Chart the new temperature and tell the senior nurse it has risen since the last round.
Note the reading as a likely thermometer fault, since he is chatting well, and continue your round.

advanced.situation: A patient after surgery has had his blood pressure drift down over three readings while his pulse rises and his urine output is low. Each reading alone looks borderline.

options.text: Encourage him to drink more fluids and recheck his blood pressure at the next scheduled time.
Call the doctor with the latest blood pressure and pulse readings and wait for instructions.
Check observations more often and call the doctor, reporting the trend and low urine output.
Chart each reading, since none is below the ward's alert level, and keep the usual schedule.

basic.situation: You are giving the morning oral medicines on a medical ward. A patient says he has not taken the new tablet before and looks worried about it.

options.text: Verify the order and his identity, explain the purpose, give it, and name effects to report.
Reassure him that many patients take it, then give the tablet from the labelled pack.
Check the order and wristband, give the tablet, and watch him for reactions during your round.
Check the order and wristband, give the tablet, and note his worry for the doctor.

advanced.situation: An hour after a new antibiotic dose, your patient is vomiting and has a new rash on his chest. A junior colleague asks whether she should give the next scheduled dose.

options.text: Tell her to check the allergy record and give the dose if none is listed.
Tell her to hold the dose, check his breathing and rash, and call the doctor together.
Delay the dose by a few hours and see whether the rash fades on its own.
Hold the next dose and call the doctor to report the rash and the vomiting.

basic.situation: You are preparing a patient for an endoscopy booked this morning. The porter is about to arrive, and you notice the patient had breakfast at 6am despite the fasting instruction.

options.text: Report the breakfast to the nurse in charge so the endoscopy team can decide on timing.
Write the breakfast time on the checklist and tell the endoscopy staff when he reaches them.
Send him as booked, since cancelling would waste the slot and delay other patients.
Ask how much he ate and send him as booked if it was a small meal.

advanced.situation: The doctor wants a stroke patient walking today, the physiotherapist says he is too weak, and his family wants him to rest. You know his condition best.

options.text: Give both your observations of his fatigue and vital signs, and propose a short supervised trial.
Keep him in bed as the family asked, since they know his habits and may complain.
Follow the doctor's order and mobilise him, as the doctor is responsible for the treatment plan.
Ask the doctor and physiotherapist to discuss it, then update the family on the outcome.

basic.situation: At a school health screening, a mother tells you her son often coughs at night. She mentions the family has just moved into a damp flat.

options.text: Reassure her that damp flats cause coughs in many children and it should pass soon.
Ask when the cough began, how often it wakes him, and what the flat is like.
Tell the mother to bring him to the clinic and leave the questions to the doctor.
Note when the cough began and how often it wakes him, then update the senior nurse.

advanced.situation: Your clinic serves a kampung with many older residents and a nearby workers' hostel. Your supervisor asks you to help plan a community health needs assessment. You must decide how to begin.

options.text: Start health talks on diabetes and blood pressure, since older residents commonly have both.
Review the clinic records, then ask residents, hostel workers and the village head about health concerns.
Use state-level health statistics to pick the main problems, then draft the checklist for approval.
Reuse the checklist from a neighbouring clinic's assessment, since it worked well and saves time.

basic.situation: You are giving a prepared talk on preventing dengue at the clinic. An older woman says she keeps water in open pails because the tap supply is often cut.

options.text: Acknowledge the water cuts, then show her how to cover the pails and scrub them weekly.
Continue the talk as scripted and advise her to avoid keeping water in open containers.
Tell her fogging by the health office controls mosquitoes, so the pails matter less.
Tell her to cover the pails and give her the dengue leaflet to read at home.

advanced.situation: Few working-age patients attend your clinic's diabetes talks, though many have poor blood sugar control. Your supervisor lets you redesign the programme.

options.text: Keep the talks for the retirees, since steady attendance looks good in the monthly report.
Advertise the existing talks more widely with posters and messages to every patient on the register.
Ask working-age patients what suits them, pilot a short evening session, and compare blood sugar results.
Make the talk longer with more detailed slides, so working patients see more value.

basic.situation: You took a patient's blood pressure and pulse at 2pm, but were called away before charting. It is now 3.30pm and you cannot recall the exact numbers.

options.text: Write the numbers you remember against 2pm and add a note that you were called away.
Retake the readings now, chart them at the current time, and note the missed 2pm entry.
Copy the 10am readings into the 2pm slot, since the patient still looks stable.
Retake the readings and chart them at the current time, then carry on with your tasks.

advanced.situation: You supervise a healthcare assistant on your ward. You notice she fills in the fluid intake chart at shift start, and today's figures differ from what patients actually drank.

options.text: Post a reminder on the ward notice board that staff should chart after each task.
Explain to her why charting follows each task and check her entries again next week.
Have her amend today's chart to match actual intake, and explain charting after each task.
Adjust her entries yourself to typical intake levels so the totals look consistent today.

basic.situation: A patient newly admitted with pneumonia asks what the prescribed treatment is for. Your senior nurse asks you to explain the basics. What do you do?

options.text: Describe the treatment purpose and invite the patient to ask questions afterward.
Read the treatment name aloud and tell the patient it is routine for pneumonia.
Ask the patient to wait until the doctor comes by to explain the treatment.
Explain the treatment in plain language, then ask what the patient wants clarified.

advanced.situation: A patient is being discharged with several follow-up needs, and staff give families inconsistent instructions. You are asked to improve how the team explains transitions. What do you do?

options.text: Send families home with the current leaflet and let each nurse explain it their way.
Remind staff to explain referrals and give families the clinic contact number.
Build a shared discharge guide with referral steps, teach staff its use, and gather feedback.
Ask senior nurses to discuss the discharge problems at the next meeting.

basic.situation: A patient receiving an intravenous infusion reports new itching, and you notice a mild rash. Your senior nurse is nearby. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the patient whether the itching feels serious before taking further steps.
Pause and assess the patient's response, then alert the senior nurse with your findings.
Record the itching and wait for the next scheduled observation round.
Tell the senior nurse about the rash and check the patient's vital signs.

advanced.situation: A monitored patient has subtle new changes on the cardiac trace and is less responsive, though the blood pressure remains stable. What do you do?

options.text: Ask another nurse to review the trace while you observe the patient.
Keep the current monitoring interval since the blood pressure is still stable.
Repeat the vital signs and share the new readings with the medical team.
Reassess the patient and trace, compare trends, and report the changes with urgency.

basic.situation: An older patient recovering from illness seems newly confused, and you are asked to check whether this is a change from their usual state. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the patient simple questions and tell your mentor how they respond.
Assume the confusion is part of ageing and continue the usual care routine.
Check the patient's recent notes and observations, then tell your mentor what changed.
Ask a family member whether the patient has seemed different today.

advanced.situation: Staff interpret a deterioration score differently across shifts, and a recent protocol update may help. You are asked to contribute to a shared assessment protocol. What do you do?

options.text: Review current guidance and shift examples, then draft shared criteria for team discussion.
Ask each shift to use familiar scoring while the shared draft takes shape.
Adopt the updated score format and invite staff feedback during tomorrow's shift.
Summarize updated guidance and propose consistent escalation criteria for a team discussion.

basic.situation: A patient with a bleeding forearm wound arrives in the acute care area, and your senior asks you to assist with initial care. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the patient to hold a cloth over the wound while you finish another task.
Apply pressure with suitable dressings, monitor the patient, and update your senior.
Check whether the patient can move their fingers before choosing a dressing.
Place a clean dressing over the wound and tell your senior when it is secure.

advanced.situation: A deteriorating patient needs coordinated urgent care, but the medical and respiratory teams disagree about the next step. You are the charge nurse. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the medical team to lead while you update the patient's family about progress.
Bring teams together to compare findings and agree on coordinated next actions.
Ask both teams to continue assessments and report findings at an agreed time.
Share the patient's changes, clarify team roles, and coordinate a joint care plan.

basic.situation: A patient recovering from surgery is uncomfortable, and their family asks what support they can provide. Your senior nurse asks you to assess their needs. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the family to keep the patient calm and wait for the next review.
Ask the patient about comfort and the family about support needs, then report both.
Explain that rest helps recovery and ask the family to speak with the doctor later.
Ask the patient to rate their discomfort and note the response for your senior.

advanced.situation: A patient may benefit from a costly therapy with uncertain gains, and the team asks you to compare the likely benefits, risks, and care burden. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the team to defer its decision until more outcome information is available.
Recommend the therapy because the patient has few other treatment choices.
Review the therapy's cost and known risks, then summarize them for the team.
Compare likely function, risks, costs, and patient priorities before presenting options to the team.

basic.situation: You set up a catheter drainage bag and record the patient's care, but the displayed output seems lower than expected. What do you do?

options.text: Ask another nurse to look at the bag while you finish your notes.
Inspect the tubing for a kink, then document the output and inform your senior.
Record the lower output and tell your senior during the next round.
Check the setup and patient, record the finding, and report the change to your senior.

advanced.situation: Several records omit patient responses after treatment changes, while an invasive device alarm has recurred on your shift. You are asked to help address both concerns. What do you do?

options.text: Clear the alarm and complete the missing response fields from memory after the shift.
Assess the alarm with the patient, document the response, and review records for recurring gaps.
Check the device connections and flag incomplete records for the nurse in charge.
Write a reminder for staff to record treatment responses and ask engineering about the alarm.

basic.situation: A patient reports poor sleep and new dizziness during intake. You need to assess her mental and physical status.

options.text: You ask about her symptom timeline and record her vital signs.
You ask about her mood and check her vital signs before proceeding.
You compare her physical findings with her symptoms and document any urgent changes.
You attribute the dizziness to anxiety and continue with the intake questions.

advanced.situation: A patient with a history of panic attacks arrives confused and shaky after missing lunch. You need to distinguish physical causes from psychological symptoms.

options.text: You record her distress as a familiar panic episode and continue the review.
You discuss her usual coping plan and note that she missed lunch.
You explore the panic symptoms and ask when she last ate.
You check orientation, medication timing, and physical findings before interpreting the distress.

basic.situation: A patient describes persistent low mood, poor sleep, and missed work. You need to assess whether the symptoms fit a common mental health condition.

options.text: You ask about duration, daily impact, and other symptoms before forming an impression.
You label the symptoms as depression based on the patient's low mood.
You focus on the sleep complaint and suggest a routine follow-up discussion.
You review mood and sleep symptoms, then record a provisional impression.

advanced.situation: Several clinics report more crisis calls from isolated residents, while staff capacity is limited. You are asked to help evaluate a community response program.

options.text: You recommend adding more crisis coverage based on the latest reports.
You keep the current approach and share the reports at the next meeting.
You collect staff views about the recent crisis calls and response workload.
You compare call patterns, response times, and follow-up needs across participating clinics.

basic.situation: A patient is due for an injection but says the last dose caused dizziness. You need to administer medication safely.

options.text: You check the medication record and ask whether the dizziness continues.
You give the scheduled injection and ask the patient to report symptoms later.
You ask when the dizziness began and check the medication record.
You confirm the medication, dose, and patient's current symptoms before giving it.

advanced.situation: A patient reports good symptom control but has missed several doses and developed nausea after a recent prescription change. You can prescribe within your agreement.

options.text: You ask about nausea and suggest taking the medication with food.
You review adherence, response, and nausea before adjusting the prescription.
You renew the current prescription because the patient reports good control.
You discuss missed doses and check the latest medication list.

basic.situation: A patient with acute anxiety becomes tearful during an individual session and says work feels unmanageable. You need to continue the session.

options.text: You move to the prepared coping worksheet to keep the session on track.
You reassure her that many people feel anxious during stressful periods.
You invite her to describe the hardest moment and explore her immediate needs.
You ask what has helped her manage similar work stress before.

advanced.situation: During family therapy for a chronic condition, relatives disagree about a patient's care and speak over one another. You need to guide the session.

options.text: You ask the family to settle on one plan before the session ends.
You summarize the disagreement and ask the family to lower their voices.
You hear from the patient's main caregiver before discussing the disagreement.
You ask each relative to describe their concern and identify shared care goals.

basic.situation: A patient gives a brief account of past treatment but cannot recall dates. You need to document her medical and psychological history.

options.text: You separate confirmed details from uncertain dates and ask focused follow-up questions.
You enter approximate dates so the history reads smoothly for the next visit.
You record her account and mark uncertain dates for later clarification.
You note the missing dates and ask her to bring old records.

advanced.situation: A patient with several chronic conditions asks how a new treatment fits with her existing medicines. You need to explain the plan and record the discussion.

options.text: You review the written plan, address her main question, and record the discussion.
You share the leaflet, discuss its key points, and note her response.
You connect the treatment to her medicines, invite questions, and document her understanding.
You explain the treatment's purpose and note how her other conditions may affect it.

basic.situation: A patient needs care beyond your service's scope after assessment. You need to arrange a referral to a suitable specialist.

options.text: You identify a suitable specialist and ask the patient to book an appointment.
You suggest the patient contact a specialist when she feels ready.
You explain the referral reason and send relevant assessment details to the specialist.
You discuss the referral with the patient and document her preference.

advanced.situation: A patient's unusual symptoms do not fit the expected response to treatment, and the next step is unclear. You need input from a psychiatrist.

options.text: You continue the current plan and bring the case to the next team review.
You share the unusual symptoms and ask the psychiatrist for guidance.
You send the latest notes and request the psychiatrist's view on treatment.
You present the timeline, findings, and treatment response when consulting the psychiatrist.

basic.situation: During a routine check, a patient's fluid output is lower than earlier in the shift. You need to monitor intake and output.

options.text: You verify the output, compare it with prior readings, and report the change.
You total the intake and output, then record the change for review.
You recheck the collection bag and ask the patient about recent fluids.
You estimate the output from the collection bag and finish the chart.

advanced.situation: A ventilated patient develops a rising temperature, falling blood pressure, and increasing oxygen needs. You need to identify possible deterioration and start appropriate interventions.

options.text: You document the readings and wait for the next scheduled medical review.
You report the blood pressure change and prepare the next observation set.
You check the oxygen setup and ask another nurse to review the readings.
You repeat key observations, alert the team, and follow the sepsis response process.

basic.situation: You are assigned to set up a cardiac monitor for a new patient and have supervision available.

options.text: You connect the leads and confirm the displayed heart rate with your supervisor.
You use the previous patient's saved monitor settings to save setup time.
You attach the leads and check that the screen shows a tracing.
You connect the leads, check the display, and confirm alarms with your supervisor.

advanced.situation: A ventilator alarm recurs after you check the tubing, and the display readings fluctuate. You need to identify possible equipment malfunction and handle the device safely.

options.text: You switch to approved backup equipment, support the patient, and report the fault.
You report the recurring alarm and request an equipment safety check.
You silence the alarm and continue monitoring the fluctuating ventilator readings.
You recheck tubing connections and record when the alarm returns.

basic.situation: A specimen is needed for a patient's laboratory test, and you have the collection instructions and supervision available.

options.text: You label the tube from the room list before collecting the sample.
You confirm the patient's identity, collect the sample, and label it at bedside.
You check the instructions and ask your supervisor to confirm the collection method.
You collect the sample and check the label against the patient's chart.

advanced.situation: A physician asks you to assist with an intubation while the patient's oxygen level is falling. You need to support the procedure within your role.

options.text: You begin handing instruments from the tray while the team gathers.
You prepare the airway equipment and confirm the team is ready.
You check the equipment list and ask the physician which item is needed first.
You prepare the requested airway equipment and track the patient's oxygen response.

basic.situation: After a patient assessment, you need to record the history and findings for the next shift.

options.text: You enter the main symptoms and assessment findings in the patient's record.
You record the patient's account and distinguish reported symptoms from observed findings.
You copy the previous history forward and update the patient's current complaint.
You note the assessment findings and leave the history for later charting.

advanced.situation: A patient's condition changes after an intervention, prompting a revised care plan. You need to document the intervention, outcome, and revision for the next team.

options.text: You link the intervention, observed outcome, and reason for the revised plan.
You document the intervention and enter the new care plan for handover.
You note the outcome and tell the next nurse about the plan revision.
You replace the old plan with the new one to keep the chart current.

basic.situation: An older patient becomes restless at night and says the ward feels unfamiliar. You need to identify age-specific needs and adapt care.

options.text: You ask about her sleep routine and adapt care with the team.
You document her restlessness and ask the day team to review possible causes.
You keep the standard night routine for consistent care across the ward.
You reassure her and dim the lights in her room.

advanced.situation: A critically ill patient is improving, but the family reports exhaustion and difficulty coping. You need to assess their needs and coordinate care planning.

options.text: You give them the unit information sheet and offer a later check-in.
You assess coping and support needs, then coordinate a care discussion with the team.
You ask the family what support would help and share their concerns.
You reassure them that the patient is improving and focus on clinical tasks.

basic.situation: A family member is distressed after a difficult update and asks what will happen next. You need to provide emotional support within your role.

options.text: You offer a quiet place and ask whether they want another relative called.
You listen and tell them the nurse in charge can answer care questions.
You listen, acknowledge their distress, and explain the next care step.
You reassure them the patient will likely improve and return to your tasks.

advanced.situation: New nurses report inconsistent understanding of alarm checks, and near misses have been discussed at handover. You are asked to help improve staff education.

options.text: You deliver a refresher on alarm checks and collect attendance records.
You remind staff to check alarms during handover and continue the current teaching.
You review staff feedback and near misses, then assess whether teaching changes practice.
You ask experienced nurses to demonstrate alarm checks during a shift.

basic.situation: A newly admitted patient on your specialty ward seems unusually tired. You have time for a brief assessment before rounds.

options.text: Ask about the fatigue, check the observations, and note what needs follow-up.
Record the patient's own description and compare it with today's routine observations.
Ask focused questions, check current observations, and flag changes against the patient's baseline.
Use yesterday's chart as your main guide and complete the standard assessment fields.

advanced.situation: A complex patient has worsening symptoms, mixed test results, and a new research finding relevant to treatment. The care team needs an updated plan.

options.text: Review the findings with the care team and revise goals around the patient's response.
Revise the plan around the patient's trends, test results, and relevant evidence, then set review measures.
Use the latest test result to adjust the plan and explain the change at rounds.
Apply the new finding to the plan and keep the existing review date.

basic.situation: A patient is unsure how to follow a new care routine after discharge. You are helping deliver a supervised education session.

options.text: Give the patient the handout and move on to the next scheduled session.
Explain the routine with the ward handout and ask what questions remain.
Ask what feels unclear, explain the routine, and invite the patient to describe it back.
Read the handout aloud and let the patient take it home for reference.

advanced.situation: Patients on your unit often misunderstand a new treatment routine. You are asked to design education and check whether it works.

options.text: Build sessions around common questions and compare patient teach-back before and after.
Prepare a detailed session, share it with staff, and collect attendance totals.
Reuse the existing slides and report how many patients attended each session.
Use a short lesson and ask patients whether it was helpful afterward.

basic.situation: During a busy shift, you prepare a dressing change and notice a colleague has left used supplies near the clean work area.

options.text: Move the used supplies aside and continue with the dressing preparation.
Prepare the dressing on the available surface and tidy the area after care.
Check the infection control steps and ask the colleague to clear the supplies.
Clear the used supplies, perform hand hygiene, and prepare a clean work area.

advanced.situation: Your unit wants to evaluate whether a revised nursing practice system has improved care quality. You are asked to propose an evaluation.

options.text: Review selected records and ask staff whether the revised system feels effective.
Ask staff to list concerns and use the responses to judge the system.
Compare a few recent records with staff feedback and summarize any recurring concerns.
Set outcome measures, sample records consistently, and compare results before and after the revision.

basic.situation: A nursing assistant is helping with routine patient care, and you have been asked to support the work under direct supervision.

options.text: Offer help with routine care and tell the assistant to call if needed.
Check the assigned care needs with the assistant and help with the agreed tasks.
Finish the assistant's routine tasks quickly so the ward can stay on schedule.
Take over the next care task so the assistant can finish documentation.

advanced.situation: Your unit is preparing for an accreditation review, and you are assigned to lead staff compliance work on updated nursing documentation requirements.

options.text: Review sample records, explain gaps, and track staff completion before the accreditation review.
Brief staff on updated requirements and ask them to verify assigned records.
Compare requirements with unit records, assign checks, and report gaps with action steps.
Remind staff about the review and collect questions for the unit manager.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to help draft a nursing service goal after several patients report delays in routine care.

options.text: Suggest a goal for timely routine care, then invite colleagues to refine its wording together.
Reuse last year's service goal and submit it as a starting draft.
Draft a measurable goal tied to reported delays and review it with your supervisor.
Write a general goal about improving patient care for the next draft.

advanced.situation: New evidence may affect a specialty nursing procedure used across your department. You are asked to update the policy draft and its review approach.

options.text: Add the new guidance as an appendix and retain the existing procedure text.
Update the procedure from the new guidance and circulate the draft for comments.
Compare the guidance with current practice, revise the procedure, and define review measures.
Replace the current procedure with a summary of the new guidance.

basic.situation: After a specialty clinic visit, you need to prepare a care report before the next patient arrives. Your supervisor can review it later.

options.text: List the main care activities and leave space for the supervisor's review.
Write a brief note that the visit went as planned and file it.
Record the care provided, the patient's response, and any follow-up needed.
Copy the visit schedule into the report and add the patient's name.

advanced.situation: A patient with complex needs is leaving the ward, and several services must coordinate ongoing specialty care. You are contributing to the discharge discussion.

options.text: Send the latest specialty note to every service involved in discharge planning.
Ask the patient to contact each service after returning home.
Coordinate service plans and document each named follow-up contact before discharge.
Share specialty concerns, then ask each service to state its follow-up plan.

basic.situation: Under supervision, you are preparing a prescribed local anesthetic for a routine procedure and notice the label is hard to read.

options.text: Use the prescription details and ask a colleague which product is usually selected.
