Choose the familiar product and prepare the prescribed volume for the procedure.
Read the label again under better light and verify the prescribed solution.
Check the prescription and product label with your supervisor before preparing the solution.

advanced.situation: During a regional block, the patient's response differs from what you expected. You are managing the anesthetic and have the unit's emergency drug protocol available.

options.text: Pause the block, assess the response, and follow the relevant emergency drug protocol.
Reassess the patient and discuss the response with the supervising anesthetist.
Continue the planned block and keep the emergency drugs close at hand.
Reduce the block dose and monitor the patient for a few more minutes.

basic.situation: A patient in recovery needs oxygen, and you are assisting with airway care under guidance. The oxygen tubing is not connected to the delivery device.

options.text: Connect the tubing to the device and check the patient's comfort.
Ask a nearby nurse to reconnect the tubing while you prepare another task.
Check the ordered delivery setup with your supervisor and connect the oxygen tubing.
Reconnect the tubing, confirm oxygen flow, and report the setup to your supervisor.

advanced.situation: A patient suddenly becomes difficult to ventilate during a procedure. You are leading the airway response and emergency support is available nearby.

options.text: Call for emergency support, assess ventilation, and coordinate airway actions with the team.
Wait for the next scheduled observation before changing the airway approach.
Check the breathing circuit and continue the current ventilation settings for now.
Reposition the airway and increase ventilation while monitoring the patient's response.

basic.situation: You are cleaning anesthesia equipment after a routine case and find residue on a removable component. Instructions for disassembly are available.

options.text: Disassemble the component as instructed, clean it, and tell the supervisor about residue.
Follow the disassembly instructions, clean the component, and check it before storage.
Ask a colleague how the component is usually cleaned and prepare the next case.
Wipe the residue from the component and return it to the equipment tray.

advanced.situation: An anesthesia monitor gives inconsistent readings during pre-case checks. You are asked to troubleshoot and coordinate any needed safety repair.

options.text: Request a repair and switch to another monitor for the case.
Compare the monitor with another reading and report any remaining discrepancy.
Reset the monitor and use it if the readings become stable.
Repeat the check, document the fault, and arrange the required safety assessment before use.

basic.situation: You are completing a pre-anesthetic screening and the patient is unsure which medicines they took this morning. The case is scheduled later today.

options.text: Record medicines the patient recalls, note uncertainty, and continue the remaining screening questions.
Ask the patient to check their medicine list and bring it before surgery.
Ask which medicines were taken and when, then clarify before completing screening.
Treat the last clinic list as provisional and ask about changes since then.

advanced.situation: A high-risk patient has a complex medical history and an ECG finding that may affect anesthesia. You are developing the care plan with the clinical team.

options.text: Base the plan on prior anesthesia records and routine checks, then discuss it.
Use the standard plan and ask the team to review the ECG before the case.
Review the history and ECG with the team, then tailor the plan to identified risks.
Discuss the history and ECG with a colleague, then share concerns with the team.

basic.situation: You are checking a patient's pulse and blood pressure after anesthesia with guidance. The readings differ from the previous set.

options.text: Record both readings with the time, then continue observations and watch for further changes.
Repeat both readings, compare the trend, and tell your supervisor about the difference.
Chart the new readings and follow the scheduled observation plan until review.
Repeat the measurements and ask your supervisor how to interpret the difference.

advanced.situation: A post-anesthesia patient develops changing ventilation readings and a falling blood pressure. You are monitoring the patient and complications are possible.

options.text: Assess the patient, address the concerning trends, and call for clinical support.
Adjust the monitor alarm limits and continue watching the patient closely.
Recheck the readings, assess the patient, and report the trend to the responsible clinician.
Increase observation frequency and document each change in the monitor readings.

basic.situation: A stable patient is ready to leave post-anesthesia care, and you are helping with discharge under guidance. The patient has a question about the anesthesia consent.

options.text: Clarify the consent question and review the usual discharge instructions with the patient.
Give the patient the discharge sheet and ask them to read it at home.
Explain the discharge instructions and ask whether the patient feels ready to leave.
Review the consent question with the patient and confirm discharge readiness with your supervisor.

advanced.situation: A new nurse asks how to respond to a post-anesthesia airway emergency. You are assigned to teach the unit's response process and anesthetic techniques.

options.text: Teach airway steps with a scenario, then observe the nurse practicing the response.
Share an airway equipment reminder during handover and invite a brief review.
Explain the airway response and invite questions about the relevant anesthetic techniques.
Review the protocol and ask the nurse to read it before their shift.

basic.situation: After a routine postnatal check, a patient says feeding is tiring and asks what care she needs before her next visit.

options.text: Discuss her priorities and warning signs, then agree on a tailored follow-up plan.
Check symptoms and readings, tailor her plan, and set a suitable review.
Use the standard recovery plan and book a routine review next week.
Use last visit's plan, update her symptoms, and set a review date.

advanced.situation: Your clinic is updating its newborn-care guidance after staff report inconsistent advice about routine feeding support.

options.text: Review current guidance, draft practical steps, and seek clinical review before use.
Ask colleagues what they do and combine the most common approaches.
Adapt the existing newborn guidance and circulate it for staff comments.
Write a new feeding protocol from your recent cases and share it.

basic.situation: At a first antenatal visit, a patient describes nausea and a past pregnancy complication while you complete her health history.

options.text: Copy the previous patient's history template and change her name.
Record her symptoms, timing, and prior complication in the history.
Enter her current symptoms and ask about the past complication later.
Ask focused follow-up questions, confirm the timeline, and document her account clearly.

advanced.situation: A patient with worsening headaches is referred for review, and the receiving clinician needs a clear account of her antenatal visits.

options.text: Mention that headaches were discussed and that she requested another appointment.
Summarize the timeline, findings, actions, and pending follow-up for the receiving clinician.
Highlight the latest headache and attach her full clinic record.
Send the visit notes together and let the receiving clinician review them.

basic.situation: During a routine antenatal visit, you are asked to listen to the fetal heartbeat and record the finding.

options.text: Listen for a short time and ask a colleague to check your note.
Explain the check, locate the heartbeat, and confirm the reading before documenting.
Use the usual listening point and record the first sound heard.
Check the patient's position, listen carefully, and record the finding and time.

advanced.situation: You are reviewing a small study proposal on breastfeeding support, and the team wants a practical plan for collecting clinic feedback.

options.text: Use the clinic's existing feedback form and summarize the responses.
Review similar studies and adapt their feedback questions for the clinic.
Choose a clear question, protect participant privacy, and use a consistent collection method.
Ask several patients what they think and report the most common answer.

basic.situation: Before a planned examination, a patient looks worried and asks what will happen and whether her partner can stay.

options.text: Hand her the standard leaflet and offer to answer questions afterward.
Say the examination is routine and start preparing the room.
Give a brief outline and invite her partner to listen too.
Describe the steps in simple terms and ask what concerns her most.

advanced.situation: A postpartum patient asks about medicine for pain, but her chart shows a possible allergy and the clinic's approved options are available.

options.text: Confirm the allergy history and discuss an approved option with her.
Verify allergy details, then choose an approved medicine and dose with her.
Review the approved list and ask a colleague which option is commonly used.
Choose a familiar medicine at the usual dose and document the discussion.

basic.situation: At an antenatal visit, a patient asks how to manage ordinary pregnancy discomfort while continuing her usual daily activities.

options.text: Share the clinic's usual comfort advice and ask her to return if concerned.
Reassure her that discomfort is common and suggest resting more.
Review her symptoms, offer suitable care, and arrange a follow-up check.
Ask about symptoms and daily needs, then agree practical care and follow-up.

advanced.situation: A patient requests an intrauterine device after discussing family planning, and your clinic provides the service by appointment.

options.text: Offer the next available appointment and explain the usual recovery advice.
Book her for insertion and record her preferred device type.
Confirm her choice, consent, and suitability before arranging insertion.
Schedule insertion based on her request and the clinic's routine workflow.

basic.situation: A first-time parent asks what to expect during the final weeks of pregnancy and when to contact the clinic.

options.text: Discuss key changes and warning signs, then check when she would call.
Review common changes and share the clinic's contact number for questions or concerns.
Offer the leaflet, summarize its advice, and suggest she read it at home.
Explain that she can contact the clinic about any new symptoms, concerns, or questions.

advanced.situation: A student nurse midwife is observing a birth and asks how you decide when to support a change in position.

options.text: Explain your reasoning as events unfold and invite the student to reflect afterward.
Ask the student to read the birth notes and discuss them later.
Tell the student to follow your movements and copy the approach next time.
Describe the position change and ask the student to repeat the steps.

basic.situation: A patient with a cough and fever asks whether a basic test is needed before you decide on care.

options.text: Use her symptoms to decide and document a likely diagnosis today.
Check her vital signs and order a basic test for review.
Order the usual blood test and review its result at follow-up.
Review her symptoms and examination, then select a suitable test if indicated.

advanced.situation: A patient with diabetes, kidney disease, and new confusion has abnormal results while another provider is available for joint review.

options.text: Review the trends and symptoms together, assess urgent risks, and collaborate on the differential.
Treat the confusion as a familiar diabetes symptom and arrange routine review.
Compare the results with her history and discuss likely causes with the other provider.
Repeat the abnormal test and wait for confirmation before discussing her case.

basic.situation: A patient with a mild urinary infection asks what treatment and follow-up to expect during a routine clinic visit.

options.text: Check symptoms and relevant history, then plan care and review warning signs.
Review her symptoms and record a plan for treatment and follow-up.
Discuss the usual care plan and give a routine follow-up date.
Offer the familiar treatment and tell her to return if symptoms persist.

advanced.situation: A patient with high blood pressure and diabetes has rising readings despite treatment and says the current plan is difficult to follow.

options.text: Increase the current treatment and schedule a check of her readings.
Review trends and barriers, then develop a guideline-based plan with her care team.
Keep the current plan and ask her to bring more readings next visit.
Discuss the readings with her and outline a revised plan for review.

basic.situation: A patient with a minor infection asks about a standard medicine, and her chart lists her age and current medicines.

options.text: Use the clinic's familiar dose and explain the expected schedule.
Choose the common medicine and let her adjust the schedule as needed.
Check her current medicines and allergies, then select an authorized dose and route.
Review the medicine list and confirm the standard dose with her.

advanced.situation: A pregnant patient has limited funds, takes several medicines, and is unsure she can follow a complex treatment schedule.

options.text: Review the interaction risks and suggest a simpler authorized regimen.
Compare safe options for interactions, cost, and schedule, then agree a workable choice.
Choose the most familiar option and explain its usual schedule.
Offer a lower-cost option and ask her to follow the printed directions.

basic.situation: A patient starting blood pressure medicine asks what side effects to watch for and how to fit doses into shift work.

options.text: Hand her the medicine leaflet and suggest reading it after work.
Explain common effects and link doses to a routine that fits her shifts.
Review the label directions and mention a few possible side effects.
Tell her the medicine is usually well tolerated and to keep taking it.

advanced.situation: A patient with a new chronic diagnosis feels overwhelmed and asks where she can find affordable support near home.

options.text: Give her a general health website and suggest searching nearby services.
Suggest she ask family members for advice about finding support.
List the clinic's usual support groups and let her choose one.
Ask what support matters, then connect her with suitable local health resources.

basic.situation: During a routine examination, a patient asks you to assess a small cut on her hand and explain whether it needs care.

options.text: Apply a dressing based on its size and complete the examination.
Review the wound and her history, then decide on treatment or referral.
Inspect the cut, clean it, document findings, and explain when she should seek care.
Measure the cut and ask a colleague which procedure is usual.

advanced.situation: A pregnant patient reports a new rash after starting medicine, and you notice she is breathing comfortably during today's examination.

options.text: Record the rash and ask her to mention it at her next visit.
Check timing, symptoms, and severity, then assess the reaction and coordinate next steps.
Document the new rash and ask whether she has taken other medicines.
Ask about the rash and review her medicines before documenting it.

basic.situation: A patient needs a follow-up for blood pressure, and the clinic schedule is filling while you complete her care record.

options.text: Book the next open slot and leave the care plan for later entry.
Update her record, set an appropriate follow-up interval, and confirm the appointment.
Enter the care plan and ask reception to contact her about a visit.
Record the plan and arrange the next available follow-up visit.

advanced.situation: Your clinic is revising infection-control procedures after staff identify uneven practice across rooms during a busy week.

options.text: Map gaps, update steps with the team, then check staff use them.
Explain the procedure and ask staff to follow it during busy periods, including room checks.
Post the existing procedure in each room and remind staff at handover.
Review the procedure with staff and record suggested changes for each clinic room.

basic.situation: During recovery after a routine procedure, you notice a patient's breathing becoming slower while the monitor readings remain stable.

options.text: You adjust the oxygen flow and watch whether the monitor readings improve.
You record the stable readings and check again after finishing another task.
You report the breathing change and continue checking the patient with your supervisor.
You assess the patient, alert the supervising clinician, and trend breathing alongside monitor readings.

advanced.situation: During a procedure, a patient develops a sudden reaction and falling blood pressure while the surgical team is focused on closing.

options.text: You ask the surgeon to pause while you review the latest readings.
You tell the team about the pressure drop and prepare the usual medications.
You call out the change, begin the established response, and coordinate support with the team.
You treat the falling pressure and tell the team when the situation settles.

basic.situation: Before a scheduled procedure, the patient says their shoulder hurts when the team positions them on the operating table.

options.text: You reposition the patient for comfort and tell the team about shoulder pain.
You report shoulder pain and help adjust the patient's arm position.
You keep usual positioning and ask the patient to report pain during surgery.
You add shoulder padding and continue preparing the patient for surgery.

advanced.situation: During sedation, a patient's airway becomes difficult to maintain and oxygen levels fall while the procedural team asks whether to continue.

options.text: You increase oxygen and urge the team to finish the procedure quickly.
You call for help, prepare airway equipment, and monitor oxygen levels.
You ask the team to pause, reposition the patient, and reassess ventilation.
You name airway difficulty, start rescue steps, and ask the team to pause.

basic.situation: The surgeon changes the expected procedure length, and the anesthetic plan may need adjustment before the next step.

options.text: You tell the theatre nurse and ask them to update the operating list.
You continue the current plan and raise the longer timing after the next step.
You tell the surgeon about timing and agree to pause for plan review.
You flag the longer procedure and ask whether the anesthetic plan still fits.

advanced.situation: A patient with several medical needs is scheduled for surgery, but specialists have given different advice about the anesthetic approach.

options.text: You share each specialist's recommendation with the lead clinician for a decision.
You bring specialists together to agree on a shared anesthetic plan.
You choose the approach used for the last similar case and tell the team.
You document the advice and ask each specialist to clarify their main concern.

basic.situation: A patient asks what small changes might help them avoid illness while recovering at home after surgery.

options.text: You advise the patient to rest and ask their family to help at home.
You hand the patient a general health leaflet and return to the theatre.
You suggest regular handwashing and ask whether the patient has questions.
You discuss practical health habits that suit the patient's recovery instructions and routine.

advanced.situation: A new staff member is unsure how to respond when a patient shows signs of an anesthesia complication during a busy list.

options.text: You pair the staff member with a colleague during a future emergency response.
You guide the staff member through emergency steps and practise initial actions together.
You explain warning signs and show the staff member where to find the protocol.
You share the protocol and ask the staff member to review it before another list.

basic.situation: You are recording anesthetic amounts during a procedure, and a brief interruption makes you unsure of the latest dose time.

options.text: You enter the amount from memory and complete the chart before handover.
You estimate the time from the monitor trend and add a note for review.
You mark the time for confirmation and continue recording the patient's condition.
You verify dose time with the team and record the confirmed details.

advanced.situation: A patient's examination and test reports do not point clearly to one cause, but the team needs your assessment before surgery proceeds.

options.text: You review the test reports and share the leading possibilities with the team.
You ask a colleague which diagnosis they would record from the available reports.
You summarize findings and explain remaining uncertainty to the team.
You select the most familiar diagnosis and prepare the usual medication plan.

basic.situation: A patient needs a routine pre-procedure blood test, and the clinic is arranging investigations before the theatre list begins.

options.text: You confirm the requested test with the care plan and place the order.
You order the usual panel and tell the team it is ready.
You review the request and ask the clinician to clarify one unclear test.
You send the patient for the test listed on last month's form.

advanced.situation: A patient has persistent pain despite the current plan, and the surgical team asks whether a medication change or specialist review is needed.

options.text: You increase the current medication and ask the patient to report back later.
You reassess needs, adjust treatment within your role, and arrange review if indicated.
You ask the surgeon whether a specialist referral would be useful before changing treatment.
You review the pain history and discuss a medication adjustment with the surgical team.

basic.situation: A patient collapses in the ward, and the monitor shows a dangerous rhythm. You are the cardiologist nearest the bedside.

options.text: I begin compressions, assign clear tasks, and relay rhythm changes to the team.
I call the response team and check the monitor before taking a role.
I ask a nurse to start care while I review the chart for history.
I take a defined task, follow the arrest protocol, and report changes.

advanced.situation: During resuscitation, the rhythm changes after treatment and junior staff give conflicting updates. You need to guide the next steps.

options.text: I ask the team to repeat the last rhythm and wait for senior review.
I continue the previous plan until the team has finished its current tasks.
I share the rhythm change and ask each colleague to continue their task.
I name the rhythm, direct the next protocol steps, and assign team roles.

basic.situation: A patient is scheduled for a pacemaker implant. You are assisting the supervising cardiologist as the patient enters the procedure room.

options.text: I confirm the patient, device plan, and sterile setup with the supervising cardiologist.
I place the pacemaker kit nearby and rely on the room team's setup.
I open the device pack while the team finishes its checks and setup.
I check the consent and equipment, then prepare the sterile field with guidance.

advanced.situation: During an angioplasty, the image shows an unexpected narrowing beyond the planned area. The supervising cardiologist asks you to review the next step.

options.text: I compare the images, summarize the finding, and agree the next step with the operator.
I extend the balloon treatment to the narrowing using the planned settings.
I review the angiogram and discuss the vessel and options with the supervisor.
I ask the operator to decide while I prepare another balloon size.

basic.situation: A patient arrives for an ECG with chest discomfort. You are asked to record the tracing while a colleague remains available.

options.text: I record the ECG and send it through the usual reporting route.
I place the leads carefully and label the tracing with patient details.
I use the prior lead positions and file the tracing with today's notes.
I verify identity, record the ECG promptly, and flag the symptoms to the clinician.

advanced.situation: An exercise ECG shows an unexpected change near peak exertion, but the tracing has movement artefact. You must decide how to handle the result.

options.text: I repeat the tracing after exercise and compare it with the baseline.
I assess signal quality, document the exertion point, and alert the reporting clinician to uncertainty.
I check the electrodes and ask the patient to rest before another recording.
I label the change as ischaemia and send the report for review.

basic.situation: An echocardiogram report includes valve measurements that differ from the prior visit. You are asked to calculate the valve area with assistance.

options.text: I verify velocity inputs, calculate the area, and show my working to a colleague.
I copy the prior valve area into the worksheet to keep records consistent.
I calculate the area and compare it with the supplied reference range.
I recalculate the area using values shown on the current report.

advanced.situation: A patient with breathlessness has subtle chamber-size changes across several reports. You need to interpret the measurements alongside the clinical record.

options.text: I call the chambers enlarged from the latest measurement alone without checking prior reports.
I repeat measurements from the latest report and flag the difference for review.
I compare measurements with standards and document the trend for clinical review today.
I check image quality, trend measurements, and relate them to symptoms today.

basic.situation: A patient asks whether walking is safe after a recent cardiology visit. You have the treatment plan and a colleague nearby for support.

options.text: I explain the activity advice in the plan and ask which parts remain unclear.
I ask the patient to follow the leaflet and bring questions next time.
I connect the plan to their question and clarify when to seek clinical advice.
I reassure the patient that walking is usually good for the heart.

advanced.situation: Several patients ask what to expect from a planned cardiac test, and staff explain it differently. You are asked to improve the patient information.

options.text: I map the test steps, check wording with clinicians, and trial it with patients.
I ask each staff member to explain the test in their own words.
I reuse an older handout and add the new test name to it.
I collect common questions and draft a clear leaflet for the clinic team to review.

basic.situation: A patient is due for an echocardiogram, but the referral has a missing history detail. You are handling the record and test request under supervision.

options.text: I confirm the patient details, clarify the missing history, and document the test request.
I check the record, note the missing detail, and ask the clinician for clarification.
I copy the history from the previous visit and send the request onward.
I enter the available history and submit the echocardiogram request for review.

advanced.situation: A patient's symptoms worsen while test results are pending, and two specialties have suggested different plans. You are coordinating updates with the care team.

options.text: I send both plans to the team and ask which approach should proceed next.
I update the physicians about worsening symptoms and request a joint treatment discussion.
I continue the current plan while the pending results are awaited by the team.
I summarize the change, results, and options for physicians to agree a plan.

basic.situation: A patient presents with an itchy, flaky scalp and asks whether it is dandruff. You are reviewing the skin findings during a routine clinic visit.

options.text: I suggest shampoo and explain when the patient should seek clinical advice.
I examine the scalp, ask about triggers, and explain likely causes and care.
I inspect the scalp, review symptoms, and discuss possible causes with my supervisor.
I label it dandruff from the flakes and enter that diagnosis in the chart.

advanced.situation: A patient's changing pigmented lesion has uneven colour and a recent growth history. You are asked to assess it during a dermatology clinic.

options.text: I reassure the patient that uneven colour is common in older moles.
I compare the lesion with prior photographs and record its dimensions and colour.
I assess its features, review the history, and discuss an appropriate diagnostic plan.
I document the lesion and arrange a routine review after comparing old photographs.

basic.situation: A patient is booked for comedo removal, and the supervising dermatologist asks you to prepare and assist with the procedure.

options.text: I set out the comedo tools and check the room is ready for treatment.
I confirm the treatment area, prepare supplies, and follow the agreed skin-care steps.
I gather the peel supplies because they are used for similar skin concerns.
I begin extraction on the most visible comedones while the room is prepared.

advanced.situation: A lesion scheduled for removal appears larger than in the referral photo, and the patient asks whether surgery can proceed today. You are the treating dermatologist.

options.text: I compare the lesion and history, then decide whether the planned excision remains suitable.
I document the new size and discuss the change with the patient.
I postpone the procedure and request another clinician's assessment of the lesion.
I proceed with the booked removal to avoid another visit for the patient.

basic.situation: A patient has a persistent rash and a history that may suggest an infection. You are considering whether a microbiologic test is appropriate.

options.text: I order a microbiologic test and note the rash duration in the chart.
I request a broad set of tests to cover several possible causes.
I review the rash history and choose a test that fits the suspected cause.
I use the last patient's test order because the rashes look similar.

advanced.situation: A changing pigmented lesion has an uncertain border and a concerning history. You are deciding whether an incisional biopsy could clarify the diagnosis.

options.text: I record the lesion features and discuss biopsy options with the patient.
I assess the lesion, choose a representative biopsy site, and document the clinical question.
I explain the uncertainty and arrange a routine review before considering biopsy.
I take a small sample from the easiest edge and send it for testing.

basic.situation: A patient with mild acne asks whether a topical treatment is suitable. You are reviewing the skin findings and medical history before prescribing.

options.text: I offer the same acne cream commonly used in the clinic.
I review the acne and history, then discuss a suitable topical option and use.
I prescribe a stronger cream so the spots clear before the next visit.
I prescribe a topical treatment and explain how often to apply it.

advanced.situation: A patient with acne has persistent symptoms and asks about hormonal treatment. Their history includes a factor that may affect prescribing choices.

options.text: I review the patient's history and discuss suitable hormonal and topical options.
I prescribe the hormonal treatment requested and review progress at follow-up.
I continue the topical plan and ask the patient to raise hormones next visit.
I assess the history, weigh relevant risks, and explain a tailored treatment choice.

basic.situation: A new patient describes recurring skin irritation and a recent change in medication. You are recording their health history before the examination.

options.text: I record the symptoms, medication change, and relevant timing in the history.
I clarify the symptom timeline, medicines, and allergies, then read back key details.
I copy the medication list from the referral and start the examination.
I ask when the irritation began and add the medication to the chart.

advanced.situation: A family doctor asks for advice about a patient's persistent rash after initial treatment. The referral includes photographs and a brief history for your consultation.

options.text: I reply that persistent rashes usually settle and recommend waiting longer.
I review the images and history, then send a focused assessment and advice.
I suggest another common cream and ask the doctor to monitor the rash.
I review the photographs and share a likely diagnosis with the doctor.

basic.situation: A patient attends for a full skin check and mentions a new spot on their back. You are conducting the examination with guidance available.

options.text: I explain the examination, check the skin systematically, and document the new spot and findings.
I focus on the back spot and leave the rest for another appointment.
I examine the skin systematically and include the new spot in my notes for later review.
I inspect the exposed areas and ask the patient to point out concerns.

advanced.situation: An intern examines a patient with a changing mole and is unsure how to describe its features. You are supervising the clinic encounter.

options.text: I describe the mole and ask the intern to add my findings to the note.
I review the intern's description and point out features they should document.
I finish the examination myself so the clinic can stay on schedule.
I demonstrate a structured description and ask the intern to apply it to the lesion.

basic.situation: A drowsy patient arrives after a fall, and the team asks you to assist with basic airway management while monitoring breathing.

options.text: I place an airway adjunct quickly, then return to charting before reassessing breathing.
I prepare suction and airway equipment, then follow instructions while watching breathing.
I bring oxygen and a bag-mask device, then await the senior clinician's direction.
I assess airway patency, position the patient, and prepare suction and bag-mask support.

advanced.situation: A patient is deteriorating during an emergency thoracotomy, and you are assigned to supervise staff assisting the procedure.

options.text: I assign clear roles, confirm sterile readiness, and monitor the team's progress against the procedure plan.
I call out the next instrument and let experienced staff manage their own tasks.
I start the next incision step while staff finish arranging equipment around the patient.
I ask each staff member to take a familiar role and focus on the procedure.

basic.situation: A patient with abdominal pain is waiting for review, and you are asked to record the history and vital signs with guidance.

options.text: I record the patient's main complaint and vital signs in the chart.
I enter a normal history from the triage note and copy the latest vital signs.
I write down the pain score and vital signs, then leave the history for later.
I record the pain history, allergies, and vital signs, then flag concerning changes for review.

advanced.situation: Your emergency department is revising assessment for older patients with communication barriers and several prior care visits.

options.text: I review prior visits and vital signs, then share common concerns at the team meeting.
I add more history fields to the form and ask staff to complete them during intake.
I map key risks, prior care, communication needs, and escalation points into a pilot assessment pathway.
I use the current adult checklist for older patients and note exceptions in free text.

basic.situation: A patient reports chest discomfort, and you are asked to request a standard diagnostic test under supervision.

options.text: I request the usual blood tests and ECG, then add the results to the chart.
I check the presenting symptoms and request an ECG under the supervising clinician's plan.
I wait for the next review before requesting any test for the chest discomfort.
I request an ECG as directed and tell the team when the tracing is available.

advanced.situation: A new clinician is learning to interpret an emergency ultrasound that conflicts with the patient's examination findings.

options.text: I compare the images with the examination, explain uncertainty, and review findings with the clinician.
I label the scan as reassuring and advise the team to rely on that result.
I let the clinician interpret the scan independently, then discuss the report afterward.
I show the clinician the key image and share my initial interpretation for discussion.

basic.situation: A patient with fever and pain has abnormal vital signs, and you are asked to suggest medication options with senior input.

options.text: I share the patient's observations and ask the senior which medication they prefer.
I review allergies, current medicines, and observations before discussing a suitable option with the senior.
I prescribe a standard dose from the chart and review the patient later.
I suggest the usual pain medicine and ask the senior to confirm the dose.

advanced.situation: The emergency department is updating treatment guidance after staff report inconsistent priorities for patients with abnormal observations.

options.text: I collect the current guidance and share a short summary at the next meeting.
I circulate recent examples and ask each shift to follow its usual approach for now.
I add a note to the guidance asking staff to use clinical judgment with abnormal readings.
I draft clear escalation thresholds and review the pathway with clinicians across common presentations.

basic.situation: A patient's breathing worsens while you assist the team with stabilization under the clinician's direction.

options.text: I finish documenting the earlier observations before mentioning the breathing change.
I tell the clinician the breathing looks worse and continue the assigned task.
I fetch oxygen and wait nearby for the clinician to decide what comes next.
I reassess breathing and vital signs, report the change, and prepare the requested support.

advanced.situation: During resuscitation, a patient develops worsening breathing and circulation problems while several teams are working nearby.

options.text: I direct each team to continue its usual tasks while I watch the monitor.
I call out the next task and ask one clinician to watch the patient's response.
I set clear team roles, track responses to interventions, and update the shared resuscitation plan.
I focus on airway tasks and let the nearby teams continue their separate work.

basic.situation: A patient needs specialist review after an emergency assessment, and you are asked to coordinate a referral with guidance.

options.text: I send assessment findings, key concerns, and the reason specialist review is needed.
I call the specialist team, share key details, and ask whether they can review.
I send a short referral explaining the patient needs specialist attention today.
I ask the specialist team to review the patient, sharing relevant emergency notes.

advanced.situation: A medically complex patient needs admission, specialist input, and social support, while the emergency department is busy.

options.text: I contact each team with the relevant details and document their replies in the chart.
I align the admission decision, specialist reviews, and social needs in one documented handover.
I send the admission request first and leave other teams to find the patient later.
I ask the admitting team to arrange the remaining referrals after accepting the patient.

basic.situation: A patient is worried about a blood test result, and you are asked to explain it and discuss the next step.

options.text: I read the result aloud and tell the patient to book another appointment.
I reassure the patient that the result looks fine and move to the next visit.
I explain what the result shows, check the patient's understanding, and discuss the planned follow-up.
I explain the result in plain language and describe the next step in care.

advanced.situation: A patient with several ongoing conditions is leaving hospital and needs follow-up from specialists and community providers.

options.text: I tell the patient to contact each specialist and provide the clinic phone numbers.
I send referrals to the listed specialists and copy the discharge summary to the clinic.
I confirm each provider's role, share the agreed plan, and check the patient knows whom to contact.
I advise the patient to wait for the specialists to call before arranging follow-up.

basic.situation: A patient returns for a follow-up visit, and you are asked to record current symptoms and vital signs under supervision.

options.text: I write down the main symptom and copy the previous vital signs into the chart.
I record symptoms, vital signs, and changes since the last visit in the patient record.
I enter today's vital signs and ask the patient whether treatment has helped.
I record the patient's main symptom and today's vital signs for the clinician.

advanced.situation: A patient with diabetes and limited transport has missed visits, and you are reviewing progress and treatment response.

options.text: I copy the previous review forward and update the date for today's visit.
I compare recent readings with the last visit and note whether the treatment changed.
I record the latest reading and ask the patient to return at the usual interval.
I review recent readings, treatment changes, missed visits, and access barriers before documenting progress.

basic.situation: A patient has a persistent cough, and you are asked to order a basic test and review its result with guidance.

options.text: I use the last patient's test request and apply it to this visit as well.
I match the test request to the symptoms and review the result with the supervising clinician.
I request the test as discussed and add the result to the patient's record.
I order the usual test and tell the patient the clinic will contact them with results.

advanced.situation: Your clinic is planning a community health programme, and local screening records show uneven attendance across neighbourhoods.

options.text: I repeat last year's programme schedule and use the existing attendance list.
I share the attendance figures and ask the team to suggest a programme focus.
I review attendance patterns, identify access gaps, and shape outreach with community partners.
I plan the same screening session at each site and promote it through clinic notices.

basic.situation: A busy clinic morning leaves several patients waiting, and you are asked to direct medical assistants under supervision.

options.text: I assign registration and vital checks, then update the clinician on the queue.
I assign patient flow and vital checks, then confirm urgent concerns reach the clinician.
I ask each assistant to handle the next patient in the waiting queue.
I let the assistants choose their own tasks while I finish the clinic notes.

advanced.situation: A new group of medical students is joining clinic, and you are asked to support their practical learning.

options.text: I ask students to follow the team and learn tasks as the clinic gets busy.
I ask experienced staff to show students the routine tasks during the morning.
I demonstrate the clinic task and invite students to observe the next patient visit.
I set learning goals, demonstrate the task, and give each student specific feedback afterward.

basic.situation: A patient asks how to improve their diet and activity while managing a new health concern.

options.text: I recommend a standard diet sheet and suggest the patient read it at home.
I tell the patient to avoid their favourite foods and exercise more each day.
I discuss a balanced diet and regular activity, then invite the patient's questions.
I ask about their routine and offer one practical food or activity change to try.

advanced.situation: Your clinic is asked to support disease prevention in a community where residents have varied schedules and health literacy.

options.text: I adapt prevention messages to local routines, check understanding, and invite community feedback.
I reuse the previous campaign slides and ask volunteers to share them online.
I distribute the existing prevention leaflet through local clinics and resident groups.
I prepare a clear health talk and offer it at the clinic's usual community session.

basic.situation: A patient is due for a routine vaccination, and you are asked to administer it under supervision.

options.text: I check the immunisation record and ask the supervising clinician to confirm the vaccine.
I check the due date and prepare the vaccine while the patient completes paperwork.
I prepare the vaccine listed in the appointment note and ask the patient to confirm their name.
I confirm the patient's history and due vaccine, explain the process, and document administration.

advanced.situation: A patient with several ongoing conditions needs a treatment review, and recent notes show a change in their medicines.

options.text: I renew the listed medicines and arrange a follow-up visit to review progress.
I check the medication list and book a review with the clinic pharmacist.
I review the latest prescription and ask the patient whether they have noticed side effects.
I reconcile current medicines, check relevant risks, and agree a treatment plan with the patient.

basic.situation: A patient with high blood pressure asks how to make healthier food choices while working long shifts.

options.text: Ask about usual meals, then suggest practical lower-salt choices for workdays.
Recommend fresh meals and regular exercise that fit the patient's work schedule.
Give a diet leaflet and discuss one change the patient can try at work.
Suggest smaller balanced meals instead of skipping lunch during long shifts.

advanced.situation: A surgeon asks about a patient's risk before an operation. The patient has several chronic conditions and recent examination results are available.

options.text: Tell the surgeon the patient seems fit based on the last visit.
Review the conditions and results, then communicate specific risks and possible precautions.
Send the surgeon a summary of the patient's chronic conditions.
Call the surgeon with your risk assessment and supporting findings.

basic.situation: During a busy clinic, two nurses are unsure which patients are due for observations before review. You are asked to coordinate the team's activities.

options.text: Tell the nurses to work through the list as time allows.
Write the patient names on a board and ask a nurse to choose.
Check the review order, assign observation checks, and confirm the handover.
Ask each nurse to check the patients nearest to them first.

advanced.situation: A colleague asks for your input on a difficult patient whose symptoms have changed despite treatment. They share recent findings and request advice today.

options.text: Suggest reviewing the current treatment at the next team meeting.
Discuss the findings and suggest one likely explanation for the change.
Share a few possible causes based on the symptoms described.
Review the course and findings, then offer a focused assessment and discuss uncertainties.

basic.situation: A patient asks how to take a newly prescribed medicine after a clinic visit. You have the treatment plan and can explain it.

options.text: Repeat the dosage instructions, then invite questions about timing and possible side effects.
Take extra medicine tonight without checking the plan or contacting the clinic.
Explain the label directions and share when to contact the clinic for help.
Review the plan together and ask the patient to explain their medicine schedule.

advanced.situation: A patient with a difficult condition has not improved on the current plan. New test results and their response to treatment are ready for review.

options.text: Review the results and response, then adapt care to the patient's current needs.
Discuss the results with the patient and continue the current plan for now.
Raise the current medicine dose and schedule a review for next month.
Compare treatment options with the results and response before proposing a change.

basic.situation: A patient gives a new medication history during review. You need to record it alongside today's examination findings.

options.text: Summarize the new history and findings clearly in today's patient record.
Copy the prior medication list without checking whether it remains current today.
Record the medication history and examination findings, then check the entry for gaps.
Record today's examination findings and add the medication history in the same entry.

advanced.situation: Your organization requests a workforce health report. Clinic records contain different dates and formats, and the submission deadline is approaching.

options.text: Use each clinic's latest reported figures to meet the deadline.
Ask clinics to resend their figures using one shared format.
Set the reporting period, reconcile records, and document any data limitations.
Compile totals, compare them with clinic records, and send a draft for review.

basic.situation: A patient is being treated for a chest infection. At review, their breathing seems worse despite taking the prescribed treatment.

options.text: Record the patient's symptoms and arrange the usual follow-up visit.
Reassure the patient that recovery can take several more days.
Ask about symptoms, check breathing and treatment use, and arrange urgent reassessment.
Assess the change, document findings, and promptly review the treatment plan.

advanced.situation: A patient has fatigue and abdominal discomfort, and the initial tests do not point clearly to one cause. Their history includes several ongoing conditions.

options.text: Check the current medicines for a possible link to the symptoms.
Treat the abdominal discomfort and reassess fatigue at a later visit.
Review the test results and ask a colleague to consider another diagnosis.
Reconcile the history and findings, consider overlapping causes, and plan targeted assessment.

basic.situation: An older patient with diabetes has recurring foot discomfort and asks whether another clinic could help. You are also due to give a scheduled immunization.

options.text: Assess the concern, arrange a suitable referral, and review immunization readiness.
Ask the patient to call a specialist clinic about the discomfort.
Give the scheduled immunization and suggest raising discomfort at the next visit.
Refer the patient for foot assessment and document the request.

advanced.situation: An older patient has diabetes, heart disease, and kidney problems. Their symptoms and recent results have changed, and they need a coordinated ongoing care plan.

options.text: Adjust the diabetes plan and review the other conditions next visit.
Discuss the changes with the patient and coordinate a revised care plan.
Integrate the changes across conditions and revise ongoing care with the patient.
Review the new results and arrange follow-up for the patient.

basic.situation: You meet a patient with recurring numbness and limited time before clinic ends.

options.text: Ask when symptoms began, then document the patient's main concerns.
Invite the patient to describe onset, pattern, medicines, and family history.
Use the referral note as the history and move to examination.
Check the symptom timeline and ask about current medicines.

advanced.situation: A patient in intensive care has absent brainstem reflexes, and the team asks you to assess for brain death.

options.text: Ask the team to verify the assessment sequence before recording findings.
Confirm prerequisites, perform accepted tests, and document each finding against protocol.
Record brain death from absent reflexes and begin the required paperwork.
Repeat the reflex checks later after reviewing the bedside notes.

basic.situation: A blood test is flagged outside the reference range, but the patient's symptoms are mild.

options.text: Interpret the result against the presentation and flag uncertainty for follow-up.
Treat the flagged value as the explanation and update the chart.
Review the result with symptoms and note its clinical limits.
Compare the value with prior tests before discussing next steps.

advanced.situation: An MRI report conflicts with new weakness, and the patient's family is waiting for an update.

options.text: Compare sequences with the examination and identify findings needing urgent review.
Tell the family the scan confirms the suspected cause and proceed.
Rely on the radiology summary while checking the current examination.
Review the images with radiology and clarify the disputed finding.

basic.situation: A patient reports brief hand tingling, and your examination shows no weakness or coordination changes.

options.text: Check whether the symptom pattern fits a common nerve problem.
Review the history and examination together before setting a working diagnosis.
Label it a nerve disorder and start the usual treatment plan.
Record a provisional impression and arrange a focused follow-up review.

advanced.situation: A patient arrives with sudden speech difficulty and weakness; the onset time is uncertain and treatment decisions are time-sensitive.

options.text: Review the history and examination, then discuss treatment options with the team.
Start a familiar stroke plan while collecting the remaining details.
Ask the emergency team to complete its assessment before you decide.
Clarify the timeline, assess findings, and coordinate urgent stroke evaluation.

basic.situation: A patient starting an anti-epileptic medicine reports feeling unusually tired after several doses.

options.text: Assess the symptom, check the regimen, and plan monitored follow-up.
Advise the patient to stop the medicine and update the prescription record.
Ask when the tiredness began and review the dose and daily routine.
Check the medication list and ask the patient to report changes.

advanced.situation: A patient with new swallowing difficulty needs rehabilitation input alongside ongoing neurological care.

options.text: Align swallowing support, nursing tasks, and neurological review around shared goals.
Send a therapy referral and leave the existing care plan unchanged.
Coordinate the therapy plan with nursing and the treating team.
Ask the patient to raise swallowing concerns at the next therapy visit.

basic.situation: After a review, you notice the patient's record omits a reflex finding and the agreed follow-up plan.

options.text: Copy the previous visit's findings and retain its follow-up plan.
Update the follow-up plan and leave the examination section for later.
Add the missing finding and plan using your examination notes.
Check the notes, enter the finding and plan, then review the record.

advanced.situation: A patient with persistent dizziness needs assessment by another practitioner, and asks why you are referring them.

options.text: Explain the concern and give the patient the referral details.
Explain the concern, referral purpose, and information sent for follow-up.
Tell the patient the referral is routine and close the discussion.
Share the referral details and ask the patient to book a visit.

basic.situation: A medical student is unsure how to check a patient's reflexes during a supervised clinic session.

options.text: Demonstrate the reflex check and explain what to observe.
Ask the student to read the notes before trying again.
Demonstrate the technique, let the student practise, and give feedback.
Complete the examination yourself so the clinic can stay on schedule.

advanced.situation: A colleague asks your view on treatment for a patient with a complex neurological problem and several other health conditions.

options.text: Recommend a specific regimen based on the neurological diagnosis alone.
Share a familiar treatment approach and suggest they review the case.
Review the diagnosis and outline options for the colleague to consider.
Discuss relevant findings, treatment trade-offs, and factors needing shared review.

basic.situation: A patient asks what a routine blood test result means while you review it with your clinic supervisor.

options.text: Compare the result with its reference range and explain its practical meaning.
Explain the result in plain language, then check what the patient understood.
Give a brief explanation and invite questions before discussing follow-up.
Read the number aloud and move on to the next appointment.

advanced.situation: The district requests a quarterly birth and disease report, but two ward registers have different totals and one contains incomplete entries.

options.text: Ask ward staff to explain differences, then use the latest register figures.
Reconcile the registers, document remaining gaps, and submit validated totals with caveats.
Submit the totals as recorded and mention that some entries are incomplete.
Use the ward total with more entries and submit the report by deadline.

basic.situation: A pregnant patient asks what daily habits may help reduce common infection risks during pregnancy.

options.text: Reassure her that routine habits matter and continue the appointment.
Suggest regular handwashing, safe food handling, and any clinic-recommended vaccines.
Ask about her daily routine, then tailor clear hygiene and prevention advice.
Share a clinic leaflet and invite her to ask about unclear points.

advanced.situation: A pregnant patient with a heart condition needs a delivery plan involving obstetrics, cardiology, anaesthesia, and the maternity ward.

options.text: Send the latest notes to each team and let them coordinate separately.
Agree shared roles, escalation signs, and a documented plan with each team.
Arrange a case discussion and circulate the cardiology team's recommendations afterward.
Ask the ward to follow the usual plan while specialists review the case.

basic.situation: A new patient arrives for antenatal care, and you are entering her medical history and examination details.

options.text: Enter the main concern and leave other history for the next visit.
Confirm key history details, distinguish reported facts from findings, and save the entry.
Copy her previous clinic summary and add today's examination findings.
Record her reported history and measured findings in their labeled fields.

advanced.situation: A patient receiving treatment for severe pregnancy-related hypertension reports a new headache, and her blood pressure has risen since the last review.

options.text: Check the chart and discuss the raised reading with the supervising obstetrician.
Assess her symptoms and readings, then promptly review treatment and escalate care as indicated.
Ask a nurse to recheck her blood pressure before deciding on next steps.
Repeat the reading later and keep the existing treatment plan for now.

basic.situation: A patient's screening result is slightly outside the clinic's usual range, and you are reviewing it before the consultation.

options.text: Mark the result as abnormal and use that label in the notes.
Compare the result with the reference range and note relevant symptoms.
Review the result, reference range, and relevant findings before recording your interpretation.
Check the range and flag the result for discussion during the visit.

advanced.situation: Your clinic is asked to plan a community programme after local records show gaps in routine screening and prevention advice for women.

options.text: Repeat last year's activities and use the same clinic handouts.
Offer a general health talk and ask attendees what topics interest them.
Set target groups, practical activities, and review measures with community partners.
Use the records to select outreach topics and schedule talks at the clinic.

basic.situation: At an antenatal visit, a pregnant patient asks whether her recent weight gain is within the expected pattern.

options.text: Review her measurements, ask about concerns, and agree practical prenatal follow-up.
Tell her to eat more carefully and return at her next appointment.
Check her weight record and share the clinic's usual pregnancy guidance.
Review her measurements and discuss nutrition and follow-up at the next visit.

advanced.situation: A pregnant patient has a new finding outside your clinic's usual care scope, and a specialist review is needed before her next visit.

options.text: Clarify the concern, contact the appropriate service, and share relevant records for referral.
Tell her to arrange a specialist appointment and continue routine antenatal care.
Prepare a referral note and ask the patient to bring it to the specialist.
Discuss the finding and provide contact details for the relevant specialist service.

basic.situation: A patient receiving treatment for a common vaginal infection asks whether she should finish the prescribed course after symptoms ease.

options.text: Tell her to stop once she feels well and book another visit if needed.
Repeat the dosing instructions and suggest she call the clinic with concerns.
Review the prescription and explain when to return if symptoms persist.
Check her understanding, explain the prescribed course, and discuss when to seek review.

advanced.situation: During a caesarean delivery, unexpected bleeding develops and the team needs you to help carry out the agreed surgical response.

options.text: Continue the planned closure and ask the team to monitor her afterward.
Call for the senior surgeon and prepare the instruments listed in the plan.
Assess the bleeding, communicate findings, and follow the team's agreed response.
Ask a colleague to check the field while you gather extra supplies.

basic.situation: During a routine visit, a child seems shorter than at the last check. You are completing the growth and development exam with guidance.

options.text: Repeat the height measurement and enter it in the growth chart.
Record today's height and tell the parent the child may catch up.
Measure height again, check the chart, and discuss the trend with your supervisor.
Compare the height with the previous visit and ask your supervisor what it means.

advanced.situation: A child has recurring fever and an unusual blood test result, while the examination is reassuring. You are interpreting findings to determine the next diagnosis.

options.text: Review the result alongside the history and examination before deciding.
Treat the fever based on the examination and review the test later.
Discuss the result with a colleague before choosing a diagnosis.
Repeat the key assessment, interpret the result with symptoms, and plan follow-up.

basic.situation: A child needs a routine vaccination, and the parent is unsure about the appointment timing. You are helping administer care under supervision.

options.text: Ask the parent to bring the record next time before arranging vaccination.
Review the record and ask the parent whether another clinic gave a dose.
Give the scheduled vaccine based on the appointment note and update the record.
Check the child's record and confirm the planned vaccine with your supervisor.

advanced.situation: Several schools report low attendance at child development sessions, and local families have different access needs. You are planning a community growth program.

options.text: Keep the current sessions and ask schools to encourage more families.
Repeat the same sessions at more schools and track attendance each month.
Use family feedback to adapt sessions, coordinate partners, and monitor participation and child outcomes.
Ask schools about barriers and adjust session times to suit families.

basic.situation: A parent looks worried before their child's blood test. You are helping explain the procedure with support from the clinician.

options.text: Ask the clinician to explain the test while you comfort the child.
Tell the parent the test is routine and prepare the child quickly.
Explain what the test involves and invite the parent to ask questions.
Describe the blood draw briefly and check whether the parent understands.

advanced.situation: A parent asks whether an unclear test result means their child needs long-term treatment. You are discussing the result and options with the family.

options.text: Say the result is concerning and recommend starting the treatment plan.
Explain the uncertainty, relate the result to symptoms, and discuss the next decision together.
Explain the result and outline the treatment option for the parent.
Describe the result and ask the parent to decide whether to proceed.

basic.situation: A child returns after starting medicine, and the parent reports a new rash. You are updating the patient's record with assistance.

options.text: Document the rash and medicine, then mention it to the clinician.
Record the rash, timing, medicine, and parent report, then alert the clinician.
Ask when the rash began and add the timing to the record.
Enter the rash in the notes and continue with the planned visit.

advanced.situation: A child with asthma has more night symptoms despite the current plan. You are reviewing progress and deciding whether treatment needs reevaluation.

options.text: Review symptoms and medicine use, then adjust the plan with the family.
Check how often symptoms occur and discuss the pattern with the family.
Review symptoms, use history, and triggers, then revise the plan with the family.
Ask the family to keep the same plan and return at the next routine visit.

basic.situation: A child has a mild cough and runny nose but is drinking and playing. You are treating minor illnesses with supervision.

options.text: Recommend fluids and rest, then ask the parent to monitor symptoms.
Suggest cough medicine so the family can manage symptoms at home.
Ask about fever and breathing, then discuss care with your supervisor.
Check breathing and hydration, then give supportive care advice with guidance.

advanced.situation: A child with a chronic condition is missing school and worsening despite regular visits. You are managing care and considering specialist input.

options.text: Discuss the decline with the family and seek specialist advice about next steps.
Review progress and arrange a specialist assessment for the ongoing concerns.
Continue the current plan and arrange follow-up to monitor symptoms and school attendance.
Refer for specialist assessment and coordinate care around the child's school and daily needs.

basic.situation: A nurse and student are both preparing for a busy clinic, and a task has been missed. You are helping coordinate the team with guidance.

options.text: Complete the task yourself and move on to keep the clinic flowing.
Ask the nurse to handle it while the student prepares the next room.
Clarify the missed task, agree who will complete it, and update the team.
Check the task list with the nurse and student before assigning work.

advanced.situation: A resident is unsure how to explain a child's growth chart, while the clinic team is preparing a complex case review. You are teaching and coordinating staff.

options.text: Teach the resident using the child's chart, then assign clear roles for the case review.
Explain the chart quickly and let the team work out the review roles.
Give the resident a growth chart handout and begin the case review.
Review the growth chart with the resident and ask staff to prepare their updates.

basic.situation: You are asked to review an autopsy case with scene notes, laboratory results, and a preliminary report that do not fully agree.

options.text: Use the preliminary cause from the referral to finish the case summary for filing.
Compare the scene notes with the autopsy findings, then flag any mismatch for review.
Check the laboratory results against the history and ask the senior about an unclear finding.
Review the report and list its main findings in the case notes for the senior.

advanced.situation: A complex death investigation has conflicting scene and tissue findings, and a junior colleague asks how to proceed with the autopsy review.

options.text: Document the unresolved discrepancy and seek a second pathologist's view before conclusion.
Ask the junior to complete the usual dissection and review the draft later.
Base the opinion on the clearest tissue finding and explain the uncertainty briefly.
Reconcile scene, imaging, and tissue findings, then guide the junior through protocol.

basic.situation: A urine analysis shows trace protein during a routine clinic workup, and a clinician asks you to review the result.

options.text: Compare the result with reference ranges and note it for clinician review.
Summarize the urine result alongside symptoms and related findings in the chart.
Record the trace protein as the likely explanation for the patient's symptoms.
Check the collection details and flag the isolated finding for context.

advanced.situation: Your laboratory is considering a new diagnostic assay, but its early results differ from the current method on several patient samples.

options.text: Compare the candidate assay with current methods using agreed samples and documented criteria.
Review performance across relevant cases, then recommend a measured validation plan.
Adopt the assay after a promising small batch and share the early results.
Ask colleagues which platform they prefer before drafting a local protocol.

basic.situation: A tissue sample has an unusual microscopic feature, and the submitting clinician has provided a brief history for your review.

options.text: Describe the observed change and correlate it with the submitted clinical details.
Label the abnormal cells as malignant based on their unusual appearance.
Review the stain quality and ask a colleague about the uncertain feature.
Compare the microscopic pattern with the clinical history and document the likely differential.

advanced.situation: A complex case has discordant clinical and histology findings, and a junior colleague asks you to guide the diagnostic review.

options.text: Recheck the sample with an additional stain before discussing the case.
Share the leading diagnosis with the team and note the discordant evidence.
Integrate morphology and clinical findings, then explain the differential to the junior.
Choose the diagnosis that most strongly fits the slide and close the review.

basic.situation: You are drafting a pathology report for a routine specimen and need to summarize its findings and conclusion for senior review.

options.text: Check identifiers, describe key findings, and link the conclusion to the specimen.
State the specimen, key findings, and conclusion in the draft for review.
Copy the preliminary conclusion into the report and send it onward.
Organize findings and note any limitation for the senior's review.

advanced.situation: Reports from several staff members vary in detail, and recurring omissions are causing extra clarification requests from clinicians.

options.text: Send the reports onward using their existing formats to meet the clinic deadline.
Draft a shared reporting guide with required elements and examples for staff.
Compare recent reports and identify recurring omissions for a team discussion.
Tell staff to follow the current template and address outliers during sign-off.

basic.situation: A surgeon asks about a preliminary margin finding while you are reviewing the specimen sections for the case.

options.text: Share the report wording with the surgeon and invite any focused questions.
Explain the finding and clarify what the specimen can establish for surgery.
Tell the surgeon the margin is clear from the first section reviewed.
Give the preliminary result and mention that the final review remains pending.

advanced.situation: A physician asks whether another test could clarify a pathology result that does not fully answer the clinical question.

options.text: Review the clinical question and findings, then discuss which test could resolve it.
Suggest repeating the same test to give the team a quicker answer.
Explain the result's limits and offer a focused alternative for discussion.
Ask the treating physician what decision the result needs to support.

basic.situation: Two histology batches are due before noon, and a colleague asks you to help coordinate the bench work.

options.text: Keep the usual sequence and update the senior if timing slips.
Move the urgent batch to the front and tell the team about priorities.
Check workload and assign the next batch according to staff availability.
Ask each technician which slide set they can finish before noon.

advanced.situation: A resident's handovers are inconsistent during a busy week, and the team is spending time tracking down missing work details.

options.text: Discuss the gap with the resident and agree on a check-in next week.
Cover the missed handover yourself and let the shift continue.
Review the roster and move one task to protect the day's service.
Set a clear handover routine, then coach the resident using a recent example.

basic.situation: During an intake, a patient shares a medical history and social detail that may affect the current assessment.

options.text: Note the key history and ask the patient to confirm the summary.
Record the patient's account and clarify any unclear dates before filing.
Copy the previous visit's history and add today's main concern.
Enter the main symptoms and leave the history section for later.

advanced.situation: A team audit finds that clinicians record patient histories in different formats, making key social details hard to locate.

options.text: Ask colleagues to use the longest existing template for future histories.
Review several records and list the most frequent missing details for discussion.
Keep each clinician's format and search records when details are needed.
Agree on core history fields and model a consistent format in team records.

basic.situation: A patient reports fatigue during an assessment, and you are asked to help complete a basic physical check.

options.text: Record the patient's answers as normal because no concern was raised.
Explain the check, record the findings, and share them with the clinician.
Complete the requested check and note any result outside the usual range.
Repeat the check once and enter the second reading in the chart.

advanced.situation: A patient has complex symptoms, and the team is considering a new diagnostic protocol to guide further assessment.

options.text: Define the clinical question and proposed checks, then discuss the protocol with colleagues.
Use the same test sequence for every patient with similar symptoms.
Add another test to the current sequence and compare the results.
Review available findings and outline where the current protocol leaves gaps.

basic.situation: Your clinic invites staff to a seminar on a new approach to understanding behavioral disorders.

options.text: Skip the session and rely on the approaches you already know.
Attend the seminar and note ideas that may inform your clinical learning.
Read the session title and share it with the clinic team.
Attend and ask the speaker how the approach was studied.

advanced.situation: You are helping plan a small study on behavioral symptoms seen in your service, and colleagues want a useful research question.

options.text: Frame a question, agree on outcomes, and plan how findings will inform care.
Review relevant studies and refine the question with the project team.
Choose a broad topic and begin gathering notes from clinic visits.
Collect memorable cases and draw conclusions from those examples alone.

basic.situation: A patient has new assessment findings, and a senior psychiatrist asks you to help draft an individualized care plan.

options.text: Reuse a previous plan and change the patient's name and dates for this case.
List key findings and ask the senior which supports could fit the patient's needs.
Record the patient's preferred support and include it in the draft care plan.
Connect the patient's goals and findings with suitable supports in the proposed care plan.

advanced.situation: A colleague asks you to review treatment outcomes across several cases because results vary between professionals using the same service.

options.text: Compare outcomes and procedures, then share specific changes for team discussion.
Keep the existing approach and wait for more cases to accumulate.
Summarize the outcome differences and ask the team what they notice.
Select the approach used in the most successful recent case.

basic.situation: A government mental health agency requests a routine case summary, and you are preparing the submission for review.

options.text: Send the previous summary again with the latest appointment date.
Check the summary against the record and include the requested case details.
Draft the key events and ask a colleague to check the details.
Include the diagnosis and current medication in a short note.

advanced.situation: A new staff member is preparing to explain a patient's care to relatives and asks you how to make the conversation clear.

options.text: Coach them to explain the care in plain language and check relatives' understanding.
Ask them to keep the conversation brief and leave details for later.
Tell them to read the clinical summary aloud and pause for questions.
Suggest they prepare the key points, explain each in plain language, and invite relatives' questions.

basic.situation: During an outpatient visit, a patient describes feeling overwhelmed and asks for help managing distress between appointments.

options.text: Listen carefully, explore coping needs, and agree on a suitable next step.
Give the patient a leaflet about stress before ending the visit.
Ask what has helped before and discuss one option together.
Offer a familiar coping tip, explain when to use it, and invite questions.

advanced.situation: A patient reports new side effects during treatment, and a junior colleague asks how to discuss the care plan with the team.

options.text: Discuss possible options with the junior before speaking with the patient.
Ask the junior to document the concern and raise it at the next review.
Review the concern with the patient and coordinate a treatment discussion with the team.
Reassure the patient that side effects usually settle and continue the plan.

basic.situation: A patient waiting for a scan asks what the procedure involves and whether it carries risks. You have been asked to explain it with guidance.

options.text: I would describe the procedure, likely benefits, key risks, and alternatives in plain language.
I would ask a senior to explain the risks before we proceed.
I would explain the scan steps and common risks, then invite her questions.
I would hand her the leaflet and start once she nods.

advanced.situation: A junior is explaining contrast imaging to a family worried about risks. You hear them struggle to describe the benefits and alternatives.

options.text: I would tell the junior to keep the explanation short and reassuring.
I would take over and tell the family the scan is safe.
I would model a clear explanation of benefits, risks, and alternatives for the junior.
I would ask the junior to repeat the leaflet details more slowly.

basic.situation: A referring doctor calls for a patient's imaging result while you are checking the draft report with supervision.

options.text: I would share the approved report through the usual clinical channel.
