I would tell the doctor when the report should be available in the system.
I would wait until approval before discussing any findings with the doctor.
I would confirm approval, then send the report securely to the referring doctor.

advanced.situation: Different hospital teams use separate routes for imaging results, and a delayed handoff has disrupted care. You are asked to help improve sharing standards.

options.text: I would map current routes and agree clear handoff points with each department.
I would ask each team to send reports through its usual channel.
I would circulate a reminder to share reports promptly across departments.
I would forward every result to all department inboxes for visibility.

basic.situation: You are preparing for a scan and the referral gives little background. The electronic record contains several earlier notes to review.

options.text: I would review the record and clarify missing details with the patient or referrer.
I would ask a colleague to locate earlier notes and summarize relevant history before the scan.
I would review recent notes, record relevant history, and flag gaps for the supervising radiologist.
I would copy the last note into today's record without checking whether it remains relevant.

advanced.situation: Your team sees inconsistent histories before similar imaging examinations, making comparisons harder. You are asked to help improve how histories are collected.

options.text: I would use one old template for every imaging referral.
I would compare sample referrals and propose consistent prompts for relevant history.
I would tell staff to check the patient's record before each scan.
I would share examples of missing details at the next team meeting.

basic.situation: Before an imaging procedure, a patient reports new pain and looks faint. You are following the department's patient-protection protocol with guidance.

options.text: I would pause preparations, alert the supervising clinician, and follow the protocol.
I would ask the patient to rest while I finish the setup.
I would check the patient and tell my supervisor what I noticed.
I would offer water and ask whether the faintness passes.

advanced.situation: Staff follow different approaches to protecting patients during procedures, and near misses have been discussed. You are asked to help strengthen local standards.

options.text: I would email the existing safety policy to all department staff.
I would ask each staff member to describe their preferred safety routine and concerns.
I would remind staff to follow the department's established protection rules.
I would review near misses and agree practical protection steps with colleagues.

basic.situation: A routine image-quality check shows an exposure issue in a sample. You are helping with the department's quality-control review.

options.text: I would mark the sample as acceptable to finish the check.
I would note the issue and ask a senior to review the sample.
I would document the finding and compare it with the check criteria.
I would repeat the check on another image from the list.

advanced.situation: Recent image reviews show recurring quality concerns, but staff disagree about where errors are most likely. You are leading a quality-improvement discussion.

options.text: I would present recurring issues, invite staff suggestions, and record agreed next steps.
I would ask staff to take greater care during image checks.
I would remove images with concerns from the meeting agenda for now.
I would review examples with staff and track agreed quality measures.

basic.situation: You review a routine image and draft report with supervision. One finding is unclear, and the referring doctor is waiting for the report.

options.text: I would send the images and ask the doctor to interpret them.
I would describe the image as normal to meet the reporting deadline.
I would flag the unclear finding and ask my supervisor to review it.
I would document visible findings and mark the uncertain point for review.

advanced.situation: New radiology staff use varied positioning and reporting styles, affecting consistency. You are asked to guide them on imaging techniques and documentation.

options.text: I would copy one colleague's reports for the new staff to follow.
I would demonstrate the standard positioning and explain the reporting examples.
I would let each staff member keep their familiar reporting format.
I would send staff the reporting template and positioning notes.

basic.situation: A patient describes a new reaction during a routine visit, and you are documenting their medical history with guidance from a senior clinician.

options.text: I would record the patient's account and ask my senior to review it.
I would note the reaction briefly and continue with the visit.
I would copy the last visit's history into the new record.
I would clarify the reaction's timing and details, then document the patient's account.

advanced.situation: A patient with allergy concerns needs input from several specialties. Junior staff are unsure how to document updates and coordinate the care plan.

options.text: I would ask each specialty to add its plan to the chart.
I would align the care plan with involved teams and coach staff on clear updates.
I would summarize the current plan and send it to the teams.
I would give the family one team's plan as the full answer.

basic.situation: A patient with suspected contact allergy needs a routine patch test. You are ordering tests under supervision and the referral has limited details.

options.text: I would ask a colleague which test they usually order.
I would place the patch test order from the referral details.
I would order a broad panel to cover possible triggers.
I would confirm the referral question and order the planned patch test.

advanced.situation: A physician asks which immunology treatment or test might suit a patient with a complicated history. You are advising within your clinical role.

options.text: I would compare relevant treatment and test options against the patient's history.
I would review the history and discuss suitable options with the physician.
I would suggest a standard prescription and testing set for the case.
I would recommend the familiar treatment to help the physician decide.

basic.situation: A patient attends for an initial allergy assessment and asks what you will check during the physical examination. You have guidance available.

options.text: I would explain the examination and check the areas relevant to their symptoms.
I would complete the usual examination and note any obvious findings.
I would skip the examination and rely on the intake form.
I would ask the patient to point out where they feel unwell.

advanced.situation: A team is preparing for a supervised food challenge, and a trainee is uncertain about examination checks during the procedure. You are guiding safe practice.

options.text: I would review the challenge steps with the trainee before starting.
I would review the challenge checks and have the trainee explain when to pause.
I would ask the trainee to watch an experienced colleague first.
I would let the trainee follow the usual challenge routine alone.

basic.situation: A patient's allergy test result is mildly positive, but their symptoms are not clearly linked to the suspected trigger. You are interpreting it with supervision.

options.text: I would compare symptoms with results and keep other causes in the differential.
I would repeat the same test before reviewing the full symptom history.
I would note the result and discuss how well it fits the patient's history.
I would label the patient allergic based on this positive result.

advanced.situation: A patient with several conditions is considering a therapy with possible benefits and risks. Colleagues disagree about its suitability, and you are asked to advise.

options.text: I would explain the team's experience and ask what matters most to the patient.
I would compare likely benefits, relevant risks, and patient priorities with colleagues.
I would discuss available evidence and patient priorities with the clinical team.
I would review similar cases, then discuss how this therapy may apply here.

basic.situation: You are reviewing recent learning materials before discussing an allergy treatment plan with your team. A colleague asks what you will study next.

options.text: I would choose learning that answers a question from recent patient care.
I would read an available allergy update and note questions for the team.
I would ask a colleague to recommend a useful article for discussion.
I would reuse old notes for the next team discussion without reviewing new guidance.

advanced.situation: Clinicians use different approaches when planning treatment for patients with persistent symptoms. You are asked to lead a peer learning session and help shape a protocol.

options.text: I would present current treatment options, invite questions, and compare concerns across the group.
I would ask clinicians to share treatment plans and explain their choices.
I would circulate one plan for persistent symptoms without inviting discussion.
I would design case discussions around shared decisions and draft a practical protocol.

basic.situation: A patient is due for a supervised allergen immunotherapy session. You are assisting with therapy and the patient asks about today's treatment.

options.text: I would confirm the planned treatment with my supervisor and explain it.
I would prepare the planned dose and let my supervisor administer it.
I would ask the patient to wait while I check the schedule.
I would use the previous visit's dose to keep the session moving.

advanced.situation: Several patients on immunotherapy have varied responses, and the team wants a clearer way to review outcomes. You are asked to guide the discussion.

options.text: I would call varied responses expected and close the review without checking patterns.
I would compare outcomes with treatment plans and share patterns for review.
I would summarize patient responses, compare patterns, and bring questions to the next team meeting.
I would ask staff to record reactions during sessions and flag concerns.

basic.situation: You review a patient admitted with fever and cough, and need to assess the likely cause and start routine care.

options.text: I treat the familiar symptoms from memory and chart the usual diagnosis.
I assess the symptoms, review observations, and document a working diagnosis for rounds.
I ask the nurse to monitor symptoms while I wait for senior review.
I compare findings with the chart, start agreed care, and flag uncertainty.

advanced.situation: A patient with kidney disease and heart failure becomes breathless and confused; the ward team needs a coordinated inpatient care plan.

options.text: I focus on the heart failure and ask the team to follow its usual pathway.
I review the changes across systems, align the ward plan, and set review triggers.
I treat the breathlessness first and document the other findings for later review.
I discuss the main findings on rounds and agree a plan with the senior doctor.

basic.situation: A patient with a urinary infection has a urine result and needs a standard medicine plan before the evening round.

options.text: I confirm the result with the nurse and ask the senior to review the prescription.
I prescribe the familiar antibiotic and check the urine result at handover.
I review the result, check allergies and current medicines, then prescribe the agreed regimen.
I use the usual antibiotic dose and note the prescription for the team.

advanced.situation: A patient with poor kidney function has changing blood results while receiving several medicines; you must adjust the inpatient regimen.

options.text: I reduce the dose based on the latest result and document the change for review.
I discuss the trend with the senior and propose a dose adjustment for approval.
I keep the current regimen and flag the results during the next ward round.
I interpret the trend, check renal dosing guidance, and tailor the regimen with review points.

basic.situation: A stable patient is ready to leave after treatment for dehydration, and you need to prepare the discharge paperwork.

options.text: I ask the nurse to check the paperwork and prepare the patient for departure.
I confirm the current plan, medicines, and follow-up before completing the discharge documents.
I complete the paperwork from the admission notes and arrange routine follow-up.
I copy the admission diagnosis and send the patient home with the standard form.

advanced.situation: A patient with several chronic conditions needs discharge, but home support and follow-up arrangements are still unclear.

options.text: I map the patient’s needs, confirm key support and follow-up, and document contingencies.
I discharge on the expected date and ask the family to arrange support later.
I coordinate the main referrals and ask the senior to review remaining gaps.
I hold the discharge plan until each service confirms its part in writing.

basic.situation: A patient with persistent dizziness needs a specialist opinion, and their primary care clinic should receive a discharge summary.

options.text: I send the primary care clinic the admission diagnosis as the discharge summary.
I refer the patient and send a concise summary of findings and pending plans.
I mention the referral at handover and leave the summary for the next shift.
I write the discharge summary and ask the senior to check the referral destination.

advanced.situation: A patient with several conditions is transferred between teams, and a changed treatment plan has not reached their primary care doctor.

options.text: I send the new plan to primary care and confirm the receiving team has it.
I send a discharge summary with the changed plan and ask the team to follow up.
I update the chart and expect the next team to pass the message onward.
I call the receiving team and note that primary care still needs an update.

basic.situation: A medical student is unsure how to present a patient's new fever during rounds, while nurses are monitoring observations.

options.text: I let the student present from the notes and move on to the next patient.
I ask the student to present the fever and review the observations together afterward.
I show the student how to connect the fever with observations, then guide their presentation.
I present the case myself and ask the student to listen during rounds.

advanced.situation: Nurses and residents use different routines for escalating concerning observations on your ward, and a new rotation starts tomorrow.

options.text: I ask the senior doctor to settle the routines before the new rotation begins.
I leave each team to use its preferred routine until the rotation settles.
I circulate the existing ward guidance and ask staff to follow their usual routines.
I agree clear escalation roles with the team and brief incoming residents using ward examples.

basic.situation: After a short stay patient returns unexpectedly, your unit is reviewing cases and arranging a specialty consultation.

options.text: I document the return accurately and bring a specific safety question to the review.
I record that the patient returned and close the unit review entry.
I attend the consultation and note the return for the quality meeting.
I join the case review and share the return details with the specialty team.

advanced.situation: Several short stay patients wait longer than planned, and your unit is asked to help improve flow while maintaining safe care.

options.text: I adjust the daily schedule to reduce waits and watch how the unit responds.
I review a sample of delays, identify a shared cause, and track a focused change.
I ask staff to move patients through faster and report any problems later.
I collect delay examples and discuss possible changes at the next unit meeting.

basic.situation: You see a patient with urinary symptoms and need to document their history before ordering a diagnostic test.

options.text: I document the symptoms and ask the senior which test they prefer.
I record the symptoms, medicines, and relevant history before placing the test request.
I copy the previous history and request the familiar test for similar symptoms.
I note the urinary symptoms and order the usual test for the clinic.

advanced.situation: A patient has a rising PSA result and an incomplete family history; a junior colleague asks how to interpret the findings.

options.text: I discuss the rising result with the junior and ask the senior to interpret it.
I point to the latest PSA value and advise the junior to arrange follow-up.
I review the trend and history with the junior, then explain what remains uncertain.
I tell the junior the result suggests cancer and record that conclusion in the notes.

basic.situation: A patient reports new urinary leakage after a procedure, and a ward doctor asks for your urology assessment.

options.text: I suggest the usual bladder exercises and ask the ward team to review later.
I diagnose routine incontinence from the brief note and recommend the usual treatment.
I clarify the symptoms, assess likely causes, and share a practical care plan.
I assess the leakage and discuss the likely cause with the ward doctor.

advanced.situation: A patient with bladder cancer has worsening urinary symptoms during treatment, and the medical team requests a urology opinion.

options.text: I review the symptoms with oncology and suggest a urology follow-up appointment.
I advise continuing cancer treatment and record the symptoms for the next clinic visit.
I recommend the familiar symptom treatment and ask oncology to review it later.
I assess the symptoms alongside treatment effects and coordinate a tailored care plan.

basic.situation: A patient has flank pain after a fall, and you need an imaging examination to assess the possible injury.

options.text: I position the patient for the usual view and record that the images were taken.
I clarify the injury question, assist with suitable views, and document the examination.
I confirm the requested view with the imaging team and assist with positioning.
I request the familiar scan and document the result as reassuring before review.

advanced.situation: Imaging suggests a complex pelvic injury after trauma, and the findings may exceed the experience of your current team.

options.text: I document the apparent injury and continue routine care while awaiting a report.
I describe the visible injury and ask the senior to decide the next referral.
I review the images, define the injury concerns, and refer for specialist input.
I send the images for another read and keep the current plan meanwhile.

basic.situation: A patient has a minor wound infection after a urologic procedure and needs a basic treatment plan.

options.text: I use the standard antibiotic from the ward supply and document the treatment.
I inspect the wound and confirm the planned treatment with the supervising doctor.
I prescribe the usual antibiotic and ask nursing staff to monitor the wound.
I check the wound and allergy history, then prescribe the agreed infection treatment.

advanced.situation: A patient taking several medicines asks about treatment for erectile dysfunction, while a complex medication regimen is being reviewed.

options.text: I review the request with the patient and ask the senior about medication choices.
I offer the familiar medicine and ask the patient to report any problems.
I prescribe the requested medicine and record it for the next medication review.
I check current medicines and relevant health risks before choosing a suitable regimen.

basic.situation: A patient with a small kidney stone is scheduled for a minimally invasive treatment, and you are assisting the urology team.

options.text: I set up the familiar equipment and proceed with the treatment from the previous case.
I arrange the equipment and ask the nurse to confirm the patient is ready.
I check the patient details, prepare the equipment, and assist with the planned treatment.
I prepare the equipment and confirm the treatment steps with the supervising surgeon.

advanced.situation: During a planned retroperitoneal operation, unexpected anatomy makes the next surgical step less clear than anticipated.

options.text: I reassess the anatomy and adjust the operative approach within my expertise.
I request another view and maintain the planned position while awaiting guidance.
I pause the next step and discuss the altered anatomy with the surgical team.
I continue the planned approach and ask the team to watch for changes.

basic.situation: You observe a prostate cancer treatment session and a new clinical staff member asks how the equipment is used.

options.text: I answer the staff member's question and ask the treatment nurse to add details.
I explain the equipment purpose and point out the steps requiring trained staff.
I ask the staff member to read the equipment guide after the session.
I describe the familiar setup and let the staff member explore the controls.

advanced.situation: Staff follow different routines when preparing patients for prostate cancer therapy, and you are asked to guide the clinical team.

options.text: I remind staff about the routine and observe the next treatment session.
I discuss the routines with staff and ask the senior to choose one approach.
I circulate the usual instructions and ask each team to use its preferred workflow.
I agree shared preparation steps with staff and use a supervised case to teach them.

basic.situation: A patient returning after a leg injury says stairs still feel difficult, so you assess strength and mobility.

options.text: Record that the patient walks well and move to the next review.
Assess strength, mobility, and the movements that challenge daily tasks.
Check leg strength and observe the patient's walking and stair movement.
Repeat the strength check and ask about pain during walking.

advanced.situation: A patient with weakness has conflicting nerve conduction and EMG findings, and the rehabilitation plan depends on the result.

options.text: Review the summary and use it to guide the current plan.
Compare the study patterns with examination findings before guiding rehabilitation.
Discuss the conflicting findings with the electrodiagnostic team before planning.
Select the finding that aligns with symptoms, then proceed with the rehabilitation plan.

basic.situation: After a mobility review, you need to record the examination findings and today's treatment plan.

options.text: Document findings, agreed treatment, and a clear measure for follow-up.
Record the main findings and planned exercises in the patient notes.
Enter the examination results and leave the plan for later.
Reuse the previous note and change the date for today's visit.

advanced.situation: A patient nearing discharge needs a long-term rehabilitation plan that includes work and community activities.

options.text: Add a return-to-work goal and ask therapy to advise on details.
Plan therapy, equipment, and community steps around the patient's goals.
Use the standard exercise plan and let the family arrange support.
Set therapy goals for home practice and review them at follow-up.

basic.situation: A patient recovering from a leg injury is ready to begin exercises to improve muscle strength.

options.text: Use the clinic's usual strengthening set and review progress later.
Prescribe simple strengthening exercises matched to the patient's current ability.
Choose a few leg exercises and ask how they feel afterward.
Ask the patient to practise the exercises from an old handout.

advanced.situation: A patient with a new mobility limitation struggles to transfer safely at home and asks about adaptive equipment.

options.text: Suggest a wheelchair model based on the patient's height and diagnosis.
Offer a standard mobility aid and check whether transfers improve.
Ask occupational therapy for equipment options and discuss them with the patient.
Assess transfers and daily needs before selecting suitable adaptive equipment.

basic.situation: A patient reports pain after therapy, and you need to record its intensity and location.

options.text: Use a consistent pain scale and record intensity, location, and duration.
Check the pain score and ask whether the patient wants a break.
Record that therapy caused pain and continue with the session plan.
Ask the patient to rate pain and mark where it occurs.

advanced.situation: A patient's pain remains high after a recent intervention, and the team is considering changes to the management plan.

options.text: Ask the patient whether the intervention has helped since the last visit.
Review the pain trend, intervention response, and relevant side effects before adjustment.
Keep the current plan and record the patient's latest pain rating.
Increase the medication dose and check the patient's pain tomorrow.

basic.situation: A recreational runner has knee pain after increasing weekly training and asks what may be causing it.

options.text: Call it a strain based on the recent increase in running.
Check the painful movements and ask when symptoms began.
Suggest rest and ask the runner to return if pain continues.
Ask about training changes and examine the knee before forming an impression.

advanced.situation: An inpatient has several disabling conditions affecting mobility, pain, and daily care, and the team needs a coordinated medical plan.

options.text: Ask each service to manage its own problem and share updates.
Review the conditions together and align medical priorities with rehabilitation needs.
Address the most visible condition and leave other issues for later.
Summarize active conditions and discuss priorities with the inpatient team.

basic.situation: A patient's new transfer difficulty affects both therapy sessions and nursing care on the ward.

options.text: Tell the nurse about the transfer difficulty and planned precautions.
Update the care team and align transfer support across ward activities.
Leave transfer guidance in the therapy notes for staff to find.
Ask the therapist to mention the issue during the next ward round.

advanced.situation: An intern asks how to assess a patient with new weakness and plan treatment for the resulting mobility limits.

options.text: Walk through assessment findings, treatment choices, and the patient's functional goals.
Ask the intern to copy the previous patient's treatment approach.
Show the intern the examination and explain key findings as you go.
Give the intern a standard examination checklist to use today.

basic.situation: At a clinic review, a patient with recurring cough works around dust and uses a household well; you need to document relevant exposure history.

options.text: Ask about work and home exposures, timing, and protective measures, then document the answers.
Ask when the cough began and whether it changes away from work.
Record the cough and work title, using the standard history template.
Note the dusty job and well water in the history for later review.

advanced.situation: Several nearby clinics report similar fever cases among market workers, but dates and exposure details differ across their initial reports.

options.text: Collect each clinic's case count and send a combined summary to the team.
Align case details and dates, then compare shared exposures before refining the investigation.
Treat the market as the shared source and focus enquiries on its food stalls.
Check work locations and onset dates, then list workers with similar reports.

basic.situation: You review a routine screening batch and notice several blood pressure results above the clinic's referral threshold.

options.text: Review the elevated results and ask the nurse to repeat questionable readings.
Mark the highest readings and mention them at the next staff briefing.
Use the previous screening list to identify patients needing another check.
Check the readings against the screening protocol and flag eligible patients for follow-up.

advanced.situation: A workplace screening finds high smoking rates among shift workers, but attendance at the existing daytime counselling sessions is low.

options.text: Ask shift supervisors to promote counselling during handover and record referrals.
Send workers a smoking factsheet and record whether they attend counselling.
Add evening sessions and compare attendance by shift next month.
Use shift-worker feedback to adapt counselling access, then track participation and smoking outcomes.

basic.situation: You are helping coordinate a clinic's vaccination education session, and two nurses have conflicting room assignments on the schedule.

options.text: Confirm staff roles and room availability with the lead, then update the shared schedule.
Check the room booking and tell each nurse which room appears available.
Move one nurse to the smaller room and note the change on your copy.
Keep both rooms listed and ask the nurses to choose when they arrive.

advanced.situation: You manage a small occupational health prevention programme, and a new site requests coverage while current staff capacity is already stretched.

options.text: Map the site's priority risks and discuss a limited pilot with the team.
Review the programme goals, staffing capacity, and site risks before proposing phased coverage.
Offer the same visit schedule used at the other sites this quarter.
Add the site to the current rota and ask staff to share visits.

basic.situation: A patient discharged after a stroke needs transport to therapy and help accessing local social support, and you are asked to coordinate referrals.

options.text: Check local agencies and share transport and support contacts with the family.
Share agency contacts and ask the patient which services they can access.
Confirm the patient's needs and coordinate suitable transport and social referrals with the care team.
Ask the therapist to identify transport services and confirm the patient's local eligibility.

advanced.situation: A district service review shows missed follow-up among older patients with diabetes, but clinic, transport, and social service records use different measures.

options.text: Compare clinic attendance totals across sites and recommend practical appointment reminders for patients.
Review missed appointments by clinic and ask social services about common transport and access barriers.
Use clinic records to extend the standard follow-up schedule across district services.
Agree shared follow-up measures, map partner data gaps, and evaluate a targeted change.

basic.situation: A new nurse asks you to explain how the clinic handles routine preventive health screening before her first community outreach shift.

options.text: Walk through the screening steps and invite questions using a routine clinic example.
Send the nurse the screening checklist and ask her to read it before outreach.
Explain the main screening steps and point out where the checklist is kept.
Tell her to follow the outreach team's usual routine and observe a colleague.

advanced.situation: Your review finds rising missed screenings across several clinics, and managers want a report to help choose practical improvements.

options.text: List clinic screening totals and recommend more frequent reminders for eligible patients.
Compare missed screening rates by clinic and summarize staff feedback about common barriers.
Share the rising trend and ask managers which clinics need extra reminders.
Summarize the pattern, assess barriers, and recommend measurable next steps for clinics.

basic.situation: A residents' group asks you to give a short talk about preventing heat-related illness during outdoor community activities.

options.text: Describe common warning signs and hand out the clinic's prevention leaflet.
Show a few prevention slides and suggest residents seek clinic advice if concerned.
Explain warning signs and practical prevention steps in plain language, then invite questions.
Read the standard heat safety leaflet aloud and finish within the time slot.

advanced.situation: A reporter asks for comment on a suspected environmental health hazard, while investigation findings and possible interventions are still being reviewed.

options.text: Describe the reported hazard and advise residents to follow official updates during review.
Refer the reporter to health authority and summarize the concern they raised for review.
Repeat preliminary findings and mention an intervention still under discussion as uncertain.
Share confirmed facts, explain uncertainty, and route technical questions through health authority channels.

basic.situation: You are assisting with cataract surgery and notice the instrument tray does not match the planned procedure. The senior ophthalmologist is preparing to begin.

options.text: Arrange the instruments by their usual sequence and prepare the field.
Check the tray against the planned procedure and alert the surgeon to the mismatch.
Use the available instruments and adapt your assistance as the case proceeds.
Pause your setup and ask the theatre nurse to confirm the tray contents.

advanced.situation: During a complex retinal operation, a junior surgeon struggles with a step that is within your experience. You are leading the case and need to guide the technique.

options.text: Pause at a safe point, demonstrate the step, and explain the key visual cues.
Describe the next movement and ask the junior to continue slowly.
Let the junior complete the step and discuss the technique afterward.
Take over the step and finish it while the junior observes.

basic.situation: A patient reports gritty, red eyes after a dusty commute. You are seeing them with a senior ophthalmologist available for guidance.

options.text: Ask when the redness began and suggest the patient rinse their eyes.
Examine the eye and share your findings with the senior ophthalmologist.
Take the symptom history, examine the eye, and discuss likely causes with the senior.
Treat the redness as irritation from dust and give routine drops.

advanced.situation: A patient has persistent eye inflammation despite treatment, and your examination raises concern beyond your experience. You need to decide how to manage the case.

options.text: Record the concern and ask the senior ophthalmologist to review the case.
Continue the current drops and review the patient at the next routine visit.
Document the findings and refer the patient for specialist assessment with relevant records.
Change to another familiar treatment and check for improvement next week.

basic.situation: A patient with a new eye diagnosis asks about options. Your senior ophthalmologist asks you to draft a plan that reflects the patient's history and priorities.

options.text: Write the usual plan for this diagnosis and leave it for review.
Summarize the history, options, and trade-offs for the senior to review.
Select the quickest treatment and note that the patient asked about options.
Record the patient's goals and ask the senior which plan to draft.

advanced.situation: Several clinics use different preparation steps for the same eye procedure, causing missed checks. You are asked to help develop a consistent service procedure.

options.text: Compare clinic steps with colleagues and draft a shared procedure for key checks.
Share a familiar checklist with clinics and invite practical feedback.
Select a brief checklist and ask clinics to review it together.
Gather clinic checklists and summarize variations for the service lead.

basic.situation: A patient asks whether their new prescription should be for glasses or contact lenses. You are reviewing the findings with a mentor available.

options.text: Confirm refraction, ask about daily needs, and review a suitable prescription with your mentor.
Ask about lens preferences and discuss options with your mentor before prescribing.
Review the patient's prior glasses prescription alongside current findings with your mentor.
Check refraction and preferences, then discuss lens options with your mentor.

advanced.situation: A patient with a difficult eye condition has not improved on the current drops and reports side effects. You need to plan therapy within your clinical role.

options.text: Document side effects and ask the senior clinician to review alternative therapy options.
Continue the drops as directed and ask whether bedtime use may reduce reported effects.
Review treatment response and side effects with the clinical team before planning therapy.
Discuss another suitable drop with the senior and arrange a follow-up review.

basic.situation: A patient reports blurred vision in one eye. You are asked to perform a basic visual system examination under supervision.

options.text: Measure visual acuity in each eye and share results with your supervisor.
Use the glasses prescription as context while checking the patient's vision.
Ask which eye is blurry, when it began, and record the patient's answer.
Check vision in each eye, examine the visual system, and record findings.

advanced.situation: A patient returns after eye surgery with new discomfort, and staff are unsure which checks belong in the follow-up. You are overseeing postoperative care.

options.text: Examine the patient and explain relevant follow-up checks to the staff member.
Ask staff to review the postoperative checklist, confirm relevant checks, and update the chart.
Reassure the patient that discomfort can occur and continue planned follow-up care.
Assess the change, review postoperative checks with staff, and document key findings.

basic.situation: A patient says their eyes feel tired after reading and asks how to maintain healthy vision. You are documenting their history with help available.

options.text: Tell the patient to use brighter lighting and return if symptoms persist.
Record the symptoms and habits, then explain practical healthy vision habits.
Suggest taking breaks from reading and note the patient's main concern.
Ask about reading habits and share your notes with the senior doctor.

advanced.situation: A patient with a complex eye condition has questions about daily care, and their family and another clinician are involved. You need to support shared understanding.

options.text: Explain daily care in plain language, check understanding, and update the clinician.
Answer the patient's main question and record key points for the care team.
Share a care leaflet, invite family questions, and note topics for next clinic visit.
Invite the other clinician to review daily care with the patient and family.

basic.situation: Before a routine knee operation, you review the referral notes and examination findings, but the medication list is incomplete.

options.text: Check the medication list against the notes, then confirm findings with your supervisor.
Rely on the referral summary and enter the planned procedure for review.
Compare allergies, examination findings, and history, then clarify mismatches before listing the case.
Use the latest clinic note to prepare the review and flag unclear history.

advanced.situation: A patient with several chronic conditions has imaging that shows a complex fracture; you must weigh operative approaches and risks.

options.text: Select the familiar procedure from the scan report and brief history.
Review the imaging alongside comorbidities, then choose an approach that protects function.
Choose the procedure from the radiology impression and move to booking.
Match imaging, examination, and medical risks, documenting why alternatives fit less well.

basic.situation: During a supervised fracture repair, the planned exposure is underway and you are asked to assist with the reduction.

options.text: Use the standard set and assist with the familiar steps as directed.
Prepare the listed instruments and follow the lead surgeon's instructions during exposure.
Confirm the operative side and instruments with the lead surgeon before assisting.
Check the imaging landmarks, maintain the planned field, and report changes promptly.

advanced.situation: A severe deformity and poor bone quality complicate reconstruction; you must select fixation that restores alignment and supports function.

options.text: Compare fixation options against bone quality, deformity, and the functional target before committing.
Reassess alignment during correction and adapt fixation to preserve stable function.
Use the established implant plan and verify reduction on the available views.
Proceed with the routine construct that has worked in similar cases.

basic.situation: A patient arrives for an elective joint procedure, and you are asked to gather examination findings for the preoperative review.

options.text: Ask whether symptoms have changed and use the answer for your note.
Examine the joint, check mobility and tenderness, and record relevant findings.
Review the referral and repeat its main findings in your notes.
Ask about pain and mobility, then record the findings for review.

advanced.situation: A patient with heart disease and prior clotting problems is being assessed for major surgery; you need to clarify surgical risks.

options.text: Use the standard risk checklist and document the overall category provided.
Review the history and examination, then list concerns for the surgical team.
Assess current function, comorbidities, and examination findings against the planned procedure's risks.
Focus on the most recent clinic assessment and record its risk summary.

basic.situation: Before a scheduled fixation, you are asked to check the instrument trays and operating room setup with a senior colleague.

options.text: Accept the sealed trays and arrange them according to the case list.
Review the tray checklist and prepare the instruments listed for the case.
Check package indicators and tray labels, then confirm any uncertainty with the senior.
Inspect seals, indicators, and room surfaces, reporting any compromised item before setup.

advanced.situation: For a long revision operation, several instrument sets arrive at different times and one package has a damaged corner.

options.text: Ask the team to use intact sets while setting the damaged package aside.
Verify each set, isolate the damaged package, and secure a sterile replacement.
Check each set's indicators and packaging, then replace any compromised items.
Set aside the damaged package and proceed with the remaining trays.

basic.situation: After seeing a patient with a painful shoulder injury, you are asked to draft the case history for senior review.

options.text: Summarize the referral and add the patient's main complaint to the draft.
Copy the referral history and add the diagnosis discussed during the visit.
Record the injury history, symptoms, examination, and relevant medical background.
Separate the patient's account from examination findings and note relevant history clearly.

advanced.situation: An unusual complication after joint reconstruction may inform future reviews, and you are preparing the detailed case history for audit.

options.text: Build a dated account linking findings, decisions, interventions, and outcome for later review.
Summarize the complication and outcome using the final discharge note.
Include the timeline, findings, treatment decisions, and outcome in the case history.
Record the final diagnosis and treatment outcome in the audit history.

basic.situation: During a routine procedure, the lead surgeon asks you to help coordinate the nurses and assistants as instruments are prepared.

options.text: Confirm the next steps with the lead and relay requests to the team.
Ask the nearest assistant to handle requests while you watch the procedure.
Clarify roles, sequence requests, and check the team has the needed instruments.
Pass along the instrument requests as they come from the lead surgeon.

advanced.situation: During a complex reconstruction, the patient develops an unexpected issue and the surgical team needs coordinated specialist input.

options.text: Assign clear team roles, share the changing priorities, and coordinate specialist input.
Continue your assigned task and wait for the lead to request help.
Ask the lead surgeon what support is needed and relay the response.
Alert the relevant specialist and summarize the issue for the lead surgeon.

basic.situation: A child is brought to clinic with a new abdominal ache. You need to examine the child and note concerns for the team.

options.text: You reassure the family that stomach aches often settle by morning.
You ask about the pain and examine the child with the parent present.
You check the child's temperature and ask when the pain began.
You focus on the child's appetite and suggest monitoring at home.

advanced.situation: A child with several health conditions is being considered for an operation. You need to review findings that may affect surgical risk.

options.text: You review the examination and test results alongside the child's medical history.
You focus on the condition that led to the surgical referral.
You use the previous clinic note to prepare the case summary.
You discuss the latest test results with the senior surgeon.

basic.situation: A child is booked for a procedure, and you are reviewing the chart before the preoperative discussion. You need to check medication allergies.

options.text: You read the allergy list and flag any recorded medication reaction.
You ask the parent about allergies during the next discussion.
You carry forward the allergy note from the last visit.
You check the allergy list and compare it with the current medication record.

advanced.situation: Preoperative tests for a child with a rare condition show mixed findings. You need to prepare the case history for the surgical team.

options.text: You organize the history, examination, and test findings around the operative question.
You include the recent test results and relevant past diagnoses.
You highlight the most unusual result in the case summary.
You reuse a previous case history and update the child's age.

basic.situation: Before a child's procedure, you are asked to check whether the instruments and operating room are ready and sterile.

options.text: You inspect all instrument packs and report any damaged seals before the procedure.
You verify instrument packaging and room readiness against sterile setup requirements.
You ask the theatre staff whether the room has been prepared.
You proceed because the instruments were prepared earlier that morning.

advanced.situation: Several operating room teams have reported setup problems before pediatric cases. You need to review how supplies and safety checks are coordinated.

options.text: You compare setup reports with staff and address recurring safety gaps.
You keep using the current setup while staff report new problems.
You remind each team to check supplies before its next case.
You list missing supplies and affected cases for discussion at the next planning meeting.

basic.situation: During a child's corrective procedure, the supervising surgeon asks you to assist with a straightforward part of the operation.

options.text: You try a new approach that seems faster for the correction.
You focus on handing instruments quickly as the case progresses.
You follow the agreed technique and keep the operative field clear.
You prepare the requested instruments and assist as directed.

advanced.situation: A child may need a transplant, and the team is reviewing a complex operative approach. You need to contribute within your surgical role.

options.text: You proceed with the transplant steps that match your assigned role.
You adapt a familiar technique to address the unusual anatomy.
You apply a technique from a different transplant case without discussion.
You review the operative findings and discuss the agreed approach with the team.

basic.situation: A parent asks what to expect before their child's planned operation. You need to explain the preparation and treatment in clear terms.

options.text: You describe the preparation steps using the clinic's usual handout.
You explain the planned preparation and invite the parent to raise concerns.
You ask the parent to read the printed instructions at home.
You tell the parent the team will explain everything on the day.

advanced.situation: After surgery, a family is unsure about the child's recovery plan and follow-up care. You need to explain the next steps and address their concerns.

options.text: You explain recovery steps, warning signs, and who to contact with concerns.
You tell the family that recovery varies from child to child.
You review the discharge instructions and answer the family's main question.
You ask the family to write down questions for the next visit.

basic.situation: A child with a heart condition is being assessed for surgery. You need to consult the child's cardiologist about whether surgery is appropriate.

options.text: You share the case details and ask the cardiologist about relevant surgical risks.
You send the cardiologist the latest test results for review.
You ask the family to describe the heart condition at the next visit.
You proceed with the surgical review using the referral note alone.

advanced.situation: A complex pediatric operation involves nurses, assistants, and specialists with overlapping tasks. You need to coordinate the team's work within your role.

options.text: You share the schedule and invite team members to review duties, timing, and handoffs.
You focus on your assigned tasks and communicate progress during the operation.
You change the task sequence yourself to save time during setup.
You confirm assigned roles and sequence agreed tasks with the team.

basic.situation: You are preparing a wrist treatment and need to locate a standard point on a patient whose arm rests at an unusual angle.

options.text: Check the point chart and mark the landmark for your senior to review.
Ask your senior to confirm the landmark before positioning the arm for treatment.
Use yesterday's measurement and mark the familiar spot before beginning the wrist treatment.
Compare posture with the chart, then confirm the landmark with your senior.

advanced.situation: A patient has a surgical scar near a planned point and reports numbness there. You are considering an adjusted location for treatment.

options.text: Choose the matching point on the opposite side and document the change afterward.
Move the point a little and proceed, following your usual needle depth.
Review the patient's anatomy and precautions, then discuss a safe alternative with your senior.
Ask your senior whether the scar changes the planned point before inserting.

basic.situation: A patient asks for a warm compress on a sore shoulder while you are assisting with a routine session.

options.text: Place the warm pack over the sore area while preparing the treatment room.
Use a heat lamp from the usual distance for the standard session time.
Ask about skin sensitivity, check the compress temperature, and monitor comfort.
Prepare a warm compress and check the temperature with your senior.

advanced.situation: A patient with reduced sensation requests heat and pressure for a painful shoulder. You have several therapy options available.

options.text: Assess sensation and skin, then choose a gentle technique suited to the findings.
Check with your senior about using pressure instead of heat for this patient.
Apply firm tuina pressure first, then add heat if the patient remains comfortable.
Use a shorter heat session and ask the patient to report discomfort.

basic.situation: You are preparing a standard herbal formula, and a patient asks how often to take the prepared dose.

options.text: Follow the recipe and ask your senior to confirm the dose instructions.
Check the formula instructions, then explain the dose and timing in plain language.
Prepare the usual amount and tell the patient to take it after meals.
Read the label aloud and let the patient decide when to take each dose.

advanced.situation: A patient taking prescribed medicine requests a herbal mixture for several symptoms. You are reviewing possible ingredients and interactions.

options.text: Ask which symptoms matter most and discuss a simpler formula with your senior.
Use the familiar mixture and advise the patient to separate it from their medicine.
Review each ingredient's risks and preparation effects, then check interactions before dispensing.
Avoid the strongest herbs and give the standard mixture with a shorter course.

basic.situation: A new patient arrives for a first visit and seems tired. You are helping collect their health history before the assessment.

options.text: Record that the patient looks tired and begin the usual intake questions.
Ask what brings the patient in and note the main complaint.
Use the intake form and ask your senior about any unclear answers.
Ask about current symptoms, medicines, health history, and daily habits.

advanced.situation: A patient's symptoms differ from their usual visits, and they bring recent medical test information. You are helping review their care.

options.text: Focus on the test result and use it to update the traditional diagnosis.
Pass the test report to your senior and document the patient's new symptoms.
Relate the test information to the symptoms and share relevant findings with the care team.
Continue the familiar assessment and mention the test at the next review.

basic.situation: After a routine visit, you need to update the patient's treatment note and record how they responded.

options.text: Record the treatment, response, and next plan using the clinic's note format.
Enter the main treatment and ask your senior to review the note.
Write the treatment performed and leave the response for your senior to add.
Copy the previous note and change the visit date for today's file.

advanced.situation: A patient reports little improvement after several visits, and their notes show changing symptoms. You are reviewing the next treatment plan.

options.text: Review progress against the goals, then adjust the plan to the changing symptoms.
Repeat the treatment that felt most effective during the first visit.
Ask your senior to review the notes before you make a treatment change.
Continue the current plan for another visit and compare the patient's response.

basic.situation: You finish a routine treatment and prepare the used instruments and room for the next patient.

options.text: Wipe the table and put the instruments in the usual tray for cleaning.
Follow the clinic's cleaning steps and check the room before resetting it.
Ask a senior to check your cleanup before the next patient enters.
Reuse the instrument tray after wiping its surface between appointments.

advanced.situation: A patient asks how to continue stretching at home after treatment, and a new staff member is unsure how to explain it safely.

options.text: Show the patient a gentle stretch, explain when to stop, and check they can repeat it.
Give the patient a stretch sheet and ask the new staff member to explain it.
Advise the patient to stretch only as far as feels comfortable at home.
Explain the stretch, then ask your senior to guide the new staff member.

basic.situation: A patient has visible staining on several teeth during a routine cleaning. You are assisting with standard instruments.

options.text: Ask your senior which instrument suits the stains before you begin.
Start with the scaler you know and change tools if progress is slow.
Check the tooth surface and use the suitable instrument with your senior nearby.
Use the instrument you handled last shift on each stained tooth.

advanced.situation: A patient has tenacious deposits near the gum margin, and a junior colleague asks which instrument to use next.

options.text: Tell the colleague to use the sharpest scaler from the tray for speed.
Recommend the scaler you usually use and watch the colleague begin.
Ask the dentist to choose the instrument while you prepare the tray.
Demonstrate a controlled instrument choice for the deposit and explain your grip.

basic.situation: A patient is due for a routine fluoride varnish application, and you are preparing the materials under supervision.

options.text: Check the patient's chart and follow the clinic's varnish application steps.
Prepare the varnish and apply the usual amount to the teeth.
Use the opened varnish left from the previous patient's appointment.
Ask your supervising clinician to confirm the materials before application.

advanced.situation: A patient with a high risk of decay asks about preventive options, and a newer colleague is learning how agents are selected.

options.text: Use the strongest agent available and explain that it offers extra protection.
Review the patient's risk and history, select a suitable agent, and explain your reasoning.
Choose the agent used for most high-risk patients and show your colleague its application.
Ask the dentist to select an agent, then let your colleague observe.

basic.situation: During a routine check, a patient points out a sore area on their gum. You are helping examine the surrounding tissue.

options.text: Ask your senior to assess the sore while you update the patient chart.
Ask whether the sore hurts, then record the patient's answer in the chart.
Examine the sore and explain that you will ask the dentist about it.
Inspect the area, note its appearance, and share your findings with the dentist.

advanced.situation: A patient has a persistent mouth sore and a tender area under the chin. You are completing the oral assessment before the dentist reviews them.

options.text: Focus on the sore and note its size in the chart for the dentist.
Examine the gums and lymph nodes, record findings, and alert the dentist for review.
Ask the dentist to check the chin area while you finish the gum exam.
Tell the patient the tenderness is likely from the sore and continue.

basic.situation: After a routine appointment, you are preparing used instruments for sterilization and checking a hand instrument's edge.

options.text: Inspect the instrument, sharpen if needed, then follow the sterilization process.
Sharpen the instrument and return it to the tray for the next patient.
Place the instruments in the sterilizer and check the edge next shift.
Ask your senior to check the edge before you prepare the sterilizer load.

advanced.situation: A sterilizer cycle ends with an indicator that does not match the expected result, and the next appointment is waiting.

options.text: Tell the dentist about the indicator and ask how to handle the load.
Set the load aside, follow the clinic's response steps, and notify the dentist.
Use the instruments for the waiting patient while the next cycle runs.
Run the load again and use it if the next indicator looks normal.

basic.situation: A new patient completes a medical history form and mentions a medicine that is not listed in the chart.

options.text: Confirm the medicine name and details, then update the history for review.
Write the medicine name in the margin and continue the appointment.
Copy the form into the chart and leave the medicine entry blank.
Ask your senior to review the medicine before you update the chart.

advanced.situation: You notice charts from several appointments have inconsistent entries for gum conditions. A colleague asks how to record findings clearly.

options.text: Share the clinic's charting guide and ask the dentist to review unclear entries.
Review the entries against the charting guide, then show the colleague a clear example.
Suggest one familiar phrase for gum findings and continue with your own charts.
Tell the colleague to copy the wording from the previous chart.

basic.situation: A patient is leaving after a routine visit, and you have been asked to remind them about their next appointment.

options.text: Send the patient the date from the previous appointment's message.
Tell the patient to call the clinic when they are ready to return.
Confirm the appointment date and remind the patient using the clinic's process.
Ask your senior to confirm the date before you contact the patient.

advanced.situation: Many patients have missed routine recalls this month, and you are planning a short oral health education activity for the waiting area.

options.text: Repeat last month's talk and send the usual recall reminders to everyone.
Ask your manager to choose a topic and continue the existing recall schedule.
Review missed recalls and patient needs, then plan a focused education activity and follow-up.
Offer a general brushing talk and remove patients who missed visits from the list.

basic.situation: A patient describes recurring headaches but is unsure when they began. You are taking their history during a routine appointment.

options.text: You note the headache and ask about other symptoms before moving on.
You enter a common headache pattern to complete the history quickly.
You copy the patient's main concern and finish the intake form.
You ask about timing, medicines, and allergies, then record the answers.

advanced.situation: A patient brings old clinic notes and describes similar illnesses in several relatives. You need to assemble a clear history for evaluation.

options.text: You summarize the family pattern and request records from prior providers.
You choose the clearest old note and base your history on it.
You compare dates, family details, and prior notes, then document gaps.
You list the relatives' illnesses and attach every available note.

basic.situation: A patient reports dizziness when standing. You are asked to perform a supervised basic examination and record the findings.

options.text: You repeat the readings across positions and note symptoms alongside them.
You enter a typical result based on the patient's general appearance.
You check posture-related observations and record each measurement with the patient at rest.
You record one seated reading and move on to the next patient.

advanced.situation: A patient's test findings do not fit their symptoms, and imaging is not available in your clinic. You are preparing the diagnostic workup.

options.text: You repeat the same function test and send its readings onward.
You rely on the symptom pattern and close the diagnostic note.
You mark the imaging as completed to keep the workup moving.
You document the mismatch and arrange imaging through an appropriate referral.

basic.situation: A patient has a mild sore throat and fatigue after a few days of poor sleep. You are reviewing symptoms and history with guidance.

options.text: You label the illness from the sore throat and finish the note.
You compare symptoms with the history and document a tentative assessment.
You list the sore throat and suggest a common seasonal illness.
You record the symptoms and history, then discuss likely causes with your mentor.

advanced.situation: Several patients report similar stomach symptoms, while a public health update mentions a local increase. You are reviewing cases and trends.

options.text: You compare case details with the update and report a possible pattern.
You share the public update with colleagues and monitor incoming cases.
You record each patient separately and leave trend review for later.
You report an outbreak based on the shared symptoms and update.

basic.situation: A patient has a small superficial abrasion after a minor scrape. You are asked to provide supervised basic wound care.

options.text: You apply a strong treatment intended for deeper injuries to save time.
You clean the abrasion, cover it, and record the care provided.
You clean the area and check its size, depth, and surrounding skin.
You cover the scrape with a dressing and continue the appointment.

advanced.situation: A patient with chronic stiffness asks whether electrotherapy could help, but their treatment response has changed. You are reviewing the regimen.

options.text: You increase the intensity to pursue relief during today's visit.
You reassess the response, pause the modality, and arrange suitable clinical review.
You review the response and adjust the therapy within your training and protocol.
You repeat the previous settings and schedule another routine session.

basic.situation: A patient asks about a vitamin supplement for low energy and mentions taking several other products. You are helping with a routine dispensing discussion.

options.text: You add the requested supplement to their list and mention it during handover.
You recommend a familiar vitamin and note their question for the clinician.
You check their current products, explain the label, and record your advice.
You discuss the label and ask them to bring their products for review.

advanced.situation: A patient asks about a synthetic medicine after a doctor changed their treatment. You are reviewing their supplement plan during a follow-up.

options.text: You suggest stopping the doctor's medicine and using supplements instead.
You review the full product list and check the plan with the doctor.
You tell the patient to keep the same supplements until follow-up.
You record the change and coordinate the supplement plan with the doctor.

basic.situation: A patient asks for simple exercise and meal advice while recovering from a minor strain. You are providing routine health education.

options.text: You recommend returning to the patient's usual exercise routine today.
You discuss food choices and leave exercise advice for another visit.
You give a simple exercise sheet and mention balanced meals briefly.
You suggest gentle activity and balanced meals, then check their understanding.

advanced.situation: A patient has worsening symptoms that may need assessment beyond your clinic. A colleague asks how to coordinate their next care step.

options.text: You suggest a nearby clinic and let the patient decide when to attend.
You share the case summary with a suitable provider and explain referral options.
You advise another round of your usual treatment before considering referral.
You explain the concern and help arrange an appropriate medical assessment.

basic.situation: A school screening pupil struggles to read the acuity chart and gives inconsistent answers. You need to complete a basic vision check and record the findings.

options.text: Explain the chart again and note that the answers were inconsistent.
Repeat the acuity test with clear instructions and record each eye's result.
Ask the teacher whether the pupil has struggled with the chart before.
Record the first chart result and move the pupil to the next station.

advanced.situation: A child with limited speech cannot follow your usual vision test instructions. You need to adapt the test communication so you can assess visual acuity reliably.

options.text: Use picture matching with simple demonstrations and record how she responds.
Offer a picture chart and ask a colleague to help communicate the task.
Repeat the standard chart instructions more slowly and record her answers.
Ask her caregiver to explain the chart and choose her responses.

basic.situation: A child with inward eye turning has test results from today's visit. You need to interpret them with guidance before contributing to a nonsurgical plan.

options.text: Compare the results with her symptoms and discuss your interpretation with the orthoptist.
Copy the measurements into the file and wait for the next appointment.
Choose a patch schedule from a familiar case and enter it in the plan.
Review the measurements and suggest a plan for the orthoptist to consider.

advanced.situation: A patient with unusual eye movements has mixed test findings and little response to earlier exercises. You need to help shape a nonsurgical plan from the results.

options.text: Compare test patterns and prior response, then propose tailored options for specialist review.
Summarize the test findings and ask the specialist to choose the treatment.
Interpret the unusual movements and suggest a revised exercise plan for review.
Repeat the exercise plan used for a similar patient and review progress later.

basic.situation: A child with amblyopia is due to begin a patch routine prescribed in the care plan. You are asked to show the family how to apply and use it.

options.text: Show the caregiver how to place the patch and explain the prescribed routine.
Explain the patch schedule and ask whether the caregiver has questions.
Hand over the patch and ask the caregiver to follow the written plan.
Suggest a longer patch routine to help the child's vision improve faster.

advanced.situation: A patient has persistent double vision despite nonsurgical treatment, and the examination raises concern beyond routine orthoptic care. You need to decide on the next care step.

options.text: Document the findings and refer her to an ophthalmic surgeon for assessment.
Continue the exercises for another month and compare symptoms at review.
Discuss the concern with your ophthalmologist and ask about referral options.
Tell her the exercises may take longer and arrange a routine follow-up.

basic.situation: An ophthalmologist asks you to assist during a tonometry procedure. The patient is anxious and keeps moving as the equipment is prepared.

options.text: Continue setting up and ask the patient to stay still for the reading.
Prepare the tonometry equipment and let the ophthalmologist handle the patient.
Reassure the patient and ask the ophthalmologist when to begin assisting.
Explain your assisting role, help position the patient, and follow the ophthalmologist's cues.

advanced.situation: A patient with abnormal eye movements has conflicting assessments from several clinics. You are coordinating input from the ophthalmologist and other specialists on ongoing care.

options.text: Discuss the conflicting findings with the ophthalmologist and record agreed actions.
Follow the latest clinic recommendation and update the patient's file.
Share each clinic's notes and ask the specialists to settle on a plan.
Summarize the differing findings, clarify shared goals, and coordinate the team's next steps.

basic.situation: A family asks how to use prescribed fusion exercises at home after a child's visit. You need to explain the treatment instructions in simple terms.

options.text: Demonstrate the exercise, explain its schedule, and ask the family to show it back.
Explain the exercise schedule and ask if they understand the instructions.
Give the family the exercise sheet and suggest they follow its pictures.
Tell them to practise the exercise whenever the child has free time.

advanced.situation: A new resident is learning how to assess binocular vision in a child who gives inconsistent responses. You are asked to train them in the clinical method.

options.text: Give the resident the testing checklist and ask them to practise with a patient.
Demonstrate the test, explain what each response means, and observe the resident's attempt.
Review the checklist with the resident and answer questions after their practice.
Explain the test steps and ask the resident to repeat them back.

basic.situation: A physician requests a summary of a patient's visual acuity and alignment results before a follow-up. You need to prepare a clear diagnostic report under supervision.

options.text: Write that the patient's vision was checked and send the report.
List each eye's acuity, alignment findings, and test date in the report.
Copy the measurements into the report and leave the interpretation blank.
Summarize the main findings and ask your supervisor to review the draft.

advanced.situation: Your clinical research group has completed an analysis of visual alignment outcomes. You are drafting a scientific paper and need to present the findings accurately.

options.text: Choose striking findings and frame the paper around them without checking supporting details.
Draft background and discussion while a colleague verifies results against the analysis.
Summarize findings and invite the research lead to review the draft before submission.
Compare methods and results with the analysis, then draft a balanced paper with colleagues.

basic.situation: You receive several biopsy samples for routine staining and mounting before the afternoon review. How do you prepare the slides?

options.text: You prepare one slide at a time, checking its label at each transfer.
You follow the staining sequence and label each slide before mounting.
You stain the batch, then compare its labels with the worksheet.
You stain the batch together, then label slides from the worksheet.

advanced.situation: A small, unusual biopsy may lose detail during routine fixation. You need to adapt preparation for microscopy. What do you do?

options.text: You test a small section across fixation conditions, then document the usable protocol.
You compare the tissue with a similar case before selecting a preparation.
You choose the familiar fixation method and prepare the full specimen.
You reuse the routine stain and note the unusual specimen in the record.

basic.situation: A routine blood sample is ready for a cell count, and the analyser flags a possible clump. How do you proceed?

options.text: You rerun the sample and enter the result if the flag clears.
You repeat the count and review the blood film for clumping.
You check the sample and ask a colleague to review the count.
You report the first count and mention the analyser flag.

advanced.situation: A body-fluid chemistry result is far outside the expected range, while the sample looks slightly cloudy. How do you investigate?

options.text: You repeat the assay and compare its reaction with the quality control.
You dilute the sample and report the value from the clearer reaction.
You rerun the assay with a fresh reagent portion and record both readings.
You review the sample condition, assay controls, and dilution response before releasing findings.

basic.situation: Before routine testing, you find residue on the spectrophotometer cuvette holder. What do you do?

options.text: You place a clean cuvette over the holder and continue testing.
You clean the holder using the routine procedure, then check its surface.
You clean the holder and note the maintenance in the equipment log.
You wipe the holder and start the first sample run.

advanced.situation: After calibration, a computer-controlled analyser gives drifting readings on a control sample. How do you troubleshoot it?

options.text: You review the calibration record, inspect the probe, and repeat controls across several levels.
You rerun one control level, record its value, and check whether the drift continues.
You adjust the calibration setting and compare the next control result with its target.
You inspect calibration records, examine the probe, and test controls at several concentration levels.

basic.situation: You enter routine test results while the laboratory system is busy. One value looks inconsistent with its worksheet. What do you do?

options.text: You enter the remaining results and leave the unusual value blank.
You verify the value against the worksheet and related findings before saving.
You compare the value with its worksheet before saving the entry.
You enter the value as shown and flag it for later review.

advanced.situation: A periodic audit finds repeat transcription mismatches between analyser printouts and the computer record. How do you examine the process?

options.text: You review recent entries and amend mismatches supported by source records.
You compare a sample of records with printouts and map where mismatches occur.
You remind staff to check each value before entering it.
You update flagged records after checking each value against its printout.

basic.situation: A routine control result is just outside its acceptable range before a batch of samples. What do you do?

options.text: You proceed with the samples and add a note about the control.
You repeat the control and check the batch only if it passes.
You prepare fresh control material and rerun the control before testing.
You hold the batch, check control records, and repeat the control.

advanced.situation: A revised preparation method improves one tissue type but gives uneven staining in another. You are asked to standardize it. What do you do?

options.text: You adopt the revision for both tissues and monitor the next batch.
You retain the current method and ask colleagues about the revised results.
You test the revised method again on samples from each tissue type.
You compare both methods across representative tissues and document performance limits.

basic.situation: A patient asks what a routine blood count measures while you are preparing samples. How do you respond?

options.text: You describe what the test measures and direct result questions to the clinician.
You explain what the measured cell counts describe in plain language.
You read the result aloud and suggest asking the doctor about it.
You tell the patient what the counts mean for their diagnosis.

advanced.situation: A new assistant repeatedly mislabels culture tubes during a busy shift. You need to support the team and protect sample handling. What do you do?

options.text: You move the assistant to simpler tasks for the rest of the shift.
You complete the remaining labels yourself to keep the shift moving.
You demonstrate the workflow, observe a practice set, and give specific feedback.
You review the labeling steps with the assistant using a real work example.

basic.situation: You are preparing routine blood specimens for cell culture and need to make fresh culture medium under supervision.

options.text: You measure the listed components and ask a colleague to review the mix.
You reuse an unlabeled bottle that looks like the needed medium.
You prepare the medium using the approved recipe and label its batch.
You use a previous batch's measurements to prepare today's medium.

advanced.situation: A rare specimen type has produced poor cultures with the routine process. You are asked to propose a preparation protocol for review.

options.text: You compare specimen needs with prior outcomes and draft a controlled protocol.
You repeat the routine protocol and set aside extra material for later.
You adjust the incubation time and discuss the result with your lead.
You replace the specimen medium with a familiar formula from another case.

basic.situation: You have prepared routine culture slides for microscopy and are following the laboratory's staining procedure under guidance.

options.text: You stain each slide, then check visibility against the procedure's expected appearance.
You follow the staining steps and label each slide before microscopy.
You stain the slides in one batch and move them to the microscope.
You use a stronger stain on every slide to make bands stand out.

advanced.situation: A difficult specimen shows faint chromosome bands after routine staining. You are reviewing which method could improve visibility for analysis.

options.text: You change the stain strength and proceed with the first clear slide.
You repeat the routine stain and ask a colleague to inspect the result.
You choose the familiar banding method used on recent cases.
You compare suitable banding methods and document the selection for this specimen.

basic.situation: You are counting chromosomes on a routine culture slide and have been asked to check your count with assistance.

options.text: You enter the expected chromosome number from the specimen label.
You count a clear spread and record the total for review.
You compare two clear spreads and record counts that need review.
