You count the first visible spread and enter its total in the worksheet.

advanced.situation: A specimen shows a possible structural chromosome change, but the spread is partly obscured. You are preparing findings for the diagnostic report.

options.text: You flag the uncertain structure and review supporting spreads before reporting.
You record the change as likely and continue with the remaining slides.
You describe the visible change and ask a senior colleague to review.
You report a definite abnormality from the partly obscured spread.

basic.situation: You are using a photomicroscope to view a routine slide and need to produce an image for review.

options.text: You capture the clearest field and tell a colleague where it is saved.
You use the previous case's image to complete today's worksheet.
You view the slide and note the field number for later imaging.
You focus the slide, capture its image, and check the saved file.

advanced.situation: A new imaging setup gives inconsistent chromosome images during a validation run. You are troubleshooting the equipment before analysis continues.

options.text: You adjust the focus settings until the images look more consistent.
You select the clearest image and continue the analysis as planned.
You check calibration records, repeat controls, and document the setup issue.
You restart the imaging system and compare the next result with controls.

basic.situation: A new specimen arrives for chromosome testing, and you are entering its details into the laboratory information system.

options.text: You enter the details and ask a colleague to review the record later.
You copy identifiers from a nearby case to speed up data entry.
You enter the patient's name and specimen type to start the record.
You enter the identifiers and requested test, then check them against the form.

advanced.situation: Several recent cases show inconsistent control results, and staff have recorded different handling notes. You are reviewing laboratory quality records.

options.text: You add a reminder to the log and continue monitoring future controls.
You amend the control entries to match the majority of staff notes.
You compare control trends and handling records, then document a targeted review.
You summarize the control failures and ask staff to repeat the checks.

basic.situation: You have completed a routine chromosome analysis and need to summarize its findings for the responsible clinician under guidance.

options.text: You draft the summary and ask a colleague to check it before sending.
You reuse a previous case summary with the same specimen type.
You summarize the result and check its wording against the reviewed worksheet.
You send the main finding and keep the worksheet available for questions.

advanced.situation: A trainee is uncertain how to describe a complex result, and the specimen collection notes show a possible transport issue. You are supporting the case.

options.text: You tell the trainee to copy wording from a similar case report.
You explain the report format and ask the trainee to revisit the notes.
You review the result with the trainee and explain how collection notes affect interpretation.
You write the report yourself and give the trainee a copy to study.

basic.situation: You screen a routine smear and notice several cells look larger than nearby cells. You have guidance available at the bench.

options.text: Compare the stain with the reference chart before recording the cell pattern.
Put the borderline smear with routine negatives to clear today’s queue.
Check a few fields, then record cell sizes on the worksheet.
Scan smear fields, note atypical cells, and flag the slide for review.

advanced.situation: An FNA has mixed cell populations, and several small clusters show subtle shape changes. A pathologist is waiting for your findings.

options.text: Mark the unusual clusters and ask a junior colleague to check their shapes.
Describe the clusters briefly and send the slide onward with the routine batch.
Map the atypical clusters, compare their patterns, and alert the pathologist with locations.
Call the clusters benign based on the dominant population and close the case.

basic.situation: You need to stain a cell sample for a routine bench task, and the protocol lists a standard dilution.

options.text: Ask a colleague to confirm the dilution before staining this tray.
Match the protocol, mix a fresh stain, and record its batch details.
Reuse yesterday's stain after checking its color against the bench card.
Prepare the stain using the posted dilution and label each rack.

advanced.situation: A special stain looks faint across several slides, and today's batch includes a sample needed for a diagnostic review.

options.text: Check controls and preparation records, isolate the batch, then document a verified adjustment.
Repeat the stain with a longer timing and compare the slides afterward.
Release the faint slides because their tissue outlines remain visible under microscopy.
Review the stain steps with a colleague before repeating this batch.

basic.situation: Your microscope image is blurry during a routine slide check, and another bench task is waiting.

options.text: Ask a nearby colleague to adjust the microscope while you prepare another slide.
Wipe the lens with a tissue and continue screening the slide.
Adjust the focus slowly, then check the image at low magnification.
Check the objective and lens surfaces, then refocus using the standard settings.

advanced.situation: A microscope stage sticks during repeated slide checks, and colleagues report similar trouble on other benches.

options.text: Clean accessible surfaces, note the symptoms, and arrange an approved service check.
Move the waiting slides to another bench and report the sticking stage later.
Lubricate the stage using available oil and resume the afternoon checks.
Compare the affected microscopes, check maintenance guidance, and document a safe corrective action.

basic.situation: A specimen arrives with a leaking container, though its label matches the accompanying request form.

options.text: Check the specimen condition and follow the lab's containment steps before handling.
Use gloves and transfer the specimen into a clean container for processing.
Set the container aside and tell the bench lead about the leak.
Wipe the container, then place it with the other samples for processing.

advanced.situation: A weekly check finds repeated specimen-label mismatches at one intake point, and staff are still sending samples onward.

options.text: Tell intake staff about the pattern and ask them to check labels more closely.
Review a sample of recent forms and send the mismatches to the lead.
Pause the affected intake, preserve mismatched items, and document each discrepancy for resolution.
Update affected labels from request forms, then continue intake as usual.

basic.situation: You are entering a specimen for a routine case and notice the request form uses a different spelling from the container label.

options.text: Enter the container spelling and attach the request form for reference.
Record both spellings in the notes and continue documenting the specimen.
Hold entry, compare identifiers, and ask intake staff to resolve the discrepancy.
Check the patient details with intake and update the entry after confirmation.

advanced.situation: A slide shows an unusual cell pattern, while the clinical note mentions a recent procedure that may affect interpretation.

options.text: Describe the unusual pattern and send the slide with the routine case batch.
Add the clinical note to the case record and flag the slide for review.
Send the slide with a concise finding and relevant clinical note to the pathologist.
Record the procedure note as the explanation and classify the pattern as expected.

basic.situation: During a guided FNA collection, the clinician asks you to prepare a slide as each sample is collected.

options.text: Prepare and label each slide as the clinician passes each sample.
Label the first slide and ask the clinician to confirm later samples.
Label each slide against the sample sequence and pass it to the clinician.
Prepare the slides in order and label them after the collection ends.

advanced.situation: Two FNAs are scheduled close together, and one colleague is delayed while slides and collection materials need preparation.

options.text: Assign preparation and labeling by case sequence, then check coverage before collection starts.
Divide the tasks between available staff and update the pathologist about timing.
Ask the available colleague to handle both cases and distribute slides afterward.
Prepare both material sets and let staff choose tasks as they arrive.

basic.situation: You are cutting a routine paraffin block, and the first sections curl instead of laying flat on the water bath.

options.text: Ask a colleague to review the microtome settings before cutting again.
Keep cutting at the same setting and choose the flattest section.
Warm the block briefly, then retry the section with the current blade.
Check the block face and blade position, then adjust sectioning gradually.

advanced.situation: A small biopsy block keeps chattering on the microtome, and only a limited amount of tissue remains for diagnosis.

options.text: Inspect the blade, block firmness, and clamping before choosing a small adjustment.
Reduce section thickness and continue until a smooth ribbon appears.
Replace the blade and test a few sections before resuming the case.
Ask a senior colleague to demonstrate a slower cutting rhythm on this block.

basic.situation: You are staining routine tissue slides, and the protocol specifies the dye sequence and rinse times.

options.text: Check the protocol and control slide, then stain and label this batch.
Ask a colleague to confirm the dye order before starting the tray.
Follow the dye sequence and rinse times, then label the completed slides.
Shorten the rinse so the slides finish before the next batch arrives.

advanced.situation: A research team requests a modified stain for a tissue type that behaves differently from your routine diagnostic samples.

options.text: Discuss the tissue differences with the researcher and run a small trial batch.
Adjust dye concentration until the tissue details look strong under microscopy.
Use the routine protocol and compare the slides with the team's images.
Set a trial protocol with controls, record conditions, and review results before wider use.

basic.situation: You are loading routine tissue samples into a computerized dehydrator after receiving direct instruction on the cycle.

options.text: Check the cycle sheet, sample positions, and run settings before starting.
Start the last used cycle and monitor the display during processing.
Load the samples and ask a colleague to verify the selected cycle.
Select the listed cycle and proceed with the posted sample order.

advanced.situation: A new tissue type needs decalcification, and the usual equipment cycle leaves similar samples too firm for sectioning.

options.text: Compare recent cycle records and propose a test run for the new tissue.
Extend the routine cycle and see whether the next block sections cleanly.
Review protocol guidance, use a controlled trial, and record the cycle conditions.
Ask a colleague to adjust the cycle and check the next sample.

basic.situation: You are checking a prepared tissue slide, and one edge looks folded while the rest appears intact.

options.text: Ask a colleague to inspect the folded area before you record anything.
Review the full slide, note the fold, and follow the lab's rejection criteria.
Check the affected edge against the slide checklist and document the defect.
Pass the slide onward because most tissue appears intact under microscopy.

advanced.situation: Several slides from one processing run show uneven tissue detail, and pathologists have returned different comments about their usability.

options.text: Compare the comments and inspect representative slides from the affected run.
Send the slides onward with a note that tissue detail varies.
Ask pathologists which slides they prefer and adopt that preference for future runs.
Set aside the slides, review control results, and document the pattern by run.

basic.situation: Your scheduled instrument check is due, and the tissue processor display shows a maintenance reminder.

options.text: Tell the bench lead about the reminder and continue other assigned work.
Review the maintenance sheet and arrange the check with available staff.
Complete the listed check and record the date and instrument reading.
Clear the reminder and use the processor for the waiting batch.

advanced.situation: A microtome fails to advance consistently after routine cleaning, delaying sectioning for several diagnostic blocks.

options.text: Check the fault guide, document symptoms, and arrange approved service if unresolved.
Inspect the feed mechanism and record the issue before requesting a service check.
Switch to another microtome and report the feed problem at shift handover.
Keep turning the feed knob while a colleague holds the block steady.

basic.situation: You are compiling slides and requisitions for a pathologist, and two cases have similar patient names.

options.text: Place the slides in name order and attach each available requisition.
Group the similar names together and let the pathologist sort them.
Separate the cases by tray and ask a colleague to check the labels.
Match each slide and requisition by identifiers, then verify the distribution list.

advanced.situation: A trainee is covering slide distribution while routine work builds up, and several pathologists have requested materials at once.

options.text: Ask the pathologists to collect their own slides from the distribution bench.
Split requests between staff and review the remaining queue before handoff.
Prioritize requests by urgency, assign clear trays, and check each handoff record.
Let the trainee choose requests and deliver the slides as time allows.

basic.situation: You receive a routine urine sample and are asked to run its chemistry panel on the analyzer with a senior nearby.

options.text: Check sample identity and controls, then run it using the approved analyzer steps.
Ask the senior to review the setup, then run the sample as directed.
Use the last patient's settings and start the run to save time.
Repeat the run with fresh reagent after checking the analyzer prompts.

advanced.situation: A chemistry analyzer flags a result that conflicts with the patient's earlier panel, and the rerun produces the same unexpected value.

options.text: Repeat testing on another analyzer and compare its result with the original value.
Ask a colleague to verify the result before releasing the report.
Review flags and controls, then compare results with the sample and prior panel.
Release repeated value because both analyzer runs produced matching results.

basic.situation: You are examining a stained blood film and notice a cell shape that may be outside the usual pattern.

options.text: Record the unusual shape and ask the senior to review the field.
Classify the film from the first striking cell and enter the result.
Mark the first unusual cell and finish the rest of the slide.
Check several fields, note the observed cells, and seek review before reporting.

advanced.situation: A junior asks how to report a rare stained-cell appearance that you have seen only once in today's samples.

options.text: Use a familiar rare-cell label so the report can be completed on time.
Show the junior the finding and agree on wording after reviewing reference criteria together.
Ask the pathologist to confirm the finding, then document the agreed description.
Tell the junior to use the usual abnormal-cell wording for consistency.

basic.situation: A ward requests a blood sample for transfusion testing, and you are collecting it with a senior technician nearby.

options.text: Use the ward list to label the tube and send it with the next batch.
Ask the senior to check the request, then collect and label the sample.
Confirm the patient's identity and labels at the bedside before collecting the sample.
Collect the sample first and match its label to the request at the bench.

advanced.situation: Two patients have similar names, and one crossmatch result is incompatible while the ward asks when blood can be issued.

options.text: Hold issue, verify identities and records, then investigate the incompatible result before reporting.
Issue compatible unit matched to the other patient's completed crossmatch.
Tell the ward results are pending while a senior checks both patient records.
Repeat the crossmatch and update the ward once results are ready.

basic.situation: You are asked to prepare a routine reagent from a written formula before the next batch of urine samples arrives.

options.text: Use another reagent's quantities and adjust the final volume by eye.
Prepare a smaller batch using the listed ratios and store it unlabeled nearby.
Check the formula and glassware, prepare the measured solution, then label it with details.
Measure the ingredients from the formula and label the reagent for use.

advanced.situation: A specimen for culture arrives with little material, and the current preparation approach may not preserve enough for analysis.

options.text: Adapt the preparation steps from a similar specimen and proceed with the available material.
Split the small sample between several routine culture conditions to broaden the search.
Use the routine preparation method and tell the reviewer that material was limited.
Record the limitation, preserve the sample, and check an appropriate preparation protocol before processing.

basic.situation: After a busy morning, you are assigned to clean a shared analyzer and check its sterility using the posted instructions.

options.text: Clean the analyzer as posted and tell the next user it is ready.
Follow the cleaning sequence and record the sterility check before returning the analyzer.
Complete the posted cleaning steps and leave the sterility result for the next shift.
Clean the accessible surfaces, then ask a colleague whether the check is due.

advanced.situation: Several analyzers drift from their calibration checks during the month, and your team asks you to improve the maintenance schedule.

options.text: Extend calibration intervals to reduce interruptions during busy laboratory work shifts.
Set check intervals from observed drift, document limits, and review findings with the team.
Add routine calibration checks and record each result beside the service date.
Keep the current schedule and remind staff to report unusual readings.

basic.situation: You find abnormal cells on a slide, and the pathologist is available to discuss the finding before a final diagnosis is recorded.

options.text: Send the slide with your observation and ask the pathologist to decide the final diagnosis.
Flag the slide as abnormal and wait for the pathologist to review it.
Describe the cells you observed, share the slide, and clarify the finding with the pathologist.
Enter the diagnosis that seems most likely and let the pathologist amend it later.

advanced.situation: A new technician records a control result outside its expected range, while the bench is busy and samples are waiting.

options.text: Treat it as a one-off and clear waiting samples before reviewing the control.
Ask the technician to notify the senior while you continue other sample checks.
Repeat the control, review its result with the technician, and demonstrate the recording process.
Pause affected reporting, review the control trend, and agree on response steps.

basic.situation: You are asked to cut routine tissue sections on the microtome while a senior technician is nearby.

options.text: Set the usual thickness and ask the senior to check your first section.
Start cutting at the standard setting and adjust if the section folds.
Check the block face and blade position, then cut sections using the guided settings.
Use the previous block's settings and trim until a section looks usable.

advanced.situation: Sections from a new tissue block keep developing uneven ribbons, though the microtome worked well on earlier blocks.

options.text: Adjust the blade angle slightly, then inspect the next ribbon for consistent thickness.
Inspect the block face, blade condition, and alignment before making one measured adjustment.
Raise the feed rate slightly to complete the block before another case arrives.
Ask a colleague to inspect the microtome settings and advise on a suitable adjustment.

basic.situation: You are embedding a routine tissue specimen in paraffin wax with a senior technician available for guidance.

options.text: Embed the specimen in the easiest position and label the block from memory.
Place the tissue in the usual position and check the label before cooling.
Follow the usual orientation and ask the senior to review the block afterward.
Orient the tissue as directed, check its label, and embed it in the prepared wax.

advanced.situation: A fragile specimen processed by the usual cycle feels unusually firm, and a junior asks whether to use that cycle again.

options.text: Ask a senior to recommend a shorter cycle before processing the next specimen.
Review specimen type and outcome, then trial a revised protocol with the junior.
Use the standard cycle again and record the firmness on the processing worksheet.
Shorten the next cycle to help keep the tissue softer for cutting.

basic.situation: You are mounting a routine tissue section and applying the standard stain with a senior technician available.

options.text: Apply the standard stain sequence and ask the senior to check the slide afterward.
Check the label, mount the section flat, and follow the stated stain sequence.
Mount the section and follow the usual stain timing for this tissue type.
Use a nearby unlabeled slide, then add case details after the staining is complete.

advanced.situation: A difficult tissue type looks faint with the routine stain, and the pathologist needs a readable slide for review.

options.text: Increase stain time for the next slide, then compare both slides carefully under the microscope.
Apply stronger stain to the same slide and prepare it for review.
Check tissue type and staining steps, then trial one controlled adjustment on spare tissue.
Record the faint result and send the prepared slide for pathologist review.

basic.situation: You need to run a routine tissue batch through the computerized processor to dehydrate it before embedding.

options.text: Select the routine program and ask a colleague to check the display.
Use the previous batch's program and start the run to keep work moving.
Confirm the batch and program, then start the processor using the posted steps.
Choose the standard program and watch for an error during the run.

advanced.situation: The processor reports a temperature error during a tissue batch, and the next run is scheduled before the cause is clear.

options.text: Pause the next run and ask a senior technician to inspect the processor fault before restarting.
Review the error and conditions, protect the batch, and consult equipment guidance before resuming.
Restart the same program and check whether the temperature returns to its operating range.
Override the temperature alert so the queued tissue batch can start on schedule.

basic.situation: You are assigned to clean the microtome after use and check it before another technician begins sectioning.

options.text: Wipe the accessible surfaces and tell the next technician it is ready.
Leave the blade in place and return the microtome to the shared bench.
Clean the outside and ask the next technician to check the blade area.
Clean the surfaces as instructed, inspect the blade area, and record the check.

advanced.situation: Staff have found residue on the tissue processor after cleaning on several shifts, and you are asked to improve its care schedule.

options.text: Extend the cleaning interval so residue has more time to loosen from surfaces.
Map residue locations, set targeted cleaning checks, and review completion records with the staff.
Add a cleaning reminder after each shift and ask staff to initial the schedule sheet.
Ask staff to clean longer when residue remains visible after a processor run.

basic.situation: You are filing today's diagnostic slides and blocks, and a case has several items with similar labels.

options.text: File the items in the usual drawer and note the case numbers on a list.
Match each item to its case record, then file it in the assigned location.
Put the similar items together and update the location list from memory.
Sort by label and ask a colleague to check the similar cases afterward.

advanced.situation: A colleague cannot find a diagnostic block during a follow-up request, and you are helping review how archived material is tracked.

options.text: Check the archive log and ask the last handler where the block was stored, then verify.
Move a similar block to the requester's tray so the case can continue.
Search the usual shelves and update the requester after checking nearby archive locations.
Trace the block through the location log, document the search, and update its record.

basic.situation: You are monitoring a patient during an ECG, and the blood pressure reading seems unusual. What do you do?

options.text: Record the reading and tell the physician when the test ends.
Check the cuff position, repeat the reading, and note both results.
Ask the patient how they feel and watch their heart rate.
Enter a typical pressure from the chart to finish the form.

advanced.situation: During a procedure, a patient's heart rate drifts downward while their skin turns pale. A junior colleague asks whether to continue monitoring. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the junior to repeat the lead check and keep watching the patient.
Alert the physician about the trend and ask the junior to observe comfort.
Pause the test, alert the physician, and guide the junior through the response protocol.
Ask the junior to record the trend while you finish the current tracing.

basic.situation: You are attaching ECG electrodes with guidance, but one keeps lifting as the patient shifts. What do you do?

options.text: Continue the test and use the clearest section of the tracing.
Reconnect the lead and begin recording to see whether the tracing settles.
Dry the skin, secure the electrode, and check its lead connection.
Ask the patient to stay still while you finish attaching the leads.

advanced.situation: A patient's ECG tracing has recurring interference despite secure electrodes. The physician is waiting for the result, and you must decide whether it is usable. What do you do?

options.text: Adjust the gain until the waveform looks closer to the previous tracing.
Save the tracing and note that movement may have affected the signal.
Inspect the lead placement and cable path, then repeat a short tracing.
Tell the physician the tracing is difficult and ask whether to proceed.

basic.situation: Before an ECG appointment, the machine powers on but its paper feed does not move. What do you do?

options.text: Restart the machine and see whether the paper feed begins moving.
Check the paper roll and feed path, then test the machine again.
Use the machine for the appointment and request service afterward.
Switch to another ready machine and tell the team about this one.

advanced.situation: A stress-test monitor intermittently loses its display, and a junior asks how to handle it. What do you do?

options.text: Show the junior the maintenance schedule and ask them to log the issue.
Move the patient to another test and leave the monitor for later.
Check the power and connections, remove it from use, and submit a service request.
Ask the junior to restart it whenever the display goes blank.

basic.situation: You are helping prepare a patient for an echocardiogram, but they are unsure how to lie on the table. What do you do?

options.text: Start the scan with the patient in their current position.
Wait for the supervising technologist to position them before starting.
Explain the position, help them settle safely, and check their comfort.
Ask them to lie back while you prepare the equipment.

advanced.situation: A patient with limited mobility needs a position that gives access for testing. A new colleague is unsure how to prepare them. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the patient what movement is comfortable, then agree a position together.
Ask the colleague to use the standard position and adjust the table afterward.
Get the colleague to prepare the table while you explain the test.
Discuss a safe position with the patient, assist within your training, and coach the colleague.

basic.situation: A patient scheduled for an ECG says they are nervous because they do not know what the test involves. What do you do?

options.text: Say it will finish soon, then start placing the electrodes.
Explain the electrode placement and sensations, then invite questions.
Tell them the test is routine and ask what concerns them.
Offer the written leaflet and begin preparing the ECG machine.

advanced.situation: A patient with hearing difficulty appears confused by your explanation of a cardiac test. A queue is forming, and a new colleague is observing. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the colleague to read the leaflet aloud while you set up.
Offer the leaflet in writing and ask what part remains unclear.
Face the patient, use plain language, and check their understanding before proceeding.
Speak louder and repeat the explanation while preparing the equipment.

basic.situation: You are copying patient details onto an ECG form, and the name on the wristband differs from the appointment sheet. What do you do?

options.text: Copy both names into the notes and ask the physician later.
Pause the entry and verify the patient's identifiers against the records.
Ask the patient to confirm their name, then continue with the form.
Use the appointment sheet and finish the form before the test.

advanced.situation: While reviewing ECG forms, you find repeated gaps in test-result entries. A trainee asks how to complete today's records. What do you do?

options.text: Show the trainee the required fields and review today's completed forms together.
Tell the trainee to copy details from the prior visit to save time.
Explain the common gaps and ask the trainee to check each entry against today's tracing.
Ask the trainee to complete the forms and flag any missing results.

basic.situation: During an ultrasound exam, a patient becomes uncomfortable on the table and asks to shift position. What do you do?

options.text: Finish the current image, then help them move on the table.
Tell them to stay still until you finish capturing the image.
Pause the scan, help them adjust safely, and check whether they feel comfortable.
Ask where they feel discomfort and adjust the cushion if needed.

advanced.situation: A patient quietly tells you a support person has been hurting them, then asks you not to tell anyone. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the patient you are concerned and ask whether they want help now.
Listen calmly, explain you must share safety concerns, and follow the reporting process.
Promise to keep it private and continue the examination as planned.
Write down their words and mention the disclosure to the next shift.

basic.situation: You are cleaning the ultrasound probe after an exam and notice residue near its handle. What do you do?

options.text: Clean it using the approved product and check the probe before reuse.
Check the cleaning instructions, then clean and inspect the handle.
Set the probe aside and ask a colleague how to clean it.
Wipe the handle quickly and prepare it for the next patient.

advanced.situation: Before a special scan, you find that only one pack of a needed supply remains. A colleague is unsure whether more are stored nearby. What do you do?

options.text: Use the remaining pack and ask the next shift to check stock.
Check the supply location, prepare the pack, and reorder through the usual process.
Look through nearby cupboards and tell the team if supplies run low.
Ask the colleague to check storage while you prepare the examination area.

basic.situation: The ultrasound image looks blurred while the patient is holding their breath as requested. What do you do?

options.text: Change the probe angle and capture another image for comparison.
Save the image and continue to the next view.
Adjust the equipment settings and check whether the image becomes diagnostic quality.
Ask the patient to hold their breath longer while you scan again.

advanced.situation: During a focused ultrasound exam, you see a finding that may need views beyond the planned scope. What do you do?

options.text: Capture nearby views beyond the planned area and send them for physician review.
Ask the physician whether the finding warrants additional views before extending the exam.
Review the finding, obtain protocol-approved views, and notify the physician about added images.
Save the images and document the finding for the physician's report.

basic.situation: You are producing an ultrasound image with guidance, but the screen view does not show the requested organ clearly. What do you do?

options.text: Change the gain and capture another image for review.
Ask the supervising sonographer to check your settings before saving.
Save the current view and move on to the next image.
Adjust the probe position and settings, then save a clear image.

advanced.situation: A scan shows an area that looks different from surrounding tissue. You must select images for the physician's review. What do you do?

options.text: Select the clearest image of the area and label its location.
Capture the area and a comparison view, then store both with clear labels.
Choose the clearest normal image to keep the image set concise.
Save several close views of the unusual area for the physician.

basic.situation: You are recording a patient's history and notice their prior ultrasound result is missing from the file. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the patient about the prior test and record what they confirm.
Leave the history blank and continue with the scheduled exam.
Copy a likely result from the referral notes to complete the history.
Record that the result is unavailable and check the file source.

advanced.situation: During a records review, you find several stored sonographs lack matching patient identifiers. A trainee asks how to archive today's images. What do you do?

options.text: Archive today's images under the appointment list and review gaps later.
Pause archiving and ask the records team how to handle the unmatched images.
Show the trainee the identifier check and verify today's images before archiving.
Ask the trainee to check each image label against the patient record.

basic.situation: A patient is unsure how to prepare for an ultrasound and where to lie. What do you do?

options.text: Help them onto the table and explain each step as you go.
Explain the procedure and ask the patient to get onto the table.
Point to the table and ask them to lie down.
Explain the exam, help position the patient, and check they are ready.

advanced.situation: A physician is preparing for an invasive ultrasound procedure while a student watches. The patient asks what will happen next. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the student to answer while you gather equipment for the procedure.
Ask the physician to describe the procedure before helping prepare the patient.
Explain your role and preparation steps, then assist the physician as directed.
Describe preparation steps to the patient and ask the student to observe your assistance.

basic.situation: You are preparing a patient for a routine tracer scan and need to position them for the requested view.

options.text: Compare the requested view with the protocol, then capture after confirming patient alignment.
Shift the patient toward the detector and repeat until the tracer appears stronger.
Use the usual preset and begin, adjusting if the first image seems unclear.
Centre the camera over the marked area, then confirm alignment with your supervisor.

advanced.situation: A cardiac function study shows an unexpected pattern, and the physician is waiting for images to guide a treatment decision.

options.text: Select the clearest curve and label it as normal for quicker review.
Check processing and image quality, then describe the pattern without making a diagnosis.
Send the first processed series while noting that the pattern looks unusual.
Review the processed curves and flag the unusual pattern for the physician's interpretation.

basic.situation: After a routine scan, you need to record the administered dose and remaining radiopharmaceutical under guidance.

options.text: Record the planned dose from the worksheet and continue with the next patient.
Record the dose and remaining amount from the worksheet for review later.
Enter the measured dose and remaining amount, then check the fields with your trainer.
Enter the administered dose in the record and leave the remaining amount for later.

advanced.situation: During a records audit, you find a mismatch between a vial's disposal entry and the stock balance before the next preparation.

options.text: Recheck the vial log and stock balance, then document the mismatch for follow-up.
Ask a colleague whether the vial was discarded, then update the balance.
Compare preparation, use, and disposal entries, then amend verified data with an audit note.
Adjust the stock balance to match the disposal entry and close the audit.

basic.situation: A patient arrives for a routine study, and you need to gather their illness history before the procedure.

options.text: Ask about symptoms, prior treatment, and relevant history, clarifying unclear answers before recording.
Confirm the main complaint and proceed if the referral lists a study.
Copy the referral summary into the history field to save time.
Ask about the current illness and relevant history, then record the patient's answers.

advanced.situation: A patient has several past treatments and an unclear referral, so the requested diagnostic procedure may not suit their history.

options.text: Map relevant treatments and symptoms against the referral, then present the conflict for physician direction.
Use the referral's listed procedure and add the past treatments to the record.
Gather the treatment timeline and key history, then ask the physician about the unclear referral.
Choose the familiar study from the referral and schedule the patient accordingly.

basic.situation: After a routine session, you must return an unused radiopharmaceutical to storage and record the disposal of waste.

options.text: Keep the vial beside the preparation area until the next shift checks it.
Return the vial to its labelled storage place and complete the waste record.
Check the label and storage instructions, return the vial, and record waste handling.
Place the vial with the routine stock and finish the waste log later.

advanced.situation: A stock preparation is delayed, and the next vial's label and shielding do not match the usual setup.

options.text: Pause preparation, check the label and shielding, and follow the approved handling procedure.
Move the vial to the usual shielded area and wait for clarification.
Check the vial label against the preparation sheet before continuing the stock preparation.
Use the familiar preparation setup and ask a colleague to check the vial afterward.

basic.situation: Before a routine injection, a patient asks what the scan involves and how they should follow safety precautions.

options.text: Give the standard explanation and start preparing the patient for the test.
Explain the steps and precautions in plain language, then check what the patient understood.
Tell the patient the scan is routine and continue with the preparation.
Describe the injection and ask the patient to read the printed precautions.

advanced.situation: During a directed radiopharmaceutical injection, the patient reports sudden discomfort and looks pale before the planned dose is complete.

options.text: Stop the injection, assess the patient, and promptly alert the physician about the reaction.
Pause briefly, offer reassurance, and resume if the patient says they feel better.
Pause the injection and tell the physician the patient looks pale and uncomfortable.
Complete the planned dose while asking the patient whether the discomfort is easing.

basic.situation: A student is learning the camera controls during a routine scan and asks you to demonstrate the basic setup.

options.text: Set the controls for the student so the scan can begin on schedule.
Ask the student to copy the last setup and continue with the patient.
Show the setup sequence, then let the student repeat it while you observe.
Demonstrate the basic controls and point out the key checks before scanning.

advanced.situation: New staff have inconsistent preparation habits, and you are asked to plan their initial training for routine nuclear medicine work.

options.text: Pair each starter with a colleague and review progress at the end of training.
Share the existing notes and let each new starter follow them during shifts.
Build sessions around preparation tasks, observed practice, and feedback on common errors.
Set a sequence of demonstrations, supervised practice, and sign-offs for each core task.

basic.situation: You are setting up a routine chest image, and the senior technologist asks you to adjust the tube distance and controls.

options.text: I would position by eye and adjust exposure after the first image.
I would match the requested view and exposure chart before positioning.
I would use yesterday's settings and expose this patient at once.
I would set the listed distance and exposure, then check the field.

advanced.situation: During catheter guidance, the live fluoroscope image shifts as the physician advances the wire, making the target harder to see.

options.text: I would hold the current view and let the physician continue guiding.
I would recenter the image and check whether the wire is visible.
I would widen the view and ask the physician to confirm the target.
I would adjust the view with the physician and keep the target visible.

basic.situation: A patient looks tense before a scan and asks what will happen once they enter the room.

options.text: I would describe the scan steps and check how the patient feels.
I would explain the procedure and watch for signs of discomfort.
I would ask a colleague to explain while I prepare the scanner.
I would say the scan is routine and ask the patient to lie still.

advanced.situation: During a quality control check, a mobile unit shows an inconsistent output reading before a busy ward round.

options.text: I would repeat the reading after the ward round and keep a note.
I would repeat the check and record the readings for the supervisor.
I would mark the unit unavailable and report the reading with the check details.
I would use the unit for the round and mention the reading later.

basic.situation: A patient arrives by wheelchair for an examination, and the room still needs its table and basic equipment prepared.

options.text: I would ask a colleague to help transfer the patient and prepare the room.
I would bring the patient in and arrange the table around them.
I would bring the patient near the room while checking available equipment.
I would prepare the table and equipment before bringing the patient in.

advanced.situation: A radiologist directs you to prepare contrast material for a delayed examination while two other rooms are waiting.

options.text: I would use the usual mixture to avoid delaying the waiting rooms.
I would verify the order and patient, prepare the material, then label it.
I would prepare the directed material and label it for the examination.
I would pause preparation and ask the radiologist which room should go first.

basic.situation: You are entering scan sequence details into the computer, and your senior technologist is guiding you through the commands.

options.text: I would follow the guidance and enter each requested sequence detail.
I would copy the last sequence and save it under this patient's record.
I would enter the main sequence now and fill minor fields later.
I would enter the sequence as shown and review the saved details.

advanced.situation: A protocol file was updated for a revised examination, but staff still retrieve the older version from the archive.

options.text: I would replace the old file with the revised protocol and note its date.
I would rename the new file and leave both versions in the same folder.
I would keep using the older file until everyone has time to switch.
I would update the current protocol file and verify the archived link points to it.

basic.situation: A patient with limited mobility needs help changing before an examination, and a senior staff member is nearby.

options.text: I would ask the patient to change alone while I prepare the room.
I would offer help and check with the senior before assisting.
I would ask the senior to handle changing while I finish setup.
I would explain each step and help the patient change with the senior nearby.

advanced.situation: Two staff members are delayed, a new hire is shadowing, and the afternoon list is backing up across several rooms.

options.text: I would assign rooms by readiness and patient flow, then brief the new hire.
I would assign open rooms by readiness and have the new hire observe an experienced colleague.
I would ask the team to choose rooms while I review the list.
I would give everyone the same room duties to keep the assignments simple.

basic.situation: You review a developed x-ray and notice that the requested area is partly outside the image frame.

options.text: I would file the image as satisfactory because most of the area is visible.
I would flag the image and show the senior technologist its cropped area.
I would compare it with the prior image before deciding what to report.
I would note the cropped area and ask whether another view is needed.

advanced.situation: A physician's request lists two body areas, while the afternoon schedule has little time between patients.

options.text: I would review both areas and arrange time that fits the schedule.
I would ask the physician to shorten the request to fit the schedule.
I would book the usual slot and let the room adjust the sequence.
I would confirm both areas from the request before scheduling the patient.

basic.situation: You connect a patient's physiological leads to the PAC unit before a routine scan. One channel shows a weak trace.

options.text: Attach the leads by color, then start scanning to save time.
Ask a colleague to confirm the channel, then test one trace.
Connect the labeled leads and verify each trace before acquisition.
Connect the PAC leads, match each label, and check signal quality.

advanced.situation: During a functional brain scan, the optical system's timing drifts from the acquisition sequence. The research team needs usable event-linked images.

options.text: Save the current run and repeat it after checking the timing logs.
Pause the sequence, check optical timing against the protocol, then resume.
Ask the researcher whether the timing shift affects the planned analysis.
Continue the sequence and note the timing drift in the scan record.

basic.situation: You take a brief medical history before a routine MRI. The patient mentions an implanted device but cannot recall its details.

options.text: Clarify the device details and follow the department's screening escalation process.
Record the device name from memory and continue the routine interview.
Ask when it was implanted and note the patient's uncertainty for review.
Ask the patient to check their records while you finish other questions.

advanced.situation: A patient with limited mobility needs an immobilization device for a scan, but the first position causes discomfort and leaves the target area misaligned.

options.text: Secure the patient in the original position and begin the planned scan.
Ask a colleague to help reposition the patient and repeat the alignment check.
Adjust the supports until the patient is comfortable, then check alignment.
Reposition with suitable supports, confirm comfort and alignment, and reassess the setup.

basic.situation: You attach physiological monitoring leads before a scan. The patient's finger lead shifts when they rest their hand on the cradle.

options.text: Secure the lead more firmly and check the displayed signal before starting.
Ask the patient to keep still while you watch the monitor closely.
Tape the lead over the glove and continue with the scheduled scan.
Reposition the finger lead, secure it, and check the signal at rest.

advanced.situation: You are preparing intravenous contrast for an ordered MRI. The patient's history includes a concern that needs clarification before the planned injection.

options.text: Document the concern and ask the ordering team to advise on the injection.
Pause preparation and clarify the concern through the department's contrast process.
Ask the patient to explain the concern while you prepare the injection.
Use the usual dose and proceed because the scan is already scheduled.

basic.situation: You count clinical supplies after a routine shift and find that the stock of monitoring leads is below the usual level.

options.text: Borrow leads from another room and leave the count for next shift.
Update the inventory and flag the low lead stock for replenishment.
Record the usual quantity so the inventory sheet stays consistent.
Tell the next shift that leads are running low and continue work.

advanced.situation: A coil fault appears during a booked scan, and another coil produces an unusual signal on the test image. The next patient is waiting.

options.text: Switch to the other coil and proceed with the booked examination.
Take the suspect coil out of use, test the alternative, and report the fault.
Check the connections and test the coil against the equipment procedure.
Restart the scanner and repeat the test image with the current coil.

basic.situation: After a routine scan, you need to create a backup copy of the images for the workstation. The transfer display reports a warning.

options.text: Retry the transfer and check that the images appear on the workstation.
Repeat the transfer and note the warning in the handover record.
Dismiss the warning and mark the image backup as complete.
Save the transfer log and ask the next shift to check the workstation.

advanced.situation: A physician asks for a summary after a difficult scan. The images show a motion issue that changed the planned sequence during the examination.

options.text: List the scan sequences and attach the image set for the physician.
Record the motion issue and sequence change in a concise procedure note.
Write that the scan was completed and send the usual brief note.
Summarize the sequence change and describe its effect on the acquired images.

basic.situation: You offer headphones before a routine scan. The patient says the fit feels loose and asks whether they will still hear the scanner noise.

options.text: Offer earplugs as another option and ask which feels more comfortable.
Tell the patient the noise is normal and start the scan as planned.
Ask the patient to hold the headphones in place during the scan.
Adjust the headphones, check the fit, and explain that scanner noise remains audible.

advanced.situation: A new staff member is preparing to help with an MRI procedure and asks how to operate the equipment while a patient is waiting.

options.text: Give a quick overview and let the staff member try the controls during the scan.
Review the main controls and ask them to observe the upcoming procedure.
Point them to the equipment guide and answer questions after the scan.
Explain the procedure, demonstrate controls, and check their understanding before patient work.

basic.situation: You draft a routine radiation field arrangement from the planning guide. One field may expose a nearby critical structure.

options.text: Use the guide's standard arrangement and send the draft for review.
Keep the field arrangement and note the structure for the team meeting.
Compare the field edges with the structure and revise the draft accordingly.
Adjust the field arrangement to reduce exposure and document the trade-off.

advanced.situation: A complex plan needs input from radiation oncology colleagues, but a junior teammate's proposed fields may leave little margin around a critical structure.

options.text: Compare alternatives with the team and explain their effects on the critical structure.
Accept the proposed fields and circulate the plan to meet the deadline.
Ask the junior teammate to revise the fields using the planning guide.
Bring the concern to the team and request comments on the proposed fields.

basic.situation: You calculate the prescribed dose for a routine course using the planning checklist. Your total differs from the prescribed course value.

options.text: Repeat the arithmetic and ask a colleague to check your total.
Recheck the inputs and calculation steps, then document the discrepancy for review.
Change the course value to match your calculation and continue planning.
Use the prescribed course value and finish the worksheet for review.

advanced.situation: A complex course has several treatment sessions and a revised prescribed total. Your verified session calculation does not reconcile with the course schedule.

options.text: Recalculate the total and ask the team to confirm the revised prescription.
Keep the schedule and adjust the final session to match the revised total.
Use the revised total and flag the session mismatch in your notes.
Reconcile the prescription, session schedule, and calculation before releasing the plan.

basic.situation: You outline bodily structures on a routine planning image with guidance. A boundary is unclear near the treatment area.

options.text: Trace the boundary from the visible image and save the outline for review.
Follow the usual outline and leave the unclear boundary unchanged.
Compare the relevant image views, mark the uncertainty, and seek review.
Check another available view and revise the contour before saving.

advanced.situation: You supervise a tumor localization simulation with a difficult target. The localization marker appears shifted on one image, and staff are waiting for direction.

options.text: Review image alignment, adjust the marker, and brief staff on the change.
Ask staff to repeat the image and compare it with the first view.
Accept the marker position and proceed with the planned simulation sequence.
Pause the simulation and ask a colleague to inspect the shifted marker.

basic.situation: You help fabricate a routine beam modifying device from the approved plan. A measured edge differs slightly from the template.

options.text: Trim the edge to fit the template and record the measurement difference.
Recheck the template and measurements, then adjust the device to match the plan.
Compare the device with the template and ask the supervisor about the difference.
Use the device as made and tell the therapist about the edge.

advanced.situation: A custom immobilization device is needed for a patient whose position differs from the usual setup. The first mold does not hold the position consistently.

options.text: Assess the positioning needs and design a revised device protocol with the team.
Use the first mold and add padding during treatment setup.
Ask a colleague to review the mold before choosing another fabrication method.
Add support material to the mold and check whether the position holds.

basic.situation: You run a routine quality assurance check on a treatment planning computer. A calibration value falls outside the expected range.

options.text: Pause use for planning, document the result, and follow the QA escalation process.
Continue planning and mention the value in your next handover.
Repeat the check and record the out-of-range value for the team.
Ask a colleague to repeat the calibration check before you continue.

advanced.situation: Your research review finds that a planning system handles a device type inconsistently. A team is considering using it in a routine plan.

options.text: Characterize the inconsistency, define a validation approach, and share findings with the team.
Tell the team about the issue and ask them to check each plan carefully.
Compare affected plans and summarize the pattern for the planning team.
Approve the routine plan and record the inconsistency for later research.

basic.situation: You record a patient's administered radiation dose in the medical record. The treatment entry and handover sheet show different totals.

options.text: Check the treatment record, resolve the discrepancy, and document the verified dose.
Enter the treatment total and flag the mismatch for the team to review.
Ask the therapist which total was delivered before updating the record.
Copy the handover total into the record so both documents match.

advanced.situation: You are teaching residents a complex dosimetry concept, and their questions show that they are applying it differently to the same planning example.

options.text: Share the answer key, then move to the next topic.
Explain with the example, then have residents apply it and discuss results.
Explain the concept again using a simpler example from the course.
Ask each resident to describe their reasoning before you clarify the concept.

basic.situation: Dispatch directs you to a residential street, and you need to drive the ambulance there during heavy rain.

options.text: Increase speed through rain to recover time on the way to the call.
Use a familiar shortcut to reach the address sooner despite the rain.
Follow dispatch's route and reduce speed for wet conditions on the residential street.
Confirm the address, follow the route, and notify dispatch if access is blocked.

advanced.situation: You are checking the ambulance before a busy shift and find a monitor battery low and several first-aid items missing.

options.text: Keep the vehicle in service and use the monitor's spare battery later.
Replace the missing supplies and note the battery issue for the next check.
Mark the checklist complete and plan to replace items after the shift.
Restock the kit, verify a working battery, and report the equipment status before service.

basic.situation: A patient is being transported, and dispatch asks for a brief update to help the receiving team prepare.

options.text: Send a quick message that the ambulance is nearly there.
Report the condition, care given, and estimated arrival through the usual channel.
Give dispatch the patient's name and say the ride is going smoothly.
Share the patient's main complaint and current condition with dispatch.

advanced.situation: At a road collision, police and fire crews are working nearby while your team prepares to transport two injured people.

options.text: Confirm responder roles, share changing patient priorities, and coordinate transport updates with dispatch.
Agree on a handoff point with nearby responders and share patient updates.
Focus on your assigned patient and let the other crews coordinate themselves.
Transport the more vocal patient first and update others afterward.

basic.situation: You arrive to find a person seated on the pavement, reporting pain after a fall and appearing pale.

options.text: Treat the fall as minor because the person can answer questions.
Help the person stand so you can see how they move.
Ask about the fall and check the painful area before reporting.
Check responsiveness, breathing, visible injuries, and pain before prioritizing care.

advanced.situation: After a vehicle collision, one patient has several injuries and becomes less responsive while your partner assesses another casualty.

options.text: Finish the current check before considering the patient's reduced response.
Recheck the patient's responsiveness and tell your partner what changed.
Reassess immediate threats, reprioritize care, and coordinate the partner's next assessment.
Continue checking the most painful injury before moving to other concerns.

basic.situation: A patient has a small bleeding cut after a kitchen accident, and your partner asks you to provide first aid.

options.text: Apply a dressing and check whether the bleeding has slowed.
Explain the care, apply a clean dressing, and reassess the bleeding.
Cover the cut with gauze and continue preparing the stretcher.
Wrap the cut firmly and move on to loading the patient.

advanced.situation: During transport, a patient becomes short of breath and your partner asks you to prepare the heart monitor.

options.text: Finish attaching the leads before checking the patient's breathing again.
Keep the patient still and wait for the next hospital update.
Set up the monitor and report the readings to your partner.
Reassess breathing, start indicated airway support, and monitor while updating your partner.

basic.situation: Your team is preparing to place a patient with back pain onto a stretcher after a fall.

options.text: Pull the patient across the sheet to reach the stretcher quickly.
Confirm the team's positions, support alignment, and move together on the count.
Lift the patient by the shoulders while your partner moves the legs.
Help position the stretcher and follow your partner's movement count.

advanced.situation: A patient with suspected spinal injury must be moved from a narrow hallway, and two responders are unfamiliar with the transfer.

options.text: Ask the stronger responder to lead while you support the patient's legs.
Check the route, assign support roles, and guide a coordinated aligned transfer.
Assign each responder a position and guide the movement on a count.
Move the stretcher closer and let the responders choose their grips.

basic.situation: A patient waiting for transport is frightened and repeatedly asks whether the injury will hurt.

options.text: Change the subject and finish preparing the transport equipment.
Tell the patient to relax because the ride will be short.
Acknowledge the fear, explain the next step, and invite questions.
Tell the patient you are checking their comfort and stay nearby.

advanced.situation: A delayed transport leaves an injured patient and a worried family member waiting together at the roadside.

options.text: Focus on equipment checks and let the family answer the patient's questions.
Update them when you can and ask what would help them wait.
Explain the delay, check concerns, and give a clear next update.
Ask the family member to keep the patient calm while you prepare.

basic.situation: A patient has chest pain, and the senior asks you to prepare the EKG while they assess him.

options.text: Check the EKG setup with the senior, then capture a clear tracing.
Ask the senior to confirm rhythm, then prepare the EKG leads.
Prepare the leads and record the tracing for the handover.
Print a quick tracing using the nearest available lead placement.

advanced.situation: A patient becomes unresponsive with a shockable rhythm, while a junior teammate hesitates over the defibrillator.

options.text: Tell the teammate to charge while you check the rhythm again.
Ask the teammate to follow the device prompts and prepare the next shock.
Take the controls, deliver the indicated shock, and direct a clear role rotation.
Deliver the shock yourself, then ask the teammate to resume compressions.

basic.situation: A patient with severe breathing difficulty needs an airway intervention before transport, and the lead paramedic asks you to assist.

options.text: Set out the familiar kit and begin arranging the airway supplies.
Bring the airway kit and wait beside the patient for instructions.
Check the patient's airway, prepare requested supplies, and stay ready to assist.
Prepare the airway kit and confirm each requested item with the lead.

advanced.situation: After a collision, a patient has worsening breathing and chest trauma; transport is several minutes away and your partner asks about intervention.

options.text: Prepare the invasive kit because chest trauma often needs early intervention.
Ask your partner to prepare the kit while you reassess breathing.
Continue airway support and discuss possible intervention during transport preparation.
Use the signs and protocol to assess the need, then brief your partner.

basic.situation: A patient needs an injectable medicine, and the senior asks you to prepare it from the treatment plan.

options.text: Prepare the medicine and leave it ready for the senior's check.
Match the order, medicine, and patient details before preparing the injection.
Check the order and label, then ask the senior to verify the dose.
Draw up the listed amount using the familiar syringe size.

advanced.situation: A patient develops new symptoms after emergency medicine, and the treatment team needs a prompt decision about further pharmacological care.

options.text: Give the planned next dose and monitor for another few minutes.
Tell the lead about the symptoms and pause further medication preparation.
Record the symptoms and continue supportive care while awaiting direction.
Reassess the patient, relate symptoms to treatment, and follow the emergency protocol.

basic.situation: At a roadside call, a patient has a painful leg injury and asks whether it is serious.

options.text: Focus on the painful area and tell the patient it seems manageable.
Check the injury and vital signs, then report your findings to the senior.
Assess the patient for urgent threats before examining the leg injury.
Ask about the injury and prepare the patient for transport.

advanced.situation: An older patient is confused after a fall, and the family gives conflicting accounts while the patient's condition changes.

options.text: Check vital signs and report the confusion to the receiving team.
Assess urgent signs, clarify key history, and prioritize care as findings change.
Use the family's clearest account to guide the initial assessment.
Ask the family for a full history before choosing procedures.

basic.situation: At a multi-vehicle crash, the team leader asks you to coordinate access with fire personnel while another patient awaits assessment.

options.text: Use the open route and tell your team where to gather.
Agree a safe route with fire personnel, then relay access and patient priorities.
Ask fire personnel for directions and pass the route to your partner.
Confirm the route with fire personnel and update the team leader before directing access.

advanced.situation: A patient is deteriorating during transfer, and the receiving clinician asks what treatment was given and how the patient responded.

options.text: Report the treatment and response, then let the receiving clinician ask questions.
Read the treatment notes aloud while the receiving team settles the patient.
Give the latest vital signs and mention the medicine during handover.
Give a concise timeline of findings, treatment, response, and current concerns.

basic.situation: Your certification course includes a new cardiac response module, and you are due to refresh your emergency skills this month.

options.text: Book the class and skim the handouts before your next shift.
Attend the module and note procedures that differ from your current practice.
Review the course summary and rely on your existing field experience.
Attend the class, practise the updated skills, and clarify uncertain steps.

advanced.situation: A new teammate is unsettled after a difficult call, and you are asked to coach them on patient reassurance during responses.

options.text: Tell the teammate to keep patients calm by speaking confidently.
Model calm reassurance, then coach the teammate through a patient-centred practice scenario.
Show the teammate a reassuring phrase and let them practise it later.
Share a few phrases that have helped patients feel calmer.

basic.situation: A patient says they have skipped breakfast several times this week, and the dietitian asks you to record their dietary history.

options.text: I would note the skipped meals and ask what the patient usually eats.
I would record that the patient eats poorly and send the note along.
I would ask the patient to remember the exact meals from each day.
I would list the skipped breakfasts and ask when the pattern began.

advanced.situation: A patient reports better appetite, but their recorded intake has fallen and their weight has changed since the last review.

options.text: I would ask the patient about meal changes and pass their account to the dietitian.
I would compare intake and weight records, then alert the dietitian to the change.
I would ask about recent meals and symptoms during today's patient check-in.
I would treat the appetite report as encouraging and continue routine monitoring.

basic.situation: You are helping choose lunch items for a menu, and the dietitian gives you a simple nutrition guideline to follow.

options.text: I would check each item against the guideline and balance the menu choices.
I would select the most popular items so patients have familiar choices.
I would choose familiar items that fit the guideline and menu theme.
I would repeat last week's menu because staff already know how to serve it.

advanced.situation: A dietitian asks you to draft meal choices for a patient with several dietary restrictions and limited options on the ward menu.

options.text: I would remove the usual restricted items and keep the remaining menu.
I would list suitable dishes and ask the dietitian to review them.
I would adapt available dishes to each restriction and check the draft with the dietitian.
I would offer a short menu of plain dishes to reduce the risk.

basic.situation: You are preparing a simple meal for the ward using a recipe and a set quantity for today's service.

options.text: I would prepare the recipe as written and ask a colleague to taste it.
I would follow the recipe and measure quantities for the planned servings.
I would follow the recipe and check the meal before it goes out.
I would use approximate amounts to finish before the meal service starts.

advanced.situation: A new dish is being considered for service, and the dietitian asks you to test its recipe yield, quality, and cost.

options.text: I would make a small batch and note the taste and ingredient cost.
I would ask kitchen staff to adjust the recipe during service.
I would prepare a full batch and estimate the cost afterward.
I would test a measured batch and record yield, quality, and ingredient cost.

basic.situation: The dietitian asks you to help supervise lunch service while trays are being assembled for the ward.

options.text: I would help staff assemble trays and check them against the meal list.
I would let the kitchen team manage trays while I finish paperwork.
I would watch tray assembly and raise service issues with the dietitian.
I would ask staff whether the trays look ready before dispatch.

advanced.situation: Several ward trays are delayed, and a staff member reports that the planned service sequence is not working today.

options.text: I would review the delay with staff and adjust the service sequence around ward needs.
I would keep the planned sequence and ask staff to work faster.
I would ask the dietitian to decide each tray's order before proceeding.
I would move available staff to the delayed trays and monitor progress.

basic.situation: A new team member starts next week, and you are helping schedule their orientation sessions around meal service.

options.text: I would schedule the sessions outside the busiest meal periods.
I would put every session on the quietest day for kitchen staff.
I would schedule sessions around service coverage and confirm the new member's availability.
I would ask the new member to attend whenever a trainer is free.

advanced.situation: Staff have raised recurring questions about portioning, and you are asked to lead an in-service education session.

options.text: I would share a reminder sheet and discuss questions during the training session.
I would shape practice around recurring staff questions about portioning.
I would ask an experienced worker to explain their usual portioning method.
I would explain today's portioning standard and invite questions from staff afterward.

basic.situation: At an interdisciplinary meeting, the team discusses a patient's meal intake and asks you to help research food service options.

options.text: I would research service models that address the meal intake concerns raised.
I would ask the dietitian which food service details would support planning.
I would record the discussion and search general nutrition articles for the team.
I would gather menus currently used by the kitchen team.

advanced.situation: The team is revising work schedules after repeated gaps in meal coverage, and the dietitian asks you to bring relevant service research.

options.text: I would keep the existing rota and ask staff to cover gaps informally.
I would research service models suited to recurring meal coverage gaps.
I would collect examples of meal schedules used in similar care settings.
I would draft a rota that prioritizes the busiest meal periods.

basic.situation: You are assigned to clean and sterilize glassware after a preparation shift, following the written procedure at the workbench.

options.text: I judge cleanliness by appearance and move the glassware batch into storage.
I rinse glassware, then repeat the cleaning routine used on the previous shift.
I follow the written cleaning steps and log the completed glassware batch.
I use the listed cleaning method and record the batch details before storage.

advanced.situation: A team is preparing a scheduled batch, and you are checking the glassware sterilization records while staff follow written mixing instructions.

options.text: I sign the batch log based on the team’s usual preparation routine.
I check the glassware labels and review the mixing notes after preparation.
I review the sterilization log and ask staff to confirm their mixing steps.
I verify each sterilization record and mixing step against the written batch instructions.

basic.situation: A customer brings a written prescription with a smudged instruction, and you are entering its details into the pharmacy system.

options.text: I use the previous prescription entry to fill the smudged instruction.
I enter the clear details and flag the smudged instruction for pharmacist review.
I hold the entry and ask the pharmacist to clarify the unclear instruction.
I enter the readable details and leave the unclear field for later.

advanced.situation: You are auditing a day’s prescription entries and find one record whose price does not match the filed prescription.

options.text: I compare entry with prescription, update permitted details, and flag the price mismatch.
I change the listed price to match the record and add a note to the file.
I flag the record for review and continue checking the remaining prescription entries.
I compare both records and send the pricing mismatch details to the pharmacist for review.

basic.situation: A delivery of medicines arrives with an invoice, and you are asked to check the received quantities before storing supplies.

options.text: I accept the invoice quantity and store the sealed boxes for the next shift.
I compare the box totals with the invoice and store the delivery.
I count the items and ask a colleague to check any doubtful totals.
I count each item against the invoice and record any quantity difference before storage.

advanced.situation: Several medicines are running low, and you are reviewing stock records before preparing the next routine supply order.

options.text: I order the usual quantities so the shelves look consistent after delivery.
I compare usage and on-hand counts, then prepare quantities that address likely shortages.
I count the low items again and draft an order from the verified totals.
I reorder the items with the lowest shelf counts using recent quantities.

basic.situation: A patient tells you about a medicine they take at home, and the pharmacist asks you to update the medication profile.

options.text: I record the medicine as reported and flag details that need pharmacist confirmation.
I add the medicine name and leave its remaining details blank for now.
I enter the reported medicine and ask the pharmacist to check the profile later.
I copy a similar patient’s medication details to complete the profile.

advanced.situation: A patient’s profile lists two medicines with similar names, and a new entry appears to duplicate one already recorded.

options.text: I remove the newer entry and note that the profile had a duplicate.
I compare the entries, preserve the source details, and flag the possible duplicate for pharmacist review.
I mark both entries for review and include their dates in a note.
I leave both entries unchanged and mention the duplicate during the next handover.

basic.situation: A customer asks where to find a non-prescription item while the pharmacist is helping another person at the counter.

options.text: I locate the item on the shelf and check the package matches the customer’s request.
I hand over the closest matching package to keep the queue moving.
I show the customer the usual shelf and offer to check another aisle if needed.
I point toward the usual shelf and return to the counter queue.

advanced.situation: A caller asks whether two medicines can be taken together, while the pharmacist is serving another customer and the phone queue is growing.

options.text: I ask the caller to hold until the pharmacist finishes serving the customer.
I take the caller’s details and arrange a pharmacist callback about the interaction question.
I tell the caller to check the medicine leaflet while they wait.
I reassure the caller that common medicines are usually fine together.

basic.situation: A customer pays for a purchase at the register, and you are learning the payment steps with a colleague nearby.

options.text: I use the last sale’s amount and take the same payment from the customer.
I enter the items and ask my colleague to check the total afterward.
I scan the items and follow the register prompts to take payment.
I enter the sale, confirm the displayed total, and tender the payment through the register.

advanced.situation: At closing, the register total differs from the payment slips, and you are responsible for checking the day’s transactions.

options.text: I adjust the register total to match the slips and close the till.
I recount the cash and compare the final figure against the register total before closing.
I compare slips with register entries, document the transactions, and report the difference.
I review the slips and register summary, then report the unmatched total.

basic.situation: With guidance, you take a patient's blood pressure and temperature before breakfast; the cuff reading seems unusually low.

options.text: You check cuff fit, repeat the measurement, and record both readings for review.
You compare the value with the prior chart and ask the nurse for guidance.
You document the low reading and share it with the nurse before breakfast.
You refit the cuff, retake the measurement, record it, and alert the nurse.
