advanced.situation: A patient's blood pressure readings are falling across checks, while their temperature remains steady during your evening round.

options.text: You document the latest value and continue the scheduled observation round.
You record the readings in sequence and tell the nurse about the downward trend.
You repeat the blood pressure and compare it with the previous charted values.
You enter the latest reading and ask the nurse to review it at handover.

basic.situation: During a routine check, a usually talkative patient becomes withdrawn and refuses lunch; the nurse asks you to report changes.

options.text: You record the meal refusal and tell the nurse the patient seems quieter.
You record the refused meal and wait to see whether the patient eats later.
You mention the patient's quiet mood when the nurse passes your station.
You tell the nurse about the withdrawal and refused meal, with the time observed.

advanced.situation: A patient becomes distressed during rehabilitation, and the doctor and therapist are reviewing how to support their participation.

options.text: You share that the patient was upset and ask the team for suggestions.
You summarize the episode, including the activity and the patient's response to reassurance.
You tell the therapist the patient had a difficult session and return to your duties.
You describe what triggered the distress and how the patient responded to each support.

basic.situation: A patient needs help washing before breakfast and becomes unsure about the next step while you assist under supervision.

options.text: You explain the next washing step calmly and help the patient complete it.
You pause the wash and ask the supervising nurse how to proceed.
You offer a clear choice, support the step the patient accepts, and preserve their privacy.
You wash the patient quickly so the morning routine stays on schedule.

advanced.situation: You are leading a prescribed group activity, but two patients lose focus when the planned conversation becomes difficult.

options.text: You shorten the discussion and offer a familiar activity from the session plan.
You continue the discussion so the group can finish the planned topic.
You end the group early and record that the patients were distracted.
You invite each patient to choose a simpler prompt linked to the session goal.

basic.situation: While helping a patient bathe, you notice the floor is wet and the patient is preparing to stand.

options.text: You call for a nearby colleague to bring a towel while you stay close.
You help the patient sit securely, dry the floor, then resume bathing at their pace.
You let the patient stand while you fetch a towel from the cupboard.
You steady the patient and ask them to wait while you dry the floor.

advanced.situation: A distressed patient moves toward another person and raises a hand; unit protocol requires two trained staff before physical restraint.

options.text: You physically restrain the patient alone to stop the movement quickly.
You guide others away, use calm de-escalation, and call trained staff under protocol.
You use the approved calming words and call trained colleagues to assist.
You call trained staff and keep a clear path between the patient and others.

basic.situation: A client wants to feel more independent with a daily routine, and you have time to demonstrate a wellness strategy.

options.text: You complete the routine for the client to keep the morning moving.
You demonstrate a simple checklist and let the client practise one step.
You show the checklist, then ask which step the client would like to try.
You describe a checklist the client could try during tomorrow's routine.

advanced.situation: A new employee asks how to approach a distressed patient during a routine evening check on the unit.

options.text: You arrange a supervised practice check and discuss what the employee observed.
You review the written procedure and identify its guidance for distressed patients.
You explain the opening steps and invite questions about approaching distressed patients.
You show the employee the unit procedure and practise its opening approach together.

basic.situation: A patient seems lonely in the common room and sits apart while you have a few minutes between routine duties.

options.text: You start a relaxed conversation about the afternoon and listen without rushing them.
You sit nearby and ask what the patient would enjoy discussing today.
You invite them to choose a group activity, then stay nearby for company.
You ask about their afternoon and listen to what they would like to share.

advanced.situation: A patient hopes to join a community activity but feels unsure about travelling there and meeting unfamiliar people.

options.text: You discuss the patient's concerns and identify a supported first step toward attending.
You encourage attendance and ask the patient to try the trip alone.
You explore what feels difficult and suggest attending with a familiar support person.
You mention the activity to the care team and ask whether it suits the patient.

basic.situation: During a routine case, the surgeon asks you for a clamp while you are arranging instruments on the sterile table.

options.text: I ask the scrub nurse which clamp the surgeon requested.
I pass the clamp from the nearest tray section.
I pass a familiar clamp to keep the case moving.
I pass the clamp after confirming its name and location.

advanced.situation: A long operation is under way, and a junior colleague cannot find the requested instrument while the usual supply tray is running low.

options.text: I guide the junior through the setup and check approved backup stock.
I take over the setup and retrieve the closest matching instrument.
I ask the surgeon to pause while I search every tray.
I direct the junior to check the usual reserve cupboard.

basic.situation: Before a routine procedure, a senior nurse asks you to scrub and glove while the team prepares the sterile field.

options.text: I follow the scrub sequence and ask the nurse to check my gloves.
I put on gloves first, then complete the scrub sequence.
I scrub at a steady pace, then put on gloves from the pack.
I ask the nurse to guide my scrub and gloving steps.

advanced.situation: During a complex case, a new colleague reaches across the sterile field while positioning a drape, and the team is preparing to begin.

options.text: I ask the colleague to pause while the nurse checks the field.
I flag the contamination risk and help restore the sterile field.
I reposition the drape and continue setting up the field.
I remind the colleague about sterile boundaries once the drape is placed.

basic.situation: After a routine operation, a nurse asks you to prepare a simple dressing for the patient under supervision.

options.text: I prepare the dressing and apply it as the nurse directs.
I use the nearest dressing pack to finish the task quickly.
I prepare gauze and wait for the nurse to apply it.
I check the wound area with the nurse before applying the dressing.

advanced.situation: A patient has a complex wound after surgery, and the team needs a dressing change that follows the documented care plan.

options.text: I choose a dressing used successfully in a similar case.
I gather listed supplies and ask the nurse to confirm the dressing change.
I prepare a standard dressing and update the nurse after the change.
I follow the documented plan and report any wound changes to the nurse.

basic.situation: During a routine case, the nurse asks you to take a patient's pulse and blood pressure and report the readings.

options.text: I take both readings and report them to the nurse.
I record the readings and compare them with the earlier chart.
I take the blood pressure and leave the pulse for later.
I estimate the pulse and report that the patient seems stable.

advanced.situation: During a long case, a patient's readings shift from earlier levels while the surgical team is focused on a difficult step.

options.text: I reduce the alarm volume to limit interruptions while the team handles the case.
I report the changed reading to the nurse and continue watching the monitor.
I note readings and tell the nurse at the next safe pause.
I call the nurse over and show the latest patient readings on screen.

basic.situation: After a routine case, a senior tech asks you to clean the used instruments and load them into the sterilizer.

options.text: I clean the instruments and load them following the sterilizer cycle instructions.
I rinse instruments, sort each piece, and load them using the tray layout.
I ask the senior tech to review my load before the sterilizer cycle starts.
I start the cycle with the instruments arranged in the tray.

advanced.situation: A sterilizer shows a fault during a busy shift, and the next case needs instruments while another unit is available.

options.text: I restart the faulty unit and run the instruments again.
I flag the fault and route the instruments through the available approved unit.
I hold the instruments and wait for the unit to clear its fault.
I move the instruments aside and tell the senior tech about the fault.

basic.situation: Before a routine operation ends, a senior tech asks you to count the sponges and needles against the checklist.

options.text: I count each item against the checklist with the senior tech.
I count the needles first and finish the sponges afterward.
I count both items and ask the senior tech to confirm totals.
I count the sponges and report the total from memory.

advanced.situation: During a complex case, a tissue specimen is ready for laboratory analysis while the usual labelled container is temporarily unavailable.

options.text: I place the specimen in a similar container and label it later.
I hold the specimen while someone fetches the usual container.
I confirm the approved container and label details before preparing the specimen.
I secure the specimen and ask the nurse which container is approved.

basic.situation: You are asked to collect a urine sample from a nervous dog and prepare it for the clinic’s laboratory test.

options.text: Set it aside and ask a colleague which label matches the request.
Write the patient’s name after preparing the sample for testing.
Label the container at collection, then match patient details with the laboratory request.
Use cage card details to label the tube before placing it with samples.

advanced.situation: Several samples arrive together before culture work, and a new technician is unsure how to label and handle them consistently.

options.text: Ask the team to use one agreed label format for incoming culture samples.
Let the technician copy a completed culture label as a reference for practice.
Write handling steps with label checks, then watch the technician apply them to one sample.
Show the current steps, then ask the technician to repeat the process.

basic.situation: After an examination, you need to clean the room before the next animal arrives, using the clinic checklist.

options.text: Follow the checklist in order and mark each completed cleaning step.
Ask a colleague to check the room while you prepare supplies.
Clean the table and floor, then mark the checklist as finished.
Wipe the main surfaces and leave the checklist for later.

advanced.situation: A review of sterilization logs shows repeated gaps on busy days, and you are asked to help reduce the risk of disease spread.

options.text: Remind staff to finish each log before leaving the sterilization work area.
Compare gaps with cleaning records and revise steps staff follow during busy periods.
Post a reminder beside the sterilizer and keep using the current checklist.
Ask the team to add a second signature to each sterilization log entry.

basic.situation: A senior technician asks you to run a blood count, but the analyzer has not been used since its last cleaning.

options.text: Load the sample and use the last settings on screen.
Run the analyzer’s routine check before loading the patient sample.
Check the analyzer’s readiness steps, then run the sample as instructed.
Wait for the senior technician to return before touching the analyzer.

advanced.situation: A blood count control is outside its expected range after routine maintenance, and a veterinarian is waiting for the patient result.

options.text: Tell the veterinarian the analyzer may be unreliable and ask what to do.
Repeat the patient sample and use whichever count looks more plausible.
Record the control result, pause patient testing, and follow the troubleshooting sequence.
Repeat the control once and continue if the next result is in range.

basic.situation: During a calm dog’s physical examination, the veterinarian asks you to steady the animal while checking its temperature.

options.text: Ask the owner to hold the dog while you watch nearby.
Keep one hand near the dog’s shoulder and follow the veterinarian’s cues.
Hold the dog firmly by its collar until the examination ends.
Use the instructed hold, watch the dog’s response, and adjust your position safely.

advanced.situation: A student is setting up for surgery and reaches across the prepared area for an instrument while the animal is being positioned.

options.text: Pause setup, mark the sterile boundary, and direct the student to an instrument outside it.
Set the instrument aside, alert the veterinarian, and prepare a replacement before setup continues.
Ask the veterinarian whether the instrument remains usable after crossing the prepared area.
Allow the student to continue so the team can keep its schedule.

basic.situation: A veterinarian asks you to prepare a vaccine for a pet and supervise the injection during a routine appointment.

options.text: Confirm the prescribed vaccine and patient details before preparing the dose.
Ask the veterinarian to prepare the dose while you hold the pet.
Read the vaccine label, prepare the dose, and confirm it with the veterinarian.
Use the vaccine prepared for the previous appointment if the label looks similar.

advanced.situation: During anesthesia monitoring, an animal’s response changes while the veterinarian is occupied with the procedure.

options.text: Record the new readings and tell the veterinarian when the procedure pauses.
Report the change and current readings, then follow the veterinarian’s anesthetic instructions.
Call the veterinarian over and wait before recording additional readings or changing settings.
Adjust the anesthetic to the previous patient’s settings, then continue monitoring and record each reading.

basic.situation: A caller wants an appointment for a limping cat, and your booking screen offers several openings this week.

options.text: Tell the caller to visit the clinic and ask the front desk there.
Book the first opening and note that the cat has a problem.
Offer two openings and write “limping” in the appointment notes.
Ask the scripted booking questions, record the concern, and offer an available appointment.

advanced.situation: A client asks how their pet is recovering after surgery while the clinical team is handling several patients and the billing queue is growing.

options.text: Reassure the client that recovery sounds normal based on the last visit.
Read the last note to the client and offer to pass their questions along.
Ask the client to call again after the billing queue clears later today.
Check recovery notes, share updates, and route concerns to the veterinary team.

basic.situation: A patient is ready for a visual acuity test, but the chart says they usually wear glasses for distance.

options.text: Measure with the glasses on and add a note about them.
Start the distance chart and record the first line they read.
Ask the patient which line seems easiest to read and note it.
Confirm the test instructions, record their correction, and measure acuity as directed.

advanced.situation: A visual field result differs from the patient’s earlier test, and the patient says they lost focus near the end.

options.text: Check fixation and test conditions, then repeat the affected section using the clinic protocol.
Keep the result and explain that visual fields can vary between visits.
Ask the physician to interpret the result before reviewing the test record.
Repeat the full test and compare the total field with the earlier result.

basic.situation: You are asked to take an axial length measurement, and the patient is having trouble keeping their gaze steady.

options.text: Ask the patient to hold still while you take another reading.
Explain the fixation target, check alignment, and repeat the measurement if needed.
Record the first displayed length so the appointment stays on time.
Take several readings and enter the closest pair in the chart.

advanced.situation: A keratometer reading differs from the patient’s previous measurement, and the physician is preparing to review the chart.

options.text: Repeat the measurement once and add the newer value to the chart.
Replace the earlier value with the new reading to keep the chart current.
Check alignment and repeat the readings, then document the values and any remaining variation.
Tell the physician the result changed and wait for further instructions.

basic.situation: After a patient visit, you need to clean the ophthalmic instrument before another patient uses it.

options.text: Clean the contact area and leave the instrument on the worktop.
Ask a colleague which wipe they used on the last shift.
Follow the instrument’s cleaning procedure and return it to its designated place.
Wipe the handle and put the instrument back on the trolley.

advanced.situation: A calibration check on an ophthalmic instrument is inconsistent, and two staff members use different maintenance routines.

options.text: Ask both staff members to outline their routines, then agree on a schedule together.
Follow the routine used by the more experienced staff member for now.
Ask each staff member to record their routine before the next team meeting.
Compare routines with equipment guidance, document shared steps, and review them with staff.

basic.situation: You are taking a patient’s medical history, and they mention using eye drops but cannot recall the name.

options.text: Write the brand name the patient recalls, and mark it as unconfirmed.
Record the reported drops and ask the patient to confirm the name later.
Leave the medication entry pending and ask the patient to check later.
Note eye drop use and the patient’s uncertainty, then request the label at follow-up.

advanced.situation: A record audit finds several post-operative calls documented without a date or summary, and you are asked to guide the team.

options.text: Share a call template covering date, recovery update, and concerns for clinician review.
Bring a dated sample note to the huddle and discuss what recovery details belong.
Ask staff to add dates and short summaries to upcoming post-operative call notes.
Remind the team to record each call’s date and key recovery details.

basic.situation: A physician asks you to give prescribed eye drops, but the patient is unsure which eye is being treated.

options.text: Use the drops in the eye that appears more irritated to the patient.
Pause and tell the physician the patient is unsure which eye should receive the drops.
Check the prescription and patient details with the physician before giving the drops.
Ask the patient which eye they recall from their previous clinic visit.

advanced.situation: During an ophthalmic procedure, the requested instrument is missing from the setup and the physician is ready to proceed.

options.text: Ask another technician to search while you monitor the setup and procedure.
Tell the physician the setup is incomplete, then ask which listed instrument should be retrieved.
Tell the physician what is missing, protect the field, and find the listed instrument.
Pass a similar instrument from the trolley to keep the procedure moving forward.

basic.situation: A patient is learning to insert a contact lens and keeps touching the lens before positioning it on their eye.

options.text: Insert the lens for the patient so the appointment can move on.
Show the patient where to place the lens on the fingertip.
Demonstrate clean handling, then guide the patient through another insertion attempt.
Tell the patient to try again while you prepare the next chart.

advanced.situation: Several patients ask similar questions about lens care, and new staff give different instructions during fitting appointments.

options.text: Draft a patient handout from clinic guidance and align staff demonstrations with its steps.
Bring current instructions to the next team huddle for a shared review.
Ask new staff to use the lens care instructions from their training.
Share one staff member’s lens care notes with the team and discuss any differences together.

basic.situation: You measure a patient's blood pressure and get a reading far above the earlier one. What do you do next?

options.text: Repeat the blood pressure after checking the cuff, then record both readings.
Enter the first number now, since the patient says they feel fine.
Take the reading again with a suitable cuff and report the change.
Ask another nurse to check the equipment before documenting the measurement.

advanced.situation: A patient becomes pale and drowsy, and their pulse and breathing have changed across two observations. What do you do?

options.text: Call the response team, share the trend, and begin permitted checks.
Recheck the observations and tell the registered nurse the pattern.
Ask a colleague to compare the chart before raising concern.
Record the latest values and wait for the next scheduled round.

basic.situation: You are preparing a prescribed oral medicine, but the patient's name on the chart differs slightly from their wristband. What do you do?

options.text: Match the chart, identity band, and medicine before giving the dose.
Ask the registered nurse to confirm the chart details before preparing the dose.
Use the dose given yesterday and record it after the round.
Read the label again and ask the patient to confirm their name.

advanced.situation: Two prescribed medicines are due close together, and a patient asks whether they can be taken at the same time. What do you do?

options.text: Give the first medicine, then review the chart before the next dose.
Tell the patient both medicines are usually given during the same round.
Check the administration instructions and clarify timing with the registered nurse.
Review the chart and explain the listed times to the patient.

basic.situation: A patient needs help bathing and dressing but feels unsteady standing beside the bed. What do you do?

options.text: Bring the items first, then ask an aide to help with dressing.
Ask the patient to stand briefly while you gather the bathing items.
Offer a seated wash and check whether the patient wants assistance.
Set up the wash items and support the patient while they dress seated.

advanced.situation: A patient with limited movement needs hygiene care, and a reddened area appears where they rest. What do you do?

options.text: Help with hygiene, then ask the registered nurse about the skin area.
Reposition the patient and document the location of the redness.
Clean the area and note the redness at the end of the shift.
Include skin checks and repositioning needs in the care discussion with the team.

basic.situation: You are asked to assemble oxygen equipment for a patient before a routine procedure. What do you do?

options.text: Check the prescribed setup, assemble the equipment, and request a readiness check.
Assemble the familiar equipment and place it beside the patient's bed.
Review equipment instructions and assemble the listed components before the procedure.
Use available tubing and ask the procedure team to review the setup.

advanced.situation: A urine sample label is smudged after collection, and the laboratory pickup is due soon. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the registered nurse whether the sample can still be sent.
Write the patient's name from the collection list onto the label.
Confirm the patient's identity and relabel the sample under local procedure.
Hold the sample and check the collection details with the patient record.

basic.situation: A patient calls the ward asking when a staff member will bring their test results. What do you do?

options.text: Ask which test they mean and connect them with the responsible staff member.
Tell them results are usually discussed during the next ward round.
Take their name and tell the registered nurse about the call.
Say you will ask the team and end the call to continue rounds.

advanced.situation: A patient is anxious about a planned wound treatment and asks what will happen during it. What do you do?

options.text: Describe the usual steps and invite the patient to discuss remaining questions with the nurse.
Explain the steps within your role, ask about concerns, and involve the registered nurse when needed.
Ask what worries them and relay their question to the registered nurse for guidance.
Reassure them the treatment is routine, then offer to ask the nurse about its expected duration.

basic.situation: A patient's food tray arrives, and the prescribed diet on the chart differs from the tray label. What do you do?

options.text: Check the diet entry and tray contents, then contact catering about the mismatch.
Serve the tray because its label matches the patient's name and room.
Compare the tray label with the checklist and note the difference.
Hold the tray and ask the registered nurse to review the diet order.

advanced.situation: After a mobility change, the patient is less steady during transfers despite the current care plan. What do you do?

options.text: Continue the current plan and record each transfer at the end of the shift.
Tell the registered nurse the patient seemed less steady during transfers.
Ask an aide to watch the next transfer and compare their notes.
Share the transfer observations with the team and review the plan's outcomes together.

basic.situation: You are assigning a diagnosis-related group, but one required detail is unclear in the discharge summary. What do you do?

options.text: Check the coding references and flag the missing detail for clarification.
Review the grouper result and query the responsible clinician for clarification.
Choose the closest group and submit the record to meet the queue target.
Use the documented diagnosis and select the matching group in the software.

advanced.situation: Two entries in a record suggest different diagnoses, and each would affect the code selection. What do you do?

options.text: Select the diagnosis repeated most often and add a note for review.
Code the clearer entry and hold the other for a later review.
Compare the documentation and ask the clinician to clarify the conflicting diagnoses.
Check the classification manual and tell the coding lead about the conflict.

basic.situation: A physician asks for a patient's earlier clinic record, but two folders have similar names. What do you do?

options.text: Check the identifiers against the request before retrieving the matching folder.
Search the index for the patient number and retrieve that record.
Take the newer folder to the physician and mention the similar name.
Ask the physician to confirm which clinic visit they need first.

advanced.situation: You notice records from one clinic are being filed under two different index labels, making retrieval slower. What do you do?

options.text: Review the affected index entries and propose one consistent retrieval label.
Add a note beside the newer label so staff can search both terms.
Keep using both labels and explain the difference when staff ask.
Map both labels to the same index entry and tell the records lead.

basic.situation: You are scanning a patient's paper record, and one page appears to belong to another file. What do you do?

options.text: Scan the page with the batch and flag it for later review.
Scan all pages in order so the batch is complete for indexing.
Pause the scan and check the page identifiers against the patient's file.
Remove the page and finish scanning the remaining patient's documents.

advanced.situation: A large batch of discharge summaries is due for entry, and several pages have faint handwriting. What do you do?

options.text: Enter the clear fields and leave the faint sections for later checking.
Ask a colleague to read the faint sections before you finish the batch.
Prioritise clear fields, queue unclear entries, and verify them against source pages.
Use the likely wording from similar summaries to complete the faint sections.

basic.situation: A record checklist shows a missing date on a treatment note, and the file is due for review. What do you do?

options.text: Complete the checklist and return the file for filing with other records.
Check nearby notes for the date and add it to the checklist comments.
Pass the file to the supervisor and mention that one field looks incomplete.
Mark the missing date and route the note for completion through the usual process.

advanced.situation: Several records contain the same unclear diagnosis wording, and the coding manual offers more than one relevant entry. What do you do?

options.text: Consult the classification manual and document which entries need clinical clarification.
Flag the wording across the records and hold them for a later review.
Check the manual and ask the coding lead how to handle the wording.
Choose the most familiar manual entry and share it with the coding team.

basic.situation: A patient is completing admission paperwork, but one contact detail differs from the referral form. What do you do?

options.text: Copy the referral detail and finish the remaining admission fields.
Leave the contact field blank and complete the other admission documents.
Confirm the contact detail with the patient and update the admission form.
Mark the field for review and ask the registration lead to check it.

advanced.situation: Several patients are waiting to book follow-up visits, and the appointment list has overlapping time slots. What do you do?

options.text: Review the available slots and contact patients about suitable appointment times.
Check the list with the clinic team before offering affected times.
Book each patient into the next open slot and adjust the list later.
Hold the overlapping slots and offer patients later appointments for now.

basic.situation: You are posting an insurance billing, but the service date on the form differs from the record. What do you do?

options.text: Hold the billing entry and add a note about the conflicting dates.
Ask the billing lead which date should be entered for this claim.
Compare the form with the record and clarify the service date before posting.
Post the date from the form and leave the record for later review.

advanced.situation: A caller asks you to send a patient's record to an agency, but their authority is unclear. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the caller to email proof of authority for the records team to review.
Record the request details and refer it to the records supervisor.
Check the release request and authorization before sending any record information.
Send the requested summary and ask the agency to confirm receipt.

basic.situation: You are fitting a finished lens into a customer's frame, and the work order is beside the bench.

options.text: I would press the lens firmly until the frame holds it.
I would seat the lens, then check whether it sits evenly.
I would check the lens against the order before seating it gently.
I would ease the lens into the frame and inspect its edge.

advanced.situation: A high-prescription lens arrives with an edge that looks uneven, and the customer needs the pair for work tomorrow.

options.text: I would recheck the grind against the specifications before approving assembly.
I would polish the edge lightly, then check how it sits.
I would inspect the lens closely and ask the team to hold assembly.
I would fit it now and let the customer judge its comfort.

basic.situation: A customer chooses a frame that looks small on their face, so you take standard measurements before suggesting a fit.

options.text: I would measure the bridge and eye size before discussing another frame.
I would order the chosen frame and see how it feels later.
I would check the frame against the customer's face and adjust it.
I would measure bridge and eye size, then compare suitable frames.

advanced.situation: A customer works at a desk and plays badminton, but their prescription feels uncomfortable at both distances.

options.text: I would discuss both activities and relate them to the prescription.
I would recommend the same lenses the customer used previously.
I would suggest a familiar frame and ask about comfort afterward.
I would ask which activity matters more before discussing lens options.

basic.situation: A first-time contact lens customer is unsure how to remove a lens before leaving the shop.

options.text: I would explain removal slowly and invite questions from the customer.
I would ask the customer to try removing it while I watch.
I would demonstrate removal, then let the customer practise safely.
I would show a care leaflet and talk through its pictures.

advanced.situation: A student optician gives mixed contact lens care advice during a busy shift, and you are supervising their client training.

options.text: I would review the advice with the student and practise a consistent demonstration.
I would hand the student a care leaflet to use with clients.
I would clarify the key points and have the student explain them back.
I would take over the client discussion and finish the fitting.

basic.situation: A customer asks you to prepare an order, but their previous record and the prescription they brought do not match.

options.text: I would prepare the order from the prescription they brought.
I would check the record and verify the prescription with the examiner.
I would ask the customer which prescription they want used.
I would copy the previous order and send it for grinding.

advanced.situation: Several staff members prepare work orders, and a complex prescription has been copied with different lens details on two forms.

options.text: I would send the clearer form to the lens workshop.
I would hold the order and ask a colleague to review it.
I would use the newer form and note the difference for later.
I would compare both forms with the prescription before releasing instructions.

basic.situation: A customer has paid a deposit, and you need to update the shop record while submitting their insurance information.

options.text: I would enter the deposit under the customer's next order.
I would submit the insurance details and update the ledger later.
I would update the payment record and submit the insurance form.
I would record the payment and check the insurance details against the form.

advanced.situation: Frame stock is moving slowly while popular lens types are running low, and you are preparing a purchase order.

options.text: I would order extra frames while the supplier has a discount.
I would compare sales and stock records before selecting order quantities.
I would repeat the last purchase and review stock next month.
I would prioritise the low lens stock and reduce frame orders.

basic.situation: The sunglass display looks untidy after a busy morning, and customers are struggling to compare the frames.

options.text: I would group similar colours together and wipe the shelves.
I would straighten the display and face each pair forward.
I would arrange the frames by type and keep their labels visible.
I would move the most popular pairs to the front.

advanced.situation: A new sunglass display is due before a weekend promotion, and junior staff ask how to arrange frames for customer browsing.

options.text: I would place new styles at eye level, keep labels visible, and explain the layout.
I would group frames by use and coach staff to keep labels visible.
I would put the highest priced frames in the largest display area.
I would arrange frames by colour and ask staff to refill gaps.

basic.situation: You are measuring a patient's lower leg for a basic orthosis, and the patient says swelling varies during the day.

options.text: I would ask the patient to return when swelling feels typical.
I would measure the limb and note when swelling changes.
I would measure the leg now and use that size for the cast.
I would take the measurement and ask when swelling feels worse.

advanced.situation: A patient has an unusual limb shape and a healed scar near the planned orthosis edge, making standard measurements less informative.

options.text: I would use the usual measurements and discuss comfort during fitting.
I would take extra measurements around the scar and note them.
I would base the design on the limb's overall length and width.
I would document the scar and limb shape when assessing appliance fit.

basic.situation: A physician's prescription requests a simple wrist orthosis, and you are drafting the design for review.

options.text: I would sketch the wrist support and check the prescription afterward.
I would map the prescription details to a simple design sketch.
I would copy the last wrist design for the new patient.
I would reuse a similar design and adjust its dimensions.

advanced.situation: A new custom device design must accommodate a patient's unusual measurements, and a recent seminar covered alternative construction methods.

options.text: I would compare the method with the prescription and patient measurements.
I would adapt a familiar design and ask a technician for feedback.
I would use the seminar method as the main design guide.
I would review the seminar notes and draft a custom design.

basic.situation: You are making a plaster cast for a patient's ankle orthosis, and the senior technician has asked you to prepare the work area.

options.text: I would use the usual cast materials and follow the last example.
I would position the limb and make the cast to guide construction.
I would make a quick cast from the limb's resting position.
I would prepare the plaster and ask the technician to check the cast.

advanced.situation: A patient's prosthetic socket needs repair, but the damaged area affects how the device sits during walking.

options.text: I would reinforce the damaged area and ask the patient to test it.
I would select a familiar repair material and check the socket fit.
I would patch the area with spare material and return the socket.
I would assess the damaged area before planning a repair with suitable materials.

basic.situation: You are fitting a patient's new knee orthosis, and they report rubbing near the edge when bending.

options.text: I would adjust the edge and ask the patient how it feels.
I would check the rubbing during movement and record the adjustment made.
I would check the standing fit and note the patient's comment.
I would ask the patient to wear it longer before changing anything.

advanced.situation: A patient reports slipping in a complex prosthesis, and the latest visit record lacks details about the adjustments made.

options.text: I would evaluate the fit during use and document the adjustments and response.
I would review the last note and check the prosthesis during walking.
I would add a brief note that the prosthesis was reviewed.
I would adjust the suspension and ask the patient about comfort.

basic.situation: A support colleague is unsure how to explain an orthosis to a ward nurse, and you have been asked to demonstrate.

options.text: I would give them a device leaflet to share with the nurse.
I would explain the main features and let them ask questions.
I would demonstrate the orthosis and practise the explanation with them.
I would answer the nurse's questions myself during the handover.

advanced.situation: Ward staff ask how a custom prosthesis works, and your new technician is preparing to explain it during a team handover.

options.text: I would outline the key features and let the technician present them.
I would coach the technician to explain its purpose and key features clearly.
I would explain the prosthesis myself and ask the technician to listen.
I would prepare a short summary for staff to read at handover.

basic.situation: A patient is learning to put on a simple ankle orthosis, and they ask whether it should feel tight.

options.text: I would demonstrate fitting, explain expected comfort, and invite their questions.
I would advise tightening straps until the orthosis feels secure and comfortable.
I would explain strap placement and ask how the fit feels.
I would show each step, then ask them to practice putting it on.

advanced.situation: A patient with limited hand strength is learning to use a new orthosis, and you are discussing device specifications with their physician.

options.text: I would explain the device options and ask which seems easier to use.
I would share the patient's handling needs with the physician when discussing specifications.
I would ask a family member to manage the straps each day.
I would teach the patient the usual steps and check their comfort.

basic.situation: You begin a pure tone screening, but the client keeps hearing hallway noise through the open door.

options.text: You record the first readings and tell the senior about the noise.
You compare both ears across tones and document the results for review.
You check otoscopy, reseat the headphones, and repeat the screening consistently.
You repeat pure tone screening after checking the room and instructions.

advanced.situation: Air and bone conduction results differ sharply between ears, and the client reports sudden changes since yesterday.

options.text: You verify test conditions, document the asymmetry, and alert the clinician promptly.
You check the transducers and ask the client to return for another test.
You repeat the full test set and summarize the pattern for the clinician.
You file the results with the usual fitting notes for later review.

basic.situation: A client is trying a hearing aid for the first time and asks how to change its volume.

options.text: You turn the volume up for the client and finish the fitting.
You point out the control and suggest checking the instruction booklet later.
You show the volume control, then invite the client to try it.
You demonstrate the control, then ask the client to adjust it independently.

advanced.situation: A client with limited hand movement and speech needs an assistive listening device for weekly family meetings.

options.text: You demonstrate the device and ask the family to practise its controls.
You show the family a quick setup and offer a printed guide.
You lend the device and let the family work out the setup.
You adapt the demonstration around the client’s movement and communication needs, then check use.

basic.situation: A recent audiology article discusses a fitting approach your clinic has not used before.

options.text: You skim the abstract and mention the approach during lunch.
You read the article and note its key points for your files.
You read the methods and findings, then compare them with current practice.
You ask a colleague whether the approach sounds useful for clients.

advanced.situation: Colleagues ask you to share a new evidence-based fitting approach, but the studies report mixed results.

options.text: You ask a senior colleague to present while you share the article.
You share the approach as a useful update for the team.
You compare study methods and limits, then lead discussion on cautious use.
You present the main findings and mention that researchers disagree.

basic.situation: You are supervised while taking an ear impression, and the client reports discomfort as you prepare.

options.text: You offer a short break, then resume the impression with supervision.
You pause and describe the discomfort to the senior before continuing.
You pause, check the client’s comfort, and ask the senior to reassess.
You continue carefully and tell the senior after the impression is complete.

advanced.situation: A returning client’s ear canal shape has changed, and the old shell no longer seals comfortably.

options.text: You arrange a supervised refit and record where the shell loses its seal.
You reuse the old impression and add material around the loose area.
You document discomfort and book a fresh impression appointment with the supervising specialist.
You take a fresh supervised impression and note canal changes for the shell design.

basic.situation: A client’s hearing aid sounds weak during a follow-up, and visible wax sits near the sound outlet.

options.text: You note the weak sound and ask the client to book service.
You push the wax inward with a pin to clear the outlet.
You clean the outlet with the approved tool and retest the sound.
You replace the battery and return the aid to the client.

advanced.situation: Several clinic aids return with intermittent sound after cleaning, and the team uses different maintenance routines.

options.text: You replace batteries in the returned aids and send them back out.
You tell colleagues to clean the aids more carefully during each visit.
You compare the returned aids and document when the sound drops out.
You inspect common fault points, record findings, and propose a shared checklist.

basic.situation: A client says they miss parts of conversation at a busy kopitiam despite wearing hearing aids.

options.text: You tell the client to avoid the kopitiam until hearing improves.
You explain that busy places can make speech harder to follow.
You suggest facing the speaker and choosing a quieter table together.
You remind the client to wear the hearing aids during conversations.

advanced.situation: A client’s family disagrees about how much help to provide as the client plans to keep working.

options.text: You encourage the family to decide which support plan seems easiest.
You give the family common communication tips and a follow-up date.
You recommend that the client stop working until the family agrees.
You ask about work conversations and agree on strategies the client can try.

basic.situation: You attach EEG electrodes, but one mark is difficult to locate through the patient’s thick hair.

options.text: You part the hair and attach the electrode at the measured mark.
You place the electrode near the mark where the hair parts easily.
You recheck the measurement, part the hair, and secure the electrode there.
You ask the patient to hold the electrode while you prepare others.

advanced.situation: A new technician is marking electrode sites, but two measurements appear inconsistent with the montage plan.

options.text: You ask the technician to finish, then review the sites together.
You move the marks to nearby spots that appear visually balanced.
You show the technician the standard landmarks and let them continue.
You check both measurements against the plan and demonstrate the landmarks again.

basic.situation: You are setting up a basic EEG montage, but the displayed channels do not match the worksheet.

options.text: You inspect the montage labels and ask the senior about the discrepancy.
You restart the setup using the usual montage and check the display.
You compare each channel with the worksheet and adjust the montage mapping.
You begin recording and ask the senior to review the display later.

advanced.situation: A channel drops out during a recording, and restarting the system could disrupt a time-sensitive study.

options.text: You check connections and settings, preserve the recording, and alert the lead.
You inspect the connection and signal path, then document the interruption.
You switch to another channel and continue with the remaining montage.
You restart the system and repeat the setup from its saved template.

basic.situation: You are assisting with an EEG setup, and the patient asks whether the test will involve pain.

options.text: You say the patient will find out once the recording begins.
You tell the patient the test is routine and continue preparing.
You ask the senior technologist to answer while you finish setup.
You explain that electrodes record signals and describe the setup briefly.

advanced.situation: You are assigned a cerebral death study under protocol, but a required recording segment contains movement artifact.

options.text: You repeat the affected segment under protocol and document the artifact.
You tell the physician about the artifact before submitting the recording.
You adjust the equipment and continue from the current point.
You mark the segment and complete the study using the remaining recording.

basic.situation: During an EEG, the patient shifts position and several channels show sudden changes on screen.

options.text: You mark the movement and tell the patient to remain still.
You note the movement in the record and continue watching the channels.
You remove the changing channels from view and keep recording.
You label the affected section and check the patient's comfort and position.

advanced.situation: Subtle rhythmic interference appears in one channel during surgery monitoring, while the other channels remain stable.

options.text: You smooth the display settings until the rhythmic pattern looks less prominent.
You mark the interference and review the electrode contact and patient movement.
You label the section as interference and keep monitoring the display.
You ask a colleague to watch the channel while you prepare a note.

basic.situation: You are drafting a technical summary, but the recorded study includes a brief section with unclear signal quality.

options.text: You summarize the usable data and flag the unclear section for review.
You leave out the unclear section and submit the remaining summary.
You ask a colleague to check the section before drafting further.
You draft the summary and mention that signal quality varied.

advanced.situation: A complex study has conflicting technical notes, and the physician needs a report before the next clinic session.

options.text: You submit the report with a note that the technical notes conflict.
You compare the notes with the recording and clarify discrepancies before submission.
You summarize the consistent findings and flag the conflicting details for review.
You ask the physician which set of notes to use for reporting.

basic.situation: Before an evoked potential test, a patient asks what the flashes and sounds are for.

options.text: You say the flashes and sounds are part of the test procedure.
You explain that the test records responses to the planned stimuli.
You ask the patient to sign in and raise questions during testing.
You reassure the patient that staff will guide them through the test.

advanced.situation: A new technician is learning patient intake, but keeps missing medication details needed to customize a test.

options.text: You review a sample intake and ask the trainee to explain medication prompts.
You tell the trainee to use the same intake questions for everyone.
You remind the trainee to review medication details during each intake.
You fill in missed medication details after the trainee finishes intake.

basic.situation: A patient struggles to read the distance chart during a routine visit. You need to measure visual acuity before the clinician sees them.

options.text: Ask the patient to try again, then note the line they can read.
Check chart distance and lighting, measure each eye, then record the result.
Record the first line read and move the patient along to save time.
Repeat the distance chart and record each response in the patient’s notes.

advanced.situation: A visual field test shows a new defect, but the patient reports losing focus halfway through. You must decide how to prepare the result for clinical review.

options.text: Save the plot and ask the patient whether they felt distracted.
Repeat the test after explaining the fixation target and checking reliability indices.
Mark the defect as confirmed because it appears clearly on the printout.
Send the plot to the clinician with the patient’s focus concern noted.

basic.situation: A clinician requests corneal curvature readings before discussing a patient’s astigmatism. You are using a keratometer with guidance.

options.text: Take readings from both eyes and record the measurements for review.
Ask the patient to hold still and note the clearest reading shown.
Align the patient, take repeat readings, and record each eye’s curvature.
Copy the first displayed value into the chart to keep the queue moving.

advanced.situation: An ocular scanner gives axial length values that differ from the prior visit. The clinician is waiting for the measurement to support planning.

options.text: Send the new value with the prior measurement attached for review.
Check the patient details and ask a colleague to review the scan.
Repeat the scan after checking alignment and compare its quality indicators.
Replace the earlier value with the latest scan to keep the chart current.

basic.situation: A patient describes recurring eye irritation during intake. You need to document their medical history for the clinician.

options.text: Record the symptoms, timing, medicines, and relevant history in their notes.
Use a previous visit’s history to fill in the current intake form.
Write down the main symptom and pass the notes to the clinician.
Ask when it began and note the patient’s answer for the clinician.

advanced.situation: Several calls report sudden vision changes, and staff describe urgency differently. You are asked to improve how the office triages these calls.

options.text: Tell staff to place every vision-change call at the front of the queue.
Collect recent call notes and ask staff which cases seemed most urgent.
Ask staff to note each caller’s symptoms and send urgent cases onward.
Draft shared urgency criteria and review sample calls with the clinical team.

basic.situation: Before a routine eye procedure, the clinician asks you to prepare prescribed drops for the patient under direct supervision.

options.text: Confirm the patient and prescribed drops, then administer them as directed.
Check the label and ask the patient to confirm their name before proceeding.
Use the drops prepared for the previous patient to save setup time.
Prepare the prescribed drops and confirm the instructions with the clinician.

advanced.situation: During a procedure, a junior colleague reaches for an instrument that was placed outside the sterile field. You are assisting the clinician.

options.text: Alert the clinician and offer a fresh instrument from the sterile set.
Remind the colleague about sterile handling and watch the next handoff.
Stop the handoff, replace the instrument, and restore the sterile field.
Pass the instrument quickly because the procedure is already underway.

basic.situation: A clinician asks you to document a patient’s corneal defect with a clinical photograph. You are setting up the camera with help.

options.text: Ask the clinician to check the image after you take the photograph.
Take the photograph and add it to the patient’s record for review.
Frame the affected area, check focus, and save the labeled image.
Use a prior patient’s image as a placeholder until your photo is ready.

advanced.situation: New staff produce retinal photographs with inconsistent focus and framing. You are asked to improve the team’s clinical photography quality.

options.text: Keep the sharpest image from each visit and discard the rest.
Set image criteria and use paired examples to coach staff on capture.
Share several clear photographs and ask staff to use them as references.
Review sample photographs with staff and discuss common focus problems.

basic.situation: After a contact lens fitting, a patient asks how to care for their lenses at home. You are helping explain basic care.

options.text: Give the patient the lens-care leaflet and point out its cleaning section.
Describe the cleaning steps and ask whether the patient has questions.
Tell the patient to rinse lenses with tap water between uses.
Explain the cleaning routine and ask the patient to describe it back.

advanced.situation: Staff record different cleaning steps for reusable instruments. You are asked to review the sterilization process and prepare guidance for the team.

options.text: Compare staff steps with the approved protocol and clarify gaps in training.
Let each staff member follow the cleaning method they learned previously.
Share the approved cleaning protocol and ask staff to read it before shifts.
Ask staff to describe their cleaning steps at the next team meeting.

basic.situation: A patient says their discharge instructions were confusing and they missed a follow-up. You are gathering details to identify the care problem.

options.text: Ask what was unclear, when follow-up was due, and what happened next.
Ask the patient to describe the confusing instruction and missed visit.
Ask whether the patient received a reminder about the follow-up visit.
Record that the patient missed follow-up and close the intake promptly.

advanced.situation: A staff member asks how to interview a patient who says they felt dismissed during care. You are sharing guidance for a sensitive conversation.

options.text: Share a sample question and ask the staff member to try it.
Model open questions, privacy, and neutral listening, then discuss the response.
Suggest meeting privately and inviting the patient to explain their concern.
Tell the staff member to reassure the patient that the team meant well.

basic.situation: A patient asks whether a family member can collect their clinic letter. You need to explain the hospital’s process with help.

options.text: Tell the family member to collect the letter using the patient’s name.
Explain the usual collection process and offer to confirm any details.
Ask a colleague whether family collection is generally allowed at the clinic.
Check the current collection process and explain what the patient should bring.

advanced.situation: Staff give patients different explanations of a complex appointment policy. You are asked to prepare a clear guide for the team.

options.text: Summarize the policy and circulate it for staff to keep nearby.
Tell staff to use the wording they find easiest during appointments.
Map the policy steps and draft plain-language examples for common patient questions.
Collect staff questions and add brief answers to the policy summary.

basic.situation: A patient says transport costs make it difficult to attend follow-up visits. You are using a checklist to refer them to local support.

options.text: Check the patient’s needs and refer them to a suitable transport resource.
Give the patient the transport support list and explain how to contact services.
Suggest cancelling follow-up visits until the patient can afford transport.
Ask which area the patient travels from and note it for referral.

advanced.situation: A patient needs care, language support, and help with transport after discharge. You are reviewing how staff handle complex referrals.

options.text: List relevant services and give the patient their contact information.
Map each need to a named service and define how staff confirm connection.
Ask staff which services they have used for similar patient needs.
Send the patient to the first service listed in the directory.

basic.situation: A patient asks why their clinic appointment is delayed and wants an update from the care team. You are handling the inquiry with supervision.

options.text: Confirm the delay with clinic staff and relay the update to the patient.
Tell the patient the clinician is running late because clinics often overrun.
Ask the patient to wait nearby while you check with reception.
Tell the patient you will pass their question to the clinic team.

advanced.situation: A patient’s complaint about a delayed referral has been passed between teams twice. You are improving how staff investigate and follow up such complaints.

options.text: Send the complaint to the referral team and request a patient update from them.
Close the complaint after forwarding it to the team responsible for referrals.
Check which team currently holds the referral and note the complaint status.
Track the referral query, assign a contact, and confirm resolution with the patient.

basic.situation: A clinic is updating a brochure about appointment preparation. You are helping draft it using the approved template.

options.text: Check the appointment steps with staff and write them in plain language.
Reuse an old brochure because its appointment instructions look familiar.
Draft the main steps and ask a colleague to check the wording.
Adapt the template wording and send the draft to staff for review.

advanced.situation: Patients receive conflicting leaflets about clinic services. You are overseeing revisions to the patient information materials across the department.

options.text: Ask teams to send their current leaflets for a shared review.
Replace the conflicting leaflets with the newest one from the clinic.
Compare the main leaflets and note where patient instructions differ.
Inventory materials, verify details with service owners, and coordinate consistent revisions.

basic.situation: You are reading current literature to keep up with patient representative practice. A colleague asks what you learned for the team.

options.text: Send the article to colleagues who may want to read it themselves.
Mention the topic and invite colleagues to discuss it at a later meeting.
Repeat a headline you remember from a recent healthcare article.
Share the article’s key points and explain how they relate to patient support.

advanced.situation: Your team wants a short session on a new healthcare development relevant to patient support. You are leading the discussion using current professional reading.

options.text: Pass along a colleague’s account as the session’s main information source.
Ask staff what they have heard and list topics for future reading.
Summarize trusted reading, discuss patient impact, and invite questions from staff.
Present a brief article summary and share the source with the team.

basic.situation: You are coding a discharge record, and the diagnosis wording needs a standard classification code.

options.text: Use the first plausible code in the classification search results.
Check the documented diagnosis and assign its matching classification code.
Choose the code used for similar cases in last week's batch.
Review the diagnosis wording, then compare two likely code entries.

advanced.situation: A discharge summary and the coded diagnosis conflict, and the record lacks a clear explanation before billing review.

options.text: Keep the existing code and flag the conflict for later review.
Send the doctor both entries and request a choice between them.
Ask the doctor a focused question and update the code from the clarification.
Compare the notes and suggest a likely code to the doctor.

basic.situation: A physician asks you to retrieve a patient's record before a clinic review, but several files have similar names.

options.text: Search by name and confirm the visit date before retrieval.
Check the clinic list and retrieve the record with the closest name.
Match the patient identifiers, then retrieve the corresponding record.
Search the name and open the first matching file for review.

advanced.situation: A healthcare app's record database slows during peak clinic hours, while a proposed change could affect access controls.

options.text: Check database logs and recommend a capacity change for the next maintenance window.
Review access controls, query load, and recovery needs before proposing a tested change.
Ask the vendor for its standard upgrade and schedule it during a quiet period.
Increase database capacity now, then review access controls after clinics close.

basic.situation: You are preparing a monthly report, and the ward census totals do not match the care data export.

options.text: Use the export totals and add a note about the census difference.
Check the ward summary against the export and report the difference.
Copy last month's totals and adjust them to match this month's trend.
Reconcile the census dates and definitions before compiling the report.

advanced.situation: Researchers request a tumor registry graphic, but two data extracts use different time periods and could change the apparent trend.

options.text: Choose the newer extract and make a chart for the researchers.
Show both extracts in separate charts and describe their date ranges.
Align the periods, validate the counts, and label the graphic's limits.
Use the longer extract and mention the date mismatch in the caption.

basic.situation: A staff member asks you to send a patient's record to a shared ward printer for a routine review.

options.text: Send it to the shared printer and ask ward staff to collect it.
Ask the requester to collect the record from the records counter.
Confirm the recipient and retrieve the record through the approved secure route.
Check the requester's name, then send the record through ward email.

advanced.situation: A standards update may affect privacy controls in your hospital's record system, and your team is planning its next review.

options.text: Forward the update to the team and ask whether anyone sees a concern.
Summarize the update and add it to the team's next meeting agenda.
Wait for the next audit and then check whether the controls changed.
Review the update's scope and map relevant controls for the system owner.

basic.situation: New clinic staff keep asking how to handle records left at shared workstations, so you are preparing an in-service handout.

options.text: Add a reminder about logging out to the existing clinic notice.
Write a short handout showing the approved steps and a practical example.
List the workstation rules and ask a colleague to check the wording.
Reuse an old privacy flyer and distribute it at the clinic.

advanced.situation: Your records team is adopting a revised indexing procedure, and staff must use it during next week's busy clinic period.

options.text: Walk through the changed steps at handover and share the new guide.
Demonstrate the new workflow with sample records and let staff practise key steps.
Replace the desk guide and ask staff to read it before their shifts.
Send the revised procedure and invite staff to raise questions later.

basic.situation: A records application query has changed, and you need to update the archived procedure used by clerical staff.

options.text: Replace the old query name and save the procedure in the archive.
Revise the archived steps, verify them against the current query, and date the update.
Keep the old procedure and tell staff about the changed query at handover.
Add the new query name to the archive and leave the earlier steps in place.

advanced.situation: Two clerical workers are covering a heavy records queue, and an urgent clinic request is waiting alongside routine filing.

options.text: Assign one worker to the urgent request and check progress before reallocating work.
Let both workers continue their usual queues until the clinic calls again.
Ask one worker to take the clinic request while you watch the routine queue.
Move the oldest routine files aside so both workers can handle the clinic request.

basic.situation: During practice, an athlete reports ankle pain after landing awkwardly, and you are asked to make an initial check.

options.text: Check the athlete's symptoms and function, then follow the care plan guidance.
Ask where it hurts and let the athlete resume at an easier pace.
Check the ankle movement and ask the coach whether this happened before.
Ask about the landing and compare swelling with the other ankle.

advanced.situation: An athlete recovering from a head injury says symptoms have eased, but the coach wants a readiness update before an important match.

options.text: Review recovery progress and established clearance guidance before advising the coach.
Check the recovery notes and recommend waiting for the next scheduled review.
Ask the athlete to describe symptoms and share the update with the coach.
Tell the coach the athlete feels better and can join warmups.

basic.situation: A physician asks you to help plan a simple return-to-running routine for an athlete recovering from a mild strain.

options.text: Ask the physician for a starting distance and note the athlete's response.
Repeat the athlete's previous running schedule at a lower speed.
Agree on gradual running steps with the physician and review the athlete's response.
Use the standard team plan and adjust it after the first session.

advanced.situation: A recovering athlete has pain with cutting drills, and a new trainer asks you to shape the next rehabilitation sessions.

options.text: Discuss the pain with the physician and have the trainer pause cutting drills.
Have the new trainer repeat straight-line drills until the athlete feels confident.
Review the physician's plan, adjust progression to the pain response, and explain the reasoning.
Ask the new trainer to reduce the cutting drills and record any pain.

basic.situation: An athlete requests ankle tape before practice, and you are applying a preventive support device under supervision.

options.text: Confirm the planned pattern with the supervisor and check comfort afterward.
Use the familiar tape pattern and ask whether it feels snug.
Wrap several firm layers so the ankle feels stable for practice.
Check the ankle and apply the agreed tape pattern with even tension.

advanced.situation: The coach asks you to recommend protective equipment for an athlete returning after a wrist injury, and another trainer is assisting.

options.text: Compare available braces with the coach and ask the trainer to check comfort.
Ask the athlete to choose a brace and tell the trainer to fit it.
Choose the wrist brace the team usually stocks and show the trainer its straps.
Discuss the sport demands and fit with the coach, then guide the trainer through checks.

basic.situation: An athlete asks how to use a new mouthguard during practice, and you are helping with equipment advice.

options.text: Show how it should fit and ask the athlete to demonstrate its use.
Explain when to wear it and remind the athlete to keep it clean.
Point out the fitting instructions printed on the mouthguard case.
Tell the athlete to wear it whenever the coach requests protective gear.

advanced.situation: Parents and coaches ask you to lead a short session on preventing common training injuries before the season begins.

options.text: Reuse last season's slides and let the coach explain prevention points.
Share familiar prevention tips, then invite parents and coaches to discuss their concerns.
Set goals, use trusted guidance, and practise prevention steps together.
Prepare a brief talk on warmups and safe progressions for the group.

basic.situation: Before practice, you are helping clean and sanitize the athletic training room after several athletes have used the treatment area.

options.text: Follow the room's cleaning steps and sanitize each used treatment surface.
Use the room checklist and ask a colleague to review any missed areas.
Wipe the main table and leave the rest for the next shift.
Clean the visible surfaces and refill supplies before practice starts.

advanced.situation: You find loose debris near a playing area before a match, while another trainer is preparing the sideline medical station.

options.text: Ask the coach to check the area and continue setting up the station.
Move the visible debris aside and tell the team the field looks ready.
Mark the debris location, arrange its removal, and recheck the playing area.
Tell the grounds staff where the debris is and wait for their reply.

basic.situation: After a weekend event, you are recording an athlete's treatment and writing a brief report with guidance from a senior trainer.

options.text: Record the care provided and event details while they are fresh.
Write a short note from memory after finishing the equipment cleanup.
Review your notes with the senior trainer and complete the event report.
Ask the athlete to confirm the main details before writing your note.

advanced.situation: Your team travels for a tournament, an injured athlete needs hospital transport, and a new staff member is handling event records.

options.text: Ask the coach to arrange transport while you finish the team paperwork.
Send the new staff member to the hospital and take over the travel records.
Accompany the athlete and ask another staff member to track team logistics.
Arrange suitable accompaniment, confirm event coverage, and guide the new staff on records.

basic.situation: You review a patient's notes before a visit and need to record a clear family history of breast and ovarian conditions.

options.text: Ask about affected relatives, their ages, and which side of the family.
Use the patient's account to draft a family tree, then confirm unclear relationships.
List the patient's closest affected relative and move on to the next section.
Copy the conditions already listed into the family history section.

advanced.situation: A patient has an unusual lab result and several relatives with early-onset disease; the physician asks you to help coordinate next steps.

options.text: Request a repeat lab test before considering the family history further.
Summarize the lab result and family history for the physician's review.
Use a familiar testing pathway based on the patient's most affected relative.
Review the result and relevant literature, then discuss suitable tests with the physician.

basic.situation: A patient asks what to expect from amniocentesis after the obstetrician offers it as one option for further testing.

options.text: Explain how the sample is collected, then outline possible risks and limits.
Describe the needle procedure and reassure the patient that it is common.
Share the clinic leaflet and invite the patient to raise questions afterward.
Focus on the test's ability to identify conditions the scan may miss.

advanced.situation: A parent receives a child's genetic result linked to a possible inherited condition and asks how it may affect the family.

options.text: Give the parent a written summary and suggest discussing it at home.
Explain what the result means, discuss inheritance, and check what the parent understands.
Describe the condition's usual course and suggest testing close relatives.
Explain the result in plain language and offer time for questions.

basic.situation: Your clinic is contributing patient information to a project on an inherited heart condition, and you are asked to gather eligible records.

options.text: Check each record against the project criteria and collect requested details.
Use the project list to identify records, then note missing details.
Ask clinic staff to flag likely records for you to review later.
Gather records with the condition code and send them to the project team.

advanced.situation: A colleague invites you to help with a medical genetics study, but its proposed data collection may not answer the stated research question.

options.text: Ask a colleague who has worked on similar studies for suggestions.
Review the question and discuss the data plan with the study team.
Compare the proposed data with the research question and suggest focused changes.
Start collecting the available data while the study team refines its plan.

basic.situation: A patient asks for a simple handout explaining what an inherited condition means for relatives who may want advice.

options.text: Draft a short explanation and ask a colleague to check its wording.
Share an existing leaflet about the condition from the clinic folder.
Print a general genetics leaflet that covers several inherited conditions.
Prepare a plain-language handout explaining inheritance and where relatives can seek advice.

advanced.situation: Your service may apply for funding to expand counseling access, and you are asked to draft the program proposal.

options.text: Describe the proposed service and request funding for additional counseling sessions.
Define the service need, target group, activities, and costs in the proposal.
Summarize the service need and outline activities for the funding application.
Use a previous proposal as a template and update the service name.

basic.situation: You are preparing for a case discussion and notice a recent genetics paper may affect how the team explains a result.

options.text: Read the abstract and note the main finding for the discussion.
Share the paper title with the team and suggest they review it.
Read the paper's findings and limitations before sharing its relevance with colleagues.
Mention the paper's conclusion based on its summary in a colleague's email.

advanced.situation: Your unit is revising its process for returning genetic results, and staff have raised concerns about inconsistent explanations to patients.

options.text: Ask each counselor to use the wording they find most comfortable.
Compare current practice with guidance and ethics, then propose clear process changes.
Suggest that the team revisit its process at the next staff meeting.
Collect examples of current explanations and identify common differences.

basic.situation: At a community health session, a visitor asks why some inherited conditions can appear in several generations of a family.

options.text: Describe genes as family traits passed down through the generations.
Use a simple family example to explain how a condition can be inherited.
Tell the visitor that inheritance patterns are explained in the clinic leaflet.
Explain that family history can help show patterns across generations.

advanced.situation: You are asked to run a short session for medical students who struggle to explain genetic test results in plain language.

options.text: Build practice cases into the session and have students explain results aloud.
Present key terminology and distribute a glossary for students to keep.
Review common results and model a plain-language explanation for students.
Ask students to read a chapter on counseling before the session.

basic.situation: Before a procedure, you are asked to help a new team member gown and glove while the scrub nurse prepares the sterile field.

options.text: Point out the gowning instructions and help if the colleague asks.
Hand over a gown and gloves and let the colleague follow the usual routine.
Guide the sequence and watch for contact that could contaminate sterile areas.
Talk through each step while the colleague gowns and gloves under supervision.

advanced.situation: During a procedure, a junior colleague's sleeve brushes the drape edge near the sterile field, and the team is waiting to continue.

options.text: Pause the exchange and tell the scrub nurse what you observed.
Identify the contacted area, protect the field, and replace affected sterile items.
Continue while reminding the colleague to keep sleeves clear of the drapes.
Move nearby supplies away and ask the colleague to adjust their gown.

basic.situation: The team asks you to arrange instruments and supplies for a routine procedure, and the setup list is beside the trolley.

options.text: Ask another team member which items are usually needed for this procedure.
Use the list to arrange instruments, then compare the trolley with it.
