Set out familiar instruments first, then add remaining supplies as requested.
Arrange the listed items and check each package before placing it.

advanced.situation: A difficult procedure changes direction, and the surgeon requests an instrument while the scrub nurse is managing a complex exchange.

options.text: Check the tray for the requested item while the nurse finishes exchanging instruments.
Track the sequence and pass the requested item with its use confirmed.
Repeat the request and prepare the named instrument for the next exchange.
Pass the closest similar instrument so the surgeon can keep working.

basic.situation: Under direct supervision, you are asked to help close a straightforward incision with sutures after the surgeon finishes deeper work.

options.text: Start placing sutures based on the spacing used in the last case.
Hand over the suture and watch while the surgeon closes the incision.
Prepare the suture and follow the surgeon's direction on each placement.
Assist with the closure and check the next suture is ready when needed.

advanced.situation: A wound needs a drain secured during closure, and the surgeon asks you to assist while the team prepares the dressing.

options.text: Hold the drain near the wound and let the surgeon adjust it later.
Prepare the dressing while another team member steadies the drain for closure.
Keep the drain positioned as directed and alert the surgeon if it shifts.
Assist with securing the drain and confirm its position before dressing.

basic.situation: During surgical entry, the surgeon asks you to assist with a clamp while a small vessel is bleeding.

options.text: Place the clamp where directed and maintain a clear view for the surgeon.
Pass the clamp and keep suction ready as the surgeon controls bleeding.
Hold a sponge over the area until the surgeon finishes the entry.
Choose a nearby clamp and apply it to the visible bleeding point.

advanced.situation: Bleeding increases during a procedure and the operative field becomes difficult to see while the surgeon works to control it.

options.text: Keep suction near the pool of blood and wait for the surgeon's next request.
Ask a colleague to bring more sponges while you prepare the suction.
Use suction as requested and pass sponges when the surgeon asks.
Coordinate suction and sponges to clear the view while following the surgeon's requests.

basic.situation: The team is positioning a patient for surgery, and you are asked to help place protective padding before the procedure starts.

options.text: Place padding at pressure points and check that the patient remains supported.
Use the padding available and adjust it after the patient is draped.
Help position the patient and confirm the padding is still in place.
Put padding under the areas the surgeon says need better access.

advanced.situation: After a long procedure, you are asked to assess the patient's skin before transfer because the patient was positioned on one side.

options.text: Look over the visible skin and record that the patient was repositioned.
Ask the team whether any skin concerns were noticed during the procedure.
Check exposed skin and pressure areas, then report any concerning changes to the team.
Inspect the skin for marks and tell the nurse if anything stands out.

basic.situation: Before the patient enters theatre, you are asked to confirm the patient's identity and operative site with a senior colleague.

options.text: Check the patient identifiers and compare the planned site with the team's records.
Ask the patient to confirm their name and point to the planned site.
Read the wristband and ask the senior colleague to confirm the site.
Use the theatre list to verify the patient and planned procedure.

advanced.situation: The team is preparing for a complex operation, and one requested piece of equipment is not yet visible in theatre.

options.text: Check the equipment list and confirm availability with the relevant team before setup.
Review the list and ask the team whether the item is already in transit.
Begin setup with available equipment and expect the missing item to arrive.
Look in nearby storage and tell the team if the item is still missing.

basic.situation: At a routine visit, you review a patient's pregnancy record and discuss the next care steps with her.

options.text: Review the record and discuss the usual care plan with the patient.
Use the last visit's plan and arrange the next routine appointment.
Check the chart and explain the next standard steps to the patient.
Review current findings with the patient and agree on an individualized care plan.

advanced.situation: Your clinic's records show repeated missed follow-ups among post-date patients, and colleagues are reviewing care approaches.

options.text: Present the count and ask colleagues whether the follow-up approach needs a change.
Share the missed visit count and suggest sending patients another reminder message.
Update the clinic summary with the latest count recorded in patient files.
Review the pattern, compare follow-up outcomes, and propose a practice change for team discussion.

basic.situation: During labor, you are asked to check a patient's vital signs and observe her contractions.

options.text: Check her vital signs and report the contraction pattern to the midwife.
Check the readings, observe contractions, and report any meaningful change promptly.
Ask the patient how contractions feel and note her response.
Record the readings and keep the usual observation schedule.

advanced.situation: During a long labor, the fetal heartbeat changes while the mother's blood pressure is rising and the room is short on supplies.

options.text: Continue the usual observations and wait for the next scheduled review.
Reassess mother and baby, communicate changes, and coordinate the needed support and supplies.
Call the senior and report the heartbeat change while checking blood pressure.
Recheck both patients and ask a colleague to fetch missing supplies.

basic.situation: A mother in labor says her current position is uncomfortable, and you are asked to help her find another.

options.text: Offer a comfortable position and ask whether she wants to try it.
Suggest the position commonly used in the birthing room.
Discuss comfortable options and help her try one that supports birth.
Help her shift position and check whether she feels steadier.

advanced.situation: A newborn is not breathing effectively after birth, and another staff member is preparing equipment while the family watches.

options.text: Lead the newborn resuscitation steps, assign roles, and communicate progress clearly.
Start newborn care and ask the other staff member to follow.
Ask the teammate to prepare the equipment while you reassure the family.
Begin the indicated newborn support and tell the teammate the next step.

basic.situation: A patient asks why her body feels different during pregnancy, and you have time to explain the changes.

options.text: Explain common pregnancy changes and invite her to share concerns.
Explain the changes in plain language and check what she wants clarified.
Suggest she read the clinic leaflet and discuss questions later.
Give a brief explanation based on what most patients experience.

advanced.situation: Several new parents ask for guidance on postpartum recovery and contraception, and the clinic plans a group education session.

options.text: Explain the handout topics and invite parents to ask questions.
Read the clinic handout aloud so everyone receives the same information.
Plan a session around recovery, contraception choices, and questions parents raise.
Use the standard handout and offer time for questions afterward.

basic.situation: A laboring patient feels tense between contractions and asks for help coping with the discomfort.

options.text: Offer breathing or massage, then adapt the support to her response.
Suggest she use the breathing method taught during her last visit.
Stay beside her and encourage slower breathing through contractions.
Guide her breathing and ask which comfort measure feels helpful.

advanced.situation: A pregnant patient with high blood pressure reports a new severe headache, and her usual monitoring values have changed since yesterday.

options.text: Use the escalation pathway and coordinate a timely clinical review.
Repeat the blood pressure and review her next scheduled appointment.
Contact the senior with the new headache and latest blood pressure.
Ask her to rest while you arrange another blood pressure check.

basic.situation: A patient's clinic visit requires a urine specimen for a laboratory test, and you are asked to collect it.

options.text: Give her a container and ask her to return the sample.
Collect the sample and leave it beside the laboratory forms.
Explain the collection steps and label the specimen with her details.
Confirm the collection instructions, identify the specimen, and record the collection.

advanced.situation: While reviewing clinic records, you find several visits with missing follow-up notes before an upcoming documentation audit.

options.text: Flag the gaps through clinic process and coach staff on complete notes.
List the missing notes, remind staff, and check that future records include follow-up plans.
Fill the gaps from memory so the audit file looks complete.
Ask the team to check their records before the audit begins.

basic.situation: You are helping a patient bathe and dress. She seems unsure about the order of the steps.

options.text: I would finish the bath quickly while she rests, then help her dress.
I would ask her daughter to choose the bathing order and assist her.
I would ask what she prefers, protect her privacy, and guide each step she can manage.
I would explain each step, offer a towel, and let her wash what she can.

advanced.situation: A patient with memory loss becomes distressed during a transfer from bed to wheelchair and resists your usual dressing routine.

options.text: I would pause, use familiar cues, and follow the transfer plan at her pace.
I would ask a family member to finish dressing her while I prepare the chair.
I would explain the transfer again and continue with the usual steps.
I would lift her into the wheelchair before she changes her mind.

basic.situation: You are changing a patient's bed linens before preparing the simple meal listed in the care notes.

options.text: I would serve quick food and replace damp linens after washing my hands.
I would change the linens, wash my hands, then prepare the listed meal.
I would prepare the familiar meal after changing linens and washing my hands.
I would check meal notes, wash hands, prepare that meal, then change linens.

advanced.situation: Two patients need meals with different dietary instructions, and laundry is piling up in a shared home.

options.text: I would prepare the meals separately and ask which laundry needs attention first.
I would serve the first meal ready and sort the laundry by patient.
I would prepare each meal from its notes, label trays, and separate clean laundry.
I would cook the same mild meal for both and finish the laundry afterward.

basic.situation: A nurse asks you to check a patient's pulse and temperature before you collect household supplies.

options.text: I would collect the supplies first and tell the nurse the readings later.
I would take the readings and note them before leaving for supplies.
I would record the pulse and temperature, then confirm the supply list with the nurse.
I would check the pulse and temperature, then head out with the usual list.

advanced.situation: You record a patient's pulse and temperature, then notice the pulse seems unusual as you are due to collect medicine from a shop.

options.text: I would ask a family member whether the pulse is usual for the patient.
I would finish the errand quickly and mention the pulse when I return.
I would tell the nurse the pulse seems unusual and wait for direction.
I would recheck the pulse, report the reading to the nurse, and confirm the errand plan.

basic.situation: A patient asks you to read aloud, then complete a simple prescribed exercise with your guidance.

options.text: I would read the passage and ask a relative to lead the exercise.
I would read a short passage, then guide the prescribed movement at a steady pace.
I would let the patient exercise alone while I finish the reading.
I would ask what they would enjoy hearing, then guide the exercise with clear cues.

advanced.situation: A patient using a prescribed brace loses focus during a longer exercise routine and asks to hear a story instead.

options.text: I would shorten the exercise and include a brief story during rest breaks.
I would complete every exercise first, then read the story if time remains in the visit.
I would pause for a story, then resume the brace exercise with prescribed cues.
I would end the exercise and spend the rest of the visit reading.

basic.situation: You notice a patient ate little lunch and seemed quieter than usual, and need to complete the care log.

options.text: I would note the meal and mood with the time, then tell the supervisor.
I would record the time, meal amount, and mood, then share these observations at handover.
I would record that lunch was small and continue with routine notes.
I would mention the quiet mood and finish recording the meal details.

advanced.situation: A patient has become less steady over several visits, and the family offers different explanations as you prepare your care notes.

options.text: I would record the family's explanation as a likely reason for the change.
I would document changes across visits and discuss the pattern with the case manager.
I would note today's unsteadiness and tell the supervisor during the next handover.
I would ask family to settle on one explanation before writing anything in the note.

basic.situation: A patient asks for a heat lamp treatment that is listed in the care instructions, while you are working under direct supervision.

options.text: I would check the plan, ask about comfort, and apply the lamp under supervision.
I would explain that I need to confirm the treatment details before starting.
I would use the lamp briefly at the usual setting and check afterward.
I would check the instructions with the supervisor and apply the lamp as directed.

advanced.situation: A patient's family is worried about caring for an ill parent at home, and the patient asks for a massage during your visit.

options.text: I would focus on the massage and suggest the family discuss concerns later.
I would listen to the family and ask the supervisor about the requested massage.
I would listen to the family and check the care plan before any massage.
I would reassure the family that they will manage and begin the massage.

basic.situation: You are asked to prepare a simple lunch and tidy the kitchen before the client returns home.

options.text: I would prepare lunch first and tidy the kitchen before the client returns.
I would make a familiar lunch and leave the dishes for the next visit.
I would check the meal notes, prepare lunch, and wash the used dishes.
I would serve a quick snack and focus on making the kitchen look tidy.

advanced.situation: You have errands for two clients, laundry at one home, and meal preparation scheduled before a family visit.

options.text: I would finish the laundry first, then fit the errands around the visit.
I would list both clients' tasks and call to confirm which errand is urgent.
I would map the timed tasks, group nearby errands, and protect each meal schedule.
I would run the closest errand first and adjust the visits as needed.

basic.situation: At a case review, the team discusses a client's meal support and increasing difficulty with household chores.

options.text: I would note that the client is managing well and leave out the concerns.
I would write that the client needs more help around the home.
I would record the meal concern and write down the team's proposed support.
I would note the needs discussed and ask the team to clarify any unfamiliar terms.

advanced.situation: At a review, team members disagree about how much help a client needs to continue living at home.

options.text: I would note differing views and ask the team to clarify its recommendation.
I would clarify client needs, summarize views, and record agreed next steps.
I would propose a longer service plan to provide the client with extra support.
I would adopt the majority view and record it as the ongoing service plan.

basic.situation: A nurse asks you to record a client's blood pressure and the time they took their prescribed medicine.

options.text: I would record the reading and medicine time, then update the nurse's log.
I would note the blood pressure and medicine time on my visit sheet.
I would record a typical reading and the usual medicine time to save time.
I would ask the client when they usually take medicine and note that time.

advanced.situation: A client's readings differ from recent records, and a new aide asks you what to enter while the nurse is away.

options.text: I would ask the new aide to use the recent reading as a guide.
I would record today's reading and tell the nurse when they return.
I would repeat the measurement, record the result, and flag the change to the nurse.
I would ask the client whether the new reading seems normal for them.

basic.situation: A client needs help bathing and dressing, and asks you to explain each step before assisting.

options.text: I would ask a relative to explain the routine while I prepare clothes.
I would guide the bath and help with dressing at the client's pace.
I would complete the bath and dressing quickly so the client can rest.
I would explain the steps, offer privacy, and let the client do what they can.

advanced.situation: A client with limited movement struggles to wash and dress, while a new aide watches your routine for training.

options.text: I would ask the aide to prepare the bathroom and assist with dressing.
I would ask the client's comfort, then coach the aide through the routine.
I would demonstrate each step beside the client, protect privacy, and invite the aide's questions.
I would follow the care plan, explain each step, and invite manageable client participation.

basic.situation: You finish a visit and need to log the help provided, including a client who seemed more tired than usual.

options.text: I would tell the next aide about unusual tiredness and complete the visit task list.
I would log tasks, describe the tiredness, and report this change to my supervisor.
I would write that the visit went well and finish the daily log.
I would list the tasks completed and note that the client seemed tired.

advanced.situation: While checking your visit notes, you find two entries with different times for the same service and a reported change in the client's condition.

options.text: I would compare source notes, verify the time, and flag the condition change.
I would choose the later time and ask the client about the reported change.
I would leave both times and ask another aide which entry they can verify.
I would report the discrepancy and condition change to my manager, then seek record guidance.

basic.situation: A client asks you to type a letter to a family member and find the address for a local support service.

options.text: I would type the client's words and confirm the service address before sharing it.
I would send a standard letter using the first address in my notes without checking.
I would type the dictated letter and look up the service address.
I would draft a friendly letter and search for a nearby support service.

advanced.situation: A family caring for a recovering client feels overwhelmed, and the client asks for help explaining household hygiene needs to relatives.

options.text: I would tell the family to divide chores fairly and reassure the client.
I would tell the relatives the client can manage alone once they leave.
I would listen to the family and explain the hygiene steps requested by the client.
I would hear concerns, share hygiene guidance, and help agree on manageable family roles.

basic.situation: You are changing a patient's bed linens with guidance. The patient is resting, and the sheet is damp from a spill.

options.text: Ask the patient to step aside, then change linens with guidance.
Pull clean linen over the damp sheet to finish before rounds.
Check the bed, gather fresh linen, and change it with guidance.
Replace the sheet promptly, then straighten the blanket and pillows.

advanced.situation: A new aide is unsure how to sanitize a patient room after discharge. You are asked to show them the routine before the next admission.

options.text: Ask the aide to wipe visible marks before the next admission.
Demonstrate the clean-to-dirty sequence, then watch the aide sanitize key surfaces.
Point out the disinfectant labels and let the aide finish the room.
Show the aide the room checklist and explain each cleaning step.

basic.situation: A patient needs a wheelchair ride to a treatment unit. Your colleague is available to assist, and the corridor is busy.

options.text: Use the quickest corridor and wheel the patient ahead of your colleague.
Take the quieter corridor and keep the transport moving steadily.
Ask your colleague to push while you walk beside the chair.
Check the route, secure the footrests, and move with your colleague.

advanced.situation: A heavier patient needs transfer from bed to stretcher, and the usual sling is unavailable. A nurse is nearby, and another aide is on the ward.

options.text: Pause, check the care plan and equipment, then agree roles with the nurse.
Ask the nurse to confirm transfer plan and gather the available team.
Bring another aide over and prepare the stretcher safely beside the bed.
Attempt a careful lift with your colleague while the patient waits nearby.

basic.situation: You are helping a patient bathe and dress with supervision. The patient seems embarrassed when a visitor enters the room.

options.text: Pause the wash, cover the patient, and ask the visitor to wait outside.
Finish washing quickly, then help the patient dress behind the curtain.
Close the curtain and continue the bath at a slower pace.
Ask the supervising nurse how to manage the interruption before continuing.

advanced.situation: A new aide is dressing a patient with limited arm movement. The patient winces as the sleeve is pulled over their shoulder.

options.text: Guide the aide to dress the less mobile arm first, supporting the shoulder.
Suggest loosening the shirt and finishing the dressing before the rounds begin.
Tell the aide to pause and ask the patient where the sleeve hurts.
Ask the patient to push through while the aide finishes the sleeve.

basic.situation: You are preparing a patient's lunch tray and have been asked to remind them about their scheduled supplement. The tray is due shortly.

options.text: Ask the patient what they usually eat, then bring that tray.
Set down the usual lunch and remind the patient about the supplement.
Prepare the listed tray and tell the patient the supplement is due.
Check the tray ticket, set out the meal, and give the reminder as directed.

advanced.situation: A new aide is distributing dinner trays. One patient's chart lists a food allergy and a texture restriction, but the usual tray looks suitable.

options.text: Check the diet information against the tray label, then arrange a suitable replacement.
Ask the kitchen for a replacement tray that matches both restrictions.
Hold the tray and tell the nurse about the allergy and texture note.
Deliver the usual tray and ask the patient to avoid problem foods.

basic.situation: You are recording a patient's weight as directed. The scale shows a result that differs sharply from yesterday's entry.

options.text: Record the displayed weight and tell the nurse about the change.
Ask a colleague whether the scale seems reliable before recording.
Use yesterday's weight for today's entry until a colleague checks the scale.
Check the scale setup and patient reading, then record and report.

advanced.situation: While coaching a new aide on vital-sign records, you notice one entry has no time and another has a value transposed from the worksheet.

options.text: Ask the aide to review both entries before the shift ends.
Compare entries with the worksheet and document any changes clearly.
Point out each discrepancy and have the aide check the original readings.
Update the values yourself and remind the aide to double-check next time.

basic.situation: A patient presses the call bell while you are helping another patient. The call light remains on, and the corridor is clear.

options.text: Tell the other patient you will return, then check the call signal.
Ask a nearby aide to check the signal while you finish safely.
Switch off the call light from the corridor and return to work.
Finish the current task, then go see what the patient needs.

advanced.situation: A patient who was settled earlier is unusually quiet and guarding one arm. You are mentoring a new aide during routine observation rounds.

options.text: Tell the aide to report the guarded arm and quietness to the nurse promptly.
Tell the aide to note the behavior and continue the observation round.
Ask about the arm, observe visible changes, and report findings to the nurse.
Ask the aide to mention the quiet behavior during the next handover.

basic.situation: A patient is striking the bedrail and the nurse is assessing the risk. You are asked to stand nearby while the nurse decides whether restraint is needed.

options.text: Stay near the patient, keep space clear, and follow the nurse's direction.
Use a calm voice, offer space, and wait for the nurse's assessment.
Apply the restraint now so the patient cannot strike the rail again.
Move nearby objects away and ask the patient to lower their hands.

advanced.situation: A patient is shouting and pacing near other patients, but has not approached anyone. A junior aide asks whether to restrain them while the nurse is nearby.

options.text: Ask the aide to hold the patient's arms until the nurse arrives.
Tell the aide to wait for the nurse's direction while you clear nearby patients.
Keep a calm distance, use one speaker, offer choices, and update the nurse.
Ask the aide to speak gently and move the group to another room.

basic.situation: A nurse asks you to help a patient dress after bathing. The patient is unsure which clothes to put on and asks you to explain each step.

options.text: Ask the nurse to repeat the directions while you wait with the patient.
Choose the clothes yourself and finish dressing before the next care round.
Lay out the clothes and guide each dressing step at the patient's pace.
Dress the patient quickly while describing what you are doing.

advanced.situation: A new aide is helping a patient with limited mobility bathe. The patient turns away when the aide reaches for a washcloth and seems distressed.

options.text: Demonstrate washing within reach, offering the cloth and covering areas between steps.
Tell the aide to complete the bath while the patient is distracted.
Ask the aide to pause and let the patient choose what happens next.
Suggest finishing the wash quickly so the patient can rest afterward.

basic.situation: A patient asks to play cards during the afternoon activity period. The group is small, and staff supervision is available.

options.text: Join the patient for a short card game and invite others to participate.
Start a quick game with whoever is nearby before the period ends.
Check the activity plan, then offer the patient a suitable card game.
Tell the patient to play alone until the next group activity.

advanced.situation: You are arranging a small recreation group, and two patients have different energy levels. A new aide will help lead the activity under your supervision.

options.text: Choose a flexible activity with seated roles, then brief the aide on adapting participation.
Let the most energetic patients play while others watch from the side.
Ask the aide to lead a familiar game while you watch the group.
Pick a familiar group game and ask the aide to keep everyone involved.

basic.situation: A patient tells you they feel lonely and asks whether anyone will visit today. A nurse is present nearby, and you do not know the visitor schedule.

options.text: Suggest a television program to help pass the waiting time.
Tell the patient visitors usually come later and stay nearby.
Listen, acknowledge the loneliness, and ask the nurse about visitor information.
Let the patient talk while you sit nearby and listen quietly.

advanced.situation: A patient in distress says they may hurt themselves tonight. You are supporting them while a nurse is working nearby.

options.text: Reassure the patient that things can improve and ask them to rest.
Listen calmly and tell the nurse the patient's exact words and current location.
Tell the patient to join an activity, then alert the nurse later.
Stay with the patient and ask the nurse to come support them.

basic.situation: During a routine ward check, a patient begins walking toward a corridor outside their assigned area. You are responsible for monitoring the group.

options.text: Ask another aide to stay with the group while you speak with the patient.
Call out from the ward doorway for the patient to return.
Calmly remind the patient of their assigned area and inform the nurse.
Walk with the patient toward the corridor and discuss where they are going.

advanced.situation: A patient who usually joins meals has stayed in their room and is pacing more than usual. You are guiding a new aide during checks.

options.text: Suggest the aide invite the patient to meals and report continued pacing to the nurse.
Ask the aide to record the pacing change and share it during handover.
Guide the aide to compare behavior with baseline and report specific changes to the nurse.
Have the aide describe the change in routine and alert the nurse.

basic.situation: You are helping enter a patient's vital signs on a ward form. The handwritten pulse value is difficult to read, and the nurse is available nearby.

options.text: Enter the value that seems most likely, then complete the form.
Enter the clear readings and mark the pulse for nurse review.
Ask the nurse to confirm the pulse reading before entering it.
Leave the pulse field blank and enter the other readings.

advanced.situation: A new aide's patient notes include an escort destination but no return time, and one vital-sign entry appears copied into a different row.

options.text: Point out the mismatched row and missing time, then check the source together.
Ask the aide to review both entries and fill in the missing time.
Review the row with the aide and remind them to add escort details.
Show the aide how to verify the source, amend the entry, and complete escort details.

basic.situation: A patient tires during a kitchen task, but still wants to practise. You need to choose an activity that fits their abilities.

options.text: Ask the patient which familiar kitchen step feels manageable today.
Choose a seated kitchen task matched to the patient's reach and stamina.
Offer a seated sorting task that uses the same hand movements.
Repeat the full kitchen task, offering a rest if requested.

advanced.situation: A patient has made little progress using the planned reach-and-place activity. You are asked to adjust it during today's session.

options.text: Swap to a familiar task that practises the same movement.
Lower the target and ask the patient whether it feels easier.
Repeat the same setup and encourage a few more attempts.
Shorten the reach and raise the target, then track the patient's response.

basic.situation: Before a session, you find a therapy board with marks from its previous use. You need to prepare it for the next patient.

options.text: Clean the board with the available approved wipe and set it out.
Wipe the board using the clinic's cleaning routine, then check its surface.
Use a dry tissue to clear the visible marks quickly.
Ask a colleague to confirm which cleaning cloth is stocked.

advanced.situation: A patient struggles to grip a standard utensil during practice. You are asked to adapt it using materials available in the therapy room.

options.text: Add a removable foam grip, then check fit with the patient.
Wrap the handle with tape to make it thicker for practice.
Trim the utensil handle to a shorter length for easier holding.
Ask the patient to try a different standard utensil first.

basic.situation: After a session, a patient completed more buttoning steps than yesterday but became frustrated near the end. You need to update your supervisor.

options.text: Mention the patient seemed frustrated during the buttoning practice.
Note the extra steps and frustration in a brief written update.
Report the added steps and frustration, with the point when it began.
Say the patient did well and seemed a little upset.

advanced.situation: At a care plan meeting, the team reviews a patient's progress with dressing. You have session observations that may affect the next plan.

options.text: Report the number of dressing steps completed across recent sessions.
Describe the patient's effort and ask what the team prefers.
Share measured dressing progress and suggest a practice goal for team review.
Recommend keeping the current plan because the patient is familiar with it.

basic.situation: A patient is unsure how to start a simple clay activity. You need to demonstrate the technique while supporting their confidence.

options.text: Make the whole shape yourself so the patient can copy it.
Show one clay step slowly, then invite the patient to try it.
Demonstrate the first few steps while the patient watches closely.
Give the patient the clay and describe the finished shape.

advanced.situation: A patient becomes angry after a difficult therapy task and says they want to quit. You are supporting them to handle the emotion constructively.

options.text: Acknowledge the frustration, then practise a calming pause the patient chooses.
Tell the patient that everyone feels frustrated during therapy sometimes.
Change the subject to a pleasant activity until the anger passes.
Acknowledge the frustration and ask what might help next time.

basic.situation: A patient is practising dressing before lunch and has trouble pulling a sleeve over one arm. You are helping with the task under supervision.

options.text: Pull the sleeve over the arm to keep lunch on schedule.
Prompt the patient to try turning the sleeve opening first.
Ask whether the patient wants help with the sleeve today.
Guide the sleeve opening and let the patient complete the pull.

advanced.situation: The occupational therapist asks you to run a small leisure group for patients practising planning and turn-taking. One participant needs more structure.

options.text: Set a simple group routine with visual turns, then adapt prompts during play.
Lead the game yourself so the group can finish on time.
Use a visual turn card and remind the group whose turn comes next.
Choose a familiar game and let participants work out the turns.

basic.situation: A caller asks to book a follow-up appointment, but the therapist's diary has two possible openings. You are handling scheduling with guidance.

options.text: Offer the earlier opening because it appears free on the diary.
Check the diary, then confirm an opening with the therapist.
Book the first opening and note the caller's preferred time.
Ask the caller which opening they prefer, then record their choice.

advanced.situation: A course on adaptive equipment is offered during your work week. You want to keep your knowledge current while meeting clinic responsibilities.

options.text: Review the course topics and arrange attendance around patient duties.
Skip the course and rely on your current equipment knowledge.
Ask a colleague to share notes from the course afterward.
Register for the course and tell the team about the date.

basic.situation: A patient attends a craft session and completes two steps with encouragement. You need to record attendance and a brief progress note.

options.text: Record attendance and the two completed steps in the client record.
Write that the patient had a good session and seemed engaged.
Mark attendance and note that the patient joined the craft activity.
Leave the note for later and rely on the attendance sheet.

advanced.situation: While checking client records, you find several notes with missing attendance details. A new aide asks how to keep their entries consistent.

options.text: Tell the aide to copy the format used by nearby records.
Fill in the missing details from memory so the records look complete.
Show the aide a sample entry with attendance and observable progress details.
Point out the missing details and ask the aide to review their entries.

basic.situation: A patient using a walking aid is ready to move from the waiting area to therapy. You are assigned to assist with the transfer.

options.text: Check the patient's aid and route, then support their pace to therapy.
Take the walking aid and guide the patient quickly to therapy.
Ask the patient whether they feel ready to walk over now.
Walk beside the patient and let them set a comfortable pace.

advanced.situation: A patient becomes unsteady while moving toward therapy and says their leg feels weak. A new aide is beside you during the transfer.

options.text: Offer a chair, then ask whether the patient feels ready to continue therapy.
Pause the transfer, support the patient, and guide the aide through clinic safety steps.
Stop in a safe place and contact the therapist to assist with transfer.
Ask the aide to contact a therapist while you steady the patient nearby.

basic.situation: A patient is learning to sort laundry by colour and asks how to begin. You are asked to demonstrate the task with guidance.

options.text: Put all the clothes into one pile so the task feels easier.
Explain the colour groups and ask the patient to start sorting.
Show one colour group, then let the patient sort a few items.
Sort the laundry yourself while the patient watches from the chair.

advanced.situation: A patient with limited hand control is learning to prepare a simple snack. You are asked to plan instruction and show another aide how to teach it.

options.text: Give the patient a picture sequence and let the aide observe.
Have the aide complete the snack while the patient watches closely.
Break snack preparation into safe steps, then model prompts the aide can adapt.
Plan short steps with pauses and ask the aide to try the sequence.

basic.situation: A patient is choosing a simple craft for the session and needs reminders to follow each step. You are supervising the activity.

options.text: Offer two suitable crafts and remind the patient of the next step.
Finish the craft for the patient so the session stays on schedule.
Let the patient pick a craft and check in near the end.
Choose the simpler craft and explain its steps as they work.

advanced.situation: A patient is building a multi-step model and repeatedly loses their place. You need to evaluate their work and adjust how you supervise.

options.text: Ask which step feels confusing and provide a reminder there.
Repeat the instructions more slowly and watch the patient continue.
Finish the model together so the patient can see the completed sequence.
Notice where the sequence breaks, then offer a step card and check progress.

basic.situation: The phone rings while you are restocking forms, and a caller asks where to send a completed clinic form. You are handling front desk duties.

options.text: Answer politely, give the clinic's standard submission route, and note the call.
Tell the caller to leave the form at the clinic reception desk.
Answer the question and return to restocking once the call ends.
Ask the caller to ring again after you finish restocking forms.

advanced.situation: Several appointments need rescheduling after a therapist's availability changes, and treatment supplies are running low. You are coordinating routine clinic administration.

options.text: Confirm suitable replacement slots, then order supplies based on current inventory.
Keep the original bookings and request a large supply order for safety.
Move bookings into open slots and order the usual monthly supply amount.
Recheck affected bookings, group caller updates, and review supply needs against use.

basic.situation: A therapist is preparing a tabletop activity and asks you to set out the materials and check the equipment. The patient arrives shortly.

options.text: Put out the materials and ask the therapist to check the equipment.
Set out the listed materials and check the equipment is ready to use.
Find a similar set of materials and start arranging the table.
Use the first available equipment and begin the activity setup.

advanced.situation: A loaned adaptive device no longer fits a patient's usual setup, and the therapist asks you to check the issue before the next session.

options.text: Adjust the device until it seems comfortable, then return it for review.
Ask the therapist to review the fit before changing the device.
Check the device settings against the patient's usual setup and report the difference.
Compare the fit with the prior setup and make a small reversible adjustment.

basic.situation: During a supervised session, you guide a patient through the therapist's simple leg exercise. The patient starts leaning and reports mild discomfort.

options.text: I finish the repetitions to keep the session on schedule.
I steady the patient, check comfort, and resume only the approved range.
I pause the exercise and tell the therapist what changed.
I remind the patient about posture and reduce the repetitions.

advanced.situation: You lead a therapist-approved breathing group. One participant becomes dizzy during deep-breathing practice while others await their next instruction.

options.text: I pause the group, support the participant, and alert the therapist.
I offer water and switch everyone to a gentler breathing pace.
I keep the group moving while the participant rests nearby.
I stop the breathing practice and ask the participant to sit.

basic.situation: A patient is ready to leave, but the sling twists as you help put it on. The therapist is nearby with another patient.

options.text: I smooth the sling, then ask the patient how it feels before securing it.
I support the arm, align the sling, and ask the therapist to review its fit.
I pause dressing, keep the patient seated, and request help with the twisted sling.
I ask the patient to hold still while I adjust the sling around the arm.

advanced.situation: A caregiver says the patient's prosthetic socket feels loose after a recent change. You are asked to show basic daily checks before discharge.

options.text: I show the caregiver how to inspect the socket and contact the therapist.
I suggest the caregiver monitor the fit during the next few days.
I demonstrate the approved daily checks and record the caregiver's concern for the therapist.
I tighten the fittings until the socket feels secure to the caregiver.

basic.situation: You help secure a patient onto a therapy table for a planned heat treatment. The patient says the strap feels tight before the therapist begins.

options.text: I reassure the patient and start the heat treatment as planned.
I loosen the strap, check positioning, and tell the therapist before treatment.
I keep the strap tight so the patient stays positioned.
I pause setup and ask the therapist to check the strap.

advanced.situation: A patient becomes pale during a therapist-directed manual exercise, and the next movement is scheduled. You are assisting with positioning.

options.text: I offer a short rest, then try the movement more slowly.
I stop the movement, support the patient, and alert the therapist.
I complete the scheduled movement, then report the patient's change to the therapist.
I pause the exercise and ask how the patient feels.

basic.situation: After treatment, you record equipment use and the patient's response. Your notes show a different treatment time from the equipment log.

options.text: I leave both entries unchanged and tell the therapist about the time mismatch.
I flag the mismatch and ask the therapist to review the original records.
I compare the equipment log with my notes, then ask the therapist to review each time.
I change the log time to match my treatment note without checking first.

advanced.situation: While reviewing a new aide's notes, you find several patient progress entries without dates. The therapist needs the records for today's review.

options.text: I flag undated entries for therapist review before using the records for today's patient review.
I add today's date to each entry so the file appears complete.
I ask the aide to date each entry from memory before review begins.
I check source notes, mark missing dates, and coach the aide on clinic dating standards.

basic.situation: A patient's family member asks how to help with the home exercise shown on a printed guide. You are assisting the therapist during discharge preparation.

options.text: I explain the guide and invite the family member to ask the therapist about concerns.
I explain the printed steps, demonstrate the approved movement, and check the family member's understanding.
I review the printed guide and ask the family member to read it at home.
I tell the family to repeat the exercise as often as possible.

advanced.situation: You are preparing a short in-service for caregivers on a therapist-approved home activity. Staff have been giving families different explanations.

options.text: I review the handout with the therapist, then present the agreed explanation and invite questions.
I check the approved plan with the therapist and share consistent steps during training.
I ask staff to describe their usual explanations before reviewing shared guidance together.
I reuse one caregiver's handout and present it as the clinic standard.

basic.situation: After a treatment, you clean the work area and find a therapy band with a small tear. The next patient is due shortly.

options.text: I remove the band, label the tear, and notify the therapist before restocking.
I set the damaged band aside and ask the therapist to assess it before use.
I put the band back so the next session can start on time.
I wipe the band and inspect whether the tear affects its safe use.

advanced.situation: You are updating the clinic inventory before a busy week. Several exercise bands are low, and one storage box contains expired cleaning supplies.

options.text: I submit an order for extra bands and check supply levels before the busy week.
I separate expired supplies, record usable stock, and submit a clinic replenishment request.
I mix the old supplies with current stock to fill the shelf.
I count the bands and request replacements through the usual clinic process.

basic.situation: You prepare a treatment space and notice the bed linens are damp after laundering. The patient is waiting nearby for the session.

options.text: I ask the patient to wait while I air the damp linens.
I replace the linens with a dry set and continue preparing the space.
I replace the linens, check the bed, and tell the therapist the setup is delayed.
I cover the damp area with a dry towel and set up the bed.

advanced.situation: You find a loose wheel on a treatment trolley during the morning equipment check. Two therapists have sessions scheduled in the area.

options.text: I park the trolley aside and tell the therapists it needs repair.
I use the trolley carefully so both sessions can start on time.
I tighten the wheel and check it by rolling the empty trolley.
I take the trolley out of service, label the fault, and report it for maintenance.

basic.situation: You are supporting a patient to stand for a therapist-directed transfer. The patient says their knee feels unsteady as they rise.

options.text: I guide the patient onward so the transfer finishes on time.
I steady the patient, pause the transfer, and alert the therapist to reassess.
I offer the patient another moment to stand before continuing.
I pause the transfer and ask the patient whether they feel ready.

advanced.situation: A patient who usually walks to treatment seems drowsy today. You are asked to bring them from the waiting area to the therapy room.

options.text: I walk beside the patient as usual to avoid delaying treatment.
I keep the patient seated and alert the therapist before choosing transport.
I use a wheelchair and tell the therapist about the drowsiness on arrival.
I ask the patient to walk slowly while I hold their arm.

basic.situation: After a session, you wipe down the therapy table and notice a small patch remains wet. The next patient is waiting outside.

options.text: I place a clean sheet over the wet patch and welcome the patient.
I let the surface dry, then prepare the table for the waiting patient.
I wipe the patch again and arrange supplies while the surface dries.
I complete disinfection, allow drying, and tell the therapist the patient is waiting.

advanced.situation: You review the cleaning log and find a missing entry for a shared therapy device. A new aide asks whether they can use it now.

options.text: I hold the device, verify cleaning, and explain the log procedure to the aide.
I enter an unverified cleaning entry and tell the aide the device is ready.
I clean the device again, record that action, and show the aide the entry.
I set the device aside and ask the therapist to confirm its cleaning before use.

basic.situation: You help a patient put on a sling under the therapist's direction. The patient says the arm feels unsupported after you fasten it.

options.text: I fasten the sling tighter so the arm stays in place.
I pause and ask the therapist to check the sling's fit.
I pause and ask the therapist to review the sling before leaving.
I reassure the patient and adjust the strap to their preference.

advanced.situation: During a therapist-directed exercise, a patient with limited movement starts sliding toward the edge of the plinth. You are assisting with the activity.

options.text: I stop the activity, steady the patient, and alert the therapist.
I pause the exercise and tell the therapist the patient is sliding.
I keep the exercise going while reminding the patient to hold still.
I move closer and help the patient finish the final repetitions.

basic.situation: You observe a patient during a therapist-directed exercise. Their breathing becomes faster than earlier, though they say they can continue.

options.text: I urge the patient to finish the set before taking a rest break.
I let the patient rest briefly and monitor breathing before asking about resuming.
I pause, note the breathing change, and ask the therapist to assess.
I pause the exercise and report the patient's changed breathing to the therapist.

advanced.situation: Across three sessions, you notice a patient needs longer rests and completes fewer repetitions. The therapist asks for your observations before planning treatment.

options.text: I compare notes and share the observed rest and repetition pattern.
I say attendance suggests progress, despite the longer rests and fewer repetitions.
I mention possible fatigue and suggest that the therapist consider shorter exercise sets.
I report that the patient needed longer rests during the most recent session.

basic.situation: A patient calls to book a therapy appointment and requests a time that is already occupied. You can see the clinic schedule.

options.text: I book the occupied time and ask the therapist to fit them in.
I check open slots, offer choices, and confirm the selected time.
I tell the patient to call back later when the schedule is clearer.
I offer the patient two available times and wait for their choice.

advanced.situation: Two therapists request the same treatment room for overlapping appointments, and one patient needs a wheelchair accessible space. You handle the clinic schedule.

options.text: I check room access, then coordinate another time with both therapist teams.
I give the accessible room to the first request without checking the patient's needs.
I ask the patient to wait while both therapists choose between the available rooms.
I move one appointment to an available slot and tell that therapist about the change.

basic.situation: A client asks for pressure-point work on a tense shoulder and winces at one spot.

options.text: I keep pressing the tender point to finish the planned sequence.
I ask how the spot feels and adjust pressure to their answer.
I move to nearby points and mention the tenderness at checkout.
I lighten my touch and complete the other points on schedule.

advanced.situation: A client with persistent tightness asks whether heat or another adjunctive therapy could complement today's massage.

options.text: I combine heat with massage and follow my usual session sequence.
I check relevant history, explain suitable options, and monitor their response.
I explain the options and ask which treatment they prefer today.
I add a familiar heat treatment because it often eases tightness.

basic.situation: A new client reports shoulder pain while you complete the health and pain-history checklist.

options.text: I ask about the pain and record the client's main concern.
I ask about medical history, pain, and what makes it better or worse.
I complete the checklist and confirm when the pain began.
I note the shoulder complaint and begin the usual massage routine.

advanced.situation: A returning client reports new stiffness after an old injury, and their shoulder movement seems reduced during assessment.

options.text: I ask when the stiffness began and avoid testing the shoulder further.
I compare both shoulders and record their movement and soft tissue findings.
I check the range of motion and ask which movements feel uncomfortable.
I focus on the tightest muscle and plan a longer massage there.

basic.situation: A client requests a massage after long desk days and says their upper back feels tense.

options.text: I recommend a firm massage because desk work commonly causes tightness.
I ask their pressure preference, then suggest a suitable massage type.
I book the same deep-pressure routine most clients choose.
I suggest a relaxation massage and ask which areas feel tense.

advanced.situation: A client with recurring tension wants a plan that balances relaxation with gradual recovery across several visits.

options.text: I outline a phased plan with massage types and review points.
I vary massage types across visits based on the client's comfort.
I repeat today's massage at each visit and review the plan later.
I promise a fixed series of sessions to resolve the recurring tension.

basic.situation: A client asks you to treat persistent symptoms that fall outside your massage training and scope.

options.text: I suggest a suitable therapist and share contact details with consent.
I recommend resting and ask the client to check back next week.
I explain that another therapist may be more appropriate for these symptoms.
I try a familiar massage approach and see whether symptoms settle.

advanced.situation: A client receiving care from a physician and psychologist wants massage included in a broader plan for ongoing stress and pain.

options.text: I agree on relevant goals and updates with both clinicians, with client consent.
I share a brief update with both clinicians after getting consent.
I send both clinicians my full treatment record to help them coordinate.
I ask the client to choose which clinician should receive my notes.

basic.situation: After a relaxation session, a client asks for a simple stretch to try at home after work.

options.text: I demonstrate a gentle stretch and let the client practise it.
I suggest a familiar stretch and send them home with its name.
I recommend holding a deep stretch until the shoulder loosens.
I show the stretch, check their form, and suggest stopping if uncomfortable.

advanced.situation: A client recovering from a soft tissue injury asks which strengthening movements to practise between appointments.

options.text: I describe a few exercises and let the client choose their pace.
I give a familiar strengthening routine and ask them to repeat it daily.
I teach each movement, check their form, and adapt effort to their response.
I demonstrate suitable movements and adjust them to the client's comfort.

basic.situation: Before the next appointment, you notice the massage area needs fresh linens and sanitised equipment.

options.text: I wipe down the main equipment and note that linens are low.
I ask the next client to wait while I gather supplies.
I replace the linens and sanitise the equipment between clients.
I change the linens and leave equipment cleaning for closing time.

advanced.situation: You finish a home visit and need to update the treatment record, clean equipment, and prepare oils for tomorrow's session.

options.text: I prepare the oil and record the session, then clean equipment at the clinic.
I record the session, clean equipment, and prepare the requested oil blend.
I clean the equipment and record the session details from memory tomorrow.
I update the record and set aside equipment to sanitise at the clinic.

basic.situation: Before a routine procedure, you are asked to prepare the patient, disinfect instruments, and set up the tray.

options.text: I set out familiar instruments and start preparing the patient.
I check the procedure list, disinfect instruments, and arrange the tray in order.
I reuse the instruments from the last tray to save setup time.
I arrange the tray and disinfect the instruments before the patient sits.

advanced.situation: A new assistant asks how you verify instrument processing records before preparing trays for a busy clinic session.

options.text: I check the cycle records and explain how each entry matches the load.
I check the latest log and tell them where processing dates appear.
I show the log fields and ask them to sign after loading instruments.
I ask them to copy yesterday's entries before we set up trays.

basic.situation: A patient is nervous before a dental x-ray, and you are asked to position them for imaging.

options.text: I ask the dentist to position the patient while I prepare the room.
I position the patient and explain how the image helps their care.
I use the same positioning as the previous patient to keep appointments moving.
I place the receptor carefully and check the patient's position before exposure.

advanced.situation: The image preview is unclear, and a junior colleague asks you what to check before the next dental exposure.

options.text: I adjust the exposure settings and ask the colleague to try again.
I review the image, identify the likely issue, then coach one correction.
I ask the colleague to repeat the same setup with steadier positioning.
I check the receptor placement and equipment indicators with them.

basic.situation: You have poured a study cast and need to trim and polish it before the dentist reviews it.

options.text: I compare the cast with the impression, then trim and polish the base.
I trim away uneven areas quickly so the cast fits the tray.
I trim the cast to its base and smooth rough edges.
I polish the cast before checking whether its base is even.

advanced.situation: A preliminary impression has a small margin defect, and you need to make a temporary restoration from it before the patient returns.

options.text: I make the temporary restoration from the clearest section of the impression.
I check the impression margins and remake it if the defect affects fit.
I show the defect to the dentist and ask whether to remake it.
I use the impression as it is and adjust the restoration chairside.

basic.situation: After treatment, the dentist gives you brief notes to enter in the patient's record before the next appointment.

options.text: I record the main procedure and leave out details that seem repetitive.
I enter the stated treatment details and check the patient record.
I enter the procedure and ask the dentist about one unclear note.
I add a familiar treatment code and leave the notes for later.

advanced.situation: While reviewing a patient's file, you notice a medical history entry differs from the signed form and a colleague asks you to fix it.

options.text: I remove the history entry so the mismatch does not confuse staff.
I ask the colleague to revise it and return to my other files.
I check the source form and follow the clinic's record amendment process with a note.
I replace the entry with the form wording and save the record.

basic.situation: A patient wants to book a follow-up and asks how much remains on the bill from today's visit.

options.text: I book the usual follow-up interval and hand over the bill.
I check the dentist's requested interval and show the bill total.
I confirm the appointment slot and explain the amount shown on the bill.
I tell the patient to call later about the bill and schedule the visit.

advanced.situation: An insurer returns a claim because a treatment detail does not match the clinic record, and the patient asks about payment timing.

options.text: I revise the claim using the record and tell the patient payment is pending.
I compare the claim with the record, clarify the detail, then update the patient.
I ask the dentist to confirm the treatment detail before resubmitting.
I resend the same claim and advise the patient to check with the insurer.

basic.situation: After a procedure, the patient asks what to do at home, and the dentist has prescribed postoperative instructions.

options.text: I hand over the printed instructions and offer to answer questions.
I add a home remedy that worked for another patient.
I summarize the main points and ask the patient to call if unsure.
I repeat the dentist's instructions and check what the patient understood.

advanced.situation: During treatment, the patient becomes faint, and the dentist directs you to help with the clinic's emergency response.

options.text: I bring the emergency kit and wait near the doorway.
I alert nearby staff and ask what equipment the dentist needs.
I follow the dentist's directions and bring the requested emergency supplies.
I leave the room to find the patient's family before helping.

basic.situation: You are asked to measure a patient's blood pressure and temperature before an appointment. The patient has just walked in from the rain.

options.text: I let the patient rest, then check cuff fit and take both readings.
I enter the first readings while the patient settles into the room.
I ask a colleague to confirm the cuff size before proceeding.
I take both readings after seating the patient and record them.

advanced.situation: A junior assistant records a patient's blood pressure far below the earlier reading. You are guiding intake while the clinic is busy.

options.text: I record both readings and let the clinician decide which one matters.
I compare the cuff and arm position, then coach a repeat measurement.
I demonstrate the standard position and observe the junior's next reading.
I ask the junior to repeat it using the same setup and pace.

basic.situation: You are preparing an examination room and notice the used instrument tray beside the clean supplies. A patient is waiting outside.

options.text: I clear used items, clean the room, and prepare fresh supplies.
I move the used tray aside and set out the clean supplies.
I pause setup and ask a colleague where the used tray belongs.
I keep the used tray separate for processing, then prepare the clean room.

advanced.situation: A junior assistant says an instrument set may not have completed sterilization, but the procedure room is nearly ready. You are guiding setup.

options.text: I ask the junior to check the sterilizer display before using the set.
I check the cycle record and hold the set until its status is clear.
I ask the junior to confirm the load finished before bringing it in.
I use the set because the instruments look dry and ready.

basic.situation: A patient is waiting for a routine examination. You need to show them to the room and help prepare them for the physician.

options.text: I point out the room so I can finish another task first.
I escort the patient, explain the next step, and prepare the room.
I escort the patient and let the physician know they have arrived.
I show the patient to the room and ask them to wait there.

advanced.situation: A physician asks you to prepare a patient for a minor procedure while two assistants are also helping. The patient seems unsure about the next step.

options.text: I confirm the physician's preparation instructions, then guide the patient and assistants.
I start the usual preparation while the assistants arrange the instruments.
I let the assistants prepare the room while I reassure the patient.
I assign each assistant a preparation task and begin with the patient.

basic.situation: A caller asks whether their insurance form has reached the clinic. You have several forms on your desk and a patient waiting.

options.text: I look through today's forms and give the caller a quick update.
I check the form log, then tell the caller its recorded status.
I ask a colleague to check the forms while I help the patient.
I tell the caller it probably arrived and return to the patient.

advanced.situation: Several examination gloves are close to running out, and a delivery is delayed. You are reviewing the clinic's supply inventory for the week.

options.text: I order the usual quantity based on last month's supply request.
I request the same amount as last time to keep the order simple.
I count remaining sizes, check recent use, and flag the shortage for ordering.
I count the boxes left and tell the office lead they are running low.

basic.situation: A patient gives you their medical history before an appointment. You are entering the details into the clinic record with guidance.

options.text: I fill unclear history fields with what seems typical for this visit.
I enter the main history details and move to the next record.
I enter the patient's stated history and check each field against the form.
I enter the details and ask the patient to review the summary.

advanced.situation: You are guiding a new assistant who has labelled two specimen containers while the collection forms remain on the trolley. The clinic is preparing samples for testing.

options.text: I check the labels for completeness and log both containers.
I use the collection order to fill any missing label details.
I match each label to its form before logging and preparing the specimens.
I ask the assistant to read each label aloud as I log it.

basic.situation: A patient arrives for an appointment and is unsure where to check in. You are at the clinic reception desk with the appointment list.

options.text: I greet the patient, confirm their appointment, and log their arrival.
I ask a colleague to check the list while I greet the patient.
I point to the waiting area and mark the patient as arrived.
I ask the patient's name and add it to the arrival list.

advanced.situation: A patient asks how to follow a physician's diet instructions, but says the written sheet is confusing. You are helping at the clinic desk.

options.text: I read the sheet aloud slowly and ask the patient to explain what remains unclear.
I tell the patient to bring the sheet to the next appointment.
I suggest a familiar diet change that seems close to the sheet.
I restate the written instructions in plain language and check what remains unclear.

basic.situation: You start a sterilizer with guidance and notice its gauge rising more slowly than during the previous load. Staff are waiting for the equipment.

options.text: I watch the gauge for another minute and note its movement.
I start the load since the gauge is still moving upward.
I check the displayed range and report the slow rise before starting a load.
I note the slower rise and tell the supervisor after the cycle.

advanced.situation: During a routine check, a colleague spots a small leak near a sterilizer fitting. You are guiding equipment checks before the next load.

options.text: I keep it out of use, identify the fitting, and report the leak for repair.
I ask the colleague to watch the fitting during the next cycle.
I report the leak to the supervisor and mark the equipment for checking.
I record the leak and report it when the next check is due.

basic.situation: A routine procedure tray is due, and you are assembling it from the provided checklist while the treatment area is busy.

options.text: I use the tray from yesterday as a guide and fill it quickly.
I match each instrument to the checklist and arrange the tray for use.
I follow the checklist and ask a colleague to review the finished tray.
I count the instruments listed and place them together in the tray.

advanced.situation: A specialty request adds several instruments to a tray used for a complex case. You are mentoring a newer preparer while assembling it.

options.text: I check the request with the newer preparer and arrange the additions together.
I copy the usual complex tray and add the extra instruments at the end.
I add the requested instruments and let the newer preparer arrange them.
I confirm the request details, map each item to the tray, and explain the layout.

basic.situation: You are cleaning a basic instrument before sterilization and find dried material near a joint. A standard cleaning solution is available.

options.text: I soak the instrument for the usual time and rinse it well.
I apply the approved solution and clean the joint until it is clear.
I clean the instrument and ask a colleague to inspect the joint.
I wipe the visible surface and send it along with the batch.

advanced.situation: A hinged instrument repeatedly arrives with residue around its joint after cleaning. You are asked to guide the team on preparing it for sterilization.

options.text: I check the instructions and verify the joint is clear before release.
I demonstrate cleaning around the joint, then ask staff to repeat the preparation steps.
I tell staff to scrub harder and send the next set through.
I have staff soak it longer before cleaning the joint again.

basic.situation: You are running an autoclave cycle with step-by-step guidance. The display shows a test result that differs from the previous load.

options.text: I ask a colleague whether the result looks normal before continuing.
I record the result and tell my supervisor it differs from the previous load.
I write down the result and continue with the scheduled load.
I record it and compare it with the cycle's acceptance range.

advanced.situation: A maintenance entry for the autoclave is missing from the load records. You are reviewing the log before the next shift takes over.

options.text: I copy the previous maintenance entry so the log looks complete.
I add a note that maintenance details need confirmation next shift.
I compare available maintenance notes with the load log and flag gaps.
I report the missing entry and leave the log for the next shift.

basic.situation: You are checking sterile supplies with a supervisor and find several packs with dates approaching their marked expiry.

options.text: I count the packs with earlier dates and tell the supervisor the number.
I ask the supervisor to decide what to do with the dated packs.
I count all packs together and note the total in the inventory sheet.
I separate the earlier dates, count them, and record the stock for review.

advanced.situation: Usage records show one sterile supply running low sooner each month, while another is often left unused. You are reviewing inventory levels.

options.text: I reduce the unused supply order and leave the faster-moving item unchanged.
I order the same quantities as last month to keep levels steady.
I compare usage and stock counts before proposing revised quantities.
I review both items' monthly use and propose revised quantities for each one.

basic.situation: You are restocking a crash cart from its checklist and notice one listed item is missing from the supply shelf.

options.text: I report the missing item and finish checking the other supplies.
I ask a colleague whether another unit has the listed item available.
I note the missing item and leave the cart ready for the next check.
I mark the gap, find the listed item, and complete the cart check.

advanced.situation: Two units use slightly different crash cart checklists, and new staff rotate between them. You are helping standardize cart stocking.

options.text: I show staff both checklists and ask them to choose the cart layout.
I compare both approved lists, flag differences, and teach staff each unit's layout.
I compare the lists and ask the lead which one staff should follow.
I use the more familiar checklist for both carts to simplify training.

basic.situation: You take a clinician’s dictation through a headset, but one phrase is muffled. You need to capture the wording for a draft report.

options.text: I replay the phrase and note its time in the recording.
I type the likely phrase from memory to keep the draft moving.
I capture the clinician’s words and mark the muffled phrase for replay.
I continue typing and ask someone nearby what the phrase sounds like.

advanced.situation: A new colleague is learning stenotype capture, and missed words are delaying drafts. You are asked to coach their next practice session.

options.text: I explain the headset controls and ask them to practise a sample passage.
I pair them with a colleague and ask them to compare notes afterward.
I share my shorthand notes and let them practise on live dictation.
I demonstrate short passages, then review their capture against the audio together.

basic.situation: You review a transcribed report using a spelling and grammar checklist. A familiar medical term looks inconsistent with the surrounding sentence.

options.text: I check the term in a trusted reference and flag the inconsistency.
I leave the term as typed and finish the remaining checklist items.
I mark the term and ask the transcriber to compare it with source audio.
I replace it with the familiar term that seems to fit this sentence.

advanced.situation: You are guiding colleagues on terminology standards. Two references give different spellings for a term in a report that must be returned today.

options.text: I choose the spelling used most often in recent reports and update the draft.
I compare the references, document the preferred form, and flag the source for confirmation.
I keep the dictated spelling and add the term to the review list.
I note both spellings and ask the team to follow one reference.

basic.situation: You have finished a dictated report and must return it for physician review. One sentence appears incomplete, but the deadline is near.

options.text: I complete the sentence using details from a similar report.
I return the draft and mention the sentence in a brief note.
I hold the report until the physician is free to discuss it.
I return the draft with the incomplete sentence clearly flagged for physician review.

advanced.situation: You are helping improve report checks after several physician corrections arrive late. A draft has a discrepancy that could affect its final wording.

options.text: I send the draft with a note asking the physician to check that sentence.
I add the discrepancy to a shared list for the next review meeting.
I revise the wording from context and send the report for signature.
I log the discrepancy, return a marked draft, and track the physician’s correction.

basic.situation: You are expanding abbreviations in a dictated report. One abbreviation has more than one possible meaning in the surrounding notes.

options.text: I use the expansion most common in the clinic’s recent reports.
I check a medical reference and flag the ambiguous abbreviation for confirmation.
I expand it using the meaning that fits the sentence in context.
I leave the abbreviation and note that its meaning needs review.

advanced.situation: You are preparing an abbreviation guide for colleagues. Staff have expanded the same shorthand differently across reports, and the source context is sometimes unclear.

options.text: I include reference links and ask staff to check uncertain entries.
I publish the most frequent expansion for each abbreviation in the guide.
I list approved expansions, context clues, and cases that require confirmation.
I collect examples from recent reports and share them with the team.

basic.situation: You are entering a lab report into a patient record with assistance. Two similar patient names appear in the search results.

options.text: I compare the record identifiers with the report before entering its details.
I open both records and compare their recent lab entries.
I pause entry and ask a colleague which record seems right.
I select the name that most closely matches the report header.

advanced.situation: You are maintaining a medical records database. Staff report that x-ray and lab files are difficult to retrieve consistently across shifts.

options.text: I rename the folders using the labels I find easiest to remember.
I add a search note to the database for the most requested files.
I standardize file labels and retrieval steps, then show staff the updated process.
I ask each shift to keep a list of its preferred file names.

basic.situation: You are filing incoming patient correspondence and typing a reply. A caller asks whether a medical case has progressed.

options.text: I tell the caller what the latest notes appear to say.
I finish filing first, then check whether someone can return the call.
I take the caller’s details and pass the inquiry to the case team.
I file the letter and refer the caller to the authorised case contact.

advanced.situation: You are coordinating incoming mail, claims, and appointments. A claim query and a patient call arrive while an appointment change needs recording.

options.text: I answer the patient call and leave reminders for the other requests.
I record the appointment change and ask a colleague to take the claim query.
I clear the mail pile first and handle calls after the appointments.
I log each request, route the claim query, and update the appointment record.

basic.situation: A customer asks where to find a non-prescription item, while the phone rings with a question you cannot answer from the shelf information.

options.text: I help the customer and take the caller’s number for a pharmacist callback.
I ask a nearby colleague to handle the customer while I answer the phone.
I show the customer the item and refer the phone question to the pharmacist.
I recommend a product from memory and answer the caller without checking the shelf information.

advanced.situation: A customer is upset that an item is unavailable and asks whether a similar product will suit them. A junior colleague is listening nearby.

options.text: I ask the junior colleague to find a substitute while I check stock.
I explain the stock position and ask the pharmacist to discuss alternatives.
I acknowledge the concern, check stock, and refer suitability to the pharmacist.
I recommend the closest alternative and offer to check its shelf location.

basic.situation: You are unpacking a delivery and find a refrigerated item in a box with other merchandise. The storage label is partly smudged.
