options.text: I separate the item, check its label, and ask the pharmacist about storage.
I read the packing slip and set it aside for the pharmacist to check.
I place it with similar products and finish counting the delivery.
I write down the item code and continue with the dry goods.

advanced.situation: During an inventory check, you find a supply close to its marked expiry date and the count is lower than the database shows.

options.text: I place the item at the front so staff use it first.
I verify the count and date, separate the item, and alert the pharmacist.
I adjust the database to match my count and move on to other stock.
I report the difference and ask the next shift to check the date.

basic.situation: You are cleaning shelves from a checklist and spot a sticky spill near items customers are browsing.

options.text: I clear the area, clean the spill, and mark the checklist when finished.
I finish the shelf first and return to the spill afterward.
I wipe the visible spot and continue with the next shelf.
I place a sign nearby and ask a colleague to clean it later.

advanced.situation: You are setting a cleaning schedule for shared work areas. Colleagues report that busy periods leave shelves and equipment waiting for attention.

options.text: I set one daily cleaning time and remind staff during the morning briefing.
I assign each shift a cleaning list and review it at handover.
I schedule checks around busy periods and record who completed each area.
I ask staff to clean whenever they notice a problem during work.

basic.situation: You are restocking a shelf and notice that one item is nearly gone, while another box has not yet been opened.

options.text: I ask a colleague where the unopened box usually goes.
I put the new box in any open space on the shelf.
I refill the low item and leave the older stock at the front.
I check the shelf label, replenish the low item, and rotate existing stock.

advanced.situation: You are guiding restocking during a busy shift. Several shelves are low, and the delivery has limited quantities of two fast-moving items.

options.text: I ask colleagues to fill low shelves and report any missing items.
I check shelf labels, replenish priority gaps, and record what remains unavailable.
I fill the easiest shelves first so the delivery gets put away quickly.
I spread the limited items across shelves to make each look fuller.

basic.situation: You are processing a customer’s cash purchase at the register. The amount displayed does not match the price on the shelf label.

options.text: I pause the sale, check the displayed price, and follow the register process.
I ask a colleague to confirm the shelf price before taking payment.
I charge the displayed amount and finish the sale to keep the queue moving.
I take the cash and write the shelf price on the receipt.

advanced.situation: You are closing a register and find a small cash difference after several card and cash sales. A new aide is waiting to learn the closing steps.

options.text: I enter the expected total and show the aide the closing screen.
I record the difference and ask the next shift to review it.
I recount the drawer, compare receipts, and explain each step to the aide.
I recount the cash and ask the aide to observe the register summary.

basic.situation: You accept a prescription for processing, but the patient’s contact details are missing. The queue is growing behind them.

options.text: I ask for the missing details and check the intake entry before routing it.
I enter a familiar contact number from the patient’s earlier visit.
I set the prescription aside while serving the next person in line.
I accept the prescription and ask the patient to provide details later.

advanced.situation: You are mentoring an aide who is collecting prescription details. The patient gives an unclear address, and the prescription needs accurate intake information.

options.text: I use the address on the patient’s old record and finish intake.
I let the aide complete the other fields while I serve the queue.
I ask the patient to clarify the address, then review intake fields with the aide.
I note the address as unclear and ask the pharmacist how to proceed.

basic.situation: You are checking a dog recovering from surgery and its temperature seems higher than yesterday. The veterinarian is examining another animal.

options.text: I would check the temperature once more and ask a colleague whether it seems concerning.
I would wait for the veterinarian's next round and mention the temperature then.
I would take its temperature and pulse again, then record both readings for the veterinarian.
I would repeat the check, note the readings and change, and alert the veterinarian now.

advanced.situation: A recovering cat becomes restless and breathes unevenly after surgery. Its chart shows earlier discomfort, but no clear instruction for this combination of signs.

options.text: I would report the breathing change and restlessness to the veterinarian, with their timing and trend.
I would record the restlessness and breathing pattern for the veterinarian to review later.
I would compare the signs with its chart and tell the veterinarian during the next check.
I would recheck the cat's breathing, then share the findings with the veterinarian.

basic.situation: You are asked to give a calm dog its prescribed oral medicine while a supervisor watches. The dog turns away after the first attempt.

options.text: I would try again while holding the dog still and then update the medication chart.
I would check the prescribed method, settle the dog, and confirm the dose was swallowed before recording it.
I would hide the medicine in a small treat and record that the dose was given.
I would pause, check the prescription instructions, and ask my supervisor to observe another attempt.

advanced.situation: Two animals have medicines due close together, and a junior assistant asks you to check the schedule. One prescription was recently changed by the veterinarian.

options.text: I would ask the junior to hold both doses until the veterinarian is available.
I would check both labels against the schedule, then brief the junior on due times.
I would confirm the changed prescription with the veterinarian and explain both schedules to the junior.
I would use the older schedule because the junior has prepared those doses.

basic.situation: A nervous rabbit needs a minor examination. You are asked to help hold it while a more experienced assistant prepares the table.

options.text: I would support the rabbit gently and keep its head steady as the examination begins.
I would hold the rabbit firmly across its body so it cannot turn during the examination.
I would keep one hand near the shoulders and ask the assistant to guide my grip.
I would follow the experienced assistant's positioning cues and support the rabbit without compressing its chest.

advanced.situation: During a longer procedure, the veterinarian changes instruments while a new assistant is unsure what to pass next. The animal remains under close monitoring.

options.text: I would anticipate the veterinarian's next instrument from the procedure and coach the assistant through each handoff.
I would pass instruments as requested and let the new assistant watch from beside me.
I would organize the instruments by type and let the new assistant pass the next one.
I would ask the veterinarian to pause while the new assistant reviews the instrument tray.

basic.situation: You are filling water bowls and cleaning cages before feeding time. One animal has a diet note on its enclosure card.

options.text: I would clean the cage, refill the water, and check the diet note before feeding.
I would check the diet instructions, prepare that feed, then clean and refill its enclosure.
I would give the usual feed first, then check the enclosure card while cleaning.
I would ask a colleague what this animal usually eats before finishing the cage.

advanced.situation: A colleague is preparing meals for several animals, including one on a special diet. The written schedule is updated, but the colleague has not seen the change.

options.text: I would compare meals with the schedule, explain the change, and check the special portion together.
I would prepare the special portion myself and leave other meals unchanged for now.
I would let the familiar meals continue, then review the special diet afterward.
I would explain the updated diet and ask my colleague to follow today's schedule.

basic.situation: You finish washing instruments after an examination. A tray is needed soon, and you are still learning the clinic's sterilizing routine.

options.text: I would wash the tray, follow the sterilizing instructions, and set it aside for use.
I would ask a colleague to confirm the cycle while I prepare another tray.
I would complete the sterilizing cycle, check the indicator, and label the tray as ready.
I would rinse the tray and return it to the clean shelf to save time.

advanced.situation: You review kennel cleaning after several staff changes. The checklist is signed, but a frequently handled latch still has visible residue.

options.text: I would accept the signed checklist and schedule another general cleaning review next week.
I would clean the latch again and remind staff to check that area during rounds.
I would ask the last cleaner to repeat the kennel cleaning before the next shift.
I would reclean the latch, trace the missed step, and update the checklist at handover.

basic.situation: You are recording feeding times and observations for several animals. A note from the morning shift is hard to read.

options.text: I would copy the feeding time from yesterday and add the clear observations from today.
I would enter the readable observations and ask the morning colleague to clarify the time.
I would record confirmed observations, flag the time as unclear, and check its source.
I would leave the feeding time blank and finish the other animals' records first.

advanced.situation: A client asks what food may suit an animal with a recent diet change. The product shelf is low, and the inventory count differs from the order sheet.

options.text: I would explain the available food options, check the diet note, and reconcile stock before ordering.
I would suggest the familiar food and update the stock count after serving other clients.
I would count the shelf again and tell the client to return after stock arrives.
I would show the client the available foods and ask a veterinarian about the diet change.

basic.situation: You are drawing blood from a patient's vein using a vacuum tube. The patient looks tense as you prepare the collection.

options.text: I would ask a colleague to talk with the patient while I prepare the tube.
I would explain the draw, check the patient's readiness, and collect the sample with steady technique.
I would begin the draw while the patient is looking away from the needle.
I would explain the next step, check the vein, and collect the sample using the tube.

advanced.situation: You are coaching a colleague through a difficult venipuncture. The first attempt did not yield blood, and the patient is becoming uncomfortable.

options.text: I would review the attempt, check patient comfort, and guide a safe next step.
I would observe, then share specific feedback with my colleague after the attempt.
I would reassure the patient and coach my colleague through a revised approach.
I would take over after checking the patient's comfort and explaining the next step.

basic.situation: You have a blood tube and requisition form from a busy collection period. The patient's name matches, but the dates differ.

options.text: I would label the tube for review and place it with the next laboratory batch.
I would update the form date to match the tube and send both to the laboratory.
I would set the tube aside and ask the collection team to check the dates.
I would hold the sample, document the mismatch, and confirm the details with the collection source.

advanced.situation: A time-sensitive specimen is ready for transport, but its tracking entry has no handoff time. The laboratory is expecting it for scheduled analysis.

options.text: I would ask a colleague to record the handoff time while I arrange transport.
I would record the actual handoff time and deliver the specimen to the laboratory.
I would contact the laboratory about the delay and update the route record.
I would confirm handoff, record its actual time, and notify the laboratory during transport.

basic.situation: You are cleaning a blood-drawing tray before the next patient. A sealed pack looks intact, but its label is smudged.

options.text: I would prepare another tray and leave the smudged pack for the next shift.
I would keep the pack out of use, verify its status, and prepare a sterile set.
I would set the pack aside and ask a colleague to check its label.
I would use the pack because its seal looks intact and prepare the tray.

advanced.situation: You are reviewing blood-drawing trays after staff report inconsistent preparation. A checklist is complete, but one tray contains an item with an unclear sterile status.

options.text: I would remove that item and remind staff to check the tray before collection.
I would hold the tray, verify the item's status, and review preparation with staff.
I would leave the tray unused and ask the next shift to verify the item's status.
I would replace the item and update the checklist at the next staff briefing.

basic.situation: After a blood draw, you have used gauze and a small amount of blood-contaminated material. The disposal bins are labelled nearby.

options.text: I would sort each used material into the labelled bin before clearing the draw area.
I would follow the labels, separate contaminated materials, and secure the waste container.
I would place used gauze in the labelled clinical waste bin and close the lid.
I would check the labels and place contaminated gauze in its designated bin.

advanced.situation: A sharps container is near its fill line during a busy clinic. A colleague asks whether one more used needle will fit.

options.text: I would press the contents down gently and close the container after this needle.
I would stop using it, secure the area, and arrange replacement under clinic procedure.
I would move the container to the supply room and ask a supervisor to replace it.
I would tell the colleague to use another container and report the fill level.

basic.situation: You are entering a patient's details and specimen information into the computer. The form has a handwritten digit that is difficult to read.

options.text: I would leave the unclear field pending and enter the specimen details.
I would pause entry and ask the patient to confirm the unclear digit.
I would enter the other details first and ask the patient to clarify the digit.
I would compare the source details and confirm the digit before saving the record.

advanced.situation: A colleague notices that two patient records may have been swapped during entry. Both specimens are still in the collection area awaiting processing.

options.text: I would pause both entries and ask a senior colleague to review the possible swap.
I would pause both entries and compare each name with the collection forms.
I would flag both records and ask the colleague to compare each patient form.
I would hold both records, verify identifiers against source forms, and guide entry updates.

basic.situation: A patient asks what will happen during a routine blood draw and says they feel nervous. You are preparing the collection area.

options.text: I would describe the needle briefly and begin while the patient is looking away.
I would ask a colleague to explain the procedure while I finish preparing supplies.
I would explain the collection, invite questions, and check the patient is ready before starting.
I would explain the steps in simple terms and ask what concerns the patient most.

advanced.situation: A physician requests a time-sensitive test result, but one value appears inconsistent with the sample notes. A colleague asks you to send the result now.

options.text: I would send the value shown and add a note that the sample details may differ.
I would ask the colleague to review the value while I prepare the next sample.
I would tell the physician the result is under review and check the sample notes.
I would verify the sample notes, confirm the result, and update the physician about discrepancies.

basic.situation: You prepare picture cards for a child's language screening, but several cards are missing.

options.text: You start with the available cards and mark the missing items after screening.
You ask the pathologist whether the available cards can support a shorter screening.
You compare the protocol materials, replace missing cards, then tell the pathologist before screening.
You check the kit list and borrow matching cards from the clinic cupboard.

advanced.situation: Two assistants record different scores during a language assessment, and the client is waiting for the next section.

options.text: You combine uncertain entries using the team's usual scoring approach and flag them later.
You pause the affected section and refer uncertain scoring to the pathologist for a decision.
You pause testing, check the protocol, and coach staff to repeat the affected item consistently.
You ask each assistant to review the scoring sheet before continuing with the client.

basic.situation: A child hesitates during a sound practice exercise, and the written plan includes a picture cue.

options.text: You repeat the instruction slowly and wait for the child to try again.
You give the child the answer and continue through the remaining sound cards.
You show the picture cue and model the target sound as the plan describes.
You move to the next sound and note the hesitation for the pathologist.

advanced.situation: A client becomes tired midway through a planned language exercise, while a junior assistant asks whether to keep going.

options.text: You stop the exercise, note the response, and check with the pathologist before changing the plan.
You offer a brief pause, then resume the same exercise at its planned pace.
You shorten the remaining practice and tell the pathologist at the next review.
You ask the junior assistant to watch for fatigue while you continue the exercise.

basic.situation: After a session, you need to record how often a client used a target word during play.

options.text: You copy the previous session's count and add a note about today's game.
You enter the observed count and example in the progress note template for review.
You write that the client used the target word several times during play.
You record the game and ask the senior clinician what count to include.

advanced.situation: A documentation audit finds that several new assistants record progress with different labels for the same treatment objective.

options.text: You flag differing labels and ask the pathologist to review them at next meeting.
You share the audit findings and ask staff to use the objective names in the guide.
You replace varied labels with one familiar phrase across the client treatment records.
You align labels with established objectives and coach staff through a shared note example.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to copy a client's weekly practice counts into a chart template.

options.text: You ask your supervisor which chart colours to use before copying the counts.
You use the latest count to fill the chart's empty weekly cells.
You enter each dated count and check the chart against the source record.
You copy the counts into the chart and add the client's name and dates.

advanced.situation: Your team compares client progress across groups, but staff have compiled weekly counts using different date ranges.

options.text: You ask the team to choose a common date range for the next report.
You place each group's existing counts in separate colours on one chart.
You standardize the date range, document the measure, and remake the comparison chart.
You label each group's date range and present the counts as separate series.

basic.situation: The pathologist asks you to prepare picture cards for a session on describing everyday objects.

options.text: You reuse the previous session's cards and add a few new pictures.
You sort cards by type and check them against the session list.
You gather familiar object cards and arrange them on the table for use.
You ask the pathologist to confirm the card set after you gather it.

advanced.situation: A speech-language research project needs picture materials, and pilot sessions show that some images confuse participants.

options.text: You pause those images and ask the pathologist how to revise them.
You replace unclear pictures, then update the research team before the next pilot.
You flag confusing images and continue collection with the existing set for now.
You review confusing images with the pathologist and revise them before collection resumes.

basic.situation: A parent asks for a handout about supporting a child's speech practice at home after a clinic session.

options.text: You ask the parent to raise the question with the pathologist at the next visit.
You share the approved handout and point out the practice steps for home.
You give the parent the handout and mention that the pathologist prepared it.
You explain a home exercise from memory while the parent reads the handout.

advanced.situation: You are preparing a community session, and families ask for ways to practise speech sounds without making children feel pressured.

options.text: You demonstrate playful speech sound games and invite families to try ideas during daily routines.
You ask families to share concerns, then refer individual treatment questions to clinicians.
You use clinician-approved examples and invite questions about adapting practice at home.
You present the planned speech sound slides and share the clinic handout afterward.

basic.situation: Before a scheduled endoscopy, you are asked to check that the scope passes the unit’s routine function checks.

options.text: Power the scope on and proceed if the image appears clear.
Follow the check sequence and record each result before the room is used.
Check the scope’s light and image, then ask a coworker about the rest.
Run the listed checks and tell the nurse about any uncertain result.

advanced.situation: During checks, a scope intermittently loses image while the room is booked for a complex case and another technician asks what to do.

options.text: Repeat the check and record when the image drops for the service review.
Ask the other technician to watch the image while you finish setup.
Reconnect the cable and keep the scope assigned if the image returns.
Switch to the spare scope and note the intermittent fault for maintenance.

basic.situation: You are preparing a room for a routine endoscopy and have the procedure list and standard setup guide.

options.text: Follow the guide and ask the nurse about any unfamiliar item.
Place the scope and standard supplies, then check the procedure list.
Set out the usual scope and supplies based on yesterday’s room layout.
Arrange the listed equipment and supplies, then check the room against the guide.

advanced.situation: A complex procedure needs extra equipment, and a newly assigned technician is helping prepare the room under your direction.

options.text: Add the requested equipment and ask your colleague to check the room.
Use the standard layout and let the nurse request additional items during preparation.
Review the procedure list, add required equipment, and tell your colleague the changes.
Set up the room from the procedure requirements and walk your colleague through the layout.

basic.situation: The nurse asks you to assist with collecting a routine specimen during an endoscopy, following the unit’s standard procedure.

options.text: Ask the nurse to confirm the specimen type before you prepare supplies.
Prepare the labeled container and follow the nurse’s instructions during collection.
Confirm the container label and collection instructions before assisting the nurse.
Use the nearest container and add the patient label after collection.

advanced.situation: During a case, the physician requests two tissue specimens from different sites, and the containers have similar labels.

options.text: Place both samples together and ask the nurse to separate them later.
Match each sample to its site as collected and verify labels before storage.
Set the containers apart and label them after the procedure ends.
Keep each sample separate and confirm its site label with the nurse.

basic.situation: Before the procedure, you are asked to place a blood pressure cuff and pulse oximeter sensor with assistance.

options.text: Place the devices and tell the nurse if either reading seems unusual.
Ask the nurse to position the cuff while you attach the sensor.
Attach the cuff and sensor where they fit comfortably on the patient.
Place both devices as instructed and check that readings appear on the monitor.

advanced.situation: A high-risk patient’s oxygen reading disappears after repositioning, and the team is preparing to continue the procedure.

options.text: Tell the nurse the reading disappeared, inspect the sensor, and confirm signal recovery.
Secure the sensor again and monitor the display while setup continues.
Check the sensor connection and placement, then report whether the oxygen reading has returned.
Replace the sensor with a spare and ask the nurse to check the reading.

basic.situation: After a routine case, you are assigned to clean and disinfect the scope using its manufacturer instructions and unit procedure.

options.text: Rinse the scope, complete the required cleaning steps, and store it for the next case.
Check the scope model instructions, complete every required step, and record the disinfection cycle.
Follow the cleaning sequence and document each completed disinfection step for the unit.
Use the usual cleaning cycle and ask a coworker to verify the scope is ready.

advanced.situation: A scope’s control feels stiff after disinfection, and the schedule is tight; the maintenance team has not yet inspected it.

options.text: Record the stiff control and ask maintenance when they can inspect it.
Test the control several times and return the scope to storage.
Tag the scope for maintenance and use another unit for the next case.
Keep the scope nearby and ask the nurse to test its control before use.

basic.situation: A nurse asks you to position a patient and pass the requested instrument during a routine endoscopy.

options.text: Arrange the common instruments and ask the nurse to adjust the patient.
Help position the patient and wait for the nurse to request each instrument.
Follow the nurse’s positioning instructions and pass the requested instrument when ready.
Position the patient as usual and place several instruments within reach.

advanced.situation: During a complex case, a junior technician is unsure which supplies remain available while the physician requests another instrument.

options.text: Check inventory, guide the junior to locate the requested instrument, and assist the nurse.
Check the inventory list, then tell the junior exactly where the requested instrument is stored.
Tell the junior to search the supply room while you watch the procedure.
Ask the nurse to manage supplies while you explain the inventory list later.

basic.situation: A sealed letter is flagged during the morning mail check. You need to decide how it should be handled under the institution’s rules.

options.text: Check the current mail rule, log the item, and route it for review.
Send it onward using yesterday's practice so the queue keeps moving.
Compare the envelope with the posted rule and log the exception for review.
Hold the item and ask a colleague what usually happens before routing it.

advanced.situation: A review finds that officers handle the same recurring procedure differently, and a recent incident exposed a gap in the written guidance.

options.text: Ask experienced officers to review recurring gaps and update the draft accordingly.
Map the current steps against policy, sample recent cases, and draft targeted revisions.
Compare written procedures with actual practice and flag gaps for management review.
Replace the checklist with a simpler version based on the team's common practice.

basic.situation: During a routine round, you are asked to confirm that an assigned area is secure before the next inmate movement.

options.text: Compare the post list with the live count and flag a mismatch.
Walk the assigned area with an officer and confirm the listed doors.
Mark the patrol complete from the prior shift's note to save time.
Check the assigned post list, confirm each area, and report any gap.

advanced.situation: A high-risk transfer is delayed after a route change, while the escort team is ready to move and the receiving area is awaiting arrival.

options.text: Keep the original route and timing so the receiving area can stay prepared.
Ask the escort team which route seems quickest, then update the receiving area.
Pause departure, confirm the route change with the duty lead, and notify the receiving area.
Confirm the revised route and receiving arrangements with the duty lead before coordinating the escort.

basic.situation: An inmate slips near the dining area and says their ankle hurts. Other inmates begin gathering while you are on duty nearby.

options.text: Clear space, check the injury, provide first aid within your training, and report it.
Ask nearby staff to watch the crowd while you notify the medical post.
Keep the area clear, check the ankle, and call the medical post for help.
Help the inmate stand and return them to their unit before the meal rush.

advanced.situation: Two inmates accuse each other of taking belongings, and their argument is drawing a crowd near a busy unit corridor.

options.text: Move one inmate aside and ask nearby officers what started the argument.
Separate them safely, settle the crowd, hear each account apart, and report the dispute.
Separate the inmates, calm the crowd, and report the unresolved dispute to the duty lead.
Tell both inmates to stop and return to their activities before the corridor blocks.

basic.situation: You are helping with a scheduled inmate count when a unit officer reports that one room's tally differs from the expected number.

options.text: Ask another officer to check the room while you update the count sheet.
Use the earlier tally so the unit can resume its planned movement.
Hold movement, compare the room tally with the count sheet, and report the mismatch.
Repeat the room count with the officer, reconcile the tally, and record the result.

advanced.situation: A laundry shift is behind schedule, and the work detail has fewer officers than planned while another unit requests help with its own movement.

options.text: Send the work detail ahead so the laundry target is met before shift change.
Ask the unit for spare staff and keep the existing work schedule meanwhile.
Rework the duty plan around safe coverage, explain the revised sequence, and track the work detail.
Adjust the schedule to retain officer coverage and notify the requesting unit of the delay.

basic.situation: During a busy visit period, you hear an officer speak sharply to a visitor who is asking where to wait.

options.text: Check the interaction, remind the officer of visitor conduct expectations, and note the concern.
Mention the exchange to another officer and ask whether it seemed unusual.
Speak with the officer after visits and record what you observed.
Ask the visitor to move along so the queue keeps flowing smoothly.

advanced.situation: A performance review is due for an experienced officer whose recent shift notes show both strong inmate support and repeated missed handovers.

options.text: Rate the officer highly based on years of service and steady team support.
Ask the officer to describe the handovers and use that account in the evaluation.
Use the shift notes to rate the handovers and discuss a follow-up review date.
Compare documented examples with the role expectations, discuss both patterns, and record agreed goals.

basic.situation: You are completing an incident form after a minor unit disruption, but the times recorded by two officers do not match.

options.text: Check the original notes with both officers, reconcile the timeline, and complete the form.
Leave the time field open and ask the next shift to finish the form.
Use the earlier time so the report can be filed before shift change.
Record both times in the notes and submit the form for review.

advanced.situation: Several new officers start next week, and recent handovers show inconsistent use of the unit log during busy periods.

options.text: Reuse last year's briefing slides and ask officers to read the log guidance.
Explain the log steps at briefing and invite questions from the new officers.
Ask a senior officer to demonstrate the log process during the next handover.
Build a short log exercise from handover examples, then check each trainee's entries against the procedure.

basic.situation: An investigator brings you two witness statements that differ on the time a shop break-in occurred and asks how to proceed.

options.text: Note the different times in the case file and ask the investigator to clarify them.
Use the more detailed statement as the timeline so the report can move ahead.
Compare the statements, identify the time gap, and guide the investigator to verify it through follow-up.
Ask the investigator to check the statements again and bring back a summary.

advanced.situation: A serious assault case has conflicting accounts, a time-sensitive lead, and an investigator proposing to interview a witness before checking the case file.

options.text: Approve the interview plan so investigators can promptly secure the witness's account.
Ask the investigator to pause while you check the file and lead.
Review the file and lead, then plan interviews to protect evidence and meet procedures.
Check key file details and agree interview timing with the investigator.

basic.situation: Two officers request the same Friday off, but your draft roster has one uncovered patrol shift that day.

options.text: Keep one officer assigned and tell both staff the request decision is pending.
Approve the first request received so the roster can be published today.
Ask both officers to arrange a swap and send you the revised roster.
Check coverage needs, discuss available swaps, and update the roster with the agreed assignments.

advanced.situation: A complaint alleges that an officer shared a duty roster outside the department. The officer says it was sent to help a partner agency.

options.text: Record the complaint and ask the officer for a written explanation before deciding next steps.
Secure the relevant records, hear the officer's account, and assess the conduct against department rules.
Ask the officer to delete the message and explain the situation to the team.
Issue a formal warning based on the complaint so the matter is addressed promptly.

basic.situation: You are checking a daily incident log before filing and notice that one entry lacks the location where the call was handled.

options.text: Flag the missing location and return the entry for the reporting officer to complete.
Check source notes with the officer, verify the location, and update the log.
Ask the desk officer which location usually applies to this call type.
File the log with the location field blank to meet the deadline.

advanced.situation: A written duty order is ready for circulation, but its search instruction appears broader than the purpose described in the supporting file.

options.text: Hold circulation and refer the scope concern to the order's author for review.
Circulate the draft order so assigned officers can prepare their station teams.
Compare the order with its basis, flag scope concerns, and request authorized revisions.
Ask a colleague whether similar operations used comparable wording in their written duty orders.

basic.situation: During a vehicle check before patrol, you notice a damaged light and see that the equipment list shows the vehicle as ready.

options.text: Ask another officer to confirm the light before changing the checklist.
Update the checklist with the defect and notify the equipment desk.
Leave the vehicle marked ready because the rest of its equipment is present.
Record the defect, report the vehicle's status, and check what replacement is available.

advanced.situation: Several patrol vehicles have recurring radio faults, and a busy weekend roster is due before the equipment requisition list is finalized.

options.text: Check the roster and fault list, then send a requisition for the affected vehicles.
Request the usual radio quantity so the roster can be finalized on time.
Ask the stores team what radios remain and reserve that number for patrol.
Review the fault records, estimate weekend coverage needs, and request matching replacement radios.

basic.situation: A school group asks your station to explain a safety programme, and a court clerk separately requests an update on an officer's attendance.

options.text: Check staff availability for the school visit and forward the court request to the liaison.
Confirm the school visit details and route the court request through the assigned liaison.
Ask the school to send its request again and tell the clerk you will check.
Promise both parties a time today so they can finalize their schedules.

advanced.situation: A community group and a nearby agency both propose a weekend safety event, but their plans overlap and each expects your station to coordinate.

options.text: Ask each group to send a separate proposal for the station to consider.
Compare the proposals, identify the overlap, and suggest a joint planning meeting.
Align both groups' aims, assign roles, and confirm a shared event plan.
Accept the first proposal and tell the other group to join that schedule.

basic.situation: A new procedure changes how officers record property received at the front desk, and several staff ask what to do on their next shift.

options.text: Tell staff to keep using the old form until everyone has time to read the update.
Send the policy notice to the team and ask them to read it before shift.
Explain the changed steps with a sample entry, then check that staff can apply them.
Brief the team on the new form and answer questions before their next shift.

advanced.situation: A complaint about an officer's conduct conflicts with two witness accounts, and the team is due for a refresher on the related procedure.

options.text: Preserve accounts, assess the allegation under procedure, and plan targeted staff learning.
Schedule a general conduct lecture and close the complaint based on the conflicting accounts.
Review the accounts, document the unresolved points, and arrange a procedure refresher for staff.
Ask the officer and witnesses for brief summaries before planning the staff session.

basic.situation: You arrive at a small shop fire with smoke near the stairwell. The senior officer asks you to assign firefighters to support a rescue and hose team.

options.text: I would hold crews at the entrance while checking access and conditions.
I would assign a rescue pair inside and a hose crew outside.
I would ask firefighters to report their skills before assigning roles.
I would send a nearby crew to assess the smoke from a safe position.

advanced.situation: Two crews reach a warehouse fire with workers reported inside and flames spreading toward stored materials. You must coordinate their first moves and update the senior officer.

options.text: I would direct one crew to search and another to protect the exposed side.
I would send both crews through the nearest entrance to search together.
I would ask crews to take tasks matching their training and current positions.
I would radio the senior officer that crews are starting work.

basic.situation: During a supervised shop inspection, you find a fire exit partly blocked by stacked boxes. You need to record the issue and take suitable corrective action.

options.text: I would mark the exit as clear because the doorway remains visible.
I would note the obstruction and ask the owner to clear it during inspection.
I would mention the boxes and leave a note for the next inspection.
I would move the boxes aside and complete the inspection checklist.

advanced.situation: Your station's vehicle checks are often recorded late, leaving crews unsure which appliances are ready. You are asked to review the procedure and suggest an improvement.

options.text: I would compare the check steps with shift handovers and flag where records lag.
I would remind crews to complete the vehicle forms before leaving shift.
I would ask the senior officer to review the procedure for the station.
I would copy last month's checklist and use it for every shift.

basic.situation: Your crew's hose coupling fails a readiness check before a scheduled shift. You have the maintenance guide and must check the equipment's condition.

options.text: I would clean it, inspect it with the hose, and report its condition.
I would set it aside and brief the next crew about the fault.
I would follow the guide, document the fault, and label the coupling unavailable.
I would return it to storage and mention the failed check to supervisor.

advanced.situation: Repeated glove damage during hose work is slowing crews, and a supplier has offered a different model. You are asked to recommend equipment changes for review.

options.text: I would tell the supplier crews prefer its newer glove model.
I would trial a sample pair and collect feedback from each crew after use.
I would recommend replacing damaged gloves with the supplier's latest model.
I would compare glove damage, crew feedback, and supplier details in a written proposal.

basic.situation: At a scheduled drill, a new firefighter is unsure how to use the assigned hose line. You are helping instruct the crew during the exercise.

options.text: I would demonstrate the hose steps, then have the firefighter practise them.
I would explain the steps while the crew continues the exercise.
I would move the new firefighter to another drill station.
I would ask a more experienced firefighter to take over the drill.

advanced.situation: Several stations report uneven turnout for required drills. You are coordinating instructors and need to update senior leadership on training progress and gaps.

options.text: I would ask instructors to send attendance totals and skill updates by Friday.
I would summarize attendance, completed skills, and drill gaps for the senior officer.
I would record the highest turnout station and include its results in the progress report.
I would reschedule the lowest turnout drill and notify all affected stations.

basic.situation: After a call at a new housing block, your crew's map lacks the updated access road. You need to maintain the operational map and record.

options.text: I would verify road details with the crew and update the operational map record.
I would confirm road details with the driver and crew before updating the map.
I would note the missing road for review and tell the mapping officer.
I would copy the road from a nearby block's map without checking access.

advanced.situation: A suspected arson case involved several calls and conflicting witness accounts. You are compiling the operational report for review by the investigating officer.

options.text: I would summarize the calls and include the main witness account.
I would ask the investigating officer which details should go in the report.
I would state that the repeated calls confirm a deliberate fire.
I would separate confirmed call facts from witness accounts in the report.

basic.situation: Two firefighters request the same leave day, while your shift needs coverage for a planned community event. You are helping schedule assignments with a manager.

options.text: I would ask both firefighters about swaps and share coverage options with manager.
I would forward both leave requests to the manager and ask for guidance.
I would map required posts, check shift coverage, and offer workable options to manager.
I would approve the first request and leave the event post uncovered.

advanced.situation: A firefighter has repeated late arrivals and says a rota change caused the problem. You are asked to recommend a personnel response after reviewing performance information.

options.text: I would review attendance records and the rota, then recommend a proportionate response.
I would recommend a formal warning based on the recorded late arrivals.
I would remove the firefighter from future shifts to prevent delays.
I would ask the firefighter to explain the pattern before making a recommendation.

basic.situation: A small bin fire is spreading toward stacked cartons, and your crew lead asks you to connect the hose. What do you do?

options.text: Attach the assigned nozzle and direct the stream at the burning material.
Check the nozzle choice with the crew lead, then direct water onto the fire.
Connect the hose and open the pump while a teammate finds the nozzle.
Use the nearest nozzle and aim at the edge of the flames.

advanced.situation: A warehouse fire reaches stored chemicals, and smoke shifts toward your hose team as the pump pressure changes. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the incident lead about the smoke and pressure change by radio.
Report the change, reassess the stream position, and follow the incident lead's direction.
Shift the stream toward the warehouse wall while watching the smoke.
Keep pumping at the same point until another crew arrives.

basic.situation: At a roadside crash, a passenger is trapped behind a door while your crew prepares the rescue equipment. What do you do?

options.text: Ask a bystander whether the passenger can open the door themselves.
Stay beside the vehicle and keep the passenger calm until directed.
Try pulling the door open while your crew unloads its equipment.
Tell the crew lead about the passenger and prepare the assigned rescue gear.

advanced.situation: A flood rescue team reaches a partly submerged car, and a survivor signals from the roof as the current strengthens. What do you do?

options.text: Move closer along the bank to hear the survivor's instructions clearly.
Report the changing current and survivor position, then follow the water-rescue lead's plan.
Enter the water with a rope so the survivor can grab it.
Keep visual contact and tell the lead where the survivor is positioned.

basic.situation: After a small room fire is extinguished, you see smoke coming from behind a cabinet. What do you do?

options.text: Report the smoke and check cabinet heat with your supervisor guiding the crew.
Mark the area and tell the crew to keep equipment clear pending inspection.
Tell your supervisor about the smoke and wait for instructions before work resumes.
Ask your supervisor before moving the cabinet to check for remaining hot spots.

advanced.situation: After a major fire, a ceiling looks stable from the doorway, but water damage has exposed cracked supports inside. What do you do?

options.text: Record the cracked supports and ask the incident lead to assess re-entry.
Report cracks and keep the area restricted pending review.
Inspect from the doorway and note whether more cracks are visible.
Re-enter briefly to check whether the supports move under light pressure.

basic.situation: After a call, your breathing apparatus has soot on its straps, and the crew is returning to the station. What do you do?

options.text: Use station cleaning steps, then report damage before the set returns to service.
Wipe soot from the straps and place the breathing set with station equipment.
Ask a teammate to clean the straps while you unload the fire engine.
Hang the set to dry and leave soot for the incoming crew to address.

advanced.situation: Fire water is entering a shop with smoke-sensitive stock, while broken glass blocks the main doorway. What do you do?

options.text: Cover the nearest stock and ask the crew to clear the doorway.
Start pumping water near the doorway while another firefighter moves glass.
Move stock away from the water first and leave the glass for later.
Coordinate salvage covers and safe access with the crew before water removal begins.

basic.situation: You reach a roadside vehicle fire and see flames near the engine, with traffic still passing close by. What do you do?

options.text: Tell dispatch that a vehicle is burning near the roadside.
Wait for the crew lead to arrive before sending a radio update.
Ask a teammate to watch traffic while you assess the flames.
Radio the fire conditions and traffic hazard so dispatch can coordinate support.

advanced.situation: After a factory fire, police ask about a possible ignition point while dispatch requests your incident notes before crews separate. What do you do?

options.text: Ask a teammate to remember the ignition area for the incident report.
Suggest a likely cause to police so they can start their inquiry sooner.
Share observed facts with police and record the timeline before the crew disperses.
Write your observations and give police the details you personally saw.

basic.situation: At a community demonstration, a resident asks how to reduce fire risk from overloaded extension sockets. What do you do?

options.text: Suggest they ask an electrician to check the sockets at home.
Hand them a leaflet and return to setting up the display.
Explain safer socket use in plain language and show the demonstration setup.
Tell the resident to avoid connecting too many devices to one socket.

advanced.situation: During a building fire-safety inspection, you find a blocked exit and a smoke alarm that does not sound during a check. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the building contact about the blocked exit and failed alarm test.
Note the blocked exit and schedule another visit to check the alarm.
Ask the building contact to clear the exit and test another alarm.
Record both hazards and report them to the building contact for follow-up.

basic.situation: A primary school class visits your station. Your colleague asks you to explain one danger of playing with matches to the children.

options.text: You show a fire poster and ask the teacher to explain the risks.
You tell the class that matches can start fires and harm people.
You describe a safe example and invite children to name a trusted adult.
You let the children pass around an unlit matchbox during the talk.

advanced.situation: After observing an evacuation drill in a crowded tuition centre, you notice families were unsure where to exit. Your team asks for procedure feedback.

options.text: You mark the drill successful because everyone eventually reached outside.
You document the bottleneck and recommend clearer route marking and drill guidance.
You recommend that staff review the exit instructions with families.
You tell staff to repeat the drill so families gain confidence.

basic.situation: At a small shop fire scene, you are assigned to collect charred wood and glass fragments for the investigation team.

options.text: You photograph the area, then collect several clear fragments without noting locations.
You collect visible fragments separately and note the room where each was recovered.
You place all fragments together in one container and label the general scene location.
You bag each marked fragment separately and note its exact recovery location.

advanced.situation: Two possible ignition areas appear in a workshop fire. You are reviewing collected fragments and scene notes before sharing a probable cause assessment.

options.text: You review the scene notes and identify the more likely ignition area.
You compare both areas with the evidence and state what remains uncertain.
You choose the area with the heaviest charring as the likely origin.
You ask another investigator which area seems more convincing to them.

basic.situation: A contractor has installed new fire alarms in a small office. You are asked to observe acceptance testing with an experienced inspector.

options.text: You mark the system accepted after hearing the first alarm sound.
You follow the test sequence and record each alarm response with the inspector.
You observe the inspector test the alarms and write down any faults.
You test one alarm and note whether it sounds in the office.

advanced.situation: During an inspection, a newly installed sprinkler system has uneven coverage in one storage area. You are preparing findings for the responsible inspector.

options.text: You record the uneven spray and request the inspector's view on next steps.
You note that coverage looks uneven and suggest another water test.
You ask the installer to adjust nearby heads until the spray looks even.
You map the affected area and recommend checks against the approved system design.

basic.situation: During a routine shop inspection, boxes partly block a corridor and an extension lead crosses the floor. You are noting visible fire hazards.

options.text: You move the boxes aside and leave a note about the extension lead.
You record both hazards, their locations, and the clear actions needed.
You note the blocked corridor and ask the owner to clear it.
You record that the shop is generally tidy and finish the visit.

advanced.situation: A warehouse stores cleaning chemicals and has submitted documents for a hazardous materials permit. You are assigned to inspect its storage arrangements.

options.text: You inspect the storage area and record visible concerns in the permit file.
You endorse the permit because the chemical containers appear orderly during your visit.
You compare storage conditions with submitted details and record gaps for the permit review.
You ask the facility contact to explain the storage plan and note their response.

basic.situation: A small shop renovation plan shows a new rear room and one exit route. You are reviewing the blueprint for basic fire safety concerns.

options.text: You trace the exit route and flag any room with no clear path out.
You mark the rear room and ask the architect to clarify its exit access.
You check that the main entrance appears wide enough on the plan.
You approve the layout because the shop already has a front door.

advanced.situation: A proposed multi-storey community centre has several halls and staircases. You are asked to review its draft fire exit plan for route clarity.

options.text: You check the main hall route and assume the other rooms follow it.
You ask the designer to explain how visitors will find the staircases.
You trace routes from each hall to exits and flag confusing stair connections.
You review the marked exits and note any route that seems unclear.

basic.situation: After a small shop fire, you are assigned to photograph damage and evidence before the investigation team clears the area.

options.text: You photograph the overall scene and close views with clear location notes.
You move loose debris aside so the damaged area is easier to photograph.
You take close photographs of the most unusual damaged items.
You photograph the damaged counter and note the shop name and room.

advanced.situation: You are preparing to testify about a fire investigation, and counsel asks you to explain how a collected fragment was handled.

options.text: You explain the usual handling process used by your investigation team.
You review your records and describe the handling steps you personally observed.
You describe the recorded handover and identify any step you did not observe.
You say the fragment stayed secure because the team followed its routine.

basic.situation: At a campsite, you see a camper's stove beside dry leaves. Your supervisor is nearby while you check compliance with forest use rules.

options.text: Tell campers to leave the site because their stove breaks campsite rules.
Explain the fire risk, ask them to clear the stove area, and check again.
Check posted campsite rules, document the concern, and brief the supervising inspector.
Ask campers to shift their stove away from dry leaves, then note it.

advanced.situation: A logging tract has dry waste near fuel storage, and inspectors report inconsistent checks. You are asked to develop prevention standards and train them.

options.text: Create a shared checklist for waste, fuel separation, and records; train inspectors with site examples.
Set hazard criteria for waste and fuel storage, then share them at briefing.
Remind teams to inspect waste and fuel storage during every site visit.
Collect current checks from inspectors and combine useful practices into shared guidance.

basic.situation: During a guided patrol, you spot a thin smoke plume beyond a ridge. Your assigned route includes a map and known landmarks.

options.text: Continue along the route and check for smoke again at the next lookout.
Ask your guide whether the plume could be cooking smoke before recording it.
Mark the ridge on your map and report the smoke to the patrol lead.
Use a known landmark to mark the smoke's direction on the map, then report it.

advanced.situation: Forecast winds may shift across a dry logging tract, while smoke sightings cluster near one ridge. You must interpret conditions and adjust patrol routes.

options.text: Use wind forecasts and smoke reports to shift patrols toward the ridge and exposed slopes.
Review the forecast and recent sightings, then add a patrol near the ridge.
Keep the existing route and ask patrol teams to report any new smoke.
Move one patrol to the ridge after checking wind direction with the team.

basic.situation: At the patrol base, you log a warm afternoon and steady wind. The daily record asks for temperature, wind direction, and observations.

options.text: Enter the temperature and wind direction, then leave the weather notes for later.
Estimate the wind speed from nearby trees and enter it as measured data.
Record the observed temperature, wind direction, and time in the daily log.
Log temperature, wind direction, time, and steady conditions during your observation.

advanced.situation: Several patrols report shifting winds, low humidity, and scattered smoke. You are compiling meteorological data for fire prediction and need consistent records.

options.text: Group readings by patrol and note where weather reports differ or lack detail.
Ask patrols to resend unclear readings before drafting the report for the base.
Combine patrol notes and use common readings to fill gaps in the summary.
Standardize units and times, flag gaps, and summarize wind, humidity, smoke trends.

basic.situation: A small grass fire reaches the edge of your line. The crew lead assigns you to help direct two crew members with hand tools.

options.text: Ask the crew lead where to place the second person before starting work.
Direct both crew members to clear a safe approach and use shovels as briefed.
Check the line, group crew, and direct shovel work from a safe position.
Send one person ahead to cut a shortcut through dry grass toward the flames.

advanced.situation: A wind shift pushes a fire toward a logging track, and two crews are working nearby. You are directing their fireline work as conditions change.

options.text: Have both crews continue their sections while you watch the fire edge.
Move the nearer crew toward the track and ask the other to stand by.
Move crews toward the track, reinforce the line, and report shifts and positions.
Tell crews to pause, check their positions, and report the shift to the lead.

basic.situation: Before a patrol, you count hoses, shovels, and extinguishers against the equipment checklist. One extinguisher is missing from its assigned kit.

options.text: Note the missing item on the checklist and continue preparing the other tools.
Mark the extinguisher missing and tell the patrol lead before departure.
Recount the kit, log the missing extinguisher, and ask about replacement.
Borrow an extinguisher from another kit and leave the checklist unchanged.

advanced.situation: A pump fails during inspection, and two hose couplings are worn before the dry season. You are coordinating repairs and equipment requests for the unit.

options.text: Set the pump aside and ask the storekeeper whether spare couplings are available.
Ask crews to keep using the pump while maintenance checks it next month.
Tag the pump, log worn couplings, and request service and replacement estimates.
Log the defects and request the pump be checked by the maintenance team.

basic.situation: A radio message reports a fallen tree blocking the recreation entrance during a fire patrol. You are relaying the location and hazard to crew members.

options.text: Tell nearby crew members there is a problem near the recreation area.
Ask another patrol member to relay the message while you continue walking.
Relay the blockage and location, then confirm crew receipt.
Pass on the tree blockage and entrance location over the radio.

advanced.situation: Dry conditions prompt temporary access restrictions in a recreation area, while visitors arrive at two trailheads. You are helping administer the restriction.

options.text: Post a closure notice at the main trailhead and answer questions there.
Use the approved notice at both trailheads and direct questions to the posted contact.
Use notices at both trailheads, explain risk, and direct visitors to open areas.
Tell visitors the area is closed and ask them to choose another destination.

basic.situation: During a hearing, a visitor keeps speaking over the proceedings. You are assigned to maintain courtroom order and can see the person is upset.

options.text: Tell the visitor to leave the courtroom and return after the hearing.
Raise your voice so the visitor stops talking over the hearing.
Give a calm warning, explain the courtroom rule, and watch whether the disruption stops.
Warn the visitor about speaking during proceedings and ask them to lower their voice.

advanced.situation: A family member approaches the jury rail while a juror looks toward them. You are helping manage a tense courtroom during trial.

options.text: Stand beside the rail and remind the visitor to respect courtroom boundaries.
Direct the visitor away from the rail and notify the lead bailiff.
Ask the visitor to sit away from the jury rail while staff assist.
Alert the judge's staff, shield the jury rail, and guide the visitor away.

basic.situation: At the courthouse entrance, an x-ray image shows a metal object in a visitor's bag. You are operating the screening lane under the usual procedure.

options.text: Ask the visitor to place the item in the tray for rescanning.
Follow lane procedure, request a bag check, and alert the security lead.
Ask the visitor to open the bag beside the machine for inspection.
Allow passage after a second scan clears the image under procedure.

advanced.situation: A new staff member is unsure how to respond when the magnetometer alarms and the x-ray lane is backing up. You are overseeing screening.

options.text: Take over alarm checks and assign the new staff member queue management.
Wave visitors through while reviewing bag images to reduce the queue.
Pause the lane, coach alarm steps, and direct visitors to alternate screening.
Have the new staff member observe your next checks before resuming screening.

basic.situation: A sequestered jury is staying at a hotel, and a guest asks which floor they are on. You are assigned to guard the lodging.

options.text: Direct the guest to hotel reception for questions about the jury's stay.
Tell the guest the floor but ask them to keep the information private.
Say you cannot discuss jury arrangements and return to your assigned post.
Decline to share the floor and alert the lead about the inquiry.

advanced.situation: A high-profile jury has received a delivery addressed to a juror, while reporters gather near the hotel entrance. You are guarding the lodging.

options.text: Decline the delivery and ask reporters to clear the hotel entrance area.
Ask hotel staff to secure the package while you address reporters outside.
Tell reporters the jury is unavailable, then leave the package at reception.
Protect jury privacy, report both contacts, and coordinate access checks with hotel staff.

basic.situation: You are escorting a prisoner from the courthouse holding area to a hearing room with an experienced bailiff nearby. The corridor is busy.

options.text: Walk ahead to open the hearing room while the prisoner follows behind.
Keep the escort route clear and maintain custody while walking beside the prisoner.
Ask the nearby bailiff to manage the corridor while you escort the prisoner.
Coordinate with the nearby bailiff and escort the prisoner through the clear corridor.

advanced.situation: A prisoner being escorted to court becomes agitated when a lift stops between floors. You are responsible for maintaining custody during the transfer.

options.text: Keep the prisoner beside you and wait for help before leaving the lift.
Tell the prisoner to stay with you while you contact control and await instructions.
Stay beside the prisoner, speak calmly, and report the stalled lift to control.
Let the prisoner leave first when doors open, then follow them out.

basic.situation: A visitor asks where to submit a form for a hearing. You know the court office location but are unsure which counter handles that form.

options.text: Walk with the visitor to the office directory and show the listed counter information.
Check the office directory with the visitor and point out the listed route.
Point out the court office and suggest asking the counter staff for guidance.
Offer the counter number you believe handles hearing forms, with a caveat.

advanced.situation: Several visitors ask about different court offices while the judge is due to enter. You are responsible for directions and the entrance announcement.

options.text: Announce the judge's entrance as assigned, then route visitors using the office directory.
Continue helping visitors and announce the judge when the entrance is clear.
Announce the judge's entrance, then direct visitors to nearby staff for help with offices.
Keep directing visitors and ask another bailiff to announce the judge's entrance.

basic.situation: During a hearing, a sealed exhibit arrives for the courtroom. You are assigned to screen and handle it under the court's established procedure.

options.text: Set the exhibit with hearing materials until the clerk requests it.
Compare its label with the hearing list and ask the lead about any mismatch.
Check the exhibit label and seal against the hearing list before secure placement.
Inspect the seal and ask the clerk where the exhibit belongs.

advanced.situation: Two exhibits have similar labels, and one seal appears disturbed before the hearing begins. You are handling them under courtroom procedure.

options.text: Ask the clerk which exhibit is expected, then keep both secured beside the bench.
Hold both exhibits aside and tell the lead one seal appears disturbed.
Use the clearer label and mention the seal concern to the lead.
Separate both exhibits, preserve labels, and report the disturbed seal to the lead.

basic.situation: You inspect incoming letters during a busy shift and notice one envelope has a cut seam and an unusual powder inside.

options.text: Ask a nearby officer to look at the seam before you continue screening.
Check the envelope exterior, then pass it along with the mail batch.
Set the letter aside, note the finding, and alert the supervising officer.
Open the envelope further and tip the powder onto the inspection table.

advanced.situation: During rounds, you find a gate latch that catches inconsistently, and the maintenance log shows two recent reports of the same fault.

options.text: Mark the fault in the log and send maintenance a repair request.
Recommend a temporary post and repair priority based on the repeated latch failures.
Try the latch several times, then record that it still feels loose.
Adjust the latch yourself so the next round can use the gate normally.

basic.situation: You are asked to escort a prisoner to the visiting room while meal trays arrive for the housing unit.

options.text: Take the trays along and deliver them after reaching the visiting room.
Ask another officer to watch the meal trays while you escort the prisoner.
Leave the trays at the unit entrance and take the prisoner upstairs.
Confirm the escort destination, maintain observation, and resume meal service afterward.

advanced.situation: A transport to a clinic is delayed, and a prisoner due for prescribed medication reports feeling unwell during the wait.

options.text: Wait for the transport slot and ask the prisoner to describe the symptoms later.
Keep the prisoner observed, contact clinical staff, and follow their medication instructions.
Call the clinic for advice and continue transport once they respond.
Give the scheduled dose from the labelled pack and note the delay.

basic.situation: You are helping with a housing-unit head count when one prisoner is not visible in the common area.

options.text: Ask your partner to check the cells while you recount the common area.
Wait a few minutes because the prisoner may return from another area.
Check assigned locations and reconcile the count with your partner before reporting.
Count the visible prisoners again and enter the expected total in the log.

advanced.situation: Two work assignments overlap with a counseling appointment, leaving one unit short of its usual cleaning detail for the afternoon.

options.text: Keep the existing roster and ask the cleaner to skip the appointment.
Ask the unit to decide who should miss work for the appointment.
Rebalance duties around the appointment and confirm coverage for essential unit tasks.
Move the cleaning detail later and tell the unit about the revised timing.

basic.situation: During a supervised cell search, you find an unlisted metal tool beneath a mattress while the prisoner watches nearby.

options.text: Pause the search, secure the tool, and follow the supervisor's evidence procedure.
Show the tool to the prisoner and ask who brought it into the cell.
Return the tool to the mattress and finish searching the other cells first.
Keep the tool in view and ask your supervisor how to document it.

advanced.situation: Two prisoners begin shoving near a crowded dining area, and one officer beside you is new to responding to physical disputes.

options.text: Push between them and restrain the nearest prisoner before assessing the scene.
Tell the new officer to separate them while you clear the dining area.
Call for support and direct nearby prisoners away from the confrontation.
Create space, use calm directions, and coordinate a clear role with the nearby officer.

basic.situation: After a brief housing-unit disturbance, you enter the daily log and notice the prisoner number on your notes is unclear.

options.text: Verify the identification against the authorized record, then enter the incident details.
Enter the name from memory and add a note that it needs checking.
Record the disturbance details and leave the identification field for review.
Use the most likely prisoner number and complete the entry before shift change.

advanced.situation: You review daily logs before handover and find two entries describing the same disturbance with different times and missing officer initials.

options.text: Choose the earlier time and add initials from the duty roster.
Keep both entries and mention the mismatch during the verbal handover.
Compare source notes, reconcile the timeline with both officers, and record the correction trail.
Flag both entries for the supervisor and keep the original versions intact.

basic.situation: A visitor arrives with a parcel for a prisoner and says an officer approved it during a phone call yesterday.

options.text: Check the visitor authorization and parcel rules before allowing the item inside.
Look at the parcel label and let the visitor explain what it contains.
Accept the parcel at the desk and tell the prisoner it has arrived.
Ask the visitor to wait while you check the approval with the duty desk.

advanced.situation: A prisoner asks for help after a family visit is cancelled, saying the change may affect an important personal matter.

options.text: Promise to restore the visit and tell the family the schedule will change.
Tell the prisoner to raise the matter during the next scheduled visit.
Listen privately, clarify the request, and connect the prisoner with the appropriate support channel.
Explain the available request process and ask what support the prisoner needs today.

basic.situation: You arrive first at a shop break-in scene, where several bystanders are near the rear entrance and a witness is preparing to leave.

options.text: Rope off the rear entrance and ask bystanders to stay near the shopfront.
Let the witness leave after taking a quick verbal account of events.
Set a clear perimeter, keep the witness separate, and note who enters the scene.
Ask the witness to wait nearby while you inspect the rear entrance.

advanced.situation: You are coordinating an outdoor search at dusk, with several officers available and a narrow lane that has poor lighting.

options.text: Divide mapped areas among officers, arrange safe lighting, and record each search boundary.
Start the search in the dark lane before the remaining officers arrive.
Ask each officer to search wherever they see useful signs first.
Assign the lane to one officer and ask others to search nearby yards.

basic.situation: You secure a deceased person at a roadside scene while curious onlookers approach before the medical examiner arrives.

options.text: Move the body behind the patrol vehicle to reduce public attention.
Maintain a respectful boundary and record any scene contact while awaiting the examiner.
Ask an officer to hold the onlookers back while you watch the body.
Cover the body with a nearby cloth and keep people several steps away.

advanced.situation: You find a small glass fragment during a search, and the evidence kit has containers for several different item types.

options.text: Pick it up with gloved hands and place it in the nearest clean container.
Place the fragment in a shared bag with nearby debris for faster transport.
Mark the location and ask the evidence lead which container to use.
Photograph its location, handle it with suitable protection, and package it separately.

basic.situation: At a vehicle collision scene, you notice a tyre mark beside a damaged kerb before the area becomes crowded.

options.text: Mark the location and photograph it from the kerb and road sides.
Take several photographs and note which vehicle appears closest to the mark.
Photograph the mark with a scale, note its position, and take measurements.
Photograph the mark after placing a marker directly across its clearest section.

advanced.situation: Your investigation report is due for a command review, but two witness times differ and one photograph has no location note.

options.text: Check source notes, clarify the time difference, and link each image to its location.
Leave the time unclear and attach the photograph with the other scene images.
Use the earlier witness time and submit the report before the review deadline.
Describe both reported times and flag the unlocated photograph for review.

basic.situation: A shop worker saw a suspect leave and is willing to give a statement, but the closing shift is starting soon.

options.text: Ask the worker to send a short summary by message after closing.
Tell the worker to leave because patrol already has the basic details.
Write down the main points and ask the worker to sign your notes.
Record the worker's account, clarify the sequence, and confirm the recording is saved.

advanced.situation: A complaint alleges repeated threats, but the initial account gives no dates, locations, or names of people who may have heard them.

options.text: Ask the complainant for dates and names, then note the answers for follow-up.
Search for general background on the accused before clarifying the complaint.
Identify the missing details and seek statements or records that can test each allegation.
Treat the complaint as confirmed and prepare a summary for the case file.

basic.situation: A suspect's file contains two possible addresses, and you have authorized access to relevant agency records for identification checks.

options.text: Compare authorized records, note source dates, and report which address needs confirmation.
Search all available files for the suspect's family and likely contacts.
Use the newest-looking address and update the case file as confirmed.
Check the agency record and ask patrol to confirm the listed address.

advanced.situation: A series of similar break-ins spans several districts, and your initial reports suggest the same vehicle may appear at different times.

options.text: Compare vehicle details across reports and suggest which leads need follow-up first.
Map the reported links, identify gaps, and propose focused steps with a workable sequence.
Treat every break-in as one case and circulate the vehicle description widely.
Ask each district to continue its usual checks and share updates later.

basic.situation: A witness reports a credible threat at the station, and the responding patrol needs support while you are nearby.

options.text: Send command a brief message that a serious threat is unfolding at the station.
Tell command the station location, threat details, and support needed for the witness.
Call command and report the threat, then stay available for questions.
Wait until you have the witness's full statement before contacting command.

advanced.situation: A neighbouring agency asks about a case detail that may affect a joint search, while your office has not confirmed what can be shared.

options.text: Confirm channel and scope with your case lead before exchanging relevant case details.
Ask what detail they need, check scope with your case lead, then send a response.
Share the search location verbally and arrange another call after the search.
Forward the full case folder so the other agency can prepare quickly.

basic.situation: You have been asked to package a recovered item for storage, and a colleague is waiting to use the bench.

options.text: I would place the item in a clean bag, label it, and log storage.
I would use the approved packaging, seal it, and record each transfer in the log.
I would confirm the item identifier, package it as directed, and log its sealed location.
I would use one bag for similar items and note their labels in the log.

advanced.situation: A sealed exhibit is due at court, but its identifier differs from the submission list. You are overseeing the handover.

options.text: I would send the sealed exhibit with the list and flag the mismatch in a note.
I would amend the seal label to match the list and meet the court deadline.
I would compare the seal and log, preserve the discrepancy, and reconcile the records before submission.
I would hold the handover, document the mismatch, and ask the evidence officer to resolve it.

basic.situation: You receive two rolls of film and several prints from an accident scene. Your supervisor is nearby but occupied.
