options.text: I would develop each roll separately, label the prints, and note the case number.
I would process both rolls together to save time, then label the clearest prints.
I would check the film type, process it, and compare each print with its source.
I would sort the materials by case, check the film type, and process each roll separately.

advanced.situation: At a busy scene, two new colleagues are ready to process evidence while several areas remain unexamined. You are leading the technical work.

options.text: I would set a processing sequence, demonstrate the protective steps, and check each colleague's notes.
I would take the first area, let each colleague choose another, and compare findings afterward.
I would divide the areas among the colleagues and check their notes later.
I would review the scene plan with the team and assign areas by experience.

basic.situation: You are called to explain a fingerprint exhibit in court, and your supervisor has offered to guide your preparation.

options.text: I would compare the exhibit record and prepare an account of each handling step.
I would review exhibit notes and rehearse its handling with my supervisor.
I would arrange the exhibit and read my report aloud before the hearing.
I would rely on memory and describe the print from the witness box.

advanced.situation: A legal team asks you to coordinate scene findings from several officers before a hearing, and one report conflicts with the others.

options.text: I would circulate the majority account and ask the officer to clarify the discrepancy.
I would map each finding to its source and share the unresolved conflict with the team.
I would ask the reporting officers to discuss the difference and summarize their replies.
I would send the reports together and flag the conflict for the legal team.

basic.situation: You are asked to lift a latent fingerprint from a glass door, and the area is still accessible to staff.

options.text: I would restrict access, select a marked area, and lift the print as instructed.
I would photograph the selected print, dust it gently, and lift it onto a labeled backing.
I would dust the whole door with a broad brush, then lift the clearest print.
I would dust the likely contact area lightly and label the lift for the case.

advanced.situation: Your team is setting a search approach for a warehouse linked to several cases, where fibers and shoe impressions may be hard to distinguish.

options.text: I would list likely fibers and impressions and let the team search those areas first.
I would draft shared search criteria, mark likely trace areas, and invite technical review.
I would ask each searcher to use the method they know from earlier cases.
I would review the case notes and assign search zones based on each person's experience.

basic.situation: A visitor needs their fingerprints taken for a routine record, and you have step-by-step guidance available.

options.text: I would follow the print sequence, roll each finger separately, and check every impression.
I would press the visitor's fingers onto the card together to finish quickly.
I would roll each finger carefully, check the impressions, and label the record.
I would use the guide to take each print and file the card for review.

advanced.situation: You are documenting a multi-room scene, and a colleague is preparing a hand-drawn sketch from your measurements.

options.text: I would let the colleague finish the sketch and add labels during the report.
I would compare the sketch with my measurements and mark any differences for correction.
I would check room measurements, build a labeled digital diagram, and guide the colleague.
I would draw the key rooms digitally and ask the colleague to add missing details.

basic.situation: You are photographing a minor accident scene for the evidence record, and your report draft is due before your shift ends.

options.text: I would photograph the main damage and attach the images to a brief report.
I would capture overall and detail views, label locations, and match them to notes.
I would photograph the damaged area and describe the scene from memory in my report.
I would take overall and detail photographs, then note their sequence in the report.

advanced.situation: During an evidence-record review, you find repeated gaps in transfer entries and are due to lead a short team training.

options.text: I would list the missing fields and remind staff to complete them in future.
I would amend the entries from memory and cover the log format during training.
I would sample records, note gaps, and train staff with a transfer example.
I would review the affected logs and ask the team to discuss common omissions.

basic.situation: A senior analyst asks you to review a local incident summary, but several dates and locations are missing.

options.text: I would separate facts from gaps and list records that may clarify them.
I would chart recorded incidents and mark breaks in the timeline for review.
I would flag missing dates and locations, then ask which records to check.
I would use similar nearby incidents to fill gaps in the summary.

advanced.situation: Recent reports show a possible shift in gang activity, and managers want a forecast before allocating patrol attention.

options.text: I would compare earlier activity with recent reports and share a cautious forecast.
I would extend the latest trend forward and brief managers on the likely shift.
I would compare time periods and source quality, then present scenarios with confidence limits.
I would call the shift certain and recommend patrol focus around the newest reports.

basic.situation: You are asked to gather public-record details about a property linked to an open inquiry, with a supervisor available for guidance.

options.text: I would search public records, save the relevant entries, and note their dates.
I would use an old address list and add likely matches to the inquiry file.
I would record the public source, access date, and exact details found for review.
I would gather the names and addresses from the first useful public pages.

advanced.situation: A known address appears in a new intelligence note, and you must check it against independent information before briefing your team.

options.text: I would treat the repeated address as confirmed and add it to the briefing.
I would compare the address with a public directory and a recent field note.
I would trace each source's origin, compare independent records, and label any unresolved conflict.
I would confirm the address with two separate databases and note the matching fields.

basic.situation: You are assigned to operate a fixed observation camera during a scheduled shift, with a colleague nearby to instruct you.

options.text: I would keep the camera on the entrance and note visible activity for review.
I would change the camera settings until the picture looks clearer and save the clips.
I would pan across the area and save useful footage for the shift report.
I would follow the camera instructions, check the view, and log any equipment issue.

advanced.situation: Your unit is drafting a technical proposal concerning foreign radio transmissions, and you have been asked to prepare an initial plan for review.

options.text: I would list likely equipment and note the foreign channels mentioned in the request.
I would start monitoring likely frequencies and add useful transmissions to the proposal.
I would describe the target frequencies and draft a timetable for technical review.
I would prepare a plan with the purpose, scope, constraints, and review points for approval.

basic.situation: A mentor asks you to chart links among several suspects using an incident list, but some names appear in more than one event.

options.text: I would connect every repeated name and label the chart with the incident dates.
I would group the suspects by their most frequent co-appearance in the list.
I would separate confirmed links from shared names and cite each event on the chart.
I would draw the clearest connections and ask my mentor to check the chart later.

advanced.situation: Several records suggest two organizations may share members, while asset links point through relatives and businesses. You are preparing a criminal profile.

options.text: I would map each record to a person or asset and mark indirect links separately.
I would connect the organizations through the closest relative and list the shared assets.
I would summarize the common names and assets and describe the likely connection.
I would compare membership records and prepare a profile with source notes.

basic.situation: You receive a set of incident figures and must draft a short written report for an analyst to review.

options.text: I would summarize the figures in a paragraph and attach the supplied table.
I would round the figures to make the trend easier to explain in prose.
I would state the time period, cite the figures, and separate findings from interpretation.
I would write the main trend and include the figures that support it.

advanced.situation: A briefing team asks you to develop a defensive response outline from intelligence about possible coordinated attacks on public facilities.

options.text: I would summarize the threat indicators and outline defensive options for the team.
I would describe the most alarming scenario and recommend a broad security posture.
I would list likely targets and suggest moving patrols toward the busiest sites.
I would connect each threat scenario to evidence, confidence, and response options for planners.

basic.situation: You are taking notes while a witness describes a meeting relevant to an inquiry, and your supervisor is observing the interview.

options.text: I would summarize the main points and let the witness confirm my notes afterward.
I would capture the names and key events and review the notes with my supervisor.
I would write the account in polished sentences while the witness continues speaking.
I would record the sequence, distinguish direct quotes from summaries, and flag unclear details.

advanced.situation: A foreign-language phrase appears repeatedly in intelligence material, and your team asks you to help interpret its significance while building language skills.

options.text: I would check a general dictionary and add the closest meaning to the notes.
I would study the language and note possible meanings for the analyst to compare.
I would translate it from similar phrases I have seen and brief the likely meaning.
I would preserve the phrase, study its language context, and seek qualified review of a draft translation.

basic.situation: During a routine foot patrol, you see fresh bait and a small net beside a stream in an assigned area. What do you do?

options.text: Secure the area, document the gear, and radio dispatch for patrol guidance.
Photograph the net and ask a nearby visitor whether it belongs there.
Leave the net in place and finish the route before reporting it.
Record the location and signs, then check the bank along your route.

advanced.situation: On a joint patrol, a shop near a protected area has several wildlife products on display, and staff give conflicting explanations about their source.

options.text: Ask the shop staff for purchase records and note their explanations.
Coordinate a joint inspection, document each item, and compare records with permits.
Finish the patrol route and mention the display at the next briefing.
Photograph the display and ask another officer to check the shop later.

basic.situation: A farmer reports that animals damaged a vegetable plot overnight and asks whether the damage came from protected wildlife.

options.text: Tell the farmer to repair the fence and close the report.
Record the damage, inspect tracks, and compare signs before advising the farmer.
Inspect the plot, photograph tracks, and record the farmer's account.
Ask the farmer which animal they suspect and note that answer.

advanced.situation: A patrol finds discoloured water and damaged vegetation downstream from a farm; the source is unclear and nearby residents rely on the stream.

options.text: Photograph the water and ask residents when they first noticed changes.
Tell residents to avoid the stream and return after the next patrol.
Ask the farm to check its drains and record its response.
Map affected areas, document water conditions, and trace possible sources before advising prevention.

basic.situation: You find a person fishing in a posted restricted area and see a rod and catch beside them.

options.text: Explain the restriction, document the catch, and file a clear report for review.
Give a verbal warning and write down the person's name.
Let the person keep the catch and leave before recording details.
Explain the restriction, record details, and prepare a violation report.

advanced.situation: After a suspected illegal hunt, you locate a vehicle, equipment, and several witnesses; your unit's procedure requires an evidence log for any seizure.

options.text: Follow seizure procedure, log each item, and record custody and witness details.
Take the equipment to the station and complete its log later.
Photograph the equipment and list witnesses for the case file.
Ask a witness to hold the equipment while you speak with others.

basic.situation: A trail crew asks you how to keep visitors from trampling a patch of native seedlings beside a busy reserve path.

options.text: Leave the path open and mention the seedlings at the next meeting.
Mark the patch and ask the crew to remind visitors nearby.
Ask the crew to put temporary tape around the seedlings.
Mark a clear buffer and place a simple sign with the crew's help.

advanced.situation: Recent patrol records show repeated crop damage near a reserve, while residents report sightings of the same wildlife along two boundary villages.

options.text: Summarise patrol records and ask residents to share dates and locations of further sightings.
Suggest warning signs near affected farms and record whether reported damage changes.
Compare damage and sighting patterns, then propose a targeted management revision for review.
Recommend limited hunting access near both villages to address recurring wildlife sightings.

basic.situation: A family at a reserve entrance asks whether they can feed macaques and where to find the marked river trail.

options.text: Tell them to follow the river and decide about feeding themselves.
Show the marked route and explain safe wildlife viewing and feeding rules.
Point out the trail and explain why feeding wildlife can cause problems.
Hand them a trail leaflet and point toward the river.

advanced.situation: A local civic group asks you to explain why proposed wildlife rules could affect visitors and nearby villages, and a reporter is attending.

options.text: Share a general conservation leaflet and invite the group to discuss it.
Tell the reporter the rules will solve the conflict across the reserve.
Describe the proposed rules, invite specific questions, and note how residents can submit feedback.
Explain the rules' aims, likely trade-offs, and where official updates are available.

basic.situation: During a search for a missing visitor, dispatch asks you to check a marked trail junction while other responders cover nearby paths.

options.text: Check the junction and radio dispatch with your location and findings.
Search beyond the marked area before telling dispatch where you went.
Confirm your search area with dispatch, check the junction, and report results.
Wait at the junction until another responder arrives to search with you.

advanced.situation: You compare this season's hunter bag counts with last season's records and notice fewer animals reported in two heavily used zones.

options.text: Recommend increasing the bag limit across all zones from these counts.
Check count coverage and zone effort, then assess whether controls need adjustment.
Compare the totals and ask hunters whether they saw fewer animals.
Summarise the counts and propose reviewing both zones after checking next season's patrol coverage.

basic.situation: A driver reports a car blocking a marked loading bay, but the plate is partly obscured from your position.

options.text: Call for a tow using the visible plate characters and bay location.
Recheck the plate safely, send dispatch the full details, and confirm the vehicle.
Radio dispatch with the location and ask whether the plate is on record.
Ask the driver to move while you make a note of the bay.

advanced.situation: Dispatch confirms a vehicle is eligible for towing, but two similar cars are parked near the same junction and a tow truck is waiting.

options.text: Ask dispatch to repeat the request while the driver waits nearby.
Read back the plate and position, then confirm the truck has that car.
Tow only after matching the complete plate to the dispatch request.
Tell the driver to verify the full plate and location before towing.

basic.situation: You find a car parked across a driveway and need to issue a citation while your handheld computer has a low battery.

options.text: Record the full plate and location, then use the backup citation process.
Write down the plate and location, then complete the citation later.
Ask a nearby colleague to lend a charger before recording the details.
Use the last battery and submit a citation with the plate you can read.

advanced.situation: A temporary colleague is learning citations during a busy shift and asks whether a partly obscured plate is enough to issue a notice.

options.text: Show the colleague a completed citation and ask them to follow its format.
Tell the colleague to enter the closest plate and keep the queue moving.
Ask them to pause citations until a senior colleague is free.
Demonstrate checking the plate, recording location details, and using the uncertain-identity procedure.

basic.situation: A driver disputes a parking notice, saying the registration shown on your handheld computer does not match their car's plate.

options.text: Compare the plate with the retrieved record, document the mismatch, and route the complaint.
Take the driver's details and ask them to return with their documents.
Tell the driver the notice stands because the handheld shows that registration.
Recheck the plate and retrieve the vehicle record again before replying.

advanced.situation: A driver contests a citation, and your registration lookup shows a different vehicle description while the appeal deadline is near.

options.text: Send the complaint to the review team with the lookup details.
Record the mismatch and send the notice and lookup details to the review team.
Ask the driver to email a photo before you route the complaint.
Close the complaint because the registration system lists the cited plate.

basic.situation: While patrolling on foot, you find a car parked in a signed no-parking area near a busy community hall.

options.text: Issue a notice using the nearest sign and leave for the next street.
Check the sign and plate, then record the violation from the footpath.
Ask a nearby resident about parking patterns, then check the posted restrictions.
Check the sign, vehicle position, and access path before recording the violation.

advanced.situation: During a vehicle patrol, you see faded lane markings and a missing temporary sign near roadworks where cars are merging into one lane.

options.text: Note the roadworks and report the missing sign after your patrol.
Place your vehicle beside the merge and wave cars through the gap.
Photograph the faded lines and ask a roadworks crew member about the sign.
Report the missing sign and marking promptly, then follow local traffic safety procedures.

basic.situation: At the end of a shift, you notice your parking activity log is missing the locations for several citations issued during a street event.

options.text: Match each citation to field notes and mark any unresolved location gaps clearly.
Review your citation notes and fill in the locations you can verify.
Ask a coworker to remember where the missing citations were issued.
Copy the event street address into every missing location field.

advanced.situation: A community event needs a temporary street closure, but the planned barricades leave a narrow gap beside a busy pedestrian crossing.

options.text: Set the barricades as planned and ask pedestrians to use the narrow gap with care.
Move the barricades clear of the crossing to keep pedestrian access open.
Ask event staff to watch the gap while you place temporary signs.
Adjust barricades to clear the crossing and guide vehicles through a visible route.

basic.situation: A visitor asks where to find public parking near the market and whether a nearby curb allows parking during peak hours.

options.text: Tell the visitor to park at the curb if other cars are there.
Explain the curb sign's time limits and direct them toward public parking.
Point out the nearest public car park and suggest checking the curb sign first.
Give directions to the market and say parking is usually nearby.

advanced.situation: At a contested citation hearing, you are asked to explain your field notes, but one entry has an unclear time and the driver disputes the location.

options.text: Read your notes aloud and describe the location as you remember it.
Say the time and location are certain so the hearing can proceed.
Ask the hearing officer for time to verify the entry and location against dispatch records.
Explain what the notes show, identify the unclear time, and answer from your records.

basic.situation: On foot patrol, you notice a side gate standing open and fresh marks near the lock. No one is nearby.

options.text: Ask a nearby guard whether the gate is usually left open.
Secure the gate and report the concern before continuing your patrol.
Record the location and time, then inspect nearby paths for signs of entry.
Notify dispatch about the open gate and marks, then observe from a safe position.

advanced.situation: During a festival shift, two patrol routes overlap while a busy exit has little coverage. You are asked to help coordinate nearby units.

options.text: Suggest that the nearest unit cover the exit while others keep their routes.
Ask each unit to keep its current route and check in at the usual time.
Move one unit toward the exit and tell the others about the change later.
Map the exit gap, propose a temporary route split, and confirm coverage with each unit.

basic.situation: After a minor collision, you are assigned to photograph the scene and speak with a witness before traffic clears.

options.text: Ask the witness to point out the damage, then photograph those areas.
Move the vehicles aside first, then take photos and collect the witness account.
Take a wide scene photo, record positions, then interview the witness separately.
Photograph the vehicles and road, then ask the witness what they saw.

advanced.situation: A suspect's account conflicts with a shopkeeper's statement and nearby camera footage. You are checking the proposed charge before the file moves on.

options.text: Match each charge element to verified evidence, flag gaps, and route the file for review.
Use the most serious charge so the case file reflects the reported harm.
Compare the statements with the footage and list the facts supporting each possible charge.
Ask the investigating officer which charge is normally used for similar reports.

basic.situation: At a roadside crash, a conscious passenger has a bleeding arm while traffic passes nearby. You are first to arrive.

options.text: Apply pressure with a clean cloth and ask another person to call for help.
Move the passenger away from traffic and ask a bystander for a cloth.
Tell the passenger to hold the wound while you direct passing traffic.
Call for medical help, keep the passenger safe, and apply firm pressure with clean cloth.

advanced.situation: Residents report recurring youth violence near a recreation area. Your station asks you to help shape a community session with local services.

options.text: Share general safety advice and distribute contact details for local services.
Ask residents about causes, then connect the session with youth services and follow-up.
Prepare a talk on penalties and ask residents to attend at the station.
Invite residents and service providers to discuss patterns and practical support options.

basic.situation: A water leak floods one lane near a junction during evening traffic. You are asked to redirect vehicles around the hazard.

options.text: Place a vehicle across the flooded lane and wait for traffic to thin.
Set a clear diversion before the junction and guide drivers past the flooded lane.
Stand near the junction and wave cars toward the open lane.
Guide vehicles around the water and ask a colleague to watch the junction.

advanced.situation: A crash closes a main road as an ambulance approaches. You are helping reroute traffic while another unit manages the crash scene.

options.text: Hold traffic at the closure and tell the ambulance which roads are blocked.
Verify the side route is open, direct traffic, and relay its status to the ambulance.
Check the marked detour for ambulance access, then direct nearby drivers and update dispatch by radio.
Wave traffic onto the side road and let the ambulance find another way.

basic.situation: A distressed adult is confused and walking toward a busy road. You are asked to help keep them safe while support arrives.

options.text: Stay beside the person, reassure them, and ask a colleague to redirect traffic while support arrives.
Guide the person to a safe area, explain the protective custody step, and request support.
Ask the person to sit nearby and wait for another unit to arrive.
Hold the person firmly and move them into the patrol vehicle for safety.

advanced.situation: You are helping locate a person named in an arrest warrant. A neighbour says the person may be inside, but you cannot confirm who is there.

options.text: Verify the warrant details, brief your team, and follow the approved approach.
Enter through the unlocked door to stop the person from leaving.
Wait outside, observe the entrance, and ask neighbours when the person usually returns home.
Share the neighbour's report with your team and wait nearby for guidance.

basic.situation: A caller reports a road hazard and asks for patrol help. Dispatch is handling several calls, and you need to relay the key details.

options.text: Send dispatch the location and hazard, then ask the caller to stay clear.
Record the location, hazard, and callback number, then relay them to dispatch.
Ask the caller for a nearby landmark before sending the report to dispatch.
Tell dispatch there is a hazard somewhere nearby and end the call.

advanced.situation: You are assigned to serve a court order at a shared address. The named recipient is away, and another resident offers to accept it.

options.text: Ask the resident when the named person is likely to return, then try again.
Check the service instructions, verify the recipient, and document the permitted outcome.
Leave the order with the resident and record the time of delivery.
Record that the recipient was absent and report the resident's offer to your unit.

basic.situation: At an airport desk, a traveler's passport details differ from the visa document. You are assigned to review them and ask about the mismatch.

options.text: Record the mismatch, compare document details, and refer unresolved concerns through the review process.
Ask about the mismatch and compare the names and dates across both documents.
Ask the traveler to explain the difference before you look closely at the documents.
Use the visa details and finish the check while the queue is moving.

advanced.situation: Several travelers present linked documents that suggest an organized entry scheme. Your team asks you to check the records and prepare findings for further action.

options.text: Compare the linked records, identify gaps, and prepare a factual referral for authorized review.
Focus on the strongest mismatch and ask another agency whether it has seen similar cases.
Treat the shared travel pattern as proof and recommend prosecution in your notes.
List the main inconsistencies and send the file to your team lead for advice.

basic.situation: A traveler declares several new watches in baggage, and the values on the receipts differ. You are assigned to inspect and assess the declaration.

options.text: Use the lowest receipt value to finish the duty calculation quickly.
Ask the traveler which receipt matches each watch before you assess the baggage.
Inspect the watches, document each value discrepancy, and calculate duty from verified details.
Check each watch against its receipt and note the declared values for assessment.

advanced.situation: A shipper disputes a duty assessment on a mixed shipment, saying several items were classified together by mistake. You are reviewing the calculation.

options.text: Keep the original total because the shipment was already assessed and released for review.
Separate the disputed items, verify their details, and document how each affects the duty calculation.
Recheck the item list and values, then compare them with the assessment basis.
Ask the shipper to provide a revised list before checking the original assessment.

basic.situation: During a baggage check, you find undeclared goods that appear restricted. A supervisor is nearby and asks you to secure the items.

options.text: Keep the goods together, record where each was found, and notify the supervisor.
Return the goods to the bag and ask the traveler to explain the declaration.
Set the goods aside, label the bag, and tell the supervisor what you found.
Hold the bag nearby while you wait for the supervisor to decide what to seize.

advanced.situation: A vehicle search reveals a concealed compartment with suspected contraband, and the driver is agitated. Your team lead assigns you to support the seizure.

options.text: Keep the driver visible, secure the area, and report the concealed compartment to your lead.
Follow the safety plan, document the compartment, and preserve suspected items for team review.
Ask the driver to step back, then photograph the compartment from a safe position.
Wait for direction before moving items, and keep the compartment area clear for inspection.

basic.situation: After a baggage inspection, your notes include the declaration, findings, and duty decision. You need to complete the incident report before shift change.

options.text: Enter the duty decision and attach the inspection notes for later reference.
Copy the main findings into the template and submit the report before shift change.
Complete the template from your notes and flag any unclear detail for review.
Check the notes against the declaration, record the decision and discrepancies, then submit the report.

advanced.situation: You notice several reports from your shift use different descriptions for the same type of baggage discrepancy. Your lead asks you to review the records.

options.text: Review a sample, note the differences, and raise them at the next briefing.
Edit the latest report's wording and ask colleagues to use that version.
Choose the most common description and replace the other entries to match it.
Compare the reports, mark inconsistent entries, and share a short documentation guide with the shift.

basic.situation: A traveler asks whether a packaged food item can enter the country. You have a published guidance sheet but are unsure how it applies.

options.text: Check item details against guidance and direct the traveler to an inspection point.
Tell the traveler packaged food is usually permitted and let them proceed.
Ask a nearby colleague what they normally tell travelers about similar food.
Read the relevant guidance and explain the listed requirement in plain language.

advanced.situation: A manufacturer asks how a proposed product change affects its import requirements. The published guidance seems unclear on one technical detail.

options.text: Summarize the guidance and ask your lead whether the product change affects requirements.
Describe a related example, explain its limits, and ask the manufacturer to consult policy staff.
Say the guidance does not resolve this detail, and avoid promising an outcome.
Explain the requirements, flag the unclear detail, and request a policy interpretation.

basic.situation: You collected a merchandise sample for examination, and your supervisor asks you to summarize how it was handled for a hearing file.

options.text: Describe the sample as matching the suspected goods based on your first impression.
Write the collection time, location, packaging, and handover details from your notes.
Ask the examining officer to tell you what details should go in your summary.
Summarize where you found the sample and what it looked like when collected.

advanced.situation: You are called to give evidence about an inspection decision that a party disputes. Your notes and the inspection record contain the relevant details.

options.text: Use the summary to fill memory gaps and present the case consistently.
Read the case summary, identify disputed points, and prepare to explain the inspection decision.
Review your notes, distinguish observations from conclusions, and prepare to explain your decision.
Review your notes and prepare a timeline of the inspection and recorded findings.

basic.situation: During a station patrol, you spot a loose cable across a walkway as passengers approach. What do you do?

options.text: Ask nearby staff whether they have seen the cable before recording it.
Move the cable aside, then continue your rounds before service gets busy.
Mark the loose cable, keep people clear, and report its location.
Record the hazard and guide passengers around it while alerting station control.

advanced.situation: A freight derailment blocks a yard track and draws a crowd near the access road. You are directing security activity. What do you do?

options.text: Keep the yard gate open for response vehicles and direct staff away from tracks.
Ask each team to cover its usual area, then update control when possible.
Set a safe perimeter, assign clear posts, and relay access routes to responders.
Close nearby access points and send one patrol to check the crowd.

basic.situation: You help document a reported theft from a station locker. The area is still busy. What do you do?

options.text: Note the reported time and item, then ask the witness to wait nearby.
Photograph the locker and record its condition after the crowd thins.
Ask a colleague to remember the details while you return to patrol.
Write down the witness's account and note who else was nearby.

advanced.situation: Several freight items are missing, and a damaged seal was found across two shifts. You are coordinating the inquiry. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the latest crew to explain the seal before reviewing earlier records.
Use the previous theft report as the likely explanation and close this inquiry.
Compare shift logs, preserve seal details, and interview staff separately.
Record the missing items and send the report to your team lead.

basic.situation: A driver stops in a marked transit lane near a station entrance, delaying a bus. What do you do?

options.text: Wave the driver through the lane to clear the entrance quickly.
Photograph the vehicle and wait for another officer to address it.
Tell the driver to move and mention the bus delay to nearby staff.
Explain the lane restriction, request that the driver move, and note the delay.

advanced.situation: A person repeatedly enters a restricted rail area after being warned, and a patrol partner sees the latest entry. What do you do?

options.text: Follow the person alone into the restricted area to stop the escape.
Approach with your partner, maintain distance, and coordinate with police for apprehension.
Keep the area watched and report the repeat entry to police.
Ask your partner to watch while you approach and repeat the warning.

basic.situation: A contractor presents an ID card at a secured station door, with your supervisor beside you. What do you do?

options.text: Let the contractor follow the next staff member through the door.
Check the name on the card against the day's contractor list.
Match the card name to the work list and confirm the entry area.
Ask the contractor's colleague to confirm the card before letting them enter.

advanced.situation: A maintenance crew needs access to a high-risk rail area, but the daily list has inconsistent names. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the crew lead to confirm names and let the crew enter together.
Hold entry for the mismatched workers and tell control which names need review.
Use a consistent name and work-zone check, recording any mismatch for review.
Accept the crew list as submitted so the maintenance work stays on schedule.

basic.situation: You are helping arrange a station fire-prevention drill, and the team needs a simple exercise plan. What do you do?

options.text: Check the planned route, note assembly points, and share the drill timing.
Choose a quiet shift and ask staff to follow last month's drill.
Confirm a drill time with staff and tell the station team.
Print the existing drill notice and place copies at staff entrances.

advanced.situation: After two near misses at different stations, you are asked to help develop a preventive safety programme. What do you do?

options.text: Share the latest warning with all stations and request staff reminders.
Wait for another incident before proposing a new prevention activity.
Compare both reports, identify shared hazards, and tailor prevention steps for each station.
Review each report and suggest the same checklist for both locations.

basic.situation: You are asked to show a small group of station staff how to keep clear of rail tracks. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the group to copy the usual staff route near the platform.
Explain the track boundary and point out the marked waiting area.
Demonstrate the safe waiting area, then ask each person to show it back.
Hand out the safety leaflet and ask staff to read it later.

advanced.situation: New officers need railroad safety training before a busy event, and you are preparing the session. What do you do?

options.text: Reuse last year's session and ask officers to sign the attendance sheet.
Cover track hazards and access rules, then invite questions at the end.
Set learning goals, use realistic rail scenarios, and check each officer's responses.
Review the current safety slides and add the event schedule to them.

basic.situation: A newly impounded dog is settled in its cage, and you are assigned its feeding and water check. What do you do?

options.text: Ask a nearby worker what food the dog usually receives, then feed it.
Check the care notes, provide the listed food and water, and record the visit.
Refill the water and offer the standard food portion before your next task.
Give the dog an extra portion so it settles while the shelter is busy.

advanced.situation: A dog captured after biting a person is drooling and highly agitated. You are assigned to move it into an enclosure. What do you do?

options.text: Offer food and approach the dog slowly to make the transfer easier.
Use the usual lead and move the dog with a coworker holding the gate.
Keep people back, follow capture guidance, and coordinate veterinary assessment before handling.
Clear the route and request experienced staff to prepare a secure enclosure.

basic.situation: A newly impounded cat has a visible limp, and you are asked to check its condition. What do you do?

options.text: Record which leg seems sore and tell the supervisor during rounds.
Note the limp, check for visible injury, and report it for treatment advice.
Let the cat rest overnight and check whether the limp improves tomorrow.
Ask the previous shift whether the cat was limping when it arrived.

advanced.situation: A dog has a deep cut and seems weak after being found outdoors. You are assessing it before shelter intake. What do you do?

options.text: Record its signs, limit handling, and arrange prompt veterinary assessment for both concerns.
Offer water and place the dog in a quiet cage until intake is complete.
Separate the dog from other animals and inform the shelter team about the cut.
Clean the cut and check whether the dog can stand after resting.

basic.situation: A resident reports seeing a dog struck near a market and offers to describe what happened. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the resident to describe what happened and write down the main points.
Tell the resident that market staff can handle the complaint from there.
Record the resident's account, note when and where it occurred, and ask about other witnesses.
Take the resident's phone number and ask them to call if they recall more.

advanced.situation: Two witnesses describe different events around an injured animal, and a nearby camera may have recorded the area. What do you do?

options.text: Use the clearer account as the main version and leave out the conflicting details.
Ask both witnesses to agree on a timeline before you write the report.
Record accounts separately, note the camera location, and preserve details for follow-up.
Write both accounts in the report and ask a senior officer how to proceed.

basic.situation: You accompany a senior inspector to check a small animal boarding facility's license and housing conditions. What do you do?

options.text: Accept the owner's assurance and finish the visit within the schedule.
Check the displayed license and note housing concerns for the senior inspector.
Ask the owner to confirm license status while counting the cages.
Review the cages and ask the owner where the license is displayed.

advanced.situation: During a facility inspection, you find several animals in crowded housing and a license detail that does not match the records. What do you do?

options.text: Give the facility a clean inspection note while the owner checks the records.
Note both findings and refer them to the senior inspector for review.
Photograph the crowded cages and ask the owner to clarify the license later.
Document the housing and license discrepancy, then explain both findings for corrective follow-up.

basic.situation: A resident asks why an unclaimed dog is being held at the shelter. You are answering public inquiries. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the resident to check the shelter noticeboard for the holding details.
Explain the holding process in plain language and direct them to the inquiry channel.
Tell the resident that unclaimed animals are held until staff have time.
Read the standard holding explanation and offer the shelter's contact number.

advanced.situation: Residents ask about an increase in reports of roaming dogs, and you are asked to prepare a short public education message. What do you do?

options.text: Tell residents that roaming dogs are a shelter problem to report later.
Post the shelter's phone number and ask residents to call with concerns.
Share a general reminder to keep pets secure and contact animal control.
Explain safe reporting steps, responsible animal care, and where residents can ask questions.

basic.situation: You have finished cleaning an animal control truck and need to update its impoundment file. What do you do?

options.text: Clean the equipment log and place the impoundment form in the pending tray.
Put the form with today's papers and rely on the next shift to file it.
File the impoundment form and tell the next worker the truck is clean.
Record the cleaning and file the impoundment details with the matching case.

advanced.situation: A case file for a prosecution is missing an impoundment date, and the owner says the pet is at the holding facility. What do you do?

options.text: Use the date from a similar case and close the owner's inquiry as answered.
Tell the owner the pet is held and ask a colleague to find the date.
Search the case file for the date and note the owner's inquiry for follow-up.
Verify the date in facility records, confirm pet location, and update the case file.

basic.situation: A client asks you to locate a former tenant, and your supervisor suggests checking public records and approved databases.

options.text: Use a recent social profile to fill gaps in the record.
Send the first matching address to the client to save time.
Check two database results and note any differences for review.
Search approved public records, then compare matching dates and addresses.

advanced.situation: Several invoices and bank entries in an insurance claim point to possible diverted payments, but the dates do not align neatly.

options.text: Label the largest unexplained transfer as fraud in your report.
Map each payment to its invoice and flag mismatches with source records.
Compare recurring amounts across accounts and list likely diversion dates.
Highlight the largest transfers and send a quick summary to the client.

basic.situation: A shop owner reports missing stock, and you have two witness accounts and a short list of staff who were present.

options.text: Record each account and ask about the missing items' usual storage.
Focus your notes on the staff member named most often.
Arrange the accounts by time and check where their details differ.
Ask the owner which staff member seems most likely responsible.

advanced.situation: Three related theft reports share unusual timing, but the locations and witness descriptions differ, and the client wants a clear lead.

options.text: Research the most distinctive witness description for a quick match.
Compare timelines, access details, and independent accounts before linking the reports.
Tell the client the same offender likely handled all three incidents.
Map the incidents by time and location, then note the strongest overlap.

basic.situation: You are asked to watch a shop entrance from a nearby parked car and record whether a person removes goods without paying.

options.text: Note the time, actions, and view limits while observing through binoculars.
Record the person's clothing and the time they entered and left.
Write that the person stole goods after seeing them leave the shop.
Keep binoculars trained on the person and note the exit time.

advanced.situation: A client suspects repeated after-hours stock removals, but a loading bay blocks part of your camera view and shifts overlap.

options.text: Describe the staff member as the thief in your evidence summary.
Zoom in on the loading bay whenever movement appears on screen.
Use a second camera angle to compare who handles each item.
Record each visible transfer with timestamps and mark the camera's blind area.

basic.situation: A small business asks you to check an applicant's public background, and your supervisor provides the applicant's consent and details.

options.text: Check relevant public records and note any identity details that differ.
Search public profiles and summarize anything that seems concerning.
Match approved public records to the applicant's details and log each source.
Forward a same-name record to the business as a likely match.

advanced.situation: A client requests a background investigation of a prospective business partner after seeing conflicting company and financial records.

options.text: Summarize the strongest concerns from the records for the client.
Check company filings and financial references for matching names and dates.
Separate verified records from leads and compare dates, names, and business links.
Send the client the most damaging record as a clear warning.

basic.situation: A client asks you to learn about a neighbour's character, and a former colleague agrees to speak with you over coffee.

options.text: Ask how they worked together and note the colleague's main impressions.
Ask whether the colleague would trust the neighbour with money.
Ask open questions about specific examples and record the colleague's own words.
Tell the client the neighbour is unreliable based on one complaint.

advanced.situation: A witness in a child custody investigation recalls a tense exchange differently from your notes, and their account may be needed in court.

options.text: Rewrite the earlier note to match the witness's latest version.
Ask whether the witness is certain their first recollection was mistaken.
Invite a fresh account, clarify the timeline, and preserve their exact phrasing.
Ask what happened before and after the exchange, then note their view.

basic.situation: After a routine missing-person inquiry, your supervisor asks for a short case summary before the next shift takes over.

options.text: Send a brief message with the latest location mentioned by a caller.
Summarize verified steps, dates, and open leads with their sources.
Write that the person was found because one contact said so.
List the calls made and the last reported sighting time.

advanced.situation: You are called to present surveillance evidence at a hearing, and counsel asks why a key timestamp differs from your written report.

options.text: Estimate the time from the shift change and explain your reasoning.
Describe the observation, flag the time mismatch, and request review of the report.
Explain your recording method, note the discrepancy, and consult source notes.
Say the timestamp is accurate because the camera usually keeps time.

basic.situation: During a quiet shift, a live table feed shows a dealer's hand briefly disappearing below the camera view.

options.text: Note the movement and check the same moment on recorded footage.
Watch the same camera closely for another similar movement.
Mark the time and compare the table view with its adjacent camera.
Report the dealer for taking chips based on that movement.

advanced.situation: A player and dealer exchange chips across two tables, while one camera angle is partly blocked by a passing group.

options.text: Call it collusion after seeing the same players meet twice.
Follow the player with the clearest camera view for the next round.
Compare both views for repeated chip movements and note the overlap.
Sync both table views and trace each chip movement across the blocked interval.

basic.situation: Your shift checklist calls for checking an identification step at a gaming table, and a busy colleague asks you to complete the log.

options.text: Observe the check against the procedure and record the result with its time.
Ask the colleague whether the identification check was completed during opening.
Mark the check complete because the table has been running smoothly.
Review the table log and flag any missing check for later.

advanced.situation: A spot audit shows repeated gaps in a gaming table's required checks, while the shift is busy and the cause is unclear.

options.text: Pause your sample and focus on the latest missing entry.
Compare sampled records with observed practice and classify each specific gap.
Tell the team the table is breaking gaming rules across the shift.
Review the affected logs and ask staff how the checks are recorded.

basic.situation: At shift start, one surveillance monitor is dark while the other camera views remain visible and recording.

options.text: Check its power and signal connections, then confirm the feed returns.
Switch to a nearby monitor and keep watching from that position.
Log the dark screen as a camera outage for the full shift.
Tell the shift lead the monitor is dark and note its position.

advanced.situation: Several feeds intermittently freeze during a busy shift, but the recording indicator remains lit and no single camera appears fully disconnected.

options.text: Switch to the clearest remaining feeds and continue the watch.
Log each freeze and ask maintenance to review the system after play.
Record affected feeds and times, then check shared connections and system status.
Restart the recording system during play to clear the frozen feeds.

basic.situation: You notice a patron repeatedly returning to the same table after leaving, and the shift log needs a short entry.

options.text: Add the patron's name and say they returned several times.
Write that the patron was scouting the table for a cheat.
Note the patron's clothing and each return time in the log.
Record times, locations, and observed actions in the shift log.

advanced.situation: Observers use different terms for chip movements, making repeated incidents hard to compare across handovers.

options.text: Share clear sample entries and propose common wording to the team.
Draft shared fields for time, table, action, camera, and follow-up status.
Replace the team log with your own labels before the next shift.
Ask each observer to add more detail to their existing entries.

basic.situation: You see a patron repeatedly reaching toward another player's chips, but the dealer redirects the play before any chips move.

options.text: Report the patron for stealing chips from the other player.
Add the patron to your notes and raise it at handover.
Tell the supervisor the patron reached toward another player's chips.
Tell the supervisor what you saw, when it happened, and the table.

advanced.situation: Footage suggests a staff member altered a transaction record, but a second angle is still being reviewed and the report is due soon.

options.text: Draft a factual timeline, identify the footage reviewed, and flag the remaining angle check.
Identify the staff member as responsible in the formal report before confirming the remaining footage.
Record visible changes, cite reviewed footage, and state that the second angle remains under review.
Send the supervisor a brief warning and postpone completing the report until later.

basic.situation: A new observer asks how to note an unusual chip movement while you are both covering the same shift.

options.text: Tell them to copy your previous entry and change details for the new observation.
Model a factual entry and ask them to record the next chip movement.
Explain the log details to include, then answer their questions about recording unusual chip movements.
Ask them to watch you write entries and follow that format for their observations.

advanced.situation: Several new observers miss subtle hand signals in practice footage, and your supervisor asks you to suggest a short training session.

options.text: Prepare annotated clips and explain the signals during a group review.
Tell trainees the missed signals are obvious once they pay attention.
Build a short practice using paired clips, clear cues, and feedback notes.
Send the team a list of signal descriptions before their next shift.

basic.situation: A visitor arrives without an appointment and says a staff member is expecting them. What do you do?

options.text: Check the visitor's identification and call the staff member to confirm entry.
Write down the visitor's name and let them proceed to reception.
Let the visitor wait in the lobby while you call the staff member.
Ask the visitor to wait while you check the staff directory.

advanced.situation: A delivery driver presents an access card that opens the service gate, but the delivery is not on today's schedule. What do you do?

options.text: Accept the access card as proof and direct the driver to the loading bay.
Keep the gate secured and verify the delivery with the receiving staff.
Let the driver park inside the gate while you check the schedule.
Ask the driver to wait while you call the receiving department.

basic.situation: On your regular patrol, you find the rear fire door slightly ajar after a busy lunch period. What do you do?

options.text: Continue your route and tell the next guard about the door.
Close the door and record the time in your patrol log.
Inspect the door and nearby area, then log its status.
Ask a nearby employee whether anyone used the rear door.

advanced.situation: You notice the same delivery van repeatedly stopping beside a poorly lit fence during your evening patrol. What do you do?

options.text: Stay near the fence until the van leaves the area.
Vary your patrol timing and report the repeated stops with their locations.
Record the van's times and location in the shift log.
Follow the van beyond the premises to learn where it goes.

basic.situation: A door alarm sounds at the staff entrance, but the corridor appears empty on your first check. What do you do?

options.text: Silence the alarm and return to your post once the sound stops.
Reset the alarm and note the time in your log.
Call the control room and ask whether anyone else saw the alarm.
Check the entrance and nearby area, then report what triggered the alarm.

advanced.situation: An alarm and a shouted call for help come from different wings, and you cannot see either location from your post. What do you do?

options.text: Go to the louder call and leave the alarm for another guard.
Radio both locations to the control room and request the nearest available response.
Check the nearer wing yourself before deciding whether to call for help.
Call the control room about the alarm and shouted call for help.

basic.situation: A visitor enters a staff-only corridor after being told to wait in reception. What do you do?

options.text: Calmly explain the access rule and direct the visitor back to reception.
Ask the visitor to return to reception while you notify your supervisor.
Let the visitor continue briefly while you find the staff member they seek.
Stand at the corridor entrance and ask what the visitor needs.

advanced.situation: A person refuses to leave a restricted lobby, raises their voice, and steps closer when you repeat the access rule. What do you do?

options.text: Repeat the direction calmly and radio a nearby guard for support.
Avoid physical contact and request support while keeping a safe distance.
Keep space, give a calm direction, and call support while watching their movements.
Ask what would help the person leave the lobby safely.

basic.situation: A visitor's bag triggers the metal detector, but the alarm stops when they step back. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the visitor to walk through again while carrying the bag for screening.
Allow entry without checking since the alarm stopped after the visitor stepped back.
Follow screening procedure and ask the visitor to present the bag for inspection.
Explain that the alarm sounded and ask the visitor to open the bag for inspection.

advanced.situation: A vehicle gate reader works intermittently, and you notice fresh marks around its control panel during your shift. What do you do?

options.text: Try the reader several times and note which cards it accepts.
Record the fault and marks, then notify the control room.
Secure the area, report the marks, and follow reader inspection procedures.
Prop the gate open while troubleshooting the reader between arriving vehicles on shift.

basic.situation: At shift end, you notice a visitor left a phone near the lobby desk, and no one has reported it missing. What do you do?

options.text: Log where and when you found it, then follow the site's lost-property process.
Keep the phone at the desk and ask visitors whether it belongs to them.
Tell the next guard where the phone was found and when.
Put the phone in a drawer and mention it during tomorrow's handover.

advanced.situation: A visitor collapses near the entrance while another person calls for help, and your activity log is due soon. What do you do?

options.text: Call paramedics and ask a colleague to note the time.
Call for help before recording the collapse in your activity log.
Call for medical help, give first aid within training, and document the response.
Ask the caller to stay with the visitor while you contact emergency services.

basic.situation: At a school crossing, children wait at the kerb while vehicles approach and your crossing point is clear.

options.text: Ask the children to cross quickly while you hold up your stop sign.
Step into the crossing and wave the children across with your flag.
Raise your stop sign and guide the children across when cars slow.
Use your stop signal, check traffic has yielded, and escort the children across.

advanced.situation: At a roadwork site, traffic backs up as a delivery truck approaches the pedestrian crossing from the far lane.

options.text: Ask pedestrians to wait while you stop the near lane with your signal.
Wave pedestrians across before the truck reaches the crossing to clear traffic.
Stop both approaches and guide pedestrians after the delivery truck passes.
Hold pedestrians at the safe point, signal both lanes, then release them when clear.

basic.situation: Several students are waiting to cross, and the traffic flow has a short gap between two groups of cars.

options.text: Watch both directions and use a gap that gives the group time to cross.
Point out the gap and let students decide when they feel ready to cross.
Wait for another gap and take the students across in smaller groups.
Check the nearest lane, then start when those cars have passed.

advanced.situation: A temporary road sign near your crossing is partly hidden by a parked van, and traffic is moving faster than usual.

options.text: Move the van's sign into view so drivers can see it again.
Hold pedestrians back, report the obscured sign, and use your assigned safe crossing point.
Tell pedestrians about the van and guide them across at your usual point.
Keep pedestrians waiting and alert the site contact that the sign is blocked.

basic.situation: You are assigned to place traffic control signs at marked points before a roadwork crew starts nearby.

options.text: Put all signs together at the roadwork entrance for drivers to see.
Set the signs near the marked points and start the rest of your duties.
Place signs at the marked points and tell the crew when finished.
Place each sign at its marked point and check it faces approaching traffic.

advanced.situation: A delivery entrance sits beyond a bend, and your plan marks sign points near the roadwork area before the crew opens the site.

options.text: Place signs at marked points, then ask a driver whether they can see them.
Follow marked points, check sign visibility near the bend, and report any blocked view.
Place each sign as planned and report the bend as a visibility concern.
Move signs closer to the bend so drivers can notice them sooner.

basic.situation: A car drives through your stop signal at a crossing, and you can see its registration plate clearly.

options.text: Record the plate, time, and crossing location, then report the infraction through your channel.
Follow the car and try to stop it so you can confirm the plate.
Write down the plate and mention the incident to the next guard.
Record the plate and crossing location, then report the driver to the site contact.

advanced.situation: Two drivers disregard signals during a roadwork shift, and one disputes your record while a queue forms behind them.

options.text: Step closer to the disputing driver to copy the plate more clearly.
Record both plates and report both incidents once the traffic queue clears.
Stay clear, note plates and times, then report both incidents to your supervisor.
Tell the driver you will report the vehicle, then continue directing traffic from your post.

basic.situation: You see a student run toward the road ahead of your crossing point while other pupils are lining up.

options.text: Alert the school official and keep the waiting pupils at the safe point.
Tell the student to return and mention it to the school official later.
Ask a nearby teacher to watch the student while you continue the crossing.
Continue the crossing and assume the student will return to the group.

advanced.situation: A roadwork shift change is planned, and your supervisor asks you to discuss traffic routing and control-point locations with the crew.

options.text: Invite crew input on control points before traffic conditions change.
Review the route and control points with your supervisor, flagging unclear pedestrian coverage.
Restate the route and control points, then check the crew understands them.
Discuss route and control points, record agreed changes, and confirm them with everyone.

basic.situation: A parent asks why students must wait for your signal before crossing at the school gate.

options.text: Wave the parent across first so they can show the students what to do.
Explain that students cross when you signal and ask the parent to wait.
Explain the crossing signal and ask the parent to wait with the students.
Tell the parent to follow the crossing rules posted near the gate.

advanced.situation: A driver asks for the detour around a roadwork closure, while pedestrians nearby also want to know how to cross safely.

options.text: Tell the driver to follow nearby vehicles and let pedestrians choose a gap.
Point the driver toward the detour sign and ask pedestrians to wait.
Explain the driver detour, then direct pedestrians to the assigned crossing point and signal.
Explain the detour route to the driver and remind pedestrians to follow site signs.

basic.situation: You are assigned a shoreline patrol during a busy afternoon. Swimmers are gathering near the marked boundary.

options.text: Patrol the full route on schedule, scanning water and access points.
Ask a nearby guard which area needs attention before moving.
Stay at the tower and watch the busiest swim zone.
Walk the assigned shoreline, scan swimmers, and note crowded sections.

advanced.situation: A large recreation area has trails, a pool, and a busy picnic zone. Staff report that visitor numbers are rising across all three.

options.text: Assign patrol routes by visitor density and set regular radio check-ins.
Send all available staff toward the busiest area for the afternoon.
Ask each team to cover its usual area and report unusual activity.
Keep the existing patrol rotation and review reports at closing.

basic.situation: Before opening, you check a rope tow using the site's checklist and spot a frayed section of visible cable covering.

options.text: Add the wear to the checklist and finish the other visual checks.
Open the tow and mention the cable at the next handover.
Mark the frayed section and report it before the tow opens.
Ask another attendant whether this amount of wear looks familiar.

advanced.situation: During a chair lift inspection, you find two seats with worn restraints and a checklist that gives no threshold for acceptable wear.

options.text: Record both findings and keep the existing checklist for this shift.
Ask inspectors to flag restraint wear and describe it in their notes.
Draft clear wear criteria with photo examples for the inspection checklist.
Use the lift's smooth operation to decide whether restraints can stay.

basic.situation: You test pool water before opening with a colleague nearby. One chemical reading falls outside the range on the facility's testing guide.

options.text: Log the reading and tell the pool lead before opening.
Retest the sample using the guide and record both readings.
Ask the colleague to confirm the reading before logging it.
Use the last acceptable reading to complete today's opening sheet.

advanced.situation: A cleanliness audit finds recurring debris near the pool deck drains, while water tests remain within the facility's stated range.

options.text: Focus the audit on pool surfaces since the readings remain in range.
Ask the cleaning team to clear the drains before the next audit.
Set routine drain checks, log findings, and review repeat debris with staff.
Note the debris and water results in today's facility log.

basic.situation: A swimmer calls for help near the pool's marked depth change. Your senior lifeguard is beside you as you prepare the rescue tube.

options.text: Move to the pool edge and prepare the tube for handoff.
Follow your senior's approach and keep the rescue tube between you.
Enter the water with the rescue tube and follow your senior's direction.
Keep the tube ready and wait for your senior to begin.

advanced.situation: A distressed person is beyond the shallow area, and a second swimmer nearby is becoming anxious. You are the senior guard on duty.

options.text: Focus on the distressed person and leave the nearby swimmer alone.
Approach the distressed person and ask another guard to watch nearby swimmers.
Direct a trained colleague to reassure the second swimmer while you approach.
Call for another guard and prepare rescue equipment at the pool edge.

basic.situation: A visitor has a deep cut and feels faint after slipping near the pool. Your trained colleague is nearby with the first-aid kit.

options.text: Call for medical help and bring the first-aid kit to the visitor.
Clean the cut and let the visitor rest before deciding what to do.
Ask your colleague to call for medical help while you assist the visitor.
Ask the visitor to sit while you look for another staff member.

advanced.situation: After a beach medical incident, staff disagree about the timeline and the weather changed during the response. You are completing the incident record.

options.text: Record the timeline, treatment, and observed beach conditions from staff notes.
Compare staff notes, clarify times, and document treatment and beach conditions.
Write a brief summary from memory and submit it before shift change.
Leave the timeline blank and record the treatment and weather only.

basic.situation: A group is entering a section closed because of rough water. You have the site's standard safety message ready to use.

options.text: Let the group enter while you find the activity leader.
Read the standard warning aloud from the sign beside the entrance.
Ask a nearby guard to repeat the warning while you watch the group.
Give the safety message and point the group toward the open area.

advanced.situation: Several groups use the recreation area, and staff deliver safety briefings differently. You are asked to improve the participant instruction materials.

options.text: Write a shared briefing outline covering hazards and safe participant conduct.
Copy the current script onto signs for each activity entrance.
Create activity-specific lessons with demonstrations and short participant checks.
Ask staff to explain safety in their own way at each activity.

basic.situation: A passenger's ticket is unclear, and they mention needing special handling before entering the screening line.

options.text: Ask a colleague to review the ticket while the passenger waits nearby.
Send the passenger through the regular line while you check the ticket later.
Check the ticket details and ask the passenger what assistance they need.
Confirm the ticket and direct the passenger to the designated assistance process.

advanced.situation: A person enters a restricted checkpoint area without a visible badge and gives an unclear reason for being there.

options.text: Let the person continue while you look for someone who recognizes them.
Ask the person about their business and request their badge for checking.
Watch the person from nearby while checking with a coworker about access.
Ask why they are there, then notify checkpoint staff about the answer.

basic.situation: A checked bag triggers an alarm on the automated screening machine. Your lead is nearby, and the bag is still on the screening line.

options.text: Pause the line and ask a coworker whether this alarm is familiar.
Set the bag aside for rescreening and tell the lead what triggered.
Tell the lead about the alarm and wait beside the screening line.
Send the bag onward because most checked bags clear the machine.

advanced.situation: A carry-on image shows a dense object that the screening guide says needs further investigation, but the passenger is waiting at the belt.

options.text: Review the image again and ask a colleague what the object might be.
Allow the bag through after checking that the passenger is in a hurry.
Set the bag aside and follow the site's process for further investigation.
Keep the bag at the belt while you reread the screening guide.

basic.situation: A hand search finds a prohibited sharp item in an opened carry-on. The passenger asks whether they can keep it in the bag.

options.text: Return the item to the bag so the passenger can continue quickly.
Explain the item cannot travel and hand it over through the disposal process.
Ask the passenger to place the item back while you check with your lead.
Confiscate the item and give it to the airline for disposal.

advanced.situation: A checked bag is flagged for possible explosive material, and the detection equipment is available. A colleague offers to open it to save time.

options.text: Let the colleague open the bag while you keep passengers back.
Move the bag aside and wait for the next screening team.
Ask the colleague to hold the bag while you contact the lead.
Use the detection equipment and swab process before any baggage search.

basic.situation: A checked bag triggers an alarm, and you have the monitoring record open while the passenger waits nearby.

options.text: Enter the bag reference and alarm type in the monitoring log.
Ask a colleague to remember the details while you clear the line.
Record the alarm details, time, and bag reference in the monitoring log.
Mark the alarm as routine and close the record for now.

advanced.situation: A person breaches a checkpoint barrier, and police are on their way. You are near the entry area with a radio.

options.text: Tell a colleague about the breach while you watch the open entrance.
Close the entry area and wait for police beside the barrier.
Close the entry area and report the breach location over radio.
Follow the person alone while leaving the entry area open.

basic.situation: The screening queue is backing up, and passengers are bunching near the checkpoint entrance during a busy morning.

options.text: Ask passengers to spread out while you remain beside the screening lane.
Watch the queue and tell a colleague when it becomes crowded.
Monitor the entrance and guide passengers into a clear waiting line.
Leave the entrance to check why the screening lane is moving slowly.

advanced.situation: During a checkpoint patrol, you spot an unattended package near a work area. Staff and passengers are moving nearby.

options.text: Tell a nearby screener about the package and ask them to report it.
Watch the package from a distance while you look for a supervisor.
Keep people clear and report the package location through checkpoint channels.
Move the package to the side so people can pass the work area.

basic.situation: A passenger has completed screening and asks where to collect checked baggage. The signs are visible near the checkpoint exit.

options.text: Ask the passenger to check the signs near the exit for directions.
Point out the baggage pickup signs and explain the route from this exit.
Send the passenger back through screening to ask another staff member.
Direct the passenger toward baggage pickup beyond the checkpoint exit.

advanced.situation: A passenger asks how to handle a prohibited item found during screening. The item cannot travel with them, and mailing services are available outside.

options.text: Explain the mailing option and the handover process if they decline it.
Allow the passenger to carry the item onward while deciding what to do.
Tell the passenger where they can mail the item to themselves.
Ask a supervisor to speak with the passenger about the item.

basic.situation: At the school gate, students crowd the bus steps while the driver waits. You need to keep boarding orderly.

options.text: Ask the driver to remind students to queue before boarding.
Let the front students board while you call out for space.
Wave the waiting group aboard so the bus can leave sooner.
Ask students to queue, then guide them aboard one at a time.

advanced.situation: During a safety drill, students hesitate at the rear exit and the route outside is crowded. You must guide their evacuation.

options.text: Guide small groups through a clear exit, checking the route as they move.
Check routes, direct students to a clear exit, and count them at assembly.
Pause briefly, then use the front exit when the crowd thins.
Rush everyone through the rear exit before checking whether the route is clear.

basic.situation: A child who uses a wheelchair is waiting at the bus. The lift is ready, and you are asked to help them board.

options.text: Ask the child to wait while you lift the chair up the steps.
Position the wheelchair at the lift and operate it using the bus procedure.
Guide the chair toward the lift and ask the child to hold still.
Ask the driver to operate the lift while you steady the chair.

advanced.situation: A student becomes distressed as other children crowd the boarding area. You need to help them board while keeping the line calm.

options.text: Ask familiar staff to support the student while you calmly manage the line.
Keep the line moving and urge the student to board quickly.
Pause the line, give the student space, and offer a calm boarding choice.
Stay nearby and ask the other children to wait patiently.

basic.situation: A passenger settles into a bus seat, but the lap belt is twisted. You are responsible for buckling passengers before departure.

options.text: Fasten the belt as it is so the bus can depart on time.
Ask the driver to check the belt before pulling away.
Buckle the belt and remind the passenger to sit back.
Untwist the belt, buckle it, and check that it sits comfortably.

advanced.situation: A wheelchair user is ready for a trip, but one tie-down strap seems loose after repositioning. You need to secure the passenger.

options.text: Check each tie-down point and refasten the loose strap before departure.
Ask the driver to inspect the straps while you steady the chair.
Hold the chair in place and ask someone nearby to tighten the strap.
Tighten the loose strap and start the trip to avoid delay.

basic.situation: The bus must reverse out of a tight school driveway. You are outside and can guide the driver from a safe position.

options.text: Ask another staff member to watch the path while you signal.
Stand where the driver sees you, signal slowly, and watch the path.
Signal from a safe position while checking the bus mirrors.
Wave the driver back quickly so traffic can pass behind the bus.

advanced.situation: Traffic is building near a rail crossing after a delay, and the driver asks whether to move forward. You need to report the situation.

options.text: Tell the driver to proceed once traffic clears, then report the delay to dispatch.
Report the delay to dispatch and wait until crossing is clear before signaling.
Check the crossing from safety, then tell the driver what you observe.
Ask the driver to assess the crossing while you contact dispatch.

basic.situation: Two students keep calling across the aisle and distracting the driver. You need to monitor conduct and maintain a safe ride.

options.text: Tell them to quiet down and sit facing forward.
Remind them of the bus rules and watch whether the distraction stops.
Move the students apart and continue the trip without speaking to them.
Ask the driver to handle them at the next stop.

advanced.situation: Two students begin arguing loudly over a seat, and one pushes the other. Other passengers are watching as you need to defuse the conflict.

options.text: Separate them calmly, check for injuries, then report the incident to their guardians.
Tell both students to stop arguing and stay seated while you continue driving.
Move one student to another seat, note the incident, and contact the school representative.
