Ask nearby passengers what they saw, then speak with both students separately.

basic.situation: After the morning route, you find wrappers and smudged windows inside the bus. You are asked to tidy the interior before the next trip.

options.text: Pick up the larger wrappers and leave the windows for later.
Sweep the wrappers into a corner so the bus is ready sooner.
Collect the wrappers and wipe the windows before the next boarding.
Ask the driver to confirm the next departure time, then clean the windows.

advanced.situation: You notice the passenger count on the trip sheet differs from your boarding tally. The bus has returned, and the daily report is due.

options.text: Ask the driver which count seems more likely before filing.
Use the trip sheet count so the report can be submitted on time.
Submit the tally and mention the difference in the report notes.
Check the boarding tally against the trip notes, then record the resolved count.

basic.situation: Your checklist shows a CCTV camera feed is blank during a routine store check. You need to verify the security system.

options.text: Refresh the monitor and mention the blank camera at handover.
Ask a colleague to confirm the blank feed before you report it.
Note the camera location, check its feed once, and report the fault.
Mark the camera as working because the other feeds are clear.

advanced.situation: A stockroom door alarm works, but deliveries leave the entrance open during busy periods. You are reviewing physical security risks.

options.text: Add a sign reminding vendors to keep the entrance clear.
Ask staff to close the door more often during delivery peaks.
Disable the alarm during delivery hours to prevent repeated alerts.
Review the door and delivery flow, then recommend a practical access control change.

basic.situation: A supervisor asks you to document a suspected missing item after a stock check. The item may have been sold or misplaced.

options.text: Ask the supervisor which details belong on the incident form.
Record the item details, time, and known checks without assigning blame.
Write down the name of the last cashier and treat it as theft.
Check the nearby shelf again and note whether the item appears.

advanced.situation: A suspected vendor fraud case includes mismatched delivery records and footage. You are supporting the investigation and asked to preserve relevant material.

options.text: Copy the relevant records through approved access and log what you collected.
Save the footage and records to your work folder for review.
Forward the footage and delivery papers to the vendor for their explanation.
Ask a senior investigator which files to retain before collecting any.

basic.situation: During a checklist audit, you notice staff skip the bag check step at one register. The manager is nearby.

options.text: Watch another transaction before deciding whether the step is skipped.
Remind the cashier about the bag check and continue the checklist.
Note the register and observed step, then discuss it with the manager.
Mark the register compliant because the other tills follow the procedure.

advanced.situation: Several stores report inconsistent checks at closing. You are asked to help identify a repeatable audit approach for the team.

options.text: Visit one store and copy its closing checklist for the others.
Tell each store to use its existing closing routine and report issues.
Ask store managers to send their current closing checklists for review.
Compare the reported gaps and draft shared checks staff can apply consistently.

basic.situation: A shelf count is short by several units after a busy shift. You need to report the stock shortage before handover.

options.text: Write the item name on a handover note for the next shift.
Record the item, count, and time, then submit the shortage report.
Change the count to match the system so the shift can close.
Ask the manager to verify the count before you file the report.

advanced.situation: Your incident reports use different descriptions for similar events, making patterns hard to review. You are asked to improve the reporting template.

options.text: Remove fields staff often leave blank so reports are quicker.
Share a sample report and ask the team to follow its format.
Add consistent fields for time, location, event, and action taken.
Tell staff to write longer narratives in the current form.

basic.situation: You notice a loose display fixture beside a busy aisle during a store walk. You need to recommend a simple safety fix.

options.text: Tell the manager where it wobbles and suggest securing the fixture.
Ask a colleague to confirm the fixture is loose before raising it.
Move nearby stock to hide the wobble until the next reset.
Put a note on the fixture for the closing team to review.

advanced.situation: Repeated refund exceptions suggest a possible financial loss pattern across departments. You are asked to recommend a response with relevant teams.

options.text: Ask cashiers to watch refunds more closely during busy periods.
Send the exception summary to finance and ask for their suggestions.
Compare the exception pattern with affected teams and propose targeted review controls.
Recommend stopping all refunds until the pattern is understood.

basic.situation: During a store evacuation drill, a staff member is unsure where to direct shoppers. You are helping with loss prevention training.

options.text: Show the staff member the exit sign once the group has passed.
Tell them to choose the nearest door and keep the drill moving.
Point them to the marked exit route and report the confusion after the drill.
Ask the team leader to guide shoppers while you observe the staff member.

advanced.situation: A severe storm causes water to enter the shop, and customers are still browsing. You are on the loss prevention team and need to respond.

options.text: Tell the duty manager about the water and wait for instructions.
Use the site response plan, move customers from the area, and report hazards.
Ask nearby staff to keep serving customers while you carefully check the water level.
Guide customers away from the water and update the manager on conditions.

basic.situation: You need to estimate ingredients for a new lunch special, but the supplier price list has just changed.

options.text: I would use last week's quantities and round each cost to a familiar amount.
I would ask a cook to check the ingredient list before I total costs.
I would weigh the listed ingredients and price them from current supplier slips.
I would compare the recipe quantities with today's prices and note the estimate.

advanced.situation: Two hotel outlets need shared ingredients for a festive menu, and one supplier warns that seasonal produce may be limited.

options.text: I would check seasonal availability, then ask outlet leads to confirm quantities.
I would total each outlet's forecast and reserve stock against expected demand.
I would align outlet forecasts, budgets, and seasonal supply before coordinating purchases.
I would combine the orders and let each outlet adjust its menu later.

basic.situation: A chilled delivery arrives before lunch service, and the invoice quantity seems different from the crates you received.

options.text: I would check the labels and ask the driver about the missing crates.
I would count the crates and check their condition against the order.
I would count the crates and tell the supervisor about the difference.
I would sign the invoice and let the kitchen adjust its prep later.

advanced.situation: During a busy shift, you notice a cleaning checklist is signed, but the slicer and nearby work surface still look unclean.

options.text: I would pause use, arrange cleaning, then check the area against standards.
I would record the area and remind the team to clean after service.
I would inspect the slicer and surface, then report the missed cleaning.
I would ask the shift cook whether the checklist was completed correctly.

basic.situation: A school group adds twenty lunches to today's bookings, and your manager asks you to help adjust the kitchen schedule.

options.text: I would add the meals to the current prep list and keep the same timings.
I would check prep times and ask the manager to adjust staff coverage.
I would map the extra meals by prep time and flag staffing gaps.
I would ask each cook to estimate how many lunches they can prepare.

advanced.situation: A hotel outlet is delayed while another has spare cooks; both are preparing dishes for the same large banquet.

options.text: I would review the two prep lists and send available cooks where needed.
I would move the spare cooks to the delayed outlet and keep menus unchanged.
I would compare both kitchens' capacity, then rebalance prep and staff by dish.
I would ask the delayed outlet to simplify its menu during service.

basic.situation: Your kitchen is low on cooking oil, and the head cook asks you to prepare a routine supply requisition.

options.text: I would order the usual amount so the kitchen can keep moving.
I would count the remaining oil and prepare the standard requisition form.
I would copy last month's quantities and send the requisition for approval.
I would check stock and expected use, then enter quantities on the form.

advanced.situation: A sales representative offers a lower price on bulk vegetables, but your storage is nearly full and this week's demand is uncertain.

options.text: I would compare unit prices, usable capacity, and forecast demand before agreeing.
I would negotiate a smaller order at the offered price for this week.
I would ask the representative to hold the quoted price while I check stock.
I would accept the bulk price and ask the kitchen to use the extra stock.

basic.situation: You are preparing a familiar soup for lunch service, and the head cook asks you to handle the vegetables and seasoning.

options.text: I would prepare the vegetables and follow the head cook's recipe closely.
I would ask a nearby cook to taste the soup while I finish prep.
I would season the full pot early so it is ready before service.
I would prepare the vegetables, cook the soup, and taste before serving.

advanced.situation: A wedding buffet needs a decorative fruit display, but the planned platter looks unstable as guests begin arriving.

options.text: I would rebuild a lower display, then check its stability and serving access.
I would move the display away from the buffet edge and alert the team.
I would remove the top fruit and arrange the remaining pieces neatly.
I would keep the display as planned and add fruit around its base.

basic.situation: A hand mixer starts making a grinding noise during prep, and the head cook asks you to help arrange a repair.

options.text: I would keep using it at low speed until the next service break.
I would tell the head cook about the noise and ask what to do.
I would unplug the mixer and place a note beside it for the team.
I would report the fault, identify the mixer, and arrange a repair request.

advanced.situation: Your team is trying a new combi oven setting for a banquet, and several cooks are unsure how the steam cycle works.

options.text: I would show the controls, explain the cycle, and watch each cook practise safely.
I would demonstrate the steam cycle and let each cook practise a batch.
I would explain the cycle and leave a short instruction sheet by the oven.
I would share the setting and ask the cooks to follow the display prompts.

basic.situation: A new kitchen worker joins your shift and needs to learn how to handle raw chicken safely during prep.

options.text: I would show the handwashing steps and explain where raw chicken belongs.
I would point to the safety poster and ask the worker to read it.
I would let the worker copy nearby staff during the lunch rush.
I would demonstrate safe handling, then watch the worker practise and discuss any gaps.

advanced.situation: Several new workers start before a weekend rush, and recent shifts have had repeated handwashing and station setup errors.

options.text: I would plan short demonstrations, practice checks, and refreshers for each shift.
I would send a reminder about hygiene and station setup to the group.
I would pair new workers with whoever is free during each busy shift.
I would run one briefing before the rush and share the safety checklist.

basic.situation: You are assigned to portion curry and rice for a lunch service using the kitchen's printed production schedule.

options.text: I would use a familiar scoop size and adjust portions if food runs short.
I would check the schedule and portion each tray with the stated serving measure.
I would read the schedule and prepare the listed number of portions.
I would ask another cook how much curry they usually serve per plate.

advanced.situation: Your kitchen's stock count shows repeated cooking oil shortages, while several teams report spills and unclear bottle returns.

options.text: I would track issues by station, then set return and spill recording steps.
I would set a sign-out sheet for oil bottles and review it weekly.
I would remind each shift to return bottles and report any spills.
I would reduce the oil order and remind cooks to use less during prep.

basic.situation: After a busy lunch, you are asked to count the till and prepare the cash deposit with a manager nearby.

options.text: I would compare the till total with receipts, then prepare the deposit record.
I would use the till display as the deposit amount and complete the slip.
I would ask the cashier to confirm the amount before I seal the bag.
I would count the notes and coins, then tell the manager the total.

advanced.situation: A staff member questions a payroll deduction, and the shift cash records also show a mismatch from the previous evening.

options.text: I would change the deduction and cover the cash difference from today's takings.
I would ask the staff member to wait while I recount the current till.
I would separate the payroll query from the cash review and document both findings.
I would check the payroll record and recount the prior shift's cash documents.

basic.situation: A family arrives during a busy dinner service, and you need to greet them and seat them at an available table.

options.text: I would greet the family, check the table is ready, and seat them with menus.
I would point them toward an open table and bring menus when free.
I would ask them to wait by the entrance until a server notices.
I would greet them and guide them to the nearest available table.

advanced.situation: A guest says their meal arrived cold, while the dining area is busy and the team has missed its usual cleaning round.

options.text: I would explain the kitchen is busy and ask the guest to wait for service.
I would acknowledge the complaint, arrange a hot replacement, and assign a cleaning check.
I would apologise, replace the meal, and ask the team to resume cleaning.
I would offer to reheat the meal and remind staff to clean after service.

basic.situation: Before opening, you are checking a food warmer and notice crumbs around its controls and a loose plug.

options.text: I would wipe the warmer and test it during the first food holding round.
I would inspect the plug and cleanliness, then report the fault before use.
I would check the warmer's plug and clean the controls before opening.
I would ask a cook whether the warmer worked normally on the last shift.

advanced.situation: A supplier offers a new reusable food container, and your team needs to decide whether it suits daily kitchen service.

options.text: I would compare cleaning, durability, and kitchen fit before recommending the container.
I would accept the sample and let the busiest station decide after use.
I would test the container during a normal shift and gather team feedback.
I would trial one container and ask cooks whether it seems convenient.

basic.situation: You are counting dry goods before dinner and find fewer rice bags than the stock sheet lists.

options.text: I would check nearby storage before asking the storekeeper about the difference.
I would recount the rice, note the difference, and report it to the manager.
I would count the rice bags and tell the manager the recorded amount is short.
I would update the sheet to match the bags currently on the shelf.

advanced.situation: A service review shows repeated late orders and rushed table clearing, and you are asked to recommend a procedure change.

options.text: I would map order and clearing delays, then recommend clear handoff steps.
I would write up the slowest worker and ask the team to follow pace.
I would observe one busy shift and share the main delays with the manager.
I would ask the team to move faster and watch the next service.

options.text: I ask the customer to wait aside while I finish serving the queue.
I check the order, arrange its replacement, and update waiting customers.
I hand over another sandwich with the popular filling to settle things.
I apologise, confirm the filling, and ask the kitchen to remake it.

basic.situation: The shelf is low on takeaway cups before the lunch rush, and you have been asked to restock supplies.

options.text: I bring cups from storage and tell the manager the shelf needs restocking today.
I check the cup size, restock that shelf, and face remaining packs forward.
I fill the shelf with nearby cups and return to the counter.
I move cups from the next shelf to make this shelf appear fully stocked.

advanced.situation: The store often runs short of takeaway packaging on weekends, while unused stock takes up space in the storeroom.

options.text: I track weekend use and leftovers by item, then adjust order quantities.
I ask staff to use fewer packages until storeroom space frees up.
I order extra packaging in every size to cover the next weekend rush.
I count weekend use and recommend more of the size customers request most often.

basic.situation: You receive a latte order, but the cup size is unclear and the queue is growing. What do you do?

options.text: Make the regular size because most latte orders use that cup.
Ask a nearby barista which size this customer usually orders.
Check the recipe card, then confirm the cup size against the ticket.
Pause the drink and ask the customer to confirm the size.

advanced.situation: You are trialling a seasonal iced coffee before a busy weekend, and two colleagues make it with different sweetness. What do you do?

options.text: Ask each barista to adjust sweetness to their usual preference.
Set measured ratios, make a sample, and coach staff through the method.
Write down your preferred recipe and share it with the team.
Make another sample and ask the shift lead to choose a version.

basic.situation: A customer orders a muffin while you are serving bagels, and the display tongs have touched a nut pastry. What do you do?

options.text: Use those tongs quickly, since the muffin is already wrapped.
Use a fresh napkin to lift the muffin from the display.
Get clean tongs and check the muffin before handing it over.
Ask a coworker to serve it while you finish the bagels.

advanced.situation: You are preparing sandwiches for a rush and notice another staff member using the same board for raw vegetables and ready-to-serve fillings. What do you do?

options.text: Finish the current sandwiches, then mention the board after service.
Pause that prep, separate the boards, and reset the affected fillings.
Ask them to switch boards and continue with the current fillings.
Tell them to rinse the board before continuing with fillings.

basic.situation: A customer asks whether the house blend is strong, but you have only practised the menu description. What do you do?

options.text: Read the menu description aloud and ask what they prefer.
Say it is very strong so the customer can decide quickly.
Ask another barista what customers usually say about the blend.
Describe the listed roast and offer a familiar drink comparison.

advanced.situation: A new colleague is demonstrating the espresso machine, and a customer asks why their shot tastes different from yesterday's. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the customer today's beans are probably less fresh than yesterday's.
Coach the colleague to explain grind and shot variation, then check the current settings.
Show the colleague how to describe the shot, then offer a remake.
Ask the shift lead to answer while the colleague continues the demonstration.

basic.situation: You are entering a takeaway order during a rush, but the customer changes one drink before you send it to preparation. What do you do?

options.text: Update the order, repeat the drinks back, and send the revised ticket.
Send the first ticket and tell the barista about the change later.
Ask the customer to confirm the changed drink before you send it.
Change the drink on screen and send the ticket without repeating it.

advanced.situation: A customer says their card was charged twice, while the till shows one completed payment and another pending entry. What do you do?

options.text: Review both till entries and ask the shift lead to confirm the next step.
Check transaction records, explain the pending entry, and follow the refund process if needed.
Refund the pending amount to address the customer's concern before checking its status.
Show the completed payment, explain the pending entry, and suggest checking the account later.

basic.situation: You are restocking cups before the morning rush and find two sleeves with different sizes mixed together. What do you do?

options.text: Leave the sleeves nearby and ask the next barista to sort them.
Use the labels you can see and place the sleeves on separate shelves.
Separate the sizes, check the labels, and restock each shelf correctly.
Put both sleeves on the busiest shelf so staff can reach them.

advanced.situation: You are arranging a retail coffee display and notice one popular bean is nearly out, while a slower seller has several bags left. What do you do?

options.text: Move the slower bags forward and order extra popular beans by feel.
Rearrange the display so both beans have equal space and visibility.
Give the popular bean more space and tell the manager it is running low.
Face the popular bean clearly, check stock records, and suggest a reorder quantity.

basic.situation: You finish steaming milk and see residue on the wand while the next drink is waiting. What do you do?

options.text: Steam briefly to clear the residue, then start the next drink.
Wipe and sanitise the wand using the station's cleaning method before steaming again.
Wipe the wand with a clean cloth before making the next drink.
Ask a coworker to clean the wand while you start the next order.

advanced.situation: You check the refrigerator during a shift and its reading is outside the store's safe range, with dated sandwiches inside. What do you do?

options.text: Record the reading, alert the shift lead, and follow the store's food-hold procedure.
Reset the dial and keep selling the sandwiches during the rush.
Move the sandwiches to another refrigerator and tell the next shift.
Hold the sandwiches and ask the shift lead what the reading means.

basic.situation: You are setting a table for two and notice one place setting is missing a clean glass. What do you do?

options.text: Bring a clean glass and check both settings against the table standard.
Ask a coworker to bring a glass while you finish the cutlery.
Use a glass from the next table, which is already set.
Bring a clean glass and place it at the empty setting.

advanced.situation: A large party is due soon, and you are clearing a nearby table while a new colleague prepares its linens and glassware. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the colleague the usual layout and clear the dishes for them.
Agree on sections, clear dishes to the kitchen, then check the full setup together.
Stack the dishes at the table edge so the colleague can keep setting.
Clear the dishes and let the colleague finish the remaining place settings.

basic.situation: You are preparing a cold drink and salad, but the service station has run low on clean napkins and cream. What do you do?

options.text: Ask a coworker to bring napkins while you finish the drink.
Borrow cream from a nearby table and finish the drink first.
Finish the salad and tell a coworker the station needs supplies.
Restock napkins and cream from the service supplies before finishing both orders.

advanced.situation: You are portioning desserts for service and notice two plates from a colleague are much larger than the menu portion. What do you do?

options.text: Serve the larger portions, since guests may welcome an extra dessert.
Check the portion guide, reset plates, and show your colleague the serving measure.
Tell your colleague the portions seem large and ask them to adjust.
Show your colleague a portioned plate as a guide before service continues.

basic.situation: A guest asks whether today's soup contains dairy, but the menu lists only its name. What do you do?

options.text: Say it is probably dairy-free because it is a vegetable soup.
Check the kitchen's ingredient information before describing the soup to the guest.
Tell the guest the menu does not list its ingredients.
Ask the kitchen whether dairy is used, then pass on its answer.

advanced.situation: A new colleague is explaining a daily special, and a guest asks how it is prepared and whether it suits their dietary needs. What do you do?

options.text: Check preparation details with the kitchen, then coach your colleague to explain them clearly.
Suggest your colleague start by describing the dish from its menu card.
Tell the guest it is popular, without checking whether it suits their needs.
Ask the kitchen about preparation, then explain the details to the guest.

basic.situation: You are writing down a table's order, but one guest changes their side dish before you send the slips to the kitchen. What do you do?

options.text: Cross out the side and write the new choice on the slip.
Ask the guest to confirm the new side before sending the slip.
Update the slip, repeat the changed order, and send the revised details.
Send the first slip and mention the side change when food arrives.

advanced.situation: A guest questions a bill that includes two coffees, though they recall ordering one, and the kitchen is still checking the table's order slip. What do you do?

options.text: Ask what the guest recalls, then adjust the check to match their account.
Check the slip and bill, then clarify the count with the guest.
Wait for the order slip check, then discuss the extra coffee with the guest.
Remove the second coffee from the check to finish the payment quickly.

basic.situation: You are sweeping near the server station and notice a wet patch where guests are walking. What do you do?

options.text: Ask a coworker to mop while you finish sweeping nearby.
Place a caution sign beside the patch and finish the nearby sweep.
Keep guests clear, dry the patch, and resume sweeping the station area.
Sweep around the patch so the floor work stays on schedule.

advanced.situation: You are checking the cleaning rota and see the same floor area marked complete twice, though the server station still has rubbish. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the assigned server whether the rubbish remains and request an update.
Ask the assigned server to clear the rubbish, then verify the station before closing.
Clear the rubbish and update the rota to reflect the work.
Mark the station complete so the rota remains current for closing today.

basic.situation: You are escorting a guest to a table when they mention that it is not the seat they requested. What do you do?

options.text: Seat them at the nearest open table to keep the entrance clear for guests.
Ask the guest which available table they would prefer for now.
Check with the host, then guide the guest to a matching table.
Apologise, then ask the host to find another table for the guest.

advanced.situation: A guest tells you their meal is late and speaks sharply while you are seating another party. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the guest the kitchen is busy and they should wait a little longer.
Acknowledge the delay, check the order status, and give the guest a clear update.
Apologise and ask a coworker to check the order when free.
Tell the guest you will check with the kitchen after seating the party.

basic.situation: You are about to send a meal cart to a ward. The tray list shows which items each recipient should receive.

options.text: I scan the list and flag missing items before delivery.
I send the trays together, trusting the kitchen's usual portions.
I match each tray to the list and hold any mismatch for correction.
I check the first tray and assume the remaining trays follow it.

advanced.situation: During lunch service, you notice a colleague using the same tongs for a special-diet meal and regular food.

options.text: I remind my colleague to use clean utensils for the special meal.
I replace the tongs and ask my colleague to keep them separate.
I finish nearby orders, then check whether my colleague changes utensils.
I pause service, replace the tongs, and review the separate serving method.

basic.situation: A lunch order asks for one sandwich, fruit and a drink on a tray. You are plating the order at the counter.

options.text: I place the listed portions on the tray and check the order slip.
I ask a colleague which fruit usually goes with that sandwich.
I plate the usual sandwich set and add a drink for speed.
I follow the slip while plating, then pass the tray onward.

advanced.situation: You are preparing soup and salad for a catered lunch when the soup thickens faster than expected and orders are waiting.

options.text: I add a large splash of water to restore the soup's flow.
I adjust the soup with measured liquid, taste it, and check its serving consistency.
I add a little stock and stir before continuing the salad orders.
I pause the soup and ask the kitchen lead to check its texture.

basic.situation: You are loading a meal tray for a resident, and the setup list calls for a spoon, napkin and condiment.

options.text: I load the listed items and check the tray.
I add a napkin and spoon, since those are usually enough.
I follow the setup list and place each accessory beside the meal.
I ask a colleague whether the condiment is needed on this tray.

advanced.situation: Before a busy lunch, you see the service station's napkin stack running low while the nearby counter remains stocked.

options.text: I leave the station unchanged until someone asks for extra napkins during lunch.
I refill the low stack from the nearby counter before service starts.
I tell the shift lead that napkins may run short at lunch.
I compare both stations with expected demand and shift stock where needed.

basic.situation: You have one tray of clean linen to carry from the service room to a nearby dining area.

options.text: I balance the tray on one hand while opening the service room door carefully.
I carry the tray steadily to the dining area and set it down.
I carry the tray along the clear route and set it down.
I wait for another worker to carry the tray with me.

advanced.situation: Two meal carts and a stack of used trays need moving through a busy corridor as residents leave lunch.

options.text: I stagger the carts and gather used trays once foot traffic thins.
I push both carts through together, expecting diners to move around them.
I collect used trays while both carts wait beside the doorway.
I move carts separately and ask a coworker to gather used trays.

basic.situation: A patron orders tea and a tuna sandwich at the counter. You need to relay the order to the kitchen.

options.text: I tell the kitchen to prepare the usual lunch set for that patron.
I ask the patron to repeat the order while the queue grows.
I confirm the order aloud and relay it to the kitchen.
I write both items down and pass the note to the kitchen.

advanced.situation: The kitchen log shows five special meals served, but your tally shows four and the next meal round is starting.

options.text: I change the log to match my tally so the counts agree.
I compare notes and tally, then record the confirmed count before service.
I check the meal tickets and update my tally if they support five.
I leave both figures recorded and mention the mismatch at handover.

basic.situation: A patron arrives for lunch and asks where they may sit. Several tables are available in the dining room.

options.text: I ask a colleague which table is usually kept for new arrivals.
I ask their seating preference and point out available tables.
I show them an open table and ask whether that suits them.
I direct them to the nearest table because it is already clear.

advanced.situation: A patron using a walking frame says the usual dining chairs are difficult to reach around in the crowded lunch area.

options.text: I ask what space would help, then arrange an accessible seat with a clear approach.
I move a chair aside and offer a seat near the aisle.
I guide them to the nearest open chair to keep the queue moving.
I ask a colleague to find a suitable place while I serve others.

basic.situation: Before lunch, you are setting a table for four using clean linens, condiments and the dining room checklist.

options.text: I ask a coworker to confirm where the condiments are kept.
I set the linens and condiments from the checklist, then check each place setting.
I place the clean linens and listed condiments at each table.
I use the usual table layout and add condiments near the centre.

advanced.situation: A new attendant is serving coffee during a crowded lunch, but several tables have not received water or rolls.

options.text: I ask the floor lead to take over the attendant's tables.
I tell the attendant to serve coffee faster so the queue moves.
I cover waiting tables and explain the service sequence to the attendant afterward.
I show the attendant how to scan tables while balancing coffee orders.

basic.situation: After a table finishes lunch, you see dirty plates, cutlery and cups ready to be taken to the kitchen.

options.text: I carry the full stack straight through so the table clears quickly.
I stack the dishes carefully and take them to the kitchen.
I scrape the plates, stack dishes securely, and carry them to the kitchen.
I take the cups first and leave the plates for another trip.

advanced.situation: During the lunch rush, dirty dishes are building up beside a narrow walkway used by customers and staff.

options.text: I ask a coworker to watch the walkway while I stack dishes nearby.
I stack all the dishes beside the walkway until the rush passes.
I clear dishes in small batches and keep the walkway open between trips.
I carry a full load to the kitchen and return for the rest.

basic.situation: After lunch, you are assigned to wipe a table and its seats before the next customers arrive.

options.text: I wipe the tabletop quickly and leave the seats for later.
I ask a coworker whether the seats need wiping too.
I wipe the tabletop and seats with the assigned cloth, then check them.
I clean the tabletop and seats with the damp cloth as instructed.

advanced.situation: A supervisor asks you to prepare the dining area for service, and you notice crumbs on tables and a sticky patch near the counter.

options.text: I clean the tables and floor patch, then check both areas.
I ask another attendant to inspect the room while I get the cleaning supplies.
I wipe the tables and mop the patch before customers return.
I mop the sticky patch and leave the tables for the next round.

basic.situation: The kitchen has finished a tray of meals for the serving counter, and you are asked to carry it there.

options.text: I carry the tray to the counter and place it beside other prepared meals.
I wait for a coworker to carry the tray with me.
I hurry the tray through the doorway to keep service moving.
I carry the tray steadily to the counter and set it down.

advanced.situation: Several cafeteria patrons are waiting for trays while a restocking cart blocks the shortest route between the counter and tables.

options.text: I take the open aisle for each delivery and return for the next tray.
I squeeze past the cart with each tray to save walking time.
I use the open aisle, group nearby deliveries, and keep the counter route clear.
I ask a coworker to move the cart while patrons keep waiting.

basic.situation: Before service, you are assigned to refill the beverage dispenser and restock the condiment cabinet.

options.text: I refill the beverage dispenser and stock the condiment cabinet before service.
I fill the dispenser and leave the cabinet for another shift.
I refill both from listed supplies, then check their levels before service.
I ask a coworker which cabinet usually needs the most condiments before stocking.

advanced.situation: A busy lunch is approaching, and you notice clean glasses are running low while the linen shelf remains well stocked.

options.text: I leave the glasses until servers begin asking for more.
I compare glass use with remaining stock and refill the service area.
I tell the shift lead the glass shelf looks low before lunch service.
I bring another rack of glasses to the service area now.

basic.situation: A couple arrives at the dining room entrance, and you are responsible for greeting and seating arriving customers.

options.text: I point them toward an open table, then return to clearing.
I greet them, ask their seating preference, then guide them to a table.
I ask a coworker to seat them while I finish my assigned task.
I welcome them and show them an available table near the dining room entrance.

advanced.situation: A customer asks for a menu item you cannot locate while the waiter is carrying several orders and another table needs help.

options.text: I check nearby serving areas and update the customer while arranging help.
I tell the customer to wait until the waiter has finished serving.
I check the usual storage spots and tell the customer what I find.
I ask the waiter to find the item after completing the orders.

basic.situation: A rack of glasses and plates arrives during lunch, and you are still learning the dishwasher controls. What do you do?

options.text: Load the glasses with plates and run the usual cycle to clear the rack.
Rinse each glass by hand first, then use the dishwasher's standard cycle.
Use the glassware rack and the marked cycle, then check the clean results.
Check the labels, separate glassware, and ask a colleague to confirm the cycle.

advanced.situation: A new colleague is washing delicate serving glasses with heavy pans, and the dinner service starts soon. How do you train them?

options.text: Tell them to use the glass rack and watch how the next load turns out.
Ask them to finish the mixed load first, then discuss delicate glasses after service.
Show how to separate delicate pieces, choose their rack, and check the cycle instructions.
Demonstrate the glass rack and have them wash one small load while you observe.

basic.situation: After a spill near the dish station, the floor is sticky while staff carry hot trays nearby. What do you do?

options.text: Sweep the area quickly and let the next shift know about the sticky patch.
Ask a nearby colleague to watch the area while you scrub and dry it.
Block the wet patch, scrub it with the approved cleaner, then dry the floor.
Mop around the spill so staff can keep using the dish station.

advanced.situation: Your agreed cleaning schedule leaves the dish station busy at the same time as floor scrubbing, and staff are skipping checks. What do you do?

options.text: Move floor scrubbing to a quieter period and review the checklist with staff.
Ask staff to clean whichever kitchen area looks busiest during their shift.
Map busy periods, stagger cleaning tasks, and add a simple sign-off for each area.
Keep the schedule unchanged and remind each shift to complete its listed checks.

basic.situation: The kitchen bins are full, and you are unsure which bags belong at the designated pickup area. What do you do?

options.text: Tie all the bags together and take them to the nearest collection point.
Check the bin labels, sort the bags, and confirm the pickup area with a colleague.
Put the full bags beside the bins until someone confirms where they belong.
Follow the labels on each bin and take the separated bags to pickup.

advanced.situation: A new waste label has confused the team, and pickup is due before the dinner rush. How do you manage the bins and removal?

options.text: Tell staff to use the familiar bins and send the bags before service.
Hold the unclear bags aside and remove the clearly sorted waste to pickup.
Clarify the label with the designated contact, brief staff, and check sorted bags before pickup.
Post the new label near the bins and check the bags before moving them.

basic.situation: Clean plates are ready to store, but the usual shelf is crowded with cooking equipment. What do you do?

options.text: Store the plates on the clear labeled shelf and keep them separated from cookware.
Place the plates on the open counter and tell the next shift where they are.
Check the labeled shelf space, make room safely, and ask where overflow belongs.
Stack the plates on top of the equipment to free the wash area.

advanced.situation: Deliveries arrive while clean utensils are being stored, and staff keep blocking the same cupboard. How do you improve stocking?

options.text: Put the new delivery wherever space appears and let staff sort it later.
Move everything to the nearest free cupboard and ask staff to remember the change.
Mark separate cupboard shelves for utensils and deliveries, then explain the labels.
Review access and labels, group frequently used items, then show staff the agreed layout.

basic.situation: A colleague asks you to move a light box of napkins from storage to the serving station during a busy shift. What do you do?

options.text: Wait until the corridor clears, then carry the box to the station.
Check the route, keep the box close, and ask a colleague to clear the doorway.
Carry the box along the clear route and place it at the serving station.
Take a hand truck for the box and wheel it through the crowded dining room.

advanced.situation: Two supply carts need to reach separate work areas before service, and a new staff member is unsure how to lift a crate. What do you do?

options.text: Plan clear routes, split cart loads sensibly, and demonstrate a safe team lift for the crate.
Use the hand truck for the crate and ask the new worker to follow you.
Send the new staff member with the heavier crate while you take the cart.
Carry the crate together after the carts arrive, keeping the supplies grouped by area.

basic.situation: You are asked to rinse a basket of apples for service, but the sink is also used for dirty utensils. What do you do?

options.text: Use the food preparation sink, rinse apples, and check them for visible soil.
Ask a colleague to identify the designated sink, then rinse the apples there before service.
Wait for the utensil sink to clear, then rinse the apples in it.
Rinse apples in the shared sink between utensil loads to save time.

advanced.situation: During a busy prep shift, staff use different methods to wash leafy vegetables, and some leaves still show grit. How do you guide the work?

options.text: Ask each worker to rinse leaves until they look clean, then start service.
Agree a consistent wash method, demonstrate it, and check a sample for remaining grit.
Demonstrate the usual wash method and ask staff to follow it for the next batch.
Keep serving the prepared leaves and review washing methods after the rush.

basic.situation: Two groups arrive together, and you are still learning which tables are ready. How do you greet and seat them?

options.text: Seat the first group at the nearest open table and greet the second afterward.
Point both groups toward open tables and let them choose where to sit.
Greet both groups, then seat them at the next tables shown as available.
Welcome both groups, check the ready table list, and confirm their party sizes.

advanced.situation: A queue forms during the dinner rush, and one server already has several new tables. How do you manage rotation?

options.text: Seat the next group wherever a table opens so the queue keeps moving.
Follow the rotation list and note which server receives each new party.
Check each server's current tables, then assign the next suitable table by rotation.
Give the next group to the server who handled the last large party.

basic.situation: A caller asks for a table for six on Friday, but you are still learning the reservation book. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the caller to ring back while you find someone familiar with reservations.
Write down the name and time, then check availability before confirming the booking.
Tell the caller the requested time is probably available and write it down.
Check the book for space, then ask a colleague to help record the details.

advanced.situation: A caller wants a large takeaway order with a food request the kitchen may need to confirm, while the phone keeps ringing. What do you do?

options.text: Take the order and request, then ask the kitchen whether it can be prepared.
Ask the caller to hold while you answer the ringing phone and seek help.
Take the order details, promise the requested change, and pass it to the kitchen.
Record the items and request, check the kitchen's response, then confirm timing and details.

basic.situation: A guest sits down and looks around for a menu while you are clearing nearby tables. What do you do?

options.text: Point toward the menu stand and continue clearing the nearby tables.
Bring the guest a menu and mention that you can answer questions about it.
Take a menu to the guest, then return to clearing the nearby tables.
Ask another guest at the table to pass over a menu.

advanced.situation: A guest asks what your café is known for, and you know several specialties but are unsure about one ingredient. What do you say?

options.text: Describe confirmed specialties and check the ingredient detail before advising the guest.
Name a familiar dish and describe its known ingredients without claiming special status.
Recommend a popular dish and explain that you can verify its ingredients for them.
Share confirmed specialties and offer the menu so the guest can compare choices.

basic.situation: You are checking the dining area before opening and find crumbs on a table beside a newly set place. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the opening team about the crumbs and continue checking other tables.
Wipe the crumbs away and ask a colleague to check the place setting.
Use the checklist, reset the table, and mark it ready after checking the place setting.
Brush the crumbs onto the floor and leave the place setting in place.

advanced.situation: New staff have missed restroom supply checks twice this week, and the dining area checklist is also inconsistent. How do you guide inspections?

options.text: Walk staff through both inspection areas and point out the supplies to verify.
Set a shared checklist for dining and restroom checks, demonstrate it, and review sign-offs.
Leave restroom supplies for the next shift and focus on the dining area checklist.
Remind the team to check restrooms and dining tables before each shift begins.

basic.situation: A guest pauses after a meal and says the service felt slow, while your section is busy. What do you do?

options.text: Acknowledge the wait, ask what would help, and pass their concern to the server.
Offer a brief apology and assure the guest the next course will be quick.
Say the kitchen is busy and return to your other tables.
Apologize for the delay and let the server know the guest was waiting.

advanced.situation: A guest says their order differs from what they requested, and the server and kitchen give different accounts. How do you handle the complaint?

options.text: Hear the guest's account, apologize for the mix-up, and ask the server to follow up.
Tell the guest the kitchen followed the ticket and ask them to speak with the server.
Ask the guest to wait while you finish seating the next arriving party.
Listen, confirm the requested details, coordinate with the server and kitchen, then update the guest.

basic.situation: A server is handling several tables while finished plates remain on one table. You have a moment to help. What do you do?

options.text: Wait until the server finishes, then ask whether they need any help.
Clear finished plates, check what else is needed, and update the server.
Move the plates to another table for the server to collect when available.
Clear finished plates, then return to your assigned station and continue service.

advanced.situation: During a busy seating, one server is waiting for drinks while another has several new tables. How do you coordinate the dining room?

options.text: Tell both servers to serve their tables in arrival order and check back later.
Review immediate table needs, redistribute available support, and keep guests updated on waits.
Ask the waiting server to help the other server before returning to drinks.
Send the busiest server to clear tables while the other handles new guests.

basic.situation: Two cleaners call in sick before a busy morning shift. You are helping prepare the schedule for a hospital ward that needs regular cleaning.

options.text: Move the available cleaners across wards and tell each person the revised start time.
Prioritise ward coverage, assign available staff by need, and confirm the revised schedule with them.
Ask one cleaner to stay late and fill the two gaps after lunch.
Keep the original schedule and ask the present team to cover every ward.

advanced.situation: A new infection-control procedure changes cleaning order in several wards, while staffing is tight. You need to brief the team and adjust today's assignments.

options.text: Brief cleaners on the new order and move staff between affected wards.
Map ward priorities and staffing, then brief cleaners on each changed sequence and duty.
Ask an experienced cleaner to cover the procedure while others use today's schedule.
Share the procedure in chat, but leave today's ward assignments unchanged.

basic.situation: A cleaner asks which product to use on a newly installed floor, and the usual detergent label does not mention that surface.

options.text: Check product guidance and ask the supplier whether it suits this floor.
Confirm a compatible product from surface guidance and share the choice with staff.
Use the usual detergent at a weaker mix, then inspect the floor afterward.
Test a small amount in a corner before treating the whole floor.

advanced.situation: A supervisor asks you to recommend a staffing level for a month with several public events and a tight supply budget.

options.text: Use last month's staffing level and order the same stock quantity.
Review event dates and recent usage, then recommend adjusted staffing and stock levels.
Share the event calendar and ask the supervisor what level to plan for.
Add a few extra shifts and supplies to cover the busiest event days.

basic.situation: During your cleaning shift, a floor machine begins vibrating more than usual. You are asked to help check the equipment before it is used again.

options.text: Ask a colleague to try the machine on a different floor first.
Wipe the machine down and return it to the charging area for the next shift.
Stop using it, check the visible parts, and tell the equipment lead about the vibration.
Tag the machine for checking, record the vibration, and note which task preceded it.

advanced.situation: Management requests a monthly report on cleaning hours, facility use, and work completed across several buildings. One site's timesheets are incomplete.

options.text: Estimate missing hours from typical weeks and submit the monthly report.
Reconcile verified figures with the site lead, noting any gaps and limits.
Hold the report until every site sends complete timesheets for review.
Submit available figures, marking the missing timesheets and affected totals clearly.

basic.situation: After a cleaner finishes a lobby, you inspect the area and notice streaks on a glass entrance beside the main walkway.

options.text: Ask the cleaner to recheck the glass and confirm when it is done.
Mark the glass for touch-up, explain the finish standard, and recheck before sign-off.
Wipe the glass yourself so the lobby is ready on time.
Accept the lobby and mention the streaks at the next team briefing.

advanced.situation: A clinic reports recurring odour after cleaning, and your inspection finds damp flooring near a service cupboard. The source is not obvious.

options.text: Mask the odour with a stronger cleaner before the clinic session begins again.
Record the complaint, inspect nearby areas, and schedule a follow-up check.
Inspect nearby surfaces, restrict access if needed, and report repair concerns.
Ask the cleaner to repeat the process and check whether odour returns.

basic.situation: A reception clerk asks whether a room is ready, while maintenance is still checking a leaking tap and housekeeping has finished cleaning.

options.text: Confirm tap clearance with maintenance and update reception on the room status.
Ask maintenance for an update and tell reception the room remains pending.
Tell reception housekeeping has finished, leaving them to decide whether the room can open.
Tell reception room ready because housekeeping finished, without checking if maintenance cleared the tap leak.

advanced.situation: Two cleaners disagree about a shared corridor handover, and a department manager asks whether the floor can reopen before a scheduled service.

options.text: Hear both accounts, confirm handover duties, and update the manager on readiness.
Ask both cleaners to clarify the corridor handover before service starts.
Tell the manager the corridor seems ready, and ask cleaners to finish promptly.
Ask each cleaner what remains, then tell the manager readiness is still unconfirmed.

basic.situation: A cleaner requests more disinfectant before a busy shift, and you are helping issue supplies from the store room.

options.text: Give the requested bottle and record it against the team's supply issue.
Issue a full spare carton so the cleaner can avoid another trip to stores.
Check needs and stock, issue a suitable amount, and update the supply log.
Tell the cleaner to take a bottle from the nearest unlocked cupboard.

advanced.situation: Your stock count shows gloves running low before a series of busy shifts, while one team has several unopened boxes in its cupboard.

options.text: Check expected demand, transfer surplus boxes, and revise the stock record.
Move unopened boxes to the busiest team and update the stock count afterward.
Wait until gloves run out, then request an urgent delivery.
Order the usual quantity and let each team manage its own cupboard stock.

basic.situation: You finish checking a park bed and notice the edging looks uneven. Your supervisor asks you to compare the work with the agreed standard.

options.text: You ask the crew lead whether the edging meets the agreed standard.
You walk the beds with your supervisor and list visible differences.
You sign off the section because most of the edging looks even.
You check each bed against the specification and mark exact sections for correction.

advanced.situation: Discolored shrubs keep appearing along one walkway after earlier treatment. You inspect the affected area and need to decide what treatment to order.

options.text: You identify the visible symptoms and order a treatment used for similar beds.
You ask the supplier to suggest a spray for the discolored plants.
You order a broad spray across the whole site to clear the discoloration.
You map affected plants, confirm the pattern, then order targeted treatment and follow-up checks.

basic.situation: A new worker is assigned to mow a small lawn while you oversee the morning crew. You need to give clear direction on the task.

options.text: You tell the worker to follow the mower tracks from yesterday.
You let the worker choose a route and check the lawn later.
You show the worker the mowing boundary and explain the expected finish.
You ask an experienced worker to explain the mowing route and pace.

advanced.situation: The crew is behind schedule because its trimmer keeps stopping, and another site needs work today. You can recommend an equipment change.

options.text: You ask the crew to share the working trimmer between the two sites.
You request a replacement trimmer matching the crew's usual model.
You keep the crew on the faulty trimmer until its scheduled service.
You compare downtime and task needs, then recommend a suitable backup trimmer.

basic.situation: A work assignment covers new planting beside a walkway. You review it before the crew starts and need to identify basic material needs.

options.text: You list the plants and supplies named in the work assignment.
You check the assignment quantities against the planting areas and list needed materials.
You order the usual plants and soil mix for a similar bed.
You ask the supplier to send the standard planting bundle for the site.

advanced.situation: A new landscaped area needs sprinkler coverage, but the layout includes different bed widths and a long pipe run. You must plan the system.

options.text: You sketch pipe routes and estimate pressure from the longest run.
You draft a pipe route and ask the installer to flag pressure concerns.
You map bed coverage, calculate pressure needs, and place valves for each zone.
You copy the valve layout from a nearby landscaped area.

basic.situation: A resident asks whether your crew can prune shrubs beside a walkway and what materials the work uses. You have the service details nearby.

options.text: You share the usual method and offer to confirm material details later.
You quote a familiar package price and say it covers the pruning.
You describe the pruning method and materials listed for this service.
You give a broad price range based on recent pruning jobs.

advanced.situation: A park event needs lawn care while another unit plans work on the same grounds. You coordinate with the other supervisor to prevent clashes.

options.text: You ask the event team to choose which unit should work first.
You tell the other supervisor your crew's planned work and ask about theirs.
You move your crew's schedule to fit the event without checking the other unit.
You align both work plans around event access, shared areas, and crew timing.

basic.situation: At the end of a shift, a worker submits a time sheet with one unclear work-hour entry. You are processing the crew's daily records.

options.text: You fill the gap with the scheduled hours and file the time sheet.
You use the crew's usual shift length to complete the missing hours.
You enter the hours from the sheet and mark the unclear entry for review.
You check the worker's shift notes and confirm the unclear hours before processing.

advanced.situation: A worker nearly slips while using a powered tool on wet paving. You are updating the crew's operating procedures and safety standards.

options.text: You remind the crew to watch their footing around wet paving.
You let each worker decide when wet paving feels safe for tool use.
You add a wet-surface procedure, explain it at briefing, and check crew practice.
You ask the crew lead to share a safety reminder at the next briefing.

basic.situation: A newly planted bed looks dry during your morning round. You are supervising the crew and need to arrange routine watering.

options.text: You ask a worker to water the bed and follow the planting notes.
You ask the crew to spray the entire bed lightly during their round.
You schedule watering for the next grounds round and tell the crew.
You water the bed yourself, then check soil moisture near the new plants.

advanced.situation: A walkway edge has cracked beside a landscaped bed, and the repair needs a new cement curb. You are assigned to carry out the installation.

options.text: You pour the curb along the old edge and smooth the surface.
You check the line and levels, prepare the base, then pour and finish the curb.
You set a string line and pour the curb to match the walkway.
You clear loose material and ask a teammate to check the curb line.

basic.situation: You are assigned to mop a small office corridor after lunch. The floor has ordinary foot marks and your team lead has left the standard supplies.

options.text: You use a damp mop across the corridor and refill the bucket once.
You check the floor and mop it using the supplied routine.
You sweep loose dirt, then mop the corridor with the labeled floor solution.
You polish the corridor with the strongest cleaner in the store cupboard.

advanced.situation: A polished floor has dull patches after routine cleaning, and the corridor includes both tile and sealed timber. You must choose a cleaning method.

options.text: You scrub both floor types with a familiar abrasive pad to lift the dullness.
You test a suitable method on each surface and check the finish before proceeding.
You ask a coworker which product has worked on similar corridors.
You use the same neutral cleaner across both floor types for consistency.

basic.situation: You are cleaning a restroom before the afternoon rush. The mirror has water spots, and the supply checklist shows the usual glass cleaner and cloths.

options.text: You ask another cleaner to confirm the mirror looks clear after wiping.
You clean the mirror with the supplied glass cleaner and cloth.
You apply the glass cleaner, wipe the mirror, and inspect it from the doorway.
You wipe the mirror with a dry cloth and leave the spots for later.

advanced.situation: A busy restroom has repeated queues, and the glass partitions show marks soon after cleaning. You are arranging the service checks during a public event.

options.text: You add extra restroom checks but leave glass cleaning until the end.
You set checks around event peaks and clean marked glass during each visit.
You clean the partitions once and restock supplies at closing time.
You ask event staff when the restroom seems busiest and adjust visits.

basic.situation: You need to prepare a cleaning solution for a marked floor. The bottle label gives dilution instructions, and your lead asks you to follow them.

options.text: You ask a coworker to check the amount before filling the bucket.
You use a little extra detergent to help lift the floor marks.
You pour detergent into the bucket and adjust it by appearance.
You measure water and detergent to match the bottle instructions.

advanced.situation: A coworker wants to use a stronger mix on a stained fixture, but the product may affect its finish. You are asked how to prepare and use it.

options.text: You suggest a stronger mix and a quick wipe on the fixture.
You ask the coworker to use the usual restroom cleaner on the stain.
You recommend the labeled mix and ask the coworker to try a small area.
You check the product directions, confirm fixture suitability, and explain the labeled dilution.

basic.situation: You are collecting rubbish from a small office wing and notice the bin liners are running low. Your shift lead asks you to keep the area ready.

options.text: You gather the full bins and request liners using the supply list.
You borrow liners from another wing and empty the bins first.
You collect the rubbish and note the low liner stock for replenishment.
You leave the nearly full bins until the next collection round.

advanced.situation: Several floors generate more rubbish during a conference, while liner stock is falling faster than usual. You need to plan collection and supplies for the shift.

options.text: You delay collection until bins are full to stretch the available liners.
You adjust rounds around busy areas and request liners using recent usage.
You keep the usual rounds and request the standard weekly liner amount.
You add a round near the conference rooms and check stock later.

basic.situation: At closing, you are assigned to check an office wing before leaving. A desk appliance is still plugged in, and several doors need checking.

options.text: You walk the wing with the closing sheet and note any door still open.
You check the appliance use and lock the doors listed on the closing sheet.
You check the appliance and ask a coworker which doors remain open.
You lock the nearest doors and leave the appliance for morning staff.

advanced.situation: You find a frayed extension cord powering a floor polisher in a busy corridor. People are passing nearby, and you are responsible for safety checks.

options.text: You report the cord at shift end and place a note nearby.
You report the cord and ask the operator to finish the nearby section.
You tell the operator about the cord and ask them to watch it.
You stop using the appliance, keep people clear, and report the hazard promptly.

basic.situation: You need to move a light box of paper supplies to a nearby storeroom. You also notice a loose door handle during your cleaning round.

options.text: You carry the box with a clear path and report the loose handle.
You move the box and mention the handle to a coworker later.
You leave the box in the corridor and note the handle on your sheet.
You ask a coworker to move the box while you record the handle issue.

advanced.situation: A storeroom door no longer closes properly, and deliveries are due soon. You notice the frame shifting while moving supplies nearby.

options.text: You push the frame back and continue moving supplies through the doorway.
You report the shifting frame and explain how it affects storeroom access.
You move the deliveries to another area and mention the door after the rush.
You tell the manager the door is difficult and ask about repair timing.

basic.situation: You are asked to polish wooden furniture, but the product label is unfamiliar and guests arrive soon. What do you do?

options.text: I check the label, test a hidden spot, then polish.
I ask a colleague which cloth suits the wooden furniture.
I use the usual spray across every surface to save time.
I dampen one cloth and polish each item as I go.

advanced.situation: A busy lobby needs waxing, and a new cleaner is unsure how to use the floor machine safely before the next shift. What do you do?

options.text: I let the cleaner follow the last shift's routine to keep work moving.
I explain the machine controls and stay nearby while they practise.
I demonstrate the machine on a small area and explain safe waxing steps.
I show the cleaner where to wax and ask them to copy me.

basic.situation: You are vacuuming a guest-room rug and notice a loose thread near the edge. The room must be ready shortly. What do you do?

options.text: I vacuum gently around the thread and report the snag for follow-up.
I ask a colleague whether the vacuum can handle the loose thread.
I move the rug aside and finish the room before telling anyone.
I vacuum quickly over the whole rug so the room is ready.

advanced.situation: Several carpeted rooms need deep cleaning before a large group arrives, and staff disagree about which areas to prioritise. What do you do?

options.text: I assign each cleaner a room and let them choose their own method.
I ask staff to list their rooms, then set a shared order.
I start with the dirtiest carpet and tell others to follow suit.
I map the affected rooms, agree priorities, and brief staff on the cleaning sequence.

basic.situation: You are replenishing guest-room towels and find fewer clean towels than the checklist requires. The next room is due soon. What do you do?

options.text: I count the towels, note the shortage, and restock from the linen closet.
I borrow towels from another cart and tell its attendant later.
I place the towels already on the cart and move to the next room.
I check the closet stock and ask a colleague to bring more towels.

advanced.situation: You are guiding a team restocking several floors, but linen counts differ from the inventory sheet and demand is rising. What do you do?

options.text: I split the available linen evenly among floors to finish quickly.
I send extra linen to the busiest floor and leave the sheet unchanged.
I recount key linen types, update the sheet, and allocate stock by floor demand.
I ask each floor to report what it needs before moving stock.

basic.situation: You are loading a washing machine and find a mixed pile of towels and delicate garments. A colleague is waiting for the next load. What do you do?

options.text: I remove the delicate items and wash the towels on their regular cycle.
I load everything together on the usual cycle to keep laundry moving.
I ask the colleague to sort the pile while I prepare another load.
I separate the garments by care needs and check labels before loading.

advanced.situation: A new cleaner's iron leaves marks on a garment, and several guest items are waiting. How do you guide the cleaner?

options.text: I demonstrate on another garment and watch the cleaner repeat the technique.
I move the marked garment aside and finish the rest of the ironing.
I tell the cleaner to use less pressure and continue with the waiting items.
I pause ironing, check the garment label and iron settings, then demonstrate a safe test.

basic.situation: You are moving clean towels and supplies to guest rooms, but your wheeled cart is crowded in a busy corridor. What do you do?

options.text: I carry the loose items by hand and leave the cart parked nearby.
I secure the load, clear the cart path, and move supplies room by room.
I ask a colleague to walk ahead while I steer the loaded cart.
I stack the remaining supplies high and push quickly before guests pass.

advanced.situation: You are helping prepare a meeting room with furniture and media equipment, but the event layout has changed and the team is short-staffed. What do you do?

options.text: I move the large tables first and fit the equipment into remaining space.
I ask a colleague to handle the equipment while I move the furniture.
I arrange the furniture as last time and ask the organiser to adjust later.
I confirm the revised layout, divide setup tasks, and check clear access paths.

basic.situation: You are emptying room wastebaskets and find broken glass mixed with paper. The disposal area is down the corridor. What do you do?

options.text: I separate the glass from the paper and alert the housekeeping lead.
I ask a colleague to watch the corridor while I carry the bag carefully.
I tie the bag tightly and carry it to disposal with the other trash.
I keep others clear, contain the glass safely, and take it for proper disposal.

advanced.situation: During a safety walk, you find a damaged guest-room lamp and a missing item reported by a guest. What do you do?

options.text: I tell the supervisor about the lamp and leave the missing item for later.
I record both findings, protect the area, and report them through the proper channels.
I note the missing item and ask maintenance to check the lamp.
I replace the bulb and close the room before the next service round.

basic.situation: You are inspecting a storeroom after droppings are found near a wall. Shelves block part of the area, and the client is waiting. What do you do?

options.text: I move one shelf aside and inspect the wall behind it.
I inspect accessible edges, note blocked areas, and ask to view them safely.
I treat the visible droppings as the source and finish the inspection.
I photograph the open area and recommend a return visit later.

advanced.situation: You are reviewing a storeroom diagram showing wall gaps and reported pest activity, but the mapped route differs from what you observed onsite. What do you do?

options.text: I compare the diagram with site evidence, record the mismatch, and refine access checks.
I ask the client which route they think pests use and update the plan.
I follow the diagram's treatment route so the team can start promptly.
I inspect the reported gaps again and tell the team to wait.

basic.situation: You are measuring a rectangular room for treatment, but stored boxes cover one wall and the client asks for an estimate today. What do you do?

options.text: I use the room's usual size and give the client a firm estimate.
I measure the open sides and estimate the covered wall from the layout.
I measure accessible sides, note the obstruction, and qualify the estimate pending access.
I ask the client for the room dimensions and prepare a provisional figure.

advanced.situation: You are estimating treatment for several connected spaces, and a revised plan adds a sealed room with unclear dimensions. The client needs a cost range. What do you do?

options.text: I separate measured spaces from the sealed room and explain what dimensions the range assumes.
I ask the client to estimate the sealed room before finalising the figure.
I give a range from measured spaces and list the sealed room as pending.
I include the sealed room at the same rate as the other spaces.

basic.situation: You are assigned to spray a treatment in a room, but the nozzle pattern looks uneven during the first pass. What do you do?

options.text: I pause and ask the supervisor whether the nozzle needs changing.
I spray more over the lighter areas until the room looks even.
I ask a colleague to watch the pattern while I finish the pass.
I pause application, check the nozzle and product directions, then resume evenly.

advanced.situation: You are guiding a new worker applying a treatment near furnishings, and the spray drifts beyond the intended area. What do you do?

options.text: I ask the worker to reduce the spray and continue the planned pass.
I stop the pass, reposition the nozzle, and demonstrate controlled application over the target.
I tell the worker to move faster so the spray reaches less furniture.
I demonstrate a slower pass and have the worker copy the motion.

basic.situation: You are cleaning a work site after treatment, and small debris remains near the doorway as the client prepares to reopen the room. What do you do?

options.text: I collect debris near the entrance and tell the client what remains.
I sweep the visible debris toward the nearest drain to finish quickly.
I clear the doorway, collect remaining debris, and check the area before leaving.
I clear the doorway and ask the client to check the rest later.

advanced.situation: You are setting cleanup expectations after work across several rooms, and one team member says the last room can wait until tomorrow. What do you do?

options.text: I let each worker decide whether their room is clean enough.
I check the busiest rooms and leave the quieter rooms for tomorrow.
I assign room checks, define what must be cleared, and review completion before handover.
I ask the team to finish the last room before closing the job.

basic.situation: You are driving a truck fitted with spraying equipment through a narrow service lane, and parked vehicles limit turning space. What do you do?

options.text: I slow down, check clearance, and choose a route with room to turn.
I stop near the lane entrance and call the office for directions.
I ask a colleague to guide me while I pass the parked vehicles.
I steer through the gap carefully to stay on schedule.

advanced.situation: You are coaching a new driver in a truck equipped with spraying gear, and they approach a crowded loading area with little room to reverse. What do you do?

options.text: I tell them to reverse slowly while I watch from the cab.
I demonstrate the turn, then let the trainee try the same route.
I ask a colleague to spot while the trainee backs into the area.
I have them pause, assess the space, and practise a spotter-guided approach.

basic.situation: You are recording a completed treatment, and the client asks how to reduce pests returning near a food storage area. What do you do?

options.text: I record the treatment and advise sealing food and cleaning the area.
I record the treatment and ask a colleague for suitable prevention tips.
I suggest moving food containers and note the client's concern for later follow-up.
I say the treatment should prevent pests and finish the work record.

advanced.situation: You are guiding a colleague who must explain treatment and prevention options to a client, then record the work completed. The client is worried about recurrence. What do you do?

options.text: I suggest they reassure the client and ask another worker for prevention advice first.
I coach them to explain options, prevention, and record the agreed work.
I have them explain treatment steps and record the products used clearly.
I tell them to promise treatment will resolve the problem and record it.

basic.situation: You are assigned to mow a narrow lawn strip with a standard power mower while a coworker supervises nearby.

options.text: Check the mower guard, clear the strip, then mow at a steady pace.
Walk the lawn first, then mow slowly around visible obstacles.
Cut the whole strip quickly before the next crew arrives.
Start mowing from the open edge and watch for people nearby.

advanced.situation: A large sod-cutting job is behind schedule, and the marked route passes near a covered irrigation line.

options.text: Move the machine to a clear section and start there first.
Ask the site lead to clarify the line location before cutting.
Confirm the route and machine settings, then cut in controlled passes.
Begin cutting along the marked route while the crew watches closely.

basic.situation: You are planting bulbs in a prepared flower bed and have a planting guide from your team lead.

options.text: Plant each bulb at a similar depth and tidy the soil afterward.
Set the bulbs at the guide's spacing and cover them with soil.
Check the guide's depth and spacing, then plant and water the bulbs.
Plant the bulbs close together to finish the bed before lunch.

advanced.situation: You are preparing a large new bed with mixed shrubs and ground cover; the planting plan specifies soil preparation and mulch.

options.text: Loosen the soil and place shrubs where the bed looks balanced.
Prepare the whole bed evenly and follow the planting marks.
Spread mulch first, then fit the shrubs into open spaces.
Check the plan's soil and spacing notes, prepare each zone, then mulch.

basic.situation: A dry patch has appeared beside a row of young plants, and you are assigned to water it with a hose.

options.text: Give the whole row a quick spray before moving on.
Water the patch evenly, then check whether nearby plants are reached.
Leave the hose running while you clear weeds nearby.
Check the dry area, water it evenly, and turn off the hose.

advanced.situation: After heavy foot traffic, the lawn has compacted areas and thatch; edging around the flower beds is also due today.

options.text: Mow the lawn closely and leave the thatch for another shift.
Remove visible thatch and edge the beds before aerating later.
Aerate compacted zones, clear thatch, and edge carefully around beds.
Aerate the lawn and tidy the edges around flower beds.

basic.situation: A hedge beside a walkway has a few uneven tips, and you have hand shears and pruners for the task.

options.text: Shear the whole hedge level to finish before visitors arrive.
Use the pruners on the largest tips and leave the rest.
Check the shears, trim uneven growth, and collect cuttings from the path.
Trim the uneven tips, keeping the walkway clear as you work.
