advanced.situation: A mature tree has crossing branches over a walkway, and you are asked to prune it with hand tools.

options.text: Remove the crossing branches in stages, keeping the walkway clear.
Assess the branch structure, prune selected crossings, and keep people clear.
Cut back several large limbs to open the canopy quickly.
Prune the lowest crossing branch first and review the remaining canopy.

basic.situation: A simple garden plan marks three shrubs along a path, and you are assigned to place them before planting.

options.text: Set the shrubs in a straight row wherever the soil is soft.
Place the shrubs near their marks and adjust them after planting.
Place the shrubs at the marked points and check their spacing.
Match each shrub to its mark, then check spacing from the path.

advanced.situation: The planting plan shows a staggered tree line on sloped ground, with support stakes noted for newly planted trees.

options.text: Line the trees up evenly and add stakes after the planting run.
Use the marks for the first trees, then continue at similar spacing.
Follow the layout marks and stake each tree on the slope.
Place the trees by the marks and attach wires to their stakes.

basic.situation: Leaves and small litter have collected across a garden path, and you are asked to clear the area before visitors arrive.

options.text: Collect litter first, then rake leaves into a disposal pile.
Rake the path clear and bag the visible litter nearby.
Push leaves and litter together behind the nearest hedge.
Rake the leaves into piles and collect litter along the path.

advanced.situation: A garden refresh includes fallen leaves, reusable compost material, and a stone border that must remain visible.

options.text: Separate litter, compost leaves, and uncover the stone border.
Collect the leaves in bags and brush soil from the stones.
Push all leaves and litter into the garden's compost corner.
Rake the leaves away from the stones and collect loose litter.

basic.situation: You are asked to start a portable sprayer for a small lawn treatment while a teammate guides you.

options.text: Start the motor and engage the pump before the team is ready.
Confirm the hose and nozzle fit, then start the pump as guided.
Check the hose connection, then start the pump with guidance.
Ask your teammate to check the pump while you connect the hose.

advanced.situation: A sprayer must cover uneven ground with a narrow treatment band, and the available nozzles produce different patterns.

options.text: Check the hose reach and use the closest available nozzle.
Choose a narrow-pattern nozzle for the treatment band and connect the hose.
Use the usual nozzle and adjust your walking pace across the slope.
Match the nozzle and hose to the band and terrain before connecting.

basic.situation: You are filling a sprayer tank for a routine job and have a written mixing formula from the crew lead.

options.text: Ask a teammate to confirm the product amount while you fill.
Measure the water and product against the written formula before filling.
Pour in the usual product amount and top up the tank.
Fill the tank with water, then add the measured product.

advanced.situation: A treatment plan calls for different mixtures on two shrub areas, and you are preparing the sprayer tanks for both.

options.text: Prepare separate labeled batches using each area's formula and measured amounts.
Use the first area's formula for both tanks to save setup time.
Fill both tanks, then check the formulas before mixing.
Measure each batch from its formula and keep the tanks apart.

basic.situation: You are helping treat a small designated patch, using a hose nozzle while a teammate directs the work.

options.text: Check the breeze, then guide the nozzle across the marked patch.
Start at the near edge and adjust the nozzle as you go.
Sweep the nozzle widely so the patch is covered in fewer passes.
Aim the nozzle across the marked patch and keep a steady swing.

advanced.situation: A treatment area slopes toward a walkway, and gusts are shifting as you apply the planned spray depth.

options.text: Pause during gusts, check the slope, then resume controlled passes.
Shorten each pass and watch the spray pattern near the slope.
Continue the full pass before the wind changes direction again.
Keep the planned depth and direct the nozzle away from the walkway.

basic.situation: You are assigned to sow grass seed over a small bare patch with a seed spreader under direct supervision.

options.text: Set the spreader high and finish the patch in one pass.
Follow the seed setting and spread evenly across the bare patch.
Start spreading at the edge and adjust after seeing the first strip.
Check the spreader setting, cover the patch evenly, and review coverage.

advanced.situation: A large seeded slope needs straw cover, and you are assigned to operate the straw blower with the crew nearby.

options.text: Begin at the lower edge and adjust the blower as needed.
Work upward in overlapping passes and watch the straw layer.
Check the mixture and wind, then cover the slope in controlled passes.
Blow a heavy layer across the slope to finish the job faster.

basic.situation: After a routine application, your teammate asks you to rinse the sprayer tank and clean its nozzle.

options.text: Pour leftover mixture into the drain before rinsing the tank.
Rinse the tank quickly and wipe the nozzle with a cloth.
Rinse the tank and nozzle, then leave the parts to drain.
Follow the cleaning steps, rinse the tank, and clear the nozzle.

advanced.situation: The sprayer pump is losing pressure during a job, and you are assigned to inspect and service the machinery.

options.text: Keep spraying at the lower pressure to finish the remaining area.
Tighten the visible hose connection and try the pump again.
Check the service points and connections, then test pressure before resuming.
Clean the filter and restart the pump to see if pressure returns.

basic.situation: A truck driver is reversing to cover a designated lawn area, and you are assigned to guide the vehicle with hand signals.

options.text: Stand where the driver can see you and signal the planned route.
Wave the truck forward while checking the coverage map afterward.
Use horn signals to guide the truck across the marked area.
Position yourself in view, signal slowly, and track the coverage boundary.

advanced.situation: Several lawn patches have discoloured leaves, and the crew asks you to identify the likely plant disease before treatment is chosen.

options.text: Inspect the leaves and note the visible symptoms for the crew.
Compare patch patterns and symptoms, then record findings for treatment planning.
Check one patch closely and identify the disease from its leaf colour.
Photograph the patches and ask the crew to choose a treatment.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to climb a low tree to reach a dead branch. You are still learning to use hooks and a belt.

options.text: I climb with my hooks and belt while my lead watches closely.
I fit my belt and hooks, then climb under my lead's close guidance.
I take the ladder up before checking its footing on the slope.
I check the ladder feet, then climb while my lead works nearby.

advanced.situation: A new trimmer is ready to climb, but one belt strap looks worn. You have been asked to check the gear and coach the first climb.

options.text: I review the main steps and let the trainee practice on a low branch.
I check the hooks and belt, then coach the trainee through a practice climb.
I let the trainee use the belt after a quick buckle check.
I inspect each connection, demonstrate the sequence, then watch the trainee repeat it.

basic.situation: You are helping trim a garden tree. A small dead branch hangs over a walkway, and your lead hands you hand pruners.

options.text: I move to the side and shorten the branch with several quick cuts.
I snip the branch where it is easiest to reach from the path.
I cut the branch near its base after my lead points out the spot.
I ask my lead to clear the walkway, then cut at the branch collar.

advanced.situation: A client wants a large roadside tree reshaped before a busy weekend. Several limbs are dead, and the crew disagrees about how much to remove.

options.text: I trim the outer crown evenly and ask the crew to follow my cuts.
I mark dead limbs and agree a light shape with the crew.
I set a cut sequence around deadwood and traffic, then brief each trimmer.
I remove the visible dead limbs and shorten the longest branches first.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to feed a stump chipper during a small cleanup. The machine is running, and brush is piling up beside it.

options.text: I feed small branches steadily while my lead watches the chipper.
I check the feed area, then pass branches singly under my lead's direction.
I push a tangled bundle through to clear the waiting pile.
I pause feeding and ask my lead which branches fit the opening.

advanced.situation: The brush chipper begins vibrating after a branch jams. The crew is waiting, and you have been asked to help troubleshoot and coach the operator.

options.text: I stop the machine, clear it by the safe procedure, then coach the operator.
I reduce the feed rate and watch whether the vibration settles down.
I stop feeding and inspect the chute while the engine runs.
I stop the feed and ask the operator to check the manual.

basic.situation: After pruning, your hand pruners are sticky with sap and the blade drags. Your lead asks you to clean and sharpen them before storage.

options.text: I wipe the blade and add oil before putting the pruners away.
I rinse the pruners and ask my lead to check the edge later.
I remove the sap, sharpen the edge carefully, then oil the pivot.
I sharpen the blade quickly and store it with sap still on it.

advanced.situation: Several crews return with dull saws near the end of a busy week. You have been asked to set a maintenance routine and show new staff how to care for tools.

options.text: I ask each crew to oil its saws when cutting starts feeling slow.
I schedule weekly sharpening and leave the cleaning steps on a noticeboard.
I set a return checklist, demonstrate care, and schedule regular blade checks.
I sharpen the saws today and tell crews to return them clean.

basic.situation: You are helping rake small branches after pruning a house garden. The truck is parked at the gate, and your lead is clearing the path.

options.text: I rake the branches into a compact pile beside the clear path.
I gather the branches near the gate and let the crew decide next.
I rake the branches to the agreed loading spot, keeping the path clear.
I push the branches into the drain to clear the walkway.

advanced.situation: A roadside pruning job is ending before evening traffic. Branch piles remain at two locations, and the truck has limited space for this trip.

options.text: I clear the traffic-side pile first, then group the rest for the next load.
I fill the truck evenly and ask the crew to tidy the remaining pile.
I stack both piles beside the road until another truck arrives.
I load the nearest pile first and send the truck on its way.

basic.situation: During a routine tree check, you spot small holes and a few discoloured leaves. Your lead gives you a checklist to inspect for visible pest signs.

options.text: I spray the leaves with a general product from the truck.
I photograph the damaged leaves and describe them to the property owner.
I check nearby leaves for signs and record the locations for my lead.
I note the holes and leaf changes on the checklist for review.

advanced.situation: A property owner asks why several mature trees are declining after noticing pests on one trunk. You are inspecting the trees and can share care information within your role.

options.text: I compare visible signs across trees, explain the limits, and suggest an arborist assessment.
I explain the checklist findings and share general tree care guidance with the owner.
I describe the visible signs and suggest watering each tree more often.
I identify the pest from the trunk and recommend a treatment product.

basic.situation: During a quiet period, you notice dust around a slot machine and crumbs on the floor beside it. You need to tidy the area.

options.text: Clean the cabinet, buttons, and nearby floor during the quiet period.
Use the approved cloth on the cabinet and clear debris around it.
Ask a colleague to cover guests while you clean the cabinet and floor.
Give the area a quick wipe, then return to the busy entrance.

advanced.situation: A slot machine repeatedly tilts after routine adjustments, and its display shows an intermittent fault. You need to record the issue and recommend next steps.

options.text: Record repeated tilts and display faults in the maintenance log for follow-up.
Reset the machine again, then record its return to service in the log.
Note the machine number and latest tilt, then forward the details to maintenance.
Log the fault pattern and machine number, then recommend removal for major repair.

basic.situation: During a busy evening, a game station is briefly uncovered while a dealer helps a guest. You need to keep service moving.

options.text: Check which stations need coverage, then assign an available qualified dealer.
Ask nearby staff to watch both tables until the dealer returns.
Move a trained dealer from a quiet table and note the coverage change.
Leave the table open briefly while the dealer finishes helping the guest.

advanced.situation: Two dealers have raised concerns about a colleague’s repeated missed procedures, while guest service remains smooth. You need to prepare a fair performance evaluation.

options.text: Mention the concern in the evaluation and recommend closer observation next month.
Record specific observed examples against the role expectations and summarize their service impact.
Repeat the dealers’ concerns as confirmed findings in the written evaluation.
List dates and observed missed procedures, then describe the pattern in neutral language.

basic.situation: You see a patron repeatedly touch another player’s cards and glance at their hand. You need to respond to a possible game irregularity.

options.text: Confront the patron at the table and tell them to leave the game.
Note the actions and table location, then alert security staff for assessment.
Ask the dealer whether the patron’s movements seemed unusual before noting anything.
Observe the behavior discreetly and notify security staff of the specific concern.

advanced.situation: A guest is shouting near a crowded walkway, and a spilled drink has made the floor slippery. You need to enforce safety rules and address the hazards.

options.text: Ask a nearby worker to mop the spill while you speak with the guest.
Block the slippery patch and call for cleanup before addressing the guest’s shouting.
Arrange prompt spill cleanup, keep guests clear, and use the venue process for the disruption.
Tell the guest to leave, then let passing staff handle the spill.

basic.situation: A guest arrives at your gaming area and looks unsure about the service. You need to greet them and check how their visit is going.

options.text: Smile and ask if everything is fine as you continue your rounds.
Ask whether the guest needs help finding a game or service desk.
Greet the guest, ask how service is going, and listen to their reply.
Point toward the gaming floor and continue checking nearby machines.

advanced.situation: A patron disputes a payout, citing a house rule that seems to conflict with the game display. You need to explain the rule and address the complaint.

options.text: Explain the usual payout rule and offer to record the patron’s concern.
Review the posted rule and machine details, then explain the applicable process in plain language.
Assure the patron the display is right and close the discussion politely.
Repeat the posted rule and suggest the patron speak with another staff member.

basic.situation: A customer asks to exchange a RM50 note for smaller bills and coins. You need to make the requested change and record the transaction paperwork.

options.text: Confirm the requested mix, count the change aloud, and complete the transaction paperwork.
Ask a nearby cashier to confirm the mix before handing over the change.
Exchange the requested denominations and fill in the transaction form afterward.
Hand over a convenient mix of small bills and record the amount exchanged.

advanced.situation: A player’s play history appears to qualify for a complimentary meal, but one session entry is missing. You need to supervise the distribution fairly.

options.text: Issue the meal using visible play totals, noting the player's name and record gap.
Compare session details with eligibility criteria before approving this meal benefit.
Review available play records and criteria, then document the decision and item issued.
Ask the player to confirm the missing session before deciding about the meal.

basic.situation: A hand-delivered jackpot has been approved, but the guest has waited several minutes. You need to monitor whether payment is progressing promptly.

options.text: Tell the guest to wait until the payment team calls their name.
Tell the guest the payment is being processed and return to your floor checks.
Check the payment status with the responsible staff member and update the waiting guest.
Ask the payment staff for an estimated completion time and note the delay.

advanced.situation: A new table game opens, and a worker asks how its limits and common cheating tactics differ from familiar games. You need to guide them using current facility knowledge.

options.text: Explain posted table limits and one tactic relevant to this specific game.
Review game guidance, explain limits and known tactics, then check the worker’s understanding.
Share recalled limits, then ask the worker to check the current game sheet for details.
Tell the worker to copy limits from a familiar table game for now.

basic.situation: A staff member calls in sick before a quiet weekday session. You need to assign the remaining team’s work schedule so the activity is covered.

options.text: Leave the shift open and ask arriving staff to divide the duties.
Ask a colleague which staff members usually cover that session before assigning shifts.
Move one available worker into the open shift and update the schedule.
Check the activity’s coverage needs and assign available staff to the required shifts.

advanced.situation: A holiday weekend has two large bookings, one planned absence, and limited trained staff. You need to schedule coverage across peak periods.

options.text: Spread staff evenly across weekend hours to balance the scheduled shifts.
Match trained staff to peak posts, then stagger breaks around the two bookings.
Adapt the previous holiday roster for the known absence and booking peaks.
Offer available staff extra shifts, prioritising the busiest booking periods.

basic.situation: A staff-led family game is due to start, but the activity area is not fully set up. You need to coordinate the workers and help the session begin.

options.text: Start the game on time and let staff finish arranging items during play.
Ask the team to finish setting up while you greet arriving families.
Confirm the activity needs, assign setup roles, and check readiness before opening.
Assign one worker to equipment and another to welcome guests before starting.

advanced.situation: A community event combines sports, a performance, and food service, but two teams have conflicting start times. You need to coordinate the program with activity leaders.

options.text: Draft a revised sequence around the sports booking and send it to the leaders.
Bring the activity leaders together, resolve timing dependencies, and share one agreed running order.
Move the performance later and tell each team about the revised time.
Keep the published times and ask teams to shorten their preparation periods.

basic.situation: During a routine inspection, you find several equipment items returned to the wrong storage area. You need to note the work issue for a staff check-in.

options.text: Move the items back and report that storage was in order.
Tell the team the area needs tidying before the next activity begins.
Note the misplaced items and mention the pattern during the staff check-in.
Record the items and locations, then compare them with the established storage standard.

advanced.situation: A staff member’s guest interactions have drawn mixed feedback, and you have observed both helpful and rushed moments. You need to evaluate performance fairly.

options.text: Ask the worker how they think their guest interactions are going.
Record examples from your observations and describe where service seemed rushed.
Compare dated observations and feedback with service standards, then document specific strengths and gaps.
Write that the worker needs to improve their attitude and guest manner.

basic.situation: A new recreation worker is unsure how to prepare equipment before a children’s activity. You need to explain the relevant procedure and policy.

options.text: Demonstrate the setup, explain its policy, then ask the worker to show each step.
Explain setup steps and connect them to the relevant activity policy.
Review the equipment list and have the worker follow its sequence.
Ask the worker to copy the previous activity setup before preparing equipment.

advanced.situation: A new shift supervisor asks for help training seasonal workers across several activities. Recent operating updates changed some procedures, and you need to support their preparation.

options.text: List the key procedures and suggest the supervisor demonstrate them during staff briefings.
Reuse last season’s training plan and distribute it to the new workers.
Share the usual training notes and ask the supervisor to adapt them for the team.
Review current updates with the supervisor, then outline practice sessions for each affected procedure.

basic.situation: A visitor asks where today’s family activities are taking place and when they start. You need to provide reliable event information.

options.text: Ask a nearby worker to verify today’s activity schedule before replying.
Review the event board together and point out today’s listed sessions.
Check today’s activity listing, then explain each location and start time.
Share the usual location and start time, while checking whether today differs.

advanced.situation: Several visitors mention long queues at the same activity across recent weekends. You need to use their feedback to improve the service.

options.text: Thank visitors for sharing feedback and forward their comments to the activity lead.
Ask staff to reduce queue delays during the next busy session.
Group comments by time and queue issue, then propose a pattern-based change.
Summarize recurring queue feedback and recommend extra coverage during peak sessions.

basic.situation: An upcoming outdoor session needs extra safety harnesses, and last month’s supply record is incomplete. You need to request equipment and record the activity data.

options.text: Check stock and session needs, request harnesses, and log the supply gap.
Confirm the expected group size with the activity lead before requesting enough harnesses.
Order a spare batch to give the session team enough equipment.
Request the previous session’s harness quantity for this outdoor activity.

advanced.situation: Attendance and staffing reports show rising demand for weekend sessions, while supply costs and vacant shifts are also increasing. You need to analyze the operations data and report useful findings.

options.text: Summarize attendance and supply trends by session, including open shifts and cost increases.
Use attendance patterns to outline a larger weekend staffing plan for review.
Recommend added weekend coverage based on rising attendance and vacant shifts.
Compare attendance, staffing, and supply trends, then report pressure points with figures.

basic.situation: Before opening, you spot damp towels and a loose shelf in a treatment room during your routine check.

options.text: You ask the attendant to tidy the room after the first appointment.
You have the attendant clean the room and flag the shelf to maintenance.
You pause room use, arrange cleanup, and log the shelf for repair.
You move the towels aside and let bookings continue as planned.

advanced.situation: Two shift leads rate a therapist's punctuality and guest manner differently, and you are asked to help align their staff reviews.

options.text: You tell both leads to use their own judgement for this review.
You compare their notes and suggest a shared rating guide for future reviews.
You ask the more experienced lead to decide the rating this time.
You agree observable criteria, then calibrate ratings against documented examples together.

basic.situation: A weekend receptionist calls in sick, and two trained attendants are available to cover the lobby desk.

options.text: You match desk skills and peak hours, then confirm a workable revised roster.
You split the shift evenly and tell both attendants the new hours.
You check coverage needs and ask the available attendants about their shifts.
You assign the first available attendant to cover the whole shift.

advanced.situation: Weekend bookings rise sharply, while staff breaks overlap and leave the reception desk short during the busiest hour.

options.text: You map hourly demand, stagger breaks, and protect minimum team coverage.
You stagger breaks around bookings and review coverage with each shift lead.
You place most breaks before lunch, when the team usually feels quieter.
You preserve familiar shifts and ask staff to trade around the busy periods.

basic.situation: Three attendants must prepare rooms before the first guests arrive, and you are asked to direct their setup tasks.

options.text: You sequence rooms by arrival time, assign clear owners, and check readiness together.
You assign each attendant one room and ask them to report progress.
You let the attendants choose rooms, then check in near opening.
You pair the newest attendant with an experienced colleague for setup.

advanced.situation: Housekeeping and reception disagree over room-ready times before a group arrival, and you are coordinating both teams on shift.

options.text: You pass housekeeping's estimated times to reception and check again later.
You tell reception to wait until housekeeping finishes its full room list.
You ask each team to send updates through their usual channels.
You map room priorities with both leads and agree one shared handover sequence.

basic.situation: A new spa attendant asks how to prepare a treatment room, and you have the opening checklist and policy notes.

options.text: You ask another attendant to show them the usual room arrangement.
You give the attendant the checklist and ask them to follow it.
You show the room once and ask them to copy your setup.
You walk through the checklist and explain the room setup policy.

advanced.situation: New attendants make recurring setup errors, and another shift lead asks you to help improve how supervisors teach the procedure.

options.text: You tell the lead to remind staff about the setup checklist at briefings.
You collect common errors and draft a practice session with clear demonstrations.
You share your usual explanation and suggest the lead use it next shift.
You ask the lead to have experienced attendants coach new starters informally.

basic.situation: An attendant says a coworker keeps changing their room assignments, and asks you what will happen next.

options.text: You suggest they wait a few shifts to see if assignments settle.
You tell the attendant to raise the issue with the coworker after work.
You report the complaint to your manager and mention the workers involved.
You listen, note the concern, and pass the details to your manager.

advanced.situation: A customer complaint points to repeated service lapses, while the worker says unclear shift instructions caused the problem.

options.text: You record both accounts and refer the matter to your manager for review.
You issue a formal warning based on the customer's account while it is fresh.
You compare accounts and shift notes, then follow the management process for next steps.
You give the worker a verbal reminder and note the complaint for follow-up.

basic.situation: A guest says an attendant was dismissive when asked about a delayed appointment, and wants the concern addressed.

options.text: You apologise for the experience and offer to pass the concern along.
You ask what outcome would help, then arrange a suitable service recovery within your role.
You hear the guest out, acknowledge the delay, and note the details for your manager.
You explain that the attendant was busy and ask the guest to wait.

advanced.situation: Monthly guest comments repeatedly mention long waits at check-in, and you are asked to help improve the service.

options.text: You share several comments at the next briefing and ask staff to be quicker.
You ask reception to remind guests about busy periods during check-in.
You summarize the wait complaints for the manager and suggest reviewing check-in.
You group feedback by time and cause, then propose a change and track results.

basic.situation: Before training, you notice a dog is quieter than usual and has left part of its meal. What do you do?

options.text: I would continue the session and check the dog's appetite tomorrow.
I would note appetite and behavior, then alert the responsible staff member for assessment.
I would offer a different treat and see if the dog eats.
I would record the changes and tell the trainer responsible for the dog.

advanced.situation: A horse in your training group has developed a recurring cough, and staff disagree about when it began. You are updating its health record. What do you do?

options.text: I would enter the first date someone remembers and notify the trainer.
I would remove the cough entries that lack a confirmed date.
I would record each observed cough with timing and inform the responsible veterinary staff.
I would ask staff to agree on a single start date for the record.

basic.situation: Your morning care list says to feed the rabbits and clean their holding area before exercise. What do you do?

options.text: I would clean the area first and leave feeding for the afternoon round.
I would feed them, clean the area, and check the care list afterward.
I would feed the rabbits and ask a coworker to confirm the cleaning.
I would check each rabbit's feed portion, clean the area, and note completion.

advanced.situation: A busy event day adds an exercise session to the usual care schedule, and the holding area still needs cleaning. You are coordinating the animal care round. What do you do?

options.text: I would schedule cleaning after the event so the animals can exercise.
I would assign care tasks by animal, timing, and area access, then check completion.
I would keep the usual schedule and fit the added exercise between rounds.
I would ask each handler to choose which care task they can skip.

basic.situation: During a first session, a dog approaches you calmly but startles at a sudden sound. You are helping assess its temperament. What do you do?

options.text: I would label the dog unsuitable based on its reaction to the sound.
I would note both responses and share them with the lead trainer.
I would record the context and responses, then observe the dog across suitable tasks.
I would repeat the sound at a lower level to see what happens.

advanced.situation: Two trainers rate the same horse's focus differently after separate sessions. You are helping review its suitability for a performance task. What do you do?

options.text: I would ask each trainer to explain the session that shaped their rating.
I would average the two ratings and record the result for the horse.
I would use the higher rating to keep the performance plan on schedule.
I would compare observations against shared task criteria and review another session.

basic.situation: A young dog hesitates when you begin a basic “sit” exercise from its training plan. What do you do?

options.text: I would ask another trainer to demonstrate the sit cue for the dog.
I would repeat the cue calmly and reward the dog after it responds.
I would move to the next command so the session stays on time.
I would follow the plan's cue and reward steps, then note the response.

advanced.situation: A dog performs a trained cue reliably in a quiet room but struggles in the busier practice area. You are adjusting its behavior training plan. What do you do?

options.text: I would return to the quiet room and repeat the cue until it succeeds.
I would increase distractions in small steps and record the dog's response at each stage.
I would remove the cue from the plan and focus on easier behaviors.
I would practise in the busy area again and offer extra rewards.

basic.situation: A visitor asks whether a particular dog would suit their household, but you know little about their daily routine. What do you do?

options.text: I would describe the dog's appealing traits and suggest they consider it.
I would ask about their household and routine before discussing the dog's needs.
I would explain the dog's needs and invite them to share their plans.
I would recommend the dog because it has been popular with visitors.

advanced.situation: A prospective owner wants a highly active dog but says they travel often and have no regular caregiver. They ask you which animal to choose. What do you do?

options.text: I would explain the active dog's routine and ask about caregiver arrangements.
I would suggest a calmer dog that fits their frequent travel schedule.
I would discuss care needs, travel, and support before suggesting a suitable match.
I would encourage choosing the active dog after they arrange reliable care.

basic.situation: Your care sheet lists a prescribed dose for a dog before its training session. What do you do?

options.text: I would verify the label, give the prescribed dose, and record it.
I would check with the responsible caregiver before changing the dose timing.
I would confirm the dose, give it as listed, and notify the trainer.
I would avoid using a dose from another facility without checking current instructions.

advanced.situation: A dog is due for prescribed medication shortly before a live demonstration, and the show caller asks for its cue time. What do you do?

options.text: I would give the listed dose and keep the original cue time.
I would skip the dose so the demonstration can start on time.
I would confirm the medication record and coordinate the cue with the caller.
I would move the cue later and let the caller know after the dose.

basic.situation: You are preparing the morning feed, and two animals have similar bowls with different portions listed on their care sheets.

options.text: I would ask a nearby caretaker which bowl belongs to each animal.
I would use yesterday’s portions because both animals ate them without trouble.
I would match each bowl to the posted schedule before serving the animals.
I would check the bowl labels and serve the listed portions to both animals.

advanced.situation: An owner asks how to combine a new exercise routine with several daily care instructions for an older pet.

options.text: I would recommend a full routine based on what worked for another older pet.
I would explain the written routine and invite the owner to call with questions.
I would review the instructions, suggest gradual activity, and flag concerns for the veterinarian.
I would suggest a gentle routine and ask the owner to watch for changes.

basic.situation: During a routine check, you notice an animal favoring one paw after returning from its exercise area.

options.text: I would mention the limp to a colleague during the next handover.
I would note the limp and tell the responsible caretaker before the next exercise period.
I would check the paw and movement, record what I see, and report the change.
I would wait through another exercise period to see whether the limp settles.

advanced.situation: A usually active animal eats less and moves quietly, but shows no obvious injury during your checks.

options.text: I would record the appetite change and ask another caretaker to watch its activity.
I would ask the team to check again later and note today’s quieter behavior.
I would compare recent appetite and activity notes, then report the pattern for review.
I would offer a favorite treat and wait to see whether its energy returns.

basic.situation: You are assigned to clean a pen after an animal leaves, and the disinfectant instructions are posted nearby.

options.text: I would remove bedding, wash the pen, and rinse the equipment with water.
I would ask a caretaker to confirm the cleaning steps before I begin.
I would spray the pen and equipment, then put them back for use.
I would clear the pen, follow the product directions, and return clean equipment.

advanced.situation: Several staff rotate through the animal quarters, and you see inconsistent cleaning after equipment is shared between pens.

options.text: I would remind the next shift to clean shared items after each use.
I would write a short cleaning sequence and demonstrate it during a shift handover.
I would ask the team lead to send a cleaning note to all staff.
I would clean the shared equipment myself whenever I notice it is due.

basic.situation: You are mixing a liquid formula, and the written instructions give a precise amount for one animal’s meal.

options.text: I would ask another caretaker to read the instructions while I prepare it.
I would measure the stated amount and check the animal’s label before mixing.
I would measure the written amount and mix the formula until smooth.
I would use the usual amount from the previous meal to save time.

advanced.situation: An animal needs a special diet, and its owner brings new feeding notes that differ from the current instructions.

options.text: I would explain the current plan and ask the owner to clarify the new notes.
I would hold the new food and record the owner’s notes for later review.
I would combine both notes into a smaller meal and observe the animal afterward.
I would follow the current instructions and share the new notes with the veterinarian.

basic.situation: You are asked to weigh an animal and update its record before the caretaker’s shift ends.

options.text: I would enter the weight in the file and tell the caretaker it is updated.
I would record the weight, time, and any visible condition notes in its file.
I would round the weight to the nearest whole number for faster entry.
I would write the weight on the shift sheet for the caretaker to enter.

advanced.situation: A treatment record shows a missed dose, and the animal’s latest observation notes a new change in condition.

options.text: I would enter the missed dose as given and add the condition note afterward.
I would document both changes and ask the next shift to follow up.
I would document the missed dose and new observation, then contact the veterinarian for direction.
I would record the observation and tell the veterinarian about the missed dose.

basic.situation: A caller asks when the animal-care centre can fit in a routine appointment, and you have the booking calendar open.

options.text: I would take the caller’s number and ask a colleague to check openings later.
I would promise the caller the first slot that usually opens each morning.
I would check the calendar, offer an available time, and confirm the caller’s details.
I would offer the next open time and ask the caller to confirm it.

advanced.situation: A worried owner asks about an animal’s recent behaviour and presses you for a health conclusion during a busy visitor period.

options.text: I would give the owner the information sheet and return to the waiting visitors.
I would reassure the owner that the behaviour is probably normal for the animal.
I would describe the behaviour notes, avoid a diagnosis, and direct health concerns to the veterinarian.
I would listen, share general behaviour information, and offer to pass on the concern.

basic.situation: You are dealing a card game with a new player, and the table is ready for the next hand.

options.text: I would ask the nearby dealer to confirm the table is ready.
I would start the hand while the last player is still choosing a bet.
I would confirm the bets, deal the required cards, and follow the game sequence.
I would deal the required cards and announce each step as the hand proceeds.

advanced.situation: During a busy baccarat round, two dealers disagree about the next dealing step while players watch closely.

options.text: I would ask the other dealer to state their understanding before continuing.
I would consult the table procedure and then announce the next step clearly.
I would pause the next deal, check the game sequence, and coordinate the team’s call.
I would follow the sequence I remember and keep the round moving.

basic.situation: A patron hands you cash for chips, and the notes are slightly folded as the table grows busy.

options.text: I would straighten and count the notes before giving the matching chips.
I would ask a colleague to check the amount while I prepare the chips.
I would give the usual chip stack for that note size to keep play moving.
I would count the notes, state the amount, and issue matching chips to the patron.

advanced.situation: A patron makes a large wager just before the game starts, and nearby conversation makes the amount hard to hear.

options.text: I would accept the chips and record the amount I think I heard.
I would count the chips carefully and enter the amount in the wager record.
I would restate the wager, verify the chips, and record the confirmed amount before play.
I would ask another dealer to listen while I count the chips again.

basic.situation: Before opening a table, you notice a card has a bent corner among the cards set out for play.

options.text: I would ask a coworker whether the card should be replaced before opening.
I would set aside the card and tell the table lead before using the deck.
I would replace the card with one from the spare deck and continue setup.
I would use the deck because the bent corner does not affect dealing.

advanced.situation: At closing, the table float count differs from the opening record, and the next shift is waiting to open.

options.text: I would adjust the closing entry to match the opening total and finish.
I would tell the next dealer there may be a difference in the float.
I would record the count, compare the opening entry, and notify the table lead.
I would count the float again and write down the new total.

basic.situation: A player asks how much they won on a straightforward hand, and the posted payout guide is available.

options.text: I would use the payout guide and tell the player the amount shown.
I would pay the amount that most players receive for this hand.
I would ask another dealer to calculate the amount while I check the guide.
I would check the wager, use the payout guide, and state the calculated amount.

advanced.situation: A patron disputes a ticket payout, and your calculation differs from the amount displayed on the ticket scanner.

options.text: I would check the ticket details and have a colleague verify the calculation.
I would rescan the ticket, compare the figures, and explain the result to the patron.
I would show the patron the scanner amount and ask whether they accept it.
I would pay the displayed amount to clear the line and review it later.

basic.situation: A visitor arrives at the gaming floor looking unsure where to go, while you are between hands at your table.

options.text: I would keep dealing and let a nearby staff member assist the visitor.
I would greet them, ask what help they need, and direct them to the right desk.
I would welcome the visitor, ask where they are headed, and point toward the cashier area.
I would greet the visitor and ask a colleague nearby to guide them.

advanced.situation: A patron has collected winnings and asks where to go next, while a new dealer watches how you handle the interaction.

options.text: I would direct the patron to the gaming cashier and mention what to bring.
I would name the gaming cashier and stay available for one follow-up question.
I would point toward the cashier, mention the gaming desk, and return quickly to my table.
I would tell the patron to ask another customer where winnings are collected.

basic.situation: A player asks whether a particular side bet is allowed, and the game rules are available at the table.

options.text: I would read the relevant rule and answer the player's question in plain language.
I would ask another dealer whether that side bet is usually accepted.
I would check the rule sheet and explain the side bet before play.
I would explain the rule as I remember it from recent rounds.

advanced.situation: A new dealer asks how a rule variation applies when a player questions the outcome of a close hand.

options.text: I would ask the floor lead to explain the variation to the dealer.
I would review the variation and explain how it applies here.
I would explain the standard rule and move on to the next hand.
I would show the dealer the rule reference and discuss the relevant variation.

basic.situation: Players are settling at your table, and the next round is ready to start. What do you do before play begins?

options.text: You check the nearest players and begin once their chips are down.
You ask the dealer whether the table looks ready, then start the round.
You scan each position, confirm every wager, then signal the dealer to begin.
You pause play briefly and ask each player to confirm their wager.

advanced.situation: Two players dispute whether a wager was placed before the hand began, while the next round is waiting. What do you do?

options.text: You ask the dealer to settle it and keep the other players moving.
You return the disputed chips and restart the hand to keep play moving.
You listen to both players and use the dealer's recollection to decide.
You pause the table, hear each account, check the layout, and apply the posted procedure.

basic.situation: You are assigned to start the numbered-ball machine for a scheduled draw. What do you do?

options.text: You start the machine, watch the draw, and call each number and color clearly.
You start the draw and call numbers as they appear on the display.
You begin the draw and call the numbers after the machine finishes.
You check the display and controls, start the draw, then announce each number and color.

advanced.situation: Before a busy session, you notice a card has a bent corner and the dealing shoe catches slightly. What do you do?

options.text: You smooth the card and test the shoe with a few cards.
You set aside the damaged card and shoe, then arrange approved replacements before play.
You inspect the card and run several cards through the shoe before deciding.
You use the set for one round and watch for any sticking.

basic.situation: A player hands you a RM100 note and asks for playing chips before the next game. What do you do?

options.text: You hand over chips near the requested amount and continue serving the player.
You exchange the note for chips and let the player count them.
You count the note and chips before finishing the exchange with the player.
You count the note, exchange it for chips, and confirm the amount aloud.

advanced.situation: A player asks you to move a winning chip stack after the next hand has started, citing the table's usual practice. What do you do?

options.text: You ask the dealer about the procedure and follow their direction.
You check the table rules and ask the dealer before moving the stack.
You move the stack as requested and tell the dealer after play.
You hold the stack, check procedure, and move it if permitted.

basic.situation: The game ends, and players are leaving while their used tickets remain on the table. What do you do?

options.text: You group used tickets by player and keep them together for table handling.
You collect each player's tickets and place them beside the game records for review.
You leave the tickets on the table until the next game ends.
You sweep the tickets into a nearby tray as players leave.

advanced.situation: A player presents a complex wager, and the apparent payout differs from the amount shown on the table layout. What do you do?

options.text: You pay the amount shown on the layout and serve the next player.
You compare the wager with the layout and verify the total before payment.
You recalculate the payout from the wager and ask the player to confirm it.
You estimate the wager total and refer the player to the cashier.

basic.situation: After a race, you have several cashed tickets and payouts to record before the next event. What do you do?

options.text: You count the tickets and write the payout total in the event record.
You enter the payout total and estimate the number of cashed tickets.
You record the ticket count and check the payout total later.
You tally cashed tickets and payouts, then record both event totals.

advanced.situation: Your collection report is due, but the cash count and ticket totals do not agree before submission. What do you do?

options.text: You compare the report with ticket records and note the mismatch before submitting it.
You reconcile ticket and cash entries, note the difference, and submit the report.
You hold the report while the next shift checks both totals.
You change the ticket total to match cash and submit the report.

basic.situation: A bingo caller is waiting to begin, and you are carrying the caller's tickets, cards, and money. What do you do?

options.text: You bring the full set to the caller's station before the game starts.
You hand over the cards and tickets first, then return with the caller's money.
You leave the items at the caller's station while they prepare.
You deliver the caller's tickets, cards, and money, then confirm the handoff.

advanced.situation: Players are waiting between games, and a patron asks to buy drinks and snacks while you are serving the gaming area. What do you do?

options.text: You list each requested item and prepare the order for the waiting patron.
You confirm each item and price, then serve the order using venue procedures.
You take a quick order and serve the usual items for that group.
You ask the patron to wait until the gaming area becomes quieter.

basic.situation: The scheduled film is ready, and you are at the booth controls before the audience enters. What do you do?

options.text: You start the projector, inspect the image, and open the shutter for the show.
You start the projector and open the shutter at the scheduled showtime as planned.
You open the shutter and adjust focus after the audience is seated.
You open the shutter once the projector powers on and check the image.

advanced.situation: Two screens show the same presentation, but one image appears dimmer and slightly out of focus before the audience arrives. What do you do?

options.text: You raise the dim screen's illumination and check its focus before opening.
You switch to the brighter screen and tell staff about the mismatch.
You adjust focus on both projectors, then compare their images from the room.
You compare both screens, adjust focus and illumination, then confirm the images match.

basic.situation: Dust has collected around the projector and on its lens between shows. What do you do?

options.text: You clean the lens with the approved cloth and remove dust from the booth surfaces.
You remove booth dust and use a soft cloth on the lens.
You clean the booth floor and leave the lens for the next service.
You wipe the lens with a tissue and sweep the booth floor.

advanced.situation: During a show, the projector begins making a grinding sound and the image briefly shakes. What do you do?

options.text: You reduce projector load and monitor whether the grinding and shaking continue.
You notify maintenance and monitor the image while the show continues.
You follow equipment procedures, stop use if needed, and report symptoms to maintenance.
You record the sound and image shake, then contact maintenance after the show.

basic.situation: You are preparing the theater, and the projector casing has a loose-looking panel before the first show. What do you do?

options.text: You inspect the panel and test the projector controls before opening.
You check the panel screws and ask a colleague whether it looks secure.
You press the panel back into place and start the projector.
You inspect the projector and controls, then report the loose panel before operation.

advanced.situation: A curtain control has responded slowly twice during setup, and the audience will enter soon. What do you do?

options.text: You run the curtain control once and note how quickly it responds.
You test the curtain controls and report their slow response before opening.
You test the control again and alert the next shift to its delay.
You use the manual control if the curtain hesitates during the show.

basic.situation: A film has started, and the picture looks clear but the dialogue seems quiet from your booth. What do you do?

options.text: You raise the volume slightly, then listen for clearer dialogue from the booth.
You raise the volume until dialogue sounds louder from the booth.
You check booth sound, compare levels with venue guidance, and adjust accordingly.
You ask a nearby colleague whether the dialogue sounds quiet.

advanced.situation: A new projectionist is monitoring a film, and several patrons report that the sound is uneven across the room. What do you do?

options.text: You raise the master volume and ask patrons if sound improves there.
You ask the projectionist to check the speakers after the film ends.
You check sound across seating areas, compare venue guidance, and coach the projectionist.
You listen from rear seats and show the projectionist how to adjust sound levels.

basic.situation: A film is paired with a pre-recorded music track, and the cue sheet says to start the track at the opening image. What do you do?

options.text: You follow the cue sheet and start the track with the opening image.
You start the track after the opening image appears, then check its timing.
You start the track with the opening image and monitor the film.
You start music as patrons settle, then sync playback with the opening image.

advanced.situation: A live presenter is speaking over a film, and the next sound effect cue is close while a music track continues. What do you do?

options.text: You hold the cue until a presenter pause, then trigger the effect while music continues.
You stop the music and wait until the presenter names the effect before playing it.
You follow the cue sheet, balancing music and firing the effect on its marked cue.
You pause the music during a presenter pause, play the effect, then resume it.

basic.situation: Your checklist says the theater doors should open shortly before the scheduled show. What do you do?

options.text: You check the schedule, open doors at the listed time, and follow closing steps.
You ask a coworker when doors usually open and follow that timing.
You open doors when patrons arrive, then close them after the film ends.
You follow the checklist to open theater doors shortly before the scheduled show begins.

advanced.situation: Two screens have back-to-back shows, and a cleaning delay may leave one theater closed when its next audience arrives. What do you do?

options.text: You move the next screening later to allow more time for theater cleaning.
You ask cleaners to finish that theater first while coordinating with the schedule.
You compare show times and turnover needs, then coordinate staff to limit delays.
You start the next show late and inform the arriving audience about the delay.

basic.situation: A family arrives at the venue entrance looking unsure while you welcome guests. What do you do?

options.text: Keep greeting at the entrance and send access requests elsewhere.
Wave them through warmly while the queue moves toward the doors.
Smile, greet them, and point out the lobby desk for questions.
Welcome the group, then ask whether anyone needs directions or access help.

advanced.situation: New ushers greet a diverse crowd, and one patron using a wheelchair is left waiting. You are asked to coach the team. What do you do?

options.text: Show staff how to greet arriving patrons and point out nearby access routes.
Suggest staff focus their welcome on patrons who approach them first.
Ask staff to use a warm greeting and offer help without making assumptions.
Tell new staff to greet everyone with the same brief phrase.

basic.situation: You are assigned to clean a lobby before doors open, and a wet patch remains near the entrance. What do you do?

options.text: Leave the patch until after opening, and tell a supervisor about it.
Place a warning sign beside the patch, then continue your assigned route.
Wipe the visible water, then check the floor around the entrance.
Mop the patch, then inspect nearby floor areas for remaining moisture.

advanced.situation: Before a sold-out show, you audit the lobby and find a blocked aisle beside overflowing rubbish bins. What do you do?

options.text: Clear the bins, reopen the aisle, and record both findings for the team.
Move the bins aside and note the overflow for the cleaning crew.
Ask a colleague to empty the bins while you inspect other areas.
Mark the blocked aisle for review after the audience enters.

basic.situation: A patron presents a ticket whose colour matches tonight's show, but the printed date appears different. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the patron to show the ticket again and compare its date.
Accept the ticket because its colour matches the current event.
Check the printed date against tonight's ticket details before admitting them.
Let them join the line while another usher checks the colour.

advanced.situation: Several tickets have matching colours but repeated print marks and dates that do not fit the event. What do you do?

options.text: Admit the holders whose tickets scan while setting aside the others.
Separate the unusual tickets and check their dates with the event list.
Ask another usher to compare a sample while you keep the line moving.
Compare the tickets with current criteria, hold disputed entries, and report the pattern.

basic.situation: A patron asks where the nearest exit is as the hall begins filling. What do you do?

options.text: Point out the nearest marked exit and give a clear route from here.
Gesture toward the exit sign above the doors across the lobby.
Tell them to follow the signs once they reach the main aisle.
Direct them toward the hall doors and let them find the exit signs.

advanced.situation: During an evacuation drill, one aisle is dark and patrons are unsure which exit to use. What do you do?

options.text: Tell patrons to wait by their seats until the drill leader arrives.
Use your flashlight to guide patrons along the clear route to the marked exit.
Point toward the nearest exit sign and ask patrons to keep moving.
Guide the nearest group toward the exit while another usher checks the aisle.

basic.situation: Two patrons claim the same seat, and both show tickets for the same row. What do you do?

options.text: Review both tickets and help the patron with the clearer seat number.
Compare both seat details with the seating plan and guide them accordingly.
Ask one patron to take an open seat nearby while you check.
Check the row with an usher and explain where each ticket leads.

advanced.situation: A parent reports a missing child during a crowded interval, while a patron also disputes a seat nearby. What do you do?

options.text: Keep the reports distinct, note the child's description, and alert the appropriate team.
Ask the parent to wait nearby while you ask staff about the child.
Ask nearby ushers to watch the doors while you resolve the seat dispute.
Tell the parent where to wait and help the seated patrons first.

basic.situation: A patron pays for one ticket at the counter, and the queue is growing behind them. What do you do?

options.text: Confirm the ticket type aloud, then process the payment at the till.
Enter the ticket type, take payment, and issue the matching ticket.
Take the cash and use a ticket from the open stack to save time.
Take the payment and hand over a ticket from the same event.

advanced.situation: A queue builds at the ticket counter while a new colleague struggles with the POS system. What do you do?

options.text: Show your colleague the sale steps while matching each payment with its ticket.
Demonstrate a few sales, then let your colleague try with your guidance.
Ask your colleague to issue tickets while you handle each payment carefully.
Take over the till while your colleague guides patrons toward the queue.

basic.situation: You are assigned to press a costume before tonight's show, and its care label is still attached. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the dresser about the fabric, then press the main panels.
Use a high setting to remove the creases before the show.
Check the care label, set a suitable heat, and press the costume.
Press the visible creases on a medium setting before returning it.

advanced.situation: Several costumes return after a show with stains, loose seams, and another performance approaching. What do you do?

options.text: Return all costumes to storage and note the problems for next week.
Repair the loose seams and send the remaining items for cleaning.
Sort items by repair and cleaning needs, then track each costume through return.
Clean the stained costumes first and leave loose seams for later.

basic.situation: A designer gives you a list of costumes to record, including one item marked for repair. What do you do?

options.text: Record each item and its condition, including the repair note.
Enter costume names first and add conditions after the rehearsal.
Add the item names to the spreadsheet and flag the repair verbally.
Record the clean costumes and leave the repair item off the sheet.

advanced.situation: A production has costumes, wigs, and makeup stored in several rooms, and status records disagree. What do you do?

options.text: Update the spreadsheet from the latest designer's list and share it.
Use the most complete room list as the current inventory record.
Check the costume racks and ask staff to confirm missing pieces.
Reconcile each room's stock against item records and note status changes.

basic.situation: You are arranging costumes for a short scene change, and two garments look alike. What do you do?

options.text: Place the first costume ready and confirm the next one with the dresser.
Keep both garments on one rack, then confirm their order with the dresser.
Arrange costumes in order and label similar garments for the quick change.
Hang both garments near the change area, marking each with its cast member.

advanced.situation: A show has rapid changes for several cast members, and rented pieces must be returned after closing. What do you do?

options.text: Keep rented pieces on the change racks until the next production.
Sequence changes by use, then separate rented pieces for tracked return.
Arrange costumes by cast member and return rented items after closing.
Order the changes by scene and ask staff to gather rented pieces later.

basic.situation: A script places a character in a past era, and you are asked to find reference images for the costume team. What do you do?

options.text: Use a familiar film's costumes as the main reference for the era.
Choose a striking image and share it with the costume designer.
Search for clothing images from the era and save the clearest examples.
Find period images from several references and note their dates and details.

advanced.situation: A script's setting is unclear, and a designer needs period references for several characters before fittings. What do you do?

options.text: Collect general period images and let the designer select relevant ones.
Ask the production team for its preferred era, then search matching pictures.
Use the earliest costume images found online as the fitting reference.
Review script clues, identify the likely period, and share sourced references for each character.

basic.situation: An actor tries on a costume and says the sleeve feels tight during movement. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the actor to try a larger costume from the rack.
Note where it pulls during movement and pass the detail to the tailor.
Write down that the sleeve feels tight and show the costume designer.
Pin the sleeve wider and send the actor back to rehearsal.

advanced.situation: Under stage lights, a costume alteration pulls at the shoulder and changes the intended silhouette. What do you do?

options.text: Photograph the costume under lights and send the image to the designer.
Ask the actor to adjust the shoulder seam before the next scene.
Explain the silhouette change and ask the tailor to review the shoulder fit.
Check fit in movement and lighting, then document the pull for alteration.

basic.situation: A senior dresser directs you to help an actor change costumes, and the dressing list shows the next item. What do you do?

options.text: Bring the costume rack near the actor and wait for further instructions.
Check the dressing list, prepare the next item, and assist as directed.
Ask the actor which costume they need and help with that change.
Choose a similar costume from the rack to keep the change moving.

advanced.situation: A production needs several wardrobe items, the designer has revised details, and cast changes overlap. What do you do?

options.text: Confirm revisions with the designer, update lists, and route purchases for approval.
Review revisions with the designer and assign each change to its cast member.
Purchase nearby items first, then share selections with the designer for review.
Update dressing lists from current notes and coordinate staff coverage for overlapping changes.

basic.situation: A guest asks whether towels are included with locker hire, and you are unsure of the facility’s policy.

options.text: Tell the guest towels are usually included with locker hire.
Check the posted policy, then explain what the locker hire includes.
Say towels are included and send the guest to the lockers.
Ask a nearby colleague what guests are usually told.

advanced.situation: A guest says a locker key failed and their clothes are missing; two junior attendants are unsure how to respond.

options.text: Ask the guest to wait while you check nearby lockers yourself.
Have one attendant note the key number and direct the guest to the desk.
Guide staff to listen, record details, and refer the complaint to the supervisor.
Tell the guest that locker keys sometimes fail and offer another locker.

basic.situation: A family arrives for swimming, and your supervisor asks you to assign lockers near the changing area.

options.text: Give them a locker number from the list you used earlier.
Ask another attendant which locker numbers are usually available.
Look at the locker board and choose an unmarked space nearby.
Check which nearby lockers are free, then assign one to the family.

advanced.situation: Several groups arrive together, and the changing area is filling; you need to allocate available lockers fairly and keep access clear.

options.text: Reserve the largest open section for the first group in line.
Group nearby assignments by party size while keeping the access route clear.
Place each group in the nearest open section and watch for crowding.
Assign lockers as guests arrive and move groups along as needed.

basic.situation: A guest asks for a clean towel at the public bath, and you are replenishing the towel shelf.

options.text: Give the guest a towel from the top of the pile.
Hand over a clean towel and note the shelf level for replenishment.
Ask the guest to take a towel from the shelf themselves.
Choose a folded towel from the clean stack and hand it over.

advanced.situation: During a busy evening, clean towels run low while used ones are accumulating; you are asked to improve distribution for the shift.

options.text: Set a simple restock point and count clean towels at regular intervals.
Ask staff to take towels from whichever shelf looks fullest.
Keep a spare stack near the entrance for busy periods.
Tell attendants to refill shelves when they notice them getting low.

basic.situation: You see a patron carrying a glass drink into the changing area, where facility rules prohibit glass containers.

options.text: Check the facility rule, then explain whether glass may enter this area.
Remind the patron glass is prohibited and ask them to leave it outside.
Show the sign and direct the patron to ask the front desk about glass.
Finish the locker check, then ask the patron to leave the glass outside.

advanced.situation: A junior attendant sees children running near wet changing-room floors during a busy shift and is unsure how to intervene consistently.

options.text: Have staff calmly remind children, clear the route, and recheck wet floor areas.
Ask staff to guide children away and keep walkways clear during the shift.
Let attendants choose whether to remind children about running near wet floors.
Ask staff to give the same calm reminder and report repeated floor hazards.

basic.situation: After a group leaves the locker room, you notice wet footprints across the floor and your supervisor asks you to clean the area.

options.text: Leave the footprints until the room is empty again.
Mop the footprints quickly before the next group arrives.
Ask a colleague to watch the doorway while you mop the floor.
Place the wet-floor sign, then mop the footprints and check the route.

advanced.situation: Locker-room cleaning is delayed during peak hours, and several attendants use different methods; you are asked to coordinate the shift’s cleaning schedule.

options.text: Ask attendants to compare busy areas and choose cleaning priorities together during quieter periods.
Schedule cleaning around peak use and give each attendant a clear area.
Let attendants follow their routines while the rush continues through the locker room.
List key areas and have staff rotate tasks according to the shift schedule.

basic.situation: You notice the clean towel shelf is nearly empty and your supervisor has asked you to check supplies before the evening rush.

options.text: Tell a colleague the shelf looks low and continue your duties.
Count the remaining towels and report the shortage for replenishment.
Wait for the next guest to request towels before checking again.
Estimate the remaining stack and tell your supervisor it may run low.

advanced.situation: Guests report misplaced belongings while staff record found items in different ways; you are asked to improve lost-and-found tracking.

options.text: Let attendants keep found items at their stations until guests ask.
Ask staff to record found items, storage locations, and handovers in the shift book.
Keep found items together and ask guests to describe missing belongings.
Use one log for item details, discovery times, and storage locations.

basic.situation: While preparing a case, you notice fluid is not draining as expected during the trocar procedure and need to continue organ preparation.

options.text: Increase the pump flow to move the fluid through faster.
Check the tube connection and ask an experienced embalmer to review it.
Reposition the trocar slightly and see whether drainage improves.
Pause the procedure, check the tubing and positioning, then reassess drainage.

advanced.situation: A case requires special preparation for overseas transport, and the paperwork notes an infectious cause of death; you are assigned part of the procedure.

options.text: Ask a colleague what extra steps are usually used for transport cases.
Check the transport notes and confirm the special steps with the embalmer in charge.
Review the case instructions and facility procedure before starting the assigned work.
Use the routine preparation steps and finish the assigned work promptly.

basic.situation: After embalming, a small incision remains open and you are assigned to close it with sutures under supervision.

options.text: Pull the edges together tightly and tie the first knot quickly.
Follow the demonstrated stitch pattern and ask for a check when finished.
Align the edges carefully and close the incision with the assigned suture method.
Place a few stitches across the opening and check the edges afterward.

advanced.situation: A visible facial injury has left uneven contours before viewing, and you are asked to assist with reconstruction using approved materials.

options.text: Assess the contours and build the shape gradually with suitable reconstruction materials.
Use plaster to fill the deepest area before checking the profile.
Cover the uneven area with a thicker layer of cotton and cosmetics.
Compare both sides and add clay where the contour appears lower.

basic.situation: The family has chosen a natural appearance for viewing, and you are asked to apply cosmetics before the casket is closed.

options.text: Apply a heavier foundation layer to cover every visible variation.
Match the requested natural look and review the finish before dressing.
Use the usual cosmetic shade and ask a colleague if it seems suitable.
Use a light application and check the appearance under viewing-room lighting.

advanced.situation: A service begins soon, and the casket and floral display are being placed while guests are arriving and choosing seats.

options.text: Coordinate the display and casket positions around the planned guest seating and clear access.
Check the seating layout, then position the flowers beside the casket.
Move the casket toward the front and let guests choose seats around it.
Place the flowers wherever there is open floor space near the casket.

basic.situation: The funeral party is ready to leave, and you are assigned to help place the casket in the hearse and organize the procession.

options.text: Follow the lead attendant and help move the casket into position inside the hearse.
Ask nearby attendants to lift while others prepare the route for the procession.
Confirm everyone is ready, then help load the casket and follow the agreed procession order.
Begin loading when the hearse door opens, without checking whether the team is ready.

advanced.situation: Two attendants disagree about the procession order while the family is waiting; you are supervising the staff on duty.

options.text: Clarify the agreed order with the team and assign each attendant a clear role.
Remind both attendants to follow the funeral plan and prepare their tasks.
Tell the attendants to choose an order and start preparing the hearse.
Ask one attendant to lead while the other helps with the casket.

basic.situation: A family asks you to help arrange an obituary notice and discuss casket choices during an intake meeting.

options.text: Ask which details belong in the notice and note the family's casket preferences.
Review casket choices, then ask the family which obituary details they want included.
Ask about casket preferences, then draft the obituary from details the family provides.
Record obituary details and present the family with available casket choices.

advanced.situation: You are checking an embalming record and notice a required field is blank before the case file is passed on.

options.text: Pass the file along and mention the blank field to the next staff member.
Hold the record for clarification and check it against the facility procedure.
Fill the field with the detail used in the previous case.
Ask the embalmer in charge what belongs in the blank field.

basic.situation: A family needs assistance during a service, and you are assigned to attend the visiting room and help as needed.

options.text: Stay in the room and offer practical help if the family needs assistance.
Leave to prepare other service items while the family visits, without checking back.
Check in with the family, then return to the corridor for other duties.
Stay nearby and tell the family where to find you during their visit.

advanced.situation: A preparation-room trolley has a loose wheel before the next case, and you are responsible for routine funeral home equipment maintenance.

options.text: Mark the trolley for repair and use another trolley for the current case.
Remove the trolley from service and arrange a repair before its next use.
Tighten the wheel by hand and use the trolley for the next case.
Ask a colleague to watch the wheel while moving the trolley slowly.

basic.situation: A family has arrived, and you are asked to help move the deceased from the transfer trolley to the preparation area.

options.text: Move the remains with your colleague using the usual trolley route.
Take the nearest available trolley and move the remains to save time.
Ask the supervisor to guide your grip, then move the remains steadily.
Lift the remains by yourself to avoid delaying the family's arrival.

advanced.situation: A new colleague is assigned a sensitive case and asks how to move the deceased while family members wait nearby.

options.text: Ask them to watch you move the remains, then repeat the same steps.
Demonstrate calm handling, explain privacy steps, and invite questions before they begin.
Tell them to follow the routine and finish before the family enters.
Have them move the remains while you give brief instructions from nearby.

basic.situation: The crematory is ready, and your supervisor asks you to place the identified remains into the machine.

options.text: Load the remains quickly so the next scheduled service can stay on time.
Check each instruction with your supervisor as you position the remains.
Use the familiar loading sequence and start once the remains are inside.
Follow the posted sequence and ask your colleague to check the position.

advanced.situation: During a scheduled cremation, the machine shows an unfamiliar fault and the next service is due soon.

options.text: Wait briefly, then retry the cycle if the warning disappears.
Check the display and ask a colleague whether they recognize the fault.
Pause the cycle, record the fault, and follow the approved troubleshooting steps.
Reset the machine using the familiar control sequence and continue the cycle.

basic.situation: Before loading, you are given the deceased's paperwork and asked to confirm the identity with a colleague.

options.text: Check the name on the form and proceed if it looks familiar.
Use the label on the trolley as confirmation and continue with loading.
Read the paperwork aloud while your colleague checks the identification.
Match the documentation details with the identification before proceeding.

advanced.situation: You notice staff use different checks when confirming identity, and a busy shift is approaching.

options.text: Ask a senior colleague to compare current forms with you.
Remind staff to review identity documents together during the shift.
Suggest one shared checklist and ask staff to record each identity match.
Let workers continue separate checks without discussing their differences.

basic.situation: After a service, you are asked to clean the preparation table and floor before the next booking.

options.text: Wipe the table and sweep the floor using the usual routine.
