Use the supplied cleaning instructions for the table and floor.
Rinse the table and floor quickly so the room can be reused.
Clean the visible marks first and leave the rest for later.

advanced.situation: You notice cleaning tasks are missed when bookings overlap, and staff use different routines for equipment and floors.

options.text: Create a shift checklist by area, then show staff how to record completion.
Share a cleaning schedule and ask staff to report missed tasks.
Clean the busiest room yourself after each service to keep things moving.
Ask staff to clean their usual areas whenever bookings allow.

basic.situation: The cremation cycle is complete, and your supervisor asks you to help retrieve the remains for the urn.

options.text: Use the familiar brush while your colleague holds the collection container.
Vacuum the chamber with the nearest equipment to finish before cleanup.
Wait for your supervisor's instructions, then sweep the chamber carefully.
Sweep the chamber quickly and check the collection tray afterward.

advanced.situation: A colleague reports that little remains material is visible after retrieval, but the family is waiting for the urn.

options.text: Check the chamber and collection area systematically before preparing the urn.
Prepare the urn with the material already gathered to meet the family's wait.
Recheck the chamber floor with a light before completing retrieval.
Ask your colleague to inspect the tray again while you prepare the urn.

basic.situation: You are asked to help load the deceased into the funeral home's vehicle for transport to the crematory.

options.text: Use the familiar route and load the vehicle as the family watches.
Load the trolley with your partner and check its position before departure.
Lift the deceased into the vehicle quickly to keep the schedule moving.
Follow your colleague's loading guidance and secure the transfer properly.

advanced.situation: Two transfers are scheduled close together, and the vehicle assignment has changed during the morning shift.

options.text: Use the original vehicle plan so staff can avoid further delays.
Send the available vehicle to the first address on the route sheet.
Confirm each transfer's destination, vehicle, and timing before dispatching.
Follow the revised schedule and tell the driver about the change.

basic.situation: Before a wake, a senior attendant asks you to help place a casket in the chapel.

options.text: Follow the senior attendant's directions while positioning the casket steadily.
Push the casket into place quickly before guests start arriving.
Move it with your partner along the clear chapel route.
Use the nearest trolley and place the casket near the front.

advanced.situation: A tight chapel entrance and a large funeral party make casket movement more complex than the earlier rehearsal.

options.text: Lead from the front and remind the team to keep the casket level.
Assign clear roles, check the route, and guide the team through each turn.
Let the strongest attendants handle the entrance while others wait nearby.
Ask the team to follow the usual route at a slower pace.

basic.situation: The family has provided flowers for the chapel, and you are asked to place them around the casket.

options.text: Put the flowers wherever they fit around the casket.
Place the larger arrangements first, then fill open spaces with smaller flowers.
Stack extra bouquets beside the casket so the chapel looks full.
Arrange the flowers where the director indicated, keeping the display balanced.

advanced.situation: Several family floral tributes arrive at once, and the chapel layout has limited space near the casket.

options.text: Arrange the largest tributes around the casket and place smaller ones nearby.
Group the tributes by size, preserve access, and confirm placements with the family contact.
Fit each tribute into the nearest open space as it arrives.
Move the earlier tributes aside to make room for every new arrival.

basic.situation: A mourner arrives at the funeral home and asks where the service is being held.

options.text: Ask another guest where the service is before giving directions.
Greet them calmly and escort them to the marked chapel entrance.
Send them toward the largest room since services are usually held there.
Point out the chapel sign and let them follow the hallway.

advanced.situation: Guests arrive together for a crowded service, while one family member needs help leaving a limousine.

options.text: Pause guest directions and help the family member exit the limousine.
Ask arriving guests to wait while you direct everyone to the chapel.
Send guests through the nearest doorway while you finish with the limousine.
Ask a colleague to assist the passenger while you greet and direct arriving guests.

basic.situation: After a funeral procession, your supervisor asks you to clean the hearse before its next use.

options.text: Clean the exterior first so the hearse looks ready for visitors.
Wipe the visible surfaces and ask a colleague to check the exterior.
Rinse the hearse quickly and park it for the next driver.
Follow the vehicle cleaning instructions and check the interior afterward.

advanced.situation: Staff report recurring chapel equipment issues, and cleaning tasks are being missed between closely scheduled services.

options.text: Ask each attendant to check assigned equipment before every service.
Keep a maintenance and cleaning log by area, reviewing open items each shift.
Handle chapel repairs when staff report them during the day.
Move faulty equipment aside and continue preparing the remaining rooms.

basic.situation: Cars begin arriving for a funeral procession, and a senior attendant asks you to help direct them near the cemetery entrance.

options.text: Follow the senior attendant's parking plan and guide cars toward open spaces.
Wave cars toward the visible open area near the entrance.
Let each driver choose a space so the line keeps moving.
Direct cars across the entrance to shorten the walking distance.

advanced.situation: A large procession is expected, and cemetery parking near the service area is limited.

options.text: Ask drivers to use the nearest spaces as they arrive.
Identify available parking areas, brief attendants, and keep the procession route clear.
Send cars toward the service area and sort parking after they arrive.
Guide the first cars into a suitable area and update the team.

basic.situation: A funeral director asks you to issue a set of chairs and a canopy for an outdoor service.

options.text: Give the director the equipment from the nearest suitable storage area.
Let the director take the equipment and return it after the service.
Record the equipment issued and show the director where to return it.
Hand over the chairs and canopy, then log the issue in the shift log.

advanced.situation: Several teams borrow funeral equipment, and items are often returned to different storage areas after services.

options.text: Let each team keep frequently used items near its own work area between services.
Set labeled storage locations and maintain a simple issue and return record.
Ask teams to return borrowed items to the usual storage room.
Count shared equipment at the end of each busy workweek for missing items.

basic.situation: A family asks to move a local burial service to the afternoon, but the cemetery opening and clergy availability are not yet confirmed.

options.text: Ask the cemetery and clergy whether the requested afternoon time is available.
Confirm cemetery hours and clergy availability before offering the family an afternoon service time.
Check the cemetery schedule and offer its nearest available time to the family.
Ask the senior director which confirmed time to offer the family.

advanced.situation: A body shipment to another state is delayed, and the receiving funeral home reports that its service time may change while flowers are already booked.

options.text: Coordinate confirmed timing with receiving home, transport provider, and flower delivery service.
Keep the original transport booking and ask the receiving home to accommodate its arrival.
Confirm timing with the receiving home, then align transport and flower delivery arrangements.
Reschedule flower delivery while the receiving home confirms its revised service time.

basic.situation: A family comparing caskets asks what is included in two service packages, and your supervisor is available nearby.

options.text: Point to the package with the lower price and say it covers the main needs.
Ask your supervisor to explain both packages while you stay with the family.
Read the package sheets aloud and let the family choose between them.
Explain the listed package inclusions and invite the family to compare their priorities.

advanced.situation: A client wants a prearranged funeral contract with a custom service, but the requested details do not clearly match the package descriptions.

options.text: Clarify the client's priorities, check which details can be included, and explain any limits before discussing terms.
Review the package terms with the client and note the custom requests for follow-up.
Offer the nearest package and ask which custom details matter most to the client.
Use the closest package wording and reassure the client that the service can be adjusted later.

basic.situation: After a service, the preparation room needs cleaning and supplies must be moved while a senior staff member is present.

options.text: Move the supplies first, then wipe the visible surfaces before the next appointment.
Follow the room's cleaning sequence and move supplies as the senior staff member directs.
Ask the senior staff member which surfaces and supplies need attention first.
Clean the worktops and floor, then place the supplies beside the room entrance.

advanced.situation: You are overseeing care of remains after a transfer, and a family has requested a particular presentation that may not suit the condition you observe.

options.text: Discuss the observed condition and available presentation choices with the family before proceeding.
Prepare the requested presentation first and let the family decide after viewing it.
Ask a senior colleague to review the requested presentation before you continue preparation.
Assess the remains respectfully, explain feasible presentation choices, and record the agreed care plan for staff.

basic.situation: Guests arrive for a service while the family van is ready, and you have been asked to help usher people and arrange transport.

options.text: Ask the driver to confirm the destination with the family contact while you usher guests.
Seat arriving guests and confirm the van's destination with the family contact before departure.
Usher guests inside and ask the driver where the family van is headed.
Send the van toward the cemetery using the destination from yesterday's service notes.

advanced.situation: Several vehicles are serving a large funeral, and an invoice total does not match the transport bookings recorded for the event.

options.text: Match bookings to the invoice and flag unmatched charges before account preparation.
Prepare the account from the bookings and leave the invoice difference for later review.
Enter the invoice total and adjust the event account to match the supplier's statement.
Compare the bookings with the invoice and ask the supplier about the difference.

basic.situation: A bereaved family member asks whether they may qualify for any benefits, then becomes tearful while discussing the service.

options.text: Listen to their concern and offer to find the relevant benefits information for them.
Acknowledge their loss, listen, and share available benefits information in a calm, private conversation.
Tell them which benefits families commonly receive and offer a leaflet to take home.
Hand over a benefits leaflet and return to the service arrangements they requested.

advanced.situation: A staff member is struggling to respond to an upset family who questions a service detail, and other families are waiting nearby.

options.text: Model a private, calm response, then coach the staff member to hear the family's concern.
Ask another attendant to speak with the family while you reassure the staff member.
Ask the staff member to repeat the service details so the family understands the arrangement.
Take over the conversation, listen to the concern, and settle the family in a quieter area.

basic.situation: A family is providing details for a death certificate, but one entry on the form differs from the document they brought.

options.text: Pause that entry and ask your supervisor how to handle the differing details.
Copy the entry from the form and pass the paperwork along for processing.
Use the detail on the document and note the family's different entry for review.
Compare the entry with the document and ask the family to clarify it.

advanced.situation: A cemetery requests grave-opening details, but the family's paperwork contains a date that conflicts with the service booking.

options.text: Use the paperwork date and tell the cemetery to continue grave preparations.
Ask the family contact to verify the date before updating cemetery details.
Confirm the service date with the family contact, then update the cemetery record.
Compare the booking with the paperwork, then hold the request until the date is confirmed.

basic.situation: A regular asks for a tidy trim before work, but their sides are growing unevenly and the shop is busy.

options.text: Match the sides to the longer side and leave the top close to its current length.
Clip the sides to the usual length and tidy the top to save time.
Ask how much length they want removed, then trim the sides and top evenly.
Confirm the requested length, even the sides with clippers, and check the shape before finishing.

advanced.situation: A client brings a photo of a layered style, but their hair texture and current length differ from the example.

options.text: Copy the photo's outline and use a dryer for a similar finish.
Discuss texture and length, then agree on layers suited to the client's hair.
Explain likely results and agree on a manageable layered version before cutting.
Suggest growing it longer, then offer a tidy trim for today's visit.

basic.situation: A client asks for a shorter beard and sharper neck line, while you are still learning the shop's razor routine.

options.text: Shape the beard with scissors and leave the neck line for another visit.
Trim the beard short and shave a sharp neck line to match the request.
Confirm the beard length, trim with scissors, and ask your supervisor to check before razor work.
Ask the client to mark the neck line and trim the beard to that outline.

advanced.situation: A client with a sharply angled beard wants both sides reshaped, and a junior barber asks you how to use the razor safely.

options.text: Trim the beard with scissors and ask the junior to watch a razor tutorial later.
Discuss the shape with the client and coach the junior through the razor routine.
Map the angles with the client, then demonstrate safe razor strokes on one side.
Copy the sharper side across both cheeks and let the junior finish the neck.

basic.situation: A client has finished, and another is waiting while the station and combs need attention between appointments.

options.text: Set combs aside for sterilizing, then wipe the station before seating clients.
Sweep the loose hair and replace the towel before the next appointment.
Clean the station, sterilize combs as directed, and prepare space for the next client.
Wipe the station and reuse the combs after brushing away loose hair.

advanced.situation: During a busy shift, you notice staff cleaning clippers in different ways and the next clients are already waiting.

options.text: Let each barber finish their current cuts and discuss clipper cleaning at closing.
Take the clippers for cleaning yourself while staff serve the waiting clients.
Remind staff to follow the shop's sterilizing procedure and check the next tools.
Pause clipper use, review the sterilizing procedure, and align staff on cleaning.

basic.situation: A walk-in asks for a haircut but is unsure what style will suit a new office role.

options.text: Ask about upkeep and workplace needs, then suggest a maintainable style.
Show several office-friendly styles and ask which one looks appealing.
Recommend the shop's popular short style and begin preparing the clippers.
Ask what length they prefer and show a couple of suitable style options.

advanced.situation: A regular asks for a styling tonic after a cut, while a junior barber is unsure how to discuss products without pressuring clients.

options.text: Recommend the highest-priced tonic and mention that regular clients often buy it.
Show the client two tonic bottles and let them choose by scent and price.
Ask the desired finish, explain a suitable tonic, and model a relaxed recommendation.
Ask about the client's styling routine and describe a tonic that may fit it.

basic.situation: A client pays for a haircut and beard trim, but the cashier ticket shows only the haircut.

options.text: Ask the barber to confirm the services and update the ticket before payment.
Add the beard trim to the ticket using the usual service price.
Check services with the client, update the ticket, and confirm the total before payment.
Charge the haircut price and add the beard trim to the next ticket later.

advanced.situation: You are helping review weekly shop records, and several supply bills appear under the wrong dates before payments are prepared.

options.text: Hold the uncertain bills and prepare payments for the remaining suppliers.
Match bills to delivery records, note date issues, and prepare an exceptions list.
Compare bills with delivery records and flag dates that clearly do not match.
Use dates on bills and prepare supplier payments to keep the week on schedule.

basic.situation: The shop's neck strips are running low, and a client is waiting while you prepare their protective cloth.

options.text: Use a spare towel as a cloth and add neck strips to next week's order.
Drape and pin the cloth securely, then check stock and record needed neck strips.
Prepare the cloth and check the supply cupboard after the client leaves.
Pin the protective cloth and tell the manager that neck strips are running low.

advanced.situation: A new styling technique is popular among clients, and junior barbers want to try it during a fully booked shift.

options.text: Ask the team to watch a styling video during their next break.
Let the juniors try the technique on walk-ins and compare their results at closing.
Study the technique, discuss suitable hair types, and schedule a practice demonstration.
Review the technique's steps and coach the juniors while they try it on mannequins.

basic.situation: A client shows you a photo and asks for a tidy trim. The senior stylist asks you to cut the sides with clippers and shape the top with scissors.

options.text: Use clippers on the sides and scissors on top, matching the photo.
Trim quickly to the requested length, then ask the stylist to check.
Confirm the guide length, then cut each section as demonstrated.
Take a small section, compare both sides, and adjust the outline.

advanced.situation: A client with tight curls wants a custom layered cut. You are shaping the outline while a junior stylist watches and asks how to avoid uneven shrinkage.

options.text: Discuss the desired layers, then demonstrate a controlled section-by-section cut.
Cut the curls dry in layers, then explain the technique to the junior.
Assess curl shrinkage, cut gradually, and show the junior how each section falls.
Ask the junior to follow the usual guide while you shape the outline.

basic.situation: A client is ready for a wash before a blow-dry. The senior stylist asks you to shampoo and rinse while checking the water temperature with the client.

options.text: Check the water with the client, shampoo gently, and rinse until clear.
Wet the hair, apply shampoo, and rinse as the senior demonstrated.
Use extra shampoo so the hair feels clean after one rinse.
Keep the water warm and move through the wash at a steady pace.

advanced.situation: A client needs a formal updo for an event, and the setting method is new to your junior colleague. You have limited time before the appointment ends.

options.text: Demonstrate section tension and roller placement, then coach the junior through the set.
Show the junior the roller pattern, then check the set before finishing.
Finish the style yourself to keep the appointment on schedule.
Set each section with rollers, then let the junior copy your finished arrangement.

basic.situation: A client asks you to tidy stray eyebrow hairs before a haircut. With the senior stylist nearby, you prepare tweezers and check the shape they prefer.

options.text: Check the shape and comfort as you tweeze small amounts from each brow.
Tidy the obvious hairs quickly so the client can start the haircut.
Confirm the preferred shape, then remove a few hairs at a time.
Follow the natural brow line and remove visible stray hairs in one pass.

advanced.situation: A performer develops redness during a facial wax before a show. You are responsible for deciding how to continue the removal safely within your role.

options.text: Ask the senior stylist to assess redness before deciding whether waxing can resume.
Pause waxing, ask about discomfort, and check product guidance before continuing.
Offer tweezers for remaining hairs, checking the performer’s comfort as you work.
Apply soothing lotion, then finish waxing while watching the skin for changes.

basic.situation: A client requests a single shade on their roots. The senior stylist gives you the prepared dye and asks you to apply it with a brush.

options.text: Apply the dye in neat sections, following the stylist's timing instructions.
Section the roots, apply evenly, and check coverage before timing as instructed.
Brush the dye over the visible roots, then begin timing the service.
Spread the dye quickly across the roots so the client stays on schedule.

advanced.situation: A client wants a major color change, but their ends are lighter than the roots. You are preparing the application while a junior stylist asks how to protect even results.

options.text: Assess the starting shades, plan separate sections, and explain the application sequence.
Apply one mixture throughout, then adjust the ends if the shade differs.
Divide the hair into sections and apply the planned color carefully.
Ask the senior stylist to approve the plan before applying any color.

basic.situation: A regular client calls to book a trim and mentions wanting the same style as last visit. You are updating the appointment book and client notes.

options.text: Offer the nearest open slot and add the client's name to the book.
Check availability, confirm the time, and record the requested style in the notes.
Put the client into the next open slot to keep the book moving.
Book the usual service time and note the client's preferred style.

advanced.situation: A client brings a reference photo for a new style, but their hair texture and face shape differ from the model's. They ask what you recommend.

options.text: Use the photo as a starting point and offer the closest suitable cut.
Suggest a similar style that suits their hair texture and explain the difference.
Recommend the pictured style, while allowing extra appointment time for careful adjustments.
Discuss their routine, assess their hair and features, then adapt the style together.

basic.situation: After a busy appointment, you clean the station, sanitize the scissors, and take payment at the register while the next client waits.

options.text: Sanitize the scissors, clear the station, and enter the payment before closing the sale.
Close the sale quickly and leave the scissors for the next station reset.
Wipe the station, sanitize the scissors, and process the client's payment.
Take the payment first, then clean the station after the client leaves.

advanced.situation: A popular shampoo is running low, and a client asks whether you have a bottle to sell. You are checking stock and completing the day's service records.

options.text: Check the shelf, sell a bottle if available, and update the stock sheet.
Tell the client it is available and update the stock sheet later.
Sell the last bottle, then note the low stock for the next order.
Check stock and records, reserve service needs, then flag the reorder quantity.

basic.situation: You read a scene where a character arrives after a long journey. The artist lead asks you to note appearance changes needed for that scene.

options.text: Use the character's usual look and add a tired expression for the scene.
Read the scene, identify its events, and list the resulting appearance changes.
Mark the journey scene and note changes to the character's hair and makeup.
Add a dusty look to the makeup notes and move to the next scene.

advanced.situation: The director's notes, costume sketches, and venue lighting suggest different looks for a period character. You are preparing points for the design review.

options.text: Show the sketches and ask the director which look should lead the design.
Compare the notes, sketches, and lighting, then present a look that resolves their differences.
Choose the strongest sketch and use it as the basis for the review.
Follow the period notes and prepare a makeup look from that description.

basic.situation: A performer is ready for a simple on-camera look. With an experienced artist nearby, you cleanse the skin and begin applying foundation.

options.text: Cleanse the skin, apply foundation in light layers, and check the finish.
Apply foundation straight away so the performer can reach set on time.
Use a generous layer of foundation to cover the skin in one pass.
Prepare the skin and apply the foundation shade the artist selected.

advanced.situation: A performer returns after a break, and the stage lighting has shifted warmer. You need to restore the character's makeup continuity before the next scene.

options.text: Add powder to reduce shine and let the lighting team handle the color shift.
Reapply the same products quickly so the scene can resume on schedule.
Refresh the makeup as before and check the result from the audience seats.
Compare the performer with reference photos under the new lights, then adjust shades and placement.

basic.situation: A performer needs a pre-made scar prosthesis for rehearsal. With the lead artist beside you, you position it and prepare to attach it.

options.text: Position the prosthesis on the marked area and secure its edges carefully.
Attach the scar where it looks convincing and move on to makeup.
Press the prosthesis firmly into place so it stays on through rehearsal.
Check the fit and placement with the performer, then attach as demonstrated.

advanced.situation: A period production needs a distinctive aged character, but the available reference images show inconsistent facial details. You are developing the prosthesis concept.

options.text: Sketch the aged features and ask the lead artist to select a design.
Use the clearest reference image and design the prosthesis around its features.
Research period references, sketch the facial changes, and shape a test model for review.
Enlarge the strongest wrinkles from the references and build those into the model.

basic.situation: After a rehearsal, you are assigned to clean the shared makeup brushes before the next performer arrives. Several brushes have visible foundation on them.

options.text: Remove visible product, clean each brush with the approved supplies, and let them dry.
Spray the brushes lightly so they look clean for the next performer.
Clean the brushes with the supplied cleaner and place them back in the kit.
Wipe the brushes with a clean towel and return them to the kit.

advanced.situation: A performer with reactive skin reports itching during makeup removal. You are helping after the show and need to decide how to handle the remaining makeup.

options.text: Ask the performer to remove the remaining makeup in their own way.
Stop using the current remover and check with the lead artist before continuing.
Switch to a gentler remover and continue with smaller cotton pads.
Pause removal, ask about the irritation, and follow the product guidance for sensitive skin.

basic.situation: A performer has finished a character look for a scene. The lead artist asks you to photograph it and record the products used for tomorrow's repeat.

options.text: Photograph the look from clear angles and note the products used for each area.
Take a front photo and write down the main products you applied.
Snap a quick photo and rely on memory for the products used.
Ask the performer to pose once, then save the photo with the scene name.

advanced.situation: A new artist will cover your character look tomorrow, and the performer has asked about a product you used. You are preparing handover notes and a demonstration.

options.text: Give the artist your product list and ask them to follow the photos.
Record the look and products, then demonstrate the application steps and answer questions.
Show the artist the finished look and pass along the product names.
Explain the products to the new artist and let them review your makeup sheet.

basic.situation: You are preparing a simple makeup job for a small performance. The lead artist asks you to list the materials needed within the agreed budget.

options.text: Write down the makeup items you expect to use for the character.
Request a full new set of makeup so the job has enough supplies.
Choose familiar products first and estimate their cost after the list is complete.
List the required makeup, check kit stock, and note any materials to acquire.

advanced.situation: A custom prosthesis job is nearing its budget limit, and the team needs additional materials for a revised design. You are preparing the materials request.

options.text: Review the revised design, check stock, and request needed materials within the budget.
Order extra materials now so the revised design can proceed without delay.
Update the materials list for the revision and check the cost against the budget.
Request the original materials and add a small allowance for the revision.

basic.situation: A client asks for a softer oval shape, but one nail is shorter than the others. You are preparing her hands for polish.

options.text: Trim uneven corners quickly, then finish each nail with a coarse board.
Match the shortest nail, then smooth the others with steady, gentle strokes.
Check her preferred oval, match the shorter nail, and smooth both hands with light strokes.
Ask which oval shape she prefers, then file gently and compare both hands.

advanced.situation: A returning client wants a long sculpted extension repaired before an event. The weakened edge flexes as you inspect it.

options.text: Use the rotary wheel lightly, then add product over the weakened edge.
File the extension shorter by hand and offer a simpler repair.
Shape the extension with the rotary wheel, then check its balance from above.
Reduce the length, shape with the rotary wheel, and check the edge between passes.

basic.situation: A client chooses a deep red polish, and you notice a pale streak after your first coat. She is waiting for her appointment to finish.

options.text: Let the coat settle, then apply a thin second layer across each nail.
Use a clear top coat to soften the streak and finish the set.
Add a thicker coat now so the pale streak disappears before drying.
Smooth the streak with a light brush pass, then apply a thin even coat.

advanced.situation: A client requests raised ornaments on two nails for a wedding. The design catches on her sleeve during a fitting.

options.text: Press the ornaments down firmly and finish both nails before she leaves.
Secure each ornament with extra adhesive, then ask her to try the sleeve again.
Remove the snagging ornaments and offer a flatter design for the event.
Reposition the ornaments within the design, secure their edges, and retest the sleeve.

basic.situation: You are applying a short artificial nail, but the paper form shifts as the client relaxes her finger.

options.text: Reposition the form under the tip, check its alignment, then apply the product.
Hold the form in place and apply powder before it shifts again.
Ask the client to steady her finger while you finish shaping the form.
Pause, realign the paper form, and apply powder once it feels secure.

advanced.situation: A client wants noticeably longer tapered extensions for a formal event. Her natural nails curve unevenly, making the paper forms sit at different angles.

options.text: Follow the natural curve on each finger and shape the tips to match.
Adjust each form to the natural curve, then build and compare the requested lengths.
Make the extensions shorter and use matching forms across both hands.
Use one form angle for every finger and build the requested length.

basic.situation: During a hand service, you see dry skin around a client's knuckles. She asks for a short massage before polish.

options.text: Apply lotion and massage the whole hand with even pressure.
Massage directly over dry patches with firm pressure to finish the service quickly.
Give a short hand massage and avoid the driest areas.
Soften loose skin gently, then massage around the knuckles with light strokes.

advanced.situation: A client asks for a hand massage, but you notice a red, flaky patch and she says it has recently spread.

options.text: Ask when it began, note the patch, and recommend medical assessment before massage.
Skip the affected hand and gently massage her other hand for now.
Massage around the patch and suggest she seek advice about a soothing cream.
Pause the massage and explain a clinician can assess the spreading patch before rescheduling.

basic.situation: After a busy manicure, you find polish dust on the table and used tools beside the clean set for the next client.

options.text: Sanitize the tools and leave the dust for the next area reset.
Wipe the table and replace the tools with a fresh set.
Move the used tools aside and wipe the visible dust from the table.
Clean and sanitize the tools, then wipe the table before setting up again.

advanced.situation: You are updating supply records before a weekend rush and notice that the polish remover stock is lower than the latest service log suggests.

options.text: Order extra remover based on the shelf count and update the inventory sheet.
Recount the remover, compare recent use, and note the verified balance in the record.
Change the count to match the service log and finish the record.
Record the current shelf count and flag the mismatch for the next stock review.

basic.situation: A client finishes her service and asks to book another slot after work next week. Two appointments are available, and the payment terminal is busy.

options.text: Ask which time suits her and hold both slots until payment is ready.
Offer both open times, confirm her choice, and process payment once the terminal clears.
Book the earlier slot and ask her to pay at the next visit.
Ask which time suits her, then note her choice while the payment terminal becomes available.

advanced.situation: A client wants a premium strengthening service but has brittle nails and asks whether a product will guarantee longer wear.

options.text: Explain that brittle nails may affect wear, and avoid promising month-long strength.
Explain that wear varies and recommend the premium service for added support.
Review care directions, set realistic expectations, and offer a suitable service choice.
Show her the premium product and describe its ingredients and intended strengthening benefits.

basic.situation: A client arrives with makeup on and asks for a gentle cleanse before her facial. You are preparing the lotions and towels.

options.text: Remove the makeup with lotion, then cleanse gently with water and fresh towels.
Apply cleansing lotion, remove it with water, and continue with the facial.
Wipe away the makeup with a damp towel, then apply cleansing lotion.
Use a toner over the makeup and start the facial as planned.

advanced.situation: A regular client says her face felt tight after the last cleanse. Today she arrives flushed after a sunny commute and requests her usual lotion.

options.text: Ask about the tightness, then select a mild lotion and cleanse gently with cool water.
Rinse with cool water and ask about her skin before applying any lotion.
Use her usual lotion and rinse gently with cool water before beginning.
Choose mild lotion, rinse with cool water, and ask how her skin feels today.

basic.situation: A client is booked for a facial mask, but she mentions her cheeks felt warm after trying a new product yesterday.

options.text: Apply the usual mask, shorten its wear, and ask about warmth during treatment.
Offer a gentle cleanse and ask whether she wants to reschedule the mask.
Ask about the reaction, choose a gentle mask, and check her comfort during application.
Test a small amount first, then check her skin and comfort after several minutes.

advanced.situation: A client requests a peel for age spots before a family event next week. She has never had a peel and wants the strongest option available.

options.text: Discuss her timing and skin history, then offer a suitable lower-intensity treatment or later plan.
Offer a facial mask for now and leave the peel discussion for another visit.
Explain that a peel may cause visible irritation and suggest booking after the event.
Choose the strongest peel and shorten the application time for her first visit.

basic.situation: A client asks for eyebrow tinting, and you are preparing the tint while a senior specialist is nearby to guide you.

options.text: Use a shorter tint time and let the client choose the shade.
Confirm the tint shade and timing with the senior, then apply it carefully.
Ask the senior to watch while you apply the chosen tint shade.
Mix the tint, apply it evenly, and check the result when time is up.

advanced.situation: A client wants facial waxing before a photo session, but the hair grows in different directions and a junior colleague is observing your service.

options.text: Ask the junior to hold the skin taut while you wax each section.
Use small wax sections and check her skin carefully after each removal.
Wax against the growth in one strip to finish before her session.
Map growth directions, use small sections, and explain your approach to the observing junior colleague.

basic.situation: You examine a client's cheeks with a magnifying lamp and see dryness around the nose. She asks what you notice.

options.text: Say the dry area proves she has a condition that needs treatment.
Suggest a richer moisturizer after seeing dryness around her nose.
Describe visible dryness, ask how it feels, and note it for service.
Ask about comfort and describe the dry area you observed around her nose.

advanced.situation: A client has a new uneven dark patch that looks different from nearby spots. She asks which brightening treatment will remove it.

options.text: Suggest a gentle brightening product and ask her to monitor the patch.
Recommend a brightening peel and offer a stronger home product.
Describe the change, avoid promising removal, and recommend medical assessment before cosmetic treatment.
Explain that you cannot assess the patch and suggest she consult a clinician.

basic.situation: A first-time client says her skin feels dry after cleansing and prefers fragrance-free products. You are writing her service record.

options.text: Record her dry feeling and fragrance-free preference in the client notes.
Record her preference for gentle products, then complete the service record before she leaves.
Note the fragrance preference and recommend a richer cleanser for home.
Record her dryness, fragrance preference, and the cleanser used during today's service.

advanced.situation: A client asks for a home routine, then shows you a painful, spreading rash near her jaw and asks which serum to buy.

options.text: Explain the rash needs assessment, document her request, and refer her to care.
Offer a simple cleanser routine while avoiding the affected jaw area today.
Pause product advice and suggest she contact a medical professional about the spreading painful rash.
Suggest a calming serum, then schedule a routine review for next month.

basic.situation: After a facial massage, you see product residue on the headrest and used tools beside the clean tray for the next client.

options.text: Clean the headrest and sterilize the tools before preparing the next service.
Wipe the headrest and return the used tools to the clean tray.
Sterilize the tools and leave the headrest for the room reset.
Replace the headrest cover and set out a fresh tray of tools.

advanced.situation: A new colleague is learning facial massage and presses firmly along a client's jaw. The client tenses but says she is fine.

options.text: Let the colleague finish this sequence, then discuss the pressure after the client leaves.
Ask whether she wants less pressure before continuing the massage sequence.
Tell the colleague to use lighter pressure for the remaining massage sequence.
Pause, check her comfort, and demonstrate gentler pressure for your colleague.

basic.situation: A guest hands you two bags for room 308 while you are learning the luggage route. What do you do before moving them?

options.text: I place the bags beside the lift while I finish another delivery.
I take the bags upstairs first, then ask the desk to confirm their room.
I load the bags onto the cart and confirm room 308 before leaving.
I check each tag against the room list, then move the bags together.

advanced.situation: Several coaches arrive together, and luggage is piling up while two guests need bags for an early departure. How do you manage the transfers?

options.text: I group bags by destination and assign clear runs to available porters.
I stagger cart departures and keep the early departure bags near the front.
I send carts in arrival order and let guests wait for their bags.
I ask porters to take the nearest bags and report back when finished.

basic.situation: A guest gives you a suitcase and says they are staying on the fifth floor, but the luggage slip is blank. What do you do?

options.text: I note the guest's name and room, then complete the check at the desk.
I attach a blank check and ask the desk to fill it in later.
I ask the guest to confirm their room, complete the check, and attach it securely.
I write the fifth floor on the claim check and attach it to the handle.

advanced.situation: Two guests claim similar suitcases, and a new porter asks how to tag the next arrivals. How do you resolve the claims and guide the tagging?

options.text: I ask the desk to settle the claims and have the porter watch my next tags.
I compare the claim details and bag descriptions, then show the porter the matching checks.
I separate the bags, verify each guest's check and description, then coach the porter through matching details.
I let each guest choose a suitcase and tag the remaining arrivals as usual.

basic.situation: A guest asks you to deliver a short message to a room while you are helping at the lobby. How do you handle it?

options.text: I ask the desk to call the room and deliver the message by phone.
I pass the message to a nearby porter and return to the lobby.
I repeat the message at the guest's door and confirm it was delivered.
I write down the message and leave it at the room door.

advanced.situation: Several guests request laundry pickups before the evening collection, and one asks for a message delivered upstairs. How do you coordinate the errands?

options.text: I log each pickup by guest and room, group nearby stops, and deliver the message.
I collect laundry by floor and keep each guest's items together for handover.
I gather laundry by floor, label bundles, and return them to the desk.
I deliver the message first, then collect laundry by guest call order.

basic.situation: A family arrives with several bags, and you are asked to escort them to their room while learning the route. What do you do?

options.text: I ask another porter to walk with them while I move the bags.
I point toward the lifts and ask them to follow the signs upstairs.
I take one bag upstairs first and leave the family waiting in the lobby.
I greet them, confirm their room, and walk with them along the marked route.

advanced.situation: A guest asks for a taxi to a busy local venue, and the hotel entrance is crowded with arriving visitors. How do you help?

options.text: I call for a taxi and ask the guest to wait near the main doors.
I point out the taxi stand and let the guest choose a car there.
I flag a passing taxi, confirm its route, and share the venue name.
I book through the usual channel, confirm the pickup point, and guide the guest there.

basic.situation: You notice wet footprints across the entrance after a rain shower, and guests are walking through the lobby. What do you do?

options.text: I mop the footprints quickly while guests walk around the wet patch.
I place a towel over the wet marks until the next lobby check.
I ask a colleague to watch the walkway while I fetch a mop.
I place a wet floor sign, then mop the entrance when the walkway clears.

advanced.situation: Rain is expected during a busy arrival period, and the entrance mat keeps shifting as guests wheel bags across it. How do you keep the area safe?

options.text: I reset the mat and check the entrance between arrival waves.
I ask arriving guests to step around the mat until the lobby quiets.
I secure the mat, post a warning sign, and check it regularly.
I remove the mat and leave the wet entrance for the cleaning round.

basic.situation: A guest asks how to use the room television and where to find the nearest pharmacy. How do you respond?

options.text: I tell the guest to try the remote and ask the desk about pharmacies.
I explain the television controls and point out the pharmacy on a nearby map.
I ask a colleague to explain the television while I return to the desk.
I show the power button and describe the pharmacy's general direction.

advanced.situation: A guest using a wheelchair asks for directions to a nearby attraction and how to adjust the room ventilation. How do you assist?

options.text: I offer a nearby route and show the guest the ventilation panel.
I explain the ventilation controls and confirm an accessible route before describing it.
I describe the usual route and tell the guest to ask staff about the controls.
I point toward the attraction and leave the controls card on the desk.

basic.situation: A guest asks you to book one rental car for tomorrow morning and gives you a preferred pickup time. What do you do?

options.text: I confirm the time and pickup details, then book through our usual provider.
I check available cars and share pickup choices before booking one.
I reserve a car and send the guest its details to review later.
I book an available car and tell the guest its pickup time.

advanced.situation: A guest's connecting train is cancelled, and they need to reach another city for a morning meeting. What do you do about their travel arrangements?

options.text: I book the first available replacement train and tell the guest the new time.
I compare viable train and car options against the meeting time, then confirm before booking.
I check the next train and offer the guest its departure time and fare.
I suggest the guest contact the railway while I keep the original booking details.

basic.situation: A guest reports a missing umbrella and asks whether a replacement can be arranged before leaving. What do you do?

options.text: I buy a similar umbrella nearby and charge it to the guest's room.
I offer an umbrella from the lobby stand and note the missing item.
I check lost property and arrange a suitable replacement if it is not there.
I tell the guest to check with the shop where they last used it.

advanced.situation: A guest needs an uncommon interpreter for a meeting later today, and the first service you contact is unavailable. How do you proceed?

options.text: I find another service and pass its contact details to the guest.
I send the guest a list of interpreter contacts and return to other requests.
I search for another interpreter and confirm availability, language, and timing with the guest.
I book the first interpreter who answers and share the meeting address.

basic.situation: A guest asks you to reserve a table for two tonight at a nearby restaurant and has a preferred time. What do you do?

options.text: I call the restaurant and ask whether the preferred time is open.
I reserve the first table I find and leave the details at reception.
I check the preferred time, confirm the party size, and call the restaurant to reserve.
I ask the restaurant for its next table and tell the guest the time.

advanced.situation: A group needs a private dinner, printed menus, and childcare for several families on the same evening. How do you coordinate the arrangements?

options.text: I arrange the dinner first and ask the group to manage the other requests.
I ask the restaurant to arrange the menus and childcare with its usual contacts.
I contact the restaurant and childcare provider, then relay their replies to the organizer.
I confirm the group's needs and timing, then coordinate each service and report confirmed details.

basic.situation: A guest asks for directions to a nearby restaurant and says they have not visited the area before. What do you do?

options.text: I tell the guest to search the restaurant name on their phone.
I point toward the main road and say the restaurant is nearby.
I check the map, explain the route, and mention a clear landmark along it.
I show the guest the restaurant's location on the lobby map.

advanced.situation: A guest using a wheelchair wants a personalized afternoon outing and asks whether a wheelchair can be provided. How do you help plan it?

options.text: I suggest a popular nearby attraction and offer the lobby wheelchair.
I offer two nearby attractions and check whether a wheelchair is free.
I ask about the guest's interests, check accessible options, and confirm wheelchair availability.
I tell the guest to choose an attraction and arrange a wheelchair later.

basic.situation: A guest gives you one suitcase for delivery to their room and asks you to take a letter to the front desk. What do you do?

options.text: I deliver the suitcase to the room and leave the letter on the desk.
I take the suitcase upstairs and keep the letter in my pocket for later.
I confirm the room, deliver the suitcase, and hand the letter to desk staff.
I take both items to reception and ask the desk to arrange delivery.

advanced.situation: Several guests arrive together with stored luggage, while two request separate errands before their rooms are ready. How do you manage the work?

options.text: I tag the bags and handle the errands in the order guests asked.
I group luggage by guest and room, log storage, then sequence errands by deadline.
I keep the bags together in one area and start with the nearest errand.
I move all the bags to storage and ask guests to remind me about errands.

basic.situation: A guest asks you to order flowers for a birthday dinner and gives you a budget and preferred colour. What do you do?

options.text: I choose a large arrangement and charge it to the guest's room.
I order a standard bouquet and leave a note about the guest's preferred colour.
I confirm the guest's budget and colour, then order a fitting arrangement.
I call the florist to ask what arrangements fit the budget.

advanced.situation: A department asks you to help plan a meeting for several guests, with a room, musicians, and printed materials to arrange. How do you organize the work?

options.text: I book a musician first and ask the department to arrange the room.
I confirm needs, coordinate schedules and vendors, and track each arrangement.
I reserve a suitable room, check musician availability, and confirm printed materials with staff.
I check vendor availability and share the responses with the department for coordination.

basic.situation: At the old railway station, a visitor asks what the platform signs mean while your group waits.

options.text: I would explain the signs using the guide notes and invite one question.
I would read the sign aloud and move on when time is short.
I would connect each sign to its station purpose, then check understanding.
I would repeat a popular story as fact to keep the group engaged.

advanced.situation: At a heritage site, visitors ask how a disputed event shaped the building, but your notes cover only its construction.

options.text: I would invent a simple link so the group leaves with a clear story.
I would steer questions back to the building's visible features and finish the tour.
I would explain what the records support, note the dispute, and invite perspectives.
I would share the construction notes and separate them from uncertain claims.

basic.situation: At a museum entrance, a family asks how to reach the accessible gallery shown on your visitor map.

options.text: I would show the main corridor and ask staff to confirm the lift.
I would suggest following other visitors toward the gallery entrance.
I would point toward the gallery and mention the nearest lift.
I would mark the gallery route on their map and describe its turns.

advanced.situation: A group must reach a hilltop viewpoint before rain, and the map shows two paths with different stair sections.

options.text: I would explain both paths' stairs and let the group decide together.
I would compare stairs, walking time, and shelter, then recommend the safer route.
I would choose the shorter path based on its distance on the map.
I would take the familiar path and check the weather at the viewpoint.

basic.situation: You are preparing a short stop at a local fort, and your senior asks you to gather basic facts about its history.

options.text: I would copy an unsourced date from a visitor comment into the notes.
I would search a travel forum and note its most repeated story.
I would check the site display and leaflet, recording where each fact appears.
I would gather dates and names from the site leaflet for review.

advanced.situation: A family requests a half-day forest walk; one child tires easily, and heavy rain is forecast for the afternoon.

options.text: I would suggest a shorter trail and mention the afternoon rain forecast.
I would promise the full loop and shorten it if the child struggles.
I would review trail length, rain exposure, and the family's stated abilities before proposing options.
I would choose a popular loop and pack extra water for the group.

basic.situation: At a lookout, visitors begin leaning over a low barrier to take photos, though signs ask them to stay behind it.

options.text: I would take their photo while they lean over, then move the group along.
I would ask them to step back and explain the barrier's purpose.
I would remind them of the barrier and point to the marked photo area.
I would mention the sign from nearby and continue counting the group.

advanced.situation: At a crowded quarry tour, a visitor crosses a marked boundary toward active equipment while the rest of your group waits nearby.

options.text: I would take the group across the boundary to retrieve the visitor together.
I would alert site staff while the group watches from the marked point.
I would call the visitor back and pause everyone at the marked point.
I would guide the visitor back along the safe path, keeping everyone behind the boundary.

basic.situation: You are escorting six visitors through a public building, and one person pauses to read a display as the group reaches a junction.

options.text: I would continue ahead and expect the visitor to catch up at the exit.
I would point out the next corridor and remind everyone to stay close.
I would ask the others to wait while the visitor finishes reading.
I would stop at the junction, count everyone, and show the next meeting point.

advanced.situation: At a busy industrial site, two visitor groups arrive together, and the marked walkway narrows near a scheduled vehicle crossing.

options.text: I would send both groups along the walkway before the vehicle reaches the crossing.
I would ask the groups to keep single file and follow the site signs.
I would hold one group at the assembly point and escort the other along the walkway.
I would wait for the crossing to clear and then lead both groups together.

basic.situation: A primary school group arrives at a nature centre, and the teacher asks you to help children notice three kinds of leaves.

options.text: I would show three leaves and ask children to name their colours.
I would guide a leaf hunt along the marked path, then compare shapes together.
I would hand out leaf sheets and ask children to find the listed shapes.
I would invite children to collect leaves from planted display beds.

advanced.situation: A school requests a half-day heritage route for mixed-age pupils, and your usual stops include a long uphill walk and a busy crossing.

options.text: I would keep the hill and schedule a rest before the crossing.
I would shorten the route and replace the hill with an indoor stop.
I would use the usual route and ask teachers to keep pupils together.
I would sequence accessible stops, avoid the busy crossing, and add age-suited activities.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to draft a one-day itinerary for visitors who want a market, a museum, and lunch near the river.

options.text: I would check opening hours, travel links, and meal timing before ordering the stops.
I would list the three stops and leave travel times for later.
I would promise all stops even if the museum closes before arrival.
I would order the stops by map distance and add a lunch break.

advanced.situation: You are drafting a four-day highland itinerary for a mixed-ability group, with two long transfers and a junior guide joining midway.

options.text: I would copy last season's route and share it with the junior guide.
I would schedule both long transfers on consecutive days to protect sightseeing time.
I would space the transfers and add a flexible rest block each day.
I would sequence transfers and stops around recovery time, abilities, and the junior guide's handover.

basic.situation: A coordinator asks you to arrange one night's accommodation and a minibus for eight visitors in a town stop.

options.text: I would check room count and pickup time with the coordinator before booking.
I would send the first available booking details to the group chat.
I would confirm rooms and pickup with providers, then share the booking details.
I would reserve rooms first and ask the driver about pickup later.

advanced.situation: You are arranging transport, camping gear, and medical support for a remote three-day trek, but a supplier has not confirmed delivery.

options.text: I would verify gear, transport, and medical availability together before confirming the departure plan.
I would check delivery status and find backup gear through another listed supplier.
I would hold the gear booking and confirm transport while waiting for an update.
I would proceed with the itinerary and expect the supplier to deliver.

basic.situation: A couple asks for a nearby place to buy local snacks and a sight they can visit before their coach leaves.

options.text: I would suggest the farthest market and say the coach can wait for them.
I would match a nearby market and sight to their time, then explain the return route.
I would point out the nearest shops and let them choose a sight.
I would name a popular market and mention its walking distance from here.

advanced.situation: A family with a stroller and two hours free asks for custom sightseeing suggestions near a crowded heritage district.

options.text: I would recommend the landmark route and warn them about the crowd.
I would suggest step-free nearby sights, quieter links, and a return point within two hours.
I would share the district map and let them pick suitable sights.
I would send them through the busiest lanes to see more landmarks.

basic.situation: A participant with limited mobility asks for help getting onto a tour boat, while the boarding ramp is wet.

options.text: I would ask crew about safe boarding and offer support if suitable.
I would steady the participant and check the wet ramp before boarding.
I would suggest boarding once other visitors have crossed the wet ramp.
I would alert the crew and wait beside the ramp with the participant.

advanced.situation: A participant falls on a walking tour, has a bleeding cut, and says they feel faint as the group approaches a road crossing.

options.text: I would keep the group back, treat the cut, and seek medical help.
I would ask a companion to stay with them as I move the group clear.
I would move the participant away from traffic and ask someone to call for help.
I would guide the group away and ask a nearby worker to assist them.

basic.situation: Your group reaches a guesthouse, but the room list has fewer rooms than the booking confirmation shows.

options.text: I would ask the guesthouse to explain the missing rooms while the group waits.
I would compare the booking confirmation with the room list and contact the guesthouse.
I would tell the group to take whichever rooms remain available.
I would ask the coordinator to call the guesthouse and hold the group nearby.

advanced.situation: A delayed ferry disrupts your island itinerary, and the hotel, driver, and visitors each have different ideas about changing the next day.

options.text: I would gather each party's constraints and offer a revised sequence they can confirm.
I would contact the hotel and driver, then update visitors with their replies.
I would keep the original plan and explain that ferry delays are outside our control.
I would tell visitors the hotel and driver can sort out the changes.

basic.situation: A visitor asks what a two-day package includes, and you have the package sheet and recent tour feedback form.

options.text: I would hand over the sheet and ask them to read it before deciding.
I would highlight included transport, mention positive visitor feedback, and explain what the package covers.
I would promise a free extra stop to help close the sale.
I would explain the package from its sheet and pass feedback to the organizer.

advanced.situation: Several recent feedback forms mention rushed visits, while a school group asks about buying your longer heritage package.

options.text: I would explain the schedule and share repeated feedback with the organizer.
I would describe the longer package and pass the feedback comments to the organizer.
I would hide the rushed-visit comments and promise this group more time at every stop.
I would offer the standard package and ask the group which stops matter most.

basic.situation: During free play, you notice one child repeatedly leaves the group and watches from the doorway. Your checklist is due before pickup.

options.text: I note the times and share the observation with the parent at pickup.
I ask another caregiver whether they noticed the child leaving play.
I record the child’s activity and mention it if the parent asks.
I mark the child as withdrawn on the checklist and move on.

advanced.situation: Over several weeks, you notice a child rarely responds when spoken to and struggles to follow familiar routines. The family asks how the child is doing.

options.text: I describe the routines that are difficult and ask what the family observes at home.
I share dated examples and suggest the family discuss them with a suitable professional.
I keep watching and wait for the family to raise the concern again.
I tell the family the child may have a developmental delay and needs assessment.

basic.situation: Your room’s plan calls for a short shape-sorting activity, but several children finish the puzzle quickly and start wandering.

options.text: I let children choose any toy while I prepare the next activity.
I repeat the puzzle and ask children to sort the shapes again.
I ask children to name each shape before putting it away.
I offer a second sorting challenge using the same shapes and plan.

advanced.situation: You are asked to draft a month of activities for mixed ages, including children who need quieter transitions, and explain the approach to new staff.

options.text: I reuse last month’s plan and add a quiet activity each week.
I write one activity for the oldest children and ask others to join.
I map shared themes to age-fit choices and note transition cues for staff.
I list age-based activities and explain each one at the staff briefing.

basic.situation: After art time, washable toys and used cups are left on the table before the next group arrives. A senior caregiver is nearby.

options.text: I separate the cups for washing and sanitize the toys as directed.
I wipe the table and leave the cups beside the sink for later.
I ask the senior caregiver which toys need cleaning before storing them.
I rinse the cups and put the toys back in their usual bins.

advanced.situation: At closing, a child’s meal entry is blank, and the medication record is due for handover. You remember giving the meal but did not see the medication administered.

options.text: I leave both fields blank and tell the next caregiver to check later.
I record the meal from memory and flag the medication entry for verification.
I write the meal entry and ask the next caregiver about the medication.
I fill both entries from the usual routine so handover stays on time.

basic.situation: You are putting away blocks when you spot a loose toy piece near the snack table. Children are about to sit down.

options.text: I ask another caregiver to clear the piece while I arrange snacks.
I put the blocks away and ask children to watch their step.
I move the loose piece out of reach and check the area before serving.
I pick up the piece and continue setting out the snacks.

advanced.situation: A planned class snack includes fruit, but a delivery arrives late and two children need their food kept separate. You are helping prepare service for several rooms.

options.text: I serve the fruit first to the largest room and bring the rest later.
I confirm the separate portions and revise the serving sequence with the room teams.
I delay all rooms until the fruit arrives, then distribute the portions.
I ask each room to collect its snack when the delivery arrives.

basic.situation: A toddler’s diaper needs changing before rest time, and you are assisting a more experienced caregiver who is guiding you.

options.text: I gather supplies, follow the caregiver’s steps, and keep the child covered.
I ask the caregiver to handle the change while I set up rest mats.
I gather supplies and ask the child to wait beside the mat.
I change the diaper quickly and bring the toddler to the rest mat.

advanced.situation: A child who uses a familiar calming routine becomes distressed before rest time after the room grows noisy. The usual caregiver is briefly helping another child.

options.text: I pause rest time and wait until the usual caregiver returns.
I offer a quiet toy and continue the rest routine nearby.
I lay the child down with the group and keep the room moving.
I reduce nearby noise and use the child’s known calming routine before rest.

basic.situation: After story time, one child leaves crayons and paper on the floor while others begin tidying their play area.

options.text: I collect the crayons so the group can move to the next activity.
I ask the child to pick up the paper before joining the group.
I invite the child to return the art materials with the group.
I remind everyone to tidy and read the next story aloud.

advanced.situation: Two children argue over turns during a group game, and one withdraws while the others wait. You need to help them rejoin play.

options.text: I speak with each child briefly, then resume the same game.
I give the next turn to the louder child so the game continues.
I pause the game and guide both children to agree on a turn-taking cue.
I choose the next player and restart the game for the group.

basic.situation: On the walk to the nearby park, your charge reaches the kerb while looking at a shop window. Traffic is moving along the road.

options.text: I ask the child to watch traffic as I guide them across the road.
I pause at the kerb, hold hands, and check traffic before crossing together.
I hurry the child across between cars without checking the crossing signal.
I call the child back and wait for the crossing signal to change.

advanced.situation: You find a sharp garden tool beside the children’s play path. The family is out, and you are due to show a relief caregiver the outdoor routine.

options.text: I move the tool to locked storage, then show the caregiver the boundary.
I warn the children about the tool and continue the outdoor routine.
I bring children indoors and tell the caregiver about the tool at handover.
I place the tool beside the shed and ask the caregiver to watch.

basic.situation: Your charge says they need the toilet just as nap time begins. The usual bathroom routine includes washing hands afterward.

options.text: I ask the child to wait until after the nap begins.
I take the child to the toilet and support the handwashing routine afterward.
I pause nap setup and help the child use the toilet.
I tell the child where the bathroom is and finish setting up mats.

advanced.situation: A child with a written medicine schedule seems unusually warm and tired before lunch. The family has asked you to follow the schedule and report changes.

options.text: I note the child’s appearance and ask the family what they prefer.
I give the scheduled medicine and let the child rest through lunch.
I wait until after lunch to check whether the child seems better.
I check the temperature, record the change, and contact the family about next steps.

basic.situation: You are preparing an afternoon snack and loading the children into the car for a scheduled appointment. A child asks for another serving.

options.text: I finish loading the bags, then serve the planned snack to everyone.
I portion the planned snack and check each child is seated before departure.
I serve the snack and ask another adult to check the car seats.
I hand out extra portions and start loading while the children eat.

advanced.situation: You are planning snacks for a week with school pickups and one appointment across town. Two children have different food preferences, and travel times overlap.

options.text: I map pickup times first, then plan portable snacks that fit each child’s needs.
I shift the appointment pickup and prepare separate snacks for both children.
I use the same snack each day and keep both pickups on the usual schedule.
I plan varied snacks and ask the family to resolve the pickup overlap.

basic.situation: Your charge finishes homework early and asks to paint. The family’s activity plan includes a short craft before dinner.

options.text: I let the child paint freely while I begin preparing dinner.
I offer the planned craft and let the child choose colours after homework.
I ask the child to complete another worksheet before starting the craft.
I check the homework is finished, then offer the planned craft before dinner.

advanced.situation: You are asked to show a relief caregiver how to run a short reading session for a child who loses focus during long stories.

options.text: I choose a short story and ask the caregiver to keep the child seated.
I ask the caregiver to read the whole story while the child listens.
I split the story into short turns and model asking for predictions.
I read a shorter story aloud and let the caregiver observe the session.

basic.situation: At pickup, the parent asks how the child’s afternoon went. The child spent time on homework, played outside, and argued over a toy.

options.text: I say the afternoon was fine and hand over the child’s bag.
I share the activities and describe what happened during the disagreement.
I mention homework and outdoor play, then ask about tomorrow’s plan.
I describe the disagreement and explain how the children resolved it.

advanced.situation: The family asks for help with repeated toy-grabbing between siblings. One parent prefers strict consequences, while the other wants the children to share freely.

options.text: I propose turn-taking and ask both parents how they want disputes handled.
I follow one parent's stricter approach during my shifts and share updates with both.
I describe how turn-taking works and invite each parent to share concerns.
I ask both parents to agree on one response and practise it together.

basic.situation: After indoor play, you find a small spill beside the toy shelf while your charge asks to start a new game.

options.text: I cover the spill with a towel and start the game nearby.
I clean the spill while the child chooses a game nearby.
I guide the child away, clean the spill, then set out the game.
I ask the child to wait while I fetch cleaning supplies.

advanced.situation: The family calendar shows two overlapping pickups, a play date, and a bill due this week. The parents ask you to update the children’s weekly schedule.

options.text: I list the clashes and ask the parents which item they want changed first.
I rearrange the pickups and note the bill reminder for the parents.
I map the pickups, play date, and bill reminder into a weekly sequence.
I keep the usual pickups and move the play date to an open afternoon.

basic.situation: A loose cable crosses the activity room floor just before opening, and two groups are waiting to enter.

options.text: I would lift the cable beside the wall and let the groups begin their activities.
I would pause bookings for that room and note the fault for the next shift.
I would block the room, redirect both groups, and report the cable for repair.
I would hold the groups outside and ask the supervisor how to handle the fault.

advanced.situation: A contractor proposes a cheaper surface for a busy recreation area, but staff have raised concerns about drainage and upkeep.

options.text: I would ask the contractor to proceed and review the surface after the first rainy week.
I would map drainage and upkeep needs, then compare surface options before recommending changes.
I would compare the proposal with staff comments and send both to the manager.
I would request another price estimate and keep the current design under consideration.

basic.situation: After a busy afternoon session, the attendance sheet has two unclear entries and the equipment count is short by one ball.

options.text: I would check the entries with the session lead and update the inventory count.
I would estimate the unclear entries from memory and list one ball as missing.
I would flag the unclear entries and ask the supervisor to review the sheet.
I would copy the sheet as written and leave the ball count for tomorrow.

advanced.situation: A partner agency asks for progress notes before a planning meeting, while one participant's recent goals have not been reviewed.

options.text: I would send recent notes and flag the goals for review at the meeting.
I would defer the update to the next review and tell the agency about the delay.
I would share existing notes and flag the unreviewed goals for the planning meeting.
I would review goals with the participant, update notes, and share relevant points with the agency.

basic.situation: A new participant arrives for a craft session and stands apart while the group starts choosing materials.

options.text: I would greet the participant, explain the rules, and point out where supplies are kept.
I would hand over the materials list and let the participant settle in alone.
I would introduce the participant to a friendly group member and explain the room rules.
I would ask another participant to show the newcomer the activity table.

advanced.situation: Staff disagree about whether beginners may use a new activity station, and participants are waiting for instructions.

options.text: I would tell staff to settle the disagreement after the group has started.
I would ask the senior staff member to decide how the station should be explained.
I would review the station guidance with staff and agree on a clear explanation for participants.
I would pause the station and offer the group a familiar activity instead.

basic.situation: You are setting up a community hall for a games evening, and the decorations are ready but the equipment layout is unclear.

options.text: I would put all equipment against one wall and let groups collect it as needed.
I would place the games near the entrance and finish decorating the stage.
I would ask the event lead where each game should go before moving equipment.
I would arrange equipment by game, keep walkways open, and finish the decorations.

advanced.situation: A community performance is due to start, but a performer is delayed and the audience is already seated.

options.text: I would invite the audience to visit the display area while the performer arrives.
I would start the next act, then review the running order with performers backstage.
I would announce a short delay and ask the audience to remain seated.
I would check available performers, adjust the running order, and brief the stage team.

basic.situation: During a supervised outdoor game, a participant scrapes a knee and asks you for help while the group waits nearby.

options.text: I would offer a clean tissue and let the participant rejoin the game.
I would rinse the scrape, apply a dressing, and follow the first aid procedure.
I would ask the supervisor to assess the scrape before I prepare supplies.
I would ask the participant to sit down until the session ends.

advanced.situation: A participant says a promised activity was cancelled without warning and asks for an explanation while other attendees listen.

options.text: I would record the complaint and refer it to management for a response.
I would offer another activity and tell the participant the schedule may change.
I would explain the schedule and ask the participant to raise concerns later.
I would listen privately, clarify what happened, and bring practical options to management.

basic.situation: Two staff members are setting up for a sports session, and neither has started preparing the equipment stations.

options.text: I would suggest splitting the stations and ask them to confirm their choices.
I would assign one staff member to each station and check their progress later.
I would start setting up the stations myself while they finish other preparations.
I would let both staff members choose their tasks as they work.

advanced.situation: In a group discussion, participants say they want to run a weekend walking club but are unsure how to organize it.

options.text: I would invite one volunteer to plan the route and share it with everyone.
I would ask members to choose roles, discuss route needs, and plan their first outing.
I would offer a list of nearby walks for participants to consider next time.
I would propose a route and invite every member to join my planned weekend walk.

basic.situation: During your evening round, you find a spill near the dormitory stairs while residents are returning from class.
