options.text: I would place a chair beside the spill and notify maintenance staff.
I would keep residents away, arrange cleanup, and report the hazard in the log.
I would warn residents about the spill and call the duty supervisor for help.
I would walk around the spill and mention it during tomorrow's handover.

advanced.situation: A drill review shows new staff missed the alarm route, and residents use two different stairwells at night.

options.text: I would post the route diagram by the alarm panel for staff reference.
I would review the alarm route with staff and ask them to confirm they understand.
I would repeat the usual drill and discuss the route with staff afterward.
I would map both routes with staff, update the protocol, and practice each route.

basic.situation: Two residents argue over shared laundry time, and one asks you to make the other leave the room.

options.text: I would ask them to take turns today and discuss a schedule later.
I would ask a nearby resident to suggest a fair laundry schedule.
I would tell one resident to leave and assign the other first use.
I would hear each resident, restate the shared concern, and help them agree on turns.

advanced.situation: After repeated noise complaints, staff disagree about a resident's response, and the resident says the warnings were unclear.

options.text: I would pause further warnings and ask the resident to keep noise down.
I would issue the next warning using the usual approach and tell staff later.
I would compare staff accounts, clarify the expected standard, and agree on a consistent response.
I would ask the senior advisor to choose a response for this resident.

basic.situation: A resident tells you that money worries are affecting their studies and asks what support is available.

options.text: I would suggest they borrow from a friend until their studies settle.
I would listen, ask what support they have tried, and offer a suitable counseling referral.
I would listen and give them the counselor's contact details for an appointment.
I would suggest they speak with their tutor about the effect on coursework.

advanced.situation: A resident's case plan mentions recurring fatigue, and you need to understand how it affects their daily routine.

options.text: I would consult medical staff about relevant background and share details with the case team.
I would note the fatigue and wait for the resident's next scheduled review.
I would ask the counselor what the fatigue means for the resident's plan.
I would ask the resident to describe fatigue and add their perspective to case notes.

basic.situation: A counselor asks you to help prepare an individual plan for a resident who has missed several study sessions.

options.text: I would ask the counselor for a suitable plan and help document its steps.
I would list missed sessions and suggest the resident attend more regularly.
I would copy the standard plan and ask the resident to follow its study schedule.
I would discuss barriers with the resident and draft study steps with the counselor.

advanced.situation: Several residents ask for evening study support, while staff report low attendance at the current educational sessions.

options.text: I would move sessions later and ask staff to see whether attendance improves.
I would keep the current sessions and remind residents about attendance.
I would add a second evening session using the existing program materials.
I would review attendance and resident needs, then adapt sessions with staff input.

basic.situation: You notice a broken corridor light near the residents' common room during a routine check.

options.text: I would tell the maintenance desk that a corridor light needs attention.
I would place a note near the switch for the next shift to see.
I would leave the light for the next maintenance round and note it later.
I would record the location, alert maintenance, and mention the dark corridor to staff.

advanced.situation: Your unit is nearing its monthly supply limit, and several commonly used items are running low before a busy intake week.

options.text: I would delay ordering until the intake numbers are confirmed next week.
I would order the usual quantities now and review spending after intake.
I would check stock and upcoming needs, then prioritize essential items within the limit.
I would ask staff which items they need most and place a smaller order.

basic.situation: A parent calls the residence hall asking about a student meeting, but you do not know which staff member is responsible.

options.text: I would ask the caller to phone again when the office is less busy.
I would take the caller's details and route the message to the assigned staff member.
I would transfer the call to the counselor who usually handles student concerns.
I would give the parent the student's room number so they can ask there.

advanced.situation: A report is due after a supervised group trip, but the supply totals in your notes differ from the checkout sheet.

options.text: I would submit the checkout total and flag the difference for later review.
I would hold the report until the trip lead returns next week.
I would reconcile both records with the trip lead and document the confirmed total.
I would copy the checkout total into the report and submit it before closing.

basic.situation: Two staff are available before the lunch rush, and the delivery arrives at the same time. You need to assign their duties while keeping the tills covered.

options.text: I would place the trained cashier at tills, then check floor coverage.
I would ask both staff to start usual duties and monitor the queue.
I would split delivery and tills, then check queue and floor coverage.
I would reuse yesterday's plan despite today's extra delivery workload.

advanced.situation: Weekend sales are rising, but extra hours are costly. You are preparing next month's shifts and must cover peak periods while keeping within the labour budget.

options.text: I would use last month's busy periods to add a few targeted shifts.
I would repeat last month's shifts and adjust them after staff raise concerns.
I would add the same extra hours to every weekend shift for consistency.
I would compare hourly sales with staff availability, then place extra cover at peaks.

basic.situation: A promotion starts this morning, and you notice two shelf labels show different prices for the same product. Customers are beginning to browse that aisle.

options.text: I would ask a nearby colleague which label they saw during setup.
I would use the lower label price to settle questions from shoppers.
I would check the promotion list and replace the label that does not match.
I would leave both labels until the next scheduled display check.

advanced.situation: A month of sales records shows one snack selling faster than forecast, while a nearby item is building up. You are reviewing stock levels for the next order.

options.text: I would cut the slow item's next order and increase the popular snack slightly.
I would raise the fast seller's order and keep the other item's usual quantity.
I would compare recent sales, stock on hand, and delivery timing before adjusting both quantities.
I would repeat the usual order so shelves stay familiar to regular shoppers.

basic.situation: You find a leaking drink bottle near the aisle entrance during a busy period. Shoppers are walking past the wet patch as you inspect nearby stock.

options.text: I would ask a colleague to watch the spot while I finish checking stock.
I would move the nearby stock first so the aisle display stays tidy.
I would block the wet patch, alert nearby staff, and follow the spill procedure.
I would place a warning sign, then arrange a prompt clean up of the spill.

advanced.situation: A new team member finds damaged cartons leaking near stored goods. The team is unsure how to handle similar spills during an evacuation drill.

options.text: I would ask the experienced team member to handle the cartons and brief others later.
I would separate the damaged cartons and tell staff to follow existing spill guidance.
I would review the spill procedure with staff and practise reporting and evacuation steps.
I would move the cartons to the back room until the next stock check.

basic.situation: A customer asks for a refund, but the receipt is missing and the department procedure describes how staff should handle that case. You are covering the service desk.

options.text: I would approve a cash refund so the queue can keep moving.
I would offer store credit to settle the request during the rush.
I would follow the missing receipt procedure and explain the available next steps.
I would use the usual refund steps and ask a senior colleague to confirm.

advanced.situation: A nearby neighbourhood has growing foot traffic, and management asks for ideas to expand sales there without adding a new store. You are preparing departmental proposals.

options.text: I would adapt another branch's promotion dates to suit this neighbourhood.
I would suggest broad discounts and estimate sales lift without checking local customer data.
I would review customer patterns and costs, then test a local promotion.
I would compare nearby sales with costs before recommending a targeted local promotion.

basic.situation: A shelf is untidy after a busy morning, and a delivery is due soon. You have been asked to help organise the display before customers arrive.

options.text: I would move slower products forward to make the shelf look full.
I would group similar products together and leave the price labels visible.
I would face the products, then check the shelf labels as I tidy.
I would follow the layout, rotate stock, and clear room for delivery.

advanced.situation: Purchase slips and sales totals often disagree at closing. You are asked to improve the records so the next stock requisition reflects what the shop actually sold.

options.text: I would keep the slips in date order and total them during the weekly review.
I would record purchases and sales daily, then send the totals for review.
I would log each purchase and sale by date, then reconcile totals before requisitions.
I would use the latest sales total to estimate the next requisition quantity.

basic.situation: A shopper asks where to find a kettle and whether it comes with a warranty. You are near the appliance aisle during a quiet part of your shift.

options.text: I would say all kettles have the same warranty and continue arranging stock.
I would direct the shopper to appliances and mention where the warranty card explains coverage.
I would greet the shopper, show the kettle section, and check warranty details.
I would point toward appliances and let the shopper browse the aisle.

advanced.situation: A customer complains that a discounted appliance stopped working, while the receipt shows a recent purchase. A new staff member asks how to respond as other shoppers wait.

options.text: I would listen, check purchase details, and coach staff on available options.
I would hear the complaint, review the receipt, and explain the available next steps.
I would ask the customer to wait while I check the receipt and policy.
I would offer a replacement first to keep the queue moving smoothly.

basic.situation: A daily sales report shows one representative below target. Your manager asks you to review the figures before the team check-in.

options.text: I would flag the low figure and ask my manager about meeting context.
I would mark the report on track to keep the team check-in brief.
I would compare the report with its target and note the main gap.
I would ask the representative about recent activity before suggesting a next step.

advanced.situation: A representative has missed targets for two months, but customer feedback remains strong. You are responsible for preparing a coaching conversation and next month's performance goals.

options.text: I would review activity and results together, then agree on a measurable improvement goal.
I would set a modest target and review progress with them at month end.
I would discuss missed targets and agree on a short term goal together.
I would review outreach activity and agree on a practical target with the representative.

basic.situation: A supplier invoice and a sales order are waiting to be filed after a busy afternoon. You have been given the team's usual filing instructions.

options.text: I would label both documents by date and file them in their matching sections.
I would place both documents in the pending tray for later sorting.
I would file the invoice and order in the same section for convenience.
I would file the documents in the usual sections and write their dates on top.

advanced.situation: A sales log total does not match the supporting receipts, and the monthly report is due this afternoon. You are checking the purchase and sales records before it is sent.

options.text: I would compare the receipt totals with the log and tell the manager about the difference.
I would change the log total to match the receipt bundle and send the report.
I would compare each entry with its receipt, amend verified errors, and note unresolved items.
I would flag the mismatch and hold the report for the next review.

basic.situation: A sales meeting asks for ideas to attract more customers to a service package. You have been asked to help draft suggestions with a senior colleague.

options.text: I would suggest a small trial offer and estimate who might respond.
I would recommend a general discount and ask the team to promote it.
I would suggest copying a competitor's package and matching its headline price.
I would review recent customer questions and propose an offer that addresses them.

advanced.situation: Sales have stalled in one district, and service teams say customers ask for different support there. You are coordinating ideas across departments to reach more potential clients.

options.text: I would extend the campaign across the district and track customer response.
I would review district sales and recommend testing the current campaign there.
I would ask departments to propose district offers that reflect local customer needs.
I would combine service feedback with sales data in a shared proposal with measures.

basic.situation: A client says a scheduled service visit was missed, and a senior colleague is available nearby. You are asked to listen and help resolve the complaint.

options.text: I would listen, check the booking with my colleague, and discuss available options.
I would apologise, check availability, and offer a realistic time for another visit.
I would invite my senior colleague to advise while I continue listening to the client.
I would hear the client, check booking details, and agree on a practical next step.

advanced.situation: A long term client disputes an invoice after a service problem, and a new staff member is unsure what to say. You are handling the complaint while guiding the staff member.

options.text: I would hear the client, review service records, and coach staff on a fair response.
I would check the invoice details and discuss a fair adjustment with the client.
I would review service records and explain the documented outcome to the client.
I would support the staff member and consult a senior colleague about next steps.

basic.situation: A manager asks you to join an interview for a sales role and take notes against the team's standard questions. The first candidate arrives early.

options.text: I would ask about the candidate's preferred salary before starting the interview.
I would take notes on the candidate's answers and share them with the manager.
I would tell the manager the candidate seems suitable before the interview begins.
I would use the standard questions and record evidence from each answer.

advanced.situation: Several new sales staff make the same errors explaining a service package, while experienced staff give inconsistent feedback. You are asked to shape training and review progress.

options.text: I would send the new staff the current guide and ask managers to watch sales.
I would build practice around common errors and review observed explanations against shared criteria.
I would run a short role play and collect feedback from the participants.
I would let experienced staff train each new hire in their own style.

basic.situation: A team schedule template has two client calls and one product briefing listed at the same time. You are helping assign today's duties before the morning starts.

options.text: I would assign the calls by availability and confirm who will attend the briefing.
I would leave the template as written and tell staff to coordinate among themselves.
I would move one call to an available person and flag the briefing overlap.
I would give both calls to the fastest representative and keep the briefing unchanged.

advanced.situation: A product change affects sales and service teams across two branches, and each team needs briefing time this week. You are coordinating staff duties and schedules.

options.text: I would map staff availability and client coverage, then coordinate shared briefings with both branches.
I would ask each branch to set its own briefing and share the times afterward.
I would send the product notes and cancel the briefings to save work time.
I would book a common briefing and ask team leads to adjust their schedules.

basic.situation: A customer pays cash for a small basket, and the register shows the amount due. You need to take payment and give the right change.

options.text: I enter the tendered amount, count the change aloud, and issue the receipt.
I use the register total, check the notes, then hand over change.
I recount the tender, confirm the displayed balance, and return exact change.
I round the change to a convenient amount and close the sale.

advanced.situation: A card payment appears twice on the register, while the customer’s bank app shows one charge. A new cashier asks how to handle the discrepancy.

options.text: I compare the transaction references, verify the settled entry, and coach the trainee through the protocol.
I ask the trainee to wait while I print the transaction history for review.
I check both register entries, follow the reversal steps, and explain the receipt trail.
I refund one entry based on the bank app and tell the trainee to do likewise.

basic.situation: A customer brings back an unopened item with a receipt and asks to exchange it for another size. You are learning the return process.

options.text: I exchange the item for the requested size and keep the receipt nearby.
I check the receipt, item condition, and exchange terms before recording the swap.
I check the receipt and item, then process the exchange in the register.
I offer store credit for the item and complete the return on screen.

advanced.situation: A customer disputes a refused return and says another cashier accepted the same item last week. The queue is growing, and you can review the transaction.

options.text: I ask a nearby cashier whether they remember the earlier return before responding.
I accept the return, keep shoppers moving, and tell colleagues the exception stands.
I check item history, record the request, and flag the pattern for review.
I explain posted terms and invite the customer to show the earlier receipt.

basic.situation: You scan a customer’s groceries, but the register total seems higher than the prices shown on the shelf labels. You need to finish the bill.

options.text: I charge the displayed total and point the customer toward the service desk.
I apply a small discount to the bill and complete the sale quickly.
I rescan the items and check whether the register shows each price clearly.
I compare the scanned prices with shelf labels and resolve any mismatch before payment.

advanced.situation: Several customers have reported that one shelf price differs from the register price. You see the mismatch while scanning another basket during a busy shift.

options.text: I use the shelf price for this basket and finish the remaining scans.
I change the item price in the register to match the label and continue scanning.
I note the affected item and ask a colleague to check the shelf label later.
I pause that item, verify the label, and alert the pricing team with the details.

basic.situation: Your checkout drawer is running low on small notes during the lunch rush. You need to keep the station ready and have a manager nearby.

options.text: I borrow notes from the next drawer and return them after the rush.
I ask a nearby cashier to watch the queue while I find more small notes.
I check the drawer balance, estimate the change needed, and ask the manager for that amount.
I tell the manager the drawer is low and request a suitable cash top-up.

advanced.situation: Two staffed lanes are short of small notes while a third has little traffic. You are helping monitor checkout stations during a weekend rush.

options.text: I ask the manager to shift cash between lanes and keep the queue moving.
I move a bundle of small notes from the quiet lane into both busy drawers.
I compare lane queues and drawer levels, then recommend a tracked top-up and temporary staff shift.
I send one cashier to a busy lane and report the low drawers to the manager.

basic.situation: A shopper asks where to find cooking oil, but you are unsure which aisle carries it. The checkout queue is short, and you can check the store guide.

options.text: I ask a nearby colleague which aisle stocks cooking oil before answering.
I tell the customer to ask at the service desk after paying.
I point toward the grocery aisles and suggest the customer look there.
I check the aisle guide and direct the customer to the listed location.

advanced.situation: A customer says a cashier gave conflicting return information over the phone, and now disputes a declined refund. Other shoppers are waiting for help.

options.text: I ask the customer to call back later when a manager is available.
I offer a refund to settle the complaint and keep the queue moving.
I clarify call details, review the receipt and policy, then explain available options calmly.
I hear the complaint, explain the posted return terms, and offer the service desk contact.

basic.situation: A drink spills beside your checkout while customers are approaching. You have cleaning supplies nearby and a paging handset at the station.

options.text: I place a warning sign and page for help, keeping shoppers clear.
I page a colleague to clean the spill while I greet arriving customers.
I mop the spill, check the floor is dry, then return to greeting customers.
I place a basket beside the spill and carry on with checkout.

advanced.situation: A blocked checkout area needs cleaning as shoppers arrive, while your team is split across lanes. You can page colleagues and organize the immediate response.

options.text: I mark the area, page a colleague, and guide shoppers around it.
I clean the visible mess first and ask a colleague to cover customer greetings.
I move loose items behind the counter and tidy when checkout quiets.
I page a nearby colleague, move the rubbish bin, and resume greeting shoppers.

basic.situation: A patron asks to exchange a small cash note for chips before play. You are at the booth and need to complete the transaction accurately.

options.text: I hand over the usual chip stack and place the cash in the till.
I enter the tender, count out the matching chips, and provide the transaction slip.
I count the cash, confirm the chip amount, and hand over the exchange.
I ask the patron to confirm the chips before I close the exchange.

advanced.situation: A new booth cashier gives a patron fewer chips than the recorded cash exchange shows. The patron notices before leaving, and the trainee asks what to do.

options.text: I check the amount, adjust the chip count, and remind the trainee to use the slip.
I ask the trainee to return the cash and restart the exchange from memory.
I add the missing chips and tell the trainee to count more slowly next time.
I recount chips, compare the slip against cash, and coach the trainee through each exchange step.

basic.situation: A slot machine alarm sounds, and a patron presents a small chip win for payoff. You need to calculate its value and issue the payout with guidance.

options.text: I count the chips together and use the usual value for the pile.
I count the chips by type, check the posted values, and prepare the payoff.
I count the pile, compare it with the alarm display, then issue payment.
I total the chips by color and ask a colleague to confirm the amount.

advanced.situation: A patron disputes a payoff after a jackpot alarm, saying the chips were counted at the wrong value. The payout record and remaining chips are available for review.

options.text: I review the payoff record and offer to ask the shift lead about the difference.
I explain that the alarm triggered payment and ask the patron to accept the amount.
I recount the chips by type, compare the payoff record, and explain the calculation to the patron.
I compare the record with the patron’s account and note the dispute for review.

basic.situation: A slot machine win is larger than the amount held in the machine. The payout receipt is ready, and the patron has not yet signed it.

options.text: I ask the patron to sign the receipt before I hand over the payout.
I hand over the winnings and ask the patron to sign after counting them.
I explain the receipt, obtain the patron’s signature, and file it with the payout papers.
I point to the signature line and wait while the patron reads the receipt.

advanced.situation: A high-value slot payout is ready, but the receipt has a blank signature field and the patron is eager to leave. You are responsible for the receipt step.

options.text: I ask the patron to sign the receipt and place it with the shift records.
I let the patron leave and add a note that the signature was requested.
I hold the receipt at the booth and ask a colleague how to proceed.
I explain that the receipt needs a signature, obtain it, and check the completed form before filing.

basic.situation: At shift change, you are asked to count a money drawer with a supervisor present. The notes and coins are arranged in the tray.

options.text: I estimate the notes, count the coins, and write down the approximate amount.
I count each denomination separately and record totals for the supervisor's review.
I count the notes by denomination and have the supervisor check the coins.
I count all the money together and tell the supervisor the total.

advanced.situation: The opening bank for the next shift is short by one bundle, and the count sheet is unclear. You are preparing the money bank for another change person.

options.text: I recount the bank by denomination, compare the sheet, and record any variance before handover.
I issue the listed bank and ask the next change person to check it later.
I pause the handover and ask another cashier whether the bundle was moved.
I recount the bundle and tell the supervisor the sheet may be inaccurate.

basic.situation: You complete a cash-to-chip exchange and need to enter it on the transaction form. A colleague has shown you the fields to fill in.

options.text: I write the amount and patron’s initials on the form, then file it.
I record the amount, exchange type, and reference on the form before filing it.
I fill the form using the transaction slip and ask a colleague to review it.
I note the cash amount on a pad and complete the form after the rush.

advanced.situation: The daily summary is short of the recorded exchange total, and two forms carry similar amounts. You are reviewing the reconciliation before the books are closed.

options.text: I compare the forms with the summary and flag the similar amounts for review.
I adjust the summary to match the drawer total and finish the close.
I match each form to its transaction reference, trace totals, and document discrepancy.
I ask the previous shift whether they recall entering both forms.

basic.situation: A patron presents identification before play, but the date is hard to read. You are checking the patron’s age at the cage with a manager nearby.

options.text: I pause the check and ask the patron to read the date aloud.
I ask the manager to look at the date and confirm the identification.
I ask for a clearer identification document and follow the age-check process.
I accept the identification because the portrait looks like the patron.

advanced.situation: A patron applies for house credit, but the reference contact gives details that do not match the application. The queue is growing at the cage.

options.text: I delay the application and tell the patron the reference could not be confirmed.
I approve a smaller credit amount and note that the reference differed.
I call the reference again and ask a colleague to review the application.
I record the mismatch, hold authorization, and use the approved reference-check route.

basic.situation: A customer rents a pressure washer for one day and asks what the total will be. You have the rate sheet and payment terminal.

options.text: Charge the amount the customer paid last time to keep the line moving.
Quote the daily rate and ask your supervisor to check the total.
Check the rate sheet, calculate the total, and confirm it before payment.
Read the rate sheet aloud and let the customer work out the total.

advanced.situation: A customer disputes a rental bill that includes an extra day. The return time is close to the cutoff, and the new clerk is unsure how to read the record.

options.text: Ask the customer to pay the bill first while you check the return time.
Review the time stamp and rental terms, then explain the charge and revise any verified error.
Use the previous customer's bill as a guide and settle this one the same way.
Check the return time and ask a senior clerk how the cutoff applies.

basic.situation: You answer a call from someone asking to rent two folding tables for Saturday. Your checklist asks for the date, quantity, and contact details.

options.text: Ask for date and quantity, then use the checklist to finish the call.
Write down the request and repeat the date, quantity, and contact details.
Reserve two tables for Saturday before confirming the caller's details or contact number.
Take the date and quantity, then ask for the caller's contact details.

advanced.situation: Several calls arrive while you record a repair order. The caller gives a model number quickly, then corrects one digit before ending the call.

options.text: Ask the caller to repeat the number, then record the repair request.
Enter the corrected number and mark the order for a later check.
Record the first number and move to the next waiting call.
Enter the corrected number and repeat it with the repair request before ending.

basic.situation: A customer wants to reserve a carpet cleaner for Friday afternoon. The rental log shows one available unit, and a manager is nearby.

options.text: Record the customer's name and Friday pickup time in the rental log.
Add the customer's name to the log and ask the manager to confirm availability.
Check the unit's schedule, confirm Friday availability, and record the reservation details.
Tell the customer it is available and leave the log for later.

advanced.situation: Two customers arrive for the same carpet cleaner after a booking was entered twice. One needs it for a paid weekend job, and you are processing returns.

options.text: Check who booked first and ask the other customer to choose another day.
Check the log and return status, then offer each customer the available options.
Give the cleaner to the first customer and update the log after the rush.
Check the return status and ask a manager which booking to honor.

basic.situation: A customer asks to rent a ladder to reach a high ceiling. Your display has several sizes, and you have been asked to discuss their needs.

options.text: Show the ladder sizes and ask the customer which one they prefer.
Ask about the height and task, then match them to the listed ladder options.
Recommend the tallest ladder because it can reach the most places.
Ask how high the ceiling is and what work the customer plans.

advanced.situation: A customer returns a wet, tagged jacket for cleaning after saying it had a torn lining at drop-off. The tag is unclear, and you are receiving articles.

options.text: Accept the jacket and use the tag's brief note to start the cleaning order.
Remove the tag and enter the jacket as routine cleaning to clear the counter.
Check the lining and ask a colleague whether the jacket can be accepted.
Compare the jacket with its tag, note the lining condition, and clarify the service requested.

basic.situation: A customer asks how to operate a rented carpet cleaner. You have a quick guide beside the machine and need to explain its basic use.

options.text: Tell the customer to press the main switch and start cleaning.
Read the operating steps from the guide and answer the customer's main question.
Point to the quick guide and let the customer read it at the counter.
Use the guide to explain the controls and basic care steps before handover.

advanced.situation: A customer asks whether a hired floor polisher suits a delicate surface. A colleague suggests the usual pad, but the product guide lists several pad types.

options.text: Check the guide for pad suitability and tell the customer which options suit that surface.
Check the guide's surface notes and recommend a suitable pad with care steps.
Suggest the usual pad because most customers use it on similar floors.
Compare the listed pad types with the customer and explain which suit delicate surfaces.

basic.situation: A customer rents a camera and is ready to leave. The rental form needs contact details, a signature, and the item information.

options.text: Fill in the item and customer details, then check the signature before handover.
Hand over the camera and ask the customer to return the form later.
Ask the customer to fill in the form while you prepare the camera.
Complete the item details, then hand over the form for the customer's signature.

advanced.situation: At closing, the rental log shows fewer customer visits than the counter tally. The next shift needs the records to reconcile daily transactions.

options.text: Enter the tally total in the log and close the record for the day.
Compare the tally with transaction records, update verified entries, and note any unresolved gap.
Adjust the log to match the tally and leave a note for the next shift.
Recount the tally and ask the next shift to compare it with transactions.

basic.situation: A customer phones for a brake part by name, but the shelf has two similar versions and you are still learning the order system.

options.text: You reserve the version that sells most often for that vehicle.
You take the order as stated and ask a colleague to verify it afterward.
You confirm the vehicle details, check the stock record, and repeat the order back.
You record the part name and ask the customer to collect it later.

advanced.situation: A customer is upset that a back-ordered part missed its expected date, and the replacement shipment has no confirmed arrival time.

options.text: You apologise, share the latest estimate, and invite the customer to call later.
You check the supplier update, explain the uncertainty, and offer available options.
You apologise and say the supplier should deliver the part soon.
You offer a similar part and suggest the customer try it meanwhile.

basic.situation: A customer is ready to pay for a part, but the card terminal asks for credit authorisation before the sale can finish.

options.text: You wait for the terminal result, then prepare the sales slip for approval.
You ask the customer to try another card while you finish the sales slip.
You check the terminal response, obtain the required authorisation, and complete the sales slip.
You complete the sales slip and tell the customer the card should clear shortly.

advanced.situation: A returned electrical component looks damaged, but the customer says it failed during normal use and asks for a refund.

options.text: You examine the component and ask a senior colleague what remedy fits.
You accept the return and offer an exchange to keep the queue moving.
You inspect the return against the sale details and apply the store's refund process.
You refund the purchase based on the customer's description of the failure.

basic.situation: A delivery of fasteners arrives while you are restocking, and several boxes have labels that do not match the shelf signs.

options.text: You check the stock system, match each label, and store boxes in assigned locations.
You keep the boxes together near the stockroom entrance until shelves are clear.
You place each box on the nearest open shelf and update the labels later.
You sort the boxes by size and ask a colleague to confirm shelf locations.

advanced.situation: A stock count shows frequent mismatches in popular filters, and you are asked to improve how the team records stock movements.

options.text: You update on-hand totals to match the latest physical count.
You review recent entries and remind staff to record every filter movement.
You ask staff to recount popular filters at each week's end.
You trace receiving and sales entries, then agree movement checks with the team.

basic.situation: A customer brings an old mower belt and asks for the replacement number, but the belt label is worn away.

options.text: You search by the belt colour and show the closest catalogue result.
You search the parts catalogue using the mower model and verify the listing details.
You find a likely listing and ask a colleague to confirm the mower model.
You measure the belt length and compare it with nearby catalogue listings.

advanced.situation: A customer needs a replacement shaft, and the old part is worn; a similar catalogue item may fit after machining.

options.text: You compare the old part's key dimensions with the candidate and check machining allowance.
You compare the shaft length with the catalogue and offer the nearest match.
You choose the closest-looking shaft and ask the customer to confirm it.
You measure the shaft and ask a senior salesperson which candidate seems closest.

basic.situation: A customer asks whether a higher-capacity filter can replace the listed part in their small workshop machine.

options.text: You recommend the higher-capacity filter based on its stated specifications.
You explain listed filter features and check machine details before suggesting a substitute.
You describe the higher-capacity filter and ask what fit the customer needs.
You show both filters and explain the differences you can verify.

advanced.situation: A customer is modifying an older pump and asks whether a non-identical fitting can work with its existing connection.

options.text: You explain the fitting differences and suggest checking the pump manual first.
You show the fitting and describe how similar pumps use it.
You check the connection details, explain the fit limits, and suggest a verified alternative.
You say the fitting may work and ask the customer to test it carefully.

basic.situation: New stock of wiper blades arrives before a weekend promotion, and the display stand has several empty spaces.

options.text: You place new boxes beside the stand until the promotion begins.
You fill empty spaces with new blades and straighten the display stand.
You put the quickest-selling blades at eye level, then sort remaining stock by type.
You arrange the new blades by type and price, then check labels.

advanced.situation: A customer needs a repaired part shipped to another state, and two carriers quote different costs and delivery windows.

options.text: You repair the part and leave it ready for the customer to collect.
You choose the carrier offering faster delivery and arrange a suitable collection time with them.
You compare costs and delivery windows, confirm needs, then track the shipment.
You book the cheaper carrier and send the tracking number to the customer.

basic.situation: Before opening, you review today's promotion sheet and a customer asks whether discounted items qualify for exchanges.

options.text: You rely on yesterday's briefing and offer the customer a likely answer.
You promise an exchange because the customer has kept the receipt.
You confirm the promotion with the manager before answering the customer.
You check the current promotion and exchange terms, then explain them clearly.

advanced.situation: A new colleague is covering the service counter during a busy weekend. You need to brief them on current payment, exchange and security procedures.

options.text: You pass on the shortcuts experienced staff usually use at the counter.
You explain the main rules and point out where the policy sheet is kept.
You share the current policy sheet and walk through likely counter scenarios together.
You tell them to approve routine requests so the queue keeps moving.

basic.situation: A customer buys two marked items with cash. You total the sale and prepare their change while your supervisor is nearby.

options.text: You total the marked prices and ask your supervisor to check the amount.
You enter both prices, confirm the total, and count the change back.
You charge the lower marked price for both items to save time.
You use the till's displayed total and hand over the change promptly.

advanced.situation: A customer disputes a card charge after returning an item, while the drawer total is short. You are handling the counter during a queue.

options.text: You check the return record and receipt, then reconcile the drawer entries before responding.
You remove the shortage from the drawer and close the return as settled.
You refund the disputed amount and note the drawer shortage for later review.
You review the return receipt and ask a colleague to recount the drawer.

basic.situation: A customer enters looking unsure and pauses near the entrance. You are free to greet them and find out what they need.

options.text: You point out the popular section and ask if they want to browse there.
You greet them, ask what they are looking for, and listen to their answer.
You direct them to the nearest aisle so you can return to restocking.
You greet them and ask whether they need help finding something today.

advanced.situation: A junior colleague recommends the first item a customer mentions. You notice the customer hesitates and has not explained how they plan to use it.

options.text: You encourage the colleague to complete the sale while interest remains high.
You suggest the colleague list the item’s features before the customer decides.
You ask the customer how they plan to use the item before advising further.
You model a follow-up question about use, then invite the colleague to listen for priorities.

basic.situation: You are arranging a delivery on a shelf using the store's display plan, which shows where each product and price ticket belongs.

options.text: You place the products by category and follow the plan for the price tickets.
You put the new items wherever space is available and leave tickets nearby.
You match each item and ticket to the plan, then check the shelf alignment.
You arrange the items by size and put tickets along the shelf edge.

advanced.situation: A seasonal promotion starts tomorrow, and you are asked to arrange a small display near the entrance using the approved products and signage.

options.text: You group the featured products at eye level and keep the approved signs easy to read.
You add nearby products that seem festive to make the display look fuller.
You place the largest products at the front and tuck smaller items behind them.
You follow the seasonal layout and check that each product has a visible price ticket.

basic.situation: A customer asks how a small kitchen appliance works. You have used it before, and a display model is available.

options.text: You show the basic controls on the display model and answer their questions.
You switch it on briefly and let the customer work out the controls.
You describe the appliance's main functions and invite them to read its box.
You explain the controls and offer to find the instruction leaflet for them.

advanced.situation: Your store has a new multi-setting appliance. A customer asks for a demonstration, and a colleague is unsure how to explain its controls.

options.text: You read the control labels aloud and offer the customer the instruction booklet.
You show the quick setting and explain when it may suit customers.
You walk through key settings and invite the customer to try the controls.
You show useful settings and link each control to the customer's needs.

basic.situation: A customer asks where to find a basic phone charger. You know the store layout but are not sure which connector their phone uses.

options.text: You point to the nearest charger display and mention that it has several types.
You ask which connector they need, then guide them to the matching chargers.
You recommend the first charger on the shelf because it is clearly labelled.
You show them the charger aisle and suggest checking their phone connector there.

advanced.situation: A customer wants a work bag for daily train travel and a laptop, but is comparing several sizes and materials.

options.text: You ask about laptop size and commute needs, then compare suitable bags.
You explain sizes and materials, noting which options fit the customer's laptop and commute.
You suggest a larger bag to leave room for the customer's extra items.
You recommend a popular bag and describe its material, pockets, and daily-use features.

basic.situation: You are presenting a standard advertising package to a local café owner, who asks how a sample social media ad would look.

options.text: You quote a larger package to make the café's small budget go further.
You show the sample, link its format to the café's audience, and invite questions.
You describe the package and promise to email a sample after the meeting.
You present the sample and explain the package's main features and price.

advanced.situation: A regional retailer wants a campaign across print and digital channels, but its goals and audience vary by location. You are preparing the presentation with a junior colleague.

options.text: You lead with the channel showing the strongest recent response figures.
You reuse one sample ad across locations to simplify the proposal.
You tailor sample ads to each location and link channels to local goals.
You explain how each available channel could support the campaign's goals.

basic.situation: You receive an assigned list of local businesses that have not advertised with your company. You need to make your first round of calls.

options.text: You email the same service sheet to each business before making calls.
You review each business briefly, then tailor your opening to its likely advertising needs.
You call from the list and use the provided introduction to explain your services.
You mark the unanswered calls as completed and move on to fresh leads.

advanced.situation: Several independent clinics in your area are opening new branches. You see a possible local advertising market and need to suggest a relevant service to your team.

options.text: You announce that clinics will need a new campaign and pitch it as settled.
You contact a few clinics with the standard package to gauge interest.
You share the emerging market and suggest adapting an existing advertising package.
You check their likely audiences and needs, then propose a focused service for discussion.

basic.situation: A small retailer asks for an estimate for a standard advertising package. You have the current rate sheet and know which options they mentioned.

options.text: You offer a low estimate before checking which options the client requested.
You quote a similar client's price and offer to revise it later.
You match requested options to the rate sheet and explain the estimate.
You quote the package price and describe its usual deliverables.

advanced.situation: A client wants a commercial taping session coordinated with a promotion involving several departments. Dates are tight and the plan is still being discussed.

options.text: You set the date before checking whether departments can support the session.
You check participants' availability and suggest a session date to the client.
You coordinate timing with the promotion plan and confirm needs with participants.
You reserve an early studio slot while the client reviews possible dates.

basic.situation: A client emails a signed advertising order and asks when the first proof will arrive. You are handling account paperwork and correspondence.

options.text: You reply with the usual proof timeline and add the order to your folder.
You tell the client the proof will arrive Friday before checking the schedule.
You acknowledge the order and forward it to the colleague handling the proofs.
You file the order, check dates, and reply with the next step.

advanced.situation: Your team is collecting documents for an advertising bid. One supplier form is missing, and the approval pack is due to be assembled today.

options.text: You reuse a similar supplier form to make the pack appear complete.
You contact the supplier, then tell the coordinator the form remains pending today.
You assemble available documents and add the form once it arrives.
You request the missing form and flag its absence in the bid pack.

basic.situation: A client has received a proof for a local promotion. They ask whether the artwork can be adjusted before they approve it.

options.text: You suggest keeping the proof because it follows the usual layout.
You explain artwork choices and ask which change would support the promotion.
You show available artwork samples and discuss the client's requested adjustment before deciding approval.
You approve the proof on the client's behalf to keep production moving.

advanced.situation: A client is launching a new service and is unsure whether to use a short video or a print advert. They ask for your creative advice.

options.text: You promise video will attract more customers before asking about the intended audience.
You explain each format's strengths, share samples, and discuss how each suits the launch.
You recommend video because it can show the service in action to viewers.
You ask about the audience and goal, then compare video with print.

basic.situation: You are preparing for a first meeting with a small furniture maker and need to understand its products, customers and past advertising.

options.text: You reuse notes from a furniture client and assume the needs are similar.
You check the client's website and use its latest product description in your notes.
You read the company profile and note the products it sells before the meeting.
You review the product range, likely customers, past advertising, and questions for the meeting.

advanced.situation: At a trade show, you hear several suppliers discuss changing buyer preferences. Your team is planning its next sales approach after the event.

options.text: You collect brochures from popular booths and pass them to the sales team.
You note repeated themes and contacts, then share implications for the sales plan.
You summarize conversations and share relevant supplier contacts with your team after the event.
You tell the team that one supplier's view represents the whole market.

basic.situation: A couple asks about life cover at a weekend booth. You have a few minutes to learn about their needs before suggesting a suitable next step.

options.text: Use the booth form to record their contact details and arrange a product call.
Ask about dependants, existing cover, and the monthly amount they can afford.
Show them the popular plan and ask whether its monthly premium feels manageable.
Ask about their income and dependants, then note their answers for follow-up.

advanced.situation: A business owner with several properties asks you to review cover after buying a warehouse. The existing schedule lists different locations and insured values.

options.text: Compare the warehouse quote with the current schedule and flag mismatched values.
Ask the owner which property worries them most and focus the review there.
Ask for the latest asset list, current policies, occupancy details, and major exposures.
Offer the warehouse plan first, then revisit the older properties at renewal.

basic.situation: A first-time buyer asks what a basic medical policy covers and whether it pays for every clinic visit. You have the approved product guide.

options.text: Describe the main benefits and say clinic visits are generally included.
Use the guide to explain covered care, exclusions, and the stated limits.
Read the benefit summary aloud and offer to clarify one point afterward.
Point out the annual limit and suggest they check the wording for details.

advanced.situation: A client says a hospital claim was partly declined and asks what the policy wording means. You can review the documents but cannot decide the claim.

options.text: Compare the decision letter with the relevant clauses and explain the stated basis.
Tell the client the insurer will probably reverse it after another review.
Explain the clause you find and suggest the client contact claims with questions.
Ask the client to send the decision letter and forward it to claims staff.

basic.situation: A shop owner asks for cover for stock and basic fire damage. You have several standard plans and a senior agent available for guidance.

options.text: Clarify the stock value and premises details, then match a standard plan with guidance.
Ask whether stock or fire protection matters more before selecting a plan.
Recommend the cheapest plan so the owner can start cover this week.
Show two standard plans and explain which listed risks each one covers.

advanced.situation: A family business wants cover for a workshop, delivery vans, and several owners. They have different renewal dates and incomplete asset details.

options.text: Recommend one insurer for every risk to simplify the business's renewals.
Map assets, owners, and renewal dates, then coordinate suitable cover across the risks.
Renew the workshop policy first and add the vans when their documents arrive.
Gather vehicle and workshop values, then ask underwriters for matching quotations.

basic.situation: A client accepts a standard policy quote and asks to pay monthly. You are following the agency's premium and payment setup instructions.

options.text: Use the monthly amount from a similar policy and set up the same method.
Enter the quoted premium and ask the client which payment method they prefer.
Set up monthly payment from the quote and send the client a confirmation.
Check the quoted premium, confirm instalment details, and enter the chosen payment method.

advanced.situation: Several business policies renew this month. One schedule has a revised asset value that differs from the renewal record, and the client needs a timely update.

options.text: Carry forward last year's value to meet the renewal date, then update it later.
Reconcile the revised value with the client record and insurer documents before processing renewal.
Ask the client to confirm the new value and update the renewal record.
Renew using the latest schedule and note the value difference for the file.

basic.situation: A client applies for a standard policy, but the form is missing a property detail required by the checklist. You are preparing the submission.

options.text: Submit the form as it stands so the underwriter can begin reviewing it.
Mark the missing field for follow-up and hold the form for completion.
Use the property detail from the client's previous application for now.
Contact the client for the missing detail and complete the form before submission.

advanced.situation: A client seeks binder cover for a renovated premises, but the underwriter's checklist requests updated details and supporting forms before confirming terms.

options.text: Check each requested item with the client, then submit the completed forms to underwriting.
Send the earlier forms and ask underwriting to bind while updates are pending.
Gather the renovation details and send them with the binder request.
Ask the underwriter which missing document is most urgent and send that first.

basic.situation: You attend a product seminar and need to explain a new personal accident plan to interested clients at the agency next week.

options.text: Note the plan's main features and questions to clarify before discussing it with clients.
Remember the headline benefit and mention it to clients during routine calls.
Ask another attendee for their notes and use those in your next calls.
Collect the handout and review its benefit summary before client calls.

advanced.situation: Your branch is losing small-business prospects to competitors. A new commercial package has launched, and colleagues ask how to present it to local traders.

options.text: Open with the starting premium, then explain how the package serves each trader.
Review the product sheet and share its key features with the team.
Match the package to prospect needs, then share clear talking points from product materials.
Ask colleagues which features resonate, then use those points in trader conversations.

basic.situation: A client asks why a commodity price moved during the week. You are tracking market positions and have notes on supply and demand changes.

options.text: Check the latest quote and mention one supply update from your notes.
Share the largest daily price change and say the market has been volatile.
Repeat the market view from yesterday's client note to save time.
Review the price movement alongside recent supply and demand information before replying.

advanced.situation: A client asks about hedging a commodity exposure while supply news and prices are shifting. Your role allows you to discuss strategies, not promise outcomes.

options.text: Track prices through the week and discuss a hedge after the trend settles.
Review the exposure and present a futures hedge with its main cost consideration.
Compare the exposure with current market drivers and outline suitable hedge choices and trade-offs.
Recommend the familiar futures hedge because it has worked for similar clients.

basic.situation: A new client asks about investing part of their savings. You have time for an initial conversation about their finances and goals.

options.text: Ask about assets, debts, cash flow, and the goals for this investment.
Describe a popular investment and ask what they hope it will achieve.
Ask how much they plan to invest and which products they understand.
Discuss their main goal, likely investment amount, and timing for this year.

advanced.situation: A self-employed client wants a plan for retirement and a home purchase, but income varies and existing investments are spread across several accounts.

options.text: Review account balances and prepare options focused on the retirement goal.
Map assets, liabilities, cash flow, and timelines before preparing a joined-up proposal.
Set a monthly investment target based on the client's highest recent income.
Ask the client which goal matters more and build around that priority.

basic.situation: A new investor asks what a market order means while considering a first share purchase. You can explain the term and available services.

options.text: Explain how a market order works and note that its execution price can vary.
Say it buys shares at the quoted price and offer to place the order.
Define a market order and suggest reading the platform's order guide.
Describe the order as a quick way to buy shares during trading hours.

advanced.situation: An experienced client asks whether to sell a particular security after a sharp price change. They want advice, and you have the latest quote and issuer information.

options.text: Recommend selling today because the price may continue moving downward.
Share the latest quote and summarize the issuer's recent financial position.
Explain the price change and ask whether the client is ready to sell.
Review why the client holds it, then discuss company facts and sale considerations.

basic.situation: A client requests a purchase of listed shares and gives you a limit price. You are preparing the bid for routing through your firm's process.

options.text: Check the security and quantity, then enter the client's stated limit price.
Ask a colleague to verify the price while you prepare the purchase bid.
Confirm the security, quantity, and limit price before entering the bid for routing.
Enter the limit price from the message and route the bid for processing.

advanced.situation: A client wants to sell a large bond holding, but current quotes differ across dealers and available volume is limited. You can discuss prices with counterparties.

options.text: Contact another dealer for a quote and update the client with the result.
Compare executable quotes and available volume, then negotiate terms against the client's instructions.
Accept the highest displayed quote before the available volume changes.
Check the leading quote's size and ask the client whether that price works.

basic.situation: A completed client transaction needs a commission figure for the billing record. Your team uses a standard schedule and calculation sheet.

options.text: Calculate the commission from the schedule and enter it for billing.
Ask billing staff for an estimate and enter it while they review the file.
Apply the stated schedule to the transaction details and check the calculation sheet.
Use the commission from the last similar transaction for this billing record.

advanced.situation: A monthly transaction report shows a client position that differs from the trade records. You are reviewing the figures before they go to your manager.

options.text: Update the report from the trade record and note that the figures differed.
Trace the reported position to trade records, resolve the discrepancy, and document the adjustment.
Send the report using the latest position figure and explain the mismatch later.
Compare the position with the trade records and flag the difference for review.

basic.situation: A client requests a sale of shares by phone. You must complete the sales order ticket before it is submitted for processing.

options.text: Write the client's requested sale in the ticket notes for processing staff.
Record the security, quantity, order terms, and client instruction on the ticket.
Enter the security and approximate quantity from the client's previous order.
Record the security and quantity, then note that the client called today.

advanced.situation: A complex client order has been completed, but the ticket and confirmation show different quantities. The day's records must be ready for review.

options.text: Flag the mismatch and ask processing staff to verify both quantities against source records.
Update the ticket from the execution record and document the quantity mismatch.
Compare all three records, amend the ticket, and retain the audit trail.
Use the confirmation quantity and remove the older entry from the ticket.

basic.situation: A couple asks for a beach holiday but has not settled on dates or spending limits. You need to clarify what they want before suggesting options.

options.text: Suggest the usual package based on their first destination and dates.
Confirm each travel need in a checklist, then summarize trade-offs for agreement.
Offer a nearby date option and note the budget difference for review.
Ask which destination, dates, transport, budget, and room needs matter most.

advanced.situation: A family wants a low-cost trip during school holidays, while one traveller needs step-free access and another can travel only on certain dates. You guide a junior agent through the discussion.

options.text: Ask the junior to list each traveller's dates, access needs, and budget.
Compare the date and access constraints, then offer feasible trade-offs for confirmation.
Recommend the cheapest holiday package and check access after they choose.
Have the junior confirm dates and access needs before checking available packages.

basic.situation: A customer has approved a flight itinerary, and you are asked to request the carrier ticket through the booking system.

options.text: Ask a colleague to review the booking before sending the ticket request.
Check passenger details against the itinerary before requesting tickets.
Request tickets from the first search result to keep the queue moving.
Compare the booking record with names and dates, then request ticketing.

advanced.situation: A booking system shows two hotel confirmations for one family after a date change. A junior agent is waiting for guidance before tickets are requested.

options.text: Inspect the booking history and identify which hotel dates match the confirmed itinerary.
Compare both confirmations with the itinerary and flag the mismatch for review.
Ask the junior to retry the hotel search with the confirmed dates.
Choose the latest hotel confirmation and continue with the ticket request.

basic.situation: A customer asks for the total cost of a flight and two hotel nights. You have the carrier fare and hotel rate details.

options.text: Quote the flight fare as the trip total to save calculation time.
Calculate each cost separately and show how both make up the total.
Use the previous customer's total as a guide for this quote.
Add the flight and two hotel nights, then check the quoted total.

advanced.situation: A family package quote is close to the agreed budget, but a hotel rate in the worksheet differs from the current rate book. You are reviewing a junior agent's calculation.

options.text: Ask the junior agent to verify another package quote before revising this one.
Keep the worksheet total and tell the family about the rate difference before booking.
Verify each package component against its source, then update the quote and budget comparison.
Recheck the hotel rate and recalculate the package total from the current rate book.

basic.situation: After arranging a trip, you need to enter the customer's contact details and chosen package into the agency's record system.

options.text: Copy details from the enquiry note into the record as written.
Enter the contact details and selected package, then review the saved record.
Fill missing contact fields with details from a similar client record.
Save the package name and add the contact details at day's end.

advanced.situation: Several agents use different labels for the same package, making client records hard to compare. You are asked to improve the team's record keeping.

options.text: Review recent records and suggest shared labels plus required fields for client details.
Invite agents to suggest clearer labels and record them in a shared guide.
Replace package labels across records after agreeing wording with the agents involved.
Map existing fields and labels, then draft a shared format with missing detail checks.

basic.situation: A customer asks what is included in a standard island tour package before deciding whether it suits their holiday plans.

options.text: Read the package script and offer the printed itinerary for reference.
Describe the inclusions and ask which parts fit their holiday plans.
Mention the package price and ask if they want to reserve it.
Promise a room upgrade to encourage the customer to book today.

advanced.situation: Your team is promoting a multi-stop package, but customers are unsure whether its extra stop is worth the added cost. You are coaching a junior agent.

options.text: Ask the junior to emphasize the extra stop and repeat the package price.
Have the junior explain the itinerary and answer questions about its added stop.
Compare the extra stop's experience and cost with the customer's priorities, then coach the pitch.
Offer a personal discount to close customers who hesitate over the price.

basic.situation: A customer is ready to pay for a flight and asks for a brochure about local customs at the destination.

options.text: Take the cash and hand over a general brochure for the region.
Record the payment against the booking and give a suitable customs brochure.
Confirm the amount due, collect payment, and provide relevant destination information.
Accept the cash and mark the booking paid before counting it.

advanced.situation: A customer pays for a group booking, but the amount received differs from the booking total. They also ask for guidance on local customs.

options.text: Reconcile the payment against the booking, explain any balance, and share relevant customs guidance.
Record the expected total as received and give the customer a destination brochure.
Check the booking balance, record the amount received, and explain the difference.
Count the payment again and ask the customer to read the brochure while waiting.

basic.situation: Before a client meeting, your manager asks what recent trade coverage says about demand for the service your team sells.

options.text: Repeat a colleague’s view that demand is rising across the sector.
Scan the headlines and report the most optimistic forecast.
Read a recent industry article and note its main market points.
Compare several recent industry sources and note repeated demand trends.

advanced.situation: A competitor has cut its service price, and a large prospect has asked for a revised quote. Your team wants your view on the market shift.

options.text: Match the competitor’s price to keep the prospect engaged during this discussion.
Ask what the competitor included before discussing a possible discount with the prospect.
Compare service scope, competitor prices, and recent market signals before advising the team on response.
Review recent competitor prices and recommend a measured adjustment to the team.

basic.situation: A customer asks for the price of a standard monthly service package and its usual start date. You have the current price sheet.

options.text: Give the monthly price and explain that the start date can be arranged.
Share the listed monthly price and typical start date from the current sheet.
Verify the package price and available start date before giving the customer a quote.
Offer last month's price to keep the discussion moving with the customer.

advanced.situation: A client requests a proposal comparing two service levels, with different setup costs and delivery dates. You are preparing the figures for review.

options.text: Use the lower monthly fee as the headline for both service levels.
List both monthly fees and delivery dates in the proposal draft.
Ask finance for a total and draft the proposal around its estimate.
Compare setup and recurring costs, then state each level’s delivery terms clearly.

basic.situation: After signing, a customer asks whether the service agreement includes weekend support. You are reviewing their purchase details.

options.text: Explain the weekend support clause listed in their signed service agreement.
Check their agreement and clarify the stated support hours and contact route.
Tell them weekend support is usually available to customers with this service.
Reassure them that the service team can provide weekend assistance if needed.

advanced.situation: A long-term client reports repeated service delays and asks whether a feature in their plan can reduce disruption. You are handling post-sale support.

options.text: Check the plan and explain how the feature may help with disruption.
Tell them the feature is part of the plan and send its setup guide.
Review the plan and vendor limits, then recommend a suitable feature and follow-up.
Suggest switching on the feature and ask them to see whether delays improve.

basic.situation: A customer has agreed to a standard service package. You are filling out the sales form before the order is processed.

options.text: Write the package and customer name on a follow-up note.
Complete the form using the package name and agreed price.
Enter the customer, package, agreed price, and start date, then check the form.
Use the previous customer's form as a template and change the price.

advanced.situation: You find duplicate customer profiles with different contact details before a renewal proposal is prepared. You maintain the customer records.

options.text: Merge the profiles using recent contact details and flag the updated customer record.
Check the source record, reconcile the details, and document the customer profile update.
Use the profile with the newest activity and prepare the proposal from it.
Ask both account owners which profile they used for recent customer contact.

basic.situation: At a local trade meeting, your team has a stand and a stack of service leaflets for visitors. You are helping with outreach.

options.text: Pass leaflets to everyone walking through the meeting area.
Offer a leaflet and briefly explain which service it describes.
Leave the leaflets on a nearby table for people to find.
Hand out leaflets to visitors who stop by the stand.

advanced.situation: Your team is promoting a new service at a trade show, but visitors vary from current clients to unfamiliar prospects. You are coordinating the stand.

options.text: Brief staff on the launch message and ask them to distribute the service leaflet.
Coach staff to ask visitor needs, tailor the service discussion, and share relevant materials.
Focus the team on collecting as many visitor contacts as possible.
Give every visitor the same leaflet and repeat the launch message.

basic.situation: A customer asks whether a standard service is available next month and what it costs. You have the current service sheet.

options.text: Quote a familiar price and say the service should be available.
Check the current price and next-month availability before replying to the customer.
Read the listed price and usual availability from the service sheet.
Send the service sheet and ask them to review the listed price and availability.

advanced.situation: A customer wants a lower price and a revised start date in a service agreement. You can discuss terms within the approved range.

options.text: Check approved terms and propose a revised price with the nearest available start date.
Clarify their priorities and negotiate a workable price and date within approved terms.
Accept the requested price and date to secure the agreement with the customer.
Offer the lowest approved price while retaining the original service start date.

basic.situation: A customer asks whether a new sensor works with an older controller. You have the product manual and need to check its specifications.

options.text: Read the product overview and give the customer its general description.
Ask a colleague about the sensor and pass along their recollection.
Check the compatibility table and share its stated limits with the customer.
Tell the customer the sensor should work based on similar models.

advanced.situation: A new technical bulletin changes a product’s operating limits, while trade publications report shifting demand. Colleagues need a grounded briefing before customer visits.

options.text: Summarize the bulletin, compare relevant market reports, and brief colleagues on implications.
Explain the bulletin’s key limits and share a relevant market article.
Describe the new limits from memory and mention the market trend you heard.
Forward the bulletin and a recent trade article for colleagues to read.

basic.situation: A customer requests a standard quote for three units and asks about the listed credit terms. You have the approved pricing template.

options.text: Offer a small discount to make the quote more appealing.
Use the template, enter three units, and state its listed credit terms.
Send the unit price and let the customer calculate the total.
Prepare the template quote and ask a colleague to check the total.

advanced.situation: A bid asks for installation costs and projected savings across several production lines. The specification uses unfamiliar assumptions and the submission deadline is close.

options.text: Prepare a proposal with the requested specifications and estimated total cost.
Apply last month’s unit costs and reuse the previous savings estimate.
Reconcile each line’s assumptions, calculate costs and savings, then flag gaps in the bid.
Calculate using the bid quantities and add a note about uncertain assumptions.

basic.situation: A small workshop wants a replacement pump for a familiar process. You can compare its stated flow needs with product specifications.

options.text: Compare two models against flow needs and ask which option fits.
Match the stated flow needs to specifications and explain a suitable model.
Suggest extra capacity only after checking expected growth and operating needs.
Review common models, then ask which features matter for this workshop.

advanced.situation: A factory’s output has fallen after a process change. The customer wants advice on product use, but the cause could involve several operating conditions.

options.text: Share common product-use guidance and ask the customer to monitor output.
Review the current product settings and suggest a cautious adjustment for a trial.
Recommend increasing the product dose to restore the earlier output level.
Map the process change to operating conditions, then recommend a product-use adjustment to test.

basic.situation: A customer reports that a unit is showing an unfamiliar warning and asks when the replacement can arrive. You can check the delivery schedule.

options.text: Suggest a restart, then share an unverified arrival estimate with the customer.
Check delivery timing and tell the customer when you can confirm warning details.
Record warning, share manual guidance, and check expected delivery date.
Send the manual and current delivery schedule for the customer to review.

advanced.situation: A customer’s production line is halted by a recurring fault, and the replacement unit’s scheduled arrival may miss a project milestone. You can review support notes and delivery updates.

options.text: Review fault notes and delivery updates, then share timing and support steps.
Send support notes and ask the customer to consult their site technician.
Promise the earlier estimate and suggest restarting between faults to maintain production.
Share the latest delivery estimate and arrange a technical follow-up about recurring faults.

basic.situation: After a routine order, you need to update the customer record and submit a travel expense report with receipts.

options.text: Save the receipts and enter one combined travel expense amount.
Submit the report with estimated amounts and update the customer record later.
Update the order details and attach matching receipts to the expense report.
Update the customer record and prepare the expense report for review.

advanced.situation: A large order’s contract has a delivery term that differs from the approved proposal, and the sales record shows another quantity. The customer is awaiting paperwork.

options.text: Use the sales record quantity and retain the proposal’s delivery term.
Submit the contract using the customer’s latest email and update the record afterward.
Check quantity and delivery terms against the approved proposal before submitting paperwork.
Check the quantity against the order and flag the delivery term for review.
