basic.situation: At a customer visit, a buyer asks whether a stocked model suits a small production line and requests a brochure to share with colleagues.

options.text: Assure the buyer the model will suit the line and leave several brochures.
Explain the model’s listed features and leave a brochure for the buyer.
Ask about the line’s needs, explain the model’s fit, and share its brochure.
Hand over the brochure and say the model is popular with small factories.

advanced.situation: A major buyer requests a lower price, faster delivery, and a longer service agreement. Your team has discussed a campaign for similar accounts, but the buyer’s priorities differ.

options.text: Accept the lower price and longer agreement to secure the order today.
Ask which term matters most, then offer an approved option and brief colleagues.
Clarify priorities, trade approved terms, and share account insights with relevant colleagues.
Offer a standard discount and explain the usual delivery and service terms.

basic.situation: At a community event, a homeowner asks about solar for a terrace house. You need to record enough information to understand their energy needs.

options.text: Ask about the electricity bill and save the homeowner’s contact details.
Give a brochure and invite the homeowner to call if interested.
Ask about the household’s electricity use, roof, and preferred contact details.
Record the homeowner’s phone number and mark them as ready for a quote.

advanced.situation: Your territory has many new housing areas, but event leads have been sparse. You need a practical way to develop solar accounts with limited travel time.

options.text: Visit every housing area and distribute flyers to build name recognition.
Ask current customers for referrals and follow up with nearby homeowners.
Map new housing areas, compare lead sources, and schedule outreach where interest is strongest.
Review recent inquiries and plan visits around the locations they mention.

basic.situation: You visit a single-storey home to note roof dimensions and direction before a solar estimate. Trees shade part of the roof in the afternoon.

options.text: Measure the roof and ask the homeowner when the shade is strongest.
Measure the sunny roof section and use it for the initial estimate.
Estimate the roof area by eye and describe it as mostly sunny.
Measure the roof, note its direction, and record the afternoon shade.

advanced.situation: A rural site has uneven ground, a tall tree, and several roof sections. Your initial compass reading conflicts with the site map used by another assessor.

options.text: Repeat the compass reading nearby and record the tree shade and roof sections.
Recheck compass orientation at clear points, map shade and roof sections, then reconcile the readings.
Record both orientations and ask the customer which roof section seems suitable.
Use the site map orientation and proceed with the clearest roof section.

basic.situation: A shop owner wants to see how a small solar kit powers lights during a demonstration. You have the display equipment and its basic instructions.

options.text: Describe the kit’s features and leave the owner with a product sheet.
Demonstrate the light and invite the owner to try the controls.
Show the kit powering a light and explain its basic operating steps.
Connect the kit quickly and say it can power the shop’s lights.

advanced.situation: A farm wants solar for cold storage, daytime pumping, and evening lighting. Its usage varies by season, and the owner asks for one package covering everything.

options.text: Separate seasonal loads, compare site and price constraints, then shape a package around priorities.
Estimate each load and offer a package for the busiest season first.
Size the package for the farm’s highest daily use and include all three loads.
Show packages used by similar farms and ask which price range feels comfortable.

basic.situation: A customer shares a roof sketch for a basic solar estimate. Nearby trees shade one side, and you need to account for this and local climate factors.

options.text: Use a nearby system’s production as a rough guide for the customer.
Estimate production from roof area, local climate, and the shaded section.
Estimate from usable roof area and note that shade may lower production.
Use the full roof area and a standard sunny-day figure for the estimate.

advanced.situation: Your territory has low solar inquiries in several districts, while other areas have many referrals. You need a sales plan for the next quarter.

options.text: Prioritize districts with more referrals and schedule additional visits there.
Distribute the same campaign materials across all districts and track responses.
Compare referral patterns, district conditions, and past outreach before targeting the quarter’s activity.
Repeat the last quarter’s campaign in every district to keep coverage consistent.

basic.situation: A homeowner accepts a standard solar package and asks for a quote using your company’s template. The roof details are available from an initial visit.

options.text: Reuse a previous homeowner’s quote and change the customer name.
Enter the selected package and recorded roof details in the quote template.
Send the package price and prepare the template after the homeowner confirms.
Prepare the template quote and ask a colleague to verify its figures.

advanced.situation: A detailed installation drawing shows panel rows close to a roof edge, while its equipment list names a different inverter than the proposal. The customer expects your review.

options.text: Check the equipment list against the proposal and hold the drawing for later review.
Flag the roof-edge spacing and ask the designer to check the inverter listing.
Approve the drawing based on the panel layout and send the proposal onward.
Compare drawing, equipment list, and proposal, then document both discrepancies for design resolution.

basic.situation: A customer asks for a basic explanation of solar warranties and wants to place an order for a standard package. You have the approved product information.

options.text: Explain the listed warranty terms, confirm the package, and record the order details.
Promise the warranty covers every part and submit the standard package order.
Read the warranty summary and note the package request for order entry.
Share the warranty brochure and take the customer’s package request by phone.

advanced.situation: A dealer asks how a system works with a financing offer and an incentive, but the customer’s site details are incomplete. The dealer also requests a quote.

options.text: Share the system specifications and ask the dealer to confirm the site details.
Send the financing brochure and ask the dealer to submit a formal quote request.
Quote the usual package and describe the incentive as available to the customer.
Explain verified system details, qualify funding information, and capture site gaps for the quote.

basic.situation: A current client mentions that nearby shops may need your product. You have a business directory and time to identify a few prospects.

options.text: Ask the client which similar outlets might welcome an introduction.
Check nearby retailers in the directory and note why each fits.
Call every listed shop with the same pitch before checking its fit.
Pick shops by location and add them to your call list.

advanced.situation: At a trade show, several buyers mention a new product feature. A competitor has also changed its prices, and your next-quarter pipeline is thin.

options.text: Call every visitor who took a brochure before the week ends.
Share the competitor's prices with the team and call familiar accounts.
Compare visitor questions with competitor prices, then qualify leads for follow-up.
Add interested visitors to your pipeline and note the competitor's new prices.

basic.situation: Your manager asks you to file this month's travel expenses and update the sales record for a completed order.

options.text: File the receipts by date and update the order after lunch.
Enter the order and attach each receipt to its expense entry.
Update the order record, then ask how to sort unusual receipts.
Submit the receipts together and estimate the trip total from memory.

advanced.situation: Several new sales staff use different formats, so monthly totals take extra time to reconcile. You are asked to prepare a shared reporting template.

options.text: Make a template with standard fields and a worked example for staff.
Send a blank spreadsheet and let each person choose useful columns.
Copy last month's workbook and rename it for the new reporting period.
Share your own report format and explain the main totals to the team.

basic.situation: A prospective shop owner asks to see a sample and catalogue for a product you have been asked to demonstrate under supervision.

options.text: Ask which product detail matters, then show the matching sample feature.
Read the catalogue highlights aloud while passing around the sample.
Hand over the catalogue and let the customer browse the sample alone.
Show the sample, explain one relevant feature, and offer the catalogue.

advanced.situation: A new colleague must demonstrate a complex product line to a buyer with limited time. The buyer wants to compare two uses before deciding.

options.text: Ask about the buyer's use, then demonstrate the two relevant features in sequence.
Ask your colleague to cover every feature while you find more samples.
Show the most popular use and offer a catalogue for other details.
Start with the standard feature tour and let the buyer interrupt with questions.

basic.situation: A customer says a product they bought does not suit their daily needs. You can review the range and recommend an alternative with guidance.

options.text: Suggest the newest model because several customers have asked about it.
Ask how they use it, then match an alternative to those needs.
Show two alternatives and let the customer choose based on price.
Offer a similar model and explain its main difference from theirs.

advanced.situation: After signing, a client reports that a product is not meeting the agreed use. Colleagues have handled similar calls differently, and you are asked to share a support approach.

options.text: Discuss the client's use with them and record the agreed next contact.
Send the client the product guide and close the support note.
Clarify the use and issue, then share a follow-up sequence colleagues can adapt.
Ask a colleague how they resolved a similar call and use that approach.

basic.situation: A regular customer asks for a quote including delivery timing and credit terms. You have current price guidance but need help with the terms.

options.text: Send the price and ask the customer to choose a delivery date.
Quote the listed price and delivery window, then confirm credit terms with your manager.
Share the price range and say you will check the delivery details.
Give the usual credit period and promise delivery by the customer's preferred date.

advanced.situation: A buyer requests a large order with staged deliveries, a warranty question, and credit terms outside your usual quote guidance.

options.text: Break out each delivery, warranty, and credit item for a reviewed quote.
Apply the usual terms to the full order and send a single total.
Map the delivery stages and ask finance to confirm the credit limit.
Estimate the total and flag the warranty detail for later discussion.

basic.situation: A customer asks whether a catalogue item is in stock and how much it costs. Your script lists the price, but stock needs checking.

options.text: Check the stock record, then answer with the listed price and availability.
Quote the scripted price and say the item should be available.
Read the listed price and offer to check stock after the call.
Ask which branch they prefer and check its stock before replying.

advanced.situation: A buyer asks whether a product can meet an unusual use, qualify for credit, and arrive before a scheduled event. The catalogue covers only standard uses.

options.text: Explain the usual credit terms and suggest a similar product for the event.
Separate the use, credit, and delivery questions, then verify each detail before replying.
Send the standard product page and quote the usual delivery window.
Answer the standard use and delivery details, then refer the credit question onward.

basic.situation: Before opening a store demo, you have a few minutes to practise the product demonstration and check that the sample works.

options.text: Turn on the sample and begin when the first customer arrives.
Review the main talking points and test the sample briefly.
Run the demonstration once, checking each step and the sample as you go.
Ask a teammate to watch the opening while you rehearse the close.

advanced.situation: A crowd gathers around a popular demo while your team has two working samples and one narrow aisle to serve from.

options.text: Pause the demo and let each interested customer try the sample in turn.
Ask a teammate to answer questions while you repeat the demonstration.
Keep demonstrating while the nearest customers pass the sample along.
Set turns with a teammate and keep the demonstration visible from the aisle.

basic.situation: At a community fair, several visitors pause near your display, but only one asks about the product's intended use.

options.text: Ask what brought the visitor over and offer details matching that interest.
Invite the nearby group to hear the main product benefits together.
Offer the brochure to the visitor who asked about the product's use.
Give every visitor the full brochure as they pass the display.

advanced.situation: A visitor needs a compact appliance for a small flat, frequent cooking, and a tight budget. You can suggest products from the range.

options.text: List two affordable models and let the visitor decide between them.
Ask which need matters most, then compare models against space, use, and budget.
Show a compact model and explain its cooking capacity and price.
Recommend the most popular model and mention its current promotion.

basic.situation: You have a small table at a store event and need to arrange the product display before visitors arrive.

options.text: Put the newest item in the centre and stack spare brochures beside it.
Place every product on the front edge so visitors see the range.
Group the products clearly, keep the sample accessible, and face labels outward.
Arrange the main products by size and leave space for the catalogue.

advanced.situation: Your team must move a large presentation backdrop and several stands to another store floor, then assemble them before the session begins.

options.text: Move the backdrop first, then assemble stands wherever space becomes available.
Sort parts by stand, move them in batches, and assemble using the guide.
Carry loose pieces together and assemble each stand from memory without sorting.
Label each bundle and ask a teammate to check stand pieces upon arrival.

basic.situation: After a store demonstration, your lead asks how many coupons you distributed. You made a tally during the session.

options.text: Round the tally to the nearest ten for a quicker update.
Use the tally to give your lead the count verbally.
Write down the number you remember from the busiest moment.
Check your tally and record the coupon count in the demo report.

advanced.situation: Your promotion records show many questions and coupon handouts, but sales varied across demo shifts. Your lead asks what the records suggest.

options.text: Use total sales for the week and recommend repeating the promotion.
Compare sales with each shift's activity and note patterns alongside the limits.
Summarize sales by shift and mention that question counts also changed.
Report the shift with the most coupon handouts as the strongest promotion.

basic.situation: You are assigned a basic demonstration for a product you have not presented before and have time to review its materials.

options.text: Read the product guide and practise explaining its main use with the sample.
Skim the package and repeat its headline when visitors ask.
Ask a teammate for the usual pitch and learn it before opening.
Review the guide's key features and keep it nearby during the demo.

advanced.situation: A customer says a competitor's model may work better for their needs. You have time to check product information before answering.

options.text: Point out your product's promotion and say it offers better value.
Mention the features you know and suggest the customer compare both guides.
Clarify the need, compare verified features, and explain where each model fits.
Check the competitor's listed features and share the differences you can verify.

basic.situation: After a demonstration, brochures, coupons, and samples remain on the table. The next session starts soon, and you need to tidy the area.

options.text: Collect coupons and samples separately, then ask where to store them.
Sweep everything into the nearest box and clear the table quickly.
Put the brochures away and leave samples for the next demonstrator.
Sort the remaining items and return each to its marked place.

advanced.situation: A customer likes a product but asks how it can be altered to fit their needs. Your product guidance includes safe, approved adjustment steps.

options.text: Explain the standard adjustment steps and offer the product guide.
Confirm the requested fit, then guide them through the approved adjustment steps.
Show the quickest adjustment and let the customer follow along.
Offer a sample coupon and suggest they ask the store after purchase.

basic.situation: During a catalog shoot, the photographer asks you to turn toward the window while the stylist adjusts your collar. What do you do?

options.text: Acknowledge the photographer's direction, then check the stylist's requested look before the next frame.
Change the pose to match the lighting, trusting the photographer can adapt later.
Ask which cue to follow, then repeat it consistently for the next frames.
Keep the first pose while the team adjusts, so the setup stays familiar.

advanced.situation: A fashion shoot is running late after a backdrop change, and the stylist and photographer need different looks from your remaining time. What do you do?

options.text: Suggest grouping frames by lighting, then coordinate quick wardrobe changes with the stylist.
Finish the current look first, then let the team decide how to use the remaining time.
Continue switching between both looks as each team member requests a different frame.
Ask the producer to choose one look and complete that setup before changing again.

basic.situation: Before a studio portrait, your makeup looks shiny under the lights, and the stylist asks you to fix your hair. What do you do?

options.text: Blot the shine, smooth your hair, and check the finish with the stylist.
Add another layer of powder and leave the hairstyle as it is.
Use a strong setting spray over your makeup and pin your hair back.
Ask the stylist to show you the needed hair shape before fixing it.

advanced.situation: Strong side lighting makes your makeup look uneven, and the client is waiting for close-up frames. What do you do?

options.text: Check the makeup under the shoot lighting, then blend the visible edges lightly.
Add foundation over the bright side, then return to the camera for another take.
Dust powder across your face to soften the shine in the close-up.
Ask the makeup artist to inspect the close-up before you adjust anything.

basic.situation: During a clothing shoot, the photographer asks you to hold a seated pose while adjusting the camera. What do you do?

options.text: Hold the seated pose and keep your expression relaxed until the photographer is ready.
Stay seated, then ask whether the photographer wants a small angle change.
Stand up briefly to stretch before the photographer takes the next frame.
Shift your legs into a more comfortable position while the camera is adjusted.

advanced.situation: A client wants a bag to feel adventurous, but the planned poses resemble the earlier formal shots. What do you do?

options.text: Offer a wider stance and turn your shoulders toward the camera for variety.
Suggest a moving pose that shows the bag clearly and conveys an outdoor journey.
Swing the bag dramatically across the frame to create a memorable action shot.
Repeat the formal pose with the bag held higher for better visibility.

basic.situation: Your agent sends a booking for a catalogue shoot, but the call time and transport allowance are unclear. What do you do?

options.text: Ask your agent to clarify the call time before you confirm the booking.
Accept the booking and ask about the allowance when you arrive at the studio.
Confirm the call time, transport allowance, pay, and shoot length with your agent.
Plan around the usual call time and assume the allowance matches past jobs.

advanced.situation: Your agency offers overlapping bookings, and one client has not confirmed the finish time or travel arrangements. What do you do?

options.text: Compare confirmed times and travel needs, then discuss a workable booking sequence with your agent.
Accept both jobs, then try to leave the first shoot early if needed.
Choose the higher-paying job and release the other booking through your agent.
Hold the earlier job and ask your agent when the second client will confirm.

basic.situation: Your shoot schedule includes an early call, and you have been given a simple sleep and exercise plan. What do you do?

options.text: Follow the planned bedtime and exercise session, then prepare your meals for tomorrow.
Exercise late tonight and sleep less so you can finish other errands first.
Skip tonight's exercise and use the extra time to rest before the shoot.
Keep the bedtime plan, and ask which exercise can fit before your call.

advanced.situation: Several shoot days are scheduled in a row, and your regular exercise leaves you tired before morning call times. What do you do?

options.text: Ask your trainer which sessions can be shortened during the shoot week.
Keep the full workouts and rely on coffee to manage the early starts.
Move each workout to the evening after the day's final shoot.
Reduce workout intensity around early calls, while protecting regular sleep and meals.

basic.situation: After a half-day catalogue job, you receive a voucher showing the pay and hours. What do you do?

options.text: File the voucher with your other papers and update your portfolio later.
Enter the hours in your log and ask your agent about the listed rate.
Check the hours and rate, then record the voucher details in your job log.
Copy the pay figure into your log and discard the voucher after the job.

advanced.situation: Your portfolio still features an old look, and two recent job vouchers show different hours from your calendar. What do you do?

options.text: Ask your agent to review both vouchers, then select recent portfolio images.
Record voucher figures as received and replace an older portfolio image with recent work.
Check each voucher against your calendar, resolve differences, and refresh the portfolio.
Refresh the portfolio with recent images and enter calendar hours as voucher totals.

basic.situation: An owner asks you to prepare a rental listing, but the advertised rent and available date are not confirmed. What do you do?

options.text: Confirm the rent and available date with the owner before preparing the listing.
Post the property with a rent range and update the date after the owner replies.
Draft the listing with the confirmed features and ask the owner about rent and date.
Use the rent from a nearby listing and publish the property details today.

advanced.situation: A buyer is keen to close, but the seller has changed the asking price and a junior agent is waiting for your direction. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the junior agent to pause the offer until the seller confirms the new price.
Share the revised price with the buyer and ask whether they still want to proceed.
Confirm the seller's revised position, then guide the junior agent through a clear offer discussion.
Tell the buyer the old price still stands while the seller considers the change.

basic.situation: An owner agrees to place a house for sale with your firm, but one listing detail is missing from the standard paperwork. What do you do?

options.text: Mark the missing detail and ask the owner to confirm it before completing paperwork.
Prepare paperwork using confirmed details and flag the blank for review.
Use details from a similar listing to fill the missing field.
Leave the field blank and send the standard form for signature.

advanced.situation: During a sale closing, the buyer and seller disagree about a settlement detail, and your office has another transaction awaiting review. What do you do?

options.text: Tell each party the other may accept their preferred settlement detail.
Check written terms and tell your manager the closing detail remains disputed.
Record disagreement, compare it with agreed terms, and coordinate discussion between both parties.
Ask both parties to restate their positions before checking the written terms.

basic.situation: You are entering a sale listing, and the owner gives you a unit number that differs from the draft property details. What do you do?

options.text: Replace the draft number with the owner's latest message and continue entering details.
Use the number from the draft and publish the listing before the viewing.
Save the draft with the confirmed details and ask the owner to clarify the unit number.
Check the unit number against the owner's documents before updating the listing record.

advanced.situation: A buyer requests a title search before making an offer, and the property record contains an unclear lot reference. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the owner to confirm the reference, then arrange the search using their reply.
Submit the unclear lot reference and let the search results identify the property.
Verify the lot reference against available property documents before arranging the title search.
Arrange the search with the current reference and flag the uncertainty to the buyer.

basic.situation: An owner asks whether their terrace house is priced fairly, and you have details of several nearby recent sales. What do you do?

options.text: Show the owner the nearby sale prices and ask which one feels most relevant.
Recommend the highest nearby sale price so the owner has room to negotiate.
Compare similar nearby sales and explain how their features affect the suggested price.
Compare the nearest recent sale and explain that more details could change the estimate.

advanced.situation: An investor asks you to appraise a small shop lot with rental income, but the lease details vary between the records provided. What do you do?

options.text: Reconcile the lease figures and assess the income potential alongside comparable property evidence.
Ask the owner to confirm the lease details before preparing an income estimate.
Use the higher rental figure to estimate income potential and reassure the investor.
Use the rent shown in the latest record and note that the estimate is provisional.

basic.situation: A purchase contract requires a document before completion, and the buyer asks whether it has been received. What do you do?

options.text: Check the file for the document and report what you find to your manager.
Ask the other party whether they sent the document and update the buyer later.
Tell the buyer it should arrive soon because similar transactions included it.
Check the transaction record and confirm receipt status against the contract requirement.

advanced.situation: You are reviewing a loan officer's file for a purchase closing and notice that a supporting figure differs from the transaction summary. What do you do?

options.text: Change the summary to match the loan file and send the closing pack onward.
Ask the loan officer to confirm which figure should appear in the summary.
Compare the source documents, document the discrepancy, and request clarification before the file proceeds.
Flag the different figures in your review notes and continue checking the remaining pages.

basic.situation: A buyer asks which mortgage options might suit a home purchase, and you are checking current information for the listing area. What do you do?

options.text: Share general mortgage options and ask which monthly payment range the buyer considers.
Recommend the mortgage type a prior buyer chose for a similar property.
Send mortgage types and let the buyer choose one to apply for.
Outline mortgage types and suggest the buyer confirm eligibility with a lender.

advanced.situation: An investor asks whether a vacant lot can support a planned business, and nearby zoning information in your notes may be outdated. What do you do?

options.text: Share your zoning notes and explain they may not reflect current local requirements.
Tell the investor nearby shops do not establish that the proposed business is permitted.
Ask a colleague to check zoning notes before discussing the lot with the investor.
Check current zoning information and direct the investor to confirm proposed use with authorities.

basic.situation: You are preparing an advertisement for a flat and arranging its first open house. The owner has provided photos and a preferred viewing time.

options.text: Use the supplied photos and details to prepare an advert for review.
Confirm key details with the owner, then prepare the advert and book the viewing.
Draft a clear advert from the supplied details and schedule the viewing time.
Post the photos with a short caption and announce the viewing on social media.

advanced.situation: A vacant shoplot has attracted few enquiries, and the owner wants a campaign that reaches suitable tenants while keeping viewing disruption low.

options.text: Refresh the listing, then promote it through channels that reach local business tenants.
Ask nearby owners to share the listing and suggest convenient viewing slots.
Keep the current advert running and offer viewings to anyone who asks.
Match the shoplot's location and permitted use to targeted adverts, then group qualified viewings.

basic.situation: A first-time buyer asks you to find a home near work but has not decided how many bedrooms they need.

options.text: Show a few popular nearby homes and ask which one feels right.
Ask about budget, commute, and household needs, then note suitable property preferences.
Ask the buyer for a budget and preferred neighbourhood before searching listings.
Send several attractive listings nearby and see which ones get a reply.

advanced.situation: A couple has a firm monthly budget, one remote worker, and a parent who may move in later. They want a shortlist near transit.

options.text: Recommend larger homes now, assuming the parent will move in permanently.
Discuss budget trade-offs, work setup, accessibility, and future household plans before ranking suitable homes.
Shortlist homes near transit within budget and flag layouts that might suit family visits.
Filter listings by price and transit access, then share the closest matches.

basic.situation: You are viewing a terrace house before showing it to a buyer. You notice a leaking kitchen tap and several cracked floor tiles.

options.text: Mention the visible defects during the showing and let the buyer decide.
Record the tap leak and cracked tiles, then notify the owner before arranging repairs.
Ask the owner whether a handyman can check the tap and tiles soon.
Photograph the defects and tell the owner they may need attention.

advanced.situation: A hillside home has an unusual extension and little recent sales data. The seller asks you to suggest a competitive asking price before listing.

options.text: Review nearby sales and note that the extension may affect the property's value.
Ask a senior agent for a price range after reviewing the nearest sales.
Use nearby asking prices and the seller's preferred figure to set a starting price.
Compare recent sales, adjust for the extension and condition, and explain the limits of the estimate.

basic.situation: During a viewing, a buyer asks whether the kitchen cabinets and water heater are included in the sale.

options.text: Tell the buyer to confirm the cabinets and heater during offer discussions.
Check the listing notes and tell the buyer what they say about both items.
Say both items usually stay and continue showing the other rooms.
Check the listing and ask the seller to confirm any unclear inclusions before replying.

advanced.situation: A seller wants to accept a lower offer today, while another buyer may secure financing soon. They ask you to advise on the market and mortgage implications.

options.text: Share recent comparable sales and suggest the seller weigh certainty against waiting.
Recommend the higher expected price because the second buyer sounds promising.
Explain comparable prices, clarify each offer's financing status, and outline the timing trade-offs.
Ask the seller which offer feels safer and share your general market view.

basic.situation: A buyer has agreed to rent a condominium, and you are preparing a standard tenancy document using the details provided by both parties.

options.text: Copy details from an older tenancy form and update the tenant's name.
Fill in the tenancy form from the agreed details and send it for review.
Check rent, dates, parties, and included items against instructions before preparing the draft.
Prepare the form using the landlord's details and ask the tenant to review it.

advanced.situation: A purchase is approaching closing, but the title search and lender paperwork show different property descriptions. Several parties are waiting for signing dates.

options.text: Tell the parties about the mismatch and ask them to check their copies.
Compare both records, flag the mismatch, and coordinate corrected documents before confirming signing.
Pause the signing schedule and ask the lender and legal team to reconcile the descriptions.
Use the lender's description in the closing documents and keep the signing date.

basic.situation: A buyer has signed a purchase offer for a landed home. The seller is at work and has asked you to present it later today.

options.text: Wait until the seller is free and then present the signed offer with its key terms.
Mention the buyer's price by phone and say the paperwork can follow later.
Tell the seller the buyer seems keen and ask for a quick answer.
Send the offer to the seller and ask when they can review it together.

advanced.situation: A buyer and seller disagree over a repair request after inspection, and both say they may walk away. You represent the buyer in the discussion.

options.text: Restate each concern and suggest a specific repair credit or work arrangement for discussion.
Separate urgent defects from preferences and suggest a focused compromise for both parties.
Explain that the buyer may withdraw unless the seller accepts every requested repair.
Ask both parties to share preferred repair terms before you reply.

basic.situation: A factory supervisor asks about a replacement pump but has not shared the required flow rate or operating hours.

options.text: Send the standard pump brochure and ask which model looks suitable.
Ask about flow rate, operating hours, and the process before suggesting pump options.
Suggest a popular replacement and offer to confirm the specifications later.
Ask for the flow rate and current pump model before checking available products.

advanced.situation: A client plans to expand a production line next year and asks whether its current control system can support extra equipment and future resale.

options.text: Recommend a full system replacement based on the planned expansion and resale interest.
Map current capacity, planned growth, and resale needs with engineering before framing options.
Review the current system and ask engineering to estimate the expansion requirements.
Ask the client for a target budget and share products used by similar factories.

basic.situation: You are attending a company seminar on a new product line and need to learn which models suit common customer requests.

options.text: Listen to the presentation and note the main product features for later.
Photograph the slides and rely on the shared deck for product details.
Collect the product brochure and review its model names after the seminar.
Take notes on model differences and ask the trainer about unclear use cases.

advanced.situation: Your team plans to introduce a packaging machine in a new regional market, but local buyers use different line speeds and material sizes.

options.text: Reuse the current sales plan and adjust its prices for the new region.
Research regional buyers and competitors, then suggest a launch plan for review.
Ask distributors which models they expect to sell and focus on their preferences.
Compare target buyers' line speeds and materials, then shape configurations and launch priorities.

basic.situation: A prospective customer visits your showroom and asks you to explain sample materials and the basic price difference between two models.

options.text: Explain that one model costs less, then ask which features matter to the customer.
Show both samples, explain their listed price difference, and invite the customer’s questions.
Compare both samples, explain price differences, and link features to the customer’s stated use.
Share the catalogue and invite the customer to compare listed prices and features.

advanced.situation: A plant manager wants a live trial of a machine on a production line during a short maintenance window with several operators attending.

options.text: Arrange the demonstration with the customer and check equipment availability beforehand.
Confirm trial goals, site constraints, and roles, then coordinate equipment and a focused demonstration.
Run the machine through its standard cycle and let the manager judge performance.
Book the trial for the window and tell operators to review the manual beforehand.

basic.situation: A salesperson asks you to join a customer call about replacing a conveyor motor but has only shared the customer's production target.

options.text: Review the production target with the salesperson and prepare relevant motor information.
Ask about the current motor and operating conditions before discussing replacement options.
Recommend the motor with the highest capacity so the target is covered.
Join the call and explain the motor models shown in the latest brochure.

advanced.situation: New sales team members describe a sensor's accuracy differently, and a customer has asked for a technical explanation before deciding on a trial.

options.text: Share the product sheet and ask each salesperson to use its stated accuracy figure.
Let each salesperson explain the sensor using language that feels natural to them.
Ask a senior salesperson to handle the customer call and brief the team afterward.
Clarify the specification with engineering, then coach the team to explain it consistently in context.

basic.situation: Your monthly forecast is due, and two account managers have updated their expected order dates for pending customer proposals.

options.text: Keep last month's dates until the pending proposals receive customer replies.
Check the revised dates with both managers and update the forecast assumptions clearly.
Enter the revised dates and note which account managers supplied each update.
Update the dates from their messages and flag the accounts as pending.

advanced.situation: A food processing client has issued a proposal request with strict line output requirements and asks for a solution using equipment from several product families.

options.text: Consult engineering across product families, then build a proposal that addresses each line output requirement.
Map output requirements to configurations, note open assumptions, and coordinate a tailored client response.
Ask the client to clarify its preferred product family before drafting the response.
Offer a familiar equipment package and adapt the proposal after the client responds.

basic.situation: After a customer call about a service renewal, you need to record the discussion and next steps in the account file.

options.text: Record the call, customer concerns, and agreed follow-up date in the account file.
Wait until the customer decides, then record the renewal activity in the account file.
Note that the customer discussed renewal and may decide soon, including any stated concerns.
Summarize the renewal call, key details, customer concerns, and next steps in recent account activity.

advanced.situation: A customer requests a service contract renewal with a changed response time, while the account record still shows the previous terms.

options.text: Draft the renewal with the requested response time, then ask sales to review the terms.
Reuse the previous contract, change renewal dates, and send it for signature.
Mark the account record as pending and wait for the signed renewal.
Check the approved offer, revise the draft, and log the changed response time.

basic.situation: A caller gives you a new order, but the street name is hard to hear over the phone. You need to enter their details into the system.

options.text: I enter the name and street now, then flag unclear fields for later review.
I confirm spelling, postcode, and payment choice with the caller, then save the verified record.
I enter the details from the call and read back the address before saving.
I use the nearest matching address and submit the order to keep the queue moving.

advanced.situation: A customer says their order confirmation shows a delivery address that differs from the contact record. The order system lists another postcode, and dispatch is due soon.

options.text: I ask dispatch to pause the parcel while I check both records.
I compare the call record and order history, confirm the address, then align both records.
I replace both postcodes with the confirmation address so dispatch can keep moving.
I update the order postcode from the latest note and leave the contact record unchanged.

basic.situation: You are calling a resident about a household service and have a prepared script. They ask what the monthly price includes while you are reading.

options.text: I quote a lower monthly figure to keep the caller interested in hearing more.
I read the next script section, then offer to explain the listed inclusions.
I use the price guide to answer, then continue with the relevant script section.
I pause the script and ask which inclusion matters most to the caller.

advanced.situation: You are revising a sales script after several callers say they rent and cannot approve building changes. The offer includes optional installation choices.

options.text: I move the installation details earlier and tailor the script around renter concerns and available choices.
I add a renter example after the standard product description and retain the other sections.
I keep the current opening and add a short line about installation choices near the end.
I remove installation from the script and focus the pitch on the monthly price.

basic.situation: A person calls after seeing an advert and asks whether a service is available in their area. Your response guide lists the coverage check process.

options.text: I take the postcode and say I will check availability after finishing the call.
I say the service probably reaches their area and continue describing its features.
I check the caller's postcode using the guide and explain the result clearly.
I read the general availability line and invite the caller to ask another question.

advanced.situation: A prospect asked for time to compare plans and has since replied with a question about a setup fee. You have their earlier preferences and one scheduled follow-up.

options.text: I send the fee details from the guide and retain the scheduled follow-up time.
I answer their fee question from the approved guide and agree a follow-up time.
I dismiss the fee as small and press them to decide during this call.
I resend the standard offer and keep the scheduled follow-up time unchanged.

basic.situation: Your team lead gives you a directory page to identify local businesses for a calling list. Several entries have similar names and multiple phone numbers.

options.text: I enter the business names now and leave the phone fields blank for review.
I copy each matching business name and its first listed number into the sheet.
I match each business name to its listed number and mark unclear entries for checking.
I choose the shortest number shown for each business to keep the list tidy.

advanced.situation: You are helping prepare a market survey for a service with several customer groups. The team wants to learn which group is most interested before planning outreach.

options.text: I ask the same broad interest question of people from the easiest available list.
I survey a few people who already asked about the service and treat their interest as representative.
I ask each group what they need and summarise the answers in separate notes.
I define the customer groups, ask comparable need and interest questions, and record responses consistently.

basic.situation: A prospect agrees to meet a sales representative next week and offers Tuesday afternoon. You have access to the shared calendar and need to book the appointment.

options.text: I promise the representative will attend at the first time the prospect offered.
I check the shared calendar, confirm an available time, and book the meeting.
I enter Tuesday afternoon and say the representative will confirm the appointment later.
I note Tuesday afternoon and check the calendar once this call ends.

advanced.situation: Two representatives share a vehicle for client visits across town, and three prospects request overlapping afternoon slots. You are coordinating their calendar bookings.

options.text: I book each prospect into the requested slot and tell the representatives to coordinate travel.
I check both calendars and offer clients the remaining open slots for their visits.
I compare locations, travel gaps, and representative availability, then offer workable slot choices to clients.
I reserve the calendar slots that appear free and sort out the vehicle once clients confirm.

basic.situation: A caller asks how much a listed product costs and whether the package includes delivery. Your product guide shows a price and a separate delivery note.

options.text: I check the guide, explain the price and delivery note, and ask if they need clarification.
I give the listed price and mention that delivery details are in the guide.
I explain the listed price and offer to check the delivery note after the call.
I quote the listed price and say delivery is probably included in the package.

advanced.situation: A customer asks whether a product will work with an older device, but the compatibility guide lists only newer models. They need an answer before choosing a package.

options.text: I tell them the guide does not cover that model and offer a callback after checking.
I share the guide's newer model list and let the customer decide whether to proceed.
I explain the guide's limits, gather the device details, and check the approved compatibility source before advising.
I say it should work because the connection type looks similar to newer models.

basic.situation: At a market stall, a shopper asks how a kitchen tool works. You have a sample and a product leaflet to show them.

options.text: Let the shopper try the tool while you serve another customer.
Demonstrate the tool's main use, then invite the shopper to try it safely.
Hand over the leaflet and say the tool is popular with shoppers.
Show the tool's main use, then point out its listed price and care details.

advanced.situation: Your team is demonstrating a cleaning product at a busy fair, and shoppers ask about its use on different surfaces. You are guiding a new colleague.

options.text: Suggest the product works on every surface to keep the line moving.
Demonstrate a suitable listed use, then coach the colleague through surface questions.
Ask the colleague to read the leaflet and demonstrate its listed use.
Show one familiar use and let the colleague handle the remaining questions.

basic.situation: A shopper asks whether a household item is worth buying at your street stall. You know its listed features and price.

options.text: Ask what matters to the shopper, then connect a relevant feature to that need.
Say the item will solve their problem even though you have not asked about it.
Describe the listed features and ask if the shopper wants to buy.
Tell the shopper the item is a bargain and encourage a quick decision.

advanced.situation: A customer likes a product but doubts its value compared with a cheaper item. You are coaching a colleague through the objection at a busy stall.

options.text: Ask the colleague to respond by emphasizing the product's popular features.
Ask what the customer values, then compare relevant features and prices.
Repeat the product's features and remind the customer of its price.
Offer a discount from your own cash to secure the sale.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to compile names of potential customers from recent stall enquiries for the sales team's follow-up list.

options.text: Enter each interested customer's contact details and product enquiry in the list.
Add every visitor's name from the sign-in sheet to increase the list.
Check enquiry notes for interest and contact details before adding prospects.
Copy names from the enquiry notes and leave contact fields for later.

advanced.situation: Your stall team has a long prospect list, but few contacts respond. You are asked to refine the list and show a new colleague how to do it.

options.text: Remove contacts who have not answered the latest sales message.
Compare enquiry and response patterns, then teach the colleague to prioritize matching prospects.
Ask the colleague to call the oldest names first and note outcomes.
Sort prospects by recent interest and show the colleague how to record it.

basic.situation: You are setting up sample merchandise on a table before a neighbourhood event. The display instructions show where each item belongs.

options.text: Put the newest items at the front, even if labels face away.
Group similar samples together and let shoppers ask about their prices.
Arrange samples by the display guide and check that each price label is visible.
Place the samples in the order shown and keep the leaflet nearby.

advanced.situation: At a busy party, shoppers crowd around one side of your merchandise stand and cannot see several samples. You are guiding a colleague through a reset.

options.text: Stack the samples higher so shoppers at the back can see them.
Ask the colleague to spread the samples out and keep the price cards nearby.
Move the popular samples to the clear side and leave the rest behind.
Reposition samples for clear access and visibility, keeping prices beside each item.

basic.situation: You have several merchandise deliveries to make on a familiar neighbourhood route and must collect payment from each customer.

options.text: Leave all parcels at the first address to finish the route sooner.
Use the familiar route and ask customers to confirm their parcels later.
Follow the route list, confirm each delivery, and record payment received.
Deliver the listed items and collect the amounts shown on each invoice.

advanced.situation: Heavy rain has slowed your delivery route, and two customers have similar addresses. You need to complete the remaining deliveries and collect payment.

options.text: Call the next customer and ask which nearby delivery should come first.
Check both addresses against the delivery list, then reorder nearby stops.
Continue the printed route and verify each customer's name at arrival.
Leave the parcels with the first available neighbour near each address.

basic.situation: A customer orders two items at your stall and pays in cash. You need to enter the order into the sales system.

options.text: Enter both items and quantities, then match the payment to the order.
Write down the items and quantities, then keep the cash together.
Enter one item now and add the second when stock arrives.
Record the total paid and ask the customer to confirm the items later.

advanced.situation: Several orders are waiting, and your stall is running low on packaging supplies. You need to record orders and arrange replenishment within your role.

options.text: Ask a colleague to estimate the packaging needed for today's orders.
Review recorded orders and current supplies, then request the needed packaging quantity.
Enter the waiting orders and note that packaging supplies are running low.
Order a large packaging batch based on the busiest day last month.

basic.situation: Management asks you to update the shared leave procedure after a form changes. You have the new form and last month's instructions.

options.text: You ask a nearby clerk to check whether the wording reads clearly.
You compare the draft with current guidance and mark unclear steps.
You copy last year's wording and circulate it before the shift.
You map each change to its owner, approval, and staff instruction.

advanced.situation: Management asks you to draft a new procedure after two teams handle returned documents differently, delaying a monthly report.

options.text: You collect examples from both teams and draft steps for review.
You compare both workflows, define handoffs, and plan staff practice sessions.
You choose the faster team's method and send it to everyone.
You ask each team to follow its current method until management responds.

basic.situation: You check a payroll summary against a checklist and notice one overtime total differs from the supporting record.

options.text: You compare each line with payroll records and ask about unclear entries.
You check the totals against the checklist and flag the mismatch.
You trace the mismatch to its source and note the reason.
You change the figure to match last week's report before filing.

advanced.situation: A monthly operations report combines shipping and payroll figures, and a late correction changes the totals before management's review.

options.text: You reconcile each changed total to its source and record the revision trail.
You ask both departments to confirm their figures before sending the report.
You keep the earlier totals and mention the correction in your email.
You update the figures and compare them with the latest source records.

basic.situation: A customer asks whether a completed request can be amended after the daily cut-off, and the procedure is unclear to you.

options.text: You check the procedure, explain the confirmed options, and record the query.
You ask a colleague what usually happens and relay their answer.
You tell the customer the cut-off probably prevents any changes today.
You say amendments are accepted and enter the request for today's processing.

advanced.situation: Several staff report that the sign-off procedure creates duplicate work, and management asks for practical changes before the next busy period.

options.text: You summarize the complaints and suggest management review the sign-off steps.
You pass on the comments and let management decide what they mean.
You recommend removing the second sign-off to speed up processing.
You group staff examples, assess impacts, and propose a tested workflow change.

basic.situation: Two clerks are available for the morning, and your template lists calls, filing, and incoming orders to assign.

options.text: You split calls and filing, then ask a clerk to watch orders.
You give both clerks filing so the easiest work gets finished first.
You assign each task by workload and note the handover time.
You assign the calls and filing, then leave orders for whoever finishes.

advanced.situation: A staff absence delays order entry just as another unit requests urgent records, and both teams need the same clerk this afternoon.

options.text: You ask the other unit which request can wait before changing assignments.
You compare deadlines, arrange coverage, and confirm revised handoffs with both units.
You tell each unit the clerk is busy and keep the current schedule.
You send the clerk to the urgent request and postpone order entry.

basic.situation: With your supervisor's guidance, you observe a clerk's weekly filing and see several records placed in the wrong folders.

options.text: You record specific examples and review them with your supervisor.
You note the errors and remind the clerk to check folder labels.
You mark the clerk's work as satisfactory since the filing is nearly done.
You move the records yourself and finish the filing before lunch.

advanced.situation: A clerk has missed several deadlines despite informal reminders, and you need to discuss the pattern and recommend a fair next step.

options.text: You discuss the examples, hear the clerk's account, and document next steps.
You remove the clerk from deadline work to protect this month's output.
You review evidence with the clerk, identify barriers, and agree measurable support steps.
You recommend a warning based on the missed deadlines and recent reminders.

basic.situation: You assist with an interview for an office clerk and are asked to keep notes on each candidate's answers.

options.text: You write brief notes on the answers and flag anything unclear.
You note the candidate's strongest answer and share your impression afterward.
You record each answer against the agreed questions and criteria.
You fill gaps in a candidate's answers to keep the interview moving.

advanced.situation: New clerks repeat errors when handling escalated complaints, so you are asked to plan training before the next roster rotation.

options.text: You brief staff on the guide and invite questions before they handle complaints.
You route escalated complaints to experienced clerks while new staff practice routine cases.
You use real cases for practice, coach responses, and check learning during shifts.
You share the complaint guide and ask clerks to review it before their next shifts.

basic.situation: You answer a caller asking for a staff member, but the directory shows two people with similar names.

options.text: You ask which department they need and confirm the person's name.
You confirm the person's department, check the listing, then transfer the call.
You transfer the call to the first matching name in the directory.
You take a message and ask the caller to try again later.

advanced.situation: Several calls arrive during a service surge, and a junior operator asks how to handle a caller whose requested extension is busy.

options.text: You tell the junior operator to offer a callback after checking the queue.
You transfer the caller to a nearby extension that usually answers.
You put the caller on hold while you clear the other incoming calls.
You explain the wait, offer a message or callback, and coach the junior operator.

basic.situation: A test alarm sounds at the switchboard, and your checklist says to notify security using the listed extension.

options.text: You check the alarm panel and ask security whether they received it.
You wait for another operator to confirm the alarm is a test.
You follow the test checklist and notify security using its listed extension.
You announce an emergency over the system before checking the checklist.

advanced.situation: A genuine alarm coincides with a busy call queue, and new operators are unsure which announcement and call route to use.

options.text: You confirm the alarm route with the senior operator and brief the team.
You ask the senior operator to handle the alarm while you clear calls.
You follow the established alarm sequence and assign operators clear call roles.
You send all callers to security and let operators choose announcements.

basic.situation: A caller leaves a message about a delivery but speaks quickly, and you need to enter the details in the standard template.

options.text: You fill in a likely delivery time based on the usual schedule.
You ask a colleague to listen and help complete the message entry.
You enter the details you heard and mark the delivery time as uncertain.
You confirm unclear details with the caller and record them in the template.

advanced.situation: A colleague's long message notes often omit the caller's requested action, and you are asked to improve clarity across the shift.

options.text: You ask colleagues to keep messages brief while stating each caller's requested action.
You share a concise example and ask colleagues to include requested next steps.
You set a format for caller, request, details, next action, and coach examples.
You revise notes into a shared format and explain how recipients can act.

basic.situation: A visitor arrives for a meeting, but the host has not yet confirmed the appointment in the visitor system.

options.text: You ask the visitor to call the host while you prepare the log entry.
You ask the visitor to wait while you check the appointment system.
You check the appointment details and contact the listed host for confirmation.
You issue a badge and let the visitor wait near the meeting rooms.

advanced.situation: A new operator is covering reception during a busy hour, and several visitors arrive while their employee escorts are away from their desks.

options.text: You ask visitors to wait together while the operator finishes each log entry.
You assign the operator a check-in order, confirm escorts, and explain the queue plan.
You let visitors follow staff through the turnstile to avoid a queue.
You show the operator the badge process and ask each escort to collect visitors.

basic.situation: Your manager asks you to update the phone directory after two staff members change extensions, using the details in an email.

options.text: You update the entries and ask your manager to check the directory later.
You update both entries and compare them with the email before saving.
You change both extensions based on the names you recognize from the email.
You update the first entry and leave the other for the next shift.

advanced.situation: Incoming parcels are sometimes recorded under the wrong department, and you are asked to improve the delivery log process.

options.text: You add a department field and tell staff to complete it for each parcel.
You ask the delivery team to review unclear entries at the end of each day.
You define a source check for departments, add a log field, and review exceptions.
You sort parcels by familiar names and update the log after delivery.

basic.situation: You collect a small payment at the counter and your supervisor asks you to prepare the petty cash record for verification.

options.text: You record the payment amount and attach its receipt for supervisor verification.
You round the amount and note the adjustment in the petty cash record.
You record the payment and ask your supervisor to check the receipt before filing.
You count the cash, match the receipt, and record the exact payment amount.

advanced.situation: A petty cash review finds repeated differences between receipts and the log, and you are asked to recommend a safer handling routine.

options.text: You adjust the log to match the cash balance before the review.
You ask staff to return receipts together at the end of each week.
You recommend recording each payment with its receipt, then reconciling balances regularly.
You remind staff to keep receipts and ask the reviewer to check totals.

basic.situation: A caller asks for the accounts desk, and its line light is blinking. You have several buttons available and a short queue waiting.

options.text: Check the lit line, confirm the extension, then connect the caller.
Place the caller on hold while checking which line is available.
Read the requested extension back before completing the connection.
Press the first flashing key and transfer the caller to reception.

advanced.situation: During the lunch rush, several callers are waiting across two switchboard lines, and a clinic asks to reach its on-call contact.

options.text: Pause new transfers briefly and clear the oldest waiting call first.
Send waiting callers to any free extension to shorten the queue.
Group routine calls by destination while reserving lines for urgent connections.
Track each caller's destination and line status before routing the next call.

basic.situation: A caller asks for a local clinic but gives only the doctor's surname. You can consult the alphabetical and geographical directories.

options.text: Check the surname in the alphabetical directory and share its clinic number.
Look up nearby clinics and ask the caller to choose a matching name.
Ask which area the caller means, then check matching directory listings.
Search the surname and offer the first clinic listed in town.

advanced.situation: A colleague finds two listings for a surname, while the caller recalls a neighbourhood name but is unsure how it is spelled.

options.text: Search both directories and ask the caller which listing looks familiar.
Use the caller's first spelling and pass on the closest result.
Check alternate spellings against the neighbourhood listings, then explain the match.
Show your colleague how to search the name and neighbourhood together.

basic.situation: A caller asks for a listing but gives a surname that sounds like two different spellings over the phone.

options.text: Ask the caller to spell the surname again, then continue the search.
Offer both spellings and ask which one matches the caller's request.
Repeat the surname back and ask the caller to confirm it.
Choose the spelling you hear most often and search that entry.

advanced.situation: A new colleague struggles with callers who know a business name but not its spelling or area. You are asked to share a useful approach.

options.text: Tell the colleague to search the name and report the closest listing.
Share a short prompt for the area and spelling, then practise it together.
Suggest asking callers to repeat the name slowly before searching again.
Demonstrate asking for an area, then checking likely name variants with callers.

basic.situation: A caller says an elderly person beside them cannot dial and needs urgent medical help. Your workplace has a procedure for emergency calls.

options.text: Transfer the call to the emergency line as soon as the caller asks.
Ask the caller to dial the emergency number from another phone.
Ask for the location and connect the caller through the emergency procedure.
Keep asking what happened before deciding whether to connect the call.

advanced.situation: A distressed caller gives a landmark but not a full address, while a new colleague hesitates during an emergency call. Your procedure covers these calls.

options.text: Ask the colleague to get a full address before routing the call onward.
Prompt the colleague to follow the emergency procedure and pass on the landmark.
Ask for a nearby landmark and keep the caller connected during the handoff.
Tell the caller to calm down, then send the call onward.

basic.situation: A supervisor gives you a verified address change for one directory entry and asks you to update the record before the next shift.

options.text: Enter the verified address, then compare the saved entry with the request.
Mark the record for updating and leave the address unchanged for now.
Replace the old address with the new one from memory.
Update the address field and save the directory entry for review.

advanced.situation: Several updates arrived today, and one business appears under two similar names with different addresses. Your team is preparing the directory for release.

options.text: Merge the similar entries using the newer address and continue publishing.
Check the source on the duplicate pair and update the clearer records first.
Sort the updates by date and enter the newest details across both records.
Compare each update with its source and flag uncertain duplicate entries for review.

basic.situation: You are typing a short meeting note from a handwritten page. One figure is faint, and the note is due before the afternoon mail run.

options.text: Ask a colleague to read the faint figure while you begin typing.
Leave a space for the figure and finish typing the other notes.
Type the note and estimate the faint figure from nearby totals.
Type the clear sections and mark the faint figure for checking.

advanced.situation: Before a mailout, you are proofreading a long departmental letter and sorting replies. Two attachments have similar names and one page appears out of sequence.

options.text: Use the first matching attachment and send the letter on schedule.
Proofread the letter and ask a colleague which attachment name looks right.
Match attachments to the letter references, check page order, and sort replies.
Sort the replies by date, then attach the newest matching files.

basic.situation: Your queue shows several past-due accounts, and one customer’s address field is blank. You have the account system and a standard follow-up checklist.

options.text: Review prior contact details, then mark the account for address verification.
Select the oldest past-due account and begin its reminder process.
Confirm the overdue balance in the account system and flag the blank address.
Review the overdue list and set aside accounts with missing contact details.

advanced.situation: A delinquent customer’s mailed notices return, and the account file has an old address. Your role allows approved address tracing through available sources.

options.text: Search a credit bureau and use its newest address for another notice.
Compare the returned mail with public records and note possible matches.
Use the first directory match and update the account address.
Check approved tracing sources and record each address lead with its source.

basic.situation: A checklist shows a customer’s instalment is overdue, and the standard reminder is ready. The customer’s account notes mention a recent billing query.

options.text: Send the standard reminder and refer the billing query for follow-up.
Review the query note, then tailor the reminder to invite a response.
Pause the reminder and ask billing to review the query first.
Email the reminder to the listed address and record the contact.

advanced.situation: A customer disputes the overdue amount and asks what may happen if payment remains late. The account notes show a recent adjustment request still under review.

options.text: State that the full balance is due and outline every available consequence.
Explain the amount shown and describe possible follow-up in general terms.
Ask the customer to pay the undisputed amount while the query is reviewed.
Review the adjustment note, clarify the balance status, and explain approved next steps.

basic.situation: A customer says the full overdue amount is unaffordable this month but can pay part of it after payday. Your team has standard repayment options.

options.text: Suggest the smallest standard instalment and note the customer's response.
Ask the customer to call again after payday with a payment amount.
Repeat the full amount due and request payment by the usual date.
Offer the standard instalment choices and ask which fits the customer's budget.

advanced.situation: A customer has irregular income and missed two agreed payments after a family expense. They ask for a schedule that varies with their monthly earnings.

options.text: Map expected income dates against essential expenses, then propose an affordable schedule within policy.
Offer a fixed standard instalment and review it after three payments.
Ask for the customer's next payday and offer a smaller first payment.
Agree to whatever amount the customer can send and update the file.

basic.situation: A customer pays part of an overdue balance at the counter and gives you a receipt. The account screen is open for posting the payment.

options.text: Post the receipt amount to the account shown and save the payment entry.
Post the payment to the open account and print a receipt copy.
Keep the payment slip with today's records for later reconciliation.
Match receipt details to the account, post the amount, and check balance.

advanced.situation: A bank transfer appears in the daily payment file, but the reference is incomplete and two accounts show the same amount due.

options.text: Hold the posting and compare the transfer details with both account records.
Apply the transfer to the older account and note the reference.
Post it to the account with the closest name and flag the entry later.
Match available transfer identifiers, document the unresolved reference, and route it for verification.

basic.situation: A customer sends a letter with a new postal address and asks that future account correspondence go there. You are updating the account file.

options.text: Verify the account reference, update the address, then compare it with the letter.
File the letter and update the address field from its details.
File the customer's letter and update the postal address field using the details provided.
Replace the address with the customer's latest letter and file it.

advanced.situation: Your assigned portfolio has returned mail, deceased-customer notices, and older correspondence awaiting filing. The team has a retention procedure for account records.

options.text: Clear the oldest files first and remove records that appear inactive.
File the correspondence by date and set aside deceased-customer notices.
Check each source notice, record address changes, and apply retention steps before purging.
Sort records by account status and follow the retention steps for each group.

basic.situation: A customer has not replied to several reminders, and the account meets the checklist criteria for escalation. Your role is to prepare the case for review.

options.text: Organize the account history and reminder log so the reviewer can assess escalation.
Verify the checklist criteria, attach contact records, and submit the case for review.
Record the reminder dates and current balance in the escalation form.
Ask your supervisor whether legal review is appropriate before sending the case onward.

advanced.situation: A non-responsive account meets internal criteria for possible service disconnection, but a recent payment may not yet appear in the system. You prepare cases for approval.

options.text: Flag the possible payment and send the case notes to the credit team.
Review recent payment records, reconcile the balance, and submit the case for approval.
Pause the case and ask the customer whether they made a recent payment.
Prepare a disconnection request using the displayed overdue account balance.

basic.situation: A customer’s single service visit is complete, and you need to prepare an itemized bill using the service note and rate sheet.

options.text: Match the service note to the approved rate, then itemize the charge.
Use the service log to list the visit, agreed rate, and amount due.
Copy last month's bill and change the customer and date.
Ask a colleague to confirm the rate before entering the service line.

advanced.situation: Several teams use different invoice layouts, and new clerks keep missing service details. You are asked to standardize the template and coach them.

options.text: Show new clerks the current template and answer questions during their first week.
Send staff a blank template based on the team's most common invoice.
Create a shared template with service, rate, and amount fields; coach staff with sample bills.
Keep your own layout and share it with new clerks as a reference.

basic.situation: A supervisor gives you a cost receipt and ledger instructions for a routine office supply purchase.

options.text: Post the amount to the account used for last week's supplies.
Enter the amount under the account named in the instructions.
Check with a teammate about the account before posting the amount.
Compare the receipt total with the instruction, then post to the named account.

advanced.situation: A monthly review finds recurring gaps between ledger entries and invoice files. You are asked to audit recent entries and improve the team’s record-keeping standard.

options.text: Sample recent entries against invoices, log recurring gaps, and update the filing checklist.
Ask each clerk to confirm that their own invoice files are complete.
Review recent entries against invoices and tell the team what you find.
Remind the team to file invoices beside the matching ledger records.

basic.situation: A routine invoice is ready for checking, and your checklist covers the customer, service, rate, and total.

options.text: Match each listed field to its source and recalculate the total.
Ask a teammate to scan the invoice before you send it onward.
Check the customer name and total, then pass the invoice along.
Tick the listed fields against the invoice and flag any mismatch.

advanced.situation: Two clerks have missed different billing errors in recent reviews. You are asked to set a verification protocol and coach the team on complex checks.

options.text: Review missed cases with staff and add those errors to the checklist.
Ask clerks to use the checklist and raise cases they find uncertain.
Map billing fields to source records, set risk-based checks, and coach staff with error examples.
Compare each invoice with the prior one processed, then note any differences.

basic.situation: A billing machine is ready for a straightforward transaction, and a colleague has shown you the basic controls.

options.text: Reuse the last transaction, change its amount, and process this customer's bill.
Ask your colleague to operate the machine while you observe the steps.
Enter the listed amount, compare the display against the bill, and then print.
Follow the machine steps, compare the display with the bill, then print.

advanced.situation: The billing machine jams during a busy shift, then shows a recurring feed fault. You need to clear minor jams and report major equipment problems.

options.text: Use the guide to clear the jam, log recurrence, and contact repair staff.
Restart the machine and continue processing the waiting bills during the busy shift.
Pause billing and ask a teammate whether the feed needs repair service.
Clear the jam using the guide, then tell repair staff that the fault returned.

basic.situation: A ledger amount differs from its matching invoice by a small amount, and your supervisor is available to guide routine checks.

options.text: Compare the source invoice with the posting and trace the differing line.
Recheck the invoice and ledger, note the differing amount, and inform your supervisor.
Ask your supervisor which figure to use before checking the documents.
Adjust the ledger to match the invoice total shown on screen.

advanced.situation: Equipment logs show repeated interruptions during billing peaks, and staff report inconsistent totals after restarts. You are asked to analyze the pattern and advise management.

options.text: Restart the machine when totals vary and record the final amount displayed.
Review equipment logs, summarize interruption patterns, and advise management about likely recurring causes.
Ask staff to report each interruption before their shift ends daily.
