I would take the smaller bag first and bring the full bag afterward.
I would carry both bags together to clear the station in one trip.

advanced.situation: Two stations need mail moved before dispatch, and the usual route crosses a crowded aisle while several bags are ready.

options.text: I would group bags by destination and move them along the clear aisle in balanced loads.
I would move the closest bags first and ask another clerk to watch the aisle.
I would wait for the aisle to clear before moving each bag separately.
I would stack the bags high and take the shortest path through the aisle.

basic.situation: A customer asks whether a small parcel can go in a post office box, and your counter reference sheet lists the service details.

options.text: I would tell the customer to ask another clerk about the box service.
I would describe the general box service and point to the printed details.
I would check the reference sheet and explain the listed parcel requirements.
I would say parcels fit if there is space in the box.

advanced.situation: A customer presents an older rate notice and questions a charge, while the team has received a newer procedure circular for counter use.

options.text: I would compare the circular with the current counter reference and explain the applicable procedure.
I would ask the customer to return after the team has discussed the circular.
I would explain the newer circular and offer the customer a copy to review.
I would follow the older notice because the customer brought it to the counter.

basic.situation: Your mentor gives you mixed letters for a short street. You need to arrange them in delivery order before bundling them.

options.text: I would sort by postcode first and check the street list afterward.
I would use the route list to order the letters, then bundle them.
I would match each address to the stop order, then bundle that sequence.
I would stack letters by street name and bundle the tray for speed.

advanced.situation: A large tray arrives late, and two streets have similar names. You need to sequence the mail quickly for a relay box cutoff.

options.text: I would sequence the larger street first and leave the smaller pile for later.
I would bundle by postcode and send the bundles to the relay box.
I would check the route sequence, separate the similar street names, then bundle by relay stop.
I would group the mail by street and ask a colleague to sequence each pile.

basic.situation: Your mentor asks you to deliver a small batch to nearby homes while they watch. One house number is partly obscured.

options.text: I would compare the number with the route sequence before placing the letter.
I would complete clear addresses and return the uncertain letter to my mentor.
I would leave it at the nearest house with a similar visible number.
I would follow the route sheet and verify the partly hidden house number.

advanced.situation: Heavy rain slows your route, and a business collection point closes soon. You need to finish deliveries and meet the return schedule.

options.text: I would keep the planned route and update the office about the delay.
I would prioritise the closing collection stop, then adjust nearby deliveries and report timing.
I would skip the business stop and complete the remaining homes first.
I would hurry through the remaining street and check the collection point afterward.

basic.situation: You and a colleague collect letters from public boxes. One item has a return address but appears to be addressed elsewhere.

options.text: I would send it back to the sender using the return address.
I would place it with the collected mail and ask my colleague at the office.
I would keep it separate, note the address issue, and bring it back for checking.
I would put it back in the box for the next collection round.

advanced.situation: At the office, collected mail includes several items marked for return, but one has an incomplete sender address and another has a forwarding label.

options.text: I would use the sender details available and place both items in separate return bundles.
I would verify each endorsement, keep the forwarding item apart, and flag the incomplete sender address.
I would put both items in the return sack for the next dispatch.
I would separate both items and ask the dispatch clerk how they are handled.

basic.situation: A resident accepts a registered letter while your supervisor observes. You need to obtain the receipt and collect the listed charge.

options.text: I would confirm the charge, obtain a signature, and record payment before handing over.
I would ask the resident to sign, record the payment, and check the receipt before handover.
I would hand over the letter and collect the charge after finishing the street.
I would take the signature and give the letter to keep the queue moving.

advanced.situation: At the end of a route, your cash-on-delivery receipts do not match the cash collected. You need to turn in both securely.

options.text: I would check the largest payments first and submit the rest for counting.
I would place the cash and receipts together in the office return pouch.
I would total each payment against its receipt and submit the full collection at handover.
I would match receipts to cash, note any difference, and report it at handover.

basic.situation: A customer asks for a change-of-address card while you are delivering nearby. You have forms in your satchel and limited time.

options.text: I would ask which change they need, provide the form, and explain its return.
I would write down the new address on a spare delivery slip for later.
I would give the customer a card and point out where to write the new address.
I would hand over the card and suggest they ask at the counter if unsure.

advanced.situation: A customer says held mail was not available on their return, while another resident asks where to collect an undelivered parcel. You have limited records.

options.text: I would ask both customers to return tomorrow when staff can review their needs.
I would direct the parcel customer to the notice location and record the complaint.
I would explain the collection notice and ask the office to check the hold request.
I would check notice details, confirm the hold request, and explain the next steps.

basic.situation: You scan a parcel at a business entrance, but the scanner display does not show a clear confirmation. Your supervisor is nearby.

options.text: I would check the label, retry the scan, and verify the delivery entry.
I would leave the scan pending and enter the delivery after the route.
I would scan the label again and ask my nearby supervisor to verify the record.
I would mark the parcel delivered on my paper list and continue the route.

advanced.situation: Several scans on your route show delayed confirmation, and a street letter box appears damaged. You need to report the unusual circumstances accurately.

options.text: I would report that the scanner and letter box both need attention.
I would note affected scan times and items, describe the box, and report both issues.
I would record the delayed scans and mention the damaged box in my route notes.
I would finish the route and report only the damaged box at the depot.

basic.situation: You are sorting a small hand-delivered batch using the posted routing scheme. Two trays have similar destination labels.

options.text: I would follow the routing chart and place each item in its labeled tray.
I would match each destination code to the chart before placing items in trays.
I would sort by the first few address letters and compare trays later.
I would put both groups in the tray with the larger mail volume.

advanced.situation: Odd-sized items arrive near dispatch, and another worker has left several unsorted pieces. Some appear to need special handling.

options.text: I would check the unsorted pieces against routing guidance, segregate exceptions, then label each destination.
I would separate the odd-sized pieces and ask a colleague to identify special handling.
I would label the odd items by destination and leave uncertain pieces for the next shift.
I would route all remaining pieces with the standard mail to meet dispatch.

basic.situation: A parcel has a smudged street name and unclear postage marking. You are checking the address before it enters the next processing batch.

options.text: I would check the address directory and ask a senior sorter about postage.
I would send it to the most likely area based on the postcode.
I would hold it aside until the next batch gives a clearer clue.
I would verify the full address in the directory and flag unclear postage for review.

advanced.situation: A redirected letter has an old address, a handwritten forwarding note, and a faint stamp mark. Dispatch is approaching while you review it.

options.text: I would send it using the handwritten address and cancel the stamp by hand.
I would verify the redirect in the directory, assess the address and postage, and separate unresolved items.
I would search the directory and ask the lead to confirm the forwarding note.
I would cancel the stamp and place the letter in the usual redirect tray.

basic.situation: You are operating a scanning machine with a supervisor nearby. A batch stops after one address is not read clearly.

options.text: I would pause the batch and ask my supervisor to check the unread item.
I would check the displayed error, realign the item, and confirm the next scan.
I would restart the machine and feed the whole batch through again.
I would bypass the unread item and let the rest of the batch continue.

advanced.situation: A sorting machine jams twice at the same point during a busy run. Staff are waiting, and you are trained to clear routine jams.

options.text: I would pull trapped mail free and restart the machine to save time.
I would clear it by procedure and flag the repeat point to operators.
I would stop the run and ask maintenance to inspect the machine.
I would follow jam procedure, log the location, and brief operators on a safe check.

basic.situation: A mail container needs moving to a loading area. You are learning the powered equipment while a trained colleague supervises.

options.text: I would confirm load stability, follow the marked route, and move at walking pace.
I would rush the container through before the loading bay fills.
I would check the route and move the container with my supervisor nearby.
I would ask a trained colleague to guide me while I move it.

advanced.situation: A truck is due soon, and parcels from a torn container need rewrapping before loading. A new worker offers to help lift the mail.

options.text: I would put the torn parcels on top and load everything before dispatch.
I would secure torn parcels, stage stable containers in order, and coach safe handling.
I would have the new worker rewrap parcels while I load the truck.
I would rewrap the parcels and ask the new worker to load the sound containers.

basic.situation: You open a container of incoming mail with a destination label attached. A colleague helps you find the correct pigeonholes.

options.text: I would match the container label to the pigeonhole list before distributing the mail.
I would place the mail in the fullest pigeonholes to clear the container.
I would read the label and place the mail in the matching pigeonholes.
I would set the mail beside the pigeonholes for the next worker to place.

advanced.situation: Several incoming containers arrive close together, and their destination labels look alike. You need to keep distribution on schedule and help a new worker label them.

options.text: I would label each container after checking its destination, then ask the new worker to sort.
I would verify destinations, label by dispatch order, and show the new worker each check.
I would separate similar labels and assign the easier containers to the new worker.
I would reuse yesterday's labels to finish the containers before the dispatch deadline.

basic.situation: A new worker is learning to sort a small batch using the posted routing scheme. Your supervisor asks you to demonstrate the basic steps.

options.text: I would sort the batch myself so the new worker can watch the pace.
I would show one example and let the new worker try the next items.
I would explain the routing chart, model one item, then check their next choice.
I would give the new worker the chart and answer questions as they arise.

advanced.situation: A senior coworker asks how to handle recurring odd-sized items, while a new worker is also learning the process. You have a shift guide to update.

options.text: I would explain the usual method to both workers and update the guide later.
I would show the new worker the standard process and refer the senior coworker to the supervisor.
I would ask the senior coworker to train the new worker while I finish sorting.
I would document the exception steps with an example, then walk both workers through them.

basic.situation: A shift finishes a batch, and the operator gives you its output and raw-material figures for the daily production log.

options.text: Match the batch sheet to the operator's figures, then enter and file them.
Copy yesterday's totals, then file the new batch sheet for later review.
Ask the operator to confirm the figures before entering them in the log.
Enter the operator's figures in the production log and file the batch sheet.

advanced.situation: A design change alters a production sequence, and managers need revised instructions and cost projections before the next shift begins.

options.text: Keep the existing instructions and ask the next shift to clarify the changes.
Document the new sequence, affected materials, and revised cost assumptions for managers.
Update the sequence notes and send the earlier cost projection to managers.
Revise the sequence instructions and flag that the cost projection needs review.

basic.situation: Your department has released tomorrow's work orders, and each production team needs its copy before the shift ends.

options.text: Leave the work orders in the shared tray for teams to collect.
Send each team its work orders through the usual department channel.
Send the full order bundle to the busiest team to pass around.
Check the team list, then send each lead the relevant work orders.

advanced.situation: A design change removes a part from tomorrow's run, while a supplier delay leaves another part short for two departments.

options.text: Keep the schedule and tell both departments to work around the shortages.
Check usable stock and delivery timing, then coordinate a feasible revised schedule.
Ask both team leads which orders they can move before changing the schedule.
Revise quantities for the design change and send the schedule to both teams.

basic.situation: A delivery due this morning has not arrived, and the line lead asks whether the supplier has confirmed its timing.

options.text: Tell the line lead the delivery should arrive around its usual time.
Check the order reference with the supplier, then share its confirmed timing.
Send the line lead the supplier's contact details to check directly.
Call the supplier to confirm dispatch and the expected arrival time.

advanced.situation: Sales forecasts rise for two product lines, but a key component has a long lead time and current orders already use much of the stock.

options.text: Raise both production commitments to match the latest forecast figures.
Compare forecast demand with stock and incoming orders before proposing timetables.
Use the forecast to draft timetables and flag the component constraint.
Keep current timetables until sales confirms the revised demand figures.

basic.situation: A new work order lists tomorrow's batch, and you need to check whether the planned crew and material quantities are available.

options.text: Compare the work order with the staffing table and material records.
Review the work order and note its listed crew and material needs.
Ask the team lead whether the listed resources seem sufficient.
Use the previous batch's staffing and material figures for this order.

advanced.situation: During a floor check, you see a batch label that differs from the specification attached to the current work order.

options.text: Ask the operator to replace the label with one matching the work order.
Pause the affected check, compare the documents, and alert the line lead.
Compare the label with the specification and record the discrepancy for review.
Mark the batch complete because its quantity matches the work order.

basic.situation: Your manager needs a midday status update showing today's production rate, material use, and remaining inventory.

options.text: Gather today's figures and send a short status update to your manager.
Send the production rate now and add inventory figures after the shift.
Estimate the remaining stock from the last inventory report and send it.
Reconcile the shift log with stock records before compiling the status update.

advanced.situation: A rush order uses overtime and extra material, and the manager asks for its estimated manufacturing cost before approving a quote.

options.text: Separate labor and material quantities, then calculate each using current schedules.
Apply the standard unit cost and send the estimate before the deadline.
Ask the manager to provide a target cost before preparing the figures.
Add overtime and extra material to the standard cost estimate.

basic.situation: The next shift's work orders call for a material that is running low in the supply area.

options.text: Requisition the listed quantity and update the inventory record afterward.
Use the remaining material first and defer the replenishment request.
Check usable stock against the work orders, then requisition the gap.
Record the low balance and wait for the next routine count.

advanced.situation: Several slow-moving supplies occupy space, while a frequently used item has arrived late twice and risks delaying next week's production.

options.text: Reduce the slow-moving supplies and raise the frequently used item's reorder level.
Compare usage, lead times, and scheduled demand before adjusting reorder quantities.
Keep current stock levels and ask the supplier to improve delivery timing.
Order extra of every item to protect next week's production schedule.

basic.situation: A pallet arrives with an invoice and manifest, and you are asked to check its contents before it goes into stock.

options.text: Count the cartons and note the total on the receiving sheet.
Match item codes and quantities to the manifest, then record the receipt.
Use the invoice total to enter the delivery before checking the pallet.
Compare the pallet count with the manifest and mark the delivery received.

advanced.situation: A new clerk finds fewer units than the manifest lists, while the invoice describes mixed cartons and one carton has a damaged seal.

options.text: Note the manifest shortage and damaged seal on the receiving record.
Record the shortage and damaged seal, then ask the clerk to finish receiving.
Enter the manifest quantities so the delivery can clear the receiving queue.
Count each carton against the manifest, isolate the damaged one, and record variances.

basic.situation: A customer order is ready to ship, and you have a price list with charges by parcel weight and service type.

options.text: Use the listed service and weight band to calculate the parcel charge.
Charge the usual amount for a parcel of this size and service.
Ask the carrier counter to confirm the likely charge for this parcel.
Check the recorded weight and service against the price list before totaling.

advanced.situation: Several weekly shipments use different routes and parcel sizes, and your lead asks you to summarize patterns for a rate review.

options.text: Total this week's shipping charges and send the amount to your lead.
Compare shipment methods, routes, and charges to identify recurring cost patterns.
Suggest one flat rate based on the cheapest recent shipment.
Summarize charges by route and parcel size for the rate review.

basic.situation: A batch of small parts needs cartons sealed and labeled before the afternoon carrier collection.

options.text: Seal each carton and apply the labels from the order sheet.
Match each label to its order, then seal and stage the cartons.
Seal the cartons now and ask a colleague to label them later.
Use a nearby carton label and seal the batch for collection.

advanced.situation: A rush batch has varied carton sizes, and new staff are sealing boxes that sometimes reopen during handling.

options.text: Ask experienced staff to seal the cartons while new staff observe.
Show the team a consistent tape pattern and check a sample carton.
Use extra tape on every carton so the batch is ready quickly.
Test suitable seals by carton size, then demonstrate the method to staff.

basic.situation: A trolley of incoming supplies must reach the correct department, but two nearby bays have similar signs.

options.text: Take the trolley to the bay that usually receives these supplies.
Check the destination on the paperwork, then deliver the trolley there.
Ask a nearby worker which bay should receive the supplies.
Leave the trolley beside the closest bay for staff to sort later.

advanced.situation: Repeated trolley trips cross a busy aisle, and a revised order means two departments need supplies before the next shift.

options.text: Group the supplies by destination and sequence deliveries around aisle traffic.
Group supplies for each department before routing the trolleys.
Send each trolley by the shortest route and tell departments to collect.
Route all supplies in one trip to clear the staging area quickly.

basic.situation: A supervisor gives you a customer order and asks you to prepare its shipping order for the carrier.

options.text: Copy the address and parcel details onto the shipping order form.
Ask the supervisor which fields need completion on the form.
Reuse a recent shipping order and change the customer name.
Check the order details, then complete the shipping order form.

advanced.situation: Several clerks prepare shipping orders differently, and recent handoffs have missed delivery instructions attached to customer orders.

options.text: Keep the existing forms and ask clerks to read each order more closely.
Draft a shared template with fields for destination, contents, and delivery notes.
Copy the most recent shipping order for each new customer shipment.
Create a template tied to the order fields and walk clerks through its use.

basic.situation: A carrier delivery arrives with a visible dent in one carton, and the receiving sheet has space for shipment notes.

options.text: Record the damage, identify the carton, and notify the receiving lead.
Mark the shipment received in full so the carrier can depart promptly.
Record the carton damage and shipment details on the receiving sheet.
Ask the carrier to note the dent on its delivery paperwork.

advanced.situation: A carrier reports a missed delivery window, while the department says the shipment is needed before its next production run.

options.text: Tell the department to use its current stock until the carrier arrives.
Ask the carrier for a new arrival estimate and relay it to the department.
Change the delivery record to the planned window so the schedule stays aligned.
Confirm the revised window with the carrier and coordinate a suitable handoff with the department.

basic.situation: You find several fittings with chipped edges while checking a delivery against the damage checklist. The receiving team is waiting to unload the next pallet.

options.text: Ask a colleague to inspect the carton while you continue receiving other items.
Set aside the carton and record the count as acceptable to keep unloading moving.
Compare each fitting with the checklist, then note visible damage for the receiving log.
Check each fitting against the checklist, separate damaged pieces, and document the affected quantity.

advanced.situation: A new batch has borderline surface marks, and different shifts classify them differently. You are asked to update the inspection guide before a large shipment is checked.

options.text: Photograph the marks and circulate them so inspectors can compare their decisions.
Use supplier specifications to define examples, then test the guide with inspectors on sample parts.
Keep the existing guide and tell each shift to use its own judgment on marks.
Ask experienced inspectors to share their usual judgments and add them to the guide.

basic.situation: You weigh a sack of resin on the receiving scale, but the display changes as the sack settles. The delivery driver is waiting for the recorded weight.

options.text: Check the scale display again and note the later weight for receiving records.
Ask a nearby colleague to read the scale while you prepare the next sack.
Record the first displayed weight and move the sack to the storage area.
Wait for the display to settle, then enter the stable reading in the log.

advanced.situation: Two scales show different weights for the same sealed batch, and dispatch needs the figures soon. You have a reference weight and access to the calibration check.

options.text: Check both scales with the reference, identify the reliable reading, and document the discrepancy.
Average both readings and enter the result so dispatch can proceed on time.
Use the scale that matches the reference and report the other reading for review.
Repeat the batch measurement on the scale used for earlier deliveries and note it.

basic.situation: You prepare identification labels for a mixed carton of parts. One label has smudged text, and the packing team is ready to seal the carton.

options.text: Replace the smudged label, then match each readable label to its part before packing.
Check the other labels against the parts and flag the smudged one for replacement.
Ask a colleague to read the label while you attach the others to parts.
Attach the smudged label and let the packing team check it during sealing.

advanced.situation: Several shifts apply batch labels in different places, slowing checks and causing occasional mix-ups. Your manager asks you to suggest a consistent method and brief the team.

options.text: Document the team's current label placement and share a short guide.
Invite the fastest shift to show its labeling method at a team briefing.
Keep each shift's familiar label placement to maintain steady output.
Compare missed label locations, agree placement with packers, then trial it across shifts.

basic.situation: You are asked to collect a sample from a sealed batch for laboratory testing. The sample container and collection instructions are ready at the workbench.

options.text: Follow the collection instructions, seal the sample container, and label it for the laboratory.
Ask a coworker to watch while you collect the sample using the instructions.
Take a small amount from the open carton and leave it near the workbench.
Collect the sample as instructed and leave the container for labeling later.

advanced.situation: Lab results vary between shifts, and you find that sampling points differ across the same production run. You are asked to draft a method for staff to follow.

options.text: Write down the sampling points used by the most experienced shift and brief others.
Have one shift collect duplicate samples while another shift reviews the handling steps.
Specify sampling points and handling steps, then compare staff samples for consistency before rollout.
Let each shift choose a convenient sampling point to keep production moving.

basic.situation: You enter received quantities and weights into the shipping record. One delivery note has a faint handwritten weight that is hard to read.

options.text: Enter the quantity and mark the faint weight for later checking by the team.
Enter the nearest readable figure so the shipping record can be completed.
Leave the weight field blank and enter the clear quantity for now.
Check the note with the receiving clerk, then enter the confirmed weight and quantity.

advanced.situation: A monthly review finds repeated differences between receiving notes and production records. You are asked to improve the recording process before the next stock count.

options.text: Copy the receiving figures into production records to keep both lists aligned.
Ask staff to review mismatched records together at the next stock count.
Add a reminder to verify weights and quantities before submitting each record.
Trace sample discrepancies to their entry points, then revise fields and instructions around those causes.

basic.situation: After weighing several deliveries, loose packaging and spilled grain remain near the scale house. The next lorry is approaching the weighing area.

options.text: Ask the driver to wait while you finish weighing the remaining delivery.
Sweep the grain away and ask a coworker to move the packaging later.
Clear the packaging, clean the spill, and keep the scale approach open for the lorry.
Move the loose packaging beside the scale and let the next shift handle it.

advanced.situation: Packaging builds up around the scale house during busy receiving periods, and staff disagree about who clears it. You are asked to improve daily upkeep.

options.text: Set clear cleanup times and assigned areas, then review the routine with each shift.
Move collection bins closer to the scale house and mention them at handover.
Add a cleanup reminder to the shift board and ask staff to follow it.
Ask the busiest shift to clear packaging whenever its workload allows.

basic.situation: You take minutes at a committee meeting with guidance from a senior colleague. Members agree to revise a report, but no owner is named before the agenda moves on.

options.text: Record the decision; ask the chair to name an owner before moving on.
Ask the senior colleague afterward whether anyone volunteered to revise the report.
Note the revision decision and mark its owner pending confirmation.
Record that members agreed to revise the report, then continue the minutes.

advanced.situation: You compile data for a board paper comparing branch performance. Two source reports use different periods, and the presentation deadline is this afternoon.

options.text: Describe both reporting periods and present the figures in separate table columns.
Choose the figures that show the clearest branch ranking for the presentation.
Align the reporting periods, document the sources, and flag any remaining limits in the paper.
Use the latest figures from both reports and explain the difference in a footnote.

basic.situation: A caller asks to speak with an executive, but gives a common name and no department. The phone script says to take a message when the recipient is unclear.

options.text: Ask the caller's name, purpose, callback number, then take a message per script.
Transfer the call to the executive's office to identify the caller.
Ask which department they need, then check the directory before transferring.
Take their callback number and ask a colleague which executive has that name.

advanced.situation: Several executives are in meetings when a visitor arrives for an unscheduled discussion about a confidential proposal. The reception desk has no written access guidance.

options.text: Ask the visitor to leave a card and offer to arrange a later appointment.
Confirm the visitor's identity and purpose, then contact the relevant executive's office for access guidance.
Ask the visitor to wait in the lobby while you check the executives' calendars.
Send the visitor to the nearest meeting room so the proposal can be discussed privately.

basic.situation: A department asks you for the latest approved travel policy. You find two similarly named files in the shared records system, each with a different date.

options.text: Check the approval details and version history, then send the current policy through the records system.
Check the filing index and ask the records contact which version is approved.
Send the newer file because its date suggests it is the latest version.
Ask the department which file title they used last time before retrieving one.

advanced.situation: Staff across departments struggle to retrieve routine correspondence, and duplicate folders have appeared. You are asked to improve the shared filing approach within your support role.

options.text: Add an index spreadsheet that lists current folder names and document dates.
Ask each department to list the files it needs most often before changing folders.
Map retrieval needs, agree naming rules with users, and trial indexed folders.
Create a new folder for each department and move the existing files into it.

basic.situation: You sort incoming emails using your manager's checklist. One message concerns a delivery delay, while another requests an executive's review by noon.

options.text: Ask a coworker which message seems more urgent before sending either one.
Forward both messages together to the executive assistant for later sorting.
Send the delivery email to operations and the review request to the executive's office.
Flag the noon deadline and route both messages to their listed recipients.

advanced.situation: A new team member will help sort executive correspondence, and urgent submissions have been reaching different inboxes. You are asked to draft distribution guidance.

options.text: List the usual recipients beside each correspondence category and share the guide.
Set urgency cues and recipient routes, then review samples with staff together.
Tell the new team member to forward uncertain submissions to the executive inbox.
Ask each department to tell the new team member where its mail belongs.

basic.situation: You receive a request to add a meeting to an executive's calendar. The proposed time overlaps a blocked appointment, and the requester asks you to keep the slot.

options.text: Ask the requester to suggest another time and hold off on changing the calendar.
Add the meeting over the blocked slot so the requester can plan around it.
Move the blocked appointment to another open time and add the requested meeting.
Check the calendar with the executive's office, then offer an open time.

advanced.situation: A board meeting needs directors, department heads, and catering arranged, but two key attendees have not confirmed. The agenda deadline is close.

options.text: Send the existing agenda and book catering using the usual board headcount.
Check attendance constraints, align agenda timing with key decisions, and confirm catering estimates.
Contact the unconfirmed attendees and ask the chair whether the agenda can wait.
Reserve a smaller catering order and add a note about the pending confirmations.

basic.situation: You are reconciling a small office supply purchase with the receipt. The amount on the bookkeeping entry differs from the receipt by a few ringgit.

options.text: Adjust the entry to match the usual supply cost without checking the receipt.
Mark the difference for the supervising colleague to review during reconciliation.
Compare receipt and entry, update the amount, and file the receipt.
Ask the supplier to confirm the charge before updating the bookkeeping entry.

advanced.situation: Supply requests are rising across departments, and several items sit unused in storage. You are asked to prepare budget input and suggest a practical ordering approach.

options.text: Ask departments to reduce requests until storage levels return to normal.
Approve the usual order quantities so departments receive supplies on schedule.
Collect each department's requests, compare totals with stock, and add figures to budget draft.
Review stock and usage, group recurring needs, and share a forecast with assumptions.

basic.situation: You are proofreading a summons from a supervisor’s draft and notice that one date differs from the case notes.

options.text: I check each field against source notes and mark unclear text.
I compare the summons with approved instructions and flag uncertain details.
I verify the date with case notes and ask the supervisor about any discrepancy.
I reuse last week's summons, changing names and dates before printing.

advanced.situation: A complex filing has conflicting names across exhibits, and junior staff are waiting for your proofreading checklist before printing.

options.text: I create a checklist linking names, exhibits, and source records for review.
I proofread the filing and tell juniors to check names carefully.
I replace each conflicting name with the most frequent version.
I use a prior filing checklist and update its case names.

basic.situation: You are photocopying client correspondence for a case file and notice that one page is missing from the stack.

options.text: I photocopy the stack again and file the newest set.
I compare the copy count with the original pages before filing.
I file the available pages and label the set complete.
I photocopy each page and check the sequence against the original.

advanced.situation: Several active matters share similar client names, and you are updating the filing guide after staff place documents in the wrong case files.

options.text: I build a filing guide using matter numbers and verified client details.
I add clearer client names to the existing file labels.
I organize files by matter number and show staff the layout.
I move misfiled documents into the folder with the closest name.

basic.situation: An attorney asks you to request a client’s employment history, and your checklist shows the dates and former employers needed.

options.text: I ask the client for a full employment file by email.
I request the employers and dates listed on the checklist.
I send the request to the employer contact from an old matter.
I request the listed dates and employers using the approved client channel.

advanced.situation: Records for a client’s claim are arriving from several sources, with duplicate dates and sensitive medical details mixed into employment documents.

options.text: I separate sources, log received items, and route sensitive records securely.
I sort documents by source and note dates before sharing them.
I forward the full bundle to the team for faster review.
I combine the records into one file and remove duplicates later.

basic.situation: A client’s application form asks for an address and contact number, but the client’s notes show two different addresses.

options.text: I fill the confirmed contact number and mark the address for checking.
I confirm the current address with the client before completing the form.
I choose the address closest to the client’s listed workplace.
I use the address appearing on the latest note.

advanced.situation: Staff are completing a lengthy client application, and recurring omissions appear in sections that depend on information from different documents.

options.text: I map each field to its source and add checks for dependent sections.
I enlarge the existing template and highlight fields needing attention.
I prefill common answers from the last client application template.
I group related fields and share a checklist with the staff.

basic.situation: You are preparing an invoice from the approved template and notice that a listed expense lacks a receipt in the file.

options.text: I match each expense to its support and flag the missing receipt.
I include the expense because it appears in the case notes.
I copy the prior invoice and update the client and total.
I prepare the supported items and mark the expense for review.

advanced.situation: A large case invoice includes multiple expenses and time entries, and the client has queried a charge that appears twice.

options.text: I remove the queried charge and resend the revised invoice.
I reconcile entries against supporting records and isolate the duplicate charge.
I compare the queried entry with the time and expense records.
I leave both charges and explain that each has a separate entry.

basic.situation: A caller asks to speak with an attorney about a hearing appointment, and the schedule shows two possible times.

options.text: I take the caller’s number and ask the attorney to return the call.
I confirm the caller’s details and check the calendar before booking.
I offer the earlier time and note the caller’s name.
I tell the caller the later time is confirmed from memory.

advanced.situation: Several calls and delivery requests arrive while an attorney is in court, including a witness asking to change an appointment time.

options.text: I confirm a new witness time based on the usual court schedule.
I answer calls in arrival order and write down brief messages.
I log each request, identify its matter, and route it by urgency.
I route the witness request and send other callers to voicemail.

basic.situation: You are filing a patient’s referral letter and notice that the file label does not match the identification details on the letter.

options.text: I change the folder label to match the referral letter.
I file the letter under the name shown on the folder.
I verify the patient identifiers against the record before filing the letter.
I set the letter aside and ask the records clerk to check it.

advanced.situation: A records audit finds duplicate folders and inconsistent labels, and you are asked to standardize filing across several clinic teams.

options.text: I merge folders with matching names to reduce the backlog.
I define identifier checks, duplicate handling, and label fields for each team.
I provide a standard label and ask teams to use it consistently.
I rename folders using the patient names already on file.

basic.situation: You are typing a clinic letter in word processing software and notice that the saved copy has an earlier draft’s date.

options.text: I copy the date from the previous letter in the folder.
I replace the date with today’s date and print the letter.
I check the date with the person who requested the letter.
I compare the saved letter with approved notes and update its date.

advanced.situation: Clinic reports are generated from spreadsheets and word processing templates, but staff keep overwriting formulas and producing inconsistent totals.

options.text: I create a shared template and show staff where totals appear.
I protect formula cells and align the report template with verified inputs.
I add a note reminding staff to preserve the formulas.
I enter the latest totals directly into each report template.

basic.situation: You are completing an insurance claim form and notice that the patient’s policy number is missing from the file.

options.text: I copy a policy number from the patient’s previous claim form.
I leave the number blank and send the form for processing.
I check the policy document and confirm the number before completing the form.
I contact the patient to confirm the policy number for the form.

advanced.situation: Several claims have been rejected for different missing details, and you are helping staff identify patterns before resubmission.

options.text: I copy details from accepted claims into the rejected forms.
I review the rejection notes and revise each form with staff.
I group rejection reasons, verify each claim against its records, and update guidance.
I resubmit each claim after adding the most commonly missing field.

basic.situation: A patient calls to book a diagnostic appointment, but the referral note lists a test without a preferred date.

options.text: I check the referral details and offer an available slot that fits them.
I book the usual test time from memory and confirm by phone.
I ask the patient which days work, note their preference, and check the referral details.
I book the first open slot and tell the patient the time.

advanced.situation: The clinic has limited consultation slots, and intake forms often arrive incomplete, delaying bookings for patients needing follow-up consultations.

options.text: I review intake forms, flag missing details, and confirm needs before scheduling patients.
I reuse the previous appointment length for each follow-up booking when needed.
I reserve open slots first, then request any missing details from patients afterward.
I check required intake details before matching follow-ups to suitable open slots.

basic.situation: A caller asks for a nurse about a test result, and you are unsure which staff member handles that clinic session.

options.text: I take a message, check today’s rota, and confirm session contact before forwarding it.
I take the caller’s details and route the message to the session contact.
I transfer the caller to the nurse listed on last week’s rota.
I tell the caller the result is probably ready for collection.

advanced.situation: Calls, visitors, and incoming laboratory documents arrive together, and staff need a reliable way to route urgent messages to the right team.

options.text: I forward every laboratory document to the clinic manager’s inbox.
I ask staff to check the shared inbox during quieter periods.
I set routing categories by message type, urgency, and responsible clinic staff.
I sort messages by clinic and tell staff to review them promptly.

basic.situation: You are ordering clinic supplies and notice that the stock sheet and cupboard count show different quantities of gloves.

options.text: I change the stock sheet to match the cupboard estimate.
I order the usual quantity and adjust the sheet later.
I check recent supply use and ask a colleague about the difference.
I recount the gloves and update the stock sheet before ordering.

advanced.situation: The clinic’s supply records are inconsistent, and monthly bills do not always match recorded orders as you prepare financial summaries.

options.text: I use the previous month’s totals to complete this month’s summary.
I reconcile orders, received stock, and bills before updating the financial records.
I compare bills with order records and list unmatched entries for review.
I enter bill totals and flag differences when the next order arrives.

basic.situation: You receive a completed staff form and must enter its details into the shared database before the afternoon filing run.

options.text: Enter the details and flag unclear fields for a later check.
Copy the previous record and change its date to clear the queue.
Enter the form details and save the record in the shared database.
Compare each field with the form, then update the matching record.

advanced.situation: Several teams use the same filing database, and duplicate staff records are disrupting reports. You are asked to review its structure before the next update.

options.text: Add a staff number field and check how duplicates affect linked records.
Merge matching names and remove the older entries from the database.
Ask teams to report duplicate records before changing the filing structure.
Map linked fields, test duplicate controls, and document safe changes for review.

basic.situation: A colleague sends a routine letter for checking before it goes to a supplier. You have the house-style checklist beside you.

options.text: Address spelling errors and leave the phrasing for the sender.
Use the previous supplier letter as the template and send this one.
Check the spelling and compare the heading with an older letter.
Read the letter with the checklist and mark spelling or grammar errors.

advanced.situation: Different teams keep returning letters with inconsistent formats and recurring grammar errors. You are asked to help improve the document review process.

options.text: Collect returned letters and fix the recurring errors before sending them.
Agree review standards, show examples, and coach staff through the checklist.
Copy the format from the latest approved letter for every team.
Share a short checklist covering house style, grammar, and common corrections.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to book a client appointment next week. The client has given two possible times, and the office calendar is open.

options.text: Ask your supervisor which of the two times they prefer before booking.
Check the calendar, select an open time, and confirm it with the client.
Book the first time and move any conflicting meeting later.
Add the first suggested time and send the client a calendar invitation.

advanced.situation: The office calendar has recurring double bookings, and staff use different tools to confirm appointments. You are asked to improve the scheduling workflow.

options.text: Move appointments into one shared calendar and send staff a quick guide.
Tell staff to check with one another before adding appointments.
Delete duplicate appointments and ask teams to submit their schedules again.
Review conflict patterns, agree booking steps, and coach staff on the calendar tools.

basic.situation: A colleague needs five copies of a signed letter for a meeting. The copier is free, and you have been shown its basic controls.

options.text: Select five copies and collect the pages when the copier finishes.
Set the copier to five copies and check the first page for clarity.
Place the signed original in the feeder and use its default setting.
Make one copy first, then adjust the setting if the page looks unclear.

advanced.situation: The shared copier repeatedly jams during a large document run, and staff need the pages for a scheduled meeting. You are responsible for arranging repairs.

options.text: Record the error, check the approved user steps, and arrange a service call.
Switch to another copier and leave the jammed machine for the next shift.
Tell colleagues to use another copier while you contact the service vendor.
Clear the visible jam, restart the run, and note whether it happens again.

basic.situation: A caller asks for a colleague who is away from their desk. You can take a message or transfer the call to the colleague's team.

options.text: Transfer the call to the colleague's team and explain that they are away.
Take the caller's name and ask them to call again later.
Give the caller the colleague's personal number to save time.
Take the caller's name and message, then pass it to the colleague's team.

advanced.situation: A visitor arrives with a delivery for a staff member but cannot explain which department requested it. The reception area is busy.

options.text: Ask for the delivery details, then contact the relevant department for direction.
Ask the visitor to wait while you check the staff directory.
Take the parcel to the reception desk and ask nearby staff about it.
Send the visitor to the largest department and return to the phone.

basic.situation: The stationery cupboard is low on printer paper, and your team has a regular supplier list and a monthly order form.

options.text: Check the stock and recent usage, then order a suitable amount from the list.
Use the last order form and submit the same quantity again.
Order extra paper now so the cupboard stays full through the month.
Count the remaining packs and order the usual amount from the supplier list.

advanced.situation: Several teams request stationery separately, and unopened supplies are piling up in one cupboard while another team runs short. You are asked to improve distribution.

options.text: Move unopened supplies to the team that requested them most recently.
Set a shared stock log, review usage, and coordinate regular team replenishment.
Ask each team to send requests before you place the regular supply order.
Combine the team requests into one order and divide supplies evenly.

basic.situation: You have entered figures from a supplier invoice and must compare them with the source before the day's batch is filed.

options.text: Compare each entered figure with its invoice source and flag any mismatch.
Review larger figures against the invoice and flag unclear entries for follow-up.
Check the invoice total against the entered total before filing the batch.
Change unusual figures based on earlier invoices without checking today's source.

advanced.situation: A batch contains recurring date and amount errors from several operators. You are asked to help set a verification routine for the team.

options.text: Share a list of recent mistakes and ask staff to watch for them.
Ask operators to check the totals again before submitting each batch.
Remove flagged entries from the batch so the team can meet its target.
Define field checks, use sample re-entry, and teach staff how to log mismatches.

basic.situation: You receive a clear sales report and must enter its dates and amounts into the designated fields before lunch.

options.text: Read each line and enter its date and amount in the matching fields.
Enter the amounts first and add the dates from the report afterward.
Enter the report's figures and leave the date fields for a later pass.
Enter the first page and save the batch before continuing with the rest.

advanced.situation: A growing stack of clear invoices must be keyed into fixed fields, and the team often reopens records to correct misplaced amounts.

options.text: Enter all amounts together, then add invoice dates in a separate pass.
Arrange invoices by date and enter each one using the same field sequence.
Ask a colleague to review the entries after each invoice is keyed.
Group similar invoices, follow the field order, and save batches at clear checkpoints.

basic.situation: The data entry machine needs a fresh paper stack for today's forms. You have been shown how to load the input tray.

options.text: Check the paper orientation, load the stack, and run a sample page.
Use the last stack's direction and load the new paper the same way.
Push the full stack into the tray and start entering the batch.
Load the paper with the printed side facing up and start the run.

advanced.situation: The machine keeps pulling two sheets at once after a paper change, and another operator is waiting to process forms.

options.text: Check the media guide, reseat the stack, and show the operator a sample feed.
Use a smaller stack and record whether the double feed continues during testing.
Pause feeding, then separate doubled pages and report the recurring machine issue.
Reduce the stack and ask the waiting operator to test a sample feed.

basic.situation: You finish keying a batch of forms and need to record the completed work in the team's activity log.

options.text: Log the batch date, record range, and completion status before filing.
Write the batch date and mark the work as completed in the log.
Leave the log blank and rely on the saved batch timestamp.
Note the batch date and your initials, then return to the next task.

advanced.situation: Different operators use free-text notes in the activity log, making it hard to see which batches are complete. You are asked to improve the log format.

options.text: Erase the free-text notes and replace them with a single completion mark.
Create standard fields for operator, batch range, status, and time, then review sample entries.
Ask operators to use the same wording when they mark batches complete.
Add a completion checkbox and tell staff to use it for every batch.

basic.situation: You finish entering a batch of invoices and must store the completed documents in the team's assigned folder.

options.text: Use the assigned folder and name the files with the supplier and date.
Save the invoices in the most recently used folder for this supplier.
Save the files to your desktop and move them after the batch.
Check the folder label and batch date, then save the invoices there.

advanced.situation: Completed files are hard to retrieve, and several operators save invoices into folders with similar names. You are asked to improve the storage arrangement.

options.text: Agree folder names, a naming pattern, and access rules, then review sample files.
Move older invoices into an archive folder and share its location with staff.
Add date labels to folders and tell operators which location stores invoices.
Delete files that appear duplicated to reduce folder clutter without checking contents.

basic.situation: A routine internal message is garbled, and the team's codebook lists a decoding procedure for this type of message.

options.text: Use the listed procedure and compare the decoded text with the message context.
Apply the first codebook method and pass the result to the next operator.
Follow the codebook steps and record which method you used.
Try the common substitution pattern and send the message once it reads clearly.

advanced.situation: A batch of coded messages contains several unclear results, and operators have recorded different methods. You are asked to help standardize the decoding process.

options.text: Set a procedure for checking inputs, recording methods, escalating unresolved messages, and coaching operators.
Share the codebook section and ask operators to record their method.
Use one codebook method for each message and maintain an exception list.
Ask operators to repeat their preferred method and compare the readable results.

basic.situation: You are typing a letter from a marked draft, but one handwritten phrase is hard to read. The letter is due before lunch.

options.text: Type the clear sections first and leave a note beside the uncertain wording.
Type the marked wording faithfully, flag the unclear phrase, and compare it with the draft.
Type the letter from the draft, then ask a colleague about one unclear phrase.
Replace the unclear phrase with wording that seems to fit the letter.

advanced.situation: You are typing a report from a voice recording and last month’s version. Several figures and names sound different, and the report goes to a client today.

options.text: Reuse last month’s figures where the recording is unclear to keep the report moving.
Type the updates, then replay the sections containing names and figures.
Type the recording first and ask a colleague to review the changed paragraphs.
Compare versions, mark every change, and replay unclear names and figures before finalizing.

basic.situation: You are updating a short meeting report. The instructions specify wider margins and more space between lines, but the page breaks look different afterward.

options.text: Use a tighter font and spacing throughout so the report fits fewer pages.
Adjust the page settings from the instruction sheet and inspect one printed page.
Set the requested spacing and margins, then preview the page breaks.
Change spacing in the named section and check its headings remain together.

advanced.situation: You are preparing a long report with inconsistent headings, tables and page breaks. Several colleagues will use your layout as their starting point for future reports.

options.text: Standardize the headings, then leave the table layouts as they are.
Fix the current report and send colleagues a short layout note.
Replace the existing styles with one preset to make the report look consistent.
Define heading, table, and page-break rules, then test them on sample pages before sharing.

basic.situation: You are scanning signed forms into a computer for editing. One page is skewed, and its printed address looks faint in the preview.

options.text: Rescan the page straight and compare its preview with the paper form.
Accept the scan and use a nearby form to fill in the faint address.
Adjust the scanner contrast and check whether the address becomes readable.
Scan the remaining forms and set the faint page aside for review.

advanced.situation: You are merging updated contact details from two office files. Several people have similar names, and other staff need to retrieve the merged records this afternoon.

options.text: Keep both files available and flag similar names for staff to resolve later.
Compare matching names with another field, then retain a review copy of the merge.
Merge the files by name and overwrite the older entries to finish quickly.
Merge by name and ask a colleague to check a few resulting entries.

basic.situation: You are checking a one-page notice with a spelling checklist. A date appears different in the heading and the body.

options.text: Mark both dates for confirmation and check the remaining spelling and punctuation.
Check spelling and punctuation, then tell the author about the date mismatch.
Change the body date to match the heading and finish the checklist.
Circle the two dates and pause proofreading until someone confirms them.

advanced.situation: You are collating a long report for review. The pages came from several files, and colleagues have found missing pages in earlier packs.

options.text: Group pages by section and check each group's opening and closing page.
Arrange pages by printed number, then ask a colleague to scan the pack.
Compare page numbers with the contents list and note any gaps.
Sort pages by filename, then prepare the pack for review.

basic.situation: You are printing a set of letters when the printer runs out of paper. The remaining letters are needed for the afternoon post.

options.text: Switch to a different tray and print the remaining pages from memory.
Load paper and restart the full set to keep the pages together.
Load paper, confirm the tray setting, and print a test page before resuming.
Load paper to the marked tray and resume the print job.

advanced.situation: You are saving completed reports in the team filing system while the printer queue shows a recurring error. Colleagues need the latest files for a meeting.

options.text: Keep the reports on your desktop and ask colleagues to use those copies.
Save the reports in the team folder and restart the printer queue.
Save dated copies in the team folder and record the printer error details.
Rename the latest files and save them over the previous versions for clarity.

basic.situation: You are sorting the morning mail and answering calls at the front desk. A caller asks whether a sealed envelope has arrived for a colleague.

options.text: Check the mail tray, then tell the caller whether an envelope is there.
Take the caller’s name and say you will ask the colleague to check later.
Check the addressee on the envelope and route it through the usual office channel.
Tell the caller the colleague’s name and check the mail tray later.

advanced.situation: You are verifying totals on a requisition before it is filed. The listed amounts add up differently from the form’s stated total, and the record may be reviewed later.

options.text: Change the stated total to match the calculator and file the requisition.
Recalculate the figures and ask a colleague whether the stated total seems plausible.
Recalculate each line, note the discrepancy, and return the form for clarification.
Check the line amounts again and flag the total for the preparer to review.

basic.situation: You are laying out a short community event flyer from supplied text. The heading looks cramped above the date and venue.

options.text: Shrink the heading until it fits, then send the page for printing.
Move the date and venue farther down the page to open the heading area.
Increase the gap below the heading and keep the supplied type size.
Choose a slightly smaller heading size and preview the spacing around the event details.

advanced.situation: You are setting a reusable layout for a multi-column guide with text and images from several databases. Other designers will adapt it for future editions.

options.text: Set column and type rules, test image placements, and share the layout guidance.
Place the images first and adjust each column to suit its page.
Apply consistent type sizes and column widths, then send the file to colleagues.
Use the first page as a model and let each designer choose later layouts.

basic.situation: You are masking a small logo on a poster image. The background is pale, and a few edges look rough in the preview.

options.text: Blur the logo edges until the pale background blends into the image.
Crop the image closer so the rough edges are less noticeable.
Refine the mask around the rough edges and review it at normal size.
Adjust the mask on the most visible edges and compare it with the source.

advanced.situation: You are retouching product photos for a printed catalogue. The color looks uneven across shots, and the client expects the items to remain recognizable.

options.text: Use one strong color adjustment across every photo to make the set look uniform.
Adjust the most uneven photos and review the full set on screen.
Compare each image with its reference, then adjust color and retouching consistently.
Match the photos by eye and smooth any marks that distract from the products.

basic.situation: You are importing text and a logo file for a small web notice. The logo appears blurred after import, while the text looks intact.

options.text: Import the text and ask for a clearer logo file before final layout.
Import the logo again and check its source dimensions before placing it.
Keep the logo at its imported size and arrange the text around it.
Stretch the imported logo until it fills the space beside the heading.

advanced.situation: You are converting a brochure for both print and web. The supplied text and artwork use different file types, and the print proof shows missing fonts.

options.text: Replace the missing fonts with similar ones, then export print and web versions.
Check font availability, then convert and review separate output files for each use.
Convert every file to one format and reuse it for print and web.
Convert the artwork first and check whether the print proof still shows missing fonts.

basic.situation: You are building a simple menu layout in desktop publishing software. A photo overlaps the price column in the proof preview.

options.text: Place the price text over the photo and export the menu for approval.
Move the price column to another page area and continue laying out the menu.
Move the photo clear of the price column and preview the whole menu.
Resize the photo slightly and check the affected part of the preview.

advanced.situation: You are producing final pages for a large event programme. The layout software freezes during export, and the print deadline is close.

options.text: Restart the export from the latest saved file and inspect the resulting pages.
Save a separate copy, isolate the failing page, and test a smaller export first.
Overwrite the working file with an older layout that exported successfully.
Export each page as an image and assemble the programme for printing.

basic.situation: You are checking a preliminary proof of a notice. The heading and body show different venue names, and printing is scheduled for later today.

options.text: Check the rest of the proof and flag the venue mismatch for review.
Change the body to match the heading and approve the proof for printing.
Mark both venue names and ask the content owner which one belongs.
Pause the proof and wait for someone nearby to confirm the venue.

advanced.situation: You are reviewing final proofs for a recurring publication. Several colleagues make inconsistent correction marks, and small errors have reached recent print runs.

options.text: Tell colleagues to check spelling, then focus your review on page layout.
Review the latest proofs yourself and send colleagues a list of common errors.
Set a shared proofing checklist, demonstrate it, and track recurring errors.
Ask each colleague to review pages using their usual method.

basic.situation: You are reviewing a simple two-color leaflet brief. The sample shows a logo and headings in different colors, and the print team needs a work sequence.

options.text: Check the brief for specified colors and draft a basic sequence of operations.
Ask the print team to choose the color count and plan the sequence later.
Treat every visible color as a separate print color and send the brief onward.
List the artwork and text steps, then confirm which elements use each color.

advanced.situation: You are studying design instructions for a large campaign with photographs, spot colors and web banners. The print and web teams need their production sequence and color specifications.

options.text: Use the print color plan for the web banners to keep campaign colors uniform.
Set the print separations and send the web team the campaign palette.
Map each output, sequence its operations, and confirm print color separations from the brief.
List the required files and ask both teams to decide their own work order.

basic.situation: You check a motor claim form against the team checklist and notice the repair date is missing before the file goes for review.

options.text: Return the form with a note asking the claimant to check every field.
Send the form onward, expecting the reviewer to spot the missing repair date.
Copy a date from the workshop estimate into the missing field.
Mark the field missing and ask the claimant for the repair date.

advanced.situation: New staff keep missing different fields on claim forms, and incomplete files are delaying reviews. You are asked to improve verification guidance.

options.text: Write a clear completeness standard and demonstrate it on typical claim forms.
Tell staff to compare forms with last month's completed claim files.
Share a field checklist with examples and practice reviewing sample claim forms.
Ask each new staff member to follow the checklist already in the file room.

basic.situation: A customer asks whether a cracked windscreen is covered. You have the policy schedule and wording, but the claim has not been assessed.

options.text: Tell the customer windscreen damage is usually covered under motor policies.
Ask the customer to send photographs before checking the policy documents.
Check the schedule for the listed cover and share that detail with the customer.
Check the policy wording for windscreen cover and explain the relevant section.

advanced.situation: An agent requests reinstatement after a missed premium, but the application and payment record show different dates. They want an answer before speaking with the customer.

options.text: Compare the dates with reinstatement criteria and explain the unresolved mismatch to the agent.
Reinstate the policy using the payment date as the most current record.
Check the reinstatement criteria and tell the agent the request is under review.
Ask the agent to confirm both dates before you continue reviewing the request.

basic.situation: You are entering a new motor policy from an approved application and notice the vehicle registration has two similar characters.

options.text: Save the policy entry and flag the registration for a later check.
Check the supporting vehicle document, then enter the confirmed registration.
Copy the registration exactly as it appears on the application.
Choose the character that matches the vehicle model you remember.

advanced.situation: A recent batch of policy records has duplicate entries and inconsistent dates. You are asked to improve the entry workflow and prepare records for audit.

options.text: Ask the team to review their own entries before submitting each batch.
Sort records by policy number and remove entries that look duplicated.
Create a standard entry sequence and add a daily duplicate check.
Compare source documents with system entries, resolve duplicates, and record the checks made.

basic.situation: A claimant calls to ask whether the workshop estimate has arrived. The file shows no estimate attached, and you can use the team's status script.

options.text: Check the file, explain that no estimate is recorded, and ask them to resend it.
Read the status script and tell the claimant the estimate is not listed.
Tell the claimant the file is still being processed and offer the usual timeframe.
Say the estimate has probably arrived and ask the claimant to wait a few days.

advanced.situation: An insured disputes a claim status because an agent said repairs could proceed, but the file shows assessment is pending. You are coaching a new colleague on the reply.

options.text: Acknowledge the mixed messages, check the file, and explain the pending assessment and next contact.
Explain that assessment is pending and suggest the insured contact the agent.
Tell the insured the agent handles repair decisions and end the call.
Ask the agent to call the insured while you continue with other files.

basic.situation: A repair invoice and the claim worksheet list different eligible amounts. You are using the provided formula to calculate the claim amount for review.

options.text: Calculate both amounts with the formula and send both figures for review.
Use the invoice total because it is the clearest amount on file.
Apply the provided formula to the worksheet amount and note the invoice difference.
Use the lower amount to avoid overstating the claim during review.

advanced.situation: A claimant disputes a valuation after an updated repair quote, while the original estimate remains in the file. You must prepare the claim for payment review.

options.text: Replace the original amount with the updated quote and send the payment request.
Ask the claimant to confirm which quote they want the insurer to use.
Compare both valuations, document the difference, and transmit the file for further investigation.
Use the original estimate and note that the claimant has submitted a newer quote.

basic.situation: A policy cancellation is recorded in the system, and you need to send the standard notice to the insurance agent and accounting department.

options.text: Use the cancellation template and verify the policy number before sending both notices.
Send the template to the agent and let accounting see the system update.
Copy the previous cancellation email and change the policyholder's name.
Send both departments a brief message with the policyholder's name and cancellation date.

advanced.situation: Audit checks found cancellation emails with missing dates and inconsistent recipients. You are asked to improve the notification template and its record trail.

options.text: Ask staff to check dates and recipients against the policy record before sending.
Ask accounting to keep a spreadsheet of cancellations reported by agents.
Update the template with required fields, recipient checks, and saved records.
Add cancellation date and policy number fields to the existing template.

basic.situation: You receive a tray of letters and need to place them into bins by destination, following the sorting guide.

options.text: Check each destination label, then place letters in their marked bins.
Group the letters by destination and check the guide after sorting.
Put each letter into the nearest open bin to keep the line moving.
Sort the letters by destination, then ask about one unclear address.

advanced.situation: A new client sends mixed mail for several offices, and the usual bins are causing delays. You are asked to propose a routing scheme and brief the shift.

options.text: Create a destination chart and explain it during the shift handover.
Map destinations to labeled bins, trial the flow, then brief staff on exceptions.
Keep the current bins and ask staff to sort unfamiliar addresses as they appear.
Use one bin per office and tell staff to move overflow later.

basic.situation: You are folding a batch of circulars and inserting them into envelopes before the outgoing collection.

options.text: Follow the sample fold, insert each circular, and check the envelope closure.
Fold the circulars together and fill envelopes as quickly as possible.
Fold each circular and insert it, checking a few envelopes afterward.
Fold each circular to fit, then insert it with the address facing out.

advanced.situation: A machine has folded a large run of letters, but several envelopes feel uneven. The collection is soon, and you are guiding a new colleague.

options.text: Show your colleague the sample, then check the next few envelopes together.
Ask your colleague to watch the output while you finish the batch.
Pause the batch, inspect sample inserts, adjust the fold, then check the restarted output.
Keep the machine running and separate any uneven envelopes at the end.

basic.situation: You are weighing a customer's parcel and using the rate chart to prepare its postage with assistance nearby.

options.text: Check the scale reading against the chart, then set the postage meter.
Weigh the parcel and ask a colleague to confirm the chart band.
Use the parcel's weight from the customer's note to set postage.
Check the chart band and apply a familiar postage amount for similar parcels.

advanced.situation: A customer questions the postage on a recurring batch and wants a cheaper service. You can review the items and explain available mailing choices.

options.text: Repeat the current charge and ask the customer to accept it today.
Offer the lowest priced service shown on the chart for the batch.
Reweigh a sample and compare it with the rate chart before replying.
Compare the batch weights and delivery needs across available services, then explain the trade-offs.

basic.situation: You start the automatic feeder for a short run and notice some sheets are not entering smoothly.

options.text: Check the sheet stack, start the feeder, and watch the first output.
Restart the feeder and see whether the sheets settle into place.
Watch the feed path, pause if sheets skew, and report the pattern.
Keep the feeder running and straighten sheets as they come through.

advanced.situation: During a high-volume run, output defects return after each restart. You are responsible for inspecting the mail machine and improving its performance.

options.text: Adjust the feed guides slightly and check whether the next stack looks better.
Compare defect timing with machine settings, isolate the likely cause, and verify a controlled restart.
Restart the machine after each defect and keep the clean pieces moving.
Check output samples and note when the defects appear during the run.

basic.situation: A delivery arrives, and you need to unload its mail containers onto the trolley for transport to the sorting station.

options.text: Check the container weight, load safely, and secure the trolley before moving.
Load the containers in arrival order and ask someone to steer the trolley.
Check the trolley load, then move each container to the sorting station.
Lift the containers onto the nearest trolley and push them onward.

advanced.situation: A courier reports a missed collection during a busy mailing period. You can contact delivery services and help coordinate the parcels awaiting collection.

options.text: Ask for another collection today and leave the parcels ready at the dock.
Send the parcels with whichever driver arrives next at the loading area.
Check parcel volume and collection window, then book a suitable courier service.
Call the courier, explain the backlog, and agree a revised pickup time.

basic.situation: You check an outgoing envelope against the checklist and notice its address is missing a unit number.

options.text: Set it aside and request the missing unit number before processing.
Add the building name from nearby mail and continue the batch.
Check the checklist again and mark the address as incomplete for follow-up.
Send it with the other envelopes and let delivery staff resolve it.

advanced.situation: A production order lists two envelope sizes, but today's output shows a mismatch. You are reviewing the mailing requirements before the batch continues.

options.text: Recheck the production order and sample, then flag the discrepancy for review.
Adjust the guide to fit the larger envelopes and check the next stack.
