Continue the run and note the size mismatch in the shift log.
Compare the order with sample output, hold mismatched items, and clarify the specification.

basic.situation: You receive a signed client form with a name on its cover and several folders nearby. You need to file it before the daily batch is collected.

options.text: Place it in the general tray until someone confirms its folder.
Use the nearest open folder so today's paperwork keeps moving.
Check the index, then file the form under its listed client folder.
File the signed form under the client name shown on its cover.

advanced.situation: A team audit finds similar project folders under different names, and staff struggle to retrieve records. You are asked to review the files and suggest improvements.

options.text: Compare folder labels with the index and map duplicate names for review.
List several confusing folders and ask the records lead what to change.
Rename the folders that seem unclear and tell the team afterward.
Add a note to each folder that staff have trouble finding.

basic.situation: You open the morning post and find an addressed invoice, a sealed personal envelope, and an unlabelled internal note. The mail tray is filling up.

options.text: Open the personal envelope to check whether it belongs to the office.
Set the unclear note beside the shared tray for later sorting.
Route the invoice by department and place the note in the internal tray.
Keep the personal envelope sealed, and check the office directory for the note's recipient.

advanced.situation: Several teams have returned letters with inconsistent formatting, and a new clerk is joining. You are asked to help standardise routine correspondence handling.

options.text: Draft a short template guide using approved examples and common proofing checks.
Ask each team to send its preferred format before preparing a guide.
Tell the new clerk to copy whichever recent letter looks suitable.
Review the latest returned letter and share it as a sample.

basic.situation: You enter monthly delivery totals from a paper sheet, and one figure looks out of line with the row's other entries.

options.text: Check the row total against the sheet and note any mismatch.
Copy the figure as written and flag the row for later review.
Enter the figure from the sheet and continue with the next row.
Recalculate the row and compare it with the paper sheet before entry.

advanced.situation: A monthly report combines figures from several teams, and totals differ from the underlying sheets. You are reviewing it before circulation.

options.text: Compare the report totals with each team's summary and list differences.
Recheck the final totals and circulate the report with a note about differences.
Adjust the report totals to match the largest team's submitted figures.
Trace each total to its source sheet and document the mismatches for resolution.

basic.situation: A colleague asks you to add a client appointment to the shared calendar, but the request gives a date and no start time.

options.text: Check the colleague's message for a time, then add the confirmed appointment.
Enter the date as a tentative calendar item and mark the time pending.
Add the appointment at the usual time and include the client's name.
Leave the appointment request in the inbox until the colleague replies.

advanced.situation: Two senior staff request the same meeting room for overlapping client appointments, and one visitor is travelling from out of town. You maintain their calendars.

options.text: Hold the room for the earlier request and note the other conflict.
Move the visitor to another open room time after checking travel constraints.
Compare calendars and room details, then suggest times around the visitor's travel plans.
Tell both staff about the overlap and ask which appointment should move.

basic.situation: You need to scan a signed form for a colleague, and the scanner screen offers several unfamiliar file settings.

options.text: Scan a test page with the standard setting before scanning the form.
Choose the first setting and scan the form for the colleague.
Check the colleague's instructions and select the matching scan setting.
Ask a nearby coworker which setting they usually select for forms.

advanced.situation: The shared copier keeps jamming, and its database shows old supply counts. You are asked to update the team's equipment and inventory records.

options.text: Record the jam and ask the team to report any missing supplies.
Update the supply counts from the database and restart the copier.
Clear the jam per the guide, record the fault, and verify available supplies.
Check the paper shelf and update the counts, then note the recurring jam.

basic.situation: A caller asks whether a routine office supply order has arrived, but you cannot see the delivery record at your desk.

options.text: Tell the caller the order should arrive today based on its usual timing.
Take a message with the order number and pass it to the supply clerk.
Take the caller's details and check the delivery record before giving an update.
Ask the caller to ring again after the delivery round finishes.

advanced.situation: A customer calls upset about a delayed stationery order while the shelf is nearly empty. You can check the order record and current stock.

options.text: Promise the customer that the delayed items will arrive tomorrow.
Apologise for the delay and ask the customer to call back later.
Check the order status and give the customer its latest recorded update.
Check order and stock records, explain the status, and offer an available alternative.

basic.situation: A print job is ready, and you need to place the originals in the feed tray while a colleague checks the copy count.

options.text: Ask the colleague which side should face up before loading the originals.
Load the originals in the tray in the order shown on the job sheet.
Place the originals face up as they arrive from the bundle.
Set the originals beside the tray while you check the machine diagram.

advanced.situation: A long booklet run needs collating, punching, and binding, and the job sheet lists several paper sizes. You are operating the auxiliary finishing machines.

options.text: Ask the requester to confirm the order before you use the finishing machines.
Run the full batch through the binder using the most common paper size.
Collate a small set and inspect its page order before finishing the batch.
Verify the page sequence and paper sizes, then test the finishing setup on a small set.

basic.situation: A job order requests 200 copies, but the copier still shows the previous job's higher count. You are preparing the next run.

options.text: Leave the previous count and write 200 on the job sheet.
Set the copy count to 200 and check the display before starting.
Ask a coworker to confirm the copy count shown on the screen.
Start the machine and stop it when the stack looks close to 200.

advanced.situation: During a large copy run, faint pages appear intermittently after a speed change. The client needs the batch today, and you are monitoring the machine.

options.text: Reduce the speed and inspect the next few pages before continuing.
Finish the current stack and note the faint pages on the job record.
Pause the run, compare sample pages, and adjust speed or ink flow before resuming.
Keep the speed and raise ink flow until pages look darker.

basic.situation: A job order asks for 80 double-sided copies on coloured paper, but the supply shelf has two similar shades available.

options.text: Set both paper shades beside the machine while you prepare the job.
Check the job order's colour description and match it to the stocked paper labels.
Use the brighter shade because it is easier to distinguish in the tray.
Ask a coworker which shade was used for similar jobs last week.

advanced.situation: A customer requests a rush print run with several paper sizes and finishing steps. You must give the supervisor billing information from the job order.

options.text: Break down quantities, materials, and finishing steps before calculating the billing details.
List the requested quantities and materials for the supervisor to price.
Reuse the price from the closest recent job and send that figure.
Estimate the total from the number of pages and mark it as provisional.

basic.situation: You finish a small print batch and find one page turned sideways among the sets. The customer is waiting at the counter.

options.text: Hand over the batch and mention that one page may be turned.
Hold the batch at the counter until the customer can inspect it.
Fix the visible set and quickly inspect the remaining stacks for the same issue.
Check the page order in each set and replace the turned page before release.

advanced.situation: A box of older papers must be prepared for microfilming, but several sheets have folds and handwritten notes near the edges.

options.text: Separate the folded sheets and ask the operator how they prefer them prepared.
Flatten the folded sheets under a weight and continue preparing the batch.
Sort sheets, flag notes, and test a sample for legibility before processing.
Trim folded edges and send the papers through with the regular batch.

basic.situation: After a copy run, toner dust is visible near the machine's removable tray, and the master copy needs to be filed.

options.text: Wipe the tray with a damp cloth and place the master nearby.
Brush away the visible dust and leave the master in the output tray.
File the master copy first, then ask a coworker about cleaning the tray.
Follow the cleaning guide and file the master copy under the job number.

advanced.situation: A machine develops a grinding noise during a high-volume run, and completed sets are due for delivery. The production log also has blank output fields.

options.text: Log completed volume and backlog, then report the unusual grinding noise.
Pack the current sets, record the noise, and alert next shift before handover.
Stop the run per guidance, log output, and report the grinding noise.
Continue at reduced speed and complete the output log after delivery.

basic.situation: You notice the stock of binding covers is low before a scheduled job. A colleague asks you to check whether more are needed.

options.text: Count the shelf stock and tell the colleague the current amount.
Order the usual carton size because the shelf looks nearly empty.
Count covers on hand and compare them with the scheduled job.
Wait for the scheduled job to start before checking the remaining covers.

advanced.situation: Several print jobs need different paper sizes this week, and the storeroom has limited shelf space. You manage supply counts and requisitions.

options.text: Order equal cartons of every size so the team has balanced stock.
Compare counts with job needs, then requisition each paper size shortfall.
Ask each operator which paper sizes they expect to use this week.
Review recent usage and replenish the sizes that ran low last month.

basic.situation: You spot a misspelled venue and a stray comma in a printed event proof due at noon.

options.text: Circle both items and ask the editor which house style applies.
Mark the venue spelling, then leave punctuation for the next proofreader.
Mark the spelling and comma with standard printers' marks, then note the query.
Fix the venue name in your file and send the proof to print.

advanced.situation: New proofreaders use different marks for deletions and insertions, and a client proof is due after their shift.

options.text: Tell colleagues to follow the last proof they handled for consistency.
Share a marksheet and ask the editor to settle any uncertain cases.
Set house rules for recurring marks, then coach peers through a calibration proof.
Draft a one-page mark guide, demonstrate examples, and review sample proofs with staff.

basic.situation: A corrected menu proof returns with changes to dish names and prices; you need to check it before it goes back to the café.

options.text: Rely on the typesetter's note that all menu changes were completed.
Check the prices against the marked copy, then pass the proof onward.
Scan visible changes, then return the page once its layout looks tidy.
Compare each marked change with the returned proof and note missed corrections.

advanced.situation: Several proof rounds for a bilingual annual report contain repeated figure changes, and the final print slot is booked this afternoon.

options.text: Use a correction log, assign page checks, and reconcile figures against the approved copy.
Review the pages with the most changes, then release the report for printing.
Ask the editor to check the last proof before the printer's deadline.
Check the cover and summary, then rely on the signed proof sheet.

basic.situation: A short staff notice has a blank caption under a photo, and the editor is in a meeting until lunch.

options.text: Leave the photo as placed and mention the blank caption when the editor returns.
Write a brief caption from the photo and place it under the image.
Record the missing caption in the query list and return the notice for review.
Flag the blank space in the margin for the editor to inspect.

advanced.situation: Across a set of monthly newsletters, you find missing image credits on several pages, while the source files contain inconsistent credit details.

options.text: Check the first newsletter closely and use it as the model for the rest.
Add the same credit line to every image and return the set for print.
Mark the missing credits you found and ask the editor to review the set.
List affected pages, compare available source notes, and query unclear credits before correction.

basic.situation: You receive a printed event schedule and its approved copy, and notice that one session time may differ.

options.text: Use the latest schedule as the source and update the approved copy.
Compare the session names and times on the first page with the copy.
Check the opening and closing times, then pass the schedule onward.
Compare each session time against the approved copy and mark any mismatch.

advanced.situation: A quarterly sales table has hundreds of entries, and a few small mismatches could change the totals in a client report due today.

options.text: Build a spreadsheet comparison against source records and review every flagged difference.
Compare the totals by eye and investigate rows that look unusual.
Match each entry to its source record, then reconcile any differing totals.
Compare the final totals with last quarter and send the report if they align.

basic.situation: A short public notice uses “its” in a sentence where you are unsure whether the word should be “it's.”

options.text: Ask a nearby proofreader which form they usually choose for notices.
Change it to “it's” because that form often appears in notices.
Check a reliable dictionary or style reference before marking the usage.
Leave a query for the editor to decide the pronoun form.

advanced.situation: Editors on a recurring report series disagree about capitalization and hyphenation, and new staff are joining the copy desk.

options.text: Let each editor retain a preferred reference and settle disagreements by email.
Ask the senior editor to answer each capitalization query as it arrives.
Collect trusted references and document the series rules with clear examples.
Choose a reference set, record agreed rules, and walk staff through tricky examples.

basic.situation: You finish marking a short article proof and need the editor to review two author queries before typesetting resumes.

options.text: Forward the proof to the editor and describe the queries in your message.
Send the proof to the typesetter and mention that queries remain open.
Send the marked proof and query list to the editor with the article reference.
Place the proof in the editor's tray and flag it for later review.

advanced.situation: An author and editor disagree over a changed paragraph in a late proof, while the typesetter is waiting for the next set of instructions.

options.text: Return the proof to the author and ask them to resolve the wording.
Forward the disagreement to the editor with both versions marked on the proof.
Record both versions, pause the passage, and ask the editor to confirm the wording.
Send the typesetter the editor's preferred paragraph to keep production moving.

basic.situation: You enter responses from a paper survey, and the coding sheet maps “not applicable” to a listed value.

options.text: Use the nearest numeric code when a response falls outside the list.
Set aside responses needing extra time, then finish the remaining forms.
Enter answers as written and ask the analyst to code them later.
Enter responses with listed codes and save the batch by survey date.

advanced.situation: Three assistants code free-text answers differently, and their combined file is due for a monthly service report.

options.text: Review a sample, then ask the team to follow whichever coding seems clearest.
Merge the files and recode entries that appear inconsistent during analysis.
Draft code definitions with examples, test edge cases, and align the team before entry.
Share a code list with assistants and answer questions as they arise.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks for the average waiting time from twelve recorded clinic visits for a weekly service summary.

options.text: Use the middle recorded time as the average for a quicker summary.
Estimate the average from the shortest and longest visits, then report it.
Add the recorded times, divide by twelve, and check the entries before reporting.
Calculate the mean with a calculator and send the result to your supervisor.

advanced.situation: A client asks whether satisfaction ratings changed between two survey rounds, but the sample sizes differ and some responses are missing.

options.text: Compare the two averages and present the difference as a confirmed change.
Use the same test as last round so the report stays comparable.
Calculate both averages and explain that the groups have different sample sizes.
Check the rating scale and missingness, then select a suitable comparison test with the analyst.

basic.situation: A survey form has a blank age field and a response outside the printed range; you are checking source forms before entry.

options.text: Mark the unusual response and enter the remaining answers for review.
Flag both issues and check the form against the source notes before entry.
Set the form aside and ask the survey lead how to classify it.
Fill the age from the respondent's nearby household details and continue.

advanced.situation: Several staff have entered survey forms with missing fields and inconsistent pen use, delaying the weekly dataset handoff.

options.text: Sample recent forms and send the team a list of common issues.
Return every form with a blank field to the interviewer for another visit.
Write clear checks for completeness and usable forms, then review examples with staff.
Tell staff to check forms more carefully before sending their next batches.

basic.situation: You need to make a bar chart from the monthly sales totals provided in a spreadsheet for a team briefing.

options.text: Copy the totals into a chart and use the spreadsheet's default labels.
Use last month's chart and replace the title with this month's date.
Check the month labels and totals, then chart them with a clear scale.
Create the chart from the totals and ask a colleague to review its layout.

advanced.situation: A client report combines production and quality figures from different source sheets, and its charts will guide next month's staffing discussion.

options.text: Arrange the source sheets in the report appendix and chart the headline totals.
Confirm units and periods, then design labeled charts that distinguish production from quality.
Keep the existing chart style and add both sets of figures to save time.
Compile the figures into separate charts and include a note about their sources.

basic.situation: A client describes a monthly dashboard in a meeting and asks for a chart showing service requests by district.

options.text: Write down the chart request and ask the client to email details later.
Note the requested districts, reporting period, and chart purpose, then confirm them aloud.
Promise a district chart and decide the reporting period after the meeting.
Ask which districts matter most and take notes on the answer.

advanced.situation: A client wants a public report comparing district performance, but the available data covers different periods and has uneven response counts.

options.text: Document the data limits and suggest reviewing them before publication planning.
Clarify the audience and comparison goal, then discuss period limits and suitable displays.
Agree to rank districts and choose a chart after the meeting.
Ask the client which chart they prefer and record the requested format.

basic.situation: You are assigned to send a short staff survey and record completed forms before Friday's team review.

options.text: Send the survey to the listed staff and count responses at week's end.
Forward the survey to nearby teams so more people can respond.
Print the survey for the office and record forms as they arrive.
Send the approved survey to the listed staff and log returns by date.

advanced.situation: A department needs feedback from staff across several shifts, but response rates have been low when surveys were sent during office hours.

options.text: Offer the survey at shift handovers and note which groups return forms.
Send another office-hours reminder and use the same response deadline.
Ask one staff member from each shift to complete a form for colleagues.
Map shift coverage, schedule distribution around work patterns, and track returns by group.

basic.situation: You see a worker step around a loose fence rail near the field path. What do you do?

options.text: I would mention the rail during the next morning's crew briefing.
I would tell the worker to use the other path and note the rail.
I would warn the worker and mark the loose rail for the repair crew.
I would ask the worker to watch the rail while continuing nearby work.

advanced.situation: During a site walk, you find workers repeatedly leaving tools across an access route. How do you address it?

options.text: I would ask the nearest worker to keep the access route clear.
I would remind the crew to clear the route at each shift change.
I would move the tools aside and continue the site walk.
I would review the repeated hazard with the crew and track agreed corrections.

basic.situation: Your daily harvest sheet and the shipping schedule show different fish counts. What do you do?

options.text: I would ask the loader which count seems closer to the shipment.
I would check the count against the harvest and shipping entries before filing.
I would record both figures and flag the difference for review.
I would use the shipping schedule count to finish today's sheet.

advanced.situation: A maintenance budget is running high after repeated fence repairs, while other infrastructure work remains scheduled. What do you do?

options.text: I would compare repair costs with remaining work before revising the forecast.
I would update the repair total and note the budget variance for review.
I would report the overspend and ask the manager how to proceed.
I would shift funds from the remaining work to cover the repairs.

basic.situation: Two workers are free after finishing their assigned tasks, while the animal quarters still need cleaning. What do you do?

options.text: I would confirm the quarters are ready, then assign workers to clean them.
I would tell one worker to begin cleaning while the other gathers supplies.
I would ask the workers to help wherever the team needs them.
I would assign the available workers to clean the animal quarters.

advanced.situation: A tractor and loading machine are needed at two work sites on the same morning. How do you coordinate their movement?

options.text: I would ask both site leads to decide which machine arrives first.
I would confirm each site's start time before assigning the machines.
I would send both machines to the site that requested them first.
I would align machine moves with site needs and the transport schedule.

basic.situation: You notice patches of pale leaves in one crop row during a routine field walk. What do you do?

options.text: I would mark the pale patch and ask a worker whether it is common.
I would record the affected row and ask the senior to inspect it.
I would compare nearby rows and note where the pale leaves begin.
I would treat the pale row with the spray used last month.

advanced.situation: Crop damage appears in several field sections, but its pattern changes near the irrigation lines. How do you plan the inspection?

options.text: I would check the irrigation lines nearest the most damaged plants.
I would harvest the damaged sections first to protect the remaining crop.
I would map damage by section and compare it with irrigation coverage.
I would mark affected sections and ask the manager to review treatment options.

basic.situation: A manager changes the morning work schedule, and the crew is already preparing for the original tasks. What do you do?

options.text: I would tell each crew lead about the updated schedule and tasks.
I would post the revised schedule by the equipment store.
I would mention the schedule change as workers pass the shed.
I would relay the new tasks and confirm workers know their assigned locations.

advanced.situation: A manager's production target conflicts with a forestry crew's planned harvest window. You are asked to coordinate the schedule. What do you do?

options.text: I would compare both plans and discuss a workable schedule with each manager.
I would ask the forestry crew to suggest a replacement harvest window.
I would share the conflict with both managers and request their preferred dates.
I would follow the production target and tell forestry about the change.

basic.situation: Workers return ladders and tools after a field job, and one ladder is missing from the issue list. What do you do?

options.text: I would update the list from memory and return the remaining tools.
I would record the missing ladder and notify the crew lead.
I would ask the crew lead whether anyone remembers using the ladder.
I would compare returned equipment with the issue list and record the gap.

advanced.situation: New workers will use a harvesting method that differs from the usual practice. How do you prepare them for the work?

options.text: I would explain the method and answer questions before the shift begins.
I would pair each new worker with an experienced harvester for the shift.
I would hand out the method sheet and begin the scheduled harvest.
I would demonstrate the method, then observe workers practising its key steps.

basic.situation: During a routine visit, you notice residue on a worktable and staff moving uncovered produce. Your checklist asks you to inspect cleanliness and employee practices.

options.text: Ask staff to clear the table, then note the practice for review.
Photograph the table and leave while staff finish the batch.
Pause handling, guide staff through cleaning, and record what you observe.
Remind the shift lead about cleanliness and return after lunch.

advanced.situation: At a processing plant audit, you find repeated sanitation failures near an active line. The manager disputes your findings, and product is due to ship today.

options.text: Accept the manager’s explanation and complete the audit using earlier records.
Record the failures, discuss a corrective plan, and check the affected line again.
Trace affected product, document evidence, and use your delegated hold process.
Ask staff to clean the area and note the manager’s response.

basic.situation: A poultry delivery arrives for routine grading. You have a scale and the standard checklist, and your supervisor asks you to verify sample weights.

options.text: Weigh each selected item, record readings, and compare them with the checklist.
Record the scale reading and compare it with yesterday’s delivery.
Check a few items by hand and record an estimated average weight.
Weigh the sample and tell your supervisor whether it seems acceptable.

advanced.situation: A processor submits a revised seafood recipe after changing an ingredient. You need to check whether the formula matches the approved version before the next production run.

options.text: Check the changed ingredient and send the full recipe for later review.
Approve the familiar recipe name and review the ingredient change later.
Compare the submitted recipe line by line with the approved formula and flag differences.
Ask production staff whether the new ingredient has worked in past batches.

basic.situation: A graded produce lot has passed its checklist. You are assigned to apply the required label and seal before the certificate is issued.

options.text: Seal the cartons and copy details from the previous certificate.
Apply the label and ask a colleague to check the certificate afterward.
Prepare the certificate first and attach the lot label before dispatch.
Match the lot details, apply its label and seal, then complete the certificate.

advanced.situation: A certificate batch contains several similar lot numbers, and one shipment is waiting. You are checking that issued grading certificates match their sealed products.

options.text: Compare every certificate with its sealed lot record and resolve mismatches before release.
Release certificates for matching grades and verify lot numbers later.
Check the urgent shipment first, then sample the remaining certificates.
Review certificate numbers against the dispatch list and report any differences.

basic.situation: Your supervisor gives you instructions to collect a plant sample from a marked field and send it for laboratory assessment.

options.text: Label the container first, collect the sample, and send it with the form.
Use the instructed container, label the sample, and route it with field details.
Collect leaves in a spare bag and write the field name afterward.
Follow the collection steps and ask the supervisor to label it later.

advanced.situation: Several farms report similar crop symptoms across a wide area. You need to plan product samples for laboratory checks and coach two junior inspectors.

options.text: Map affected sites, set a consistent sample plan, and demonstrate labeling and handling.
Set site priorities and have inspectors follow the standard collection steps.
Ask each inspector to collect from the nearest farm and combine the samples.
Choose the most affected farms and send inspectors the usual collection notes.

basic.situation: A grower asks how to correct a record-keeping gap noted during inspection. Your supervisor is present, and the applicable standard is in your guidance notes.

options.text: Explain the relevant record standard and show how to update the missing entries.
Describe the missing entries and provide the guidance note for later reference.
Suggest copying a nearby farm’s records as a temporary example.
Read the guidance aloud and ask the supervisor to explain the details.

advanced.situation: A processor is planning a larger facility and asks for advice on plant layout and food safety systems. You have inspection experience and their draft plans.

options.text: Mark crowded areas on the draft and suggest adding more space.
Review product flow, identify likely cross-contact points, and explain layout improvements.
Discuss equipment needs and send written comments on the draft plans.
Recommend copying the current plant layout to speed up construction planning.

basic.situation: During a routine check, you see a damaged water pipe spraying onto exposed produce. Your instructions say to report safety concerns to the manager.

options.text: Finish the inspection route and mention the pipe at the next briefing.
Call the manager and describe the leak near the produce line.
Tell a nearby worker and continue checking the other rooms.
Alert the manager, identify the affected produce, and record the location.

advanced.situation: A routine test suggests a batch may be unsafe, and more product is moving through the plant. Your delegated procedure allows you to initiate a temporary production hold.

options.text: Ask the line lead to pause work while you check the test record.
Wait for the next test before raising the concern with plant staff.
Notify the manager and mark the current batch for later review.
Initiate the temporary hold, trace affected lots, and record the test evidence.

basic.situation: During morning rounds, you notice a goat limping and eating less. Your supervisor asks you to check for visible signs of injury or illness.

options.text: Check the leg briefly and mention the limp at feeding time.
Record the limp and ask a coworker whether it looks familiar.
Offer extra feed and wait to see whether its appetite returns.
Observe its movement and appetite, record signs, and tell your supervisor.

advanced.situation: Several animals show unusual weakness after a feed change, and one has a swollen leg. You need to assess signs and coordinate veterinary care.

options.text: Check temperatures where trained and tell the supervisor about the weakness.
Treat the swollen leg with a familiar remedy and watch the group overnight.
Ask the veterinarian about the group and send a brief symptom summary.
Separate observations by animal, record the feed change, and contact the veterinarian.

basic.situation: You are choosing a breeding pair from the herd using genealogy charts and the farm’s stated goal for healthy offspring.

options.text: Ask the owner which pair has produced the most young recently.
Check the charts for close relatives and then suggest a pairing.
Compare both pedigrees and traits with the stated goal before proposing the pair.
Choose the largest animals because size is easy to compare.

advanced.situation: The farm wants stronger disease resistance without losing its desired growth traits. You are reviewing pedigrees and proposing a breeding plan for the next cycle.

options.text: Use last cycle’s pairings and adjust one selection for stronger resistance.
Pair the fastest-growing animals and see whether resistance improves over time.
Map available pedigrees and compare resistance and growth traits across candidate pairings.
Select resistant animals first, then check whether their growth records are acceptable.

basic.situation: You are observing a group of cows during the morning check and have been asked to note signs that heat may be approaching.

options.text: Ask the handler whether any cow seemed restless during feeding.
Mark the most active cow as ready and update the breeding list.
Watch the group again later and tell the supervisor what you noticed.
Watch for changes in behavior, record each cow, and share the observations.

advanced.situation: Breeding dates are slipping because signs of heat vary across the herd. You are managing the observation and exercise schedule under the farm’s approved protocol.

options.text: Keep an animal-level log and adjust exercise times as signs change.
Track signs by animal, schedule protocol-based exercise, and review changes daily.
Ask handlers to report signs and revise the schedule at week’s end.
Exercise the whole herd together and use the first observed sign for timing.

basic.situation: A young calf needs an identification tag. Your supervisor has given you the tag number and asks you to apply it under direct supervision.

options.text: Write the calf’s description down and wait for another tagging session.
Use a spare tag now and update the number in the record later.
Confirm the tag number, apply it with supervision, and record the calf details.
Apply the assigned tag and ask the supervisor to check the record afterward.

advanced.situation: A herd count reveals several animals with unreadable tags, and breeding records are due today. You are responsible for checking identification links and updating the register.

options.text: List the unreadable tags and ask handlers to identify those animals from memory.
Reconcile visible tags with animal records and flag uncertain identities for checking.
Assign new numbers to unclear animals and revise their breeding records.
Check readable tags against the register and hold unclear entries for review.

basic.situation: You are assigned to feed and water the rabbits, then clean their hutches using the farm’s step-by-step routine.

options.text: Top up feed generously and sweep the visible bedding from each hutch.
Use the feed chart and clean the hutches before refilling water.
Follow the feed amounts, refresh water, and clean each hutch as instructed.
Refresh water and clean the hutches, then ask about feed amounts later.

advanced.situation: A larger group of goats is arriving, and the current pen layout is wearing down. You are asked to build a durable fenced yard and adjust feeding routines.

options.text: Plan sturdy fencing and feeding access around the group’s space and daily routine.
Build a stronger fence first and review feeding after the goats arrive.
Extend the nearest fence and place feed bins wherever space remains.
Measure the yard and position feed bins near the existing gate.

basic.situation: After weighing the young animals, you need to enter their weights and diets in the provided record template before the end of the shift.

options.text: Enter each weight and diet under the matching animal identifier, then review entries.
Record the weights now and add diet details during tomorrow’s rounds.
Enter average weights for the group and copy yesterday’s diet notes.
Use the template and enter weights before noting the group’s common diet.

advanced.situation: Feed costs have risen, and growth records vary across pens. You are reviewing animal data and stock levels before preparing the next supply order.

options.text: Check stock counts and order less feed for pens with slower growth.
Compare growth and diet records by pen, then match needs to current stock.
Order the usual feed quantity and review growth patterns next month.
Reduce each pen’s feed amount and check whether costs fall next week.

basic.situation: You hear an unfamiliar rattling from the tractor engine while working a field row.

options.text: I would ease the load and compare the rattle with its usual engine sound.
I would park nearby and inspect the belt and engine area before restarting.
I would stop at a safe edge, note the rattle, and tell the lead.
I would finish the row, then check the engine after reaching the field edge.

advanced.situation: Two tractors develop intermittent power loss during a busy planting shift, and operators describe different warning sounds.

options.text: I would pause affected tractors, compare their symptoms, and brief operators on safe checks and reporting.
I would inspect the air filters and ask operators to try another gear.
I would compare each sound with the operating load, then record patterns for maintenance.
I would ask each operator to keep working while I listen during the next pass.

basic.situation: You are asked to load a specified seed blend into the planter, but the labels on two bags look similar.

options.text: I would check both bag labels against the work sheet before loading the blend.
I would ask a nearby operator which bag they used on the last job.
I would use the bag that looks familiar and fill the planter for this pass.
I would check one label and ask the supervisor to confirm the other bag.

advanced.situation: A crop block needs a different sprayer mix than yesterday's, but the new instruction has no clear batch amount.

options.text: I would prepare a small trial batch and ask the lead to inspect it.
I would check the written instruction and ask the farm lead to clarify batch amount.
I would scale yesterday's mix to today's acreage and start filling the tank.
I would pause mixing, confirm the rate and volume, then brief the loader on handling.

basic.situation: You are driving a tractor with guidance when the planter begins leaving uneven rows in a familiar field.

options.text: I would adjust the steering and ask my guide to watch the next row.
I would slow down and check planter alignment with my guide before continuing.
I would lower the speed and watch whether the rows become more even.
I would adjust the steering slightly and finish the field pass at this pace.

advanced.situation: Heavy rain softens a field during seeding, and the tractor starts slipping near a sloped section.

options.text: I would keep the same route and increase throttle to clear the soft patch.
I would lower the implement and try crossing the slope at an angle.
I would stop at firm ground and ask the field lead about changing the route.
I would reduce speed and assess traction before choosing a safer route for the next pass.

basic.situation: You are unloading harvested vegetables by hand when crates begin stacking near the edge of the loading area.

options.text: I would ask a coworker to steady the stack while I finish unloading.
I would lower the top crates and ask the team to leave a walkway.
I would move crates away from the edge and keep the path clear.
I would keep stacking crates quickly and clear the space after unloading.

advanced.situation: A truck is waiting while two teams load crop crates through a narrow area, and the hand truck queue is growing.

options.text: I would ask the waiting team to stack crates nearer the truck.
I would pause incoming crates, clear the route, and set one-way traffic at loading.
I would assign one team to load while the other moves crates along the route.
I would stagger the teams and keep hand trucks clear of the loading area.

basic.situation: You are using a hand sprayer on a crop row when wind begins carrying the spray toward a nearby work path.

options.text: I would pause spraying, move away from the path, and resume when drift is lower.
I would pause briefly and check whether the spray is still moving toward the path.
I would continue spraying and finish the row before the wind changes again.
I would lower the sprayer and aim closer to the plants as I finish.

advanced.situation: Several crop rows show signs of disease after recent spraying, and the next planned treatment is due during a windy afternoon.

options.text: I would follow the planned timing and cover the affected rows before evening arrives.
I would reduce spray pressure and treat a short section as a trial.
I would ask the farm lead whether treatment should wait for calmer weather.
I would inspect rows, check product guidance, and reschedule for suitable conditions.

basic.situation: You are attaching a disc implement to a tractor with help, but one hitch pin does not line up with its hole.

options.text: I would ask my helper to guide the tractor back slightly before retrying the pin.
I would stop, realign the tractor and implement, then secure both hitch points.
I would force the pin through and tighten the remaining hitch connections.
I would ask my helper to shift the implement while I hold the pin.

advanced.situation: A sprayer implement must be changed for a new crop, and inspection reveals a leaking hose near the hitch.

options.text: I would ask maintenance whether the hose can remain in service today.
I would connect the sprayer and watch the hose during its first pass.
I would replace the hose, check each connection, and test the sprayer safely.
I would tag the leak for repair and ask the lead to assign another sprayer.

basic.situation: You spot unfamiliar leaf damage while checking weeds in a crop bed, and the treatment guide lists several possible pests.

options.text: I would compare several leaves with the guide and ask the lead to confirm.
I would mark the bed for review and check nearby plants for similar damage.
I would match damage to a guide picture and note the likely pest.
I would check affected plants, record signs, and confirm the pest before treatment.

advanced.situation: New seasonal workers are grading harvested produce, but several disagree about whether bruised items belong in the saleable crates.

options.text: I would let each worker use their usual judgement and review the crates later.
I would ask experienced workers to explain their choices and discuss them with new staff.
I would separate disputed produce, review grading examples, and check a sample with the team.
I would explain the grading rule and review several crates with the team.

basic.situation: You are cleaning a greenhouse walkway when a delivery of produce arrives and the loading area becomes crowded.

options.text: I would clear the walkway first, then help load from the designated area.
I would pause cleaning and ask the loading lead to keep traffic away from the walkway.
I would ask a coworker to watch the walkway while I join the loading team.
I would leave the walkway debris and help move the produce to the truck.

advanced.situation: A truck to storage is due soon, but produce crates are arriving faster than your small team can load them.

options.text: I would ask the driver to wait while the team catches up with the queue.
I would load the nearest crates first and update the lead about the delay.
I would load crates as they arrive and sort out the truck space when it is full.
I would group crates by destination, keep a clear loading route, and tell the lead what remains.

basic.situation: You are hand-harvesting tomatoes when several fruits split as you pick them from the same row.

options.text: I would set the split tomatoes aside and finish the row before reporting it.
I would keep picking at the same pace and put split fruit in with the others.
I would slow my picking, separate split tomatoes, and tell the lead about the row.
I would ask a coworker to check the next few plants while I continue picking.

advanced.situation: New seasonal workers are harvesting ripe fruit, but their crates contain mixed ripeness and some stems are being pulled roughly.

options.text: I would let each worker continue at their own pace and sort the crates later.
I would ask an experienced picker to watch the team and mention any problems.
I would show the team ripe examples and a gentle picking method, then check early crates together.
I would explain the ripeness standard and check the first crates before they leave the row.

basic.situation: You are operating irrigation equipment under supervision when water begins pooling at one end of the bed.

options.text: I would reduce the flow and watch whether the water spreads more evenly.
I would keep the irrigation running and check the pooling after this cycle.
I would check the lines and outlets with my supervisor before restarting the system.
I would pause the system and tell my supervisor where the pooling appeared.

advanced.situation: You are operating a tractor-drawn cultivator across changing soil, and the last pass left uneven rows near a wet patch.

options.text: I would assess row spacing, adjust settings, and inspect the next pass.
I would slow down and watch the cultivator while crossing the field.
I would keep the settings and repeat the pass across the wet patch.
I would ask the lead whether to change settings before making another pass.

basic.situation: You are entering today's crop yield in the farm template, but the handwritten total is difficult to read.

options.text: I would estimate the total from the previous day's yield and note it for review.
I would enter the closest number and submit the crop sheet with today's records.
I would check the tally with the person who recorded it, then enter the confirmed yield.
I would compare the tally with the crate count and ask the lead to review it.

advanced.situation: During a maintenance round, you find a loose implement fitting and discover that recent repair entries are missing from the farm log.

options.text: I would secure the equipment, inspect the fitting, and compare entries with available work notes.
I would note the fitting and schedule a log review after finishing the maintenance round.
I would report the fitting and ask the lead to compare missing entries with work notes.
I would tighten the fitting and add the repairs I remember to the log.

basic.situation: You are checking a crop bed and notice the plants are growing unevenly across one section. What would you tell the farm manager?

options.text: I would report that the crop looks uneven and continue with my assigned work.
I would tell the manager which section looks uneven and offer to check it again.
I would say the crop is doing well because most plants look healthy.
I would report the affected section, describe the uneven growth, and share a few observations.

advanced.situation: Seasonal workers are falling behind during harvest, and the manager needs a progress update before deciding how to use the remaining crew.

options.text: I would tell the crew to speed up and send the manager an update after harvest.
I would report the delay and ask the manager to decide how the team should proceed.
I would report completed rows and the remaining work, then ask the manager about priorities.
I would report completed rows, remaining work, and crew pace, then suggest a task split.

basic.situation: You weigh a young calf and notice a shallow cut near its leg during the morning check.

options.text: Skip the note and use yesterday's weight while the calf settles.
Record the weight and cut, then flag the calf for the planned check.
Reweigh the calf later and tell the lead about the visible cut.
Clean the cut with the yard's usual wash and update the weight sheet.

advanced.situation: Several animals are breathing heavily after handling, and one has stopped eating. You are asked to guide the next health checks.

options.text: Give the group the usual mineral supplement and watch through the afternoon.
Ask workers to check temperatures and report any unusual readings to you.
Move the animals to a quiet pen and note who continues breathing heavily.
Check each animal's breathing and appetite, record changes, and separate concerns for veterinary review.

basic.situation: A senior worker asks you to tag three new goats before they join the marked herd.

options.text: Apply the tags in the order the goats entered the pen.
Match each tag to the herd list, then apply it as shown.
Tag the goats first and copy their numbers onto the list afterward.
Use the spare tags from yesterday and note the goats as new arrivals.

advanced.situation: Two workers report duplicate tag numbers in separate pens, and today's transfer list is due before the herd moves.

options.text: Pause those animals' transfers, compare tags with the herd register, and log confirmed corrections.
Write down both numbers and ask the crew to remember the affected animals.
Retag the animals with the next available numbers and update the register.
Check the register, mark the duplicate entries, and send the list on time.

basic.situation: You are told to separate this morning's piglets by age, using the pen labels already prepared.

options.text: Put the quickest piglets together and finish the remaining group afterward.
Check each label, then guide piglets into their matching age pens.
Sort the piglets by size, since the larger ones look older.
Follow the pen labels and move piglets in small batches.

advanced.situation: A group of market lambs varies in weight, age, and condition, and the scale queue is backing up before dispatch.

options.text: Set separate groups by recorded weight and condition, then sequence weighing before dispatch.
Use the weight records to create batches, then keep the dispatch order moving.
Mix lighter lambs into full batches to clear the pens before dispatch.
Send the largest-looking lambs first and weigh the rest as space opens.

basic.situation: After feeding, you are assigned to wash a pen and its water trough with the supplied cleaning solution.

options.text: Rinse the trough and scrub the pen with the solution left nearby.
Scrub both areas with the supplied solution and rinse the surfaces afterward.
Wash the trough and leave the pen floor for the next cleaning round.
Remove debris, wash the pen and trough, then rinse them as directed.

advanced.situation: A shared wash area is used by staff cleaning two pens, and the next group is due soon. You are coordinating the cleanup.

options.text: Assign tools by pen, clean from the lower-risk area outward, and track completed surfaces.
Ask each worker to finish one pen quickly before the next group arrives.
Post a cleaning order and have workers initial each completed pen.
Reuse the same brushes across both pens to keep the wash area clear.

basic.situation: You need to guide one restless cow from its stall to the nearby holding pen while a senior worker assists.

options.text: Walk ahead and tug the halter toward the holding pen entrance.
Follow the senior worker's pace and keep the cow moving toward the pen.
Open both gates and let the cow choose the wider route.
Clear the path, move calmly beside the cow, and follow the senior worker's signals.

advanced.situation: A large group of cattle must reach the scales before loading, but one passage is crowded and another gate is under repair.

options.text: Move small groups through the clear passage, spacing cattle at the scales.
Send the whole herd through the clear passage to keep loading on schedule.
Move smaller groups through the clear passage, with workers guiding cattle around each turn.
Wait until the scales clear, then move groups through the open passage.

basic.situation: You are assigned to refill water troughs and distribute the morning feed to a small group of goats.

options.text: Pour the usual feed amount and refill the nearest trough afterward.
Refill the troughs and distribute the usual feed portions to the goats.
Give the goats extra feed now so the group stays settled until noon.
Check each trough's level, refill water, then distribute the measured feed portions.

advanced.situation: The feed delivery is short, a tractor route is muddy, and several pens need their scheduled portions before the next shift.

options.text: Check remaining stock, prioritize scheduled rations, and use a safe route for delivery.
Use the dry route and divide available feed fairly among pens according to headcount.
Hand-carry feed to the far pens while the tractor route dries out.
Drive the tractor across the muddy shortcut and finish the nearest pens first.

basic.situation: After landing, you are asked to wash the deck and knives with the crew's supplied brushes and detergent.

options.text: Clear loose catch, scrub the deck and knives, then rinse both areas.
Wash the deck first and stack the knives beside the sink to soak.
Scrub the deck and knives with detergent, then rinse both surfaces.
Rinse the knives and leave the deck for the next crew member.

advanced.situation: A deck conveyor jams during unloading, and the crew needs it working before the next catch is brought aboard.

options.text: Clear the jam by hand while another crew member watches the controls.
Isolate the conveyor's power, inspect the jam, and make a minor repair within your training.
Use a hooked tool to pull out the catch and restart the conveyor slowly.
Ask the crew to pause unloading while you inspect the conveyor and its belt.

basic.situation: You are travelling by boat with an experienced crew member to reach a familiar fishing area before daylight.

options.text: Follow the familiar route and ask the crew member when landmarks are unclear.
Follow the other boat toward the area and keep the shoreline in view.
Check the marked route, follow the crew member's guidance, and monitor the boat's position.
Head toward the usual area and adjust course when the crew member calls.

advanced.situation: Dark clouds build across the route, the sea is roughening, and the vessel begins handling differently as you approach the fishing grounds.

options.text: Reduce speed, check instruments, and ask the crew to watch sea conditions.
Compare weather and vessel response, turn toward shelter, and update the crew.
Continue toward the grounds while watching the clouds and checking vessel instruments.
Turn back along the known route and monitor vessel response while returning.

basic.situation: You are shown how to attach floats and weights to a net before it is set for the day's fishing.

options.text: Match each float and weight to the marked positions, then check the attachments.
Attach the floats first and add weights wherever the line sags.
Tie the floats to one side and let the crew adjust the weights later.
Follow the demonstrated pattern and connect the floats and weights along the net.

advanced.situation: The crew is preparing traps for two target species with different sizes and habits, and you are asked to guide the setup.

options.text: Use the familiar trap layout for both species to keep setup moving.
Place the traps in separate areas and let each worker choose the bait.
Set separate layouts for each species, matching bait and trap placement to their known habits.
Use the usual bait for each species and mark traps by target group.

basic.situation: You remove fish from the nets and are asked to measure them against the minimum size marked on the boat's guide.

options.text: Measure each fish against the guide and separate undersized catches for release.
Measure the catch and set aside fish that appear below the marked size.
Place the fish in the sale basket and check sizes after unloading.
Measure the larger fish first and keep smaller ones in a separate tub.

advanced.situation: A mixed catch includes several species, some close to the size guide's limits, while the crew is preparing to transfer it ashore.

options.text: Sort by species and measure fish that look close to the guide's limits.
Measure every fish quickly and stack the catch by approximate size.
Transfer the full catch ashore and sort it when the landing crew is ready.
Sort by species, measure borderline catches against the guide, and keep unverified fish apart.

basic.situation: During net retrieval, a crew member asks which line to pull while the supervisor is occupied on deck.

options.text: Tell the crew member to pull the line nearest the winch.
Point to the next line in the sequence and keep watch on the retrieval.
Check the agreed retrieval sequence and direct the crew member to the next line.
Ask another experienced deckhand which line the crew usually pulls next.

advanced.situation: Two crew members disagree about retrieval order as the catch shifts and the deck becomes crowded.

options.text: Restate retrieval order and have each crew member confirm their assigned line.
Let the more experienced crew member choose the order while others keep working.
Pause conflicting pulls, assign positions, and restart in the agreed order.
Move the catch clear first, then hear both crew members' suggestions.

basic.situation: You are helping prepare a fishing trip and need to list the supplies and gear the crew will need.

options.text: Check the trip plan, count usable gear, and list supplies that need replenishing.
Copy the previous trip's list and add extra fuel for the boat.
List the usual gear and ask the crew to bring any missing items.
Review the trip plan and write down the expected supplies and gear.

advanced.situation: Several trips are planned, replacement nets are delayed, and the remaining supply budget must cover essential gear and routine items.

options.text: Delay routine purchases and use remaining funds for replacement nets first.
Compare trip needs with usable stock, prioritize essential replacements, and record the budget trade-offs.
Check current stock and costs, then draft a purchase list for the planned trips.
Order the usual net quantity now so crews have familiar equipment for each trip.

basic.situation: You are cutting trees marked for thinning, and two nearby trunks have similar paint marks. How do you select the next tree?

options.text: Cut the tree whose paint mark looks clearest from your current position.
Follow the nearest painted mark and keep the thinning line moving.
Check the tree's mark and size against the work instructions before cutting.
Match the paint mark to the instructions, then cut that tree.

advanced.situation: A tree has discoloured foliage and a cracked limb near a work area. You have a power saw and are assigned to remove diseased trees. What do you do?

options.text: Inspect the defect, clear the fall zone, and use the saw from a safe position.
Cut it while workers pass nearby, keeping the saw at a steady speed.
Check the tree's condition and fall area, then remove it with the power saw.
Ask nearby workers to move, then cut the diseased tree from its current side.

basic.situation: After clearing a campsite, you find a pile of dry brush beside a fire break. You are assigned to dispose of brush for fire protection. What do you do?

options.text: Leave the pile beside the fire break until the next crew arrives.
Move the brush to the designated disposal area and keep the fire break clear.
Carry the brush away from the fire break to an open patch.
Move the brush beside the nearest path for easier collection later.

advanced.situation: A fire officer directs you to help with a prescribed burn, but wind gusts begin shifting smoke toward the crew's access route. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the officer smoke is shifting, then hold position while awaiting further direction.
Continue the planned burn pace while telling the officer smoke is nearing the route.
Report the smoke shift to the officer, then move clear as directed.
Keep tending the assigned edge while monitoring where gusts carry the smoke.

basic.situation: You are planting a reforestation plot and have seedlings with different root lengths. How do you choose seedlings and prepare each planting spot?

options.text: Use the manual tool to set each suitable seedling at its proper depth.
Plant the seedlings quickly wherever the soil looks soft enough.
Plant the largest seedlings first in the easiest ground to reach.
Choose sound seedlings and loosen each spot with the manual planting tool.

advanced.situation: You are operating a skidder to pull scarification equipment across a regeneration site. The ground softens near a marked boundary. How do you proceed?

options.text: Slow down and watch the tracks while pulling across the softer section.
Check the ground and boundary, then adjust the route before pulling the equipment.
Keep to the planned line and pull the equipment across the soft ground.
Assess the soft patch and pull the scarifier around its edge.

basic.situation: You are assigned to spray vegetation with insecticide, and the wind picks up across the plot. What do you do?

options.text: Spray along the row quickly before the wind changes again.
Check the product instructions and wind, then spray from the planned position.
Pause at the row edge and wait for the wind to ease.
Check the instructions and wind direction, then position yourself to limit drift.

advanced.situation: You are tallying trees examined during marking. A rain-wet page has a smudged entry, and the crew is ready to move on. How do you handle the count?

options.text: Copy the visible total and move the crew to the next area.
Rewrite the visible figures on a dry page before the crew leaves.
Ask the marker to confirm the unclear entry, then copy the tally.
Check the smudged entry against the marked trees and update the tally clearly.

basic.situation: Before field work, you check a brush cutter and notice its guard is loose. What do you do?

options.text: Start cutting slowly and watch the loose guard during the first pass.
Tighten the guard and check that the cutter runs smoothly before work.
Tag the cutter for repair and use the next available machine.
Check the guard and controls, secure the loose part, then test operation.

advanced.situation: You sort seedlings against a standard chart before planting, and one tray contains roots that look damaged. What do you do?

options.text: Keep the seedlings that look sturdy and set aside the visibly damaged roots.
Use the chart to remove obvious rejects, then sort the rest by size.
Set aside the damaged roots and plant the rest of the tray.
Compare the tray with the chart and discard seedlings that fail its criteria.

basic.situation: Before thinning starts, workers disagree about cutting heights and one escape route is partly blocked. What do you do?

options.text: Discuss the cutting heights and clear the blocked route with the crew.
Pause the start and ask each worker what height they prefer.
Agree the cutting height, clear the route, and confirm the crew's shared plan.
Start at the agreed height and ask others to clear the route later.

advanced.situation: A camper asks whether a small fire is allowed near a dry brush area. You are helping explain and enforce campsite fire rules. What do you say?

options.text: Tell the camper to keep the fire small and watch it closely.
Explain that fires belong in the designated area and ask them to move.
Explain the site rule and direct the camper to the designated fire area.
Ask the camper to check the posted fire guidance before lighting it.

basic.situation: You are assessing a tree for felling and notice rot near its base and a heavy limb on one side. What do you check next?

options.text: Check the rot and heavy limb, then plan around the trunk's apparent lean.
Look from the open side and estimate whether the tree can be felled.
Check the rot, limb growth, and lean before sharing your assessment.
Focus on the rot and leave the limb and lean for the felling crew.

advanced.situation: A new faller asks you to help assess a twisted tree on sloping ground after rain. How do you guide their felling assessment?

options.text: Review the twist and slope with them, then state your chosen fall direction.
Point out the twist and slope, then suggest the usual direction of fall.
Show the faller how twist, lean, ground, and weather shape the felling assessment.
Tell the faller to use your chosen direction and prepare the saw.

basic.situation: Under close supervision, you begin an undercut and back cut on a tree with a clear fall line. What do you do?

options.text: Check the scored line, then make the undercut and back cut as directed.
Keep the cuts close to the line and watch for movement as you saw.
Make the undercut on the line, then finish the back cut to meet it.
Follow the scored line and leave enough sound wood in the back cut.

advanced.situation: On a sloped site, your saw begins binding while you make a planned felling cut. You have wedges available. What do you do?

options.text: Force the saw through the cut before the tree shifts on the slope.
Tap a wedge into the cut while keeping the saw running nearby.
Pause the saw and check whether the tree has started to move.
Stop cutting, assess the bind, and place a wedge to keep the kerf open.

basic.situation: You are measuring a felled tree for specified log lengths, but a section has a split near the cut mark. What do you do?

options.text: Measure the lengths and mark each cut where the log looks sound.
Ask the supervisor where to cut, then measure the remaining sections.
Measure the specified lengths and check the split before cutting the section.
Cut the listed lengths quickly and sort out the split afterward.

advanced.situation: You are cutting logs for two buyer specifications, and a trunk has variable quality along its length. How do you choose the cut sequence?

options.text: Mark lengths by buyer specification and place the soundest sections in higher-grade logs.
Cut uniform lengths across the trunk to keep the crew's pace steady.
Cut the standard lengths first, then sort the logs by visible quality.
Measure each buyer's lengths and mark the trunk before starting cuts.

basic.situation: You are clearing brush from an escape route and spot an unstable tree nearby. What do you do?

options.text: Clear around the tree and tell the next crew about its condition.
Clear the route, mark the unstable tree, and keep workers clear of it.
Cut the unstable tree first so the route stays open afterward.
Mark the unstable tree with ribbon, then finish clearing the route.

advanced.situation: You are asked to plan brush clearing near several marked trees and escape routes on uneven ground. How do you set the work sequence?

options.text: Map the escape routes and marked trees, then order clearing to protect both.
Set the escape routes first, then clear brush around marked trees.
Start clearing the widest area so the crew can work faster.
Clear the easiest route first and check marked trees as work progresses.

basic.situation: You are helping load logs onto a truck, and one log could roll as the loader raises it. What do you do?

options.text: Help load it from the truck side while watching closely for any movement.
Ask the loader operator to lift slowly while you guide the log.
Attach a chain and lift the log before the truck queue grows.
Support the log, then help load it from a clear position.

advanced.situation: A crew is dragging logs with a tractor while another team loads nearby. The cable path crosses their work area. How do you coordinate the move?

options.text: Secure the cable and coordinate a clear path before the tractor moves.
Check the cable attachment and ask loaders to stand clear during the pull.
Attach the cable and start dragging while the loaders finish nearby.
Signal the tractor operator to pull slowly past the loading crew.

basic.situation: After a shift, you are cleaning and oiling your chainsaw and notice a dull chain. What do you do?

options.text: Oil the chain and check whether it cuts smoothly next shift.
Wipe the saw and put it away so the crew can leave on time.
Clean and oil the saw, then set aside the dull chain for later.
Clean and oil the saw, then sharpen the chain to the proper profile.

advanced.situation: A chainsaw stalls repeatedly during a shift, and a newer worker asks how to maintain it. What do you do?

options.text: Show the worker how you clean the saw and ask them to try again.
Adjust the engine settings until the saw holds a steady idle.
Swap to another saw and leave this one for the next maintenance round.
Diagnose the fault within your training and show the worker routine checks.

basic.situation: You need to move marked logs from a felling site to the landing before the next load arrives. The marked route passes close to a soft patch.

options.text: Check the marked trail, then use the winch to bring logs in sequence.
Drag the nearest logs through the soft hollow to keep the route short.
Ask the landing crew to guide the tractor while you move each log.
Drive the tractor along the marked route and winch logs to the landing.

advanced.situation: Rain has softened one skid trail, while the landing queue is growing. You must choose a tractor route that keeps logs moving and limits soil damage.

options.text: Take the shortest line through the saturated patch to clear the queue.
Study ground firmness and slope, then route loaded skids over durable ridges.
Follow yesterday's route and keep the tractor moving at a steady pace.
Compare soil conditions at two crossings, then alternate traffic to protect ground.

basic.situation: A harvester is cutting a straight, sound tree into the requested lengths. You notice the next stem is close to the marked cutting area.

options.text: Use the harvester to limb the stem and cut each requested length.
Cut the stem to the usual lengths to keep the harvester cycle quick.
Swing the boom clear, then limb and cut the stem to its marked lengths.
Continue the current cut pattern and move the stem past the marked area.

advanced.situation: On sloping ground, a harvester stem has a bend near the butt and a branch beside the cut zone. The buyer's length specification is unchanged.

options.text: Cut from the current position and sort any damaged lengths at the landing.
Adjust the head position for the slope, then check the bend before cutting.
Keep the usual settings and cut the stem into the requested lengths.
Move the head past the branch and use a shorter cut sequence.

basic.situation: Brush is blocking a short section of the designated logging road. Your tractor's blade is ready, and a loaded truck is due soon.

options.text: Clear the brush in small passes and leave the road surface even.
Move the largest brush first so the truck can pass sooner.
Use the blade to clear brush from the marked road section.
Push the brush into the nearest roadside drain to clear the lane.

advanced.situation: A logging road has ruts after heavy rain, and trucks are losing traction on a steep section. You are operating the tractor assigned to road repairs.

options.text: Push loose soil downhill to reopen the truck lane before the next load.
Check rut depth and drainage, then repair the slope in stable layers.
Grade the ruts first and ask the next driver how the slope feels.
Fill the visible ruts and smooth the steep section in one pass.

basic.situation: Before your shift, you find a loose guard near a tractor's moving linkage during the pre-use inspection. The machine has not started.

options.text: Tighten the guard, then check that it stays clear of the linkage.
Start the tractor slowly and listen for any unusual sound.
Tell the mechanic about the loose guard and wait for advice.
Mark the guard with chalk and check it again after the first run.

advanced.situation: During inspection, you hear a new grinding sound and see fresh metal dust near a tractor joint. The next crew is scheduled to use it after your shift.

options.text: Grease the joint and note that it sounded rough during inspection.
Record the noise and dust, then flag the joint for a focused maintenance check.
Wipe away the dust and run the tractor briefly to hear the joint again.
Add grease and tell the next operator to watch the joint during use.

basic.situation: A stack contains logs of mixed lengths and visible knots. Your tally needs a board-foot total before the load leaves the landing.

options.text: Use the average length and count the stack as one group.
Grade each log by the checklist, then use the conversion table for totals.
Sort similar lengths together and calculate each group from the table.
Count the logs and apply the usual conversion for this landing.

advanced.situation: Two operators disagree about a knotty batch's grade, and the buyer's measurement is due shortly. The company checklist gives criteria for knot size and straightness.

options.text: Use the stricter operator's grade so the batch can be tallied soon.
Compare samples against knot and straightness criteria, then explain the grade decision.
Review the checklist against one sample, then use that grade for similar logs.
Ask both operators to grade separate parts and average their results.

basic.situation: Your shift report asks for the number of loads and any machine downtime. You have the tally book and notes from a short stoppage.

options.text: Copy the load count and downtime from your notes into the report.
Ask a coworker to confirm the load count before completing the form.
Enter the usual load count and leave the stoppage field blank.
Reconcile the tally and stoppage notes, then complete each report field.

advanced.situation: While reviewing shift reports, you find one load count differs from the tally book and another report has a blank downtime entry. The records are not yet filed.

options.text: Ask the operators to resend their reports after their next shift.
Revise both reports using the tally and notes, then record each change.
Use the tally book count and leave the downtime entry as submitted.
Copy the higher load count into both reports and file them together.

basic.situation: A log has a large knot near one end and otherwise looks straight. You need to assign its grade using the checklist at the landing.

options.text: Check knot limits on the checklist, then assign the log's grade.
Use the grade most common for logs from this cutting area.
Set the log aside for another grader to review at the landing.
Compare the knot with a similar log graded during this shift.

advanced.situation: A new batch has unusual knot patterns, and two graders are assigning different grades. The existing criteria cover knot size and straightness but give limited examples.

options.text: Review the criteria with the other graders and compare several sample logs.
Use the lower grade for all disputed logs to keep the tally moving.
Compare disputed samples with both criteria and document how each feature affects grade.
Ask the most experienced grader to choose the grade for the batch.

basic.situation: You inspect a load before tallying it and spot a split end and several large knots. The driver is waiting to unload at the landing.

options.text: Check the split end and let the knots pass as normal.
Point out the defects to the grader and ask them to confirm the load.
Mark the split logs and finish the remaining load inspection later.
Inspect the split and knots, then note each visible defect for grading.

advanced.situation: A coworker finds no obvious damage in a batch, but several logs have subtle twists and curves. The tally is due before the truck leaves.

options.text: Show the coworker how to sight along each log and compare its curve with the criteria.
Demonstrate sighting along a few logs, then have the coworker inspect the rest.
Ask the coworker to mark any logs that look unusual for your review.
Inspect the most curved logs and let the rest follow the batch pattern.

basic.situation: A felled log must be bucked to the marked specification. Your tape measure is ready, and the saw operator is waiting for the length call.

options.text: Use the previous log's length and mark this bole at the same point.
Measure from the butt and mark the specified bucking length clearly.
Measure quickly from the nearest end and call out the result.
Check the specification, measure the bole, then mark the cut point.

advanced.situation: A buyer's volume total differs from your tally for a mixed load. One log length was entered twice, and a second measurement is close to the cutoff.

options.text: Recheck the close measurement, remove the duplicate, and recalculate from the log entries.
Use the buyer's total so the truck can continue to the mill.
Compare the totals and ask the buyer which measurement method they used.
Remove the duplicate and recalculate the load from your recorded lengths.

basic.situation: A batch includes two grades of the same species. The marking guide assigns a different paint color to each grade, and you are asked to mark the logs.

options.text: Use the color from the first log across the full batch.
Separate the grades first, then paint each group using the guide.
Check each grade on the tally, then paint its specified identification color.
Ask the marker beside you which color they used for each grade.

advanced.situation: A species not listed on the usual marking sheet arrives with two apparent grades. Your supervisor has provided provisional colors for this batch, but examples vary.

options.text: Keep the batch aside until a revised marking sheet becomes available.
Mark clear examples by provisional grade and group uncertain logs for review.
Use the color assigned to the nearest listed species for every log.
Apply provisional colors by recorded grade, noting any logs that remain unclear.
