basic.situation: You tally individual logs and a truck's before-and-after weights during a busy landing shift. The terminal asks for supplier identity and load volume.

options.text: Record the weights and volume now, then add the supplier from the ticket.
Enter each log and both weights, then match them to the supplier record.
Write the supplier and total on paper for entry after the queue clears.
Enter the total volume and reuse the supplier from the previous truck.

advanced.situation: A review shows repeated volume entries in one terminal and missing supplier identities in another. The original tally sheets and weighbridge slips are available.

options.text: Match entries to tally sheets and slips, resolve duplicates, and flag missing identities.
Remove repeated volumes and copy the last supplier name into blanks.
Ask the terminal user to review the entries when their shift ends.
Compare duplicate volumes with tally sheets and list blank supplier fields for later review.

basic.situation: A loader is preparing to move a log beside two coworkers. You have a clear view of the path and are assigned to signal the movement.

options.text: Wait for the loader to choose a direction, then signal the lift.
Check the path, then signal the loader with agreed hand signs.
Ask one coworker to watch the far end as you signal the move.
Give the usual signal while the coworkers step out of the way.

advanced.situation: A truck is due at the mill while several logs need regrading or recutting. You are checking the logs and relaying movement signals to the crew.

options.text: Hold the logs in place until the truck driver chooses a mill.
Identify logs needing rework, check their destination, and signal the crew to move those first.
Send all affected logs to the nearest mill to clear the landing.
Sort logs by action, signal safe moves, and confirm each mill destination.

basic.situation: Two workers are absent from a small site crew. Your supervisor asks you to assign the day's tasks while a concrete delivery is expected.

options.text: I assign available workers to the urgent tasks and update my supervisor.
I send the full crew to the first task on the board.
I match workers to the delivery and urgent tasks, then confirm access timing.
I keep the usual assignments and ask the present crew to work faster.

advanced.situation: A delayed material delivery overlaps with another contractor's planned access. Your crews have a tight deadline, and you are coordinating the work schedule.

options.text: I keep the original sequence and have both crews share the access route.
I agree a revised access window, then resequence crews around available work.
I move my crew onto available work and notify the contractor.
I hold my crew at the workface until the delivery arrives.

basic.situation: You are helping set out a small equipment pad. The drawing gives two measurements, and your supervisor asks you to mark the location.

options.text: I measure from the nearest reference and mark the pad corners.
I check both drawing dimensions from the stated reference before marking corners.
I copy the first measurement and ask my supervisor to confirm the other.
I mark the corners from the fence line because it looks square.

advanced.situation: A plan shows a structure close to a sloping boundary, but the ground markers seem offset. Your crew needs a location before starting excavation.

options.text: I ask the crew to begin the accessible section while I review the plan.
I shift the marks toward level ground and tell the crew the change.
I recheck the dimensions from the plan reference and flag the mismatch.
I compare plan references and field marks, then pause excavation pending clarification.

basic.situation: You are checking a small work area before a task begins. A worker has left a power tool cord across the main walking route.

options.text: I step over the cord and start the inspection at the far end.
I have the cord rerouted, then check the walking route is clear.
I ask the worker to move the cord before the task starts.
I place a cone beside the cord and tell workers to watch their step.

advanced.situation: During a site check, you see a temporary platform beside ongoing work. Its access is partly blocked by stacked materials, and workers are approaching.

options.text: I ask the crew to move the materials and keep the work area open.
I clear the access route and inspect the platform before workers proceed.
I place a barrier near the platform while the crew finishes nearby work.
I tell workers to use the platform carefully around the materials.

basic.situation: Your crew is preparing a small concrete repair. You are asked to list the materials needed, and the measured area is smaller than first expected.

options.text: I reduce the estimate by a small amount and note the change.
I list the planned quantity and tell my supervisor about the smaller area.
I order the original quantity so the crew has extra material.
I recalculate from the measured area and check the list with my supervisor.

advanced.situation: Two work fronts need the same supply, and storage space is limited. A delivery is due soon, while one crew's quantities have changed.

options.text: I request the usual quantities for both crews to protect their progress.
I request a large buffer so neither crew runs short during the work.
I compare both crews' updated needs and stagger orders against available storage.
I ask each crew to send revised quantities before placing the supply request.

basic.situation: At the end of a shift, you are completing a daily report. One worker's hours are missing, but the crew has already left site.

options.text: I enter the usual hours so the report can be sent on time.
I check the attendance record, enter supported hours, and mark any gap clearly.
I leave the hours blank and send the report to my supervisor.
I record the hours I know and flag the missing entry for follow-up.

advanced.situation: Your weekly reports show different output totals for two similar work areas. Management wants the figures for a progress review, and you maintain the records.

options.text: I report the higher total and mention the difference in a note.
I send both totals to management and ask which figure to use.
I highlight the inconsistent totals and provide the source reports for review.
I compare source entries, reconcile the totals, and explain any remaining gap.

basic.situation: A new worker is learning to use a hand tool for a simple task. You are asked to demonstrate the method while other crew members prepare the work area.

options.text: I hand over the tool and ask the worker to copy my last cut.
I demonstrate the grip, explain the safe motion, then observe a practice cut.
I show the grip and cutting motion, then let the worker practice nearby.
I explain the tool parts and let the worker try on spare material.

advanced.situation: A recurring handoff problem is slowing two crews, and a new supervisor is learning your methods. You are asked to recommend a practical improvement.

options.text: I ask each crew for its concerns and report them to management.
I assign the blame to the slower crew and recommend a personnel transfer.
I tell the new supervisor to remind both crews to communicate more.
I map handoff steps with both crews, then coach the supervisor on shared check-ins.

basic.situation: You visit a home where trees shade part of the roof. The customer asks whether the roof can support a small solar system.

options.text: I would photograph roof obstructions and record usable dimensions before recommending a layout.
I would compare roof space, shading, and meter details with the site checklist.
I would sketch the roof, note shade, and ask about daytime use.
I would estimate from roof area and send the usual panel layout.

advanced.situation: A warehouse roof has shaded sections and limited access. Your first layout exceeds the budget, and the client asks you to reduce costs.

options.text: I would ask the supplier for a lower price on the same panel package.
I would compare layouts that avoid shade and access hazards, then price their trade-offs.
I would reduce the panel count and revise the quote around the new layout.
I would move panels onto shaded sections to preserve the planned panel count.

basic.situation: You are helping quote a small home installation. The site notes include roof measurements, an inverter choice, and a clear access route.

options.text: I would reuse last month's quote and adjust the total slightly.
I would list panels, rails, inverter, and labour from the site notes.
I would check quantities against roof measurements, then price each listed item.
I would include access gear and crew hours, then flag assumptions clearly.

advanced.situation: A commercial job needs a revised budget after a delivery delay shifts the installation schedule and the client asks whether the margin can hold.

options.text: I would preserve the original schedule and budget to keep the proposal stable.
I would add a general delay allowance to the current project budget.
I would compare revised labour and equipment costs against the new schedule assumptions.
I would map schedule options to crew, equipment, and cost impacts before revising margin.

basic.situation: You see an installer preparing to work on a roof section. Their fall-protection gear is nearby, but they have not put it on.

options.text: I would remind the installer about the gear and watch the next task.
I would check the gear with the installer and remind the crew of the site rule.
I would ask the crew to finish this section first, then check their gear.
I would pause that roof task, confirm the gear is fitted, and resume once ready.

advanced.situation: A subcontractor's crew is installing rails along a revised roof line, but their work no longer matches the approved layout or planned sequence.

options.text: I would record the rail position and discuss the layout difference with the lead.
I would ask the crew lead to realign the rails before work continues.
I would pause the rail work and compare the layout with approved drawings.
I would review the changed section with the lead and agree a safe sequence.

basic.situation: The home installation is ready for a building inspection, and the customer asks when the inspector can visit.

options.text: I would give the customer an estimated visit window after checking the booking schedule.
I would book an open slot and notify the site team afterward.
I would confirm readiness, request an open slot, then share timing with customer and crew.
I would check the site team's readiness before requesting an inspection appointment.

advanced.situation: A commercial PV layout differs from the drawings used for inspection planning. The change affects equipment access and the installation sequence.

options.text: I would compare the revised layout with the applicable project requirements and update the inspection sequence.
I would keep the original inspection plan and explain the layout change onsite.
I would check the revised layout against the approved drawings before planning inspection steps.
I would ask the installer which inspection steps seem affected by the change.

basic.situation: You are assisting with startup at a home installation. The crew has completed wiring and asks you to begin the initial system checks.

options.text: I would start the inverter and watch for its normal display.
I would energize the system before checking the commissioning notes.
I would follow the startup checklist with the supervisor and record each reading.
I would check the inverter display and report any warning to the supervisor.

advanced.situation: During a commercial system check, output is below the expected level, though the inverter shows no warning and several strings share the same roof zone.

options.text: I would inspect visible cables and panel surfaces for obvious issues.
I would reset the inverter and record whether the output improves.
I would compare system, string, and component readings to isolate the underperforming section.
I would compare the system output with the expected figure and inform the lead.

basic.situation: A small installation needs a lift for one day. You are asked to arrange suitable rental equipment within the job budget.

options.text: I would book the familiar lift for the requested day after confirming availability.
I would compare rental dates and daily rates against the job allowance before booking.
I would match lift capacity to site access, then confirm its rental cost.
I would check route access and compare lift rental rates before reserving equipment.

advanced.situation: Installers report that a planned inverter model does not fit the site's electrical arrangement. The delivery is scheduled soon, and the crew needs guidance.

options.text: I would compare system requirements with compatible models and advise the crew.
I would check the order record and tell the crew to hold the inverter installation.
I would tell the crew to adapt the connections to fit the delivered inverter.
I would confirm the model details and ask the supplier for a compatible alternative.

basic.situation: You need to mark cutting lines on a steel plate from a template, but the first measurement differs slightly from the drawing.

options.text: Copy old plate marks and cut to them before checking the drawing.
Measure from the drawing datum and mark cut lines with a square.
Mark the template lines, then ask a fitter to check the first mark.
Use the template and tape measure, comparing marks with the drawing.

advanced.situation: Two assembly drawings show different locations for a boiler connection, and the plate layout is due before the shift ends.

options.text: Compare revision details and dimensions, then flag the conflict before laying out that area.
Mark the location from one drawing and note the other dimension for review.
Use the newer drawing and mark the connection location for the team.
Follow the drawing used on the last boiler and keep the layout moving.

basic.situation: A delivered boiler plate has a shallow bend near its edge, and you are asked to straighten it with a jack.

options.text: Apply steady jack pressure, then inspect the edge from the side.
Strike the bend with a hammer until the edge looks level.
Ask a nearby fitter to hold the straightedge while you make small adjustments.
Use the jack at the bend and check the plate against a straightedge.

advanced.situation: A new chute must fit around existing pipework, but the available plate differs slightly from the dimensions on the premises sketch.

options.text: Measure the clearances, revise the pattern, and shape a trial section before finishing.
Cut the chute to the sketch dimensions and bend the edges to fit.
Adjust the pattern from a site measurement and shape the chute in stages.
Trim the plate edges slightly and use the available clamps to pull it into place.

basic.situation: You are bolting a small boiler support bracket in place, and one hole seems slightly out of line.

options.text: Tighten bolts lightly, then check the bracket sits flat against its support.
Check hole alignment and hand-start each bolt before applying even tightening.
Start bolts loosely, then ask fitter to verify bracket position before tightening.
Use a drift pin to align the holes, then tighten each bolt evenly.

advanced.situation: A repair team finds a tube-end joint leaking during a test, and the surrounding tubes make access difficult.

options.text: Have a welder repair the joint and record the location for retesting.
Add weld over the visible leak and ask for another pressure test.
Tell the crew to use the same repair sequence as the last tube joint.
Assess access and joint condition, then agree a repair sequence with the crew.

basic.situation: You are assisting with a hoist lift of a boiler frame section, and the signal line is partly blocked by stacked materials.

options.text: Ask a coworker to watch the load while you signal from beside it.
Pause the signal, clear the sightline, and resume when the operator acknowledges.
Give the usual lifting signal from your current position beside the stacked materials.
Move to a visible position and confirm the operator can see your signal.

advanced.situation: A heavy boiler section is nearly aligned with its frame, but the marked landing point is obscured and the crew is waiting for your signal.

options.text: Have the crew identify the landing point, then guide the section with agreed signals.
Use a tag line to pull the section toward the frame marks as it lowers.
Ask the operator to hold while you check the frame marks from a clear position.
Signal the operator to lower slowly while the crew estimates the section's alignment.

basic.situation: You are visually checking a newly assembled vessel and notice a small irregularity near one fitting.

options.text: Look over the nearby fittings and record the irregularity for the work sheet.
Assume the mark came from handling and continue to the next vessel.
Wipe the area and check the fitting closely for visible damage or leakage.
Mark the irregularity and tell the fitter after the assembly is moved.

advanced.situation: During a pressure test, the gauge reading drops slightly while the crew sees no obvious leak around the vessel.

options.text: Check the gauge connection and test setup, then follow the approved test procedure.
Record the drop and ask the test lead whether to repeat the test.
Inspect visible joints for seepage and take another gauge reading after a short wait.
Continue the test at the same pressure and note the lower gauge reading.

basic.situation: After scraping residue from a vessel fitting, you need to clean the tool and nearby work area before the next task.

options.text: Spray solvent on the tool and set it beside the work area to dry.
Wipe the tool on a rag and leave the area for the next shift.
Brush the tool and wipe the work area using the approved solvent.
Brush the tool clean and collect the residue before returning it.

advanced.situation: A maintenance crew is cleaning a vessel with stubborn deposits, and the usual brush-and-solvent method leaves residue in narrow seams.

options.text: Ask each worker to clean the seams using the tool they prefer.
Repeat the usual brushing and let the maintenance crew inspect the result.
Choose a suitable scraper and brush sequence, then inspect the seams before release.
Mark the affected seams and ask the crew to give them extra brushing.

basic.situation: You need to mark a wall guideline from a reference point before the crew starts laying bricks. How do you set it out?

options.text: Copy the previous course's line so the crew can start laying sooner.
Set the datum with a level, then compare both ends before marking.
Use the marked reference, set the level, and ask the mason to check alignment.
Measure from the nearest wall and mark a line matching its edge.

advanced.situation: A drawing shows a stepped wall beside an existing footing. You must estimate brick quantities and check the planned alignment before ordering materials. What do you do?

options.text: Measure the footing and use its length to scale the wall quantities.
Count each wall section from the drawing and add a small allowance for cuts.
Use the longest wall length and order a rounded quantity from the supplier.
Break the drawing into sections, calculate each quantity, and check dimensions against site references.

basic.situation: You are asked to prepare a batch of mortar powder and sand for a routine bricklaying job. How do you mix it?

options.text: Measure the stated sand and powder, add water gradually, and mix under the foreman's guidance.
Fill the bucket by eye and stir until the batch looks workable.
Use the previous batch's proportions and add a little extra water for easier spreading.
Follow the stated amounts, then ask the foreman to check the texture before use.

advanced.situation: Hot, windy weather is drying mortar quickly during a long wall job. You are showing a new worker how to prepare the next batch. What do you do?

options.text: Add extra water so the mortar stays soft while the crew lays bricks.
Use the normal batch size and remind the worker to cover the mortar between uses.
Mix the usual amount and ask the worker to watch its consistency in the heat.
Keep the approved proportions, mix smaller batches, and explain how to limit drying time.

basic.situation: A brick needs trimming to fit the end of a short course. You have a hammer and a trowel edge. What do you do?

options.text: Mark the cut line, support the brick, and tap along it with the hammer.
Score the line with the trowel, then ask the mason to guide the break.
Tap the brick at the edge until a piece breaks off to fit.
Use the nearest spare half brick and leave the gap for mortar.

advanced.situation: A visible brick feature needs several narrow pieces, and chipped edges would spoil the finish. Which cutting approach do you choose?

options.text: Use a hammer for every piece because it is already beside the work area.
Use a power saw with a suitable blade and support each piece through the cut.
Ask another mason which tool they used on a similar feature last month.
Test one cut with the saw, then use the same method for the remaining pieces.

basic.situation: You are fastening a short brick section to an existing structure with wire clamps. How do you proceed?

options.text: Use extra mortar around the joint instead of fitting the wire clamp.
Fasten the clamp where the brick meets the structure and continue the course.
Fit the clamp as shown and ask the mason to inspect the connection.
Position the clamp at the marked point, secure it, and check the brick sits firmly.

advanced.situation: A long wall must meet a corner pole, and small alignment errors could carry across several courses. How do you set up the work?

options.text: Use the existing wall edge as the guide and adjust the corner bricks by eye.
Set the pole with a level, then have the mason check the first few courses.
Set the corner pole plumb, build a short pyramid, and check each course against the line.
Raise the corner quickly and let the crew fill between it and the next corner.

basic.situation: Fresh mortar is squeezing out between bricks as you finish a short wall section. What do you do?

options.text: Wipe the mortar across the face and tidy the bricks at the end.
Remove the squeeze-out with a trowel and ask the mason to finish the joint.
Trim the excess with a trowel, then smooth the joint with the jointing tool.
Scrape away the visible mortar with the trowel and leave the joint as it is.

advanced.situation: Two apprentices are finishing a visible wall, and their joints vary in depth and shape. How do you guide the next section?

options.text: Ask them to finish quickly, then smooth the whole wall yourself later.
Tell them to make the joints look similar to the last wall.
Demonstrate the jointing tool once and let each apprentice continue at their pace.
Show a finished sample, set the joint profile, and check the next section together.

basic.situation: A small damaged patch of mortar must be removed before repointing. You have a chisel and hand tools. What do you do?

options.text: Set the chisel on the damaged mortar and work along the patch with controlled taps.
Chip out the visible patch with firm blows and clear the loose pieces.
Start at the patch edge and ask the mason to guide the chisel angle.
Break out the nearby brick as well so the repair area is easier to reach.

advanced.situation: Several bricks around a damaged section sound loose, and the wall carries a nearby load. How do you approach removal?

options.text: Mark the loose bricks and ask the mason to review the removal sequence.
Mark the damaged area, check its extent, and arrange the approved safe support before removal.
Clear the loose mortar around the bricks so the crew can judge the damage better.
Remove the visibly cracked bricks first and see whether the wall settles afterward.

basic.situation: A stone slab needs trimming to fit a prepared opening. You are assigned the power saw with guidance. What do you do?

options.text: Cut freehand, then grind uneven edges after checking how the slab fits.
Mark the cut, secure the slab, and follow the mason's saw setup guidance.
Align the saw with the opening, then trim the slab edge to fit.
Mark the edge, then ask the mason to check saw setup before cutting.

advanced.situation: A polished stone panel has a chipped corner and a visible crack nearby. You are asked to repair the damaged area. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the mason which mastic was used on the previous stone panel repair.
Fill the chip with available mastic, then polish near the visible crack.
Assess the crack and chip, choose a compatible repair method, and test it discreetly.
Clean the chip, apply the usual mastic, and inspect the finish after curing.

basic.situation: One masonry unit in a wall is broken, and you are helping replace it under supervision. What do you do?

options.text: Pull out the broken piece and place a replacement into the open gap.
Remove the unit and ask the mason to check the replacement before bedding it.
Remove the broken unit carefully, clear its bed, and fit the replacement to the course.
Cover the crack with mortar so the wall looks even for now.

advanced.situation: A furnace lining needs a replacement section while production is scheduled to resume soon. You are helping build the masonry lining. What do you do?

options.text: Confirm the lining pattern, prepare the units, and coordinate each course with the crew.
Check the drawing and prepare enough units for the first course.
Fit the quickest available units and adjust the joints to meet the schedule.
Use the old section as a guide and rebuild it with available units.

basic.situation: You need to mark a stone wall pattern on the prepared base using a straight edge and staked lines. What do you do?

options.text: Follow the base edge, adjusting the pattern as stones are placed.
Mark the pattern from the drawing, then ask the mason to inspect stake placement.
Stretch a line between nearby stakes and mark the pattern along its edge.
Place stakes at marked points, stretch a line, and verify with the straightedge.

advanced.situation: A curved stone feature must meet a straight wall, and small alignment errors will show at the join. How do you set the alignment?

options.text: Set curve and wall reference points, checking stones against pattern and level.
Set initial stones by eye and let the next worker blend the join.
Start at the join and adjust each stone until the curve looks balanced.
Mark wall and curve references, then check the first few stones with a level.

basic.situation: You are mixing grout for stone slabs and cleaning residue from the finished surface. How do you handle the work?

options.text: Mix until the grout looks smooth and wipe the stone after the joints are filled.
Use extra water for easy spreading and rinse the surface when the crew finishes.
Measure the grout as specified, spread it evenly, and clean residue with a damp sponge.
Follow the stated mix and ask the mason when to clean the stone.

advanced.situation: Rain threatens a stone jointing job, and the crew is finishing an exposed section. How do you keep the mortar work consistent?

options.text: Cover the work and remind the crew to keep their joint depth consistent.
Add cement to the mortar so it sets faster before the rain arrives.
Use approved mix, shield fresh joints from rain, and show the target finish.
Keep the usual mix and ask the crew to finish the exposed joints first.

basic.situation: You are digging a shallow trench for a monument foundation and have a pick and shovel. How do you start?

options.text: Start with the pick at the marked end and shovel out the loosened soil.
Dig where the foundation seems centered and adjust the trench as needed.
Follow the marked trench line, maintain even depth, and clear spoil from the edge.
Use the shovel along the marked line and check depth with the mason.

advanced.situation: A large monument project needs anchor holes across several stone sections. You are helping plan the drilling sequence. What do you do?

options.text: Use the first stone as a template and transfer its hole spacing across the others.
Map hole positions from the layout, check each stone, and group drilling by setup.
Mark all holes from the drawing and prepare the drill for the first section.
Drill the first hole on each stone and adjust later positions to match.

basic.situation: A stone monument section is on the truck bed, and you are helping guide it onto skids. What do you do?

options.text: Check the skid path, take the guide position, and follow the lifting crew's signals.
Stand beside the foundation and point the section toward its final position.
Push the stone toward the skid as the crane starts lifting it.
Clear loose items near the skids and ask where the crew wants you positioned.

advanced.situation: A heavy monument section must move from a truck onto a narrow foundation using a hoist and skids. You are coordinating the ground work. What do you do?

options.text: Begin moving once the hoist takes the weight and guide the section by hand.
Clear the landing area and ask the operator when to guide the section.
Lay the skids in place and have one worker watch each side during the move.
Confirm route and landing points, clear the area, and coordinate signals with the operator.

basic.situation: You are preparing a timber frame from a simple sketch, and the boards are longer than the listed dimensions. What do you do?

options.text: Use the usual board length and adjust the cut once the frame is assembled.
Compare the sketch with the stock, then mark the required lengths for cutting.
Ask a nearby carpenter to read the sketch while you prepare the timber.
Check the sketch dimensions, then mark the timber after confirming the measurement.

advanced.situation: Two architectural views show different frame positions near a doorway, and cutting is due soon. How do you resolve the layout?

options.text: Lay the drawing sheets together, mark the conflict, and confirm dimensions before cutting.
Follow the larger dimension and trim any overlap after the frame is fitted.
Compare key dimensions across views, then mark a workable layout for lead review.
Ask the site lead which view to use while you hold the material.

basic.situation: You have marked a straight cut on a board and have a hand saw ready. What do you do?

options.text: Hold the board by hand and follow the line to save setup time.
Clamp the marked board, then saw steadily along the pencil line.
Ask a coworker to steady the board while you saw through the mark.
Check the saw angle against the line, then cut with steady strokes.

advanced.situation: A hardwood frame needs a close-fitting joint, and the drawing shows a shaped cut. Which cutting method do you choose?

options.text: Check the joint drawing and timber grain, then choose a suitable saw and test cut.
Compare the cut profile with the tool limits, then confirm the method with the lead.
Select a fine-tooth blade for the hardwood and cut slowly through the joint.
Use the fastest available saw, then adjust the joint with a chisel.

basic.situation: You are joining two timber pieces for a small frame, with nails and glue available. What do you do?

options.text: Nail the pieces together and add glue along the visible edge.
Align the pieces, apply glue at the joint, then nail them together.
Apply glue to the joint and ask a coworker to hold the pieces.
Nail the pieces together while checking that their edges stay aligned.

advanced.situation: A large project needs temporary timber supports around an opening, and several crews are working nearby. What do you do?

options.text: Build the supports from the opening dimensions and check each connection as you assemble.
Use the spare timber to assemble a familiar support frame beside the opening.
Ask the site lead to choose the frame while you prepare the timber.
Review the support layout against the opening and work sequence, then assemble to suit.

basic.situation: A coworker is nailing a plank into position, and you are asked to hold it steady. What do you do?

options.text: Keep the plank level while your coworker nails through the marked point.
Hold the plank against its marks and keep your hands clear of the nail path.
Hold the plank near the edge while your coworker starts the first nail.
Grip the plank where it feels steady and let your coworker set the nail.

advanced.situation: You are setting support poles where the soil feels loose and damp. The planned hole positions are marked. How do you proceed?

options.text: Check the ground at each mark, then select bracing suited to the site conditions.
Set the poles at the marked positions and add timber wedges for support.
Ask the lead about the soil, then set the poles with the standard braces.
Use the usual anchor rods at each mark and tighten them firmly.

basic.situation: You have finished cutting timber, and wood scraps are scattered across the work area. What do you do?

options.text: Sweep the area, sort the scraps, and place them in the designated bins.
Collect the larger pieces and sweep the smaller scraps toward the bins.
Sweep the main walkway and put the larger scraps in a nearby bin.
Push the scraps into a pile near the workbench for the next shift.

advanced.situation: A timber section has cracked again after a recent repair. The surrounding frame is still in use. What do you do?

options.text: Fit a similar timber section and continue work once it looks secure.
Inspect the cracked section and nearby joints, then report your findings to the lead.
Mark the cracked area and ask the lead to decide on the repair.
Remove the cracked section, note how it failed, and alert the lead before replacement.

basic.situation: At the end of your shift, you need to record the timber frame work completed today. What do you write?

options.text: Tell the next carpenter which sections you finished before leaving the site.
Record the frame sections completed, materials used, and any work still pending.
List the sections you finished and note any delay that affected the work.
Write that the frame work is done and leave the rest for tomorrow.

advanced.situation: Several carpentry tasks depend on delivered materials, and two crew members have different availability tomorrow. How do you plan the work?

options.text: Ask the lead to assign the crew while you write down the task list.
Reuse today’s crew list and assign the same tasks for tomorrow.
Map task dependencies, check crew availability, and update the schedule with likely blockers.
Check each worker’s availability and draft a schedule for the lead to review.

basic.situation: You are measuring a small room from a floor sketch before the carpet arrives. What do you do?

options.text: Measure the longest and widest points, then multiply them for an area estimate.
Use the sketch dimensions and round the area to a convenient carpet amount.
Measure each wall and write the dimensions beside the matching sketch edges.
Check the sketch, measure each wall, and note the room dimensions for the material estimate.

advanced.situation: A large room has alcoves and a busy doorway, and the carpet rolls are limited. How do you plan the layout?

options.text: Plan seams away from the doorway and mark the alcoves on the floor sketch.
Draw the room dimensions, then estimate the carpet needed from the floor area.
Measure the alcoves, map traffic flow, and place seams to suit wear and roll sizes.
Start from the longest wall and fit seams around the alcoves as you go.

basic.situation: You have a straight carpet sample marked to size and a carpet knife ready. What do you do?

options.text: Secure the sample, then cut along the marked line with steady pressure.
Check the marked length, then guide the knife steadily along the line.
Ask a coworker to hold the sample while you cut across the mark.
Hold the sample flat and cut along the line to finish quickly.

advanced.situation: A carpet must fit around a column and doorway projection, with bound edges at both cuts. How do you handle it?

options.text: Mark both projections from the sketch, cut with fitting allowance, then bind the finished edges.
Cut close to each projection and bind the edges before checking the fit.
Mark the column and doorway, then ask the lead where to finish each edge.
Measure each projection and cut the carpet, leaving extra material for fitting.

basic.situation: You have measured a room and need to cut padding before laying carpet. What do you do?

options.text: Mark the padding from the room dimensions and cut along the marks.
Cut the padding from the first measurement and trim it after laying.
Ask a coworker to hold the padding while you cut it to size.
Check the room measurements, cut the padding to size, and fit it in place.

advanced.situation: A busy corridor has an irregular alcove and padding with different thicknesses is available. How do you prepare it?

options.text: Measure the alcove carefully and cut available padding to follow its irregular shape.
Check the corridor profile and traffic, then fit padding and strips around the alcove.
Choose padding for corridor traffic and adjust strips to fit around the alcove.
Use thick padding and standard strips throughout the corridor, including its alcove regardless of traffic.

basic.situation: You are helping stretch carpet toward a wall while a coworker aligns it. What do you do?

options.text: Pull evenly toward wall marks and hold carpet as it engages the tack strips.
Keep the carpet aligned with the wall marks as your coworker stretches it.
Pull hard toward the nearest wall and let the carpet settle without checking its alignment first.
Hold the carpet near the tack strips while your coworker adjusts its position.

advanced.situation: The carpet bunches near a doorway where it meets tile, and the edge must stay secure. What do you do?

options.text: Cover the bunch with a metal tread and fasten it across the doorway without checking tension.
Ease tension, refit the doorway edge, and secure it with the specified transition strip.
Stretch the carpet toward the doorway and fit a tread over the edge.
Ask the lead which adhesive to use while holding the carpet at the doorway.

basic.situation: Two carpet edges meet across a small room, and seam tape and a heated iron are ready. What do you do?

options.text: Set the edges together and run the heated iron quickly along the tape without checking alignment.
Align edges, tape the seam, then heat it evenly while holding it straight.
Apply the tape and move the iron steadily along the aligned carpet edges.
Check the edges meet evenly, then ask a coworker to guide the iron.

advanced.situation: A carpet seam will run through a bright lobby entrance, and a new installer is watching. How do you proceed?

options.text: Align pile and edges, test the method, then demonstrate steady seam joining.
Join the entrance edges and let the installer copy your pace without checking pile direction.
Check the pile direction and align the edges before joining the seam.
Ask the lead to demonstrate the seam while you prepare the heated iron.

basic.situation: You have finished installing carpet and small remnants are scattered around the room. What do you do?

options.text: Vacuum carpet, collect remnants, and place waste in the designated area.
Vacuum the carpet and ask a coworker to collect the remaining scraps.
Collect the large remnants and vacuum the carpet around the work area.
Push the scraps beside the doorway and vacuum only the visible carpet after work.

advanced.situation: You have removed old carpet and padding from a furnished office, and installation is due to start. How do you prepare the handover?

options.text: Remove the old carpet and padding, then vacuum the exposed floor area.
Ask the installer where to put the old padding before clearing the room.
Move furniture aside and stack old carpet near the room entrance, leaving padding in place.
Clear furniture and old materials, sort waste, and check for leftover pieces.

basic.situation: You are preparing a small bedroom floor, and dried dirt and a raised patch could show through the new covering. What do you do?

options.text: Sweep around the patch and let the covering bridge it.
Scrape and sweep the base, then check it feels even.
Sand the patch lightly and sweep the loose dust away.
Scrape the raised patch, then sweep the base before laying.

advanced.situation: A large subfloor has several ridges and cracked areas beneath a planned sheet covering. You spot them before the adhesive arrives. What do you do?

options.text: Fill the cracks and sand ridges, then check the base across the room.
Cover the worst ridge with extra adhesive and continue the installation.
Sand the ridges and fill the visible cracks before covering.
Sand the highest ridges and leave shallow cracks for the sheet.

basic.situation: You are fitting a flooring sheet around a pipe in a small room. Your first mark leaves little spare material. What do you do?

options.text: Cut a wide opening so the sheet clears the pipe easily.
Cut a small test notch, check the fit, then trim carefully.
Mark the pipe edge again, then cut slowly around it.
Cut to the mark and press the sheet around the pipe.

advanced.situation: A client requests a repeating border pattern from a sketch, but one dimension is faint and the flooring is costly. What do you do?

options.text: Mark the pattern from the clear dimensions and check the layout.
Confirm the unclear dimension, then mark and cut a sample section.
Cut one border piece and adjust later pieces to match it.
Cut the full pattern from your closest reading of the sketch.

basic.situation: You are due to install flooring in a kitchen, but a recently washed area still looks darker than the rest. What do you do?

options.text: Check the surface is firm and dry before starting installation.
Start along the dry side and work toward the darker area.
Press the darker area and wait briefly for it to lighten.
Check for softness and let the darker area air for a while.

advanced.situation: A hallway has heavy foot traffic near its entrance and a quieter side passage. You are deciding where to place sheet seams. What do you do?

options.text: Place the seam across the entrance for the shortest material use.
Keep the seam away from the entrance, using the quieter passage.
Put the seam along the hallway center for a balanced appearance.
Place the seam near the wall, away from the main entrance.

basic.situation: After laying a floor covering, you notice small ridges of excess cement along the finished edge. What do you do?

options.text: Leave the ridges until the next crew cleans the room.
Rub the cement with a dry cloth until the edge looks neat.
Wipe the ridges with a damp cloth and check the edge.
Scrape the cement gently, then wipe the finished surface clean.

advanced.situation: An old floor covering must be removed before a room refit, and an appliance and wall fixture are in the work area. What do you do?

options.text: Clear the covering first, then arrange safe disconnection before moving fixtures.
Ask the site lead who is responsible for disconnecting the fixtures.
Remove the covering around the fixtures and leave them in place.
Remove the covering and move both fixtures to clear the room.

basic.situation: You are marking a straight guide across a small room before laying a plain floor covering. The starting points are clear. What do you do?

options.text: Measure both ends, snap a chalk line, and check its alignment.
Snap a chalk line from the doorway to the opposite wall.
Measure the ends and snap a line between the marks.
Mark the line by eye and begin laying from the doorway.

advanced.situation: You are marking a diagonal repeat pattern from a layout drawing, and the room has an uneven corner. What do you do?

options.text: Mark a central guide from the drawing and extend the pattern outward.
Start at the uneven corner and continue the repeat across the room.
Use the corner as a guide and adjust each diagonal line by eye.
Set measured reference points from the drawing, then snap checked guidelines.

basic.situation: You are positioning a sound-deadening underlay in a bedroom, and the chalk guideline is visible. What do you do?

options.text: Lay the underlay quickly, then trim any exposed edges afterward.
Start from the doorway and smooth the underlay toward the wall.
Position the underlay along the guide, check its edges, then press it down.
Align the underlay with the guideline and press it down evenly.

advanced.situation: You are laying a decorative floor pattern across a large room, and the first course appears slightly angled against the guideline. What do you do?

options.text: Adjust the next course to bring the pattern closer to the guideline.
Press the first course down and trim the visible edge later.
Continue the next courses and let the border hide the angle.
Lift the first course, realign it with the guideline, and check the repeat.

basic.situation: You are sanding beside a doorway where the floor machine cannot reach, and a rough strip remains. What do you do?

options.text: Rub the strip with spare sandpaper until it feels less rough.
Use a hand scraper on the strip, then check its surface.
Sand the strip with suitable hand tools, then check it against the floor.
Leave the strip and let the finish coat blend the roughness.

advanced.situation: A new worker is sanding tight corners beside an open doorway, and the floor edge has delicate trim. You are asked to show the technique. What do you do?

options.text: Show careful hand sanding near the trim and explain how to check the edge.
Ask the worker to copy your pace while you sand the corner.
Demonstrate the scraper first, then let the worker try the same corner.
Have the worker use the floor machine close to the trim for speed.

basic.situation: You are guiding a sanding machine over a room floor under supervision. A faint uneven patch remains near the center. What do you do?

options.text: Overlap the next pass slightly and continue across the room.
Make another pass over the patch at the same steady pace.
Guide another even pass over the patch and inspect the surface.
Move the machine faster across the patch to finish the room sooner.

advanced.situation: You are guiding sanding across a large hall, and another worker's passes leave visible ridges between lanes. What do you do?

options.text: Set an even pace, overlap passes, and show the worker how to check each lane.
Let the worker finish, then discuss the ridges and adjust the sanding technique.
Ask the worker to slow down and overlap passes across the ridged lanes.
Demonstrate overlapping passes, then inspect the next section together for visible ridges.

basic.situation: You are checking a sanded room floor with your supervisor, and one area feels rough under your hand. What do you do?

options.text: Walk across the area again to see whether it still feels rough.
Mark the rough spot, then ask your supervisor to check it with you.
Tell your supervisor the floor feels rough in that area.
Brush away the dust and assume the rough feel will disappear.

advanced.situation: You are inspecting a large sanded floor before finishing, and smoothness varies between the middle and edges. What do you do?

options.text: Check representative middle and edge areas, then mark uneven spots for sanding.
Check the middle and approve the floor if that area feels smooth.
Check the middle and edges, then report any rough areas.
Check the edges and ask another worker whether the middle feels smooth.

basic.situation: You are preparing a sanded floor for finish, and fine dust remains near the wall. What do you do?

options.text: Vacuum the middle and let the finish crew handle the edges.
Buff and vacuum around the wall before the finish is applied.
Sweep the dust toward the doorway before applying the finish.
Buff and vacuum the floor, then check for remaining dust.

advanced.situation: You are cleaning a large floor before finish application, and sanding dust keeps settling near the entry. What do you do?

options.text: Repeat vacuuming the entry and continue once the dust seems reduced.
Buff the entry and open the door to clear the remaining dust.
Vacuum the floor, then check the entry and nearby surface again.
Vacuum the entry first and begin coating while the floor looks clear.

basic.situation: You are cleaning a wood floor joint after fitting, and a small bead of glue remains. What do you do?

options.text: Let the glue dry, then scrape it off with a chisel.
Wipe the glue across the joint with a damp cloth, spreading it.
Use a knife to lift the bead carefully from the joint.
Trim the bead with a knife, then inspect the joint edge.

advanced.situation: A coworker asks how to remove glue from a tight wood joint without marking the boards. What do you advise?

options.text: Soften the glue with water before scraping the tight joint.
Use a knife carefully along the joint and check the wood surface.
Scrape with a sharp chisel at a shallow angle, following the grain.
Scrape across the grain with a knife to clear glue from the joint.

basic.situation: You are preparing a sanding machine for a floor, and its roller needs fresh sandpaper before work begins. What do you do?

options.text: Attach the sandpaper to the roller before starting the machine.
Fit the paper loosely so it can settle while the roller turns.
Wrap the new paper over the old sheet and start sanding.
Attach the sandpaper evenly and check it sits firmly on the roller.

advanced.situation: You are applying filler and finish to a wood floor, and the timber varies in tone across the room. What do you do?

options.text: Select a suitable finish and apply it evenly across the room.
Use the same finish as the last room and coat the floor evenly.
Apply extra filler over the darker boards before using the finish.
Choose a compatible finish, test a small area, then guide an even application.

basic.situation: You are preparing a small bathroom wall where several old tiles have come loose. How do you clear the area for replacement tiles?

options.text: Set new tiles over the loose edges to finish the wall faster.
Remove the old tile and adhesive with a scraper, then clean the surface.
Scrape off the loose grout and adhesive, then sweep the exposed wall.
Lift the loose tiles and brush away visible debris before continuing.

advanced.situation: A tiled shower wall has uneven masonry and a metal section near the mixer. You need to prepare both areas before the installation begins.

options.text: Secure suitable lath over the metal, then apply mortar to create a stable base.
Cover both areas with waterproof paper before beginning the tile installation.
Build up the masonry with mortar while leaving the metal section uncovered.
Level the masonry with mortar and cover the metal section with waterproof paper.

basic.situation: A floor tile needs a straight cut to fit beside a doorway. You have marked the measurement and are using a manual cutter.

options.text: Score the marked line and snap the tile with the manual cutter.
Snap the tile across the nearest grout line to save time.
Score the tile once and snap it, then test it at the doorway.
Check the mark against the doorway, then score and snap the tile.

advanced.situation: A patterned floor needs tiles cut around several curved pipe covers. A new coworker is waiting to use the wet saw.

options.text: Trace each cover and make several small relief cuts around the curve.
Mark each curve from a template, then make controlled cuts and explain safe saw handling.
Measure each curve carefully, then ask the coworker to copy your cuts.
Mark the curves by eye and let the coworker cut the first tile.

basic.situation: You need a small mortar batch for replacement tiles on a dry kitchen wall. The mix is ready to spread.

options.text: Spread mortar across the wall and set the tiles while it remains workable.
Use the leftover mortar from yesterday and press the tiles into it.
Apply a generous mortar layer and tap the tiles until they seem secure.
Spread a thin bed and press each tile into place with the trowel handle.

advanced.situation: The crew is setting tiles on a warm, breezy balcony. The adhesive on the first section is skinning before all the tiles are placed.

options.text: Keep spreading the same adhesive farther ahead to maintain the crew pace.
Use shorter sections of the same adhesive and check the bed as you work.
Spread smaller workable sections and select an adhesive suited to the balcony conditions.
Ask the crew to press tiles harder into the skinned adhesive bed.

basic.situation: You are placing the first tile beside a marked line on a small kitchen backsplash. The adjacent cabinet edge provides a clear reference.

options.text: Set the tile by the cabinet edge and check it with a level.
Place it where the grout gap looks even from across the kitchen.
Align the tile with the cabinet edge and continue to the next row.
Set it beside the cabinet and compare its edge with the marked line.

advanced.situation: A client has chosen a diagonal pattern for a prominent lobby floor. The blueprint marks the room center, but the walls are not square.

options.text: Measure from the center mark and follow the nearest wall for each row.
Set a pattern grid from the marked center and check lines against room walls.
Start the diagonal at the nearest wall and trim the opposite edge after laying tiles.
Mark diagonal guide lines from the room center and adjust the edge cuts.

basic.situation: You have finished grouting a small section of a kitchen backsplash. A thin film is forming on the tile faces.

options.text: Let the film dry fully, then scrape it away with a sharp metal blade.
Wipe tile faces with a damp sponge, rinsing it as grout builds up.
Dab the grout film with a wet cloth after finishing the whole wall.
Wipe the faces with a damp sponge, changing to a clean side often.

advanced.situation: A tiled shower niche is ready for sealing, and the owner expects frequent use. The grout joints must resist water and staining.

options.text: Choose a sealer labeled for grout and wet areas, then follow its application directions.
Select a grout sealer rated for wet areas and water resistance, then cover each joint.
Apply the general purpose sealer already open on the workbench across all grout joints.
Use leftover floor polish to coat grout joints and tile edges before the owner arrives.

basic.situation: Pre-cut stone pieces are ready for a small entrance feature. You are helping position them according to the marked plan.

options.text: Follow the marks and keep stone edges close to each planned joint.
Place each stone on its mark, checking edges against neighboring pieces.
Set larger stones first, then fit smaller pieces around their marked positions.
Use spare pieces only in marked spaces, keeping gaps aligned with the planned feature.

advanced.situation: A foyer mural uses several mosaic colors around a stone column. One row appears to drift from the approved pattern as the work progresses.

options.text: Pause, compare the laid pieces with the pattern, and reset the guide line.
Fill the remaining spaces with nearby colors to keep the row moving and preserve your pace.
Shift the pieces in the next row to balance the mural by eye.
Check the pattern at the next section and realign the upcoming row carefully.

basic.situation: A small slab is being poured, and concrete is collecting more heavily near one edge. You are helping spread it with a rake.

options.text: Rake the nearest mound flat and leave the far edge for later.
Spread concrete across the slab and ask the finisher to check the level.
Pull concrete toward the low area and check the spread with a straightedge.
Push the excess toward the edge and smooth the middle with a shovel.

advanced.situation: A truck is ready to pour a long driveway form, and several laborers are waiting with shovels. The chute is not yet aligned with the starting section.

options.text: Position the chute at the start and direct the crew to spread evenly along the form.
Signal the driver to pour at the nearest end and let the crew catch up.
Align the chute with the start and have the crew spread the concrete forward.
Ask the driver to pause while laborers spread the first load by hand.

basic.situation: A small concrete patch has firmed enough for rubbing. The surface has a few shallow ridges that need smoothing.

options.text: Wet the patch and rub ridges with a stone until smooth.
Wet the surface and rub raised areas with a stone.
Rub each ridge with a dry stone while the patch remains soft.
Brush dry cement over ridges and leave the patch to set.

advanced.situation: A concrete walkway near a drain remains damp after rain, and the owner asks you to restore its weathered surface with a compound.

options.text: Apply the leftover indoor floor coating to the wet walkway.
Select a concrete sealer and apply it across the walkway surface.
Brush a general repair compound over the weathered areas after rain.
Choose a compound suited to damp exterior concrete and follow its application directions.

basic.situation: You are setting forms for a short path beside a house. The plan gives a shallow pitch toward the drain.

options.text: Set the forms to the planned pitch and check depth and alignment along the path.
Set the forms level and let water find its own way to the drain.
Set the forms to the marked pitch and check their depth at both ends.
Place the forms at the drain end and estimate the pitch toward the house.

advanced.situation: A repair around an irregular concrete corner needs a wooden mold. The existing surface has several angles that do not match standard boards.

options.text: Clamp straight boards around the corner and fill the visible gaps later.
Measure the boundary, shape a mold, and clamp it around the repair.
Shape a quick mold from spare boards and hold it while filling.
Cut boards to the main angles and clamp them around the repair boundary.

basic.situation: You are repairing a small chip in a concrete step. The area is dusty and has a few loose edges.

options.text: Wet the whole step and spread grout across the chip and nearby surface.
Brush away loose concrete, then press grout into the chipped area.
Cover the dusty chip with grout and smooth it flush with the step.
Brush away loose concrete, wet the area, and fill the chip with grout.

advanced.situation: A deep crack in a concrete landing may need reinforcing rods. You are assigned to prepare the damaged section for repair.

options.text: Fill the crack with grout and smooth the top to match the landing.
Drill the rod holes and position reinforcement across the cracked section.
Cut out the loose edge and cover the crack with a surface slurry.
Cut back damaged concrete, drill rod holes, and position reinforcement.

basic.situation: Fresh concrete is ready for a neat edge along a short garden path. You have an edging tool and straightedge.

options.text: Guide the edging tool along the straightedge, checking the joint depth.
Press a shallow line by eye and smooth over any uneven sections later.
Make the edge with the tool, following the path border by sight.
Use the straightedge to guide the edging tool along the path.

advanced.situation: A fresh concrete entrance slab needs anchor bolts at marked points for a door sill. The concrete is still workable and the crew is finishing nearby.

options.text: Place bolts at the marks and check their spacing before finishing the surface.
Set each bolt at its mark, check projection, and secure it.
Set the bolts by eye and ask the installer to adjust the sill later.
Press the bolts into convenient spots and cover their bases with concrete.

basic.situation: You are mixing a small batch of grout for a patch. The dry mix and water are ready beside the mixing machine.

options.text: Mix the dry material with water and check the consistency before use.
Pour in all the water and add dry mix until it looks loose enough.
Add water gradually to the dry mix and blend until the grout is even.
Run the machine briefly, then use the batch while some dry pockets remain.

advanced.situation: A slab is curing on a hot, windy afternoon. The surface is drying faster than expected, and your crew is monitoring the pour.

options.text: Check the surface regularly and keep the crew ready to protect it.
Spray the slab once and stop checking while the crew clears tools.
Leave the slab exposed so the wind can dry the surface evenly.
Monitor surface conditions and apply planned curing protection as needed.

basic.situation: You are preparing a routine terrazzo batch. The job sheet lists quantities, and the scales and graduated containers are ready beside the mixer.

options.text: Measure the cement and chips, then estimate the water from the last batch.
Use the graduated containers for liquids and scales for dry ingredients.
Measure the listed quantities and ask a coworker to confirm the batch amounts.
Measure each ingredient to the job sheet and check the scale between materials.

advanced.situation: A terrazzo installation includes a narrow color band and a different stone mix from the standard floor. The usual grout formula leaves little working time.

options.text: Use the usual formula and speed up placement before the grout stiffens.
Adjust the mixing and grouting method to the stone and band requirements.
Ask the lead which formula was used on a similar color band.
Check the product guidance and adapt the batch timing for the narrow band.

basic.situation: Before a terrazzo base is poured, you are asked to position the moisture membrane and wire mesh over a prepared floor.

options.text: Align the membrane and mesh with the layout marks before fastening them.
Lay the membrane flat, overlap seams, and secure the mesh as instructed.
Place the mesh first and tuck the membrane around its edges.
Position both layers and ask your coworker to check their alignment.

advanced.situation: A large floor has damp patches and several cracks before terrazzo bonding. The pour is scheduled today, and the surface varies across the room.

options.text: Wet the whole floor and fill visible cracks with the standard slurry.
Fill the larger cracks first and let the crew decide about damp patches.
Check the surface moisture and fill cracks before wetting the floor evenly.
Assess damp areas and cracks, then prepare each section for reliable bonding.

basic.situation: A routine terrazzo base is ready to spread in a marked section. Your coworker is mixing while you have a rake and shovel.

options.text: Shovel the mix into the section and let the trowel crew level it later.
Spread the mix evenly with the rake, then smooth it to the marks.
Rake the mix across the section and check its depth at several points.
Spread the mix quickly with the shovel to keep the batch moving.

advanced.situation: You are forming a terrazzo edge beside a doorway where the floor changes height. The expansion joint must meet an existing straight line.

options.text: Shape the edge by eye and press the joint strip into the wet mix.
Set a straightedge to the joint line and shape the edge to the height change.
Place the joint strip on the line, then shape the edge with an edging tool.
Follow the existing line and ask a coworker to check the edge.

basic.situation: After a concrete pour sets, you find a raised ridge near the wall. A hand chisel and other finishing tools are available.

options.text: Scrape the ridge with a finishing tool and inspect the surrounding area.
Chip the ridge gradually with the hand chisel, checking the surface as you go.
Use the hand chisel on the ridge and check the level afterward.
Strike the ridge hard with the chisel to bring it down quickly.

advanced.situation: A polished terrazzo stair has curved corners that the surfacing machine cannot reach. The surrounding floor is finished and must stay unmarred.

options.text: Hand grind the corners, then blend them with the nearest floor pass.
Use a portable grinder on the corners, keeping it clear of the floor.
Run the large surfacing machine close to each curved corner.
Use a portable hand grinder carefully, matching the stair’s curve and finish.

basic.situation: A polished terrazzo surface is ready for its routine wash. The cleaner and sealer instructions are available at the work area.

options.text: Wash the surface with cleaner and ask the lead about sealer timing.
Wash with the specified cleaner, then apply sealer as the instructions describe.
Wash with cleaner and water, then prepare the sealer for application.
Rinse the floor with water and leave sealing for another shift.

advanced.situation: After cleaning a chipped terrazzo area, one patch feels rough while nearby sections look smooth. The floor is due for finishing later today.

options.text: Ask a coworker whether the patch feels acceptable before finishing.
Brush the area, feel and inspect it, then address any roughness before finishing.
Inspect the patch under work lights and note the rough area for finishing.
Brush the patch quickly and proceed with the rest of the floor.

basic.situation: A customer’s terrazzo design calls for a plain field with a band of colored marble chips. The base is ready for the finishing chips.

options.text: Sprinkle the specified colored chips evenly across the marked band.
Ask the lead to confirm the color before sprinkling the band.
Scatter the chips across the nearby floor to use the open batch.
Apply colored chips along the band and smooth them into the base.

advanced.situation: A lobby design changes from one terrazzo color to another around a curved feature. The division strips and chip colors are on site.

options.text: Set strips to the design curves, then place each chip color in its field.
Mark the curve on the base, then press the strips in and add chips.
Follow the color drawing and ask a coworker to check the curved sections.
Place the strips freehand and adjust the chip colors as the work progresses.

basic.situation: You are asked to mark a short trench from a plan. The drawing gives a clear starting point and distance, and the crew is waiting to begin.

options.text: I would find the marked start and measure the distance with a tape.
I would pace out the distance from the nearest visible corner and mark it.
I would check the plan and measure from the marked starting point.
I would ask a nearby worker where the trench starts and mark from there.

advanced.situation: A large work area has several openings, and the latest drawing gives dimensions that differ from an older site sketch. You are asked to record layout marks.

options.text: I would use the older sketch and mark the openings from its measurements.
I would read the current specifications, verify references, and record each opening.
I would measure from the current drawing and ask the lead about each opening.
I would mark the clear openings first and leave conflicting ones for later.

basic.situation: Loose timber and packaging are scattered beside the walkway where materials are being carried. The lead asks you to clear the work area.

options.text: I would collect loose debris and place it at the site's waste point.
I would sweep the walkway and stack the timber beside the work area.
I would ask the carrier crew to step around the debris until cleanup.
I would move the timber aside and leave the packaging near the walkway.

advanced.situation: A leaking hose has left a slick patch beside a machine, and oily rags are near the same area. Workers are still passing through to collect tools.

options.text: I would place a warning cone and clean the spill with the site's materials.
I would block the slick patch and notify the lead to arrange cleanup.
I would tell workers to watch their footing until the hose is repaired.
I would wipe the floor with nearby rags and put them back by the machine.

basic.situation: A delivery of cement bags and hand tools arrives at the site. The plan marks separate storage spots, and you are asked to distribute the items there.

options.text: I would unload everything beside the gate for the crews to sort.
I would take the cement to storage and leave tools near the unloading area.
I would group the materials by type and check the plan before moving them.
I would read the plan and carry each item to its marked spot.

advanced.situation: Two crews need materials from a narrow access lane, and a pallet blocks the route to the far work area. You are distributing items from the project plan.

options.text: I would check destinations and time the deliveries by crew to keep the lane clear.
I would move the pallet to the nearest open space and send both crews through.
I would send the lighter tools first and move the pallet after the bags.
I would take each load along the marked route as the crews request it.

basic.situation: You are helping dig a shallow trench with a shovel. The string line marks its route, and the lead asks you to keep the trench close to grade.

options.text: I would shovel along the string and check depth at intervals.
I would follow the string and compare the trench depth with the grade marks.
I would remove loose soil first and wait for the lead to check depth.
I would dig quickly along the string and let the lead fix the depth.

advanced.situation: A longer trench crosses a sloped section, and the marked grade changes along its length. Your crew is digging and compacting the earth to the specified levels.

options.text: I would follow the grade marks and check levels as the crew progresses.
I would compare each section with grade marks before digging and after compaction.
I would dig the high end first and let the compacted soil set the slope.
I would keep the same depth throughout and compact the trench firmly.

basic.situation: A crew needs a generator for hand tools. You have been shown its controls, and the lead asks you to start it while they check the cable run.

options.text: I would wait for the lead to return before touching the controls.
I would start the generator and tell the lead when the engine runs.
I would pull the starter and connect the tools as the engine catches.
I would start it using the shown controls and check the power output.

advanced.situation: A generator starts but its output drops when a compressor is connected. The crew needs both tools, and you are responsible for tending the equipment.

options.text: I would tell the lead the output drops and wait for direction.
I would keep restarting the generator until both tools hold power.
I would check the fuel and connections, then tell the lead output is low.
I would disconnect the load, check the controls and fuel, then report trouble.

basic.situation: A crane operator cannot see the load's landing spot clearly. You are assigned to guide a short lift using the site's agreed hand signals.

options.text: I would stand where visible and give the agreed signals for movement.
I would use the agreed signals and watch the load throughout the lift.
I would wave the operator forward and point toward the landing spot.
I would give the agreed movement signal and step aside to clear the route.

advanced.situation: A lift must pass a material cart while another machine is backing nearby. The operators have different sightlines, and you are helping coordinate their movements.

options.text: I would guide the crane past the cart and ask the other operator to pause.
I would ask both operators to wait while the cart is moved away.
I would signal the crane through first while the other machine reverses.
I would agree a sequence with the operators and signal one movement at a time.

basic.situation: You are starting the paver beside a road form, and the crew lead asks you to guide it along the marked line.

options.text: You ask the lead to check your line before continuing at the same pace.
You engage the clutch, align the screed with the form, and manage drift.
You start the paver and steer by the truck's path near the edge.
You ease the paver along the form, checking the guide line as you go.

advanced.situation: The asphalt mat is wavering beside a tight curve, while trucks keep feeding the hopper and the crew is watching your pass.

options.text: You keep the current settings and steer harder through the curve to finish the pass.
You balance the hopper feed and screed settings, checking the mat after each adjustment.
You slow the paver and adjust the screed, then watch the mat through the curve.
You reduce speed and ask the truck driver to pause while you inspect the surface.

basic.situation: Before paving starts, you are asked to light the machine burners and bring the screed to its working temperature.

options.text: You ask a nearby operator whether the screed seems ready for the first load.
You turn on the burners and begin paving once the surface feels warm.
You light the burners and check the screed temperature as it warms.
You follow the start-up sequence and confirm the screed gauge is rising steadily.

advanced.situation: A cooler-than-usual mix is arriving for a long pass, and the screed starts leaving shallow low spots as the queue grows.

options.text: You mark the low spots and adjust heat while watching the mat on the next section.
You raise the screed heat and increase asphalt flow to fill the low spots.
You reduce travel speed and ask the lead to review the mix before changing settings.
You check screed temperature, tune heat and flow gradually, and compare each section's finish.

basic.situation: After your shift, asphalt has hardened near a guard and the machine's hand lever feels stiff during cleanup.

options.text: You clean around the guard with hand tools and report the stiff lever.
You secure the machine, clean the guard, and check the lever for visible blockage.
You note the stiff lever for the next shift and finish the routine cleanup.
You force the lever through its range, then wipe the visible asphalt away.

advanced.situation: The paver's screed begins vibrating unevenly mid-shift, and a newer operator is ready to resume after a quick check.

options.text: You report the vibration and keep the machine parked until the lead reviews it.
You ask the operator to listen for changes while finishing the current short section.
You stop the machine, inspect likely connections, and explain the checks to the operator.
You tighten nearby fittings and let the operator continue at reduced speed.

basic.situation: You are rolling a fresh road section under guidance, and the foreperson points out a narrow strip that still looks loose.

options.text: You make a controlled pass, then review the strip's finish with the foreperson.
You speed up so the crew can clear the lane sooner.
You make a steady pass over the strip, keeping the roller aligned.
You shovel a little blacktop over the strip before making one pass.

advanced.situation: A finished road section crosses soft ground near a drainage edge, and repeated roller passes are leaving uneven marks.

options.text: You vary the roller route and inspect each pass for changes in the surface.
You pause rolling and ask the foreperson whether the marks need another pass.
You add more passes across the entire section until the marks fade.
You use the grade reference to plan passes, then guide the crew around soft ground.

basic.situation: Your crew is setting up the paving machine beside an open lane, and the lead asks you to place traffic controls before unloading.

options.text: You unload the machine first, then place the signs beside the work area.
You check the planned work area, place signs and barriers, then help set up equipment.
You place the warning signs, then help position the machine and barriers.
You ask a coworker to watch traffic while you start placing the equipment.

advanced.situation: A paving job needs a lane shift near a side-road entrance, and delivery trucks are due while the crew tears down equipment.

options.text: You shift the signs around the entrance and wave each truck through as it arrives.
You coordinate the sign layout with the lead and keep the entrance clear during teardown.
You pause teardown when a truck approaches and let the driver choose the route.
You sequence the teardown around arrivals and maintain a clear, consistent route through the shift.

basic.situation: At the end of the paving shift, you are asked to drive the machine onto a truck trailer with a spotter guiding you.

options.text: You confirm the trailer position, agree on signals, and move steadily as directed.
You ask the spotter to stand closer and then use a slower approach.
You follow the spotter's signals and drive the machine slowly onto the trailer.
You line up by eye and drive onto the trailer before the queue grows.

advanced.situation: Two dump trucks arrive together at a narrow paving site, while the loader must keep the hopper supplied without blocking the exit.

options.text: You assign a clear holding point and sequence dumps around hopper demand and the exit route.
You direct both trucks to queue beside the loader and unload as space opens.
You ask the drivers to take turns and keep the loader near the hopper.
You schedule one truck to unload while the other waits clear of the exit.

basic.situation: You are starting a bulldozer for a clearing pass, and the operator beside you is guiding your first movements.

options.text: You ask the operator to take over once the machine begins to move.
You start the engine, check the blade response, and follow the operator's signals.
You start the engine and drive forward while testing the blade lever.
You start the engine and move the blade controls as the operator directs.

advanced.situation: Your crew is clearing rocky ground in successive bulldozer passes, and a shallow ridge remains near the boundary stakes.

options.text: You adjust the blade and guide the next pass to follow the boundary stakes.
You assess the ridge and ground, then set a controlled blade angle for the next pass.
You make another pass at the same blade angle and watch the ridge line.
You lower the blade sharply and push through the ridge in one pass.

basic.situation: Before excavating beside a marked service corridor, you notice one section has faded and the crew is preparing to begin.

options.text: You follow the visible marks and begin at the clearer end of the corridor.
You point out the faded mark and ask the crew to keep the bucket shallow.
You pause the excavation and ask the lead to confirm the service location before digging.
You compare the site markings with the work plan and flag the unclear section.

advanced.situation: During a busy shift, you see a worker enter the loader's turning area while another machine approaches the same work zone.

options.text: You signal both operators to slow down and check the turning area after the pass.
You alert the nearby operator and guide the loader around the worker's position.
You call a pause and have the crew review the approach between the machines.
You stop the movement, clear the worker, then agree on separation before restarting.

basic.situation: You are positioning a tractor-drawn machine beside reference stakes, and a crew member gives you hand signals from the ground.

options.text: You stop near the stake and ask the crew member to check your position.
You agree on the signals, watch the signaler, and check alignment against the guideline.
You move toward the stake while watching the machine instead of the signaler.
