You follow the hand signals and align the machine with the nearest stake.

advanced.situation: Two machines are moving a load through a tight work zone, and the ground crew's audio cues conflict with one operator's hand signals.

options.text: You call a stop, agree on one signal method, and resume with clear positions.
You follow the hand signals and ask the ground crew to repeat its audio cues.
You pause the movement and ask the lead to clarify the signals before proceeding.
You tell both operators to keep moving slowly while the crew sorts the signals.

basic.situation: You are attaching a grader blade to a tractor, and a coworker is helping connect the hydraulic hoses and fasten the hitch.

options.text: You connect the hoses and fasten the hitch while your coworker holds the blade.
You inspect the hose ends, connect them, and secure the hitch with your coworker.
You connect the hoses and ask your coworker to check the hitch before use.
You fasten the hitch first and connect the hoses after the blade is raised.

advanced.situation: A newly fitted attachment jerks during a test lift, and the crew needs the tractor for a sloped section later in the shift.

options.text: You test the attachment again on level ground before deciding whether to report it.
You retry the lift with less throttle and tell the next operator to watch closely.
You report the jerking movement and keep the attachment out of service for review.
You check the hose and hitch connections, then explain the test to the newer operator.

basic.situation: You are loading loose rocks into a truck with a loader, and your supervisor is watching the first few bucket loads.

options.text: You scoop the rocks and tip each bucket into the truck as it waits.
You fill the bucket high and tip from the side to finish sooner.
You load smaller buckets and ask the supervisor to watch the truck's balance.
You check the truck position, scoop steadily, and place each load within the bed.

advanced.situation: After a small demolition, mixed debris is scattered across a parking area while a delivery route must stay open for vehicles.

options.text: You pile all debris near the entrance so the trucks can collect it together.
You clear debris from the delivery route and move the remaining material afterward.
You map a clear vehicle route, then sequence debris removal around that access.
You move the largest debris first and leave a narrow route through the area.

basic.situation: At the end of a shift, you need to record the grader's hours and note that its blade control felt sluggish.

options.text: You record the hours and leave the blade issue for the next shift to notice.
You enter the hours and note that the blade control needs attention.
You record the hours, conditions, and blade-control symptoms in the equipment log.
You record the operating hours and describe when the blade control felt sluggish.

advanced.situation: Several loaders show recurring hydraulic leaks across recent shifts, and operators record the problems in different places.

options.text: You copy the latest leak note into every loader's log for easier tracking.
You ask operators to keep using their usual notes and collect them monthly.
You gather the recent notes and list each loader's leak history for the lead.
You set a shared log format for hours, leaks, and repairs, then explain its use.

basic.situation: You are laying out a small room and the drawing shows panel types and dimensions. You are unsure which dimension applies to one wall.

options.text: I check the nearby room dimensions before marking the wall.
I mark the stated wall length and follow the panel note.
I compare the wall dimensions and panel note, then mark the layout.
I use the drawing's scale to estimate that wall and mark it.

advanced.situation: A ceiling detail conflicts with a structural note about a support location. You are setting out the ceiling grid before the other trades arrive.

options.text: I mark the conflict on the drawing and ask the site lead which detail governs.
I shift the grid around the support and note the adjustment for review.
I compare both notes, mark the affected grid area, and request a coordinated detail.
I set out the grid from the ceiling detail and flag the support later.

basic.situation: You are fastening lath to a short wall frame, and one edge feels loose under your hand.

options.text: I test the frame, then fasten the lath evenly across its supports.
I add a few fasteners near the corner before finishing the wall.
I add screws along the loose edge and check how the lath sits.
I fasten the lath at the usual spacing and move on to the next bay.

advanced.situation: The plan calls for a suspended ceiling grid across a large hall, but a service route crosses several planned hanger points.

options.text: I install the grid to plan and let the services team work around it.
I show the service route to the lead before fixing hangers in that area.
I move the affected hangers around the service route and continue the grid.
I map the clashes, preserve clear routes, and coordinate revised hanger positions with the lead.

basic.situation: You are fitting a wallboard panel to a bedroom frame, and the panel edge does not sit flush.

options.text: I shift the panel slightly and fasten its edge to the nearest stud.
I fasten the panel at the closest studs and finish the next sheet.
I check the frame and reposition the panel before fastening it evenly.
I ask a nearby installer to hold the panel while I fasten it.

advanced.situation: You are hanging ceiling panels with a lift in a busy school corridor, and the next delivery is due before the area clears.

options.text: I ask the delivery crew to wait while I finish this row.
I sequence panels by bay and confirm each lift path with the crew.
I finish this bay, then pause until the corridor clears.
I keep the lift moving as the crew clears the next delivery area.

basic.situation: You need to cut a panel opening for a wall outlet, but the marked outline looks slightly off the box.

options.text: I ask the electrician to confirm the box location before cutting.
I cut the marked opening and adjust the panel around the box.
I measure from the panel edge and cut to the marked outline.
I recheck the box position and mark the opening before cutting.

advanced.situation: A ceiling border narrows irregularly beside a column, and the remaining tiles are limited for this room.

options.text: I make a cardboard template and cut tiles one at a time.
I start with the narrowest section and trim tiles as I reach it.
I cut each tile to the column and use spare pieces to fill gaps.
I template the changing edge, plan the cuts, and dry-fit the border tiles.

basic.situation: You are sealing the ceiling edge in a small room, and the gap varies along one wall.

options.text: I fill the gap in short sections and smooth each bead as I go.
I cover the visible part with a quick bead before leaving the room.
I run sealant along the full edge using the same bead size.
I check the gap width, then apply and smooth a suitable bead along it.

advanced.situation: Several rooms have uneven ceiling-to-wall gaps, and a junior installer asks how to seal them consistently before inspection.

options.text: I tell the installer to size each bead to the visible gap.
I set a sample, show varied gaps, and review early rooms with the crew.
I demonstrate a bead, then inspect each room after the crew finishes.
I ask the junior to follow the label while sealing each room.

basic.situation: You are removing old plaster from a small room, and a loose section sits above a doorway.

options.text: I ask a coworker to hold a sack beneath the section as I remove it.
I clear the area below, then remove the loose section in controlled pieces.
I pull the doorway section down first and clear it as it falls.
I break the loose section into smaller pieces before moving debris away.

advanced.situation: Drywall finishers are booked after your crew, but one room will not be ready when they arrive because panel hanging is delayed.

options.text: I finish the delayed room before contacting the finishers about readiness.
I tell finishers to start in the delayed room and catch up later.
I notify finishers of the delay and suggest they start in another room.
I update the lead and agree a revised room handover sequence with finishers.

basic.situation: You are asked to check continuity on a new lighting circuit before handover. The breaker is on because other trades are using the same board for their tools.

options.text: Run the continuity test with the breaker on, since switching off would stall other trades.
Measure the voltage at each fitting while the breaker is on and note the readings.
Switch off and lock the circuit breaker, then test the conductors' continuity with the meter.
Test continuity at the first fitting, since the rest share the same cable run.

advanced.situation: A cold-room compressor motor trips its breaker twice daily. Your insulation test readings are lower than last month's, and the owner is pressing to keep it running for a big delivery.

options.text: Isolate the motor, then test windings and supply cable separately to locate the fault.
Reset the breaker after each trip and log the times to build up a pattern.
Fit a larger breaker so the motor stops tripping and the cold room stays running.
Clean the motor terminals, retest insulation, and keep running if readings improve through the delivery.

basic.situation: During a guided inspection of a kopitiam kitchen, you notice a wall socket with a cracked cover and a scorch mark near the cooker.

options.text: Isolate the socket's supply and report the scorch mark to your supervisor for repair.
Wipe off the scorch mark and list the socket as acceptable since it still works fine.
Replace the cracked cover with a spare from your kit and carry on with the inspection.
Record both defects on the checklist and ask the owner to stop using that socket.

advanced.situation: An old switchboard at a small factory has overheated breakers and brittle wiring. The manager asks if the line can keep running for a big export order this week.

options.text: Recommend reduced load this week and schedule the board replacement once the export order ships.
Explain the specific defects and fire risk, and recommend isolating the board until repaired.
Tell the manager you will watch the board and report if the heat gets worse.
Tighten the loose terminals and tell the manager the line can run for the order.

basic.situation: You are marking socket positions from a blueprint for a classroom. The drawing in your hand is dated earlier than the one pinned on the site office wall.

options.text: Mark the positions at the usual standard heights and spacing so the work keeps moving.
Mark from your drawing and compare with the pinned one afterwards, correcting any positions that differ.
Mark from your drawing, since it was handed to you by your supervisor for this task.
Confirm which drawing is the current revision, then mark the positions from that one.

advanced.situation: A restaurant owner wants a rough price to rewire the dining area and add kitchen circuits. You have visited once, and no drawings are available yet.

options.text: Give a low figure now to secure the job and cover extras later as variations.
Quote a price per point from your last restaurant job, adjusted a little for this site.
Give a price range, list your assumptions, and say the final quote follows the drawings.
Count the points and cable runs, then give one total figure for the owner.

basic.situation: You are pulling cable through conduit already buried in a wall, helped by a workmate. The wires keep snagging halfway along a long run with two bends.

options.text: Add some lubricant on the wires and keep pulling steadily while your mate feeds them in.
Pull a few wires at a time, so there is less friction at the bends.
Run a draw wire first, then pull the conductors together with lubricant and steady force.
Tie the wires to a rope and winch them through the bends in one strong pull.

advanced.situation: A conduit run must turn around a steel beam in a tight ceiling space, and no ready-made fitting in the van suits the offset.

options.text: Squeeze the standard bend into the gap and clamp it tight against the beam.
Measure the offset, bend a matching piece with your bender, and test-fit before fixing.
Bend a piece by eye against the beam and trim it if it is long.
Run a flexible conduit around the beam, since it bends easily and saves fabrication time.

basic.situation: You are fixing a box for a new socket on a plasterboard partition wall. Your screws spin in the board and will not grip.

options.text: Use larger screws in the same holes and tighten until the box stops moving.
Fit a plasterboard-type box with grip clips, then tighten the clips until it sits flush.
Hold the box with a bead of adhesive and let the faceplate screws finish the job.
Slide a small timber offcut behind the board and screw the box into it.

advanced.situation: After connecting a pump motor, your earth continuity test shows a high reading. The client wants it running for the afternoon.

options.text: Retest with a different meter in case the first reading was affected by its leads.
Keep the motor off, then trace and remake the poor earth joint and retest.
Note the reading as acceptable for this old motor and release it for the afternoon run.
Run an extra earth lead from the frame to the board's earth bar, then retest.

basic.situation: You are replacing a cracked socket outlet in an office under supervision. The circuit is isolated, and the new socket's terminals are marked differently from the old one.

options.text: Copy the old socket's terminal positions onto the new one, then have the supervisor check.
Wire each conductor to its marked terminal and tighten the screws, then switch on to check.
Wire each conductor to its marked terminal, tighten the screws, then test before restoring power.
Connect the cables in the order they leave the wall, then switch on to check.

advanced.situation: A new apprentice on your team keeps stripping too much insulation from cable ends when terminating. Work is busy and the client inspects tomorrow.

options.text: Give the apprentice a written strip-length guide and check the finished terminations before the inspection.
Redo the apprentice's terminations yourself this evening so the inspection goes smoothly tomorrow morning.
Move the apprentice to carrying materials until the inspection is finished this week.
Demonstrate the strip length on a spare piece, then watch the apprentice do the next few.

basic.situation: You are measuring a shopfront opening, and the plan lists two glass thicknesses for nearby panels.

options.text: I choose the thinner glass and mark the opening from the plan.
I compare the panel callouts with the opening and confirm the unclear thickness.
I measure the opening and note both listed thicknesses for the installer.
I use the thickness shown beside the closest panel and take the opening size.

advanced.situation: A large facade drawing shows glass panels above a sloped entrance, but the access notes do not show where equipment can stand.

options.text: I ask the site lead to review possible lift positions near the entrance.
I plan panel lifts from the ground beside the sloped entrance.
I mark access limits and compare staging needs with panel sizes and site levels.
I note the slope and suggest staging from the wider entrance side.

basic.situation: You are scoring a small replacement pane, and the marked line runs close to one edge.

options.text: I shift the mark slightly inward and score the glass there.
I score near the edge and snap the excess by hand.
I score the line once and break the excess with a notched tool.
I check the edge clearance, then score and break along the marked line.

advanced.situation: A curved display pane needs a shaped edge for a frame, and the cut leaves a rough section near the corner.

options.text: I polish the rough section until it looks even, then pack the pane.
I ease the corner with the grinder and ask for a fit check.
I check the curve against the frame, then grind and polish the edge to fit.
I grind the rough corner lightly and check the pane in the frame.

basic.situation: You are fitting a small pane into a timber sash, and a thin gap remains along one edge.

options.text: I check the pane seating, adjust it, then seal the edge with putty.
I add putty along the edge and smooth it into the gap.
I press the pane toward the clips and apply putty around the edge.
I pack the gap with extra putty and leave the pane in place.

advanced.situation: You are assembling a metal-framed shower enclosure, and a corner joint does not line up with the gasket.

options.text: I add sealant over the corner and check for visible gaps.
I trim the gasket at the corner and fasten the enclosure together.
I check frame alignment, reseat the gasket, and confirm the joint closes evenly.
I loosen the corner, reposition the gasket, and tighten the frame again.

basic.situation: You are moving a small mirror from the delivery truck, and the route to the room has a narrow turn.

options.text: I ask a coworker to steady the mirror as we guide it through the doorway.
I attach suction cups and guide the mirror slowly around the narrow turn.
I grip the mirror sides and guide it carefully around the narrow turn.
I clear the turn and guide the mirror with suction cups and a coworker.

advanced.situation: A crane is ready to lift a heavy glass panel above a loading area where workers are finishing another task.

options.text: I wait for the crew to finish before starting the planned lift.
I verify the load and route, clear the lift area, and coordinate signals.
I pause nearby work and confirm the route with the operator before lifting.
I signal the crane operator after workers clear the area below.

basic.situation: You are preparing a furnished office for mirror installation, and the floor beneath the work area is polished tile.

options.text: I unload the mirror first and shift the furniture if it blocks access.
I place a drop cloth under the mirror work area and begin unloading.
I move nearby furniture, cover the floor and furnishings, then unload the mirror.
I cover the floor with cardboard and set the tools beside the desk.

advanced.situation: Your truck has several mirrors for different rooms, and a client asks for one room to be completed first while furniture is being moved.

options.text: I ask the client which room needs priority, then identify and unload its mirror first.
I move the furniture first and keep the mirrors secured on the truck.
I unload the first mirror by the entrance and sort the rooms later.
I confirm room order, protect the route, and stage mirrors near destinations.

basic.situation: You are helping assemble a short scaffold beside a window opening, and one brace does not reach its fitting easily.

options.text: I check the frame connections and brace fit with the lead before use.
I push the brace into place and tighten its fitting before climbing.
I show the lead the brace and wait before continuing the assembly.
I leave the brace loose and ask the lead to inspect the scaffold.

advanced.situation: You are helping erect scaffold and hoisting gear for an upper-level glass installation, but the landing area is tighter than shown on the setup drawing.

options.text: I adjust the scaffold footprint while keeping the planned hoist position in place.
I compare the landing area with the setup, note clearances, and coordinate a revised arrangement.
I report the tight landing area and ask the lead to revise the setup.
I move hoist gear toward the wall to make more landing space available.

basic.situation: You find two insulation types noted near a wall section and need to identify which applies.

options.text: I match the wall callout to the schedule and check the material with my foreman.
I compare cavity depth and heat needs with plan notes before choosing a listed insulation type.
I use the type shown nearest the wall and prepare that material for fitting.
I ask a nearby installer which type the crew used in similar walls.

advanced.situation: A complex wall detail lists two materials for different zones, and newer workers ask which one belongs around a narrow service chase.

options.text: I check the plan's zone callout before selecting material for the service chase.
I identify the listed material for that zone and explain its heat performance.
I trace the chase boundary, compare clearance and heat needs, then explain the plan's specified material.
I ask the site lead which plan callout covers the chase before advising workers.

basic.situation: You need to cut several pieces of insulation to fit a straight wall bay before the crew starts fixing them.

options.text: I ask a coworker to hold the tape while I mark and cut the piece.
I estimate the length from the next bay and trim the piece to fit.
I measure the bay and cut the piece, then compare it with the opening.
I measure the bay, mark the piece, and cut along the marked line.

advanced.situation: A wall bay narrows around a brace, and several fitted pieces are needed before the afternoon delivery arrives.

options.text: I copy the first notch across the stack and check the last piece in place.
I map each bay width and brace position, then mark each piece to its own measurements.
I measure both sides of the brace and mark a matching notch on each piece.
I cut straight pieces first and trim their edges at the brace during fitting.

basic.situation: You are fitting rolled insulation to a ceiling section, and your foreman asks you to staple it in place.

options.text: I fit the roll into the section and staple it at the supporting edges.
I fit the roll evenly, keep its thickness intact, and staple it along the supports.
I pull the roll tight across the section and staple it at each end.
I hold the roll in place while a coworker staples the nearest edge.

advanced.situation: Your team is lining a large ceiling with rolled insulation, and early sections show inconsistent coverage around supports.

options.text: I let each installer adjust the roll as needed to keep the work moving.
I review the uneven areas at the end and ask the crew to repair them.
I plan support cuts and coverage, then check each section during installation.
I ask each installer to check the next section against the roll width and supports.

basic.situation: You are assigned to fill the blower hopper and start insulation flow for a small ceiling space under supervision.

options.text: I load the hopper and start the blower while my supervisor watches the nozzle.
I ask the supervisor to confirm the controls before I fill the hopper.
I fill the hopper, check the hose connection, and start the blower at the agreed setting.
I fill the hopper and start the blower at the setting used on the last job.

advanced.situation: Insulation flow from the blower pulses while your trainee is filling a ceiling cavity, and the crew is waiting for completion.

options.text: I pause feeding, inspect the hose for a kink, and explain its effect on flow.
I ask the trainee to steady the nozzle while I check the hopper level.
I lower the flow setting and ask the trainee to keep filling at a measured pace.
I lower the setting and watch whether material spreads across the cavity more evenly.

basic.situation: You are sealing an insulated access opening with tape and a cover before the area is handed to another crew.

options.text: I align the cover, press the tape along every edge, and check for lifting.
I ask a coworker to hold the cover while I tape two sides.
I fit the cover over the opening and tape its edges against the surface.
I stretch the tape across the opening and press down its centre.

advanced.situation: An insulated surface near a damp service area needs finishing, and the available sealant labels describe different uses.

options.text: I use the labelled sealant and plan to inspect the joint after it dries.
I use the sealant from the previous dry area and cover the joint with tape.
I compare the labels' stated uses with the damp exposure and recommend a suitable sealant.
I check the sealant label and ask the foreman whether it suits the area.

basic.situation: You are preparing a clean wall section for insulation, and the foreman asks you to attach metal pins before fitting begins.

options.text: I mark the pin positions, attach them, and brush dust from the surrounding surface.
I attach pins where the surface feels firm and start laying insulation.
I ask the foreman to mark the wall before I attach each pin.
I brush the wall and attach pins at the spacing shown by the foreman.

advanced.situation: During removal, an old insulation layer looks unlike the newer material, and dust begins to fall as the crew approaches it.

options.text: I pause removal and tell the foreman the older layer needs checking first.
I lift a small section to check whether it matches the newer insulation.
I wear the usual dust mask and continue removing the newer insulation nearby.
I stop nearby work, clear others, and report the suspect layer for assessment.

basic.situation: You are reading a simple pipe insulation drawing and need to identify the work required on one line.

options.text: I match the pipe label to notes and confirm listed work with my lead.
I follow the nearby line note and prepare insulation for that pipe.
I ask a coworker which note applies to this pipe size.
I trace the pipe callout and compare its note with the job list.

advanced.situation: Two drawing sheets show different insulation details where a pipe system crosses a vessel, and the fitters need guidance before cutting.

options.text: I hold the cuts and ask the site lead which drawing applies.
I use the vessel detail and explain its insulation note to the fitters.
I follow the thicker detail and mark the pipe for cutting.
I compare both sheets, trace the crossing, and brief fitters on the applicable detail.

basic.situation: A short pipe section needs insulation, and the job notes list two common materials with different heat performance.

options.text: I match pipe heat needs and location to listed material properties before choosing.
I use material already opened for the nearby pipe run.
I choose a familiar material and check its label before cutting.
I compare heat performance notes and check the pipe location with my lead.

advanced.situation: A pipe runs through a hot exposed area, and the specified material is costly and less familiar to the crew.

options.text: I replace it with the cheaper stock material and tell the crew it should be adequate.
I check the listed performance and quantity, then explain the specified material's fit for the exposure.
I compare exposure, shape, performance, and required quantity against available types before advising the crew.
I ask the supplier which material is most commonly used for hot pipes.

basic.situation: You are asked to measure and cut straight insulation pieces for a short pipe run beside a workbench.

options.text: I measure the run, mark the insulation, and cut along the mark with a knife.
I ask a coworker to read the tape while I cut the insulation.
I use the last piece as a guide and trim the new piece after fitting.
I measure the pipe section and cut the insulation, then check its length.

advanced.situation: A pipe fitting creates an irregular shape, and you need several insulation pieces with minimal waste before the team resumes work.

options.text: I measure the fitting and each straight section before marking the cuts.
I measure the fitting once and copy its outline across all the pieces.
I leave extra material around each curve and trim it during fitting.
I map each obstruction and measure each section, then mark cuts to reuse suitable offcuts.

basic.situation: You are preparing a pipe surface for insulation, and the foreman asks you to brush it and apply adhesive.

options.text: I brush the surface clean, apply an even adhesive layer, and check for missed areas.
I spread adhesive over the dusty surface so fitting can start sooner.
I brush off loose dirt, spread the adhesive evenly, and let my foreman check it.
I ask my coworker to brush while I prepare the adhesive for application.

advanced.situation: A shaped vessel surface has old adhesive patches, and the crew is waiting for you to prepare it for insulation.

options.text: I check the surface condition, clear loose residue, and apply the specified adhesive evenly.
I spread fresh adhesive over the patches and start fitting the insulation.
I brush the visible areas and apply adhesive where the insulation will touch.
I inspect the patches and ask the foreman whether they need further preparation.

basic.situation: You are fitting insulation around a simple pipe elbow, and your lead asks you to shape the piece to sit neatly.

options.text: I shape the insulation around the elbow and check that its edges meet.
I shape the piece to follow the elbow and check for gaps along the curve.
I ask my lead to mark the elbow before I trim the insulation.
I force the straight piece around the elbow and tape the open seam.

advanced.situation: You are repairing insulation around a large vessel with several nozzles, and each covering must fit around the obstructions.

options.text: I cut one large opening around the nozzle group and seal the remaining space with tape.
I measure each nozzle, shape the insulation and covering, then check all joints.
I leave extra space around the nozzles and ask the lead to review the finish.
I cut matching openings for the nozzles and cover any visible gaps with spare material.

basic.situation: You are fitting a protective sheet metal cover over insulation on a short pipe section before the area is exposed to weather.

options.text: I ask a coworker to hold the cover while I place screws along the seam.
I fit the cover closely, secure the seam with screws, and check the exposed ends.
I wrap the cover loosely and add one screw near the middle.
I fit the sheet metal around the insulation and secure the seam with screws.

advanced.situation: A sealed access opening on an insulated system is near a high-exposure area, and several covering products are available.

options.text: I apply the familiar sealant and plan to inspect the cover at shift end.
I use the tape used on the last access opening and press it around the cover.
I check the sealant label and ask the lead whether it suits this area.
I compare the exposure and surface with product labels, then apply a suitable listed sealant.

basic.situation: You find greasy fingerprints and light mildew on a bedroom wall before repainting.

options.text: You wash the wall and sand rough spots, then ask someone to check it.
You cover the marks with primer and continue before the room is needed.
You wash and treat the marks, then let the wall dry before sanding.
You sand the marks, then start painting once the wall looks smoother.

advanced.situation: A repair crew is preparing a peeling exterior wall with old coatings and damaged patches before a scheduled repaint.

options.text: You map defects, set removal and repair standards, then inspect test patches before releasing sections.
You assign each worker a wall section and review the surface when the crew finishes.
You let the crew sand every area quickly so the repaint can stay on schedule.
You ask the crew to strip peeling areas and report any difficult patches to you.

basic.situation: A customer wants a muted blue for a small office, and the sample tin looks too bright.

options.text: You mix a small test batch and ask the customer to view it wet.
You adjust measured amounts, blend evenly, and compare a dry sample with the request.
You add a little black paint and stir until the blue appears less bright.
You pour in white paint until the mixture looks close to the office sample.

advanced.situation: Several painters need the same custom green for a large renovation, but small batches have varied between rooms.

options.text: You mix a larger batch and ask the team to keep it covered.
You record approved ratios and ask painters to use them for every batch.
You label a dry standard, record ratios, and train painters to compare each batch.
You let each painter adjust the green until their room looks close enough.

basic.situation: You are painting a bedroom wall beside a bed, tiled floor, and light switches.

options.text: You place a dropcloth on the floor and begin rolling near the bed.
You start painting carefully and plan to wipe any splashes from the tiles.
You cover the floor and bed, mask switch edges, then check the protected area.
You cover the floor and bed with cloths before opening the paint tin.

advanced.situation: A crew is painting a busy lobby with artwork, light fittings, signs, and a stone floor near public walkways.

options.text: You let the crew paint around the artwork and move it if needed.
You assign one worker to watch the floor while others begin around the lobby.
You cover the floor and artwork, then ask painters to work around the fittings.
You map exposed items and walkways, assign covers and fixture removal, then check before work starts.

basic.situation: You are priming a small bare metal handrail before its finish coat.

options.text: You apply a thin primer coat with a brush and leave visible gaps for later.
You brush on primer across the rail and ask a coworker to spot missed areas.
You skip primer and apply the finish paint to save time before lunch.
You clean the rail, apply primer evenly, and check corners before the finish coat.

advanced.situation: A crew is coating an exposed building exterior with several repaired areas and narrow ledges that are hard to reach.

options.text: You ask painters to roll the ledges and spray the broad wall sections.
You divide the wall among painters and review the finish after their shifts.
You select methods for each area, set coverage checks, and pace work around access.
You let the crew spray each section at its own preferred speed and distance.

basic.situation: You find a narrow crack and two small nail holes before applying a simple sponge finish.

options.text: You fill the holes with putty and sponge over the crack while it dries.
You add extra sponge texture over the holes to blend them into the wall.
You fill the crack and holes, then start sponging once the patches feel firm.
You fill each defect, smooth the patches, and let them dry before sponging.

advanced.situation: A client requests a layered faux finish across a feature wall, and the sample shows visible differences between workers.

options.text: You note the layer order and ask painters to match the sample photograph.
You ask the experienced painter to handle the most visible wall section.
You make a reference panel, set layer order and texture cues, then coach painters.
You let each painter apply glaze in their own style across their assigned wall sections.

basic.situation: A work order lists two bedroom walls for repainting, but gives no paint quantity or access details.

options.text: You confirm the walls and finish, measure their areas, then list materials and access needs.
You estimate paint from the room size and collect the usual brushes and ladder.
You measure the walls, estimate paint, and send the quantities for a supervisor's review.
You buy extra paint and begin with the nearest wall while checking the order later.

advanced.situation: You are preparing a cost estimate for repainting a multi-level building with limited access and several coating choices.

options.text: You price the familiar coating and add a general allowance for ladders and supplies.
You verify the work order, measure surfaces, compare coating needs and access, and record quantities.
You use the last building estimate and adjust the total for the larger site.
You measure the building, price likely materials, and ask a senior painter to review access costs.

basic.situation: You find rough wall patches and small nail holes before hanging new paper in a bedroom.

options.text: You sand the rough areas and fill the largest holes before starting.
You smooth visible rough patches and ask a coworker whether the holes matter.
You fill the holes, smooth the patches, and check the wall before hanging paper.
You sand the rough patches and cover the nail holes with wallpaper.

advanced.situation: An old wallcovering has lifted over damp-looking patches, and the substrate feels uneven in several areas.

options.text: You remove loose paper and test repairs after checking damp patches and uneven areas.
You add thicker paper over uneven areas to conceal the visible surface defects.
You remove loose paper, smooth raised spots, and ask the lead about damp patches.
You inspect the wall, map defects, and trial suitable repairs before choosing materials.

basic.situation: You are hanging prepasted paper in a small room and need to activate several strips.

options.text: You follow the product directions, wet each strip evenly, and wipe off excess adhesive.
You dip each strip briefly and hang it while the paste still feels dry.
You brush a little mixed paste onto the driest edges as you hang each strip.
You wet the strips and let them rest while you prepare the next wall.

advanced.situation: A porous bathroom wall needs wallcovering, and the selected material is intended for a damp room.

options.text: You thin glue and brush it over the porous wall before hanging the covering.
You check the surface and product guidance, then apply suitable thinned glue evenly before hanging.
You apply ordinary paste to the wall and hang the material before it dries.
You add extra paste powder to the mix so it grips the wall more firmly.

basic.situation: You have measured wallpaper strips and notice one edge is ragged before hanging them.

options.text: You align a straightedge, trim the rough edge, and check the strip before pasting.
You fold the ragged edge under so it will disappear at the seam.
You trim the ragged edge with a knife while holding the strip by hand.
You trim the rough edge on the pasteboard and set the strip aside.

advanced.situation: A patterned wallcovering has a large repeat, and the next strips must meet across a doorway.

options.text: You leave extra length on every strip and trim the pattern edges at the doorway.
You cut one measured strip and use it as a guide for the remaining drops.
You match the repeat on the roll, measure each drop, and mark cuts before trimming.
You cut several strips to wall height and plan to align the pattern during hanging.

basic.situation: You are starting a wallpaper run on a bedroom wall with an uneven corner.

options.text: You ask a coworker to hold the strip while you line it up by eye.
You begin at the corner and straighten each strip by eye as you work.
You place the first strip near the corner and check its edge with a level.
You mark a vertical guideline, align the first strip, and smooth it onto the wall.

advanced.situation: You are covering a high ceiling with a repeating pattern, and several long strips must meet across the room.

options.text: You start with the clearest edge and have workers smooth strips as they go.
You plan the layout from the room center, mark references, and coordinate strip placement against the repeat.
You hang the long strips from one end and adjust each pattern as it reaches the seam.
You mark one reference line and have the team align each strip to it.

basic.situation: You have placed a paper strip and notice a small air bubble near the center.

options.text: You press the bubble firmly with a fingertip and continue to the next strip.
You roll the bubble toward the nearest edge and check the joint afterward.
You leave the bubble to settle while the paste dries around it.
You smooth from the center toward the edges with a roller and inspect the surface.

advanced.situation: A visible wrinkle crosses a patterned strip in a hotel lobby shortly before the area reopens.

options.text: You smooth over the wrinkle with firm strokes and hope the pattern settles.
You assess the wrinkle, lift the affected section as needed, then smooth and realign the pattern.
You press the wrinkle flat with a brush and ask a coworker to check it.
You roll the wrinkle toward the nearest seam and inspect the strip from the doorway.

basic.situation: You have finished a wall and can see that one seam looks wider than the others.

options.text: You press the seam down and check whether it looks narrower from the doorway.
You leave the seam and focus your check on the wall's central pattern.
You check the pattern at eye level and record the wide seam for the installer.
You inspect alignment and seams, then flag the wide joint for review.

advanced.situation: Several rooms use repeating wallcovering, and a final review finds uneven seams and pattern shifts in some corners.

options.text: You tell the team to tighten seams and compare patterns at every corner.
You review each room and ask installers to fix obvious mismatches they notice.
You set checks for alignment, repeat matching, and seam neatness, then sample rooms.
You check the most visible rooms and accept small shifts in less used spaces.

basic.situation: You are digging a marked service trench, and the foreman asks you to reach the stated depth before the crew brings pipe.

options.text: You measure against the depth marks as you dig, correcting shallow spots before continuing.
You dig steadily, checking the depth at the end of each section.
You follow the trench line and use the first measured section as your guide.
You check the marked depth at intervals and ask the foreman about any uneven stretch.

advanced.situation: The trench base crosses mixed soil, and a pipe crew is waiting for a uniform grade that meets the drawing's fall.

options.text: You tamp each section to the grade marks, then check the fall across the full base.
You compact the middle first, then smooth the remaining base by eye to keep the crew moving.
You let the helper compact the soft areas while you prepare the next pipe section.
You use the tamping machine evenly, following the grade marks and showing a helper the same pattern.

basic.situation: A pipe section needs a measured length for today's run, and you are using a hand saw with guidance from a senior worker.

options.text: You use the previous section as a length guide and trim this pipe to match it.
You measure and mark the pipe, then cut it while holding it steady against the bench.
You mark the length, secure the pipe, and saw along the mark with the senior worker nearby.
You cut to the mark, then compare the section with the drawing before passing it on.

advanced.situation: Two pipe runs meet at a slight angle beside a tight excavation, and the welder is ready to join them.

options.text: You bring the ends together and adjust supports until the gap looks even.
You align both ends to the planned angle and check the joint gap.
You set the layout angle and check the joint with a straightedge.
You tack one edge first, leaving the far side for later alignment.

basic.situation: You are connecting two compatible pipe pieces with the sealant specified for the job, while a senior worker guides you.

options.text: You prepare both ends as directed, apply the specified sealant evenly, and connect the pieces squarely.
You add a little extra sealant at the visible gap and tighten the connection by hand.
You follow the senior worker's preparation steps, then check that the joint is fully seated.
You apply sealant to the joining end and press the pieces together firmly as shown.

advanced.situation: A joint must be sealed in damp conditions, and your crew is unsure whether the planned method will hold on the prepared pipe ends.

options.text: You use the planned method and coach the crew to keep the ends clean and aligned.
You compare the specified method with the pipe and site conditions, then prepare the joint accordingly.
You apply extra sealant to the joint and let the crew continue with the planned method.
You check the product instructions for damp conditions, then explain the preparation steps to the crew.

basic.situation: The site plan marks a short pipe route, and your senior directs you to use a backhoe to move earth beside the work area.

options.text: You confirm the marked route with your senior, then move earth in controlled passes as directed.
You ask your senior to confirm the first pass, then continue along the marked route.
You start moving earth along the visible stakes and check with your senior at the next pause.
You follow the clearest open path and move the soil toward the pipe staging area.

advanced.situation: A revised route passes close to an existing service in a narrow work area, while a loader is needed to clear soil.

options.text: You confirm the revised marks with the supervisor and keep the loader movements slow and deliberate.
You clear the open side first and shift the loader closer once the route becomes visible.
You follow the revised marks and use short loader passes, watching the service as you work.
You review the route with the supervisor, confirm clearance, and move soil in controlled passes.

basic.situation: You are checking a newly laid pipe's slope with a level, and the foreman asks whether it matches the marked requirement.

options.text: You take readings at both ends and report them for the foreman's review.
You compare several level readings with the marks and report any variation.
You check the slope near the joint and tell the foreman if readings match.
You check the middle section and use its reading to describe the slope.

advanced.situation: A stormwater line still backs up after a repair, and indicator readings point to more than one buried section as a possible fault.

options.text: You compare indicator readings, inspect likely sections, and plan repairs around confirmed faults.
You compare readings across points and report the likely fault area to the foreman.
You follow the strongest reading and prepare that section for inspection.
You reopen the last repaired section because it is nearest the backup.

basic.situation: The pipe has passed inspection, and you are asked to cover it with earth while a new worker watches the finishing work.

options.text: You push the nearby soil over the pipe in one pass to clear the work area.
You place the earth in steady layers, checking the pipe remains covered as the work progresses.
You cover the pipe, then check the visible surface and ask the new worker to tidy it.
You shovel earth over the pipe and ask the new worker to spread it across the trench.

advanced.situation: A new worker is ready to tap a pipe for an auxiliary line while others are finishing the cover nearby.

options.text: You mark the opening and direct the cover crew while the worker drills.
You demonstrate each tapping step, then closely supervise as the worker repeats the sequence.
You explain the connection point and ask the worker to follow the marks.
You pause covering, explain the sequence, and supervise preparation of the marked opening.

basic.situation: A short pipe run needs a coupling, and you are assembling the sections with guidance before the next crew arrives.

options.text: You check the ends, fit the specified coupling, and tighten the connection as shown by your lead.
You fit the coupling as shown and use the first connection as a guide for the next one.
You fit the coupling and tighten it firmly, then ask your lead to check the finished joint.
You tighten the coupling until it feels secure and move on to the next section.

advanced.situation: A threaded steel connection sits near a hot work area, and the drawing calls for a durable joint in a tight space.

options.text: You use familiar brazing equipment and ask the lead to check fit before joining.
You shorten a support for welding access and join the pipe without checking the route.
You confirm the joint and access, then prepare ends for its specified joining method.
You check the drawing, select its joining method, and prepare the pipe ends.

basic.situation: A pipe section must be attached to a wall beside a fixture, and your supervisor has shown you the bracket locations.

options.text: You secure the pipe at the easiest bracket points and adjust the fixture connection to meet it.
You fasten the nearest bracket first and use it to hold the pipe while fitting the next.
You place the brackets at the marks, support the pipe, and tighten each clamp evenly.
You attach the clamps at the marks and check the pipe alignment after tightening.

advanced.situation: An underground water line must pass around a foundation obstruction, and the planned route also includes a flow-saving fixture connection.

options.text: You shift the route to the clearest trench and extend the pipe to reach the fixture.
You route the line around the foundation and fit the specified water-saving fixture at the end.
You mark a route around the obstruction and check its clearance with the supervisor before laying pipe.
You verify the revised route and fixture connection against the plan, then install the line clear of the foundation.

basic.situation: You have filled a new pipe section with water, and your lead asks you to watch the gauge for signs of leakage.

options.text: You watch the gauge and tell your lead if its reading starts to fall.
You note the starting gauge reading, watch for changes, and report leaks or pressure loss.
You record gauge readings at the start and end, then share them with your lead.
You inspect the joints and report any water appearing around the connections.

advanced.situation: During a pressure test across several branches, one gauge drops while the others hold steady, and helpers are waiting for direction.

options.text: You compare branch readings, direct checks on the dropping branch, and track pressure changes.
You ask a helper to inspect the dropping branch while you record each gauge reading.
You send helpers to inspect every branch joint while you record the gauges.
You release test pressure and refill, then check whether the same gauge drops.

basic.situation: You are reviewing a plumbing drawing before work starts, and your lead asks which fittings the marked section needs.

options.text: You read the notes beside the section and tell your lead which fittings are listed.
You choose fittings that match the pipe size shown and start setting them out.
You trace the marked section, check its notes, and list the required fittings.
You use the fitting list from the previous section to prepare this one.

advanced.situation: A planned pipe route crosses a beam and a fixture wall, and the installation sequence may need to change to fit the space.

options.text: You check beam clearance and ask the lead whether the planned sequence fits.
You start at the fixture wall and adjust the route when the beam blocks it.
You compare site clearance with drawings and flag the beam conflict before starting work.
You review drawings with the lead, propose routing around the beam, and revise the sequence.

basic.situation: A sink drain is clogged, and your supervisor asks you to shut off the water and clear the simple pipe section.

options.text: You try a drain tool first, closing the valve if water begins backing up.
You loosen the nearest pipe joint to check whether a blockage sits there.
You close the valve, verify flow stops, then clear the section with a suitable tool.
You close the valve, clear the accessible section, and report what you find to your supervisor.

advanced.situation: A facility reports recurring leaks across several repaired lines, and you are assigned to replace a defective component and record the work.

options.text: You tighten the leaking connection and close the work order as repaired.
You choose a worn-looking component, replace it, and record repairs under the line's usual label.
You replace the failed part, recording its location, part number, and repair outcome.
You replace the component and record its location and date in the work log.

basic.situation: You are marking a pipe route on a wall from the drawing, and your lead asks you to place the fixture connection points.

options.text: You measure from the drawing's reference points, mark each connection, and recheck the spacing before drilling.
You use the fixture dimensions to estimate the marks, then compare them with the drawing.
You line up the marks by eye with nearby fixtures and start laying out the pipe.
You measure the first point from the corner and mark the remaining connections at shown intervals.

advanced.situation: A plant room needs a revised pipe layout around equipment, and the project lead asks you to estimate materials and labour for the change.

options.text: You estimate pipe length from the drawing and reuse the previous job's labour allowance.
You measure the route, check specified materials, and estimate quantities and labour for review.
You order extra pipe and supports for the route and possible future changes.
You measure the revised route and estimate pipe, fittings, and labour for the lead's review.

basic.situation: You find a damp patch and a loose cable near the planned collector route. Before installation, you need to identify the site hazards.

options.text: Move the work line away and record the cable hazard for review.
Continue fitting brackets around the pipe and mention the cable later.
Photograph the cable and pipe, then ask the lead to assess both.
Mark both hazards on the site plan and keep nearby work clear.

advanced.situation: A client wants collectors moved to a shaded roof section to shorten the pipe run. You must design the system and advise the crew on orientation.

options.text: Place collectors at the requested angle and route pipes by the shortest path.
Compare exposure, tilt, pipe losses, and system type, then brief the crew.
Check exposure and tilt, then compare output with the shorter pipe route.
Sketch two layouts and ask the lead which orientation the crew should use.

basic.situation: You are helping mount a flat-plate collector on a tiled roof. One bracket sits unevenly as the crew prepares to secure it.

options.text: Reposition the bracket on a sound tile and check its alignment.
Ask the experienced installer to check the bracket before fastening it.
Add a small shim and ask a colleague to inspect the fit.
Tighten the bracket against the uneven tile to keep the work moving.

advanced.situation: A commercial roof has mixed tile and built-up sections, and the collector array spans both. You need to plan mounting and weather sealing with the crew.

options.text: Mark anchor points on both sections and prepare the usual flashing kit.
Use the same anchors across both sections to simplify the mounting run.
Check the roof details and ask the lead to confirm the fixing plan.
Map each roof section, match fixings to its surface, and seal every penetration.

basic.situation: You are cutting plastic pipe for a small solar loop, and a fitting sits loose after your first glue joint. The crew is waiting for the section.

options.text: Ask the supervisor to inspect the joint before you connect the loop.
Apply another bead of glue around the fitting and hold it steady.
Cut back the joint, dry-fit the pieces, and remake it squarely.
Mark the section for review and cut a fresh pipe piece.

advanced.situation: A pump and storage tank are being added to a long solar loop, but the crew's proposed piping route has several tight turns and awkward service access.

options.text: Review flow, fittings, and access, then mark a serviceable route for the crew.
Keep the proposed route and add extra bends where the pipe meets obstacles.
Reroute around the tightest turns and note where access remains limited.
Check the fitting list and ask the lead to review the route.

basic.situation: You are installing a temperature gauge and flow meter from the manual. The diagram shows two sensor positions, and the pipe labels are hard to read.

options.text: Trace the labelled pipes, match sensor positions to the diagram, then verify readings.
Fit one sensor first and compare its reading with the manual.
Fit the gauges where the pipe labels seem closest to the diagram.
Ask a colleague to confirm the pipe labels before fitting both sensors.

advanced.situation: After a controller upgrade, the pump cycles while the collector is cooler than the tank. You need to troubleshoot the control setup before the client handover.

options.text: Review the controller settings and ask the lead to confirm the threshold.
Raise the start threshold until the pump stops cycling during the demonstration.
Swap the sensor plugs and observe whether the pump timing changes.
Compare sensor positions and controller settings with the schematic, then test a full cycle.

basic.situation: You have filled a solar storage tank, and a checklist prompts a leak check. A joint looks damp, but no water is dripping yet.

options.text: Place a cloth below the joint and inspect it after the next task.
Wipe the joint and tell the lead it looked damp during filling.
Dry the joint, watch it under pressure, and record whether dampness returns.
Mark the joint as dry after wiping it so the checklist can close.

advanced.situation: A new solar loop passes a cold-water check, but the pump and controller have not been tested together under operating conditions. The commissioning record is due today.

options.text: Run an operating cycle, check pump and control responses, and record each result.
Record the cold-water result and schedule the remaining checks for later.
Mark the system operational based on the successful cold-water check.
Test the pump manually and ask the lead to approve the commissioning record.

basic.situation: You are tagging valves and sensors before handover. Two similar pipes run beside the storage tank, and the labels on the drawing are faint.

options.text: Tag the clear components and leave the two pipes for a later check.
Copy the faint labels onto the nearby pipes and finish the tag set.
Trace each pipe from its component and label it to match the drawing.
Ask the installer to confirm the two pipe labels before tagging them.

advanced.situation: A shop's solar system has recurring low flow, and its staff will take over routine care. You need to plan maintenance and show them how to diagnose the issue.

options.text: Give staff a general maintenance sheet and ask them to report flow problems.
Show staff the flow meter and arrange a maintenance refresher next month.
Ask staff to reset the controller whenever the flow reading falls.
Set inspection intervals around the fault, teach flow checks, and document escalation signs.

basic.situation: You are applying a textured finish coat to a lounge wall, and the client asks for a light brushed pattern across the surface.

options.text: Test the brush pattern on a spare board, then apply it consistently.
Brush broad strokes across the full wall to finish before the plaster sets.
Start the pattern in a corner and show the client the result.
Use a small trowel to vary the pattern as you cover the wall.

advanced.situation: A hotel entrance requires a repeating ornamental plaster border across a curved wall, with visible joins under bright lighting. You are leading the finish work.

options.text: Make a sample panel and ask the project lead to approve its appearance.
Mark the border height and begin the motif from the entrance corner.
Divide the wall into measured sections and continue the motif across each join.
Apply the motif freehand around the curve and blend joins as they appear.

basic.situation: You are mixing plaster for a small room, and the first batch feels stiff while the crew waits to begin the coat.

options.text: Add a little water and check the feel with the mixing paddle.
Ask the plasterer to check the mix before anyone starts applying it.
Add a large splash of water and mix until the plaster loosens.
Check the mix against the product guidance and adjust water gradually.

advanced.situation: You are estimating plaster and mortar for several blocks, and the delivery slot is tight. Site measurements differ slightly from the drawings.

options.text: Reconcile site measurements with drawings, calculate quantities, and order with a workable allowance.
Order for the larger measured area and hold the excess for later work.
Check the measured area and ask the supplier to suggest order quantities.
Use the drawing quantities and place one order to secure the delivery slot.

basic.situation: You have finished plastering a small room, and offcuts, dust, and empty bags remain near the doorway before the next trade arrives.

options.text: Sort reusable tools, bag debris, and clear the doorway before handover.
Sweep the floor and move the empty bags beside the work area.
Push the offcuts and bags into a corner so the doorway stays open.
Collect the bags and ask the next crew to take the offcuts.

advanced.situation: A renovated shop has patched plaster over old paint and fresh drywall joints. You need to prepare the surfaces and clear the work area before a large finish coat.

options.text: Clean the whole wall and begin coating over the patched areas.
Review the patches with the lead and sweep the floor before coating.
Check bond and dust, prepare each substrate, then clear debris before coating.
Sand the drywall joints and cover the painted sections with a bonding coat.

basic.situation: You are helping set up a low scaffold beside an exterior wall. One leg rests on uneven ground, and the plasterer is ready to climb up.

options.text: Place a loose board under the leg and let the plasterer climb up.
Hold the frame steady while the plasterer climbs onto the platform.
Level the base on firm ground and check the scaffold before anyone climbs.
Ask the plasterer to check the scaffold before using the platform.

advanced.situation: A façade crew is installing prefabricated insulation across a tall shopfront, and scaffold bays must move around openings. You are coordinating the setup and work sequence.

options.text: Review the scaffold layout with the lead and stage insulation panels nearby.
Set the bays to reach the openings and check the frames after relocation.
Move bays as needed and keep panels stacked on the nearest platform.
Plan bay access around openings, secure insulation edges, and check each setup before use.

basic.situation: You are spraying stucco beside a shop window, and a light breeze keeps lifting the plastic sheeting from one corner.

options.text: Continue spraying past the window and clean any splashes afterward.
Add tape to the lifted corner and begin spraying the next section.
Secure the sheeting along its edges and check the window stays covered.
Ask a coworker to hold the loose corner while you spray nearby.

advanced.situation: You are planning an exterior stucco job across a busy shopfront with doors, windows, and a shared sidewalk. Spraying will happen while the shop remains open.

options.text: Cover the full sidewalk and direct customers through the work area entrance.
Cover the nearest windows and move the sheeting as each section is sprayed.
Map splash zones, cover openings and walkway edges, and keep the entrance clear.
Cover the windows and doors, then ask the shop staff about access.

basic.situation: You are preparing an undercoat for a finish layer, and the plasterer asks you to scratch a small test area before the coat sets.

options.text: Scratch even grooves across the test area while the undercoat is workable.
Scratch a few lines in one direction and check the surface by hand.
Make deep grooves quickly so the finish coat has plenty to grip.
Ask the plasterer to show the groove depth before you start scratching.

advanced.situation: A finish coat has pulled away from several patched areas on a curved wall. You need to adjust the undercoat roughing method before the remaining sections are finished.

options.text: Increase groove depth across the remaining wall and continue the finish coat.
Compare failed patches, test scratch patterns on a spare area, and use the matching texture.
Vary the scratch direction on the curved sections and inspect the next coat.
Ask the lead to inspect the failed patches before you change the scratcher.

basic.situation: You are checking a simple beam plan before tying bars, and one callout is faint.

options.text: You compare the callout with the bar schedule and mark the size.
You ask a nearby fixer to read the callout before you proceed.
You trace the bar mark across the plan and confirm its location.
You use the nearest bar size and keep the tying crew moving.

advanced.situation: A structural sketch shows bars crossing a beam opening, while the section detail places them at different levels. The crew is waiting for your read.

options.text: You compare the bar marks and dimensions, then report the clash with a marked sketch.
You follow the section detail and have the crew place the bars there.
You compare both views and flag the conflicting levels before placement starts.
You check the bar schedule and ask the site supervisor which view to use.

basic.situation: You have several marked rods to cut to length with a hand cutter, and your lead is nearby.

options.text: You use the first rod as a guide and cut the rest to match.
You measure each mark and cut the rods as your lead watches.
You cut the first rod, check its length, then cut the remaining marked rods.
You check the cutter setting and confirm one mark with your lead.

advanced.situation: A coated, high strength bar is needed at an exact length, and the usual bar cutter leaves a rough end.

options.text: You use a fine toothed saw and measure each finished bar carefully.
You switch to a torch and trim each bar to the marked length.
You confirm the specified cutting method, then check a sample end and length.
You ask the lead which cutter handles this bar, then prepare the batch.

basic.situation: You are supervised while bending a small batch of rods to the same simple hook shape.

options.text: You ask your supervisor to confirm the bend angle before starting the batch.
You copy the shape from the first rod and bend the rest alike.
You use the bending tool marks and make each hook to the drawing.
You bend one rod to the marked shape, check it, then repeat the bend.

advanced.situation: A complex welded rod joint is needed near a congested beam cage, and two workers ask you how to set up their bends.

options.text: You ask the site lead to approve a bend pattern before the workers start.
You set a bend pattern from the sketch and tell both workers to follow it.
You review the joint detail and explain the bend sequence to both workers.
You check the joint detail, make a trial fit, then brief both workers on the sequence.

basic.situation: You are tying a small floor mat with wire and pliers, following the spacing shown on the drawing.

options.text: You ask a coworker to check the first few ties before you continue.
You tie the crossings firmly and keep the bars aligned to the marks.
You tie each crossing and check the spacing against the drawing as you go.
You tie the corners firmly and let the middle bars follow their positions.

advanced.situation: A large cage has several crowded intersections, and a delivery delay leaves you helping check spacing and ties before the pour.

options.text: You check marked spacing, retie loose crossings, and demonstrate the pattern.
You inspect the main bars and ask the crew to secure loose crossings.
You tighten the accessible ties and tell the crew the cage is ready.
You focus on the congested intersections and report any spacing concerns to the lead.

basic.situation: You are fitting wire mesh into a small concrete form, and your lead has marked its intended position.

options.text: You ask your lead to review the cut before placing the mesh.
You follow the marks and fit the mesh along the form edges.
You cut to the marks, fit the mesh, and check its coverage before fastening.
You trim the mesh to fit the nearest edge and place it in the form.

advanced.situation: Two mesh sheets meet across a broad slab form, and the marked layout leaves a narrow strip near an edge.

options.text: You shift the sheets toward the edge and trim the overlap to use less mesh.
You map the sheet edges against the layout, then ask the lead about the uncovered strip.
You overlap the sheets at the marked join and position them to cover the slab.
You check the layout and edge coverage, then adjust the join while preserving the specified overlap.

basic.situation: You are placing blocks under floor rebar to hold the bars off the deck before the concrete pour.

options.text: You place blocks at the marked points and keep the bars level.
You place blocks near the ends and leave the middle bars resting on the deck.
You place blocks under the bars and check their support along the marked run.
You ask a coworker to check the first row of blocks before continuing.

advanced.situation: A congested form has several tied bars that may shift during the pour, and you are helping secure them before concrete arrives.

options.text: You add ties at the easiest points and ask the crew to watch for movement.
You identify likely movement points, secure those bars, and recheck the clearances.
You add ties to the loose bars and check that the cage stays in place.
You tell the lead which bars look loose and wait for direction on securement.

basic.situation: You are clearing pooled rainwater and loose leaves from a low roof before roofing work begins.

options.text: You sweep away the leaves and drain the visible water from the roof.
You ask the lead to look over the roof after you clear the water.
You push the leaves toward the roof edge so the crew can start sooner.
You clear the leaves and water, then check the surface for remaining debris.

advanced.situation: A waterproofing crew is waiting while you smooth rough patches around drains and a parapet on a wide roof.

options.text: You smooth the rough patches around each drain and parapet with suitable hand tools.
You walk the transitions, smooth raised spots, and recheck drains and edges for snags.
You fill over the rough patches with coating so the waterproofing crew can proceed.
You mark the rough areas and ask the crew lead to choose which ones to smooth.

basic.situation: You are attaching roofing paper in overlapping strips on a simple roof section under a lead's guidance.

options.text: You follow the chalk line and lay the strips over the roof section.
You ask your lead to inspect the first strip before you attach the rest.
You align each strip to the chalk line and check the overlap as you work.
You lay each strip edge to edge to cover more of the roof quickly.

advanced.situation: You are installing a single-ply membrane around several roof penetrations, where the roof surface changes slope near an edge.

options.text: You check the system detail, fit a sample around one penetration, and review the transition.
You mark the tight areas and ask the lead which seam to finish first.
You cut each sheet around the penetrations and bond the seams as planned.
You stretch the membrane across the slope change and trim excess at the edge.

basic.situation: You are covering exposed nailheads with roofing cement on a small repair under supervision.

options.text: You dab roofing cement over the visible nailheads on the repair area.
You ask your supervisor to check the first covered nailhead before continuing.
You spread cement across the nearby shingles to finish the repair faster.
You cover each exposed nailhead and check that the cement seals its edge.

advanced.situation: A roof joint meets a wall beside a drain, and you are sealing the flashing before rain is forecast.

options.text: You flag the drain area for the lead and seal the wall joint first.
You cover the joint with a wide bead of sealant to keep water out.
You inspect the flashing laps, seal the drain transition, and check the full joint continuity.
You add sealant along the visible joint and finish the exposed flashing edges.

basic.situation: You are cutting felt around a vent on a small roof section, with the cut line marked.

options.text: You cut a wide opening so the felt clears the vent with room to spare.
You cut along the mark and test the felt fit around the vent.
You follow the marked line and place the cut felt around the vent.
You ask the lead to check the marked line before you cut the felt.

advanced.situation: A roof valley meets a wall and vent, and you must cut flashing strips to fit all three angles.

options.text: You mark the difficult angles and ask the lead which edge to cut first.
You cut one broad piece to cover the valley, wall, and vent in one pass.
You cut each strip to the visible angle and fit it around the vent.
You mark each transition, make a template, and test the pieces before fixing them.

basic.situation: You are applying reflective coating to an existing roof under guidance, and the surface is ready for the first section.

options.text: You ask the lead to check coating thickness before continuing with the next section.
You add a thicker coat near the edges to use the remaining material.
You coat the marked section evenly and check the surface for missed patches.
You spread reflective coating evenly across the marked roof section, checking for thin areas.

advanced.situation: A client wants more daylight and ventilation in a finished roof, and you are helping install a skylight near an existing vent.

options.text: You check the roof layout and product details, then mark clearances for lead review.
You measure space beside the vent and report the available opening size to the lead.
You review the roof layout and ask the lead where the skylight can fit.
You place the skylight beside the vent and cut an opening sized to fit its frame.

basic.situation: You are setting up scaffold access for a roof repair, and your lead has shown you the planned work area.

options.text: You place the scaffold close to the roof edge so workers can reach across.
You ask the lead to inspect the scaffold after you assemble its frame.
You assemble the scaffold to the site setup and check access before use.
You follow the setup instructions and position the scaffold beside the work area.

advanced.situation: A leak appears on a roof with several patched areas, and you are asked to inspect it and estimate the repair materials.

options.text: You record the leak location and ask the lead to define the repair scope.
You inspect the wet patch and nearby seams, then list materials for the repair area.
You trace leak signs across patched sections and estimate materials for each area.
You inspect patched areas and estimate materials for the clearest visible damage.

basic.situation: You are preparing a replacement panel from a simple drawing. Its note lists a material and gauge, but the stock labels look similar.

options.text: I would take the sheet marked with the listed material and gauge.
I would compare the drawing note with the stock labels before choosing the panel material.
I would cut the available sheet that fits and note its gauge afterward.
I would use the gauge from the drawing and choose the closest-looking metal sheet.

advanced.situation: Two blueprint views show different duct dimensions near a beam. You need to brief the fabricators before they cut the first section.

options.text: I would ask the team to pause that section while I flag the mismatch for review.
I would compare both views and trace the affected dimensions before briefing the team.
I would use the dimension that matches the stock and start cutting the first section.
I would follow the dimension on the larger view and brief the fabricators.

basic.situation: You are marking a rectangular roofing panel from a drawing. The first edge is square, and the dimensions are written beside it.

options.text: I would measure from the squared edge, then check the diagonals before cutting.
I would mark the lengths from the nearest edge and compare the corners afterward.
I would mark each dimension from the same squared edge using the ruler and scribe.
I would copy the dimensions onto the panel by eye and cut the outline.

advanced.situation: Several roofing units share a long run, and apprentices are marking reference lines from different ends. The final overlap must stay consistent.

options.text: I would set one datum, demonstrate the layout sequence, and have each apprentice verify a sample.
I would let each apprentice keep their familiar reference and compare overlaps later.
I would give the apprentices the same dimensions and ask them to coordinate their marks.
I would specify a common starting edge and inspect the first marked unit from each apprentice.

basic.situation: You are shaping a small sheet-metal bracket over a block. The marked bend is close to the edge, and your lead is nearby.

options.text: I would strike the bend firmly once, then adjust the bracket to fit.
I would begin with a light bend and ask my lead to check the shape.
I would hammer the bracket flat against the block until its edge turns.
I would make light hammer passes over the block, checking the bend against the mark.

advanced.situation: A retrofit needs a custom HVAC duct section around a tight beam clearance. The first trial piece nearly fits, and airflow matters across the run.

options.text: I would adjust the section around the beam and test its fit before repeats.
I would map clearance, preserve the duct path, and test one revised section.
I would repeat the trial dimensions and trim each duct section on site.
I would flatten the nearby fold slightly so the trial section clears the beam.

basic.situation: You are riveting a simple seam on a small casing. The edges line up, but one rivet hole seems slightly offset.

options.text: I would align the seam, confirm the hole fit, then rivet the joint as instructed.
I would check the seam alignment and ask my supervisor how to handle the offset hole.
I would widen the hole slightly with a drill and fit the rivet.
I would drive the rivet through at an angle to secure the seam quickly.

advanced.situation: A new welder is finishing casing seams for a batch. Several joints look smooth, but one has a visible gap at the edge.

options.text: I would show the welder the gap and ask them to recheck each seam.
I would grind the visible gap smooth so the batch can move ahead.
I would inspect the batch, mark the gap, and ask the welder to rework it.
I would mark seam checkpoints, show an acceptable sample, and have the welder compare joints.

basic.situation: You are helping move prefabricated duct sections to a renovation site. The route narrows at a doorway, and the next section is bulky.

options.text: I would tilt the section through the doorway while a coworker guides its far end.
I would push the section through first, then turn it once its ends clear.
I would check the route, then move the section with a coworker safely.
I would carry the section alone by its narrow end to save a trip.

advanced.situation: You are fitting a run of duct assemblies through a crowded ceiling. The support framework shifts slightly when the last section is offered into place.

options.text: I would ease the section into place and tighten its nearest support as needed.
I would shift the neighboring assembly first, creating room for the final section.
I would check framework positions, then install the run in a sequence that preserves support.
I would pause that section, inspect its support, and ask the site lead about movement there.
