basic.situation: After cutting panels, you are cleaning the portable shear. Its blade area has metal scraps, and a fastener looks loose.

options.text: I would brush away the scraps and tell my lead about the loose fastener.
I would leave the scraps in place and put the shear back on the rack.
I would clear scraps safely, inspect the fastener, and report the looseness before storage.
I would tighten the fastener with the nearest wrench and return the shear.

advanced.situation: You are helping onboard an apprentice who will maintain shared hand tools. The team has recurring loose handles and no regular inspection routine.

options.text: I would teach the apprentice to inspect handles and report looseness during their shift.
I would set routine checks, demonstrate safe handle repairs, and record recurring faults for follow-up.
I would show the apprentice how to tighten handles and let them handle future repairs.
I would replace loose handles as they appear and ask the apprentice to watch.

basic.situation: You are checking a simple steel frame drawing before members are staged. A beam size is printed beside the grid location you need.

options.text: I would stage the available beam that looks closest to the drawing.
I would read the beam size and ask the lead where it belongs.
I would match the beam callout to its grid location before staging the member.
I would stage the beam with the size printed nearest its mark.

advanced.situation: The steel framing plan and architectural drawing show a brace crossing a service opening. The crew is about to prepare the affected members.

options.text: I would follow the steel plan and ask the crew to prepare the brace.
I would shift the brace slightly to clear the opening and keep work moving.
I would flag the clash, compare both drawings, and brief the crew on pending review.
I would compare both drawings, note the crossing, and hold those members for review.

basic.situation: You are checking a column's vertical alignment with a plumb bob. It appears close, but the beam connection is not yet bolted.

options.text: I would push the column until its plumb line appears centered from the front.
I would check both faces with the plumb bob and report readings before bolting.
I would check one face with the plumb bob and request supervisor confirmation.
I would bolt the connection while the column appears nearly vertical.

advanced.situation: Several columns are being set along an uneven slab. New crew members use different laser references, and small alignment differences are appearing between bays.

options.text: I would ask crews to use their levels and address visible lean during checks.
I would set one datum, demonstrate two-direction checks, and ask crews to verify a sample bay.
I would set a shared laser reference and inspect each pair's first column.
I would let each pair use its laser, then compare columns at the end.

basic.situation: You are assisting with a beam lift under direct supervision. The chains are ready, and the beam has marked lifting points.

options.text: I would attach the chains near the beam ends and ask the supervisor to check.
I would loop the chains around the beam wherever they sit securely.
I would fasten the chains to the marked points and wait for the supervisor's signal.
I would attach the chains at the marked points and show the supervisor before lifting.

advanced.situation: A long girder must be hoisted past a tight access area. The planned cable arrangement may let one end swing near a scaffold.

options.text: I would adjust the cable arrangement and ask the operator to lift slowly past the scaffold.
I would revise the rigging with the lift lead and set a clear signal plan before hoisting.
I would use the usual cable setup and have the crew guide the girder past.
I would review the route and rigging arrangement, then brief the crew on lift signals and swing control.

basic.situation: You are helping position a steel member for bolting. It is close to its mark, but the holes are not yet lined up.

options.text: I would pull the member toward the nearest hole and try the bolt again.
I would ease the member with a hand tool while monitoring the holes.
I would push the member firmly until the holes appear close enough to bolt.
I would check the marks and ask the lead whether the member needs repositioning.

advanced.situation: A prefabricated steel unit is unloaded beside the assembly area. The crane queue is tight, and its orientation will affect the next two lifts.

options.text: I would unload the unit where space is open and let the crew turn it later.
I would position the unit for the next lift and keep the crane queue moving.
I would stage the unit beside the crane, then rotate it during the next lift.
I would check orientation against the sequence and stage the unit for upcoming lifts.

basic.situation: You are tightening bolts on a pre-aligned beam connection. One bolt turns smoothly, while another begins to bind before seating.

options.text: I would use a longer wrench to seat the binding bolt with the others.
I would loosen the nearby bolts slightly and try seating the binding one.
I would pause that bolt and ask the supervisor to check the fit.
I would check the bolt and hole alignment before continuing with the connection.

advanced.situation: You are checking a bolted beam connection while coaching a new worker. Several bolts look seated, but the crew has used different tightening sequences.

options.text: I would review the instructions with the worker and inspect bolts that appear uneven.
I would cover the uneven bolt heads with paint so the connection looks finished.
I would ask the worker to tighten each bolt firmly, then inspect the connection.
I would demonstrate the specified sequence and ask the worker to follow the instructions.

basic.situation: You are cutting a small steel strip to a marked length with shears. The strip is part of a frame, and the first cut is still ahead.

options.text: I would cut at the nearest mark and file the strip to fit afterward.
I would secure the strip, check the mark, and cut along the measured line.
I would trim the strip freehand to match the neighboring piece.
I would hold the strip steady and cut along the mark as drawn.

advanced.situation: You are helping erect a large steel tank section. Its edge meets the next section unevenly, and the crew wants to continue joining the structure.

options.text: I would pull the sections together with a jack and continue the assembly.
I would grind the high edge until both sections meet across the seam.
I would pause the joint and ask the erection lead to inspect the uneven edge.
I would compare the fit with drawings, identify the mismatch, and hold the joint.

basic.situation: A roof has a shaded edge, several vents, and limited access; the senior asks where to begin the panel layout.

options.text: I would choose the easiest section to reach and note its shade for later.
I would mark the clear section and ask the senior installer to review it.
I would compare sun exposure, clear area, and roof condition before suggesting a location.
I would place panels across the vents to use the largest open area.

advanced.situation: You are preparing a layout for three connected buildings, and one roof's condition and utility connection details are still uncertain.

options.text: I would size the arrays from roof area and refine connection details during installation.
I would compare each roof and connection, then develop a layout suited to each building.
I would use the same array layout on all three roofs to simplify the drawing.
I would map each roof, note site features, and flag uncertain structural details for review.

basic.situation: The drawing shows a support rail spacing that differs from the marks on the roof, and you are assembling the first module row.

options.text: I would follow the roof marks and ask the senior to check the row afterward.
I would keep the marked spacing and mount the row as planned.
I would pause that row and compare the marks with the drawing before mounting.
I would shift the rail to match the nearest module edge and continue.

advanced.situation: On a metal roof, a support point moves slightly under load and the next crew is waiting to mount modules.

options.text: I would add a nearby fastener and keep mounting while the support shifts.
I would move modules elsewhere and continue without checking the shifting support point.
I would mark the point and ask the senior installer to inspect the support.
I would pause that section, record the movement, and request an approved repair detail.

basic.situation: You are checking the first string's wiring with a senior nearby, and the polarity labels do not match your meter reading.

options.text: I would check another string first, then return to this reading with the senior.
I would reconnect leads to match labels and finish the string check.
I would record the reading and ask the senior to verify the string polarity.
I would repeat the meter reading at test points and show the senior installer.

advanced.situation: After rain, you find a wet cable entry beside an array that is being prepared for testing on a large installation.

options.text: I would avoid that route and test a dry section while it remains isolated.
I would mark the wet entry and ask the lead installer to review it.
I would isolate the section, inspect the seal, and arrange repair before testing.
I would wipe the entry dry and continue with the scheduled test.

basic.situation: You are checking an inverter's operating voltage under guidance, and the first reading sits near the acceptable limit.

options.text: I would note the reading and ask the senior whether it needs another check.
I would adjust the inverter setting until the displayed voltage looks steadier.
I would record the reading and repeat it at the specified test points.
I would finish the remaining checks and revisit the voltage at the end.

advanced.situation: A site controller has separate daytime and backup modes, but its output falls during a cloudy test and the readings vary.

options.text: I would repeat the cloudy test later and leave the current settings unchanged.
I would compare readings with the design requirements and check each mode against its intended settings.
I would raise the output set point so the controller can recover faster.
I would check the current mode and report the variable readings to the lead.

basic.situation: You are visually checking a small array before activation, and one module has a cracked corner near its frame.

options.text: I would mark the module and ask the senior installer to inspect it before activation.
I would photograph the corner and continue checking the other undamaged modules.
I would activate the array and watch the display for a warning.
I would document the crack, exclude that module, and report it for assessment.

advanced.situation: You are demonstrating a large site's emergency shutdown to a new crew, but the displayed performance readings do not return to their prior pattern.

options.text: I would repeat shutdown and startup, then describe the expected display to the crew.
I would reset the display and continue demonstrating emergency mode to the crew.
I would finish the demonstration, then tell the site lead about the changed readings after training.
I would compare readings with the operating record and explain each mode to the crew.

basic.situation: You are cleaning modules with a senior's guidance, and several have visible dust while one has a loose cable clip.

options.text: I would clean the dusty modules and note the loose clip for the senior.
I would photograph the clip and clean nearby modules with extra care.
I would clean every module first so the array looks consistent for inspection.
I would avoid the loose clip, clean the other modules, and record its location.

advanced.situation: You are updating maintenance records for several sites, and repeated inverter faults appear to cluster after scheduled cleaning visits.

options.text: I would compare fault dates with service notes, then propose targeted changes for review.
I would list recurring faults by site and leave the current schedule unchanged for now.
I would revise each site's schedule using the latest inverter fault reports now.
I would flag the recurring pattern across sites and ask the lead to review all records.

basic.situation: You are mixing mortar for a small wall repair, and the batch looks stiffer than the standard formula shown on the board.

options.text: I would pause and check the formula with the mason before adjusting the batch.
I would add water until the mortar spreads easily across the board.
I would tell the mason the mix looks stiff and ask what to do.
I would mix it longer and see whether the texture improves.

advanced.situation: You are moving grout for a polished stone job, but the narrow access route and the product instructions call for a different handling method.

options.text: I would take smaller loads along the clear route to keep grout moving.
I would carry the batch in manageable loads rather than risk the narrow route.
I would check product guidance and use a covered trolley along the clear route.
I would ask the mason which clear route they prefer before moving grout.

basic.situation: You are wiping fresh grout from tile joints, and a damp sponge begins pulling material from the edges.

options.text: I would use a lightly damp sponge and follow the joint direction with gentle passes.
I would tell the mason the sponge is pulling grout and ask for guidance.
I would wait a little longer, then wipe the tile faces again.
I would press harder so the tile faces are clean before the grout sets.

advanced.situation: You are cleaning dried residue from textured stone and a mixing machine, and the usual water rinse leaves marks on both surfaces.

options.text: I would test mild cleaner on one small area and ask the mason to review it.
I would extend the machine run and scrub the stone with a wire brush.
I would rinse both surfaces again and wipe each dry with clean cloths.
I would identify residue and surfaces, then choose a compatible cleaner and tool for each.

basic.situation: You are helping move a marble slab on a dolly, and the route narrows near a stack of tile boxes.

options.text: I would tilt the slab and guide the dolly around the boxes.
I would secure the slab, clear a safe path, and move it with a spotter.
I would stop at the clear area and ask the mason to check the route.
I would hold the dolly steady while a coworker shifts the boxes.

advanced.situation: You are helping position a large stone slab with a hoist, and its lower edge starts swinging near a finished wall.

options.text: I would pause the lift, steady the load from a safe position, and coordinate the move.
I would guide the swinging slab by hand and hurry it into position.
I would call for the operator to pause while I check the slab's clearance.
I would move nearby tools clear and wait until the slab stops swinging.

basic.situation: You are supplying bricks from a numbered sequence, and the mason asks for the next stack while two labels look similar.

options.text: I would show the two labels to the mason and ask which stack is next.
I would check the number on the drawing and match it to the stack label.
I would take the stack with the closest label and bring it over.
I would bring both stacks nearby so the mason can choose at the wall.

advanced.situation: You are supplying stone for a patterned entry, but the drawing changes direction at a threshold and the next pieces are similar in color.

options.text: I would follow the previous row and supply pieces in that same order.
I would mark the threshold change on the drawing and stage pieces in its shown sequence.
I would ask the mason to confirm the first pieces before I stage the rest.
I would set out the next pieces by color and let the mason place them.

basic.situation: You are removing loose mortar from a small repair area, and the wire brush reveals a crack beside the tile edge.

options.text: I would chip around the crack until the loose material falls away.
I would mark the crack and ask whether to keep brushing nearby.
I would brush the whole repair area lightly and check the edge again.
I would stop near the crack, clean the loose area carefully, and show the mason.

advanced.situation: You are preparing a wall for a stone finish, and removing damaged mortar exposes a loose section where an anchor is planned.

options.text: I would clear loose material, show the area, and confirm a sound anchor location.
I would drill at the marked point and patch around the exposed loose section.
I would shift the anchor toward firm material and carry on after a visual check.
I would pause drilling and ask the mason to inspect the loose section and anchor area.

basic.situation: You are cutting a tile to the marked width, and the first cut leaves a narrow chip along the visible edge.

options.text: I would fit the piece as cut and cover the edge with grout.
I would install the tile with the chipped edge turned toward the wall.
I would trim another piece to the mark and compare the finished edge before fitting.
I would show the chip to the mason and ask whether the piece can be used.

advanced.situation: You are applying sealant around a stone counter, and the gap widens near a corner where the cut pieces meet.

options.text: I would apply a thicker bead across the corner to fill the widened gap with care.
I would pause at the corner and ask the mason how to finish it.
I would seal the straight runs first and return to the corner later.
I would check the joint width, adjust the bead consistently, and smooth the corner neatly.

basic.situation: You are helping fasten a timber frame, and the carpenter asks you to hold a beam while they check the nail line.

options.text: Ask the carpenter to confirm the line, then brace the timber firmly.
Shift the timber to match the panel edge before fastening starts.
Drive the remaining nails where the carpenter points to save time.
Hold the timber steady while the carpenter checks the nail line.

advanced.situation: A scaffold section shifts slightly while you help set it beside a busy work area, and the crew is waiting to continue.

options.text: Keep workers clear and check the scaffold base, braces, and connections.
Check the braces and connections before asking the crew to use it.
Tighten the nearest fitting and let the crew continue their work.
Add a loose timber brace where the section seems to move most.

basic.situation: You are securing stakes to a footing grid when one stake leans as the concrete crew prepares the form.

options.text: Drive the stake deeper until it looks steady from your position.
Ask a nearby worker to hold the stake while you nail it.
Straighten the stake against the grid and secure it firmly.
Check the grid mark, realign the stake, and secure it again.

advanced.situation: A long form must be raised to its marked elevation, but its far end sits low and the pour crew is nearly ready.

options.text: Raise the low end until it matches the nearest visible form edge.
Add a shim beneath the low end and tell the crew it is ready.
Lift the low end while a coworker watches the far support.
Use the elevation marks to guide the lift and check both ends.

basic.situation: You are holding a sighting rod for a reference line when the carpenter says the mark seems slightly off.

options.text: Move the rod toward the mark until the carpenter says it looks aligned.
Keep the rod where it is so the crew can maintain its pace.
Reposition the rod at the marked point and keep it plumb for checking.
Hold the rod steady while the carpenter checks the mark again.

advanced.situation: You are marking tie spacing along a panel, but the final interval does not match the drawing dimension.

options.text: Measure the final interval again before changing any of the marks.
Ask a coworker to compare the last mark with the nearby tie.
Recheck the drawing and measure each interval from the same datum.
Adjust the last mark to make the spacing appear even across the panel.

basic.situation: You finish sanding near a walkway, and sawdust and offcuts remain beside the machine.

options.text: Ask the next crew to tidy the scraps when they arrive.
Push the sawdust away from the walkway with a scrap board.
Sweep the walkway and gather the offcuts before leaving the area.
Clear the walkway, collect offcuts, and clean around the machine.

advanced.situation: Two teams need lumber from storage, and a narrow access route is already crowded with tools and materials.

options.text: Wait until the access route looks quieter, then bring the lumber through.
Carry the requested lumber through the clearest gap to save a trip.
Move the lumber in smaller loads after checking with the nearby team.
Choose the needed stock and plan a clear route before moving it.

basic.situation: You are sanding a panel edge before installation, and a ridge remains visible under the work light.

options.text: Sand the ridge with the same pressure used on the surrounding edge.
Coat the edge now so the ridge blends into the finished panel.
Sand the visible ridge until it feels smooth to your hand.
Check the surface under the light and sand the ridge evenly.

advanced.situation: A shaped timber piece is slightly oversized at one end, and the matching piece is already fitted on site.

options.text: Compare the piece with its mate, mark the difference, then trim gradually.
Sand the end until it fits, checking the joint after several passes.
Measure the oversized end and make one careful cut to match.
Trim the end by eye until the pieces look close together.

basic.situation: You are drilling a hole in a timber, and the bit begins to wander from the marked point.

options.text: Ask the carpenter to steady the timber while you continue drilling.
Keep drilling slowly and steer the bit back toward the mark.
Ease off the pressure and check the bit against the mark again.
Pause and realign the bit with the mark before continuing.

advanced.situation: You are helping square a large form, and diagonal measurements differ while the concrete team waits nearby.

options.text: Shift one corner until the form looks square from your position.
Compare both diagonals and adjust the form before checking its level.
Measure the diagonals again and hold the form while the carpenter adjusts it.
Check the form's level and ask the carpenter which corner to move.

basic.situation: You strip a wire end for a terminal, then notice a small nick in the exposed conductor before handing it over.

options.text: Trim the end back and strip it again, then show the sound conductor.
Attach the wire as prepared and tell the electrician about the nick.
Put the wire aside and prepare another end while the electrician checks it.
Show the nicked end to the electrician and ask how they want it handled.

advanced.situation: You are threading conduit for a complex assembly, and a coupling catches because the threaded end feels uneven.

options.text: Inspect the thread, dress the uneven end properly, then test the coupling by hand.
Try the coupling by hand again, then report the catch to the electrician.
Force the coupling past the rough threads so assembly can continue today.
Mark the conduit end and tell the electrician the coupling seats unevenly.

basic.situation: You are bolting tower components together, and one bolt begins to bind before the parts sit flush.

options.text: Hold the parts together while another worker checks the bolt alignment.
Ease the tool pressure and tell the electrician the parts are not flush.
Back the bolt out, realign the parts, and start it by hand again.
Push the parts together and tighten the binding bolt to finish the assembly.

advanced.situation: You are helping rig a hoist for an elevated installation, and the load begins to swing as it clears the ground.

options.text: Lower the load to the ground and tell the electrician it swung during lifting.
Keep raising slowly while a coworker guides the load by hand.
Reduce the hoist speed and ask nearby workers to clear the lifting path.
Pause the lift, steady the load with a tag line, and check the rigging.

basic.situation: You are pulling wiring through a drilled opening, and the cable jacket catches on a rough edge.

options.text: Reduce tension and tell the electrician the cable has caught on the opening.
Ease the cable back, protect the edge, then pull while watching the jacket.
Pull harder so the wiring clears the opening before the crew changes tasks.
Ask a coworker to feed the cable while you guide it through the opening.

advanced.situation: You are stringing cable through a long conduit run, and resistance rises sharply before the cable reaches the next access point.

options.text: Stop the pull, check the route at the access point, and resume with controlled tension.
Ease the pull and tell the electrician resistance increased along the conduit run.
Pull harder with the crew so the cable reaches the access point on time.
Add another worker to the pull and watch for movement at the conduit entrance.

basic.situation: You are checking an electrical unit for loose connections, and one terminal moves when you touch the wiring.

options.text: Tighten the terminal with a hand tool and report the movement to the electrician.
Hold the wire still while another worker tightens the terminal connection.
Tell the electrician the terminal moved and wait beside the work area.
Stop handling the unit, keep clear, and alert the electrician to the moving terminal.

advanced.situation: You are tracing a suspected short with a test meter, but the reading changes when the circuit setup shifts.

options.text: Check the meter setup and circuit condition, then repeat the test before identifying the fault.
Use the first reading and replace the part that seems most likely faulty.
Try a different meter range and note whether the reading settles down.
Repeat the reading and tell the electrician it changes when the setup shifts.

basic.situation: After electrical work, you are washing parts when a small component slips onto the wet floor near the work area.

options.text: Pick up the part and finish washing it safely at the sink.
Tell the electrician the part fell and leave it for the cleanup round.
Secure the area, retrieve the part, and dry the wet floor before resuming.
Step around the part and continue washing the remaining components at the sink.

advanced.situation: You are digging a conduit trench, and the marked route crosses a busy walkway used by other crews.

options.text: Start at the far end and leave the walkway section until later.
Dig quickly across the walkway before more crews pass through this morning.
Tell crews about the trench route and ask them to use another path.
Mark and barricade the route, then coordinate a safe crossing before digging there.

basic.situation: You are moving tools on a handtruck, and the load shifts as you reach a sloped path to the work site.

options.text: Slow the handtruck and ask a coworker to walk beside the load.
Tell the electrician the load shifted and ask them to meet you at the site.
Hold the handle tightly and push down the slope at a steady pace.
Stop on level ground, secure the load, then choose a stable route to the site.

advanced.situation: You are positioning equipment with a hoist, and its load begins drifting toward a nearby stack as you raise it.

options.text: Pause the lift, control drift with a tag line, and check the path.
Reduce the hoist speed and have a coworker watch the nearby stack.
Lower the load to a clear spot and tell the electrician where drift began.
Keep raising while a coworker pushes the equipment clear of the nearby stack.

basic.situation: You are masking a bedroom before painting, and the homeowner's polished floor meets the wall.

options.text: You cover the floor fully, seal the edge, and check the route to the doorway.
You mask the wall edge and ask where the remaining floor sheets are stored.
You lay a narrow strip along the wall and begin carrying paint tins.
You tape the floor edge quickly, then start helping with the first coat.

advanced.situation: You are helping protect a busy renovation area where painters and plasterers share a narrow hallway beside finished flooring.

options.text: You tape the nearest doorway and let each crew cover its own section.
You spread sheets across the hallway and ask the crew to watch their footing.
You cover the hallway floor and mark a clear route for workers carrying materials.
You ask the painters where their floor sheets are before covering the hallway.

basic.situation: You are assisting at a stripping tank, and a supervisor points out the tagged cabinet panels waiting nearby.

options.text: You lower the panels into the nearest open tank to keep the line moving.
You place the tagged panels in the tank after checking the supervisor's instructions.
You ask the supervisor to confirm the tank before placing the panels.
You check the panel tags and place them in the tank marked for that batch.

advanced.situation: You are loading tagged metal pieces into a stripping tank when the schedule changes and another batch is waiting nearby.

options.text: You follow the revised schedule and check each tag before loading the tank.
You hold the pieces aside and ask which batch should go in next.
You compare the tags with the batch list, then load the matching pieces.
You load the waiting batch first because the tank is already prepared for work.

basic.situation: You are supporting a plasterer who is smoothing a wall and asks for a clean trowel and another pail of mix.

options.text: You pass a clean trowel and place the pail beside the work area.
You bring the pail first and search for a clean trowel after plastering.
You hand over the clean trowel and bring the pail within reach.
You hand over a used trowel and leave the pail request for later.

advanced.situation: You are supplying two crews on a renovation floor, and both request the same type of ladder before their next tasks.

options.text: You park the ladder by the doorway so either crew can collect it.
You give the ladder to the crew that asked first and move on to supplies.
You check each task and position the ladder where it avoids blocking the shared passage.
You confirm each crew's timing, then assign the ladder to the earlier task.

basic.situation: You are carrying plaster to a plasterer, who says the next batch should be mixed using the marked instructions.

options.text: You carry the dry materials over and let the plasterer mix them there.
You mix the batch to the marked instructions and carry it over steadily.
You prepare the batch and ask the plasterer to check its consistency before carrying.
You add extra water so the plaster is easier to carry to the wall.

advanced.situation: You are helping remove metal furniture from a stripping tank, and the prescribed waiting period ends as the work area becomes crowded.

options.text: You wait for the aisle to clear before taking the first piece out.
You prepare a clear landing area, then remove the pieces when their time is due.
You lift the pieces out as soon as space opens beside the tank.
You follow the prescribed timing and move each piece to the designated clear area.

basic.situation: You are helping erect a small scaffold for a painter, and the supervisor asks you to position its next frame.

options.text: You carry the frame to the work area and wait for another instruction.
You set the frame in place as directed and check its fit with the supervisor.
You position the frame beside the others and ask whether its alignment looks right.
You wedge the frame against the wall so the painter can start sooner.

advanced.situation: You are helping erect scaffold sections on uneven ground, and a painter is waiting to reach a high wall.

options.text: You hold the frame steady while the painter climbs to test its reach.
You check that the frame connections are seated, then flag the uneven base.
You place a loose board under one leg so the section sits level.
You pause at the uneven base and ask the supervisor how to set the section securely.

basic.situation: You are sanding a patched plaster wall, and the painter asks you to smooth the area around a repaired crack.

options.text: You sand the patch evenly and feel the edges before passing the surface on.
You ask the painter to check the patch before sanding the final section.
You smooth the patch and inspect the surrounding area under the work light.
You sand the centre quickly and leave the raised edge for later.

advanced.situation: You are preparing several plaster repairs for painting, and one filled crack feels raised while nearby patches look smooth.

options.text: You sand every patch for the same amount of time before the painter arrives.
You run your hand over each patch and mark the areas that still need sanding.
You compare the raised repair with nearby surfaces and sand it flush.
You apply another coat of paint over the raised crack to hide the line.

basic.situation: You are cutting pipe for a fitter, who gives you a length and marks the cut point.

options.text: You measure the length once, cut it, and ask the fitter to check the result.
You cut at the nearest mark and carry the pipe to the fitter.
You measure from the marked end, cut at the line, and pass the pipe safely.
You hold the pipe steady while another helper finds a tape measure.

advanced.situation: You are preparing threaded pipe for a tight installation, and the fitter's sketch shows two sizes close to one another.

options.text: You compare pipe labels with the sketch before cutting each measured length.
You cut a sample piece and ask the fitter to inspect it.
You choose the larger pipe because it seems safer for this connection.
You match each pipe to the sketch and check thread engagement with the fitter.

basic.situation: You are helping dig a shallow service ditch, and the supervisor marks the route and depth for the pipe.

options.text: You dig along the marked route, check the depth, and keep the trench clear.
You follow the marked route and ask the supervisor to check the depth before laying.
You start digging where the ground is softest and reconnect with the mark later.
You dig a deeper trench so the pipe has extra room beneath it.

advanced.situation: You are helping lay pipe in a long sewer ditch, and the grade marks become harder to see near a change in direction.

options.text: You follow the ditch base and join the next pipe section at the turn.
You pause laying at the turn and recheck the grade marks before joining the next section.
You set the next pipe aside and ask the crew where the grade continues.
You use the last visible grade mark to align the next pipe section.

basic.situation: You are assisting a fitter with a valve installation, and they ask you to hold the coupling while they tighten it.

options.text: You hold the coupling steady while keeping the tools within the fitter's reach.
You grip the valve body and turn it to help tighten the coupling.
You hand over a wrench before the fitter finishes positioning the coupling.
You hold the coupling aligned and pass the requested hand tool when signalled.

advanced.situation: You are helping assemble a water line with several couplings and a valve, and the fitter's layout leaves little room to turn a wrench.

options.text: You sort the fittings by connection and stage the likely tools beside the line.
You arrange the couplings and tools in assembly order, keeping the wrench access clear.
You hold the next coupling while the fitter clears space around the valve.
You pass parts as requested and shift the valve closer to the wall for room.

basic.situation: You are collecting pipe and tools for a fitter, who says the crew needs supplies at the work site before the next task.

options.text: You check the requested sizes and carry the pipe and tools to the marked work area.
You take the nearest pipe lengths and bring them over with the tool box.
You bring the tools first and return for pipe after the fitter begins.
You read the request, gather the listed pipe sizes, and load the tools for transport.

advanced.situation: You are supplying two plumbing crews, and both request pipe and tools while the storage area has limited room for loading.

options.text: You load the longer pipes first because they take up the most storage space.
You compare both requests, separate the pipe by size, and load each crew's tools together.
You label the pipe bundles by crew and gather the tools beside them.
You ask each crew to collect its supplies when a space opens.

basic.situation: You are holding a pipe bracket against a wall while a fitter prepares to drill its fixing holes.

options.text: You hold the bracket on marked points and keep it steady during drilling.
You shift the bracket slightly so the drill can reach the wall from that angle.
You hold the bracket near the wall while the fitter marks the holes.
You keep the bracket steady and ask the fitter to confirm its position.

advanced.situation: You are helping mount several pipe hangers across a ceiling, and one marked position conflicts with an existing beam.

options.text: You drill a new hole beside the beam so the hanger stays near its marked position.
You mark a nearby clear spot and tell the fitter about the change.
You flag the conflict and ask the fitter to confirm another support point.
You hold the hanger in place while the fitter checks the beam location.

basic.situation: You are cleaning after pipe work, and a fitter asks you to clear the floor and wipe the tools before the next job.

options.text: You sweep larger scraps aside and leave the smaller pieces beside the workbench for now.
You collect debris, wipe tools with approved solvent, and clear the floor.
You wipe the tools first and ask the fitter to clear the floor debris.
You sweep the floor and group the used tools for a later wipe-down.

advanced.situation: You are helping with a leaking pipe repair, and water appears again near a section the fitter has just examined.

options.text: You report the returning water and mark the damp area before removal continues.
You place a bucket beneath the leak and move the tools aside.
You loosen the nearest pipe joint to give the fitter access to the wet section.
You tell the fitter water has returned and point out the damp section.

basic.situation: You are laying roofing felt before tile installation, and a gust lifts one edge while the roofer measures the next section.

options.text: Hold the lifted edge while the roofer checks the overlap.
Cover the loose edge with cement and continue the next felt run.
Secure the felt with approved fasteners and align its overlap before continuing.
Lay the next felt strip across the lifted edge and keep moving.

advanced.situation: Rain has stopped, but a leak remains near a metal roof seam. The roofer asks you to help with a temporary repair before the next shower.

options.text: Hold the patch materials ready while the roofer checks the seam.
Nail a spare metal sheet over the seam to cover the drip.
Mark the leak area and help the roofer fit a compatible temporary patch.
Spread roofing cement across the wet seam and cover it with felt.

basic.situation: You are helping hoist roofing bundles to a roof when a coworker calls for another load, and the rope begins to twist.

options.text: Pause the lift and untwist the rope before guiding the next bundle up.
Send another bundle up on the same twisting rope to save a trip.
Ask the coworker to pull faster so the bundle clears the edge.
Keep the load steady while the coworker guides the rope from below.

advanced.situation: You are heating chopped tar in a kettle when the temperature rises faster than expected and another worker brings more material to add.

options.text: Lower the heat and add smaller pieces as the kettle settles.
Tip the new tar into the kettle so the batch heats together.
Ask the roofer to check the heat while you keep chopping tar.
Stop adding tar and alert the roofer while you check the kettle controls.

basic.situation: You are sweeping a roof before new felt goes down, and loose nails are mixed with leaves near the work area.

options.text: Brush the nails and leaves into the open drain to clear the surface.
Sweep the debris into a pile for the roofer to collect.
Gather the nails and leaves into separate containers before clearing the roof.
Push the leaves and nails toward the roof edge with a broom.

advanced.situation: You are clearing a gutter after heavy rain when water backs up at a downspout and the blockage is out of easy reach.

options.text: Clear the reachable gutter section and report the backup to the roofer.
Push debris farther down with a long tool to reopen the flow.
Check safe access, then clear reachable debris without sending it into the downspout.
Ask the roofer to check the downspout before trying to move the blockage.

basic.situation: You are helping check a finished roof for leaks, and the roofer asks you to report what you see during a hose test.

options.text: Tell the roofer the roof passed after checking the driest room.
Check the ceiling after the hose test and note any damp patches.
Report any visible drips as the roofer moves the hose along.
Watch the interior for drips while the roofer wets each roof section in turn.

advanced.situation: You are helping inspect an older tiled roof before repair work, and one slope has worn areas near several tile edges.

options.text: Mark visible worn tiles across the slope and note each area for the roofer.
Mark worn areas by location and alert the roofer for closer checks.
Tell the roofer that several tile edges look worn and need checking.
Call the roof sound after checking only the easiest part of the slope.

basic.situation: You are holding a roofer's tools during a flashing repair when they ask for a snip, but two similar tools are beside you.

options.text: Pass both snips so the roofer can choose while cutting.
Pass the tin snips they named and keep the flashing steady.
Ask which snip they need and keep the other tools steady.
Hand over the nearest snip and hold the flashing in place.

advanced.situation: You are assisting with a complex roof repair, and the roofer needs a flashing piece held in place while checking how it meets the wall.

options.text: Fasten one corner temporarily so the roofer can inspect the fit and adjust it.
Hold the flashing at its mark while the roofer checks the wall joint.
Press the flashing firmly against the wall so it stays in place.
Hold the flashing steady while the roofer checks the wall joint.

basic.situation: You are cleaning tools after a roofing shift when a hammer has tar on its handle and a roofer is waiting to use it.

options.text: Scrape off the tar and return the hammer for the next task.
Wipe the handle with a rag and place the hammer with the clean tools.
Dip the hammer in solvent and return it while the handle dries.
Clean the handle and check the hammer head before returning it.

advanced.situation: You are checking equipment for the next shift when a rope pulley feels stiff and the crew plans to hoist roofing bundles soon.

options.text: Use the pulley for one bundle and watch for any change in movement.
Tag the stiff pulley and place a working spare beside the hoisting area.
Test the pulley gently with a light bundle before the crew uses it.
Tell the roofer about the stiffness and ask them to check the pulley before hoisting.

basic.situation: You are checking a small building plan against the safety checklist and notice that a stair detail is missing from the submitted sheet.

options.text: Compare the submitted sheets with the checklist and record the missing detail clearly.
Mark the plan as complete because the stair appears on another drawing.
Record the missing stair detail and ask the senior inspector how to note it.
Note that the stair detail is unclear and return the plans for review.

advanced.situation: You are comparing a revised plan with earlier comments, and a fire exit detail appears to conflict with a safety requirement in the checklist.

options.text: Mark the revised detail as acceptable because the exit is still shown.
Send the revised sheet and earlier comment to the senior inspector.
Trace the revised detail against the cited requirement and prepare both for senior review.
Ask the designer to clarify the exit detail before recording the concern.

basic.situation: You are observing a site with your mentor when workers begin carrying materials through a walkway beside active work.

options.text: Record the work as safe because the workers are carrying materials carefully.
Record the walkway conflict and alert your mentor while observing the route.
Ask a nearby worker if the walkway can be cleared during the task.
Note the busy walkway in your log and mention it after the round.

advanced.situation: You are monitoring a crowded site where deliveries, lifting work, and pedestrian access overlap at different times during the day.

options.text: Treat the site as controlled because a spotter is present during lifts.
Watch the lifting zone closely and note any near misses during the round.
Report that deliveries and pedestrians share the same area during busy periods.
Map route overlap times and share monitoring points with the senior inspector.

basic.situation: You are watching a plumbing installation with a mentor and notice a pipe joint that appears loose before the wall is closed.

options.text: Wait until the pressure test to see whether the joint leaks.
Point out the joint and record its location for the mentor to check.
Check the joint against the plan and tell your mentor before it is covered.
Sign off the plumbing check because the pipe follows the planned route.

advanced.situation: You are reviewing a complex wiring installation, and the equipment layout differs from the approved drawing near a service access panel.

options.text: Accept the layout because the equipment is installed and working.
Show the contractor the changed layout and ask for their explanation.
Compare the installed layout with the drawing and document how access is affected.
Record the equipment locations and refer the drawing conflict to your senior.

basic.situation: You are measuring a new doorway with your supervisor and find one side differs from the plan measurement.

options.text: List each measurement, then ask your supervisor to compare readings against the plan.
Repeat both side measurements and record each reading beside the plan dimensions.
Record the frame appearance and request another measurement before assessing plan alignment.
Check the doorway level, then note whether its frame appears straight and aligned.

advanced.situation: You are inspecting a bridge repair and notice a new crack beside a joint during a scheduled check, with no prior note about it.

options.text: Photograph the crack, note its location, and flag it for structural review.
Close the scheduled check as satisfactory since the bridge remains open.
Measure crack width and compare it with the nearby joint during inspection.
Record the crack in your notes and alert the senior inspector before closing.

basic.situation: You are preparing a building permit file and notice the application lists a floor area that differs from the attached plan.

options.text: Return the file to the applicant with a note that details differ.
Mark the area difference and prepare a query for the senior inspector to review.
Enter the larger area so the application can move to processing.
Compare both area figures, note mismatch, and hold the file for review.

advanced.situation: You are reviewing a revised building plan after a dispute about a required specification, and the submitted sheet does not address the earlier comment clearly.

options.text: Mark the plan as approved because a revised sheet was submitted.
Send the revised sheet and earlier comment to the authorized reviewer for a determination.
Ask the applicant to explain how the revised sheet addresses the comment.
Compare the revised sheet with the cited specification and list unresolved points.

basic.situation: You are filling out a daily inspection log when your supervisor asks you to add photos of a partially completed wall.

options.text: Note the wall's progress and request a photo reference from your supervisor.
Take photos from two angles and label them with the inspection location.
Attach an older photo of a similar wall to complete today's log.
Photograph the wall and add images to today's inspection log.

advanced.situation: A contractor asks why a recorded inspection item needs remedial work, and you have the cited requirement and site photos in the file.

options.text: Explain the cited requirement alongside the matching site photo and recorded finding.
Tell the contractor the item can be closed because the work looks improved.
Repeat the cited requirement and point the contractor to the inspection record.
Ask the contractor to discuss the item with your senior inspector.

basic.situation: You are auditing a small shop and need a morning baseline; the owner can pause nonessential loads for a short meter reading.

options.text: Use one quick reading and enter it as the shop's typical daily use.
Check the meter setup, capture readings across the busy period, and label each interval.
Record the meter reading, time, and active equipment, then repeat after the shop settles.
Log readings at agreed intervals and note equipment changes that could explain variation.

advanced.situation: Your weatherization plan seals attic gaps in an occupied home, but the inspection notes show damp patches near the roof framing.

options.text: Photograph the damp area and ask the crew to check it during installation.
Mark the plan ready based on the clear access and keep the crew booking unchanged.
Record the damp patches and raise them with the project lead before confirming the work sequence.
Flag the moisture concern, document its location, and request a qualified assessment before that work proceeds.

basic.situation: A café gives you twelve months of electricity bills, but one month is missing and the tariff changed during the year.

options.text: Compare billed usage by month, note the tariff change, and flag the missing bill.
List each bill by month and mark the missing period for follow-up.
Average the available bills and use that figure as the full-year baseline.
Separate usage from charges, compare months across the tariff change, and flag the missing bill.

advanced.situation: A workshop runs a day shift, but its cooling bills peak on weekends; the manager wants to know when the building needs cooling.

options.text: Map operating hours and cooling loads by day, then check weekend peaks against occupancy records.
Chart the weekend bills beside normal weekdays and note the cooling peak for discussion.
Compare monthly bills and ask the manager which weekends had unusual activity.
Treat the weekend peak as a billing anomaly and use weekday hours for cooling estimates.

basic.situation: During a small office audit, your blower-door test shows airflow near a closed rear door, and the tenant has time for one follow-up check.

options.text: Record the total test reading and list the rear door as a likely leak location.
Mark the door as the source and recommend replacement from the first reading.
Check the door edges with a smoke pencil during the test and record the airflow direction.
Repeat the test, compare pressure readings near the door, and note the test conditions.

advanced.situation: A contractor has installed a high-efficiency pump, and its display shows normal operation although the audited flow reading is below the specification.

options.text: Photograph the display and ask the contractor to explain the lower flow reading.
Record the flow and settings, compare them with the specification, and request a targeted adjustment check.
Sign off from the display reading and leave the flow check for the next service visit.
Repeat the flow reading under the same conditions and share the result with the installer.

basic.situation: A homeowner accepts attic insulation, and you need to prepare a job sheet that lets the installer quote and plan the work.

options.text: Note the attic size from the owner's estimate and name the insulation upgrade.
List the proposed insulation and attic access details, then request a site measurement.
List the attic area, proposed insulation, access notes, and a site measurement reference.
Write attic insulation on the sheet and let the installer choose the work details.

advanced.situation: A commercial building has sharp afternoon demand peaks, and you are assessing whether its management system can control selected loads.

options.text: Inspect the control panel and peak-load list, then note any obvious barriers.
Recommend peak control from the bill pattern and leave equipment compatibility for later.
Check the control system and loads, then ask the facilities team about operating limits.
Review the control system, target loads, and operating constraints before judging feasibility.

basic.situation: A small office keeps its air-conditioning running after staff leave, and you are prioritizing practical energy-saving measures for the owner.

options.text: Share a reminder about switching units off and leave prioritization for the owner.
Suggest a shutdown schedule and note that after-hours operation may waste energy.
Suggest a shutdown schedule and estimate savings from the known after-hours run time.
Recommend replacing the air-conditioning units as the first measure for the office.

advanced.situation: A rural clinic has frequent power interruptions and high cooling costs; the manager asks which efficient technology or alternate source merits review.

options.text: Share examples of solar and efficient cooling, then invite the clinic to choose a direction.
Recommend rooftop solar from the available roof space and current electricity bill.
Review efficient cooling options and ask the manager whether alternate supply is a priority.
Compare efficient cooling and alternate supply options against the clinic's load and site limits.

basic.situation: A tenant asks whether a portable heater costs more to run than a ceiling fan, and you have their appliance wattages and usage hours.

options.text: Use the heater's wattage alone to say which appliance costs more to run.
Estimate each appliance's energy use from wattage and hours, then explain the difference.
Tell the tenant that the heater usually costs more and suggest shorter use.
Compare the appliances using wattage and hours, then explain the cost estimate and assumptions.

advanced.situation: You are overseeing pipe insulation at a home, and the installer has begun covering a section where the pipe route differs from the work sheet.

options.text: Record the route change and ask the installer to confirm the next section's fit.
Pause covering that section, compare the route with the job sheet, and document the agreed correction.
Let the installer finish the section and describe the route change in your report.
Photograph the route, compare it with the sheet, and discuss a correction with the installer.

basic.situation: You are checking a lift after a service call, and a test meter shows an inconsistent brake switch reading during a floor stop test.

options.text: Replace the switch from the first reading and record the lift as tested.
Repeat the switch test, compare readings with the wiring diagram, and record the result.
Repeat the switch test and note whether the inconsistent reading returns during a floor stop.
Check the switch connection and meter leads, then report the reading to the senior technician.

advanced.situation: A lift intermittently misses floor calls after a control panel replacement; a junior technician asks you which checks to run first.

options.text: Review fault history, trace the call circuit, and guide one measured check at a time.
Check call wiring and panel connections with the junior, then record loose terminals.
Ask the junior to repeat the panel test and record any displayed error codes.
Replace the suspected board only after checking its connectors and documenting the call failure.

basic.situation: You are fitting guide shoes on a lift car, and the rollers feel uneven as the car moves along a short test section.

options.text: Recheck the roller spacing, adjust the uneven side, and test the travel again.
Inspect the roller positions and ask the senior fitter to confirm the adjustment.
Check the shoe seating and roller alignment against the assembly reference before fastening.
Tighten the rollers until the car feels steady and continue assembly.

advanced.situation: You are overseeing an escalator assembly, and a landing section arrives with a slight frame offset that could affect alignment with the next section.

options.text: Hold the connection, measure the offset, and ask the lead fitter about alignment limits.
Draw the sections together with the hoist and adjust the trim after assembly.
Inspect the landing frame and mark the offset for correction during final alignment.
Measure the offset, check the frame references, and sequence alignment checks before connecting sections.

basic.situation: A lift door hesitates at closing, and you are assigned to adjust its mechanism under a senior technician's supervision.

options.text: Inspect the mechanism and discuss a small adjustment with the senior technician before testing.
Check the door travel, make the supervised adjustment, and test the safety response afterward.
Record the hesitation and ask the senior technician to make the adjustment.
Turn the door adjustment until closing looks smooth, then return the lift to service.

advanced.situation: During a scheduled repair, a junior technician is ready to dismantle a worn door lock while the lift is isolated for maintenance.

options.text: Review isolation and dismantling steps with the junior, logging checks and parts during work.
Show the junior lock removal steps and update the repair log after reassembly.
Ask the junior to photograph the lock and note its condition before removal.
Let the junior remove the lock, then record the part number in the repair log.

basic.situation: You are reviewing a lift installation blueprint before staging equipment, and the machine room layout differs from the site sketch.

options.text: Stage equipment using the site sketch, then resolve the layout difference during installation.
Review blueprint symbols and ask the lead which layout should guide equipment selection.
Use the blueprint to list the main components and note the sketch discrepancy.
Compare blueprint and site sketch, mark differences, and confirm equipment layout with the lead.

advanced.situation: A service report says a newly installed lift passed its checks, but the attached records do not show a door alignment measurement.

options.text: Compare installation checks, flag the missing measurement, and request its record.
File the report as complete because the installer recorded a passing result on site.
Note the missing measurement in your review and send the report to the lead.
Ask the installer for the alignment measurement and attach it to the service report.

basic.situation: You are helping fit an outer lift door frame on one floor, and its opening appears slightly out of square before the door is hung.

options.text: Hang the door and adjust its closing force to compensate for the frame.
Check the frame level and ask the installer whether the opening needs adjustment.
Mark the uneven edge and let the lead fitter decide how to set the frame.
Measure the opening, check the frame alignment, and report the out-of-square condition before fitting.

advanced.situation: You are coordinating outer door frame work across several floors, and two crews need the same lift shaft access tomorrow.

options.text: Sequence floors by access and readiness, confirm crew slots, and track alignment checks.
Let both crews start and sort out the shaft access when they arrive.
Ask each crew to report its progress and adjust the schedule during the day.
Assign separate floor ranges to each crew and confirm their start times.

basic.situation: You are pulling plastic-covered control wires through shaft conduit with a senior technician, and the pull begins to snag at a bend.

options.text: Pause the pull, tell the senior technician where it snags, and wait for direction.
Check conduit path and pull tension, then ease wire back before retrying.
Ease the wire back, inspect the bend, and retry with the senior technician watching.
Pull harder with a second worker so the wires reach the control panel.

advanced.situation: A control panel wiring route has changed after a site obstruction, and a new electrician asks where to run the conduit through the lift shaft.

options.text: Review shaft route, mark the revised path, and guide the electrician during pulling.
Show the electrician the old route and ask them to identify a workable conduit path.
Mark the obstruction on the drawing and ask the lead to approve a revised route.
Route conduit along the nearest clear wall and update the drawing after the pull.

basic.situation: You have a fence drawing, tape measure and string. The crew is ready to dig, and you need to mark the posthole positions along the planned line.

options.text: I stretch the string between end marks and measure each hole location.
I pace out the line and mark holes from those rough points.
I mark the planned posts, then shift one to suit easier digging.
I mark each post from the drawing and recheck the tape spacing.

advanced.situation: A customer wants a fence across an unfamiliar yard. You see utility covers near the proposed route, and the crew is waiting for layout marks.

options.text: I start digging along the proposed route before checking service locations.
I check the service plans and move marks clear of mapped lines.
I arrange a utility locate, then mark a route clear of identified services.
I ask the site contact about services, then mark the proposed route.

basic.situation: You have dug a marked posthole. Your lead asks you to place the fence post upright while they check the work.

options.text: I dig the marked hole, then hold the post while the lead checks it.
I brace the upright post and check it with a spirit level.
I widen the hole until the post can sit firmly at the bottom.
I set the post by eye and pack soil around its base.

advanced.situation: Rain has softened the soil on a sloped fence line. Several posts are shifting as you set them, and the concrete is ready to pour.

options.text: I pause the pour, stabilize the posts, and recheck alignment as concrete goes in.
I add more concrete around each post and check the line afterward.
I deepen the holes and tamp the soil around the posts for support.
I brace each post and check its vertical position before pouring concrete.

basic.situation: A rail needs to fit between two posts. You have a hand saw and a measurement from the fence drawing.

options.text: I clamp the lumber and check the marked length before sawing.
I cut the lumber near the measured length and trim it later.
I mark the length from the drawing and saw through the lumber.
I measure the space between posts and mark the lumber once.

advanced.situation: A customer approves a fence design with angled rails and curved ends. You must prepare several matching pieces from the drawing.

options.text: I shape the pieces by eye to match the first finished rail.
I cut each piece from the drawing's dimensions as I work.
I mark the angles on every rail and cut them in one batch.
I make a full-size template from the drawing before cutting matching pieces.

basic.situation: The posts are in place and your lead has marked the rail height. You are asked to nail the top rail to the posts.

options.text: I support the rail, check its level, and nail it at the marks.
I hold the rail at the marks and nail it to each post.
I tack the rail in place and ask the lead to check its height.
I nail the rail where it sits most easily against the posts.

advanced.situation: You are assembling a louvered fence on a sloped boundary. The customer expects the panels to follow the approved pattern and keep consistent spacing.

options.text: I install the louvers from the drawing and check the pattern at the end.
I set a spacing reference and check each louver against the slope and drawing.
I match the louver angles to the nearest panel as I build.
I fit each louver to the last one and adjust gaps at the end.

basic.situation: A metal fence frame needs one short joint welded. Your qualified lead is nearby and has asked you to assist with the portable gas equipment.

options.text: I weld across the gap so the frame can move to assembly.
I clean the joint and make a short weld under the lead's guidance.
I tack the pieces together and let the lead finish the weld.
I fit and steady the joint, then weld under the lead's guidance.

advanced.situation: A custom gate has several tight metal joints. You are qualified to weld them, and the frame must stay square as it is assembled.

options.text: I weld each joint, then check the frame dimensions afterward.
I tack the joints, weld in a balanced sequence, and inspect them.
I fill visible gaps with extra weld, then grind the joints smooth.
I follow the cut list and weld the joints in sequence.

basic.situation: A customer asks for a fence quote at a kopitiam meeting. They mention a gate and privacy, but have not chosen a material or fence length.

options.text: I ask about length, gate access, privacy, and material, then record the answers.
I note the fence style and ask the customer to send measurements later.
I quote a standard fence package and let the customer choose its options.
I write down the preferred style and give a rough price from memory.

advanced.situation: A customer wants a detailed quote for a long boundary fence with two gates. The ground changes level, and they are comparing metal and timber options.

options.text: I estimate the cheaper material and explain that the final price may change.
I use the site measurements and price list to prepare a quote for both materials.
I send a single total based on a typical fence of similar length.
I measure the boundary, itemize both materials and gates, and explain the cost assumptions.

basic.situation: You are assigned to remove a small patch of suspect asbestos from a surface. Your lead has prepared the work area and asks you to use hand tools.

options.text: I use the assigned tool within the prepared controls and collect debris carefully.
I follow the work steps and collect the removed material as I go.
I pause when the surface crumbles and ask the lead how to proceed.
I scrape the surface into a waste bag and keep working at pace.

advanced.situation: A spill has spread suspect hazardous material beyond the marked work area. You are the senior removal worker on shift and must help limit contamination.

options.text: I alert the response lead and help mark a wider controlled area.
I collect the visible material first and update the response lead afterward.
I extend the boundary around the visible spill and start cleanup there.
I stop nearby work, isolate the affected route, and coordinate containment with the response lead.

basic.situation: Your crew has bagged hazardous debris from a removal job. You are asked to move the bags into the site's designated storage area.

options.text: I move the sealed bags to the marked storage area and update the count.
I check each bag label, place it in the assigned bay, and log its location.
I stack the bags near the storage entrance until the next collection.
I load the bags onto the trolley and ask the storekeeper where to leave them.

advanced.situation: At a licensed reactor facility, you are trained to operate the basin equipment. A shift handover shows one irradiated fuel basket has an unclear storage location.

options.text: I check the handling record and equipment position, then reconcile its location with the shift log.
I move the basket to an open slot and record its location on the board.
I compare the shift log with the location board and flag the mismatch.
I ask the next operator to verify the basket during their scheduled handling round.

basic.situation: After a small cleanup, contaminated equipment needs washing with the site's approved detergent. Your lead has shown you the cleaning station.

options.text: I clean the equipment with the approved detergent and check the surface before reuse.
I follow the station steps and tell the lead when the wash is done.
I wash the equipment with detergent and return it to the work area.
I rinse the equipment quickly and put it beside the clean tools.

advanced.situation: A planned abatement area includes porous debris and a shared corridor nearby. You are asked to build containment before removal begins.

options.text: I move the debris away from the corridor and add plastic sheeting around the room.
I seal the work room and start removal once the entry is covered.
I set a barrier at the work room and place warning signs at the entry.
I map the work boundary, protect the corridor route, and set controlled entry before removal.

basic.situation: A sealed waste container must be loaded onto a truck using the site's forklift. Your lead is nearby while you prepare the lift.

options.text: I lift the container and guide it toward the truck at a steady pace.
I check the load and route, then lift it with the assigned forklift.
I move the forklift into position and ask the lead to confirm the load.
I raise the container high enough to clear the truck side and drive over.

advanced.situation: At a reactor facility, you are qualified to operate the crane moving a canister. A signaler reports a changing clearance near the planned travel path.

options.text: I hold the load, confirm the signaler's route, and resume when the path is clear.
I pause the crane and request a new route from the shift lead.
I ask the signaler to guide the canister past the tighter section.
I continue the lift slowly while watching the clearance from the cab.

basic.situation: You are driving a truck carrying sealed contaminated waste to its designated ground disposal location. Your route sheet lists the approved destination.

options.text: I take a shorter site road and unload at the nearest marked area.
I follow the route sheet and record the container count at arrival.
I follow the approved route, confirm the destination, and record the waste details on arrival.
I call the site contact for directions if the route sheet seems unclear.

advanced.situation: At a designated disposal site, several waste containers have been received. Your shift record shows the container total, but not the waste types or amounts.

options.text: I note the missing details and ask the delivery driver to resend the manifest.
I verify the labels against the received containers and record their types and amounts.
I copy the types and amounts from the delivery paperwork into the shift record.
I enter the total count and leave the type fields for the next shift.

basic.situation: A surface may contain lead before removal starts. You have been assigned a monitoring device and your lead is available to assist.

options.text: I mark the surface as clear based on its appearance and begin work.
I check the device setup, sample the assigned area, and record readings for review.
I ask the lead to take the reading while I prepare removal tools.
I take a reading at the surface and note the result for the lead.

advanced.situation: A site plan calls for bioremediation of a contained hazardous waste area. You are responsible for applying the approved treatment and keeping the work records.

options.text: I follow the approved treatment plan, log application and site conditions, and flag deviations.
I spread the treatment across the area and report that work has started.
I apply treatment at the listed rate, record site conditions, and file the completion note.
I hold the treatment until the supervisor reviews the site plan again.

basic.situation: You are clearing litter from a roadside verge with a crew nearby and traffic passing. How do you collect the rubbish safely?

options.text: Ask the lead worker where to gather litter, then clear the verge.
Walk into the lane to collect a plastic sheet before it blows.
Gather the loose rubbish near your work area for the crew.
Bag visible litter along the shoulder, keeping clear of passing traffic.

advanced.situation: After heavy rain, rocks and mud cover part of the shoulder near a bend. You are assigned to help remove debris while the crew assesses the area.

options.text: Clear the bend with a loader before checking whether the slope is still shifting.
Move loose rocks from the shoulder, then report any larger unstable material.
Set a safe work boundary with the crew, then remove stable debris in stages.
Shift the smaller stones first while the lead checks the slope above.

basic.situation: You are helping clean a roadside drain after rain. The water is receding, and your lead asks you to inspect the inlet before clearing it.

options.text: Check the inlet for visible blockage, then clear debris from the opening.
Rinse the inlet with a hose so the leaves move downstream.
Reach deep into the inlet to pull out a branch quickly.
Clear loose leaves from the grate and tell the lead what remains.

advanced.situation: During a routine bridge check, you spot a fresh crack near a drain outlet. Your crew is preparing to clean the structure nearby.

options.text: Clean around the crack carefully and mention it after the shift.
Mark the area with a cone while the crew finishes other cleaning.
Photograph the crack with a location reference and report it before nearby work proceeds.
Tell the lead about the crack and pause cleaning beside it.

basic.situation: You are helping patch a small pothole with asphalt. Your lead has prepared the area and asks you to spread and tamp the mix.

options.text: Spread the asphalt evenly, then tamp it with the tool as shown.
Dump the full load into the pothole and tamp the top once.
Add a little asphalt at a time and ask the lead to check the depth.
Spread the mix across the hole and let the truck wheels press it down.

advanced.situation: A washout has left a long low section beside the road shoulder. You are helping place gravel while the crew keeps a lane open.

options.text: Spread gravel across the low section, then have the lead review the finished shape.
Place gravel in manageable layers and check the shoulder profile as you progress.
Push all the gravel into the washout quickly before traffic builds.
Fill the deepest area first and compact it with the truck tires.

basic.situation: You are assigned to flag motorists near a crew repairing a roadside drain. A vehicle approaches while workers are moving tools.

options.text: Use the agreed flag signal to slow the vehicle before tools cross.
Ask a nearby worker to watch traffic while you move the tools.
Wave the vehicle through so the crew can finish carrying tools.
Hold your position and signal the vehicle to slow as shown.

advanced.situation: A repair crew must work beside two lanes, and the approved diversion layout reaches a junction. You are setting out signs and cones with the team.

options.text: Start placing cones from the crew outward while another worker handles signs.
Set the signs at the junction and place cones along the work area.
Place the signs and cones in the approved sequence, checking that each approach is visible.
Put cones around the crew first, then add diversion signs if drivers hesitate.

basic.situation: You are driving a truck to take a maintenance crew and tools to a nearby work site. The load is secured, and the crew is ready.

options.text: Follow the site entrance listed on the work sheet and posted signs.
Ask a passenger to navigate while you focus on driving safely.
Check the route with the lead, then drive the crew at a steady pace.
Use the quickest familiar road to help the crew reach the site sooner.

advanced.situation: You are operating a road sweeper with a mower attachment on a rural shoulder. The grass is thick, and a drainage inlet is partly hidden.

options.text: Slow down and watch the shoulder closely as you approach the inlet.
Stop before the inlet and ask the lead how to clear that patch.
Raise the mower near the inlet, then resume at a safe distance along the shoulder.
Keep the mower low and cut through the thick grass in one pass.

basic.situation: Before a morning job, you are asked to check a maintenance truck. You notice one tyre looks softer than the others.

options.text: Drive slowly to the site and watch for changes in how the tyre handles.
Tell the lead the tyre looks low before the truck leaves the yard.
Add air until the tyre looks similar to the others on the truck.
Use the assigned gauge to check tyre pressure, then report the reading.

advanced.situation: A loader repeatedly loses hydraulic power during routine work. You are a mid-level operator asked to diagnose the fault and brief a newer crew member.

options.text: Log power loss timing, inspect visible fluid levels, and brief the mechanic and trainee.
Note when power drops and share the pattern with the loader mechanic.
Ask the trainee to top up the reservoir and test whether hydraulic power drops again.
Replace the hydraulic filter you suspect is causing the loader's repeated power loss.

basic.situation: You are helping level a short track section with a maintenance machine. Your lead asks you to adjust the controls while watching the indicator arms.

options.text: Watch the indicator arms and tell the lead when they appear level.
Adjust one control slightly and wait for the lead to confirm the result.
Make the small control adjustment shown, then watch the indicator arms settle.
Move the controls farther until the rail appears level from your seat.

advanced.situation: A long section shows uneven readings across several indicator arms. You are setting machine adjustments to meet the work specification and guide a newer operator.

options.text: Change controls near the largest deviation, then recheck the indicator arms.
Compare readings with specifications, adjust in stages, and explain each change.
Reuse settings from the last section to keep the machine moving.
Review specifications, adjust controls, and ask the operator to watch the indicator arms.

basic.situation: You are using a track wrench to tighten bolts at a rail joint. Your lead has shown you the sequence, and the crew is waiting nearby.

options.text: Tighten the joint bolts in the shown sequence and check each one as you go.
Tighten the bolts you can reach and tell the lead about the rest.
Turn each bolt until it feels tight, then move to the next joint.
Ask the lead to inspect the joint after you tighten the visible bolts.

advanced.situation: A spike driver leaves one spike sitting higher than the others near a joint. You are troubleshooting the fastening and helping a newer operator use the machine.

options.text: Apply full pressure and drive the spike again to lower it quickly.
Shift the machine slightly, then make another pass over the raised spike.
Inspect the raised spike and ask the operator to check the machine setting.
Check machine setup and tie position, then demonstrate a controlled correction.

basic.situation: You are asked to cut a replacement rail to a marked length with a rail saw. Your lead is beside you as the crew prepares the joint.
