options.text: Measure the marked section and ask the lead to confirm before cutting.
Cut at the nearest mark so the crew can fit the rail sooner.
Start the saw and trim the rail slightly after checking the fit.
Confirm the mark with the lead, then cut to the specified length using the saw.

advanced.situation: A newly fitted rail joint feels uneven during a check, and the crew is ready to move on. You are asked to grind the rail ends smooth.

options.text: Use the grinder on the higher side, then continue the scheduled work.
Make a light pass on the uneven end, then ask the lead to review it.
Inspect joint contact, grind high areas in controlled passes, and recheck the surface.
Grind both rail ends broadly until the joint looks smoother from above.

basic.situation: You are helping drill a marked hole through a fishplate for a rail joint. Your lead has set the drill and is checking the alignment.

options.text: Hold the drill on the mark and follow the lead's feed guidance.
Press firmly so the drill bit passes through the plate faster.
Start drilling quickly before the mark becomes hard to see.
Check the bit sits on the mark, then ask the lead to watch.

advanced.situation: A welded switch section has several joints to complete before the track is returned to service. You are coordinating the welding sequence and mentoring a newer worker.

options.text: Set the joint order and have the worker observe as you weld each section.
Plan joint access, then teach the worker to inspect each finished weld.
Weld the easiest joints first to show visible progress to the crew.
Let the newer worker choose the order while you focus on welding.

basic.situation: You are assigned to lubricate a track machine before the shift. The maintenance sheet lists the service points and specified fluid levels.

options.text: Top up reservoirs that look low before using the machine.
Follow the sheet's service points and fill reservoirs to their stated levels.
Add lubricant to the easiest points and start the machine for the crew.
Service listed points and ask the lead to check fluid levels.

advanced.situation: A track machine keeps losing pressure after servicing. You are diagnosing the fault and leading two workers through the scheduled checks.

options.text: Compare pressure loss with service records, inspect for leaks, and assign worker checks.
Check for visible leaks and ask both workers to review the service sheet together.
Replace the reservoir hose that seems most likely to be leaking.
Ask both workers to top up fluid and test the machine again.

basic.situation: You are patrolling your assigned track section and spot a cracked tie near a switch box. The crew is working farther down the line.

options.text: Put a loose ballast stone beside the tie so the crew notices it.
Record the location and condition, then report the damaged tie to the lead.
Step over the tie and finish the patrol before mentioning it.
Tell a nearby worker that a tie looks cracked near the switch box.

advanced.situation: Snow and debris keep collecting around several switch boxes on your assigned section. You are defining a patrol check and coaching staff on what to report.

options.text: Set a route for each box, teaching staff to report blockage and location.
List each switch box and ask staff to record debris, location, and condition.
Have workers clear snow first and discuss a patrol routine afterward.
Ask staff to clear whichever switch box looks most blocked during patrol.

basic.situation: A crew is ready to dig near a manhole, and you need to measure from the marked reference point and mark the sewer excavation site.

options.text: Estimate from the kerb and mark the likely pipe route.
Follow old paint marks and tell the crew where to dig.
Check the plan, measure from the reference point, and mark the excavation.
Use the tape measure from the marked manhole, then mark the dig point.

advanced.situation: A locator gives conflicting readings near a busy access road. You are training a new worker to find and mark the damaged pipe.

options.text: Use the strongest reading as the dig mark and explain the equipment.
Compare the readings, mark the fault, and show trainees how you checked it.
Show trainees the locator once and let them mark the first signal.
Demonstrate a repeat scan from another access point, then record the agreed mark.

basic.situation: A household drain is blocked, and your supervisor asks you to use a power rodder while they watch the job.

options.text: Feed the rodder steadily and check progress with your supervisor nearby.
Check the rodder setup, clear the blockage in controlled passes, and report flow.
Run the rodder in short bursts and ask your supervisor about resistance.
Push the rodder hard through the bend to clear the blockage faster.

advanced.situation: A large sewer line remains blocked after an initial pass. You are assigned to configure the water jet for the next attempt.

options.text: Review the blockage, choose a suitable nozzle, and set a controlled jet pressure.
Use the previous nozzle and lower pressure for a slower pass.
Check the flow and nozzle, then repeat the pass at the current setting.
Raise the jet pressure and make another pass through the line.

basic.situation: A shallow sewer line is exposed for repair. Your supervisor asks you to dig out the remaining soil by hand with a shovel.

options.text: Use the shovel carefully and follow your supervisor's directions.
Dig quickly along the pipe to finish before the crew arrives.
Remove the loose soil first, then check the pipe before digging again.
Clear soil in measured layers and keep the exposed pipe visible.

advanced.situation: Water is seeping through a septic tank wall during a repair. You are responsible for coordinating the assigned crew’s work on the structure.

options.text: Direct the crew to patch the visible seep and continue the repair.
Pause work near the seep, inspect the affected area, and agree a repair sequence.
Ask the crew to clear the wall and prepare the usual patch materials.
Have the crew clean the area, then repair the visible section together.

basic.situation: After clearing a drain, your supervisor asks you to clean the power rodder and tools before they are stored in the truck.

options.text: Rinse the tools, check the rod and attachments, then store them dry.
Wipe the tools, coil the rod, and return the kit to the truck.
Load the rodder first and clean the tools at the next job.
Brush off the rod and pack the kit with the other gear.

advanced.situation: Several crews share sewer-cleaning equipment, and a junior worker is unsure how to care for the attachments between jobs.

options.text: Ask the junior worker to clean each attachment before the next shift.
Keep using the attachments while they still clear drains reliably.
Show the junior worker the usual cleanup and return the attachments to storage.
Set a simple service schedule, log checks, and coach staff on attachment care.

basic.situation: Your supervisor is riding along as you drive a truck carrying pipe sections and tools to a nearby sewer repair site.

options.text: Secure the load, follow the planned route, and drive at a steady pace.
Check the mirrors and drive carefully toward the repair site.
Drive the familiar route while your supervisor keeps an eye on the load.
Take the quickest road and arrive before the crew needs supplies.

advanced.situation: Two repair sites need equipment, and the truck is carrying a heavy jetting unit. You are planning the crew’s delivery route and loading order.

options.text: Secure the unit and drive to the closest site before deciding the next stop.
Load the jetting unit first and follow the usual route to both sites.
Take the shortest route and ask the crew to unload quickly at each site.
Choose a route around road constraints, secure the unit, and sequence both stops.

basic.situation: Your crew finds a blockage during a sewer job. Your supervisor asks you to send a radio update on the work status.

options.text: Tell the supervisor that the crew has nearly finished clearing the line.
Say the drain is still blocked and the crew is working.
Report the blockage and ask whether the crew should keep working.
Radio the location, blockage status, and the crew's next action.

advanced.situation: Crews send radio updates in different formats, and repair notes are hard to compare. You are asked to help new workers communicate and record jobs clearly.

options.text: Set common fields for radio updates and repair logs, then coach workers through examples.
Share a short update format and coach workers to use it on each job.
Ask new workers to copy the last completed repair note for their jobs.
Let each worker keep notes in the format they already prefer.

basic.situation: You are preparing a small path where loose, uneven soil remains beneath the planned paver area, and the crew is waiting for the base.

options.text: Grade the visible surface so the crew can begin laying pavers.
Cover the soft patches with extra bedding sand and start laying.
Rake the area level and ask the crew to check the grade.
Remove loose soil, grade the area, and compact it under guidance.

advanced.situation: After rain, a large paving area has weak saturated patches where bedding sand may migrate. You are helping prepare the base for installation.

options.text: Add a thin layer of base material across the whole area.
Identify weak patches, remove unsuitable material, and stabilize and grade the base.
Compact the wet patches firmly and continue with the planned sand layer.
Drain standing water and recheck the surface before placing the bedding sand.

basic.situation: You are placing bedding sand and edge restraints for a short walkway, with the crew lead nearby to guide the work.

options.text: Spread the sand across the walkway and fit the restraints afterward.
Place the restraints first, then spread bedding sand evenly within them.
Spread a rough sand layer and let the paver crew adjust it.
Set the edge restraints and spread sand near the walkway center.

advanced.situation: A large paving site has several work zones and deliveries arriving at different times. You are coordinating placement of base materials, restraints, and bedding sand.

options.text: Send each delivery to the nearest open zone and place materials as they arrive.
Track deliveries by zone and ask crews where they want each load placed.
Keep a delivery list and spread available materials across the active zones.
Match delivery timing and quantities to each zone's sequence and storage space.

basic.situation: You are marking joint lines and stringlines for a small rectangular patio, and the paver crew is ready to start.

options.text: Stretch a stringline and mark the visible joints for the crew.
Follow the existing marks and start the pavers along that line.
Mark the joints from one edge and check the stringline across the patio.
Mark the first joint line and let the crew continue the pattern.

advanced.situation: A large plaza design combines several paver patterns and directional markings. You are creating joint references for crews working in separate zones.

options.text: Mark the main directions and ask crews to work out their local joints.
Map each zone's pattern and align directional references across shared boundaries.
Draw the zone patterns and mark stringlines for each crew to follow.
Extend one pattern across the plaza and let each crew adapt the joints.

basic.situation: You are setting pavers along a straight garden path, and the crew lead has asked you to keep the spacing even.

options.text: Set the pavers in a straight line and adjust gaps at the end.
Place each paver against the last and check the joints as you go.
Lay the pavers close together to finish the path sooner.
Follow the stringline and keep a similar gap between each paver.

advanced.situation: You are setting a herringbone section beside a drain cover, where the pattern changes direction and several workers are placing pavers together.

options.text: Mark the drain edge and let each worker continue the nearest row.
Set the pattern from the drain edge and have workers check alignment together.
Turn pavers to fit around the cover and fill remaining gaps later.
Establish the pattern reference at the cover, then guide workers on each direction change.

basic.situation: A row of pavers meets a straight garden border, and you are assigned to cut the edge pieces with a splitter.

options.text: Measure each gap, mark the paver, and cut it with the splitter.
Cut the pavers slightly short so they fit along the border.
Mark the visible edge and split each paver to match the row.
Use one edge piece as a guide for the remaining splitter cuts.

advanced.situation: A curved border needs several shaped cuts, and the jointing sand has been swept in. You are finishing the edges before the final compaction.

options.text: Cut the edges in sections and sweep sand into the visible joints.
Cut the curves to fit and compact the area once the pieces are placed.
Use the same splitter angle for every curved edge and compact the joints.
Mark each curve, cut to fit, refill the joints, and compact the pavement.

basic.situation: You are screeding bedding sand for a small patio, and the crew lead asks you to recheck the level before pavers are set.

options.text: Pull the screed across once and ask the crew lead to inspect it.
Rake the high spots flat and let the paver crew begin.
Spread extra sand over low spots and start laying the pavers.
Screed the sand evenly, then check the surface with the crew lead.

advanced.situation: A paved entrance is ready for final compaction, but sand remains on the surface and some joints look shallow. You are helping prepare the area for use.

options.text: Fill the visible joints and cement the edges before compacting the paving.
Compact the area, sweep loose sand, and open the entrance to users.
Sweep the surface and compact once, then check the joints and edges.
Refill shallow joints, compact the pavement, and sweep the surface before opening.

basic.situation: You are adding loose-fill insulation in an attic, and the marked depth is hard to see near the eaves.

options.text: Ask the lead to mark each section before you spread the insulation.
Fill the whole attic evenly, then note the estimated depth in your log.
Spread insulation near the hatch first so the visible area looks complete.
Check the depth markers as you work and compare coverage across attic sections.

advanced.situation: A wall cavity has irregular gaps around pipes, and your chosen board insulation would leave visible voids.

options.text: Fit the boards around the pipes and fill the remaining gaps with scraps.
Press the boards into place and cover visible gaps with trim.
Ask the lead which approved material suits the cavity before cutting anything.
Use a suitable cavity foam, following product directions and checking the finished coverage.

basic.situation: You are patching a small wall hole with spackling, but the first layer sinks as it dries.

options.text: Apply another thin layer after drying, then sand the patch flush.
Add a thicker layer now and sand it once the surface feels firm.
Paint over the settled patch so the wall is ready for handover.
Show the lead the patch and ask whether another layer is needed.

advanced.situation: A loose section of drywall surrounds a damaged timber edge, and you have basic tools available for a minor repair.

options.text: Ask the lead to inspect the timber before you choose a repair method.
Remove loose material, secure sound edges, and patch within your repair scope.
Cover the damage with a larger drywall patch and finish its edges.
Fill the opening with compound and sand it smooth after drying.

basic.situation: You are assisting with a combustible appliance test, and the reading changes between two checks.

options.text: Write down the lower reading and continue with the remaining checks.
Use the appliance's usual performance as a guide for the report.
Tell the lead the readings differ and ask them to review the test.
Repeat the check using the same setup and record both readings for review.

advanced.situation: Your furnace efficiency equipment shows uneven airflow across rooms after a recent duct repair, but the readings are not stable.

options.text: Adjust the nearest vent and use the next reading as your diagnosis.
Check the setup and repeat readings at each point before tracing the airflow pattern.
Report the lowest reading as the main fault so repairs can proceed.
Share the fluctuating readings with the lead and ask which area to check.

basic.situation: A resident asks to move tomorrow's weatherization appointment because a family member will be home then.

options.text: Confirm the resident's preferred window, check the crew schedule, and update both records.
Move the visit to the next morning and send a brief confirmation.
Offer the next open slot and note the new time in your schedule.
Keep the original slot and ask the resident to arrange access.

advanced.situation: A building owner asks which weatherization measures meet applicable requirements, but the building has an unusual wall system.

options.text: Assure the owner that the usual approach will satisfy the requirements.
Share general conservation measures and ask the lead about the wall system.
Explain the factors you can verify and refer the wall details for technical review.
Recommend the familiar insulation package and explain its usual energy savings.

basic.situation: You are helping write a report after a small weatherization job, and one material quantity is missing from the work notes.

options.text: Use the standard quantity from a similar job and finish the report.
Check the work notes with the installer and describe any remaining estimate clearly.
Enter a rounded quantity so the report can be sent today.
Leave the quantity blank and ask the lead how to complete the report.

advanced.situation: You are drafting a bid estimate for several buildings, and one building's access conditions may increase labour time.

options.text: Separate the uncertain access allowance and state the assumption in the estimate.
Ask the lead for a labour figure before finalising the bid draft.
Use the average labour allowance from the other buildings in the bid.
Use the lowest allowance so the proposal stays competitive with other bids.

basic.situation: You completed duct wrapping today, but the activity log has separate fields for materials and work performed.

options.text: Add the material quantity to the work field for a quicker entry.
Enter the work performed and material used in their matching fields.
Copy yesterday's entry and change the date to save time.
Record the duct wrapping in the notes field and finish the entry.

advanced.situation: While reviewing activity logs, you find the same completed job recorded under two different dates by different crew members.

options.text: Delete the older entry so the log shows one completed job.
Ask both crew members which entry they want to retain.
Compare job details, identify the supported date, and amend the duplicate entry.
Keep both entries and add a note that the dates differ.

basic.situation: You are cleaning a derrick component before use and notice oily residue collecting around one joint.

options.text: Clean the joint, check its condition, and report any continuing seepage.
Cover the residue with grease so the component stays protected.
Wipe the joint and add fresh oil before the next task.
Tell the senior operator about the residue before continuing the cleaning.

advanced.situation: Before a derrick is lowered, your inspection reveals a visible crack near a supporting connection.

options.text: Photograph the crack and ask the lead whether inspection should continue.
Report the crack and hold your inspection input for the responsible lead's review.
Mark the area and tell the crew to watch it during lowering.
Proceed with lowering at a slower pace to reduce strain on the joint.

basic.situation: You are mixing drilling mud with a portable mixer, and the measured clay amount differs from the work sheet.

options.text: Ask the senior operator to confirm the amount before adding more clay.
Add enough clay to make the batch look like its usual consistency.
Pause the batch, recheck the clay weight, and record the amount used.
Use the worksheet amount and check the mixture after the next sample.

advanced.situation: A drilling-fluid sample is outside the expected range, and a new crew member asks how to handle an additive.

options.text: Tell the crew member the usual mixing order and prepare a routine report.
Use the familiar additive amount and note the adjustment after circulation.
Refer the additive question to the senior operator and log the sample result.
Check the approved handling instructions, guide the additive step, and report the sample readings.

basic.situation: You are checking mud pumps and hear a new vibration while the readings remain within their usual range.

options.text: Reduce the pump speed until the vibration sounds less noticeable.
Record the normal readings and continue listening during your next round.
Ask the senior operator to listen while you note the current readings.
Note the vibration, compare nearby pump conditions, and alert the senior operator.

advanced.situation: During circulation, pump vibration rises while fluid flow becomes uneven, and a routine reading does not explain the change.

options.text: Compare pump symptoms and system readings, then communicate the pattern to the lead.
Keep circulation steady and wait for the next scheduled monitoring round.
Use the routine reading as the likely cause and update the mud log.
Ask the lead to inspect the pump while you keep recording flow.

basic.situation: You are helping repair a mud pump, and a replacement fitting does not match the removed part.

options.text: Set the mismatched fitting aside and ask which spare to try next.
Fit the replacement with an adapter from the parts shelf.
Compare the fitting details and ask the lead to confirm a compatible part.
File the fitting edges until it seats firmly in the opening.

advanced.situation: A mud tank repair keeps leaking after a fitting change, and the rig needs the tank back in service soon.

options.text: Cover the wet area with a temporary patch and return the tank to service.
Trace the leak source, inspect the connection, and report repair needs to the lead.
Fit another spare fitting and check the connection for seepage during a controlled test.
Tighten the fitting slightly, then test the tank while monitoring the repaired connection.

basic.situation: You are stringing a hoisting cable through pulleys, and it begins to twist near a block.

options.text: Pause the pull, ease the twist out, and check the routing before continuing.
Call the crew lead over to check the cable before the next pull.
Pull the cable through steadily and untwist it at the far end.
Guide the cable around the block edge to keep the job moving.

advanced.situation: During derrick alignment, one element sits out of line and the crew is waiting on the platform for your next instruction.

options.text: Tell the crew to climb higher and pull the element across by hand.
Ask the lead to choose the next adjustment while the crew holds position.
Check the alignment points and communicate a controlled repositioning sequence to the crew.
Have the crew push the element into line while you watch its movement.

basic.situation: You are steadying a pipe during connection, and it shifts as a crew member guides it toward the elevator.

options.text: Push the pipe toward the elevator before it shifts further.
Hold the pipe firmly and let the crew member guide it into place.
Signal the crew member to pause, steady the pipe, and realign together.
Ask the crew lead to guide the pipe while you maintain your hold.

advanced.situation: While mud is circulating through the drill pipe, flow drops and a pipe connection shows fresh seepage.

options.text: Record the flow drop and ask the lead to inspect the connection.
Keep circulation unchanged and note the seepage at the next check.
Increase pump speed to restore the flow while watching the connection.
Report the seepage and flow change, then follow the lead's direction on circulation.

basic.situation: After the rig is stopped for routine maintenance, you are asked to clean and oil pulleys, blocks, and cables. One cable has visible grit near a sheave.

options.text: Oil the cable and pulleys quickly, then note the maintenance in the shift book.
Brush away the grit, apply oil along the cable, and return the pulley to service.
Wipe the cable and sheave, oil the moving parts, then tell the lead what you found.
Check the cable condition with the lead, clean the sheave, oil approved points, and report wear.

advanced.situation: You are showing a new crew member routine rig maintenance when a pulley guard is loose and a cable shows fraying. The next shift is waiting for the rig.

options.text: Ask the crew member to watch while you handle the loose guard and finish the oiling.
Demonstrate the maintenance checks, keep the damaged cable out of use, and explain the repair handoff.
Show the crew member how to tighten the guard and oil the cable before the next shift.
Pause that task, explain the fraying concern, and show how to report it for repair.

basic.situation: At the end of a drilling run, you need to record footage drilled and the time taken. The depth notes and shift handover time differ slightly.

options.text: Use the latest depth note and estimate the time from the run sequence for the log.
Check the depth and time with the driller, then record the confirmed figures in the log.
Record the drill notes, flag the time difference, and ask the next shift to confirm it.
Enter the depth from the drill notes and use the handover time for the shift record.

advanced.situation: You are checking a drilling log before handover. Its footage total conflicts with the daily entries, and the listed strata change has no matching note.

options.text: Trace footage to the source entries, verify the strata note, and record queries before handover.
Recalculate the footage from daily entries and ask the driller about the missing strata note.
Change the total to match the daily entries and complete the strata field from the nearby note.
Mark both entries for review and hand over the log with the discrepancies highlighted.

basic.situation: You are helping connect drill pipe sections with hand tools. One connection feels tighter than the others, and the next section is ready to be joined.

options.text: Back the section off, remove visible dirt, and reconnect it with the same hand tool.
Stop joining, inspect and clean the threads, then align and connect as the procedure requires.
Clean the threads, line up the sections, and ask the lead to check the tight connection.
Apply more force with the hand tool until the connection feels firm enough to continue.

advanced.situation: During a complex assembly, a pump and engine connection will not line up with the flow line. The crew is waiting to begin the next operation.

options.text: Recheck the flow line ends and try the connection again after loosening the nearest joint.
Check the alignment points, compare the assembly sequence, and coordinate a safe correction with the lead.
Ask the lead to review the alignment and hold the next connection until it is checked.
Loosen the nearby bolts, shift the pump slightly, and reconnect the flow line for a fit.

basic.situation: You are assisting with a core sample during drilling. The core is loose in the barrel, and the next section is due to be removed.

options.text: Ask the driller to confirm the depth, then help guide the sample onto the tray.
Pull the core out by hand and add the depth label once the tray is ready.
Hold the run, confirm depth with the driller, and remove the core carefully into its labeled tray.
Ease the core out onto the tray and label it with the current depth from the notes.

advanced.situation: A fractured formation is producing a fragile core that is breaking at the barrel mouth. You are managing extraction while the crew prepares another run.

options.text: Ask the crew to prepare a tray and reduce the pull speed while you guide the core out.
Continue the pull steadily, then place the fragments together and label the tray by depth.
Slow the extraction, support the core as it emerges, and keep fragments grouped by depth.
Pause the pull, reposition the tray, and resume with one person watching the barrel mouth.

basic.situation: During a routine run, you are watching the pressure gauge and controlling drill speed with the throttles. The reading begins to fluctuate as the bit enters a new layer.

options.text: Ease the throttle, watch the gauge settle, and tell the driller about the fluctuation.
Compare the reading with operating limits, adjust the throttle gradually, and report the trend.
Hold the same speed and wait for another reading before making a control change.
Reduce drill speed a little and note the gauge reading at the next check.

advanced.situation: A bit is lost downhole during a difficult run. You are helping recover it with fishing tools, while pressure readings vary and the crew awaits your next move.

options.text: Review the loss details, match the fishing tool to the bit, and coordinate the recovery sequence.
Check the pressure trend and inspect available fishing tools before choosing a likely match.
Choose a familiar fishing tool and start the recovery while monitoring the pressure gauge.
Ask the lead which fishing tool to use and prepare the recovery equipment for the crew.

basic.situation: You are counting drill rod sections to estimate borehole depth. A tally mark is unclear, and the crew is preparing to report progress.

options.text: Ask a crew member to read the tally, then record the depth from their interpretation.
Count the visible rods, estimate the unclear mark, and enter the depth on the progress sheet.
Recount the rods with a crew member and compare the total with the tally before recording.
Record the visible count and flag the unclear mark for the lead to check during handover.

advanced.situation: Drilling progress slows as the formation changes, and the current bit shows wear. You are monitoring the run and helping guide the crew's next bit choice.

options.text: Switch to the usual next bit and tell the crew to keep the planned drilling pace.
Compare formation signs and bit wear, then recommend a suitable bit and monitor the change.
Discuss the changed formation with the lead and prepare the replacement bit they prefer.
Slow the run and inspect the bit before asking the crew which replacement they have used.

basic.situation: You are checking equipment gauges before a routine service run. One reading differs from the usual range, while the engine sounds steady.

options.text: Continue checks while monitoring the gauge against its usual range.
Record the reading, compare it with the equipment range, and notify the supervisor.
Recheck the gauge, compare related readings, and report the change before service.
Ask a colleague about the reading and note it on the check sheet.

advanced.situation: A well reading shifts while the rotary chain makes an unusual sound. You are assessing the condition before the crew selects a repair approach.

options.text: Report the reading and sound to the supervisor and wait for a repair direction.
Compare the gauge trend with the chain sound, inspect equipment, and share evidence for repair planning.
Use the gauge change as the main clue and suggest checking the likely obstruction depth.
Treat the sound as routine chain noise and continue checking the gauges during service.

basic.situation: You are assisting with installing a pressure-control device onto a wellhead. The sealing surfaces look clean, but the connection alignment is slightly off.

options.text: Tighten the connection gradually until the device sits close to the wellhead.
Pause, realign the device, inspect mating surfaces, and confirm fit before securing.
Clean visible surfaces and use fasteners to draw the device into place.
Align the device, inspect seals, and ask the supervisor to verify fit.

advanced.situation: A broken casing obstruction is confirmed downhole, and you are helping select fishing tools. The first proposed tool may not match the casing size.

options.text: Choose the tool that has worked on similar wells and begin preparing the fishing assembly.
Ask the lead to confirm the casing size and set aside the proposed tool until then.
Review the available fishing tools and choose one with a close match to the casing size.
Verify casing details and obstruction depth, then compare compatible fishing tools with the lead.

basic.situation: You are threading a replacement cable through derrick pulleys with hand tools. The cable catches at one pulley while the crew waits to resume service.

options.text: Stop the pull, check the cable path, and guide it through the pulley with the lead's help.
Ease the cable back, inspect the pulley opening, and try threading it again slowly.
Pull the cable through firmly while guiding it past the pulley with a hand tool.
Ask a colleague to watch the pulley while you draw the cable through at low tension.

advanced.situation: You are operating a rig control to level the derrick while pumps circulate fluid. The rig shifts slightly and circulation becomes uneven during the adjustment.

options.text: Reduce the control movement and ask the pump operator to watch the circulation during leveling.
Pause the adjustment, check rig position and circulation indicators, then coordinate a measured correction.
Hold the derrick control steady and inspect the pump readings before continuing the adjustment.
Finish leveling with small control movements, then check whether the fluid circulation settles.

basic.situation: You are driving a truck-mounted service unit to a well site with a co-driver. A turnoff is muddy, and the route notes show a firm access road nearby.

options.text: Pause at the turnoff, review the route notes, and ask the co-driver which access looks safer.
Take the muddy turnoff slowly and ask the co-driver to watch the truck's clearance.
Follow the muddy turnoff behind another site vehicle and keep a steady pace to the well.
Use the firm access road, confirm the route with your co-driver, and approach the site cautiously.

advanced.situation: You are driving a truck-mounted unit toward a remote well site after heavy rain. The main access is soft, and daylight is fading as the crew waits.

options.text: Continue along the main access slowly and use the truck's traction to reach the site.
Slow down, avoid the deepest ruts, and reassess the access after the next bend.
Check ground conditions with the co-driver, choose a firmer route, and update the crew on arrival timing.
Ask the crew about the access and wait for their guidance before taking the main track.

basic.situation: You are filling in a service log after a routine visit. The tool list is clear, but the recorded hours differ from the crew's time sheet.

options.text: Record the time sheet figure and flag the difference for the senior operator to review.
Enter the time sheet hours, list the tools used, and submit the service log.
Use the rounded hours from the service notes and finish the tool list for billing.
Compare the log with the time sheet, confirm the hours with the crew, and record the result.

advanced.situation: You are reviewing service reports before billing. One report lists a tool absent from the issue record, and its recorded time overlaps another crew's entry.

options.text: Remove the tool entry and adjust the overlapping time to match the other crew's report.
Check the tool issue record and compare crew hours before deciding which entry seems likely.
Trace entries to source records, ask crews about gaps, and document agreed updates.
Mark the report for review and send the two discrepancies to the senior operator.

basic.situation: You are gathering pipe size information before a service job. Two colleagues give different sizes, and the well notes list a third measurement.

options.text: Record all three measurements in the handover notes and let the crew choose later.
Use the size mentioned by the more experienced colleague and add it to the job notes.
Tell the lead about the mismatch and ask which measurement to use for the job.
Check the well notes with both colleagues and confirm which pipe size applies to this job.

advanced.situation: During a service discussion, the pump crew and well crew report different borehole conditions. You are gathering details to help them agree on suitable pipe and tool sizes.

options.text: List the conflicting conditions and pipe sizes in the service notes for later discussion.
Ask each crew to repeat its borehole observations, then pass both accounts to the lead.
Compare both crews' observations, clarify pipe and tool sizes, and summarize the agreed condition for planning.
Share the latest report from the pump crew and ask the well crew to prepare matching tools.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to start the drill and bring it to the planned speed, but the controls feel unfamiliar.

options.text: Ask your supervisor to point out the controls before you start the machine.
Start the machine at a familiar speed and adjust it after drilling begins.
Use the last shift's speed setting and begin drilling to save setup time.
Check the control labels, confirm the planned setting, then start at the agreed pace.

advanced.situation: The drill slows in hard rock, and the pressure gauge rises as the crew falls behind schedule.

options.text: Reduce the feed, review the rock response, and tune pressure and speed together.
Ease the downward pressure and see whether the drill steadies in the rock.
Pause the adjustment and ask the supervisor to choose the next setting.
Raise the pressure and keep the rotary speed unchanged to recover lost time.

basic.situation: During your shift check, a lubrication point is dry and a simple guard bolt looks loose.

options.text: Lubricate the listed point and report the loose bolt for an approved repair.
Apply the specified lubricant, secure the bolt to guidance, and note the maintenance.
Add extra lubricant and tighten the bolt firmly before the next shift starts.
Wipe the point clean and leave the bolt for the next scheduled service.

advanced.situation: Your notes show a new fractured layer, but the drilling log is nearly full and the next crew needs a clear handover.

options.text: Use the remaining space for progress totals and skip the formation detail.
Record the formation, depth, and drilling progress in the approved log, then flag its capacity.
Summarize the fractured layer in the log and leave space for the next shift.
Keep drilling notes on a loose sheet and transfer them when the log is replaced.

basic.situation: After a short bore, you are asked to flush cuttings from the hole while your coworker checks the setup.

options.text: Use a stronger flow to clear the hole faster before the crew moves on.
Confirm the hose connection, flush at the set flow, and check that cuttings clear.
Flush briefly, then tell the crew the hole is ready for the next step.
Connect the standard flushing equipment and clear cuttings at the agreed flow.

advanced.situation: On uneven ground, your marked boring position appears slightly off after the rig settles, and the hole is nearing target depth.

options.text: Shift the rig toward the stake and continue at a slower feed rate.
Pause the run, verify depth and alignment against the stake, then resume.
Compare the bore position with the stake and tell the crew about the offset.
Reach target depth, then log the measured offset before moving the rig.

basic.situation: The soil changes from loose material to compact gravel, and you are preparing the next standard bit with guidance.

options.text: Fit the bit specified for compact gravel and confirm the rod connection.
Keep the current bit for one more section to avoid a changeover delay.
Choose the next available standard bit and fit it for a short trial.
Ask your supervisor which listed bit suits the compact gravel before fitting it.

advanced.situation: A bore crosses mixed fractured rock, and the bit is wearing faster than expected while a junior waits for your recommendation.

options.text: Recommend the bit used on the previous bore and monitor its wear closely.
Compare the formation notes with bit wear, then recommend a suitable drill configuration.
Review the formation notes and ask the supervisor to confirm your bit choice.
Choose a harder bit based on the wear and resume at a cautious pace.

basic.situation: You are helping position a casing pipe and assemble a rig component with hand tools before drilling starts.

options.text: Check the component fit, use the specified tool, and coordinate the casing position.
Position the casing with the crew and tighten the component using the specified tool.
Use a nearby power tool to finish the component while the crew holds the casing.
Set the component in place loosely and let the next crew finish assembly.

advanced.situation: A retrieval tool meets resistance in the bore, and the crew asks you to decide whether to keep working the stuck equipment.

options.text: Pull harder with the current setup to free the equipment before changing tools.
Pause retrieval, assess the tool setup and resistance, then choose a controlled recovery approach.
Switch to another available retrieval tool and test it with a steady pull.
Ease the pull and ask the supervisor which retrieval tool to use next.

basic.situation: A spotter guides your truck-mounted drill into a level work area, but the access track narrows near the site entrance.

options.text: Choose a wider line around the entrance and ask the spotter to catch up.
Keep the truck moving slowly and let the spotter signal if space gets tight.
Follow the spotter's signals and steer steadily through the narrow entrance.
Follow the spotter's signals, pause at the narrow point, and confirm clearance.

advanced.situation: At a remote site, the rig reaches a sloped pad with soft ground on one side and no clear level position.

options.text: Hold position, assess ground and slope, then coordinate a stable setup location.
Check the slope and ask the spotter to suggest where to position the rig.
Reverse to a flatter-looking area and level the rig after positioning.
Use the firmest visible patch and extend the rig once the truck is parked.

basic.situation: You are marking blast-hole locations from the approved pattern when a drill operator asks whether one mark is several centimetres off.

options.text: Check the mark against the pattern before giving the operator an update.
Move the mark toward the operator's estimate so drilling can start.
Recheck the pattern and mark against its stated reference points.
Ask the operator to hold while you compare the mark with nearby holes.

advanced.situation: A drilled hole measures deeper than the blast plan indicates, and the crew is preparing the next stage of work.

options.text: Measure the hole again after the crew finishes setting up nearby.
Record the depth and flag the difference for the site lead's review.
Hold work at the affected hole and report its measured depth through site procedure.
Treat it as close enough and keep the crew on the planned sequence.

basic.situation: During a supervised loading shift, you notice the assigned hole differs from the marked plan before the crew continues.

options.text: Tell a nearby coworker and wait for their view of the plan.
Show the mismatch to the supervisor before resuming the assigned task.
Continue with the planned loading while the supervisor is nearby.
Pause your assigned work and report the mismatch through the site procedure.

advanced.situation: A specialist loading component does not match the job paperwork, and the team is waiting to prepare the equipment.

options.text: Pause preparation, secure the mismatch as procedure requires, and notify the lead.
Set the component aside and check its details against the job paperwork.
Use the component that appears closest to the listed specification.
Ask a coworker to identify the component before deciding whether it fits.

basic.situation: You are assigned to connect a circuit component, but its label differs from the one on the job sheet.

options.text: Compare the component label with the job sheet before making the connection.
Ask a coworker whether this label appeared on earlier jobs.
Pause the connection and report the label difference using site procedure.
Connect it based on the matching colour shown on nearby components.

advanced.situation: You find a damaged section in a laid line while the crew is preparing to complete the planned circuit.

options.text: Report the damage and wait for direction before completing that section.
Stop work around the section, keep others clear, and notify the lead.
Tell a nearby worker and ask them to watch the damaged section.
Mark the damaged section and continue laying the remaining line.

basic.situation: You are placing warning cones around the blast area when workers start using a gap in the boundary as a shortcut.

options.text: Close the gap, alert the workers, and signal the site lead about the breach.
Tell the workers about the boundary and point them to a safe route.
Move the cones closer together around the gap where workers crossed the line.
Leave the cones in place and ask the crew to use the other path.

advanced.situation: During a planned blast sequence, a worker reports that a section of the exclusion area is not clear.

options.text: Repeat the warning signal and check whether workers respond from their stations.
Ask the worker to check the section again while preparations continue.
Hold the firing sequence and report the uncleared section through site procedure.
Tell the site lead about the report and wait nearby for an update.

basic.situation: You are moving a scheduled explosives inventory, and one container's identification does not match the movement record.

options.text: Pause the movement and report the mismatch using storage procedures.
Ask a coworker to compare the container with the latest inventory list.
Move the other containers first and leave this one for later.
Use the closest matching record and complete the planned movement.

advanced.situation: The stock record shows fewer supplies than the next scheduled work requires, while the current shift is preparing its inventory update.

options.text: Order the listed shortfall based on the current stock figure.
Review the stock figure and inform the lead that supplies may run short.
Check the recent issue entries and prepare a replenishment request through procedure.
Record the shortage and tell the next shift to follow up.

basic.situation: You are preparing a truck for an explosives transport run when a warning light appears during the routine check.

options.text: Report the warning and follow the vehicle procedure before loading.
Ask another driver whether the same warning appeared on their truck.
Start the route slowly and watch whether the warning stays on.
Note the warning and tell the lead before the scheduled departure.

advanced.situation: A blasting instrument fails a function check, and the schedule leaves little time before the crew needs equipment.

options.text: Try a quick adjustment with a hand tool and repeat the check.
Set the instrument aside and ask the maintenance worker to assess it.
Tell the lead about the failure and wait for the next instruction.
Tag the instrument for service and arrange an approved replacement.

basic.situation: You are ready to begin a routine cut, and the shift card shows the machine position and startup sequence. What do you do?

options.text: Check the machine position and start the conveyor before checking cutter alignment.
Start the cutter and conveyor in the sequence shown on the shift card.
Confirm the face position, then start each control in the marked sequence.
Start both controls together to save time before the face is fully aligned.

advanced.situation: The rock feels harder than on the last shift, and output has slowed. You can adjust settings within the approved range. What do you do?

options.text: Lower feed to ease the cutter, then continue with the current speed setting.
Raise cutter speed and feed together to recover output during the shift.
Keep the previous settings and ask the next operator to review the slower cut.
Reduce feed slightly, watch the cut, and record output before another adjustment.

basic.situation: With your supervisor beside you, you check roof and rib supports before mining the face. One support looks slightly out of line. What do you do?

options.text: Keep the crew clear of that area and show your supervisor the support change.
Continue the planned cut because the support is still standing in place.
Mark the support location and finish checking the other supports before reporting it.
Point out the shifted support and wait nearby while your supervisor checks it.

advanced.situation: Before a face entry, you hear a new creak and spot a fine roof crack near a support. The crew is preparing equipment. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the crew the support looks sound and start the equipment checks.
Notify the supervisor about both signs while the crew finishes nearby preparations.
Ask the crew to pause nearby work and show the crack and sound location.
Report the crack and creak to your supervisor before the next entry.

basic.situation: You are helping hang ventilation tubing toward the face, and the crew gives you the planned route. What do you do?

options.text: Hang the tubing along the route and leave the final end near the face.
Secure the tubing along the marked route and check its end reaches the planned face position.
Secure the tubing along the marked route and tell the crew when finished.
Keep the tubing folded until someone else confirms the route at the face.

advanced.situation: The face now has an offset branch, and the approved ventilation plan shows a route around it. You are laying out tubing and curtains. What do you do?

options.text: Follow the approved route and hang curtains around the branch as mapped.
Ask the crew to place curtains while you lay tubing along the original line.
Compare the branch with the plan, then place tubing and curtains along the approved route.
Route tubing through the nearest opening, then hang curtains across the branch.

basic.situation: You are learning to use the gas detector with a supervisor nearby before the next face entry. What do you do?

options.text: Check the detector status, take the face reading, and report it to your supervisor.
Use the detector without checking its status, then report the displayed result.
Take a face reading, note the detector display, and tell your supervisor the result.
Ask your supervisor to take the reading while you watch the detector display.

advanced.situation: Your methane readings have risen across several checks, though each remains within the site's stated limit. The next face check is due. What do you do?

options.text: Repeat the gas test, check trends, and alert your supervisor before face entry.
Log the reading, take another sample, and compare it with the previous checks.
Compare recent results and tell your supervisor the readings are trending upward.
Continue scheduled checks and raise the rising pattern during the shift handover.

basic.situation: A provided face map marks the locations and depths for your next set of holes. You are preparing the machine. What do you do?

options.text: Mark the locations now and ask a coworker to check the depths later.
Choose the easiest hole positions near the marked line to save setup time.
Mark the hole locations from the map and begin setting up the cutter now.
Mark hole locations from the map and check depth notes before cutting.

advanced.situation: You uncover a harder rock band where the map places the next cut. The approved boundaries remain clear, and the machine can be repositioned. What do you do?

options.text: Mark the changed band, reposition for the mapped next cut, and record the obstacle.
Revise the next cut location within approved boundaries and reposition the machine for it.
Keep the mapped cut depth and increase feed to move through the harder band.
Pause the cut and wait for another shift to decide where the machine should move.

basic.situation: A technician is beside you while you oil a machine part and adjust a loose fitting with a wrench. What do you do?

options.text: Oil the part and tighten the fitting while the technician watches.
Ask the technician to finish the adjustment while you prepare the oil can.
Apply specified oil, adjust the fitting with the technician, and check seating.
Tighten the fitting firmly and add extra oil before returning the machine.

advanced.situation: A cutter keeps binding after routine oiling, and a newer operator asks how to check the teeth. A technician is available nearby. What do you do?

options.text: Replace the visibly worn tooth and show the operator how to inspect it.
Inspect for tooth damage, involve the technician in recurring binding, and explain the checks.
Replace the teeth and explain the repair to the operator before checking whether binding returns.
Show the operator how to replace each tooth and return the machine to service.

basic.situation: You are drilling bolt holes along a marked roof line, with the specified spacing on the work plan. What do you do?

options.text: Mark the row and start drilling while a coworker checks the spacing afterward.
Drill the row at a quicker spacing to finish before the next crew arrives.
Drill each hole at the marked spacing and check its position against the plan.
Drill the holes at the marked spacing and tell the crew when the row is ready.

advanced.situation: A changing rock band crosses the marked bolt row, while the support plan gives spacing for the usual formation. What do you do?

options.text: Note the changed band, then drill the row at the usual spacing for now.
Mark the changed band and request a pattern review before drilling that section.
Follow the usual spacing, record the band, and tell the next shift about it.
Use the usual spacing and drill through the changed band to keep the row straight.

basic.situation: You are using a hydraulic bolting machine to force a bolt into a prepared hole, with a coworker nearby. What do you do?

options.text: Use the hydraulic mechanism to seat the bolt and signal when it is in.
Seat the bolt with the hydraulic mechanism and check its position against the hole.
Push the bolt in quickly and move the machine toward the next hole.
Ask the coworker to guide the bolt while you operate the hydraulic control.

advanced.situation: The ceiling span is wider than usual, and the support plan specifies a resin bolt type for this section. What do you do?

options.text: Use a familiar bolt type and tighten it to the usual feel for this span.
Ask a coworker to choose a bolt while you prepare the bolting machine.
Check the specified resin bolt and installation steps, then fit it across the planned span.
Fit the specified resin bolt across the span and tell the crew when done.

basic.situation: You are positioning a bolting machine and fitting a drill bit into its chuck with guidance from an experienced coworker. What do you do?

options.text: Push the bit into the chuck and start positioning the machine at the face.
Fit the bit, check that it is seated, and position the machine at the marked point.
Ask the coworker to position the machine while you fetch another drill bit.
Position the machine at the marked point and seat the bit in the chuck.

advanced.situation: The bolting machine is vibrating more than usual after a bit change, and the roof conditions differ from the previous section. What do you do?

options.text: Increase the drilling setting and continue to match the harder roof conditions.
Check the bit seating and machine position, then adjust within the approved setup range.
Adjust the machine setting within range and watch whether the vibration changes.
Pause the setup and ask the next crew to assess the vibration and roof.

basic.situation: Before operating the bolting machine, you are assigned to check its controls and guards with a supervisor present. What do you do?

options.text: Ask your supervisor to inspect the guards while you check the controls.
Check the controls and guards, then report any concern to your supervisor.
Start the machine and test the controls while the crew prepares nearby.
Inspect each assigned control and guard, then confirm the machine is ready to operate.

advanced.situation: A coworker has missed a control check twice, and methane testing is due before the next entry. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the coworker to verify controls while you conduct the methane test and record results.
Ask the coworker to finish the controls check while you start methane testing.
Request supervisor guidance while preparing the machine for both required checks before entry.
Check controls and test methane yourself, then brief the coworker on results before entry.

basic.situation: You are using a torque wrench to test a bolt against the tension specified on the work sheet. What do you do?

options.text: Test the bolt and ask a coworker whether the result seems within range.
Test the bolt and note whether the wrench reaches the specified tension.
Turn the wrench until the bolt feels tight enough for the roof section.
Check the specified value, test with the torque wrench, and record the reading.

advanced.situation: Several tested bolts are below the specified tension, though nearby bolts pass. You are checking a new section with a torque wrench. What do you do?

options.text: Retest the low bolts and note the new readings for the shift record.
Check the specified tension, test the new section, and flag repeated low readings to the lead.
Test the new section at the usual setting and record whether most bolts pass.
Record the passing bolts and leave the low results for the next inspection round.

basic.situation: After bolting, you are asked to hang a ventilation curtain and dust loose rocks in your work area. What do you do?

options.text: Hang the curtain on the marked line and dust the rocks as assigned.
Move the curtain aside and dust the rocks to clear the work area faster.
Secure the curtain along the marked line, check its coverage, and dust the rocks.
Dust the rocks first and leave the curtain for the next crew to hang.

advanced.situation: A larger work area needs curtains and tubing around two active sections, followed by dusting after bolting. You are assigned to plan your crew's setup. What do you do?

options.text: Finish the first section's curtain and dusting before planning the second section later.
Run tubing along the shortest route and schedule dusting after both sections finish.
Hang curtains at both sections, run tubing from the nearest point, and dust after bolting.
Map both sections, route tubing and curtains to each, then schedule dusting after bolting.

basic.situation: You check the marked rock level before loading a shuttle car, but the reading is near its limit.

options.text: Use the last car's amount as a quick guide for this load.
Pause loading and confirm the marked level with your supervisor before adding more.
Compare the reading with the car limit and ask for a second check.
Load the remaining rock to finish this pass before the shift change.

advanced.situation: New operators use different rock-level readings, and one loaded car nearly exceeds its specification during a busy shift.

options.text: Tell the crew to follow the existing mark and report unusual loads to you.
Post a reminder to check the rock level before each shuttle car leaves.
Set a shared measuring point and demonstrate how operators verify each car against its specification.
Ask each operator to use the method that feels quickest during loading.

basic.situation: A conveyor boom needs a small adjustment to place the next load into a mine car while your supervisor watches.

options.text: Push the lever farther so the load reaches the car in one movement.
Ask your supervisor to make the adjustment while you watch the controls.
Move the boom in small lever adjustments while watching where the material lands.
Move the boom to the usual position used for the previous car.

advanced.situation: Two shuttle cars are approaching a long conveyor, and uneven loading could delay the next collection cycle.

options.text: Increase conveyor speed to clear the waiting material before the next cars arrive.
Adjust conveyor distribution as loading progresses, watching both car fill and belt flow.
Keep the current setting and ask the lead operator to review it after this cycle.
Use the setting from the last cycle and watch for any spill at the transfer point.

basic.situation: After a loading run, rock has spilled around a hopper and onto the nearby track during your assigned cleanup.

options.text: Clear larger walkway pieces first, then collect smaller rock with approved tools.
Start at the hopper, then ask your supervisor which spillage needs clearing next.
Sweep track spillage toward the hopper after checking this route is safe.
Clear hopper and track with approved tools, checking the walkway as you work.

advanced.situation: A shuttle car's discharge control behaves inconsistently during a loaded run, and a ramp is approaching.

options.text: Park clear of traffic and ask the mechanic to inspect the control before discharge.
Stop at a safe position, report the control fault, and follow the site's maintenance process.
Ask a nearby operator to watch the discharge while you proceed to the ramp.
Continue to the ramp and use the control gently while a mechanic is notified.

basic.situation: With your supervisor nearby, you spot loose material on a roof section above the machine's travel path.

options.text: Knock the piece down quickly so the machine can pass before the shift changes.
Pry the visible loose piece from where you are standing and watch it fall.
Use the crowbar from the approved position and move the loosened material into the machine path.
Ask your supervisor to check the roof and confirm where you should stand.

advanced.situation: A loaded machine is due through a roadway where a fallen rock and fresh roof fragments partly block the travel path.

options.text: Mark the blockage and take the machine along the nearest alternate route.
Hold the route, assess the obstruction and roof, then coordinate clearance before travel resumes.
Move the fallen rock aside and let the machine pass at reduced speed.
Ask the operator to wait while you check the fallen rock and roadway edges.

basic.situation: A trailing cable crosses a clear section of walkway near your machine, and your supervisor is available to guide you.

options.text: Pull the cable across the walkway by its nearest section to clear the route.
Ask your supervisor to move the cable while you hold the machine controls.
Wear rubber gloves and move the cable clear using the guided handling method.
Step over the cable and shift it when your loading pass is finished.

advanced.situation: A cable must be hung near a high-voltage source, and the installation plan is unclear about the safe work boundary.

options.text: Check the route with a coworker, then wait for the electrical lead before hanging the cable.
Stay clear; ask the electrical lead to confirm the safe boundary and approved cable method.
Use the usual hanging route and tell the crew the cable may be energized.
Review the plan and mark a likely safe area for the crew to work around.

basic.situation: A conveyor's lubrication point is due for service, and you have hand tools and a supervisor's guidance available.

options.text: Use specified lubricant and hand tool, then check for even coverage.
Ask your supervisor to demonstrate the lubrication point before you begin.
Oil the visible moving parts and tell your supervisor when you are done.
Apply the lubricant used on the last conveyor to save setup time.

advanced.situation: A hydraulic hose on a gathering arm shows a fresh leak during a shift, and a replacement hose is available in the workshop.

options.text: Ask the mechanic to inspect the leak while you keep the machine nearby.
Park the machine safely, report the leak, and follow the approved hose replacement procedure.
Park clear of traffic and ask the mechanic to replace the hose before reuse.
Finish the current pass, then replace the hose during the next planned pause.

basic.situation: A marked stone section needs a small piece removed, and your supervisor is beside you as you prepare a jackhammer.

options.text: Break away the largest piece first to clear the face for the next worker.
Ask your supervisor to point out the section before you start the jackhammer.
Check the marked section with your supervisor, then remove the piece using the guided tool method.
Start at the nearest edge and follow the visible crack with the jackhammer.

advanced.situation: A narrow stone section is not separating cleanly, and a new worker asks how to drive the wedges without damaging the block.

options.text: Demonstrate one controlled strike, then let the worker continue at the same pace.
Show the worker how to seat wedges evenly, checking the split after each strike.
Use the usual wedge spacing and continue the split at a steady pace.
Ask the worker to strike harder so the resistant section separates in fewer blows.

basic.situation: You are drilling along a chalk outline with a jackhammer while a more experienced quarry worker guides your position.

options.text: Drill quickly through the marked area so the splitting crew can prepare.
Ask your guide to mark the first hole before you start drilling.
Drill holes at even intervals and adjust toward the outline near the end.
Follow the outline and check each hole position with your guide as you work.

advanced.situation: A complex split needs charges, but the blast area has workers nearby and the firing plan is still being confirmed.

options.text: Keep the crew back and review the written plan before handling charges.
Hold charge work until the authorized lead confirms the plan and the area is clear.
Ask the lead to confirm the charge layout before you prepare the holes.
Place the charges at the planned holes while the crew clears the area.

basic.situation: A stone slab needs a shallow groove along its marked outline, and a senior cutter is available to guide your chisel work.

options.text: Cut the groove in a few deep strokes to finish before the next slab.
Ask the senior cutter to confirm the groove line before you begin.
Chisel along the marked line, checking groove depth as you work.
Use the existing groove as a guide and compare the result when finished.

advanced.situation: Several slabs are queued for floor sheets, and a junior cutter is unsure how to keep cuts consistent across the batch.

options.text: Review the first cut together, then ask the junior to repeat that method.
Ask the junior to mark each sheet clearly before starting the cuts.
Tell the junior to use the last slab's settings throughout this batch.
Set a repeatable sequence and show checks against marked dimensions for each sheet.

basic.situation: Before cutting a stone block, you need to locate its grain lines, but the pattern is faint under the quarry dust.

options.text: Clean the face and trace the visible grain before choosing a split.
Mark a split line from the faint pattern and begin cutting along it.
Use the block's outer edge as a guide for the likely split direction before cutting.
Ask an experienced cutter to point out the grain line before cutting.

advanced.situation: A large block shows intersecting grain lines, and the planned cut could produce several costly slabs if the split runs off course.

options.text: Follow the strongest visible line and tell the crew to allow for a rough edge.
Mark the most visible line and keep the planned slab dimensions for now.
Trace the intersecting lines and review the likely split with the lead.
Ask a senior cutter to inspect the block before you mark a split direction.

basic.situation: A broken stone piece needs holes for dogs before removal, and your supervisor is guiding the drilling position.

options.text: Confirm marked positions, drill each hole, and test that every dog seats securely.
Drill holes at the marked positions and insert dogs before lifting the piece.
Ask your supervisor to confirm the hole positions before you begin drilling.
Attach the sling at the nearest edge and direct the piece toward loading.

advanced.situation: A large block is ready for removal, but the sling angle differs from the previous lift and the crew awaits your direction.

options.text: Ask the rigging lead to verify the angle while the crew stays clear.
Pause the crew and reposition the sling after confirming the safe alignment.
Reuse the earlier lift direction and ask the crew to move the block slowly.
Inspect the anchor points and sling angle before authorizing the block's removal.

basic.situation: A customer order calls for a stone counter cut to marked dimensions, and you have a rule and chalk line ready.

options.text: Measure each side once and draw the chalk lines from those readings.
Copy the dimensions from a similar counter and mark the stone quickly.
Measure from the reference edge and verify both dimensions before marking.
Ask a senior worker to confirm the measurements before you draw the outline.

advanced.situation: A batch of stone sheets needs consistent outlines, and a new worker will mark the next pieces while you prepare the cutting queue.

options.text: Ask the worker to note dimensions beside each sheet's chalk marks.
Tell the worker to copy the first sheet's chalk lines across the whole batch.
Review the first outline together, then let the worker mark the remaining sheets.
Set a common edge and verify each outline's dimensions before cutting.

basic.situation: You are tightening a tubing joint with a hand wrench, and the thread starts to bind before the shoulder seats.

options.text: You add a longer handle and force the joint until it seats.
You back off, clean the threads, and restart with guided hand pressure.
You ask your partner to hold the pipe while you turn steadily.
You pause, check the thread alignment, then resume with the wrench.

advanced.situation: You are coordinating a pipeline section, and the route crew reports a ground shift near the planned trench.

options.text: You shift the section slightly around the soft ground and continue laying.
You compare the marked route with current ground conditions, then reset the section plan.
You keep the planned route and lower the section before the ground changes again.
You pause lowering and ask the site lead to confirm the route adjustment.

basic.situation: You are dismantling an oil field pump under supervision, and several similar bolts come off in sequence.

options.text: You label separate trays by pump section and arrange parts in removal order.
You place each set of bolts beside its matching part as you work.
You stack the bolts by size and ask your supervisor to identify them later.
You put all the bolts together in one tray to save bench space.

advanced.situation: You are repairing a boiler assembly, and inspection shows uneven wear across several mating parts after dismantling.

options.text: You set a shared inspection sequence and record wear before approving each part for repair.
You replace the visibly worn parts and return the assembly to the crew.
You compare the parts with a similar assembly before choosing repair work.
You inspect each mating surface and discuss the findings with the repair crew.

basic.situation: You are cleaning a field truck after a muddy shift, and grit has collected around the footwell and controls.

options.text: You sweep the cab quickly and leave the mats for the next shift.
You remove the mats, clear grit from the footwell, then wipe controls dry.
You clear loose grit, then wipe the controls with a damp cloth.
You use a brush on the footwell and wipe the steering wheel afterward.

advanced.situation: You are planning cleaning for several field trucks, and the team reports that mud builds up faster after wet shifts.

options.text: You schedule checks after wet shifts, prioritise heavily soiled trucks, and track completion.
You keep the current weekly schedule and ask drivers to mention heavy mud.
You leave the trucks for the weekly wash to keep the rota unchanged.
You set a daily cab-cleaning rota for every truck and keep a simple completion log.

basic.situation: You are moving pipe from a truck with a partner, and the next length is awkward to lift by hand.

options.text: You ask the supervisor to set the winch before you guide the pipe down.
You ask your partner to lift one end while you guide the other.
You clear the landing area, secure the pipe, and guide the truck winch with help.
You pull the pipe toward the truck edge so it drops onto the ground.

advanced.situation: You are planning pipe loading for transport, and the truck has limited deck space with lengths of different sizes.

options.text: You group similar lengths together and leave the driver to arrange the final load.
You check the deck capacity and arrange the lengths in the planned loading order.
You map pipe lengths, support points, and load sequence before directing the winch crew.
You load the longest pipes first to use the deck space efficiently.

basic.situation: You are bolting a pump part together with step-by-step help, and one bolt catches before the faces meet.

options.text: You turn the bolt harder until both faces pull together against the catch.
You back out the bolt, align the faces, then restart it gently by hand.
You ask your helper to steady the part while you tighten the bolt.
You check face alignment, then turn the bolt slowly while watching the joint.

advanced.situation: You are guiding engine assembly, and two new workers are fitting matching parts in different sequences.

options.text: You set out parts in assembly order and demonstrate the fit and bolt sequence.
You ask them to finish quickly so the engine can return to the work area.
You show each worker the parts and let them follow the sequence they know.
You review the sequence with both workers before they continue fitting parts.

basic.situation: You are signaling a crane operator under supervision, and a suspended load begins to swing near the deck edge.

options.text: You signal the operator to keep moving while the swinging load settles.
You signal a pause, clear the route with your supervisor, then guide a slow move.
You signal a slower pace and choose a clear place to watch the load.
You signal the operator to pause and watch the load settle before proceeding.

advanced.situation: You are directing a deck lift, and the planned path crosses a busy work area while the load is ready.

options.text: You hold the lift, clear the route, and confirm signals with the operator and crew.
You ask the operator to pause while you check the load and nearby crew.
You redirect the load around workers using short moves and clear hand signals.
You ask nearby workers to watch the suspended load while the operator follows its planned path.

basic.situation: You are watching extraction equipment, and its usual rhythm changes while material is moving through the process.

options.text: You watch the next cycle and note whether the changed rhythm continues.
You ask a nearby worker whether the equipment sounds unusual to them.
You alert the operator to the change and share what you observed.
You adjust the controls slightly to bring the rhythm back to normal.

advanced.situation: You are monitoring extraction equipment, and pressure and vibration readings change together during a busy run.

options.text: You reset the pressure control to its usual setting and resume monitoring.
You report the readings and ask the operator to decide what to check.
You record both readings and tell the crew to keep watching the equipment.
You identify the combined change, alert the operator, and guide a check against normal readings.

basic.situation: You are organizing materials for a drilling job, and several similar items are due at different work areas.

options.text: You send all the items to the first area so the crew can begin.
You sort the items by work area and label each prepared group.
You arrange the items in separate piles and tell the crew where each belongs.
You place the items together near the equipment to save carrying time.

advanced.situation: You are preparing specialized materials for a complex boring job, and a new worker is unsure which items belong together.

options.text: You give the worker the job list and ask them to sort materials by use.
You group the materials, then show how to match each label with the job list.
You arrange materials by task and invite the worker to check the labels with you.
You ask the worker to pair similar materials and compare labels against the list.

basic.situation: You are clearing debris after extraction, and scrap and loose soil are mixed across the work area.

options.text: You sweep the mixed debris into one pile for collection later.
You push the debris to the edge so equipment can leave the area.
You sort scrap from loose soil as you clear the work area.
You follow the site's waste directions, separate scrap, and clear the work area.

advanced.situation: You are coordinating cleanup before boring begins, and old debris remains near the marked work zone.

options.text: You begin boring around debris and assign a crew to remove it during the shift.
You set a shared cleanup standard and direct crews to the designated waste points.
You plan the cleanup order, assign debris destinations, and inspect the zone before work starts.
You ask each crew to clear nearby debris and move it to the assigned waste points.

basic.situation: You are unloading a machine part with hand tools under supervision, and it shifts against the truck bed.

options.text: You check where the part is resting, then use a secure tool to ease it free.
You ask your partner to steady the part while you pull with the tool.
You wedge a loose board beneath the part and pull it toward the edge.
You stop pulling and ask the supervisor to check how the part is resting.

advanced.situation: You are planning heavy material loading into equipment, and the parts differ in shape and the order of use.

options.text: You sequence parts by use, check load balance, and coach the crew.
You group parts by size and ask the crew to agree on loading order.
You check part weights and ask workers to follow a planned loading sequence.
You load heavy parts first, helping the crew finish the job quickly.

basic.situation: You are helping set up excavation equipment, and one support foot does not sit level on the prepared ground.

options.text: You inspect the ground and foot with your supervisor before making setup adjustments.
You tell the supervisor the foot is uneven and wait for guidance.
You ask a coworker to check the foot's level before changing its position.
You pause setup and ask your supervisor how to address the uneven foot.

advanced.situation: You are configuring excavation equipment, and a test run shows the cutting head drifting from the marked line.

options.text: You keep the current setting and tell the crew to compensate during excavation.
