You adjust the head in small increments while watching the next test run.
You pause the run, check alignment and supports, then make a measured adjustment.
You ask a coworker to watch the head while you adjust the controls.

basic.situation: You are helping repair drilling equipment with hand tools, and a removed cover exposes several worn fasteners.

options.text: You set worn fasteners aside and ask your supervisor before continuing cover work.
You compare worn fasteners with toolbox stock and ask before replacing them.
You label fasteners by location and confirm suitable replacements with your supervisor.
You sort fasteners by size and ask your supervisor which ones need replacement.

advanced.situation: You are maintaining drilling equipment, and repeated repairs are needed on the same component across several shifts.

options.text: You keep a repair log and ask workers to report further problems.
You ask the team to inspect the component during scheduled maintenance rounds each shift.
You log repairs and guide inspection of the component's recurring wear points.
You replace the component again so the equipment can return to service.

basic.situation: You finish checking a repaired bracket before it returns to service. The job order lists its required dimensions.

options.text: I inspect visible joints and ask the technician to recheck one doubtful point.
I check the repaired bracket with a ruler against the job order.
I sign off after the fitter says the measurements were within range.
I compare key measurements with the stated tolerance, then record any mismatch.

advanced.situation: A technician is injured when a lift slips during repair work. You are asked to investigate and report what happened.

options.text: I collect witness accounts, inspect the lift, and separate observed facts from possible causes.
I write the report from the injured technician's account and the shift notes.
I note the injury and ask the team to resume after replacing the lift.
I inspect the lift and summarize the likely cause for the manager.

basic.situation: A routine service needs two replacement seals and an hour of labour. Your price list gives the rates.

options.text: I use the last similar job's total to save time on the estimate.
I add the two seal prices and round the labour charge upward slightly.
I list two seals and one labour hour, then calculate each at listed rates.
I multiply the seal price by two and add the listed labour charge.

advanced.situation: A shutdown project needs several repair crews, outside contractors, and parts with uncertain delivery costs. Management requests an estimate.

options.text: I copy a previous shutdown estimate and update the largest parts prices.
I total the main parts and add a broad allowance for the other work.
I price parts and labour separately, then use the last contractor quote.
I build separate cost lines for labour, parts, and contractors, with stated assumptions.

basic.situation: A workshop trolley has a loose handle and a sticking wheel during routine maintenance. You have hand tools available.

options.text: I oil the wheel and tighten the handle before the next trolley run.
I secure the trolley, tighten the handle, and test the wheel by moving it.
I tighten the handle and free the wheel with the supplied hand tools.
I wedge the handle in place and return the trolley to the work area.

advanced.situation: A hydraulic press stalls under load during a deadline repair. A junior technician is waiting to learn the repair method.

options.text: I test the valve and repair the press, then explain the main steps afterward.
I isolate the press, check its fault sequence, and demonstrate the repair steps as I work.
I replace the suspected valve and ask the junior to watch the repair.
I ask the junior to swap the valve while I update the job board.

basic.situation: A repair job needs a technician, a quality check, and a part from a supplier before the afternoon shift ends.

options.text: I confirm the part arrival with the supplier and share the work sequence with quality.
I tell the technician to start and let quality know when the repair is ready.
I ask the technician to wait until the supplier calls with an update.
I start the repair and assume the supplier will deliver before the shift ends.

advanced.situation: Engineering changes a repair sequence while quality and a supplier have different views on the replacement part. You need to coordinate the next steps.

options.text: I forward engineering's sequence to quality and ask the supplier for a revised quote.
I ask quality to confirm the part before updating engineering and the supplier.
I tell the supplier to send the usual part so the repair can proceed.
I bring engineering and quality's requirements to the supplier and relay agreed constraints.

basic.situation: One mechanic has fallen behind on routine jobs for several shifts. You need to review the work level and report the issue.

options.text: I note the missed jobs and ask the manager to review the mechanic's pace.
I move the unfinished jobs to another mechanic and close the shift sheet.
I compare completed jobs with the shift plan and report the continuing shortfall.
I tell the mechanic to speed up and mention the delay at handover.

advanced.situation: A mechanic's repeated mistakes continue after coaching, and a transfer or disciplinary measure may be considered. You must recommend a personnel action.

options.text: I discuss the pattern with the mechanic and recommend more coaching to the manager.
I document the coaching and work examples, then recommend an action through the usual process.
I suggest a transfer so the current team can meet its repair targets.
I recommend discipline based on the latest mistake and the team's frustration.

basic.situation: Two urgent repairs and a routine inspection need the same mechanic today. The assignment board lists each job's priority and required skills.

options.text: I match both urgent repairs to the mechanic and move the inspection to tomorrow.
I assign the urgent repair first and leave the inspection for the next open slot.
I compare job priority and skill needs, then sequence assignments around the mechanic's capacity.
I assign the mechanic to the repair with the closest deadline and review the board later.

advanced.situation: After two near misses with a shop tool, you are asked to review the maintenance procedure and brief the team on safe use.

options.text: I review the near-miss details, revise the relevant steps, and demonstrate them during the briefing.
I add a safety note to the procedure and schedule a brief talk next week.
I remind everyone to use the tool carefully and keep the current procedure posted.
I update the procedure's safety steps and ask an experienced worker to brief the team.

basic.situation: A customer reports that an office printer stopped feeding paper. You are sent to the site with a service order and basic tools.

options.text: I call ahead to check the printer model, then travel with common supplies.
I ask the customer to bring the printer to our workshop for service.
I travel with the listed tools and start with the printer's paper path.
I confirm the reported fault with the customer and follow the service order at the site.

advanced.situation: Two client offices report critical machine failures at once. You are the nearest repairer, and each site needs an estimated arrival time.

options.text: I head to the closer office first and update the second client after arrival.
I ask both clients to restart their machines while I drive to one site.
I confirm each symptom, estimate travel and repair needs, then sequence visits by impact.
I call both offices for symptoms and send the nearer client an arrival estimate.

basic.situation: A receipt printer jams repeatedly. You open its casing to inspect the feed gears and wiring for visible wear.

options.text: I inspect the gears and wiring with a light before removing any parts.
I remove the feed cover and check the gears with my hand tools.
I check the wiring first and leave the feed gears for another visit.
I replace the feed gears using the usual kit and close the casing.

advanced.situation: Performance records show an ATM receipt printer failing after long runs. You need to inspect worn parts and trace its power connections.

options.text: I trace the power connections and replace the most worn-looking feed gear.
I compare failure timing with component wear, then trace the power connections against the layout.
I review the failure logs and inspect the cable and feed gear for wear.
I replace the printer's cable and feed gear, then check the next run.

basic.situation: A copier produces faint prints after a settings change. The service sheet lists the normal density setting and test procedure.

options.text: I raise the density setting and ask the user whether prints look clearer.
I restore the previous setting from memory and return the copier to use.
I compare the current density setting with the service sheet and run its test page.
I read the service sheet and set the listed density before printing a sample.

advanced.situation: A copier's control circuit fails intermittently after a board replacement. Diagnostic readings point to two possible signal paths.

options.text: I reproduce the fault, compare both paths, and trace readings through the schematic.
I reseat the board, run its test, and check whether the fault returns.
I compare signal readings and use the schematic to choose a test path.
I replace the board again and close the repair after startup.

basic.situation: You replace a worn roller in a copier and must reassemble the cover before checking print quality.

options.text: I reassemble the cover using the service steps and check that it sits evenly.
I reassemble the cover in sequence and run a test copy to check feeding.
I close the cover loosely so the user can test the roller later.
I fit the cover and ask the user to report any feeding problem.

advanced.situation: A document scanner's alignment drifts after transport. You have its calibration specifications and a test sheet before a client handover.

options.text: I align scanner settings and verify results across the supplied test sheet.
I check calibration settings and run the test sheet after making adjustments.
I adjust the scanner and check that its edges appear even across the test sheet.
I adjust alignment across the test sheet until every scanned page appears centered and clear.

basic.situation: You refill a shared office printer's toner after a service call. The repair form has fields for the part and work completed.

options.text: I record the toner used and the refill on the repair form before leaving.
I note the toner refill in my job book and continue to the next call.
I enter the toner refill on the repair form after finishing the next call.
I refill the toner and leave the form for the next technician to complete.

advanced.situation: Several repair jobs need different parts, and the stock count is lower than the inventory sheet shows. You must order supplies and update records.

options.text: I review open job parts, verify stock counts, record gaps, and order missing supplies.
I compare stock with job needs, order confirmed shortages, and update inventory records.
I recount shelf stock, then order parts needed for the jobs due soon.
I check each job's parts, compare shelf stock, and order supplies for confirmed needs.

basic.situation: A customer says a copier jams on double-sided jobs but works on single pages. You need details before troubleshooting.

options.text: I ask how often jams happen and whether another tray works.
I ask the customer to clear the jam and restart the copier.
I ask when jams happen, paper type, and what the display shows.
I tell the customer to use single-sided mode until the next service visit.

advanced.situation: A new repairer is learning to reinstall copier software after a settings fault. You are asked to train them on the procedure.

options.text: I talk through the reinstall while the trainee watches me change the settings.
I explain the procedure, demonstrate a reinstall, then have the trainee practise on a test machine.
I hand over the reinstall guide and ask the trainee to follow it during the repair.
I demonstrate the reinstall and ask the trainee to explain the main steps back.

basic.situation: You receive a tower work order and a site drawing before starting. What do you check to identify the required work?

options.text: Read the work order and list the equipment named for installation.
Use the previous crew's notes to decide what this visit covers.
Start with the antenna shown nearest the tower access point.
Compare the work order with the drawing, then mark each required item.

advanced.situation: A completed antenna mount has loose hardware, and its weather seal looks uneven after rain. What do you do during the installation audit?

options.text: Record the gaps and loose hardware, then request a focused rework before sign-off.
Mark the mount complete since the antenna stayed in place during rain.
Ask the crew whether the mount passed their final inspection.
Tighten the accessible bolts and photograph the uneven seal for the file.

basic.situation: Your senior asks you to connect a tower grounding lead, and the clamp is beside the marked connection point. What do you do?

options.text: Fit the grounding lead to the marked point and check the clamp is firm.
Attach the lead to the nearest bare metal point on the frame.
Check the marked point with your senior, then fit and secure the lead.
Clean the clamp and set the lead beside the marked point for review.

advanced.situation: A sweep trace shows a sharp return loss change after a connector was replaced, but the transmit path passes a basic check. What do you investigate?

options.text: Compare the sweep trace with the saved baseline and inspect the replaced connector.
Check nearby jumpers and ask the crew which connections they touched.
Repeat the sweep across the affected line and record the readings.
Accept the path because the basic transmit check passed after replacement.

basic.situation: You are helping bolt a small equipment bracket onto a rack using the supplied hand tools. What do you do?

options.text: Start two bolts loosely, then ask your partner to check the fit.
Align the bracket with its holes, then tighten each bolt with the supplied tool.
Hold the bracket steady while fitting and tightening the supplied bolts.
Use a longer wrench from the truck to finish the bolts faster.

advanced.situation: A heavy equipment crate must reach a remote tower site before rain, but the access track is narrow and uneven. How do you plan the transport?

options.text: Load the crate onto the available trailer and take the shortest route.
Use the utility truck and ask the site crew to guide the trailer in.
Ask the driver to inspect the track before loading the crate.
Check the route and trailer limits, then coordinate a suitable vehicle and delivery window.

basic.situation: Your supervisor assigns you to run a coaxial cable along the approved route and keep it separate from the power cable. What do you do?

options.text: Bundle both cables together at the supports to keep the run tidy.
Follow the marked route, keep the cable separated, and secure it at the supports.
Lay the coaxial cable near the route and ask the supervisor to inspect it.
Run the coaxial cable along the marked route and clip it at each support.

advanced.situation: An approved tower plan calls for a surge arrestor and TMA, but the delivered line components differ from the drawing. What do you do before installation?

options.text: Install the supplied parts in the planned positions to keep the crew on schedule.
Set out the components by their labels and confirm the connections with the lead technician.
Check the component datasheets against the approved drawing and flag any mismatch before fitting.
Fit the components that match the connectors and note the remaining difference.

basic.situation: You have been asked to photograph an antenna replacement before the crew packs up. What photos do you take?

options.text: Use the clearest photo from the previous site visit for the record.
Photograph the old and new antenna, including the mount and its connections.
Photograph the new antenna label and the crew working nearby.
Take a wide photo of the installed antenna and the tower section.

advanced.situation: You are coordinating an antenna replacement, and the audit requires photos that show the old unit, new unit, and finished connections. How do you manage the record?

options.text: Submit one crew overview photo as the replacement record for the audit.
Ask the crew to photograph removal, installation, and finished connections from multiple clear angles.
Use a stage shot list and verify images show the unit and connections.
Take ground photos of the finished antenna and file them with the job notes.

basic.situation: You have finished a scheduled tower visit and need to enter the work details in the reporting software. What do you record?

options.text: Record the crew's arrival and departure times, then attach the visit checklist.
Save the work details in a draft and ask a teammate to enter them.
Enter the completed work, visit date, and any outstanding item in the report.
Mark the visit complete using the standard status and leave the notes for later.

advanced.situation: Several tower jobs are nearing handover, and your progress report will help plan maintenance visits. What information do you include?

options.text: Include completed work, open issues, and conditions affecting follow-up visits.
List each job's completion status and the date of its last site visit.
Describe the largest open issue and attach the latest site photos.
Copy the previous progress report and update the job completion fields.

basic.situation: A senior asks you to use a meter to check a circuit connection on a telecom unit. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the senior to confirm the meter setting before you take a reading.
Set the meter as directed, check the connection, and record its reading.
Use the nearest meter range and report whether the circuit seems live.
Use the meter setting from the work note and check the connection.

advanced.situation: A repaired unit passes its power check, but readings across several circuits vary from the service notes. How do you assess the results?

options.text: Check the connectors and ask the repairer which parts were changed.
Repeat the readings on each circuit and record the results for the team.
Release the unit because its power check passed after the repair.
Compare each reading with the specifications and isolate the circuit that remains outside range.

basic.situation: You are asked to connect two wires on a communication unit using the supplied diagram. What do you do?

options.text: Follow the diagram and secure each wire at its marked terminal.
Match each wire to the diagram, then secure the connections and check their seating.
Connect wires by matching their colors to the nearest terminal labels.
Prepare the wires and ask a teammate to confirm the terminal labels.

advanced.situation: A work order changes a switching circuit, and two wiring diagrams show different routes through the frame. How do you handle the layout?

options.text: Trace the approved diagram against the frame and mark the revised route before rewiring.
Use the latest dated diagram and label each changed connection as you work.
Keep the existing route and move only the connections named in the order.
Map both routes on paper and ask the team which one fits better.

basic.situation: A senior identifies a faulty plug-in circuit module and asks you to replace it. What do you do?

options.text: Bring the spare module to the senior and wait for a second check.
Confirm the module label, swap it as directed, and update the equipment record.
Fit the closest spare module so the equipment can return to service.
Replace the module with the matching spare and tell the senior afterward.

advanced.situation: A recurring fault returns after two module swaps, and the equipment record shows the same symptom at earlier visits. How do you investigate?

options.text: Review the service history and test related circuits before setting a repeatable repair procedure.
Ask the previous repairer which module they replaced at the last visit.
Replace another matching module and close the repeat fault entry afterward.
Run the usual circuit checks and document the results before another swap.

basic.situation: You are with a supervisor at a cable vault, where loose wire pieces remain after inspection. What do you do?

options.text: Pick up the loose wire pieces and place them with the site waste.
Tell the supervisor about the debris and wait for their direction.
Gather the wire pieces, keep the access clear, and check the area before leaving.
Move the wire pieces to the side of the vault entrance for later collection.

advanced.situation: A telecom fault requires access through a narrow vault entrance, and the usual ladder cannot be set safely on the wet ground. What do you do?

options.text: Assess entry and ground conditions, then arrange suitable access equipment with the crew.
Relocate the ladder to firmer ground and have a coworker steady it during access.
Use the ladder at the entrance and keep the first inspection brief.
Clear nearby debris and ask the supervisor whether the ladder can be repositioned.

basic.situation: You find a cable whose color differs from the maintenance note. What do you do before continuing the equipment check?

options.text: Note the cable color and ask a teammate to check the manual section.
Mark the cable for review and continue with a separate equipment check.
Record the observed color and compare it with the diagram before tracing the cable.
Use the color in the maintenance note to identify the cable in your entry.

advanced.situation: A manual and site specification describe different maintenance steps for a switching unit. How do you determine which instructions apply?

options.text: Check the unit model and site specification, then clarify conflicts before starting maintenance.
Follow the unit model manual, record the site specification difference, and flag it for review.
Compare both instruction sets and ask a senior which one the crew uses.
Use the shorter maintenance procedure to keep the equipment available for service.

basic.situation: Your base asks by radio for an update while you are checking a customer communication unit. What do you report?

options.text: Give the unit status, the check still underway, and the next expected update.
Reply that the unit is under check and return to the test bench.
Report the unit status and say that testing is still underway.
Ask the customer whether the unit worked before the current fault.

advanced.situation: A customer reports that calls still fail after your on-site checks, and the usual reset has not helped. What do you do next?

options.text: Call the technical service center and describe the failed reset and call issue.
Summarize the checks and symptoms, then contact technical support for the next diagnostic step.
Ask a coworker to repeat the reset while you explain the delay to the customer.
Tell the customer the line should recover once the current checks finish.

basic.situation: You are helping review a flight test log, and one radio reading briefly drops below its usual range.

options.text: Ask a technician to check the trace before you write a finding.
Check related channels and test conditions to see whether the dip repeats.
Compare the reading with nearby test data and note the exact time.
Record the dip as a confirmed radio fault and request a replacement.

advanced.situation: After a thermal run, flight test data show intermittent failures across two avionics systems. The team needs your analysis before the next test window.

options.text: Repeat the last test sequence and note which system fails first.
Review each system's traces and flag the recurring fault times for the engineer.
Replace the component named in the latest fault log before the next run.
Compare fault timing with temperature and shared supply readings across both systems.

basic.situation: You are laying out a small avionics assembly from a blueprint, and two mounting points look close together.

options.text: Check the drawing scale and dimensions, then mark both points for review.
Mark both points from the blueprint and ask for a check before cutting.
Use the first point as a reference and place the second by eye.
Measure the points from the assembly edge and compare them with the drawing.

advanced.situation: A test connector cannot reach a panel during a planned avionics check. You are asked to fabricate a temporary aid before the test window.

options.text: Sketch a simple extension and make it from stock with matching connectors.
Ask the test team for a spare lead and check whether it reaches.
Review the panel layout and test needs, then design an aid with secure access.
Measure the panel gap and fabricate an extension with the required connector spacing.

basic.situation: You are assembling a switch box from a wiring diagram, and a terminal label is hard to read.

options.text: Check the diagram and ask your guide to confirm the unclear terminal label.
Pause assembly and set the unclear wire aside for the next shift.
Trace the wire path on the diagram and verify the terminal before joining.
Connect the wire to the terminal that matches its color and length.

advanced.situation: A prototype circuit works on the bench, but its indicator flickers during vibration testing. You are preparing the next version for evaluation.

options.text: Replace the indicator with a brighter model and repeat the vibration test.
Inspect solder joints and connector seating, then record the flicker conditions.
Vary vibration and supply conditions separately, then revise the prototype around the result.
Resolder the indicator connections and ask the test team to run another cycle.

basic.situation: You are using a voltmeter to check an avionics assembly, and the first reading is lower than expected.

options.text: Repeat the reading once and record both values for your supervisor.
Record the first reading and tell your supervisor the assembly has failed.
Check the meter range and probe contact, then repeat the measurement.
Note the reading and ask your supervisor whether to check it again.

advanced.situation: A ground test shows a radio fault only when another system is powered. Your next test slot is short, and several causes are possible.

options.text: Swap in a serviceable radio unit and see whether the fault clears.
Test each system separately and together, logging conditions and instrument readings.
Repeat the full test and note whether the radio fault appears again.
Inspect the radio connections and report any visible damage before testing again.

basic.situation: You are installing an avionics component with hand tools, and its cable route appears to cross a nearby panel edge.

options.text: Secure the cable along the shortest route and finish the installation.
Check the installation drawing and show your guide the cable route before securing it.
Compare the route with the drawing and check clearance at the panel edge.
Pause the installation and ask another technician to review the route.

advanced.situation: You are fitting a radio system during a tight maintenance window. The wiring diagram and installed connector positions do not seem to align.

options.text: Compare connector labels with the diagram and mark the mismatch for the lead.
Adjust the cable path to reach the connector and complete the installation.
Check the diagram revision and trace each connector before routing the cables.
Hold the installation and ask the lead which connector positions to follow.

basic.situation: You have finished a small avionics repair, and the maintenance log is due before the aircraft moves to another bay.

options.text: Enter the repair and part used, then leave the check for the next shift.
Write that the radio was repaired and close the job record.
Log the repair and part used, then ask your supervisor to review it.
Record the repair, part, and test result, then check the entry against your notes.

advanced.situation: Two technicians need the same avionics test bench, while an engineer is waiting for one result to plan the next maintenance step.

options.text: Check both job priorities and bench needs, then agree a sequence with the team.
Let the first technician use the bench and tell the engineer to wait.
Ask the technicians to split the bench time and update the engineer afterward.
Set a bench order with the technicians and give the engineer an estimated time.

basic.situation: You are reassembling a repaired motor, and the service notes mention a washer whose position is not obvious.

options.text: Compare the notes with the layout and show your guide the washer position.
Pause and ask your guide to confirm where the washer belongs.
Check the notes and compare the washer position with the parts layout.
Place the washer where it fits and continue tightening the housing.

advanced.situation: You are reassembling a large motor after bearing work. The specified end clearance is close to your gauge reading, and the job is due today.

options.text: Ask the senior repairer to interpret the reading before you continue reassembly.
Use the first clearance reading and close the housing to meet the deadline.
Recheck the gauge setup and repeat the clearance measurement before closing the housing.
Repeat the clearance measurement at several points and compare it with the specification.

basic.situation: You are soldering a replacement lead to a small motor connection, and the joint looks dull after cooling.

options.text: Set the motor aside and ask the next shift to assess the joint.
Inspect the wire seating and joint, then ask your guide to review it.
Add solder over the joint and return the motor to the repair bench.
Reheat the joint with the wire seated firmly, then inspect the cooled connection.

advanced.situation: Several repaired connections fail a pull check across one batch. You are helping a junior worker prepare the next set of motor leads.

options.text: Inspect a sample of joints and discuss the pull check results with your junior.
Use more solder on each lead and continue with the next batch.
Review the failed joints and demonstrate a repeatable seating and heating method.
Ask the supervisor to check the iron temperature before the next batch.

basic.situation: You are cleaning a small motor part, and old grease remains near a surface that will be inspected.

options.text: Buff the whole part until the grease marks are less visible.
Check the part surface, choose a suitable cleaning method, and inspect the area afterward.
Wipe the area with solvent and ask your guide to check the surface.
Set the part aside until someone confirms which cleaning method to use.

advanced.situation: A motor assembly has grease on painted and bare metal areas, with inspection scheduled soon. You are choosing how to clean both surfaces.

options.text: Separate the surfaces, check cleaning guidance, and choose a suitable method for each.
Clean the painted area gently and buff the bare metal, then inspect both.
Use solvent on both areas and wipe until the grease is gone.
Use the buffing wheel on both areas to finish the cleaning quickly.

basic.situation: You are disassembling a small motor on the bench, and its housing screws are tight after routine service.

options.text: Use a longer wrench to loosen each screw and remove the housing.
Check the screw heads and use the matching hand tool to loosen them.
Inspect the screw heads, then tell your supervisor they are tight.
Pause and ask your supervisor whether you should try a different tool.

advanced.situation: A generator must be opened for repair, and its rotor assembly is too heavy to lift by hand. The crane operator is waiting nearby.

options.text: Check the lift points and weight, then coordinate signals and clearance with the operator.
Agree on signals with the operator and clear nearby tools before the lift.
Signal the operator to lift while you guide the rotor from its edge.
Ask the operator to wait while you find a senior repairer.

basic.situation: You are adjusting a motor contact with a gauge, and the gap is slightly outside the service guide range.

options.text: Adjust the contact in small steps and recheck the gap with the gauge.
Use the gauge to adjust the contact, then ask your guide to check it.
Bend the contact until the gap looks close to the guide range.
Record the gap and wait for your supervisor to advise on adjustment.

advanced.situation: A motor runs unevenly after contact and spring adjustments. Two technicians have used different gauge readings on similar units this week.

options.text: Recheck a unit with your gauge before adjusting any further contacts.
Record both readings and ask technicians to use one gauge on future checks.
Compare readings and test results, then agree on a measured team adjustment method.
Use one gauge to check the contacts, then note the running result.

basic.situation: You are repairing a power tool, and its service guide lists two possible causes for the same symptom.

options.text: Read the guide and ask your supervisor which listed cause to check first.
Replace the part that is quickest to reach and close the repair.
Read the guide and note both possible causes on the work order.
Check the guide and inspect the wiring diagram for the listed causes.

advanced.situation: A repaired motor still draws high current under load. The wiring diagram shows several connections, and the work order notes an intermittent stoppage.

options.text: Inspect the wiring and relay connections, then record any visible wear.
Measure current and inspect the connections against the diagram under load conditions.
Read the work order again and ask a senior repairer what to inspect.
Replace the relay named in an older work order and rerun the motor.

basic.situation: A vehicle lighting circuit is reported faulty. You have a meter and schematic, and your senior has asked you to check its basic electrical function.

options.text: Use the meter on the isolated circuit, then note the reading for your senior.
Swap the fuse first, then test whether the equipment starts again.
Ask a nearby technician to confirm the meter setting before you record results.
Check the supply and ground readings against the schematic before reporting.

advanced.situation: A trainee is using diagnostic software on an intermittent transport control fault. You need to teach them a sound way to investigate it.

options.text: Ask the trainee to follow the software prompts and write down each result.
Show the trainee how to compare fault logs with the schematic and test results.
Walk through one similar fault report and explain the likely software readings.
Let the trainee clear the stored faults and rerun the software scan.

basic.situation: A work order calls for a rated outlet on a transport unit. Your senior has marked the position and asked you to fit it with hand tools.

options.text: Compare the outlet label with the work order before selecting tools.
Mount the specified outlet firmly, then report the installation to your senior.
Use a smaller outlet that fits the opening and complete the work order.
Fit the specified outlet and ask your senior to check mounting and cable entry.

advanced.situation: A replacement power source and terminal board are ready for a transport unit. Commissioning checks are still pending while you coordinate the installation.

options.text: Use the approved drawing to sequence the board connections and coordinate each check.
Check terminal labels against the drawing, then ask the team to continue fitting.
Connect the power source now so the team can confirm the board layout under load.
Stage the power source and board while the team waits for the pending checks.

basic.situation: A transport unit has a blown lighting fuse. Your senior directs you to replace it after checking the listed fuse rating.

options.text: Fit a higher-rated fuse so the lighting circuit can stay in service.
Ask your senior to confirm the fuse rating before you open the holder.
Replace the fuse with one matching the label, then tell your senior.
Check the listed rating, fit that fuse, and record the repair for review.

advanced.situation: A transport safety control circuit has an intermittent relay fault. You are repairing it and guiding a peer while the unit remains out of service.

options.text: Replace the suspect relay and ask your peer to inspect the connection.
Bridge the relay contacts for a road check, then replace the relay afterward.
Compare the relay terminals with a similar unit before choosing a repair.
Trace the relay wiring against the diagram, repair the defect, and explain your checks.

basic.situation: The drawing marks an outlet box opening on a transport panel. Your senior has shown you the drill and asked you to prepare the opening.

options.text: Confirm the box size and marked position, then drill under your senior's direction.
Drill through the marked spot before checking the panel's reverse side.
Mark the drawing position, then drill the opening with your senior nearby.
Ask your senior to recheck the mark before you set up the drill.

advanced.situation: Several fixtures must be installed in a crowded transport panel. You are choosing drilling locations while the routing behind the panel is not fully clear.

options.text: Map the rear clearances and fixture spacing, then mark a workable drilling layout.
Ask the installation team where they expect the fixtures to sit before marking.
Drill the neatest locations first and adjust the fixture spacing afterward.
Space the fixtures evenly on the face and check each opening as you drill.

basic.situation: A fixture lead has come loose on a transport unit. Your senior asks you to splice and solder the wire while they supervise.

options.text: Strip matching lengths, solder the splice, and show your senior the finished joint.
Solder the joined ends neatly, then return the fixture lead to its place.
Ask your senior to confirm the wire length before you begin stripping it.
Twist the wire ends together and cover the joint with electrical tape.

advanced.situation: New staff are joining fixture wires for transport equipment. You are setting a soldering standard after finding inconsistent splice quality in recent work.

options.text: Demonstrate a sound joint, then watch each new worker solder one practice wire.
Set a sample joint and teach staff to inspect wetting, insulation clearance, and pull strength.
Teach a quick soldering sequence and let each person decide when a joint looks sound.
Give new staff the soldering notes and answer questions during their first shift.

basic.situation: You replaced a transport unit fuse under supervision. The service log asks for the part and work performed, but you are unsure how to phrase the entry.

options.text: Ask your senior how the log names this fuse before making an entry.
Mark the job complete so the unit can return to the service queue.
Enter the fuse type and work performed, then ask your senior to review.
Record that you replaced the fuse and leave the part field for later.

advanced.situation: You are auditing transport equipment service logs and find entries that look duplicated, though some may describe separate repairs to the same unit.

options.text: Compare dates, unit identifiers, and work details, then flag confirmed duplicates for correction.
Sort entries by unit and date, then send the apparent duplicates for review.
Delete the repeated-looking entries and keep the newest record for each unit.
Ask the service team whether repeated entries usually reflect separate repairs.

basic.situation: An operator reports that a packaging machine stops mid-cycle. You have the work order and can speak with them before checking the equipment.

options.text: Ask when the stoppage occurs, then compare the answer with the work order.
Read the work order and ask the operator what changed before the stoppage.
Ask another operator whether the machine has stopped during their shift.
Restart the machine several times to see whether it completes a cycle.

advanced.situation: A production team needs a device to add a new inspection signal to an existing line. You are assessing whether standard equipment can meet the requirement.

options.text: Ask the line engineer to clarify the signal before researching device options.
Recommend a familiar device model so the line team can order it promptly.
Translate the signal needs into functional specifications and compare suitable standard equipment.
Review available devices and describe which ones appear close to the request.

basic.situation: Your scheduled maintenance list calls for cleaning and checking a conveyor sensor before the next shift uses the line.

options.text: Clean the sensor, check its mounting, and record the maintenance findings.
Wipe the sensor face and mark the scheduled task complete.
Ask the operator whether the sensor has caused any recent stops.
Clean the sensor and check whether its indicator responds as expected.

advanced.situation: A line needs an electronic control module changed to meet a revised operating specification. You are assigned to modify the device using the approved design details.

options.text: Map each approved requirement to the circuit changes, then verify the resulting functions.
Change the module settings until the line appears to match the requested output.
Apply the listed circuit changes and run the module through its normal cycle.
Review the design details with an engineer before starting the module changes.

basic.situation: A replacement controller is ready for a production line. You need to study its manual and schematic to determine how it should be installed.

options.text: Read the manual's installation section and prepare the listed tools.
Compare the manual and schematic, then note the installation steps for this controller.
Ask a colleague which installation steps they used on the last controller.
Follow the wiring shown on a similar controller and begin fitting this unit.

advanced.situation: A repaired control unit must be installed at a restricted industrial site with a different mounting layout. You are coordinating the installation with the site team.

options.text: Use the installation drawing and arrange a functional test after mounting the unit.
Adapt the mounting and cable route to the site team's available space.
Ask the site contact to confirm access and mounting arrangements before delivery.
Review site constraints against the drawings, then coordinate setup and functional tests.

basic.situation: A repaired motor control cabinet is ready for return to service. You are checking its components for assembly defects before handover.

options.text: Check each connection and wire condition against the assembly points, then note defects.
Ask the repairer which components they changed before you inspect those areas.
Look at the cabinet exterior and sign off if the cover sits flush.
Inspect visible wiring for loose connections or fraying before handover.

advanced.situation: Different shifts inspect similar control cabinets, but their defect notes vary. You are proposing a shared component inspection standard for the team.

options.text: Define common inspection points, defect examples, and a shared recording format.
Tell each shift to use its usual inspection method and compare results monthly.
List the components to inspect and ask shifts to note anything unusual.
Collect recent defect notes and circulate them as examples for the shifts.

basic.situation: A technician has updated a control schematic after a repair. You are entering the revised drawing into the computer system for storage.

options.text: Save the revised schematic under the unit's identifier and check it opens.
Ask the technician which folder they usually use for revised drawings.
Overwrite the first similar schematic file so the folder stays tidy.
Enter the revision date in the file name and store the updated drawing.

advanced.situation: A production line needs a spare drive, and another unit has been sent for specialist repair. You are managing the parts record and repair tracking.

options.text: Check stock and repair status, update both records, and arrange any needed follow-up.
Order a replacement drive and close the external repair entry as resolved.
Check the spare count and update the inventory record before ordering.
Ask the repair shop for an estimate before changing either record.

basic.situation: Another technician is replacing a sensor while you handle nearby equipment checks. You need to coordinate work so the installation and maintenance do not conflict.

options.text: Agree on the work sequence and share any access constraints with the technician.
Continue your checks and let the technician finish the sensor work independently.
Tell the technician when your checks should be clear of the shared area.
Ask the operator which task should happen first on the line.

advanced.situation: Management asks for advice after operators report repeated slowdowns on a machine. You have collected performance notes and customer feedback from recent shifts.

options.text: Ask operators to gather another week of notes before sending management an update.
Share a clear data pattern and propose a practical improvement for management to review.
Recommend evaluating machine replacement after reviewing the recent operator complaint and performance notes.
Summarize slowdown counts and operator feedback so management can compare recent shift patterns.

basic.situation: A relay circuit fails its routine check. You have a meter and wiring diagram, but one reading is unclear.

options.text: You compare the meter reading with the diagram and note the likely section.
You test each accessible point and ask a technician to confirm an unclear reading.
You isolate the test points, check meter range, then compare readings with the wiring diagram.
You replace the relay because its contacts look worn during a quick inspection.

advanced.situation: After a relay modification, test results show uneven signal quality across several cables. You need to assess whether performance changed.

options.text: You compare each cable's recorded results with its baseline and flag changes by location.
You map individual signal and connectivity results against the baseline and modification points.
You repeat the signal checks on the weakest cables and record the new readings.
You use the overall average to report that cable performance is acceptable.

basic.situation: During supervised maintenance, a breaker compartment is dusty and a brush appears worn. You have been assigned routine cleaning and part replacement.

options.text: You replace the brush based on its appearance and close the compartment for service.
You clean the compartment, then ask the supervisor whether the brush needs replacing.
You clean the compartment and leave the worn brush for the next service round.
You clean the compartment and replace the brush using the approved work steps.

advanced.situation: A relay fault has returned after adjustment, and two junior technicians are available. You are asked to guide the repair approach.

options.text: You demonstrate an adjustment on one relay and let the juniors repeat it.
You let each technician use the repair method they know from past jobs.
You set shared checks for contact condition and adjustment, then review each repair result.
You ask the more experienced junior to handle the relay and share notes afterward.

basic.situation: A breaker trips during a routine check, and the wiring diagram is available. You are unsure which branch to trace first.

options.text: You focus on the branch that seems most likely from the trip pattern.
You trace the diagram from the breaker and compare it with the equipment labels.
You trace the diagram and ask a technician to check your branch choice.
You trace the diagram and mark the branch that appears connected to the trip.

advanced.situation: Test data after a system modification shows slower relay response but fewer interruptions. Operations asks whether the new setup is functioning well.

options.text: You compare response and interruption data with baseline conditions and identify the trade-off.
You repeat the response test and report whether the slower result occurs again.
You highlight the slower response and ask engineering personnel how to interpret it.
You report fewer interruptions as evidence that the modification improved performance.

basic.situation: You finish a routine relay test and repair with guidance. The log needs the result, repair details, and date before the next shift.

options.text: You record the date and test result, then ask a colleague to check the repair entry.
You enter the date and repair performed, using the result shown on your notes.
You write that the relay was repaired and leave the test result for later.
You enter the test result, repair performed, date, and equipment reference in the log.

advanced.situation: A maintenance review finds missing test details in several relay logs. You are asked to help bring records up to the site's documentation standard.

options.text: You return incomplete logs with a list of fields that need attention.
You ask staff to add details wherever they remember what happened.
You address clear omissions and flag unclear entries for supervisor review.
You check each log against the required fields and coach staff using specific examples.

basic.situation: A routine relay inspection requires a planned equipment shutdown. You have the approved timing and a list of affected facility staff.

options.text: You tell nearby staff that some equipment will be unavailable during maintenance.
You post the shutdown time on the noticeboard and assume staff will see it.
You notify affected staff of the shutdown time and equipment before work begins.
You notify the listed staff of the shutdown time and ask them to share it.

advanced.situation: A planned substation shutdown affects several facility teams, and the work window may shift if testing takes longer. You are coordinating staff updates.

options.text: You brief affected teams on scope and timing, then send updates if the window changes.
You tell each team the original shutdown time and let them check back later.
You post the latest expected time in the control room for staff to read.
You share the expected window and ask team contacts to relay timing changes.

basic.situation: You are counting relay spares with guidance before a routine service. The shelf label and part descriptions do not quite match.

options.text: You count the parts and ask a colleague which shelf label to use.
You count each part type, note the label mismatch, and check descriptions against stock.
You use the shelf label as the count category and submit the total.
You count the visible items and list the total under the closest label.

advanced.situation: Relay repairs have used several spares faster than expected, while another part has sat unused. You are preparing the inventory and requisition list.

options.text: You request extra units of the fast-moving parts to prevent another shortage.
You reorder the parts that are currently out of stock first.
You review recent usage and ask the supervisor which parts to requisition.
You match stock with planned work and requisition parts for maintenance.

basic.situation: A customer's car has intermittent audio, and the diagnostic screen shows a stored fault. You are assigned to replace a simple component under supervision.

options.text: You clear the stored fault and tell the technician the audio worked earlier.
You confirm the fault location, replace the component, then record the diagnostic result.
You replace the component named by the stored fault and return the car for testing.
You show the stored fault to the technician and wait for repair direction.

advanced.situation: A hybrid vehicle has an intermittent electronics fault after a component replacement. You are coaching a junior through the diagnostic protocol.

options.text: You walk the junior through the diagnostic steps and review the recorded results together.
You show the junior the test that found a similar fault last week.
You ask the junior to replace the component again and see whether the warning clears.
You guide the junior through the approved sequence and connect each result to the fault symptoms.

basic.situation: A customer reports a window switch that works intermittently. You have a voltmeter and guidance to check the basic circuit.

options.text: You check voltage at the switch and note whether it rises when pressed.
You measure the circuit and ask the technician whether the reading looks normal.
You check the circuit at the specified points and record the readings for review.
You test the switch once and tell the technician it seems faulty.

advanced.situation: A fleet vehicle needs a complex electrical repair, and the customer wants an estimate before approving work. Parts and labor may vary by fault found.

options.text: You separate confirmed parts and labor from possible costs, then explain the estimate assumptions.
You price the parts now and leave labor out until the repair is complete.
You quote the highest likely total so the customer can budget for the repair.
You estimate parts and labor from the likely repair and note that findings may change.

basic.situation: You are installing a basic stereo with step-by-step help. The trim is off, and the harness connectors look different from the guide.

options.text: You check the stereo dimensions against the opening before continuing the install.
You fit the stereo into the opening and see whether the harness reaches.
You ask the supervising installer which connector should match the stereo.
You compare the harness connectors with the installation guide before fitting the stereo.

advanced.situation: A customer wants navigation and communication equipment fitted into a high-end interior with limited space. You are planning the custom layout.

options.text: You check available space for both units and choose the easiest positions to fit.
You map equipment positions against access, cable routes, and interior clearances before fitting.
You sketch the layout and ask the senior installer to review the positions.
You place the navigation unit where the screen looks most balanced.

basic.situation: A speaker fixture needs a new opening in a trim panel. You have a power drill and supervision, but the marked position is near an edge.

options.text: You test the drill on a spare trim piece before working on the panel.
You drill at the marked point and adjust the opening if the fixture sits tight.
You check the fixture position and edge clearance with the supervisor before drilling.
You measure the marked point from the panel edge and ask whether to continue.

advanced.situation: A bespoke speaker enclosure must fit a curved vehicle boot, and an apprentice is helping. The first template leaves little clearance for the trim.

options.text: You ask the apprentice to hold the template while you mark the enclosure blank.
You refine the template against the boot shape and check trim clearance before cutting material.
You cut the enclosure from the first template and sand the edges to fit.
You revise the template for the curve and show the apprentice how to check its fit.

basic.situation: A single speaker wire needs splicing during a routine installation. You have pliers and soldering guidance, and the cable ends are accessible.

options.text: You solder the wire ends together and cover the joint with tape.
You twist the wire ends together and tuck the join behind the trim.
You splice and solder the wires, then ask the installer to inspect the joint.
You strip the ends, make the splice, solder it, and check the connection with guidance.

advanced.situation: A vehicle upgrade needs new speaker and power cables through a crowded interior. You are planning routes for several systems before trim is refitted.

options.text: You route the new cables through the existing trim gaps and secure them as you go.
You sketch separate routes for speaker and power cables and check them with the installer.
You map each cable route around moving parts and existing wiring, then label both ends.
You run the power cable along the shortest route and bundle the other cables beside it.

basic.situation: A customer says the car alarm sometimes activates overnight. You have a checklist and need to understand when the malfunction occurs.

options.text: You record that the alarm activates overnight and book the car for a check.
You ask whether the alarm has been troublesome for a while and note the answer.
You ask when it happens, what warning appeared, and what changed before the fault began.
You follow the checklist on timing and warning signs, then summarize the customer's account.

advanced.situation: A customer describes an intermittent security fault differently from the service notes. You are helping a junior gather details before diagnosis.

options.text: You ask for an example, clarify timing and recent changes, and coach the junior.
You rely on service notes and start intake without confirming the customer's account.
You coach the junior to ask about timing, symptoms, and recent changes.
You ask the customer to repeat symptoms while the junior records key details.

basic.situation: A projector loses one input during setup. You have its circuit diagram and service manual, and your senior is nearby.

options.text: Compare the symbol and connector labels with the manual before naming the likely part.
Check the drawing against the chassis labels and mark the suspected circuit for review.
Trace the diagram labels to the unit, then ask your senior to confirm the part.
Swap the matching board from stores and see whether the fault clears.

advanced.situation: A venue's video wall fails intermittently across several inputs. You are asked to use engineering drawings to guide the team's troubleshooting.

options.text: Replace the board serving the most frequently used source after confirming its connections.
Trace the shared signal path in drawings, then check its common connections first.
Review the service manual and assign checks around the suspected input board.
Have technicians inspect separate inputs and compare their fault notes together.

basic.situation: At a customer's home, a television has no sound after a recent move. Your service call is supervised by a senior technician.

options.text: Ask when the sound stopped, check the connections, and show your senior what you find.
Tell the customer the television likely needs a new speaker and note it for return.
Try another source and cable, then suggest a shop repair if sound stays absent.
Check the volume and mute settings, then ask the customer to test a channel.

advanced.situation: A home theatre fails intermittently during a customer's event. The fault returns after a reset, and your van has limited spare parts.

options.text: Replace the available cable and schedule another visit if the problem comes back.
Record when the fault returns, check the service steps, and recommend a shop return with evidence.
Reset the receiver again and ask the customer to monitor it after you leave.
Check the cable connections and try a known working source before discussing next steps.

basic.situation: A microphone level meter reads low before a small event. Your senior asks you to calibrate it using the bench instrument and hand tools.

options.text: Adjust the trim using the service manual, then note the meter's new reading.
Turn the trim screw until the reading matches the other meter on the bench.
Check the manual's reference setting, adjust the meter, and compare it with the bench instrument.
Ask your senior to check the reference setting before you adjust the trim screw.

advanced.situation: Several technicians report inconsistent readings from the same test meter model. You are asked to set calibration guidance and coach the team.

options.text: Compare the meters with one another and circulate the range they produce.
Review the manual with the team and ask them to repeat their usual checks.
Set a manual-based reference check, record results, and demonstrate the method on each meter.
Share your own meter's settings and let each technician use them as a reference.

basic.situation: You are helping mount two speakers in a meeting room. The console and wiring points are marked, and your senior is supervising the installation.

options.text: Use the marked positions, then compare each speaker's wiring with the console labels before connecting.
Place both speakers evenly at marked positions and connect them to nearby console outputs.
Ask your senior to confirm the marked positions before mounting either speaker in the room.
Confirm the marked positions, secure both speakers, and connect each to its labelled console output.

advanced.situation: A production room needs new speakers, consoles, and signal wiring before rehearsal. You are coordinating the installation from approved drawings.

options.text: Assign speaker and console tasks separately, then review every connection with technicians before rehearsal.
Use approved drawings to map speaker runs and console links before assigning work.
Mount speakers first and route cables along the quickest available paths.
Follow the drawings for speaker placement and ask the team to arrange console links.

basic.situation: A receiver has a loose internal wire and a worn connector. Your senior has approved the repair and asked you to record the work order.

options.text: Replace the connector, record its part number, and send the receiver for testing.
Replace the connector and note that the unit works on its work order.
Resolder the wire, replace its connector, then test the receiver before returning it.
Replace the connector, secure the wire, and log parts and test results.

advanced.situation: Your team has several open repair records with missing test results. You are asked to standardize repair notes and check the maintenance log.

options.text: Use a completed repair note as a guide, updating details for each unit.
Create a template listing parts, faults, and test results for open repairs.
Ask technicians to add missing details they recall before the next shift begins.
Review open records and flag missing test results for technicians to complete before closure.

basic.situation: A customer says a speaker cuts out during video calls but works for music. You are asked to learn more before your manager explains the repair.

options.text: Invite your manager to speak with the customer while you inspect the speaker.
Ask whether it happens on another device, then share that information with your manager.
Ask when the issue occurs, which connection they use, and prior troubleshooting steps.
Suggest a cable replacement based on symptoms and offer to arrange the part.

advanced.situation: A new colleague must explain a complex receiver repair and safe operation to a customer who is worried about recurring faults.

options.text: Model a plain-language fault explanation, link it to safe operation, and have the colleague practise.
Explain the fault to the customer yourself and ask the colleague to observe the discussion.
Give the colleague the service manual and ask them to explain the repair in their own words.
Tell the customer the repair is routine and pass the colleague a short safety leaflet.

basic.situation: A motion sensor triggers repeatedly in a small storeroom. Your senior asks you to adjust its sensitivity using the programming keypad.

options.text: Check the room layout and manual guidance, then adjust sensitivity and test the sensor.
Use the manual's suggested setting, then record whether the sensor triggers again.
Ask your senior which keypad setting to change before entering it.
Lower the sensitivity several steps and see whether the alerts stop.

advanced.situation: Sensors in a client’s glass-fronted lobby trigger inconsistently. You are asked to guide two juniors on sensitivity settings for the room structure.

options.text: Have each junior try a different sensitivity level and keep the one with fewer alerts.
Set a level from the manual and ask the juniors to watch for further alerts.
Compare room features with manufacturer guidance, set a test approach, and coach the juniors through keypad adjustments.
Review the guidance with the juniors and let them choose a setting for the lobby.

basic.situation: A new contact needs a cable through a partition wall. The work order marks the outlet, and your senior is supervising the drilling.

options.text: Ask your senior to mark the hole and confirm the route before drilling.
Drill beside the outlet and push cable through the nearest open space.
Check the marked route, drill the approved hole, and feed cable toward the outlet.
Use the work order to mark the hole, then ask where cable should run.

advanced.situation: A cable must cross a roof space and reach several alarm fixtures. The route passes near existing services, and the installation team needs a safe sequence.

options.text: Ask a senior to choose the route, then prepare the cables for the team.
Mark outlet locations first and let each installer choose a path to them.
Feed cables through the shortest cavity path and secure them after reaching the fixtures.
Trace a route around existing services, plan access points, and sequence cable feeds to each outlet.

basic.situation: A shop owner asks why the entrance alarm triggered during closing. You are demonstrating the system with your supervisor present.

options.text: Ask what happened at closing, explain likely triggers, and demonstrate arming the system safely.
Tell the owner the sensor may be faulty and offer to arrange a check.
Ask your supervisor to explain the alarm while you demonstrate the keypad.
Show the owner how to arm the system and explain how doors can trigger alerts.

advanced.situation: A clinic manager wants stronger security for a room holding valuable stock. You are gathering requirements and coaching a junior on the client discussion.

options.text: Review sensor coverage with the manager, then show the junior how to explain each area.
Ask the manager about access patterns and share key details with your junior.
Ask about access, hours, and concerns, then coach the junior to match needs with features.
Promise the room will be fully protected so the manager feels reassured.

basic.situation: A work order calls for a replacement door contact. You have the site notes, a parts list, and instructions from your supervisor.

options.text: Order the listed part and record its expected delivery date for the team.
Ask your supervisor which supplier to use before placing the order.
Order the nearest matching contact from the supplier catalogue to save time.
Check the work order and site notes before selecting the listed contact.

advanced.situation: A planned alarm installation needs several sensor types, and a supplier has announced a newer model. You are updating the materials plan for the team.

options.text: Share the product notice with the team and retain the current parts list pending review.
Check the new model's specifications and send the team a summary of its features.
Replace the listed sensors with the newer model so the team uses current equipment.
Compare the new model with site needs, then update the team parts plan.

basic.situation: A door contact and control panel are ready for a small office installation. Your senior has marked their positions and is guiding the work.

options.text: Ask your senior to position each part while you prepare the mounting tools.
Mount both parts at the marked positions and check the wiring labels afterward.
Mount the panel near the power point and connect whichever wires reach comfortably first.
Follow the marked layout, mount the contact and panel, connect labelled wiring.

advanced.situation: A multi-room office needs panels, contacts, cameras, and sensors installed from electrical layout drawings. You are coordinating the installation team.

options.text: Match devices and wiring to drawings, sequence room tasks, and check connections.
Follow drawings for device placement and inspect wiring after each room is finished.
Assign devices by room and ask the team to report any installation conflicts early.
Install cameras in visible areas first, then fit remaining devices where space allows.

basic.situation: A monthly check shows a backup battery test failed, though the keypad and siren appear normal. Your senior is available to supervise further checks.

options.text: Check battery connections and test results against the checklist, then report the fault.
Repeat the battery test and note whether the same warning appears again.
Ask your senior to retest the battery while you record the keypad status.
Reset the keypad and mark the battery check as passed if the siren sounds.

advanced.situation: A site reports brief alarm failures that disappear before technicians arrive. You are asked to shape a diagnostic checklist and coach junior installers.

options.text: Ask juniors to inspect wiring first and note any loose connections they find.
List common fault symptoms and share diagnostic notes with the junior team before practice today.
Have juniors reset the panel whenever alarms clear and record whether the fault returns.
Create a checklist for fault timing, wiring, battery, keypad, and siren, then coach juniors.

basic.situation: During a routine walkaround, you see a worn patch on an airframe panel that is not mentioned in the work notes.

options.text: Clean the area and continue the walkaround, expecting the next check to clarify it.
Ask a senior technician to look, then note the finding in your sheet.
Mark the worn spot, compare nearby surfaces, and record its location for review.
Touch up the worn patch with matching coating before returning the aircraft.

advanced.situation: You are assigned to inspect completed maintenance before release, but one step in the work record has no result entered.

options.text: Ask the technician to complete the record, then sign after a quick visual check.
Sign the release based on the technician's verbal summary and the completed checklist.
Review the work record and inspect the completed item before signing its release.
Verify the step against approved data, inspect the work, and resolve the gap before signing.

basic.situation: A service check finds a worn replaceable component, and you have the specified replacement, hand tools, and gauges ready.

options.text: Use the closest matching component from the parts tray to keep the job moving.
Fit the replacement, then check its seating and gauge reading against the work card.
Install the new component and ask a colleague to confirm the gauge reading.
Replace the part and compare its gauge reading with the last recorded value.

advanced.situation: A hydraulic unit has recurring leakage after a component replacement, and you are assigned to rebuild it using the approved repair data.

options.text: Ask a colleague to inspect the unit after you replace the seal and run it.
Rebuild the unit to the repair data, checking each fitted part and test result.
Fit a seal from available stock and monitor the unit during the next service.
Strip the unit, replace the visibly damaged seal, and reassemble it for a run.

basic.situation: A replacement panel is ready, and your work card calls for marking its reference lines with a template before fitting.

options.text: Mark the lines from the template, then ask a colleague to check them.
Mark the lines by eye so the panel can reach the fitting bench sooner.
Align the template to the panel datum, mark the lines, and check measurements.
Trace the old panel's visible marks onto the replacement before fitting it.

advanced.situation: A damaged section needs a custom replacement, and its final alignment must match the drawing before the assembly is riveted.

options.text: Shape a close-fitting section from the damaged piece, then adjust it during riveting.
Make the section to the drawing and ask the lead to check alignment.
Fabricate to the drawing, clamp the section in alignment, and recheck reference points.
Fabricate a section to the drawing, then compare its edges with the opening.

basic.situation: The work area needs supplies for an engine removal, and you are assigned to check stock and prepare the parts request.

options.text: Check the shelf, then ask the stores team to send the usual engine kit.
Take supplies from the nearest open job trolley to avoid delaying the removal.
Request the listed supplies and let the stores team resolve any stock differences.
Count the required supplies against stock and request the missing items by part description.

advanced.situation: During an engine installation, a heavy part starts to sit off line as the hoist takes its weight and the fitting team waits.

options.text: Pause the lift, communicate the misalignment, and coordinate a controlled reposition with the team.
Tell the team about the offset and let the hoist operator decide the next move.
Lower the engine onto its mounts and adjust the position with the fitting team.
Ask the fitter to guide the part while you watch the hoist clearance.

basic.situation: A maintenance request describes a small skin repair, and you need to check whether the manual gives a feasible repair method.

options.text: Use the method from the last skin repair since this damage looks similar.
Search the manual for a similar repair and tell the lead what it describes.
Find the matching manual section and compare its limits with the described damage.
Read the repair heading and estimate whether the work seems manageable.

advanced.situation: An engineering order changes a structural detail, and you are assigned to modify the part using its drawing and written instructions.

options.text: Use the previous modification as a guide and adapt its dimensions to this part.
Compare the drawing revision with the order, then mark the modification references on the part.
Mark the part from the drawing and ask the lead to verify the change.
Read the order and mark the key dimensions from its attached drawing.

basic.situation: After control cable work, you are asked to measure the cable tension with the available instrument and record the result.

options.text: Use the same setting as the last cable and enter the reading in the log.
Measure the cable near the fitting and note the displayed value for review.
Take a reading and ask a colleague whether it looks reasonable before recording.
Measure at the specified point, check the instrument range, and record the reading.

advanced.situation: An engine run shows an unstable system reading, and you are assigned to test its operation before maintenance release.

options.text: Complete the run and enter the final steady reading as the system result.
Record the unstable reading and ask the lead whether another run is needed.
Repeat the test under the specified conditions, compare readings with limits, and document the result.
Check the test equipment setup and note whether the reading settles on another run.

basic.situation: A small dimple remains on a steel body panel, and you have pick hammers and punches available at the repair bay.

options.text: Support the panel with a dolly and work the dimple with controlled hammer taps.
Fill the dimple and move on to the next body area in the estimate.
Strike the panel firmly with a punch to flatten the dimple in one pass.
Use the pick hammer on the dimple, then ask a colleague to inspect the surface.

advanced.situation: A deep dented door panel hides damage behind its outer skin, and you are assigned to remove the panel and identify its plastic trim.

options.text: Remove the panel carefully and ask a senior repairer to identify its plastic family.
Heat the trim to soften it, then pull the panel clear of the damage.
Check the panel edges and remove it with a trim tool for inspection.
Check the trim markings, remove the panel in sequence, and protect clips for refitting.

basic.situation: A replacement bracket is ready for fitting, and the repair card calls for welding it into place on the vehicle body.

options.text: Fit the bracket, check its position, then weld and smooth the joint.
Weld the bracket in place and ask a colleague to check the joint afterward.
Fit and weld the bracket, then grind the joint smooth for finishing.
Tack the bracket quickly and cover the rough joint with filler for painting.

advanced.situation: A collision repair requires cutting out a damaged body section and installing a replacement that must meet the surrounding panel edges.

options.text: Follow the repair plan to cut out the section and install its replacement.
Mark the planned cut, remove the section, and check replacement fit before joining.
Cut out the damage and position the replacement for a colleague to check.
Cut along the visible damage and weld the replacement into the opening.

basic.situation: A shallow dent remains after the panel has been worked, and the repair plan calls for filling before surface preparation.

options.text: Clean the dent, apply filler in controlled layers, and shape it after curing.
Spread a thick layer across the dent to reduce the number of sanding passes.
Fill the dent and sand it level once the material has set.
Apply filler to the dent and ask a colleague to check its shape later.

advanced.situation: A repaired body area is ready for paint preparation, with nearby windows, bumpers, and trim that must stay clear of overspray.

options.text: Sand the body area and cover the nearest trim with masking paper.
Sand the repair and leave the bumpers exposed for the painter to cover.
Sand the repair evenly, clean the dust, and mask nearby trim and glass.
Mask the trim and windows, then ask the painter to check the surface.

basic.situation: A small damaged area needs a fiberglass repair, and you are assigned to mix polyester resin and hardener for the matting.

options.text: Measure both materials to the repair instructions and mix a fresh batch.
Mix the resin and hardener, then ask the repairer to check its consistency.
Add extra hardener so the mixture sets sooner during the busy shift.
Combine the materials in the usual proportion and prepare the matting.

advanced.situation: A plastic panel has a shallow crease, and the repair plan calls for warming and pressing it back into shape.

options.text: Use the hot-air gun and ask a colleague to judge when the panel is soft.
Warm the panel evenly, test its flexibility, and press it gradually against its contour.
Warm the panel with hot air and press the crease back by hand.
Heat one spot until pliable, then press firmly to flatten the crease.

basic.situation: A damaged frame section is secured on the alignment machine, and you are assigned to chain it before hydraulic correction.

options.text: Position the chains at the marked points, secure them, and check their tension.
Secure the chains at the marked points before the hydraulic pull begins.
Chain the frame to the machine and ask the lead to check the setup.
Attach the chains to the closest solid points so the machine can start sooner.
