advanced.situation: A commercial cooling system passes startup, but its readings differ from the approved plans. The building manager expects you to sign off today.

options.text: Repeat the measurements and share the results with the building manager.
Ask the manager whether the observed readings are acceptable for the building.
Compare the readings with plans, check the setup, and report unresolved deviations.
Record the startup readings and sign off based on normal operation.

basic.situation: During a routine repair, you find a small leak at a soldered joint. The unit is shut down and the joint is accessible.

options.text: Prepare the joint, resolder it, and check for leaks after cooling.
Tighten the nearby fitting and see whether the leak becomes smaller.
Resolder the joint and record the repair on the work order.
Add solder over the damp joint and restart the unit to check.

advanced.situation: You are aligning a heavy condenser with two assistants when the hoist shifts slightly. The unit is close to its mounting points.

options.text: Lower the condenser slightly and reposition the assistants before lifting again.
Keep lifting while the assistants guide the condenser into place.
Ask one assistant to watch the hoist while you continue the lift.
Pause the lift, secure the load, and realign the hoist before continuing.

basic.situation: You need to route a condensate drain through a wall for an indoor unit. The marked area is clear, and your drill is ready.

options.text: Move the hole slightly if the drill meets unexpected resistance.
Confirm the route with the site contact before drilling the wall.
Drill through the marked spot and fit the drain pipe afterward.
Check both sides of the wall, then drill at the marked route.

advanced.situation: Several units need control adjustments after a tenant fit-out. The supplier's delivery is delayed, and the current stock list may be out of date.

options.text: Check unit needs and stock, then order quantities that cover planned adjustments.
Ask the supplier which materials are available before preparing an order.
Order the quantities from last month's maintenance list to save time.
Estimate the materials from the new unit count and send a purchase request.

basic.situation: You replace a failed thermostat during a service call. The work order asks for time, materials, and the fault found.

options.text: Record the time and replacement thermostat on the work order.
Record the time, thermostat used, and fault found on the work order.
Enter the visit time and close the work order after the replacement.
Note the thermostat fault and tell the office what part was used.

advanced.situation: A compressor has failed, and the repair requires an overhaul and refrigerant recovery. The replacement unit is due later today.

options.text: Start dismantling the compressor while a colleague prepares recovery equipment.
Follow recovery procedures, then overhaul the compressor and document the work.
Recover the refrigerant into an open container while preparing the overhaul.
Arrange the recovery equipment and begin the overhaul when the unit is ready.

basic.situation: A shop manager says the air conditioning stopped cooling after lunch. You are at the unit and can ask about what they noticed.

options.text: Reset the thermostat and see whether the shop feels cooler afterward.
Ask what changed and when the cooling stopped before inspecting the unit.
Ask when cooling changed and what the controls showed, then check the unit.
Tell the manager the unit may need a new filter and schedule maintenance.

advanced.situation: Two assistants are cleaning rooftop units before a busy week. One is unsure how to isolate power, while the other is ready to start washing.

options.text: Demonstrate isolation to both assistants, then have them clean in pairs.
Ask the unsure assistant to read the procedure while the other prepares tools.
Pause the cleaning, explain power isolation, and check each assistant's understanding.
Let the experienced assistant start washing while the other watches.

basic.situation: A washer trips its breaker after a customer reports an intermittent fault. You have the circuit diagram and a circuit tester.

options.text: I would ask a senior technician to point out the likely short before testing.
I would test each wire against the diagram, then isolate the suspect branch.
I would test the circuit section by section and record where continuity changes.
I would replace the fuse and see whether the appliance runs through its cycle.

advanced.situation: A stove has a weak flame and an electrical fault after servicing. The customer smells gas, and you are asked to check pressure and wiring.

options.text: I would secure the area and trace the leak, pressure, and electrical faults separately.
I would check the appliance pressure, then report the reading for review.
I would adjust the pilot and test the stove again to compare its flame.
I would isolate the supply, check for leaks, and test the electrical fault separately.

basic.situation: You install a refrigerator in a customer's kitchen. Its door swings shut unevenly, and the dispenser water line still needs connecting.

options.text: I would tilt the refrigerator slightly and tell the customer to watch the door.
I would level the refrigerator, adjust its doors, and connect the water line.
I would connect the water line and leave the door adjustment for another visit.
I would adjust the feet until the door sits evenly, then connect the line.

advanced.situation: A customer reports a gas smell beside a newly installed stove. Other appliances are in use nearby, and you are the first repairer to arrive.

options.text: I would warn occupants, avoid ignition sources, and isolate supply if safe.
I would turn off the stove and call the office for instructions.
I would stop stove use, ventilate, and follow the site's gas response procedure.
I would test the stove ignition and see whether the smell clears.

basic.situation: A work order says a dryer stops mid-cycle, but gives no other details. You are at the customer's home and need to establish the malfunction.

options.text: I would ask what happens before it stops and compare that with the work order.
I would tell the customer that dryers often stop when their cycles finish.
I would ask when it stops, then note the customer's answer on the work order.
I would start a cycle and watch for the point where the dryer stops.

advanced.situation: A washer shows no familiar error code, yet vibrates only during one spin setting. The manual has two possible causes, and a teammate asks what to check.

options.text: I would inspect suspension during that spin setting and share my observations.
I would compare the schematic with the spin cycle, then test circuit and mechanical causes.
I would replace suspension parts named in the manual, then retest the washer.
I would ask my teammate to repeat the cycle while I listen for vibration.

basic.situation: A customer's washer leaks near its pump. You need to open the cabinet to inspect the pump before deciding whether a part needs replacement.

options.text: I would pry the cabinet clips loose quickly and set the panel aside.
I would check the manual, then remove whichever panel seems easiest.
I would remove the front panel first and place its fasteners nearby.
I would open the cabinet in sequence and keep fasteners grouped for reassembly.

advanced.situation: A washer's transmission has failed, and a replacement circuit board is available. A junior colleague is watching while you prepare the repair.

options.text: I would fit the board, then assess whether the failed transmission still needs replacement.
I would ask the junior to remove the transmission while I inspect the board.
I would explain transmission removal while following the service guide and checking each step.
I would replace the transmission following service steps and explain key checks to my junior.

basic.situation: You have replaced a dryer belt and cleaned lint from the cabinet. The panels and drum are ready to be reassembled before testing.

options.text: I would clean the cabinet and reinstall the panels in their original order.
I would close the cabinet quickly and skip turning the drum by hand.
I would put the panels back and let the customer clean the cabinet later.
I would reinstall the parts, check the drum turns freely, and clean the cabinet.

advanced.situation: Several repaired dryers return with squeaks after reassembly. You are asked to finish today's repair and suggest a practical cleaning and lubrication routine.

options.text: I would follow service guidance for affected parts and record any remaining squeaks.
I would clean and lubricate specified moving parts, then share the routine with colleagues.
I would clean accessible parts and apply lubricant sparingly near the noisy area.
I would heavily lubricate every moving part to keep the squeaks away longer.

basic.situation: You finish a washer repair and need to bill the customer. The work order lists a part and labour, but the customer asks what the total covers.

options.text: I would explain each listed charge, confirm the total, and collect payment.
I would state the total and ask whether the customer can pay by card.
I would collect the amount shown and offer to explain the bill afterward.
I would lower the labour charge to settle the customer's question quickly.

advanced.situation: A customer disputes a repair bill because the replaced part differs from the estimate. You have the work record and are asked to help resolve the complaint.

options.text: I would compare the part and labour entries with the estimate before discussing payment.
I would repeat the final total and ask the customer to pay the undisputed amount.
I would explain the difference using the work record and check the estimate with the office.
I would offer a small discount so the customer can close the bill today.

basic.situation: A conveyor stops after an operator reports a flickering indicator. You have a voltmeter and can test its basic electrical connections under supervision.

options.text: I would reset the conveyor and see whether the indicator stays steady.
I would test the indicated connection and compare its reading with the manual.
I would bridge the connection to keep production moving during the shift.
I would test the connection and note whether the voltmeter reading changes.

advanced.situation: A packaging line stops intermittently, and the error log shows several codes after each restart. Operators report that the fault appears during heavier runs.

options.text: I would restart the line and note which fault code returns.
I would review code sequences and ask operators when stops occurred.
I would compare codes with operator reports and test data to trace patterns.
I would inspect the component named in the latest error message.

basic.situation: A guard latch on a packing machine is cracked. The replacement part and a step-by-step guide are available before the next scheduled run.

options.text: I would secure the cracked latch with tape until the next service window.
I would swap the latch and ask the operator to check it during production.
I would replace the latch using the guide and set the old part aside.
I would follow the guide to replace the latch, then check its fit.

advanced.situation: A repaired pump still vibrates during a test run. Its coupling was replaced, but the vibration begins only after the pump warms up.

options.text: I would lower the pump speed and observe whether vibration changes.
I would run a normal cycle and compare vibration readings with repair records.
I would operate the pump briefly and listen for changes in vibration.
I would retest at normal speed and record whether the pump still vibrates.

basic.situation: During an inspection, you find a bent metal bracket that needs replacing. The drawing gives its dimensions, and standard cutting tools are available.

options.text: I would mark the drawing dimensions and cut the replacement bracket carefully.
I would mark the dimensions clearly, cut the bracket, and check its fit.
I would copy the bent bracket's outline and cut a replacement to match.
I would cut a larger bracket and force it into the mounting points.

advanced.situation: A production line needs a replacement guard frame that is no longer in stores. You have the drawing, suitable stock, and access to the workshop tools.

options.text: I would tack the stock together quickly and ask production to test the frame.
I would use the drawing to cut and weld the new frame to size.
I would copy the old frame dimensions and weld the stock into a replacement.
I would cut stock to the drawing, weld the frame, and check its fit before reassembly.

basic.situation: A packing machine is due for routine upkeep before the afternoon shift. Your checklist calls for cleaning and lubricating its accessible moving parts.

options.text: I would add lubricant to the moving parts and leave the cleaning for later.
I would clean and lubricate the accessible parts, then tell the next shift.
I would pour lubricant over the assembly so every part gets some.
I would clean the listed parts, apply the specified lubricant, and mark the checklist.

advanced.situation: Two shifts report repeat stoppages after routine cleaning on one machine type. You are asked to suggest a consistent maintenance approach for the crew.

options.text: I would shorten the cleaning time so the crew can finish every machine sooner.
I would compare stoppage reports with the maintenance steps and propose a revised checklist.
I would remind the crew to clean the machines carefully at each shift change.
I would standardize the existing cleaning sequence and ask the crew to follow it.

basic.situation: A new operator asks how to start a mixer after a routine repair. The machine manual is available at the work station.

options.text: I would point out the manual and ask the operator to find the startup section.
I would find the startup section and walk the operator through its listed steps.
I would show the operator the startup section and summarize its main steps.
I would tell the operator to use the same startup sequence as the older mixer.

advanced.situation: A replacement conveyor motor has a different mounting layout from the old unit. The blueprint and manufacturer manual are available, and an operator needs a handover.

options.text: I would use the manual's mounting steps and show the operator the controls.
I would compare the blueprint and manual, then explain the installation points during handover.
I would study the blueprint and tell the operator where the motor sits.
I would align the motor with the old bolt marks and demonstrate a restart.

basic.situation: You replace a worn belt on a production machine. The maintenance log is open, and the store needs a record of the part used.

options.text: I would log the repair and belt details before closing the job.
I would take the spare belt from stores and update the log next week.
I would write down the belt type, machine number, repair date, and store issue details.
I would note that the machine was repaired and leave the part entry blank.

advanced.situation: A repair is complete, but the parts shelf count differs from the log after several urgent jobs. You need to update the records and request needed stock.

options.text: I would request a replacement stock order using the count in the maintenance log.
I would adjust the stock count to match the shelf and submit a reorder.
I would reconcile job records with shelf counts, log parts used, and request confirmed shortages.
I would record parts used and ask stores to verify the shelf count before requesting stock.

basic.situation: You start the conveyor after the morning check and hear a new rhythmic knock while its belt runs under a light load.

options.text: You reduce the load and check whether the knock becomes less noticeable.
You keep it running through the shift and mention the sound during handover.
You stop the test, note when the knock occurs, and report the sound for inspection.
You listen near the guard and ask a colleague whether the sound is familiar.

advanced.situation: A repaired pump runs, but pressure pulses and the coupling warms during your check; production is waiting for your maintenance findings.

options.text: You repeat the run at low pressure and compare the readings with the work order.
You record the readings and heat, then suggest checking the coupling and pump internals before release.
You log the pressure pulses and coupling temperature for the supervisor to assess.
You mark the coupling for replacement and tell production the pump can return to service.

basic.situation: You are assigned to clean a gearbox cover with solvent and cloths, but old grease remains around the edges.

options.text: You use an air gun to blow remaining grease away from the cover.
You apply approved solvent and let grease soften before wiping the edges again.
You scrape the edges with a nearby screwdriver to finish before the next job.
You follow solvent instructions, wipe the edges, and discard cloths in the designated waste bin.

advanced.situation: A press slide has hardened residue near a fitted surface, and the usual cloth cleaning has not cleared it before reassembly.

options.text: You select a fine abrasive for the residue and keep it away from the fitted surface.
You try a hand scraper around the edge and leave the deeper buildup for later.
You use a coarse disc across the whole slide to remove the residue quickly.
You identify the fitted surface, choose a suitable abrasive, and test a small area before cleaning further.

basic.situation: A worn filter box is due for change during a routine service, and the replacement is beside the machine.

options.text: You confirm the box type from work instructions, fit it, and check its seating.
You compare the old and new boxes, then install the one with matching connections.
You ask the experienced fitter to confirm the replacement before you install it safely.
You fit a similar-sized box from stores and restart the machine for the next batch.

advanced.situation: You are reinstalling a guard attachment after repair; the work order lists a revised bracket, but the machine drawing shows the earlier version.

options.text: You compare both brackets and ask the supervisor which revision production expects before proceeding.
You verify the bracket revision with the work order owner, then fit it.
You attach the revised bracket loosely and check whether the guard aligns with its mounts.
You use the earlier bracket because it matches the drawing and aligns with bolt holes.

basic.situation: A motor housing needs moving to the repair bench, and a dolly is available in the aisle.

options.text: You move the housing slowly and ask someone to watch the front wheels.
You ask a nearby worker to help push the housing to the repair bench.
You push the housing on the dolly alone to clear the aisle before other workers arrive.
You secure the housing and guide the dolly with a colleague along a clear path.

advanced.situation: A large mixer must be dismantled with a hoist; its control response becomes uneven while the suspended frame begins to turn.

options.text: You raise the frame higher to clear the supports before its turn becomes harder to control.
You stop hoisting and ask the crane operator to inspect the uneven control response.
You halt hoisting, steady the frame, and request a control check before continuing dismantling.
You guide the frame by hand while the operator lowers it toward the supports.

basic.situation: Your checklist calls for greasing two bearing points, and one grease nipple looks partly blocked during the routine service.

options.text: You clean around the nipple, try the grease gun again, and record the result.
You force grease through the blocked nipple and mark both bearing points as serviced on checklist.
You grease the clear point, note the blocked nipple, and record service status for follow-up.
You lubricate the clear point and leave the checklist open for the next shift.

advanced.situation: During an overhaul, you replace a torn liner in a parts chute, but the maintenance log has conflicting entries for the material used.

options.text: You copy the material entry into the log and close the record after checking its source.
You record the liner replacement and flag the material discrepancy for supervisor review.
You verify liner material from the job record, update the log, and note repair details.
You leave the material field blank and finish the repair entry for now.

basic.situation: A colleague asks you to help move a pump casing from the service bay to a nearby work area during repairs.

options.text: You lift your end as soon as your colleague starts moving the casing.
You agree on route and lifting cues, then move the casing with your colleague.
You ask your colleague where to grip, then help move the casing at their pace.
You fetch a trolley and help guide the casing across the service bay.

advanced.situation: A repair team needs two replacement bearings before the next service window, and the storeroom count differs from the parts register.

options.text: You check the shelves and tell the supervisor the register may be out of date.
You request two bearings from the register count so the service window stays covered.
You reserve the bearings shown in the register and tell the team to plan around them.
You recount stock, check issued parts, and update the register before requesting replenishment.

basic.situation: You are assigned to dismantle a small gearbox with hand tools, and one cover bolt resists turning during the routine strip-down.

options.text: You check the tool fit, support the cover, and work the bolt loose with controlled pressure.
You tap the wrench handle with a hammer and continue removing the cover.
You extend the wrench with a pipe to break the bolt free before lunch.
You apply penetrating oil and ask the fitter to check the bolt if it stays stuck.

advanced.situation: Your team is dismantling a large drive for shipment, and a lifting point looks worn while the planned maintenance task is still outstanding.

options.text: You use the worn point briefly, then finish maintenance after loading the drive.
You pause the lift, replace the worn point, then schedule maintenance before shipment resumes.
You move smaller parts first and defer the main drive to next shift.
You report the worn point to the lead and hold dismantling until inspection.

basic.situation: You connect a power unit to a pump for a guided test, but the pump turns more slowly than the work instructions suggest.

options.text: You note the slow speed and ask the fitter whether the connection looks right.
You increase the power setting until the pump reaches its usual speed.
You run the pump again and compare its speed with another unit nearby.
You stop the test, check the connection against the instructions, and report the speed difference.

advanced.situation: A hydraulic press moves unevenly after a repair, and your checks show a pressure drop alongside an intermittent electrical signal.

options.text: You repeat the press cycle at reduced speed and watch for another pressure drop.
You record both symptoms and ask the electrical technician to inspect the signal first.
You isolate the fault area, document pressure and signal readings, and define separate hydraulic and electrical checks.
You replace the pressure sensor and clear the fault for the next production run.

basic.situation: You are attaching a moving subassembly to a basic unit with hand tools, and the fasteners are mixed in an open tray.

options.text: You identify the specified fasteners, attach the subassembly, and check its movement with the fitter.
You attach the part with matching threads and leave the movement check for later.
You use the nearest bolts that fit and tighten the subassembly before the fitter returns.
You sort the bolts by size and ask the fitter which set belongs on the unit.

advanced.situation: A large assembly is nearly fastened to its foundation, but two bolts do not align with the specified holes on the drawing.

options.text: You widen the two holes slightly so the remaining bolts can be installed on schedule.
You pause fastening, compare the assembly with the drawing, and realign it before tightening.
You hold those bolts and ask the lead to review the drawing and alignment.
You tighten the aligned bolts and leave the remaining two for the next crew.

basic.situation: You help position a steel beam under a bedplate, and the level shows one side sitting slightly high.

options.text: You tell the fitter which side reads high and wait for their adjustment.
You tap the high side down while your colleague watches the level and signals closely.
You check the level again, steady the beam, and adjust support with fitter guidance.
You place a loose steel offcut beneath the low side to level the beam.

advanced.situation: A machine line must meet a tight centerline tolerance, but laser readings drift after a nearby hoist moves the frame.

options.text: You secure the nearby hold-down bolts evenly, then take another laser reading.
You stabilize the frame, repeat laser readings, and record reference points before alignment.
You average drifting readings and set the machine using that estimated centerline.
You record the drift and ask the lead to review readings before choosing a reference.

basic.situation: You are helping build a simple machine foundation, and the timber base shifts when you place the steel support.

options.text: You hold the shifting timber with your foot while placing the steel support.
You ask the fitter to stabilize the base while you position the steel support.
You add a timber support beneath the base to limit movement during placement.
You steady the base, verify its layout position, and secure it before setting support.

advanced.situation: A custom guard bracket is cracked near a weld, and the machine is due back in service after your repair shift.

options.text: You inspect the crack, measure fit, and confirm repair dimensions and method against job requirements.
You measure the bracket and ask the lead whether repair or replacement suits the job.
You make a matching bracket from spare steel and compare it with the original.
You weld over the crack, then grind the bracket until it clears the machine.

basic.situation: You are moving a gearbox with a dolly and notice fresh grease around one bearing during the routine maintenance check.

options.text: You lubricate the bearing, then move the gearbox carefully with the dolly.
You ask a colleague to guide the dolly and report the grease during handover.
You secure the gearbox, guide its dolly, and report the bearing leak.
You wipe away the grease and continue moving the gearbox to the next area.

advanced.situation: You are preparing a preventive maintenance plan for several machines, while one unit has recurring alignment adjustments and frequent production use.

options.text: You review service history and production demands, then plan checks for recurring alignment changes.
You ask the team to report any new alignment changes during routine machine checks.
You schedule added alignment checks for the busy unit and review its service history.
You assign every machine one monthly check date to simplify routine scheduling.

basic.situation: You are preparing refractory mortar for a routine ladle repair. The work sheet lists the amounts of sand, clay, mortar powder, and water.

options.text: I would compare the sand and clay amounts with yesterday's successful batch.
I would measure each ingredient to the work sheet before starting the mixer.
I would use the nearest shovel measure and start mixing the batch.
I would add water gradually, then check whether the mortar holds together.

advanced.situation: A cupola repair needs a mortar mix for higher operating temperatures than your usual work. The approved job sheet gives a specialized ratio.

options.text: I would weigh the ingredients to the approved ratio and record the batch.
I would adjust the water until the specialized mortar feels workable.
I would add extra powder to help the mix withstand the heat.
I would make a small trial batch using the listed specialized ratio.

basic.situation: A ladle has cooled and is ready for maintenance. You are assigned to chip slag from its lining with a hammer and chisel.

options.text: I would use firm hammer blows to clear the slag in fewer passes.
I would use a heavy hammer to break the slag away quickly.
I would tap the loose slag with a chisel and check the lining between passes.
I would remove the visible slag and ask the crew to inspect afterward.

advanced.situation: During a ladle inspection, several areas are cracked and one section sounds loose. You must decide whether the lining can be repaired or needs full removal.

options.text: I would patch major cracks and schedule a follow-up inspection after the repair.
I would assess the loose section and compare its condition with removal criteria.
I would map cracks and loose areas, then assess the lining against removal criteria.
I would mark each damaged area and compare findings with the repair criteria.

basic.situation: You are filling a routine mold with refractory clay. The work sheet gives the clay amount, and a coworker is ready to help with tamping.

options.text: I would fill the mold to the marked level and tamp each area evenly.
I would pour in the clay until the mold looks full and move it along.
I would fill the mold and let my coworker handle the tamping.
I would dump the clay into the center and spread it with the tamper.

advanced.situation: A mold has a narrow bend and a thick section that must hold its shape. You are responsible for tamping the clay to a consistent density throughout.

options.text: I would fill the bend first, then tamp the mold with even overlapping passes.
I would pack the bend, then fill and tamp the thicker section evenly.
I would tamp in measured layers and check density across both mold sections.
I would tamp measured layers, checking density through the bend and thick section.

basic.situation: You are carrying a spray hose up scaffolding for a cupola repair. A coworker is guiding you and the equipment is ready below.

options.text: I would pause at each level and ask my coworker to reposition the hose safely.
I would carry the hose over my shoulder and keep climbing steadily.
I would control the hose and follow my coworker's guidance while climbing.
I would pull the hose behind me to reach the work platform sooner.

advanced.situation: You are spraying a large cupola area with refractory mixture. Coverage looks uneven near a seam, and the crew wants the repair finished before the next shift.

options.text: I would hold a steady spray and overlap each pass carefully across the seam.
I would increase flow to finish the remaining area before the next shift begins.
I would adjust the nozzle angle and check coverage along the seam after each pass.
I would test the spray setup, then work in sections with even overlap.

basic.situation: You are coating a stopper head and rod with mortar before sliding a brick sleeve over the rod to form a refractory jacket.

options.text: I would spread an even mortar layer, then slide the sleeve into position.
I would cover the head first and add mortar to the rod afterward.
I would apply mortar to the head and push the sleeve over the rod.
I would coat the head and rod, then check the sleeve fit as it slides on.

advanced.situation: A stopper rod has an unusual profile, and the standard brick sleeve leaves a gap. You need to prepare a custom refractory jacket for the assembly.

options.text: I would measure the rod and modify a standard jacket to match its full outline.
I would measure the rod profile and fit a jacket to its clearances.
I would use the standard sleeve and build up the gap with extra mortar.
I would adapt the nearest standard sleeve and check whether it slides on.

basic.situation: A new lining is ready to dry over a burner. A senior worker is helping you place it inverted above the burner.

options.text: I would place the lining as directed and ask my senior to check its position.
I would center the lining by eye while my senior holds the other side.
I would position the lining over the burner and check that it sits steadily.
I would start the burner while we finish settling the lining into place.

advanced.situation: A complex new lining is curing, and readings near its thick section are rising faster than elsewhere. The work schedule specifies a gradual heating curve.

options.text: I would compare section readings with the heating curve and adjust the rate gradually.
I would raise the burner setting to bring slower areas up to temperature steadily.
I would record readings at checkpoints and hold the scheduled heat setting.
I would monitor the thick section and lower burner output if readings rise.

basic.situation: You are preparing to check equipment at a work site, and your lead asks you to set up barriers before testing.

options.text: Begin testing near the line while a coworker fetches the barrier tape.
Set barriers and inspect the tester with my lead before starting work.
Check visible equipment, then start when the crew gathers at the site.
Check the tester, confirm barriers, and report unsafe readings before entry.

advanced.situation: You are teaching junior workers to use testing instruments on a transmission fault, and their readings disagree about the suspected span.

options.text: Model meter setup, compare trainee readings, and trace the fault path together.
Ask trainees to copy the last meter settings and test the suspected span.
Pair trainees on readings and review their notes after the fault check.
Show the instrument sequence, then let each trainee repeat one test.

basic.situation: You are helping pull cable from a truck reel into a trench, and the crew calls for a steady pace around a bend.

options.text: Coordinate hand signals, control reel tension, and pause at each trench bend.
Keep the reel moving at the crew's pace and watch the trench edge.
Pull hard through the bend so the cable reaches the crew before lunch.
Follow the spotter's signals and ease the cable around the marked bend.

advanced.situation: You are guiding junior workers through a cable splice when the cable label and the prepared joint sleeve appear to specify different types.

options.text: Use the familiar joint method and ask the crew to check the cable label.
Match the cable specification to the joint method, then demonstrate the approved sequence.
Continue the joint with the available sleeve to avoid wasting the prepared ends.
Let the experienced splicer finish while you compare the two cable labels.

basic.situation: You are attaching cross-arms and insulators to a pole before installation, and your lead asks you to prepare the hardware.

options.text: Attach the parts quickly so the crew can move the pole to position.
Check the hardware, align each insulator, and confirm the attachment points with my lead.
Lay out the cross-arms and insulators, then attach them in the familiar order.
Prepare the cross-arms and insulators, then attach them as my lead directs.

advanced.situation: You are overseeing repairs on a distribution section, and a replacement component appears to differ from the work specification.

options.text: Install the replacement and note the difference for the completion report.
Ask the crew to finish other repairs while you check the parts list.
Pause that component's installation and compare its rating and fit with the work specification.
Check the replacement against the work pack and flag the difference to the crew.

basic.situation: You are using a bucket truck to reach pole equipment, and your lead asks you to position the bucket near the work area.

options.text: Wait for the lead's signal, then use the bucket to reach the equipment.
Move the truck closer and raise the bucket once the work area looks clear.
Check the truck position with the ground crew, then raise the bucket as guided.
Raise the bucket toward the equipment while the ground crew finishes positioning.

advanced.situation: You are helping plan a new pole line where the route crosses a narrow access track and a section slated for underground cable.

options.text: Mark the pole locations and trench route, then share the plan with the crew.
Use the track for equipment and adjust the trench route around the narrow section.
Map access, pole locations, and trench sections before sequencing the crew's work.
Set the pole positions along the shortest route to reduce crew travel time.

basic.situation: You are helping cover exposed conductors with insulating material before a repair, while a senior worker guides the placement.

options.text: Place the insulating cover where the senior worker points and keep the crew clear.
Hold the cover in place while a coworker finishes the nearby repair.
Check the cover's fit with the senior worker and secure it over the exposed joint.
Lay the cover over the exposed section and continue once it appears settled.

advanced.situation: You are reviewing the team's high-risk repair procedure after a fallen line is reported near a road and the crew prepares to work.

options.text: Ask the crew to move the barriers farther from the road before starting.
Remind the crew to use grounds and check the barrier placement during work.
Set a sequence for isolation, grounding, barriers, and a crew check before repair.
Start the repair after the line appears settled and traffic has slowed.

basic.situation: You are driving a utility truck with tools to a repair site, and rain has made the access road slippery.

options.text: Check the access conditions with the crew, secure the load, and adjust your speed.
Keep to the usual speed so the crew reaches the repair before daylight fades.
Drive slowly along the usual access road and keep the tools secured.
Secure the tools and follow the truck ahead along the access road.

advanced.situation: You are coordinating drivers and vehicles for inspections at several line sections, with changing weather and limited daylight affecting the schedule.

options.text: Prioritize nearby sections, while checking daylight and weather before dispatching each crew.
Group routes by access, confirm vehicle readiness, and schedule driver check-ins.
Assign drivers routes, then request progress updates at agreed check-in times.
Review weather forecasts with drivers and agree on a safe inspection sequence.

basic.situation: A line crew gives you a short damaged drop cable to splice while a senior installer checks nearby.

options.text: Prepare each conductor with the specified tool, make the splice, then verify its seal.
Match the cable ends, follow the work card, and ask for a check.
Use the hand tools shown, then tape the joint for the senior installer.
Twist the conductors together and cover the joint to finish before lunch.

advanced.situation: Two installers are preparing a long aerial run, and their first splice looks uneven as they pull the cable taut.

options.text: Ask the most experienced installer to show a splice while you monitor the run.
Demonstrate the specified splice and tension checks, then observe each installer applying both.
Let the crew finish the run, then review the joints together at the depot.
Show the crew the splice sequence, then have each person practise on a short cable.

basic.situation: You are asked to dig a short trench for a cable beside a marked customer boundary, with a senior worker nearby.

options.text: Use the nearest clear path and fill the trench once the cable is covered.
Confirm the marked route, dig carefully to the stated depth, and show the trench for review.
Start digging along the marked line, then ask the senior worker to check depth.
Follow the markings and dig steadily, keeping the removed soil beside the trench.

advanced.situation: A crew must lay cable through ducts under a busy access road, but the proposed trench route crosses a drain cover.

options.text: Mark the proposed route and have the crew start opening the trench at one end.
Check the duct path and crossing constraints, then revise the layout before directing the crew.
Shift the trench around the cover and keep the crew moving with the original schedule.
Walk the route with the crew and flag the drain crossing for the site lead.

basic.situation: At a customer site, you and a coworker need to pull cable by hand from a reel mounted on the truck.

options.text: Check the reel feed, agree on steady pulls, and pause when resistance changes.
Ask your coworker to hold the cable while you pull from the truck.
Give the cable a sharp tug to free it, then keep pulling together.
Pull steadily while your coworker watches the reel and calls out snags.

advanced.situation: A truck carries several cable reels for customer jobs, and the team is unsure which reel is assigned to the next site.

options.text: Count the reels with the team and tell them which sizes are available.
Review the job list, match reel labels to sites, and record each movement.
Write down the reel sizes after crews load their trucks for the day.
Ask each crew to take a reel that looks suitable for its next job.

basic.situation: A customer reports weak reception, and you are asked to measure signal strength at the nearest utility pole with guidance.

options.text: Record the meter reading and compare it with the work card range.
Use the last recorded reading as today's result and close the job notes.
Take a reading at the pole and send the number to your senior installer.
Check the meter setup, take a fresh reading, and record the pole location.

advanced.situation: Several customers report intermittent service, and your cable test results show different faults along the same transmission route.

options.text: Retest the first fault and arrange repairs there before checking the other results.
Share the readings with the crew and ask them to check nearby sections.
Use the strongest reading to choose a section for the crew to inspect first.
Map the readings by route section, compare patterns, and set repeatable test steps for the crew.

basic.situation: You arrive at a customer's flat to connect a receiver, and the customer is waiting to check the service before leaving.

options.text: Follow the connection steps, test reception, and show the customer the working setup.
Connect the receiver to the easiest socket and leave once its power light appears.
Check the cable ends, connect the receiver, and tell the customer how to switch it on.
Connect the receiver using the setup steps, then ask the customer to check reception.

advanced.situation: A customer says the newly connected receiver loses reception whenever another device is switched on in the living room.

options.text: Check the connections and test the setup with each device state, then explain the finding.
Ask the customer to reproduce the issue while you inspect the receiver connections.
Replace the receiver with a spare unit and see whether the complaint stops.
Tighten the visible connections and ask the customer to monitor reception tonight.

basic.situation: After a pole job, your senior asks you to clean the test meter and leads before they go back into the kit.

options.text: Clean the meter and leads with approved materials, then check for visible damage.
Wipe the meter case and wind the leads before returning everything to the kit.
Use a dry cloth on the meter and coil the leads neatly for storage.
Put the meter away with dust on the case so the crew can leave on time.

advanced.situation: A crew is preparing a bucket truck for work above a shop lot, and you notice one worker has not checked the climbing equipment.

options.text: Remind the worker to check the gear while the truck is positioned below the lines.
Pause setup, confirm gear checks, and review the access plan with the crew.
Check the truck controls yourself and let the worker finish checking their gear.
Ask the crew to check each other's gear before anyone uses the bucket truck.

basic.situation: A customer says a camera image looks soft, and you are asked to check whether its lens focuses correctly.

options.text: Test focus with the gauge and tell the customer whether it seems usable.
Adjust the focus ring until the image looks sharp through the viewfinder.
Check the mount, test focus with the gauge, and record the measured result.
Use the focus gauge, record the result, and compare it with the service specification.

advanced.situation: A specialist video camera fails its transport test, and the engineering drawing shows several linked mechanisms that may need repair.

options.text: Read the drawing and mark the likely repair areas before opening the camera.
Start with the transport mechanism and list parts that appear worn during inspection.
Trace the drawing's mechanism links, confirm symptoms with measurements, and order the repair sequence.
Ask a senior technician to identify the first assembly to inspect from the drawing.

basic.situation: A camera's viewfinder sits off-centre after a customer reports difficulty framing pictures, and you are asked to adjust it with guidance.

options.text: Ask the senior technician to set the viewfinder while you observe the adjustment.
Check the reference mark, make the guided adjustment, and compare the viewfinder alignment.
Turn the adjustment screw until the frame looks centred through the viewfinder.
Use the service reference, adjust in small increments, and verify alignment after each change.

advanced.situation: Two light meters give different readings before a busy repair shift, and a junior technician is preparing to use one for calibration work.

options.text: Set aside the meter with the larger reading and use the other for today's jobs.
Have the junior repeat readings on both meters and note any differences for review.
Choose the meter with the newer label and let the technician begin the work.
Compare both meters against the timing reference, document the results, and coach the junior through verification.

basic.situation: A customer returns a camera with fingerprints on the lens, and you are asked to clean it using the workshop materials.

options.text: Apply cleaning fluid to the lens and polish until the fingerprints fade.
Use the approved lens cloth and inspect the glass under the bench light.
Remove loose dust first, use lens-safe material, and check the glass under light.
Wipe the lens with the nearest cloth, then return the camera to the customer.

advanced.situation: A team is cleaning a set of delicate lenses, and a new technician suggests using the same cloth across every lens.

options.text: Give each lens its own cloth and ask the technician to work carefully.
Let the technician finish the set, then inspect the lenses for marks afterward.
Set a dust-first cleaning sequence, assign clean materials, and demonstrate the inspection step.
Ask the technician to change cloths whenever one looks dirty during the task.

basic.situation: You need to remove an external camera cover to reach a reported fault, and a senior technician has shown you the hand tools.

options.text: Use the shown tool, remove the cover, and place the screws in a tray.
Check the fasteners, use the shown tool, and group each screw by location.
Pry the cover open with a screwdriver and keep the screws on the bench.
Remove the visible screws and leave the cover beside the camera for later.

advanced.situation: A commercial video camera has an intermittent fault, and reaching its transport assembly requires removing several delicate internal panels.

options.text: Study the service diagram, map panel order, and separate fasteners before opening the assembly.
Ask a senior technician to remove the delicate panels while you label each tray.
Remove panels in the order they appear accessible and keep the screws together.
Photograph each layer as you remove panels and place its screws in a tray.

basic.situation: A small camera bracket is bent, and your senior asks you to shape a replacement part on the bench grinder with help.

options.text: Ask the senior to mark the stock before you grind it to the line.
Grind a replacement from similar stock until it fits the bracket opening.
Measure the bracket, shape the stock gradually, and compare the fit with guidance.
Use the sample bracket to guide the grind, then ask for a fit check.

advanced.situation: A discontinued camera model needs a replacement drive component, and the original part is unavailable for direct ordering.

options.text: Use an old service drawing to estimate the part and machine one for review.
Ask a supplier to search its catalog for a compatible drive component first.
Shape a replacement from the closest stock and test whether the drive turns.
Measure the mating parts, draft dimensions, and machine a sample for careful fit checks.

basic.situation: A camera repair needs a listed shutter spring, and you are asked to request the part using the workshop catalogue.

options.text: Check the spring name in the catalogue and ask the senior to confirm the request.
Request the spring using the closest catalogue description and include the repair number.
Choose a spring that looks similar and request it to keep the repair moving.
Match the catalogue part number to the repair list, then submit the request.

advanced.situation: Several repairs need specialized parts, and one vendor has delayed a previous shipment while the workshop's stock is running low.

options.text: Check stock and lead times, group confirmed needs, and track each vendor response.
Request the same quantities from that vendor and update the team after confirmation.
Ask the vendor for an updated delivery estimate before preparing the requisitions.
Send requests to two vendors and let the workshop choose whichever replies first.

basic.situation: You are installing a monitor in a ward bay with a senior technician nearby. The room has limited space and several power outlets.

options.text: I check the outlet rating, then position the unit beside the bed.
I review the setup checklist with the senior, then install to specification.
I confirm power and clearance needs, then ask the senior to check placement.
I unpack the unit and connect it where the room has space.

advanced.situation: A clinic is choosing between two infusion pumps for rooms with different power and space limits. You must assess which specifications suit the intended use.

options.text: I compare the pump specifications and ask the ward which model feels easier.
I compare flow ranges and alarms, then recommend the pump matching clinical needs.
I choose the model with the wider display and familiar controls for staff.
I match clinical requirements, power demand, and room constraints across both pump specifications.

basic.situation: During a supervised check, you find a treatment-room cable with worn insulation near a trolley. The equipment is due for use soon.

options.text: I secure the area, keep the unit out of use, and document the cable hazard.
I tape the worn section and tell staff they can use the equipment carefully.
I keep the equipment out of use and show the senior the damaged cable.
I move the trolley aside and check the cable against the equipment manual.

advanced.situation: A facility audit finds a portable suction unit near a wet cleaning area, with its route and power connection unclear. You are reviewing the room setup.

options.text: I place a warning label nearby and ask staff to watch the unit.
I assess the wet-area risk, power path, and intended use before proposing relocation.
I trace the power route and compare the room layout with the safety guidance.
I move the unit onto a dry shelf and note the change for staff.

basic.situation: A bedside monitor gives inconsistent readings during a routine check. With a senior nearby, you have a multimeter and the manufacturer's test steps.

options.text: I swap the component with a spare and see whether readings settle.
I repeat the reading and record whichever value appears most often.
I follow the manual and measure the component with the multimeter.
I check the meter leads, follow the manual, and compare readings with limits.

advanced.situation: A department marks several older monitors as excess. You are asked to assess their condition and serviceability before the equipment list is updated.

options.text: I mark the oldest monitors for disposal based on their age and appearance.
I test each monitor and classify its condition against service criteria.
I review records, test function, and document condition before recommending disposition.
I ask the ward which units they want to keep for backup.

basic.situation: A portable monitor cuts out when its cable moves. With a senior supervising, you open the approved service area and find a loose connection.

options.text: I replace the cable assembly and note the change for the senior.
I secure the unit, repair the joint, and retest cable movement afterward.
I reflow the joint quickly and return the monitor to the ward.
I inspect the joint and solder it using the approved setup.

advanced.situation: A welded joint on a stainless hospital trolley has cracked under load. You are asked to repair it before the trolley returns to service.

options.text: I assess the break, prepare the joint, weld it, then test trolley stability.
I fit a brace over the crack and ask staff to limit trolley loads.
I weld over the crack, let it cool, then return the trolley to service.
I clean the joint, weld it, and inspect the finished repair before release.

basic.situation: You are completing preventive service on a clinic scale. The manual calls for cleaning and lubrication, and the maintenance log is open on your bench.

options.text: I clean and lubricate the scale, then record the work performed.
I wipe the scale and mark the maintenance box as complete.
I follow the manual, clean and lubricate, then record condition and work.
I clean the scale and enter the date in the service log.

advanced.situation: A repair record shows a replacement part was fitted, but the required follow-up update is missing. You are reconciling records before the monthly service review.

options.text: I note the missing update and leave the record for later review.
I copy the previous service entry and change its date and part.
I add the part number and close the record for the review.
I check the repair notes, confirm the update, and complete the equipment history.

basic.situation: A nurse is about to use a newly installed pulse oximeter and asks how to start a reading. You have the operation checklist with you.

options.text: I explain each control and answer questions while the nurse follows the quick guide.
I review the checklist and demonstrate how to start a reading for the nurse.
I demonstrate the steps, then ask the nurse to repeat them using the checklist.
I show the start button, then let the nurse practice a reading with the checklist.

advanced.situation: A new technician is learning preventive care for a ward monitor. You are asked to demonstrate the service steps and identify a suitable replacement sensor source.

options.text: I show cleaning and inspection, then note a sensor supplier in the parts list.
I explain routine care and ask the technician to search the parts catalogue.
I demonstrate the manual steps and verify sensor compatibility before recording its source.
I demonstrate the service steps and share the first sensor listing I find.

basic.situation: A customer needs a guitar tuned before collection. You have a digital tuner and hand tools, and one string sounds flat during the check.

options.text: I compare each string with the tuner and adjust tension in small turns.
I tighten the flat string until its pitch matches the tuner display.
I adjust the flat string with the tuner, then check it once again.
I tune the guitar by ear to the pitch I remember from yesterday.

advanced.situation: A replacement saddle leaves a guitar with uneven intonation. You have access to a lathe and must shape the part while preserving its contact surface.

options.text: I compare fretted notes with the tuner, then make one lathe adjustment.
I measure the existing setup, shape the saddle incrementally, and test intonation across frets.
I shape the saddle from the old part's outline and polish the surface.
I remove a small amount from the saddle and test the open-string pitch.

basic.situation: A customer says a borrowed violin sounds dull after travel. You can play it and have guidance from a senior repairer nearby.

options.text: I retune the violin and tell the customer it should sound fine.
I play open strings and a scale, noting where the dullness or rattle occurs.
I play a short scale and listen for uneven notes or rattling.
I ask the customer to play it and describe what sounds different.

advanced.situation: An older cello may need restoration, and its owner asks for an estimate of value and work. You must inspect it before discussing a repair scope.

options.text: I note visible wear and suggest a standard restoration package for its age.
I inspect the body and fittings, then discuss likely restoration needs with the senior.
I check the cello's condition and compare it with similar instruments in the shop.
I inspect condition, play it for defects, and document value factors and restoration scope.

basic.situation: A customer's guitar has a broken high string before a lesson. With guidance available, you need to replace it and leave the instrument ready to play.

options.text: I tie on a spare string and hand the guitar back for the lesson.
I fit a matching string and tune the guitar using the electronic tuner.
I replace the string with the nearest available gauge and tune it by ear.
I confirm the string gauge, fit it securely, stretch it gently, and retune.

advanced.situation: A piano key returns slowly before a recital, and inspection points to a worn felt part. You have time to replace the component and test the action.

options.text: I trim the worn felt and reinstall it to save the existing fit.
I match the felt, fit it cleanly, and compare key return with adjacent keys.
I loosen the key action and leave a note for the next repairer.
I replace the felt, then play the key several times to check its return.

basic.situation: A wooden clarinet has a small crack near a joint. With a senior repairer guiding you, you prepare filler and clamps for the repair.

options.text: I clean the crack, apply the specified filler, and clamp it evenly.
I inspect the crack, prepare it, apply filler, and check the joint after curing.
I apply filler over the crack and clamp the joint until it sets.
I cover the crack with extra filler and polish the area smooth.

advanced.situation: A metal trumpet has a fine crack near a brace, affecting its response. You have a soldering iron and must repair the crack without shifting the brace.

options.text: I heat the crack and add solder, then check the brace position.
I support the brace, prepare the crack, solder it, and test the joint.
I add solder along the crack and polish the area for the customer.
I mark the brace position, solder the crack, and inspect the joint afterward.

basic.situation: You are reassembling a small wooden instrument after repair. The work card gives a glue mixing ratio, and clamps are ready at the bench.

options.text: I mix the glue by eye and clamp the pieces until they hold.
I measure the glue using the work card and clamp the joint evenly.
I use the remaining glue from the last repair and clamp the pieces firmly.
I measure the glue to the card, align the joint, and clamp evenly.

advanced.situation: A repaired instrument needs reassembly with a new glue choice for a delicate joint. You must select and mix a suitable adhesive before clamping.

options.text: I compare the joint materials and repair needs, then select and measure suitable glue.
I use the shop's usual glue and apply a thin layer to the joint.
I choose the quickest-setting glue and mix enough for the whole instrument.
I select a familiar glue, mix a small batch, and test its spread.

basic.situation: A customer brings in a guitar with a loose bridge for repair. You need to remove the relevant parts carefully before adjustment, with guidance available.

options.text: I remove the strings and loosen the bridge area using the repair checklist.
I lift the bridge first so I can inspect beneath it quickly.
I loosen the strings and place the removed parts together on the bench.
I document the setup, release string tension, and remove parts in sequence.

advanced.situation: A customer requests a high-gloss finish on a polished brass instrument. You are preparing the surface and have access to polishing compounds and a buffing wheel.

options.text: I choose a suitable compound, buff evenly, and inspect the finish under clear light.
I use the usual compound and buff the instrument in overlapping passes.
I buff the surface with compound until the brass looks bright under bench lights.
I polish the visible panels by hand and leave the fittings for later.

basic.situation: You open a customer's watch for a routine inspection and see uneven wear near the balance wheel. What do you do?

options.text: I ask the bench lead to confirm whether the wear matters.
I replace the worn pivot with one from a similar watch.
I run the watch briefly and judge its sound and motion.
I compare the parts under a loupe and record visible wear.

advanced.situation: A rare watch has uncertain service history and an intermittent fault. The owner asks for a repair estimate before authorising work. What do you do?

options.text: I quote a low figure to secure the repair booking today.
I document the tests, likely parts, labour range, and valuation basis.
I inspect the movement and give an estimate after identifying the fault.
I price a full overhaul using the usual rate for similar watches.

basic.situation: You have opened a routine mechanical watch for service, and the movement is ready for lubrication under supervision. What do you do?

options.text: I apply a small amount of the specified oil to moving points.
I spread oil across the gears so the movement runs smoothly.
I add oil to the easiest visible moving parts first.
I ask the supervisor to show me the oiling points again.

advanced.situation: A discontinued watch needs a small replacement part, and no compatible stock part is available. You have access to the workshop lathe. What do you do?

options.text: I ask a senior watchmaker to choose the stock and dimensions.
I measure the original, then turn a matching part from suitable stock.
I select a close stock part and check its fit on the lathe.
I file down a near-match part until it fits the watch.

basic.situation: You have finished a routine service and need to reassemble the watch with a replacement glass face before returning it. What do you do?

options.text: I ask a colleague to check the glass before I close the case.
I press the replacement glass firmly until the case closes.
I install the glass and reassemble the watch using my usual sequence.
I fit the glass evenly, reassemble the case, and check closure.

advanced.situation: A customer's watch gains time after a service, and its rate varies between positions. What do you do before returning it?

options.text: I adjust the regulator against rate readings across several positions.
I move the regulator until the watch sounds more even.
I check the rate once, then adjust the regulator slightly.
I make a small regulator change and check the rate again.

basic.situation: You are cleaning disassembled watch parts using the workshop's provided solutions and machine. What do you do before reassembly?

options.text: I clean the parts, then let them air dry on the bench.
I clean, rinse, and dry each part using the stated cycle.
I ask the senior technician to confirm the cycle before starting.
I run the parts through one wash and assemble them damp.

advanced.situation: A delicate watch part has light corrosion, and the usual cleaning solution may affect its finish. What do you do?

options.text: I check the material and corrosion, then select a compatible solution.
I ask the workshop lead which solution is usually used for corrosion.
I soak the part in the strongest available cleaning solution.
I use the regular solution briefly and inspect the part afterward.

basic.situation: A customer brings in a watch that stops overnight and cannot recall its last service. What do you ask at intake?

options.text: I ask when it stops, how it is worn, and about past service.
I ask when it stopped and whether it was recently serviced.
I ask whether it runs after winding and note the answer.
I record that it stops overnight and send it to the bench.

advanced.situation: A returning customer asks whether an older watch should be serviced again, but its service records are spread across several visits. What do you do?

options.text: I review the latest invoice and suggest the usual service interval.
I reconcile the service history and explain care based on its condition.
I tell the customer to service it now to protect its value.
I list the recorded visits and ask a senior colleague for advice.

basic.situation: A routine watch repair needs a replacement crown, but the parts drawer is low. You can consult the supplier catalog. What do you do?

options.text: I check the catalog for crowns listed for the same watch brand.
I order the most common crown size to keep the repair moving.
I compare the old crown with a catalog image before ordering.
I match the model details to the catalog and confirm the crown size.

advanced.situation: Several watch models need different batteries, and stock is low before a busy month. What do you do when preparing the next order?

options.text: I compare usage and stock by battery type before placing a balanced order.
I ask the supplier for a bulk discount on the common battery size.
I buy a large quantity of the battery used most often.
I replenish each battery type to the same shelf quantity.

basic.situation: During a routine check, you find low fluid and a clogged filter on a small workshop machine. What do you do?

options.text: I check the fluid level again before telling the maintenance lead.
I top up with the nearest available fluid and restart the machine.
I check the checklist, verify the fluid type, and record both findings.
I refill the fluid and replace the filter using the checklist.

advanced.situation: A production machine has an intermittent fault, and the repair estimate depends on a hard-to-find cause. What do you do?

options.text: I test likely causes, document evidence, and give a range with assumptions.
I inspect the machine and estimate after finding the most likely fault.
I estimate from a similar repair and ask the team to check the cause.
I quote the cheapest likely repair so production can approve it quickly.

basic.situation: You are fitting a simple pipe section after a routine repair, with the correct components and a guide available. What do you do?

options.text: I ask the experienced technician to confirm the fitting sequence first.
I align the fittings, assemble them to the guide, and check for leaks.
I tighten the fittings as far as possible to prevent leaks.
I follow the guide and tighten each fitting with the usual wrench.

advanced.situation: Repeated repairs require holding a machine guard steady, and the current support slips. You have time to propose a repair aid. What do you do?

options.text: I wedge timber beneath the guard so the next repair can proceed.
I ask the workshop lead to approve a stronger standard prop design.
I measure the guard and suggest a fixed metal support for it.
I sketch a stable adjustable support around the guard and repair access needs.

basic.situation: After a routine machine repair, you are assigned to clean dust from the nearby workshop floor and benches. What do you do?

options.text: I ask which benches need attention before starting the cleanup.
I sweep dust toward the machine base to finish the area quickly.
I dust the benches and sweep the open floor area.
I clear dust from benches and floor, then leave walkways unobstructed.

advanced.situation: A commercial building uses older lighting, and a routine maintenance review identifies an opportunity to improve energy efficiency. What do you do?

options.text: I compare compatible efficient fittings and expected operating needs before proposing replacement.
I order the highest output efficient fittings available for the rooms.
I note the existing fittings and suggest a standard efficient replacement.
I ask the facilities lead which efficient fittings are usually installed.

basic.situation: A small patch of peeling paint is visible on an interior wooden door during routine maintenance. What do you do?

options.text: I ask the maintenance lead which paint was used on the door.
I prepare the patch, apply a compatible finish, and check the edges.
I paint over the peeling patch to cover it before inspection.
I sand the loose paint and apply the closest matching color.

advanced.situation: A repair needs a custom shaft sleeve, and the machine shop has a lathe and the relevant drawing. What do you do?

options.text: I set the lathe from the drawing and check dimensions during machining.
I ask a machinist to confirm the setup before cutting the stock.
I machine the sleeve to match the old part by eye.
I use the drawing to set the tools and inspect the finished sleeve.

basic.situation: You have completed a small repair to a door latch and need to enter the work in the maintenance log. What do you record?

options.text: I note the latch repair and total charge in the maintenance log.
I write the repair type in the log and attach the receipt.
I enter the total charge under general repairs for the month.
I record the latch repair, parts used, labour, and cost in the log.

advanced.situation: A hospital laundry machine has recurring faults, and the shift is busy. You are assigned to inspect it for maintenance needs. What do you do?

options.text: I replace the part commonly changed on this machine without checking other causes.
I ask the laundry operator about fault patterns and repairs that helped during recent shifts.
I inspect the machine, note symptoms, and report a likely repair to my supervisor.
I review service notes, inspect the fault, and record findings before repair.

basic.situation: A routine repair needs a replacement belt, and the supplier catalog lists several similar sizes. You have a supervisor available for guidance. What do you do?

options.text: I check the old belt's label and order the same listed item.
I show the catalog options to my supervisor and ask which belt to order.
I order the belt with the closest listed size to avoid delay.
I match the machine details and belt size to the catalog before ordering.

advanced.situation: A maintenance team uses different checks for the same recurring repair, and subcontractors are due on site next week. What do you do?

options.text: I let each contractor choose a repair method based on speed and available parts.
I create a repair checklist and review it with team leads and contractors.
I ask team leads to explain agreed repair steps at each shift handover and contractor briefing.
I share the current maintenance notes with subcontractors before their scheduled site visit.

basic.situation: You are checking a turbine electrical component with a multimeter under supervision, and its reading differs from the service sheet.

options.text: Restart the generator to see whether the warning clears before recording the reading.
Check the meter against a known source, then log the reading for the lead technician.
Repeat the measurement once and ask the lead technician what the value means.
Record the meter reading, compare it with the checklist, and flag the difference.

advanced.situation: Several turbines show inconsistent converter readings after an update, and you must plan tests and analyse the results with engineers.

options.text: Sample two operating states and compare converter readings with recent service records.
Design controlled test cases across operating states, separating sensor drift from converter behaviour.
Repeat the run at rated output and report whichever readings look stable.
Plot each turbine's readings by operating state and discuss outliers with engineers.

basic.situation: A turbine generator shows a recurring fault alert during your shift, and the senior technician asks you to help diagnose it.

options.text: Ask a nearby technician whether this alert appeared on another turbine recently.
Review the alert history and compare it with the generator's recent operating readings.
Clear the alert and restart the generator to see if normal output returns.
Check the alert code against the service guide and record matching symptoms.

advanced.situation: A variable-speed control fault returns after a repair, while the turbine is needed for a scheduled service window.

options.text: Compare the fault timing with pitch and speed-control records from the last run.
Map the fault against control inputs, then document a repeatable diagnostic sequence for the team.
Replace the most recently serviced control component and see whether the fault returns.
Reset the converter settings to their previous values and restart the turbine.

basic.situation: You are assigned to climb a turbine tower and inspect equipment after a routine service visit.

options.text: Ask a colleague to carry the heavier tools while you climb with the rest.
Inspect your harness, connection points, and tools before climbing to the work area.
Check your climbing equipment and follow the site's access steps before ascending.
Use the ladder while carrying your tools in one hand to save a trip.

advanced.situation: Rain has stopped, but the tower ladder remains damp and your team is due to inspect equipment before the next shift.

options.text: Reassess ladder conditions against site procedures, then brief the team on the agreed controls.
Resume the climb now that the rain has stopped and keep the inspection brief.
Delay the climb until the ladder looks drier and update the shift handover.
Brief the team on the wet ladder and review the site's climb conditions together.

basic.situation: You are completing a routine turbine maintenance checklist and notice a loose panel fastener during your inspection.

options.text: Mark the panel as checked and leave the fastener for the next service visit.
Tighten the fastener to the listed setting and note the maintenance completed.
Ask a colleague to confirm the fastener feels secure after you tighten it.
Check nearby fasteners, secure the loose one to specification, and update the checklist.

advanced.situation: Repeated maintenance visits across several turbines are finding similar wear, and you are asked to improve the wind field schedule.

options.text: Move the affected turbines earlier in the existing schedule and track the next findings.
Compare wear by turbine and service interval, then adjust the schedule around the pattern.
Ask each technician to report wear sooner so the team can plan visits.
Keep the current intervals and handle each turbine when its next service date arrives.

basic.situation: A new technician is watching you commission a turbine, and the lead asks you to demonstrate the basic startup checks.

options.text: Show each startup check, then have the trainee perform it while you observe.
Walk through the startup checklist and explain what each check confirms.
Give the trainee the checklist and answer questions after the startup is complete.
Start the turbine while the trainee watches, then point out the completed steps.

advanced.situation: Technicians at several sites report inconsistent test results, and you are asked to develop training for the commissioning procedure.

options.text: Build a practice session around common errors, with demonstrations and observed test runs.
Ask experienced technicians to share their preferred methods at the next team meeting.
Share the current procedure and invite technicians to discuss difficult steps.
Send a short reminder covering the steps most often missed in recent reports.

basic.situation: You are counting replacement sensors and tools after a turbine repair, and the shelf total differs from the inventory list.

options.text: Ask the technician who used the kit whether any sensor was taken.
Count the shelf again and record the quantity that matches the physical stock.
Adjust the list to the shelf count so the inventory task can be closed.
Recount each item type, check recent issue notes, and log the discrepancy for review.

advanced.situation: Your inventory records show frequent sensor shortages at several turbines, and you are asked to recommend stock levels for the next service cycle.

options.text: Increase the sensor order slightly and monitor whether shortages continue next cycle.
Compare usage, lead times, and shortages across sites before recommending stock levels.
Review shortage counts by site and discuss likely needs with procurement.
Order the same extra quantity for every site with a recorded shortage.

basic.situation: You are restocking a snack machine at a busy office and notice the product count differs from the route sheet.

options.text: Count each product, compare the route sheet, and record any mismatch before filling.
Change the route sheet to match the machine before completing the restock.
Fill the listed products and note the count difference on the route sheet.
Ask the site contact which products sold quickly since the last visit.

advanced.situation: Several office machines run out of popular drinks before your next route visit, and you must recommend supply quantities across locations.

options.text: Load each machine near its full capacity to reduce future refill trips.
Review recent sales by location and raise quantities where sales were strongest.
Compare sales and refill timing by location, then set quantities around demand patterns.
Add the same extra drink quantity to each machine on the next route.

basic.situation: You are cleaning and oiling a vending machine's moving parts, and a colleague points out residue near the product mechanism.

options.text: Ask your colleague to check the mechanism after you finish oiling it.
Remove the residue, clean the surrounding parts, and apply the specified oil sparingly.
Add extra oil so the mechanism moves smoothly after the cleaning.
Wipe the residue and apply the oil listed for the moving parts.

advanced.situation: Residue keeps returning in several machines after cleaning, and you are asked to improve the team's cleaning schedule and guidance.

options.text: Ask technicians to share which cleaning products they prefer for each machine.
Add more frequent cleaning visits for the machines with repeat residue.
Track residue locations and cleaning intervals, then train staff on the affected parts.
Keep the current schedule and remind staff to clean the visible surfaces.

basic.situation: A card reader fails during a service visit, and the senior technician asks you to replace its worn reader head.

options.text: Ask the site contact whether the reader worked before the fault appeared.
Swap the head quickly and return the machine to service for customers.
Fit the replacement head and check that it sits securely in place.
Match the replacement part, fit it carefully, and test a sample transaction.
