advanced.situation: A replacement reader head fits, but several machines still reject cards after similar repairs, and you are asked to guide the team.

options.text: Compare failed units and repair steps, then demonstrate a verified replacement method.
Tell the team to replace the reader head again when card rejection continues.
Review the repair notes and ask technicians which installation step feels difficult.
Share the common rejection symptoms and review the replacement steps together.

basic.situation: A vending machine's product tray sticks during a service visit, and you are using its repair diagram with guidance.

options.text: Ask the site contact whether the tray has stuck during earlier visits.
Inspect the guide for obstruction, adjust it to the diagram, and test movement.
Pull the tray firmly until it releases and continue the service visit.
Check the diagram and adjust the tray guide until it moves freely.

advanced.situation: A recurring amusement machine fault returns after several repairs, and you are asked to help technicians improve their repair approach.

options.text: Repeat the last successful adjustment across the machines with similar symptoms.
Have technicians try a different adjustment and report whether the fault returns.
Compare symptoms and repair outcomes, then document a tested adjustment sequence for staff.
Review recent repair notes and ask technicians which adjustment they tried last.

basic.situation: You are recording a vending machine's cash total after service, and the amount differs from the transaction log.

options.text: Document the counted amount, attach the transaction log, and note the difference on the form.
Ask a nearby technician whether the machine had a cash issue earlier.
Recount the cash, compare transaction entries, and tell the designated contact about the discrepancy.
Change the recorded total to match the cash before closing the service form.

advanced.situation: Repair logs from several routes use different descriptions for the same fault, making it hard to track repeat service visits.

options.text: Leave each route's wording unchanged and compare the logs by machine number.
Collect examples from each route and send them to the service coordinator.
Ask technicians to include the machine location and date in each repair entry.
Review repeated entries, agree on shared fault terms, and update the logging guide.

basic.situation: You inspect a vending machine after a customer reports a stuck product, and the display shows no fault code.

options.text: Try another product selection and leave the machine available if it releases.
Inspect the channel, clear a visible jam, and test a product release.
Ask the customer which selection they tried before checking the machine.
Check the product channel and clear any visible obstruction you find.

advanced.situation: A group of machines fails intermittent payment tests, and you must identify likely causes and prepare parts requests for repairs.

options.text: Ask the route technician which machines seemed most difficult to test.
Compare test results by machine, then list parts tied to confirmed faults.
Order replacement readers for every machine that failed a payment test.
Review payment failure counts and request readers for the most affected machines.

basic.situation: You inspect a dock pile with a checklist and spot a narrow crack near its waterline. What do you do?

options.text: I compare the marked pile with the checklist and report visible damage.
I mark the pile as sound because most of its surface looks intact.
I photograph the crack, record its location, and ask the lead diver to review it.
I mention the crack during the debrief after finishing my visual sweep.

advanced.situation: Your non-destructive test on an offshore platform leg gives readings that differ from the previous inspection, and the report is due today. What do you do?

options.text: I note the difference in the report and ask the site lead what to do.
I check the test setup, map the new readings, and flag the discrepancy for review.
I repeat the test at the marked points and document both sets of readings.
I use the earlier readings to complete the report and meet the deadline.

basic.situation: A routine dock inspection is ready to start, but you have not confirmed the planned depth or registered the dive. What do you do?

options.text: I confirm depth plan and registration with dive lead before gearing up.
I compare planned depth with my limits and ask the lead about registration.
I pause gearing up until another diver confirms the registration details.
I rely on last week's depth and head for entry without checking registration.

advanced.situation: A current has strengthened since the dive plan was briefed, and two divers are approaching their planned bottom time. What do you do?

options.text: I check the surface conditions and ask the dive lead whether to shorten the work.
I relay the changed current and diver times, then follow the agreed return plan.
I ask the team to pause entry and review conditions, limits, and exit plans together.
I keep the schedule and tell the divers to watch their gauges closely.

basic.situation: Under your supervisor's direction, you are preparing to cut a small steel bracket underwater, but the work area has shifted. What do you do?

options.text: I reposition the jig with the supervisor and confirm the cut line before starting.
I pause the cut and tell the supervisor the bracket moved from its marks.
I check the cut line and ask the supervisor to confirm the bracket position.
I keep the original line and adjust my torch angle around the shifted bracket.

advanced.situation: A repair drawing shows a steel seam for underwater welding, but the prepared joint does not match the drawing. What do you do?

options.text: I mark the mismatch and wait for the supervisor before setting the welding jig.
I pause the weld and ask the supervisor to clarify the seam dimensions.
I weld the prepared joint and record the drawing mismatch for the shift report.
I photograph the joint, compare its dimensions with the drawing, and seek technical review.

basic.situation: You are helping place sandbags beneath a temporary dock support, and the guide rope begins pulling away from the marked position. What do you do?

options.text: I check the mark again and ask the lead to confirm the rope position.
I keep lowering the bags and note the shift after the support is settled.
I hold the placement, recheck the mark with the lead, and guide the rope back.
I pause placement and tell the diver lead the guide rope shifted off the mark.

advanced.situation: A bridge piling is being lowered, and the seabed mark differs from the position shown on the placement plan. What do you do?

options.text: I ask the crane operator to keep the piling steady while I check the mark again.
I signal a hold, record the mark and plan difference, and request a placement check.
I use the seabed mark as the guide and continue the lowering sequence.
I report the mismatch to the installation lead while the piling remains suspended.

basic.situation: During a routine gear check, your depth gauge needle sticks before a planned training dive. What do you do?

options.text: I tag the gauge for checking and tell the equipment lead before it is issued.
I compare the gauge with a teammate's and mention the sticking needle at briefing.
I clean the gauge face and check the needle again with the equipment lead.
I use the last recorded depth reading as a guide for today's dive.

advanced.situation: A seawater valve on a dive support line will not close fully after cleaning, and the next crew is due soon. What do you do?

options.text: I check the valve movement again and ask the lead whether to replace it.
I adjust the valve stem and tell the next crew it should hold for now.
I isolate the line as trained, check the valve seating, and log the fault for repair.
I report the valve fault to the equipment lead and leave the line untouched.

basic.situation: You are helping rig a sunken metal crate to a crane line, and the sling starts sliding as tension comes on. What do you do?

options.text: I tell the crane operator about the sliding sling and keep the line lightly tensioned.
I keep tension on the line and ask the lead to watch the sling closely.
I signal a stop, reset the sling with the lead, and check its seating before lifting.
I ask the lead to inspect the sling before the crane takes more weight.

advanced.situation: During an underwater search, a diver's planned return time passes and the search line is snagged near wreckage. What do you do?

options.text: I free the search line first, then check whether the diver has returned.
I alert the surface team about the overdue diver and ask them to check the line.
I report the overdue diver and snag, then follow the team's lost-diver response plan.
I check the diver's last line position and tell the lead about the snag.

basic.situation: You are installing a deposit safe from a blueprint, but the marked floor position conflicts with the doorway clearance. What do you do?

options.text: I anchor the safe at the floor marks and tell the site contact about the tight clearance.
I measure the clearance, compare the blueprint, and hold drilling for an agreed position.
I check the blueprint dimensions and ask the site contact to confirm the marked position.
I mark the doorway clearance and ask the installer lead where to shift the safe.

advanced.situation: A vault door frame arrives with lifting points that differ from the installation drawing, and the crew is ready to raise it. What do you do?

options.text: I check the drawing and have the crew hold the frame while the lead reviews it.
I ask the crane operator to use the new points and raise the frame slowly.
I map the lifting points against the drawing and pause the lift for a rigging review.
I photograph the points and ask the installation lead whether the lift can proceed.

basic.situation: You disassemble a customer's mechanical door lock and find a worn spring beside the work tray. What do you do?

options.text: I label the spring and tell the lead it may need replacement.
I keep the spring with its lock, note its position, and alert the lead.
I fit a similar spare spring and test the key before returning the lock.
I set the spring aside and inspect the tumblers before reassembly.

advanced.situation: An electronic lock intermittently fails after you replace a worn component, while the customer needs the door secured before closing. What do you do?

options.text: I test several lock cycles and note when the same failure returns.
I tell the lead the fault persists and ask whether replacement is needed.
I record failure conditions, test cycles, and explain the unresolved fault to the lead.
I repeat the repair, then test the lock with the customer's key.

basic.situation: A customer needs a duplicate for a worn house key, and the first cut does not turn smoothly in the sample cylinder. What do you do?

options.text: I make another duplicate from the original and ask the customer to try it.
I check the blank alignment and run one more duplicate through the machine.
I compare the cut with the original and adjust the machine before trying another blank.
I file the new key by feel until it turns in the sample cylinder.

advanced.situation: A code-cut key for a restricted office cylinder differs from the supplied code card, and the requester is waiting. What do you do?

options.text: I cut from the supplied code and test the key before handing it over.
I verify the machine code entry and ask the lead to review the card.
I hold the cut and tell the requester the code card needs checking.
I compare card details with the work order and ask the requester to resolve mismatch.

basic.situation: You are changing a safe combination under guidance, and the replacement tumbler does not sit flush in its slot. What do you do?

options.text: I compare it with the removed part and ask the lead to confirm.
I check the tumbler orientation and ask the lead to inspect its fit.
I stop fitting it and ask the lead whether another tumbler is needed.
I press the tumbler into place and test the dial before closing the safe.

advanced.situation: After adjusting a vault door component, the door binds near the frame, and the client has scheduled a handover today. What do you do?

options.text: I check the frame gap today, report the binding point, and ask before another adjustment.
I demonstrate the binding to the lead and ask whether handover should be delayed.
I mark the binding point, check clearances, and document it for lead review.
I adjust the hinge again until the door closes smoothly and prepare the handover.

basic.situation: You are installing a door closer, and the supplied template places one fixing over a glass panel edge. What do you do?

options.text: I measure the clear fixing area, compare the template, and mark a revised position for approval.
I pause the drilling and show the lead where the template meets the glass edge.
I drill at the template marks and fit the closer before the tenant arrives.
I check the template against the door and ask the lead to confirm a safe fixing position.

advanced.situation: A master key works on a door that the access schedule lists as excluded, and the tenant move-in is tomorrow. What do you do?

options.text: I hold the key issue and ask the lead whether the door should remain excluded.
I remove that door from the schedule and tell the tenant the key is ready.
I test the affected keys against the schedule and report the unintended access for correction.
I confirm the door's schedule entry and tell the lead the key opens it.

basic.situation: A customer asks you to pick a jammed office door lock, but the job record does not show who authorized entry. What do you do?

options.text: I review the work order and call the site contact if the authorization is missing.
I check the work order with the site contact before attempting to pick the lock.
I tell the customer the record is unclear and ask the lead to confirm access.
I ask the customer to confirm their name and then try the lock picks.

advanced.situation: You are assigned to open a vehicle lock, but the customer cannot show ownership documents and the vehicle is blocking a shared loading bay. What do you do?

options.text: I check the work order and call the listed contact to confirm the request.
I record the request, verify authority with the contact, and await confirmation.
I use the vehicle tool and ask the customer to settle ownership details afterward.
I tell the customer the documents are missing and ask the lead for guidance.

basic.situation: You receive a work order for a leaking unit and a parts diagram. You need to list parts and estimate their cost before the crew starts.

options.text: Price visible items, then ask the supplier about any gaps.
Cross-check the work order against the diagram, then price required parts.
Order familiar parts from the last job to save preparation time.
Use the diagram to list matching parts and price them.

advanced.situation: Several joined units have water damage, and the work order lists only two affected rooms. You are preparing a cost estimate for the project lead.

options.text: Add a broad repair allowance to cover damage beyond the listed rooms.
Estimate the listed rooms and flag uncertain damage for later review.
Compare each unit's damage notes and diagrams, then separate confirmed and uncertain costs.
Use the first unit's repair list as the estimate for every unit.

basic.situation: A window sticks after installation. You are asked to open and close it and check whether its edges need trimming.

options.text: Open and close it several times, noting where it catches.
Plane the edge that looks tight, then try the window again.
Ask a colleague to test it while you prepare a jackplane.
Check the frame and sash, then test movement before marking any tight edge.

advanced.situation: After a repair, several units show intermittent water pressure and one fixture has a slow drain. You are asked to guide the inspection checks.

options.text: Repeat the first unit's checks on every unit to keep the process moving.
Compare fixtures under similar conditions, record results, and set checks around each symptom.
Test the affected fixtures and record which units show each symptom.
Inspect the slow drain first, then ask the team to check pressure.

basic.situation: A mobile home is ready to move onto its lot, and you are helping the crew position it on the prepared supports.

options.text: Follow the crew's signals and help guide the home onto its supports.
Check the support positions against the layout, then guide the home with the crew.
Ask the operator to pause while you clear loose items near the supports.
Guide the home toward the nearest clear space to save time.

advanced.situation: Two prefabricated units must be set up together on a sloped lot. You are coordinating the hardware reset as the crew aligns them.

options.text: Wait until both units arrive, then reset their doors and drawers together.
Reset each unit's hardware after the crew finishes positioning and leveling it.
Start with stiff doors while the crew levels the second unit on site.
Coordinate the reset after both units align, checking every door and drawer for fit.

basic.situation: You connect a replacement water hose to a unit's inlet pipe and need to test the kitchen fixture before handover.

options.text: Connect the hose and ask the occupant to watch for drips.
Tighten the hose by feel and leave the tap running briefly.
Connect the hose, run the tap, and inspect beneath the joint for leaks.
Seat the hose, run the fixture, and inspect the joint for leaks.

advanced.situation: A replacement appliance system has several connections and a shared water inlet. You are installing it while a trainee prepares the fixtures for testing.

options.text: Connect the shared inlet first, then fit the remaining parts as space permits.
Plan connection order, fit joints, and show the trainee how to test fixtures.
Install the appliance, then ask the trainee to check each fixture and report concerns.
Fit the appliance components, then ask the trainee to check loose connections.

basic.situation: A modular unit has an open side before shipment. You are assigned to cover it with polyethylene sheeting and secure the sheet with nails.

options.text: Lay the sheet evenly, overlap its edges, then nail it firmly in place.
Nail the sheet at the corners and finish the packing task.
Stretch the sheet evenly over the opening, then nail it securely along every edge.
Hold the sheet taut while a coworker nails the nearest edges.

advanced.situation: Several exterior panels are damaged and a frame member is soft near a leak. You are helping organize repairs across a large modular unit.

options.text: Trace the leak, assess the frame, then sequence member repair before panel replacement.
Remove loose panels and ask the lead to decide what repairs follow.
Cover the damaged area with a new panel to keep work on schedule.
Replace the damaged panels and seal around the visible leak.

basic.situation: You find a small water leak at a plastic pipe joint in a unit. You are asked to make a simple repair with guidance.

options.text: Ask a coworker to hold a cloth beneath the joint during testing.
Dry the joint, apply sealant, and check it after water flows.
Add sealant around the damp joint and return the fixture to service.
Shut the supply, inspect the joint, repair it, then test for seepage.

advanced.situation: A unit has intermittent lights and a plumbing leak near the same service area. You are asked to locate faults and plan repairs with the crew.

options.text: Keep the area clear, isolate affected services, and diagnose each fault before repair.
Ask the crew to avoid the area while you test both systems.
Check wiring and piping separately, then record each fault and clearly note its location.
Repair the leak first, then test wiring while the crew works nearby.

basic.situation: A crate must be lifted onto a platform. You are helping attach it to the rigging under the crew lead's direction.

options.text: Check the load points and sling alignment before confirming the attachment with the lead.
Fit the available shackles and ask the lead to inspect them.
Attach the slings to the nearest corners to save setup time.
Choose the marked lifting points and attach the slings as directed.

advanced.situation: A temporary hoist needs repaired pulling gear and a block fixed to an overhead beam. You are assigned to prepare the rigging for a planned lift.

options.text: Inspect gear and beam attachment, then repair and arrange equipment for the planned lift.
Replace worn gear and secure the overhead block before preparing the planned lift.
Repair worn pulling gear and mount the block using the planned rigging layout.
Replace worn gear and ask a coworker to check the block bolts before lifting.

basic.situation: A suspended machine needs to pass a low beam. You are handling a rigging line while the crew lead directs the move.

options.text: Pull the line harder to clear the beam in one movement.
Take up the line gradually as the lead guides the machine past.
Watch the beam closely and call out if the machine gets near it.
Coordinate line tension with the crew, pausing as the machine clears the beam.

advanced.situation: A long load must turn around pipework using several suspension points. You are managing the lines as the crew moves it through a tight bay.

options.text: Adjust each line as needed while watching the load's clearance.
Ask one worker to watch the pipework while you manage the main line.
Coordinate line changes in small stages, keeping the load level and checking clearances.
Pull the front line to start turning, then catch the rear swing.

basic.situation: Before a routine lift, you are asked to test the rigging with a supervisor and record any problems you find.

options.text: Follow the test procedure, check each connection, and report any failure before use.
Check the visible rigging parts and note anything unusual for review.
Use the rigging if it looks serviceable and finish the check later.
Ask the supervisor to test the main sling while you inspect the hooks.

advanced.situation: A new team is preparing several rigging sets for repeated lifts. You are guiding their checks after finding inconsistent inspection records.

options.text: Review the records at the end of the shift and discuss missed checks.
Use the quickest set as a reference and let workers follow its condition.
Have each worker check a rigging set and record any visible defects.
Set a shared check sequence, demonstrate it, and compare records before releasing each set.

basic.situation: You need cables and a winch for a scheduled lift. The load size and work area are listed on the job sheet.

options.text: Ask the store for available cables, then choose one for the load.
Choose gear from the listed load and check its fit with the work area.
Match cable and winch capacity to the load, site, and planned work window.
Use the cable from the previous lift to keep preparation moving.

advanced.situation: Two lifts with different loads share one work area and a narrow time window. You are asked to identify the rigging gear needed for both.

options.text: Ask the crew to bring spare cables while you confirm the winches.
Compare each load, facility limits, and timing, then plan compatible gear between lifts.
Reserve the largest winch for both lifts to simplify the schedule.
List the cables and winches for each load, then check availability.

basic.situation: A machine is ready to load onto a truck after transport. You are asked to clean its exposed surfaces and component parts.

options.text: Brush off loose dirt and load the machine before the truck leaves.
Clean the surfaces, dress marked areas as directed, and keep parts organized.
Wipe exposed surfaces and brush debris from accessible machine components before loading.
Ask a coworker to clean the parts while you prepare the truck bed.

advanced.situation: Several machines need to pass through a narrow opening before loading. You are coordinating their movement and the equipment cleanup between moves.

options.text: Move each machine through with chainfalls, then clean its exposed surfaces.
Use the shortest route and adjust the machine as it reaches the opening.
Clean the machine parts first while another worker guides each move.
Plan clearances, sequence machine moves, and clean exposed parts between passes.

basic.situation: A load is being hoisted onto a platform. You are assigned to signal the workers while the crew lead watches the load.

options.text: Stand visibly, signal clearly, and confirm workers acknowledge each direction.
Use the agreed hand signals and watch the load's path.
Call out directions from beside the platform as the load rises.
Keep signaling upward while workers reposition around the platform.

advanced.situation: A machine must be aligned, leveled, and anchored after a tight hoist. You are coordinating the crew before dismantling and storing the rigging.

options.text: Ask the crew to level the machine, then store the rigging nearby.
Store the rigging while the crew shifts the machine into place.
Have one worker call alignment while you collect the loose rigging.
Coordinate alignment, leveling, and anchoring checks before clearing and storing the rigging.

basic.situation: At a crossing, a signal lamp flickers during a routine check. You are working with a supervisor nearby and have testing equipment ready.

options.text: I would compare the circuit response with the indication while my supervisor observes.
I would reset the interlock and return the signal to service for traffic.
I would test the gate contacts and note any movement that seems delayed.
I would clean the lens, then watch one crossing cycle from the verge.

advanced.situation: An interlock fails intermittently during a busy shift, and a junior technician is ready to replace a relay before the fault is understood.

options.text: I would replace the relay that seems most likely, then monitor the next shift.
I would review recent fault notes and ask the junior to inspect wiring connections.
I would test the interlock through several cycles and record when indications change.
I would reproduce the failure, trace circuit indications, and brief the junior on each safe check.

basic.situation: You are helping test a track circuit after a routine inspection, and the standard diagnostic meter is available at the site.

options.text: I would take a meter reading and compare it with the usual range.
I would follow the test sequence, observe each indication, and log the readings.
I would check the connections and repeat the meter reading with my senior.
I would bridge the circuit briefly to confirm whether the track indication clears.

advanced.situation: A track circuit passes its initial test but drops intermittently when a train passes. The team needs a reliable way to investigate the fault.

options.text: I would adjust the circuit until the indication stays steady during one passage.
I would inspect the connections and record readings during repeated train passages.
I would repeat the initial test and ask another technician to watch the display.
I would compare readings across operating conditions and set a repeatable team test log.

basic.situation: A crossing lamp is out during a scheduled service visit. You have a replacement bulb and a senior technician is available for guidance.

options.text: I would replace the bulb and check that the lamp illuminates during a test.
I would clean the lens and leave the lamp for the next service visit.
I would fit the available bulb and note whether it lights after switching.
I would check the lamp connection and ask the senior to confirm the bulb type.

advanced.situation: A replacement lamp stays dark, and you find a loose connection beside brittle wiring. A junior technician is waiting for your repair guidance.

options.text: I would isolate the repair area, replace damaged wiring, and show the junior safe checks.
I would tighten the connection, then ask the junior to check the lamp response.
I would secure the loose joint with tape and return the crossing to service.
I would replace the connection and record the lamp test result for the senior.

basic.situation: A gate-crossing mechanism moves noisily during a scheduled visit. You have lubricant and your senior has shown you the service points.

options.text: I would apply a small amount at the nearest hinge and note the noise.
I would listen through another cycle and ask the senior where to lubricate.
I would add lubricant near the noise and leave the gate for later checks.
I would lubricate the marked moving parts and watch the gate complete a cycle.

advanced.situation: Several crossing gates show increasing resistance between service visits. A new technician asks how you would plan lubrication work for the route.

options.text: I would review service dates and ask the new technician to record gate resistance.
I would add more lubricant at the stiffest gates and review them next month.
I would schedule every gate for the same monthly lubrication and brief the new technician.
I would list the mechanisms and propose service intervals based on observed movement and wear.

basic.situation: During a scheduled visit, you inspect a signal battery with a senior technician and notice its connection appears loose.

options.text: I would note the loose connection and plan to check it next visit.
I would inspect the terminals with the senior, secure the connection, and recheck it.
I would replace the battery now and place the old one with general scrap.
I would tighten the connection and record the battery condition for the senior.

advanced.situation: Several signal batteries are nearing replacement, but recent condition notes vary by site. You are preparing a route plan with a senior technician.

options.text: I would replace the oldest batteries first and record the new installation dates.
I would schedule replacements by age and update the route sheet for the team.
I would swap batteries across sites to spread the remaining service life evenly.
I would check each battery condition, compare service notes, and propose replacements by need.

basic.situation: You drive to a signal repair site and help record the track inspected, mileage, and a lamp replacement on the service sheet.

options.text: I would write the track section and repair, then check mileage with the driver.
I would enter the mileage, track section, and lamp repair before returning the sheet.
I would note the mileage and ask the senior to fill in the repair details.
I would record the repair and estimate the mileage from the route map.

advanced.situation: A maintenance audit finds several route sheets with mismatched mileage and missing replacement notes. You are asked to coach staff on future records.

options.text: I would send the mismatched sheets to the senior and pause further audit work.
I would list missing fields and ask each technician to review their own sheets.
I would compare sheets with available trip details and teach staff a consistent entry format.
I would amend the mileage from memory and tell staff to add clearer notes.

basic.situation: A pump sounds uneven during a routine shift. You are assigned to observe its operation and have a basic meter nearby.

options.text: I would observe the cycle, check the visible readings, and report any change.
I would adjust the wiring until the pump runs quietly through one cycle.
I would watch one more cycle and record the sound for maintenance staff.
I would note the sound and ask the operator whether it is usual.

advanced.situation: A machine trips intermittently after a component replacement. You are a helper with electrical experience, and the maintenance team needs the fault diagnosed.

options.text: I would bridge the suspected component so production can continue during the shift.
I would compare the wiring with the machine plan, test safely, and verify operation.
I would trace the supply and component connections, then document the fault conditions.
I would swap the component again and monitor whether the machine trips later.

basic.situation: After a repair, your bench and hand tools are dusty, and another job is waiting for the same work area.

options.text: I would brush the tools and clear the bench before setting up.
I would wipe the tools and bench with a clean cloth before the next job.
I would clean the hand tools and ask the next worker to clear the bench.
I would sweep the bench and leave the tools beside the next machine.

advanced.situation: A repaired steel assembly will sit in a damp store before installation. You are asked to apply protection and choose a suitable product from the approved supplies.

options.text: I would ask the storekeeper which coating was used on similar assemblies.
I would coat the visible face with the first available spray and stack it away.
I would check the approved product guidance, prepare the surfaces, and cover exposed areas.
I would apply the usual oil to the assembly and label the treatment date.

basic.situation: A technician asks for a wrench and replacement washers at a work station. You are carrying supplies from the nearby tool store.

options.text: I would bring the requested wrench and washers to the station and check quantities.
I would take the wrench over and ask which washers are needed there.
I would bring the wrench and washers listed on the job slip.
I would leave a mixed box of tools near the station for quick access.

advanced.situation: Two repair jobs are due tomorrow, and the stock count shows few replacement filters. You help maintain the parts inventory and can prepare a reorder request.

options.text: I would check stock and job needs, then request enough filters with a count record.
I would borrow filters from another work area and update the count later.
I would count the filters and ask the lead what quantity to order.
I would request the usual quantity and update the stock sheet after delivery.

basic.situation: A machine guard has a loose handle, and a replacement handle and hand tools are ready at your work station.

options.text: I would fit the handle with the supplied fasteners and check its movement.
I would secure the handle with spare wire so the machine can run.
I would remove the old handle and ask the technician to fit the replacement.
I would tighten the handle bolts and ask the operator to check the guard.

advanced.situation: A gearbox has been repaired by a skilled worker and is ready for reassembly. You are assigned to support the work using the parts and hand tools provided.

options.text: I would follow the disassembly order, fit the parts, and check movement with the worker.
I would reassemble the gearbox from memory and test it after installation.
I would install the returned parts and ask the worker to inspect the assembly.
I would pass the parts as requested and keep the work area clear.

basic.situation: A technician is fitting a small pump onto a marked base. You are asked to hold the pump steady and supply the next tool.

options.text: I would hold the pump at the marks and pass the requested tool when ready.
I would hold the pump steady and ask which tool comes next.
I would pass the tool first and steady the pump after the adjustment.
I would release the pump to reach the tool tray beside the base.

advanced.situation: A large machine must align with anchor marks before installation. You are helping position it with a technician using jacks and hand tools.

options.text: I would check the marks and guide the technician during each positioning adjustment.
I would check anchor marks, guide each jack adjustment, and verify position with the technician.
I would shift the machine toward the marks and let the technician check alignment.
I would coordinate jack adjustments against marks and confirm position with the technician.

basic.situation: A disconnected hose and a labeled wire must be reconnected after a routine service. You have the correct hand tools and the work plan.

options.text: I would connect the wire to the nearest terminal and tighten the hose clamp.
I would reconnect both parts by their labels and record the work completed.
I would match the labels and plan, reconnect both parts, and check their fit.
I would reconnect the labeled wire and ask the technician to confirm the hose.

advanced.situation: A custom bracket is needed to fit a replacement assembly. You are asked to fabricate it from a mechanical plan using the workshop's approved welding setup.

options.text: I would measure the old bracket and ask the technician to review my layout.
I would check the plan dimensions, mark the stock, and fabricate the bracket to match.
I would cut matching scrap metal and weld a bracket based on the old part.
I would prepare the stock and weld a close-fitting bracket for the assembly.

basic.situation: You are helping lay a geothermal loop pipe, and the trench depth looks different from the marked plan. What do you do?

options.text: I would lay the pipe at the current depth to keep the crew moving.
I would check the depth with my senior, then lay the pipe together.
I would compare the depth with the plan before laying pipe.
I would measure one section and use that depth along the trench.

advanced.situation: A long loop trench crosses uneven ground, and the pressure test is due before backfill. How do you oversee the work?

options.text: I would review depths, inspect joints, and confirm pressure results before backfill.
I would ask the crew to finish backfill, then review the test sheet.
I would check the pressure readings and sample several trench sections.
I would inspect the joints and ask the crew about any depth changes.

basic.situation: A small property needs heating, and you are comparing compressor options for the proposed geothermal system. What do you do?

options.text: I would match compressor capacity to the stated heating need and seek review.
I would compare the compressor options with the senior's equipment guidance.
I would list the available compressors and ask which one is common.
I would choose the familiar compressor to keep the proposal moving.

advanced.situation: A commercial site has uneven heating needs across several buildings. You must recommend a geothermal loop type. What do you do?

options.text: I would compare loop types against the site's heating and cooling profile.
I would select the loop type used on the nearest commercial site.
I would ask the team which loop type has worked well on similar jobs.
I would map building loads, site limits, and loop choices in one comparison.

basic.situation: You are assisting with a residential heat pump, and its control wiring differs from the installation drawing. What do you do?

options.text: I would check the drawing with my supervisor before changing any wiring.
I would connect the matching wire colours and continue the installation.
I would compare the terminals with the drawing and note the difference.
I would ask a nearby installer how this model is usually wired.

advanced.situation: A geothermal heat pump serves space heating and a hot water tank, but the tank temperature keeps falling. What do you do?

options.text: I would trace the heat exchange connections and test each system's operation.
I would raise the pump setting to restore hot water more quickly.
I would inspect the tank connections and ask the building operator about usage.
I would check the tank sensor and compare readings with the controller.

basic.situation: During your shift, a geothermal plant gauge reading drifts from its usual range. What do you do?

options.text: I would compare this reading with the previous shift's log before adjusting.
I would record the reading and ask the senior technician to review it.
I would compare the gauge with the operating range before making an adjustment.
I would note the reading and adjust the control to its usual setting.

advanced.situation: Power demand rises while plant output approaches its usual limit. You are adjusting production systems within your shift authority. What do you do?

options.text: I would raise output to meet the new demand before the next reading.
I would check the latest load data and make a measured output adjustment.
I would ask the control room which output setting handled similar demand.
I would review load readings and adjust output within the plant's operating limits.

basic.situation: A newly installed geothermal loop is ready for flushing, but the water still looks cloudy. What do you do?

options.text: I would continue flushing until the water appears clearer to the team.
I would follow the flushing procedure and check its stated completion conditions.
I would stop flushing and mark the system ready for the next check.
I would record the cloudy water and ask the supervising technician what follows.

advanced.situation: A scheduled switchgear check is due, and one gauge reading is outside its usual range. What do you do?

options.text: I would record the reading and arrange a gauge check during this round.
I would log the reading, check the procedure, and compare related indicators.
I would compare the gauge with its last recorded value before noting it.
I would enter the usual reading so the maintenance log stays consistent.

basic.situation: Your shift log needs the geothermal plant's operating data, but one meter reading is hard to read. What do you do?

options.text: I would copy the reading after asking a coworker what the meter shows.
I would record the visible reading and mark the unclear digit for checking.
I would note the meter issue and record the other operating data.
I would estimate the unclear reading from the previous shift's entry.

advanced.situation: Weekly plant reports show power output falling while flow readings stay steady. You are asked to prepare a team report. What do you do?

options.text: I would ask the team which readings should appear in the weekly report.
I would list this week's output and flow readings in the report.
I would compare dated output and flow records, then show the trend clearly.
I would report the lower output and carry forward last week's flow figure.

basic.situation: At shift end, you record attendance and output, but one operator’s hours are missing from the handover sheet.

options.text: Ask the operator to confirm the hours, then finish the entry.
Check the shift log and time record, then flag any mismatch for review.
Leave the hours blank and note that the entry needs follow-up.
Enter the hours from yesterday’s sheet so the daily report can go out.

advanced.situation: A safety audit finds inconsistent machine checks across shifts, while production records show repeated stoppages on one line.

options.text: Copy the latest completed sheet for shifts with missing machine checks.
Remind each shift to complete its existing machine check sheet more carefully.
Ask the line leads to explain the gaps before updating the audit notes.
Compare check sheets with stoppage records and propose a consistent log for each shift.

basic.situation: A parts delivery is delayed, and the next shift asks whether its scheduled work can still start on time.

options.text: Check nearby departments for available stock, then share the confirmed start plan.
Tell the next shift the delivery is late and ask them to wait for instructions.
Repeat the supplier’s estimated arrival time and keep the current schedule posted.
Tell the next shift to borrow parts from the nearest line for now.

advanced.situation: Two departments dispute responsibility for a recurring handover error, and both supervisors say their workers are being blamed unfairly.

options.text: Review both accounts and handover records, then agree on a shared fix with both supervisors.
Reassign the named worker after hearing both supervisors’ accounts and checking shift needs.
Ask each supervisor to discuss the complaint with their workers and report back.
Meet both supervisors, review a recent example, and assign the next handover check.

basic.situation: A work order calls for a set output, and you notice a gauge reading near the line’s marked limit.

options.text: Check the work order and gauge range, then alert the operator to the reading.
Ask the operator whether this reading is normal for the current batch.
Record the reading at the next routine check and keep the line running.
Continue the run while watching the gauge at the usual intervals.

advanced.situation: Three batches show similar defects, but the work orders differ and the machine gauge readings vary between shifts.

options.text: Compare defect samples, work orders, and shift readings to identify a pattern for review.
Ask each shift to watch the gauge more closely during the next run.
Review the latest batch readings and request a repeat inspection of its output.
Use the average gauge reading from all shifts as the new monitoring target.

basic.situation: A new operator repeatedly pauses to check each step, slowing the line during a routine task you are observing.

options.text: Record the pauses in shift notes and discuss the pattern during the next review.
Ask what feels unclear, demonstrate the step, and observe one more attempt.
Flag today’s pace for review after checking the expected time for this task.
Compare task output with a trained operator doing the same routine task.

advanced.situation: A team meets its output target, but equipment stoppages and rework are rising, and one experienced operator is struggling with a changed method.

options.text: Review output, stoppages, and rework with the operator; agree on a measurable plan.
Raise the output target to recover time lost to stoppages without first checking causes.
Ask maintenance for stoppage figures before reviewing the operator’s recent results.
Coach the operator on the changed method and check progress next week.

basic.situation: One operator calls in sick, and you need to assign today’s jobs while keeping the posted production sequence.

options.text: Keep assignments unchanged and ask the team to increase pace across today’s jobs.
Move the available operator to the urgent job and tell the team about changes.
Check training coverage, then adjust assignments while preserving the posted production sequence.
Assign the absent worker’s jobs to whoever finishes their current task first.

advanced.situation: A new product may fit the line, but a pilot would require different sequencing, extra setup time, and a cost estimate for management.

options.text: Plan pilot sequencing, setup needs, and cost assumptions for management review.
Schedule the product on the current line and track actual costs during production.
Ask operators to suggest a sequence before preparing a rough cost estimate.
Estimate extra labour hours and ask management whether the product fits the budget.

basic.situation: A new worker is assigned to a familiar machine, but has not yet practised its start-up and shutdown steps.

options.text: Demonstrate the sequence, then watch the worker practise the start-up and shutdown.
Give the worker the machine guide and ask them to read it before starting.
Explain the main controls and let the worker learn the sequence during the shift.
Walk the worker through start-up and ask an experienced operator to cover shutdown.

advanced.situation: A revised job order changes the installation sequence, and several workers are unsure which specification applies to their assigned units.

options.text: Read the revised job order aloud, then confirm each worker’s assigned specification and sequence.
Use the prior sequence only after confirming it still matches the revised order.
Ask experienced workers to explain the drawing to their own teams.
Check the revised order against the approved drawing, then brief teams on sequence.

basic.situation: You are assembling a prefabricated bracket subassembly, and the shift is nearly over.

options.text: Use the closest matching bolts and finish the subassembly before the shift change.
Check the parts against the drawing, then assemble them in the shown sequence.
Ask a nearby assembler to confirm each fitting while you build the unit.
Fit the parts by hand, then tighten fasteners evenly to keep work moving.

advanced.situation: You are leading a complex subassembly build with two new assemblers and several joining points.

options.text: Split the subassembly into stations and review fit at the handoff points.
Let experienced staff choose fasteners from their usual kits to save time.
Demonstrate one difficult joint, then have each assembler repeat the sequence.
Walk the team through the drawing sequence, checking interfaces before each join.

basic.situation: You are locating a bracket from a simple assembly drawing before marking its position.

options.text: Compare the part number and view label before choosing the bracket location.
Position it beside the similar bracket and copy that spacing for now.
Ask a teammate to point out the bracket on the assembly drawing.
Use the blueprint callout to identify the bracket, then mark its location.

advanced.situation: Two specification views place a bracket differently, and your team is waiting for layout marks before cutting nearby material.

options.text: Use the clearer view and keep the team moving with its layout.
Shift the bracket marks slightly so both views appear to align.
Compare both views and ask the lead which datum controls this location.
Check revisions, trace dimensions to the stated datum, and flag the conflict before marking.

basic.situation: You are assigned to check a newly installed panel for fit and alignment before the next assembly step.

options.text: Check the main gap with a ruler and tell the assembler if it looks tight.
Run a quick visual check and pass the unit along for the next step.
Measure the installed unit against the drawing dimensions and record the fit.
Use a caliper at the specified points and compare readings with the work sheet.

advanced.situation: During a critical system audit, you find crews recording different checks on otherwise similar installations.

options.text: Align checks with approved criteria, record evidence, and propose one shared checklist.
Use the familiar crew sheet as the shared reference for inspection checks.
Sample critical units against approved criteria and track every identified gap.
Draft a checklist from crew entries and ask the lead to review it.

basic.situation: Your work card calls for cleaning and light oiling a valve part before it joins a subassembly.

options.text: Use the open degreaser nearby and apply light oil to save setup time.
Ask a teammate which bottle is used, then prepare the part for assembly.
Wipe the valve with an approved cloth and oil its moving surfaces.
Confirm the part marking, use the named cleaner, then apply specified oil.

advanced.situation: New staff are preparing a sensitive component whose work card specifies cleaning steps and a particular oil.

options.text: Show new staff the usual wipe and oil routine before their shift starts.
Reuse the general component checklist and add the sensitive part's oil name.
Pair each trainee with an assembler who already knows the preparation sequence.
Draft a component specific checklist from its work card and demonstrate each preparation step.

basic.situation: A work card gives a trim dimension for a small panel edge that must clear an adjoining part.

options.text: Measure from the drawing datum, mark the trim line, and cut to length.
Cut the edge to match the adjoining panel by eye and continue assembly.
Use the neighboring panel as a quick size guide before filing the edge.
Trim to the marked line, then file the edge smooth for a trial fit.

advanced.situation: Approved edge dressing is allowed, but two panels still interfere near a fastener row.

options.text: Measure the interference and ask the lead to confirm the allowed removal.
Enlarge the fastener opening slightly so the panels pull together during fitting.
Use transfer marks to find contact, remove permitted material, then recheck clearance.
File the visible high spot lightly and fit the panels again.

basic.situation: You have a template and jig for marking installation points on a replacement access panel. The template looks reversible, and drilling follows your marks.

options.text: Check the template orientation against the panel datum, then mark each point.
Ask the fitter to confirm which side of the template faces outward.
Trace the template from its reverse face to save resetting the jig.
Line up the jig with the panel edge and mark its reference points.

advanced.situation: A major repair uses an unfamiliar panel layout, and the approved repair drawing gives several datums and a staged replacement sequence.

options.text: Lay out each panel section from its nearest edge and share the marks.
Mark the primary datum first and ask the lead to review the sequence.
Map the datums and sequence from the approved drawing, then brief the repair team.
Copy the nearest model's layout and adjust marks to match the damaged panel.

basic.situation: You are asked to start a coiling machine for a routine batch. The setup card lists the wire and winding settings for this job.

options.text: I ask a nearby operator to confirm the machine is ready before starting.
I use the previous batch settings and start winding while the line is ready.
I check the wire type and start the machine using the displayed settings.
I check the setup card and wire, then start the machine as instructed.

advanced.situation: A coil’s turns are uneven, and the machine has paused twice. The work card lists the target winding settings, but the next batch is due soon.

options.text: I inspect the wire feed for snags and report both pauses to the lead.
I use listed settings and monitor the first coil after restarting the machine.
I compare the winding pattern and settings with the card, then inspect the feed path.
I adjust tension by eye until turns look even, then restart the batch.

basic.situation: You are trimming wire leads from a finished coil. The sample shows the required length, and the coil is waiting for inspection.

options.text: I trim both leads to the sample length and inspect each cut end.
I compare one lead with the sample, then trim the other to match.
I cut both leads near the sample length and place the coil in the tray.
I trim both ends evenly and ask a nearby operator to check the coil.

advanced.situation: Several coils have wire leads of uneven length after trimming. The batch is still at your station, and the finishing guide gives a target length.

options.text: I measure a sample against the guide, then rework and recheck each affected coil.
I shorten every lead to the same length I see on the neatest coil.
I sort the coils by appearance and rework the shortest leads first.
I show the finishing guide to the team and ask them to trim more evenly.

basic.situation: You receive a work order for a coil batch. It lists wire type and insulation, and the materials are stored in similar-looking reels.

options.text: I compare both reel labels with the work order and ask the lead about mismatches.
I check the wire label and ask a teammate which insulation reel is used.
I choose the reel resembling the last batch and start preparing the coil.
I match the wire and insulation labels with the work order before selecting reels.

advanced.situation: A work order lists a wire type that differs from the type named in its attached specification. Production is waiting for you to confirm the materials.

options.text: I ask the lead which document production normally follows for this coil type.
I use the wire listed on the work order because it controls the batch.
I compare the order and specification, then flag the mismatch before materials are issued.
I set aside the wire reels and prepare the insulation while waiting for guidance.

basic.situation: You are loading a coiling machine for a routine run. The setup sheet identifies the wire reel and the guide used for this batch.

options.text: I compare the reel and guide with the sheet, then load them in sequence.
I load the reel used for the previous run and set the guide beside it.
I match the reel and guide to the setup sheet before loading them.
I check the reel label and load the guide that is already at the machine.

advanced.situation: Two machines need different wire reels, and a changeover is due during your shift. Both setup sheets are available, and an operator is new to the sequence.

options.text: I stage the earlier reel first and keep the second reel near its machine.
I stage both reels by the machines and let the operator load whichever is ready.
I label each reel from its setup sheet and ask the operator to follow the posted sequence.
I sequence the reels by each machine’s changeover needs and walk the operator through the labels.

basic.situation: A completed coil is ready to remove from the machine. The machine has stopped, and the work instruction names a hand tool for release.

options.text: I use the named tool to release the coil and support it onto the tray.
I use the named tool and place the coil on the nearest open surface.
I pull the coil free by its lead wires and set it beside the machine.
I release the coil with the tool and ask a teammate to receive it.

advanced.situation: Finished coils are accumulating after a machine stop, and a new operator is helping with removal. The hand tool and padded tray are at the station.

options.text: I ask the operator to use the tool and place each coil on the tray.
I let the operator pull the coils free quickly so the machine can restart.
I show the operator the release tool and tray, then review the first removal.
I remove the waiting coils myself and leave the operator to watch the next one.

basic.situation: You are completing the production form after a coil run. The machine counter and batch card show the quantities, and one field asks for rejected coils.

options.text: I enter both quantities from the batch card and pass the form along.
I estimate the rejects from the tray and complete the remaining fields.
I copy the total and reject count from the records, then check the entries match.
I enter the total from the counter and leave the reject field for later.

advanced.situation: You notice several production forms use different names for the same machine stop. The shift records are due, and the downtime totals may be affected.

options.text: I compare each entry with the shift notes, clarify ambiguous stops, and record the agreed terms.
I use the most common label for each form and submit the shift records.
I standardize the labels from memory and update the downtime totals on each form.
I flag the different labels and ask the lead how the team should record them.

basic.situation: A simple work order lists a control unit and wiring, but you are unsure which parts to stage. What do you do?

options.text: Mark unclear symbols and confirm the required materials before issuing parts.
Use the familiar cabinet layout and begin with available components.
Ask a nearby assembler which parts usually fit this model.
Check the work order against the drawing, then stage listed parts.

advanced.situation: A schematic revision and the connector labels on a delivered batch disagree, while the line is waiting. How do you handle the discrepancy?

options.text: Ask engineering to interpret the drawing while teammates continue unaffected work.
Record each mismatch by reference and hold affected assemblies for correction.
Compare the schematic revision with the physical connector labels first.
Fit the connector that matches most pins, then flag remaining mismatch.

basic.situation: A tray of parts has oily residue, and you are asked to prepare them for wiring. What do you do?

options.text: Clean parts with approved solution, then dry and arrange them on cloth.
Blow away residue and send the parts to the wiring station.
Confirm the solution with the lead, then clean and dry parts as directed.
Wipe the visible surfaces and place the parts on a labeled tray.

advanced.situation: Misaligned parts have caused repeated wiring delays on your team’s station. How could you improve their positioning and preparation flow?

options.text: Let each assembler position parts using their preferred order and tools.
Ask the lead to remind the team to align parts more carefully.
Trace the misalignments to handling steps, then standardize tray orientation and checks.
Move the alignment check closer to the wiring station during each batch.

basic.situation: A bracket needs two mounting holes marked on its drawing. You have a drill and calipers, with a lead nearby. What do you do?

options.text: Use the old bracket to mark hole locations, then drill them.
Mark the locations from the drawing and prepare the drill for review.
Verify the drawing dimensions with the lead, then mark and drill the holes.
Measure the marked locations with calipers and ask the lead to check.

advanced.situation: Several brackets show holes drifting from their specified positions, and new staff are joining the job. How do you address the fabrication work?

options.text: Compare drift patterns with setup steps, then demonstrate a checked marking sequence.
Ask staff to follow the marks they find easiest to reach.
Tell the lead that the drill setup may need a fresh check.
Check a few brackets with calipers and share the measurements at handover.

basic.situation: You are fitting a small unit and its wiring into a casing, but one bolt does not seat smoothly. What do you do?

options.text: Set the unit aside and assemble another casing while checking the parts.
Check the assembly drawing and seat the unit with the specified bolts.
Use a nearby longer bolt to secure the unit and continue wiring.
Pause fitting, compare the bolt and casing holes, then ask the lead if unclear.

advanced.situation: A batch of assembled units fails its fit check at the casing joint, though wiring appears correct. How do you help resolve the assembly issue?

options.text: Inspect the joint and compare fastening points with a passing unit.
Tighten each joint further and send the units back for checking.
Trace the failed joint through fit and fastening steps, then share the verified method.
Ask the lead to review the joint while the team checks wiring.

basic.situation: A unit fails a check because one component is faulty, and the repair guide shows a replacement procedure. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the lead to confirm the listed replacement before opening the unit for repair.
Follow the guide to replace the component, then record the repair.
Match the replacement to the guide and verify the unit’s check.
Ask the lead to confirm the replacement before you open the unit.

advanced.situation: The same loose connection has returned on several units after repair. You are asked to help reduce repeat defects. What do you do?

options.text: Compare repair records and assembly points, then share the verified fix.
Tighten each connection slightly more before running the next check.
Tell the lead that the recurring connection needs another review.
Repair the next connection and record affected units, symptoms, and each repair result.

basic.situation: A work order changes the assembly sequence, and you are unsure whether your station should begin with wiring or casing. What do you do?

options.text: Show the changed sequence to the lead and relay confirmed steps to peers.
Review the revised work order and ask the lead to confirm the station sequence.
Ask a nearby assembler how they interpret today’s revised sequence at this station.
Use yesterday’s sequence to keep the station moving until the lead clarifies.

advanced.situation: Two stations use different assembly sequences, causing repeated handoff delays. You are asked to help the team review the issue. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the lead which station should revise its sequence first today.
Map handoff steps with both stations and agree on shared update points.
Tell each station to keep its sequence and work around delays.
Collect examples of delayed handoffs from both stations and share them with the lead.

basic.situation: You are starting a small motor frame and need to identify the bracket and bolts shown on its assembly drawing.

options.text: Use the kit contents sheet to choose a likely bracket and bolts.
Compare the bracket label with the parts list before asking the lead.
Take the bracket that looks closest and begin the frame assembly.
Check the drawing's part number, then collect the listed bracket and bolts.

advanced.situation: A drawing shows two different sequences for fitting a motor cover, and the next shift is waiting for your staging plan.

options.text: Check the revision and related views, then propose a sequence for specified interfaces.
Use the first sequence shown to keep the team moving.
Pause at the callout, compare views, and record the sequence conflict for review.
Ask the lead which view to use before staging parts.

basic.situation: You have been asked to attach a name plate to a control box, and the work sheet marks its location.

options.text: Measure from the marked edge and attach the plate at the shown location.
Place the plate near the marked area where it reads clearly.
Check the work sheet location, then align the plate with the box edge.
Attach it where the previous box's plate appears to sit.

advanced.situation: A new product line uses three similar housings, and two assemblers have marked their identification plates in different places.

options.text: Copy placement from the closest existing model after checking its drawing.
Set a shared location from the drawing, then show how to mark plates.
Mark one sample housing, then have others follow that plate position.
Let each assembler use a flat spot that seems clear on the housing.

basic.situation: You are checking a shaft diameter with a caliper, and the work sheet gives the target dimension.

options.text: Take a reading and ask the supervisor whether it seems acceptable.
Measure the shaft once and use the nearest whole number on the display.
Zero the caliper, measure the shaft, and compare the reading with the target.
Check the target first, then take a caliper reading for the supervisor.

advanced.situation: A precision instrument reads differently from the reference block, while a batch of motor shafts is waiting for tolerance checks.

options.text: Check calibration status and the reference block, then hold readings pending review.
Adjust the instrument to match, then measure the waiting shafts.
Use a second caliper on several shafts and note the mismatch.
Repeat the reference reading and record the difference for the quality technician.

basic.situation: You are fitting a small cover to a motor frame, and the assembly steps show which edge should line up.

options.text: Seat the cover against the shown edge, then fasten it with the specified screws.
Fit the cover by eye and tighten the screws to finish quickly.
Align the cover with the frame and start each screw by hand.
Start the screws while holding the cover close to the frame edge.

advanced.situation: A tight gearbox bracket shifts as you tighten it, and a junior assembler is waiting to learn your fastening method.

options.text: Hold the bracket steady as the junior tightens the nearest screws.
Loosen the screws, realign the bracket, then tighten them in turn.
Reseat the bracket on reference faces, fasten evenly, and explain the method.
Tighten one side firmly first to keep the bracket from moving.

basic.situation: You are connecting a cable to a motor control box, and its label matches one port listed on the wiring sheet.

options.text: Check the port label, then ask another assembler to confirm the match.
Match the cable label to its listed motor port before connecting.
Follow the wiring sheet and check the port label before you connect the cable.
Use the port that fits the plug and route the cable neatly.

advanced.situation: Two wiring diagrams show different connector routes on a new unit, and the test bench is booked for the afternoon.

options.text: Trace both routes against connector labels and report the conflict with a sketch.
Flag both routes and ask the lead to choose the documented path.
Compare diagram revisions and connector labels, then map the confirmed route before connecting.
Use the shortest route shown and continue the unit's assembly.

basic.situation: You are helping open a motor unit so a damaged fan can be replaced, and the senior assembler is supervising.

options.text: Follow the disassembly order and keep removed parts grouped for refitting.
Lay out a tray and remove the listed cover fasteners in sequence.
Ask the senior which fasteners to remove before opening the unit.
Remove the fan cover first because it is closest to the damaged part.

advanced.situation: A completed unit has a noisy fan before crating, and the packing team needs your inspection findings and disassembly notes.

options.text: Run the fan again and crate the unit if noise fades.
Inspect the fan area and list each fastener to remove before crating.
Record the noise, inspect checks, and note parts removed for crating.
Tell packing about the noise and ask them to hold crating.

basic.situation: You are assembling an engine mount and need to identify the plate and bolts shown on its blueprint.

options.text: Choose the plate with the closest shape and begin fitting the mount.
Match the part numbers on the blueprint before collecting the plate and bolts.
Use the stock list to pick the most likely plate and bolt set.
Compare the stock list with the drawing, then check a doubtful part with the lead.

advanced.situation: The engine assembly plan shows different fitting orders for a fuel pipe bracket, and your team is staging parts for the next build.

options.text: Follow the order on the first page so staging can continue on schedule.
Compare revisions and connected views, then propose the order that fits the assembly interfaces.
Trace each bracket view and note where the two fitting orders differ.
Mark the conflicting steps and ask the lead which order to use.

basic.situation: You are checking a machined pin with a caliper, and the blueprint lists its target diameter.

options.text: Measure once and round the display to the nearest whole number.
Take a reading, then ask the senior worker if it looks acceptable.
Check the target diameter, then take a caliper reading for review.
Zero the caliper, measure the pin, and compare the reading with the blueprint.

advanced.situation: A gauge disagrees with its reference, and several engine bushings are waiting for your dimensional checks before assembly.

options.text: Adjust the gauge until the reference reading matches and check the bushings.
Repeat the reference check and record the readings for the quality technician.
Use a second gauge on a few bushings while noting the mismatch.
Verify the gauge status and reference condition, then hold measurements until the discrepancy is understood.

basic.situation: You are positioning a heavy engine cover with a hoist, and the assembly drawing shows its locating face.

options.text: Lower the cover near the mount and adjust it once it rests.
Align the locating face to the drawing and guide the cover into place.
Check the locating face, then signal the hoist operator to lower slowly.
Lower it where the bolt holes look close enough to line up.

advanced.situation: A long engine rail needs several drilled holes, and the first layout mark is close to the edge shown on the plan.

options.text: Measure the first mark again and ask a teammate to compare it.
Recheck the plan dimensions and edge references, then confirm the layout before drilling.
Drill from the first mark and adjust later holes to fit the rail.
Mark the hole pattern, then review the spacing with the senior assembler.

basic.situation: You are installing a short pipe section on an engine subassembly, and the work sheet identifies its fittings and fasteners.

options.text: Start fastening the listed fittings and check the work sheet afterward.
Match each fitting to the work sheet, then secure the pipe section.
Check the fitting list against the work sheet before fastening the pipe section.
Use the fittings that sit most neatly against the pipe section.

advanced.situation: A wiring bundle and fixture share a crowded engine frame, and your junior colleague is unsure which fasteners to install first.

options.text: Fasten the fixture first, leaving the bundle room to move around the frame.
Route the bundle as specified, position the fixture, then secure both safely.
Check the specified route and fastener locations before securing the fixture in place.
Ask the junior to hold the bundle while you fasten the fixture securely.

basic.situation: You are smoothing a rough spot on a machined bracket so it will fit its mating part.

options.text: File the rough area gently, checking its fit against the mating part.
Use the power grinder to remove the spot in a few passes.
Use the specified hand tool lightly, checking the mating fit as you smooth.
Smooth the spot with a hand file, then compare it with the mating part.

advanced.situation: A curved engine cover has rough edges near a sealing surface, and a teammate asks which finishing method to use.

options.text: Recommend a fine file near the seal, then inspect the full edge afterward carefully.
Ask the teammate to try a file on a small section first.
Protect the seal, use a controlled hand tool, and check the finished fit.
Use a fine abrasive on the rough edge, keeping clear of the sealing surface.

basic.situation: You are inspecting a completed pump assembly, and its test sheet lists the checks to complete before handover.

options.text: Run the listed checks and record any result that differs from the sheet.
Check the pump casing and ask the senior whether it seems ready.
Operate the pump briefly and pass it along if it sounds normal.
Review the test sheet, then inspect the pump casing for any visible defects.

advanced.situation: A tested engine assembly fails its clearance check after repair, and another unit is waiting on the same bench.

options.text: Record the failed reading and ask the lead which part needs further inspection.
Repeat the clearance check, trace parts, and record the cause before repair.
Adjust the closest part until the clearance reading falls within range.
Recheck clearance and inspect the related assembly for signs of visible damage.

basic.situation: You need plate for a small bracket, and the blueprint shows dimensions and a material note. You are unsure which stock matches the drawing.

options.text: I compare the material note with available stock and ask a fitter about the dimensions.
I check the drawing revision and dimensions against the job sheet before selecting stock.
I match the drawing dimensions and material note to the stock label.
I use the grade from a similar bracket job and cut that stock.

advanced.situation: Two drawing views give different hole locations on a support frame. Your crew is waiting to mark the pieces, and the latest revision is unclear.

options.text: I trace dimensions and revision notes, then explain the agreed reading to the crew.
I compare both views and revision notes, then flag the conflict before marking.
I pause marking and ask the lead fitter which view the crew should follow.
I follow the clearer dimensions and tell the crew to proceed.

basic.situation: A flat steel strip needs a simple cut line for a bracket. You have the drawing, a ruler, and a guide, but the stock edge is rough.

options.text: I measure the length with a ruler and mark a straight line from the stock end.
I mark from the rough edge and keep the line close to the drawing size.
I square one clean edge, measure the drawing length, and mark with the guide.
I measure from the nearest edge and ask a fitter to check my mark.

advanced.situation: Several brackets must be cut from one sheet, with different bend lines and narrow margins. You are asked to lay them out before the shear is set.

options.text: I mark each bracket from a shared edge and check the first layout.
I place largest brackets first, then fit smaller pieces into open areas.
I arrange the parts by eye, leaving room for the shear blade.
I map cuts and bend allowances, then verify clearances against the drawing.

basic.situation: A small steel plate needs a straight edge cleaned on the grinder. Your senior has set up the machine and asked you to finish the piece.

options.text: I hold the plate firmly and grind until the edge looks smooth.
I use the grinder from a similar job and remove the rough edge quickly.
I follow the mark and pause to compare the plate with the drawing.
I grind the marked edge in short passes, checking the shape as I go.

advanced.situation: A drill press starts cutting off-centre on a batch of frame plates. The crew needs the parts soon, and you are responsible for the machine setup.

options.text: I adjust the table by eye and finish at a slower feed.
I stop cutting, secure a test piece, and compare setup with the drawing.
I check workholding, table alignment, and drill condition, then test scrap before resuming.
I stop the press and ask the lead to inspect alignment.

basic.situation: A short angle must sit on a jig for welding. You are helping position it, and the senior fitter asks you to secure the piece.

options.text: I align the angle with the jig edge and ask the fitter to check.
I clamp the angle against jig stops and check that it sits flat.
I place the angle on the jig and tighten one clamp.
I clamp the angle where it looks close and let the welder adjust.

advanced.situation: A long frame rocks on the standard fixture because its legs vary slightly. You need to brace it for welding while keeping the joints aligned.

options.text: I map contact points, support low legs, clamp in sequence, and recheck joint alignment.
I brace beneath the longest leg and ask the welder to inspect joints.
I tighten nearby clamps and check whether the frame still rocks.
I reposition the frame and add adjustable supports beneath uneven legs.

basic.situation: Two short plates need to meet squarely before tack welding. You are holding them with clamps while the welder prepares the torch.

options.text: I pull the plates tight with one clamp and let the welder tack them.
I clamp the plates together and check the joint with a square before tacking.
I hold the plates flush and let the welder judge the angle.
I clamp the edges where they meet and ask the welder to tack them.

advanced.situation: A welded subunit meets a mating frame at one corner but sits out of line at the other. The drawing tolerance is tight, and final assembly is due soon.

options.text: I compare the diagonals and mating points, adjust with a jack, then recheck before tacking.
I loosen the clamps and ask a senior fitter to confirm the alignment.
I use a drift pin to pull the far corner into place and tack it.
I measure both corners and use a jack to bring the subunit into line.

basic.situation: A small metal component needs to move across the workshop to the fitting bench. You have a hand truck and a clear route.

options.text: I lift the component onto the truck and check it is stable.
I ask a coworker to steady the component while I wheel it across.
I check route, secure component, and guide the truck to the bench.
