I balance the component securely on the truck, then push it to the bench.

advanced.situation: A large frame must be moved by overhead crane through a busy bay. You are helping plan the lift and spot the crew from the floor.

options.text: I ask the operator to lift slowly while I watch the frame pass.
I review lift points, clear people from the path, and agree signals with crew.
I guide the crane operator along the shortest clear route through the busy bay.
I check frame balance points and clear the route before the lift.

basic.situation: You are gathering precut fiberglass mat and wood bracing for a small cabin panel. The work sheet lists the materials, but the bundles look similar.

options.text: I take mat and bracing from the nearest open bundles.
I compare labels with the sheet and ask about one unclear item.
I match the worksheet labels and separate the listed materials.
I choose bundles that look closest in size and set them aside.

advanced.situation: Several finished panels are ready for inspection, and one appears slightly uneven near a seam. You are checking dimensions and visible defects before release to the next stage.

options.text: I measure the panels and inspect the seams, then flag the uneven one.
I check the panels that look uneven and send the smooth ones ahead.
I inspect the seams closely and ask the lead to measure the unusual panel.
I compare each panel's measurements and visible surfaces with its specifications, recording any variance for review.

basic.situation: You need to saturate a small piece of cloth with resin for a panel. The project sheet gives the mix instructions, and a coworker is nearby to guide you.

options.text: I measure catalyst from the sheet, mix it, and ask my coworker to check.
I follow sheet directions, measure catalyst, mix resin, and brush cloth evenly.
I use a nearby batch's proportions and saturate the cloth with resin.
I add catalyst by feel, then brush the resin across the cloth.

advanced.situation: A large panel requires resin-saturated cloth in several batches. The previous batch felt thicker than expected, and you need to keep saturation consistent across the panel.

options.text: I reuse the same catalyst amount and brush harder to thin the resin.
I check project directions and record each batch while saturating cloth sections.
I mix smaller batches from project directions and ask a laminator to compare texture.
I compare the thick batch with project directions, confirm proportions, and record measured amounts.

basic.situation: You are spraying chopped fiberglass and resin onto a prepared small mold under supervision. The surface looks patchy as you cover the first section.

options.text: I follow the supervisor's pass pattern and check coverage across the mold.
I steady the gun, overlap passes evenly, and inspect each section as I work.
I slow the gun and ask whether the patchy area needs another pass.
I keep spraying until the patchy section looks covered from above.

advanced.situation: A large mold has wrinkles and air pockets where saturated cloth meets a sprayed layer. The next layer is due, and the surface must stay even.

options.text: I cover uneven spots with another layer and continue across the mold.
I press cloth with a brush, smoothing wrinkles before adding another layer.
I work from centre outward, pressing wrinkles and bubbles flat before the next layer.
I lift the loose edge and ask a senior laminator how to replace it.

basic.situation: You are bonding a wood reinforcing strip to a small cabin structure. The project sheet identifies its position, and a senior laminator is helping you prepare it.

options.text: I ask the senior laminator to position the strip while I prepare cloth.
I place the strip at its marked position and press it into saturated fiberglass.
I align the strip with marks, bond it in fiberglass, and check its seating.
I place the strip where it fits and cover it with saturated cloth.

advanced.situation: A cabin structure needs wood reinforcing strips across several joints. One joint has a narrow contact area, and you must keep each strip aligned while bonding it.

options.text: I bond strips where convenient and add cloth over the narrow joint.
I place a strip across the narrow joint and ask the lead to inspect.
I compare joints with layout, seat strips, and check contact before covering.
I follow the sheet for each strip and check that cloth holds it.

basic.situation: A small mold has excess fiberglass along one edge after curing. You have hand shears and a marked trim line to follow.

options.text: I follow the marked line with shears and check the cut edge as I progress.
I secure the piece and check the marked edge while trimming with shears.
I ask a coworker to hold the piece while I trim along its mark.
I trim the overhang by eye, staying close to the mold edge.

advanced.situation: Several molded parts need trimming, and the edge allowance varies around the curves. You are preparing the first part so the crew can follow a consistent approach.

options.text: I trim to mold edge and ask crew members to follow my approach.
I review the marked allowance, then trim the first part slowly with a knife.
I mark curves, trim measured sections with shears, and compare edges against the drawing.
I use shears on straight edges and ask another laminator to handle curves.

basic.situation: A small seam on a fresh laminate has a visible air bubble. You have a roller and a senior laminator nearby to guide you.

options.text: I add another layer over the seam to hide the visible bubble.
I roll beside the bubble toward the edge, then inspect for trapped air.
I ask the nearby senior laminator to roll while I hold the mold steady.
I roll toward the edge from beside the bubble and inspect the seam.

advanced.situation: A long curved seam has tiny bubbles and a ridge that is easy to miss under workshop lighting. You are smoothing it before the next layup stage.

options.text: I inspect under work light and roll visible bubbles toward the edge.
I roll the full seam firmly and move on when the surface feels level.
I ask a coworker to point out bubbles while I roll along the ridge.
I use angled light, roll bubbles outward, and recheck the curve.

basic.situation: You are fitting a small wheel under guidance, and it does not sit flush in the movement.

options.text: Fit the wheel by eye, then ask a colleague to check.
Press the wheel into place to keep the bench moving.
Use the loupe to align the wheel, then fit it gently.
Check the drawing, seat the wheel, and confirm free movement.

advanced.situation: A new technician is learning a complex train assembly, and one tiny component repeatedly shifts during fitting.

options.text: Ask them to press the part firmly until it stays seated.
Fit the component yourself and ask them to watch closely.
Show the fitting sequence under magnification, then have them repeat it.
Let them follow the diagram while you finish your own work.

basic.situation: A watch loses time during a routine check, and you are asked to inspect its movement with a loupe.

options.text: Look over the parts, then report anything that seems unusual.
Record the timing result and ask the technician what to inspect.
Open the movement and adjust the part that looks loose.
Compare the movement's operation with the checklist and note irregularities.

advanced.situation: A chronometer passes one bench test but later stops intermittently, and the usual checklist shows no clear cause.

options.text: Adjust the escapement based on the single test result.
Repeat timed tests across operating positions and log when stoppages occur.
Inspect the balance under magnification and share your observations with staff.
Ask another technician to inspect the movement and suggest a cause.

basic.situation: You are cleaning a small gear with guidance, and a trace of old oil remains near its teeth.

options.text: Use the approved solvent and buff stick, then inspect the teeth.
Ask your guide which solvent is approved for this gear.
Wipe the gear with a cloth and return it to the tray.
Apply a little fresh oil to loosen the old residue.

advanced.situation: Several technicians use different amounts of oil on similar assemblies, and you are asked to set a shared maintenance approach.

options.text: Tell everyone to use the amount that has worked for them.
Ask the senior watchmaker to choose an oiling method for everyone.
Compare the parts' needs, then document cleaning and oiling steps for each.
Demonstrate your method and invite technicians to ask questions.

basic.situation: A bridge sits slightly uneven during reassembly, and your supervisor guides you to correct its fit with tweezers.

options.text: Check the contact points, then make a small adjustment with tweezers.
Ask a nearby technician to check whether the bridge looks even.
Use tweezers for a small bend, then show your supervisor.
Bend the bridge further until it lies flat on the plate.

advanced.situation: A junior technician is correcting a hairspring that still coils unevenly after an initial adjustment, with a customer repair awaiting completion.

options.text: Take over the adjustment so the repair can meet its deadline.
Tell them to straighten the spring until its coils appear uniform.
Show one correction, then ask them to repeat it on the spring.
Have them inspect the coil, identify the distortion, and adjust incrementally.

basic.situation: You are taking apart a simple clock movement with step-by-step instructions, and several screws look similar.

options.text: Follow the sequence and place each screw in its marked tray.
Follow the guide and ask which tray suits the screws.
Remove the screws together and sort them by size afterward.
Take a quick photo before removing the screws from the plate.

advanced.situation: You are preparing a disassembly guide for a chronometer with a layered mechanism, and a new technician will use it during repairs.

options.text: Have the trainee remove the layers in order as you call them out.
Document the sequence, part locations, and checks at each delicate stage.
Write down the main steps from memory and share the notes.
Ask an experienced technician to demonstrate while you take notes.

basic.situation: A specified screw is worn on a watch, and you are replacing it with direct assistance at the bench.

options.text: Compare the screw visually with the removed one before fitting it.
Fit the specified screw and ask your guide to review it.
Use a similar screw from the parts tray to finish promptly.
Match the replacement to the specification, then check its fit under magnification.

advanced.situation: A chronometer repair needs a replacement component, but the supplied part fits loosely during your final bench check.

options.text: Compare the supplied part with the specification and note the looseness.
Recheck the part specification and fit before recording the repair result.
Hold the repair for a second opinion on the loose fit.
Seat the part firmly and return the chronometer for collection.

basic.situation: Your work order lists a bracket size that differs from the measurement shown on the assembly drawing.

options.text: Follow the work order because it is attached to your station.
Compare revision details, record the conflict, and get the approved dimension.
Use the drawing measurement and keep the line moving.
Check both references and ask the lead which dimension governs.

advanced.situation: Two blueprint views appear to give different hole positions for a bracket, and several units are due for assembly today.

options.text: Use the dimensions on the clearest view and note your choice.
Ask the lead to confirm which hole position the team should use.
Check drawing revisions and view references, then flag the mismatch for clarification.
Compare the views and report the differing positions to the lead.

basic.situation: A checklist asks you to inspect finished brackets, and one edge appears rough under the bench light.

options.text: Check the edge against the checklist and mark the bracket for review.
Pass the bracket because its overall shape looks usable.
Inspect the edge again and tell the lead what you noticed.
Ask a colleague whether the edge seems acceptable before recording it.

advanced.situation: Similar scratches keep appearing on assembled panels, and newer inspectors disagree about which ones fail inspection.

options.text: Ask the quality lead to explain the scratch limits to everyone.
Review examples against product criteria, then document clear defect guidance.
Show the team recent scratched panels and discuss the differences.
Tell inspectors to use their own judgment on each panel.

basic.situation: Your assigned assembly steps are taking longer than planned, and another station is waiting for your completed parts.

options.text: Check the schedule, finish your assigned batch, and update the next station.
Ask the lead whether the waiting station can receive partial output.
Continue your steps and tell the next station about the delay.
Skip a check to send the parts ahead on time.

advanced.situation: A shortage of one component disrupts today's assembly sequence, and two nearby stations have different tasks ready.

options.text: Move workers to whichever station has the largest unfinished pile.
Ask the lead to assign everyone while you maintain your station.
Shift one worker to the ready station and inform the lead.
Check dependencies and available parts, then reorder tasks to keep work flowing.

basic.situation: Small packing scraps collect beside your station during a shift, and your checklist calls for a clear floor.

options.text: Sweep the scraps into the designated bin and check the walking area.
Push the scraps under the bench until the next cleanup round.
Ask a colleague to sweep while you finish your current batch.
Sweep the visible scraps and tell the lead the area needs attention.

advanced.situation: Scraps and loose packaging keep gathering near several stations, and you are asked to help improve the team's cleaning routine.

options.text: Tell each assembler to clean whenever their own station looks untidy.
Map recurring waste spots and set a shared cleanup sequence with the team.
Move the packaging behind stations so the floor looks clear.
Clear the busiest walkway yourself before the next shift change.

basic.situation: You are assigned to rotate from fitting handles to checking finished units, and the next worker is waiting for your station.

options.text: Leave the unit unfinished so you can reach the next station sooner.
Ask the next worker to finish your unit after you rotate.
Finish your current unit, record progress, and hand over the station clearly.
Complete the unit and tell the next worker what remains there.

advanced.situation: A colleague is rotating through a production process for the first time, and the final inspection station is backing up.

options.text: Review station readiness, guide the rotation, and balance coverage at inspection.
Keep the colleague at the fastest station until inspection clears.
Walk them through the next station and ask where they need help.
Tell them to follow the posted sequence while you clear inspection.

basic.situation: A new colleague is unsure how to secure a panel, and you are asked to demonstrate the procedure during a busy shift.

options.text: Show the procedure once and invite them to ask questions.
Secure the panel for them so the batch can continue promptly.
Explain the steps while they continue working on the panel.
Demonstrate the sequence, then watch them secure one panel themselves.

advanced.situation: Several assemblers make the same fastening error after training, and the shift lead asks you to improve how the procedure is taught.

options.text: Tell assemblers to work faster so the fastening step stays consistent.
Review the error pattern and update the training demonstration accordingly.
Demonstrate each step, then check every assembler's practice.
Repeat the current demonstration to the team before the next batch.

basic.situation: A tray of buns is ready for baking, and the oven is warming up. You need to set the temperature and load the tray.

options.text: Set the oven to the recipe temperature, then load the tray carefully.
Use yesterday's oven setting and slide the tray onto the rack.
Set a familiar temperature and watch the buns as they bake.
Check the recipe temperature, then ask a colleague to confirm it.

advanced.situation: During a busy shift, the oven fan makes a new rattling sound and heat seems uneven. You are responsible for checking equipment before the next batch.

options.text: Ask a coworker to listen, then decide whether the oven seems usable.
Pause loading, note the fault, and report it through the bakery's maintenance process.
Tell the shift lead about the rattle and wait for guidance.
Turn the heat down and continue baking while watching each tray.

basic.situation: You are preparing cookie dough, and the recipe calls for a measured amount of flour. The scale is free beside your mixing bowl.

options.text: Use the marked container and add extra flour to finish the batch.
Weigh flour and check its reading against the recipe before mixing.
Estimate the flour in a bowl and begin mixing the cookie dough.
Tare a clean bowl, then weigh flour to the recipe amount.

advanced.situation: A larger order needs several batches of batter, and the mixer has different speed settings. You need to choose a workable mixing method.

options.text: Run every batch at high speed to finish before the delivery cutoff.
Use the recipe's speed and timing, then record how each batch turns out.
Set the mixer speed and time from the recipe, then check the batter's consistency.
Ask an experienced baker to select the mixer settings for the order.

basic.situation: You are preparing a tray of cookies from chilled dough. The pieces need even shapes before they go into the oven.

options.text: Cut the dough into similar pieces and place them across the sheet.
Break off rough chunks and crowd them together on the baking sheet.
Roll evenly, cut matching pieces, and space them across the sheet.
Roll a few pieces first, then shape the rest by eye.

advanced.situation: Several pastry orders share one oven, and another baker is shaping dough at a different pace. You need to coordinate the baking sequence.

options.text: Load the largest order first and fit the remaining trays around it.
Agree on tray timing and oven space with the other baker.
Ask the other baker to pick a sequence while you continue shaping dough.
Compare each tray's bake time, readiness, and available space before setting the oven sequence.

basic.situation: A delivery of flour arrives before the morning bake. You need to check its condition and record what the bakery received.

options.text: Count the bags and record the quantity before putting them away.
Check the bags for damage and tell the baker what arrived.
Put the bags into storage and enter the delivery's full invoice quantity.
Inspect the flour bags, note any damage, and record the accepted quantity.

advanced.situation: A last-minute event order is smaller than planned, and some prepared items may not sell. You need to adjust ingredient quantities and update production records.

options.text: Keep the original batch size and store any extra products for later sales.
Reduce the ingredient amounts and note the change in the production record.
Recalculate ingredients for the confirmed order and update the production record before baking.
Ask the team to estimate demand and bake a smaller batch.

basic.situation: A tray of cooled buns is ready for a light glaze before display. You have a pastry brush and a bowl of glaze.

options.text: Brush a thin, even glaze over the cooled buns before arranging them.
Brush glaze over the buns, then move them straight to display.
Dab glaze on the tops with a spoon to save time.
Pour the glaze across the tray and let it run between the buns.

advanced.situation: A customer requests a simple new decoration for a celebration cake, and a junior baker is helping you finish it during a busy shift.

options.text: Show the junior a sample cake and explain how to repeat its decoration.
Let the junior try the piping while you finish another cake nearby.
Pipe the design yourself while the junior watches from nearby.
Sketch the design, then coach piping practice with spare icing.

basic.situation: A delivery of baking trays arrives while you are preparing for the morning shift. You need to check the shipment against the order.

options.text: Check the tray sizes and ask a colleague whether the count looks right.
Count the trays and tell the supplier if the total seems short.
Sign the delivery slip and stack the trays near the ovens.
Compare the tray count and sizes with the order before signing the receipt.

advanced.situation: Two bakery deliveries are due during the morning rush, and one driver reports a delay. You need to coordinate which orders leave first.

options.text: Check readiness and routes, then brief both drivers on the sequence.
Ask both drivers to review the deadlines and agree which delivery leaves first.
Hold both deliveries until the delayed driver reaches the bakery.
Send the nearest driver with the first order packed by the team.

basic.situation: A customer orders several beef portions for a family meal. You have a boning knife and need to trim the cuts to size.

options.text: Measure the first portion, then cut the remaining pieces to match it.
Ask a coworker to check the portions while you continue cutting.
Cut portions quickly from the larger piece and tidy their edges afterward.
Trim each portion to size, keeping the boning knife steady on the board.

advanced.situation: A customer requests a tied roast with an even shape for an event. You are preparing it while the counter is busy.

options.text: Shape the roast evenly, lace it with twine, and secure both ends.
Ask a senior cutter to finish the lacing while you serve customers.
Shape the roast and tie it firmly at regular intervals.
Tie the roast at both ends and send it to the counter.

basic.situation: You have wrapped a chicken portion for a customer. The counter scale and label printer are ready for use.

options.text: Use the usual weight and attach a label from the last order.
Print a label after weighing and ask the cashier to verify the price.
Weigh the wrapped cut, print its matching price label, and check it before handover.
Weigh the package and print a label using the displayed price per kilogram.

advanced.situation: A customer has ordered a special cut for a family gathering, and several similar packs are on display. You need to prepare and present their order.

options.text: Prepare the requested cut, label its weight, and keep it distinct from display packs.
Prepare the requested cut and set it beside the other wrapped orders.
Choose the closest display pack and wrap it for the customer.
Ask the customer to identify their pack from the display options.

basic.situation: A chilled meat delivery arrives with several cartons. You need to inspect them and store the accepted stock appropriately.

options.text: Open one carton for inspection, then store the remaining delivery chilled.
Check carton condition and temperatures, record concerns, then chill accepted stock promptly.
Inspect the cartons and temperatures, then place accepted stock in the chiller.
Chill the cartons first, then inspect packaging and delivery details when time allows.

advanced.situation: A junior colleague receives a meat delivery with one carton that looks damaged. You are responsible for guiding the incoming inspection.

options.text: Guide the junior through the checklist while they inspect and record the carton condition.
Ask the supplier driver about handling, then check the damaged carton with your junior.
Isolate the damaged carton, inspect contents with the checklist, and document findings before acceptance.
Accept the delivery, then ask the junior to record carton details before chilled storage.

basic.situation: A cook collects beef from the chiller for lunch service. You need to record the quantity issued from stock.

options.text: Record the quantity the cook reports in the stock sheet with the collection time noted.
Weigh the beef, record its quantity against the cook's collection, and verify the entry.
Write down the estimated amount after the cook has left the chiller.
Note the collection time and update the stock total after lunch service.

advanced.situation: A supplier offers a different pack size for next week's meat order. You have authority to discuss order details but not approve a new contract.

options.text: Ask the supplier to repeat last week's order terms for the new pack.
Compare the quoted unit costs and ask the supplier to hold the offer.
Accept the larger pack at the quoted rate to secure next week's stock for the team.
Compare pack sizes and costs with expected use, then confirm details within your authority.

basic.situation: A supervisor asks you to tenderize a batch of beef portions with a meat mallet before they are prepared for cooking.

options.text: Tenderize each portion evenly with the mallet, keeping the pieces intact for cooking.
Tenderize the thicker portions more and leave the thinner ones as they are.
Strike the portions firmly until their surfaces become ragged and thin.
Use a few measured mallet strokes on each portion and check the texture.

advanced.situation: A team is preparing a smoked meat batch using the shop's established method. You are asked to show a junior colleague the preservation steps.

options.text: Walk the junior through the smoking steps while you prepare the next batch.
Demonstrate the recorded method, explain key checks, and supervise the junior's practice.
Give the junior the seasoning mix and let them manage the batch alone.
Ask the junior to observe your work and take notes for later reference.

basic.situation: Two meat cutters are assigned different tasks, and one asks which cuts should be prepared first for the lunch service.

options.text: Ask the senior cutter to decide the order while you prepare stock.
Review the service list, clarify tasks, and check cutter progress during the shift.
Tell both cutters to start with whichever meat is nearest the bench.
Assign each cutter a task from the list and ask them to report back.

advanced.situation: A new cutter is struggling to trim portions consistently, while the display needs replenishing before a busy period. You are coordinating the team.

options.text: Demonstrate the trim standard, watch the cutter practise, and rebalance tasks for display coverage.
Explain the trim standard and ask the cutter to continue on the current batch.
Pair the cutter with a colleague and ask them to finish the display first.
Move the cutter to display work and finish the trimming yourself.

basic.situation: You are removing skin from a carcass for processing, and the knife starts drifting from the marked seam. The next section is due soon.

options.text: I would copy the previous cut and keep the pieces moving for the packer.
I would secure the carcass, follow the guide, and pause if the bone line shifts.
I would follow the marked seam and ask the lead to check my next section.
I would pull the skin firmly and slice through the joint to finish this side.

advanced.situation: A new cutter is removing bones quickly, but their sections are uneven and leave meat on the frame. You are asked to coach them during a busy shift.

options.text: I would explain the target section size and remind them to check their cuts.
I would show the bone line, demonstrate one cut, then watch their next section.
I would finish their section myself and let them return to trimming later.
I would ask them to copy the fastest cutter to catch up with the line.

basic.situation: You are trimming a retail cut for packing, and the fat edge is thicker than the sample. The packer is waiting for your next tray.

options.text: I would copy the thickness from the last tray and keep cutting.
I would trim a little from the edge and ask the packer to check it.
I would leave the edge as it is and move the tray to packing.
I would compare the cut with the sample and trim the extra fat steadily.

advanced.situation: Two experienced cutters produce different sizes from the same primal part, and a retail order needs consistent portions. You are guiding the next run.

options.text: I would let each cutter use their usual method and sort portions afterward.
I would show the target weight and have each cutter check a portion periodically.
I would ask the faster cutter to demonstrate their method to the others.
I would set a sample cut, explain the trim points, and check the first portions together.

basic.situation: You spot a bruise and a strip of excess fat on a meat cut before packing. The line is moving and you have been asked to inspect it.

options.text: I would trim the bruise and ask the lead whether the fat strip needs removal.
I would turn the bruise underneath and send the cut along with the tray.
I would trim the bruise and excess fat, then compare the cut with the sample.
I would remove the fat strip and leave the bruise for the next inspection.

advanced.situation: Several new staff remove different amounts of bruised meat from similar cuts. You are coaching the team during inspection before packing.

options.text: I would let each person follow their own judgment and sort the cuts at packing.
I would define the visible defect boundary, demonstrate a sample trim, and review their next cuts.
I would have the most experienced cutter remove bruises from the next batch.
I would explain the sample standard and ask staff to compare each cut as they work.

basic.situation: You are feeding meat trimmings into the grinder, but pieces are collecting unevenly near the feed opening. The next batch is waiting.

options.text: I would stop feeding, check the opening with the lead, and follow the grinder guide.
I would use smaller pieces and keep the grinder running at its current pace.
I would slow the feed and ask the lead to watch the next few pieces.
I would push the pieces through quickly so the waiting batch can start.

advanced.situation: A ground-meat batch has a different lean-to-fat balance from the sample, and the team is preparing another run. You are guiding production.

options.text: I would add fattier trimmings now and review the finished batch afterward.
I would pause the next run and check the blend target with the team.
I would repeat the last recipe to help the team keep its rhythm.
I would compare trim mix with sample, adjust blend, then test a small run.

basic.situation: You are cutting fish into bite-sized pieces for a ready-to-heat tray. Some pieces are larger than the sample and vegetables are ready.

options.text: I would match the sample size, then arrange the fish and vegetables in the tray.
I would mix the larger fish pieces among the vegetables in each tray.
I would trim the largest pieces and ask the lead to check the tray layout.
I would place the larger pieces on top so the tray looks full.

advanced.situation: You are coaching staff assembling a ready-to-heat fish tray. The fish, vegetables, and sauce vary across trays, and the next batch is for a large order.

options.text: I would state portion targets and remind staff to keep sauce within each tray.
I would assign an experienced worker to assemble trays for this order.
I would ask stations to follow one layout and inspect trays during assembly.
I would set a sample tray with measured portions and sauce placement, then coach staff.

basic.situation: You are weighing a meat container and tagging its contents. The scale reading differs from the number written on the packing sheet.

options.text: I would write the sheet's weight on the tag and send the container onward.
I would check the scale reading with a colleague before completing the tag.
I would use the nearest whole number and finish tagging the container.
I would reweigh the container and match its tag to the verified contents and weight.

advanced.situation: You are coaching staff who weigh and tag sealed meat containers. A spot check finds mismatched weights on several tags before dispatch preparation.

options.text: I would trace containers, verify weights, and show staff how to match tags.
I would explain the tagging rule and check a few containers alongside staff.
I would ask one careful worker to check tags on the next batch.
I would retag affected containers using the packing sheet, then check labels against recorded weights.

basic.situation: You are assigned to shackle an animal before it is raised, and the area is busy. What do you do?

options.text: Wait for a quieter moment and ask a coworker to watch the setup.
Use the familiar shackle position and keep the line moving steadily.
Check the restraint setup with your lead, then shackle as directed.
Confirm the restraint is secure and follow the taught handling sequence.

advanced.situation: A new coworker is learning the stunning and shackling sequence while the line is running. How do you help them work safely?

options.text: Demonstrate the sequence, watch a practice run, and coach their handling.
Explain the steps during the next pause and demonstrate the controls.
Let the coworker copy the person ahead to learn the sequence.
Ask the lead to pair the coworker with an experienced operator.

basic.situation: You are assigned to open a carcass and remove its organs under supervision. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the supervisor to confirm the opening point before starting the cut.
Make the usual opening cut and place organs in the nearest tub.
Check the assigned cut and receiving containers, then remove organs carefully.
Follow the taught cut line and keep edible portions separated as you work.

advanced.situation: Blood is draining unevenly along your section, and the next carcass is approaching. How do you respond within your role?

options.text: Ask a nearby worker whether the uneven drainage looks familiar today.
Check the cut and drainage path, then alert the line lead to the pattern.
Pause your section, identify the affected carcass, and report the drainage issue.
Continue the usual cut sequence and let the next station sort it.

basic.situation: You are asked to wash a carcass after singeing, but one area still has visible residue. What do you do?

options.text: Ask a coworker to look at the area before you continue washing.
Move the carcass along and expect the next station to clean it.
Wash the area again and check the surface before passing it onward.
Recheck the area, use the taught cleaning method, and report persistent residue.

advanced.situation: Several hides from your section have uneven trimming, and the team is preparing another batch. How do you help improve the work?

options.text: Ask workers to trim each hide in whichever order feels efficient.
Share one example of uneven trimming during the next team handover.
Review the uneven sections and tell the lead where trimming varied.
Compare the hides with the taught method, then demonstrate consistent trimming points.

basic.situation: You are asked to trim head meat under supervision, and the cut line is less clear than usual. What do you do?

options.text: Follow the familiar cut and place the trimmed meat in its tray.
Confirm the cut boundary and receiving tray, then trim along the taught method.
Check the cut line with your supervisor before trimming the head meat.
Mark the unclear area for review and prepare the next head meanwhile.

advanced.situation: A carcass split is drifting from the marked line, and later portions may be uneven. How do you help the cutting team?

options.text: Continue the split along its current path to finish this carcass.
Ask another cutter to compare the split with the marked line.
Pause your cut, realign to the mark, and share the adjustment with the team.
Check the current split against the mark and report the drift to the lead.

basic.situation: You are washing viscera and separating edible portions from offal, but two pieces look similar. What do you do?

options.text: Use the familiar sorting pattern and place the similar pieces together.
Set the pieces aside while you wash the remaining viscera in the batch.
Compare the pieces with the taught sorting guide, then separate them into labeled tubs.
Keep the pieces apart and ask the lead to confirm their sorting.

advanced.situation: A supervisor asks you to review sorting after edible portions were found mixed with offal. How do you help check the process?

options.text: Ask workers to sort by appearance and keep the line moving.
Watch one worker sort a batch and mention anything that looks unusual.
Inspect a few tubs and report any mixed portions to the supervisor.
Trace the sorting steps, check tub labels, and share any recurring mix points.

basic.situation: You are wrapping meat cuts for the next stage, and the labels and wrap are ready at your station. What do you do?

options.text: Match cuts to labels, wrap them securely, and stage the batch.
Wrap each cut neatly, check its label, and place it with the prepared batch.
Use the nearest label for each wrapped cut to keep pace.
Ask a coworker to check the first wrapped cut before continuing.

advanced.situation: Your team is preparing premium cuts while another batch needs grinding, and staff vary in their cutting approach. How do you help coordinate the work?

options.text: Set out the cut sequence, demonstrate the target portions, and align grinding inputs.
Let each cutter choose portions and send remaining meat to grinding.
Review the cut list and give the team a clear order for the batch.
Ask the lead to assign one cutter to premium portions today.

basic.situation: The oven temperature is drifting above the work order range, and your supervisor is nearby. You need to check the gauges and respond.

options.text: Leave the setting unchanged until another product sample is ready.
Read both gauges, then adjust the thermostat with nearby guidance.
Match readings against the batch sheet, then adjust within its limits.
Ask the operator beside you which valve suits the reading.

advanced.situation: During a large coffee roast, temperature looks normal but pressure keeps pulsing. A junior operator asks what to change while the batch continues.

options.text: Check the pressure trend and sample, then explain a cautious adjustment.
Review recent readings with the junior before choosing a control.
Lower the heat slightly and watch the next pressure reading.
Tell the junior to keep the present controls through this roast.

basic.situation: A conveyor carrying nuts slows and makes a repeated scraping sound. You are tending the line while your supervisor is nearby.

options.text: Reduce the feed briefly and watch whether the sound changes.
Keep feeding nuts at the usual rate through the slowdown.
Listen again and check the material flow before reporting the scraping.
Tell the supervisor the conveyor is scraping and slowing down.

advanced.situation: A dryer has intermittent spillage and a faint new vibration, though output still looks steady. You are asked to brief the next shift.

options.text: Ask the next operator to listen closely during routine checks.
Mention the spillage and vibration during the shift handover.
Wait for output quality to change before raising the vibration.
Record both symptoms, the operating conditions, and a clear reporting trigger.

basic.situation: The work order lists two biscuit varieties and different quantities. You are unsure which line should receive the larger batch.

options.text: Ask a nearby operator which variety usually uses that line.
Send the larger quantity to the line running biscuits now.
Compare product names and quantities, then confirm the line assignment.
Read each product name and quantity aloud against the work order.

advanced.situation: A work order has a handwritten quantity that could read either 80 or 30 trays. The first tray is due soon, and a new operator is beside you.

options.text: Use the clearer product line as a guide for this quantity.
Hold the disputed quantity and clarify it through the order channel.
Ask the new operator which quantity the handwriting resembles.
Compare the writing with earlier entries and flag the uncertainty.

basic.situation: A biscuit sample looks darker than the earlier trays, and you have been asked to check its texture and appearance with guidance.

options.text: Set the sample aside and check another biscuit from the tray.
Pack the darker biscuits with the earlier trays for consistency.
Compare the sample's colour and texture with the stated standard.
Ask your supervisor to compare this biscuit with the earlier tray.

advanced.situation: A cocoa batch has a bitter note and uneven colour, but the texture seems acceptable. A junior colleague asks how to assess the next samples.

options.text: Approve the batch based on its acceptable texture and appearance.
Ask the junior to describe each sample before sharing your view.
Compare taste and colour with standards, then show consistent sampling.
Taste several samples and explain what differences you notice.

basic.situation: The scale hopper shows a different weight from the last check while you measure roasted beans. Your supervisor is working at the next station.

options.text: Pause filling and take one more reading from the hopper.
Ask your supervisor to verify the hopper reading before filling.
Continue filling at the earlier rate to meet the schedule.
Check the hopper display and compare the weight with the batch target.

advanced.situation: The scale conveyor readings vary between two checks, and the batch target is close. You need to determine whether the weighing setup is reliable.

options.text: Repeat the weighings and average the displayed results for the batch.
Ask a teammate to repeat the weighing on the same conveyor.
Use the first reading because it matched the target more closely.
Check the scale's calibration status and compare a known test weight.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to start a dryer conveyor and light the oven for a routine grain batch while they watch.

options.text: Check batch settings, then start the conveyor and light the oven while your supervisor watches.
Wait beside the oven while your supervisor confirms startup steps and checks batch settings.
Start the conveyor after checking the grain batch label and confirm oven settings with your supervisor.
Light the oven using yesterday's grain run setting without checking today's batch instructions.

advanced.situation: A mixed nut batch needs a longer roast, but trays are arriving unevenly and a junior operator is unsure when to load the next cart.

options.text: Keep the usual roast time and load each cart as it arrives.
Set the batch time, pace tray loading, and signal each handoff clearly.
Extend the roast and ask the junior to follow the usual loading pace.
Extend the roast and record the time for the next shift.

basic.situation: You are helping start a mixer for a routine filling batch, and the operator asks you to set its basic controls.

options.text: Check the recipe sequence, then start the mixer with guidance.
Ask which switch starts the mixer before touching the controls.
Turn the speed knob to the setting used for yesterday's batch.
Press the start switch while the operator watches the first mix.

advanced.situation: A thick batch is forming lumps as it leaves the vat, and the discharge valve is open. You need to adjust operation while keeping the mix consistent.

options.text: Reduce the discharge flow and check texture against the recipe target.
Close the valve slightly and watch how the next portion moves.
Ask the operator to suggest a valve position for the thick mix.
Keep the valve open to clear the vat before the next batch.

basic.situation: The mixing chamber thermometer is nearing the recipe limit during a supervised batch. You are watching the gauges and valves.

options.text: Tell the supervisor the temperature is nearing the stated limit.
Leave the valve where it is until the next scheduled check.
Compare the thermometer with the recipe limit and adjust the valve.
Turn the valve slightly and watch the thermometer for movement.

advanced.situation: A mixing chamber temperature is steady, but a faint leak and intermittent plugging sound begin during a large batch. The line is still producing.

options.text: Ask a nearby operator whether the sound is familiar to them.
Continue mixing at the current pace while listening for another sound.
Report the leak to the supervisor before the next batch starts.
Note the leak and plugging pattern, then report it with batch conditions.

basic.situation: A filling sample looks paler and feels softer than the previous one. You are asked to examine it with guidance before production continues.

options.text: Blend this sample into the next vat to keep output moving.
Taste another portion and describe its texture to your supervisor.
Tell the supervisor the filling looks paler and feels softer.
Compare colour and texture with the recipe sample before reporting.

advanced.situation: A new sauce recipe has clear colour but a faint aroma and changing texture across samples. Your team needs a consistent way to assess it.

options.text: Set sample notes for aroma and texture against the recipe targets.
Ask each worker to record which sample they prefer most.
Approve the batch based on its clear colour and smooth appearance.
Taste several portions and describe the aroma differences to coworkers.

basic.situation: You are weighing sugar for a small batch, and the balance scale reading differs from the amount on the recipe sheet.

options.text: Ask your helper to read the recipe amount while you weigh.
Check the recipe amount, then weigh sugar with your helper.
Pause and recheck the balance display before adding sugar.
Use the amount from the previous batch to keep mixing on schedule.

advanced.situation: A new recipe lists flour in kilograms and flavouring in ounces, and the batch is due soon. You are responsible for measuring both ingredients.

options.text: Use the familiar flour measure and estimate the flavouring portion.
Ask a teammate to convert the flavouring amount while you weigh flour.
Convert each listed measure carefully, then weigh ingredients separately.
Look up the unit conversion and prepare both scale readings.

basic.situation: A simple fruit mixture calls for adding sugar before the heated liquid. You are following the sequence with a supervisor nearby.

options.text: Add all ingredients together to save time before heating begins.
Ask the supervisor whether the sugar can go in after heating.
Add the sugar first, then wait for the supervisor's next instruction.
Follow the recipe order and check each ingredient as added.

advanced.situation: A cooked mixture tests less firm than the target, and the next forming cycle is due. You can adjust the operation based on sampling results.

options.text: Use the sample result to adjust the cooking cycle toward target firmness.
Keep the current cycle so the forming line stays on schedule.
Ask the forming operator whether the softer mixture feels workable.
Extend cooking slightly and check firmness after the next sample.

basic.situation: After a batch, your assigned vat and work area need cleaning before another product is prepared. A supervisor is nearby.

options.text: Wash the vat while your supervisor checks the work area.
Rinse the vat and start the next batch to save time.
Ask a coworker which cleaning step usually comes after rinsing.
Clean and sterilize the vat and area using the posted sequence.

advanced.situation: A batch record is missing its test result, and two coworkers are waiting for directions on the next mixing stage. You are coordinating their work.

options.text: Give each worker a clear stage, then complete the missing test entry.
Ask one worker to check the result while you direct the other.
Tell both workers to continue the usual mixing sequence for now.
Fill the record from memory before giving the next stage directions.

basic.situation: You are setting a cooker for a routine batch and have the recipe's temperature and time settings beside you.

options.text: I set recipe temperatures and times, then check the displayed readings.
I copy settings from yesterday's similar batch and check the result.
I raise the heat until the mixture looks ready to move.
I enter the listed settings and watch the first batch closely.

advanced.situation: The cooker temperature drifts during a large run, and the product flow changes as the gauge fluctuates.

options.text: I compare gauge trends with product flow, isolate the drift, and refine settings.
I check the gauges and adjust one control at a time during the run.
I keep production running while the gauge settles on its own.
I reset the controls to the usual values and restart the batch.

basic.situation: You are weighing ingredients for a routine recipe, and a coworker is available to help check the scale.

options.text: I weigh the ingredients and compare each amount with the work order.
I use the marked jug for dry ingredients to save setup time.
I add a familiar scoop count based on the last batch size.
I tare the scale, weigh the listed amount, and ask for a reading check.

advanced.situation: Several batches are due before lunch, and recent loads have varied in size and left excess ingredients in the cooker.

options.text: I use a larger load when the cooker has spare capacity.
I sequence measured loads by recipe and check each batch for carryover.
I adjust loading pace to keep the hopper steady between batches.
I top up short loads by eye to keep the line moving.

basic.situation: A routine batch has finished cooking, and your supervisor is nearby as you prepare to remove the product.

options.text: I use the usual scoop and set the product beside the cooker.
I pull the material out while the machine cycle is finishing.
I follow the release steps and clear cooked product into the assigned tray.
I wait for the signal, then remove the cooked material with care.

advanced.situation: A high-volume cooker is ready to drain, but the cooling tank is filling and another batch is queued.

options.text: I open the drain fully to clear the vessel before the next batch.
I coordinate pump timing with cooling space and watch the transfer level.
I pace valve transfers against tank capacity and confirm the receiving vessel.
I keep the pump moving and redirect overflow into a spare container.

basic.situation: After a routine batch, you are assigned to wash the cooker and nearby work area using the supplied cleaning solution.

options.text: I wash the equipment and cooking area using the labeled cleaning solution.
I rinse visible residue first and use the solution near shift end.
I hose down the cooker while warm residue is still loosening.
I apply the supplied solution, rinse surfaces, and follow the posted sequence.

advanced.situation: Several shifts have missed cleaning tasks between batches, so residue has been found during handovers.

options.text: I post the existing cleaning steps near equipment and remind the team.
I set a weekly cleaning rota and explain chemical labels during briefing.
I ask the next shift to cover missed cleaning during their setup.
I map each cleaning task to changeovers, assign owners, and demonstrate checks.

basic.situation: You are asked to collect a sample from a routine batch and check its color and consistency with help.

options.text: I compare a quick sample with the last batch before recording it.
I collect the sample and compare its color and consistency with guidance.
I rely on the kettle view instead of collecting a separate sample.
I take a labeled sample at the stated point and check its texture.

advanced.situation: Test results from two recent batches vary, while cooker readings remain steady and today's production is underway.

options.text: I review the test results and tune the cooker toward the product target.
I relate test trends to batch readings, then adjust the affected control.
I repeat the test and hold settings at the current production values.
I use the latest result to change the temperature across all vats.

basic.situation: You receive a routine work order and need to record the batch's processing time and temperature readings.

options.text: I record the planned values now and fill in results after cooking.
I match the work order to recipe settings and record readings as they occur.
I read the order and write batch times and temperatures on the sheet.
I copy the previous batch record, then update its date and number.

advanced.situation: Before handover, you notice gaps in several production records while the next run is being prepared.

options.text: I reconcile batch records against test results and flag gaps before handover.
I carry forward complete figures from yesterday to finish the record.
I check totals and ask operators to fill gaps during the shift.
I review entries for missing readings and align workers around the next run.

basic.situation: A routine extrusion run is underway, and you are asked to measure samples for defects against the product specification.

options.text: I sort by appearance and keep borderline pieces with the good stock.
I check the product dimensions and note any visible surface defects.
I measure one section and compare it with the previous accepted piece.
I measure samples against the specification and mark each defect location.

advanced.situation: The same surface defect returns on several runs despite minor control changes, and a large order is due today.

options.text: I continue the run and sort out the same defect downstream.
I clean the affected area and increase the line speed slightly.
I trace the recurring defect to its control pattern and make a measured correction.
I inspect the die and controls, then adjust the likely source carefully.

basic.situation: A routine changeover requires a listed die and sizing ring, and your supervisor is available while you install them.

options.text: I reuse the previous die because the line is already warm.
I confirm the die number, fit it with guidance, and check alignment.
I install the listed die and sizing ring using the setup checklist.
I use the closest matching die to avoid delaying changeover.

advanced.situation: A new production line needs a complex die assembly, and its material and dimensions differ from the last product.

options.text: I fit the familiar assembly while the new product sheet is pending.
I adapt the closest assembly and adjust the line after startup.
I match the assembly to material and dimensions, then verify fit before setup.
I select the specified die set and check the sizing ring sequence.

basic.situation: You receive a setup checklist for a routine product and need to select the specified machine die and parts.

options.text: I check the requested die and parts against the current product order.
I gather the usual parts before checking the product specifications.
I use the last setup list for this similar product family.
I follow the setup sheet and match each selected part to its specification.

advanced.situation: A complex new product has a detailed drawing and unusual dimensions, and you are asked to define its setup procedure.

options.text: I define the setup sequence from product specs and validate each part choice.
I adapt a familiar procedure and check dimensions during first production.
I draft the procedure around the approved drawing and required material.
I select the standard parts set and refine it after the first run.

basic.situation: You are finishing a routine run and have been asked to clean your immediate work area before handover.

options.text: I push loose offcuts beside the machine to clear the walkway.
I sweep around the machine after the current production run ends.
I clear scrap, wipe surfaces, and keep walkways open during the shift.
I clean my assigned area and place scrap in the marked bins.

advanced.situation: Scrap and dust have collected across several stations, and you are asked to guide the team on cleaner work areas.

options.text: I place labeled bins and remind the team during the shift.
I let each operator choose when to clear scrap from their station.
I set a cleaning checklist by shift and show operators how to verify it.
I clarify the posted cleanup steps and review them at handover.

basic.situation: You are starting a routine extrusion run and have the approved setup sheet beside the machine controls.

options.text: I start extrusion with the standard controls to save changeover time.
I start the machine and set controls from the approved setup sheet.
I set listed vacuum and temperature values, then check startup.
I copy the previous run settings and watch the first product.

advanced.situation: A difficult material responds unevenly at the current speed, and you are helping another operator tune the controls.

options.text: I raise temperature to improve flow and sort rough sections later.
I use the nearest material preset and trim speed during the run.
I balance heat, pressure, and extrusion speed against the material response.
I adjust the controls in small steps while checking the product dimensions.

basic.situation: You are reeling a routine product order and have guidance on the specified roll length and weight.

options.text: I use the usual roll setting and weigh it near completion.
I keep winding until the roll looks close to the requested size.
I reel the product and check roll length against the work order.
I set roll length from the order and check winding tension.

advanced.situation: A high-volume run needs many rolls, and frequent changeovers have been leaving excess material between rolls.

options.text: I coordinate reel changes with line speed and track roll weights throughout.
I adjust the roll length after checking the material left on the line.
I run longer rolls to reduce changeovers and trim excess afterward.
I plan roll changes around target lengths and inspect winding as production runs.

basic.situation: You start a press for a sample run, and the first piece looks slightly uneven. What do you do?

options.text: I stop the sample and ask the setter to review the press.
I run several more pieces to see whether the uneven shape settles.
I adjust the ram depth until the next sample looks flatter.
I compare the setup settings with the work order before another sample.

advanced.situation: During a tight-tolerance run, the ram stroke drifts and the press gives an unfamiliar vibration. What do you do?

options.text: I halt the run, isolate the setup issue, and verify stroke settings against specifications.
I reduce the pressure and watch whether the vibration becomes less noticeable.
I ask a nearby operator whether this vibration happened on earlier runs.
I continue at the current settings and check the next finished pieces.

basic.situation: A work order lists two operations, and you are unsure which comes first before the sample is measured. What do you do?

options.text: I ask the experienced operator to explain the operation sequence on the order.
I begin with the operation that matches the machine already set up.
I read the work order, then verify the first step with the operator.
I follow yesterday's sequence because the part number looks familiar.

advanced.situation: A new forging blueprint gives a tight tolerance, but the inspection sheet uses a different reference edge. What do you do?

options.text: I compare the drawing datums and tolerance callouts, then flag the mismatch before inspection.
I ask quality staff which reference edge they used on similar products.
I use whichever edge gives a measurement within the tolerance range.
I measure from the inspection sheet edge and record the result for review.

basic.situation: A workpiece starts to drift as you guide it through the dies under supervision. What do you do?

options.text: I pause feeding and ask the supervisor to check its alignment.
I keep feeding pieces while nudging each one toward the center.
I guide the next piece closer to the die's center by hand.
I stop the feed, mark where drift begins, and report it to the supervisor.

advanced.situation: After a die change, the hammer timing seems out of step with the cam during a precision run. What do you do?

options.text: I pause and verify cam timing and hammer synchronization against setup references.
I adjust the stop guide to compensate for the timing difference.
I ask the die fitter to confirm how the previous installation was timed.
I continue the run and sort out pieces that appear out of shape.

basic.situation: The production run ends, and the die is still warm in the press. You are asked to help remove it. What do you do?

options.text: I confirm the press is secured and follow the operator's removal sequence.
I loosen the visible fasteners while the operator prepares the hoist.
I pull the die free as soon as the hoist takes its weight.
I wait for the press operator to say when removal can begin.

advanced.situation: A complex forging needs trimming near its tolerance limit, and the usual trim would remove extra material. What do you do?

options.text: I trim the edge evenly and check dimensions before releasing the forging.
I ask the lead hand about settings used on a similar forging.
I use the usual trim, then inspect the forging against its dimensions and drawing.
I compare trim allowance with tolerance and adjust the sequence to retain material.

basic.situation: During a supervised die check, you find a worn replaceable insert and have a spare ready. What do you do?

options.text: I ask the supervisor to confirm the insert before replacing it.
I fit the spare insert that appears closest in size.
I compare the spare with the removed insert before supervised replacement.
I leave the worn insert in place for the next short run.

advanced.situation: A critical die has needed the same repair twice this month, and the next run is scheduled soon. What do you do?

options.text: I review repair history and wear points, then propose checks before the run.
I tell the maintenance lead that the die may need closer attention.
I wait for the next visible defect before planning another die repair.
I schedule the same repair before every run and record each date for review.

basic.situation: A setup sheet shows one ram depth, while a coworker mentions a different value for the same job. What do you do?

options.text: I choose the midpoint value so the press can start on time.
I compare both values with the setup sheet and ask what changed.
I ask the coworker to explain why their value differs from the sheet.
I use the coworker's value since they ran this job last week.

advanced.situation: Two operators read different operation sequences on a revised forging order, and the first sample is due soon. What do you do?

options.text: I compare the revised order, resolve differences, and align the team on its sequence.
I ask both operators to state which sequence they used on earlier runs.
I start with the sequence that keeps the press available for the next scheduled job.
I choose the shorter sequence and tell the team to proceed with it.

basic.situation: You set the roll gap and guide distance by hand, but the first sample is wider than the order specifies. What do you do?

options.text: I compare the roll gap and guide points with the order before changing them.
I measure the gap and guide distance again against the setup sheet.
I keep the current points and trim the sample edges afterward.
I widen the guide slightly and run another sample to compare.

advanced.situation: A new alloy order needs three mill stands, and the planned draft leaves the final strip outside its target dimension. What do you do?

options.text: I ask the mill operator which stand usually handles this alloy's final reduction.
I recalculate draft space and roll speed across the stands, then revise the sequence.
I run the planned sequence and sort out strips that miss the target.
I reduce the final stand gap until the strip reaches its target width.

basic.situation: You start the rolling mill for a sheet run, and the strip begins to feed unevenly. What do you do?

options.text: I check the dial indicators and adjust the controls to steady the feed.
I ask the nearby operator whether this feed pattern is typical.
I lower the speed and watch whether the strip feeds more evenly.
I keep the mill running and plan to inspect the coil at the end.

advanced.situation: A sheet shows a repeating thickness mark, and speed adjustments have not removed it. What do you do?

options.text: I reduce speed further and check whether the mark becomes less visible.
I inspect the setup and adjust the relevant controls, then check a fresh sample.
I keep the current settings and send the marked sheet for sorting.
I ask maintenance whether a roll change could explain the repeating mark.

basic.situation: A rolling order lists a new strip width and temper, and you are preparing the mill setup. What do you do?

options.text: I use the last order's dimensions because the alloy is the same.
I read the order for dimensions, temper, and sequence before setup begins.
I set the mill to its usual width and check the strip later.
I ask the operator which setup they used for the previous order.

advanced.situation: The finished strip looks uniform, but two width readings differ near the order limit. What do you do?

options.text: I consult quality staff and share both readings before deciding on disposition.
I use a suitable gauge at consistent points and record each width reading.
I take fresh readings at set points, then compare them with the order limit.
I hold the strip for review because its readings approach the order limit.

basic.situation: You are positioning a coil on the arbor, and it appears slightly off the center mark. What do you do?

options.text: I secure the coil in place, then adjust its guide to match alignment.
I ask a coworker to verify the coil's position before securing it.
I align the coil to the mark, then secure it on the arbor.
I feed the coil and monitor its tracking along the line.

advanced.situation: A heavy spindle must be repositioned while a coil is waiting, and another worker is ready to help. What do you do?

options.text: I signal the worker to move the spindle while I watch its clearance closely.
I guide the spindle into place while the coil remains queued nearby.
We agree on signals and clearances before I guide the spindle into position.
I ask the worker to wait while I check the available space.

basic.situation: The lubricant gauge is low during a run, and the oil cup looks nearly empty. What do you do?

options.text: I open the valve further so more lubricant reaches the workpiece.
I refill the oil cup, adjust the valve, and confirm the gauge response.
I leave the valve setting and finish the run before checking supply.
I refill the cup and note the low gauge reading for the operator.

advanced.situation: Coolant flow drops and the mill temperature begins rising during a long run. What do you do?

options.text: I lower the mill speed and watch whether the temperature stabilizes.
I check the coolant gauge and adjust the valve to restore steady flow.
I tell the operator the temperature is rising and ask how they respond.
I continue the run and record the temperature at the next scheduled check.

basic.situation: A coworker asks you to help position a replacement roll, but they are unsure where to stand. What do you do?

options.text: I point out the agreed safe position and assist the lead's roll change signals.
I start guiding the roll while the coworker finds a clear place.
I tell the coworker to stand where they can see the roll clearly.
I ask the lead where they want each person positioned for the roll change.

advanced.situation: A new worker is assigned to help remove a coil, but has not used the mill's loading signals before. What do you do?

options.text: I ask the lead to demonstrate the signals before the coil is moved.
I let the worker follow the others once the coil starts moving.
I give the worker a copy of the loading notes to read during setup.
I show the worker the signals and have them repeat the sequence before movement.

basic.situation: You are setting a saw for a routine order, and the work order lists a cutting speed and table angle. Your supervisor asks you to make the initial settings.

options.text: Use the usual speed and angle from the last similar order.
Start with a familiar setting and adjust it after the first piece.
Set the listed speed and angle, then check the display before starting.
Turn the controls to match the order and ask the supervisor to check.

advanced.situation: A new material runs inconsistently across two production batches despite matching speed settings. You are asked to troubleshoot before the next batch begins.

options.text: Compare both batches against the specifications, then test settings with a gauge.
Repeat the first batch settings and ask maintenance to inspect the machine.
Increase feed rate slightly and watch whether the next pieces improve.
Keep the current settings and sort out any inconsistent pieces later.

basic.situation: You are asked to start a shear on a routine order while your experienced coworker watches. The first sheet is ready at the machine.

options.text: Ask your coworker to watch the cycle while you prepare the next sheet.
Start the shear, watch its first cycle, and record the operating data.
Start the cycle and record the output after several sheets are cut.
Run the usual cycle and enter an estimated count at shift end.

advanced.situation: You tend two cutting machines during a busy shift. One begins cycling more slowly while the other is due for its next sheet.

options.text: Ask a nearby operator to watch one machine while you check the other.
Keep both machines running and check their output at the next break.
Finish loading the second machine, then inspect the slower cycle.
Pause feeding the slower machine, check its cycle, and log both outputs.

basic.situation: A simple work order lists plastic sheet stock and a marked cutting line. You are preparing the first piece and need to confirm what to cut.

options.text: Use the sheet already loaded and follow its visible edge as the line.
Use the same stock and line as the previous similar job.
Check the material and cutting line against the work order before cutting.
Read the material entry, then ask a coworker where the line falls.

advanced.situation: A production schedule lists two stages for a metal order, but the second stage's cutting line appears inconsistent with the listed dimensions. Work has not started.

options.text: Compare both stages' dimensions and lines, then flag the conflict before setup.
Use the second stage line because it appears later in the schedule.
Follow the first stage and leave the second stage for the next shift.
Ask the planner which line to use before preparing either stage.

basic.situation: You finish a small batch of cut pieces. The work order gives one dimension, and your supervisor asks you to check a piece with a ruler.

options.text: Check the edge by eye and set aside any piece that looks uneven.
Measure the first piece and use that result as the batch reference.
Measure one piece, then ask your supervisor whether the result seems acceptable.
Measure the stated dimension on a piece and compare it with the order.

advanced.situation: A micrometer reading varies between checks on a close-tolerance piece. The production order is waiting, and you are responsible for verifying its dimension.

options.text: Check the micrometer condition, repeat the measurement, and compare it with specification.
Switch to calipers and continue measuring the remaining pieces.
Take another reading and ask a coworker to confirm the dimension.
Use the midpoint of the readings and release pieces near that value.

basic.situation: You are sorting finished pieces from a routine order. One edge has a visible chip, and your coworker is waiting to pack the batch.

options.text: Set it aside and tell your coworker the edge looks damaged.
Separate the chipped piece and mark the flaw type for sorting.
Place it with the sound pieces and let packing continue.
Put it in a general reject tray for later review.

advanced.situation: Several finished pieces show similar marred surfaces, all from one part of the batch. You are sorting defects and the next run is approaching.

options.text: Tell the next shift about the marks and finish sorting this batch.
Set marked pieces aside, then continue sorting the rest of the batch.
Separate heavily marked pieces and flag the remaining batch for review.
Group marred pieces, record their batch location, and share the pattern with the operator.

basic.situation: You are loading plastic sheets for a routine run. After the last piece, scraps and dust remain on the work surface.

options.text: Load the sheets in order, then clear scraps and wipe the work surface.
Ask a coworker to load while you wipe the surface and clear scraps.
Push the scraps aside, load the sheets, and wipe down later.
Load the next sheet and leave the scraps for the cleaning round.

advanced.situation: Two material lots are ready for a long run, but frequent changes between them have caused delays. Scraps are also accumulating near the loading area.

options.text: Load both lots together and sort them as each piece reaches the machine.
Ask the lead which lot should run first, then clear nearby scraps.
Load whichever lot is nearest and move scraps after production ends.
Arrange each lot in run order and clear the loading area before feeding.

basic.situation: A simple job order lists a hole dimension and finish requirement for a metal part. You are preparing to set up the drilling machine.

options.text: Prepare the usual tool and check the finish after the first hole.
Read the dimension and ask a coworker to confirm the finish requirement.
Check the hole dimension and finish requirement against the job order before setup.
Use the dimensions from the last similar part and begin setup.

advanced.situation: A blueprint shows a hole location that seems inconsistent with a dimension on another view. A junior operator is waiting for your setup guidance.

options.text: Ask the junior operator to use the usual hole location for this part.
Follow the view with the clearest hole symbol and explain that choice.
Point out the conflict to the junior operator and request a drawing check.
Compare the views and dimensions, then clarify the conflicting location before setup.

basic.situation: You have machined a part with one listed bore dimension. Your supervisor asks you to check it with calipers before the next part.

options.text: Measure the bore once and use that reading for the next part.
Measure the bore and compare the caliper reading with the listed dimension.
Check the bore visually and continue if it seems even.
Take a reading and ask your supervisor whether the bore looks acceptable.

advanced.situation: Two operators report different readings on a close-tolerance bore using a telescoping gauge. You are checking the machined batch before it moves on.

options.text: Check the gauge use, take repeat readings, and compare results with the specification.
Take another reading yourself and ask one operator to recheck it.
Use a different bore gauge and continue the inspection with it.
Average both readings and record the result for the batch.

basic.situation: You need to secure a small metal workpiece on the table for a routine drilling job. Standard clamps are available, and your supervisor is nearby.

options.text: Place the piece near the usual mark and tighten one clamp firmly.
Use the standard clamps and ask your supervisor to check the position.
Set the piece against the table edge and tighten both clamps.
Position the piece to the plan and secure it with the standard clamps.

advanced.situation: A long irregular workpiece must be held for boring, and the usual clamps leave one end unstable. You can choose available jigs, shims, and clamps.

options.text: Arrange suitable supports and clamps to steady the part across its length.
Tighten the usual clamps further and start with a shallow cut.
Position the part on available shims and ask a coworker to watch it.
Hold the free end by hand while the machine begins boring.

basic.situation: The coolant flow is low during a routine drilling job, and a worn cutting tool needs changing. Your supervisor is present for the adjustment.

options.text: Keep drilling with the worn tool and top up coolant after this part.
Change the worn tool with a wrench, then direct coolant over the cutting area.
Open the coolant valve further and finish the current hole first.
Ask your supervisor to change the tool while you adjust coolant flow.

advanced.situation: A new alloy cuts inconsistently, and the current tool shows wear. You are responsible for settings on the next run and must select suitable cutting parameters.

options.text: Change the tool, then reduce the feed rate slightly for the next run.
Increase coolant flow and keep the current speed and feed settings.
Review the machining instructions, select suitable parameters, and replace the worn tool.
Reuse the last alloy settings and ask the next operator to watch the cut.

basic.situation: A simple part needs a hole at the intersection of two edges. You have a scribe and square and are asked to mark its reference point.

options.text: Measure from one edge and mark the approximate hole location.
Use the square to locate the edges, then scribe their intersection accurately.
Mark the point by eye from the nearest edge and begin layout.
Scribe one edge and ask a coworker to mark the crossing point.

advanced.situation: An intricate part has several machining locations, and its reference lines appear slightly out of alignment with the table axis. You have a dial indicator mounted in the spindle.

options.text: Check one reference line with the indicator and ask a coworker about the rest.
Redraw the visible lines with a square and continue marking locations.
Check the reference lines with the indicator, then adjust alignment before layout.
Keep the current alignment and shift each location mark as needed.

basic.situation: A small plastic part is positioned beneath the drill. You are asked to lower the tool and engage the feed while your supervisor observes.

options.text: Engage the feed as the tool approaches, and watch the cut for changes in sound.
Lower the tool quickly and let the automatic feed complete the hole.
Ask your supervisor to lower the tool while you prepare the next part.
Lower the tool to the part, then engage the feed while watching its progress.

advanced.situation: A heavy workpiece needs a hoist for the next drilling run. The current tool is dull, and the machine's feed has started to sound uneven.

options.text: Stop the feed and inspect the tool before asking for hoist help.
Continue the run, then sharpen the tool before lifting the next piece.
Ask a crane operator to position it while you sharpen it and report feed noise.
Pause the run, arrange hoist positioning, and inspect tool and feed before resuming.

basic.situation: You are setting up a grinding machine for a routine batch, and the work order gives the required settings. What do you do before starting?

options.text: I use the last batch's settings and start, since the parts look similar.
I set the listed controls, then ask the operator beside me to check them.
