I match each control to the work order and verify the setup before starting.
I ask a senior operator to set the controls before I start the batch.

advanced.situation: After a wheel change, test pieces vary in finish despite matching the work order. Production is behind, and a new operator asks you what settings to use.

options.text: I restore prior settings and run several pieces to see whether the finish improves.
I suggest a slight feed increase and check the finish on another test piece.
I compare settings with the work order, adjust one, and review another test piece.
I check the wheel and settings, then make a small adjustment for another test piece.

basic.situation: A new work order includes a blueprint and machining notes for a part you have not made before. You need to identify the required finish.

options.text: I check the blueprint and work order together, then confirm the finish requirement.
I read the finish callout and ask a colleague to confirm what it means.
I ask the shift lead to read the blueprint before I prepare the machine.
I use the finish from a similar part and begin preparing the machine.

advanced.situation: A blueprint gives two different dimensions for a shoulder, while the machining notes show a sequence that depends on that shoulder. The batch is due today.

options.text: I compare the views and notes, mark the conflict, and request clarification before setting the machine.
I compare the views and notes, then ask the lead which dimension should govern.
I follow the dimension shown in the main view and continue preparing the setup.
I ask an experienced operator which dimension is normally used for this shoulder.

basic.situation: You finish a ground shaft, and the work order calls for a diameter check with a micrometer. The next piece is waiting.

options.text: I measure the shaft and write down the reading for the batch record.
I ask a nearby operator to measure the shaft before I continue.
I compare it by eye with the last shaft before moving on.
I check the micrometer, measure the shaft, and compare the reading with the work order.

advanced.situation: Two operators get different readings on a tight-tolerance part, and the next batch is queued. You are asked to show the team how to inspect it.

options.text: I let each operator use their usual method and record both readings.
I check the micrometer, demonstrate consistent measuring pressure, and compare repeat readings with the tolerance.
I show the operators how I hold the micrometer and take one reading.
I demonstrate the micrometer technique, then ask each operator to take a reading.

basic.situation: A routine polishing job calls for lubricant on each workpiece. You have the specified compound and a spray bottle ready.

options.text: I coat the pieces and ask a colleague to inspect the first one.
I spray each piece evenly, using the specified amount and checking coverage before polishing begins.
I ask the lead to apply the compound while I prepare the next order.
I apply an even coat and confirm lubricant covers the full work surface.

advanced.situation: A difficult part needs a finer finish than usual, and the coolant stream keeps missing the contact area during a test run.

options.text: I select a finer tool and ask the lead where the coolant should flow.
I choose a suitable finishing tool and redirect coolant onto the contact area for another test.
I run the next piece with the same tool and coolant setting to meet the queue.
I keep the current tool and increase coolant flow for the next piece.

basic.situation: You need to load a heavy workpiece into a grinding machine hopper, and a hoist is available. The batch is waiting.

options.text: I use the hoist with a colleague, then secure the piece in the hopper.
I lift one end by hand and slide the piece into the hopper.
I wait for the senior operator to load the workpiece before starting.
I guide the hoist into place and ask a colleague to check the position.

advanced.situation: An irregular workpiece rocks on the machine table, and the usual clamp points obstruct the grinding path. A new operator is watching your setup.

options.text: I add an edge clamp and ask the operator to watch for movement.
I shift clamps to clear areas, test stability, and explain the setup.
I clear the grinding path with clamps, then show how I check stability.
I use usual clamp points and ask the operator to steady the workpiece.

basic.situation: During a grinding run, you hear a new rattling sound and see the workpiece shift slightly. The machine is still running.

options.text: I stop the cycle and tell the lead about the sound and movement.
I ask a nearby operator if the rattling is familiar and record what they say.
I stop the cycle, inspect the workpiece and machine, and report my findings.
I finish the current piece and mention the rattling at shift change.

advanced.situation: A recurring vibration returns after a minor adjustment, and a machine cover is visibly loose. The next run is scheduled soon.

options.text: I stop the run, report both symptoms, and wait for maintenance to inspect the machine.
I stop operation, secure the area, and report the vibration and loose cover.
I note the vibration and ask the lead whether the machine can run the batch.
I tighten the cover with a hand tool and run another piece to check vibration.

basic.situation: You need to load a steel bar into a lathe, and the hoist and hand tools are ready. The next job is waiting.

options.text: I use the hoist to place the bar, then ask a colleague to check it.
I push the bar into the machine by hand to save setup time.
I wait for the senior operator to secure the bar before the job starts.
I position the bar with the hoist, secure it, and check that it sits firmly.

advanced.situation: A turning job uses an unfamiliar fixture and cam to feed an irregular part. The drawing is clear, but the first setup leaves little tool clearance.

options.text: I install the fixture and cam, then check alignment and clearance through a hand-turned cycle.
I install the fixture as shown and ask a colleague to watch the first powered cycle.
I use the standard fixture and adjust the tool path to clear the part.
I align the fixture and cam carefully, then check the stock movement by hand.

basic.situation: A job order names a steel grade and bar size, but you have not run this part before. You need to prepare the lathe.

options.text: I ask a colleague which bar is usually used for this part.
I read the material and size on the job order, then confirm the stock label.
I check the job order and write down the material and bar size.
I use the bar left by the previous shift because it looks similar.

advanced.situation: A print omits one shoulder dimension needed to set a turning stop. You can derive it from two shown dimensions, but the stock allowance is tight.

options.text: I derive the dimension from the print, check the allowance, and set the stop.
I use a similar job's dimension and set the stop from it.
I derive the value and ask the lead to confirm it before setup.
I subtract the shown dimensions and set the stop to that value.

basic.situation: You finish a sample turned part, and the job order gives a diameter tolerance. A micrometer is available at the bench.

options.text: I ask a nearby operator to check the sample before I move on.
I compare the part by eye with one from the last batch.
I check the micrometer, measure the diameter, and compare it with the stated tolerance.
I measure the diameter and record the reading for the next operator.

advanced.situation: A tight-tolerance job needs timing and clearance checks. You are asked to crank the lathe through a cycle before the next run.

options.text: I crank through the cycle and check the tightest clearance with an indicator.
I turn the handwheel through one cycle and watch for any obvious contact.
I start the machine at low speed and listen for contact during the cycle.
I crank the machine by hand through the cycle, checking timing and clearances at each point.

basic.situation: You are assigned a routine turning job with a listed speed, depth, and feed rate. The lathe is set up and ready.

options.text: I check the speed and feed, then ask a colleague to start the lathe.
I match the listed settings, start the lathe, and watch the first cut.
I use yesterday's speed and feed because the stock looks similar.
I ask the lead to review the settings before I start the lathe.

advanced.situation: Measurements from the first turned parts drift toward the tolerance limit. The job order specifies strict dimensions, and the lathe is still running.

options.text: I track dimensions, adjust the tool slightly, then recheck the next part.
I adjust the tool slightly and measure the next piece against tolerance.
I reduce feed slightly and measure several more pieces before changing settings.
I ask the lead if the trend warrants a tool adjustment for this batch.

basic.situation: After a turning run, chips and oil remain around your lathe and tools. The next operator will use the station soon.

options.text: I cover the chips with a rag so the bench looks tidy for now.
I clear the chips safely, wipe the tools, and leave the station ready for handover.
I clear the chips and ask the next operator to wipe the tools.
I sweep the chips into a tray and leave the tools for the next operator.

advanced.situation: A worn tool leaves a poor finish on a steel part. The tooling instructions list alternatives, and you need to choose a replacement for the next run.

options.text: I choose a steel-suited tool and ask a colleague to confirm it.
I reuse the last steel job's tool without checking whether it suits this cut.
I fit a fresh rack tool and see whether the finish improves.
I match the listed tool to the steel and cut, then inspect it.

basic.situation: The lathe's coolant level is below its marked operating range before your shift's first job. A refill container is available.

options.text: I run the first part, then refill coolant after the current job is complete.
I ask the lead to check coolant before I begin the first job.
I refill to the marked range and verify the coolant level before starting.
I top up the coolant and record the refill for the next shift.

advanced.situation: A repeat production run needs a revised CNC program for a slightly longer bar. You have the approved program and the new dimensions in the job order.

options.text: I ask the lead to make the program change before production begins.
I update the bar dimension, compare program and order, then test one piece.
I revise the bar dimension and review program lines before running the machine.
I copy the prior program, change the bar dimension, then start the production run.

basic.situation: A routine milling job is ready, and you need to secure a metal block before cutting its first face.

options.text: Seat the block against the stop and check its position with a rule.
Center the block with a dial indicator, then tighten the fixture evenly.
Clamp the block against the stop and begin the first pass.
Ask a nearby operator to confirm the setup before tightening the clamps.

advanced.situation: A large irregular casting needs a special cutter and several clamps; a newer operator asks how to secure it for a deep cut.

options.text: Show the operator how to seat the cutter and add clamps at the overhang.
Use the usual clamp pattern and let the operator fit the cutter.
Ask the operator to follow the setup sheet and check the clamps afterward.
Review the contact points, then guide the operator to support and clamp the casting evenly.

basic.situation: A work order arrives for a replacement plate, and you need to identify its size and hole locations before setup.

options.text: Check the plate size, then ask a colleague about the hole spacing.
Start from a similar plate and copy its hole pattern for this order.
Read the work order dimensions and mark the plate's required hole locations.
Use the listed size and hole spacing to prepare the workpiece layout.

advanced.situation: A drawing shows a thin alloy housing with stepped bores and tight clearances; you must determine dimensions and a workable tooling sequence.

options.text: Use the standard bore sequence and adjust the final pass to fit.
Map the stepped bores from the drawing and list tools in cutting order.
Calculate the clearances from the drawing, then plan the bore sequence around the thin walls.
Check the bore dimensions and ask the lead to choose the tooling sequence.

basic.situation: You are setting up a routine steel cut, and the machine controls need the specified speed, feed, and tool position.

options.text: Set the listed speed and feed, then position the cutter before starting.
Use the previous job's settings and start the machine for a quick cut.
Match the listed settings and check cutter position before starting the machine.
Set the speed from the sheet and ask someone to confirm the feed.

advanced.situation: A difficult alloy job is running hot, and you need to choose a suitable speed, feed, cut depth, and coolant flow.

options.text: Check the alloy guidance and lower the feed while maintaining coolant flow.
Reduce the cut depth, then tune speed and feed while watching heat and coolant flow.
Keep the current feed and raise the speed to clear the cut faster.
Ask the lead for a setting and leave coolant at its current flow.

basic.situation: You are milling a shallow slot on a simple part, with a guide nearby and the handwheel controlling the cutter travel.

options.text: Move the cutter in short turns and check the slot near the end.
Turn the handwheel quickly to finish the slot before the next job.
Follow the guide's pace and watch the cutter as you move the handwheel.
Advance the handwheel steadily while checking the slot against the marked line.

advanced.situation: During a long cut on a stepped surface, the automatic feed begins leaving uneven marks as the cutter approaches a narrow shoulder.

options.text: Keep the automatic feed running and ask the lead to inspect the finished surface.
Switch to handwheel travel near the shoulder and watch the surface marks.
Pause the feed, inspect cutter engagement, and resume with controlled travel before the shoulder.
Increase the feed slightly so the uneven section passes the cutter sooner.

basic.situation: A finished block comes off the mill, and you need to check its thickness against the work order before it moves onward.

options.text: Measure the block with calipers and record the reading for the next shift.
Measure the thickness with calipers and compare it with the work order.
Check the thickness with a rule and note whether it seems close.
Send the block onward because the final pass looked even across the face.

advanced.situation: A precision assembly requires a milled base to align with two reference edges, and the measured gap differs slightly across the length.

options.text: Measure the gap at both ends and note the difference for the fitter.
Repeat the end measurements and ask the fitter whether the gap is acceptable.
Check both reference edges with a gauge and compare the readings across the length.
Use the smaller gap as the alignment figure and release the base for assembly.

basic.situation: The cutter on your machine is visibly dull during a routine job, and a replacement tool is available at the bench.

options.text: Ask a colleague to replace the cutter while you prepare the next workpiece.
Bring the replacement cutter over and check its size before changing tools.
Continue the pass with the dull cutter to avoid pausing the job.
Replace the dull cutter with the specified tool using the hand tools provided.

advanced.situation: Several cutters have dulled early on a high-volume run, and you need to record output and help plan sharpening work.

options.text: Record the output and sharpen cutters when operators report poor finishes.
Sharpen every cutter at the end of each shift to keep the routine simple.
Ask the lead to set the sharpening schedule and enter the latest output.
Compare output records with tool wear, then schedule sharpening around the run's workload.

basic.situation: A routine lathe job is ready, and you need to align and secure its holding fixture and cutting tool before loading stock.

options.text: Secure the fixture and check the tool position against the setup sheet.
Align the fixture to the spindle, then secure the tool and stock.
Fit the fixture and tool using the usual positions from the last job.
Ask a colleague to check the fixture before you tighten the tool holder.

advanced.situation: A repair needs a nonstandard shaft held securely for machining, and the existing fixtures cannot support its offset features.

options.text: Sketch a support around the shaft and check its fit before machining.
Adapt the nearest fixture and begin a light pass to see how it holds.
Measure the shaft features and sketch a fixture that supports the offset during cutting.
Ask the engineer to provide a fixture design before preparing the shaft.

basic.situation: You are machining a replacement pin on a lathe, and the drawing gives its finished diameter and length.

options.text: Check the drawing, then ask a machinist to confirm the lathe settings.
Machine the diameter to specification, then check the pin's length afterward.
Turn the pin to the drawing dimensions and check both finished measurements.
Turn the pin to a familiar size and leave a little extra length.

advanced.situation: A small sleeve needs a precise internal finish, and the standard lathe setup is causing chatter on the trial piece.

options.text: Ask the lead to choose a precision tool while you hold the trial piece.
Continue with the standard setup and polish the sleeve after machining.
Reduce the feed and make another pass with the current setup.
Set up the suitable precision tool and test a controlled pass on sample stock.

basic.situation: A bar must be cut into three blanks, and you need to mark each cut location from the drawing before machining.

options.text: Check the drawing dimensions and ask a colleague to mark the stock.
Measure each length from the drawing and mark the three cut positions clearly.
Mark three equal sections by eye and leave room for trimming later.
Measure the first section and use it as a guide for the remaining marks.

advanced.situation: A turned pin is near its tolerance limit, and you need to verify its diameter with a precision instrument before acceptance.

options.text: Repeat the diameter reading and record the result for the inspection sheet.
Check the pin with calipers and ask the inspector whether it seems acceptable.
Measure at several points with a micrometer and compare each reading with tolerance.
Use the first micrometer reading and release the pin if it looks smooth.

basic.situation: A drawing arrives for a small bracket with two milled faces and drilled holes, and you need to plan the operation sequence.

options.text: Drill the holes first, then choose the facing setup during machining.
Ask a colleague for a sequence and prepare the bracket for the first step.
List the facing and drilling steps in the order shown on the drawing.
Study the drawing and sequence facing before drilling to keep the references stable.

advanced.situation: A repeat job meets dimensions, but its current machining sequence requires frequent repositioning and adds idle time between cuts.

options.text: Ask the lead to revise the sequence and continue the current setup meanwhile.
Raise the feed rate so the existing sequence finishes sooner each run.
Track feed and idle periods, then recommend a shorter tool path.
Review the sequence and propose a fixture change that combines compatible cuts.

basic.situation: A machine tool has a scheduled service check, and you need to keep it in operational condition during the shift.

options.text: Ask a colleague to complete the check while you continue production.
Check the machine's usual lubrication points and tell the lead if needed.
Clean the machine, check lubrication points, and record any service needs.
Keep running parts and note the service check for the next shift.

advanced.situation: A machine tool starts vibrating and leaving inconsistent finishes after a recent adjustment, and you need to determine whether it needs repair.

options.text: Check adjustment settings, compare the vibration, and report findings to maintenance.
Ask the lead to assess repair needs before inspecting the machine settings.
Pause the run, inspect the adjustment and vibration, then document findings for maintenance.
Change the feed to improve the finish, then continue production.

basic.situation: After a routine machining run, metal offcuts and oily waste are left at your station for disposal under shop procedures.

options.text: Move the offcuts aside and ask which container takes the oily waste.
Sort the offcuts and oily waste into their designated disposal containers.
Check the disposal labels and place the waste in the marked area.
Put all waste into the nearest bin to clear the station quickly.

advanced.situation: A run produces reusable metal drops, mixed scrap, and containers with residue, and you need to separate them for recovery or disposal.

options.text: Separate clean reusable drops, mixed scrap, and residue containers by their handling routes.
Send all metal drops with the clean scrap so collection can happen sooner.
Check the waste labels and ask the storekeeper where to place each pile.
Keep clean drops apart and label the mixed scrap for the next collection.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to inspect the furnace surface before the next shift. You notice a small crack near a panel seam.

options.text: Tell your supervisor about the crack and wait for further instructions.
Continue the check and mention the crack during the shift handover.
Mark the crack's location and tell your supervisor before work continues nearby.
Wipe the area clean and note that the surface looks sound.

advanced.situation: During a planned inspection, you find a widening seam and powdery lining near a burner. The furnace is still within its operating range.

options.text: Photograph the seam and add it to the next routine inspection record.
Report the powdery lining and seam to the shift supervisor for assessment.
Brush away the powder and keep the furnace on its current schedule.
Compare the wear with recent inspection notes and report the trend for maintenance review.

basic.situation: Your senior operator asks you to shovel a specified fuel amount into the furnace. The scale display is hard to read.

options.text: Add a full shovel now and record the amount as the specified charge.
Ask the senior operator to confirm the scale reading before charging the fuel.
Use the last charge as a guide and shovel in a similar amount.
Check the written charge amount and ask a nearby operator to read the display.

advanced.situation: A crane operator is ready to load a mixed charge, but one container's label is smudged and the furnace is waiting.

options.text: Hold that container outside the load and confirm its identity against the charge sheet.
Ask the crane operator to pause while you check the smudged label.
Use the container that matches the usual mix and note the label issue afterward.
Load the clearly labelled materials first and ask the shift lead about the other container.

basic.situation: Your senior operator tells you to adjust the fuel valve. The temperature gauge is moving more quickly than usual.

options.text: Turn the valve as instructed and tell the senior operator the gauge is moving quickly.
Wait for the gauge to settle, then make the requested valve adjustment.
Turn the valve farther to bring the rising gauge down more quickly.
Make the instructed small adjustment and watch the gauge for the response.

advanced.situation: A new metal mix is heating unevenly, with temperature and coolant readings shifting together. You are operating the controls during the shift.

options.text: Keep controls within the approved range and report both changing readings to the senior operator.
Pause further adjustments and ask the senior operator to assess the unusual mix and readings.
Increase fuel flow until the metal color matches the previous batch, then check both readings.
Adjust fuel flow in small steps while monitoring the temperature gauge and coolant readings.

basic.situation: You are assisting with a workpiece discharge. The controls respond slowly, and the workpiece has not cleared the furnace opening.

options.text: Keep the controls engaged briefly and watch for the workpiece to move.
Pause the movement and tell the senior operator the workpiece has not cleared.
Press the discharge control again to help the workpiece clear the opening.
Release the controls and ask a nearby operator whether the workpiece is moving.

advanced.situation: A large pour is entering a mold when the flow begins to surge and the metal approaches the rim. Your crew is waiting for your signal.

options.text: Ask the crew to stand clear while you monitor the flow for another moment.
Reduce the flow and watch the metal level near the mold rim.
Signal the crew to pause the pour while you check flow and mold alignment.
Increase the pour speed to fill the mold before the metal reaches the rim.

basic.situation: A chemist asks you to draw a metal sample, but the sampling tool is still warm from the previous draw.

options.text: Draw the sample now and note that the tool was warm on its label.
Wait briefly, then draw the sample and label it for the chemist.
Tell the chemist the tool is warm and ask whether to use another.
Let the tool reach its approved condition, then draw and label the requested sample.

advanced.situation: A lab result shows the batch is off specification, and a previous adjustment used a different mix. You are asked to calculate the next addition.

options.text: Ask the chemist to confirm the result before using the previous adjustment as a guide.
Recheck the result against this batch's charge record before calculating a measured adjustment.
Repeat the previous addition amount so the furnace can return to schedule.
Use the current lab result and calculate an addition from the standard mix sheet.

basic.situation: You are copying production figures onto the shift log. One scale reading is faint, and the next batch is ready to weigh.

options.text: Ask a nearby operator to read the display and write down the weight.
Enter the closest visible figure and flag the reading for shift handover.
Copy the previous batch's weight and keep the line moving for now.
Check the scale display again and enter the verified weight in the shift log.

advanced.situation: Your log shows rising fuel use across several shifts, but one day's production total is incomplete. The team is reviewing possible process changes.

options.text: Fill the missing total from the daily average and summarize the fuel increase.
Compare the recorded fuel use across shifts and flag the missing production total.
Separate the incomplete day, compare verified shifts, and present the fuel trend with its limits.
Report the rising fuel use as a process problem and suggest cutting the next charge.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to check a mold before pouring. You find dirt caught in a shallow groove.

options.text: Coat over the groove and mark the mold ready for pouring.
Brush the visible dirt away and mention the groove during handover.
Tell your supervisor about the dirt and wait for the next instruction.
Point out the groove and help clean it before checking the mold again.

advanced.situation: A mold looks smooth, but you find a thin residue under its coating before a costly casting. The pouring crew is nearly ready.

options.text: Ask the supervisor whether the residue needs cleaning before the crew pours.
Wipe the visible residue and tell the crew to inspect the coating again.
Accept the smooth surface and continue preparation for the scheduled casting.
Hold the mold from release and show the residue for cleaning and reinspection.

basic.situation: You are loading specified metal and flux into a furnace. The metal amount is clear, but the flux label is partly torn.

options.text: Load the clear metal amount and keep the flux beside the furnace for now.
Ask the senior pourer to read the torn label before you load the flux.
Pause the flux loading and confirm its amount against the charge instruction.
Use the usual flux amount and note the damaged label on the shift sheet.

advanced.situation: A complex casting is filling unevenly, and the flow is nearing a thin section. A junior pourer asks whether to speed up the ladle.

options.text: Keep the current rate and ask the junior to monitor the thin section.
Reduce flow to protect the thin section and explain the fill pattern to the junior.
Speed up the ladle so metal passes the thin section with less delay.
Slow the ladle briefly and check the casting plan with the crew.

basic.situation: The chemist asks for a metal sample during pouring. A worker is nearby, but you cannot see whether they heard the request.

options.text: Signal the worker clearly and confirm they acknowledge the sampling request.
Tell the nearest worker about the sample while continuing your other task.
Assume the worker heard the chemist and continue with your current task.
Repeat the sampling signal and watch for the worker to respond.

advanced.situation: Two workers are positioning a ladle and pouring nozzle for a tight casting. Their hand signals differ, and the equipment is not yet aligned.

options.text: Use the clearer signal and tell the second worker to follow it.
Continue positioning while watching both workers for signs of confusion.
Ask each worker to repeat their signal before moving the equipment again.
Pause positioning, agree on one signal with both workers, then confirm alignment together.

basic.situation: You are moving a single ingot to storage with a forklift. The marked aisle is partly blocked by a pallet.

options.text: Ask a nearby worker to watch the pallet while you edge past with the ingot.
Wait for a clear moment and guide the forklift around the pallet slowly.
Set the ingot down beside the pallet and return for it after the shift.
Stop before the blockage and ask for the aisle to be cleared before moving the ingot.

advanced.situation: Several ingots are ready for storage, and the usual route is crowded with other moves. You are coordinating forklift trips during a busy period.

options.text: Send forklifts one at a time along the usual route and watch for congestion.
Group trips by destination and confirm each route is clear before dispatching a forklift.
Ask operators to use the nearest open aisle and report any delays afterward.
Keep all forklifts moving on the usual route to clear the ingots sooner.

basic.situation: You are adjusting a furnace flame under supervision. The temperature gauge rises past the target while the metal is still melting.

options.text: Ease the flame down as instructed and watch the gauge settle near target.
Tell the supervisor the gauge has passed target and ask about the flame.
Turn the flame off briefly so the temperature can drop below target.
Reduce the flame slightly and check the metal color before changing it again.

advanced.situation: A trial melt for a new alloy heats unevenly, and the gauge and metal color suggest different temperatures. The batch is valuable.

options.text: Ask the senior operator to assess color as you recheck the gauge and compare batch readings.
Compare both indicators within approved limits, then report the mismatch before changing heat.
Raise heat until the metal color matches the usual appearance for this alloy.
Make a small flame adjustment and track whether the gauge moves toward the target.

basic.situation: You are removing excess metal from an ingot with a rake. A piece of scrap falls beside the collection tray.

options.text: Move the scrap into the recycling tray and check the ingot edge before continuing.
Pick up the scrap and place it in the tray before finishing the ingot.
Continue raking, then collect the loose scrap when the ingot is finished.
Push the scrap beneath the workbench to clear the space around the tray.

advanced.situation: Several ingots leave uneven excess metal and slag, and the scrap tray fills before the shift ends. You are reviewing removal work with the crew.

options.text: Sort scrap by type, then ask the crew which ingots created the most excess.
Record scrap by source and review removal methods with the crew.
Use a larger tray and collect scrap as the crew cleans each ingot.
Leave remaining scrap beside the tray and clear it at shift end.

basic.situation: You receive a simple sketch for a small bracket, but you are unsure which dimension shows its width before cutting the stock.

options.text: Use the first dimension shown and cut the stock to keep work moving.
Check the sketch with a ruler, then mark the stock for cutting.
Compare the views and identify the width dimension before marking the stock.
Ask a nearby maker to point out the main dimensions before you mark.

advanced.situation: A multi-view drawing shows a tight-fitting model part, and its hole position appears inconsistent across views as you plan the production sequence.

options.text: Follow the main view and begin machining the holes before checking the other views.
Plan the sequence from the main dimensions and check the hole after setup.
Compare the views and flag the hole location for engineering clarification before machining.
Use the section view to estimate the hole position and machine a test piece.

basic.situation: You are setting up a drill press for a prototype plate, and the marked hole is close to the edge.

options.text: Clamp the plate and start with a smaller bit before opening the hole.
Hold the plate firmly by hand and drill slowly to keep it steady.
Ask a colleague to check the setup while you select a suitable drill bit.
Clamp the plate, align the mark, and confirm the drill size with your supervisor.

advanced.situation: A CNC job for a complex model part is due today, but the tool path approaches a thin wall with little clearance.

options.text: Run one part at reduced feed and measure the wall before continuing.
Review the tool path, verify clearances, and run a controlled first piece.
Ask the programmer to explain the close pass before you start the machine.
Run the posted program at production speed to protect the delivery time.

basic.situation: You need to drill a bolt hole in a prototype tab, and the mark sits near a finished edge.

options.text: Drill on the mark while holding the tab flat against the table.
Center the mark, clamp the tab, and drill the specified hole with guidance.
Clamp the tab and make a small pilot hole before using the specified bit.
Ask a coworker to steady the tab while you drill the marked hole.

advanced.situation: A ground model surface must meet a close tolerance, but your first measurement falls just outside the drawing limit.

options.text: Grind the surface again until the reading falls inside the stated tolerance.
Check the instrument and datum, then make a controlled pass and remeasure.
Take another reading from the same datum before deciding on a light pass.
Ask an experienced finisher to read the measurement before you touch the surface.

basic.situation: You are fitting two simple model sections with bolts, but one pair of holes does not line up cleanly.

options.text: Loosen the fit, adjust the sections by hand, and try the bolts again.
Tighten the bolts in sequence to pull the sections into alignment.
Ask a coworker to hold one section while you start each bolt.
Check the mating faces and hole alignment, then fit the bolts with guidance.

advanced.situation: A new model needs a holding jig, and its irregular shape may shift during machining if the supports are poorly placed.

options.text: Copy the last jig dimensions and adjust the clamps to fit the new shape.
Map stable contact points, then build and test a jig on a sample setup.
Position adjustable supports and check for movement before setting the cutter.
Build a quick jig around the easiest surfaces and begin machining the model.

basic.situation: A small prototype piece is ready for inspection, and the drawing gives its length while you have a ruler at your bench.

options.text: Use the ruler to check the piece and pass it along if it looks close.
Measure the length once and tell the maker whether it seems within range.
Ask a nearby worker to confirm the length before you mark the piece.
Measure the length against the drawing and record the reading for review.

advanced.situation: Several parts from a rework batch show slightly different readings, and the team needs consistent checks before the next run.

options.text: Set a shared datum and method, then record the batch acceptance range for everyone.
Recheck each part against the drawing and record variation before approving the next run.
Use one instrument for every part, logging readings that fall outside drawing limits.
Compare recorded readings with the team and identify parts needing a second measurement.

basic.situation: You are marking reference points on a metal blank for a model part, and the drawing uses an edge as its dimension reference.

options.text: Write down the point locations after marking them for the next operation.
Measure from the stated edge, mark the points, and note the dimensions used.
Use the drawing dimensions to mark the points and ask someone to check them.
Mark from the nearest convenient edge and carry on with the layout.

advanced.situation: A machined model part interferes with its assembly, and engineering asks you to describe the problem before considering a modification.

options.text: Suggest removing material from the interfering area and tell engineering the part is ready.
Record the interference location and measurements, then discuss the drawing with engineering.
Write down the assembly issue and continue with another model part for now.
Describe where the parts touch and ask engineering what change they prefer.

basic.situation: You are preparing a simple casting pattern, but the blueprint uses two dimensions that you cannot confidently relate.

options.text: Check the dimension references across views before calculating the pattern size.
Ask a patternmaker to point out which dimension controls the part size.
Use the larger dimension for the pattern and continue preparing the stock.
Compare the views and mark the dimensions you can identify for review.

advanced.situation: A complex casting drawing gives conflicting dimensions between a section and an overall view, affecting the pattern sequence you are planning.

options.text: Use the section view as the working reference and flag the conflict for review.
Follow the overall view and machine the pattern to meet the scheduled sequence.
Pause the sequence and ask a senior patternmaker which view to follow.
Compare the dimension origins, document the conflict, and confirm the design intent before sequencing.

basic.situation: You are checking a simple pattern dimension against its work order with calipers, but the reading is close to the stated limit.

options.text: Check the calipers at zero, remeasure the same faces, and note the reading.
Record the first reading and send the pattern onward to keep the queue moving.
Ask a coworker to check the dimension with a scale before you decide.
Take another caliper reading and tell the supervisor whether it seems acceptable.

advanced.situation: Two calipers give different readings on a complex pattern, and you need to help the team check dimensions consistently across the run.

options.text: Set the datum and contact points, verify the instruments, and document a shared method.
Choose the caliper with the more familiar display and use it for the batch.
Use one caliper for all pieces and note any dimensions that differ from the drawing.
Ask the team to compare readings and agree on a caliper for the run.

basic.situation: A sample part needs a simple template, and you are unsure which face should guide the outline.

options.text: Trace the sample outline in pencil and ask for a check before cutting.
Compare the sample faces with the work order, then trace the specified outline.
Ask a coworker which sample face usually guides a simple template.
Trace the easiest visible edge and cut the template to save preparation time.

advanced.situation: A high-precision run needs a complex core box, and the available wood and resin could behave differently through repeated production.

options.text: Ask the lead patternmaker which material they would select for the run.
Choose resin based on prior jobs and check the first core box against the drawing.
Use the available wood and adjust the core box after the first batch.
Compare material stability with the run needs, then design and validate the core box.

basic.situation: You are creating a simple digital model from a work order, but one dimension is unclear before you save the file for pattern production.

options.text: Enter the visible dimensions and save the model for the production queue.
Model the part using the sample proportions and ask someone to review the file.
Ask a coworker to explain the dimension before you create the model.
Build the clear features and mark the unclear dimension for confirmation before release.

advanced.situation: A complex digital pattern model is ready, but a junior colleague will use the file to prepare a production pattern with several mating features.

options.text: Check feature references and naming, then walk the colleague through key model controls.
Send the file as saved and let the colleague explore the mating features.
Offer to answer questions after the colleague starts working in the file.
Send the model with a short note naming the mating features to inspect.

basic.situation: You are preparing a pattern for lacquer, and the surface has a few marks that may show through the finish.

options.text: Apply the first coat over the marks and assess the surface after drying.
Prepare the surface as instructed, then apply a light coat for review.
Smooth the visible marks and apply the lacquer in the usual sequence.
Ask a coworker to inspect the marks before you begin coating the pattern.

advanced.situation: A plastic pattern has a difficult surface that will be sealed for repeated use, and the usual lacquer may not suit the material.

options.text: Check material compatibility, test the sealing coat, and assess the cured finish.
Use the familiar sealing wax and inspect the finish after it sets.
Ask the finishing lead which sealant has worked on similar patterns.
Apply the usual lacquer in a thicker coat to cover the difficult surface.

basic.situation: You are helping assemble two pattern sections, but glue residue keeps the mating faces from sitting flush.

options.text: Clean the mating faces, check their fit, and assemble with the specified fasteners.
Ask a coworker to hold the sections while you fasten the joint.
Scrape away the visible residue and tighten the bolts evenly across the joint.
Tighten the bolts to pull both faces together and finish the assembly.

advanced.situation: A critical pattern section is damaged before a CNC run, and the replacement must fit its existing assembly and holding fixture.

options.text: Ask the CNC operator to advise whether the repaired section can run.
Measure the mating features, repair to the drawing, and verify fit before release.
Repair the section to its drawing dimensions and check it with the CNC fixture.
Patch the damaged area to match the visible outline and resume machining.

basic.situation: You are packing a mold section for a routine casting and notice the pattern has several narrow contours.

options.text: Take leftover sand from another batch and ram it to save time.
Pack each section evenly with screened sand, checking the pattern contours.
Follow the usual ramming passes, then ask a coworker to inspect.
Fill low areas first and adjust pressure as the mold firms.

advanced.situation: A trial mold shows uneven density near a deep contour, and the next casting is a large customer order.

options.text: Use extra sand from an unverified pile to fill the deep contour.
Repeat the same ramming routine and watch the next casting closely.
Increase the ramming pressure throughout the mold for firmer packing.
Compare sand condition and ramming across the affected areas, then adjust the pattern.

basic.situation: You are smoothing a core box before a routine run and spot a shallow rough patch along its inner face.

options.text: Use a quick scrape across the full face to make it look even.
Brush the surface, then smooth the rough patch with a suitable hand tool.
Clean the box as usual and ask a coworker to check the patch.
Brush the whole box and leave the patch for the next shift.

advanced.situation: A complex mold has recurring rough spots near its parting surface, and the next batch needs consistent cores.

options.text: Set a smoothness check for the affected area and repair spots before release.
Repair the visible spots and rely on the usual visual check afterward.
Cover rough areas with extra repair material to speed preparation.
Grind the full parting surface to remove any possible roughness.

basic.situation: You are placing a pattern in a mold section under supervision and see that one edge sits close to the cavity wall.

options.text: Set it by eye and tighten the clamps firmly for stability.
Place the pattern near the marks and ask a coworker to confirm.
Center the pattern against its marks, then clamp the sections together.
Shift the pattern slightly toward the wall to make room.

advanced.situation: You are aligning a multi-part pattern for a large mold, and the section marks appear slightly offset from one another.

options.text: Shift the upper pattern until the seam appears straight from your side.
Clamp the sections using their marks and inspect the seam afterward.
Align each section to the pattern references, checking fit before clamping.
Force the sections together and tighten the clamps to close the gap.

basic.situation: You are forming a slab core around a pattern and have been asked to place wire reinforcement with hand tools.

options.text: Use a short wire piece and secure it with glue at the edge.
Skip the wire and make the slab thicker to save time.
Form the slab first, then press wire into the nearest open area.
Shape the slab around the pattern, placing wire where support is needed.

advanced.situation: A large slab core has cracked during handling, and you are assembling its replacement around a complex pattern.

options.text: Place reinforcing wire along vulnerable spans, securing it within the assembled core.
Remove the wire and rely on a thicker slab core alone.
Use the same wire layout and handle the replacement more gently.
Add more glue along the crack line and assemble the core again.

basic.situation: You are preparing a pattern for removal and have been asked to apply parting agent to its surfaces.

options.text: Spray the agent heavily around the edges to ease the lift.
Apply a light, even coat across the pattern surfaces before removal.
Use leftover agent from an unlabeled container to finish quickly.
Use the usual amount and ask a coworker to check coverage.

advanced.situation: A detailed pattern has resisted removal twice, and another rough lift could damage the mold surface.

options.text: Repeat the familiar coating and have a coworker guide the lift.
Use more of the current agent and increase the lifting force.
Apply a suitable parting agent evenly, then lift the upper section steadily.
Lever the pattern free against the mold edge to save the section.

basic.situation: You are cutting a simple sprue hole into a mold under supervision and need to keep the opening clear.

options.text: Use the usual cut and ask a coworker to inspect it afterward.
Cut the sprue hole to the marked position, keeping its opening clear.
Cut through the nearest thin wall to finish the opening quickly.
Cut a wider hole so the metal can enter more easily.

advanced.situation: A complex mold needs a runner hole, and your first cut appears too narrow for the planned metal flow.

options.text: Keep the narrow opening and ask the pour team to compensate.
Widen the hole slightly and watch how the next casting fills.
Cut a much larger hole to prevent any chance of restricted flow.
Check the channel layout, then adjust the runner hole to its specified dimensions.

basic.situation: You are setting a molding machine from a checklist and the temperature dial is close to its listed setting.

options.text: Set the listed temperature and speed, then confirm the cycle time.
Turn the temperature dial until the display looks close enough.
Use the previous run's values to avoid delaying the machine.
Set temperature and speed, then ask a coworker to check them.

advanced.situation: A complex part run is starting, and the work order lists a new cycle time alongside changed temperature and feed settings.

options.text: Enter all listed values and ask an operator to check the display.
Match listed settings to the work order, then observe a stable trial cycle.
Use settings from a similar part and begin a monitored trial.
Update temperature and feed values, then retain the listed cycle time.

basic.situation: You are checking molded parts from a routine run and notice a faint mark on one surface.

options.text: Polish the mark off so the part matches the others.
Set the marked part aside and continue checking the next ones.
Check the mark by eye and use the usual pass judgment.
Compare the mark with the specification and measure the part's key dimension.

advanced.situation: Several parts show the same shallow surface flaw, while machine gauges remain within their usual ranges.

options.text: Keep inspecting visually and set aside parts with obvious marks.
Share the repeated flaw with the team and continue routine checks.
Record the pattern and measurements, then compare them with the specification and readings.
Adjust the gauges to make the readings reflect the surface flaw.

basic.situation: You are preparing a machine for a simple order and the work sheet lists a temperature and cycle time.

options.text: Enter the temperature and use the cycle time from the last run.
Read both listed settings back against the order before entering them.
Copy the two values and ask a coworker to review them.
Use a familiar temperature and cycle time to start sooner.

advanced.situation: A blueprint for a new part shows two dimensions that seem inconsistent with the work order's setup notes.

options.text: Compare the drawing references and notes, then clarify the conflicting setup before entry.
Follow the work order notes and keep the drawing nearby during setup.
Choose the dimension that fits the current mold and continue preparation.
Use dimensions from a similar part and proceed with the setup.

basic.situation: You are cleaning a mold after a run and notice residue along its inner surface.

options.text: Use a grinding wheel across the full surface to clear it quickly.
Apply oil over the residue to ease the next production run.
Brush the visible residue and leave the mold ready for the next run.
Brush and scrape the residue, then check the inner surface for remaining buildup.

advanced.situation: A mold needs frequent cleaning because residue returns after runs, and you are preparing the team's routine care notes.

options.text: Add extra oil after each run to reduce the visible residue.
Document cleaning steps, note residue patterns, and brief the team at each shift start.
Track recurring buildup and cleaning intervals to guide routine care checks.
Skip scheduled cleaning when the mold looks usable to save time.

basic.situation: You are connecting a water hose to a die cooling system using hand tools and notice the fitting feels loose.

options.text: Tighten it firmly and start the machine to check for leaks.
Ask a coworker to check the fitting after you connect the hose.
Seat the fitting securely and check the hose connection before use.
Wrap the loose fitting with spare tape and continue the setup.

advanced.situation: After a production run, you need to remove a die and its cooling hose connection seems stuck.

options.text: Verify isolation, follow procedure, and seek a lead's help with the stuck hose.
Inspect fitting for a release method and consult a lead before choosing a tool.
Keep the die supported and request help rather than pulling against the attached hose.
Ask a coworker to steady the die while you loosen the connection.

basic.situation: You are watching an automatic molding machine and notice its cycle pauses longer than usual between parts.

options.text: Note the pause and check for a jam or warning.
Restart the machine to restore the usual production pace.
Tell the supervisor the cycle slowed and note when pauses began.
Wait through several cycles to see if the delay clears.

advanced.situation: The machine has had several brief jams this week, though each cleared before the next scheduled check.

options.text: Slow the machine slightly to reduce the chance of another jam.
Log jam times and compare them with cycle readings for recurring patterns.
Report repeated jams to the supervisor and keep monitoring cycle readings for patterns.
Clear each jam and resume production as soon as it stops.

basic.situation: A new bar stock order is ready, and you need to secure the first piece in the chuck before machining.

options.text: I would seat the bar against the stop and ask a nearby operator to check it.
I would clamp the bar by eye and start the first cut to save setup time.
I would position the bar against the stop and tighten the chuck evenly.
I would align the bar with the fixture stop, secure it, then request a setup check.

advanced.situation: A new die requires a different feed sequence, and two newer operators are waiting for you to guide their setup.

options.text: I would review the feed sequence with both operators and answer their setup questions.
I would demonstrate the sequence in stages and have each operator confirm the settings before running.
I would explain the setup steps and point out the feed controls before they begin.
I would give the team yesterday’s setup sequence and ask them to adapt it for this die.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to start the drill press and engage its coolant flow for a routine batch.

options.text: I would ask a coworker to watch the coolant while I start the press.
I would start the press with the coolant valve closed and open it after drilling.
I would open the valve, confirm coolant reaches the tool, then start the press.
I would start the press and open the coolant valve while watching the first piece.

advanced.situation: A part jams in an automatic feed while another machine is running, and you must clear the jam without disrupting the batch.

options.text: I would stop the affected feed, use the lift bar, and check the other machine’s cycle.
I would stop the affected machine and use a wire hook to free the part.
I would pause both feeds, then pull the jammed part free by hand.
I would stop the feed and ask a coworker to watch the running machine.

basic.situation: The first turned piece looks uneven, and you need to check its length against the job template before the batch continues.

options.text: I would measure the piece with a rule and ask the operator to review.
I would measure the piece against the template and record its length.
I would compare the piece with the template and note visible variation.
I would place the piece beside the template and compare both ends.

advanced.situation: A gear drawing gives several dimensions, and the machinist needs your calculation for a revised machine setting before cutting a costly blank.

options.text: I would use the previous gear’s setting and adjust it by feel for this blank.
I would calculate the setting from the drawing and check the dimensions against the machine chart.
I would work through the dimensions with the machinist before suggesting a setting.
I would calculate the setting from the drawing and write it down for the machinist.

basic.situation: A routine job order arrives for a batch of plastic parts, and you need to identify the stated size and tooling instructions.

options.text: I would read the size and tooling notes, then ask the lead about unclear markings.
I would scan the order for the part size and pass it to the setup operator.
I would note the stated size and tooling, then verify unclear markings with the lead.
I would copy the previous batch settings and start tooling without checking the order.

advanced.situation: A detailed order combines drilling and turning steps, but one tooling note conflicts with the sequence shown on the drawing.

options.text: I would list the drilling and turning steps, then ask the lead about the conflict.
I would plan the familiar turning steps first and leave the tooling note for later.
I would map each operation to its drawing note and flag the conflict before preparing the sequence.
I would follow the order sequence and treat the conflicting note as an old revision.

basic.situation: After a routine run, metal chips and dust remain around the machine bed, and your lead asks you to clean and oil it.

options.text: I would stop the machine, brush away chips, and oil the marked points.
I would clean the bed after stopping the machine and oil the marked points.
I would wipe the bed and ask the lead where the oil points are.
I would brush away chips and apply the specified oil while the machine runs slowly.

advanced.situation: A loose switch connection causes intermittent starts, and a worn cutter is also affecting the finish on the current batch.

options.text: I would tape the switch connection, replace the cutter, and continue the batch.
I would stop using the machine, report the switch fault, and note the worn cutter.
I would replace the worn cutter and report the switch fault for qualified service.
I would change the cutter and ask the lead to inspect the switch before restarting.

basic.situation: A small steel bracket has light rust and sharp edges after storage, and you are asked to finish it by hand.

options.text: I would file the sharp edges and ask the operator to handle the rust.
I would brush off rust, file the sharp edges, and inspect the bracket.
I would cover rust with paint and wrap the sharp edges for delivery.
I would use a file on the edges, brush off rust, and check the bracket.

advanced.situation: A finishing run produces rough edges, and the pressure readings and stroke lengths vary from the last accepted batch.

options.text: I would note the varying readings and ask the operator which finishing tool to use.
I would compare readings with the accepted run and choose a tool for the edges.
I would record pressure and stroke readings, then select a finishing tool for the rough edges.
I would keep the current settings and buff the rough edges before recording a final reading.

basic.situation: A simple sketch arrives for a replacement punch, and you need to identify its shape and basic dimensions before work begins.

options.text: I would look over the sketch and ask the lead which dimensions matter.
I would read the sketch dimensions and note the punch shape for the machinist.
I would copy the last punch dimensions and prepare the stock from memory.
I would read the dimensions and shape, then check the notes for stock requirements.

advanced.situation: A die assembly has several fitted components and detailed notes, and you need to plan the operation sequence before machining begins.

options.text: I would list the operations from the notes and review the order with the lead.
I would group similar machining steps together and ask the lead about fit order.
I would order the operations from the notes and check each step against the assembly drawing.
I would machine the largest components first and fit the rest as they arrive.

basic.situation: You need to mark a simple straight cut on metal stock using the ruler and protractor specified for the job.

options.text: I would mark the length from the stock edge and cut at the nearest angle.
I would use the protractor to mark the angle and ask the lead about the length.
I would mark the length from the reference edge and confirm the angle with the protractor.
I would mark the length with a ruler and ask a coworker to check the line.

advanced.situation: A multi-part die specification lists clearances and fitted dimensions, and you need to work out whether the assembly will move freely.

options.text: I would add the listed clearances and compare the total with the assembly drawing.
I would calculate the tolerance stack and compare the resulting clearances with the assembly drawing.
I would use the previous die’s clearance and adjust the new parts during fitting.
I would measure the mating parts and ask the lead whether the movement seems acceptable.

basic.situation: A small plate needs two tapped holes for a simple assembly, and you are assigned the drill press under supervision.

options.text: I would clamp the plate, check the marked positions, then drill and tap each hole.
I would align the plate, clamp it, and drill both holes from the marked positions.
I would hold the plate by hand and drill the holes from the marks.
I would clamp the plate and ask the supervisor to confirm the drill size.

advanced.situation: A CNC mill is set for a tight-finish part, but the first trial shows chatter near a curved edge.

options.text: I would ask the lead to review the chatter before changing the CNC settings.
I would inspect the trial surface, adjust the setup, and run another test piece.
I would reduce the feed and continue the full run to see whether chatter fades.
I would lower the feed slightly and inspect the next trial piece for chatter.

basic.situation: A metal blank is longer than the drawing calls for, and you need to trim it to the marked rough length with hand tools.

options.text: I would trim to the nearest convenient length and leave fitting for assembly.
I would mark the cut and ask a coworker to hold the stock steady.
I would check the marked length, cut the blank, and file the edge smooth.
I would cut at the marked line and file the edge to remove burrs.

advanced.situation: A replacement die block will face heat and repeated impact, and you must select a suitable metal from the available stock.

options.text: I would use the alloy from the last die block and confirm its stock size.
I would compare hardness and heat tolerance with the specifications before selecting stock.
I would compare the listed hardness values and ask the lead about heat exposure.
I would choose the hardest available alloy because impact parts need strong material.

basic.situation: A small machined guide must be held on the worktable while you check its fit against a mating part.

options.text: I would set the guide on the table and hold it while checking the mating part.
I would support the guide with a v-block, secure it, and check the mating fit.
I would position the guide in a vise and check its fit against the mating part.
I would ask the lead which clamp to use before setting the guide on the table.

advanced.situation: A complex part shifts during repeated milling, and the team needs a work aid that holds its angle for later pieces.

options.text: I would design a fixture that locates the faces and holds the angle repeatably.
I would sketch a fixture from the setup and ask the lead to review it.
I would secure the part and pause milling to check why it shifts.
I would add a shim beneath the shifting side and inspect another piece.

basic.situation: A flat steel surface has file marks after shaping, and you are asked to smooth it before the parts are assembled.

options.text: I would cover the visible file marks with a coat of paint before assembly.
I would ask the fitter whether the file marks will affect assembly.
I would smooth the surface with a file and check it under the bench light.
I would file down high spots, use emery cloth, and inspect the flat surface.

advanced.situation: A completed die produces parts with a slight contour mismatch during its test run, and the customer specification is strict.

options.text: I would adjust the die by eye and run the production batch to confirm the contour.
I would set aside the test parts and ask the lead whether the mismatch matters.
I would measure the test part against the contour specification, adjust the tool, and retest.
I would inspect the contour, make a small tool adjustment, and run another test part.

basic.situation: You are asked to weld two flat steel plates using the standard shop machine. The job sheet lists the joint size, and a senior worker is nearby for guidance.

options.text: You tack the plates first, then finish the weld after checking their fit.
You use a familiar setting and weld the plates before checking the job sheet.
You set the machine from the job sheet and weld the joint in steady passes.
You check the settings with the nearby worker, then complete the weld at the listed size.

advanced.situation: A stainless bracket must be welded overhead to a cast iron support. The joint is awkward, and the drawing gives limited guidance on the sequence.

options.text: You ask a senior welder to confirm the rod, then follow their sequence for the joint.
You choose a familiar rod and complete the overhead weld in one continuous pass.
You check the alloy and joint details, select suitable equipment, and weld in controlled passes.
You use the stainless setting and reduce the heat while welding the support.

basic.situation: After welding a small frame, you need to check whether its sides match the dimensions on the work sheet before it moves to the next station.

options.text: You use a template on the frame and mark any side that seems out of line.
You compare the frame with the last one and pass it along if they look alike.
You measure the longest side and check the main dimensions on the sheet.
You measure each side with a straightedge and compare it with the work sheet.

advanced.situation: During a run, you spot a fine crack on a finished weld and notice the machine gauge fluctuating. The next piece is ready for inspection.

options.text: You recheck the weld and gauge, then set the piece aside for inspection.
You hold the piece and report the crack and gauge fluctuation to the supervisor.
You tag the cracked piece, note the gauge change, and alert the supervisor before restarting.
You smooth the crack and continue, monitoring the gauge during the next piece.

basic.situation: You are about to grind rust from a plate before welding. Dust is gathering around the bench, and your face shield is on its hook.

options.text: You put on the face shield, clear nearby material, and grind the plate at the bench.
You move the plate to the side and grind it while keeping your face turned away.
You make a few quick passes, then put on the shield if dust spreads.
You put on the shield and ask a nearby worker to clear the bench for you.

advanced.situation: A drawing shows a long, angled joint on a stainless assembly with little access for the torch. You must choose a welding method before preparing the surfaces.

options.text: You compare the drawing with a similar joint and ask a senior welder to confirm the method.
You review the joint angle, alloy, and access, then select a method suited to the assembly.
You use the method from the last stainless job and prepare the same way.
You choose a torch method for the tight access and clean the joint before welding.

basic.situation: Two short plates need to meet squarely for a tack weld. The bench has rules, a square, and clamps available.

options.text: You clamp the plates near the ends, then check their alignment with a square.
You mark the joint with a rule and ask a coworker to hold the plates for tacking.
You align the edges with a square, check the rule marks, and clamp both plates.
You hold the plates by hand and tack them where the edges look even.

advanced.situation: A heavy frame must be set on a welding table using the shop hoist. The sling is available, and other workers are moving through the area.

options.text: You hook the frame at one corner and lift it onto the table in a short move.
You pause foot traffic, then lift the frame with the sling while watching its balance.
You clear the lift path, secure the frame with the sling, and guide it onto the table.
You secure the sling and ask a coworker to guide the frame as you lift it.

basic.situation: A thin sheet has a small bulge near its edge after fitting. You have a hand hammer and a flat support at the bench.

options.text: You support the sheet flat and tap the bulge in small, controlled passes.
You tap around the bulge, checking the edge against the bench after each pass.
You strike the raised area hard until the sheet looks flat.
You hold the sheet down and hammer the highest point until it flattens.

advanced.situation: A bent guard needs repair, but its attached bracket blocks access to the damaged section. The assembly must fit its original mounting points afterward.

options.text: You pull the guard into shape with the bracket attached, then check its fit.
You cut away the bracket, straighten the guard, and form a replacement from spare stock.
You remove the bracket and straighten the guard, leaving reassembly for the next shift.
You remove the bracket, straighten the guard on a press, then refit and check its mounting points.

basic.situation: After a short weld, dried slag and spatter remain around the joint. The part is due for a visual check at the next station.

options.text: You brush the joint with a wire brush and clear loose residue before passing it on.
You brush the visible slag and ask the next station to check the remaining area.
You wipe the part with a rag and send it along to keep the queue moving.
You use a scraper on the larger pieces and leave small specks for inspection.

advanced.situation: A thick weld bead exceeds the drawing profile, and the area is crowded. An arc-cutting set is available for removing excess weld material.

options.text: You cut quickly along the bead to bring it near the drawing profile.
You remove the highest section first, then inspect the profile against the drawing.
You mark excess weld, clear nearby items, and cut the bead in controlled passes.
You gauge the profile and ask a coworker to watch the area while you cut.

basic.situation: You receive a work order for a batch of brazed brackets. The drawing and schedule are at the machine, and the first piece is ready.

options.text: You read the work order and ask a coworker to confirm the joint details.
You check the schedule for the batch size and prepare the machine for the first piece.
You use the setup from yesterday's bracket batch and start the first piece.
You check the drawing and work order for the joint and batch instructions before starting.

advanced.situation: The schedule moves a job forward, and two operators are waiting for setup instructions. The work order lists a revised sequence for the machine.

options.text: You review the revised sequence and give both operators clear setup and use directions.
You read the revised sequence aloud and ask each operator to confirm their task.
You tell them to use the prior setup so the schedule stays on track.
You explain the first setup step, then let the operators coordinate the remaining sequence.

basic.situation: A new steel strip is thinner than the last batch. You need to select the torch tip and alloy material from the shop data chart.

options.text: You reuse yesterday's tip and alloy to start the first piece.
You choose a smaller tip and use alloy stored beside the machine.
You check the chart and choose the listed tip and alloy for this strip.
You check the chart for a tip, then ask a coworker about alloy.

advanced.situation: A run of small curved parts shifts during brazing, and the standard jig cannot hold their shape. You can make a fixture from available shop stock.

options.text: You shape a fixture to support each curve and hold parts aligned during brazing.
You wedge parts against the machine guide and continue brazing the run.
You clamp a plate beside the jig to steady each part during brazing.
You add a jig stop and check each part's position before brazing.

basic.situation: The machine is ready for a routine weld, and the work order gives the required cycle. You are at the control panel with a coworker nearby.

options.text: You turn the main control and start the machine, then watch the first piece closely.
You set the listed cycle on the controls and start the machine for the first piece.
You read the cycle from the work order and ask the coworker to check the panel.
You use the last cycle setting and press start to save setup time.

advanced.situation: A trial run shows uneven brazing across the joint. The machine is stable, but the bead suggests the heat cycle may need adjustment.

options.text: You slow the feed and continue testing at the current heat setting.
You adjust heat slightly and ask a coworker to review the next trial.
You sharply raise the heat setting and start the production run.
You compare the sample with specifications, adjust the cycle, and run another trial.

basic.situation: A work order calls for two metal plates to be joined at marked points. You have a rule, square, and template at the bench.

options.text: You mark points by eye and begin fitting both plates together.
You use the rule to mark points, then ask a coworker to check.
You mark weld points from the template and check spacing with a rule.
You place the template on both plates and mark edges for alignment.

advanced.situation: A replacement plate must fit a frame with a slight offset shown on the drawing. The parts are already cut, and you need to lay them out for bonding.

options.text: You mark the offset on the frame and fit the plate against the marks.
You align the plate edges evenly and tack them before checking the drawing.
You calculate the offset from the drawing, then fit and connect the plates to match it.
You check the offset on the drawing and ask a coworker to confirm your layout.

basic.situation: A completed welded bracket is held in the machine. The cycle has ended, and hand tools are available beside the fixture.

options.text: You pull the bracket free while the holding device remains closed.
You release the holding device and remove the bracket with the available hand tool.
You loosen the fixture and lift the bracket out by its cooler edge.
You check that the cycle ended and ask a coworker to release the fixture.

advanced.situation: A machine begins feeding wire unevenly during a batch, and the next component is already loaded. You can adjust its controls or stop the machine.

options.text: You stop the cycle, secure the loaded part, and check the feed controls before restarting.
You pause the machine and ask a coworker to inspect the feed before restarting.
You finish the current part at a slower speed and then inspect the feed setting.
You increase the feed setting during the cycle and let the batch continue.

basic.situation: Your shift has finished a short production run, and the report needs the machine's operating information before the next operator takes over.

options.text: You record today's run details and ask the next operator to review the report.
You copy the previous shift's figures into the report to finish it quickly.
You note total pieces produced and leave remaining report fields for later.
You enter run details in the report and compare entries with the machine display.

advanced.situation: A batch must meet a tight dimensional specification, and the machine gauge drifts during the run. You have measuring tools and time for a sample check.

options.text: You watch the gauge closely and check one finished piece before the batch ends.
You measure a sample against the specification and tell the supervisor the gauge is drifting.
You test sample pieces against specifications, note gauge drift, and report the concern.
You keep the run going and record the final piece count at shift end.

basic.situation: A work order lists a soak time that differs from the posted furnace chart, and the first batch is waiting.

options.text: You check the work order against the chart and ask the lead which cycle applies.
You compare both records, find the current approved revision, and confirm the cycle before loading.
You pause the batch and check the work order again for a clearer time.
You use the posted chart so the waiting batch can enter the furnace.

advanced.situation: A new product has a three-stage heat cycle, but its work order omits the cooling interval and production is due today.

options.text: You hold the order, identify the missing interval, and request an approved cycle before scheduling.
You schedule the first two stages and leave the cooling interval for the next shift.
You compare the stages with similar approved orders and ask the lead to clarify cooling.
You copy the previous product cycle and mark the new work order for review.

basic.situation: You are loading small stock with guidance when one piece sits unevenly near the furnace door.

options.text: You stop the conveyor, keep clear, and reposition the piece with the approved handling method.
You push the piece farther inside with a bar so the door can close.
You ask the supervisor to check the stock position before continuing the load.
You hold the next piece back and wait for the stock to settle.

advanced.situation: A crane is lowering a large ingot toward a soaking pit, but its path is close to stacked stock.

options.text: You signal the operator to lower the ingot quickly before the next load arrives.
You guide the crane operator along the usual route and watch the stacked stock.
You ask a coworker to watch the stock while you guide the ingot down.
You pause the lift, clear the travel path, and signal the operator through the safe approach.

basic.situation: Under supervision, you are lighting a gas burner and the flame weakens as you adjust the controls.

options.text: You ask the supervisor to check the gas and water settings before adjusting further.
You increase the gas control until the flame looks strong enough for heating.
You reduce the water flow slightly and watch whether the flame steadies.
You compare the gauges with the set points and adjust the controls as instructed.

advanced.situation: During a long cycle, the temperature chart fluctuates while gas and water readings remain within their usual ranges.

options.text: You compare chart readings with instrument checks, then make small measured control adjustments.
You raise the gas control carefully and record the temperature response.
You record the fluctuation and ask the lead which control needs adjustment.
You select a familiar control setting and monitor the cycle response closely.

basic.situation: With assistance, you remove a treated part after its specified furnace time, and the work order says to air cool it.

options.text: You use handling tools to place the part in the marked air cooling area.
You place the part in a water bath, though order specifies air cooling.
You ask your coworker to confirm the cooling method before placing the part.
You set the part on a clear metal surface and let it cool there.

advanced.situation: A specialized alloy finishes its cycle, but the work order names an oil bath and the nearby bath labels are unclear.
