options.text: You select a clearly labelled bath and begin cooling the alloy as directed.
You use an oil bath from earlier shifts for similar parts during production.
You confirm the specified oil bath with the lead before cooling the alloy.
You set the alloy aside and ask the lead to identify the specified oil bath.

basic.situation: You are following a setup sheet to start a heat treating machine, but its bath setting is hard to read.

options.text: Use yesterday's run setting to start the machine without checking the source.
Pause startup and request a clearer setup sheet before entering bath settings.
Start the machine and enter its bath setting after checking the display.
Ask an experienced operator to read the bath setting and confirm it.

advanced.situation: You tend an induction unit and a flame hardening machine, and both are ready for jobs with overlapping deadlines.

options.text: You run the easier job on both machines to clear the queue quickly.
You check each setup sheet, confirm machine readiness, and sequence the jobs around safe tending.
You start the induction job first and leave the other machine at its current setup.
You ask the lead which machine should take the job with the earlier deadline.

basic.situation: You remove a part after its furnace cycle, but another task is waiting and the time is not yet on the record sheet.

options.text: You write an estimated time so the record sheet is complete before handover.
You record the removal time from the clock before moving to the next task.
You ask a coworker to note the time while you handle the waiting task.
You tell the next operator the removal time and finish the record later.

advanced.situation: A new worker is learning furnace operation while the shift is busy, and they reach toward a control before checking the setup sheet.

options.text: You stop the adjustment, show the setup sequence, and have them demonstrate it before resuming.
You take over the controls and let the worker observe the rest of the cycle.
You remind them to check the setup sheet after they finish the control step.
You ask the worker to pause, then explain the relevant control and safety steps.

basic.situation: A flat plate needs straight cut lines and hole marks, and the next station is waiting for your layout.

options.text: You mark the visible edges and estimate the hole spacing with a ruler.
You copy the spacing from a similar plate and punch the hole centers.
You measure from the drawing and mark the lines and holes with a scribe.
You confirm the drawing datum, measure each point, and mark lines and centers for checking.

advanced.situation: An irregular plate needs a curved cut line and welding symbols, but its reference edge is partly trimmed.

options.text: You establish a usable datum, transfer the curve, and mark each symbol from the drawing.
You follow the curve from the template and add symbols near the weld area.
You copy the curve from a similar plate and mark the welding symbols by eye.
You mark the curve from the remaining edge and ask the fitter to check symbols.

basic.situation: A workpiece is ready for checking, and your ruler measurement appears slightly different from the drawing dimension.

options.text: You ask another worker to check the same edge before deciding what to report.
You measure from the drawing datum, record the reading, and flag the difference for review.
You round the reading to the drawing dimension so the part can move on.
You recheck the dimension with a square and tell the fitter about the difference.

advanced.situation: A template seems centered on an irregular workpiece, but a dial indicator shows different readings at opposite ends.

options.text: You ask a coworker to repeat the indicator readings before you move the template.
You adjust the template until the readings look closer, then continue marking.
You verify the datum, reset the template, and compare both ends with the specified tolerance.
You record the higher reading and proceed with the layout as planned.

basic.situation: A simple blueprint shows a bracket with two dimensions and a hole symbol, and the cutting station needs your layout.

options.text: You identify the drawing datum, dimensions, and hole symbol before marking the bracket.
You mark the outer edges first and ask the cutter about the hole location.
You read the dimensions and hole symbol, then mark the bracket from the drawing.
You copy the hole spacing from a bracket already on the bench.

advanced.situation: You are adding dimensions to a drawing, and a bend line appears to conflict with a nearby hole location.

options.text: You move the hole dimension to match the bend line and send the drawing onward.
You add the visible dimensions and ask the drafter whether the hole needs moving.
You dimension the hole from the nearest edge and leave the bend line unchanged.
You mark the conflict, preserve the shown geometry, and seek design clarification before adding dimensions.

basic.situation: You need to cut a paper template from a provided pattern, but its center mark is faint.

options.text: You trace the outline and estimate the center mark from its nearby edge.
You clarify the faint mark against the pattern, then cut and label the template.
You cut the template and place the center mark where it seems balanced.
You ask a coworker to check the pattern before cutting the paper template.

advanced.situation: A specialized frame needs a metal template with several cutouts, but the operation sequence is unclear on the drawing.

options.text: You adapt a similar frame template after checking its dimensions against this job's drawing.
You ask the fitter to confirm cutout order before preparing the template for this frame.
You review the drawing, confirm reference points and sequence, then prepare a matching template.
You prepare a plain template, then add cutouts after confirming their order with the fitter.

basic.situation: With help, you are placing a small workpiece on a surface plate, but it rocks on one corner.

options.text: You fit a parallel block, then check the workpiece rests steadily.
You ask your coworker to hold the piece while you add a support block.
You press the rocking corner down and mark the workpiece in place.
You move the piece to a flatter area and ask for another check.

advanced.situation: A large hull section needs temporary bracing for welding, but one brace shifts as the part settles.

options.text: You tack the brace in place so the section stays aligned for welding.
You ask a coworker to steady the brace while you check the alignment.
You pause welding, clear the area, then reset the brace with help.
You tighten the brace and continue the fit up while watching the joint.

basic.situation: You are aligning a fabricated bracket to a marked surface, but its edge leaves a small gap at one end.

options.text: You clamp the bracket at one end and fill the gap during welding.
You hold the bracket flush and ask the welder whether the gap is acceptable.
You compare the bracket with the marks, adjust its position, and recheck the contact.
You tap the bracket toward the marks and check the gap once more.

advanced.situation: You are fitting a fabricated bulkhead section, and its frame alignment conflicts with the plate edge at two points.

options.text: You trim the plate edge at the two tight points and continue fitting the section.
You check the frame and plate against the layout, then ask the fitter to review the conflict.
You clamp the frame at the better aligned point and see whether the other gap closes.
You document both mismatch points, recheck the layout references, and hold fitting for clarification.

basic.situation: You are starting a zinc plating run, and the checklist asks you to confirm the tank and machine status.

options.text: Use yesterday's settings and start before confirming the tank contents.
Check each checklist item, then start and watch the first cycle.
Ask a nearby operator to confirm the setup before you start.
Start the machine after checking the listed guards, tank level, and gauge readings.

advanced.situation: The plating line's gauge fluctuates and the coating looks uneven. You need to decide whether to adjust settings or stop the machine.

options.text: Turn the current dial until the gauge settles, then finish the batch.
Stop the machine, record the readings, and check the setup against the fault procedure.
Ask the shift lead to review the gauge before changing machine settings.
Reduce the current slightly and keep watching the gauge and coating.

basic.situation: During a routine plating run, your supervisor asks you to adjust the current dial after the voltage reading changes.

options.text: Ask your supervisor to point out the dial before making the change.
Turn the dial toward the usual setting and check the next reading.
Follow the instructed adjustment, then verify both current and voltage readings.
Move the current dial several marks to bring the voltage reading down.

advanced.situation: A customer order needs a thicker nickel deposit, but the current and voltage readings drift during the run. You are assigned to adjust the controls.

options.text: Increase voltage until the deposit looks thicker, then recheck the current.
Set current and voltage from the last similar order and continue.
Raise current in small steps and compare readings with the target.
Pause adjustments, log both readings, and follow the approved settings procedure for this order.

basic.situation: After a coating run, you are asked to rinse finished parts in cleansing liquid and dry them before they move to packing.

options.text: Ask a coworker which cleansing liquid was used on the last batch.
Dip the parts briefly and dry them together to keep packing on schedule.
Rinse each part as directed and dry it with the assigned cloth.
Use the specified rinse, then inspect each part before drying and moving it onward.

advanced.situation: Several complex parts still show stubborn residue after rinsing, and the next coating stage is waiting for them.

options.text: Grind the visible residue off each part and return them to the line.
Try the approved cleaning method on one part and check its surface before treating the rest.
Repeat the rinse cycle and let the coating team know about the delay.
Use an air hose to clear the residue, then send the parts onward.

basic.situation: You are helping with a routine batch and must immerse each workpiece in the coating solution for its specified time.

options.text: Use the previous batch's timing so the workpieces move through together.
Lower the workpieces together and estimate the time from the wall clock.
Ask the experienced operator to confirm the immersion time before you begin.
Follow the specified immersion time and keep each workpiece in view.

advanced.situation: A mixed-material order has different specified immersion times, and the bath queue is backing up while you manage the workpieces.

options.text: Use the longest time for every material to keep the queue moving.
Ask the next operator to watch the bath while you check the order sheet.
Group pieces by material and track each group's specified immersion time.
Start with the shorter times and extend pieces that look unfinished.

basic.situation: You are checking a newly coated batch and notice a few bubbles on the surface before the parts move to the next station.

options.text: Mark the bubbled parts and let the next station decide what to do.
Pack the parts with minor bubbles so the batch can leave on time.
Set the bubbled parts aside and show the operator the affected areas.
Check the remaining parts for bubbles, then report the count to the operator.

advanced.situation: A high-value batch looks smooth, but earlier checks found inconsistent deposit thickness. You have a micrometer and the order specification.

options.text: Measure one part and use its result to clear the full batch.
Measure several parts and share the readings with the quality technician.
Measure representative parts, compare results with the specification, and record any outliers.
Inspect the surface under good light and report any visible changes.

basic.situation: At the end of a routine plating run, you need to complete the production record with the batch details and machine readings.

options.text: Record the readings you noted during the run and submit the form.
Copy the previous batch record, then update its product name, quantity, date, and operator details.
Enter batch details and readings from the run sheet, then review the form.
Fill in the batch number and ask a coworker to add the readings.

advanced.situation: Weekly records show longer plating runs on one shift, and your manager asks you to identify a useful pattern for the team.

options.text: Compare run times by shift and product, then share the pattern with records.
Point out the longest runs and ask the shift lead what happened.
Tell the team the slower shift should work faster next week, without checking product differences.
Average all run times and suggest shortening each run by that amount.

basic.situation: You are mounting a grinding wheel for a routine job, and the specification lists the wheel type and machine setup.

options.text: Mount the wheel that was used on the last similar job.
Ask a coworker to confirm the wheel type before you mount it.
Choose a wheel of similar size and tighten it with the usual hand tools.
Check the wheel specification, mount it with hand tools, and confirm it is seated.

advanced.situation: A blueprint shows several angled surfaces and tight tolerances. You need to plan the grinding sequence and setup before the machine is available.

options.text: Ask the lead to review your setup plan before the machine is prepared.
Start with the largest surface and decide the sequence as you go.
Set up for the first angle and keep the remaining blueprint nearby.
Plan the setup from the blueprint, noting each angle, wheel choice, and sequence.

basic.situation: The grinding wheel begins to run dry during a routine job, and you are responsible for directing coolant flow with the valve.

options.text: Keep grinding at the same pace and watch for a smoother finish.
Turn the coolant valve until flow reaches the wheel and workpiece steadily.
Open the valve fully so the wheel gets plenty of coolant.
Ask the operator to check the coolant flow before you adjust the valve.

advanced.situation: A replacement cutting tool must meet a specified angle and width, but your first measurement differs from the blueprint dimensions.

options.text: Recheck the measurements, compute the required angle and width, then adjust the tool.
Adjust the tool to the measured angle and begin a trial cut.
Ask a coworker to verify the blueprint dimensions before you adjust anything.
Use the closest available angle setting and check the first workpiece afterward.

basic.situation: A routine workpiece needs a filed edge before inspection, and the job instructions name the hand file to use.

options.text: Use the nearest file and smooth the edge until it feels acceptable.
Use the prescribed file and finish the edge with even, controlled strokes.
Ask the inspector which file they prefer before finishing the edge.
File the edge quickly with a coarse tool to clear the queue.

advanced.situation: An intricate die surface has a small burr near a narrow groove, and the workpiece must retain its specified shape.

options.text: Ask the lead to confirm the finishing approach before touching the groove.
Use a coarse file to remove the burr before checking the groove.
File the accessible edge and leave the groove for another operator.
Choose a suitable prescribed hand tool and work the burr in controlled passes.

basic.situation: You remove finished pieces from the grinder and notice one feels rougher and measures wider than the others.

options.text: Ask a coworker to feel the rough piece before you rack it.
Measure the pieces against the specification and set the outlier aside.
Set the rough piece aside and rack the remaining pieces for inspection.
Place all pieces on the rack and mention the rough one at handover.

advanced.situation: Several operators disagree about acceptable surface feel on a tight-tolerance batch. You are asked to guide the next inspection checks.

options.text: Compare sample surfaces and dimensions with the specification, then explain the checks to operators.
Tell each operator to use their usual judgement and keep the line moving.
Use the smoothest sample as the standard and ask operators to compare by feel.
Ask the quality lead to settle the disagreement before anyone checks more pieces.

basic.situation: At the end of a routine shift, you are assigned to clean and lubricate accessible machine parts.

options.text: Wipe the visible surfaces and leave lubrication for the next shift.
Clean the parts listed for upkeep, then apply the specified lubricant points.
Clean and lubricate the parts you recognise before handing the machine over.
Ask the next operator which parts they usually lubricate during handover.

advanced.situation: A grinding machine makes a new vibration, and inspection shows a worn component that your assigned maintenance task allows you to replace with hand tools.

options.text: Stop the machine, identify the worn part, and replace it using the maintenance instructions.
Tighten nearby fasteners and restart to see whether the vibration fades.
Ask the maintenance lead to confirm the replacement part before you begin.
Replace the worn part with a similar spare and monitor the next run.

basic.situation: During a routine grinding run, you hear an unusual scraping sound and see the workpiece shift slightly.

options.text: Slow the feed and finish this pass while watching the workpiece.
Ask a nearby operator whether that sound is normal for this machine.
Pause the feed and check whether the scraping sound continues.
Stop the machine and report the sound and movement before restarting.

advanced.situation: A machine's vibration has slowly increased over several runs, though there is no obvious defect yet. You are monitoring operation during a precision job.

options.text: Tell the lead about the rising trend and ask whether to stop the machine.
Continue the run and check the finished workpiece for signs of vibration.
Compare vibration with recent readings; stop the machine if it exceeds limits.
Reduce the grinding speed slightly and listen for any change in vibration.

basic.situation: You are checking a supplied photograph before plate making and notice a faint mark near the edge.

options.text: You approve the thumbnail because the image looks clean on screen.
You compare the image with its original and flag obvious imperfections.
You inspect the image at working size and magnification, then note defects.
You scan the image and flag visible edge marks for review.

advanced.situation: A finished plate's dots look slightly different from the master, and the job is due soon. How would you check it?

options.text: You compare both plates under the light box and record microscope dot measurements.
You release the plate because the difference seems small from arm's length.
You measure several dots with the microscope and compare them to the job notes.
You check the plate under a light box and mark any visible mismatch.

basic.situation: You proof a brochure page and spot a possibly mistyped price beside a product image.

options.text: You read the page once and mark wording that seems unusual.
You check the price against the supplied copy and flag any mismatch.
You compare the price with the product list and mark visible text errors.
You approve the page because the layout looks consistent with earlier pages.

advanced.situation: A proof looks washed out in the shadows, though the client expects deep tones. How would you assess the original?

options.text: You inspect the highlights and shadows with a densitometer before advising a change.
You use a densitometer on the shadows and compare the reading with the proof.
You measure density across highlights, middle tones, and shadows, then note the readings.
You raise the density setting until the proof appears darker to you.

basic.situation: You are asked to make plates from an approved file, and the laser equipment is ready for a supervised run.

options.text: You select a recent file from the job folder and begin the run.
You load the approved file, check the plate position, and start the supervised run.
You confirm the file name and begin the run with the equipment settings shown.
You load the file and start the equipment while watching its status display.

advanced.situation: A long press run is planned, but the requested plate type is not clearly stated on the job ticket.

options.text: You match the expected run length to plate durability and document the selected type.
You check available plate stock and choose a type used for similar jobs.
You use the plate type left from the previous job to keep production moving.
You choose a durable plate commonly used for long runs and note the choice.

basic.situation: A customer requests a smaller copy of a supplied layout, and you need to calculate the reduction for a proof.

options.text: You use the proportion wheel on the width and apply that reduction to the copy.
You measure the target width and use the proportion wheel to calculate a reduction.
You measure the original and target sizes with a proportion wheel, then set the reduction.
You reduce the copy until it looks small enough on the screen.

advanced.situation: A client wants to approve a brochure on screen before the print run, but its colors may shift in print. What would you prepare?

options.text: You send a low-resolution screen preview to speed up client approval.
You export a digital proof and review images and text at normal viewing size.
You generate a digital proof using output settings and inspect key color areas.
You make a digital proof with current document settings and share it for review.

basic.situation: You receive several approved job files and need to store them on the computer-aided equipment for the next shift.

options.text: You save the files in the current job folder and record the job reference.
You enter the job details and save the files using the date as the label.
You enter the job details, save files under the job reference, and confirm retrieval.
You overwrite the older folder with the new files to keep the list short.

advanced.situation: A supplied image looks soft, and the job ticket specifies a fine screen ruling and exact size. How would you prepare the scan?

options.text: You set the scanner's size, ruling, density, and exposure to the job specifications.
You use the previous job's scanner preset because its image looked sharp.
You set the scanner's size and ruling, then check the scan for softness.
You adjust scanner exposure and density until the scan looks clear on screen.

basic.situation: After a short run, you are asked to clean the equipment before the next job.

options.text: You wipe the accessible surfaces and tell the next shift the equipment is ready.
You clean the surfaces listed in the instructions and return the tools.
You leave the cleaning for the next shift because the run was short.
You clean the assigned surfaces, check for residue, and report any adjustment needed.

advanced.situation: A page has too much copy for its assigned space, and the text size needs adjusting before output.

options.text: You adjust text size and position to fit copy while preserving reading order.
You reduce text size until the copy fits inside its assigned space.
You remove the final paragraph so the remaining copy fits the page.
You move the text block and make a small size change to fit.

basic.situation: You are loading a new paper size for a supervised run, and the feed guides need setting.

options.text: You load paper and set the guides to match the job ticket.
You use the previous paper setting because the new stock looks similar.
You load the stock, set guides to its size, and check the feed path.
You load the stock and ask the senior operator to check the guides.

advanced.situation: Registration drifts across the sheet after a plate change, and the cylinder alignment is uncertain.

options.text: You check plate seating and cylinder alignment against register marks, then adjust carefully.
You adjust the cylinder in small steps while checking the register marks.
You reseat the plate and check registration on the next sheet.
You increase feed tension until sheets appear to register more closely.

basic.situation: The job ticket calls for a named ink color, and the matching paper stock has arrived. How would you prepare the materials?

options.text: You use nearby ink already in the fountain to save setup time.
You match paper and ink to the ticket, then fill the fountain.
You check the ticket color and confirm the paper label before setup.
You verify the stock and fill the fountain from its labeled ink container.

advanced.situation: A custom brand shade is required for a large run, and the available paper has a different finish from the sample.

options.text: You use a close premixed shade and proceed on the available stock.
You mix from color notes and compare the shade with the sample under lighting.
You test the mixed shade on available paper and refine it by eye.
You mix a measured shade and check a proof on stock before filling.

basic.situation: An automated press alert reports uneven ink flow during a run, and the sheets are becoming pale.

options.text: You raise the ink flow slightly and watch the next few sheets for improvement.
You check the alert details, adjust fountain flow in small steps, and inspect a sheet.
You ask a senior operator to review the alert before changing the flow.
You clear the alert and keep the current flow to avoid slowing production.

advanced.situation: Humidity has risen during a long run, and ink transfer is becoming inconsistent. How would you respond?

options.text: You check humidity, tune ink flow, and track transfer changes on samples.
You adjust ink flow gradually and monitor the next samples for transfer consistency.
You check the room humidity and adjust the press setting listed for the job.
You increase ink flow to cover the inconsistent areas across the sheet.

basic.situation: The press has started, and your first proof may show a registration shift. How would you check it?

options.text: You pull a proof and check its alignment and registration against the job marks.
You approve the first sheet because the colors appear close to the sample.
You inspect the proof's registration and ink coverage before continuing the run.
You pull a proof and inspect coverage, alignment, and registration against job marks.

advanced.situation: Random samples show slight density variation during a long run, and newer operators are unsure what to inspect.

options.text: You tell the operators to keep samples that look similar to the last approved sheet.
You show the operators how to compare sample density and registration across sheets.
You explain the job's acceptable appearance and demonstrate sample checks for density and registration.
You ask each operator to inspect a sample and report any visible density change.

basic.situation: A completed run leaves ink in the fountain and residue on a plate. You have the cleaning instructions.

options.text: You clean the fountain and plate using the listed materials and steps.
You clean the fountain and plate as instructed, then check both for residue.
You wipe the fountain and plate, then put away the cleaning materials.
You leave the plate in place and clean the fountain at the next setup.

advanced.situation: A press handle feels loose after cleaning, and the next shift starts soon. What would you do within your maintenance duties?

options.text: You inspect the handle, tighten it with a suitable tool, and record the repair.
You remove the press guard to reach the handle faster and tighten it.
You report the loose handle and leave a note for the maintenance team.
You tighten the handle with a suitable hand tool and brief the next shift.

basic.situation: A job order lists quantity, paper size, and two ink colors, and the workstation needs its settings.

options.text: You enter the quantity and stock, then ask a colleague to check the colors.
You enter the quantity, stock size, and colors from the job order.
You enter quantity, stock, and colors, then compare settings with the order.
You reuse the settings from the last job with a similar paper size.

advanced.situation: Two jobs need the same stock, and remaining inventory looks low against the orders. How would you support production planning?

options.text: You reserve the remaining stock for the larger job and update the count later.
You compare orders with stock, record needs, and request replenishment for shortages.
You check the stock count and alert the planner that supplies may run short.
You review the orders and ask stores whether more stock is available.

basic.situation: You are setting up the glue machine for a short booklet run, and the reservoir is low while the flow setting is unclear.

options.text: You check the glue level, confirm the specified temperature, and test flow on scrap sheets.
You raise the flow until the first sheets feed smoothly, then continue the run.
You top up the reservoir and keep the previous flow setting for this short batch.
You ask the lead to confirm the flow setting before starting the warmed machine.

advanced.situation: A mixed-size book order needs a knife and roller change, and the first setup leaves one size slightly misaligned.

options.text: You set the knife for the largest book and trim the smaller sizes afterward.
You compare the knife and roller positions with the order, then ask the lead about the mismatch.
You use the prior job's guide positions and check the first book from each size.
You adjust the guides and rollers to the work order, then test each size before the run.

basic.situation: You are gluing endpapers onto a small batch, and a few sheets lift slightly as you brush the signatures.

options.text: You pause and ask an experienced binder to confirm your brush technique.
You add glue to lifted edges and press the batch together.
You align endpapers, brush evenly, and check the first bonds as they set.
You reapply glue to lifted sheets, then finish the remaining signatures.

advanced.situation: A large run is due today, and the first pressed books show uneven edges after trimming to the work order size.

options.text: You compare order dimensions with the machine stop, then consult the lead about uneven edges.
You check the trim reference, reset the stop, and sample books before continuing.
You trim the remaining books to match the first copy, then check their edges.
You slow the feed and inspect several trimmed books for even edges.

basic.situation: You are checking a sample stack of bound booklets before packing and notice one torn page and a loose thread.

options.text: You inspect several copies for the same faults and separate affected booklets for review.
You show the sample to the lead and ask how many copies to inspect.
You remove the torn booklet and continue with the rest of the stack.
You check the next few booklets for torn pages and loose threads.

advanced.situation: A bound batch passes a quick page check, but samples show faint glue marks that appear only near the spine under angled light.

options.text: You check more copies under angled light and hold the marked samples aside.
You inspect samples under consistent light, note where marks recur, and share the pattern with production.
You approve the batch because the marks are faint and the pages stay attached.
You record the glue marks and ask the lead whether the batch should be held.

basic.situation: After a shift, you are assigned to clean a bindery machine and apply lubricant as shown on the maintenance sheet.

options.text: You wipe the accessible parts and apply lubricant to the marked points.
You check the sheet with the lead before cleaning and lubricating the machine.
You clean the listed parts, apply the specified lubricant, and record the completed care.
You lubricate the moving parts generously before wiping away visible residue.

advanced.situation: The binder starts making a new clicking sound and its output slows, though no jam is visible during your shift.

options.text: You keep the machine running at reduced speed until the order is complete.
You tell the lead about the sound and ask whether a mechanic should inspect it.
You stop to inspect the accessible parts, clean or lubricate as instructed, and report the sound.
You clean around the rollers and restart the machine at its usual pace.

basic.situation: You finish a routine booklet batch and need to enter its output and rejected copies on the daily production form.

options.text: You ask the shift lead to review figures against the tally before submitting the form.
You enter the completed and rejected counts from the tally, then check the form totals.
You copy both counts from the tally sheet onto the daily form.
You enter the completed count and estimate rejects from the waste stack.

advanced.situation: Two work orders share a paper size but require different spine widths, and the next job must start before the current run ends.

options.text: You flag the spine difference and wait for the next order before staging guides.
You read both work orders and ask the lead which guide set to stage.
You compare order dimensions and spine details, then stage matching guides for changeover.
You use the current guide positions for both jobs because the paper size matches.

basic.situation: Finished books are ready for dispatch, and you need to wrap them and stack the cartons on a pallet for collection.

options.text: You wrap the books and place each carton on the pallet in neat rows.
You wrap the books securely, label each carton, and stack stable pallet layers.
You check the dispatch list with a colleague before wrapping and stacking cartons.
You stack cartons tightly and wrap the pallet for the collection team.

advanced.situation: A new worker is assigned to an automatic binder before a rush run, and you are asked to show the safe setup and startup steps.

options.text: You walk through the setup sheet and ask the worker to repeat the steps.
You demonstrate the setup and ask the lead to watch the worker's first run.
You show the worker the startup buttons and let them follow your last setup.
You demonstrate setup, explain guards and stop controls, then supervise a practice run.

basic.situation: You are starting a washer with a new load, and the guide specifies valve and soap settings. What do you do?

options.text: Ask a coworker which valve position worked on a similar load.
Use the last load's settings and start the washer to keep the queue moving.
Follow the guide's valve and soap settings, then start the washer.
Set the valves and soap from the guide, then check the cycle before loading.

advanced.situation: A dryer displays an unfamiliar error during a busy shift, and a new worker asks what to do. How do you respond?

options.text: Show the new worker the reset steps, then restart the dryer.
Pause loading, check the guide, and explain the safe response for this error.
Hold the load and report the error before starting another cycle.
Ask the worker to monitor another dryer while you test a restart.

basic.situation: A cotton shirt has a fresh food stain, and its care label permits water treatment. How do you pre-treat it?

options.text: Pre-soak and gently work the stain with the approved solution, then check the result.
Put the shirt straight into the regular wash with the rest of the load.
Apply the approved neutralizer and scrub the spot firmly before washing.
Dab the stain with neutralizer and let it soak before washing.

advanced.situation: A dark jacket has an oily mark near a delicate trim, and its fabric label is unclear. Which spotting approach do you take?

options.text: Use a mild spotting solution on the mark and watch for color change.
Identify the fabric and stain first, then choose a suitable solvent and test discreetly.
Apply the familiar solvent to the whole marked area and blot it dry.
Send the jacket for standard cleaning and inspect the trim afterward.

basic.situation: You need a detergent solution for a routine laundry batch, and the mix sheet gives the amounts. How do you prepare it?

options.text: Use the amount from yesterday's batch and pour the solution into the washer.
Measure each ingredient from the mix sheet, then label the prepared solution.
Follow the mix sheet and stir the solution before adding it.
Measure the detergent and ask a coworker whether the strength looks suitable.

advanced.situation: A customer needs a close color match on a test swatch, and the standard dye mix looks too warm. How do you adjust the trial?

options.text: Check the swatch under steady light, then adjust a measured trial by approved method.
Add bleach to the dye vat until the test swatch appears cooler.
Prepare a revised dye sample and compare it with the target swatch.
Add a small amount of cooler dye from a similar job to the trial.

basic.situation: A mixed laundry delivery includes light and dark items with different dirt levels. How do you sort it into lots?

options.text: Check color, fabric, and soil level against the checklist before assigning lots.
Combine the similar-looking items and send them through the usual wash.
Sort by color first, then check the dirt level on each group.
Separate the light and dark items, then ask a coworker about the rest.

advanced.situation: A garment's label is missing, and its trim may have a fragile dye. Your procedure permits testing a small sample. What do you do?

options.text: Treat it as a delicate fabric and inspect the result after gentle cleaning.
Use the approved sample test and choose treatment based on the observed reaction.
Take an approved sample, test it by the procedure, and record the result before treatment.
Use a flame test on a hidden garment edge to identify the fabric.

basic.situation: You are hanging trousers on stretch frames to dry, and one frame seems wider than the garment. What do you do?

options.text: Stretch the trousers firmly over the frame so they dry without creases.
Adjust the frame to fit the trousers, then hang them evenly to dry.
Hang the trousers on this frame and loosen the fit after a short time.
Use a smaller frame from the rack and check the garment's shape later.

advanced.situation: A delicate blouse needs pressing, and another worker is unsure how much heat to use. How do you guide the finish?

options.text: Check the garment guidance, choose a suitable press setting, and demonstrate a test area.
Show the worker the low setting and ask them to watch the finish.
Use the usual press setting and tell the worker to keep the blouse moving.
Demonstrate a short press on a hidden area, then inspect the fabric.

basic.situation: A dryer filter has lint buildup, and the care guide lists cleaning and lubrication steps. What do you do?

options.text: Remove the lint and check the filter before returning the dryer to use.
Clean the filter, then ask the next shift to handle lubrication.
Follow the care guide to clean the filter and lubricate the listed parts.
Brush off visible lint and restart the dryer for the next load.

advanced.situation: A new coworker will clean filters across several machines, and one model has a different lubricant point. How do you organize the care routine?

options.text: Show the model-specific guide, then check each filter and lubrication point with them.
Give them the guide and ask them to report any unfamiliar machine.
Have them use the same lubrication point on every machine to finish sooner.
Demonstrate one machine's filter cleaning and ask them to follow the guide for others.

basic.situation: You are lowering a pressing head over a shirt panel, and the queue is building. How do you position it for pressing?

options.text: I would ask a nearby operator to confirm placement before lowering the head.
I would align the panel beneath the head, then press at the listed setting.
I would check clearance, align the panel, then lower the head for its timed cycle.
I would lower the head quickly to keep the queue moving during the rush.

advanced.situation: An evening gown has delicate beading near a wrinkled hem, and the finishing deadline is close. How do you press it by hand?

options.text: I would use a hand iron on the hem, checking the beading after each pass.
I would test a hidden area, shield the beading, and use controlled hand-iron passes.
I would press the whole hem at the usual heat to finish before dispatch.
I would lower the heat and press the hem slowly around the beading.

basic.situation: A shirt panel is bunched on the ironing board before its turn at the press. How do you prepare it?

options.text: I would pull the panel flat by its corners and feed it onward.
I would place the panel under the press as it lies to save time.
I would smooth the panel from the centre outward, then align its seams.
I would straighten the panel and check its edges against the board guide.

advanced.situation: A cleaned knitted cardigan is shorter than its measurement sheet, and steam has softened the fibres. How do you reshape it by hand?

options.text: I would use the block to restore length, then compare the finished cardigan with its sheet.
I would pull the cardigan longer by hand until it looks close to its former shape.
I would stretch it to the listed length, then let it dry on the block.
I would block it to the original measurements, checking length and width as it settles.

basic.situation: The press has released a finished tablecloth, and another item is waiting. How do you handle the cloth?

options.text: I would remove it, hang it to cool, and route it for the next step.
I would fold the warm cloth now so the next press can start.
I would remove the cloth and hang it to cool before checking its tag.
I would remove the cloth and stack it with the warm pieces for cooling.

advanced.situation: You spot an oily mark on a customer's jacket before dispatch, and the care label is unclear. How do you treat the spot?

options.text: I would identify the mark, then apply a fabric-safe spotter in small dabs.
I would check the fabric and ask the senior finisher which spotter to use.
I would identify the stain and test a suitable treatment on a hidden area first.
I would dab the mark with the usual solution and return the jacket to pressing.

basic.situation: A pressed blouse is ready for customer collection, but its tag has slipped off the hanger. How do you prepare it?

options.text: I would hang it with the other blouses and attach a replacement tag.
I would fold the blouse neatly and place it with the tagged orders.
I would hang the blouse, replace its tag, and match it to the order slip.
I would put it in a garment bag and leave the tag for the counter.

advanced.situation: A heat-sensitive blouse and a sturdy pair of trousers need finishing on the same shift. Which pressing machines do you select?

options.text: I would press the blouse first on a cooler machine, then assess the trousers.
I would choose a lower-heat option for the blouse and a suitable press for the trousers.
I would use the same press for both items to keep the work flowing.
I would check the care labels and choose presses suited to each garment.

basic.situation: A cotton shirt has a stubborn crease, and the steam iron is unavailable. How do you soften the fabric?

options.text: I would ask a coworker to mist the shirt while I prepare the iron.
I would spray water over the crease and press it at the usual setting.
I would spray the crease lightly, smooth the shirt, then iron that section.
I would dampen the whole shirt so the crease releases during pressing.

advanced.situation: A rayon blouse and a thick cotton shirt both need smooth finishes, and neither can use steam. How do you choose the moisture?

options.text: I would dampen cotton first, then assess whether the blouse needs a light spray.
I would mist the rayon lightly and target cotton creases, checking each fabric's response.
I would begin with a light mist on each garment and inspect the creases.
I would spray both garments lightly, then compare their surfaces before pressing.

basic.situation: A work order lists a pressing temperature, and the machine is set lower from the previous job. How do you set it?

options.text: I would raise the temperature well above the listed setting to warm the plate faster.
I would ask the shift lead to set the temperature before I start.
I would raise the temperature to the work order setting and begin pressing.
I would set the listed temperature, check the display, and confirm it stabilizes before pressing.

advanced.situation: A lined jacket is leaving shiny marks, and the pressure reading fluctuates during a rush order. How do you adjust the controls?

options.text: I would ease pressure slightly, then inspect the next jacket and check whether shine decreases.
I would pause the run, check order settings, adjust one control, and test a sample.
I would lower temperature and pressure together until the shiny marks begin to fade.
I would ask a senior operator to review the controls before resuming this order.

basic.situation: You are setting up a sewing machine for a routine seam, and a new thread spool is ready. How do you prepare it?

options.text: I would mount the spool and thread the needle, then start the seam slowly.
I would place the spool, thread each guide, and check the bobbin before sewing.
I would follow the threading path and insert the bobbin as shown on the machine.
I would thread the needle directly from the spool to save setup time.

advanced.situation: A machine keeps skipping stitches after a style change, and a new operator is waiting to learn setup. How do you respond?

options.text: I would check needle fit, guides, threading, and attachment settings, then show the operator each check.
I would increase the speed so the machine can push through the skipped stitches.
I would ask maintenance to inspect the machine while the operator watches the setup.
I would replace the needle, rethread the machine, then teach the operator the routine setup.

basic.situation: A pocket piece has chalk marks that must line up beneath the needle. How do you position it for sewing?

options.text: I would align the chalk marks with the template, then guide the piece steadily.
I would line up the marks with the template and secure the piece before sewing.
I would sew across the pocket piece first and trim it to fit later.
I would place the piece under the needle and follow the chalk marks by eye.

advanced.situation: A curved sleeve section twists as you guide it, and a new colleague is learning the seam. How do you manage the piece?

options.text: I would stretch the sleeve edge and ask my colleague to observe.
I would pull the sleeve flat and sew the curve in one pass.
I would mark alignment points, guide the curve in sections, and explain cues.
I would ease the sleeve through short sections and show my colleague the method.

basic.situation: You are assigned a straight seam on a single-needle machine, and your supervisor is nearby. How do you begin operating it?

options.text: I would start quickly so I can finish the seam before the next batch.
I would start at a steady speed, keep the seam aligned, and watch the stitching.
I would ask the supervisor to operate the machine while I watch the seam.
I would sew at a moderate speed and check the seam after the first section.

advanced.situation: A complex collar style puckers on the first sample, and two operators are waiting for guidance. How do you adjust the machine?

options.text: I would raise tension and speed, then tell both operators to use them.
I would check style requirements, adjust settings on a sample, and coach both operators.
I would lower speed, adjust tension, and inspect another sample before continuing.
I would ask the line lead to select settings while operators continue sewing.

basic.situation: A batch has two shades of blue fabric, and the pieces must match before sewing. How do you prepare the sequence?

options.text: I would ask the sewing operator to confirm the shade as each piece arrives.
I would separate the shades and check the pattern before bundling the pieces.
I would sort by shade and pattern, then compare each bundle before sending it onward.
I would stack the pieces by size and let sewing sort the shades later.

advanced.situation: Finished shirts show occasional broken stitches, and a new inspector asks what to check. How do you guide the inspection?

options.text: I would check several shirts for broken thread and show the inspector where to look.
I would inspect seams against the checklist and demonstrate how to spot broken stitches.
I would pass smooth shirts for now and focus on the next style.
I would sample across the batch, compare seams with standards, and teach defect logging.

basic.situation: A sewn garment has loose thread ends and is still held in the machine. How do you finish the piece?

options.text: I would remove the garment and trim the visible thread ends neatly.
I would pull the garment free and leave thread ends for the next station.
I would cut the threads while the machine is running to save a handling step.
I would remove the garment, trim loose threads, and check the seam ends.

advanced.situation: A new line adds elastic to curved waistbands, and finishers are leaving uneven joins. How do you organize the finishing work?

options.text: I would show one finisher how to align the elastic and ask them to share the method.
I would tell each finisher to attach elastic by feel and inspect at the end.
I would set a sample waistband standard and have finishers compare their joins to it.
I would define checkpoints for elastic alignment and join quality, then coach finishers using sample pieces.

basic.situation: Your shift ends after a run of shirts, and the machine needs routine cleaning. How do you close out the work?

options.text: I would record the quantity and ask the supervisor which cleaning supplies to use.
I would record the quantity, clean and oil the machine, and note any needle wear.
I would wipe the table and leave the quantity for the next shift to record.
I would clean and oil the machine, then enter the processed quantity in the log.

advanced.situation: The production log and thread stock count differ after a busy shift, and the machine is due for cleaning. How do you reconcile the closeout?

options.text: I would compare the log with the stock count, then tell the supervisor the difference.
I would check the entries against job slips, note the mismatch, and clean the machine.
I would adjust the production log to match the stock count, then finish cleaning before handover.
I would recount materials, trace entries, document the difference, and complete cleaning checks.

basic.situation: A customer needs replacement shoe panels, and the leather varies slightly in texture. You must trace the approved pattern onto suitable material.

options.text: Trace the pattern on a spare leather piece before checking the main material.
Check the pattern area for consistent texture, then trace it on suitable leather.
Trace the pattern on the closest matching leather and start cutting the panels.
Ask a colleague to choose the leather, then trace the pattern on it.

advanced.situation: A custom therapeutic shoe needs firm, matching leather panels. The first hide has uneven strength near the planned seam, and the order specifies a consistent finish.

options.text: Ask the senior worker which hide seems suitable, then lay out the panels.
Compare strength, color, and texture across candidate panels before tracing the pattern.
Place the pattern on the first hide and avoid the visibly uneven seam area.
Use the strongest-looking section and note the uneven area for the maker.

basic.situation: You are cutting two matching leather tabs from a simple paper pattern. The hide shifts slightly as you position it on the bench.

options.text: Ask a colleague to steady the hide while you cut around the pattern.
Hold the pattern flat and cut both tabs along its marked outline.
Cut the tabs freehand, using the paper pattern as a nearby size guide.
Pin the pattern at one corner and cut around its remaining edges.

advanced.situation: A premium repair needs a heel profile to match the shoe precisely. After shaping, one edge looks slightly uneven against the existing sole.

options.text: Buff the heel until the uneven edge looks less visible from above.
Sand the uneven edge lightly and return the heel for fitting.
Compare the profile with the shoe, reshape the edge, then buff it smooth.
Ask the senior repairer to inspect the profile before you finish sanding.

basic.situation: You are joining two simple leather pieces for a shoe repair. Their marked edges meet, but the pieces move slightly as you prepare to stitch.

options.text: Add a small amount of glue before stitching the marked edges together.
Stitch along the nearest edge and trim the pieces after joining them.
Hold the marks together and stitch slowly along the joined edge.
Secure the aligned pieces, check the marks, then stitch the joined edge.

advanced.situation: You are attaching an outsole to a custom shoe, and the upper sits unevenly on the last. A new operator is ready to help with the assembly.

options.text: Ask the operator to hold the upper while you attach the outsole.
Show the operator the seam line, then attach the outsole as positioned.
Have the operator apply the outsole while you check the heel placement.
Realign the upper on the last, explain the alignment, then attach the outsole.

basic.situation: A customer brings in dusty leather shoes with light scuffs and asks for a basic clean and polish before collection this afternoon.

options.text: Apply polish over the dusty areas and buff the shoes for collection.
Brush off dust, clean the leather, then apply a matching polish.
Ask a colleague to check the leather before you choose a polish.
Wipe the shoes with a damp cloth and use the available polish.

advanced.situation: A leather handbag has a torn seam near its handle, and the lining is loose. The customer needs it for travel tomorrow and asks whether you can repair it today.

options.text: Re-sew the visible seam and tuck the loose lining inside the bag.
Explain the timing and repair the seam while securing the lining separately.
Check the seam and handle attachment, then repair the damaged stitching and lining.
Repair the seam first, then ask the customer to return for lining work.

basic.situation: A customer requests a standard shoe insert. You have a simple specification and need to record the foot measurements before preparing the order.

options.text: Take both measurements and check them against the listed size range.
Measure both feet with a tape and record the larger measurement.
Read the specification, measure both feet, and record each result clearly.
Ask a colleague to confirm the size after you take one measurement.

advanced.situation: A prescription and foot cast specify a custom lift, but the measurements appear inconsistent with the cast. You are preparing inserts for a therapeutic shoe.

options.text: Use the cast for the insert and mention the measurement difference at handover.
Ask the senior fitter to review both sources before you prepare the insert.
Make the lift from the written measurement and keep the cast nearby.
Compare the prescription and cast, note the discrepancy, and clarify before shaping.

basic.situation: You are adding a buckle to a leather belt. The marked holes sit close to the edge, and the customer expects the belt today.

options.text: Punch the marked holes and attach the buckle with the available hardware.
Check the marks against the buckle, then punch and attach the hardware.
Move the holes slightly inward and fit the buckle using the same hardware.
Ask a colleague to confirm the hole spacing before you attach the buckle.

advanced.situation: A custom leather panel needs stamped decoration, cushioning, and a protective lining. The sample stamp is crisp, but the lining edge may show after assembly.

options.text: Check the assembled edge, adjust the lining position, then stamp the panel consistently.
Set the stamp spacing from the sample, then attach the lining and cushioning.
Stamp the panel and glue the lining over the cushioning as planned.
Stamp the panel and trim any exposed lining after the glue has set.

basic.situation: You are preparing a stitching machine for a short shoe-panel run. The thread guide diagram is nearby, and the bobbin is not loaded.

options.text: Follow the guide slots, thread the needle, and load the matching bobbin.
Ask a colleague to check the thread path after you load the bobbin.
Thread the needle from memory and load a bobbin from the spool rack.
Load the bobbin, then thread the needle through the nearest guide slots.

advanced.situation: A new operator reports skipped stitches after changing thread. You spot the thread outside one guide slot while the next batch is waiting.

options.text: Ask the operator to rethread from the diagram while you prepare the next bundle.
Review the diagram with the operator and check the thread path together.
Trace the full thread path, adjust the guide, then show the operator the setup.
Reseat the thread in that slot and restart the batch at the current settings.

basic.situation: You are stitching a shoe part, but it shifts as the presser foot lowers. A colleague is waiting to pass the next part.

options.text: Lower the foot, steady the part, then start stitching along the seam.
Ask your colleague to hold the part while you lower the foot and stitch.
Reposition the part, lower the foot to secure it, then begin stitching.
Start stitching while your colleague holds the part near the marked edge.

advanced.situation: A thick leather panel is puckering under the needle, and the next batch uses thinner material. A new operator asks which settings to use.

options.text: Adjust stitch length and tension on a sample, then show the operator the result.
Lengthen the stitch and raise tension for both materials to save setup time.
Test a small adjustment on scrap, then tell the operator the settings used.
Ask the operator to reduce tension slightly and begin with the next panel.

basic.situation: You are placing a shoe upper under the needle. Its seam marks are visible, but the material curls slightly at one edge.

options.text: Ask a colleague to hold the curled edge while you align the seam marks.
Follow the seam marks and let the presser foot flatten the curled edge.
Align the seam marks, smooth the curled edge, and position the part under the needle.
Position the part by its straight edge and stitch toward the seam marks.

advanced.situation: A curved shoe design has a seam line that shifts between sizes. The team is waiting for your aligned parts before stitching the first production batch.

options.text: Align each part by eye and ask the stitcher to flag any mismatch.
Check a sample from each size, then explain the seam references to the team.
Compare each size's marks, record the alignment points, and position parts to them.
Use the smallest size markings as a guide for every curved part.

basic.situation: You remove a finished shoe from the machine. The checklist calls for a visible seam and stitch channel inspection before the pair moves on.

options.text: Remove the shoe and send it forward so the next station can inspect it.
Ask a colleague to check the channel while you remove the next shoe.
Look over the upper and pass the shoe along if the stitches appear even.
Check the seam and stitch channel against the checklist before passing the shoe.

advanced.situation: Several finished pairs show slight stitch drift near the toe. You are checking the batch against specifications before it goes to packing.

options.text: Set aside the visibly uneven pairs and inspect the rest of the batch.
Accept pairs with even-looking stitches and note the toe drift for later.
Check the affected pairs closely and ask the line lead what to do next.
Compare toe stitches with the specification, separate affected pairs, and record the defect pattern.

basic.situation: You finish a short run and find loose thread ends on several shoe parts. The machine has visible dust around its work area.

options.text: Ask a colleague to clean the machine while you trim the thread ends.
Trim thread close to each seam and leave dust for the next shift.
Cut the loose thread ends and brush dust from the machine's work area.
Follow the cleaning routine, then trim the thread ends with scissors.

advanced.situation: A replacement needle is needed after a break, and thread scraps are collecting near the machine. A newer operator asks how to prevent repeat stoppages.

options.text: Show a safe needle change, clear scraps, and set a check with the operator.
Replace the needle and clear scraps, then resume the queued work.
Replace the needle, clear scraps, and tell the operator to watch for breakage.
Replace the needle, explain scrap removal, and suggest checking it each shift.

basic.situation: A work order lists a leather type and thread color for a small shoe batch. You are unsure whether the tagged material matches the order.

options.text: Read the order and tag together, then check the material description before setup.
Use the tagged material and ask the next operator to confirm the thread color.
Ask a colleague to read the order while you prepare the tagged material.
Check the leather type on the order and tell the next operator the thread color.

advanced.situation: Two work orders show different thread colors for similar shoe parts, and the machine passed its startup check. The team is ready to begin stitching.

options.text: Use the color on the largest batch and note the other order for review.
Start with the color shown on the first order and sort the parts later.
Compare both orders and tags, clarify the color conflict, then brief the team.
Ask the line lead which color to use while the team stages the parts.

basic.situation: A customer’s lining has opened at a short seam, and you have been asked to close it before collection.

options.text: Sew the lining closed quickly, following its visible edge.
Match the seam allowance, secure the layers, and sew evenly.
Pin the lining and sew a straight seam at a steady pace.
Baste the lining, then check its edge before finishing.

advanced.situation: A decorative fagoting stitch on a formal garment keeps loosening, and a newer worker needs to learn a reliable method.

options.text: Ask the worker to copy a finished section as a guide.
Have the worker repeat the stitch until it looks consistent.
Teach the stitch sequence, then check the first few repeats together.
Show the worker your usual stitch, then let them practise.

basic.situation: You are cutting a simple fabric shape for a small repair, and the paper pattern has clear measurements.

options.text: Trace the pattern, then cut along its marked outline.
Pin the paper pattern and cut around its outside edge.
Cut around the paper edge as it sits on the fabric.
Check the measurements, secure the pattern, and cut carefully.

advanced.situation: A client says a made-to-measure jacket pulls at the shoulder, while its marked pattern and finished measurements appear to differ.

options.text: Check the client’s movement, compare pattern marks, then pin a test adjustment.
Compare the shoulder markings, then pin a small adjustment for fitting.
Pin the shoulder seam higher and ask the client to try it.
Cut the shoulder line to match the finished jacket shape.

basic.situation: You need to hand-sew a loose button back onto a shirt, but the thread supplied is a different thickness from the original.

options.text: Use several strands of the supplied thread for extra strength.
Compare the thread thickness, choose a close match, and thread the needle.
Thread a needle with the supplied thread and sew the button.
Choose a nearby thread colour and thread one needle strand.

advanced.situation: A delicate embroidered cuff needs a replacement thread that will blend in, pass through tiny holes, and hold during wear.

options.text: Use the strongest thread in the drawer for a lasting repair.
Select fine thread that passes through the cuff holes easily.
Compare colour and thickness, test a short length, then thread the needle.
Choose a matching colour thread, then test it through one hole.

basic.situation: You are attaching a narrow trim to a straight fabric edge, and the guide marks are visible.

options.text: Line up the trim with the guide marks and pin it.
Start pinning the trim at one end and follow the edge.
Match the trim to the marks and sew as you go.
Measure the edge, align the trim to marks, and pin evenly.

advanced.situation: A patterned garment panel must meet a narrow cuff exactly, and slight misalignment would show across the finished seam.

options.text: Measure the cuff and align its centre before pinning both ends.
Align the pattern at the seam, pin the cuff, and sew steadily.
Pin both ends, then ease the fabric together while sewing.
Match the pattern points, measure the seam, and secure several checkpoints.

basic.situation: You are preparing a square of fabric for a simple hand-sewn hem, and its edge needs a neat fold.

options.text: Press the fabric edge into a fold, then pin it loosely.
Measure the fold width, press it, and secure it with pins.
Fold the edge once and hold it with a few pins.
Fold the edge by eye and begin stitching near the corner.

advanced.situation: You are preparing slippery lining and outer fabric together for a curved seam, and the layers keep sliding apart.

options.text: Match the curve at several points, then secure the layers with fine pins.
Fold both layers together and add pins along the curved edge.
Pin the layers at both ends, then stretch them around the curve.
Align the ends and centre, then pin the layers before sewing.

basic.situation: After hand-sewing a hem, you are asked to smooth the seam before returning the garment to the work rack.

options.text: Use a warm iron and press the seam from one side.
Press the seam with a cloth between fabric and iron.
Run a hot iron across the seam to flatten it quickly.
Press the seam gently, checking the fabric label first.

advanced.situation: A handmade ribbon knot on a display piece slips loose when handled, and the client expects it to stay neat through delivery.

options.text: Retie the knot tightly and trim the ribbon tails close.
Retie the knot with even loops and leave longer tails.
Test the ribbon tension, retie the knot, and secure its tails discreetly.
Add a small hidden stitch where the knot meets the ribbon.

basic.situation: You are hemming a pair of trousers, and the customer’s marked line shows the requested length.

options.text: Pin the hem at the line, then sew it evenly.
Cut the trouser legs at the marked line before hemming.
Check both marked lengths, fold the hems, and sew evenly.
Fold each leg at its mark and stitch around the opening.

advanced.situation: A high-end jacket sleeve has a curved lining and outer seam that must be joined neatly before the final fitting.

options.text: Match the seam points, distribute the lining ease, and baste before stitching.
Pin the sleeve layers at the ends and sew along the curve.
Baste the sleeve layers, check the curve, then machine stitch them.
Pull the lining tight and stitch both layers together quickly.

basic.situation: A customer’s trousers feel loose at the waist, and you have been asked to take in the side seams.

options.text: Remove the side seam stitches and take in a small amount.
Pin the waist to fit, confirm with the customer, then unpick.
Unpick the side seams and cut away the extra fabric.
Mark the new seam, then remove the old stitches carefully.

advanced.situation: Several staff are altering suit jackets, but their shoulder adjustments produce inconsistent fit across different customers.

options.text: Set shared fitting checkpoints, demonstrate adjustments, and compare trial results.
Show staff a shoulder adjustment, then review finished jackets weekly.
Ask each tailor to follow their preferred shoulder alteration method.
Share a sample jacket and invite staff to discuss its shoulder fit.

basic.situation: You are measuring a customer’s sleeve for shortening, and the customer is waiting while you record the alteration.

options.text: Measure from the shoulder, mark the sleeve, and note the length.
Mark the sleeve at its current cuff and record that measurement.
Ask the customer to show the preferred cuff position, then measure and record it.
Measure the sleeve from the cuff and write down the result.

advanced.situation: A customer’s jacket fits differently when they move their arms, and you need to establish the shoulder alteration before marking it.

options.text: Pin both shoulders evenly and record the adjustment for later.
Measure the shoulder seam while the customer stands naturally.
Watch the customer move, compare both shoulders, and mark a test alteration.
Measure both shoulders and mark the side that appears longer.

basic.situation: You are cutting a simple sleeve panel, and its paper pattern has clear outlines and a grain direction mark.

options.text: Cut around the pattern before checking its grain direction.
Pin the pattern where it fits and cut around the paper edge.
Place the pattern on the grain, pin it, and cut carefully.
Check the grain direction, secure the pattern, and cut along its outline.

advanced.situation: A patterned fabric has limited usable width, and the jacket front and matching pocket pieces must be cut with the motif aligned.

options.text: Match the motif across fronts, reserve pocket placement, then cut pieces.
Lay out all pieces by grain, then adjust pockets to match nearby motifs.
Cut the jacket fronts along the grain and mark pockets afterward.
Place the jacket fronts first, then fit pocket pieces into remaining fabric.

basic.situation: A customer brings a simple shirt design and asks whether it can be made with the fabric they selected.

options.text: Adapt the design to the fabric and give a rough cost range.
Review the design details, check fabric needs, and estimate sewing time.
Promise the same price as a basic shirt before reviewing details.
Copy the design and estimate fabric use from a similar shirt.

advanced.situation: A customer wants an original formal outfit with layered fabric and hand-finished details, but has not set a spending limit.

options.text: Design the outfit, then quote a low price to secure the order.
Sketch a layered design and price it from a similar outfit.
Clarify priorities, develop a design, and cost materials and labour separately.
Draft a design and offer a broad estimate for the full outfit.

basic.situation: A customer brings in a jacket for a zipper replacement, and you need to record the requested work on its tag.

options.text: Attach a blank tag so the alteration team can check the jacket.
Read the garment tag, confirm the zipper request, and write it down.
Write “replace zipper” on the tag and attach it to the jacket.
Note the zipper issue on a tag and place it by the jacket.

advanced.situation: A customer requests a style change to a suit, but the alteration tag and spoken instructions describe different lapel shapes.

options.text: Hold the suit and ask a colleague to compare the tag with the customer's request.
Show both descriptions to the customer, confirm the lapel choice, and revise the alteration tag.
Ask the customer to choose a lapel, then tell the sewing team and record it.
Proceed using the alteration tag, then check the finished lapel against the customer's request.

basic.situation: A fabric roll comes off the dye line, and you notice a faint patch that looks different from the surrounding shade. Your trainer is nearby.

options.text: Use the approved sample to compare the patch, then flag the affected section.
Set the roll aside and mention the patch when the next check is due.
Mark the patch and ask the trainer to compare it with the approved sample.
Pass the roll forward since the shade difference looks small from here.

advanced.situation: Two inspectors disagree about a subtle shade shift across a long roll, and several similar orders are scheduled. You need to set a consistent inspection standard.

options.text: Keep the existing checks and let each inspector judge the shade from experience.
Define a sample-based shade threshold, document it, and coach inspectors using borderline examples.
Ask both inspectors to use the same lighting and compare marked samples against the order standard.
Add another visual check at the roll end and record any disagreement for review.

basic.situation: Before a dye run, you see a loose-looking guard beside a moving roller. The operator is preparing to start the machine.

options.text: Tell the operator what you saw and ask them to check the guard before starting.
Start the run at a slower speed and watch the guard during the first minutes.
Note the guard in the shift log and continue with the planned setup.
Keep clear of the roller and show the supervisor the guard for an inspection.

advanced.situation: A dye machine has uneven tension and a recurring vibration after a recent adjustment. You are asked to inspect it before a high-value production run.

options.text: Check the accessible rollers and tension settings, then report the vibration pattern for repair assessment.
Compare the vibration with prior settings, inspect likely wear points, and document findings for repair planning.
Ask the mechanic to replace the tension parts before checking the roller alignment.
Run a short trial at reduced speed and see whether the vibration settles down.

basic.situation: You are weighing dye for a small batch when the scale reading shifts slightly as you add powder. The formula card is beside you.

options.text: Ask a nearby operator to read the scale while you continue adding dye.
Add a little more powder until the displayed amount seems close to the target.
Pause the addition, steady the container, and recheck the weight against the formula card.
Wait for the display to settle, then compare the weight with the formula card.

advanced.situation: A complex shade mix uses several small dye weights, and a batch record shows one entry was copied from an earlier order. You must verify the measurements.

options.text: Use the earlier order's weights since the shade name and fabric match closely.
Check each recorded weight against the current formula and mark the copied entry for confirmation.
Ask the mixer to confirm the copied amount and proceed with the remaining ingredients.
Reconcile every measured amount with the current formula before releasing the mix for use.

basic.situation: While watching a dye run, you see the temperature display flicker near the edge of its marked range as fabric enters the machine.

options.text: Tell the operator about the flicker and check the displayed temperature against the range.
Write down the flicker and ask a coworker whether the display does that often.
Check the temperature again after the next section of fabric enters.
Keep watching the cloth and mention the display at the end of the run.

advanced.situation: Temperature is within range, but dye flow keeps pulsing and the cloth entering the machine shows uneven color. You are monitoring a large order.

options.text: Compare flow and temperature trends against ranges, then alert the operator about the linked anomaly.
Observe another cloth section and record whether its color variation continues through the machine.
Adjusting flow without guidance could affect the batch, so report the variation first.
Record pulsing flow and alert the operator while checking the cloth entering the machine.

basic.situation: Your trainer asks you to start a washing machine for a routine fabric load. The controls are set, and the drum is empty.

options.text: Confirm the trainer's setup, then start the machine while they watch the cycle begin.
Start the machine and call the trainer over once the drum begins turning.
Wait beside the controls until your trainer is ready to watch you start.
Ask a coworker nearby to confirm the controls before you start the machine.

advanced.situation: A delicate fabric order is running at its specified speed, but tension rises as the roll thickens. You are authorized to adjust controls for this run.

options.text: Adjust tension toward its specified range and record the change for the shift handover.
Reduce speed first and see whether the rising tension settles across the next section.
Keep the current settings and report the tension change after the roll finishes.
Use the fabric guidance to balance tension and speed, then watch the next section closely.

basic.situation: You are told to add water to a tank for a routine solution, but the order card gives two different batch volumes. A coworker is waiting to soak fabric.

options.text: Use the smaller volume and tell the team after the fabric is ready.
Ask the coworker which volume they used for the previous similar order.
Check the order details with your coworker before adding water to the tank.
Hold the water addition and show the conflicting volumes to the supervisor.

advanced.situation: A large batch needs a stronger dye solution, but the tank's flow seems erratic and the soak time is due to begin. You are preparing the solution.

options.text: Ask a coworker to confirm the planned soak time while you prepare the stronger mix.
Pause chemical additions and tell the supervisor the tank flow is behaving unusually.
Check the established formula and soak plan, then report the flow problem before adding chemicals.
Increase the dye concentration to offset the uneven flow and start the soak on schedule.

basic.situation: You are placing a paper pattern on a single fabric layer when the edge shifts near the marked cutting line. A trainer is supervising.

options.text: Stop cutting, align the pattern with marks, and ask your trainer to check placement.
Ask a coworker to steady the pattern while you cut beside the nearest mark.
Pause and show your trainer where the pattern shifted before continuing layout.
Cut along the visible line, then trim uneven edges after lifting the piece.

advanced.situation: A multi-layer stack has limited fabric remaining, and several pieces must fit around a flaw near one edge. You are planning the cutting sequence.

options.text: Cut the largest pieces first and fit smaller pieces into whatever fabric remains.
Arrange pieces around the flaw, then check grain direction and layer alignment before cutting.
Ask the team which pieces are most urgent and lay those out first.
Map the flaw and grain direction, compare nesting layouts, and confirm the stack before cutting.

basic.situation: Your trainer has set a cutting machine for a routine order. The first test piece comes out slightly shorter than the specification.

options.text: Ask a coworker to measure the piece while you prepare the next layer.
Run the next piece at the same setting to see whether the length repeats.
Stop the test, compare the setting with the specification, and show your trainer the piece.
Tell your trainer the piece is short and wait for instructions before restarting.
