advanced.situation: A cutter produces inconsistent lengths on two fabric types despite using the same speed. You are authorized to adjust settings and troubleshoot the setup.

options.text: Keep the shared speed and ask the operator to monitor further variation.
Check tension settings and record which fabric shows a length difference.
Compare fabric settings and dimensions, then adjust controls for each setup.
Adjust speed for the thicker fabric, then compare pieces with order dimensions.

basic.situation: A finished fabric piece looks clean, but its cut edge seems uneven against the checklist sample. You are checking the batch before packing.

options.text: Ask a coworker whether the edge looks acceptable before completing the checklist.
Measure the edge against the specification and separate the piece if it falls outside.
Pack the piece with the batch since the uneven edge is barely visible.
Compare the edge with the checklist sample and mark the piece for a closer check.

advanced.situation: Inspectors disagree about whether a faint edge fray meets the standard across several fabric types. You are asked to define a consistent check and coach the team.

options.text: Assign a second inspector to disputed pieces and record both decisions.
Use the current sample and have inspectors compare fraying under shared viewing conditions.
Set a measurable fray limit for each fabric, then coach inspectors with borderline pieces.
Ask experienced inspectors to decide cases and save examples for team discussion.

basic.situation: During cleaning, you notice a loose cover near a cutter's blade area. The maintenance checklist says to inspect the machine before use.

options.text: Note the cover on the checklist, then continue cleaning the remaining machine parts.
Wipe around the cover and start the machine to see whether it rattles.
Keep clear of the blade and show the loose cover to the lead.
Ask a coworker to hold the cover while you finish cleaning around the blade area.

advanced.situation: A cutter repeatedly loses alignment after routine cleaning, and a replacement part appears worn. You are inspecting it before the next shift begins.

options.text: Inspect alignment points and the worn part, then document findings for repair planning.
Tighten accessible parts and return the cutter to service for the next shift.
Report the worn part and leave the cutter tagged for a mechanic's review.
Replace the worn part and ask the next operator to monitor alignment during cutting.

basic.situation: At shift end, you must record work completed and machine settings, but the last order's speed entry is missing from your notes.

options.text: Leave the speed blank and tell the next shift it was unrecorded.
Use the previous order's speed and complete the log before handover.
Ask a coworker which speed was used and add it to the order record.
Check machine records or ask the operator, then log the verified speed and order.

advanced.situation: Several shifts report recurring length variation, but their logs use different labels for settings and machine stops. You are asked to improve the record template.

options.text: Create a shared template linking order, settings, measured lengths, and stop reasons across shifts.
Add common labels for settings and stops, with a short example beside each field.
Collect the existing logs and summarize the length issues in a separate sheet.
Keep the current log and ask each shift to add more detail in free text.

basic.situation: You are unsure whether an order needs a straight or angled cut, and the next fabric layer is ready. A coworker handled a similar order yesterday.

options.text: Check the order details with your coworker before placing the next layer for cutting.
Use the straight cut from yesterday's similar order and keep the line moving.
Ask the coworker what they remember and begin arranging the layer while they answer.
Pause the layout and ask the coworker to show you yesterday's order notes.

advanced.situation: Two coworkers give conflicting details about a cutting order, and a machine fault has delayed the next stack. You need to coordinate the issue with the team.

options.text: Share fault status, compare order details with job information, and agree the next stack sequence.
Tell the team that the machine is delayed and ask each coworker to restate order details.
Use details from the coworker who prepared the last stack, then restart the cutting run.
Ask the supervisor to check order details with coworkers before discussing the machine delay.

basic.situation: You start a loom with guidance, and the first cloth looks slightly uneven. What do you do while monitoring the run?

options.text: Start the loom at the approved speed and watch the first cloth closely.
Ask a nearby operator to confirm the setting before starting the loom.
Keep the previous shift's speed and check the fabric at break.
Start the loom slowly, then adjust tension when the cloth looks uneven.

advanced.situation: After a complex loom adjustment, your test cycle produces a sample with a faint line. The next order is waiting. What do you do?

options.text: Save the sample and begin the order at a slower loom speed.
Run another test cycle and compare its sample with the order specifications.
Ask the supervisor to inspect the sample before you make another adjustment.
Nudge the tension and start production, since the line is faint.

basic.situation: You inspect a woven roll with a simple order specification and spot a small variation in the cloth. What do you do?

options.text: Check several points on the roll against the stated width and appearance.
Pass the roll because most of the cloth appears consistent.
Measure the first section, then continue if that part matches the order.
Mark the variation and ask a co-worker whether it looks acceptable.

advanced.situation: A woven roll meets the width target but shows faint repeating bars under close inspection. You must decide whether the loom needs adjustment. What do you do?

options.text: Accept the roll because its measured width meets the order target.
Pause the inspection and ask the next shift to review the bars.
Look closely at one bar and adjust the loom if it seems severe.
Compare bar spacing across the roll with the detailed product specification.

basic.situation: A loom stops during a routine run. You see loose filling yarn near the shuttle area. What do you do to identify the cause?

options.text: Inspect the filling path and note findings before asking the supervisor about restarting.
Stop the loom, secure the loose yarn, and tell the supervisor before restarting.
Check nearby guides for snags, then report your observations to the supervisor.
Ask a trained co-worker to inspect the shuttle area while you keep others clear.

advanced.situation: A loom repeatedly stops after a harness break, and a mechanical defect may also be present. What do you do to help prevent another stoppage?

options.text: Replace the broken harness part and resume the run at reduced speed.
Inspect the harness and related mechanism, then report the findings for repair assessment.
Inspect the broken harness closely and note whether another strand looks worn.
Ask the repair staff to check the loom and share the repeated stop pattern.

basic.situation: You are learning to thread yarn through a loom's guides and needles for a routine fabric order. One guide is hard to see. What do you do?

options.text: Use the usual route and ask the supervisor to check the needles afterward.
Ask a nearby operator where the hidden guide sits before continuing.
Thread the yarn through the visible guides and start at low speed.
Follow the threading diagram and check each guide as you pass the yarn.

advanced.situation: A new order needs a complex fabric path through several guides and rollers. The sample thread catches once near a roller. What do you do?

options.text: Pull the thread past the roller and run the order at reduced speed.
Check the roller where it caught and adjust the thread angle there.
Trace the specified path through every guide and roller before testing again.
Ask an experienced operator to confirm the path while you hold the thread.

basic.situation: You find a visible filling defect in a cloth section assigned for repair. What do you do to remove it with help?

options.text: Ask a co-worker where to cut, then pull out the marked filling.
Pull the filling at the visible spot and inspect the cloth afterward.
Cut several nearby filling threads so the visible mark disappears.
Mark the defect and cut out the affected filling with the guide's help.

advanced.situation: A cloth roll has an intricate defect crossing several filling threads near a patterned area. What do you do to remove it efficiently?

options.text: Start at the defect's edge and pull filling threads one by one.
Cut through the patterned section and remove enough filling to clear it.
Ask a co-worker to point out which threads appear to carry the defect.
Map the affected filling, then cut and pull those threads with care.

basic.situation: During your shift, a loom develops an unfamiliar mechanical rattle but continues running. What do you do?

options.text: Ask a co-worker whether the sound seems normal for this loom.
Note the sound and report it if the loom stops or slows.
Tell the supervisor or repair staff what changed and when it began.
Keep the loom running and mention the rattle during the handover.

advanced.situation: Two looms produce uneven cloth after a shared yarn change, and the next order is due soon. What do you do to help resolve the process problem?

options.text: Tell the supervisor both looms are producing uneven cloth and await direction.
Compare the order and yarn details with co-workers, then share the pattern found.
Ask the yarn operator about the change and pass their answer to the supervisor.
Adjust each loom's tension until the cloth looks closer to the sample.

basic.situation: You are threading a new yarn package through the machine guides, and the strand keeps slipping from one roller during startup.

options.text: You ask a nearby operator to check the thread path before restarting.
You reseat the strand at the loose roller and watch the first bobbin.
You pull the strand taut and start the machine at normal speed.
You stop the thread, reseat it through the guides, and check tracking at low speed.

advanced.situation: A long order needs consistent strength across several yarn lots, but trial bobbins show uneven twist after a setting change.

options.text: You lower speed slightly and inspect the next trial bobbin for twist consistency.
You compare trial bobbins across lots, adjust twist settings, and verify uniformity before the run.
You compare the samples with the specification and ask the lead which setting to retain.
You keep the faster setting and sort weaker bobbins out after production.

basic.situation: You are checking finished yarn with help, and a sample bobbin looks fuller than the stated size on its tag.

options.text: You compare several bobbins with the specification and note any size variation for adjustment.
You pass the bobbin because its yarn feels even when handled.
You ask the experienced operator whether the fuller bobbin is acceptable.
You measure that bobbin and check the next one against its tag.

advanced.situation: A run meets the usual checks, but slight thick spots recur on bobbins from one frame while other frames look even.

options.text: You mix affected bobbins with even ones to keep the shipment consistent.
You inspect more bobbins from that frame and set aside ones with thick spots.
You compare frame samples, record thick spots, and share the pattern for a focused check.
You report thick spots and ask the supervisor about checking that frame further.

basic.situation: After an adjustment, you are asked to run a test cycle and provide a yarn sample, with guidance nearby.

options.text: You run the cycle and bring the sample to the operator guiding you.
You run the cycle quickly and leave the sample beside the machine for review.
You check the setup sheet with the guide before running the test cycle.
You run the test cycle at set conditions, label the sample, and report its results.

advanced.situation: A test run shows irregular vibration after a roller change, and the next production shift starts in an hour.

options.text: You inspect the roller area and ask maintenance to check the vibration before restart.
You inspect the roller seating and machine condition, then record findings for repair planning.
You report the vibration to maintenance and request an inspection before the shift.
You tighten the visible bolts and return the machine to production at full speed.

basic.situation: You finish winding a routine shift's output and need to record the number and types of bobbins produced.

options.text: You tally bobbin types and enter shift figures in the production record.
You confirm the shift totals with the outgoing operator before completing the production record.
You enter the total count and list the bobbin types produced that shift.
You enter the total bobbins and divide them evenly among listed types.

advanced.situation: Several shifts recorded more bobbins but also more stoppages, and you are compiling this shift's production figures for review.

options.text: You report the higher output as improved efficiency and omit the stoppages from the summary.
You record counts by bobbin type and note the stoppage pattern for the shift review.
You compare the shift totals with earlier records and ask the lead to interpret the stoppages.
You record the output counts and mention that stoppages rose during the shift.

basic.situation: Your winding machine stops twice during a routine run, and restarting it does not keep the yarn moving.

options.text: You restart it again and finish the remaining bobbins before reporting the stops.
You tell the supervisor the stop pattern, what you observed, and when it began.
You note the two stops and ask a nearby operator whether theirs also stopped.
You tell the supervisor that the machine stopped and wait for instructions.

advanced.situation: A recurring thread break follows a roller change, and production asks you to explain the pattern before maintenance arrives.

options.text: You report when breaks occur, which machine position is involved, and the recent roller change.
You say the yarn lot is poor and ask production to switch to another lot.
You report the thread breaks and the roller change to the mechanic.
You check with production about the lot and then notify the mechanic of the breaks.

basic.situation: The yarn package feeding your machine is nearly depleted, and a full replacement package is available at the supply point.

options.text: You replace the depleted package, thread the yarn through its guides, and check the feed.
You tie the remaining strand to the new package and keep the machine running.
You tell the nearby operator the package is low and ask them to change it.
You replace the package and watch the strand for the next few turns.

advanced.situation: Several machines are running a long order, and the last full yarn packages are at the supply point as two feeders run low.

options.text: You check stock with the storekeeper and ask the lead to prioritize refills.
You replace both low packages, check stock, and alert the team about upcoming needs.
You move a full package between machines and let the first machine run empty.
You replace both low packages and request more yarn before supplies run low.

basic.situation: You need to adapt an existing bodice pattern for a sample with a slightly altered neckline. The designer is available to clarify the change.

options.text: Copy the outline quickly and send it for cutting before checking notches.
Trace the closest existing size, then compare key seams with the sample.
Ask the designer about unclear shape changes, then draft and label each part.
Use the sample to draft each outline, checking seam lines and notches.

advanced.situation: A designer wants a jacket pattern across a full size range, and the fabric stretches differently across the grain. The first graded sample fits unevenly.

options.text: Adjust each size from the sample, then review the grade with the designer.
Grade from the approved base, account for stretch, and check key sizes against measurements.
Ask the designer to choose new measurements before drafting the range.
Reuse the previous size chart and release the full range for sampling.

basic.situation: You are asked to make a cardboard template from a paper sleeve pattern before the sample room closes. A teammate offers to help cut it.

options.text: Trace around the paper and cut the cardboard as soon as possible.
Mark the main outline and cut the cardboard, leaving small notches for later.
Ask your teammate to confirm the outline, then cut the cardboard template.
Trace the paper outline onto cardboard, then check the edges before cutting.

advanced.situation: A limited roll must cover several jacket sizes, and the approved pieces have directional nap. You need to mark a layout for cutting today.

options.text: Nest the pieces tightly, then mark the fabric while preserving the nap direction.
Turn selected pieces across the nap to fit more shapes on the roll.
Map all sizes with nap direction aligned, then mark the lowest waste layout.
Lay out the largest pieces first, then fit smaller pieces into open areas.

basic.situation: You are marking a blouse pattern after a fitting. The sample has a pocket and two pleats, and the sewing team needs clear join points.

options.text: Add the pocket and pleat marks to one piece, then send it onward.
Mark the pocket, pleats, and matching join points on each pattern part.
Ask the sample sewer to confirm the join points before marking the details.
Mark the pocket position and leave the pleats for the sewing team.

advanced.situation: A lined coat has hidden pockets, several pleats, and a collar assembled in stages. You must prepare sewing and assembly instructions for a trial run.

options.text: Specify each stage, joins, pocket placement, pleats, and checks for the trial sample.
List the new pocket and collar details, then let the sewer plan remaining steps.
Write the assembly sequence, matching points, and details for each coat section.
Reuse the last coat instructions and change the style name for this trial.

basic.situation: You are labelling a finished sample pattern before it goes to the cutting room. Its size and style code are written on the work order.

options.text: Write the size and style code on the largest pattern piece.
Mark the size, style code, section, and sewing notes on each pattern part.
Copy the style code onto the parts and send them to cutting.
Confirm the work order, then label the size and style on the pattern.

advanced.situation: A design combines stretch panels with a woven lining across several sizes. The specification lists shapes but leaves one panel dimension unclear.

options.text: Estimate the unclear panel from the sketch, then calculate fabric for each size.
Check the sample and specifications, resolve the dimension, then calculate each part's quantities.
Ask the designer about the panel, then calculate material from the confirmed dimensions.
Use the base size dimensions, then scale the remaining parts by the size chart.

basic.situation: A sample skirt pulls slightly at the side seam during fitting. You are asked to adjust the paper pattern before another sample is made.

options.text: Shift the seam line by eye and cut a replacement sample for the next fitting.
Pinpoint the pull, adjust the side seam, and compare both sides before recutting.
Ask the fitter where it pulls, then adjust the side seam accordingly.
Open the side seam a little and send the revised pattern for sampling.

advanced.situation: A fitted jacket sample twists at the armhole and strains across the back when the wearer reaches forward. Two pattern assistants ask how to revise it.

options.text: Ask the assistants to mark the strain, then revise the back panel together.
Compare the strain and twist, isolate affected panels, then guide a controlled fitting revision.
Release the sample as close enough and note the fit issue for production.
Increase the back width and tell the assistants to repeat that change on each size.

basic.situation: A senior patternmaker asks you to enter the approved waist measurement into the pattern system. The screen shows several fields with similar labels.

options.text: Enter the measurement in the first waist field and save the pattern.
Check the field labels against the work order, then enter the approved measurement.
Follow the system guide and enter the measurement, then review the saved value.
Ask a teammate which waist field they usually use, then enter it.

advanced.situation: Several patternmakers enter specifications in the shared system, and recent files use inconsistent units and field names. You are asked to guide the team's next batch.

options.text: Send a note listing preferred units and fields for the next batch.
Ask each patternmaker to follow their familiar setup for the current batch.
Share a simple field guide with units and examples, then check a sample batch together.
Convert the files that look unusual and tell the team to continue entering specifications.

basic.situation: You are checking a dining chair before reupholstery. One spring sags slightly, and the work order asks you to note visible frame and webbing defects.

options.text: Ask the upholsterer to inspect the frame after you note the spring.
Check the loose spring and estimate the covering material from the old chair.
Inspect the frame, springs, and webbing, then record the sagging spring for repair planning.
Note the sagging spring and start removing the cover for faster progress.

advanced.situation: A custom curved sofa has an unusual frame and patterned fabric. The work order gives a sketch, but the required covering quantity is uncertain.

options.text: Order the usual roll length now so the upholstery team can start tomorrow.
Measure the frame, compare the sketch, and calculate material needs with pattern matching allowance.
Use the last sofa order as a guide and add a little extra fabric.
Confirm the sketch dimensions with the designer, then estimate the covering quantity.

basic.situation: You are removing an old chair cover, and several tacks sit close to the wood frame. A senior worker is nearby to guide you.

options.text: Use a tack puller carefully, keeping removed cover and fasteners sorted for review.
Ask the senior worker to point out the safest tacks before you begin pulling.
Pry the nearby tacks hard so the cover comes off in one pull.
Pull the cover free with the hammer claw and collect loose tacks afterward.

advanced.situation: An older armchair has loose webbing and scratched exposed wood near a repaired joint. You are assigned the restoration work before new padding goes on.

options.text: Ask a senior upholsterer to check the joint before you repair and refinish it.
Cover the scratched wood with trim and fasten new webbing over the old.
Check the joint, repair the frame, refinish exposed wood, then secure replacement webbing evenly.
Tighten the loose webbing and touch up the visible scratches afterward.

basic.situation: You are replacing worn padding on a small footstool. The new foam is cut, and the webbing needs securing before the cover is fitted.

options.text: Add extra foam over the worn area and cover the stool as scheduled.
Ask a coworker to check the webbing tension before you secure the foam.
Secure the webbing evenly, then build smooth padding over the supported surface.
Place the foam over the webbing and staple the edges for the cover fitting.

advanced.situation: A sofa seat dips unevenly, and several springs move under load. You need to adjust the spring system and secure it before replacing the padding.

options.text: Secure the loose springs as found and refit the padding to meet the schedule.
Ask the lead to identify the moving springs, then replace and fasten them.
Replace the visibly loose spring and add padding to level the seat surface.
Compare spring tension across the seat, adjust the system, and secure each connection before padding.

basic.situation: You are fitting a plain fabric panel to a small chair frame. The corners need folding, and a coworker is available to guide your stapling.

options.text: Ask your coworker to hold the panel while you staple around the frame.
Staple the corners down first and trim away any uneven fabric later.
Pull the fabric tight and staple the nearest edge before checking alignment.
Center the panel, fold the corners evenly, and staple along the frame edge.

advanced.situation: A curved chair frame needs leather fitted around a tight corner, with adhesive and staples both specified. The visible edge must stay smooth.

options.text: Ask the lead which tool to use, then fit the leather around the corner.
Stretch the leather firmly around the corner and staple through the visible edge.
Use adhesive on the curve and add staples wherever the leather lifts.
Test adhesive placement, ease the leather around the curve, then secure hidden edges with staples.

basic.situation: A small tear has opened along a loose seam on a cushion cover. You are asked to sew it before the cover returns to the chair.

options.text: Pull the edges together tightly and sew across the fabric beside the tear.
Ask a coworker to hold the edges while you sew the rip closed.
Close the gap with several quick stitches and return the cushion cover.
Align the torn edges, stitch them securely, and check the seam under light tension.

advanced.situation: A button tuft has loosened on a high-tension sofa back, and a nearby tear is lengthening. The customer expects the pattern to match the other tufts.

options.text: Tighten the tuft and cover the growing tear with a matching fabric patch.
Assess the tear edges and tuft tension, then repair both to match neighboring points.
Sew the tear closed first, then tighten the loose tuft to match the next button.
Retie the tuft at its old point and sew the tear with a short surface stitch.

basic.situation: You are attaching buttons to a removable chair cover. The placement marks are clear, and the hand tools are set out for you.

options.text: Fasten the buttons along the marked row and check their spacing by eye.
Place the buttons where they look balanced and fasten them before sewing.
Match each button to its mark, secure it, and check the cover side.
Attach the buttons at the marked points and pass the cover to sewing.

advanced.situation: You are restoring a custom bench with a worn seat and decorative trim. The frame is ready, and the client expects the new finish to match the original design.

options.text: Replace the seat fabric and ask the lead where the decorative trim should go.
Plan fabric, padding, and trim together, then compare the finish with the original.
Fit new padding and fabric, then use the trim to cover any uneven edges.
Reuse available fabric and attach trim where it can hide worn seat edges during fitting.

basic.situation: Your lead asks you to set up a power saw with guidance and says its guard must stay fitted during cutting.

options.text: You check the guard, fence, and clear offcut path with your lead before cutting.
You check the fence against one board, then begin cutting the batch.
You hold the guard back so the first boards pass through more quickly.
You line up the fence and cut the marked boards at the requested length.

advanced.situation: A long production run uses several saw settings, and a test piece comes out slightly short before the batch starts.

options.text: You compare the drawing and test cut, adjust the setting, then verify another sample.
You ask the operator who ran the last batch which setting they used.
You change the length setting and run the full batch to keep production on schedule.
You rerun the posted settings and start production after the first piece looks close.

basic.situation: A cabinet panel has a rough edge after cutting, and you have a plane and guidance available before assembly.

options.text: You press hard and plane the full edge in one quick pass.
You run the plane along the edge until it looks smooth from above.
You plane a small area with the grain, then check the surface with your lead.
You ask your lead to show the plane angle, then try a short pass.

advanced.situation: A fitted cabinet joint has a slight gap at one corner, and the visible face must remain clean for finishing.

options.text: You mark the tight area and pare it once before checking the fit again.
You pare the high spot in small passes, checking the joint fit after each cut.
You add glue to the gap and clamp the joint firmly for finishing.
You sand the mating edges until the joint closes across the full face.

basic.situation: Two small cabinet rails need gluing, and you have clamps ready while a colleague finishes the matching parts.

options.text: You clamp the dry rails together and leave them for the next shift.
You use extra glue so the joint stays filled when the clamps tighten.
You apply glue and clamp the rails where their ends appear aligned.
You dry-fit the rails, spread an even glue layer, and clamp them square.

advanced.situation: A tall display cabinet has several subassemblies, and its doors bind when the frame is clamped for final assembly.

options.text: You release the clamps, check the frame diagonals, and realign before fastening.
You trim the door edges slightly, then test whether they swing freely.
You drive the fasteners tighter to pull the frame closed before fitting the doors.
You check the hinges and adjust their positions to improve the door swing.

basic.situation: A simple cabinet drawing shows a rectangular side panel and shelf, and you need to identify their shapes before assembly.

options.text: You trace the panel and shelf outlines, then compare their labels with the drawing.
You call both pieces rectangles and set them beside the cabinet frame.
You mark the pieces as square because their corners look alike.
You ask a colleague to point out the panel and shelf shapes.

advanced.situation: A detailed drawing shows a cabinet with a recessed back and overlapping joints, but the assembly sequence is not stated.

options.text: You sketch a likely assembly order and ask a nearby carpenter to review it.
You choose a familiar sequence and begin cutting the joint parts from the drawing.
You list the visible joints and prepare the parts in drawing order.
You map the joint order against the drawing, then confirm clearances before cutting.

basic.situation: You need to mark a shelf blank to the length written on the cabinet plan before it goes to the saw.

options.text: You measure from the end, mark the length, and check the tape alignment once.
You use the nearest edge as your starting point and mark the length quickly.
You measure the plan length and mark the shelf blank with a pencil.
You measure twice from the same end and mark the matching point.

advanced.situation: A cabinet opening varies slightly across its height, and a fitted door must sit evenly without catching.

options.text: You measure the opening once at the center and trim the door to that width.
You sand the door edges until it moves freely inside the opening.
You measure the opening at several points and compare the door clearances before trimming.
You check the door against the opening and mark the tight side for adjustment.

basic.situation: A cabinet door has a rough patch before finishing, and you have sandpaper and a supervisor nearby for guidance.

options.text: You ask your supervisor which grit to use, then sand the rough area.
You sand across the grain to remove the rough patch in fewer strokes.
You sand the patch with the grain, then feel it and check with your supervisor.
You rub the patch briskly until its color matches the surrounding wood.

advanced.situation: A repaired cabinet door needs a new hinge position because the old screw holes have loosened and the door sags.

options.text: You add wood filler to the old holes and reuse them after it dries.
You drill new holes close to the old ones and tighten the hinge screws firmly.
You inspect solid wood, mark the hinge position, then bore pilot holes before fitting.
You shift the hinge slightly and test the door before tightening its screws.

basic.situation: A small table has raised grain before staining, and you have sandpaper and steel wool with guidance available.

options.text: You ask your lead to show the grit, then sand one small area.
You rub the table with steel wool until it feels less rough.
You sand with the grain, feel the surface, and check its finish.
You sand across the grain quickly to cover raised areas in fewer passes.

advanced.situation: A customer wants a distressed antique look on a cabinet, while the matching doors need consistent shading across the set.

options.text: You vary the tool pressure across the doors until each one looks suitably aged.
You scrape deeper on the first door so the remaining doors match its character.
You use the same abrasive passes on each door and compare them under the shop lights.
You distress a hidden sample, agree its texture and shade, then repeat the method across the doors.

basic.situation: An old chair has peeling finish, and your lead asks you to remove it with hand tools and approved solvent.

options.text: You test the solvent on a hidden spot, then loosen the finish with a scraper.
You sand the peeling finish until most of it has come away.
You apply solvent across the chair so the old finish lifts evenly.
You scrape the peeling areas and wipe the surface with the approved solvent.

advanced.situation: A carved cabinet has brittle coating and delicate details, and a trainee asks which stripping method to use.

options.text: You select a solvent based on the coating's appearance and begin at the back.
You start with hand scraping on a hidden edge and show the trainee the result.
You test a small hidden area, assess the coating response, and choose a gentle removal method.
You demonstrate scraper use on a carved section so the trainee can follow along.

basic.situation: A dining chair arrives with a visible split and worn finish, and you need to assess it before choosing repair work.

options.text: You inspect the split and ask a colleague whether its depth needs further assessment.
You examine the split and record its length for the repair notes.
You inspect the split and nearby joints, then record damage before discussing repairs.
You choose a matching stain, since the worn finish stands out most.

advanced.situation: A veneer cabinet has blistering, dark patches, and a loose corner, so the restoration method depends on the materials and damage.

options.text: You inspect the blistering and loose corner, then note what needs repair.
You map damage, check the loose joint, and assess veneer before repair.
You choose a close stain and test it on the cabinet's back before use.
You sand the dark patches until they blend with the surrounding veneer.

basic.situation: A customer sample is slightly warmer than the stain on hand, and you are asked to mix a small matching batch.

options.text: You tint a sample, compare it beside the reference, and record the formula.
You pour extra tint into the full container so the batch looks warmer.
You mix a small batch, then compare it with the sample in daylight first.
You add tint until the wet sample looks close under bench lighting.

advanced.situation: Several cabinet doors need a custom shade, and an earlier test looks different after drying than it did when wet.

options.text: You increase the colorant in the full batch so the dry finish should look richer.
You adjust a test, let it dry, compare with the reference, and record its formula.
You make another small sample, let it dry, and ask a colleague to compare it.
You add a small amount of color to the batch and compare the wet shade again.

basic.situation: A cabinet door has removable handles and glass that must stay clear while you prepare it for finishing.

options.text: You remove the handles, cover glass edges, and check the mask before finishing.
You mask around the handles and glass, then leave the hardware attached during preparation.
You finish the door with the handles attached and wipe them clean afterward.
You remove the handles and mask the glass before handing over the door.

advanced.situation: An ornate cabinet has removable trim, delicate brass fittings, and narrow glass borders that must stay free of finish.

options.text: You remove trim and fittings, placing each piece together in a labeled tray for later.
You leave the trim fitted and spray around its edges to save preparation time.
You label removable parts, then mask glass borders and protect the fittings.
You label each removed part and mask the glass before preparing the cabinet.

basic.situation: A wooden tray has a small crack and needs a clear finish, and your supervisor is available to guide the repair.

options.text: You use extra finish across the crack so it appears less noticeable.
You fill the crack and apply finish once the filler feels dry.
You brush clear finish over the tray, then fill and smooth the crack afterward.
You fill the crack, smooth it after setting, and apply a thin coat.

advanced.situation: A carved cabinet has a stained patch and a chipped decorative border, and the restoration should preserve its original appearance.

options.text: You repaint the border and blend the stained patch while both colors remain wet.
You test stain on the back, then touch up the border to match nearby carving.
You assess contours, test a color match, repair the chip, then compare details.
You fill the chip and apply darker stain across both damaged areas.

basic.situation: You receive a blueprint for a wooden pump model, and the flange size is needed before cutting the stock.

options.text: You use the nearest printed size and start cutting the flange blank.
You compare the marked dimensions with the written specification and note the flange size.
You measure a similar model and use its flange as a working reference.
You trace the flange view, check its scale, and confirm the dimension before marking stock.

advanced.situation: A pump housing drawing shows two different curves across its views, and the designer's note does not explain which profile the pattern needs.

options.text: You choose the curve that appears in the clearest view and mark it for shaping.
You shape the curve from the side view and flag the other view for review.
You follow the curve from the last similar housing to keep the job moving.
You ask the designer which curve governs and record the confirmed profile before setup.

basic.situation: You need to mark a square end and a 45-degree cut on a timber blank for a small display stand.

options.text: You transfer both lines from a matching offcut, then compare them with the plan.
You sketch the end by eye, then compare the diagonal with the plan.
You use a square for the end and estimate the angle from the plan.
You mark the end with a try square and set the cut using a bevel gauge.

advanced.situation: You are laying out a full-scale curved casing mock-up, but the stock width leaves little room for repositioning the outline.

options.text: You draw the outline from the blueprint scale and review the crowded areas afterward.
You map the full outline from fixed reference points and check the contour with a template.
You sketch the outline on the stock and shift it where the curve feels tight.
You place the main curve first, then fit the smaller sections around it.

basic.situation: You are preparing a bandsaw to cut a straight wooden pattern section, and the stock is ready beside the machine.

options.text: You use the previous job's guide setting and feed the timber steadily.
You check the blade guard and guide setting, then make a test cut on scrap.
You ask a nearby operator to check the guide before you cut the stock.
You set the guide near the blade and begin cutting the pattern stock.

advanced.situation: A dense hardwood blank chatters on the planer, and the pattern needs a tight, even thickness across its full length.

options.text: You take lighter passes, support the blank, and check thickness along its length.
You reduce the feed and measure thickness at both ends afterward.
You keep the current setting and slow the feed across the blank.
You make another full pass at the same setting to even the surface.

basic.situation: You are joining two simple wooden blocks for a small pattern, and the parts fit closely on the bench.

options.text: You nail the blocks together first and fill the visible seam with glue.
You dry-fit the blocks, apply glue, and nail them while the faces align.
You hold the blocks against the bench edge and glue them in place.
You spread glue, press the blocks together, and add nails at the corners.

advanced.situation: A large sectional mold has several dowelled joints, and the first dry assembly shows a slight step at one mating edge.

options.text: You shift the dowels slightly and clamp the sections until the seam looks even.
You recheck the mating faces, reduce the step, then assemble with dowels aligned.
You mark the raised area and ask the lead maker how to adjust it.
You clamp the sections together and sand the raised edge after fastening.

basic.situation: A small wooden model has rough edges after trimming, and the next task is to smooth its surfaces by hand.

options.text: You file the rough spots quickly and leave the dust for the next step.
You use a scraper on the rough edges and inspect them under the bench light.
You sand the rough edges with broad strokes until they look even.
You sand with the grain and check the edges by touch between passes.

advanced.situation: A hand-shaped wooden turbine model has a narrow concave curve that must match a template without flattening the adjacent ridge.

options.text: You file the hollow in small passes, checking the curve and adjacent ridge against the template.
You sand the curve with folded paper and inspect the ridge at the end.
You use a curved scraper in short passes and compare the profile with the template.
You plane across the hollow to remove the high spots in fewer strokes.

basic.situation: You finish a wooden template that will go to a machine operator, and its matching parts need a clear assembly mark.

options.text: You write the product name on the template and hand it to the nearest operator.
You mark the template code and assembly direction, then check them against the job sheet.
You mark the job number on the template and place it in the issue rack.
You add a colored mark and tell the operator which side faces up.

advanced.situation: Two operators request the same pattern for separate runs, while the record shows one copy and its last issue is unconfirmed.

options.text: You ask the operators to take turns and note their names on the job sheet.
You tell both operators the pattern is unavailable until the record is updated.
You check the issue record, confirm the pattern's location, then arrange a tracked handoff.
You issue it to the first operator and update the record after the run.

basic.situation: You receive a simple bracket drawing and need its length and outline before selecting pattern stock.

options.text: You read the dimension labels and match the outline to the front view.
You use the longest visible line as the bracket length and mark the stock.
You compare the outline with a similar bracket kept in the shop.
You check the drawing title and use its stated overall length.

advanced.situation: A multi-view casting drawing shows a stepped cavity and a curved edge, but one section view is partly obscured by a revision mark.

options.text: You compare the views, identify the missing profile, and request a legible revision before setup.
You follow the overall outline and leave the stepped cavity for later shaping.
You infer the hidden curve from the nearest section and lay out the setup.
You plan the setup from the clear views and flag the obscured section for review.

basic.situation: You finish a straight-sided wooden pattern and need to check its length and one right-angle corner before assembly.

options.text: You measure the length with a ruler and check the corner with a square.
You compare the length with the drawing and estimate the corner by eye.
You mark the pattern complete based on its cut edges and move it to assembly.
You use a ruler for the length and compare the corner against another pattern.

advanced.situation: A curved pattern nearly matches its template, but caliper readings differ near one end and assembly is due this afternoon.

options.text: You recheck the end against the template and calipers, then adjust the local deviation.
You compare the curve with the template and hold assembly for a fit check.
You average the readings and send the pattern to assembly on schedule.
You smooth the end slightly and see whether the sections fit together.

basic.situation: You are cutting a rectangular pattern blank from timber and need to mark its outline before rough shaping.

options.text: You measure the length with a ruler and draw the other edges freehand.
You mark the length by eye and cut the blank to save setup time.
You trace a similar blank and trim the timber to match its edges.
You mark the dimensions from the drawing with a square and cut outside the line.

advanced.situation: A lathe-turned pattern needs a narrow curved section to match a drawing, and the hardwood blank begins to vibrate at speed.

options.text: You stop shaping and ask another maker to finish the curved section safely.
You reduce feed, support the cut, and check the curve against the drawing between passes.
You keep the speed and take a deeper pass through the curved section.
You slow the cut and shape the curve from the visible outline between passes.

basic.situation: You are joining two flat wooden sections for a small pattern, and the edges appear to meet evenly on the bench.

options.text: You nail the sections together and cover any open seam with extra glue.
You apply glue, hold the edges together, and nail near each corner.
You dry-fit the sections, apply glue, and nail them while checking alignment.
You clamp the sections against the bench edge while the glue sets.

advanced.situation: A sectional pattern has several glued joints and interior angles, and a narrow gap remains where a fillet should sit.

options.text: You add glue to the gap and press the sections together until it closes.
You trim a fillet to the angle and glue it into the open seam.
You fit a fillet to the angle, then clamp the sections against their alignment marks.
You clamp the sections first and shape a fillet to fit afterward.

basic.situation: A completed wooden model needs a simple protective finish before it is returned to the pattern rack.

options.text: You brush on wax and leave the model beside the rack to dry.
You rub the model with a cloth and return it to the rack.
You apply an even coat of wax and check the surface for missed areas.
You add a thick coat of paint to cover the rough marks quickly.

advanced.situation: A pattern used in repeated molding has a worn surface, and the next batch needs a finish that will hold up in the mold.

options.text: You paint over the wear marks so the pattern is ready for the next batch.
You use the familiar lacquer and add extra coats for a harder surface.
You select a suitable coating from the shop's approved supplies and apply it evenly.
You assess the worn surface, choose a compatible coating, and apply a thin even finish.

basic.situation: You finish using a wooden pattern and need to return it with the remaining lumber to its assigned storage area.

options.text: You put the pattern with similar shapes and leave the lumber near the saw.
You check the pattern code, return it to its location, and store lumber by size.
You return the pattern to its usual rack and stack the lumber beside it.
You place the pattern and lumber on the nearest open rack for the next shift's work.

advanced.situation: Several castings show the same shallow defect, and you suspect the pattern needs a small correction before another run.

options.text: You smooth the suspected area lightly and inspect the next casting result.
You record the casting issue and ask the lead maker to assess the pattern.
You map defects to the pattern and propose a measured change for review.
You sand the matching pattern area and return it for another run.

basic.situation: You receive a work order for a short run of boards, but two cut dimensions are listed. You need to confirm the required size before setup.

options.text: I check the drawing notes and confirm which dimension applies to this run.
I compare the listed dimensions with the pattern and mark the likely one for review.
I ask the nearby operator which dimension the team normally uses for these boards.
I use the dimension from yesterday’s similar order and begin setting the stops.

advanced.situation: A work order combines several board patterns and machine setups. A late revision changes one piece, and the first run is due this shift.

options.text: I follow the earlier pattern and keep the machines running to protect the shift target.
I separate the patterns by setup and check each dimension against the revised order.
I pause the changed piece and set the remaining machines from the matching order pages.
I map each pattern to its machine settings, then verify the changed piece before release.

basic.situation: You are marking boards for a batch of shelf supports. The first board has a faint pencil line that is hard to see against the grain.

options.text: I ask a coworker to hold the square while I mark the board from its edge.
I extend the faint line by eye and use it to mark the other boards.
I measure from the end with a ruler and mark the cut using a square.
I check the ruler reading twice, then mark each board from the same end.

advanced.situation: A finished panel must fit a tight opening, and the first measurements are close to the work order limits. You have a caliper rule available.

options.text: I compare the panel with the sample piece and continue if the edges appear aligned.
I recheck the widest point with the caliper rule and record the reading for the batch.
I measure several points with the caliper rule and compare them with the specified dimensions.
I use the ruler to check the panel length and set aside any visibly uneven pieces.

basic.situation: You are sorting lumber for a small order. One board has a dark knot near the planned cut, and the remaining stock is limited.

options.text: I ask the next operator to decide whether the knot matters for this batch.
I use the board for the order because the knot looks small from this side.
I put the board aside with other pieces that have visible marks or knots.
I inspect the knot’s position and mark the board for a cut that avoids it.

advanced.situation: A mixed stack of lumber must cover several parts, and some boards have uneven grain or edge defects. You need to plan cuts with little spare stock.

options.text: I cut the boards to the largest part size and use offcuts where they fit.
I group boards by visible quality and match sound sections to the parts needing them.
I map each board’s defects against the part sizes and plan cuts to retain sound sections.
I take the clearest boards first and leave the harder pieces for a later run.

basic.situation: You are replacing a worn blade before a routine run. The machine is stopped, and the new blade is beside the shaft.

options.text: I seat the blade on the shaft and tighten its bolts with the specified wrench.
I align the blade by eye and tighten the bolts with the nearest wrench.
I tighten the bolts evenly and check that the blade turns without rubbing.
I fit the blade and ask a coworker to check the mount before setup continues.

advanced.situation: A work order calls for a new wood profile and a finish cut. The available blades differ in tooth pattern, and the run includes costly stock.

options.text: I use the blade from the last profile run and adjust the guide for this stock.
I check the work order for the profile and choose a blade with a similar tooth pattern.
I match the blade type and cutting procedure to the profile and finish requirements.
I compare the available blades and ask the lead which one is usually used.

basic.situation: You need to position a board on the saw table for a routine straight cut. The stock shifts slightly when you line it up against the stop.

options.text: I hold the board firmly by hand and start the feed at a slow pace.
I seat the board against the stop and clamp it before starting the cut.
I align the board with the stop and check that it sits flat on the table.
I line the board against the guide and ask a coworker to watch its position.

advanced.situation: A work order calls for a bevel and a curved cut on a costly panel. The pattern is narrow, with little room for a second attempt.

options.text: I check the pattern against the panel and make the curved cut at a steady feed.
I follow the curve by eye and adjust the panel as the blade reaches each turn.
I trace the pattern, confirm the bevel settings, and guide the panel through the specified cut.
I ask the lead to confirm the angle while I prepare the panel for the curve.

basic.situation: Your shift ends after a routine run, and sawdust and offcuts have collected around the machine and waste bin.

options.text: I collect the offcuts and wipe the table before handing over the machine.
I clear the offcuts into the designated waste bin and clean the machine surfaces.
I sweep the offcuts into the nearest bin and leave the machine for the next shift.
I clear the floor around the saw and place loose pieces beside the waste bin.

advanced.situation: During a run, the saw begins to pull unevenly and the band tension reading has drifted. A jam could damage the next boards.

options.text: I clear the current jam and ask the lead to review the tension later.
I increase the feed speed so the boards pass before another jam develops.
I check the tension and feed behavior, then adjust the setting within the machine procedure.
I reduce the feed rate and watch whether the tension reading settles during the run.

basic.situation: You are setting up a mortising machine for a routine batch. The guide sits slightly off the mark, and the senior operator is nearby.

options.text: I tighten the guide where it sits and start a trial piece for the batch.
I use a hand tool to align the guide with the marked position before fastening it.
I loosen the guide and shift it until it looks parallel with the workpiece.
I check the guide against the mark and ask the senior operator to verify the setup.

advanced.situation: A new workpiece shows a repeated edge defect across two machines. You suspect their guides are misaligned, and a small setup error could waste the remaining stock.

options.text: I compare both guide positions with specifications and realign them before another trial piece.
I check the first machine’s guide and make a trial piece to see whether the edge improves.
I hold the remaining stock and ask the senior operator to review the two guide settings.
I adjust the second guide to match the first and continue with a short run.

basic.situation: You are starting a routine run on a drill press. The first trial hole appears slightly shallow against the sample piece.

options.text: I continue the batch because the first hole looks close to the sample.
I ask the senior operator to check the depth control before I continue production.
I compare the depth setting with the specification and make another trial hole.
I adjust the depth slightly and inspect the next hole against the sample.

advanced.situation: A CNC router run combines several cut depths and shapes. The first pieces show drift on one profile, while the rest of the order is time-sensitive.

options.text: I review the program path and offsets, then verify the corrected profile on a trial piece.
I increase the feed rate so the router completes the order before the shift ends.
I change the affected offset and run a short sample to check the profile.
I pause the affected profile and finish the other shapes while checking the display.

basic.situation: You are helping feed short boards into a shaping machine. A board begins to tilt as it approaches the guide.

options.text: I push the board through quickly before the tilted edge catches the cutter.
I steady the board against the guide and feed it at the pace the machine accepts.
I slow the feed and keep the board pressed against the guide through the pass.
I ask the coworker beside me to hold the far end as I feed the board.

advanced.situation: A high-volume line is backing up before the sanding machine. Board sizes vary, and offcuts are accumulating near the feed conveyor.

options.text: I group boards by size and sequence the feed to keep the conveyor moving steadily.
I feed each board as it arrives and clear offcuts whenever the conveyor pauses.
I set aside the mixed boards and ask the line lead to decide the next order.
I sort sizes, plan the feed order, and use suitable stock sections to limit offcuts.

basic.situation: You are checking finished chair legs after sanding. Some surfaces feel smooth, but the angles look different from the sample piece.

options.text: I stack the legs that feel smooth and let the next station check their angles.
I compare each angle with the sample and set aside pieces that look uneven.
I ask a coworker to look at the angles while I check the sanding marks.
I compare the angles with the sample and examine the surface before stacking the legs.

advanced.situation: A new delivery of woodstock will supply a long run. Several pieces appear undersized, and using them could affect finished dimensions across the order.

options.text: I sort visibly small pieces into a separate stack for a later review.
I use the stock that looks closest to size and check finished pieces during production.
I measure the questionable stock against the size specification and separate pieces that fall short.
I tell the machine operator that some pieces may be undersized before loading starts.

basic.situation: You are cleaning around a planer after a routine shift. The guard is in place, but the drive belt looks loose from the walkway.

options.text: I check that the guard is secure and tell the senior operator about the belt.
I finish cleaning the floor and ask a coworker whether the belt looks loose.
I wipe the table and leave the belt for the next scheduled inspection.
I keep clear of the belt and report its condition before the machine runs again.

advanced.situation: During a routine inspection, you notice a worn belt and an overdue lubrication entry on the machine log. The next shift is scheduled for a long run.

options.text: I flag the belt as a pre-run concern and log the lubrication due for scheduled upkeep.
I note the overdue oiling and let the next shift report any belt problems.
I ask the next operator to inspect the belt and check the oiling log at startup.
I record both findings and arrange the worn belt replacement and lubrication with the maintenance lead.

basic.situation: You are packing completed wood parts for the next workstation. The pallet is nearly full, and several pieces have different lengths.

options.text: I place the remaining parts on top and send the pallet when it is full.
I sort the parts by length and stack them neatly on the pallet.
I stack the parts by length in the marked pallet area and check their labels.
I place the shorter parts in a box and leave the longer pieces beside the pallet.

advanced.situation: A batch of wood parts needs trimming to specification, but the remaining stock is tight. Several pieces have rough edges that could require extra sanding.

options.text: I ask the finishing operator which pieces need more sanding before trimming.
I check the specification and trim the pieces with a plane where needed.
I sand the rough edges until they look even and set the parts aside.
I mark each trim to specification and remove the rough edge with a controlled pass.

basic.situation: During a routine shift, the flux reading drifts from its expected range while you are assigned a supervised adjustment under the approved procedure.

options.text: I would make the usual small adjustment, then compare the next flux reading.
I would pause the adjustment and ask the control room supervisor to confirm the target.
I would use the previous shift's setting and record the change after the reading settles.
I would check the approved procedure, confirm the target, and make my assigned adjustment.

advanced.situation: A trainee sees flux fluctuate during a planned power change and asks you to guide the response while the unit remains within procedure limits.

options.text: I would make the adjustment myself and explain the chosen setting once the trend steadies.
I would follow the trainee's preferred setting and update the log after the power change.
I would tell the trainee to repeat the last adjustment and watch the trend.
I would walk the trainee through the procedure's decision points and trend checks before any move.

basic.situation: During a routine round, a turbine indicator moves outside its usual band while you are monitoring auxiliary equipment under guidance.

options.text: I would call the control room operator and ask whether the reading needs attention.
I would compare the indicator with its normal range and report the reading to the operator.
I would note the turbine reading and mention it during the next routine handover.
I would adjust the turbine setting to match yesterday's reading and log the result later.

advanced.situation: Boiler and turbine readings remain within their limits, but a scheduled auxiliary load change could affect both efficiency and operating margin.

options.text: I would align the auxiliary changes with the approved operating plan and track the resulting readings.
I would change both settings to their most efficient marks and record them afterward.
I would optimize the turbine first, then review the boiler readings at the next check.
I would ask the shift operator to choose the sequence while I monitor the readings.

basic.situation: During a routine system check, one gauge differs from the nearby instrument while output appears steady.

options.text: I would tell the supervisor that the gauges differ and ask for a review.
I would compare both gauges with the checklist and report the difference with the readings.
I would reset the unusual gauge to match its neighbor and enter the reading later.
I would write down the unusual gauge reading and mention it at handover.

advanced.situation: You are asked to refine a routine inspection after several minor instrument discrepancies appeared across different areas during recent rounds.

options.text: I would ask the supervisor which areas should receive another inspection round.
I would repeat the full inspection route more often and note anything unusual.
I would add targeted checks for the affected instruments and record each comparison consistently.
I would mark the affected instruments as normal based on their latest readings.

basic.situation: A pump alarm appears during your watch, and the operating procedure calls for reporting the abnormal condition before corrective action.

options.text: I would clear the alarm and restore the pump setting before reporting it.
I would report the alarm time and indicators, then follow the procedure's next step.
I would acknowledge the alarm and monitor its status during the next operating round.
I would contact the supervisor, describe the alarm, and ask which step to take.

advanced.situation: A maintenance team requests clearance for equipment after an abnormal indication, and the approved isolation points are listed but one status is unclear.

options.text: I would hold the clearance and ask the control room operator to check the unclear point.
I would pass along the listed points and let maintenance confirm the unclear status.
I would mark the clearance complete using the expected status and send the team in.
I would verify each listed isolation status and resolve the unclear point before clearance proceeds.

basic.situation: You are recording a completed surveillance test, and one result is hard to read on the source sheet.

options.text: I would copy the last test's result and submit the completed log today.
I would verify the unclear result with the source record owner before entering it.
I would enter the nearest readable value and flag the entry for review.
I would leave the result blank and tell the supervisor that the source is unclear.

advanced.situation: While reviewing a draft operating procedure, you find a step that uses an unclear term during a routine equipment transition.

options.text: I would flag the term and ask the owner to explain its intended meaning.
I would mark the unclear term and invite colleagues to comment on the draft.
I would remove the step and circulate the shortened procedure to the team.
I would suggest clearer wording to the owner, tied to the approved sequence.

basic.situation: You are assigned to prepare for a supervised fuel element transfer, and the handling team needs the sequence and timing relayed by radio.

options.text: I would tell the team to start with the familiar sequence and update them later.
I would ask the supervisor to relay the sequence while I prepare the transfer area.
I would relay the approved sequence and timing, then repeat back the team's acknowledgement.
I would send the timing first and share the sequence when the team is ready.

advanced.situation: A planned fuel element transfer depends on two support teams arriving in sequence, and one reports a delay while you coordinate assigned communications.

options.text: I would keep the first team ready and ask the delayed team for an arrival estimate.
I would tell the ready team to proceed with the transfer and catch up the other team later.
I would inform the supervisor of the delay and hold the team communications for guidance.
I would confirm the delay, update both teams on the approved sequence, and coordinate the revised timing.

basic.situation: A transformer fault interrupts service on one feeder, and your dispatcher checklist calls for rerouting current around the affected area.

options.text: I would follow the checklist route and confirm the affected feeder status before relaying the change.
I would use the familiar alternate route and watch the feeder readings afterward.
I would switch to the last used route and update the board once service returns.
I would call the senior dispatcher to confirm which route the checklist indicates.

advanced.situation: A transmission line fails during high demand, and two alternate routes have different service impacts as you coordinate the response with a junior dispatcher.

options.text: I would choose the route with fewer switching steps and monitor demand after the change.
I would compare route capacity and service impacts, then brief the junior on the chosen approved path.
I would check the route options with the senior dispatcher before directing the junior.
I would send the junior to use the route from the previous line outage.

basic.situation: During a routine shift, the distribution control display shows an unexpected status change while you operate the controls under supervision.

options.text: I would verify the display against the control checklist before making the assigned change.
I would select the last used control setting and record the status after the shift.
I would pause and ask the senior dispatcher whether the status needs a control change.
I would make the usual adjustment and watch whether the display returns to normal.

advanced.situation: Two distribution controls affect the same service area during a planned configuration change, and a trainee asks you to explain the sequence.

options.text: I would show the trainee the faster control and explain its usual setting.
I would let the trainee choose the control order and review the display afterward.
I would operate the controls myself and tell the trainee what each display means.
I would explain the approved sequence and have the trainee verify each displayed state before proceeding.

basic.situation: A routine load shift changes demand between two substations, and you are assigned to make a guided adjustment to the power flow.

options.text: I would copy the previous shift's flow split and note the result later.
I would move a small amount toward the busier substation and watch the readings.
I would compare both substation readings with the schedule before adjusting the flow.
I would ask the senior dispatcher which substation should receive more flow.

advanced.situation: Peak demand is forecast across several substations, and a planned transmission schedule leaves limited room for balancing service as conditions shift.

options.text: I would direct more flow toward high demand and review the schedule later.
I would balance flow against the schedule and readings, then reassess as demand shifts.
I would keep yesterday's flow pattern and report overloads during handover.
I would ask the senior dispatcher to choose a plan for peak demand.

basic.situation: A weather update suggests warmer conditions this afternoon, and you are estimating the expected load from the provided charts.

options.text: I would apply the chart's weather adjustment and check the estimate against recent demand.
I would use yesterday's afternoon load as today's estimate and note the forecast.
I would ask the planner which chart value to use for warmer weather.
I would enter the usual peak estimate and send the equipment request before checking the chart.

advanced.situation: Several weather and demand forecasts differ before a busy period, and you are preparing a load estimate for equipment requirements.

options.text: I would submit the lowest estimate to keep the equipment request within the usual plan.
I would compare the forecast assumptions with recent demand and show a range for planning.
I would ask the planner which forecast should anchor the equipment estimate.
I would use the forecast that most closely matches last week's peak demand.

basic.situation: A maintenance crew requests isolation for a small work area, and you are drafting a switching order from the standard template and system drawing.

options.text: I would trace the work area on the drawing and fill the matching order steps.
I would ask the crew to confirm the boundary before I complete the template.
I would send the previous order to the crew and revise the drawing before seeking approval.
I would copy the last similar order and replace its work location details.

advanced.situation: A planned system upgrade affects several work areas and scheduled transmission commitments, and you are asked to draft the switching plan.

options.text: I would reuse the last upgrade order and change the area names before sending it.
I would map work boundaries to the drawing and check scheduled commitments.
I would ask the engineer to identify the affected areas before drafting the order.
I would sequence the usual isolation steps and review the schedule after drafting.

basic.situation: During your shift, a control board reading differs from the trend sheet, and you are compiling the routine operational data report.

options.text: I would report the mismatch to the dispatcher and leave the reading pending.
I would copy the trend sheet value and add it to the report.
I would recheck the board reading and record both the value and its time.
I would replace the board entry with the trend value and submit the report.

advanced.situation: A new dispatcher is compiling meter readings and notices several entries lack times after a busy period with frequent handovers.

options.text: I would copy the previous report's times into the blank entries and file it.
I would teach the dispatcher to reconcile entries with board notes and add times.
I would add the missing times from the nearest handover and finish the report.
I would ask the dispatcher to flag blank times and note them for the next shift.

basic.situation: You receive the shift instruction to start a generator, and its auxiliary pump is due to run first. What do you do?

options.text: Check the shift instruction and confirm the auxiliary pump is ready before starting.
Start the generator from the panel to save time before checking the pump.
Ask the outgoing operator to confirm the unit state, then start as logged.
Follow the approved start sequence, watching pressure and status indicators at each step.

advanced.situation: A generator is ready to join a grid panel, but its frequency is drifting while demand is rising. What do you do?

options.text: Match the displayed frequency and connect once the reading appears stable.
Adjust output in small steps, watching frequency and phase before closing the breaker.
Ask a colleague to watch phase while you match frequency at the panel.
Close the breaker now, then adjust generator output to settle the readings.

basic.situation: You are assigned to shut down an auxiliary unit after the main unit stops. The procedure lists valves and switches in order. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the outgoing operator which switch usually comes first, then proceed.
Close the nearest valve first, then check the procedure for the remaining steps.
Use the written sequence and mark each valve and switch as you operate it.
Read the shutdown steps, then operate the valves and switches from memory.

advanced.situation: A site microturbine is supplying a production line, and its output fluctuates as the load changes. What do you do?

options.text: Raise output to cover the latest load increase and check the next reading.
Set output to the turbine's highest marked level so production keeps running.
Track load and output together, then adjust the microturbine within its operating limits.
Check the microturbine display and ask production staff whether the line is steady.

basic.situation: During your routine round, a pump indicator differs from its usual reading, though the plant is still running. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the control room the pump reading looks unusual and ask them to check.
Reset the indicator to its usual range so the board looks normal.
Record the unusual value and continue the round to finish on schedule.
Compare the reading with nearby indicators and the previous log, then report the change.

advanced.situation: At the scheduled reading interval, a chart shows water level moving toward the operating boundary. What do you do?

options.text: Call the control room and report the chart direction before adjusting the feedwater.
Take the scheduled reading, compare its trend with limits, and regulate level within procedure.
Wait for the next scheduled round before making any change to the feedwater.
Adjust the feedwater based on the latest gauge reading and note the change.

basic.situation: On a routine round, you find dust around a pump and it is due for cleaning and lubrication. What do you do?

options.text: Clean and lubricate the pump at the scheduled points, then record the maintenance.
Wipe the exposed casing and leave lubrication for the next maintenance round.
Check the maintenance notes, clean the pump, and tell the next shift about lubrication.
Apply lubricant to the running pump so the unit stays available for production.

advanced.situation: You notice a small leak at a pump gland joint during a round, with no change in pump readings. What do you do?

options.text: Turn the joint until the visible leak stops, then return to the round.
Tighten the joint slightly and watch the next pressure reading for a change.
Confirm the joint is safe to access, tighten it to procedure, and recheck for leakage.
Tell the control room about the leak and ask whether they want it tightened.

basic.situation: At shift end, you must enter the day's operating readings on the plant log, but one value is hard to read. What do you do?

options.text: Enter the readings you can read and leave the unclear field for handover.
Enter the clear readings and check the source instrument for the unclear value before submitting.
Copy the unclear value from yesterday's log to complete the daily form.
Ask a colleague to read the note and enter the value they think it shows.

advanced.situation: Management asks for a monthly operating summary, and the logs show several short output dips during busy shifts. What do you do?

options.text: Group the dips by day and ask the shift team what may have caused them.
List each dip in the report and leave management to find the pattern.
Include the lowest output reading and describe it as the month's typical performance.
Compile the readings by shift and compare the dips with recorded operating conditions.

basic.situation: A planned pump changeover will affect the next shift's rounds. You need to pass the operating plan to plant personnel. What do you do?

options.text: Post the changeover time on the shift board and tell the nearest operator.
Tell the next shift the changeover time, pump status, and expected round impact.
Leave the pump in changeover and let the next shift discover its status on rounds.
Mention the changeover during handover and let the next shift check the board.

advanced.situation: The logbook says a standby pump was tested, but an operator reports it sounded abnormal afterward. What do you do?

options.text: Check the pump indicators and tell the control room about the operator's concern.
Ask the operator to repeat the sound description and add it to handover.
Use the logbook entry to mark the standby pump as ready for the shift.
Compare the test entry with the operator's account and inspect current status indicators.

basic.situation: Your shift instruction calls for starting a biomass generator after the boiler reaches its stated operating condition. What do you do?

options.text: Start the generator when the boiler display looks close to its stated condition.
Check the boiler condition against the instruction, then follow the generator start sequence.
Read the start steps and ask the outgoing operator whether the boiler is ready.
Check the boiler indicator and start the generator according to the written steps.

advanced.situation: During cogeneration, steam pressure trends down while generator output remains steady and production demand is unchanged. What do you do?

options.text: Compare pressure and output trends with operating limits, then regulate the unit within procedure.
Tell the control room about the falling pressure and ask for their suggested setting.
Raise firing based on the falling pressure and check whether the trend improves.
Increase firing to the marked maximum so steam pressure recovers for production.

basic.situation: A delivery of wood chips arrives for the next run, and you are assigned to measure the feedstock before loading. What do you do?

options.text: Measure the assigned quantity, note the material condition, and load it as instructed.
Check the delivery note and estimate the quantity before loading the hopper.
Measure the chips and ask the operator whether the quantity seems suitable.
Load the amount that filled the hopper during the previous run.
