advanced.situation: Two biomass loads differ in moisture and particle size, and the next run's mix is not yet prepared. What do you do?

options.text: Blend equal amounts of each load to keep the feed preparation moving.
Use the delivery notes to calculate a ratio and begin mixing the loads.
Ask the boiler operator which load should make up most of the feed.
Measure both loads, calculate the instructed mix, and check the blend before feeding.

basic.situation: During a routine inspection, you find a loose guard bolt on a conveyor, and the maintenance guide lists a minor repair. What do you do?

options.text: Check with the operator, then tighten the bolt once the conveyor is stopped.
Follow the maintenance guide, secure the guard bolt, and record the repair.
Tighten the bolt while the conveyor is moving so the line keeps running.
Tell the next shift about the bolt and continue with the other checks.

advanced.situation: You find repeated vibration marks near a biomass conveyor bearing, and the inspection notes show they appeared again after a recent repair. What do you do?

options.text: Compare the marks with recent notes, inspect nearby components, and report the recurring pattern.
Adjust the bearing mount until the vibration marks stop appearing on the housing.
Tell maintenance the marks returned after repair and ask them to inspect the bearing.
File the new mark as a routine inspection note and continue the round.

basic.situation: You are helping record boiler pressure and temperature readings, and one gauge is difficult to read from your position. What do you do?

options.text: Write down the nearest marked value so the shift sheet is complete.
Record the clear gauge and leave the difficult reading for another round.
Ask a colleague to read the gauge and enter the number they call out.
Read the gauges from a safe position, record each value, and flag any unclear reading.

advanced.situation: Weekly logs show steam pressure rising before several generator output drops, though each reading stayed within its marked range. What do you do?

options.text: List the pressure and output readings in the weekly report for management review.
Report the highest pressure and lowest output as the week's main operating pattern.
Ask the shift operators whether they noticed a link between pressure and output.
Compare readings across shifts and summarize when pressure changes align with output drops.

basic.situation: You are assigned to replace a filter, and the equipment manual shows a sequence you have not used before. What do you do?

options.text: Skim the manual and ask a colleague which steps are usually skipped.
Use the sequence from the similar filter you replaced last month.
Read the manual and ask the outgoing operator to clarify the unfamiliar step.
Read the manual sequence, identify the required settings, and follow it during the task.

advanced.situation: A biomass process drawing shows a water sampling point near a boiler, but the labels differ from the current equipment tags. What do you do?

options.text: Use the nearest tagged valve as the sampling point to keep the test on schedule.
Trace the drawing connections against site tags and confirm the sampling point before testing.
Follow the drawing labels and take the sample at the indicated connection.
Ask a colleague which tagged point has been used for recent boiler tests.

basic.situation: After a feedstock spill near the loader route, you are assigned to clean the work area before loading resumes. What do you do?

options.text: Sweep the loose material away from the immediate loader path and continue.
Clear the route using the site's cleanup method, then check the area before resuming.
Ask a nearby worker to watch traffic while you clean the visible spill.
Push the spill aside with the loader bucket so trucks can pass.

advanced.situation: A fuel flow meter reading differs from the transfer log before a scheduled calibration check. What do you do?

options.text: Check the meter setup and calibration steps, record the difference, then follow site procedure.
Repeat the reading once and enter that new value in the shift record.
Tell the supervisor about the difference and ask whether the calibration check should proceed.
Change the display to match the log, then record the adjusted value for this shift.

basic.situation: On a routine round, you find a turbine bearing temperature above its usual range. What do you do?

options.text: I verify the reading on another instrument, compare nearby readings, and report the change.
I recheck the bearing temperature and report the reading to the shift supervisor.
I reduce the unit load slightly and watch whether the temperature falls.
I enter the usual temperature in the log to keep handover moving.

advanced.situation: Over several shifts, output falls as water head changes, while one unit's vibration rises. A junior asks what to adjust.

options.text: I compare head, output, and vibration trends, then explain a cautious adjustment to the junior.
I ask the junior to raise output until the unit matches its earlier figure.
I keep the current setting and note the vibration for the next shift.
I review the output trend and suggest a small load change for the unit.

basic.situation: A senior technician asks you to stop a generating unit after its scheduled run. What do you do?

options.text: I stop the unit using the sequence I remember from training.
I stop the nearest unit so the scheduled shutdown can stay on time.
I confirm the unit and stop sequence with the senior, then operate the controls.
I ask the senior to point out the unit, then stop it as directed.

advanced.situation: Dispatch sends a switching order while another unit is changing load. You are assigned to carry out the order.

options.text: I check the order against the current unit state, then carry out each authorized step.
I carry out the listed switch positions from memory to save time.
I read back the order and follow its sequence while watching the unit load.
I pause the switching sequence and ask dispatch to resend the order later.

basic.situation: A pump trips during a routine check, and its breaker indicator remains lit. What do you do?

options.text: I note the indicator, keep the pump stopped, and report the trip to the supervisor.
I reset the breaker and restart the pump to restore service after checking clearance.
I wait for the next round and check whether the breaker indicator has cleared.
I check the alarm and indicator, keep the pump isolated as instructed, and report findings.

advanced.situation: A generator control fault returns after a cable termination repair, and the unit is needed for the evening peak.

options.text: I replace the cable termination again using the earlier repair method.
I bridge the faulty control point so the unit can return for peak demand.
I trace the fault indications and wiring, then document evidence for a controlled repair.
I report the repeated fault and ask maintenance to inspect the cable run.

basic.situation: You are helping bolt a replacement pump bracket in place under a technician's supervision. What do you do?

options.text: I hold the bracket steady and ask which bolts to fit first.
I check the bracket alignment with the technician, then fit the specified bolts.
I fit the easiest bolts first and leave the awkward ones for later.
I start tightening the bolts while the technician finishes aligning the bracket.

advanced.situation: A hoist is ready to lift a replacement motor, but its route passes close to installed pipework. What do you do?

options.text: I review the lift plan with the crew and watch the motor pass the pipes.
I direct the lift along the planned route and adjust once the motor is moving.
I clear and confirm the lifting route, then coordinate the lift with the assigned crew.
I ask the crew to lift slowly and steer around the pipework.

basic.situation: A senior gives you the lubricant and steps for changing oil in an auxiliary pump. What do you do?

options.text: I follow the steps and check the lubricant label before refilling the pump.
I follow the steps, then ask the senior to check the refill.
I change the oil using the same amount as the previous service.
I drain the pump and refill it using the lubricant already at hand.

advanced.situation: Several auxiliary pumps share a maintenance window, and recent oil changes have been missed on one unit. What do you do?

options.text: I set a recurring schedule from the service interval and track each pump's completed work.
I ask each technician to service a pump when they have spare time.
I list each pump's last oil change and remind the team during handover.
I service the overdue pump, check other units, and flag their dates for the next shift.

basic.situation: During your round, you record water level and flow readings in the plant log. One value looks unusual.

options.text: I write the unusual reading on scrap paper for the next round.
I record the observed value and flag it for the supervisor to review.
I enter the reading I expect from yesterday so the log stays consistent.
I recheck the instrument, record the observed value, and note the time.

advanced.situation: A handover log shows a flow reading that differs from the control room record. A new technician asks which value to copy.

options.text: I compare the timestamps and source notes, then guide the technician to record the discrepancy.
I show the technician both entries and ask the senior which to use.
I tell the technician to copy the control room value into both records.
I ask the senior which reading to record, after showing both records and noting their mismatch.

basic.situation: During your round, a boiler pressure gauge reads higher than it did earlier. What do you do?

options.text: I record the higher pressure and tell the shift engineer during handover.
I check the gauge response and related readings, then report the change promptly.
I wait for another round to see if the pressure settles.
I tap the gauge and enter the earlier pressure to keep the log steady.

advanced.situation: Boiler water tests show a gradual chemistry shift, while feedwater levels vary between rounds. What do you do?

options.text: I adjust treatment to match the last shift's amount and update the log.
I compare test results and levels over time, then recommend an adjustment within procedure.
I report the chemistry shift and request another water test before changing treatment.
I add the usual treatment amount and watch the next test result.

basic.situation: A senior asks you to open a boiler feedwater valve to the marked setting. What do you do?

options.text: I turn the valve until the boiler level looks close to normal.
I open the valve to the marked setting and confirm the level response.
I open the valve fully so the boiler level recovers faster.
I ask the senior to watch while I set the valve mark.

advanced.situation: A burner control is in automatic mode during a planned inspection, and you are assigned to prepare it for isolation.

options.text: I switch the control to manual and ask the senior what to isolate next.
I switch to manual and begin the inspection while the burner is stable.
I follow the isolation procedure and confirm the control state before inspection.
I tell the team to pause and check the isolation points together.

basic.situation: You are asked to start an auxiliary pump after a routine stop. What do you do?

options.text: I start the pump and check its sound after it reaches speed.
I ask the senior to confirm the pump before I start it.
I confirm the pump is clear and ready, then start it as instructed.
I start the pump while the senior finishes checking the nearby line.

advanced.situation: A steam boiler and its feed pump are running unevenly during a demand rise. You are monitoring both systems.

options.text: I raise the feed pump output and watch whether pressure improves.
I increase firing and pump output together to meet demand quickly.
I ask the senior which system to adjust while I monitor the gauges.
I check both readings and make a controlled adjustment to the system needing it.

basic.situation: You are assigned to clean and lubricate an auxiliary fan during a planned maintenance stop. What do you do?

options.text: I clean the fan and use a small amount of available lubricant.
I clean the fan and ask the senior to check the lubricant before applying it.
I check the service instructions, clean the fan, and apply its specified lubricant.
I apply the lubricant used on the last fan and restart the equipment.

advanced.situation: A boiler valve leak returns after a gasket change, and a major maintenance window starts tomorrow. What do you do?

options.text: I fit another gasket from stores and return the valve to service.
I tighten the valve further and schedule a new gasket during the window.
I record leak conditions and inspect valve parts before selecting repair steps.
I arrange a valve inspection and prepare replacement parts for the window.

basic.situation: You measured the fuel used during your shift, but the scale reading changed once. What do you do?

options.text: I repeat the measurement, record the stable reading, and note the time.
I use yesterday's fuel figure so the daily log remains complete.
I record both readings and ask the engineer which figure to report.
I enter the first reading and finish the shift log.

advanced.situation: Your daily logs show boiler test results and maintenance entries, but two shifts use different units for fuel. What do you do?

options.text: I revise earlier entries against source records and record each fuel unit conversion used.
I flag the unit difference and propose one shared format for upcoming shifts.
I compare results, standardize fuel units, and document conventions for later entries.
I note differing units beside figures and preserve the original entries.

basic.situation: A steam engineer gives you operating instructions, but one valve position is unclear. What do you do?

options.text: I ask the engineer to clarify the valve position before I continue.
I set the valve to its usual position and continue the round.
I repeat the instruction back and confirm the valve position before acting.
I wait for the next handover so another operator can explain the setting.

advanced.situation: A compressor keeps tripping after routine checks, and the equipment manual points to a specialist service question. What do you do?

options.text: I report the trips to the senior and request specialist contact.
I contact the manufacturer with the trip details and checks already completed.
I reset the compressor repeatedly while waiting for the trip to clear.
I ask the next shift to contact the manufacturer when they have time.

basic.situation: You are assigned a routine sample at the plant’s marked collection point and have a bottle, test kit, and colour chart. What do you do?

options.text: Take a fresh sample and repeat the test before recording the chart colour.
Rinse the sampler, collect the labelled point, and compare the result with the chart.
Collect with the supplied bottle, then ask a senior to check your chart reading.
Use yesterday's reading for the shift sheet and keep the line moving.

advanced.situation: Two test results differ near a treatment adjustment point, and a trainee is waiting for your sampling guidance. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the trainee to repeat the test while you review the latest chart.
Repeat the approved sample method and share results with the shift lead.
Use the higher result to adjust treatment and brief the trainee afterward.
Compare both results, repeat the sample, and explain the approved adjustment process.

basic.situation: A senior operator gives you the approved chlorine dose for a routine batch and asks you to add it. What do you do?

options.text: Add the full dose at once, then note the amount on the shift sheet.
Measure the stated amount and ask the senior to watch while you add it.
Add a little less than stated and wait for the next routine check.
Check the chemical label and dose instruction, add the stated amount, and record it.

advanced.situation: A change in incoming water is affecting chlorine readings during your shift, and a junior asks how to adjust the dose. What do you do?

options.text: Pause additions and confirm the changed reading at the next scheduled test.
Raise the dose using the previous shift's rate and brief the junior.
Compare readings with the approved range, adjust within authority, and coach the junior.
Check the reading, make an authorised adjustment, then recheck the next sample.

basic.situation: You are covering a routine filter run, and a senior has shown you the control sequence for starting the purification equipment. What do you do?

options.text: Start the unit using the shown sequence and check the panel indicator.
Press start, then ask the senior to confirm the flow reading.
Use the previous shift's settings and start while the senior is busy.
Wait for the senior before touching controls or starting the equipment.

advanced.situation: A filter outlet flow falls while the panel shows a rising level, and the shift is busy. What do you do?

options.text: Check the control sequence, compare inlet and outlet readings, and make an authorised adjustment.
Reduce the feed slightly and watch whether the outlet flow begins recovering.
Hold current settings and ask the next operator to investigate the changing trend.
Open the outlet further to restore flow, then record the rising level afterward.

basic.situation: Your checklist shows routine meter and gauge readings are due during a stable shift. What do you do?

options.text: Check the main pressure gauge and ask a colleague about the other readings.
Walk past the gauges and return after completing the other shift tasks.
Copy the last readings onto today's checklist to finish the round quickly.
Read each meter and gauge at the listed points, then enter the current values.

advanced.situation: A pump’s gauge is drifting from its usual pattern, though the alarm has not activated. What do you do?

options.text: Log the drift and tell the shift lead that the pump needs inspection.
Record the value and continue the round while the alarm remains quiet.
Take another reading later and decide whether the change persists.
Compare related readings, note the trend, and report a pump check.

basic.situation: A routine cleaning is due for a filter bed, and a senior has assigned you the hand tools. What do you do?

options.text: Clean the bed with the available tools, then ask the senior to check the area.
Sweep around the bed first and wait for the senior to resume the cleaning.
Clear the visible debris and leave the remaining bed for the next shift.
Use the assigned tools to clean the bed and return them to the marked store.

advanced.situation: Several pumps are due for routine lubrication, and a junior operator is available to help. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the junior to lubricate scheduled pumps while you update the maintenance sheet.
Lubricate the loudest pump first and leave other units for another round.
Check the schedule, sequence due pumps, and show the junior lubrication points.
Work through the listed pumps and note any unit needing attention.

basic.situation: At shift change, you need to enter the current meter readings and attendance on the standard forms. What do you do?

options.text: Fill the form from notes and ask the next operator to verify entries.
Read the meters, confirm attendance, and complete the matching fields on each form.
Copy previous meter values and enter the attendance names from today's list.
Enter readings from memory and complete attendance after finishing the round.

advanced.situation: You notice one shift’s operating form has a reading that conflicts with the meter trend, and plant management needs the report. What do you do?

options.text: Trace the entry, flag the discrepancy, and send a verified report with notes.
Change the reading to match the trend and send the report before its deadline.
Mark the entry unclear and ask management to review the discrepancy.
Ask the shift operator to confirm the entry and hold the report pending reply.

basic.situation: A routine product sample is due from a marked point, and your supervisor has provided the test kit. What do you do?

options.text: Take the labelled sample, run the specified test, and record the observed result.
Run the test on a nearby sample point and note where it came from.
Use the previous batch result to complete the form and keep production moving.
Collect the sample and ask a senior operator to confirm the test steps.

advanced.situation: A lab report conflicts with a sight-glass observation, and a junior asks how to interpret the difference. What do you do?

options.text: Change the process to match the sight glass and explain that reading.
Ask lab to repeat its test and share observation with shift lead.
Check sample timing and process trends, compare indicators, and explain each result's limits.
Use the latest lab value as an indication until another report arrives.

basic.situation: A senior has shown you the approved panel setting for a routine speed adjustment on a production unit. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the senior to confirm the setting again before moving the control.
Wait for the next shift to make the adjustment at handover.
Use the last batch's setting and change the speed to match it.
Move the setting by the stated amount and check the displayed speed.

advanced.situation: A reaction is running unevenly, and product quality is nearing its operating limit. What do you do?

options.text: Increase speed sharply to push the reaction back into its operating range.
Hold the setting and ask the next operator to assess the reaction trend.
Trim the setting slightly using the main indicator, then watch the next reading.
Compare panel readings with the approved range, then make a measured authorised adjustment.

basic.situation: Your checklist calls for a routine inspection of the operating tower and its nearby tank. What do you do?

options.text: Mark both units as normal based on the previous inspection sheet.
Inspect the tower and ask a colleague whether the tank looked normal.
Check the listed indicators and inspect both units for normal operation.
Walk the area and check the tank after finishing the rest of the round.

advanced.situation: A tank level is rising faster than usual while the panel lights remain steady. What do you do?

options.text: Dismiss the concern and continue the route because the panel lights remain steady.
Record the rising level and tell the shift lead inspection may be needed.
Compare level trends with flow indicators, inspect the tank, and report follow-up.
Take another level reading at the next scheduled round before raising concern.

basic.situation: A senior has assigned you to start a pump and set a valve to the marked flow for a routine rinse. What do you do?

options.text: Start the pump, set the marked valve position, and check the flow indicator.
Wait until the next rinse cycle to start the pump and set the valve.
Open the valve fully to finish the rinse as quickly as possible.
Set the valve and ask the senior to check the flow after startup.

advanced.situation: A rinse pump is running, but flow through the vessel has dropped while a nearby line remains active. What do you do?

options.text: Check pump indication and valve path, make an authorised adjustment, then recheck flow.
Stop the rinse and leave the valve position for maintenance to review.
Open the vessel valve fully to regain flow and finish the rinse.
Slightly adjust the valve and watch for a response on the flow gauge.

basic.situation: A routine reading is due, and a damaged panel label needs replacing with a spare part under your senior’s guidance. What do you do?

options.text: Enter the previous shift's reading, then fit the spare label as instructed.
Record the displayed value and ask the senior to verify the replacement label.
Read the instrument, record its current value, and replace the label as instructed.
Replace the label first, then enter the reading from memory when finished.

advanced.situation: Several repair records show inconsistent pump readings, and one minor part replacement is due during your shift. What do you do?

options.text: Flag inconsistent readings and replace the part using the listed maintenance work note.
Set the repair aside and ask the next shift to reconcile readings.
Trace each reading to its source, preserve entries, and coordinate replacement.
Standardise readings to the common value and close the repair record.

basic.situation: A pump alarm signals a malfunction during production, and the supervisor’s shutdown instruction is posted at the panel. What do you do?

options.text: Ask a nearby operator to watch the alarm while you finish another task.
Call maintenance and wait for their advice before following the posted instruction.
Reset the alarm and keep the pump running until the next round.
Follow the posted shutdown instruction and notify maintenance with the alarm details.

advanced.situation: During a response drill, an alarm affects production and maintenance reports a second equipment concern. What do you do?

options.text: Shut affected units using posted directions and relay both concerns to the lead.
Tell response lead about the alarm and ask maintenance to check the concern.
Reset the first alarm so production can continue while maintenance checks the other unit.
Wait for maintenance to finish its check before sharing the alarm details.

basic.situation: You are assigned to start a compressor after routine maintenance, and the control panel shows the unit is ready.

options.text: Review the startup sheet, then begin the compressor sequence.
Use yesterday’s sequence to start the compressor and save time.
Start the compressor after checking the panel and telling the next operator.
Start the compressor using the approved sequence and confirm each step.

advanced.situation: Gas purity has slipped while compressor demand is high. You can adjust the compressor and scrubber within your operating limits.

options.text: Compare scrubber readings with the operating range and adjust in small steps.
Hold the current settings and report the purity change at shift handover.
Raise compressor pressure first, then check purity after the next sample.
Adjust the scrubber gradually and record the next purity result.

basic.situation: During your rounds, the gas feedline pressure gauge reads above its usual range while temperature and flow appear steady.

options.text: Check the pressure trend against limits and alert the control room.
Record the readings and compare them with the prior round.
Copy the usual readings into the log to finish the round.
Repeat the gauge check before entering the result in the log.

advanced.situation: Several days of logs show rising scrubber moisture readings, though each result remains within the normal operating range.

options.text: Check the trend against recent gas tests and flag the pattern.
Ask the next shift to watch the readings during routine rounds.
Treat each in-range result as routine and close the log review.
Compare the latest logs with the prior week and note the rise.

basic.situation: A routine inspection finds dust around a hand-accessible filter housing, and the unit can be safely isolated for cleaning.

options.text: Wipe the housing quickly while the unit remains in service.
Isolate the unit as directed, clean the housing, and log completion.
Check the isolation status, then clean the housing with hand tools.
Brush the housing clean and tell the next operator about it.

advanced.situation: Feedline pressure repeatedly dips when demand rises, while nearby units remain stable and your adjustment authority is limited to setpoints.

options.text: Lower the feed rate slightly and log whether pressure stabilizes.
Compare pressure patterns across units and recommend checking the line capacity.
Keep the setpoint unchanged and report the repeated pressure dips.
Raise the setpoint to mask each dip during peak demand.

basic.situation: You finish a shift with several temperature and flow readings, plus a gas test result, ready for the daily operations log.

options.text: Enter the readings and test result before handing over the log.
Use the previous shift’s values for readings you missed.
Enter each reading with its time and unit, then check the log.
Write the readings in the log and add the test result later.

advanced.situation: Compiled monthly logs show small pressure swings during similar demand peaks, but no single reading exceeds its operating limit.

options.text: Group the readings by demand period and summarize the recurring swings.
Compare peak-period swings across units and propose a targeted standard review.
List the monthly pressure swings and share them at handover.
Keep the summary focused on readings that crossed operating limits.

basic.situation: A delivery of flammable product is being moved into storage, and you notice a vehicle parked near the marked transfer area.

options.text: Tell the driver about the transfer area and watch the delivery.
Pause the transfer, clear the area through site procedure, then resume.
Ask the driver to move before the delivery continues.
Continue the transfer while the driver finishes unloading nearby.

advanced.situation: A new storage team is unsure how to handle a flammable product transfer after a near miss involving a hose connection.

options.text: Review approved handling steps and demonstrate hose checks before the team starts the transfer.
Invite experienced operators to explain transfer controls and compare them with approved procedures.
Read the approved procedure together and clarify each person's checks before transfer begins.
Discuss the near miss, then ask the team to describe safeguards for the hose connection.

basic.situation: You are assigned to direct an auxiliary cooling unit check while another operator watches the main control panel.

options.text: Signal the worker, confirm the cooling check, and report its status.
Assume the worker heard the signal and log the unit as checked.
Signal the worker and note the cooling check for handover.
Signal the worker to check cooling and continue your panel round.

advanced.situation: A gas unit develops unstable flow while maintenance is checking an auxiliary valve and another operator monitors the panel.

options.text: Tell the panel operator about the valve check and wait for updates.
Coordinate the panel readings and valve check before agreeing on the next adjustment.
Make a small panel adjustment while the valve check continues.
Ask maintenance to finish the valve check, then review the flow trend.

basic.situation: During a tank round, an automatic gauge shows a higher oil level than your last reading, while the inlet meter continues to run.

options.text: Record the level, compare it with the inlet meter trend, and note any change.
Enter the current reading and flag its difference from the previous round sheet.
Verify the gauge against the meter, then report the unusual rise to the supervisor.
Take a second gauge reading, then record both values for comparison.

advanced.situation: A product meter’s readings drift from the tank gauge over several rounds, though both instruments remain within their marked ranges.

options.text: Record both readings and mention the mismatch at shift handover.
Repeat both readings and note whether the mismatch remains.
Use the meter reading as the movement total for this shift.
Compare the readings across rounds and flag the meter discrepancy for verification.

basic.situation: The process schedule calls for a modest pressure change, and the control panel shows the unit is stable before the adjustment.

options.text: Set the scheduled pressure and check the panel response against the target.
Adjust the panel gradually and check the pressure once it settles.
Use the previous shift’s pressure setting to avoid slowing production.
Make the pressure change and record the new panel reading.

advanced.situation: Distilling demand changes while an auxiliary pump is due for service, and you are coordinating controls across two processing units.

options.text: Check the service update, then adjust the busier unit’s controls.
Shift flow toward the available unit and monitor its pressure response.
Balance both units against the schedule and confirm the auxiliary pump status first.
Keep both units at their current settings until the next round.

basic.situation: At shift end, you have instrument readings and a laboratory result to enter in the operating record before handover.

options.text: Enter the instrument readings now and attach the lab result later.
Enter each result with its time and source, then check the record.
Record the readings and laboratory result for the incoming operator.
Use the prior shift’s laboratory result until today’s copy arrives.

advanced.situation: A pump vibrates more than usual during your inspection, and the next scheduled transfer depends on that unit.

options.text: Check the unit’s condition, report the vibration, and note the transfer impact.
Run the next transfer at the usual rate and note the vibration afterward.
Report the vibration and ask maintenance to inspect the pump.
Reduce the transfer rate and write the vibration in the log.

basic.situation: The schedule calls for moving one product from a processing unit to storage, and the line map shows two available routes.

options.text: Follow the scheduled route and watch the receiving tank level.
Check the line map and confirm the destination tank is available.
Use the route from yesterday’s transfer to save setup time.
Check route capacity and line connections before following the scheduled movement.

advanced.situation: Two scheduled products need the same line window, and storage levels leave little spare capacity across the connected tanks.

options.text: Sequence both transfers from the schedule and report any delay afterward.
Check the shared line window, then propose a revised transfer order.
Compare routes with line capacity and tank space before sequencing.
Review product demand, available tank space, and transfer timing before choosing sequence.

basic.situation: You are starting a scheduled oil transfer into a tank, and the receiving level is within its expected range.

options.text: Confirm the destination tank and level before starting the pump.
Check the tank level before starting the pump and opening the valve.
Open the valve to the usual tank and start the pump.
Start the pump and watch the tank level during transfer.

advanced.situation: A scheduled sample is needed during a transfer, and the product line has handled a different grade earlier in the shift.

options.text: Check the sampling point and collect the scheduled product sample.
Take a quick sample from the nearest bleeder valve to meet timing.
Confirm the line is flushed for this grade before sampling.
Collect the sample and label it with the current product grade.

basic.situation: The pumphouse asks you to start a pump while another worker checks the line temperature for the same transfer.

options.text: Signal the pump start and ask for the temperature reading afterward.
Start the pump on schedule and tell the pumphouse afterward.
Confirm the line and temperature check, then signal the pump start.
Ask the worker for the temperature reading before signaling the pump.

advanced.situation: Two pumphouses must hand off a shared line between products, and a delayed status update leaves the next transfer window unclear.

options.text: Delay your side’s change and tell the other pumphouse the window is unclear.
Ask the other pumphouse to send its latest status before the transfer.
Confirm both line statuses and agree on the handoff before changing product flow.
Keep the planned flow moving while the other pumphouse sends an update.

basic.situation: You are assigned to measure refined feedstock before a routine batch, and the loading sheet lists the target volume.

options.text: Ask a trained operator to confirm the scale before you load.
Measure twice with the calibrated vessel, then record the transfer total.
Use yesterday's volume and start loading to keep the batch moving.
Check the tank reading, measure the target, and log the amount.

advanced.situation: During a feedstock transfer, the loading meter and tank reading disagree, and the next batch is waiting for material.

options.text: Tell the shift lead about the mismatch and wait for instructions.
Compare the meter and tank readings, then adjust the logged total to match.
Pause the transfer, check the meter setup, and document both readings.
Recheck the tank level and note the difference on the batch sheet.

basic.situation: You are assigned to record routine processing data for a biofuels batch, and the panel shows temperature, flow, and batch time.

options.text: Record the readings with units and the time shown on the panel.
Check the panel trend, then log each reading with its time and units.
Copy the displayed readings and time into the batch log.
Use the previous batch values to complete the log quickly.

advanced.situation: A hybrid run switches from batch mixing to continuous flow, and flow readings fluctuate while stored product awaits transfer.

options.text: Keep the existing checks and record each mode change in the log.
Review readings by process mode and set checks around each transition.
Ask the lead to review the flow trend before transfer proceeds.
Use one hourly flow reading to simplify monitoring during the run.

basic.situation: You are helping with a routine production run, and an operator asks you to start the feed pump after checking the line.

options.text: Wait for the operator to return and start the pump together.
Confirm the line is ready, then start the pump as instructed.
Check the valve position and pump direction, then start and watch flow.
Start the pump and adjust the valve until feed begins moving.

advanced.situation: A centrifuge extraction rate falls during a high-volume run, while the feed remains steady and the next fraction is due soon.

options.text: Ask the lead which centrifuge setting to use for this fraction.
Hold the current setting and record the lower extraction rate for review.
Compare feed and output rates, then adjust within the approved operating range.
Raise the centrifuge speed to recover extraction before the next fraction.

basic.situation: During a routine walkaround, you notice a loose guard on a biofuels pump and have the inspection checklist with you.

options.text: Record the loose guard and report it through the maintenance process.
Keep clear, note the pump location, and tell the operator before use.
Tighten the guard with available tools and mark the checklist complete.
Finish the checklist, then mention the guard at the shift handover.

advanced.situation: A pump seal keeps leaking after routine maintenance, and a replacement component is available during a scheduled production pause.

options.text: Ask maintenance to take over the pump repair during the pause.
Inspect the seal seating and related wear, then document the repair findings.
Fit the available seal and restart once the leak appears smaller.
Replace the seal using the maintenance instructions and report the repeat leak.

basic.situation: You are asked to collect a routine biofuels sample and check its quality using the laboratory procedure for the batch.

options.text: Test the nearest open sample to save time before the next batch.
Use a clean labeled container and confirm the batch before testing.
Take the sample and run the listed test using the batch label.
Ask a lab colleague to collect the sample while you prepare the bench.

advanced.situation: A biofuels additive sample shows an unexpected result, and the batch is scheduled for reprocessing later in the shift.

options.text: Repeat the test with a fresh sample and compare it with the procedure limits.
Hold the sample result for review and note the planned reprocessing time.
Approve the additive based on its normal appearance and keep the schedule.
Record the result and ask the lead whether the additive can be used.

basic.situation: Before a routine run, you are assigned to clean the processing area and help check a liquid flow meter calibration.

options.text: Wait for a colleague to finish cleaning before you check the meter.
Clear the work area, follow the cleaning steps, and prepare the meter.
Wipe the visible surfaces and mark the area clean on the sheet.
Use the listed cleaning method, then record the meter check result.

advanced.situation: After calibration, two flow meters feeding the reaction vessel show different rates during the same steady-water check.

options.text: Repeat the water check and record the difference for the shift lead.
Adjust the lower reading until both meters display the same rate.
Check each meter against the reference flow and document both results.
Use the higher reading for the run and schedule another check later.

basic.situation: You are adjusting a reactor during a routine batch, and its temperature is drifting slightly above the written set point. What do you do?

options.text: I compare the gauge with the set point, then trim the feed slowly.
I ask a nearby operator which control usually steadies this reading.
I turn the feed down to settle the reading before checking the target.
I check the written set point and adjust one control in small steps.

advanced.situation: A reaction is not reaching its expected pressure, and a junior operator asks what to do while the batch remains active. What do you do?

options.text: I reduce feed and watch whether pressure begins to recover.
I stop feed and ask the junior to prepare for documented shutdown.
I check the procedure and guide the junior through documented shutdown steps.
I ask the junior to repeat the last setting while I watch pressure.

basic.situation: During your routine round, a flowmeter reading differs from the normal operating range on the process sheet. What do you do?

options.text: I check the nearby gauge and note both readings for the next round.
I adjust the valve until the flowmeter looks closer to its usual position.
I ask a coworker whether that flowmeter often moves around during a batch.
I record the reading and compare it with the operating range on the sheet.

advanced.situation: You notice a faint leak near a pump, while its readings remain stable and the next area is busy. What do you do?

options.text: I mark the area, report the leak, and assess whether the pump needs shutdown under procedure.
I ask a coworker to watch the readings while I finish the round.
I note the location and continue the round, planning to report it later.
I report the leak to maintenance and keep watch on the pump readings.

basic.situation: At the specified stage of a routine batch, you need to draw a sample for a basic pH check. What do you do?

options.text: I draw the sample and tell the technician it came from this batch.
I fill a clean container and leave it beside the testing bench.
I take the sample at the stated stage and label it for the pH check.
I collect a small sample and ask the technician which test to run.

advanced.situation: A lab result differs from the expected concentration, while the batch colour looks normal and production is waiting. What do you do?

options.text: I adjust the ingredient feed to bring concentration closer to target.
I repeat the test with the same method and compare both readings carefully.
I ask the lab whether earlier batches showed a similar concentration.
I verify the sample identity and method, then flag the batch for review.

basic.situation: After a routine run, your lead asks you to flush a tank with water using the posted cleaning sequence. What do you do?

options.text: I start the water flow and ask a coworker when the tank usually looks clean.
I use the posted sequence and tell the lead when the flush is finished.
I rinse the tank until the water runs clear, then move to cleanup.
I follow the posted flush sequence and confirm the tank is drained afterward.

advanced.situation: A filter needs frequent cleaning between runs, and you have been asked to help reduce recurring stoppages. What do you do?

options.text: I log cleaning intervals and condition, then suggest a schedule from the pattern.
I ask the next shift to clean the filter whenever production slows down.
I clean the filter after each run and track whether stoppages become less frequent.
I suggest cleaning the filter more often based on recent stoppages.

basic.situation: You are preparing a routine transfer near flammable materials and notice a hot surface beside the work area. What do you do?

options.text: I move nearby containers farther away before starting the transfer.
I tell the lead about the hot surface and wait for direction.
I pause the transfer and follow site precautions for controlling ignition sources.
I ask a coworker to watch the surface while I complete the transfer.

advanced.situation: A process alarm indicates a release, and a nearby operator is unsure which emergency response applies. What do you do?

options.text: I alert the control room and ask the operator to stand by the response sheet.
I ask the operator to check the alarm panel while I look for the response sheet.
I silence the alarm and ask the control room whether a release is likely.
I activate the posted response, alert nearby staff, and guide them to the designated safe area.

basic.situation: You finish a routine batch and need to enter its temperature and processing time in the log. What do you do?

options.text: I enter the usual temperature and run time for this product in its log.
I ask the previous operator to confirm the temperature before completing the log.
I write the temperature and time from my notes before handing over.
I compare instrument readings with the batch sheet before entering them.

advanced.situation: Two shifts recorded different amounts of a powdered ingredient used in the same batch, and stock counts are due. What do you do?

options.text: I reconcile issue records against entries and document verified use and variance.
I note the mismatch and postpone the count until the next stock review.
I use the larger amount in the stock count to keep the balance cautious.
I compare both entries and ask each shift to clarify its recorded amount.

basic.situation: You are preparing a batch and the written checklist says to start the transfer pump after checking the outlet valve. What do you do?

options.text: Start the pump while checking the outlet valve as flow begins.
Ask a nearby operator to confirm the outlet, then start the pump.
Check the checklist, confirm the outlet is clear, then start the pump.
Check the valve position and start the pump as the checklist directs.

advanced.situation: A new batch gives uneven flow despite the usual control settings. You are asked to adjust the machine for better yield before the next run. What do you do?

options.text: Review the control limits, then adjust the flow setting and observe.
Ask the senior operator which control they would change first.
Check the process readings, adjust one control, and record the result.
Change several settings together and compare the next batch's yield.

basic.situation: During a run, the pressure gauge moves above its usual mark. Your supervisor is nearby. What do you do?

options.text: Record the reading and continue watching the gauge for a few minutes.
Read the gauge aloud and ask your supervisor to check it with you.
Compare the reading with the checklist range and alert your supervisor.
Turn the pressure control down to bring the needle back toward normal.

advanced.situation: You notice a small leak and a faint vibration that were absent last shift. The machine still runs steadily. What do you do?

options.text: Log both signs, mark their locations, and report the changed pattern.
Ask the next shift to listen for vibration during their rounds.
Report the leak and vibration to maintenance for a machine check.
Tighten the nearby fitting and see whether the vibration settles.

basic.situation: The lab requests a sample from the settling tank during your shift. The batch is still processing. What do you do?

options.text: Fill a container from the nearest open drain and send it along.
Collect a tank sample now and write the shift on its label.
Take the sample from the tank's usual point and label the container.
Confirm the tank and timing, collect the sample, and label its batch.

advanced.situation: Two operators collect samples at different points, producing conflicting clarity results. You are asked to help make verification more consistent. What do you do?

options.text: Agree on a shared point and remind both operators to label samples.
Ask each operator to use the point that seems most representative.
Set one sampling point and timing, then document how to label samples.
Use the tank outlet for the next samples and compare their clarity.

basic.situation: After a batch, your checklist calls for rinsing a tank and its inlet pipe with a hose. What do you do?

options.text: Rinse the tank and pipe, then ask a coworker to check the result.
Rinse the tank and pipe in the order shown, then check both surfaces.
Rinse the tank and inlet pipe until the visible residue clears.
Rinse the tank first and leave the inlet pipe for the next cycle.

advanced.situation: A rinse line has recurring residue after cleaning, while other tanks are due for the next batch. You are asked to improve the cleaning schedule. What do you do?

options.text: Add the rinse line to a timed cleaning schedule and record completion checks.
Add extra rinses to every tank at the end of each shift.
Schedule a rinse-line clean before each batch and track the results.
Ask operators to clean the rinse line whenever residue appears.

basic.situation: You need to load a specified amount of refined material into a storage container. The scale and container are ready. What do you do?

options.text: Pour until the container looks close to the usual fill level.
Weigh the specified amount, load it steadily, and label the container.
Check the batch amount and load it into the prepared container.
Load the amount shown on the batch sheet and ask someone to check.

advanced.situation: Two materials are ready for loading, and one shared conveyor serves both lines. A delay on either line could hold up production. What do you do?

options.text: Ask both line operators which material should go onto the conveyor first.
Load the larger batch first so the conveyor stays busy longer.
Sequence loads by batch need and changeover, confirming the conveyor path each time.
Check each line's due time and load the earlier batch first.

basic.situation: You are entering temperature readings in the shift log, and one entry is hard to read on the paper sheet. What do you do?

options.text: Check the gauge record with the operator, then enter the confirmed reading.
Enter the most likely number and finish the remaining log entries.
Mark the entry unclear and ask the previous shift to confirm it.
Ask your supervisor to interpret the unclear entry before entering it.

advanced.situation: Your weekly log shows flow readings rising before several slow batches, but entries use different abbreviations. What do you do?

options.text: Compare dated readings with batch outcomes, then suggest consistent log terms.
Review the readings with the team and agree on common abbreviations.
Standardize abbreviations in the next log and review the trend afterward.
Tell the next shift that rising flow readings can slow production.

basic.situation: Your supervisor is nearby as you prepare to start a grinder for a scheduled batch. The work order lists the material and settings.

options.text: Check the material label and ask a nearby operator which controls to use.
Read the work order, confirm the listed settings with your supervisor, then start the grinder.
Use the last batch's settings and start the grinder to keep production moving.
Match the material and settings to the work order, then start the machine as directed.

advanced.situation: The grinder's output becomes uneven, and the conveyor flow slows during a production run. You are an experienced operator with a newer colleague beside you.

options.text: Pause feed, inspect visible causes, and guide your colleague through safe adjustment.
Adjust grinder settings to match the sample without checking the cause.
Pause feed and ask the supervisor to assess uneven output before adjustments.
Check output and conveyor, then make a routine adjustment while monitoring production.

basic.situation: A batch of polished parts is ready for a routine check. Your checklist shows the sample size and the required visual features.

options.text: Look over the top layer and mark the batch acceptable if it appears consistent.
Use the checklist to inspect the sample and note any parts that need another look.
Inspect several parts and ask a coworker whether the finish seems within range.
Compare sampled parts with the listed features and record any visible defects on the checklist.

advanced.situation: A few parts show faint surface marks that were missed on earlier shifts. You are asked to guide operators on inspection standards for the next production run.

options.text: Gather marked parts and ask operators to describe the visible differences.
Keep the checklist and inspect the completed batch closely after production ends.
Show marked examples, explain sample comparisons, and review operators' findings during the run.
Ask operators to reject parts with visible marks under normal inspection lighting.

basic.situation: A new work order is at your station before a crushing run. The line is ready, and you need to identify the production details.

options.text: Read the order and ask a coworker to point out the production quantity.
Read the material, target quantity, and listed settings, then confirm any unclear item before starting.
Check the listed quantity and material, then keep the order beside the controls.
Start with the previous order's settings and compare the first product afterward.

advanced.situation: During a long run, the conveyor flow pulses and the motor sound changes slightly. Production continues, and you are tracking equipment performance.

options.text: Monitor conveyor flow through the run and report the sound during handover.
Record changes in flow and sound, then request a maintenance check before restarting.
Raise feed to steady output while the motor sound settles.
Note the sound change and ask the supervisor to arrange an equipment check.

basic.situation: A scheduled batch has finished, and your work area needs cleaning before the next run. Hand tools and the cleaning instructions are available.

options.text: Follow the cleaning instructions, use the provided tools, and clear residue from the work area.
Sweep visible dust toward the aisle so the next operator can begin sooner.
Ask the next operator which surfaces need cleaning before you put the tools away.
Clean the main surfaces with the provided tools and tell the next operator what remains.

advanced.situation: Recurring residue builds around a machine after each run, and different operators clean it differently. You are helping the team plan equipment care.

options.text: Ask operators to clean the residue whenever they have spare time between runs.
Add residue checks to handover notes and ask the supervisor to agree a cleaning schedule.
Show the team how you clear the residue with the usual hand tools.
Use equipment instructions to set a routine, demonstrate safe cleaning, and review results.

basic.situation: Your shift has finished a short grinding run. The production form asks for output, test readings, and any adjustments made.

options.text: Copy the output from the display and ask a coworker where the readings belong.
Fill in the output and test readings, then leave adjustments for the next operator.
Enter the recorded output, readings, and adjustments in their matching fields, then check the form.
Write the total output in the comments box and submit the form before shift change.

advanced.situation: Recent production forms show inconsistent units and missing adjustment notes across shifts. You are reviewing the logs and asked to improve how operators record run data.

options.text: Use one shift's units as standard and copy notes from similar runs.
Compare readings, clarify units and adjustment fields, then share a recording guide.
Add a reminder explaining how operators should complete each field on the form.
Review logs for patterns, then show staff clear examples of complete run records.

basic.situation: A belt begins slipping during a run, and the machine output becomes uneven. Your supervisor is working nearby, and the line is still operating.

options.text: Tell a nearby operator what changed and ask them to monitor the belt and output.
Let the supervisor know the output changed and ask whether the belt needs attention.
Report the slipping belt and uneven output to your supervisor using site procedures.
Keep the run going and mention the belt at the next scheduled break.

advanced.situation: A machine starts vibrating sharply, and a second operator sees the same change on another line. You are responsible for reporting repair needs during the shift.

options.text: Ask operators to record unusual vibration, note each affected line, and send logs for maintenance review.
Notify the supervisor about both vibrations and remind the team to report changes promptly.
Report the vibration on your line and ask the other operator to tell their supervisor.
Notify the supervisor with both machine locations and symptoms, then brief operators on the reporting route.

basic.situation: You are sanding a flat steel cover before coating. Your lead shows you the sample finish and asks you to remove the visible marks.

options.text: Use a coarse wheel to remove the marks in fewer passes.
Match the sample finish with even strokes, then check the surface under good light.
Sand the visible marks until the surface feels smooth to your hand.
Sand the marked area with light, even strokes using the sanding block.

advanced.situation: A contoured metal part has a tight groove and curved edges. The blueprint gives exact dimensions, and a rushed polish could remove material from either feature.

options.text: Use a coarse file to bring each feature close before polishing.
Polish the whole contour lightly, then compare it with the blueprint.
Use the matching file and follow the template around each curved edge.
File the groove and curves to match the template, checking dimensions between passes.

basic.situation: You finish a small metal part, and the work order gives a target width. A caliper and ruler are available at your bench.

options.text: Estimate the width against a similar finished part on the bench.
Check the width with the caliper and mark the reading on the job card.
Measure the width with the ruler and set the part aside.
Use the caliper to check the width against the work order.

advanced.situation: A finished die has several grooves and curved edges. The template and job dimensions are available, but the first measurement differs slightly from the drawing.

options.text: Check the template fit, then measure the area that differs from the drawing.
Measure the overall width again and compare the surface by sight.
Compare each feature with the template and record its measured dimensions.
Polish the close areas until they look consistent with the neighboring grooves.

basic.situation: After a shift using hand files and scrapers, your bench is dusty. The tools are due back in the shared cabinet before the next job.

options.text: Put the dusty tools back together so the next shift can find them.
Clean the files and scrapers, then return them to the labeled cabinet.
Brush the tools clean, check their handles, and return them to their labeled places.
Wipe each file quickly and place the set together in the cabinet.

advanced.situation: A grinding wheel has become uneven during a long run. The machine is available for dressing, and the next batch needs a consistent surface finish.

options.text: Ask a nearby operator which dressing tool suits this wheel before restarting the batch.
Continue with lighter pressure and inspect the next piece for a consistent surface finish.
Dress the uneven face, then resume the batch at its usual setting and inspect one sample.
Dress the wheel evenly, inspect its face, and test the finish on a sample piece.

basic.situation: A small metal workpiece needs light deburring. Several files are available, and the job card describes its material and shape.

options.text: Select a file suited to the metal, then test it on one small edge.
Choose a fine file suited to this metal and its small edges for deburring.
Take the largest file nearby and remove material quickly across all small workpiece edges first.
Use a medium file that seems suitable for this type of metal part.

advanced.situation: A heavy irregular casting must be moved to a work table, then secured for hand finishing. The marked lifting points and available moving device are shown on the job sheet.

options.text: Use marked lifting points and the device, then secure the casting before finishing.
Ask a colleague to guide the move while you lift one side by hand.
Move it with the device and position it near the table edge for easier access.
Transfer it with the moving device and clamp it near the marked work area.

basic.situation: Before sanding a timber panel, you spot a narrow crack near the edge. The work order asks you to mark defects for repair.

options.text: Sand the crack lightly so the area looks smoother before marking it.
Mark the edge area where you can see the surface change.
Mark the crack clearly and note its position for the repair team.
Circle the crack and show the panel to the repair team.

advanced.situation: A complex layout shows a shaped template with several notches. You need to mark a metal blank for finishing, and two reference lines are close together.

options.text: Use the drawing to mark the template shape and every notch with care.
Mark the outline, then estimate where the two close reference lines meet.
Trace from drawing datums, verify both reference lines, then mark each notch.
Start marking each notch from the nearest blank edge to save time during setup.

basic.situation: You are asked to start a polishing machine for a small batch. The workpiece is secured, and your lead has shown you the start and stop controls.

options.text: Start with the shown control and watch the first pass closely.
Use the nearest switch and run the batch at full speed.
Use the marked start control, then inspect the workpiece after its first pass.
Start the machine and polish the batch at a steady, familiar pace.

advanced.situation: During a long polishing run, the finish begins to look uneven. The controls allow speed adjustment, and the job card specifies the target surface finish.

options.text: Increase the speed and make another pass, then inspect the finish across the full area.
Keep the setting and polish remaining areas with lighter pressure, checking each pass.
Lower speed slightly and compare the finish with the job card target.
Adjust speed slightly, then inspect the next polished area against the target.

basic.situation: You are running a mixer for a routine batch. The work order gives the mixing time, and the supervisor has shown you the start and stop controls.

options.text: Run the mixer until the mixture looks uniform to you.
Start the mixer and time the run against the work order.
Let the mixer run while you prepare the next batch nearby.
Use the shown controls and stop the mixer at the stated time.

advanced.situation: A mixer sounds different during a batch and the blend looks uneven. The work order sets a run time, and you are trained to use its controls.

options.text: Stop mixing and tell the lead that the blend appears uneven.
Continue the timed run and inspect the blend after it leaves the mixer.
Stop the mixer safely, inspect the batch and settings, then report the change.
Lower the speed slightly and monitor whether the unusual sound continues.

basic.situation: A work order calls for a measured amount of powder in the mixer. The weighed container is at your station, ready to load.

options.text: Check the container label, then use the funnel to add the powder.
Add scoops until the mixer appears adequately filled, then begin mixing.
Pour it in and record the amount once the batch is underway.
Verify the work order amount, then load the weighed powder into the mixer.

advanced.situation: Two mixtures must move from separate work areas to different processing lines. A new operator is helping, and the route is busy with hand carts.

options.text: Plan separate cart routes, label each load, and show the operator the safe sequence.
Ask the operator to follow your cart while you carry the labels.
Label each load and guide the operator along the marked route.
Move both loads along the shortest route and sort them at the lines.

basic.situation: You are preparing a routine dough mix. The written recipe lists each ingredient and amount, and the supervisor is nearby to guide you.

options.text: Add ingredients by handfuls until the mixture looks familiar, then proceed with mixing.
Measure the listed amounts and add them to the mixing bowl.
Measure each recipe ingredient and add them in the listed sequence.
Use the recipe amounts, rounding small measures to simpler scoops.

advanced.situation: A new dye formula lists several additions, and the product specification has changed slightly. Your role permits formula preparation, but not approval of a new formula.

options.text: Check each addition against the formula and note the specification change.
Adjust dye amounts until a small trial sample matches the newly requested shade.
Prepare the listed formula and flag the changed specification for review.
Use the closest existing formula and prepare a smaller batch first.

basic.situation: A batch of dry ingredients arrives at your station. The work order gives a target weight, and you are asked to check it before mixing.

options.text: Ask a coworker to review the reading against the recipe target before mixing begins.
Weigh the ingredients, then compare the reading with the target listed on the work order.
Weigh the container and record its displayed amount beside the work order target.
Inspect the filled container visually, then start mixing the batch according to schedule.

advanced.situation: A work order calls for a specific colour and texture. A new operator sees a slight difference between two containers and asks how to check them.

options.text: Compare both containers with the work order, then check each texture against the sample.
Select the closer-looking container and continue mixing while noting the visible difference.
Ask the operator to compare both samples by touch and describe their texture differences.
Review the work order and compare each container's colour and texture with the sample.

basic.situation: The mixture has reached the stated quality, and the work order calls for transfer to the next area. Your lead has shown you the valve and pump controls.

options.text: Wait for the next operator to handle valve opening and transfer.
Stop mixing at target quality; use the shown valve and pump controls.
Stop the mixer and start the pump to send the mixture onward.
Open the valve and start the pump while the mixer runs briefly for transfer.

advanced.situation: A conveyor feeding the mixer slows, and material begins collecting at its inlet. You can access its normal controls, but clearing the issue may affect the running batch.

options.text: Pause feed using normal controls, inspect the inlet, and report persistent faults.
Tap the conveyor guard lightly, then check whether material starts moving again.
Tell the lead the conveyor has slowed and watch the material level.
Raise the feed setting so the conveyor clears material at its inlet faster.

basic.situation: After a production run, powder remains on the floor around your station. The work area must be cleaned before the next batch arrives.

options.text: Push the powder toward the edge so the next shift can collect it.
Wipe around the machine and leave the loose powder for later.
Sweep the area and place the powder in a nearby bin.
Sweep the powder into its designated waste container and clear the work area.

advanced.situation: A production form shows a different output total from the container labels. You also notice residue on a mixer part during the shift change.

options.text: Record the discrepancy, check the source entries, and clean the part as instructed.
Note the difference on the form and clean the mixer part.
Change the form total to match the labels and wipe the visible residue.
Leave the form for the next shift and clean the mixer part now.

basic.situation: You receive an order for canvas pouches in two sizes. You need to confirm the dimensions and quantities before cutting.

options.text: I match each size and quantity to the order before laying pieces.
I copy the listed size and quantity onto my cutting ticket.
I use yesterday's batch marks to begin cutting the matching fabric.
I check the order with a nearby cutter before marking the fabric.

advanced.situation: A work order combines several fabric sizes and colors, with limited material for each. You must plan the cuts to meet quantities and reduce waste.

options.text: I follow the order line by line and cut each listed piece separately.
I start with the largest pieces and adjust the smaller cuts afterward.
I group matching sizes and plan each color's cuts against available lengths.
I map all sizes onto each color's available lengths before choosing cut order.

basic.situation: You are marking straight cut lines on a roll of fabric for a small batch. The work order gives the piece dimensions.

options.text: I measure from the last line and use the same pencil mark each time.
I measure each piece with a ruler and mark its line in pencil.
I check the ruler's start point, measure each dimension, and mark the lines.
I mark the first line by eye, then repeat its spacing across the fabric.

advanced.situation: A new cutter is marking curved templates on costly fabric, and several pieces must fit within one narrow length. You are guiding the layout.

options.text: I mark one template together, then have the cutter place the rest.
I let the cutter reuse yesterday's chalk marks to save setup time.
I set shared alignment points and demonstrate checks for curves and fabric yield.
I show how to align templates and check key points before marking.

basic.situation: You receive finished pieces in several sizes and shades. A packing list shows which groups belong together.

options.text: I stack pieces by size and ask packing staff to check the shades.
I separate sizes first, then verify each shade against the packing list.
I place similar-looking shades together and copy the packing list later.
I sort each piece by its listed size and shade before stacking.

advanced.situation: During sorting, you find several pieces with small stains and inconsistent shade. The batch is needed for an order with strict appearance requirements.

options.text: I mark affected pieces clearly, group by shade, and record the defect counts.
I move the stained pieces into the closest shade group for later review.
I separate the stained pieces and note their shade for the quality log.
I place the pieces at the bottom of the batch to keep work moving.

basic.situation: You are asked to unroll a fresh fabric length onto the cutting table before a routine batch. The surface is ready.

options.text: I unroll the fabric evenly and smooth it before the cutter begins.
I pull the roll quickly across the table and start laying templates.
I smooth the middle and ask the cutter to check the edges.
I align the fabric edge with the table guide and smooth the length.

advanced.situation: Two fabric lengths must fit on the table for a mixed batch. A new coworker is helping, and the available material is costly.

options.text: I use the full table length for the larger pieces and fit the rest later.
I lay the lengths side by side and let the coworker position templates.
I show the coworker how to unroll both lengths and smooth the surface.
I plan the layout around the templates, then coach the coworker through alignment.

basic.situation: A finished product has a few loose thread ends along one seam. You have scissors and a supervisor nearby.

options.text: I trim the loose threads close to the seam with scissors.
I ask the supervisor to show me where to trim the first thread.
I hold the fabric flat and trim each end with a small margin.
I pull each thread taut and snip it quickly beside the fabric.

advanced.situation: You are cutting a delicate, curved textile shape for an urgent batch. A new worker is watching and wants to try the hand tool.

options.text: I support the fabric, cut the curve in short passes, and coach their grip.
I let the worker cut the urgent piece while I sort the next batch.
I cut the curve myself and explain how the blade follows its outline.
I demonstrate a steady cut on a sample, then supervise their turn.

basic.situation: Your hand saw begins to drag while trimming a batch. The workbench has a spare saw and a sharpening station.

options.text: I press harder so the saw can finish the current batch.
I set the saw aside and wait for someone to sharpen it.
I switch to the spare saw and tell the lead about the dull one.
I tag the dull saw for sharpening and use the ready spare tool.

advanced.situation: Several hand saws are shared across shifts, and dull blades have delayed work twice this month. You are helping organise tool care.

options.text: I check the saws at shift start and sharpen any that feel slow.
I ask each shift to tell me when a saw starts dragging.
I set a check schedule, label tool status, and record sharpening dates.
I sharpen every shared saw at the end of each shift.

basic.situation: You are fitting a replacement blade and rollers for a routine paper run. The work order lists the required components.

options.text: I fit the blade first and ask a coworker about the rollers.
I fit the listed blade and rollers using the specified hand tools.
I choose a similar blade and use the existing roller positions.
I match each component to the order, fit it, and check its seating.

advanced.situation: After a blade change, test cuts drift across the sheet even though the listed parts are fitted. The next batch is a high-value order.

options.text: I shift the guide until one test sheet follows the cut line.
I compare the setup points, adjust alignment gradually, and verify repeat cuts.
I reduce the speed and ask the next shift to check the drift.
I check the blade seating and make a small guide adjustment.

basic.situation: A routine batch is ready, and the machine is set for the listed material. You are asked to start the cutting run with guidance.

options.text: I use the pedal and feed the stock as the blade moves.
I press the start button as the guide points to it.
I start the machine and watch the first piece leave the bed.
I confirm the stock is aligned, then use the start control.

advanced.situation: A long production run is behind schedule, and the cut edges vary as stock feeds. You can adjust speed and pressure within the set range.

options.text: I keep the current settings and ask the next operator to watch the edges.
I review feed alignment, then tune speed and pressure against repeated samples.
I raise speed to recover time and check the next stack of cuts.
I reduce pressure slightly and compare several cuts before changing speed.

basic.situation: The first pieces from a new job are on the table. The work order gives a target width, and you have a ruler.

options.text: I measure several pieces and compare their widths with the order.
I compare one piece with the sample and note its ruler reading.
I stack the pieces and rely on their edges lining up.
I measure the first piece and continue if it looks close.

advanced.situation: Measurements show that cut widths vary near the order limit across several runs. You are checking the output and can adjust machine components.

options.text: I widen the stop until most pieces match the sample sheet.
I measure a fresh sample and adjust the stop to the average width.
I mark the affected pieces, compare settings with the order, and test adjustments.
I remove the narrow pieces and tell the lead the widths are varying.

basic.situation: During a routine run, you notice residue on a conveyor and the checklist calls for cleaning and lubrication after shutdown.

options.text: I stop at the checklist point, clean the residue, and apply listed lubricant.
I wipe the visible residue and leave lubrication for the next shift.
I finish the batch, then clean and lubricate the conveyor as listed.
I spray lubricant over the residue to clear the conveyor quickly.

advanced.situation: Operators report recurring residue and occasional feed pauses on the same conveyor. You are asked to help improve routine equipment care across shifts.

options.text: I schedule conveyor checks, record pauses, and show shifts the cleaning steps.
I remind operators to add more lubricant before each run.
I clean the conveyor at week's end and note any remaining residue.
I ask each shift to clean the conveyor when residue appears.

basic.situation: A cutting run has finished, and several types of sheets need stacking for the next process. A cart is available beside the machine.

options.text: I stack sheets by size and place a note beside each group.
I place all sheets in one stack to clear the machine area.
I sort the sheets by type and size, then stack them on the cart.
I move the sheets onto the cart and ask processing staff to sort them.

advanced.situation: Cut stock, scrap, and two product sizes are leaving the machine at once. The shared aisle is busy, and the next process needs steady supply.

options.text: I label the carts and move finished stock as space becomes available.
I stage carts by product size and keep scrap beside the machine.
I push every cart into the aisle until the machine area clears.
I map cart positions by size, route scrap aside, and feed the next process steadily.

basic.situation: Your shift has produced several sizes of cut sheets. The production log asks for quantities, types, and dimensions.

options.text: I list the sizes produced and estimate the quantity from each stack.
I write the total quantity and leave the dimensions for later.
I enter each type, quantity, and dimension in the production log.
I record the quantities by type and check the dimensions with the lead.

advanced.situation: Recent logs show mismatched totals for several sizes across shifts. You are reviewing production records and want to improve their consistency.

options.text: I compare totals by size, flag gaps, and revise the entry format.
I remind each shift to double-check totals before handing over.
I review one shift's log and share its clearer format with others.
I fix the largest mismatch and leave smaller differences for review.

basic.situation: A panel light changes from green to amber during a routine cycle. The equipment still runs, and your shift checklist lists the normal indicators.
