options.text: Keep the cycle running and note the amber light at shift handover.
Reset the panel so the green light display returns for the cycle.
Check the checklist for the amber light and tell the lead what changed.
Tell the lead the light changed and continue watching the panel.

advanced.situation: The kiln temperature stays within its normal range, but its readings have crept upward across several checks. The panel shows no alarm yet.

options.text: Tell the lead the temperature is rising and ask about continuing the run.
Lower the setpoint to bring the latest temperature back toward its earlier reading.
Compare the trend with the operating limits and alert the lead to the drift.
Keep logging each reading and wait for the next scheduled inspection.

basic.situation: Your work order lists two products and a delivery sequence. You are unsure which batch is assigned to your kettle, and the next load is waiting.

options.text: Load whichever batch is closest so the waiting area stays clear.
Ask a nearby operator which product usually runs first on this shift.
Load the first product listed and keep the order beside the kettle.
Check the kettle assignment and sequence on the order before loading a batch.

advanced.situation: Two work orders share the same kettle window, but their specifications and production sequences differ. You can stage your assigned loads, while the supervisor controls schedule changes.

options.text: Stage your assigned load for the listed slot and tell the supervisor about the overlap.
Swap the orders to fit the kettle window and update the schedule board.
Compare both specifications and sequences, then stage your assigned load for its listed slot.
Hold your load until the supervisor confirms which order should use the window.

basic.situation: Your operator shows you how to collect a routine sample from the processed batch. The lab label and sampling point are printed on the work sheet.

options.text: Collect from the listed point and label the sample with the batch details.
Collect the sample as shown and bring it to the lab bench for labeling.
Take a sample from the nearest container and ask the operator to label it.
Collect from the listed point and leave the sample beside the lab labels.

advanced.situation: Quality varies between the start and end of a long batch. The approved sampling method allows samples at defined intervals and from the specified points.

options.text: Ask the lab which sample from the batch they prefer to receive.
Collect at the approved intervals and send the samples to the laboratory separately.
Take one sample midway through the batch and use it to represent the full run.
Use the approved intervals and points, then compare results across the batch sections.

basic.situation: A cart of packaged output must go to the marked storage area. Your supervisor has shown you the route and the cart's load limit.

options.text: Push the cart to storage along the shown route and watch for people.
Pile extra packages on top so the delivery takes one trip.
Check the load fits the limit, then take the cart along the shown route.
Ask a coworker to carry several packages while you push the cart.

advanced.situation: Two loads need to reach separate work areas before the next kettle cycle. The usual corridor is crowded, and you can choose a safe route for the cart.

options.text: Check the clear marked route, then deliver the time-sensitive load before the next cycle.
Wait until the corridor clears, then take the loads one at a time.
Use the marked route and deliver the loads in the order they are waiting.
Take the usual corridor with both loads and move quickly between groups.

basic.situation: The work order gives the kettle's target setting and startup sequence. You are shown the controls, and the batch is ready to begin.

options.text: Set the listed target and follow the startup sequence on the work order.
Set the control to the usual target and ask the operator to check it.
Press start now and adjust the setting after the batch begins heating.
Use the target shown on the panel and start the kettle in sequence.

advanced.situation: A long drying run is using more energy than the previous batch, though the output still meets its specification. You may adjust settings within the work order limits.

options.text: Keep the setting unchanged and record the higher energy use for the next shift.
Raise the temperature above the listed range to shorten the drying time.
Check work order settings, adjust within limits, and monitor the next output sample.
Lower the setting slightly and check whether the next output sample remains within specification.

basic.situation: You need to enter a gauge reading and test result in the shift log. The gauge fluctuates slightly, and the test sheet shows the sample time.

options.text: Use the previous shift's test result because today's value is not ready.
Copy the latest gauge value and test result into the shift log.
Enter the reading, time, and matching test result from the sheet.
Write the current gauge value in the log and add the test result later.

advanced.situation: Recent log entries show longer heating times across three shifts, while output tests remain within specification. The next production record is being prepared.

options.text: Copy the latest shift's heating time into the new production record.
Keep the usual record format and mention the longer times at handover.
Compare times and output, then log the pattern with batch details.
Record longer heating times and ask the lead to review them.

basic.situation: You prepare a batch of fittings for a routine test and notice a few pieces look different from the rest. What do you do?

options.text: I would set the unusual pieces aside and label them for review.
I would mix the unusual pieces into the test tray to finish faster.
I would select pieces across the batch, keeping unusual ones separate and labelled.
I would take the easiest pieces to reach and note the batch number.

advanced.situation: A new product has several sizes, and the team disagrees about which defects justify rejection. You are asked to plan sampling and explain the criteria.

options.text: I would use the last product's sampling plan and share its rejection guide.
I would sample one size and apply the same rejection rule to every size.
I would write down the agreed rejection criteria and ask staff to follow them.
I would sample each size, document defect examples, and coach staff on the criteria.

basic.situation: During a run, the pressure dial sits near the stated limit. You have the manual and a supervisor nearby. What do you do?

options.text: I would adjust the setting until the dial looks closer to the usual reading.
I would record the pressure and continue watching the dial for a while.
I would compare the dial with the manual's operating range and report the reading.
I would note the pressure and ask my supervisor what the limit means.

advanced.situation: A new material produces inconsistent readings across two lines. You review the equipment data and procedures before proposing inspection settings.

options.text: I would average both lines' readings and use that value for production settings.
I would compare both lines' data, isolate affected conditions, then propose a controlled setting trial.
I would copy settings from the line reporting fewer rejected parts for this material.
I would compare readings and recommend the steadier line's current settings for both lines.

basic.situation: You measure a batch of brackets with a ruler, and one dimension seems close to the specification limit. What do you do?

options.text: I would set the bracket aside and ask a colleague to recheck it.
I would recheck the dimension and show the ruler reading to my lead.
I would use a gauge, confirm units, and record the measured result.
I would mark each bracket accepted based on my first ruler reading alone.

advanced.situation: A complex part has curved surfaces, and two inspectors get different dimensions with calipers. You must choose a measurement approach and guide the team.

options.text: I would accept the larger measurement and mark the parts to keep production moving.
I would average both measurements and record that as the part's dimension.
I would agree the reference points, select a suitable instrument, and demonstrate repeatable technique.
I would have each inspector repeat the caliper measurement and compare results.

basic.situation: You find a small burr on an unfinished metal part before inspection. Your station has an approved hand tool and a work instruction.

options.text: I would scrape the burr off with the nearest metal edge and stack the part.
I would remove the burr and pass the part to the next station.
I would remove the burr with the approved tool, then inspect the surface again.
I would mark the burr and leave the part for the next shift.

advanced.situation: A gauge drifts after calibration, while parts show a rough finish near the tolerance boundary. You are asked to check the instrument and finishing standard.

options.text: I would pause gauge use, record the drift, and ask the technician to review it.
I would verify the gauge against its reference, review recent readings, and document the finishing limit.
I would turn the calibration screw until the gauge returns to its usual reading.
I would use another gauge and compare the readings on several parts for consistency.

basic.situation: You weigh a set of packaged parts and record the figures on the inspection sheet. One entry looks different from the rest.

options.text: I would flag the entry and ask the next inspector to confirm the weight.
I would leave the entry blank and finish recording the other packages.
I would copy the nearby weight into the unusual entry to complete the sheet.
I would reweigh that package, note both readings, and flag the difference.

advanced.situation: Your team's weekly inspection sheet shows more weight variations in one product line. You must report the pattern and suggest a reporting improvement.

options.text: I would report the rising variation and suggest more frequent weighing on that line.
I would remove the unusual readings and report the remaining average to management.
I would compare like batches, describe the trend, and recommend recording line and shift consistently.
I would average the weekly readings and share the mean as the line's result.

basic.situation: You spot repeated scratches on products coming off your line, and the next batch is due soon. What do you do?

options.text: I would mention the scratches to a nearby operator and keep inspecting.
I would mark the scratched products as acceptable and continue the usual inspection.
I would finish checking the current tray, then tell the line lead about scratches.
I would notify the line lead, describe the scratches, and identify the affected batch.

advanced.situation: The same surface defect returns after two adjustments. You are asked to advise the production lead using your inspection results.

options.text: I would map defects by batch and station, then recommend checking the shared contact point.
I would show the repeated results and recommend another adjustment at the same station.
I would recommend reducing the line speed to lower the number of defects.
I would report the first adjustment as successful and close the defect record.

basic.situation: You examine a cut gemstone under a loupe and notice a faint mark near one facet. The stone is due for grading. What do you do?

options.text: I would record the mark on the plot diagram and check its location again.
I would call the mark a surface flaw and move the stone onward.
I would polish the marked area before grading to make the stone look clearer.
I would tell the grader there is a mark and let them decide its significance.

advanced.situation: A rare stone shows unusual internal features under the microscope, and its outline is hard to distinguish. You must document what you can observe.

options.text: I would compare it with a reference image and record the closest match.
I would capture the microscope view and ask a senior gem worker to review it.
I would label it as the rarest matching stone in the reference guide.
I would use suitable optical views, record the features, and separate observations from identification.

basic.situation: You sort a tray of rough diamonds into size and shape groups. One stone is smaller but has an unusual outline.

options.text: I would put it with the closest shape group and note its size separately.
I would place it in the largest group so it stays with valuable stones.
I would set it aside, label its size and shape, and ask for a grouping check.
I would place it with the nearest size group and leave the shape unmarked.

advanced.situation: Two junior staff assign different polish and symmetry grades to similar stones. You must guide a consistent review using the established grading system.

options.text: I would ask each worker to explain their grade and then record the difference.
I would review the criteria with both staff and compare their grades against shared examples.
I would explain the criteria again and have each worker grade the stones separately.
I would choose the more experienced worker's grade and ask the other to follow it.

basic.situation: A customer asks for a price range for a common gemstone, and your guide lists several grades. What do you do?

options.text: I would check the stone's grade and compare it with the guide's matching range.
I would give the full range and let the customer choose a figure.
I would share the guide's middle price and explain that grades affect value.
I would use the highest listed price because customers prefer a clear figure.

advanced.situation: A client is choosing a high-value center stone for a custom ring and asks how to use its unusual shape well. What do you advise?

options.text: I would recommend the most expensive setting to match the stone's value.
I would explain two setting ideas and ask which style the client prefers.
I would discuss settings that suit its shape and preserve the client's design priorities.
I would suggest a familiar setting that displays the stone prominently.

basic.situation: You are preparing a small gem for a routine cut. The work instruction calls for a dop, and the stone must be secured first.

options.text: I would ask a colleague to check my setup before I cut the stone.
I would press the stone into the dop and start with a light pass.
I would hold the stone by hand against the wheel for the first cut.
I would secure the stone in the dop, check its hold, then begin cutting.

advanced.situation: A custom gem has a delicate edge and needs a new shape. You must choose a wheel and abrasive for the cut and finish.

options.text: I would select the wheel used for the closest recent custom job.
I would match the wheel and abrasive to the material, edge, and desired finish.
I would choose a fine wheel and polish compound to protect the delicate edge.
I would use the coarsest wheel to shape the gem quickly before polishing.

basic.situation: You measure a gemstone's bore hole and get a reading close to the stated size. What do you do?

options.text: I would record the first reading and send the stone onward for setting.
I would repeat the measurement and compare it with the stated size.
I would ask another worker to measure the bore hole when they have time.
I would check the instrument's scale, measure again, and record the result.

advanced.situation: Measurements of a batch of bore holes differ between two instruments, affecting a custom order. You are asked to resolve the discrepancy.

options.text: I would repeat measurements on several holes using both instruments and share the results.
I would compare both instruments with a reference, then remeasure sample holes consistently.
I would average both instruments' readings and report the batch measurement.
I would use the instrument that gives readings closest to the order specification.

basic.situation: After polishing, you are assigned to clean the exterior of the lapping equipment before the next shift uses it.

options.text: I would brush residue toward the machine opening so the bench stays clear.
I would wipe the control panel and leave the rest for scheduled cleaning.
I would wipe the exterior, clear visible residue, and return the cleaning cloth.
I would wipe the exterior and tell the next shift the machine is ready.

advanced.situation: The team is assigned routine internal cleaning of a polishing machine. You are asked to help organize the cleaning and show a newer colleague the process.

options.text: I would set monthly cleaning reminders and have the colleague watch my next dismantling.
I would show the colleague how to dismantle the machine from memory and clean it.
I would follow the machine's cleaning sequence, record due dates, and demonstrate each approved step.
I would share the cleaning dates and ask the colleague to use the manual.

basic.situation: A case arrives with a clear prescription and tooth model. You need to identify the product before starting bench work.

options.text: I match the crown type on the prescription to the model before labelling the case.
I use the usual crown pattern and send the model to casting.
I identify the crown type, then ask a colleague to confirm the model.
I read the prescription and record the stated crown type on the case sheet.

advanced.situation: A bridge prescription specifies a material that conflicts with a note about the available clearance. You need to resolve the design before fabrication.

options.text: I send the dentist the conflicting details and ask for design clarification.
I ask a senior technician which instruction seems more workable for the case.
I ask the dentist which requirement should guide the bridge design and record the reply.
I follow the material note and shape the bridge to the available clearance.

basic.situation: You have mounted a tooth model on an articulator with guidance. Your next check is whether its basic movement looks right.

options.text: I move the articulator through its range and note any contact that seems unusual.
I mark the first contact and send the model onward for finishing.
I follow the guided movement check and compare contacts through the full range.
I ask my colleague to move the articulator while I watch the teeth.

advanced.situation: Two technicians report different occlusion results on similar appliances. You are asked to help them test a case due for dispatch today.

options.text: I accept the result from the technician who has handled more cases.
I ask each technician to repeat the check and report the result.
I review the contact marks with both technicians and agree a shared check.
I compare their setup steps, then demonstrate a consistent articulator check on the case.

basic.situation: A colleague guides you through preparing plaster for a tooth model. The case sheet gives the material and amount needed.

options.text: I prepare the stated amount and ask my colleague to check the paste.
I mix a small batch first and adjust it by how it feels.
I measure the plaster and liquid as instructed, then mix until smooth.
I add extra liquid so the plaster flows quickly into the mould.

advanced.situation: A complex prosthesis needs acrylic paste, and a junior asks whether to change the mix because the workshop feels warmer today.

options.text: I ask the junior to wait while I check with another technician.
I check the product instructions, explain the safe handling steps, and follow its stated mix.
I use yesterday's mix ratio and pour the acrylic before it thickens.
I check the instructions with the junior and follow the stated mix together.

basic.situation: A simple framework has excess material along one edge. With guidance, you need to remove it and polish the surface.

options.text: I ask my guide to mark the area before I start polishing.
I polish the edge until it looks smooth under the bench light.
I press the framework firmly against the wheel to finish the edge faster.
I use the polishing machine gently and check the edge against the model.

advanced.situation: A porcelain prosthesis has a rough patch after polishing, and a junior is waiting to use the machine on another case.

options.text: I buff the whole surface once more, hoping the rough patch blends into the finish.
I try a gentler polishing pass, then inspect the patch under good light.
I ask the junior to wait while I test the machine on scrap.
I inspect the patch, refine my approach, and teach the junior to assess it.

basic.situation: A crown case needs a simple component assembled under close supervision. The prescription and prepared parts are at your bench.

options.text: I fit the parts in the order that seems quickest for this case.
I assemble the parts in sequence and check the fit before handover.
I follow the prescribed order and ask my guide to inspect the assembly.
I arrange the parts on the model before asking which one goes first.

advanced.situation: A custom orthodontic appliance needs a small alteration to match the prescription. A junior asks how to shape the component at your bench.

options.text: I show the junior how to shape the component using the case model.
I copy the shape from a similar appliance and finish the component.
I ask the junior to prepare the component while I find a reference case.
I shape the component to the prescription and check its fit.

basic.situation: A new colleague is unfamiliar with the polishing machine. Your lead asks you to demonstrate its basic use at the bench.

options.text: I point out the machine guide and stay nearby for questions.
I let the colleague start polishing a case after a quick explanation.
I demonstrate the machine's controls, then watch the colleague practise safely.
I show the controls and ask the colleague to explain them back.

advanced.situation: Several new bench workers need training on model preparation, and their lead asks you to help them learn the workflow over the next week.

options.text: I ask the lead to choose which worker should practise each step.
I map key steps, demonstrate them, and track workers' practice.
I prepare a short workflow guide and coach workers as cases arrive.
I pair each new worker with whoever has time at the bench.

basic.situation: A prescription arrives for a patient device, but you have not handled this product type before. You need to identify what the workshop must prepare.

options.text: I match the device with listed materials and tools before preparing the job.
I read the prescription and note the device type, materials, and required tools.
I identify the device type and ask a colleague about usual materials.
I choose a familiar pattern and begin cutting the available material.

advanced.situation: A complex brace specification lists two materials that seem unsuitable for the same section. You need to guide the workshop before fabrication starts.

options.text: I send the conflicting material details to the prescriber and request clarification.
I use the stocked material for that brace section without checking compatibility.
I ask another technician which material worked for similar braces.
I compare material notes, then ask the prescriber to resolve the listed conflict.

basic.situation: You are asked to take a patient's lower-leg measurement for a brace pattern, with a colleague supervising the appointment.

options.text: I ask my colleague to position the limb while I take the measurement.
I measure over the patient's clothing and use that figure for the pattern.
I take the guided measurement and write the figure on the case sheet.
I explain the measurement, position the limb as guided, and record the reading.

advanced.situation: During a brace fitting, the patient reports pressure at the ankle after you make an adjustment. The clinician is available for questions by phone.

options.text: I tighten the straps to keep the brace stable during fitting.
I check the pressure point, adjust within fit limits, and confirm patient comfort.
I reassess the fit and ask the clinician about further adjustment.
I loosen the brace and ask the patient to walk again.

basic.situation: A simple orthotic device needs a thermoplastic section shaped from a limb cast. A technician guides you through the workshop steps.

options.text: I check the cast orientation, heat the material as guided, and shape it to the pattern.
I prepare the cast and wait for my guide to set the material.
I heat the sheet until flexible and shape it around the cast by eye.
I follow the pattern and ask my guide to check the formed section.

advanced.situation: A custom device combines a metal support with a padded cover, and the limb cast has an uneven contour. You are responsible for fabricating the sections.

options.text: I ask a colleague to choose padding thickness while I trim the support.
I shape the support against the cast and add padding where contact feels firm.
I shape the support to the cast, then fit padding to reduce pressure ridges.
I cover the support first to hide the uneven cast contour.

basic.situation: A simple brace component has a rough edge after shaping. You need to smooth it with supervision before assembly.

options.text: I press the component firmly against the wheel to remove roughness quickly.
I buff the component evenly, then compare its contour with the template.
I ask my supervisor to mark areas needing more smoothing.
I smooth the edge and check its contour against the template.

advanced.situation: A curved support needs to match a prescribed contour, but a previous bend left a shallow flat spot. The device is due for assembly today.

options.text: I bend the flat spot back and compare the curve closely with the sample.
I compare the curve with the contour, refine the bend, then recheck it.
I reshape the area carefully and check it against the template afterward.
I ask a colleague to hold the component while I adjust its curve.

basic.situation: You need to mark rivet positions on a simple device part using its template, with a colleague nearby to guide you.

options.text: I mark the holes by eye and drill them before the bench clears.
I use the template to mark the positions, then ask my colleague to inspect them.
I place the template on the part and wait for my colleague to mark it.
I align the template, mark each position, and check the spacing with the measuring tool.

advanced.situation: Several parts of a custom brace must be joined, and the layout marks are close to an edge. You need to assemble the device for a fitting.

options.text: I check edge clearance and alignment, then join the parts using the specified fasteners.
I drill the marked holes and rivet the parts while they still line up.
I align the parts and confirm the marks before drilling and fastening them.
I ask a colleague to hold the parts while I start the first rivet.

basic.situation: A finished brace moves unevenly on the alignment fixture. Your lead asks you to help inspect it before the device is returned.

options.text: I ask another technician to repeat the fixture check while I watch.
I adjust the brace until its movement feels smoother on the fixture.
I test its movement on the fixture and record where the alignment shifts.
I check its alignment on the fixture and tell my lead what I observe.

advanced.situation: A patient returns with a prosthetic device they are unsure how to use. The clinic asks you to demonstrate its prescribed use and note any fit concerns.

options.text: I show the patient a quick way to put on the device safely before leaving.
I demonstrate the prescribed steps and ask whether the patient has questions.
I demonstrate prescribed steps, have the patient practise, and note fit concerns for clinic.
I ask the clinic to repeat the instructions at the next appointment.

basic.situation: A batch of lens blanks arrives, and you notice a faint haze on one surface while checking them against the work order.

options.text: I would polish the hazy area now so the blank can stay with the batch.
I would inspect the surface under the lamp and mark the blank for checking.
I would ask a nearby technician to confirm the haze before sorting the batch.
I would compare the hazy blank with the checklist and set it aside for review.

advanced.situation: A new technician measures mounted lenses for a high prescription order, but readings vary across repeated checks.

options.text: I would ask them to repeat readings using the instrument guide.
I would pause that pair and ask a colleague to review both readings.
I would demonstrate lens seating, then repeat each reading against the work order.
I would log the first reading and keep the order moving on schedule.

basic.situation: You are preparing a lens blank for grinding, and the holding tool has several positions that look similar.

options.text: I would ask a coworker which position they usually use for similar blanks.
I would align the blank with the fixture marks and secure it as shown.
I would clamp the blank in the nearest open position to keep setup moving.
I would check the work order and confirm the blank sits securely before clamping.

advanced.situation: A specialized lens order needs a different curve, and the usual grinding setup leaves a test blank outside the work order dimensions.

options.text: I would adjust the cutting depth from the last successful run and start production.
I would compare the order with the machine setup guide and tune the curve and depth.
I would check the curve setting and run another test blank before deciding on changes.
I would ask the shift lead to review the test result before changing settings.

basic.situation: You are polishing a lens by hand, and its surface begins to look uneven under the work light.

options.text: I would ease the lens off the wheel and ask for a finish check.
I would keep the lens against the wheel until the surface looks clearer.
I would adjust my hold to keep the lens evenly supported across the wheel.
I would lower the pressure and continue briefly while watching the surface.

advanced.situation: A colleague is polishing a difficult lens surface, but the finish shows faint rings near one edge before the order deadline.

options.text: I would reduce pressure and inspect the finish after another pass.
I would keep the same pace and polish longer to remove the rings.
I would pause and compare the finish with a sample lens.
I would guide a varied lens path while maintaining even contact across the wheel.

basic.situation: You are attaching nose pads to a frame, and one pad sits at a different angle from the other.

options.text: I would support the frame and align both pads while checking their contact points.
I would compare both pad angles and adjust the uneven side with pliers.
I would bend the uneven pad until both sides look level from the front.
I would tighten the pad screw firmly so the angle stays in place.

advanced.situation: A colleague assembles a frame whose lenses sit slightly twisted, and the temples no longer rest evenly on the bench.

options.text: I would show how to check lens seating and frame alignment before tightening each side.
I would have them check the frame with a second pair of pliers.
I would bend the higher temple until the frame rests flat on the bench.
I would ask the colleague to loosen the frame and realign the lenses.

basic.situation: You are selecting a lens blank and polishing wheel for an order, and two blank labels look similar on the rack.

options.text: I would match the blank and wheel to the production specifications on the checklist.
I would take the blank with the closest-looking label and start cleaning it.
I would set both possible blanks aside and ask which one the team used yesterday.
I would check the blank label against the work order before choosing a wheel.

advanced.situation: A complex prescription needs a less common blank, and the usual wheel choice leaves little usable material after trial shaping.

options.text: I would ask a colleague which blank they used on a similar prescription.
I would compare the prescription specifications with available blanks and suitable wheel options.
I would select a blank with extra stock and keep the usual wheel for now.
I would choose the familiar wheel and allow extra material for another trial.

basic.situation: A customer frame sits crooked after minor handling, and you are asked to adjust its alignment with hand tools.

options.text: I would ask a nearby technician to look at the frame before I adjust it.
I would use the pliers to nudge the raised side and check the result.
I would twist the higher temple until the frame looks level on the counter.
I would inspect how the frame rests, then make a small supported adjustment.

advanced.situation: A colleague repairs a delicate optical assembly with a loose joint, while nearby components could shift under heat from the soldering iron.

options.text: I would suggest using less heat and checking the joint after soldering.
I would shield nearby parts, secure the joint, and apply controlled heat.
I would ask them to pause and bring the assembly to the repair bench.
I would steady the assembly, inspect nearby components, then solder the joint before they shift.

basic.situation: You are starting a filling machine with a new package size, and the controls have several similar settings.

options.text: I would ask a coworker which control they use for this package size.
I would check the labels and engage the closest matching control for a short run.
I would select the setting from the last run and engage the controls.
I would match the package size to the setup guide before engaging the controls.

advanced.situation: A faster line speed raises output, but filled packs begin arriving warm and uneven after a product change.

options.text: I would restore the earlier speed and check the next filled packs for consistency.
I would lower the speed slightly and see whether the packs settle down.
I would compare the product settings with the operating range, then tune flow, speed, and temperature.
I would keep the faster speed and let the next checks show whether quality improves.

basic.situation: You are watching a packing line, and several sealed packs look slightly different from the sample at the station.

options.text: I would compare a pack with the sample and separate any clear mismatch.
I would check several packs against the sample and note what changes along the line.
I would leave the packs moving while I finish the current carton.
I would ask a nearby operator whether the packs usually look this way.

advanced.situation: Pack weights drift upward across several checks, while the line is also building a small pile-up near the carton feed.

options.text: I would sample weights and trace where the pile-up starts before changing the line.
I would adjust the feed setting to reduce weight and keep watching the pile-up.
I would slow the line and check whether weights and carton flow improve.
I would flag the weight drift and ask the lead to review the feed setting.

basic.situation: You are closing finished bags by hand, and the ties on several packs feel looser than the sample.

options.text: I would compare a tied bag with the sample and adjust the tie before stacking.
I would secure the next bag with the same tie length as the last one.
I would ask a coworker to check one tie before continuing the bags.
I would pull each tie tighter and stack the bags for packing.

advanced.situation: Cartons of fragile packs are arriving with crushed corners, and the wrapping pattern leaves little space between stacked items.

options.text: I would reduce the stack height and ask the packer to watch for damage.
I would add another layer of wrapping around each pack before stacking.
I would stack the cartons higher so the wrapping station can keep up.
I would change the wrap pattern to cushion corners and keep packs stable in cartons.

basic.situation: You are preparing the packaging station, and the supply rack has mixed carton sizes beside the conveyor.

options.text: I would take the nearest cartons and begin assembling them for the run.
I would ask the previous shift which carton stack they used last.
I would sort the cartons by size and restock the rack from the run list.
I would check the run list and set aside cartons that appear to fit.

advanced.situation: The hopper empties twice during a busy run, while spare ingredients and packaging supplies are stored across the work area.

options.text: I would track supply use and stage refills near the feeder.
I would move nearby supplies closer and refill the hopper as it empties.
I would bring extra ingredients to the hopper and keep the line running smoothly.
I would ask a coworker to watch the hopper while I fetch supplies.

basic.situation: You are sorting finished packs, and one package has a torn seal while the rest look intact.

options.text: I would remove the pack from the line and note it at handover.
I would separate the pack and record it in the rejected items log.
I would set the pack aside and check whether its seal meets the standard.
I would place the torn pack aside and flag it during carton count.

advanced.situation: Rejection counts rise on one shift, and several cartons carry labels that do not match the printed lot details.

options.text: I would separate the mismatched cartons, record rejects, and compare the label pattern by run.
I would stop using the suspect labels and record the rejection total for the shift.
I would tell the lead about the labels and continue counting accepted packs.
I would replace the labels with the most common lot number and count the rejects later.

basic.situation: A small jam stops the packaging machine, and the guide is accessible beside the guarded feed area.

options.text: I would call the lead and wait beside the machine for help.
I would pause the machine and ask a coworker to check the feed area.
I would stop the machine and follow the jam clearing steps in the guide.
I would reach past the guard and pull out the trapped pack.

advanced.situation: A guide rail loosens during a run, and your colleague wants to make a small adjustment before packs begin drifting.

options.text: I would stop the line, then tighten the rail with the usual tool.
I would tighten the rail while packs pass and inspect the next carton.
I would stop the machine, secure the rail, and check its position.
I would call maintenance before touching the loose rail during the run.

basic.situation: A dusty batch of aluminium panels arrives before a routine clear coat. Your lead asks you to prepare the surfaces.

options.text: You check the label, use the approved cleaner, then dry a test panel.
You wipe each panel with a dry cloth and begin the scheduled coat.
You rinse the panels with water and send them along to coating.
You brush off dust, then ask which solvent suits the aluminium finish.

advanced.situation: A mixed batch includes aluminium and an old lacquered panel, and the coating has failed before. You need to choose a cleaning method.

options.text: You use the familiar solvent on every panel to keep the line moving.
You use a mild cleaner on the batch and inspect it before coating.
You clean a spare panel with the usual solvent and compare its appearance.
You identify each surface, check product guidance, and test a compatible cleaner discreetly.

basic.situation: A wooden display shelf needs a routine coat of lacquer. Your supervisor asks you to brush the visible faces.

options.text: You brush a thin, even coat along the grain and check for missed edges.
You brush the faces carefully and ask your supervisor to check the finish.
You load the brush generously and cover each face in broad strokes.
You apply lacquer to the front faces and leave the edges for later.

advanced.situation: A carved cabinet has fine grooves and a dark decorative pattern. You must apply the finish before the next shift begins.

options.text: You spray the entire cabinet evenly to finish before the shift change.
You trace the pattern with a coating pen, then inspect the carved details.
You test the pen on a sample, then follow the pattern with controlled strokes.
You use the usual brush and fill the grooves with steady strokes.

basic.situation: You find a small nick on a painted chair leg before the final coat. Your lead asks you to fill it.

options.text: You mark the nick and ask the lead to confirm the repair method.
You brush extra paint over the nick and move the chair onward.
You dab putty into the nick and leave the excess for sanding later.
You apply a small amount of putty, smooth it, and let it set.

advanced.situation: A cabinet door has several dents beside a glossy repaired area. You need to restore the surface before its finish coat.

options.text: You fill the visible dents and check the surface under angled light.
You map the dents, apply filler in thin layers, and level each repaired area.
You spread a thick filler coat across the door and sand it later.
You sand around the dents and cover the remaining marks with finish.

basic.situation: A finished table arrives at your station with a checklist. You are asked to check its surface before packing.

options.text: You check the top and edges, then note anything that needs attention.
You inspect the table from a distance and touch up obvious marks.
You inspect each face against the checklist and retouch any small defect.
You look over the top and pack the table if it appears smooth.

advanced.situation: Several workers are missing faint runs on glossy panels. You are asked to help make checks more consistent across the shift.

options.text: You inspect the panels yourself and tell workers about any missed runs.
You add run examples to the checklist and review the next batch.
You agree on viewing angles and defect examples, then practise checks together.
You ask workers to inspect panels more carefully before they leave.

basic.situation: You are preparing a routine coating batch from a job order that lists the ingredients and mixing instructions.

options.text: You pour in the ingredients and stir until the colour looks uniform.
You use the previous batch amounts and stir until the mixture seems smooth.
You measure each ingredient as listed, mix steadily, and check its consistency.
You measure the main ingredients and ask your lead about the final texture.

advanced.situation: A specialised coating order calls for a specified mix, but the first batch looks thicker than the sample. You are preparing the next batch.

options.text: You remix the listed ingredients and check the flow with a sample.
You use less of the thick ingredient and stir until the texture improves.
You verify the written ratios, mix a measured sample, and compare its flow.
You add solvent to the next batch until it pours like the sample.

basic.situation: After a routine coating run, your brushes and small parts need cleaning before the next batch starts.

options.text: You rinse the tools and ask where the cleaned parts should be stored.
You wipe the brushes with a rag and leave them beside the workbench.
You clean the tools with the approved solvent, wipe them, and store them safely.
You soak every tool in solvent while setting up the next batch.

advanced.situation: A coated batch needs a set drying time, while spray tools are due for cleaning. Another order is waiting for the equipment.

options.text: You start the drying cycle and rinse the sprayer before the next order.
You clean the sprayer first and place the batch in the dryer afterward.
You shorten the dryer cycle and leave the sprayer for the next shift.
You follow drying time, clean the sprayer, and log its condition before reuse.

basic.situation: A routine coating run is ready, and your lead asks you to start the conveyor machine using its controls.

options.text: You turn the speed dial and start the conveyor for the waiting batch.
You press the start button and watch the conveyor begin moving.
You check the setup indicator, then start the machine using its control button.
You confirm the machine is ready and ask your lead before starting it.

advanced.situation: Spray dispersion changes after a nozzle swap, and the line pressure fluctuates. You need to restore the setup for the next batch.

options.text: You inspect the nozzle and adjust pressure in small steps while monitoring spray.
You replace the nozzle again and restart at the previous pressure setting.
You increase pressure until the spray looks even across the test panel.
You stop the run, check the nozzle fit, then adjust pressure against the setup sheet.

basic.situation: A prepared metal panel is ready for its specified primer. Your lead asks you to spray the surface during a routine run.

options.text: You hold the gun steadily and overlap each pass across the prepared panel.
You hold the gun close and apply extra primer along visible areas.
You spray the centre first, then cover the panel edges with another pass.
You move the spray gun quickly across the panel to keep the line flowing.

advanced.situation: A sealed frame has narrow seams and recessed corners that a spray gun cannot reach evenly. You need to complete its coating.

options.text: You angle the spray gun across the frame until the recessed areas look covered.
You spray the accessible faces, then brush the seams and recessed corners.
You spray several extra passes over the frame to reach the recessed corners.
You brush the seams, then inspect the corners before releasing the frame.

basic.situation: A sample panel comes off the line with a slightly uneven sheen. You are asked to check it before the batch continues.

options.text: You compare the sheen with a known panel and report the difference.
You look at the sheen and pass the sample if the colour appears consistent.
You compare the sample with its specification and check the coating with a viscometer.
You inspect the panel visually and set it aside for another review.

advanced.situation: Viscosity readings vary between batches, though finished panels look similar. You are asked to help resolve whether the run meets its specification.

options.text: You repeat a reading and record it for your lead to review.
You confirm viscosity readings using one method and compare results with the order limits.
You accept the batches because dried panels appear similar to each other.
You adjust the next batch to match the previous viscosity reading.

basic.situation: A routine spraying job is finished, and your team needs the work area and tools cleaned before the next order.

options.text: You rinse the tools and sweep the visible overspray from the floor.
You clean the floor and ask where the used tools belong afterward.
You wipe the bench and leave the used sprayer for later.
You collect residue, clean the work area, and wipe the tools as instructed.

advanced.situation: A sprayer has uneven output after a long run, and the next order is queued. You are assigned to clean and reassemble it.

options.text: You replace the nozzle and clean the exterior before the next order.
You isolate the equipment, clean removable parts, then reassemble and check the connections.
You disassemble the sprayer, clean its parts, and reassemble it carefully.
You flush the sprayer quickly and return it to the waiting line.

basic.situation: The coating hopper is low during a routine run. Your lead asks you to refill it from the labelled material container.

options.text: You add a small pail of material and let the operator monitor it.
You check the label and refill the hopper while watching the level.
You pour in the nearest open container to keep the line running.
You confirm the material label, then refill the hopper to its marked level.

advanced.situation: A container of leftover coating is labelled for disposal, while a fresh hopper refill is waiting. You are responsible for handling both materials.

options.text: You place the waste container near the collection area and refill from fresh stock.
You seal the waste and follow its labelled disposal route before refilling.
You set the waste aside, refill the hopper, and check disposal instructions afterward.
You pour the leftover coating into the hopper to avoid wasting material.

basic.situation: A finished vehicle panel has a light haze after coating. Your lead asks you to buff and wax it before release.

options.text: You buff the panel lightly and compare its sheen with a nearby panel.
You buff the panel firmly until the haze is less noticeable.
You apply wax over the haze and inspect the panel under the booth lights.
You check the finish, then buff and wax the panel with the approved materials.

advanced.situation: Streaks keep appearing near the end of each run. You are monitoring the line and need to help address the recurring flaw.

options.text: You buff each streaked panel and keep the line moving at its current pace.
You log when streaks appear, inspect the process settings, and test a focused adjustment.
You slow the line slightly and monitor whether the next panels improve.
You add extra coating to panels where streaks appear during the run.

basic.situation: You inspect a wafer under a microscope with guidance and notice several faint marks near the circuitry.

options.text: I wipe the wafer before checking so loose particles cannot confuse the view.
I scan the wafer under the microscope and note visible surface marks.
I recheck marked areas at higher magnification before entering the inspection result.
I compare the whole wafer with the defect guide and log each suspect location.

advanced.situation: Two technicians disagree about faint surface marks, and a new trainee is waiting for guidance before inspecting a production lot.

options.text: I raise the allowable defect limit so the lot can move forward on schedule.
I ask each technician to use their usual judgement and collect the results for comparison.
I write down the current inspection limits and demonstrate the microscope to the trainee.
I set measurable defect examples, compare sample wafers, and train the team on instrument use.

basic.situation: You are assigned to clean a wafer in a chemical bath, and the next batch is due soon.

options.text: I check the work instruction, confirm the bath label, then clean the wafer as specified.
I follow the posted bath sequence and use the blow-off wand as instructed.
I shorten the rinse so the next batch can enter the bath sooner.
I use the familiar bath cycle and inspect the wafer after the rinse.

advanced.situation: The cleaning bath is nearing its change point, and you are asked to improve the protocol while keeping chemical waste handling within team procedures.

options.text: I compare cleaning results across approved cycles and document a controlled protocol recommendation.
I refresh the bath on the posted schedule and remind coworkers about the waste labels.
I track bath use and ask the lead which approved cycle seems most efficient.
I extend the bath's use when wafers look clean and record the extra cycles.

basic.situation: You need to unload a finished wafer carrier and take it to the next processing area with a senior technician nearby.

options.text: I stack the carrier with the nearest finished lot to save a trip.
I ask the senior technician to verify the label before I move the carrier.
I carry the sealed carrier to the next area and confirm its label there.
I check the carrier label and route, then carry it using the handling guide.

advanced.situation: Carriers from two process areas are arriving together, and you need to improve the handoff route while keeping lot identities clear.

options.text: I send each carrier through the shortest open aisle and sort the lots afterward.
I share the current route and remind staff to keep carriers separated by lot.
I ask the team which route feels easiest and update the handoff notes.
I map the approved route, identify staging points, and teach staff to verify carrier labels.

basic.situation: You are placing a wafer into a processing holder with tweezers while a senior technician supervises your first attempt.

options.text: I place the wafer into the holder and check that it appears level.
I check the holder orientation, grip the wafer gently, and seat it as instructed.
I follow the senior's placement demonstration and inspect the wafer afterward.
I press the wafer down firmly so it stays in the holder during processing.

advanced.situation: A new hire reports that wafers sometimes sit unevenly in one holder, and the next processing load is approaching.

options.text: I inspect holder alignment, check wafer seating, and guide the new hire through placement.
I seat each wafer and let the next cycle show whether placement holds.
I test another holder and record whether the wafer sits evenly.
I demonstrate a steady tweezer grip, then ask the new hire to practice.

basic.situation: You have a work instruction for a routine processing cycle and are asked to start it on the control panel with guidance.

options.text: I match the panel settings to the work instruction before starting the cycle.
I press the familiar start sequence and watch the panel for a status change.
I reuse the prior lot's settings to start the cycle on time.
I ask the technician nearby to confirm the settings before I press start.

advanced.situation: A complex cycle stops at a control panel warning, and the next lot is waiting while you troubleshoot within your technician role.

options.text: I review recent panel entries and ask the lead about next steps.
I log the warning, check cycle instructions, and follow approved recovery steps.
I consult the alarm guide, verify its reset applies, and document the panel response.
I restart with the same settings and note whether the warning returns.

basic.situation: You are filling in the production log after a routine wafer run, and one inspection result is not on the shift sheet.

options.text: I enter recorded run details and flag the missing result for confirmation.
I ask the supervisor for the result before entering anything in the log.
I complete the available fields and leave the inspection entry for later review.
I copy the prior run's inspection result to finish the log before shift handoff.

advanced.situation: During a records review, you find repeated gaps in inspection entries and a new technician asks how to complete the production log.

options.text: I explain the required fields, review recent logs with the team, and record recurring gaps.
I verify each gap against source records, then route changes through the log process.
I use nearby lot records to fill gaps and complete the audit copy.
I list the gaps and send them to the lead for review.

basic.situation: You need to load a customer's camera images onto the lab computer, and several folders have similar names.

options.text: I open each folder preview and copy the requested image set into its job folder.
I ask a coworker which folder looks right and load that set.
I copy the folder with the newest date and check the images afterward.
I rename the newest folder with the customer's job number to keep work moving.

advanced.situation: A transfer job produces duplicate files and missing previews, and another operator needs to move images from a camera before printing.

options.text: I remove the duplicate files and continue with the images that have previews.
I check file counts and previews against the source, then teach a verified transfer sequence.
I repeat the transfer using the usual cable and explain the steps to the operator.
I switch to another card reader and ask the operator to retry the transfer.

basic.situation: A customer order calls for a small batch of standard prints, and you are loading paper into the machine for the first time today.

options.text: I load the standard paper and check the first print against the order.
I load the usual paper and make a sample print before continuing.
I use the paper left in the tray and run the full batch.
I confirm the order size and paper type, then load the paper as instructed.

advanced.situation: A customer requests a large enlargement from a small negative, and you need to adjust machine controls to produce usable prints.

options.text: I increase enlargement and sharpening until the image appears crisp on screen.
I use the requested dimensions and adjust settings after checking one trial print.
I check the negative and requested dimensions, then adjust settings and review a test enlargement.
I enlarge with the usual settings and review the first print for softness.

basic.situation: You are checking developed prints from a routine order and spot a faint blur on one image.

options.text: I compare the print with the order sample and mark the blurred image for review.
I include the blurred print with the rest so the customer receives the full set.
I look across the prints and set aside any image that seems soft.
I check the image again under the inspection light before packing the order.

advanced.situation: Digital previews and paper prints show inconsistent color, and you are asked to help staff apply shared quality criteria.

options.text: I share the current print checklist and ask staff to review a sample order.
I ask staff to note color differences and collect their comments after review.
I approve the previews that look balanced on the monitor and release the order.
I define review criteria with matched previews and prints, then coach staff using defect examples.

basic.situation: You are preparing a routine processing solution from a supplied formula, with the measuring equipment and safety gear ready.

options.text: I use the remaining solution from the previous batch to finish preparation.
I follow the usual formula and check the mixture color before filling the tank.
I check the formula and solution label, measure each amount, and mix as directed.
I measure the listed amounts and mix the solution using the usual sequence.

advanced.situation: Several solution containers are low before a busy shift, and you need to guide coworkers through preparation and disposal under facility procedures.

options.text: I count containers and ask the lead which solution needs preparation first.
I combine compatible-looking leftovers to stretch supplies and clear the bench.
I check stock, assign formula-based preparation, and verify waste labels with coworkers.
I remind coworkers to follow posted formulas and place waste in marked containers.

basic.situation: A processing machine is ready for a routine run, and you notice residue near the tank after the previous batch.

options.text: I clean around the tank and note the residue for the next shift.
I rinse the visible residue, then check the tank before starting the next batch.
I top up the tank with fresh solution and begin processing.
I inspect the tank and remove residue with the approved rinsing solution.

advanced.situation: A printer's output intermittently shows lines, and you are responsible for checking equipment operation and advising the maintenance schedule.

options.text: I clean accessible parts, then check whether later printed pages show visible improvement.
I restart the printer and ask another operator whether they also see lines.
I continue printing and set aside pages showing lines for the maintenance review.
I compare output with machine checks, log patterns, and plan preventive inspection.

basic.situation: A work order arrives for a photo set, and you need to identify the process and materials before preparing it.

options.text: I read the requested print size and choose the standard paper for the job.
I use the settings from the last similar order and begin processing.
I ask a coworker to identify the process and prepare the listed materials.
I read the order for print size and finish, then confirm the required materials.

advanced.situation: Orders are backing up before delivery, and you are asked to improve work-order flow while keeping quantities and customer charges accurate.

options.text: I combine similar orders and enter one shared charge to speed up delivery.
I remind staff to update quantities and charges before packing each order.
I map order stages, reconcile quantities and charges, then train staff on the handoff records.
I sort orders by delivery time and ask the team to clear the oldest first.

basic.situation: You are setting up a routine part and need to enter its initial dimensions into the machine control panel.

options.text: I enter the drawing dimensions into the control panel fields.
I copy dimensions from the previous job, then adjust visible differences.
I check units and datum against the drawing before entering dimensions.
I enter the listed dimensions and confirm the panel shows them.

advanced.situation: A revised part program must reach the CNC module before the next run, and two similar revisions are on the server.

options.text: I send the latest file from the shared folder to save setup time.
I transfer the revised file after checking its job number and revision.
I match the approved revision and machine, then transfer the file and verify receipt.
I confirm the revision with the programmer before sending it to the CNC module.

basic.situation: You finish a batch and need to measure a workpiece dimension against the job specification before releasing it.

options.text: I measure the feature and ask a colleague whether the reading seems acceptable.
I compare the workpiece visually with the sample and release the batch.
I measure the feature with a caliper and record its reading.
I zero the micrometer, measure the feature, and compare it with tolerance.

advanced.situation: A new blueprint has several operations and tight dimensions; you must set the machine sequence before production starts.

options.text: I map dimensions, datums, tools, and operation order against the blueprint.
I set the familiar sequence first and resolve any dimension conflicts during the run.
I reuse the last job sequence and change the final cutting step.
I list the operations and set the sequence from the blueprint notes.

basic.situation: You are mounting a routine workpiece in a fixture and need to secure it before the machine cycle begins.

options.text: I clamp the workpiece and check that it sits square in the fixture.
I secure the workpiece with the fixture clamps and inspect their grip.
I tighten the nearest clamps and start the setup measurement.
I use the previous setup position and tighten the clamps for this part.

advanced.situation: A heavy workpiece must be lifted onto the machine, and its centre of gravity is offset from the usual lifting point.

options.text: I confirm the hoist capacity and use the usual lifting points with a spotter.
I attach the hoist at the marked point and guide the workpiece onto the bed.
I check the load balance, sling points, and travel path before guiding the lift.
I ask a nearby operator to steady the workpiece as the hoist raises it.

basic.situation: At the end of a routine run, you need to clean oil and residue from the machine parts using the approved solvent.

options.text: I use the solvent on the visible surfaces and return the machine to service.
I use the strongest available solvent to clear the residue quickly.
I wipe the parts with the approved solvent and a clean rag.
I confirm the solvent suits the parts, then wipe and inspect them.

advanced.situation: A cutting tool is chipped during a run, and the machine is stopped for replacement before the next part is made.

options.text: I install the spare and run the next part at reduced feed.
I fit a similar tool from the rack and resume the saved program.
I replace the tool with the matching spare and check its seating.
I confirm the tool specification, fit it securely, and check its offset.

basic.situation: During a routine cut, you hear a new vibration and suspect the cutting tool may be dull.

options.text: I pause the cycle safely and inspect the tool and workpiece setup.
I keep the cycle running and plan to check the tool after the batch.
I lower the feed slightly and listen for a change in vibration.
I listen again and note when the vibration occurs in the cycle.

advanced.situation: Repeated parts show the same unexpected dimension, and a control adjustment has not resolved the production error.

options.text: I send the readings and program details to the supervisor for review.
I hold affected parts, document readings, and review the error with the programmer.
I adjust the offset again and see whether the next part improves.
I use the first acceptable reading to continue the batch at the current setting.

basic.situation: A routine batch has finished, and you need to load the items onto the conveyor for the next station.

options.text: I load the items in sequence and watch that the conveyor moves them.
I place the finished items evenly on the conveyor and check spacing.
I load the items quickly in a single pile to clear the machine area.
I stack the items at the conveyor entrance for the next operator to spread.

advanced.situation: A revised material requires a different cut position, and you need to calculate speed and feed ratios before the next run.

options.text: I use the previous ratio and adjust the cut position to match the drawing.
I check the material figures, calculate speed and feed, then verify cut position.
I calculate the new feed ratio from the job figures and enter it.
I retain the previous speed and feed to keep the production schedule on track.

basic.situation: You are entering hole coordinates and commands into the controller for a routine part, with a senior programmer available for guidance.

options.text: I enter the coordinates carefully and store the program for the next run.
I match each coordinate to the drawing, enter commands, then verify the display.
I enter the coordinates from the prior part and change the hole count.
I enter the listed coordinates and ask for a review before storing them.

advanced.situation: A proven program has a long tool path, and you are asked to improve efficiency while keeping the part dimensions unchanged.

options.text: I revise the longest moves and keep a copy of the original program.
I shorten repeated moves and ask a colleague to review the revised path.
I remove pauses that look unnecessary and save the faster program for production.
I compare the path changes against dimensions, then validate the revised program.

basic.situation: A program check shows a coordinate that differs from the drawing, and you need to revise it with supervision.

options.text: I replace the coordinate with the nearest value used in a prior program.
I trace the coordinate to the drawing, revise it, and retest the program.
I change the coordinate and ask the supervisor to check the edited line.
I revise the flagged line and save the program for the next trial.

advanced.situation: Several programs have recurring coordinate errors, and you are asked to help colleagues resolve them consistently.

options.text: I send colleagues the corrected files so they can reuse the proven values.
I explain the recurring issue and offer to review colleagues' next edits.
I outline a source-to-edit retest routine and demonstrate it on a sample error.
I share recent fixes and suggest colleagues compare edits with the source drawings.

basic.situation: You have a controller printout for a routine part and need to compare its instructions with the blueprint under supervision.

options.text: I compare the printout's hole locations with the blueprint and note differences.
I compare the printout with a similar part's file and accept matching entries.
I check the first and last coordinates, then file the printout.
I match each listed coordinate and dimension against the blueprint before signoff.

advanced.situation: You are asked to review a colleague's encoded instructions after an earlier printout mismatch caused a rejected part.

options.text: I compare the full instruction set with source specifications and record discrepancies.
I copy the prior review notes and mark the current file as checked.
I sample several coordinates and share any differences with the colleague.
I review the changed lines and approve the file if those entries match.

basic.situation: A routine drawing shows two cuts and a drilled hole, and you need to choose their sequence and cutting tools with guidance.

options.text: I list the cuts and hole, then match tools to each operation.
I use the tool order from a similar job and adapt the hole step.
I order the operations around the workpiece setup and select matching tools.
I start with the familiar drill step and choose tools as the job proceeds.

advanced.situation: A complex part has several faces, tight dimensions, and limited setup changes; you need to plan an efficient sequence for a junior programmer.

options.text: I follow the prior sequence and let the junior adjust tools for access.
I schedule the fastest cuts first and keep the same setup throughout.
I map datums, tool access, and setup changes before sequencing operations for the junior.
I group operations by face and explain the tool changes to the junior.

basic.situation: You observe a trial run for a routine part and need to check that the program and machine produce the intended item.

options.text: I watch the tool path and note any unexpected movement during the trial.
I follow the path, check clearances, and compare the trial part with specifications.
I run the familiar trial path at production pace to save setup time.
I watch the first tool movement and report that the trial started smoothly.

advanced.situation: A new part combines several tool changes and close clearances, and you are asked to plan its simulation before a trial run.

options.text: I test tool changes and close clearances in simulation before observing a cautious trial.
I simulate the first operation and rely on the familiar later sequence.
I simulate the full path and note any tool changes that appear unusual.
I simulate each operation separately and review the tool list afterward.

basic.situation: You need to prepare a simple geometric layout from a part graphic for a routine job, with a colleague available to assist.

options.text: I reuse the last layout and change its title for this job.
I sketch the visible outline and fill in details from the previous layout.
I draw the main shapes from the graphic and ask for a review.
I transfer the key dimensions and check the layout against the graphic.

advanced.situation: Several shop orders use different sizes of the same sheet material, and you need to group them to reduce waste and setup changes.

options.text: I group the largest orders first and assign leftover sheets to smaller jobs.
I compare part layouts and group compatible orders to use sheets efficiently.
I run each order in arrival sequence and use the next available sheet.
I group similar orders by material and note the remaining sheet space.

basic.situation: A new order calls for a narrower strip and a different glue amount. You are preparing the machine with guidance before the first run.

options.text: I would ask an operator to set the machine while I stage materials.
I would check the order, then set width and glue with guidance.
I would reuse yesterday's settings to keep this routine batch moving.
I would compare each adjustment with specifications before starting the run.

advanced.situation: A trial with a layered material produces uneven bonds. You are asked to refine machine settings and show a new operator how to set up the next run.

options.text: I would adjust glue and pressure in small trials, recording results against the work order.
I would keep the current settings and ask the operator to watch the bond line.
I would compare controlled trials, confirm a stable setting, then demonstrate the setup sequence.
I would use the closest standard setting and explain how to watch for uneven bonds.

basic.situation: The feeder is nearly empty and finished pieces are piling up beside the line. You are asked to reload material and stack the completed products.

options.text: I would grab the nearest roll and keep feeding while clearing the pile.
I would match roll label to order, reload it, and stack by batch.
I would ask a coworker to reload while I move pieces to the rack.
I would refill the feeder from labelled stock and stack pieces neatly by batch.

advanced.situation: Two material deliveries arrive as the line speeds up, and a new colleague is helping move stock. You need to keep supply flowing and finished batches separated.

options.text: I would verify labels, stage each delivery by sequence, and show the colleague safe routes.
I would move the first delivery closer and let the colleague organize the second.
I would stage both deliveries near the feeder and brief the colleague on lifting safely.
I would send the colleague to move stock while I keep the feeder supplied.

basic.situation: During a run, the pressure gauge is higher than the reading on your previous shift. You are checking the panel while a supervisor is nearby.

options.text: I would turn the pressure control down slightly and watch the next pieces.
I would note the reading and ask the supervisor whether it matches this order.
I would keep the feeder moving because the products still look smooth.
I would compare the gauge with the order settings, then report any mismatch before continuing.

advanced.situation: Pressure readings drift during a long run, and the same alarm has appeared on several shifts. You are monitoring the panel and asked to help refine checks.

options.text: I would log readings at intervals and compare them with the alarm threshold.
I would reset the alarm after each alert so production can continue smoothly.
I would map readings against run conditions, flag the drift, and propose clear check points.
I would ask the next shift to watch the gauge more closely during production.

basic.situation: The first bonded panels are off the line, and the order lists a target width. You have a tape measure and a supervisor available to check your results.

options.text: I would stack the panels because their edges look even from here.
I would measure a panel and ask the supervisor to confirm my reading.
I would measure several panels against the target and flag any variation for review.
I would measure the top panel and continue if it matches the target.

advanced.situation: A test run meets the width target, but bond strength varies between samples. You are responsible for checking the run and helping the team respond to the specification failure.

options.text: I would group failures by run time, verify the method, and share findings.
I would accept the average strength because most samples meet the target.
I would adjust glue amount and test another sample from the line.
I would repeat the strength check and report the range to the line lead.

basic.situation: A strip jams at the feeder, stopping the run. You are asked to help clear it and restore normal operation with an experienced operator nearby.

options.text: I would pull the strip free and restart at the same speed.
I would remove the visible strip and ask the operator to check the feeder.
I would follow the machine's clearing procedure, inspect alignment, then restart with the operator.
I would stop the feed and ask the operator to guide me through clearing it.

advanced.situation: The same material jams twice after small alignment changes. You are asked to clear the latest jam and suggest how to reduce repeat stoppages.

options.text: I would compare jam points with settings, then recommend checks for likely causes.
I would clear the jam and ask maintenance to inspect the feeder later.
I would clear the strip, note the alignment, and suggest checking it each shift.
I would widen the feed gap and keep the line running at speed.

basic.situation: You have finished a batch and must record its quantity, width, and thickness. The figures are on the order sheet and the measuring station.

options.text: I would copy the previous batch figures to finish the entry quickly.
I would reconcile my count and measurements with the order sheet before recording them.
I would record the quantity now and add dimensions after the next run.
I would enter the quantity and dimensions from my notes before the next run.

advanced.situation: A shift audit finds duplicate entries and inconsistent thickness values across several batches. You are asked to review the production records and suggest a clearer entry process.

options.text: I would trace entries to source sheets, resolve discrepancies, and propose duplicate checks.
I would copy the latest values across similar batches to align the record.
I would remove obvious duplicates and share the revised sheet with the team today.
I would mark uncertain values for the next shift to review during entry.

basic.situation: A thermometer reading rises above the usual range during a cleaning cycle. You are checking the machine with a supervisor nearby.

options.text: I would compare the reading with its range and report the rise first.
I would reread the thermometer and ask the supervisor to review the setting.
I would keep the cycle running while the cleaning liquid still looks clear.
I would lower the temperature slightly and watch the next reading.

advanced.situation: A pump's pressure fluctuates and the same warning has appeared on several shifts. You are checking the machine and helping newer operators respond consistently.

options.text: I would ask a senior operator to inspect the pump after this batch.
I would reset the warning and continue the cycle at its current setting.
I would record each warning and ask the next shift to watch the pressure.
I would compare pressure trends with cycle conditions, report the pattern, and set shared check points.

basic.situation: The tank needs a fresh cleaning solution, and the instruction sheet gives the amounts. You have a calibrated rod and the measured chemicals ready.

options.text: I would measure the main chemical and top up the tank to its usual mark.
I would measure each amount with the calibrated rod and follow the sheet.
I would check the sheet, measure each chemical, and confirm the tank level before mixing.
I would use the same proportions as the last tank to save time.

advanced.situation: A new operator is preparing solution for a larger tank, and the usual mix gives uneven cleaning. You are asked to review the ratio and coach the operator.

options.text: I would ask the operator to measure carefully and record the next tank's results.
I would compare trial results with the instructions, confirm a stable ratio, and demonstrate measuring it.
I would use the old ratio and increase the cycle time for this batch.
I would show the operator the usual ratio and ask them to mix a trial tank.

basic.situation: A batch of metal parts needs a set temperature and cycle length from the work instruction. You are preparing the controls with guidance before starting the conveyor.

options.text: I would match both controls to the instruction and confirm them before starting the conveyor.
I would start the conveyor and adjust the temperature while the parts enter.
I would use the previous batch's cycle because the parts look similar.
I would set the listed temperature and cycle time, then ask for a check.

advanced.situation: Two product types share the line but need different cycle lengths. A queue is building, and you are asked to improve flow without mixing their settings.

options.text: I would group each type and use its listed cycle as queues move.
