I would sequence batches by type, verify settings, and track time against output.
I would use the shorter cycle for both types to clear the queue.
I would alternate types and ask a coworker to monitor the controls.

basic.situation: The scheduled tank change is due after the current batch. You are assigned to drain, clean, and refill it using the supplied cleaning solution.

options.text: I would drain and rinse the tank, then refill it to its usual level.
I would drain the tank and clean it using the supplied solution as directed.
I would drain, clean, check residue, and refill to the mark.
I would refill the tank now to reduce the line's waiting time.

advanced.situation: Several tanks need draining and cleaning during a busy week. You are asked to plan the sequence and help the team keep each tank change on schedule.

options.text: I would make a weekly list and ask operators to initial each tank change.
I would schedule the busiest tank first and let the team handle the rest.
I would schedule tank changes around downtime and track each refill.
I would clean the tanks when the line has spare time between batches.

basic.situation: A batch of glass products is ready for washing, and the machine is set for the listed cycle. You are loading the items with supervision.

options.text: I would fill the machine quickly so the waiting batch can start sooner.
I would load the glass in one layer and ask the supervisor to start.
I would load the glass evenly and check the batch label before starting.
I would confirm the batch, space items, then start the listed cycle.

advanced.situation: A mixed batch of tin plate surfaces shows uneven cleaning after washing. You are asked to handle the next batch and keep results consistent across the run.

options.text: I would load the next batch evenly and inspect several surfaces after washing.
I would slow the conveyor and check whether the next surfaces look cleaner.
I would separate surface types, standardize loads, and compare samples from each group.
I would run the mixed batch again using the same loading pattern.

basic.situation: You are asked to log the tank temperature, material used, and cycle time after a batch. The gauge and work sheet are still at the line.

options.text: I would copy the gauge reading and cycle time onto the log sheet.
I would copy the previous batch's readings to complete the log on time.
I would write the temperature now and fill the other fields after the next cycle.
I would record the reading, material, and time against the work sheet.

advanced.situation: A review finds repeated gaps in cycle times and inconsistent material names across production logs. You are asked to analyze the records and improve how operators enter them.

options.text: I would fill gaps with typical cycle times so the monthly log is complete.
I would list the missing fields and remind the team to complete each log.
I would group gaps by shift, standardize material labels, and prompt time entry.
I would ask each operator to review their own entries at month end.

basic.situation: You are asked to start a pump and conveyor to move a batch into the freezer. The line is clear, and your supervisor has given the settings.

options.text: Check the route, then start the pump and conveyor at the given settings.
Open the valve fully and run both machines to finish the transfer sooner.
Start the pump first, then turn on the conveyor after flow begins.
Start the pump and conveyor, then watch the batch enter the freezer.

advanced.situation: A freezer line produces uneven product after a speed change, and a new operator asks how to restore steady flow before the next batch.

options.text: Compare feed and freezer speed, adjust in small steps, and explain the response.
Watch the outlet closely and lower the speed if unevenness continues.
Return to the last settings and ask the operator to watch the line.
Increase the feed rate and see whether the product becomes more even.

basic.situation: During a batch, the flowmeter reading moves above its marked range. You are monitoring the panel and have been shown the normal range.

options.text: Compare the flowmeter with the normal range, adjust feed, and check pressure too.
Read the flowmeter again and adjust the feed control toward its marked range.
Ask your supervisor to read the gauge while you keep watching the batch.
Turn the feed control down sharply until the needle drops into range.

advanced.situation: New operators read a density dial differently during a changing mix. You are asked to help them monitor the panel and maintain the specified conditions.

options.text: Ask operators to check density more often and report unusual readings.
Tell each operator to use the dial that seems clearest to them.
Use density and temperature together, explain the target ranges, and log each check.
Set a shared reading interval and compare density with the specified range.

basic.situation: A run of containers seems underfilled after a filler change. You are weighing packages and have the specified amount beside the scale.

options.text: Increase the filler setting until the packages look full enough to ship.
Raise the filler setting slightly and check the next container on the scale.
Weigh several containers and adjust the filler valve toward the specified amount.
Check the scale, weigh samples across the run, then adjust and recheck the filler.

advanced.situation: A new ingredient lot gives inconsistent acidity readings, though the recipe is unchanged. You are sampling the mix and checking results before release.

options.text: Use the first acceptable reading to record the batch as within range.
Calibrate the pH meter, take fresh samples, and compare results with the specified range.
Repeat a sample with the pH meter and compare it with the batch record.
Blend the batch longer and check acidity again near the end.

basic.situation: The mix is cooling unevenly, and you are assigned to stir it with a paddle before the next filling step.

options.text: Stir the whole surface quickly so filling can begin on schedule.
Stir from the edges inward and check the temperature at the center.
Stir the center well and ask a coworker whether the edges feel cooler.
Stir steadily across the vat, then check whether the mix cools evenly.

advanced.situation: A sticky mix begins clinging to the scraper during a busy run. You are operating the agitator and need to keep the batch moving evenly.

options.text: Increase the agitator speed and keep the scraper running until sticking stops.
Keep the beater running and scrape the accessible buildup between batches.
Check the approved setting, clear visible buildup safely, and restart while watching the mix.
Pause the beater, inspect the mix, then restart at the approved setting.

basic.situation: You are positioning containers in a freezer rack before cooling. The marked guides show where each container should sit.

options.text: Load the containers by eye and start once the rack looks reasonably full.
Use the guides for each container and leave a little space between rows.
Place each container against its guide and check spacing before starting.
Position the containers along the guides, then ask a coworker to glance over them.

advanced.situation: A pipe fitting leaks slightly after a line change, and the next batch is waiting. You are assembling the equipment with hand tools.

options.text: Tighten the fitting firmly and start the line to see whether it holds.
Ask a coworker to check the fitting while you prepare the next batch.
Check the fitting alignment, reseat it, and confirm the joint before restarting.
Retighten the fitting, then watch for drips during a short run.

basic.situation: Frost is building around a freezer edge after a run. You have been shown the approved hand tool for scraping it away.

options.text: Scrape the buildup with the approved tool, then check the edge again.
Scrape the accessible frost and tell your supervisor the edge needs checking.
Use a metal scraper quickly so the freezer is ready sooner.
Scrape the frost carefully and check whether any remains near the seal.

advanced.situation: After flushing a product line, the return water still looks cloudy before the next batch. You are responsible for the cleaning record and line check.

options.text: Ask a coworker to assess the cloudy return before deciding whether another flush is needed.
Flush again, inspect the return, and record its appearance before releasing the line.
Log the flush, then hold the line while checking the cloudy return water.
Repeat the flush and document the extra cleaning before preparing the line for production.

basic.situation: You are setting the worktable height for a simple engraving cut. The job sheet gives the required depth, and a senior operator is nearby.

options.text: Set the table depth from the job sheet, then verify the gauge reading.
Match the gauge to the job sheet, then request a senior operator's review.
Adjust the table to the specified depth, then check the first cut.
Use the similar job's table setting after checking its material and depth.

advanced.situation: A repeat engraving is too shallow on one edge despite matching the recorded settings. You are checking the machine before a costly plate is run.

options.text: Check the arm gauge across the worktable, adjust the height, and test a sample.
Ask the operator to watch the next cut while you adjust the arm gauge.
Repeat the recorded settings and run another plate to confirm the pattern.
Lower the worktable a little and inspect the next test cut.

basic.situation: You need an etching solution at the concentration on the job sheet. The formula and measuring equipment are ready, and a senior worker is available.

options.text: Measure water and acid using the formula, then label the prepared solution.
Measure the acid carefully and add water until the amount looks right.
Follow the formula and ask the senior worker to check your measurements.
Pour the acid into the water by eye, then check the mixture color.

advanced.situation: An etched workpiece needs neutralizing before inspection, but traces of acid remain near the design. You are assigned to rinse and prepare it for review.

options.text: Use the specified rinse, inspect the design area, and repeat until clear.
Rinse the design area carefully, then ask a senior worker to review it.
Wipe the visible acid away with a brush and move the piece along.
Rinse the whole piece with water and set it aside for inspection.

basic.situation: A small metal plate needs clamping for engraving. The fixture marks show its position, and you have been asked to set it up.

options.text: Align the plate carefully and ask a coworker to check its position.
Clamp the plate near the marks and begin once it appears steady.
Align the plate to the fixture marks, clamp it, and check for movement.
Place the plate in the fixture and tighten the clamps as far as possible.

advanced.situation: A thin glass workpiece shifts in its fixture during a test pass. You are preparing a high-value piece and need a stable hold before engraving.

options.text: Add a soft pad and retighten the clamps before trying another pass.
Pause and ask a senior operator to suggest a safer fixture arrangement.
Tighten the fixture harder and continue the pass at reduced speed.
Reposition the glass on its support points, secure it gently, and test stability.

basic.situation: You are tracing lettering onto a plate using a supplied template. The plate is clean, and the layout marks are visible.

options.text: Copy the lettering freehand onto the plate to keep the job moving.
Trace the lettering from the template and compare it with the sketch afterward.
Position the template by eye and mark the letters lightly for speed.
Align the template to the marks, then trace the lettering with a scribe.

advanced.situation: A client changes the size of a detailed engraving after the first pattern is prepared. You are using design software to update the transfer file.

options.text: Change the scale setting and ask the operator whether the preview looks suitable.
Resize the existing pattern and send it to the machine for engraving.
Update the dimensions, check proportions and lettering, then export a revised pattern.
Resize the file to the new dimensions and review the preview before export.

basic.situation: You are guiding a stylus over a template to duplicate a simple logo on a brass plate under supervision.

options.text: Trace the outline first, then complete the smaller details at a slower pace.
Move quickly over the main lines and touch up any obvious gaps later.
Guide the stylus steadily along the template and check the cut as you proceed.
Follow the template at a steady pace and inspect the engraving afterward.

advanced.situation: A detailed glass design includes narrow lettering and broad exposed areas. You are sandblasting it, and a test piece shows uneven depth.

options.text: Ask a coworker to watch the lettering while you complete the broad areas.
Compare the test depth across areas, adjust the spray, and verify another sample.
Reduce the spray pressure slightly and inspect the lettering during the next pass.
Increase the spray pressure and finish the exposed areas in one pass.

basic.situation: A customer sketch and sample show different lettering widths on an engraving job. You are reviewing the requirements before the plate is prepared.

options.text: Use the sample as the guide and tell the operator the lettering looks wider.
Follow the sketch dimensions and keep the sample nearby for reference.
Compare the sketch and sample, note the width difference, and clarify the intended dimension.
Choose the wider lettering because it will be easier to read.

advanced.situation: A proof looks accurate, but inspection finds shallow cuts in several small characters. You are checking the engraving before it is sent onward.

options.text: Ask another inspector to review the proof and decide whether the cuts matter.
Inspect the small characters again under magnification and mark the shallow areas.
Measure the shallow cuts, compare them with the design, and arrange focused rework.
Polish the surface and send the plate onward since the proof matches.

basic.situation: You are fitting a tube into a mold for a routine casting. The work order gives its position and depth, and a depth gauge is nearby.

options.text: I would align the tube by eye and begin once it looks centered.
I would match the work order, seat the tube, and verify its depth with the gauge.
I would seat the tube, then have a senior check the depth gauge.
I would press the tube in until it feels snug and start filling.

advanced.situation: A repaired mold keeps producing castings with a thin edge. You find a crack near the cavity and a coworker asks how to fix it before the next run.

options.text: I would inspect the crack, repair the edge, and explain the method.
I would smooth the cracked edge with tools and run a small batch.
I would patch the edge with clay and ask the coworker to watch.
I would cover the crack with loose sand and continue the pour.

basic.situation: A routine casting has a thin ridge of excess material along one edge. You have a scraper and the finished dimensions on the work order.

options.text: I would remove the ridge with a scraper, then ask a coworker to check the edge.
I would scrape the ridge in small passes, then check the finished edge against the work order.
I would trim the ridge with a knife in one pass to save time.
I would cut the whole edge back to the next visible line and pack it.

advanced.situation: A brittle mold mixture chips under the usual trimming method, and several orders need the same profile. A new worker is ready to copy your approach.

options.text: I would test short scraper passes on a sample, then demonstrate the stable method to the new worker.
I would use a knife on one sample and show the new worker the result.
I would use the usual band saw setting and let the new worker trim the batch.
I would trim the pieces with shorter knife strokes and ask the worker to follow.

basic.situation: You are smoothing a mold surface with sandpaper before a routine run. A shallow rough patch remains near the edge, and the finish sample is available.

options.text: I would scrape the patch deeply so the next mold surface looks uniform.
I would sand the patch lightly, then compare the surface with the finish sample.
I would sand the rough patch and ask a coworker whether it feels smooth.
I would sand the whole edge until it feels even under my fingers.

advanced.situation: Two workers finish the same type of mold differently, and the surface variation is appearing on customer parts. You are asked to guide the next shift.

options.text: I would compare samples, explain the finish target, and teach checks by touch.
I would suggest finer sanding and check one sample with the team together.
I would demonstrate a sanding method and ask the next shift to follow.
I would let each worker finish as usual, then review the parts together.

basic.situation: A work order lists two parts with similar names but different quantities. You need to identify which sections to produce before preparing the molds.

options.text: I would read both part names and confirm the sections with a coworker.
I would match names and quantities to the order, then mark each section.
I would start with the larger section because it appears on the order first.
I would prepare the section matching the most familiar part name first.

advanced.situation: A new batch uses a formula that gives inconsistent material texture, while the finished parts must meet tight dimensions. You are asked to propose an adjustment.

options.text: I would add water until workable, then release parts that seem close to target.
I would reduce one ingredient slightly, then check several parts with calipers.
I would repeat the formula and measure several finished parts before making changes.
I would record formula results, adjust one measured ingredient, and verify dimensions.

basic.situation: You finish a routine run and find dried material on a mold part. The cleaning instructions call for cleaning and lubrication before storage.

options.text: I would clean the residue, inspect the part, and apply the specified lubricant before storage.
I would wipe the visible residue away and place the part on the storage rack.
I would clean the part and ask a coworker to confirm it is ready for storage.
I would apply lubricant over the residue so the part is ready for the next run.

advanced.situation: Filled molds are ready for the curing oven, but space is limited and several are different sizes. A newer worker asks how to load them safely.

options.text: I would load the largest molds first and ask the worker to follow that order.
I would group molds by size, follow loading instructions, and show stable placement.
I would stack molds as high as the rack allows to fit the batch.
I would place smaller molds on top and check the rack before moving it.

basic.situation: You are preparing a routine mold surface with a parting agent before casting. The work instruction specifies a light, even coating.

options.text: I would spray extra agent near the edges where sticking often starts.
I would apply a light, even coat and check coverage across the mold surface.
I would coat the cavity heavily so the casting releases with less effort.
I would spray the mold and ask a coworker whether the surface looks covered.

advanced.situation: A solidified casting resists release, and a loose core is still inside. The surface looks intact, but forcing it may damage the product.

options.text: I would pull the core firmly while keeping the casting steady on the bench.
I would ease the core out gradually, checking the casting as it releases.
I would tap the mold lightly, then try withdrawing the core once more.
I would check the casting and core, then withdraw it along its release path.

basic.situation: You are trimming a rough stone block to match a simple diagram. A small ridge remains near the marked edge, and the supervisor is working nearby.

options.text: I would shape the ridge and ask the supervisor to check the outline afterward.
I would remove the ridge with one deep cut and smooth the block after.
I would trim the ridge in small cuts, then compare the edge with the diagram.
I would cut back to the next visible line so the edge looks even.

advanced.situation: A monumental stone design has several deep curves and a narrow raised detail. The pattern is clear, but one surface is harder than the sample you practised on.

options.text: I would shape from pattern marks in stages, checking raised details between passes.
I would follow marked curves with a pneumatic tool and inspect the surface afterward.
I would shape the raised area first, then ask a coworker to check curves.
I would deepen main curves first, then blend the raised section by eye.

basic.situation: You have finished smoothing a small carving. A sample with the required finish is on the bench, and your fingers feel one slightly rough patch.

options.text: I would leave the patch, since the surrounding carving feels smooth.
I would feel the patch and nearby surface, comparing both against the sample.
I would sand the full face lightly to make the finish feel even.
I would recheck the patch by touch and ask a coworker to compare it.

advanced.situation: Two carvings feel different after separate shifts worked on them, though both use the same finish sample. You are asked to guide the next shift's surface checks.

options.text: I would ask the next shift to check the rougher carving and compare it with the sample.
I would ask the next shift to sand both carvings until they feel alike.
I would demonstrate my surface check, then ask the team to repeat it consistently.
I would compare both carvings with the sample and standardize finger checks across each face.

basic.situation: You have carved a set of shallow cuts from a blueprint. The listed depth is available, and a measuring gauge is ready for checking.

options.text: I would measure the deepest cut and compare its reading with the others.
I would gauge each cut and compare readings with the listed blueprint depth.
I would gauge one cut, record its depth, and ask a coworker to review.
I would mark the set finished because the cuts look even from above.

advanced.situation: A carving's depth readings differ from the model near a detailed corner. You must determine how much stone remains before the next shift continues.

options.text: I would mark shallow readings and ask a coworker to compare them with the model.
I would remeasure with a gauge, record depth, and ask the next shift to verify.
I would measure from model reference points, record readings, and brief the next shift.
I would deepen the corner until its profile looks close to the model.

basic.situation: A simple stone design has a broad flat face and one shallow groove. You need to choose tools and order them before starting the work.

options.text: I would use the broad chisel first and choose the groove tool once I reach it.
I would choose a suitable chisel for the face, then a narrower tool for the groove.
I would use the narrowest chisel for both areas to keep the work consistent.
I would start with a familiar chisel and ask a coworker about the groove tool.

advanced.situation: A large carving combines broad planes, fine grooves, and a textured edge. The pattern is detailed, and a junior worker asks which tools to prepare first.

options.text: I would match tools to features, sequence broad shaping before details, and explain each transition.
I would lay out chisels for grooves and ask the worker to select tools for planes.
I would start with the sandblasting nozzle across the face, then carve the grooves.
I would prepare common chisels and show the worker how to begin safely.

basic.situation: A diagram shows a straight groove and two drilled holes in a stone piece. You have marked the locations and are preparing the drill.

options.text: I would cut the groove first and adjust its ends to meet the holes.
I would check marks against the diagram, then drill holes and cut the groove.
I would drill both holes slightly wider so the groove connects cleanly.
I would drill the marked holes and ask a coworker to review the groove line.

advanced.situation: A stone panel has an intricate molding that narrows around a corner, with grooves following a pattern. A junior worker is ready to cut the first section.

options.text: I would mark the corner and ask the worker to finish straight grooves first.
I would cut main grooves from the pattern, then review the corner with the worker.
I would deepen corner grooves first so the pattern stays visible during finishing.
I would transfer corner details, cut in stages, and check each molding transition.

basic.situation: You need to transfer a small design from tracing paper onto a stone face. The sketch includes two dimensions and a clear centerline.

options.text: I would copy the outline freehand and adjust it to fit the face.
I would align the tracing to the centerline, transfer the marks, and check both dimensions.
I would trace the outline and ask a coworker to check its placement.
I would trace the design near the center and begin carving while the marks remain clear.

advanced.situation: A large stone panel has a complex design with several aligned motifs and a narrow border. The tracing paper is available, and another worker will continue after your layout.

options.text: I would align tracing with panel references, transfer key points, and verify motif spacing.
I would transfer the main motifs, mark border width, and ask the next worker to verify both.
I would trace motifs where they appear to fit and begin the outer border.
I would mark the border and ask the next worker to confirm motif spacing.

basic.situation: A batch of small glass cups is cooling, and one rim looks wider than the drawing allows. You need to check its dimensions before it moves on.

options.text: I would compare the caliper reading with the drawing tolerance, then mark the cup for review.
I would use the last cup's reading to clear this one and keep the line moving.
I would check the rim with a ruler and ask the next operator to confirm it.
I would measure the rim twice and note the result beside the batch number.

advanced.situation: A client sketch combines a narrow neck with a heavy base. You are asked to develop the blueprint specifications for a new glass vessel.

options.text: I would turn the sketch into a dimensioned draft, noting glass thickness and forming constraints.
I would draft the outline and label its key dimensions for the production team.
I would estimate the base thickness from a similar vessel and add it to the drawing.
I would copy the sketch dimensions into a blueprint and send it to the shop floor.

basic.situation: A mold is ready for a short production run, and the first glass piece stuck during release. You need to prepare the mold for the next piece.

options.text: I would apply a light, even coat of mold oil before the next piece.
I would swab the sticking area and continue with the next piece.
I would use the mold again and release the next piece with extra force.
I would ask a nearby operator to oil the mold while I prepare glass.

advanced.situation: A thick-walled glass type is soft on one side but stiff on the other after heating. You need to adjust the heating process before shaping it.

options.text: I would raise the oven setting until both sides look equally soft.
I would rotate the glass more often and watch how evenly it softens.
I would check the glass type, adjust the oven setting gradually, and monitor both sides.
I would extend the heating time and ask the shaper to test the piece.

basic.situation: A straight glass section needs a shallow bend for a small order. You are shaping it with paddles and hand tools while it remains workable.

options.text: I would press the section firmly once to reach the requested bend quickly.
I would use the paddle to form the bend, then ask a coworker to inspect it.
I would make a small bend with the paddle and compare it by eye.
I would press the bend gently with a paddle and check its angle against the sample.

advanced.situation: A customer sketch shows a hollow glass ornament with a twisted neck. You need to shape a trial piece using a blowpipe and hand tools.

options.text: I would twist the softened neck sharply to match the sketch in one motion.
I would form the ornament in stages, rotating the gather to control the hollow shape.
I would blow the body to size and shape the neck with the hand tools.
I would shape the body first and leave the neck twist for the final stage.

basic.situation: A batch of narrow glass tubes needs air pressure to keep them open while they are shaped. You are preparing the tubing ends.

options.text: I would seat a rubber hose on each end, then charge the tubing evenly.
I would charge the tubing first, then push the hoses onto the ends.
I would fit one hose and check the air flow before setting up the rest.
I would fit the hoses and charge the tubes one at a time as needed.

advanced.situation: Optical blanks from the press show slight shape variation across a run. You are asked to improve mold placement and press settings for the next batch.

options.text: I would compare blank measurements, mold seating, and press settings before a controlled adjustment.
I would adjust the press stroke until the next blank matches the target.
I would increase press pressure for the whole run to tighten the blank shape.
I would reseat the mold and ask the operator to watch the next blank closely.

basic.situation: A work order calls for short tubing sections, and the cut pieces must fit a glass assembly. You are setting the length with a cutting wheel.

options.text: I would mark each length from the work order and cut along the marks.
I would score the tubing at the mark and finish the break by hand.
I would cut the tubing to the usual length for this assembly.
I would measure and mark the tubing, cut one piece, and verify its length.

advanced.situation: The next order uses a glass type with a different working range, and recent pieces have varied in thickness. You need to set the press and oven.

options.text: I would verify glass type, adjust stroke and oven temperature, then inspect a trial.
I would reuse prior settings and inspect the first piece for variation.
I would adjust press stroke for thickness and monitor the existing oven setting.
I would raise press pressure and oven heat to reduce thickness variation.

basic.situation: A shift ends with several glass products completed in different sizes. You are recording the production details for the handover.

options.text: I would copy yesterday's figures and update the total for today's batch.
I would note the quantities and sizes on the batch sheet before leaving.
I would record the total quantity and leave size details for the next shift.
I would total the pieces by size and type, then record them against the shift.

advanced.situation: A finishing machine leaves rough edges on a glass batch, and a new operator is waiting to learn the polishing process. You need to respond.

options.text: I would keep the machine running and ask the operator to polish each edge longer.
I would inspect the abrasive and machine condition, then demonstrate a consistent polishing sequence.
I would lower the feed rate and show the operator the polishing sequence.
I would replace the abrasive and ask the operator to try another piece.

basic.situation: You have a ball of clay ready for a small bowl, and the potter's wheel is waiting. You are positioning the clay before starting the motor.

options.text: I would start the wheel first and press the clay toward the middle.
I would center the clay on the wheel before starting it at a steady speed.
I would set the clay down and ask a coworker to check its position.
I would place the clay near the center and start the wheel slowly.

advanced.situation: A trainee is throwing a tall pitcher, but its walls thin unevenly as it rises. You are guiding the work and setting a standard for the form.

options.text: I would ask the trainee to make another pitcher and compare the two forms.
I would set a wall thickness and profile target, then coach gradual, even lifting.
I would reshape the upper wall quickly so the pitcher meets the planned height.
I would have the trainee slow the wheel and steady both hands as the walls rise.

basic.situation: A leather-hard cup has shallow tool marks on its side. You are smoothing the surface with a rubber scraper and a wet sponge.

options.text: I would pass the wet sponge over the cup until the marks soften.
I would use the scraper lightly and ask someone to check the finish.
I would smooth the marks with a scraper, then blend the area using a damp sponge.
I would press hard with the scraper to flatten every mark in one pass.

advanced.situation: A new team member is attaching handles to mugs, and several handles meet the bodies at uneven angles. You are asked to coach the finishing standard.

options.text: I would show the target handle angle and demonstrate even joins on a sample mug.
I would point out the uneven angles and ask the team member to adjust them.
I would press each handle into place and leave the trainee to finish the mugs.
I would demonstrate one handle attachment and let the team member copy it.

basic.situation: A finished bowl looks slightly uneven near its base. You need to examine it for defects and check its dimensions before it is shelved.

options.text: I would compare the bowl with another one and set aside any obvious mismatch.
I would shelf the bowl if its glaze looks smooth from the front.
I would inspect the rim and measure the bowl's width with a rule.
I would check the base and rim, then record any visible defect and dimensions.

advanced.situation: A set of bowls must match a display template, but fired pieces vary slightly in width. You are asked to verify shape accuracy and refine inspection checks.

options.text: I would sort the bowls by eye and keep the closest-looking pieces together.
I would use calipers at set points and compare each bowl with the template.
I would compare each bowl with the template and measure the widest point.
I would measure a few bowls with a rule and use them as the reference.

basic.situation: A small batch of pottery is ready for a colored glaze, and the spray gun has been cleaned. You are mixing and applying the glaze with supervision.

options.text: I would apply equal spray passes to each piece for a consistent coating.
I would follow workshop directions, mix the glaze, and spray an even test coat.
I would adjust glaze thickness only after checking workshop guidance with my supervisor.
I would mix the glaze, test one piece, and check results before continuing.

advanced.situation: A gallery has offered a narrow display shelf for your pottery range. You are planning the display and guiding a coworker on glaze presentation.

options.text: I would arrange the pieces by height and coach the coworker on a shared color story.
I would fill the shelf with the newest pieces and ask the gallery to rearrange them.
I would group the pieces by glaze color and show the coworker the layout.
I would place the largest pieces at the back and let the coworker arrange colors.

basic.situation: Several freshly thrown plates are ready to leave the wheel, and the drying area has space. You are moving them for drying.

options.text: I would slide the plates together onto one board to save trips.
I would move the plates one at a time and check for clear space.
I would carry the plates carefully and set them on the nearest drying boards.
I would lift each plate with support and place it level in the drying area.

advanced.situation: A gallery order is due for packing, while the studio is low on wrapping material. You are coordinating supplies and preparing pottery for shipment.

options.text: I would check the order count and ask a coworker to find more wrapping.
I would pack the order with available wrapping and request more supplies later.
I would count the order, protect each piece, and update the wrapping stock record.
I would use thin paper for the whole order and dispatch it on schedule.

basic.situation: A pug mill is ready, and a clay batch needs blending before it can be extruded. You are operating the mill under supervision.

options.text: I would feed the batch at a moderate pace and ask the supervisor to inspect it.
I would push the full batch into the mill quickly to finish the run.
I would feed the clay steadily and watch the blended output as it emerges.
I would start with a small amount and add more when the mill clears.

advanced.situation: The pug mill begins feeding clay unevenly, and a coworker is waiting to learn kiln and mill safety. You are responsible for the run and training.

options.text: I would stop adding clay, inspect the feed path, then demonstrate the controls.
I would reduce the feed and explain the mill controls during the run.
I would keep the mill running while my coworker watches clay move through its feed path.
I would pause feeding, check for blockage, and explain controls to my coworker.

basic.situation: You are fitting a folding attachment for a new carton order, and your supervisor is nearby to guide you.

options.text: I would force the attachment into place and start a short run.
I would compare the attachment with the work order before fitting it.
I would ask the nearby lead to confirm which attachment belongs there.
I would fit it by sight, then run several sheets.

advanced.situation: A calibrated cutter leaves uneven folds after an attachment change, and the next batch is due before the shift ends.

options.text: I would check the guide positions, then ask a senior setter to review them.
I would loosen several guides and rerun the machine at production speed.
I would compare the setup measurements with specifications and adjust one point at a time.
I would move the folding bar slightly and inspect the next few cartons.

basic.situation: A fresh paper roll is ready at the feed track, and you have been asked to thread it through the rollers.

options.text: I would place the roll on the track and follow the usual threading route.
I would ask my coworker to steady the roll while I follow the threading path.
I would check the roll direction and feed path before threading it through.
I would push the roll onto the track and pull the paper through quickly.

advanced.situation: Paper keeps drifting toward one side during a large run, while a new operator is waiting to load the next roll.

options.text: I would shift the roll guides and show the new operator the adjustment.
I would keep the line moving and ask the new operator to watch the edge.
I would check the paper path and have the operator reload using the usual method.
I would stop feeding, inspect tracking and tension, then coach the loading sequence.

basic.situation: Finished paper cores are coming off the machine, and your coworker asks you to help move them to the conveyor.

options.text: I would slide the cores across the floor toward the conveyor with care.
I would ask my coworker to guide each core as we carry it.
I would lift each core together and set it onto the conveyor.
I would stack the cores beside the conveyor until the batch is finished.

advanced.situation: Several cores are leaving the line at once, and the transfer conveyor is nearly full as the next batch arrives.

options.text: I would stack cores higher to clear the machine and keep output moving.
I would pause transfers, clear space, and place each core in a stable pattern.
I would keep transferring and put any awkward cores on the side.
I would move the cores in smaller groups and watch for damage.

basic.situation: The forming machine is running while your supervisor works nearby, and you notice a carton with an uneven fold.

options.text: I would watch the next cartons for the same fold and report the pattern.
I would set the carton aside and tell the supervisor what I observed.
I would adjust the forming guide slightly and see whether the fold improves.
I would feed the carton back into the hopper with the others.

advanced.situation: Cartons are entering the gravity chute unevenly, but the hopper has not jammed yet and output is building quickly.

options.text: I would slow the machine and tap cartons toward the chute center.
I would stop the feed using the normal control and inspect the entry point.
I would reach into the chute while cartons continue dropping to keep them moving.
I would track the feed pattern and clear the chute at the next safe pause.

basic.situation: Your checklist calls for checking a carton batch, and you find several pieces with smudged date stamps.

options.text: I would check the work order and sample more cartons for stamp quality.
I would set aside the smudged cartons and report them to the operator.
I would check a few more cartons before deciding whether the stamp is faulty.
I would stamp over the smudges and return the cartons to the batch.

advanced.situation: A customer order requires a clear date mark, but the stamp is fading midway through a high-volume batch.

options.text: I would pause stamping, tell the operator, and hold cartons since the last check.
I would replace the stamp pad and resume the run at the same setting.
I would keep stamping and sort out faint dates after the full batch.
I would adjust the stamping device and check a sample against the order.

basic.situation: A small order needs hand cutting, and your supervisor has shown you the specified dimensions and cutter.

options.text: I would cut one piece, then ask the supervisor to check its size.
I would mark each piece and compare it with the specified dimensions before cutting.
I would cut a stack together to finish the order in fewer passes.
I would cut the pieces one by one using the ruler beside the cutter.

advanced.situation: A pressure roll is losing tension during production, and the next order needs a different synchronized speed setting.

options.text: I would lower the speed setting and see whether tension becomes steadier.
I would follow the setup procedure, change one control, and verify the speed and tension.
I would pause the run and ask the maintenance lead to inspect the pressure roll.
I would adjust tension while the rolls are moving, then check the next sheet.

basic.situation: You are learning to wind plies on a drum, and your trainer is beside you as the first tire body begins.

options.text: I would press the pedal quickly so the plies wrap before shifting.
I would follow the ply count and use the pedal at the trainer's pace.
I would keep the drum turning slowly and check the ply edges as I go.
I would count the plies aloud while the trainer watches the drum rotate.

advanced.situation: A tire body shows a slight shift during winding, and a new builder is waiting to operate the drum on the next unit.

options.text: I would show the new builder the pedal sequence and ask them to watch alignment.
I would stop the rotation, check the ply alignment, then coach the next setup.
I would keep the drum turning and press the shifted ply back into place.
I would pause and ask an experienced builder to confirm whether the shift matters.

basic.situation: You are fitting an inner tube and final rubber layer onto a tire, with a senior builder available nearby.

options.text: I would ask the senior builder to check the tube before I add rubber.
I would fit the tube first and smooth the rubber layer afterward.
I would push the tube in quickly and stretch the rubber over it.
I would fit the tube and rubber layer, checking that each sits evenly.

advanced.situation: A rebuilt casing has a section that lifts slightly after rolling, and several more casings are due for vulcanization.

options.text: I would press the lifted area down and send the casing with the others.
I would set the casing aside and ask a senior builder to review the bond.
I would roll the area again with extra pressure and recheck the surface.
I would inspect the bond, rework the area to specification, and verify adhesion.

basic.situation: A worn tire is waiting for retreading, and you have been asked to check its surface for visible faults.

options.text: I would look over the surface and measure the tire before sending it onward.
I would inspect the tread and sidewall, then note each visible fault.
I would check the tread closely and ask the senior inspector about a mark.
I would pass the tire along if the tread looks usable.

advanced.situation: Two worn tires have similar tread wear, but one has a small cut near the shoulder and a mold size is needed.

options.text: I would measure both tires and compare the cut with the inspection criteria.
I would select the tire with the deeper tread and mark the size needed.
I would buff the shoulder lightly and see whether the cut remains visible.
I would measure the tire and ask the senior inspector to judge the cut.

basic.situation: You are cutting a ply at its marked splice point, and a coworker is ready to help press the ends together.

options.text: I would cut near the mark and press the ends together firmly.
I would cut at the mark, then ask my coworker to check the join.
I would cut at the mark and press the ends flush with my coworker.
I would trim a little extra and overlap the ends to hold them together.

advanced.situation: A different rubber stock is producing uneven tread splice ends, and the production queue is growing behind your station.

options.text: I would slow the drum and make smaller cuts until the ends look even.
I would pause the drum and ask a senior builder to review one cut.
I would check the stock guidance, adjust the cut, and verify a sample splice.
I would trim each end by eye and keep the drum running.

basic.situation: You are applying cement to drum edges before winding plies, with the required materials laid out at your station.

options.text: I would ask the nearby builder to check my cement coverage afterward.
I would apply a thicker stripe so the plies have enough cement.
I would rub the stick quickly along the center of each drum edge.
I would rub the cement stick evenly along the drum edges as shown.

advanced.situation: A batch of plies needs solvent coating, and the first pass looks uneven before the next layer is due.

options.text: I would repeat the solvent pass over the whole batch and keep the same direction.
I would brush the visible gaps and proceed once the surface looks covered.
I would hold the next layer and ask a senior builder to check coverage.
I would compare the coating with the process instructions and address uneven areas in sequence.

basic.situation: You are placing a tire into a mold for new tread, and your trainer is available to guide the positioning.

options.text: I would align the tire with the mold guides before lowering it into place.
I would lower the tire quickly and shift it until it sits inside the mold.
I would center the tire by eye and compare the sides afterward.
I would place the tire and ask my trainer to check its position.

advanced.situation: A repaired tire has a filled cut near the edge, and the next tire is ready for the mold station.

options.text: I would press the fill edges again and check that they feel smooth.
I would cover the filled cut with fresh rubber and send the tire onward.
I would ask a senior builder to review the filled area before moving it.
I would inspect the fill against work criteria before positioning the next tire.

basic.situation: You are checking a batch against a simple checklist before packing. One item has a small mark that is not shown on the sample.

options.text: Check a few pieces and tell the lead about any visible defect.
Mark every listed feature and separate any questionable items.
Compare each item with the checklist, then set aside any mismatch.
Pass the batch onward when most pieces look close enough.

advanced.situation: A new helper asks how to check a recurring defect, while today's batch contains pieces with the same unclear mark as yesterday's non-conformance.

options.text: Tell the team to pass pieces that look similar to the sample.
Explain the sample to the new helper and report the repeated mark.
Use the written standard, separate affected pieces, and record the defect for review.
Show the team the sample, then let them continue checking the batch.

basic.situation: You are watching a conveyor during a routine run. It briefly slows, then returns to its usual pace while items are moving.

options.text: Watch the belt for another cycle and note any repeated slowing.
Tell the operator about the slowdown and where it happened.
Keep feeding items at the usual pace since the belt recovered.
Pause your loading and ask a nearby helper whether they saw it.

advanced.situation: During a long run, the machine's usual hum changes slightly and its indicator flickers once. A new operator is nearby, and production is on schedule.

options.text: Keep production running while watching the indicator and listening for further changes.
Ask the operator to review the indicator after the current production run ends.
Show the operator the flicker and ask them to consult the maintenance guide.
Record the sound and indicator change, then guide the operator through the preventive check.

basic.situation: After a routine production run, you see dust and a few scraps on your assigned work surface before the next batch arrives.

options.text: Ask a nearby helper to wipe the surface while you fetch supplies.
Brush the scraps aside so the next batch can start on time.
Wipe the surface and sweep the scraps into the marked bin.
Sweep the scraps now and leave the surface for the next break.

advanced.situation: A shared machine has several surfaces and attachments that need cleaning between product types. The team is unsure which areas are due during this shift.

options.text: Set a shift checklist by surface and attachment, then review completion with the team.
Use the usual wipe-down order and leave unfamiliar parts for maintenance staff.
Tell the next shift which parts looked dirty during today's run.
Clean the visible surfaces and ask the team to remember the attachments.

basic.situation: A light carton of finished products needs moving from storage to the packing area. A hand truck is free, and the route is clear.

options.text: Place the carton on the truck and push it quickly around the nearest aisle.
Ask a coworker to move it while you finish your current task.
Load the carton securely on the hand truck and follow the clear route.
Carry the carton yourself to avoid spending time setting up the hand truck.

advanced.situation: Several pallets must reach two work areas before a shift change. A new helper is unsure how to move the lighter cartons through a crowded aisle.

options.text: Move the urgent pallets first and tell the helper to follow your route.
Give the helper the shorter route and let them learn the lifting method.
Map a clear route for each area and demonstrate safe lifting and truck use.
Explain the lifting method, then send the helper with one carton.

basic.situation: You are placing items on a conveyor using the posted steps. One item sits crooked as the next pieces approach.

options.text: Hold the next item and ask the operator to check the crooked one.
Straighten the item and check its spacing against the posted steps.
Keep loading and let the next item push it into line.
Move the item closer to the belt edge to make room.

advanced.situation: At a faster line speed, items begin arriving unevenly and one catches briefly at the conveyor entry. The operator is occupied across the line.

options.text: Slow your loading rhythm and tell the operator about the catch.
Free the item only after checking the entry, then resume at a controlled pace.
Keep the same rhythm so output stays close to the shift target.
Space items evenly, pause feeding, and report where the catch occurred.

basic.situation: You are packing finished items into boxes. One piece of packaging waste has fallen beside the packing table as the next box is ready.

options.text: Box the item, then put the packaging waste in its marked bin.
Move the waste beneath the table to keep the walkway clear.
Ask a nearby coworker to collect the waste while you finish packing.
Finish a few more boxes, then collect the fallen waste during a quieter moment.

advanced.situation: A run is ending with several product sizes left to pack. The waste bin is nearly full, and the next shift needs a clear packing area.

options.text: Group sizes by box, use space well, and sort waste into marked streams.
Pack mixed sizes together to save boxes before the shift ends.
Pack the remaining sizes in sequence and leave the cleared area ready for handover.
Clear the bin, then pack each size as it arrives in sequence.

basic.situation: The daily schedule lists three workers for loading and two for receiving. One loader calls in sick before the morning delivery arrives.

options.text: Check who can switch roles, then report the gap to the manager.
Ask the remaining loaders to cover the delivery at their usual pace.
Move one scheduled receiver to loading and tell the team the revised duties.
Start the delivery with the available loaders and update the manager later.

advanced.situation: Two large deliveries are due close together while several workers are assigned to a slower task. You need to adjust today's plan without leaving another area uncovered.

options.text: Estimate each delivery's time and staffing, then stagger assignments around essential coverage.
Move two workers to the earlier delivery and review coverage later.
Shift all available workers to deliveries and ask another area to wait.
Keep the schedule and ask the delivery teams to work faster.

basic.situation: A pallet has arrived for a scheduled job. The work order lists a material size, and the label is difficult to read.

options.text: Set the pallet nearby and wait for the supervisor to review it.
Load the pallet since its label appears close to the listed size.
Ask a coworker to read the label while you prepare the next pallet.
Compare the label with the work order and flag the unreadable size.

advanced.situation: During a busy shift, a forklift's fork shows wear near its tip, and a loaded pallet is waiting. A newer worker asks whether the equipment meets specifications.

options.text: Ask the worker to report the fork wear before handling the waiting pallet.
Ask the worker to check the fork against inspection criteria before moving the waiting pallet.
Compare the fork with inspection criteria, record wear, and keep it out of service pending review.
Show the worker the worn tip and notify the equipment lead before use.

basic.situation: You are checking work during a routine shift and see a worker walking through a marked forklift lane while looking at a load sheet.

options.text: Remind the worker to use the marked walkway and tell the supervisor.
Ask a nearby worker to remind them while you continue the inspection.
Finish checking the next area, then mention the lane issue at handover.
Wait to see whether the worker notices the lane markings.

advanced.situation: Near shift end, a crowded unloading area has repeated near misses around a blind corner. Workers use different hand signals, and another load is expected soon.

options.text: Set a shared signal and route, brief the team, then monitor the next unloading cycle.
Continue unloading and record further near misses at shift end for the supervisor's review.
Tell workers to slow near the corner and use one agreed hand signal.
Ask experienced operators to guide each incoming load and reinforce the agreed signal.

basic.situation: You are recording shift hours when a worker says their recorded finish time is wrong and asks you to change the time sheet.

options.text: Check the roster and time record, note the concern, and refer it for confirmation.
Record the worker's concern and ask the manager to check the time.
Tell the worker you will ask the manager after payroll is prepared.
Change the time to what the worker remembers and complete the sheet.

advanced.situation: During a performance review, a worker disputes a rating and says a recent complaint was left out of the record. The appraisal is due today.

options.text: Add the complaint to the file, then ask the manager to review it.
Pause the appraisal, explain what evidence is needed, and set a follow-up date.
Review the supporting records together, record the worker's response, and refer open points.
Check the records with the worker, note their response, and explain review channels.

basic.situation: You receive a work order for a morning shift with two loading tasks and one changed storage location. Workers are gathering before duties begin.

options.text: Read out the tasks and point workers toward the updated storage area.
Ask a senior worker to explain the changed location after loading starts.
Tell workers to start the familiar loading tasks and check the location later.
Read the order aloud and explain each task and the changed location.

advanced.situation: A delivery arrives with fewer pallets than the order lists, and two departments are waiting for materials. Your team is about to begin its shift briefing.

options.text: Continue the briefing and let each department discover the short count.
Tell both departments the short count and share the revised delivery plan.
Ask the waiting teams to keep working on their current tasks for now.
Notify the receiving team about the short count and check other teams later.

basic.situation: A new worker is assigned to help with moving materials. They are unsure which walkway to use and ask you before their first trip.

options.text: Point out the walkway sign and let the worker follow the others.
Ask an experienced worker to give the new starter a quick briefing.
Show the marked route and walk through the safe handling steps together.
Tell the worker to take the nearest clear path with the load.

advanced.situation: Two applicants have relevant experience, but one has less documented equipment work. The hiring manager asks you to review their credentials and recommend who should be interviewed.

options.text: Review both applicants against interview criteria, then recommend a fair interview order.
Compare their equipment experience with role requirements before recommending either applicant for interviews.
Summarize each applicant's relevant experience and ask the manager to make the interview decision.
Compare both applicants' stated experience with the role criteria and recommend interviews fairly.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to draft a recycling goal for a new office collection plan. The budget is tight, and last month's collection figures are available.

options.text: Match the target to collection figures and budget, then set a monthly review.
Promise a large diversion target in the plan to help secure staff support.
Draft a modest target from last month's figures and flag the budget limits.
Reuse last year's target and adjust it slightly for the new office.

advanced.situation: A food court asks whether your programme can collect used cooking oil. You have no local collection data, and the nearest processor has not confirmed its requirements.

options.text: Add the oil stream to next month's collection plan and ask staff to track volumes.
Tell the food court you can collect the oil and confirm details later.
Ask the processor about its requirements and draft a possible collection proposal.
Map likely volumes and handling needs, then check processor requirements before proposing a trial.

basic.situation: Two drivers call in sick before the morning collection. Several stops have narrow access, and you need to help assign the available drivers and technicians.

options.text: Assign familiar routes by driver experience and note which stops need a smaller vehicle.
Send the full route sheet to the first available driver to save time.
Split the uncovered stops between available drivers and call about tight-access locations.
Give each available driver a route from the printed schedule and inform the team.

advanced.situation: A new technician is assigned to a baler after a minor jam. The team has different ways of isolating equipment before clearing it, and the next load is waiting.

options.text: Ask the experienced technician to clear the jam while the newcomer observes.
Pause the task, demonstrate the site procedure, then watch each technician practise it.
Review the written isolation steps with the team before the next load.
Let the newcomer copy the quickest method used by nearby staff.

basic.situation: A processor changes its receiving hours for Friday. Your collection team has already planned several loads, and you are asked to help update the material movement schedule.

options.text: Keep the old schedule and mark the processor's new hours for next week.
Move all Friday loads to the earliest available slot on the shared schedule.
Shift the affected loads to the new hours and tell drivers about the change.
Rework Friday's collection slots around receiving hours and confirm space with the processor.

advanced.situation: A grant-funded waste programme is halfway through its timeline, but one site has delayed installation. The sponsor's reporting date is near, and you must prepare a progress update.

options.text: Submit the completed milestones and note that one installation remains pending.
Compare milestones with site evidence, explain the delay, and outline a dated recovery plan.
Ask the site for a new date and hold the update until it replies.
Report the planned installation date and add the delay after the site confirms it.

basic.situation: A forklift load of sorted cardboard needs moving to a marked storage bay. Your supervisor is nearby, and another pallet is waiting in the aisle.

options.text: Check the marked bay and load stability, then move the pallet with your supervisor nearby.
Follow the floor arrows and move the pallet into the first open marked bay.
Move the pallet to the nearest open space so the aisle clears quickly.
Ask your supervisor to confirm the bay, then move the pallet at a steady pace.

advanced.situation: After a baler processes a mixed load, the shipping weight on the bill of lading differs from the dispatch log. The truck is due to leave soon.

options.text: Change the bill to match the dispatch log so the truck can leave on time.
Recheck the scale ticket against the log and bill, then update the matching record before release.
Hold the bill, compare the scale ticket and log, and report the mismatch.
Use the scale ticket as the shipping weight and file the mismatch for later review.

basic.situation: A shop requests an extra recycling pickup because its usual bin is full. You can see the service schedule, but the caller has not said what material is overflowing.

options.text: Ask which material and how much is overflowing, then arrange a suitable collection slot.
Book the usual truck for another pickup at the shop's normal time.
Ask what is overflowing and pass the details to the collection team.
Mark the request as handled because the shop already has a scheduled pickup.

advanced.situation: A resident reports repeated dumping beside a recycling drop-off point. Your inspection finds fresh bags nearby, but no clear link to a particular household or business.

options.text: Record dates, locations, and observations, then check the site and follow the investigation process.
Name the nearest shop in the report so enforcement can respond quickly.
Photograph the bags and note the resident's account for the case file.
Ask nearby businesses whether they saw anything and add their replies to the file.

basic.situation: You are preparing a short presentation for a residents' group that keeps mixing recyclable items with food scraps. The organiser has asked for practical examples.

options.text: Tell residents that all dry household items belong in the recycling bin.
Build the talk around local sorting examples and show where residents can check collection guidance.
Use the leaflet's examples and invite the group to ask questions at the end.
Read the sorting rules from the existing leaflet and finish within the time slot.

advanced.situation: A waste contractor proposes a longer collection term with a revised rate. You are authorised to discuss service terms, and your manager needs a clear comparison before approving any agreement.

options.text: Ask for more time and compare the monthly rates with the current contract.
Summarise both offers, ask the contractor to clarify service scope, and note implications for collection coverage.
Accept the lower monthly rate by email so the contractor holds the offer.
Compare rates, service scope, and exit terms, then seek an offer aligned with programme needs.

basic.situation: The morning shift schedule lists three loading jobs and two available operators. You are asked to assign the jobs using the posted sequence and equipment plan.

options.text: Use the posted sequence to split the jobs and tell operators their start times.
Assign both operators to the first job so it finishes ahead of schedule.
Give the first operator the earliest job and send the other operator to the next one.
Match operators to the listed equipment and sequence, then check each understands the first job.

advanced.situation: A late delivery changes the order of a loading plan, and one machine is due for servicing during the shift. You need to revise the work sequence around both constraints.

options.text: Check the revised delivery date and service slot before updating the job sequence.
Recheck shipping dates and machine availability, then sequence jobs to protect urgent loads and service time.
Keep the original sequence and ask the next shift to absorb any unfinished loads.
Move the late delivery to the end of the sequence and keep other jobs unchanged.

basic.situation: Before a shift, you notice a loose guard on a vehicle used to move pallets. A new operator is waiting, and your supervisor is checking other equipment.

options.text: Tell the supervisor about the guard and wait for their direction before assigning it.
Ask the new operator to use the vehicle slowly for one short trip.
Keep the vehicle parked, record the loose guard, and ask maintenance to inspect it.
Tag the vehicle for checking and use another machine for the first pallet.

advanced.situation: A field crew is moving oversized metal stock, but the load dimensions differ from the handling note. The work area is busy, and a second vehicle is approaching.

options.text: Use the handling note and continue the move before the other vehicle arrives.
Ask the crew to remeasure the stock and tell the approaching vehicle to wait.
Pause that move, verify dimensions and handling needs, then coordinate a clear path for the load.
Have the crew shift the stock to the side while you check the dimensions.

basic.situation: At shift end, your activity log is missing one operator's finish time. The crew has left, and the daily report is due before handover.

options.text: Check the time sheet or dispatch log, enter the supported time, and flag any gap.
Enter the time from yesterday's shift because this crew usually finishes together.
Mark the time as pending and tell the manager the report needs follow-up.
Use the scheduled finish time so the report can be submitted before handover.

advanced.situation: Weekly reports show a rise in handling delays, but crew logs use different labels for the same stoppages. Your manager asks you to identify where the time is going.

options.text: Remove unclear stoppages from the totals so the report has a clean trend line.
Standardise stoppage categories, reconcile past entries, then compare delay patterns by job and shift.
Ask each crew to explain its labels and postpone the analysis until replies arrive.
Group similar labels and compare the weekly totals by shift for the manager.

basic.situation: A supervisor asks you to move a parked yard vehicle to the next loading bay. You have operated it before, but the bay is crowded with pallets.

options.text: Ask a nearby worker to guide you while you move slowly toward the bay.
Drive through the shortest gap and ask nearby workers to move pallets as needed.
Check the route and bay clearance, then move the vehicle at a controlled pace.
Wait for the bay to look less busy before moving the vehicle across.

advanced.situation: A loader begins losing hydraulic pressure while lifting a routine pallet. You are qualified to operate it, and the next load is waiting nearby.

options.text: Stop the lift, lower the pallet, and call the supervisor to inspect the loader.
Lower the pallet and switch to another machine while noting the loader's symptoms.
Finish the lift at reduced speed and report the pressure issue after the load is placed.
Lower the load safely, park the loader, and report the pressure change for maintenance review.

basic.situation: A new worker asks how to secure a load before a short trip across the yard. The checklist is posted nearby, and you are covering the shift briefing.

options.text: Tell the worker to copy the last load because it made the same short trip.
Point to the checklist and tell the worker to follow its instructions for this load.
Use the checklist to demonstrate each securing step, then ask the worker to show the sequence.
Review the checklist with the worker and answer questions before the trip starts.

advanced.situation: Several new operators are joining the night shift, and recent work orders require a different sequence for handling fragile stock. You can arrange training tasks and requisition supplies.

options.text: Assign the new operators to fragile stock on their first shift to build confidence quickly.
Demonstrate the sequence on one load and ask an experienced operator to coach the group.
Send the operators the written procedure and ask them to read it before their first shift.
Build practice around the work orders, check operators' performance, and request needed handling supplies.

basic.situation: Two operators disagree over who caused a delayed loading job, and the argument is slowing the next task. You are the shift supervisor on duty.

options.text: Ask each operator to explain the delay, then pass their accounts to the manager.
Separate the operators and ask the senior manager to resolve the disagreement later.
Tell both operators to stop arguing and assign the next task to the faster worker.
Hear each account briefly, restate the next task, and agree who will handle each part.

advanced.situation: A radio report says a vehicle has stalled at a busy loading entrance during a shift change. You have two available workers and one spare vehicle to coordinate.

options.text: Send both workers to move the stalled vehicle before shift traffic builds.
Ask one worker to assess the vehicle and radio back before assigning help.
Dispatch a trained worker in the spare vehicle and keep the entrance clear.
Use the spare vehicle to assist, while gate staff direct traffic around the entrance.

basic.situation: Before boarding, you check a batch of seat-belt extensions and find one with frayed stitching. What do you do?

options.text: Use the checklist to inspect every extension and report the frayed stitching.
Mark it serviceable after a quick glance and continue the boarding process.
Ask a colleague to review it, then note their view for the shift.
Compare each extension with the checklist, set the damaged one aside, and notify the lead.

advanced.situation: Different teams record the same cabin-equipment defect in different ways, delaying follow-up. You are asked to guide a consistent inspection process.

options.text: Copy last month's checklist and ask teams to use it for every item.
Write clear defect categories and show attendants how to record each finding.
Let each team keep its preferred notes and reconcile them after the shift.
Set inspection criteria, define defect escalation, and coach teams through sample findings.

basic.situation: During boarding, an attendant's uniform appears untidy, and a passenger says the greeting felt abrupt. Your supervisor is nearby.

options.text: Record the specific observations and passenger feedback, then review them privately with your supervisor.
Record the attendant as fully compliant so the shift report stays uncomplicated.
Note what you observed and ask your supervisor to review the service standard with you.
Tell the attendant to improve their appearance before the next boarding begins.

advanced.situation: An attendant has repeated service complaints, but your manager asks you to gather evidence before any formal disciplinary review.

options.text: Issue a formal warning yourself so the recurring complaints receive prompt attention.
Ask nearby colleagues for general impressions and summarize the shared view.
Organize dated evidence, invite the attendant's account, and present both for the review.
Compile dated examples against service expectations and submit them for the review.

basic.situation: A passenger says an attendant gave confusing directions to the transfer gate. Your supervisor asks you to help record the complaint.

options.text: Ask the passenger what was said and note the time, location, and concern.
Listen without interrupting, note the details, and ask what help would resolve the concern.
Apologize for the confusion and tell the passenger the attendant was busy.
Close the complaint as resolved because the passenger found the gate eventually.

advanced.situation: Several passengers report confusion about transfer directions at the same counter during peak hours. You are reviewing feedback for service improvements.

options.text: Treat each comment as a separate case and close it after replying to passengers.
Compare feedback across shifts, pinpoint the confusing step, and propose a targeted service change.
Group the comments by time and counter, then suggest clearer transfer signs.
Ask the counter team to remind passengers about transfers during busy periods.

basic.situation: At the end of a busy shift, your supervisor gives you a form to record attendants' late arrivals and completed trips.

options.text: Enter estimated arrivals and trips so the report reaches the manager on time.
Fill the form from memory while the shift details are still familiar.
Match each entry to the shift notes, mark unclear details, and submit the verified totals.
Check the shift notes, enter each arrival and trip, and total the figures.

advanced.situation: Supervisors receive weekly activity reports with inconsistent labels for delays and service incidents. You are asked to improve reporting across shifts.

options.text: Ask each shift to add clearer notes using its current report format.
Create shared labels and a template, then explain how teams should enter figures.
Define common fields, add simple validation prompts, and train staff using sample reports.
Merge the different reports into one file and leave the labels unchanged.

basic.situation: A new attendant is unsure how to secure a passenger's carry-on bag before departure. You have been asked to demonstrate the task.

options.text: Explain the steps verbally while the attendant watches the boarding queue.
Demonstrate the approved steps, observe a practice run, and discuss missed points.
Tell the attendant to copy a nearby colleague's approach during boarding.
Show the approved steps, then let the new attendant practise with feedback.

advanced.situation: A new policy changes how attendants support passengers who need extra time boarding. Experienced staff have questions about applying it consistently.

options.text: Summarize the policy and ask experienced attendants to share their usual approaches.
Send the policy link and let each attendant review it before the shift.
Build short practice cases around the policy and coach staff on consistent responses.
Tell staff to continue their usual routines until passenger feedback shows a problem.

basic.situation: Two attendants are assigned to the same gate while another gate is short-staffed. Your supervisor asks you to coordinate coverage for boarding.

options.text: Leave the roster as shown and let the gate teams work it out.
Check the roster and ask your supervisor where to move one attendant.
Check both boarding schedules, coordinate a temporary move, and update the supervisor.
Move an attendant to the quieter gate so both teams have some support.

advanced.situation: One team is covering repeated peak departures while another has quiet periods. You can propose shift adjustments and small service improvements.

options.text: Review departure peaks and rotate duties so attendants share demanding periods.
Give the busiest team fewer breaks so departures remain fully covered.
Keep current assignments and ask the busy team to maintain its pace.
Match staffing to departure peaks, rotate duties, and invite team input.

basic.situation: During the pre-flight walkaround, you notice a damaged access-panel latch. Your senior pilot is reviewing the checklist with you.

options.text: Mark the panel as serviceable and continue preparations to keep departure on schedule.
Ask the ground crew whether the latch usually looks like that before boarding.
Record the defect, pause acceptance, and seek the maintenance disposition through your senior pilot.
Record the latch damage on the checklist and report it to your senior pilot.

advanced.situation: A recurring warning appears during checks after a recent repair, but the maintenance entry is unclear. You are preparing to accept the aircraft.

options.text: Accept the aircraft since the warning did not affect the previous flight.
Ask maintenance control to clarify the entry and note the response for the crew.
Hold acceptance until maintenance records a clear disposition, then brief the crew on it.
Review the previous flight notes and see whether another crew reported the warning.

basic.situation: During a flight, you notice fuel use differs from the planned figure. Your senior pilot is monitoring the other instruments.

options.text: Call out the fuel reading and compare it with the planned figure.
Note the reading, then tell your senior pilot at the next check.
Change the log entry to match planned fuel use and continue monitoring.
Call out the reading, track its trend, and alert your senior pilot to the variance.

advanced.situation: An engine indication begins fluctuating while fuel use rises above its recent trend. You are monitoring the instruments with the captain.

options.text: Focus on the engine display and ask the captain to watch fuel use.
Report both trends, cross-check related indications, and support the captain's checklist actions.
Silence the alert and keep the flight profile unchanged until the next waypoint.
Call out both indications and suggest checking the relevant abnormal procedure.

basic.situation: During a training leg, your instructor asks you to hold a steady heading while following the planned route.

options.text: Turn toward a landmark you recognize and leave the planned route for now.
Ask the instructor to repeat the heading while you maintain the current controls.
Hold the assigned heading on instruments, report any drift, and follow the instructor's corrections.
Make small control inputs and check the heading against the instruments.
