advanced.situation: Cloud thickens and outside references disappear during a route segment. You are pilot flying and have functioning flight instruments.

options.text: Cross-check attitude and navigation instruments, hold the cleared route, and call out any deviation.
Steer toward the last visible landmark until the outside view improves.
Use the instruments to maintain the cleared route and advise the other pilot.
Reduce attention to the instruments while searching briefly for a break in cloud.

basic.situation: During approach, the captain assigns you a checklist call while the cabin crew reports a passenger issue. You are the monitoring pilot.

options.text: Acknowledge the checklist call and tell the captain the cabin report is pending.
Complete the assigned call, acknowledge the cabin report, and relay it when workload permits.
Finish the checklist item first and ask the cabin crew to call again later.
Skip the checklist response and handle the passenger issue through the cabin phone.

advanced.situation: During cruise, two crew members give conflicting timing for a cabin service change, and the captain asks you to coordinate the response.

options.text: Tell the cabin team to follow whichever timing they used on the previous flight.
Ask each crew member to explain their timing and relay both accounts to the captain.
Choose one timing without telling the other crew member to avoid further debate.
Confirm the captain's direction, communicate one timing to both crew members, and check their acknowledgment.

basic.situation: You are preparing for departure and need a takeoff clearance. Your senior pilot is beside you as you tune the radio.

options.text: Check the assigned frequency, request clearance, and read back the instruction received.
Ask your senior pilot to make the call while you monitor the radio panel.
Transmit readiness and taxi toward the runway before receiving clearance from control.
Tune assigned frequency, request clearance, read it back, and confirm with your senior pilot.

advanced.situation: A system warning appears in flight and the crew begins the relevant checklist. You are assigned to make the radio call and coordinate with dispatch.

options.text: Ask dispatch for advice before telling control about the warning or position.
Wait for the warning to clear before reporting it to control or updating dispatch.
Tell control the warning, position, and intentions, then update dispatch when workload allows.
Report the warning and aircraft position to control, then update dispatch when able.

basic.situation: After landing, you need to enter the flight time, distance, and fuel use in the log book before handing it over.

options.text: Fill in the figures from the flight plan while the details are familiar.
Copy the previous flight's time, distance, and fuel figures into today's log book before handover.
Use the recorded flight data to enter times, distance, and fuel consumption.
Reconcile recorded times, distance, and fuel use, then flag any uncertain entry before handover.

advanced.situation: You are assigned to brief newly approved trainee pilots on route planning, and one trainee asks how to balance speed and smoothness.

options.text: Explain how route, altitude, and speed choices shape a smooth flight, using an approved example.
Share your recent route choice and explain how it balanced speed and passenger comfort.
Discuss planning tradeoffs with an approved example, then ask about one route choice.
Tell the trainee to choose the fastest available route for each trip.

basic.situation: During a guided pre-flight check, you notice an engine reading fluctuating near its usual range. The departure is scheduled soon.

options.text: Ask a mechanic to inspect it before you release the aircraft.
Run the checklist again, then treat the brief vibration as normal.
Compare the reading with limits and report the finding to the captain.
Repeat the engine check with the checklist and record the vibration.

advanced.situation: During a scheduled in-flight equipment test in rough weather, a control response differs from the expected result, and visibility is falling.

options.text: Repeat the test at the next planned altitude and note the response.
Record the result and tell the captain before continuing the test.
Complete the remaining checks, then summarize all results after landing.
Pause that test and ask the captain whether to repeat it.

basic.situation: You are helping prepare a flight plan when updated weather and fuel figures arrive, changing the expected departure time.

options.text: Use the earlier figures and mention the update during the briefing.
Update the plan with the new figures and flag the timing change.
Ask the dispatcher which figures should go into the flight plan.
Recheck fuel, weather, and schedule together before drafting the route.

advanced.situation: Two routes are available: one is faster but crosses forecast turbulence, while the other adds time and has more stable conditions.

options.text: Choose the faster route and brief the crew about the turbulence.
Take the stable route and keep the planned speed and altitude.
Keep the filed route to avoid delaying the departure schedule.
Compare route, altitude, and speed options against safety and timing.

basic.situation: With a senior pilot beside you, you are assigned to start the engines and operate the controls during a routine departure preparation.

options.text: Start the engines and move through the controls at your usual pace.
Wait for the senior pilot to handle the controls while you observe.
Follow the start sequence while confirming each control response aloud.
Use the checklist and ask about any control response that feels unfamiliar.

advanced.situation: During a scheduled co-pilot leg, the captain asks you to take the controls while following the filed plan in changing visibility.

options.text: Take control and keep the aircraft aligned with the flight plan.
Confirm the handover, then fly by instruments and call out deviations.
Take the controls and check the instruments against the planned track.
Ask the captain to retain control until visibility becomes clearer.

basic.situation: On a routine flight, you and the co-pilot notice fuel consumption running slightly above the planned figure.

options.text: Check fuel flow and system indications, then update the co-pilot.
Compare fuel use with the plan and tell the co-pilot the trend.
Recheck the gauge after a short interval before raising it.
Record the reading at the next scheduled monitoring point.

advanced.situation: Several hours into a flight, a system warning appears alongside rising fuel use, but the indications do not point to one clear cause.

options.text: Review related indications and brief the captain on the combined trend.
Track the fuel trend and ask the captain to review the warning.
Check the warning guide and wait for another reading before reporting.
Reset the warning and watch whether fuel use settles down.

basic.situation: You are using the radio with guidance and need takeoff clearance, but the tower transmission is partly obscured by static.

options.text: Wait for the next transmission before contacting the tower again.
Ask the tower to repeat the clearance and read it back clearly.
Tell the senior pilot the message was unclear and ask them to call.
Request the clearance again and note the runway they mention.

advanced.situation: A weather change affects your route while traffic is building, and the planned altitude may no longer be suitable.

options.text: Request a route change and include the weather reason and preferred level.
Ask for a different route and follow the clearance received.
Request a lower altitude first, then explain the weather concern.
Alter course toward clearer skies while monitoring nearby traffic.

basic.situation: After a routine flight, you are completing the flight record with a senior pilot and notice the fuel figure differs from your notes.

options.text: Enter the figure from memory and finish the record before debrief.
Mark the fuel entry for review and complete the other fields.
Check the notes against the instrument reading and enter the supported figure.
Ask the senior pilot which fuel figure seems more likely.

advanced.situation: A crew member reports a recurring equipment issue after landing, and the next flight is planned before a major maintenance slot opens.

options.text: Ask the crew member to repeat the check before deciding what to record.
Tell the captain and record the crew member's description of the issue.
Note the issue for the next crew and keep the aircraft schedule intact.
Record the reported issue and arrange the required maintenance through the captain.

basic.situation: You are directing a pilot toward a runway, but another aircraft is still taxiing across the route you planned to use.

options.text: Hold the taxiing aircraft clear and confirm the crossing before directing the pilot.
Ask the crossing aircraft to report when it has passed the route.
Direct the pilot to wait near the runway entrance for a gap.
Send the pilot along the planned route while monitoring both aircraft.

advanced.situation: Several aircraft are taxiing near a maintenance vehicle, and a departing flight is building pressure on the runway queue.

options.text: Route the nearest aircraft around the vehicle and watch the queue.
Sequence the taxiing aircraft around the vehicle, then update the runway queue.
Ask ground crews to move the vehicle before releasing more traffic.
Hold all aircraft until the vehicle leaves the taxi area.

basic.situation: During a routine shift, a pilot reports weak radio reception while you are checking the assigned frequency equipment.

options.text: Inspect the radio connections and tell the pilot you are checking.
Ask the pilot to repeat messages while you continue monitoring.
Switch to a nearby frequency and continue the exchange there.
Check the frequency setting and test reception with the pilot.

advanced.situation: An adjacent control unit reports a developing traffic conflict near your boundary while one of your pilots requests a route update.

options.text: Tell the pilot to maintain course while you contact the adjacent unit.
Coordinate the boundary traffic with the adjacent unit before updating your pilot.
Give the pilot a route change based on your display, then call the unit.
Ask the adjacent unit to call again after you answer the pilot.

basic.situation: You are completing the daily activity report and notice that one aircraft message has no time recorded in your notes.

options.text: Check the message log for its time and complete the report entry.
Mark the entry for follow-up and finish the remaining report fields.
Ask a colleague whether they remember when the message arrived.
Leave the time blank and submit the report before shift change.

advanced.situation: While reviewing a shift report, you find two conflicting altitude entries and a message summary that could be read in two ways.

options.text: Choose the altitude that appears most consistent and file the report.
Flag both entries for review and keep the report in draft.
Rewrite the summary in simpler words and ask a colleague to check it.
Compare the entries with source records and clarify the summary before filing.

basic.situation: You are monitoring radar during a routine arrival when one aircraft's track briefly becomes less distinct near the edge of your display.

options.text: Check the track against available radar and visual references, then keep monitoring.
Keep watching the display and wait for the track to sharpen.
Assume the aircraft has left your sector and turn to arrivals.
Note the brief change and tell the next controller at handover.

advanced.situation: A pilot requests a higher altitude while traffic is crossing above and weather is reducing visibility at another level.

options.text: Check the requested level for traffic and then advise the pilot.
Check traffic and conditions across the requested level before responding.
Ask the pilot to remain level while you review the crossing traffic.
Approve the climb based on the clear space shown at your level.

basic.situation: A pilot reports wind and visibility worsening near the destination, with another aircraft nearby on the approach.

options.text: Wait for another pilot report before sending a weather update.
Report the visibility concern and ask the pilot to confirm receipt.
Share worsening visibility and wind, noting nearby traffic on approach.
Tell the pilot conditions are worsening and suggest slowing down.

advanced.situation: An aircraft overdue on a routine arrival has not responded to calls, and search coordination is beginning across nearby sectors.

options.text: Keep calling the aircraft while waiting for another sector to take charge.
Notify adjacent units of the overdue aircraft and its planned route.
Ask a nearby unit whether it has seen the aircraft recently.
Share its last known details with adjacent units and coordinate search coverage.

basic.situation: You are organizing plans for aircraft expected to enter your assigned airspace, and two arrival times now overlap on the same route.

options.text: Keep both expected times and monitor the arrivals as they approach.
Ask the next shift to decide which aircraft should enter first.
Flag the overlap and prepare to adjust one entry time.
Review both plans and organize their entry timing for manageable traffic.

advanced.situation: A new controller is learning to organize incoming flight plans during a busy period and asks you how to handle overlapping entries.

options.text: Tell them to copy the previous shift's timing pattern for now.
Answer their question briefly, then return to your own traffic screen.
Walk through a sample overlap and explain how you sequence the entries.
Give the new controller a written checklist to use during the shift.

basic.situation: An aircraft has landed, but its parking stand is still being confirmed. You need to relay its arrival status to the controlling agency.

options.text: Tell maintenance the aircraft landed, then update control when confirmed.
Share the estimated time from the last radio call to save time.
Send the confirmed arrival time and stand assignment to the control desk.
Check the latest movement log, then relay the verified arrival and stand.

advanced.situation: Runway snow clearance is falling behind while taxiway work continues. You are coordinating updates between operations, maintenance, and air traffic control.

options.text: Compare crew progress reports, then align clearance priorities with control and maintenance.
Ask maintenance to finish its current pass before sharing a revised runway estimate.
Tell control the runway is clear so arrivals can keep moving.
Send control the latest maintenance estimate and ask crews to confirm progress.

basic.situation: A crew asks which stand is assigned and whether the usual flight-planning information is available before departure. You are supporting the airfield desk.

options.text: Suggest a likely stand based on the usual aircraft parking pattern.
Read the stand from yesterday's sheet and pass it to the crew.
Share the current stand, then direct the crew to the operations desk.
Give the crew the confirmed stand and current airfield information for planning.

advanced.situation: A mobile airfield inspection finds a lighting fault as a crew requests flight-planning information. You are managing the operation with several agencies involved.

options.text: Tell the crew about the fault and request an updated departure estimate.
Keep the mobile team moving and tell the crew to check back later.
Coordinate the fault response across agencies, then give the crew verified planning details.
Mark the affected area clear so the crew can depart on schedule.

basic.situation: An arriving aircraft is taxiing toward its assigned parking area, where another aircraft is still being serviced. You are monitoring its arrival and parking.

options.text: Ask the crew to use the nearest open stand and update the log.
Confirm the serviced aircraft has vacated, then monitor arrival at the assigned stand.
Record the assigned stand as occupied by the arriving aircraft now.
Track the taxi and update the log once the aircraft parks.

advanced.situation: Two aircraft arrive close together; one needs refueling before loading, and the other is waiting to depart. You are monitoring their movement and servicing.

options.text: Mark both aircraft serviced and departed to clear the movement board.
Update the board after refueling, then watch the waiting departure.
Track each aircraft's position and service status, updating the board as movements change.
Let the departing aircraft queue behind the arriving aircraft for refueling.

basic.situation: During a perimeter walk, you find a gate standing open and have a checklist for the airport property inspection.

options.text: Close the gate, note its location, and report the access issue through procedure.
Finish the checklist, then return to the gate after the perimeter walk.
Record the open gate and tell the next shift to check it.
Mark the gate secure because the surrounding fence looks intact.

advanced.situation: A routine inspection finds uneven pavement near a taxiway edge, and the checklist does not clearly describe its severity. You are recording airfield conditions.

options.text: Document the uneven pavement and ask the inspection lead how to classify it.
Describe the defect, compare it with inspection criteria, and report its location for assessment.
Record the area as compliant because aircraft are still using the taxiway.
Photograph the pavement and note its location for a later inspection.

basic.situation: A vehicle stops near an aircraft stand after a worker reports feeling faint. You are on duty and need to assist with the response.

options.text: Stay with the worker and radio for help from the operations desk.
Ask a nearby colleague to check the worker while you finish your task.
Call the emergency contact, keep the area clear, and follow airfield procedures.
Move the worker to the nearest vehicle and drive them to the clinic.

advanced.situation: A bird flock gathers near an active runway while an aircraft is approaching. You are responsible for helping manage wildlife around the airfield.

options.text: Record the flock for the next patrol as the aircraft approaches the runway.
Report the flock to operations and control, then follow established wildlife procedures.
Advise control the runway is clear despite the flock near the active runway.
Notify control about the flock and monitor its movement from a safe position.

basic.situation: A small pavement repair is planned near a taxiway, and the site team asks where to stage equipment. You are helping plan the construction activity.

options.text: Tell the team to stage equipment beside the taxiway for easier access.
Ask the team to choose a spot and add it to your notes.
Confirm the work area and equipment staging with the site team and operations.
Share the proposed staging location with operations for a quick review.

advanced.situation: New operations staff are unsure how to complete the movement log, and several entries have been inconsistent. You are responsible for their training.

options.text: Show one example, then let staff learn the log during live operations.
Explain the log steps and answer questions during the next shift briefing.
Demonstrate the log, observe practice entries, and give specific feedback before duty.
Give staff the log guide and ask them to read it before duty.

basic.situation: A family is boarding, and a child is unsure which seat is theirs. You are helping passengers find their assigned seats.

options.text: Show the family the seat numbers and let them find the row.
Check the family’s boarding passes and guide them to their assigned seats.
Point them toward the nearest open row to keep boarding moving.
Ask another passenger where the family should sit, then guide them.

advanced.situation: During turbulence, a nervous passenger raises their voice while a nearby passenger asks for help stowing a bag. You need to keep the cabin calm and assist both.

options.text: Ask the nervous passenger to settle down while you stow the nearby bag.
Tell the nervous passenger everything is fine and continue serving the cabin.
Acknowledge the concern, explain the crew's guidance, and arrange help with the bag.
Reassure the passenger about turbulence, then ask a colleague to help nearby.

basic.situation: Before boarding, you notice crumbs and a loose panel in the cabin during your cleanliness and visible-problem check.

options.text: Wipe around the panel and mark the cabin ready for boarding.
Record both findings for the cabin team before passengers board.
Tell the cleaning team about both issues and wait for their update.
Clean the crumbs, report the panel, and follow the cabin check process.

advanced.situation: A passenger keeps reaching into a bag after the cabin check, and an emergency equipment seal appears disturbed nearby. You are monitoring cabin safety.

options.text: Observe the behavior, check the equipment through procedure, and alert the lead to findings.
Tell the lead about the behavior and disturbed seal for assessment.
Ask the passenger to put the bag away and continue the cabin walk.
Record the kit as ready because its compartment remains closed for now.

basic.situation: At the preflight briefing, the crew reviews emergency procedures and routes for the flight. You need to understand your role.

options.text: Use the route you remember from the last flight to save briefing time.
Review the briefing notes and confirm your assigned emergency route with the crew.
Listen to the briefing and write down the emergency route details.
Ask a colleague to explain the route after the briefing ends.

advanced.situation: After an emergency landing, passengers need assistance evacuating while one person appears distressed. You are coordinating crew actions during the response.

options.text: Pause passenger movement until the distressed person can explain what happened.
Follow the crew's evacuation roles and guide passengers to the designated usable exit.
Ask another crew member to manage the distressed passenger while you guide the aisle.
Direct passengers toward the usual exit and check the distressed person afterward.

basic.situation: The flight is delayed, and passengers ask when departure will resume. You have the latest approved update and need to announce it.

options.text: Ask passengers to check airport screens for the latest timing information.
Announce the approved delay update using standard cabin wording to passengers.
Share the approved delay update and say when passengers can expect another announcement.
Tell passengers the flight should leave soon based on the schedule.

advanced.situation: Several passengers appear unsure during the safety demonstration, including some who do not follow the spoken instructions easily. You are giving the briefing.

options.text: Ask a nearby passenger to explain the instructions to others afterward.
Repeat the demonstration more slowly while pointing out each safety feature.
Finish the standard demonstration at its usual pace to keep boarding on time.
Use clear gestures and simple wording, then invite questions about key safety steps.

basic.situation: A passenger's ticket destination is hard to read as you check travel details for the cabin report. You need to verify the information.

options.text: Set the ticket aside and complete the rest of the cabin report.
Ask the passenger to confirm the destination and note their answer.
Check the ticket against the passenger's itinerary, then record the verified destination.
Enter the most likely destination from the flight's usual passenger list.

advanced.situation: Recent cabin reports mention repeated audio problems in different sections. You are reviewing reports to identify a pattern for operational follow-up.

options.text: Count the reports and tell the team audio has been a problem lately.
Summarize the repeated audio reports and share them with the cabin lead.
Mark the audio system as working because the latest flight had sound.
Compare report dates and cabin sections, then summarize the recurring audio issue.

basic.situation: A passenger buys a beverage during service and offers cash. You need to collect payment using the provided system.

options.text: Ask a colleague to hold the cash while you continue serving.
Enter the beverage sale in the payment system and give the passenger a receipt.
Keep the cash with the service notes and enter the sale later.
Record the cash amount on the tally sheet for the cabin report.

advanced.situation: Blankets are running low on one flight, while unopened packs often return unused on another. You are checking supply levels across flights.

options.text: Keep the standard blanket quantity and note the shortage after service.
Tell crews to report blanket needs before the next flight loads.
Load extra blankets on every flight so crews have a larger reserve.
Record current counts and adjust future loading to match observed use.

basic.situation: You are driving an ambulance with a senior attendant beside you. A junction is busy, and the route card directs you to turn left.

options.text: Follow the senior driver's route and keep a steady, safe speed.
Keep to the route card and ask the senior to watch intersections.
Take a shortcut through a busy market lane to save time.
Match speed to road conditions, signal clearly, and confirm route changes with the senior.

advanced.situation: A newly assigned driver is taking an ambulance to hospital in heavy rain. You are accompanying them and notice they are approaching bends too quickly.

options.text: Ask them to maintain the posted speed and continue the trip as planned.
Tell them to follow the vehicle ahead and keep the warning lights on.
Review the safe-driving protocol with them after the ambulance reaches hospital safely.
Explain how to slow before bends, increase following distance, and adjust speed to visibility.

basic.situation: You and another attendant need to place a patient with a painful leg injury onto a stretcher before loading the ambulance.

options.text: Coordinate with your partner, explain each move, and support the injured leg during transfer.
Lift together on a count and secure the patient before loading the stretcher.
Slide the patient onto the stretcher quickly so the ambulance can leave.
Ask the patient to move toward the stretcher while you guide their injured leg.

advanced.situation: A distressed patient is trying to leave the ambulance bay. Your partner suggests restraints, and you need to help manage the patient safely.

options.text: Ask your partner to hold the patient while you prepare the stretcher.
Keep space, speak calmly, and follow the approved restraint procedure with your partner.
Move close and hold the patient's arms while your partner fetches restraints.
Use calm words and ask the patient to sit while your partner stands nearby.

basic.situation: An EMT asks you to help bandage a patient's forearm cut while they assess the patient at the scene.

options.text: Wrap the cut firmly with gauze and return to the equipment bag.
Apply a clean bandage as the EMT directs and report any change you notice.
Ask the EMT to check your bandage placement before you secure it.
Place gauze over the cut and hold it while the EMT continues assessment.

advanced.situation: At a roadside collision, an EMT is treating a patient with a bleeding arm while another patient waits nearby. You are asked to support first aid.

options.text: Keep the arm supported and ask the EMT where your help is most useful.
Hold gauze on the arm and ask a bystander to watch the other patient.
Check both patients, report urgent changes, and assist the EMT with directed first aid.
Finish bandaging the arm before checking the other patient or updating the EMT.

basic.situation: Before a shift, your checklist shows the ambulance washer fluid is low. You have been shown how to top it up.

options.text: Ask a colleague to confirm the recommended fluid before topping it up.
Top up the washer fluid as shown and record the check on the vehicle sheet.
Mark the washer fluid as low and tell the next shift to refill it.
Add water from a nearby bottle and leave the checklist for later.

advanced.situation: You are checking several ambulances after a busy shift. One has a loose mirror, while a new attendant is unsure how to inspect minor faults.

options.text: Ask the attendant to check mirrors while you inspect fluids and lights.
Demonstrate checks for visible faults, record findings, and report repairs beyond your role.
Inspect each vehicle yourself and note the loose mirror for maintenance staff.
Show the attendant the checklist and ask them to initial each vehicle after inspection.

basic.situation: After a patient transfer, you find soiled linen on the stretcher and the ambulance is due for another call soon.

options.text: Replace the linen, clean the contact area, and restock the used disposable items.
Fold the soiled linen into a bag and use the spare sheet for now.
Remove the linen and ask your partner to replace the disposable items.
Replace the linen and note the used supplies for the next vehicle check.

advanced.situation: A new attendant is cleaning the ambulance after a spill and replacing supplies. You have been asked to guide their hygiene routine between calls.

options.text: Demonstrate the cleaning sequence, then verify restocking before the ambulance returns to service.
Let them finish the cabin and check the supplies at the end of the shift.
Give them the hygiene checklist and ask them to initial each section.
Ask them to spray the spill area and replace the nearest used items.

basic.situation: After a minor roadside collision, hospital staff ask what you observed while transporting the patient. You have the trip details and times.

options.text: Tell them the collision happened nearby and the patient seemed shaken.
Say the other driver caused it and provide the patient's arrival time.
Share the trip times and ask the hospital staff what else they need.
Give the observed facts and times, separating them from what others told you.

advanced.situation: A colleague asks you to draft an account of a complex emergency call for hospital staff. You saw the transfer but heard some details from others.

options.text: Write the main events from memory and send the account for a quick review.
Record the times you witnessed and ask colleagues to add their own observations.
Draft the timeline, label firsthand observations, and attribute details reported by others.
Write a smooth narrative that combines the team's observations into one account.

basic.situation: You are driving a delivery truck on a familiar route when a roadworks sign directs traffic onto a narrow side street.

options.text: Slow down, follow the signed diversion, and check your route sheet before turning.
Follow the signed diversion, then call dispatch from a safe stopping place.
Wait for a safe gap, then turn back toward the original route.
Take the side street cautiously and leave space behind the vehicle ahead.

advanced.situation: You are planning deliveries after a bridge restriction changes the truck route. A customer needs a time-sensitive order, and the detour adds distance.

options.text: Use the posted detour and tell the customer the order may arrive later.
Ask dispatch for a revised sequence after checking the truck-accessible detour.
Follow the car navigation's shortest route and keep the delivery sequence unchanged.
Check the restriction, recalculate the route, and update delivery estimates using safe truck roads.

basic.situation: During a scheduled stop, you notice a drink machine is dirty inside. Your supervisor has shown you the cleaning steps.

options.text: Use the cleaning cloth and finish the inside before you restock the drinks.
Wipe the visible front and refill the machine for the next customer.
Clean the machine using the shown steps and check the surfaces before refilling.
Ask a colleague to clean it while you complete the delivery paperwork.

advanced.situation: A machine stops dispensing drinks during your route. A new coworker is with you, and you know basic cleaning but have not handled this fault before.

options.text: Reset the machine several times and ask the coworker to watch for a change.
Show the coworker the basic checks, then report the unresolved fault for service.
Review the notes, make a basic check, and report the fault if it continues.
Ask the coworker to check the power while you review the machine notes.

basic.situation: You are loading a delivery truck from a customer list. Two nearby orders have similar names and different quantities.

options.text: Ask a coworker to read the list while you load both orders together.
Check the names against the list and keep the similar orders apart.
Load the larger order first and sort out the labels at the stop.
Match each order to its address and quantity before placing it in the truck.

advanced.situation: A truck has chilled and fragile goods for several stops. A last-minute order is added, and you need to revise the loading sequence.

options.text: Place the new order on top and rearrange the stops during the route.
Keep the original load sequence and ask dispatch to deliver the new order later.
Reorder the load by stop, keeping chilled and fragile goods protected and accessible.
Move the fragile goods aside and fit the new order near the rear doors.

basic.situation: A regular customer places an order for two cases, but the written form shows three. You are completing the order before leaving.

options.text: Confirm the quantity with the customer and update the order form before dispatch.
Use the form quantity and note the customer's spoken amount on your route sheet.
Call the office to check the previous order before completing this form.
Ask the customer to initial the form beside the changed quantity.

advanced.situation: Your daily delivery record shows a cash sale that does not match the signed customer receipt. You are closing the route paperwork.

options.text: Check the receipt total and leave a note for the next day's paperwork.
Compare the receipt and record, document the difference, and report it through the usual process.
Keep both figures and ask the office to review them during reconciliation.
Adjust the daily total to match the cash counted at the end of the route.

basic.situation: A customer pays cash for a delivery, but you are unsure whether the change is right while other customers wait.

options.text: Hand over the change you calculated and move on to the next customer.
Count the payment and change aloud, then record the amount on the receipt.
Ask the customer to confirm the change amount while you prepare the receipt.
Recount the notes and coins before completing the customer receipt.

advanced.situation: At the end of a vending route, the coin collection is lower than the machine's sales record. You also need to remove aged merchandise.

options.text: Record the counted coins, note the variance, and separately log removed aged merchandise.
Remove the aged items and ask another driver to check the cash figures.
Count the coins again and report the difference with the machine reading.
Adjust the machine total to the cash collected and remove the dated items.

basic.situation: A regular office customer asks whether a new sandwich is available and how its price compares with their usual order.

options.text: Share the sandwich price and ask whether they want details about it.
Explain the new sandwich and price, then let the customer choose what suits them.
Read the product script and offer the customer a menu to review.
Recommend the new sandwich and take it as their order for today.

advanced.situation: A customer says their delivered drinks were warm and asks for a refund during a busy stop. You can record the complaint but cannot approve refunds.

options.text: Listen, record the order details, and explain how the refund request will be reviewed.
Apologize, note the order number, and pass the complaint to the office.
Tell the customer that refunds are handled by the office and continue the route.
Offer a replacement from the truck and close the complaint as resolved.

basic.situation: Before a morning delivery, you use the checklist and find a rear tyre looks worn while the brake pedal feels soft.

options.text: I use yesterday's check and leave once the warning light clears.
I follow the checklist, test each light, and flag weak braking before departure.
I check lights and tyres, then ask the supervisor about soft brakes.
I top up the tyre and note its condition for the next check.

advanced.situation: During a pre-trip check, brake pressure drops twice, and a newer driver asks whether the tractor-trailer can still reach the depot.

options.text: I record the pressure drop and park the truck pending a qualified inspection.
I show the driver the pressure change and explain the check sequence.
I repeat the check and take the truck if pressure holds on the third try.
I ask the newer driver to watch the gauge while I check the lights.

basic.situation: You read the bill of lading for a first delivery and see two addresses with similar street names in the same town.

options.text: I check the town and street name, then call dispatch about the number.
I compare the bill with the map and confirm the street number with dispatch.
I read the bill again, then ask another driver which address looks familiar.
I choose the address nearest the town centre and follow the map.

advanced.situation: A road closure appears on your GPS after loading, while a new driver is checking the delivery papers and the customer expects an afternoon arrival.

options.text: I check the closure, compare truck-suitable routes, and verify the delivery timing with dispatch.
I ask dispatch for a route and review the new driver's paperwork afterward.
I review the papers with the new driver and ask dispatch about another route.
I reroute through the shorter road and tell the new driver to follow.

basic.situation: After unloading at a warehouse, you spot loose packaging and small debris across the trailer floor before the next load arrives.

options.text: I sweep the visible debris toward the trailer door for the next shift.
I clear the floor and check the corners before the next load enters.
I pick up the larger pieces and tell the next crew about the rest.
I clear the packaging and ask the warehouse crew to inspect the floor.

advanced.situation: At a busy loading bay, a pallet shifts as the crew uses powered equipment, and loose debris is visible near the trailer's rear wheels.

options.text: I pause the loading, clear the debris, and help reposition the pallet with the crew.
I ask the crew to finish loading, then sweep around the rear wheels.
I move the debris aside and tell the crew to watch the shifting pallet.
I alert the crew about the pallet and ask them to clear the debris.

basic.situation: At the depot, you need to reverse the tractor-trailer into a bay while a loading crew member gives hand signals from beside the dock.

options.text: I follow the signals while checking both mirrors as the trailer turns.
I pause if signals vanish, then ask the crew member to guide me again.
I ask the crew member to move clear of the dock before I reverse.
I reverse slowly, checking both mirrors and the crew member's hand signals.

advanced.situation: Rain and spray reduce visibility on a loaded route, and a newer driver radios that the weigh station entrance is approaching.

options.text: I slow down and ask the driver to watch for entrance signs.
I maintain speed and follow the truck ahead toward the weigh station entrance.
I ask the driver to use the next exit and circle back to the station.
I ease off, increase distance, and guide the driver toward the marked entrance.

basic.situation: During your daily log entry, you notice the service record has no note for the oil you added before leaving the depot.

options.text: I mention the oil top-up in tomorrow's log when I have more time.
I enter the oil top-up and keep the receipt with the service record.
I write that I added oil, then ask the manager where receipts belong.
I save the receipt in the cab and leave the service record unchanged.

advanced.situation: A tyre loses pressure on a delivery route, and your work-hours log is close to its required break entry while the truck is on a shoulder.

options.text: I call roadside assistance, note the time, and arrange a safe repair.
I secure the area, assess safe repair options, and record work time accurately.
I position the truck safely on the shoulder and check available tyre tools.
I change the tyre on the shoulder and complete the log after delivery.

basic.situation: At a shop delivery, the receiver signs the bill but says the cartons appear short and asks you to leave before checking them.

options.text: I call dispatch from the shop and ask whether to take the signed bill.
I note the receiver's concern on the delivery copy and report it to dispatch.
I leave the signed bill in the cab and call the receiver later.
I ask the receiver to count the cartons and wait for their answer.

advanced.situation: Your CB radio reports a collision ahead, and another driver asks you to relay the message while your GPS shows a possible detour.

options.text: I ask the other driver to check the map while I keep listening for updates.
I relay the collision location and direct the driver toward a nearby side road.
I share the collision location and ask dispatch to confirm a suitable detour.
I share the location, check for a truck-suitable detour, and clearly report uncertainty.

basic.situation: Before leaving for a delivery, you check the van with the checklist and find a dim headlight and low tyre pressure.

options.text: I use yesterday's check and leave once the dash warning clears.
I adjust the tyre pressure and note the dim light for later.
I check the light and tyre, then ask the supervisor about the pressure.
I follow the checklist, assess headlight visibility, and adjust tyre pressure before departure.

advanced.situation: A newer driver says the van's brakes feel different after several stops, though the dashboard shows no warning during your supply check.

options.text: I inspect the tyres and ask the driver to describe the brake feel.
I record the symptom and arrange for the van to be checked before use.
I ask the driver to keep the route short and monitor the brake feel.
I check the brake fluid level and share the checklist with the driver.

basic.situation: You have written directions to a new industrial area, but two roads have similar names and the dispatcher is handling another call.

options.text: I compare the written directions with the map and confirm the turn by phone.
I call dispatch when free and ask which road matches the address.
I choose the road that appears first on the map and continue.
I check the road names on the map and ask a nearby driver.

advanced.situation: Three deliveries share a district, and a road closure changes your route while a newer driver asks how to sequence the remaining stops.

options.text: I ask dispatch for a revised order and pass it to the driver.
I take the nearest stop first and ask the driver to adjust afterward.
I keep the printed order and tell the driver to follow the same streets.
I check the closure, compare the addresses on the map, and explain the revised sequence.

basic.situation: You unload boxes from a van and notice the last carton on the shipping paper is missing from the stack.

options.text: I compare the paper with the remaining boxes and report the missing carton to the receiver.
I note the missing carton and tell the receiver before signing the shipping paper.
I continue unloading and sign the shipping paper without checking the carton count.
I ask a coworker to search the van while I finish unloading the stack.

advanced.situation: A heavy item must be unloaded with a tight schedule, and the inventory sheet lists two similar cartons with different destinations.

options.text: I move both cartons to the nearer bay and sort them after unloading.
I separate the cartons by label and ask a colleague to check the sheet.
I verify the carton labels against the sheet, then stage each by destination.
I ask the receiver which carton should go to each bay.

basic.situation: You are driving a light truck through steady rain, and a delivery entrance appears just after a busy junction.

options.text: I drive past the entrance and ask dispatch for another way in.
I follow the traffic speed and signal before turning into the entrance.
I brake near the junction and turn into the entrance at once.
I slow with traffic, signal in good time, and enter when the lane is clear.

advanced.situation: A newer driver radios from a wet road where spray obscures lane markings, and asks whether to pass a slow vehicle before the next exit.

options.text: I advise the driver to stay behind until the road markings are clear.
I advise staying behind, easing speed, and waiting for clear markings before changing lanes.
I ask the driver to check mirrors and decide whether the gap is enough.
I tell the driver to pass before the exit while the gap remains.

basic.situation: You complete a delivery and see that the vehicle log has yesterday's mileage copied into today's entry.

options.text: I leave today's entry unchanged and tell my manager mileage may be copied.
I ask my manager whether to update today's mileage after checking the odometer.
I check the odometer, then update today's mileage and note the change.
I compare the odometer with today's entry, then update and document the mileage.

advanced.situation: While reconciling vehicle logs, you find a delivery entry with missing cargo details and a billing statement already prepared from that record.

options.text: I ask the driver to recall the cargo and enter the details from memory.
I compare the log with delivery papers and flag missing cargo details before statement submission.
I send the statement and fill in the cargo details after the next run.
I reconcile delivery papers and log details, then review the billing statement.

basic.situation: At a delivery, the van's temperature warning appears and the customer asks you to unload the chilled boxes before they warm up.

options.text: I stop unloading and call my supervisor about the warning before proceeding.
I photograph the warning, then send it to my supervisor and await advice.
I park safely and call my supervisor before deciding whether to unload the chilled boxes.
I unload the boxes, then report the temperature warning to the depot supervisor.

advanced.situation: A customer disputes the quantity on your delivery bill, while another waiting customer asks for their receipt and the van is blocking a loading area.

options.text: I issue the waiting customer a receipt and ask the first customer to call dispatch.
I note the dispute and ask dispatch how to handle payment before leaving.
I collect payment for the listed total and leave the signed bill with the customer.
I record the disputed quantity, present the bill, and contact dispatch about the account.

basic.situation: You approach a junction where traffic has slowed and a car is stopped near the crossing. You need to continue your school route safely.

options.text: You keep the timetable by following the moving traffic through the junction.
You slow early, leave space, and follow the crossing guard's signals.
You ease off the accelerator and let the queue settle before continuing.
You steer around the stopped car when a small gap appears.

advanced.situation: Rain and roadworks have narrowed your route, and cars are trying to merge beside your bus. You must pass safely with students aboard.

options.text: You slow down and leave space for a nearby car to move ahead.
You keep pace and watch nearby traffic for a safe opening to pass.
You speed up past waiting cars before the lane narrows beside your bus.
You hold your lane, ease your speed, and let vehicles merge one at a time.

basic.situation: A student starts stepping off the bus while another is still climbing aboard at the stop. You need to keep boarding orderly.

options.text: You remind both students to take turns and watch their footing.
You pause boarding and let the exiting student clear the doorway first.
You let the students sort out the doorway while you watch from your seat.
You ask the boarding student to wait beside the bus for a moment.

advanced.situation: At a busy stop, students need to cross a two-way street after leaving your bus, while impatient traffic queues behind you.

options.text: You keep students beside the bus until traffic stops, then guide them together.
You hold the students near the bus and ask a staff member for help.
You ask students to wait for a gap and cross in pairs.
You tell the quickest students to cross first while the queue is stopped.

basic.situation: A written route sheet lists a familiar street, but a temporary closure blocks your usual turn. You need to reach the next pickup safely.

options.text: You follow the posted diversion signs and compare them with your route sheet.
You turn into the next side street and hope it reconnects nearby.
You pause at a safe spot and call dispatch for another direction.
You check the map for a nearby open road before continuing the route.

advanced.situation: Two nearby pickups are running late after a road closure, and another driver asks which order avoids backtracking without missing students.

options.text: You compare the map and pickup times, then share the shorter feasible order.
You suggest visiting the closest stop first to reduce extra driving.
You check the route sheet and recommend its listed stop order.
You tell the driver to follow your usual route and adjust along the way.

basic.situation: Before departure, your checklist shows a rear light is not working. Students are waiting, and you need to report the vehicle issue.

options.text: You mark the checklist complete because the other lights are working.
You note the failed light and report it before the bus leaves.
You write the light fault in the log for the next check.
You report the light fault and ask whether the bus may operate.

advanced.situation: A new driver reports a soft brake pedal during the morning check, while the bus is due to collect students in ten minutes.

options.text: You record the brake concern and report it before the bus is assigned.
You suggest trying the brakes in the yard before deciding about the route.
You advise the driver to keep the trip short and watch the brakes.
You ask the driver to describe the pedal change and note the details.

basic.situation: A traffic jam will delay your afternoon route, and the school office needs an update while students are waiting on the bus.

options.text: You tell dispatch that traffic is heavy and the route is behind.
You radio dispatch with your location and estimated delay before proceeding.
You wait until reaching the next stop before reporting the delay.
You keep to the schedule and tell the office after the route ends.

advanced.situation: A student repeatedly leaves their seat while you are driving, and the behavior is disrupting the trip. You need to inform the school administration.

options.text: You report the repeated behavior to the school with the route and timing details.
You radio the school that a student is disrupting the trip.
You leave the behavior off the report since the trip is nearly over.
You wait until dismissal and mention the student to a staff member.

basic.situation: After a trip, you find wrappers and a spilled drink in the bus aisle, and the next group is due soon.

options.text: You clear the aisle, clean the spill, and leave the interior ready for students.
You ask the next group to keep clear of the dirty area.
You cover the wet patch with a floor mat until the next stop.
You wipe the spill and place the wrappers in a rubbish bag.

advanced.situation: Your trip report shows mileage that differs from the route record, and fuel use appears higher than usual after today's runs.

options.text: You check the odometer reading against your trip notes before submitting.
You compare the trip entries with the route record and report the unresolved difference.
You submit the mileage figure and mention the fuel increase in your notes.
You use the route record's mileage so the report matches the planned trip.

basic.situation: Your pre-departure checklist shows the oil level is below its usual mark, and passengers are waiting at the terminal.

options.text: You check the dipstick once more on level ground before departure.
You tell dispatch the oil looks low and wait for their reply.
You leave on schedule and note the oil reading in your log later.
You record the low reading and report it before taking the vehicle out.

advanced.situation: A maintenance log shows repeated tyre pressure concerns on a coach, and a new driver is preparing to take it on a long route.

options.text: You ask the driver to use yesterday's pressure reading for today's log.
You check the latest entry and remind the driver to inspect the tyres.
You review the entries, check current pressures, and report any remaining concern.
You show the driver the repeated entries and explain the pressure check.

basic.situation: An older passenger is carrying a bag and hesitates at the bus steps while other passengers are queuing behind them.

options.text: You ask the passenger to board quickly so the queue can move.
You offer an arm and help the passenger board with their bag.
You ask whether the passenger would like help with the steps.
You carry the passenger's bag aboard and ask them to follow.

advanced.situation: A passenger using a wheelchair asks whether they can reach a stop that is not shown on the route display, as boarding continues.

options.text: You check the route information and explain the stop options before they board.
You tell the passenger the usual route and suggest checking with the driver.
You ask a colleague to confirm the stop while you explain the boarding area.
You say the bus probably serves that stop and let them board.

basic.situation: At a busy terminal, the marked loading bay is partly blocked by a parked car, and passengers are waiting to board your bus.

options.text: You position near the bay entrance while keeping the passenger door closed.
You wait in a safe holding area and ask staff to clear the bay.
You stop beside the parked car and let passengers step aboard.
You wait briefly for the car to leave before approaching the bay.

advanced.situation: A road closure has put your coach behind schedule, and a narrow detour has several low branches near the next stop.

options.text: You stop safely and ask dispatch whether another route is available.
You follow the signed detour slowly and watch for low branches.
You take the narrow detour to recover time and avoid another delay.
You check the detour for vehicle clearance, then follow a safe route update.

basic.situation: A collision ahead blocks your route, and passengers are asking why the coach has stopped. You need to report the delay to dispatch.

options.text: You reassure passengers that the coach should move again soon.
You turn onto a side road and update dispatch after moving.
You report your location, the blocked route, and the likely delay to dispatch.
You tell dispatch there has been a collision and wait for instructions.

advanced.situation: A passenger becomes faint during a crowded intercity trip, while traffic is moving slowly and other passengers are asking for updates.

options.text: You pull over safely, check the passenger, and contact dispatch for assistance.
You ask dispatch for advice while looking for a suitable place to stop.
You ask a nearby passenger to check on them while you continue slowly.
You stop at the next safe place and ask the passenger what support they need.

basic.situation: Passengers say the rear of the coach feels stuffy, and the ventilation setting is lower than usual on a warm afternoon.

options.text: You turn the fan off briefly, then restore the previous setting.
You raise the ventilation setting and check whether air reaches the rear.
You increase the fan setting and ask passengers if it feels better.
You open the front vents wider to improve airflow through the coach.

advanced.situation: During a long trip, the rear cabin remains warm despite higher ventilation, while front passengers say the airflow is already strong.

options.text: You check rear vents and adjust airflow to balance cabin comfort.
You raise the fan setting and ask passengers for feedback.
You explain the airflow difference and lower front vents slightly.
You keep current settings until reaching the next scheduled stop.

basic.situation: A passenger hands you cash for a fare, but the amount is unclear while several people are boarding behind them.

options.text: You count the cash, state the fare, and return the remaining change.
You ask the passenger to confirm the amount they handed over.
You accept the notes and move to the next passenger to keep boarding.
You place the cash aside and ask the passenger to pay again later.

advanced.situation: At the end of a busy run, your cash total is short of the recorded fares, and the next departure is approaching.

options.text: You recount the cash once and tell the next driver about the shortfall.
You recount the cash against the fare record and note any remaining difference.
You report the shortage and submit the figures as recorded.
You add personal cash to match the recorded fare total before leaving.

basic.situation: A passenger asks to get out beside a marked bus lane while traffic is moving. What do you do?

options.text: You slow down and ask the passenger to wait for a safer place.
You stop beside the bus lane so the passenger can get out quickly.
You continue to a legal bay, then help the passenger exit safely.
You explain the safe stopping point and pull over there.

advanced.situation: A passenger using a wheelchair is ready to board, but the lift area is slightly sloped and another vehicle is waiting behind you. What do you do?

options.text: You ask the passenger to wait while you move to a flatter nearby spot.
You deploy the lift and ask the passenger to board while you hold the brake.
You find level ground, secure the vehicle, and operate the lift as trained.
You ask a companion to help guide the wheelchair onto the lowered lift.

basic.situation: Before a morning shuttle run, you notice one tyre looks softer than the others. What do you do?

options.text: You compare it with the other tyres and tell the depot it seems low.
You add air until the tyre looks firm enough for the trip.
You check its pressure and inflate it to the vehicle's stated level.
You ask a colleague to check it while you prepare the passenger list.

advanced.situation: A brake warning appears during your pre-trip check, while a booked group is waiting. What do you do?

options.text: You ask dispatch whether another driver has used the shuttle without trouble.
You test the brakes again in the yard and report the warning to maintenance.
You keep the shuttle parked and report the warning for a mechanic's assessment.
You clear the warning and take the group on a short route to assess it.

basic.situation: At the end of a shuttle run, your route sheet has a blank for the last neighbourhood stop. What do you do?

options.text: You enter the last stop from your trip notes and check the route order.
You ask another driver which stop was listed on the shared route.
You fill the blank with the neighbourhood you usually visit last.
You write the likely stop and flag the blank for your dispatcher.

advanced.situation: A minor collision delays your shuttle, and dispatch needs an incident report before the shift ends. What do you do?

options.text: You report the delay now and add the collision details at shift end.
You record the time, location, damage, and events while details are fresh.
You describe the collision from memory after finishing the remaining passenger runs.
You submit a short report saying there was contact and no one complained.

basic.situation: Dispatch radios a new pickup address while you are approaching a busy roundabout. What do you do?

options.text: You continue driving and call dispatch once the surrounding traffic eases.
You tell dispatch you are driving and will respond from a safe place.
You tell dispatch you will confirm the address after you clear the roundabout.
You repeat the address while steering carefully through the roundabout.

advanced.situation: Your shuttle develops a steering vibration on an expressway, and a group is due at a meeting shortly. What do you do?

options.text: You report a vehicle problem and continue to the next scheduled stop.
You ask the passengers whether they feel comfortable continuing to the venue.
You pull over safely and call dispatch with your location and the vibration.
You tell dispatch your location, symptoms, and passenger status, then follow its safe-stop guidance.

basic.situation: An older passenger reaches your shuttle with a suitcase and struggles with the high step. What do you do?

options.text: You offer an arm and let the passenger decide how to board.
You ask the passenger to wait while you find another staff member.
You steady the passenger and place the suitcase securely before departure.
You lift the suitcase aboard and ask the passenger to climb in alone.

advanced.situation: A visitor asks for a nearby dinner recommendation, while the shuttle's air conditioning feels too cold to several passengers. What do you do?

options.text: You ask the visitor what food they prefer before naming a nearby area.
You suggest a nearby option and adjust ventilation after checking passenger comfort.
You adjust the air conditioning and suggest asking hotel staff about dinner.
You name the first restaurant you remember and leave the controls unchanged.

basic.situation: A written direction names a neighbourhood street you do not recognise, and your next pickup is approaching. What do you do?

options.text: You call dispatch for directions while continuing along the main road.
You ask dispatch to confirm the street name before choosing a turn.
You check the map while stopped and confirm the route before moving on.
You turn toward a familiar road and hope it reaches the neighbourhood.

advanced.situation: You are behind schedule for two neighbourhood pickups when one passenger reports feeling faint. What do you do?

options.text: You tell dispatch about the delay and pull over at the next stop.
You stop safely, assess the passenger, and use your first-aid knowledge as needed.
You continue to the next pickup and ask dispatch to send help there.
You ask the passenger to sit quietly while you finish the short route.

basic.situation: A passenger pays with a large note for a short trip, and several people are waiting behind them. What do you do?

options.text: You return what seems like the right change and move the queue along.
You check the meter total and count out the change carefully.
You ask the passenger to confirm the change before you close the meter.
You state the fare, count the change, and offer a receipt.

advanced.situation: A passenger disputes the metered fare after a long traffic delay, and the next passenger is already waiting. What do you do?

options.text: You explain the meter reading and review the trip details before accepting payment.
You show the meter total and ask dispatch how to handle the complaint.
You repeat the total and ask the passenger to pay before discussing it further.
You lower the amount to the passenger's offer to keep the queue moving.

basic.situation: You are carrying a passenger through unfamiliar city streets when a turn appears sooner than expected. What do you do?

options.text: You ask the passenger to point out the missed turn while you drive.
You continue safely and check the route before choosing another turn.
You take the next safe turn and follow the main road back around.
You brake sharply and turn across the lane to stay on route.

advanced.situation: A new driver asks how to handle a passenger who wants to board from a busy traffic lane. What do you do?

options.text: You advise moving to a safe legal pickup point before allowing boarding.
You suggest stopping briefly if the passenger can board quickly.
You tell the driver to ask dispatch whether the lane is acceptable.
You remind the driver to watch traffic and keep the passenger informed.

basic.situation: A passenger with two bags reaches your taxi stand and struggles to open the rear door. What do you do?

options.text: You place both bags inside while the passenger gets into the cab.
You ask the passenger to hold one bag while you open the door.
You open the door, help with the bags, and check the passenger is settled.
You leave the bags on the pavement and ask the passenger to board first.

advanced.situation: A visitor asks for a quiet hotel near a clinic, but you know several areas and are unsure which hotel fits. What do you do?

options.text: You ask the visitor to search for hotels while you finish the trip.
You describe nearby areas and let the visitor choose a hotel online.
You name the quietest hotel you remember and reassure the visitor it is nearby.
You suggest a nearby area and recommend checking hotel details with the clinic.

basic.situation: Dispatch offers you a fare request while you are parked, but the pickup street sounds unfamiliar. What do you do?

options.text: You accept the request and check the street on your map before leaving.
You repeat the pickup street and ask dispatch to confirm the location.
You ask dispatch to send another request with a clearer street name.
You accept the request and start toward the nearest familiar landmark.

advanced.situation: Your assigned taxi develops a fault light before a booked pickup, and dispatch is assigning nearby drivers. What do you do?

options.text: You report the warning, vehicle location, and pickup status so dispatch can reassign.
You continue to the pickup and mention the warning after the trip.
You ask a nearby driver whether that warning appeared on their taxi.
You report the warning and ask dispatch whether to take the booking.

basic.situation: Before starting your shift, you find one tyre below its usual pressure and the air pump is available. What do you do?

options.text: You compare it with the other tyres and add a small amount of air.
You check the recommended pressure and inflate the tyre to that level.
You note the low tyre and wait for the next service visit.
You add air until the tyre looks round enough for city driving.

advanced.situation: A taxi's wipers leave streaks during a sudden downpour, and you are due to collect a passenger. What do you do?

options.text: You stop safely, check the wipers, and arrange servicing if they remain ineffective.
You drive slowly to the pickup and use the wipers on their fastest setting.
You ask the passenger to wait while you wipe the windscreen by hand.
You test the wipers while parked and report the problem to the garage.

basic.situation: After a rainy fare, you notice muddy marks across the rear floor before your next passenger arrives. What do you do?

options.text: You vacuum the floor mats and wipe the marked area before the next fare.
You wipe the obvious marks and vacuum the cabin after your next fare.
You shake the mats outside and leave the remaining marks for later.
You cover the muddy patch with a spare floor mat and begin the next trip.

advanced.situation: A colleague asks how to prepare the taxi for a hotel pickup after a passenger spilled a drink on the seat. What do you do?

options.text: You explain the cleaning steps and let the colleague finish the seat.
You clean the seat yourself and ask the colleague to prepare the exterior.
You show the colleague how to clean the spill and check the seat before pickup.
You place a towel over the seat and tell the colleague to collect the fare.

basic.situation: You receive the conductor's starting signal, but this freight train is heavier than your practice consist. How do you begin moving?

options.text: Confirm the signal, ease the throttle, and monitor brake response as the train moves.
Use brisk throttle to keep schedule, expecting the brake line to settle.
Release the brakes and use steady throttle, checking gauges after departure.
Use a small throttle and check the train's movement before adding power.

advanced.situation: You must assemble a long freight consist in a busy yard, and two cuts of cars are ready on adjacent tracks. How do you plan the moves?

options.text: Move the nearer cut first, then adjust the consist if the yard gets busy.
Couple both cuts as they stand, then sort out their order before departure.
Ask the conductor which cut matters more and work on that one first.
Check the switching plan, sequence both cuts, and coordinate each move with the conductor.

basic.situation: During a routine run, the air-pressure gauge dips briefly as you approach a station. What do you do while monitoring the readings?

options.text: Compare the reading with the normal range and tell the conductor what changed.
Watch the gauge for another moment and mention the dip at the next stop.
Reduce power slightly and ask the conductor to watch the gauge too.
Continue at the current pace and check the gauge again after the station.

advanced.situation: You spot a subtle rail alignment change ahead while your speed gauge stays normal. The track is clear, but the defect's extent is uncertain. What do you do?

options.text: Slow down and ask the conductor whether the alignment looks unusual too.
Reduce speed, report the location to control, and follow their operating direction.
Continue slowly, noting the location for the next routine inspection.
Keep speed steady while checking for another sign of track trouble.

basic.situation: Your pre-run checklist shows the locomotive's water level is near the lower mark, and the next service point is some distance away. What do you do?

options.text: Start the run and plan to refill at the next service point.
Top up the water and note the amount on the inspection checklist.
Tell the conductor about the level and ask whether to arrange water.
Mark the level as adequate so the departure can stay on schedule.

advanced.situation: During the pre-run check, you find a recurring mechanical warning alongside a fresh fluid mark beneath the locomotive. The run is due soon. What do you do?

options.text: Check the fluid level and warning again, then decide based on the readings.
Record both signs and tell the maintenance crew before the locomotive leaves.
Record both signs, compare them with the manual, and report the locomotive for assessment.
Wipe the mark, reset the warning, and see whether it returns after departure.

basic.situation: A train order gives you a route, but you are unsure whether the signal ahead applies to your track. How do you handle the instruction?

options.text: Take the route that matches your usual run and confirm the order later.
Hold your movement, check the order, and call out the signal for confirmation.
Follow the route in the order and watch the signal as you approach.
Ask the conductor to read the order again while you prepare to move.

advanced.situation: A written train order and a signal appear to call for different actions near a junction. Your assistant is waiting for your callout. What do you do?

options.text: Proceed at reduced speed while the assistant watches for another signal change.
Hold the train and ask the conductor which instruction should guide the movement.
Call out the signal, hold movement, and clarify the conflict through the proper channel.
Use the written order as your guide and tell the assistant to prepare.

basic.situation: A signal problem delays your train outside a station, and the conductor asks you to update traffic control by radiophone. What do you say?

options.text: Report the location, signal problem, and delay, then confirm control received it.
Wait until arrival and include the signal issue in your later report.
Say the train is running late and provide details if control asks.
Tell control the train is delayed by a signal issue near the station.

advanced.situation: Two trains report conflicting signal problems in your area, and traffic control asks for a written account after your stop. How do you prepare it?

options.text: Present the first report as a possible cause, and include the second report's details.
Build a timeline from memory, noting key signal details reported by both trains.
Log each report's time, location, and wording, separating observations from crew accounts.
Summarize both reports separately, so control can compare details during its review.

basic.situation: At a shunting station, you are asked to check that the brake examination test is complete before the locomotive continues. What do you do?

options.text: Check the test marker and confirm completion with the crew before departure.
Record the check after the crew confirms the examination is complete.
Verify the result with the responsible crew member, then record the completed check.
Ask the crew to confirm completion, rather than relying on routine or appearance.

advanced.situation: During a run, a breakdown leaves your locomotive stopped near a busy track, and the crew looks to you for the next safety action. What do you do?

options.text: Secure the locomotive, alert control and the crew, then follow the emergency procedure.
Secure the locomotive and ask the conductor to notify control about the breakdown.
Restart the locomotive to clear the busy track before reporting the breakdown.
Move clear of the locomotive and wait for control to give instructions.

basic.situation: Your pre-use checklist shows low air pressure on a yard engine, while the other gauges look steady. What do you do before starting work?

options.text: Start the engine and recheck the air gauge after the first move.
Check the gauge again after a short wait and decide whether it seems stable.
Hold the engine from use, record the reading, and request a mechanical check.
Compare the reading with the normal range and tell the supervisor what you found.

advanced.situation: You find a switch defect and a fresh engine fault during the yard inspection, with cars waiting nearby. How do you handle the findings?

options.text: Report both locations, protect the affected area, and keep the engine out of service pending assessment.
Use the other track and continue the engine's work while maintenance is busy.
Inspect the switch again and run the engine briefly to see whether the fault clears.
Tell the yard conductor about both findings and ask which needs attention first.

basic.situation: A car's knuckle stays closed as your crew prepares to couple it, and a coworker offers to help. What do you do?

options.text: Check the car is secured, then open the knuckle with the coworker's guidance.
Push the knuckle with a tool so the coupling can proceed on time.
Ask the coworker to steady the car while you pull the knuckle open.
Try the lever once more, then ask the coworker to take a turn.

advanced.situation: After coupling, an air hose connection leaks and the drawbars sit slightly out of line. The next yard move is waiting. What do you do?

options.text: Reposition the cars, align the drawbars, and reconnect the hose before checking the seal.
Tighten the hose fitting and try the connection again for the next move.
Tell the conductor about the leak and ask maintenance to inspect the connection.
Cover the leaking joint with tape and continue with the waiting move.

basic.situation: You are asked to release a car's hand brake before a short yard move, with a supervisor nearby. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the supervisor to watch as you release the car's hand brake.
Release the brake while crew members are still positioning around the car.
Release the brake, then signal the crew to begin the short yard move.
Confirm the crew has secured the car, then release its hand brake as directed.

advanced.situation: A locomotive must reach the service track, but the usual switch is unavailable and two routes appear open. How do you route it?

options.text: Wait for the conductor to choose a route, then operate the switches as directed.
Take the clearer route and adjust the switches if the service track is blocked.
Check the switching instructions, confirm the route with the conductor, and operate the switches accordingly.
Ask a nearby operator which route they used most recently and follow it.

basic.situation: The daily car schedule lists a switch you have not handled before, and the conductor is available nearby. What do you do?

options.text: Follow the listed sequence and check each car against the schedule before moving.
Review the schedule with the conductor, then repeat the unfamiliar car sequence back.
Ask the conductor to explain which car should move first, then confirm the sequence.
Compare the schedule with yesterday's sequence and discuss any differences with the conductor.

advanced.situation: Train operations changes a switching instruction while customer service asks for the expected completion time. What do you relay to the crew?

options.text: Pass the new instruction to the crew and estimate the finish from the current schedule.
Tell the crew about the change and send customer service the previous estimate.
Relay the new instruction and ask customer service to check back later for timing.
Relay the change, confirm crew readback, and update customer service with a revised estimate.

basic.situation: A color light signal changes as your yard engine approaches a loading spot, and your mentor is beside you. What do you do?

options.text: Follow the movement you expected and check the signal after spotting the car.
Move slowly toward the spot while watching for another signal change.
Call out the signal aspect, compare readings with your mentor, and respond accordingly.
Ask your mentor to explain the color indication before moving closer to the signal.

advanced.situation: A hot box detector sounds as your engine approaches a customer siding, and the crew is preparing to spot cars. What do you do?

options.text: Finish spotting the nearest car, then report the detector alert to the conductor.
Tell the crew about the alert and ask them to watch the cars closely.
Stop movement, report the detector alert, and follow response steps before spotting cars.
Report the alert to the conductor and await a decision on the siding move.

basic.situation: You need to guide a short engine move with hand signals, but one crew member is partly obscured by a car. What do you do?

options.text: Give the movement signal from where you stand and proceed at a crawl.
Move to a visible position, signal the move, and check the crew member acknowledged.
Use the last signal and begin the move while the crew member clears the view.
Ask the conductor to watch the obscured crew member while you signal.

advanced.situation: Two crews are switching adjacent tracks, and their radio calls overlap while your crew awaits a hand signal. How do you coordinate the movement?

options.text: Signal your crew to start on the schedule while the adjacent crews sort out their call.
Use hand signals with your crew and keep listening for the other radio call.
