Ask your conductor to repeat the last instruction and wait for a clear radio channel.
Pause your crew, establish which call applies, then signal after confirming the adjacent move is clear.

basic.situation: The yardmaster assigns a cut to track four, but the radio crackles as you watch the engineer prepare to move.

options.text: I repeat the track and car numbers, then signal when clear.
I signal the engineer toward the usual track from memory.
I acknowledge the yardmaster and check the written switch list.
I ask a nearby crew member which track the order named.

advanced.situation: During a tight switching sequence, two crew members give conflicting hand signals while the engineer is easing cars toward a coupling.

options.text: I ask one crew member to repeat the signal from their position.
I radio the yardmaster to confirm the next switching step.
I signal the engineer to hold and clarify the movement with the crew.
I use the last signal received and keep the sequence moving.

basic.situation: Under a senior worker's guidance, you need to raise a lever to uncouple two cars in the yard.

options.text: I check the cars have stopped, then raise the lever as directed.
I pull the lever as the cars begin rolling apart.
I ask the senior worker to demonstrate the lever movement again.
I raise the lever while the senior worker watches the coupling.

advanced.situation: A train makeup order changes, and you must connect air hoses between cars before the planned departure window.

options.text: I finish the hose connections, then ask the senior worker to inspect them.
I connect each hose and check its fitting as I work along the cut.
I connect the first hose and assume the remaining fittings match.
I tighten the visible hoses and leave the less accessible ones for later.

basic.situation: Before departure, you inspect a coupling and air hose with a supervisor and notice one fitting feels loose.

options.text: I ask the supervisor to check the fitting while I inspect the handbrake.
I mention the fitting to the supervisor after checking the other cars.
I flag the loose fitting and ask for guidance before the car moves.
I check the hose visually and continue with the inspection.

advanced.situation: During a pre-service inspection, you find worn locomotive parts and the engine is due to return to service shortly.

options.text: I note the worn parts and ask the engineer whether service can continue.
I make a minor adjustment with hand tools and recheck the part.
I describe the wear and report the locomotive for repair assessment before service.
I record the wear and return the locomotive to the service queue.

basic.situation: A senior engineer asks you to start a diesel engine for warm-up before the day's run.

options.text: I confirm the locomotive is assigned, then start it as instructed.
I ask the senior engineer to repeat the starting steps beside me.
I start the nearest diesel engine to begin the warm-up.
I start the engine and tell the senior engineer once it is running.

advanced.situation: While operating a locomotive in an emergency, you see a crew member move near the track ahead.

options.text: I sound the warning and continue at the current speed toward the clear section.
I reduce movement and follow the emergency procedure while tracking the crew member.
I ask the crew member to move before changing the locomotive's direction.
I stop the locomotive and radio the engineer with the person's location.

basic.situation: During a run, the oil gauge moves above its usual range while the locomotive is working uphill.

options.text: I note the reading in the log after the uphill section.
I ask the engineer whether this reading is normal for the climb.
I watch the gauge for a few minutes before mentioning it.
I report the gauge reading and follow the engineer's operating instructions.

advanced.situation: Your train makes an emergency stop on a route, and visibility is poor as you prepare warnings for oncoming trains.

options.text: I place the approved warning devices at the front and rear as procedure directs.
I place the nearest flag behind the train and return to the cab.
I ask a crew member to take the front warning while I cover the rear.
I set a lantern at the rear, then check whether more devices are needed.

basic.situation: You see a signal along the route that differs from the one you expected, and the engineer asks what it shows.

options.text: I tell the engineer it appears to match the previous signal.
I give the engineer the meaning I remember from training.
I describe its color and position, then ask the mentor to confirm.
I report the signal as seen and verify its meaning with my mentor.

advanced.situation: From the locomotive's left side, you spot debris near the rail while an unfamiliar signal is visible farther ahead.

options.text: I focus on the signal and assume the debris is beyond the rail.
I report the debris and describe the signal without interpreting it.
I mention the debris after confirming the signal meaning with a mentor.
I report the obstruction and signal separately so the engineer can assess both.

basic.situation: The written plan assigns a crew to couple two cars, and you need to direct their basic switching work.

options.text: I read the plan aloud and ask the crew to confirm the cars.
I give the crew the track and car numbers from the written plan.
I tell the crew to handle the coupling listed on the board.
I point the crew toward the usual coupling area for that job.

advanced.situation: Two switching crews need the same track, and a junior worker is unsure which movement should happen first.

options.text: I direct both crews to begin and sort out the track conflict as they work.
I ask the junior worker to check with the other crew before moving.
I let the first crew finish, then direct the other crew afterward.
I sequence the moves around track access and brief both crews on the order.

basic.situation: The dispatcher gives you a route instruction over the radio, but the track number is hard to hear.

options.text: I acknowledge the route and check the schedule for the track number.
I relay the track number from the last route used on this run.
I read back the route and ask the dispatcher to confirm the track number.
I ask the engineer which track number they heard from the radio.

advanced.situation: A dispatcher reports a rail defect affecting your planned route, and the engineer asks about an alternative.

options.text: I pass on the defect report and let the engineer choose a route.
I tell the engineer to use the route taken on the previous run.
I discuss the defect and available route choices with the engineer before relaying a request.
I ask the dispatcher which alternative route they recommend for this train.

basic.situation: An engineer waits for your hand signal before starting a train run from the yard.

options.text: I radio the engineer to confirm they are ready to move.
I signal the train to start as soon as the yard gets quiet.
I give the starting signal when the engineer looks toward me.
I check the movement is ready, then signal the engineer to begin.

advanced.situation: Several trains are moving through a busy area, and an engineer asks you to signal a speed change near a junction.

options.text: I confirm the intended movement and signal the speed change using the agreed method.
I signal the speed change to the train nearest the junction.
I radio the engineer to confirm the junction before signaling the change.
I use a hand signal while checking which train is approaching the junction.

basic.situation: You are recording car contents and destinations from the train documents before the cars leave the yard.

options.text: I copy the destinations from the way bills onto the train sheet.
I use the previous train sheet for cars with familiar destinations.
I match each car number to its contents and destination before recording.
I enter the cargo details first and check car numbers later.

advanced.situation: An unscheduled stop delays the train, and you need to document what happened for the operations report.

options.text: I record the stop time, location, reported cause, and any timing updates.
I record the delay duration from the schedule and file the report.
I note the stop and ask the engineer for the reported cause later.
I enter the expected arrival time as the stop time in the report.

basic.situation: A way bill lists a freight car's cargo and unloading point, and you need to review its loading destination.

options.text: I use the previous car's unloading point for this similar load.
I note the unloading point shown beside the cargo description.
I match the car number and unloading point against the way bill.
I ask a coworker which siding usually handles this cargo.

advanced.situation: Several freight cars have different unloading points, and the switching order may delay a planned departure.

options.text: I review the waybills and suggest grouping cars by unloading point before switching.
I compare destinations and switching order, flagging any sequence that risks delay.
I follow the listed order and note any delays after switching.
I move the easiest cars first to keep the crew busy.

basic.situation: Before departure, an engineer asks you to verify the timekeeping instrument against the scheduled departure time.

options.text: I ask the engineer what reading the instrument should show before departure.
I set the instrument to match the time on my watch.
I read the instrument aloud and ask the engineer to confirm its scheduled time.
I compare the reading with the schedule and confirm it with the engineer.

advanced.situation: During a run inspection, you find a car defect that may affect service, while the train is nearing its next stop.

options.text: I document the defect and arrange removal of the car at the stop.
I ask the engineer to assess the car when the train reaches its next stop.
I mention the defect to the engineer and continue checking other cars.
I mark the car for review at the next scheduled inspection point.

basic.situation: At a station, your train stops beside a busy platform and passengers wait to board. You are learning the door controls with a senior operator nearby.

options.text: Confirm the train is stopped and the platform side before opening doors.
Check the platform indicator, then open the doors for boarding.
Open both sides briefly so waiting passengers can board faster.
Ask the senior operator which controls to use before opening doors.

advanced.situation: A temporary route variation adds a slow section before a crowded station, while dispatch asks you to recover lost time on your scheduled run.

options.text: Follow the posted restriction, then recover time at later permitted sections.
Keep the usual timing and ask dispatch about the variation at the next stop.
Use extra speed through the slow section to regain the schedule.
Confirm the variation and limits with dispatch, then pace each section within them.

basic.situation: During a supervised run, an obstruction light changes as your train approaches a crossing where cars are waiting near the tracks.

options.text: Continue at the usual pace because the cars remain behind the barrier.
Call out the changed light and follow the required cautious response with your senior.
Slow down and ask your senior what the changed light means.
Watch the light and keep your senior operator informed as you approach.

advanced.situation: On a busy approach, a signal aspect appears dimmer than usual while another train's lights are partly obscured by rain and glare.

options.text: Ask dispatch to confirm the signal while maintaining close visual watch.
Treat the faint aspect as clear and maintain the planned approach speed.
Reduce speed under operating rules, report both observations, and await confirmed movement authority.
Report the dim signal and keep watching the other train's position.

basic.situation: A passenger asks whether a ticket covers a transfer to another line, and you are making a supervised trip announcement at the next stop.

options.text: Direct the passenger to the station staff for transfer advice.
Check the fare information and explain the transfer in plain language.
Tell the passenger the ticket should work for any connecting line.
Confirm the destination and fare guidance, then explain the transfer and next stop.

advanced.situation: A visitor asks for a route to a hospital after a service delay changes the usual connection, while other passengers wait for your announcement.

options.text: Confirm the affected connection, give the revised route, and announce the delay clearly.
Explain the delay and direct the visitor to a route map at the station.
Announce the delay and suggest the usual transfer point for the hospital.
Tell the visitor to follow the crowd to the next interchange.

basic.situation: At the end of your shift, your supervisor asks you to complete a summary that includes a brief delay and the time service resumed.

options.text: Ask the incoming operator to fill in the missing details later.
Enter an estimated resumption time to finish the summary before the handover starts.
Check the event log, record both times, and note the service impact.
Record the delay and resumption times from your shift notes.

advanced.situation: A passenger incident caused a short service interruption, and your report may help the team review how staff responded during the disruption.

options.text: Describe the timeline and actions you observed in the report.
Separate observed facts from uncertainty and document timing, response, and conditions.
Leave out uncertain details and submit the report before the deadline.
Write a brief account and ask your supervisor to add safety findings.

basic.situation: Your train is held at a station by a minor door fault, and passengers are waiting while you contact the supervisor by radio.

options.text: Tell passengers the train is delayed, then resume when the door closes.
Ask a nearby operator to radio the fault while you check the doors.
Report the door fault, location, and delay estimate over the radio.
Report the door fault and wait for instructions before estimating time.

advanced.situation: Smoke is reported near a platform during peak service, and dispatch asks for updates as another unit approaches the affected area.

options.text: Report the smoke near the platform and ask dispatch what to do next.
Wait for a clearer report before using the radio during peak traffic.
Tell dispatch about the smoke and let the approaching unit assess it.
Report the exact location, observed conditions, and affected movements to dispatch.

basic.situation: At a safety meeting, the team discusses a recent passenger near-miss and asks operators to share how it affects daily work.

options.text: Skip the discussion and ask a colleague for the main takeaway later.
Listen to the discussion and note the main safety points.
Attend and record the meeting topic for your shift notes.
Share a relevant observation and ask how it changes platform checks.

advanced.situation: A station evacuation begins after smoke is reported, and you are the nearest operator available to guide passengers toward a safe exit.

options.text: Direct passengers toward the nearest exit and keep the walkway moving.
Wait for a manager to arrive before giving passengers any directions.
Point passengers toward the visible exit and ask staff to help guide them.
Use the designated route, check for hazards, and coordinate passenger flow with staff.

basic.situation: During routine engine maintenance, an engineer asks you to help adjust a stiff pump coupling. You notice the parts are still warm.

options.text: Fetch the tools and help turn the coupling as requested.
Wait for the engineer to identify the safe adjustment, then assist.
Check the work instructions and temperature with the engineer before assisting.
Loosen the coupling now so the engineer can finish faster.

advanced.situation: After a winch repair, a load test shows uneven movement. The deck team is waiting, and you need to verify the adjustment before returning it to service.

options.text: Record the uneven movement and ask the engineer to review the setting.
Compare the adjustment with specifications and test movement through the operating range.
Ask the repair team whether the winch feels ready for use.
Repeat the test with a lighter load and watch the winch movement.

basic.situation: Before a short deck task, a mooring line has a frayed section. A senior crew member asks you to splice a replacement section with hand tools.

options.text: Check the line type, prepare the strands, and follow the guided splice method.
Use the familiar splice and ask the senior crew member to inspect it.
Tie the ends together with spare twine to save preparation time.
Copy the last splice you saw and trim the ends neatly.

advanced.situation: A towing wire has a damaged section before departure, and the replacement splice must carry a heavy load. You are guiding a less experienced crew member.

options.text: Describe the splice steps and inspect the finished wire before use.
Match the splice to the wire, demonstrate strand control, and inspect each tuck.
Have the crew member copy your usual splice and check its appearance.
Let the crew member finish the splice before checking it together.

basic.situation: During your bridge-wing watch near a marked channel, a small craft crosses ahead while a buoy is difficult to see in rain.

options.text: Keep watching the buoy and wait for the next watch handover.
Call out the craft and turn toward the buoy for a clearer view.
Report the craft and unclear buoy to the officer on watch.
Report the craft's position and the obscured buoy, then keep scanning ahead.

advanced.situation: During an engineering watch, a pressure gauge rises above its logged range while lubricant flow appears uneven. The vessel is approaching a narrow passage.

options.text: Log both readings and compare them with their normal range after clearing the passage.
Record the pressure and report uneven lubricant flow to the watch officer.
Ask a crew member to verify the gauge while you monitor the lubricant flow.
Check both readings against limits, record the trend, and notify the watch officer.

basic.situation: At a sheltered berth, your mate asks you to help tie two barges into a tow unit. One line looks slack as the tug begins to take up tension.

options.text: Signal the mate to pause, then help secure the line under direction.
Call the mate and watch the line while the tug eases tension.
Pull the slack line tight as the tug continues taking up tension.
Add a second turn around the fitting and tell the mate afterward.

advanced.situation: On arrival at a busy berth, the tow unit is due for disconnection, but one barge sits unevenly and traffic is moving nearby.

options.text: Begin disconnecting the accessible lines while the tug holds position.
Ask the tug to hold steady while you inspect the nearest connection.
Check the tow unit's position and line loads with the mate before disconnection.
Tell the mate the barge looks uneven and wait for instructions.

basic.situation: After a small oil spill on deck, your crew lead asks you to wash the area before foot traffic resumes.

options.text: Mark the area and ask the crew lead which cleaning method to use.
Cover the oil with absorbent pads and resume nearby deck work.
Wash the visible oil toward the scupper with a deck hose.
Contain the oil, clear debris, then wash the deck as directed.

advanced.situation: You are directing wheelhouse cleaning before a voyage, and the paint team needs access to a nearby surface with fresh coating.

options.text: Have cleaners start at the far end and move around the paint.
Tell the team to clean the wheelhouse before the painters arrive.
Send the cleaners through the wheelhouse and ask painters to work around them.
Set a cleaning sequence around the fresh paint and assign clear work areas.

basic.situation: During a supervised cargo lift, a passenger approaches the loading area as the crew prepares to move a vehicle aboard.

options.text: Pause the lift and guide the passenger clear with the crew lead.
Tell the crew lead about the passenger and hold the vehicle in place.
Move the passenger aside while the crew keeps the vehicle moving.
Ask the passenger to wait while the vehicle is moved aboard.

advanced.situation: A cargo transfer hose begins to vibrate strongly as a tank approaches its planned fill level. You are operating the pump under the duty officer's direction.

options.text: Tell the officer about the vibration and keep the pump at its current rate.
Reduce the pump rate and watch the tank level for another minute.
Keep the pump running and mention the hose vibration at handover.
Stop the pump, report the vibration, and check the transfer status with the officer.

basic.situation: You are preparing a routine coastal passage and have the chart, a weather report and navigation equipment available. How would you decide the ship's movement?

options.text: Set the course from the chart and check the weather later.
Check the chart and latest weather, then steer toward the marked channel.
Keep the previous course even though the chart shows a shoal nearby.
Follow the familiar route from the last similar passage.

advanced.situation: Near a headland, the electronic sounder reading and chart contour lines seem inconsistent. You must calculate the land sighting before confirming the ship's position.

options.text: Compare sounder readings with contour lines and calculate the sighting before updating position.
Use the latest sounder reading to estimate the land sighting.
Enter the sounder estimate as the ship's position and continue.
Read the contour lines, then use the sounder reading as the sighting.

basic.situation: During a routine leg, you are asked to steer using the radar, depth finder and channel lights.

options.text: Steer toward the nearest channel light and keep a steady speed.
Follow the radar track, then check the depth finder at the next marker.
Keep the wheel steady and use the last depth reading for this stretch.
Use the radar and lights to hold the channel, checking depth as you steer.

advanced.situation: A vessel is entering a narrow lock with crosswind and limited room to adjust. You are handling the approach under the mate's direction.

options.text: Increase speed to counter the crosswind before entering the lock.
Ask the deckhand to watch one side while you maintain the approach.
Hold steady, then make one adjustment as the lock walls draw near.
Reduce speed, align early, and use short corrections while watching clearance.

basic.situation: Before departure, a gauge shows hydraulic fluid below its usual range. The vessel is alongside and the equipment is not yet in use.

options.text: Note the reading and check it again during the next watch.
Check the reading against the normal range and report it before use.
Top up the reservoir from a nearby container and proceed.
Ask a crewmate whether that gauge usually reads this low.

advanced.situation: During a vessel inspection, you find a fire extinguisher with a damaged seal and uncertain service status. Departure is planned soon.

options.text: Record the defect, check the service status, and raise it before departure.
Move the extinguisher to the ready area and mention the seal later.
Ask the crew if anyone recalls when it was last serviced.
Record the damaged seal and ask the officer whether departure can proceed.

basic.situation: At the end of your watch, you must record the ship's position, movement and weather conditions. What would you enter?

options.text: Copy the previous entry and update the position and time.
Record the position and weather, then add movement from memory later.
Leave the record unchanged until the next watch confirms the details.
Enter the observed position, movement, weather, and time in the daily record.

advanced.situation: A navigation display fails a startup check before a passage, and a fire extinguisher bracket is loose. You are assigned onboard maintenance.

options.text: Secure the extinguisher, troubleshoot the display, and record both maintenance actions.
Log both defects and leave repairs for the next maintenance round.
Check the display connections and report the loose bracket for repair.
Tighten the bracket and restart the display before noting the fault.

basic.situation: Before cargo work, a deckhand is waiting for direction to rig a tow line. The vessel is alongside and the area is clear.

options.text: Ask the deckhand to start rigging while you prepare the next assigned task.
Signal the deckhand to rig the tow line and report when ready.
Point toward the tow line and ask the deckhand to begin.
Signal the deckhand to pull the line across the walkway for now.

advanced.situation: A vessel is arriving at a berth with a crosswind, and the crew await your docking directions. You are serving as docking master under port procedures.

options.text: Call for the bow line first and adjust the approach as needed.
Tell the crew to prepare the lines while the vessel closes the berth.
Set the windward approach and direct line handling in a clear sequence.
Order both side lines secured as soon as either reaches the berth.

basic.situation: At night, a passing vessel is approaching on a course that may cross yours. You are keeping watch and have lights and a whistle available.

options.text: Sound the whistle and ask the lookout to track the vessel.
Keep the lights steady and assume the other vessel has seen you.
Use the whistle and lights to signal, then monitor the vessel's response.
Flash the lights once and continue the watch as planned.

advanced.situation: A small craft is taking on water near your vessel, and its crew are signalling for help. You are on watch with rescue gear available.

options.text: Approach at full speed so the crew can reach the craft sooner.
Alert the bridge, assess hazards, and coordinate the rescue.
Report the distress and keep the craft in sight while awaiting direction.
Turn toward the craft and have the crew ready the rescue gear.

basic.situation: On a calm morning trip, you are steering along a familiar marked channel. How would you hold the boat on course?

options.text: Hold the last heading even when the markers begin to shift.
Follow the markers and make small steering corrections when needed.
Keep the tiller centered and check the shore as a guide.
Steer by the compass and check the channel markers as you go.

advanced.situation: A ferry route bends around a shoal, and a gust pushes your boat off the electronic track. What would you do to regain the route?

options.text: Use the compass to regain the heading, then check the display.
Check the aid's position, adjust gradually, and verify clearance from the shoal.
Turn toward the displayed route and steady the throttle.
Increase throttle and steer sharply back across the track.

basic.situation: Passengers are boarding with bags while the boat is alongside. One person wants to stand near the side rail.

options.text: Ask passengers to keep bags clear and take seats away from the rail.
Ask the person to move away from the rail and take a seat.
Seat passengers first, then ask them to stow bags clear of the aisle.
Ask the person to sit down and keep the boarding aisle clear.

advanced.situation: A passenger reports smoke near the engine cover, and two crew members are unsure where to assist.

options.text: Open the engine cover so the crew can see whether anything is burning.
Ask passengers to move forward while you look for the smoke source.
Direct the crew to alert passengers, ready extinguishers, and keep clear access for response.
Send one crew member to check the cover while the other watches passengers.

basic.situation: After a day trip, mud and salt residue cover the hull above the waterline. You have brushes and cleaning supplies.

options.text: Paint over the residue so the hull looks clean before inspection.
Scrub the marked areas and rinse them before stowing the brushes.
Rinse the hull and leave stubborn residue for the next cleaning round.
Rinse the hull, scrub the residue, and check for visible damage as you clean.

advanced.situation: During routine service, you find milky oil and unusual resistance when turning the engine by hand.

options.text: Change the oil and test the engine briefly at low throttle.
Top up the oil and record the unusual resistance for later review.
Drain the oil and inspect the filter before deciding on next steps.
Stop the service, document both signs, and arrange a qualified engine assessment.

basic.situation: Before departure, you check the boat's fenders, lines and fire extinguisher. One fender is missing from its usual rack.

options.text: Locate a replacement fender and check the lines and extinguisher are ready.
Tell the crew to bring a spare fender and inspect the lines.
Ask another boat to lend a fender for this short trip.
Record the missing fender and cast off on schedule.

advanced.situation: A scheduled gear check finds a fire extinguisher with an unreadable pressure gauge and a pump that cycles unevenly.

options.text: Tag the extinguisher for checking and clean the pump intake.
Mark both items for service and replace the extinguisher with ready equipment.
Tap the gauge and run the pump again to see if readings settle.
Record both faults and tell the next operator to watch the equipment.

basic.situation: Passengers are boarding for a short crossing, and several are standing near the stern. What would you tell them?

options.text: Point out open seats and ask passengers to leave bags beside them.
Let them choose places while the crew finishes boarding.
Direct them to available seats and keep the boarding path clear.
Ask them to sit near the stern until the remaining passengers board.

advanced.situation: At a busy river crossing, one crew team loads goods while another boards passengers. The departure time is close. How would you coordinate them?

options.text: Ask both teams to speed up and report when their work is complete.
Let the goods team load through the passenger queue to save time.
Have the passenger team pause while the goods team finishes loading.
Set separate loading zones and sequence boarding around the goods movement.

basic.situation: You are securing the boat at a dock after a routine trip. The wind is light and the mooring lines are ready.

options.text: Fasten a line to a nearby dock cleat, then step ashore carefully.
Secure lines to dock points, then check the boat rests safely alongside.
Tie the bow line first and add the stern line when ready.
Use one available line and ask a crewmate to watch the boat.

advanced.situation: Before a longer trip, the boat needs fuel, a pump repair and replacement lines. The supplier can deliver in separate trips. How would you arrange the work?

options.text: Confirm the repair window, then coordinate fuel and lines to arrive before departure.
Order fuel and lines first, then ask the mechanic to fit the repair between trips.
Book the pump repair and ask the supplier for one delivery estimate.
Use the current lines and depart while the pump repair is pending.

basic.situation: You check a technician’s routine pump repair before the vessel leaves port. The checklist has one unchecked connection test.

options.text: Look over the pump and ask the technician whether the connection feels secure.
Review the completed items and sign the checklist to keep departure preparation moving.
Ask the technician to run that test, then record the result on the checklist.
Check the pump against the checklist and ask the technician to explain the repair.

advanced.situation: A junior team is repairing a recurring engine fault before a long voyage. Earlier repairs used different checks, and the cause remains uncertain.

options.text: Ask the team to repeat the last repair method and compare the engine readings afterward.
Set repair checks around the fault, guide the team through tests, and review their findings.
Approve the familiar repair steps so the team can finish before the voyage deadline.
Have the team use the usual checklist and report any new symptoms at the end.

basic.situation: During a routine safety round, you check the lifebuoys and find one locker seal broken. The equipment appears to be inside.

options.text: Check the locker contents against the list, then record the seal and equipment condition.
Note the broken seal and continue the round since the locker appears stocked.
Open the locker, check the lifebuoys, and note the seal condition for the supervisor.
Mark the locker as stocked on the checklist and tell the next watch about the seal.

advanced.situation: During an emergency drill, a crew member cannot reach the muster point because a passage is partly blocked by stores. The drill is underway.

options.text: Ask the crew member to use another passage and note the blocked route afterward.
Pause movement in that passage, redirect the crew safely, and record the obstruction for clearing.
Move the nearest stores aside so the crew member can reach the muster point.
Finish the drill using the usual route, then mention the stores during the debrief.

basic.situation: A departure time changes after a shore-side delivery is delayed. The captain asks you to update the shore contact, and the new time is confirmed.

options.text: Tell the shore contact the vessel may leave later and share the confirmed time afterward.
Pass the new time through a nearby crew member to save a call.
Send the confirmed departure time and ask the shore contact to acknowledge the update.
Call the shore contact with the new time and note who answered.

advanced.situation: A port slot moves forward while a spare-parts delivery is still pending. The captain wants to keep the schedule, and shore staff need an updated plan.

options.text: Compare the revised slot with the delivery timing, then agree a workable sequence with shore staff.
Keep the original plan and tell shore staff the delivery may arrive late.
Ask the supplier to speed up delivery while the vessel prepares for the new slot.
Send shore staff the new slot and ask them to advise on the delivery.

basic.situation: You assist a senior engineer with a small pump repair. After replacing a seal, the pump runs, but a joint still shows a slow drip.

options.text: Stop the pump for a safe recheck, then tell the engineer where the joint is dripping.
Watch the joint for a few minutes and report whether the drip changes.
Show the engineer the drip and ask whether the seal needs another adjustment.
Wipe the joint dry and finish the repair entry while the pump runs.

advanced.situation: A ventilation fan trips repeatedly during a hot afternoon. You find a warm motor casing and a loose panel, but the cause is not yet clear.

options.text: Tell the engineer about the heat and trips, then wait for repair instructions.
Record the trips and casing temperature, then ask the engineer to inspect the fan.
Reset the fan and leave the panel open to improve airflow around the motor.
Isolate the fan under procedure, record the symptoms, and help the engineer check likely causes.

basic.situation: You copy engine gauge readings into the watch log. One reading is smudged, and the next watch needs the figures for its handover.

options.text: Use the previous watch’s figure for the smudged reading and complete the log.
Recheck the gauge, enter the legible reading, and mark the unclear figure for confirmation.
Ask the outgoing watch to read the smudged entry before you submit the log.
Copy the clear figures and leave the unclear space blank for the next watch.

advanced.situation: While checking monthly machine-operation records, you find two oil-use entries that do not match the engine-room stores tally. The next order is being prepared.

options.text: Trace both entries to their source records, reconcile confirmed use, and flag any unresolved difference.
List the mismatch in the records and ask the stores clerk to check the tally.
Compare the entries with the last order and tell the stores clerk about the mismatch.
Adjust the oil tally to match the log so the order can be submitted on time.

basic.situation: With the senior engineer present, you start an engine for a routine departure check. The pressure gauge rises, while the temperature reading remains steady.

options.text: Follow the start sequence, compare both readings with the operating range, and report them.
Start the engine, watch the gauges, and tell the senior engineer what they show.
Start the engine and note the steady temperature for the watch handover.
Start the engine and report that the temperature looks steady to the senior engineer.

advanced.situation: During a scheduled liquid transfer, the off-loading pump’s flow drops while the tank level is nearing its planned limit. The deck team is waiting for your update.

options.text: Hold the current pump setting and tell the deck team that flow has slowed.
Check pump and valve readings, slow transfer near tank limit, and update deck team.
Check the valve position and tell the deck team the tank is nearing its planned limit.
Report the slower flow and ask the deck team to monitor the tank level.

basic.situation: You watch an approaching fishing vessel near the lock entrance. Its speed seems higher than nearby traffic, and you need to judge its approach.

options.text: Compare its position at two moments and give the operator a cautious speed estimate.
Watch its position for a short interval and report whether it seems to be closing fast.
Estimate its speed by eye and tell the operator it is moving quickly.
Track its movement against fixed landmarks and report the estimated speed to the lock operator.

advanced.situation: Two vessels approach from different directions as a third clears the lock. Their arrival times are close, and available spaces are limited.

options.text: Watch the closest vessel and hold the other estimates until it clears.
Track each vessel’s position and progress, then report a sequence that fits the available spaces.
Report each vessel’s estimated arrival time and let the operator choose the order.
Use the usual arrival order and report it to the lock operator.

basic.situation: A vessel requests passage under the drawbridge. The road is clear, and you are assigned to activate the navigation lights and traffic signals.

options.text: Activate the signals and lights, then report what the control panel displays.
Activate the navigation lights and tell the operator the bridge is ready.
Check the assigned controls, activate the signals and lights, then confirm their indications.
Switch on the signals and lights, then continue with the next routine check.

advanced.situation: A long vessel is ready to pass, but the drawbridge indicator pauses midway through its opening sequence. Road traffic is waiting at the barriers.

options.text: Tell the traffic operator about the pause and ask which control to use.
Hold at the safe state, follow procedure, and report the indicator fault.
Continue the opening sequence and monitor whether the indicator catches up.
Pause the controls and report the stalled indication to the bridge operator.

basic.situation: A small vessel approaches the bridge area while another is moving clear. You have been asked to direct the approaching vessel using the loudspeaker.

options.text: Hold the vessel until the other clears, then direct its approach.
Ask the vessel to hold position while you check the other vessel’s progress.
Ask the vessel to reduce speed and wait for your next signal.
Tell the approaching vessel to proceed slowly toward the bridge area.

advanced.situation: Two vessels arrive together at a narrow bridge area, and one is already turning to leave. Their crews are waiting for your signals.

options.text: Signal both vessels to move slowly and maintain separation in the narrow area.
Direct the turning vessel out, then signal the second once space opens.
Signal the turning vessel to continue and tell the second to hold position.
Ask both crews to wait while you check which vessel can turn first.

basic.situation: A cargo vessel passes through the lock during your watch. You can read its name and type, but its destination is not on the passage note.

options.text: Record the visible details and leave the destination for the next watch to find.
Enter the vessel name and type, then fill the destination from the last passage.
Record the visible name and type, then confirm the destination with the operator.
Record the name and type, and mark the destination as pending confirmation.

advanced.situation: Your weekly lock log shows more vessels arriving during one time period than others. A manager asks for a summary to help with shift planning.

options.text: Count arrivals by period and send totals to the manager.
Ask the manager whether this pattern matches recent staff observations on shift.
Recommend a shift change based on the busiest period shown in the log.
Check entries for gaps, compare counts by period, and summarize patterns with caveats.

basic.situation: You are sweeping the lock facility yard before a busy shift and find loose leaves collecting beside a drain grate.

options.text: Sweep the open yard and leave the leaves by the drain for the next round.
Sweep the leaves into a pile beside the drain for collection later.
Clear the leaves from the grate, sweep the yard, and report any blockage that remains.
Move the leaves away from the grate and finish sweeping the yard.

advanced.situation: Several routine maintenance jobs are due at the facility, including repainting a walkway and repairing a loose handrail. Staff use both areas daily.

options.text: Submit separate requisitions for each job and include clear facility locations.
Rank jobs by access and safety impact, then submit requisitions with locations.
Submit one general requisition for all jobs and let maintenance choose the order.
Ask staff which job causes more disruption and submit that requisition first.

basic.situation: A vehicle clips a bridge barrier during your watch. No one appears hurt, and the driver gives you the time and location for the accident report.

options.text: Note the time, location, and driver’s account, then submit the accident form.
Record the time, location, vehicle details, and observed damage, then submit the report through procedure.
Record the time and location, then ask the driver to send details later.
Write that a vehicle hit the barrier and submit the brief note before shift change.

advanced.situation: After a minor bridge-area collision, two witnesses describe different vehicle movements. Your report is due before the watch ends.

options.text: Ask both witnesses to agree on one version before completing the report.
Include both accounts in one summary and submit the report on time.
Use the account that aligns with damage, then finish the report before handover.
Record accounts separately, note observations, and flag differing details in the report.

basic.situation: A guest arrives during a busy lunch rush and asks for help with a wheelchair and directions to the lift. You are assigned to greet arriving drivers.

options.text: Welcome the guest, ask where they need to go, and guide them along the accessible route.
Point toward the lift and explain that the accessible entrance is beside it.
Open the driver's door, hand over a parking map, and return to the queue.
Ask a nearby colleague to greet the guest while you finish the next car.

advanced.situation: A driver reports feeling faint beside a car while another guest asks for directions. You are the senior attendant on duty with two newer staff nearby.

options.text: Ask a colleague to fetch first aid while you keep waiting guests informed.
Ask one colleague to call emergency services while you guide the driver somewhere safe.
Tell the driver to sit inside while you finish helping the waiting guests.
Stay with the driver and ask a colleague to direct guests and call responders.

basic.situation: A customer hands you a numbered tag at the collection desk, but the matching vehicle is not in the first row you check.

options.text: Ask the customer to wait while you check the next few rows for the vehicle.
Search the nearby rows using the tag number, then update your supervisor on what you find.
Check the tag log, confirm the vehicle number, and ask your supervisor to help locate it.
Take a car that looks similar to the customer’s description and bring it forward.

advanced.situation: Two new attendants are preparing for a busy evening collection period, and recent handovers have included mismatched keys and numbered tags.

options.text: Set a key and tag logging routine, then review several entries together.
Ask attendants to follow desk steps and report mismatches during collection.
Demonstrate key and tag matching, then ask staff to verify each log entry.
Let staff use personal tag shorthand to speed up the collection queue.

basic.situation: A customer is waiting while you check a car before parking it, and you notice a fresh-looking scrape near the rear bumper.

options.text: Record the scrape and show the customer before moving their car.
Note the scrape on the form and point it out before parking.
Park first, then add the scrape to your inspection notes before shift handover.
Tell a colleague about the scrape, then continue the remaining visible checks.

advanced.situation: You are reviewing several damage reports after customers questioned whether scratches were present at drop-off; the team uses different descriptions for similar marks.

options.text: Write common descriptions for visible marks and audit a sample of team reports.
Agree shared photo and location prompts with the team, then compare reports against those prompts.
Use the most detailed report as the team's example and ask others to copy it.
Ask each attendant to add more detail to the damage notes on future cars.

basic.situation: A customer pays a small parking charge with a large note, and several cars are waiting behind them at the payment desk.

options.text: Round the change to the nearest ringgit and serve the next driver.
Use the displayed fee, make change, and log payment after the queue clears.
Make change, log the amount, and give the customer a receipt.
Count the note, state the change, and record payment before serving another car.

advanced.situation: At closing, your cash drawer is short by RM20 after a busy shift, and you are helping a newer attendant learn the balancing routine.

options.text: Compare receipts with the cash log, note the shortage, and explain your findings.
Ask the trainee to recount notes while you complete closing paperwork.
Recount cash against transactions, record the shortage, and show the trainee each check.
Add RM20 from your wallet to cover the shortage before handover.

basic.situation: You are tidying the parking area and spot food wrappers near a bay that drivers are using to turn around.

options.text: Sweep the wrappers into the next bay before the arriving cars turn in.
Move the wrappers to the edge so cars can pass, then collect them later.
Clear the wrappers from the bay and place them in the nearest bin.
Pick up the wrappers, check the turning path, and leave the bay clear for drivers.

advanced.situation: After rain, litter gathers around two busy rows, and attendants have been parking carts where they narrow available bays during peak hours.

options.text: Schedule row checks, name a cart holding area, and review access weekly.
Ask attendants to tidy rows between cars and store carts beside office.
Have staff clear busy rows when customers report blocked bays during peak periods.
Review peak demand, assign cart storage, and check that bays stay open.

basic.situation: A customer asks you to park their car in a marked bay and wants to know the fee before leaving the keys.

options.text: Take the keys and park in a convenient space before checking the fee board.
Park in the nearest open bay and tell the customer the usual charge.
Confirm bay, fee, and key handover details before parking the car.
Park in the marked bay and point out the posted fee to the customer.

advanced.situation: A customer disputes a parking charge because their ticket is smudged, while a queue forms and you are expected to coach a new attendant on fee complaints.

options.text: Check entry records, explain the fee calmly, and coach staff to document resolution.
Charge the lowest visible amount and ask another attendant to handle the disagreement.
Review ticket details, explain the posted fee, and record the customer's complaint.
Apply the usual charge, note the smudged ticket, and invite later follow-up.

basic.situation: A car is due for a routine check before service, and your checklist shows tire pressure and fluid levels still need checking.

options.text: Check the tires and fluid levels, then tell the mechanic about anything low.
Top up the visible fluids and set tire pressure from the last service note.
Check the front tires and engine oil first, then move the car into the service bay.
Check each tire and listed fluid against the checklist, then record any level needing attention.

advanced.situation: A vehicle has a falling coolant level and a wet patch beneath it, while a junior attendant asks whether to refill it before the next service booking.

options.text: Ask the junior to refill coolant before the car's next booking.
Record the coolant loss and leak, then ask the mechanic about refilling.
Top up to the mark and ask the junior to monitor for leaks.
Note the low coolant and leak, then refer the vehicle for mechanic assessment.

basic.situation: A scheduled service includes an oil change, and your mechanic has left the steps and supplies ready at the work bay.

options.text: Use the remaining oil from the open container and finish the change quickly.
Drain the oil and fit the new filter before checking the service instructions.
Follow the service steps, confirm the specified oil, and record the completed change for the mechanic.
Use the prepared oil and follow the listed steps, then tell the mechanic when finished.

advanced.situation: A customer reports vibration after a tyre rotation, and a junior attendant is unsure whether the wheel nuts were tightened to the service specification.

options.text: Recheck wheel fit and specified tightening, then hold the car for mechanic review.
Tell the customer vibration may settle after a short drive, then release the car.
Check the wheel nuts against specifications and ask the mechanic to assess vibration.
Ask the junior to repeat the rotation and check whether vibration changes.

basic.situation: Your checklist calls for greasing a vehicle's specified joints, and the grease gun and service notes are ready at the bay.

options.text: Apply grease to the easiest joints first and check the list after the bay clears.
Match each specified joint to the notes, apply grease with the gun, and record the service.
Grease the listed joints with the prepared gun, then tell the mechanic the work is done.
Use the grease gun on every visible joint so none are missed during service.

advanced.situation: A vehicle returns with a dry-looking joint soon after scheduled greasing, and a junior asks whether to add more grease before the next booking.

options.text: Grease nearby joints too so the vehicle can leave on schedule.
Inspect the joint, record its condition, and request a maintenance review.
Apply specified grease and ask the junior to monitor the joint next check.
Check the joint record, note dryness, and refer it to the mechanic.

basic.situation: A driver requests a specific fuel amount and asks you to replace a worn wiper blade while the pump queue is short.

options.text: Fill the tank to the next whole ringgit and fit the nearest blade size.
Start fueling while checking which wiper blade looks closest to the old one.
Confirm fuel type and amount, then fit the matching requested blade.
Fill the requested amount and install the replacement blade from the matching shelf.

advanced.situation: Several vehicles arrive for fuel while a customer needs a replacement headlamp bulb, and a newer attendant asks how to keep the work moving safely.

options.text: Ask the attendant to fit the bulb while you manage fueling and payments.
Continue fueling and let the customer choose a bulb from the shelf.
Separate fueling from fitting, confirm requests, and show the attendant the bulb check.
Fuel waiting cars while the attendant checks the requested bulb and confirms its fit.

basic.situation: A customer pays for a small service in cash and asks which road leads toward the nearest town centre.

options.text: Keep the cash on the counter and wave toward the main road as the customer leaves.
Give the customer the usual town direction and enter the payment after the next sale.
Confirm the amount, give the receipt and change, then explain the marked route toward town.
Take payment, issue the receipt, and point out the town direction on the road map.

advanced.situation: A customer says their card was charged twice after an accessory purchase, and a newer attendant is waiting for your help at the counter.

options.text: Offer a cash refund for the second charge and ask the attendant to document it.
Review receipts with the customer, explain the payment record, and document their complaint.
Review receipts and payment records, explain the findings, and guide case documentation.
Ask the customer to check their banking app while you serve the queue.

basic.situation: A delivery of wiper blades arrives, and the shelf is nearly empty while the daily accessory sales report is due before closing.

options.text: Put the boxes beside the shelf and finish the sales report from yesterday's figures.
Check the delivery against its list, shelve stock, and update the records.
Shelve the delivered blades and enter their verified quantity in the stock record before closing.
Add the expected delivery quantity to the shelf count and complete the report quickly.

advanced.situation: Your monthly accessory records show popular wiper blades often run out, while some slow-selling bulbs remain on the shelf for weeks.

options.text: Compare sales with stock counts, then adjust reorder suggestions and explain the entry process.
Use last month's order quantities as a starting point, then review them against current demand.
Review sales totals, recommend extra blades, and show staff how to update stock records.
Order extra blades from recent requests while monitoring current bulb quantities on the shelf.

basic.situation: You are assigned a cabin turnaround and find loose rubbish and fingerprints on the passenger windows.

options.text: Spray cabin cleaner on the windows to finish the wipe-down faster.
Wipe the windows and leave the rubbish for the next cabin team.
Vacuum the aisle and wipe the windows, then report any rubbish left.
Pick up the rubbish, then wipe the windows with the approved cloth.

advanced.situation: After an exterior wash, dark exhaust streaks remain near a panel, and the approved cleaning fluid is available.

options.text: Rub the streaks with a general-purpose solvent to save turnaround time.
Ask the lead which fluid suits the streaks before treating the panel.
Test the approved fluid on a small area and wait for the lead's reply.
Apply the approved fluid to the streaks, then check the panel for residue.

basic.situation: You are assigned to refill an aircraft's potable water tank, and the service hose is ready.

options.text: Confirm the hose label with a colleague before beginning the refill.
Connect the potable-water hose, refill the tank, and record the service.
Inspect the hose connection, then refill the tank as time allows.
Use the nearest service hose to complete the refill before boarding.

advanced.situation: After a fluid change, you spot a fresh drip beneath a connection while the aircraft is still in the service area.

options.text: Pause the fluid service and trace the drip to its connection before release.
Record the drip and finish the fluid change for the next shift.
Tighten the connection with a nearby tool and finish the fluid change.
Wipe the area and ask the technician to recheck the connection.

basic.situation: You are assigned to empty the lavatory system during a turnaround and have the service cart nearby.

options.text: Open the drain valve to empty the tank before connecting the cart.
Connect the service cart, empty the system, and replenish sanitizer as assigned.
Connect the cart and empty the system, then leave sanitizer for later.
Check the cart fittings with a teammate before starting the service.

advanced.situation: During lavatory servicing, the indicator stays lit after emptying, and the sanitizer level appears below the marked range.

options.text: Replenish sanitizer and ask the next shift to check the indicator.
Reset the indicator and send the aircraft onward after the emptying cycle.
Tell the cabin team about the lit indicator and low sanitizer level.
Check the servicing indicators, replenish sanitizer to its marked range, and report the fault.

basic.situation: You are in the raised basket for a scheduled de-icing pass, with a team lead guiding the application.

options.text: Confirm your starting surface with the lead before applying fluid.
Apply fluid to the nearest wing section while the truck is positioned.
Follow the lead's pass pattern and apply fluid across the assigned surfaces.
Cover the visible upper surfaces and tell the lead where you stopped.

advanced.situation: Freezing rain is increasing during a de-icing shift, and the lead asks you to prepare another fluid mixture.

options.text: Follow approved mixture instructions for these conditions and confirm the batch with the lead.
Check the approved mixture chart, then prepare and label its listed batch.
Prepare a smaller batch at the earlier ratio and watch its coverage.
Reuse the earlier mixture ratio to keep the next aircraft moving.

basic.situation: You are assigned to guide an arriving aircraft toward its marked stand using hand signals and batons.

options.text: Check stand markings with a teammate before guiding the arriving aircraft.
Wave the aircraft toward open space beside its marked stand.
Take the assigned position and give agreed signals as the aircraft approaches.
Give approach signals from the marked stand entrance as the aircraft arrives.

advanced.situation: A tug assignment changes while another aircraft is approaching the shared apron lane, and dispatch requests an update by radio.

options.text: Radio dispatch with the new assignment, then wait outside the lane for guidance.
Ask dispatch to confirm aircraft priority before moving the tug into the shared lane.
Pause tug movement and radio dispatch about the approaching aircraft and shared lane.
Use the shorter route only after checking the shared lane remains clear of aircraft.

basic.situation: While cleaning, you notice a small visible crack on an aircraft component and must complete the shift form.

options.text: Record the crack's location on the form and tell maintenance staff.
Note a crack on the form and finish the cabin handover.
Mark the form as clear so the cleaning handover stays on schedule.
Ask a colleague to inspect the component with you before completing the shift form.

advanced.situation: During a surface check, you find a fresh fluid trace near a panel, while the service form says the area was inspected.

options.text: Ask the previous shift to clarify the inspection entry before handover.
Add a note that fluid was seen near the panel.
Record the trace and panel location, then flag the mismatch for maintenance review.
Change the form to show no leak so the records match the inspection.

basic.situation: You are counting vehicles at a junction during the morning peak when a delivery truck blocks your view for several minutes.

options.text: Keep counting visible vehicles and note when the truck blocked your view.
Estimate the hidden vehicles from the next signal cycle and complete the sheet.
Mark the obstructed interval, then resume counting when your view clears.
Move closer to the junction to see around the truck.

advanced.situation: A planned traffic study spans several junctions, but field teams use different time intervals and one radar device gives inconsistent readings.

options.text: Give teams a common interval and record which radar readings seem unusual.
Combine the available counts and flag the radar readings for review.
Set shared intervals, device checks, and exception codes before collecting comparable data.
Ask teams to submit their sheets and reconcile the totals afterward.

basic.situation: A signal timing worksheet has updated approach counts, and your assigned task is to calculate a standard setting for the junction.

options.text: Round the counts first, then calculate a convenient signal setting.
Reuse the last setting because the junction layout has not changed.
Use the standard formula and check the inputs against the count sheet.
Enter the new counts into the standard formula and record the result.

advanced.situation: A proposed shopping development may increase traffic near two junctions, while the council is reviewing parking needs for the surrounding area.

options.text: Base the strategy on current parking complaints near the entrance.
Compare the traffic forecast with current counts and note likely junction pressure.
Review projected flows and parking demand across the affected area and time periods.
Use the developer's peak-hour forecast to estimate a parking target.

basic.situation: You are placing an automatic traffic counter beside a busy road, and the fastening bracket shifts when you tighten it.

options.text: Place a wedge under the bracket and continue with the installation.
Tighten the bracket harder so the counter stays in place.
Secure the area, reposition the bracket, then check its stability with guidance.
Stop fastening and ask your supervisor to check the bracket placement.

advanced.situation: A traffic counter stops recording during a field survey, and the next scheduled count period begins soon at a nearby site.

options.text: Check power and connections, replace a faulty part, then verify a live count.
Swap its battery and restart the counter at the same settings.
Move the device to the next site and report the failed count later.
Record the outage and ask a colleague to test the counter.

basic.situation: You visit a roadwork site and find the temporary signs placed behind parked vehicles, reducing drivers' view of the lane closure.

options.text: Photograph the signs and record the parked vehicles in your site notes.
Ask a nearby worker whether approaching drivers can see the signs clearly.
Shift the signs toward the road edge after checking with the site contact.
Compare visibility with the plan, then raise the obstruction with the site contact.

advanced.situation: A large housing project proposes a new access road near a busy junction, and your site review must inform the traffic impact assessment.

options.text: Focus the review on the proposed entrance and its sight lines.
Compare projected trips, junction capacity, and nearby access effects across peak periods.
Review the junction counts and note where queues currently form.
Use the access plan to estimate traffic and recommend a nearby signal change.

basic.situation: Your manager asks for a chart of observed vehicle delays at a junction, but one observation period has missing entries.

options.text: Leave out the incomplete period and title the chart as a full-day view.
Chart the complete periods and label the missing interval clearly.
Fill the missing interval with the average from nearby periods.
Prepare the chart and mention the missing interval in your notes.

advanced.situation: A review meeting needs drawings of a proposed signal installation, but the latest site measurements differ from the older base plan.

options.text: Copy the old drawing and adjust the signal location by visual estimate.
Draw the signal layout from the latest measurements and submit it for discussion.
Use the base plan and note that field dimensions may have changed.
Update the drawing from verified measurements and mark unresolved dimensions for review.

basic.situation: A resident calls asking whether a lane closure will affect access to a local clinic, but your work order lists only the road segment.

options.text: Tell the resident the clinic will remain accessible during the closure.
Check the current closure notice, then explain confirmed access details plainly.
Direct the resident to the site office for information about clinic access.
Read the listed closure details and offer to check the access question.

advanced.situation: A utility crew reports that its permitted street closure is blocking a bus route, and a traffic technician asks you how to handle the closure.

options.text: Suggest shifting barricades to reopen one bus lane, after confirming it is safe.
Ask the crew to pause while you refer the route conflict to your manager.
Check permit conditions, coordinate a safe route adjustment, and brief the technician.
Keep the closure in place and ask the technician to monitor bus traffic.

basic.situation: You inspect a freight bay before departure and notice that one pallet has shifted against its blocking. What do you do?

options.text: Photograph the bay and record the loose pallet for the shift report.
Check the blocking against the load plan and note any gaps.
Ask the loader to reposition the pallet, then recheck its blocking.
Accept the wrap as adequate and move on to the next bay.

advanced.situation: A heavy crate shifts during loading, and the remaining freight is already braced around it. You are asked to clear the bay for dispatch. What do you do?

options.text: Keep the current arrangement and ask dispatch to watch the crate during transit.
Add another strap across the crate and record the extra restraint.
Have the crew unload the adjacent freight and rebuild the bracing around the crate.
Tell the crew to reload the crate and check its blocking before dispatch.

basic.situation: During an inspection, you find a cargo handling device with a worn contact surface. What do you do?

options.text: Mark the device unavailable and arrange a condition check before further use.
Check the device condition against its maintenance guidance and note the wear.
Continue the inspection and mention the worn surface in your notes.
Use the device for lighter cargo since the surface still holds a load.

advanced.situation: You find a cargo restraint that does not meet the handling procedure, but the shipment is due shortly. What remedial procedure do you recommend?

options.text: Recommend adding a second restraint beside the existing one for added support.
Recommend pausing this shipment until the crew can inspect the restraint again.
Record the restraint finding and let the shipment proceed on schedule.
Recommend a suitable restraint change and verify it against the handling procedure.

basic.situation: A shipment plan cites a loading procedure you have not used before. You need to check the permitted cargo arrangement. What do you do?

options.text: Check the cargo list against a similar shipment plan from last week.
Review the capacity page and flag any figures that appear unusual.
Ask the planner which arrangement they normally use for this cargo.
Find the cited procedure and match its limits to the planned arrangement.

advanced.situation: A vessel plan lists draft markings and cargo limits that leave little room for a heavy item. What do you review before advising on the shipment?

options.text: Check the stability guidance and suggest reducing the heavy item's quantity.
Use the last approved load as a guide and keep this cargo quantity.
Compare the cargo plan with stability limits and draft markings before advising.
Read the draft markings and tell the planner the available depth looks tight.

basic.situation: You check a storage area holding moisture-sensitive cargo and find the humidity above its stated range. What do you do?

options.text: Move the cargo to a suitable area and record the condition change.
Record the humidity and check the cargo guidance for the allowed range.
Open the loading doors to air the room before the next check.
Place a fan nearby and check the humidity again later in the shift.

advanced.situation: A sudden humidity change affects a high-value shipment, and the usual storage area is no longer suitable. What storage protocol adjustment do you make?

options.text: Adjust the storage schedule and notify the team of the changed humidity range.
Keep the shipment in place and compare readings with the next routine check.
Cover the shipment and ask the team to check conditions at shift change.
Move the shipment to a stable area and log the new conditions for monitoring.

basic.situation: After a freight shipment, you find a torn package and a delay during loading. What do you include in your report?

options.text: Include handling details and explain how they affected the shipment schedule.
Note the loading delay and package condition for the incoming shift to review.
Describe the torn package and loading delay in the shipment report summary.
Record the torn package, loading delay, and time each issue occurred.

advanced.situation: Your recent shipment reports show repeated delays at the same loading point. What do you do with the recorded details?

options.text: Count the delayed shipments and share the total at the next handover.
Compare delay times and handling notes across reports to identify the recurring pattern.
Summarize the delays from memory and suggest the team work faster.
Send the latest report to the loading team and ask what happened.

basic.situation: A shipment needs a special handling step that is listed on its cargo instructions. What do you tell the workers?

options.text: Cover the special handling step during the next team update with the workers.
Leave a note by the shipment and ask the lead worker to brief colleagues.
Explain the special handling step and confirm workers understand the cargo instruction.
Show workers the instruction sheet and review the required handling step together.

advanced.situation: A crew is preparing a mixed load with dangerous and heavy cargo, and the stow plan has a difficult sequence. How do you guide them?

options.text: Review the stow plan with the crew and answer questions as they work.
Tell the crew to follow the plan and report any problems during loading.
Share a familiar stow method and let the crew adapt it to the cargo.
Demonstrate the sequence and explain how the heavy cargo affects dangerous cargo stowage.

basic.situation: You inspect an aircraft exterior and find a small dent near an access plate. What do you do?

options.text: Check the area against the inspection checklist and record the dent's location.
Ask the mechanic whether this dent was present during the last service.
Mark the dent on the worksheet and continue with the remaining exterior checks.
Treat the dent as cosmetic and finish the inspection on schedule.

advanced.situation: After a modification, an aircraft has an unfamiliar instrument reading during an authorized inspection. What do you do before assessing its airworthiness?

options.text: Record the reading and ask the maintenance team what value they expected.
Accept the modification since the aircraft started and the instrument settled.
Compare the reading with approved test guidance and document the aircraft response.
Repeat the observation using the approved procedure and compare the readings.

basic.situation: During an authorized ground test, you see a gauge reading fluctuate outside its expected range. What do you do?

options.text: Record the test conditions and reading, then follow the approved test steps.
Finish the test and mention the fluctuation at the end of the shift.
Ask the mechanic whether this gauge often fluctuates during ground checks.
Repeat the reading once and note whether the fluctuation happens again.

advanced.situation: A reported aircraft incident has conflicting witness accounts and a damaged component. What do you do within your investigation role?

options.text: Write up the first account received and add the other details later.
Document both accounts and note where their timelines differ.
Interview the witnesses again and ask them to agree on a timeline.
Preserve the component details and compare each account with available records.

basic.situation: You review a maintenance record and see that a service entry has no matching date in the flight log. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the operator to confirm which date they intended to enter.
Note the mismatch and continue reviewing the remaining service intervals.
Compare the entries and flag the date gap for record verification.
Use the maintenance entry date and complete the interval review.

advanced.situation: A competency review shows that several trainees struggle with the same repair procedure. How do you use the finding in your role?

options.text: Pass the results to the training team for its next routine update.
Schedule another general review session and repeat the same practice exercise.
Compare examination results and identify which parts of the procedure need stronger training.
Review the training materials and note where the procedure is covered.

basic.situation: Your inspection finds a cracked cover on an aircraft instrument. What equipment recommendation do you record?

options.text: Keep the aircraft on its planned schedule and revisit the cover later.
Record the crack and ask maintenance to decide on the next action.
Recommend replacing the cover and include its location in the report.
Recommend replacement or an approved repair based on the inspection finding.

advanced.situation: Inspection records show a recurring equipment issue across different operating conditions. What recommendation can you make within your role?

options.text: Recommend changing the standard based on the latest inspection report.
Compare the records by condition and recommend a targeted standards review.
Share the issue count and suggest that the current policy be reviewed.
Ask the operations team whether they have seen the same equipment issue.

basic.situation: You complete an inspection form and notice that one repair detail is missing from the work record. What do you do?

options.text: Submit the form as complete because the repair passed inspection.
Use the mechanic's verbal summary to complete the repair field.
Check the repair record and enter the verified detail in the inspection report.
Leave the field open and note that the repair detail is pending.

advanced.situation: An investigation report is being prepared after several inspectors documented the same defect in different ways. What reporting approach do you recommend?

options.text: Let each inspector keep a personal report style for faster completion.
Ask each inspector to use the format from the most recent report.
Share a sample report and ask the team to follow its section order.
Set shared reporting fields for the defect, evidence, action, and certification basis.

basic.situation: You review an airworthiness certificate application and find one supporting record missing. What do you do within your delegated review role?

options.text: Return the file for completion and note the absent supporting document.
Ask the applicant to resend the application with the missing attachment.
Check the checklist, identify the missing record, and brief the authorized decision maker.
Withhold endorsement and document why satisfactory inspection findings cannot replace missing records.

advanced.situation: Two applications raise the same airworthiness concern, but their supporting records differ. How do you guide junior inspectors on the certification review?

options.text: Compare both records against applicable criteria and explain how evidence shapes each review.
Review both files with the junior inspectors and discuss the shared airworthiness concern.
Copy the earlier application's outcome for both reviews without checking differing records.
Ask each inspector to note a proposed outcome before the group discussion begins.

basic.situation: During a walk-around, you see a fresh fluid stain beneath a parked service vehicle before its next trip.

options.text: I would check the stain's location, inspect nearby parts, and record what I find.
I would ask a nearby technician to confirm the stain before I complete the form.
I would clear it based on its clean exterior and keep the inspection queue moving.
I would walk around the vehicle and note visible damage on the inspection sheet.

advanced.situation: A vehicle passes its usual checks, but you spot an altered fuel line and an unfamiliar engine part during inspection.

options.text: I would document each change, assess its system impact, and base my finding on evidence.
I would review the service record and routine checks before deciding on vehicle status.
I would record the changes and compare each part with available vehicle specifications.
I would flag the vehicle for review and ask the owner about these changes.

basic.situation: You are assigned an emissions inspection, and the OBD scanner is ready beside a vehicle waiting in the bay.

options.text: I would record the previous vehicle's result and keep the inspection queue moving.
I would connect the scanner and begin the emissions check using its standard screen.
I would reconnect the cable after an error and save the displayed result.
I would match vehicle details, secure the cable, and confirm the scanner reads its data.

advanced.situation: A remote inspection feed briefly freezes while a handheld controller shows the vehicle moving near a marked test area.

options.text: I would pause the check and record the brief interruption in my inspection notes.
I would pause the remote check, restore a clear view, and resume after steady device response.
I would ask a colleague to monitor the screen while I operate the controller.
I would rely on the last clear image and finish the current check.

basic.situation: During a routine check, a diesel vehicle releases a visible plume as you inspect its exhaust area.

options.text: I would observe the plume, inspect emission equipment, and record both findings.
I would note the smoke and compare visible emission equipment with my checklist.
I would ask the driver when smoke began and include the answer in my notes.
I would record a pass because the engine sounds steady during this check.

advanced.situation: A workshop says it has repaired a steering fault, but the replacement part and adjustment differ from the earlier inspection notes.

options.text: I would inspect the repair, verify the steering response, and document any remaining concern.
I would ask the workshop to explain the different part before I close the check.
I would sign off from the workshop's repair note and return the vehicle to service.
I would check the repair against the original notes and inspect the changed parts.

basic.situation: A passenger submits a complaint that a vehicle's step shifted while boarding, and you are assigned to gather initial details.

options.text: I would close the complaint since the vehicle completed its route safely.
I would record the complaint and ask the driver what happened during boarding.
I would ask the driver to inspect the step and report after the next trip.
I would record the passenger's account, time, location, and available vehicle details.
