advanced.situation: Two vehicles report similar brake warnings after recent servicing, and you are asked to investigate the equipment failures.

options.text: I would compare service notes and report the matching warning to the workshop.
I would inspect one affected vehicle and use its findings to guide the second case.
I would map failures by vehicle, service date, and warning conditions before review.
I would treat each warning as routine wear and close both incident files.

basic.situation: A driver's log has a blank entry during a delivery day, while the related shipping paper lists several stops.

options.text: I would copy the previous day's entry into the blank to finish the file.
I would flag the gap, match the listed stops, and record which details need clarification.
I would mark the blank and compare the log with the shipping paper.
I would ask the driver to fill the blank from memory before filing the papers.

advanced.situation: A carrier's training file has current attendance sheets, but its qualification guidelines appear inconsistent across several vehicle roles.

options.text: I would compare role guidelines with attendance records and note unclear requirements.
I would accept the sheets as sufficient evidence without comparing role guidance.
I would ask the carrier to explain role differences and record its response.
I would trace each role's guidance through training records and document unmet requirements.

basic.situation: You finish a routine inspection after finding a cracked mirror, and the form asks for findings and actions taken.

options.text: I would record the mirror's condition, inspection details, and the action taken before filing.
I would add a brief note and tell the next shift about the cracked mirror.
I would describe the crack and note that the vehicle needs mirror attention.
I would mark the form clear because the rest of the vehicle looked sound.

advanced.situation: Several inspections find the same lighting defect, and you are asked to guide colleagues on corrective notices and reporting.

options.text: I would draft each notice and send it to colleagues as a reference.
I would share a sample notice and invite colleagues to adapt wording for each finding.
I would close repeat cases as minor and keep the inspection queue moving.
I would set an evidence and action template, then coach colleagues to tailor notices.

basic.situation: A passenger with a walking stick reaches the coach door as the queue begins to form behind them.

options.text: I would point them toward an open seat and keep boarding on schedule.
I would greet them, ask what help they prefer, and guide them aboard at their pace.
I would open the door and offer an arm while they choose a seat.
I would ask another passenger to hold the queue while I assist them.

advanced.situation: A passenger using a wheelchair boards with a companion, while the remaining seats include one space near the door.

options.text: I would ask the companion where the chair should go and follow their direction.
I would place the wheelchair where it fits and fasten the nearest straps.
I would offer the seat near the door and prepare the wheelchair straps.
I would ask about seating and transfer needs, then secure the chair using the available tie-downs.

basic.situation: A new passenger asks whether the next bus stops near the market, while you are greeting people at the door.

options.text: I would avoid assumptions and check the route card before guiding them aboard.
I would ask a colleague to confirm the market stop, then share that information.
I would check the route card, identify the nearest market stop, and explain boarding.
I would greet them, check the route card, and name the nearest market stop.

advanced.situation: A passenger says the advertised timetable conflicts with an earlier staff answer and asks how they can still reach their appointment.

options.text: I would compare the timetable with the earlier answer and explain the listed departure.
I would check current service details, resolve the conflicting advice, and offer workable routes.
I would acknowledge the conflict and avoid promising that the earlier time remains valid.
I would confirm the departure with a colleague, then explain the appointment options.

basic.situation: At a busy stop, you count boarding tickets and need to record how many passengers leave the vehicle.

options.text: I would record ticket sales and ask the driver to estimate departing passengers.
I would tally people leaving, compare the ticket count, and record both figures.
I would copy the previous stop's count to finish the log quickly today.
I would count departing passengers as they exit and record that total alongside tickets.

advanced.situation: Your boarding total differs from the seat reservations, and another attendant has already recorded a matching total for disembarking.

options.text: I would compare the reservation list with my boarding tally and record the difference.
I would ask the other attendant to confirm their total before I submit mine.
I would retrace boarding and disembarking counts against reservations, then record any unresolved variance.
I would change my tally to match the reservation list and finish the report.

basic.situation: Before departure, you notice a loose handrail during the equipment check, and passengers are waiting to board.

options.text: I would alert the driver and request a pause to assess the loose handrail.
I would test the rail, note the defect, and follow the safety procedure.
I would keep boarding moving since the handrail still seems usable for now.
I would document the loose handrail and continue the remaining safety checks.

advanced.situation: During pre-departure checks, a door warning appears only when the vehicle turns, a fault absent from your checklist.

options.text: I would record the warning and finish the listed checks before raising the issue.
I would ask the driver when the warning appeared and note its trip history.
I would clear the warning once it fades and prepare the bus for scheduled departure.
I would safely recreate the warning while parked and report it for review.

basic.situation: A family boards while you are due to explain the seatbelt procedure before the coach leaves.

options.text: I would explain the belt steps, demonstrate one, and invite a fit check.
I would ask an experienced attendant to demonstrate the belt and answer family questions.
I would read the safety script and point out each belt while speaking.
I would tell passengers to buckle up and keep the boarding line moving.

advanced.situation: Several new attendants give different explanations of the emergency hammer, and passengers ask when to use it.

options.text: I would let each attendant use their own wording to explain the hammer.
I would demonstrate the approved procedure and explain when passengers should use the hammer.
I would explain the hammer to each group myself and let colleagues observe.
I would share the approved script and show staff where the hammer is stored.

basic.situation: At a regular roadside stop, the bus is ready to pull away and the driver is watching your signal.

options.text: I would wave the bus forward since this stop is running late today.
I would call the driver over and ask whether the bus can safely leave.
I would give the agreed hand signal and watch for the driver's response.
I would check the passenger path, signal clearly, and confirm the driver responds.

advanced.situation: Two buses share a crowded terminal bay, and one driver begins edging forward while passengers cross between them.

options.text: I would ask an attendant to watch passengers while I signal the first bus.
I would wave the waiting bus ahead to free space in the bay.
I would signal the nearer driver to pause and clear the crossing path.
I would stop both buses, clear the crossing, then coordinate departures in sequence.

basic.situation: A conveyor light turns amber, and its dial nears the posted limit. The station procedure says to stop the belt if the light turns red.

options.text: I would ask a nearby operator to watch the light while I finish loading.
I would reset the warning dial and keep production moving at its usual pace.
I would check the dial again and tell the senior operator about the amber light.
I would watch the dial and stop the belt if the light turns red, as posted.

advanced.situation: The belt runs normally, but one gauge has crept upward across three checks. A large order is due before the shift ends.

options.text: I would note the latest reading and wait for the next scheduled check.
I would record each reading and compare the trend with the operating range.
I would compare the trend with earlier readings, then flag the change before the next run.
I would adjust the gauge until its reading matches the usual shift level.

basic.situation: Your supervisor has stopped the belt after a small carton jam. You have a hand tool and can see the carton near the guard.

options.text: I would wait nearby until another operator has time to clear the carton.
I would reach past the guard and pull the carton free while the belt coasts.
I would use the hand tool from the safe side while the supervisor watches.
I would ask the supervisor to confirm the belt is stopped before using the tool.

advanced.situation: A torn sack is wedged deep beneath the conveyor roller, and the line is backing up. Your supervisor has stopped the belt and asked you to assess it.

options.text: I would select a suitable bar, ease the sack clear, and check the roller before restart.
I would identify the wedged material and describe its position before choosing a tool.
I would lever the sack loose with a long bar and restart the line quickly.
I would ask the supervisor to bring the usual pole for the wedged sack.

basic.situation: A senior operator asks you to hand-load boxes onto a conveyor. The marked loading area is nearly full, and more boxes are waiting nearby.

options.text: I would ask where the next boxes should go before adding them.
I would wait for the area to clear before moving any more boxes.
I would place the boxes across the belt to clear the waiting stack.
I would load a small batch where the senior operator points and check spacing.

advanced.situation: Delicate cartons arrive faster than the conveyor clears them. Several corners are already dented, and the next pallet is due in minutes.

options.text: I would space the cartons and slow my loading to match the belt flow.
I would move the next pallet closer so cartons are easier to reach.
I would inspect the damaged corners, then space cartons and adjust the loading pace.
I would feed cartons at the arriving pace to keep the belt fully supplied.

basic.situation: A lift is available to move supplies to a work station, but you have not used this model before. A senior operator is nearby.

options.text: I would load the supplies and follow the senior operator's lift guidance.
I would ask the senior operator for lift guidance and secure the supplies.
I would take the lift alone to deliver supplies before the station runs short.
I would carry the lighter supplies by hand and leave the rest for later.

advanced.situation: Two stations need supplies before the next production run, and one narrow aisle is already busy with incoming materials.

options.text: I would check which station is lowest, then plan deliveries around aisle traffic.
I would send both loads through the busy aisle to finish deliveries together.
I would deliver to the low station first, then find a clear route.
I would wait for the aisle to clear before moving either load.

basic.situation: You weigh the shift's first batch of materials and must enter its type, quantity, and storage location in the logbook before the next batch arrives.

options.text: I would enter the type, weight, quantity, and location from the batch ticket.
I would reuse yesterday's entry and change the quantity to save time.
I would copy the weight and quantity from the ticket into the logbook.
I would record the weight and location, then leave the type for later.

advanced.situation: Your logbook shows several slowdowns beside similar motor warnings this month. The maintenance team is planning its next service window.

options.text: I would mention the repeated warnings at the next routine team meeting.
I would remove the warning notes that seem unrelated to keep the log brief.
I would group warnings by date and suggest checking the motor before similar runs.
I would total the slowdown minutes and send the number to maintenance.

basic.situation: You notice a conveyor motor making a new scraping sound during a routine run. The line still moves, and your supervisor is at the nearby station.

options.text: I would report the sound, its timing, and any change in the motor's operation.
I would increase the line speed so the motor sound becomes easier to hear.
I would finish the current task before mentioning the new sound.
I would tell the supervisor about the sound and when it began.

advanced.situation: A conveyor hesitates twice, then resumes. A junior coworker heard the same fault but is unsure what details the supervisor needs.

options.text: I would ask the coworker to mention the fault at the shift handover.
I would help the coworker report the hesitations, timing, and restart response.
I would tell the supervisor it stopped twice during the run.
I would suggest telling the supervisor the belt was fine after restarting.

basic.situation: A delivery arrives with a steel bundle whose weight is marked on its paperwork. You are checking it against the crane’s capacity with your supervisor nearby.

options.text: Use the marked weight and ask your supervisor to confirm the chart reading.
Check the paperwork weight against the crane’s chart before rigging begins.
Read the bundle weight and compare it with the chart at this radius.
Use the bundle’s usual weight from the last delivery to plan the lift.

advanced.situation: A long beam will be lifted from two points, and its weight is split unevenly. The crew wants to proceed, but the load chart is close to its limit.

options.text: Treat the beam as evenly shared and begin while the crew watches.
Check the total beam weight against capacity and ask the rigger about balance.
Calculate each pick point’s share, then compare the heaviest share with capacity at radius.
Review the lift drawing and chart, then use the marked beam weight.

basic.situation: Before a routine lift, you notice fraying on one crane cable during your inspection. A replacement cable is available, and the shift is waiting.

options.text: Stop that cable’s use and arrange replacement before the next lift.
Show the wear to your supervisor and wait for their replacement decision.
Tell the operator about the fraying and ask them to watch the cable.
Mark the frayed section and continue with lighter loads for this shift.

advanced.situation: During setup, a lifting accessory moves unevenly under a light test and has no obvious damage. The planned load is valuable and the work area is tight.

options.text: Adjust the accessory tension by feel and proceed with the planned lift.
Pause setup and report the uneven movement for a maintenance check.
Try a smaller test load and watch whether the accessory settles evenly.
Compare the movement with the setup guide, then adjust and retest unloaded.

basic.situation: A truck arrives with bundled timber for unloading. Your spotter is ready, but another delivery is waiting behind it in the yard.

options.text: Unload the whole truck quickly so the waiting delivery can enter.
Ask the driver which bundles should come off first, then begin unloading.
Unload the bundles in the marked sequence while your spotter guides placement.
Start with the nearest bundle and let the spotter guide each move.

advanced.situation: Two containers need moving to storage bins, but the first bin is partly blocked and the second has limited clearance. The next truck is due soon.

options.text: Move the containers to whichever bins are open, then update the staging list.
Ask the yard lead which container should move first, then follow their order.
Check each bin’s clearance and route, then place containers by the staging plan.
Clear the first bin and send both containers there to save travel time.

basic.situation: You are under direct supervision, moving a small load from a truck to a marked area. The supervisor gives a signal to raise the boom slowly.

options.text: Wait for the supervisor’s signal, then move the lever in short increments.
Move the lever smoothly, follow the signal, and watch the load’s path.
Raise the boom at a steady pace while watching the hook.
Raise the boom quickly to clear the truck before the next signal.

advanced.situation: You are operating a crane in a narrow work area where a suspended load must pass near scaffolding. The signaler’s view is partly blocked.

options.text: Hold position and reposition the signaler before resuming the lift.
Pause the lift, restore clear signals, and use controlled movements through the gap.
Ask the signaler to give shorter calls while you move the load carefully.
Continue slowly using the last signal and judge clearance from the cab.

basic.situation: Your maintenance guide calls for cleaning and lubricating a crane pulley after the shift. Dust has gathered around the cable groove.

options.text: Check the guide’s lubrication point and clean the pulley before applying lubricant.
Clean the groove and apply the guide’s specified lubricant to the pulley.
Apply a small amount of available grease and clean the pulley afterward.
Wipe away the visible dust and leave lubrication for the next service.

advanced.situation: A grappling device slips during a routine check, and inspection shows a worn pivot pin. Your maintenance instructions include approved replacement parts and repair steps.

options.text: Remove the device from use and request an approved pin for repair.
Replace the pin with its approved part, then follow the repair checks.
File the worn pin to fit, then return the device to service.
Tighten the pivot and test the device with a light load before release.

basic.situation: A helper is placing blocking under a crane on level ground. You have the placement instructions and can see the support point clearly.

options.text: Read the placement instruction aloud and check where the helper sets it.
Point out the support point and direct the helper to seat the blocking there.
Ask the helper to choose a spot that looks stable under the crane.
Tell the helper to place the blocking near the marked support point.

advanced.situation: Several helpers are setting outriggers on soft, sloping ground. One pad begins to settle as the crane is positioned for a lift.

options.text: Ask the nearest helper to watch the settling pad during positioning.
Stop positioning, direct helpers to reset blocking, and check each outrigger’s seating.
Pause positioning and direct the crew to inspect the settling pad together.
Have the helpers add loose boards under the settling pad and continue setup.

basic.situation: Your supervisor directs a small adjustment so the suction boom stays over the marked excavation line.

options.text: Swing the boom quickly across the marker to catch up with the line.
Use small lever movements and check the boom against the marker after each adjustment.
Make a broad lever movement to bring the boom back across the marker.
Follow the supervisor's signal and move the lever toward the excavation line.

advanced.situation: A narrow channel turn needs precise dredge positioning, and two operators ask how to coordinate boom rotation and pump engagement.

options.text: Set a shared sequence for positioning, boom rotation, and pump engagement, then confirm each move.
Have each operator follow the last signal they heard while you watch the channel edge.
Ask the more experienced operator to take over the positioning decisions for this turn.
Tell both operators to rotate the boom as needed while keeping the pump running.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to start the dredge engine, but a deckhand is still beside the intake.

options.text: Start the engine now so the crew can begin the shift on schedule.
Wait for the deckhand to finish nearby, then check with the supervisor about starting.
Start the engine at low speed while the deckhand steps away from the intake.
Ask the deckhand to move clear, then start when the supervisor confirms readiness.

advanced.situation: After a brief stop, the dredge engine turns slowly on restart and the crew is waiting to resume excavation.

options.text: Ask a crew member to watch the engine while you try one more restart.
Pause briefly, check the usual starting indicators, and try one controlled restart.
Record the slow turn, stop repeated attempts, and follow the crew's engine fault procedure.
Keep trying the starter between short pauses until the engine catches.

basic.situation: With guidance from the lead, you need to pull in a manual cable to shift the dredge slightly.

options.text: Take in the cable at a steady pace and watch the drum as it winds.
Pull quickly to remove slack before the lead finishes checking the cable path.
Pull in the cable in short bursts, pausing when the line feels tight.
Pull the cable steadily while the lead watches its route and tension.

advanced.situation: A dredge shift requires two winches and a shore cable to move through a tight reach; newer operators need guidance.

options.text: Let the most confident operator control both winches while others handle the shore cable.
Have one operator call the movements while the crew watches cable tension.
Assign each winch a clear signal and review the cable route before coordinated movement.
Ask operators to keep their winches moving slowly and report any cable slack.

basic.situation: The lead asks you to pump water through a dredge pipeline after flow drops during routine work.

options.text: Start the water flow gradually and watch the outlet for returning movement.
Run the pump at full flow until the usual clearing time has passed.
Increase the pump setting a little and let it run while you watch the gauge.
Pump water at the usual setting and check whether the outlet flow improves.

advanced.situation: Pipeline flow has fallen twice this week, and you are coordinating junior staff around a busy dredging schedule.

options.text: Keep the current pumping schedule and assign one junior to monitor the pipeline gauge.
Set regular water-clearing intervals around planned pumping and brief staff on flow checks.
Increase water pumping between shifts so the pipeline stays clear through busy periods.
Ask staff to clear the line whenever flow drops and note the next shift's results.

basic.situation: A lead asks you to help place a shore anchor and cable before another pipe is laid from the dredge.

options.text: Help set the anchor at the marked point and let the lead check the cable.
Guide the crew to place the anchor at the marked point, then check cable alignment.
Hold the cable while another worker sets the anchor where the ground feels firm.
Place the anchor near the marked point so the pipe crew can keep moving.

advanced.situation: At a difficult bank, the planned shore anchor point is soft and the team must place an anchor and extend pipe safely.

options.text: Ask the crew to shift the anchor slightly toward firmer ground and check the pipe reach.
Pause placement, identify a firmer point with the lead, and reroute the cable and pipe.
Move the anchor a short distance and keep the original cable path for the pipe extension.
Have the crew use the planned point and add cable tension to steady the anchor.

basic.situation: With your supervisor nearby, you lower an anchor pole to verify the depth at a routine excavation point.

options.text: Ask the supervisor to read the gauge while you hold the pole steady.
Lower the pole to the marked point and read the depth gauge after it settles.
Lower the pole quickly and record the first depth reading it shows.
Lower the pole at the point and compare the gauge with the expected depth.

advanced.situation: Two depth gauge readings differ near a channel edge, and the excavation record is due before the next dredge move.

options.text: Use the deeper reading so the record is ready before the next move.
Repeat the scan at the same point, compare readings, and record the consistent result.
Enter both readings with a note that the channel edge needs another check.
Average the two readings and mark the channel edge for a later review.

basic.situation: With a lead nearby, you receive a hand signal to start the hoist drum and raise a routine load.

options.text: Start at a low speed while watching for the lead's hand signal.
Move the control smoothly after confirming the lead's start signal.
Wait for the hand signal, then start the drum at a steady speed.
Start the drum as soon as the load team looks ready to move.

advanced.situation: During a tight lift, hand signals and the dial indicator suggest different hoist speeds while the load passes near a platform.

options.text: Use the dial reading to increase speed and clear the platform before the next lift.
Hold the current speed until the signaler and dial reading agree on the movement.
Ease the drum speed and follow the clearest signal while tracking the dial indicator.
Follow the signaler's speed instruction and check the dial as the load moves.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to start the diesel winch that moves a cableway, with the crew ready at their stations.

options.text: Confirm the diesel controls are set, then start with the supervisor nearby.
Ask a nearby operator whether the cableway is clear, then start the engine.
Start the winch now so the cableway can keep to its planned schedule.
Start the diesel winch after checking that the crew is at its stations.

advanced.situation: A compressed air winch must move a cableway through a narrow span, and you are covering the controls during a busy shift.

options.text: Keep pressure steady and ask the crew to monitor cable movement closely.
Increase winch speed to shorten the crossing time during the busy shift.
Check air supply response under load, then adjust winch pace for the span.
Set a steady pace and monitor cable movement across the span.

basic.situation: You are watching the hoist gauge while another worker signals that a routine load has reached its marked height.

options.text: Check the gauge against the worker's signal before confirming the load height.
Rely on the gauge reading and tell the crew the load has reached its mark.
Ask the worker to repeat the signal while you note the gauge reading.
Confirm the marked height when the worker signals, then keep watching the gauge.

advanced.situation: During a deep lift, the indicator reading and a worker's hand signals disagree about the load position near the landing point.

options.text: Continue toward the landing using the depth reading as your main position cue.
Follow the signaler's direction slowly while checking the indicator reading.
Use the indicator as reference and tell the worker the reading you see.
Pause movement and confirm the indicator reading with a clear signal before proceeding.

basic.situation: A routine delivery arrives, and you need to select a load that fits the hoist's posted weight and size limits.

options.text: Select a large load only after checking it against the stated limits.
Compare the load's listed weight and dimensions with posted limits before selection.
Choose a load within the posted weight and size limits, leaving a safety margin.
Choose the pallet's heaviest load to reduce the number of lifts.

advanced.situation: Two bundled materials fit the platform, but their labels show different weights and the lift plan sets a strict maximum.

options.text: Ask the delivery crew which bundle they usually send for this hoist.
Use the heavier bundle because the platform has space and the load looks stable.
Choose the bundle whose labeled weight and dimensions meet the lift plan's limits.
Select the lighter bundle and compare its label with the lift plan before loading.

basic.situation: You are helping load materials, and a coworker waits for your signal before the hoist takes the next item.

options.text: Signal as soon as the item reaches the platform to keep loading moving.
Check that the item looks steady, then signal the coworker to continue.
Signal the coworker once the item is settled and the loading area is clear.
Tell the coworker to get ready while you finish arranging nearby materials.

advanced.situation: Several materials must be loaded in sequence near a shared landing area, and workers are giving overlapping signals.

options.text: Ask everyone to repeat signals slowly and watch the landing area between lifts.
Let each worker signal their own material so the crew can work in parallel.
Have workers wait for a gap in the signals before moving each load.
Agree on one signal caller and confirm each load is clear before the next move.

basic.situation: With a lead nearby, you need to attach a cable to a routine load using the available hand tools.

options.text: Attach the cable with a suitable hand tool and signal readiness for the lead's check.
Fasten the cable firmly, then check that it sits straight on the load.
Fit the cable with the assigned tool, then check its connection before lifting.
Use the specified hand tool and ask the lead to inspect the attachment.

advanced.situation: A heavy hoist must be repositioned near stored materials, and its cable connection needs to be reset for the next lift.

options.text: Move the hoist clear of stored materials, then reconnect and check the cable seating.
Shift the hoist a short distance and check that the cable remains attached.
Reposition the hoist carefully and have a coworker watch its clearance from materials.
Reconnect the cable first so the hoist is ready once the crew clears space.

basic.situation: You are positioning a pallet of boxed stock for a marked bay. The pallet looks uneven, and your lead is nearby to guide you.

options.text: Follow the marked fork pockets and ask for a spotter while raising the load.
Ask the lead to confirm fork spacing, then position the pallet for the marked bay.
Slide the forks under one side and lift before checking the pallet balance.
Check the pallet entry points and load balance, then place both forks evenly before lifting.

advanced.situation: A trainee is preparing an irregular crate for transport, and its weight sits toward one end. You are asked to coach the securing step.

options.text: Have the trainee identify shift points, choose rated restraints, and test stability before release.
Demonstrate two cross straps and ask a spotter to watch the first movement.
Show the trainee how to add rated straps across the crate, then check tension.
Use one convenient strap around the middle and let the trainee move it slowly.

basic.situation: You are moving an empty forklift to the assigned loading bay with supervision. A pedestrian crossing is on the route.

options.text: Check the aisle is clear, use the assigned route, and move at walking pace.
Back through the crossing while looking toward the pallet instead of aisle traffic.
Ask your supervisor to guide your first turn while you carry the empty forks.
Follow the usual aisle and slow near the crossing while watching pedestrians.

advanced.situation: A new operator must raise a long beam with a swivel hook near a storage rack. You are guiding the lift from the floor.

options.text: Lift the beam quickly over the rack while the operator stands beneath its path.
Check the beam's balance and clearance, then guide a slow lift from a safe viewing point.
Ask the operator to raise the beam slightly while you check its swing from the side.
Review the controls and hand signals, then guide the operator through the rack approach.

basic.situation: You are weighing two similar pallets before dispatch. Their old tags are hard to read, and a scale and blank tags are available.

options.text: Weigh both pallets, record each reading against its pallet ID, and make fresh tags.
Copy the clearer old tag and send both pallets with matching labels.
Weigh each pallet and write its reading on a temporary note for the lead.
Use the scale for one pallet and apply that weight to the similar one.

advanced.situation: A load audit finds repeated differences between pallet counts and dispatch tags. You are asked to recommend a simple accuracy check for the shift.

options.text: Approve loads when their pallet tags match the dispatch sheet for the shift.
Sample several pallets, compare tags with counts and weights, and log each mismatch.
Check a few tags against the dispatch sheet and report any differences.
Ask the team to reweigh the pallet with the largest difference before dispatch.

basic.situation: Your forklift is due for routine cleaning and lubrication. The maintenance checklist names the points to service and the truck is parked nearby.

options.text: Clean the listed points and lubricate them while following the checklist sequence.
Park the truck securely, then clean and lubricate the listed points as directed.
Ask your lead to confirm the lubricant before cleaning the specified points.
Clean around moving parts while the truck is running to save setup time.

advanced.situation: A battery warning returns after charging, and your maintenance log shows this has happened twice. You are preparing the truck for the next shift.

options.text: Bypass the warning and send the truck out since charging restored power.
Keep the truck out of service, record the recurring warning, and arrange inspection.
Recharge the battery once more and see whether the warning returns during use.
Review the maintenance log and schedule a battery inspection before assigning the truck.

basic.situation: You are tending an automatic stacking machine using a step-by-step card. A box has shifted at the feed, while the machine is still moving.

options.text: Slow the machine and watch whether the next box pushes it back into line.
Reach through the guard and straighten the box while the stacker runs.
Stop the cycle and ask the lead to check the shifted box before restarting.
Pause the feed, realign the box from outside the guard, then resume per instructions.

advanced.situation: Cartons are skewing on an automatic packaging line, slowing output. You are allowed to adjust its marked feed and speed settings and coach the shift team.

options.text: Raise the speed to clear the backlog before checking the skewed cartons.
Reduce the speed and show staff how to watch carton alignment during the run.
Test permitted feed settings on a sample, confirm alignment, then coach staff on checks.
Ask maintenance to inspect the line while staff continue packaging by hand.

basic.situation: You are releasing granules from a storage bin into the marked hopper with supervision. The chute and receiving area are clear.

options.text: Open the valve halfway based on the last load and watch the hopper fill.
Open the chute before confirming which hopper is connected to the bin.
Confirm the connected hopper, then open the valve gradually while watching the flow.
Follow the posted sequence and monitor the hopper level as the granules flow.

advanced.situation: Granules surge during a bin release, and the receiving hopper's high-level alarm sounds. You are operating the assigned controls while the lead is nearby.

options.text: Keep releasing material despite the alarm, then tell the lead after clearing the bin.
Reduce valve opening, watch the alarm, and let the hopper catch up.
Stop the feed, check hopper level with the receiving operator, and get restart clearance.
Close the valve, note the alarm, and tell the lead before resuming work.

basic.situation: You are scrubbing a painted vehicle panel with oily marks. The job card calls for mild cleaner, and brushes and pads are available.

options.text: Apply mild cleaner and scrub the painted panel using a standard brush in steady passes.
Use mild cleaner and a soft brush, then inspect the panel in good light.
Scrub the paint with an abrasive pad until the oily marks fade and the surface looks even.
Rinse the panel first, then repeat the cleaner pass if oily marks remain visible.

advanced.situation: Stubborn grime remains on a vehicle component, and the work card identifies it as aluminium. You are choosing among labeled cleaners and abrasives.

options.text: Apply the available acid cleaner across the aluminium to break down the grime.
Choose a labeled cleaner based on the surface and apply it across the component.
Use a strong abrasive pad to remove the grime before the next job arrives.
Check product guidance for aluminium, test a compatible method on a hidden spot, then proceed.

basic.situation: You need to mix a cleaning solution for a parts wash. The posted recipe gives measured amounts, and a marked jug and labeled concentrate are ready.

options.text: Estimate each amount from the container markings, then mix a small batch carefully.
Measure recipe amounts in the marked jug, mix in posted order, and label the solution.
Use the marked jug to measure both ingredients, then mix the posted amounts.
Add extra concentrate to the bucket so the wash might work faster during the job.

advanced.situation: Grease remains on steel parts after the standard dilution, and another batch is due soon. The cleaner label lists an approved dilution range.

options.text: Add extra concentrate beyond the label range to clear the grease quickly.
Increase the concentration within the label range and inspect the next batch.
Test a measured dilution within the labeled range on a sample, then check results.
Ask the lead which approved dilution to try for the steel parts.

basic.situation: You have rinsed a batch of small machine parts. Drying racks and clean cloths are available, and the next batch is waiting.

options.text: Place the rinsed parts across the drying rack with gaps between them.
Wipe the parts with a clean cloth and put them on the rack.
Stack the wet parts together on the rack to clear the wash area.
Space the rinsed parts on a clean rack and check they drain freely.

advanced.situation: A cleaning bay has loose debris and salvageable scrap after a job. The site waste plan marks separate containers for each stream.

options.text: Sort debris and salvage by the waste plan, then clear the bay.
Shovel the loose material into separate containers and ask where to take them.
Use the labeled containers for each stream and clear the work area afterward.
Sweep the debris and scrap into the nearest general container for removal.

basic.situation: You are starting a standard parts-cleaning machine. The load is inside, the cover is closed, and the posted card names the normal cycle.

options.text: Press the high-pressure cycle button to finish the parts faster.
Ask a coworker to confirm the cycle before you activate the machine.
Check the closed cover and selected cycle, then press the start button.
Select the posted cycle and press start while watching the indicator lights.

advanced.situation: A sprayer's pressure has fallen during a wash, though its gauge remains in the marked operating range. You can adjust the flow valve and inspect visible hoses.

options.text: Switch to a lower-flow cycle and finish the vehicle with slower passes.
Open the flow valve slightly and see whether the spray improves.
Check the gauge and hoses, adjust the valve within range, then retest.
Turn the pressure control past its marked limit to restore the spray.

basic.situation: You are checking a vehicle after washing it. A visible streak remains on the rear panel, and the delivery queue is building.

options.text: Check the rear panel again after the next vehicle is finished.
Mark the streak for another pass, then recheck the panel before release.
Record the streak and tell the wash operator before the vehicle leaves.
Sign off the vehicle as clean so the delivery queue keeps moving.

advanced.situation: Several cleaned vehicles return with streaks, and you are asked to improve the team's cleanliness checks for the next shift.

options.text: Ask staff to pass vehicles with light streaks so the queue can recover.
Update the checklist with visible streak examples for each vehicle area.
Set panel criteria, inspect a sample, and coach staff to apply them.
Inspect one returned vehicle and tell the team what you noticed.

basic.situation: You are connecting a wash hose to a pump before driving the van to a nearby job. The labeled hose and pump fittings are available.

options.text: Start the pump with the hose loosely attached to check the flow.
Connect the matching fittings and coil the hose beside the pump.
Ask a coworker to hold the hose while you start the pump.
Match fittings, secure the hose, and check its route before leaving.

advanced.situation: You are preparing tomorrow's van loads and suggested stops. One site needs a specific cleaner, and stock is low across the two jobs.

options.text: Pack common cleaners and follow the usual route order for both scheduled jobs.
Check the stock sheet and map both sites, then plan the shortest route between them.
Count stock, reserve the needed cleaner, and order stops by site needs and location.
Use last week's stock count and assign the scarce cleaner to the first stop scheduled.

basic.situation: Your work order lists two pallets for Bay 3, but the handwritten bay number is smudged. Where should you take them?

options.text: Take both pallets to the bay used for this product yesterday.
Choose the nearest open bay and mark the work order complete.
Ask the nearby lead to confirm the bay before moving either pallet.
Read the legible item details and move the pallets toward Bay 3.

advanced.situation: A work order lists three crate sizes, two drop-off points, and shared padding. You have one trolley and a tight dispatch window. How do you plan the materials?

options.text: Check the sequence and quantities, then stage padding by each drop-off point.
Take the first crate listed and return for materials as each stop arises.
Gather all listed padding and start with the closest delivery point.
Load the largest crates first and ask dispatch to sort out the stops.

basic.situation: You are tagging containers for a routine stock transfer. One label has the right item name but the wrong destination. What do you do?

options.text: Set that container aside and tag the other containers first.
Keep the label as printed and send the container with the batch.
Add the right destination beside the existing label in marker.
Replace the label with the destination shown on the transfer sheet.

advanced.situation: A new returnable container has two similar sizes and will pass through several shifts. Your tags must distinguish them during a busy handover. What do you do?

options.text: Mark sizes with different ink colours and record the choice for handover.
Write the item name on every tag and sort by size at dispatch.
Use the size and item identifiers from the order on each container tag.
Reuse the old tags and tell the next shift which size is which.

basic.situation: You find spare hand tools on the floor beside a storage rack during your shift. What do you do to protect the stored inventory?

options.text: Return the tools to their marked storage spot and clear the rack access.
Push the tools under the rack to clear the visible floor space.
Stack the tools neatly beside the rack and note them for later.
Place the tools on the nearest shelf until the aisle is free.

advanced.situation: Rainwater is reaching a lower rack where boxed stock and spare equipment share space. You can rearrange items within your assigned storage area. What do you do?

options.text: Shift the boxes to another wet corner and note their new location.
Move the boxes higher and place equipment in the open aisle temporarily.
Cover the lower boxes with spare plastic and leave the rack arranged.
Move boxed stock to a dry rack and keep equipment accessible for inspection.

basic.situation: You are assembling a small crate from precut lumber, and one side panel rocks after fastening. What do you do before packing the item?

options.text: Check the other joints and ask a teammate to steady the panel.
Add padding inside so the item presses against the loose panel.
Realign the panel and refasten it before placing the item inside.
Pack the item and strap the crate tightly for the short trip.

advanced.situation: A long, fragile part must be repacked after its crate corner splits. You have precut lumber, padding, and hand tools. How do you assemble a safer container?

options.text: Wrap the part heavily and close the old crate with extra nails.
Lay the part diagonally in the old crate and fill the spare space.
Build a square frame around the part and pad each contact point.
Replace the split corner and add padding where the part touches wood.

basic.situation: You are sorting mixed cartons before loading. Several contain glass, and the truck will travel over uneven roads. What do you do?

options.text: Load the glass cartons near the door for easier unloading later.
Separate the glass cartons and ask the loader to place them carefully.
Group the glass cartons together and add padding before loading them.
Mix the glass cartons between sturdy boxes to fill the gaps.

advanced.situation: A high-value machine has an uneven base, and the transport crew expects a bumpy route. Your assigned task is to fit the available bracing and straps. What do you do?

options.text: Pad the uneven base and ask the driver to avoid rough roads.
Add extra straps across the machine and check them at the dock.
Brace the base, pad contact points, and tension straps across stable surfaces.
Place loose padding underneath and tighten one strap over the casing.

basic.situation: You need to move several cartons from storage to a nearby production area. A hand trolley is available, and the cartons fit securely. What do you do?

options.text: Stack every carton high on the trolley to finish in one trip.
Carry the top cartons by hand and leave the trolley for others.
Move half the cartons by trolley and return for the rest.
Load a stable stack and wheel the cartons along the clear aisle.

advanced.situation: A team is moving a suspended load toward a storage bay, and the operator has limited visibility. You are assigned to attach the sling and guide the load. What do you do?

options.text: Hook the nearest sling point and walk ahead to clear the bay.
Check the sling placement and stand where the operator can see you.
Attach the sling at approved points and guide using clear agreed signals.
Attach the sling where convenient and rely on the operator's view.

basic.situation: You are sorting paper and plastic at the yard. A few damp sheets are stuck to plastic packaging. How do you handle them?

options.text: Separate the paper from the plastic and place each in its marked bin.
Set the stuck pieces aside and finish sorting the loose materials first.
Put the stuck pieces in the paper bin for the next sorting round.
Place the bundle in whichever bin has more room at the moment.

advanced.situation: A mixed metal delivery includes copper, brass, and aluminium pieces that look similar under dusty light. Your team is sorting it for recycling. What do you do?

options.text: Put the dusty pieces with the largest metal group to clear the bay.
Wipe sample surfaces and separate each identified metal into its marked container.
Group the similar pieces together and let the facility separate them later.
Sort clear pieces first and set uncertain items aside for a closer check.

basic.situation: You are operating a baler with guidance, and a bundle finishes compressing. The indicator still shows pressure. What do you do next?

options.text: Ask the assigned guide to confirm the pressure reading before release.
Release the chamber latch so the finished bundle can be removed.
Follow the baler's release sequence and check the panel before opening it.
Wait a short while, then open the chamber when the bundle looks firm.

advanced.situation: A grinder begins vibrating more than usual during a shift, while material is still feeding steadily. You are trained for routine checks. What do you do?

options.text: Reduce the feed rate and keep running until the batch is finished.
Increase the feed briefly to see whether the vibration settles down.
Pause the feed and tell the lead about the vibration before resuming.
Stop feeding, follow the shutdown steps, and inspect accessible areas for buildup.

basic.situation: You are moving a wrapped pallet with a pallet jack. The load tilts slightly as you turn into the shipping lane. What do you do?

options.text: Keep the handle low and complete the turn before the lane fills.
Turn more slowly and keep the pallet close to the lane edge.
Ask a nearby teammate to watch the pallet as you finish the turn.
Pause in a clear area and reposition the pallet before continuing.

advanced.situation: A new teammate is using a forklift to load bales onto a truck. The first bale shifts as it rises. You are experienced with the loading area. What do you do?

options.text: Have the driver lower the bale and check its balance before lifting again.
Signal a pause and coach the driver to reposition the forks under the bale.
Ask the driver to lift more slowly and guide the bale from nearby.
Tell the driver to continue upward while you steady the bale by hand.

basic.situation: You are preparing a discarded refrigerator for chemical extraction with specialized equipment. The checklist flags a damaged connection. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the trained operator to review the connection before continuing the setup.
Connect the extraction hose carefully and proceed at a slower pace.
Pause preparation and follow the checklist for a damaged connection before extraction.
Set the unit beside the machine and prepare the next appliance first.

advanced.situation: During extraction from an air conditioner, the machine reading changes and the chemical line looks damp. You are operating the specialized equipment. What do you do?

options.text: Wipe the line dry and continue while monitoring the machine display.
Pause extraction and follow the equipment procedure for a damp chemical line.
Stop the cycle and tell the lead what the reading and line show.
Reduce the extraction rate and finish the current unit under close watch.

basic.situation: You are placing sorted recoverable materials on a conveyor belt. A small metal piece falls near the moving belt. What do you do?

options.text: Push the metal piece onto the belt with another light item.
Place the next materials on the far side of the belt from it.
Tell the belt operator about the piece before placing more materials.
Pause feeding and follow the site's method for removing the loose piece.

advanced.situation: A batch of metal parts arrives with oily residue, and the next batch must meet the site's cleaning requirements. You are assigned to clean the materials. What do you do?

options.text: Set the batch aside and ask which cleaning method applies to oily metal.
Rinse all the parts together and send them forward to dry.
Wipe visible oil from the parts and place them with the clean batch.
Separate the oily batch and clean it using the site's metal requirements.

basic.situation: You are sweeping the recycling yard and spot broken glass beside a barrel. Workers are moving nearby. How do you handle the area?

options.text: Mark the spot and finish sweeping the rest of the yard first.
Keep people clear and collect the glass using the site's cleanup method.
Push the glass under the barrel until nearby work has finished.
Sweep the glass toward the barrel so it stays out of the walkway.

advanced.situation: Your site log shows two missed equipment-cleaning entries, and loose paper is gathering near the machinery. You are assigned to record logs and maintain the yard. What do you do?

options.text: Clear the paper and record the missed entries as unverified for follow-up.
Sweep the paper away and mark both cleaning entries as complete.
Clear the paper and ask the equipment team to confirm both cleaning entries.
Record the missing entries and leave the paper for the next cleanup round.

basic.situation: You spot a dent on a product while checking a batch against the shift checklist. The conveyor is moving steadily.

options.text: I note the defect pattern and hold matching items for a second check.
I compare each item with the checklist and set aside visible defects.
I feed the marked batch onward so the next station can sort it.
I check a few items, then keep the line moving at its usual pace.

advanced.situation: Different shifts classify the same surface marks differently, and a large order is due today. You are asked to guide defect checks.

options.text: I approve the marks so the waiting order can leave on schedule.
I show the team a few examples and ask them to follow my judgments.
I define defect limits from the specification and train staff with sample items.
I write a short guide showing the marks that the team should flag.

basic.situation: A new stack of materials arrives with two similar grades, and your work card shows the required labels for each.

options.text: I match each grade to the work card and label its stack clearly.
I place both grades together and let the next station identify them.
I check a sample label and mark the remaining stacks by appearance.
I label the first stack, then copy those marks onto the second stack.

advanced.situation: Several similar products move between stations, and staff have mislabeled samples during a busy shift. You are asked to improve marking practice.

options.text: I reuse the old sample labels to keep the line supplied during the shift.
I ask each station to add a different color beside its usual label.
I set one label format with clear product identifiers and teach staff to verify it.
I tell staff to write the product name more neatly on every label.

basic.situation: Your work card gives a target weight for each bundle, and the scale is ready beside the line.

options.text: I weigh each bundle and compare its reading with the work card.
I weigh a bundle from each group and check the readings against target.
I weigh one bundle, then use it as a guide for the rest.
I record the target weight and send the bundles onward by feel.

advanced.situation: A new product has a narrow weight range, and two scales show slightly different readings during your shift. The batch is waiting.

options.text: I compare both scales with a known check weight before measuring more items.
I use the faster scale and record its readings for the batch.
I ask another operator which scale has worked better for them lately.
I pause batch measurements and report the differing readings to the lead.

basic.situation: A conveyor is feeding a machine, and the next materials are stacked nearby with a hand truck available.

options.text: I place the next stack beside the machine and let it feed itself.
I load the easiest stack first to avoid slowing the conveyor.
I move the next stack closer and check its label before loading.
I load the next materials in the order shown on the work card.

advanced.situation: Two materials must enter a machine in sequence, and a new coworker is helping during a busy changeover. You are responsible for loading.

options.text: I let the coworker choose which stack to load to build their confidence.
I show the coworker the sequence and agree on clear hand signals before loading.
I demonstrate the first load and ask the coworker to copy my movements.
I load both materials quickly while the coworker watches from the side.

basic.situation: At the end of your run, residue is visible on the machine guard and the floor beside your station.

options.text: I leave the residue in place so the next batch can start sooner.
I clean the guard and floor using the posted routine before leaving.
I wipe the guard and ask the next shift to handle the floor.
I sweep the floor and leave the guard for the next cleaning round.

advanced.situation: Residue has appeared at the same machine several times this week, while cleaning checks vary between shifts. You are asked to improve the routine.

options.text: I set a shift cleaning schedule with clear checks for the residue area.
I audit cleaning records and walk the area against a shared checklist.
I sign off the cleaning sheet so the next run can begin on time.
I remind staff to clean the machine when they have a spare moment.

basic.situation: A finished stack needs to move from the machine to the marked staging area, and a hand truck is available.

options.text: I leave the stack beside the machine for the next crew to move.
I move the stack to the staging area and check that it stays balanced.
I push the stack along the shortest open path to save time.
I secure the stack on the hand truck and follow the marked route.

advanced.situation: Two machines need regular material deliveries through a narrow aisle, and a hand truck transfer caused a near collision this week.

options.text: I tell operators to move carefully and keep deliveries close to each machine.
I keep the current route and send both deliveries together to save trips.
I set a delivery route and sequence that keep the aisle clear during transfers.
I stagger the deliveries and ask the operators to watch for each other.

basic.situation: You notice a loose seam on a packed item while checking containers against the order checklist.

options.text: I check the next few items and keep packing the rest as usual.
I set the item aside and compare nearby seams with the checklist.
I pack the item with the finished cartons so the order stays complete.
I mark the item for review and continue checking the next one.

advanced.situation: Two packers disagree about which carton dents matter, and a large order is nearly finished. You are asked to guide the checks.

options.text: I define acceptable marks from the packing specification and train staff with examples.
I collect disputed cartons and write down the marks staff have questioned.
I ask each packer to use their own judgment and flag uncertain cartons.
I show the packers a few cartons that seem acceptable to me.

basic.situation: You are packing two similar products, and the work card lists a different container label for each.

options.text: I use the label from the first container on the next several cartons.
I check a label sample and mark the remaining cartons by product color.
I match each product to its work card and apply the listed label.
I leave the cartons unmarked for the next station to identify later.

advanced.situation: Similar containers use different product labels, and several team members rotate between packing stations during the shift.

options.text: I reuse spare labels from the previous product to keep the line moving.
I write a short guide showing where each station should place its labels.
I use a shared label layout with product identifiers and teach staff to verify each container.
I ask each station to add a color mark beside its current label.

basic.situation: You are sealing a carton with the specified fasteners, and one side does not stay closed after assembly.

options.text: I add a strip of tape over the loose side and continue packing.
I set the carton aside and ask a nearby packer to check the seam.
I send the carton along because the other sides are still closed.
I check the seam and reseal the carton with the specified fasteners.

advanced.situation: Cartons are opening during handling, and newer packers assemble them differently during a busy order. You are asked to improve the method.

options.text: I let cartons move on and rely on careful handling to keep them closed.
I demonstrate a consistent fold and fastener sequence, then watch staff practice it.
I ask each packer to add extra fasteners wherever a carton feels loose.
I post a reminder to fold the cartons firmly before sealing them.

basic.situation: Your order sheet gives a target count per carton, and the packed items are ready for checking.

options.text: I count each carton against the order sheet before sealing it.
I count cartons from each group and note any difference from target.
I count one carton from the stack and use it as my guide.
I seal the cartons now and let dispatch count them later.

advanced.situation: A weighing scale gives inconsistent readings for packed orders, and staff are waiting to complete a shipment.

options.text: I use the lower reading so the shipment can be completed on schedule.
I pause weighing and report the inconsistent readings to the shift lead.
I compare the scale with a known check weight before weighing more orders.
I ask a coworker which scale they trust for heavier cartons.

basic.situation: Packed cartons for two orders are ready near your station, and the work cards show separate staging areas.

options.text: I check each work card and move cartons to the matching staging area.
I move one order at a time and check its staging sign.
I move the nearest cartons first and leave the work cards behind.
I place both orders together and sort them again near dispatch.

advanced.situation: Several orders share a narrow packing aisle, and cartons are building up near the staging areas during a busy shift.

options.text: I move cartons in order and ask nearby staff to clear space.
I move one order at a time and tell staff what comes next.
I ask packers to keep the aisle open while we move each order.
I group cartons by order and set a clear route through the aisle.

basic.situation: You finish packing an order and need to clean your tools and record its packaging details on the shift form.

options.text: I clean the tools and ask a coworker to fill in the form.
I clean the tools and record the order details on the specified form.
I leave the form blank and put the tools back for the next packer.
I write the order details down and clean the tools after the next run.

advanced.situation: Several shift forms have missing packaging details, and residue has appeared on shared tools. You are asked to improve the routine.

options.text: I sign off the forms together so the next order can start sooner.
I ask each packer to check their own form and tool before leaving.
I check completed forms against order details and inspect shared tools during cleaning rounds.
I remind staff to complete forms and clean tools before leaving the station.

basic.situation: You unpack a delivery of fast-moving cartons while a narrow aisle is busy. Where would you place them so coworkers can find and reach them?

options.text: Stack cartons across the aisle until the rush passes.
Place the cartons on an open upper rack to save floor space.
Put fast-moving cartons near the aisle for quicker picking.
Group frequent picks in reachable bays, label them, and keep paths clear.

advanced.situation: You are relocating slow-moving cartons and supplies sensitive to damp conditions. You need to free a busy picking bay while keeping stock usable.

options.text: Place slow cartons in a dry, labeled upper bay after checking safe access.
Group the cartons in a dry corner, keeping damp-sensitive supplies covered for counting.
Shift slow stock to a nearby clear floor area until a suitable bay opens.
Move slow stock away from picks and cover damp-sensitive cartons during storage.

basic.situation: A coworker asks you to retrieve cartons from a high shelf using the forklift. The aisle is open, and you have a spotter nearby.

options.text: Check the route and load, then operate with your trained spotter guiding you.
Wait for a clearer moment, then use the forklift with guidance.
Raise the forks and drive toward the shelf to save time.
Ask the spotter to guide you while you retrieve the cartons.

advanced.situation: After a shift, you notice a frayed strap on a pallet jack and dust around its wheels. The next crew needs the equipment soon.

options.text: Wipe the wheels and leave the strap for the next shift.
Clean the jack and tell the next crew about the strap.
Clean the jack, tag the damaged strap, and report it for repair.
Replace the strap with spare packing tape and return the jack.

basic.situation: A customer has bought glass jars and boxed groceries. You are packing the order at a busy counter with bags and cartons ready.

options.text: Put the jars loose on top so the customer can see them.
Separate the jars in a small bag and place it beside the carton.
Place the jars between the boxes to keep everything together.
Wrap the jars with packing paper, then secure them inside a carton.

advanced.situation: A weekend promotion starts soon, and a popular item has moved to a new shelf. You need a sign and display that customers can spot easily.

options.text: Move the item to a busier shelf and reuse its current sign.
Put the item near the aisle and add a handwritten sign.
Make a clear price sign and place the item at eye level together.
Copy last week's sign and place it above the old shelf.

basic.situation: A picking slip lists a catalog number, two sizes, and several quantities. You are filling the order before the dispatch cut-off.

options.text: Match catalog numbers, sizes, colors, and quantities against each line.
Pick by item description and check the total quantity at packing.
Take the first matching color from each shelf and finish quickly.
Check the catalog numbers and sizes, then count the picked items.

advanced.situation: While checking stock for an order, you find several scuffed units and one with a cracked casing. Dispatch is due shortly, and the items look similar.

options.text: Pick another unit and leave the damaged items near the order bench.
Set aside the cracked unit and alert your supervisor about the damage.
Inspect each unit, separate damaged stock, and report findings before picking replacements.
Send the scuffed units and cracked unit together to meet dispatch.

basic.situation: A coworker brings a requisition for packing supplies while another team is waiting nearby. You have the requested cartons and tape in stock.

options.text: Check the requisition and prepare the requested supplies for pickup.
Match the requisition, issue its quantities, and record the handover.
Give out extra cartons so the coworker has a buffer.
Hand over the cartons and tape, then note the issue later.

advanced.situation: A shelf holds slow-moving packaging with dated labels and several visibly defective units. You are asked to review stock and suggest what should happen next.

options.text: Move all the packaging to a back bay until space is available.
Recommend disposal for the whole shelf to clear storage space.
Recommend a discount for the slow stock and set aside damaged units.
Separate defective units and recommend reviewing the slow stock before disposal.

basic.situation: A delivery arrives with cartons listed on a packing note. You count the items as they are unloaded and must complete the receipt before shelving them.

options.text: Count the cartons and record the total on the receipt.
Compare each item with the note and record any difference.
Sign the receipt from the packing note, then count cartons as shelving begins.
Record the listed quantity and check a few cartons before shelving.

advanced.situation: A stock-handling cart returns with a damaged wheel, and a coworker reports it veered during use. The next shift is waiting for the cart.

options.text: Record the wheel damage and identify which shift used the cart before handover.
Leave the cart in rotation and mention the wheel at handover.
Log the wheel damage and ask the next shift to watch it.
Log the damage, veering report, and time; tag the cart for repair.

basic.situation: You are helping start a compressor and auxiliary pump during a routine shift. The operator asks you to move the controls and turn the marked valves in sequence.

options.text: Turn the marked valves and move each control as directed.
Confirm the marked sequence, then adjust controls while watching the readings.
Open the outlet valve fully before starting the compressor.
Start the auxiliary pump first, then follow the operator's directions.

advanced.situation: Pressure readings begin fluctuating while a remote station reports reduced flow. You can adjust the control room settings and relay instructions within your shift duties.

options.text: Compare readings, make a measured control adjustment, and coordinate a remote check.
Raise the pressure setting to restore flow at the remote station.
Ask the remote crew to check their local gauge and report back.
Hold the current setting and monitor the pressure for another cycle.

basic.situation: You are assigned to transfer a routine batch using a power-driven pump. The line is connected, and the experienced operator is nearby to guide the run.

options.text: Check the batch direction and indicated settings, then monitor the transfer.
Ask the nearby operator to confirm the transfer direction first.
Start the pump and watch the flow during transfer.
Run the pump at full power to finish the batch quickly.

advanced.situation: Two scheduled transfers share a pumping area, and the higher pressure line is ready first. You are operating the pump with an experienced operator nearby.

options.text: Pause both transfers until the nearby operator chooses a sequence.
Use the scheduled order and monitor the gauge during each transfer.
Check line labels, confirm the scheduled batch, and sequence the transfer within limits.
Start the higher pressure transfer and adjust flow as needed.

basic.situation: During a routine shift, you read the gas meter and need to record the amount received since the previous entry.

options.text: Write the meter reading and time in the operating log.
Compare the current and prior readings, then log the amount and time.
Copy the previous amount to keep the log consistent.
Record the current meter reading after finishing the round.

advanced.situation: Your shift ends after several operating changes and meter readings. The daily report is due, and the manager needs a clear account of facility operations.

options.text: Send the previous day's report and update the date.
List the major changes and submit the report before handover.
Submit the log summary with the latest meter reading included.
Reconcile readings with logged changes, then submit a concise daily report.

basic.situation: You are assigned to clean a dusty hand tool and nearby equipment after routine use. The shift lead has given you step-by-step instructions and supplies.

options.text: Confirm the cleaning sequence with the lead, then start using the supplied materials.
Use the assigned supplies to clean residue from the equipment and tool surfaces.
Follow the cleaning steps, use specified supplies, and inspect the tool before storing it.
Wipe the tool and equipment, check for residue, then return both items to storage.

advanced.situation: A routine inspection shows a worn gasket and a filter due for replacement. You have the assigned hand tools and maintenance instructions for the equipment.

options.text: Replace the filter and report the gasket condition to the lead before handover.
Replace the gasket and filter, then restart equipment to assess the repair under supervision.
Follow maintenance steps, replace both parts, and check fittings before handing over equipment.
Replace both parts as instructed and record completed maintenance for the next shift.

basic.situation: A routine sample is due for a gas quality check. You have the labeled sampling container and the laboratory submission instructions at the station.

options.text: Check the form, collect the sample, and leave it for scheduled dispatch.
Collect the labeled sample and send it with the completed laboratory submission form.
Confirm the labeled point, collect the sample, and complete the form.
Use the nearest open point and fill the labeled container for testing.

advanced.situation: A laboratory result shows moisture above the usual range, while a repeat sample is pending. You need to interpret the result and coordinate detailed analysis.

options.text: Discuss the first reading as preliminary while awaiting the repeat laboratory result.
Ask the laboratory to repeat moisture analysis using the new sample and report findings.
Compare sample details, request repeat analysis, and coordinate interpretation with the laboratory.
Share the preliminary result as unconfirmed while the repeat sample remains pending.

basic.situation: You are preparing a routine transfer between a pump and a container. The connection points are marked, and a senior operator is supervising the setup.

options.text: Ask the senior operator to inspect each connection before starting the transfer.
Use the marked connection and wait for the senior operator's transfer direction.
Match the marked line, secure the connection, and request a supervisor check.
Connect the marked lines to the container and begin filling under supervision.

advanced.situation: A high-volume transfer uses two marked containers and a shared pump manifold. You are assigned to connect the pipeline while the senior operator coordinates the transfer.

options.text: Trace the marked route, connect the intended container, then check each joint.
Confirm the assigned container with the senior operator before fitting the hose securely.
Connect both containers to the manifold to reduce changeover time during transfer.
Connect the scheduled container and check the hose seating before transfer begins.

basic.situation: You are checking a storage tank with your supervisor nearby when its level gauge sits close to the marked limit.

options.text: You adjust the gauge to match the expected level and report the check as complete.
You compare the gauge with the flowmeter and ask your supervisor to confirm the reading.
You note the level, then keep the transfer running at its scheduled rate.
You pause the transfer and verify the level with the calibrated dip gauge before restarting.

advanced.situation: During a transfer, the pressure gauge pulses slightly while flow remains steady; the site procedure calls for a check before continued pumping.

options.text: You reset the gauge needle and continue at the scheduled rate once it looks steady.
You reduce the rate, compare the gauge with a second reading, and report the trend.
You pause pumping under the procedure, compare instruments, and inspect the pressure trend before resuming.
You record the pulses and keep monitoring while the transfer continues at its current rate.

basic.situation: Your supervisor asks you to test a process sample with the standard bench kit, and the colour falls between two chart bands.

options.text: You note the result as between bands and ask your supervisor how to report it.
You repeat the test with a fresh sample and show both results to your supervisor.
You choose the chart band that keeps the batch within its usual range.
You record the nearer chart band and pass that result to the next shift.

advanced.situation: A solution test is outside its usual range, but a repeat is closer to target; the batch is due for transfer soon.

options.text: You flag the first result and ask your supervisor whether the batch can wait for review.
You hold the sample for another test and inform the operator that results are still pending.
You use the repeat result and tell the operator the batch is ready to move.
You check the kit and sample conditions, repeat the test, then report the full result pattern before transfer.

basic.situation: Your schedule assigns a product transfer to a line that also serves another tank, and the operator asks when you can start.

options.text: You start the transfer now because the assigned slot appears open on your sheet.
You ask the operator to wait until the other tank has finished using the line.
You compare the line connections and capacity with the schedule, then agree a workable start time.
You check the line schedule and confirm the next available slot with the operator.

advanced.situation: Two units need the same transfer line during a short operating window, and one has a larger scheduled volume than usual.

options.text: You keep the existing order and ask both operators to work around the shared line.
You reserve the line for the larger volume and mark the smaller transfer as completed.
You give the larger transfer the first slot and move the smaller one later.
You compare capacities and downstream availability, then propose a sequence that fits both transfers.

basic.situation: During a scheduled clean, your supervisor shows you the pump points to lubricate and asks you to follow the equipment instructions.

options.text: You lubricate the points that look dry and return the tools to the bench.
You follow the marked points and tell your supervisor when the lubrication is done.
You apply lubricant to the listed points, then check them against the equipment instructions.
You add lubricant to every fitting so the pump is ready for the next shift.

advanced.situation: The same pump has needed repeated lubrication between planned services, and you are preparing its next routine maintenance entry.

options.text: You record the lubrication entry and note the repeated need for the next shift.
You flag the repeated need and request a pump check during the next planned service.
You log the repeat lubrication need and retain the current interval pending review.
You review service history and operating signs before proposing a targeted inspection.

basic.situation: Your supervisor instructs you by radio to start a transfer, but the receiver has not confirmed that its valve is ready.

options.text: You hold the start and ask your supervisor to repeat the instruction over the radio.
You repeat the instruction and start the pump while the receiver checks its valve.
You tell the receiver to prepare and wait for its reply before starting the pump.
You request confirmation from the receiver, then relay the start instruction when it is ready.

advanced.situation: Two unit operators give conflicting radio instructions about a transfer amount, while the written operating schedule lists a different quantity.

options.text: You pause the transfer and read back the schedule and both requested amounts.
You compare the schedule with both requests, then relay one confirmed transfer amount.
You verify the schedule and radio requests with both operators before confirming any amount.
You ask both operators to confirm one amount before the transfer begins.

basic.situation: You are connecting a hose for a scheduled transfer, and the checklist requires the connection to be checked before pumping starts.

options.text: You inspect the joint visually and record the hose connection for the operator.
You tighten the hose connection and tick the checklist before pumping starts.
You connect the hose, check the joint, and record the setup before pumping.
You mark the connection checked and start pumping to keep the schedule on time.

advanced.situation: Your shift log shows a quantity that differs from the gauging sheet, and the next shift is using the record to plan a transfer.

options.text: You compare entries, retain both figures, and brief the next shift about the difference.
You keep both figures and ask a coworker to review source entries before planning the transfer.
You amend the log to match the gauging sheet and omit the earlier figure.
You flag the mismatch and ask the next shift to verify the quantity before planning.
